A user opening a tab can now reach the helper. That sentence was false for the whole of level 1 until this landed.

THE FINDING. internal/helper/client had no Spawn and no Attach; proto.OpSpawn and proto.OpAttach were served by internal/helper/session/service.go and called by nobody outside internal/helper and its tests; every terminal session went through session.Reg.Open. So nocx-k6p18.3, .4, .5, .15, .16, .17, .18, .6, .7 and .13 were correct, tested, and reachable from cmd/nocx-helper's main and from tests — and from nothing a person does.

WHY THE EVIDENCE MISSED IT, and this is the part to keep. nocx-k6p18.3 proved its acceptance "end to end over the real frame protocol with a real shell under a real PTY: a coordinator spawns a per-second marker loop, is killed, and its replacement finds the session in the inventory". That coordinator was a TEST coordinator. And its -whylive chain — main -> Host.frame -> Host.request -> Service.Call -> Service.spawn — is exactly right about cmd/nocx-helper's main. `-whylive` answers "is this reachable from SOME main"; it cannot answer "can a user get here". Rule 2 of AGENTS.md says cmd/nocx-server runs the SHIPPED coordinator, not a harness beside it, and that is the distinction the whole bead turns on.

VERIFIED BY THE COORDINATOR, not taken on report:

  deadcode -tags gtk3 -whylive '…/internal/helper/client.Client.Spawn' ./cmd/nocx-server
    cmd/nocx-server.main -> run -> WSServer.handleControlFrame$1
      -> WSServer.sessionSpecs$1$1 -> openHandlers.handleOpen
      -> capability.openOperation.Dial -> operation.Run -> handleOpen$2
      -> app.helperRegistry.OpenHosted -> helper/client.Client.Spawn

Two mutations, both red on TestShippedOpenUsesHelperMintedSessionID, tree byte-identical after each revert:
  Adopt mints its own id instead of preserving the helper's
  the open branch never consults the helper opener at all

NO SECOND POLICY WAS INVENTED, which was the main risk. The open path resolves through the SAME resolver git.open uses — newResolver + Machine{Fingerprint, Mode}, keyed by the verified host public key, with the same refusal states (unsupportedPlatform, execForbidden, deployFailed, ConsentRequired). The resolver was already parameterised by which surface is reaching for the helper and said so in a comment; session-open is simply the second surface. Two predicates for "is this machine helper-hosted" would have agreed everywhere anyone looked and disagreed once.

AD-7 IS AMENDED IN docs/architecture.md rather than routed around, and narrowly: "for a helper-hosted session, the execution host's helper mints the id and the server adopts and returns that same authoritative sessionId; otherwise the server assigns it." One authority, never the frontend — AD-7's purpose survives verbatim; only the holder changes. session.Reg.Adopt preserves the minted id rather than generating a second one, and refuses a nil channel or an empty id.

THE EQUALITY NOW HAS A NAME. internal/app/helper_inventory.go:39 and frontend/src/panes.ts both join the coordinator session id against HostSessionID.Session, and both were merged depending on that silently. TestShippedOpenUsesHelperMintedSessionID drives the real WSServer socket and asserts it: `open sessionId = %q, want helper-minted %q`.

Also carried: the discovery lease now threads the host key fingerprint, because the resolver keys on it and the open path needs it before a session exists.

go test -race on transport (3 packages), helper (7 packages) and session: all ok. deadcode chain above. Merged into feat/relay-pty-owner.

WHAT THIS UNBLOCKS: nocx-1u0am (recording {host, account, generation} at open — the triple now arrives synchronously), nocx-k6p18.13, nocx-k6p18.8, and the epic's end-to-end nocx-k6p18.9, which could not have been written honestly before.

title: The session binding nocx-k6p18.15 reads has no production writer
description:
Found 2026-09-01 while judging nocx-k6p18.13's block, and verified by reading rather than
by report. It is the nocx-rtg0 shape, which AGENTS.md names as the failure this repository
has already paid for once: a reachable READ path hiding an unreachable WRITE path in the
same package.

## The two writers of `sessions`, and only one of them runs in production

`ensureLedgerContext` (`internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:137`) is production-
reachable — `ledger_command.go:199` and two agent-capture paths call it. It inserts the
row with `ON CONFLICT(id) DO NOTHING` and the payload
`captureEnsuredSessionMarker` = `{"ensure":"agent-capture"}`.

`CreateSession` (`ledger_sqlite.go:39`) is the writer that sets the durable binding
nocx-k6p18.15 built — `{generation, host, account}` in `sessions.payload`. **Every one of
its callers is a test.** `internal/content/ledger.go:24` says so in the file itself:
"WHAT IS STILL TEST-REACHABLE ONLY: CreateSession, DeleteSession, ListEntries,
DeleteEntry, AppendArtifact, AddEdge and RunState."

## What that costs, and it is the whole of nocx-k6p18.15

Session rows DO exist in production. They carry no generation, no host and no account,
because the only writer that sets those is unreachable. So `carryOver` reads an empty
generation, `reconcile.go` says "empty means no inventory may judge it", and every session
is `unknown` forever. The chain nocx-k6p18.15 built — helper client adapter, DTO,
`sessions.inventory` RPC, schema, generated renderer type, the ordering that asks only the
helper that owns the id space — is correct, tested, and reads a binding nothing writes.

The tests pass because they call `CreateSession` themselves. That is the same reason
nocx-rtg0's ContentDB.Add looked fine.

## Why this also blocks the surface

nocx-k6p18.13's worker blocked because `sessions.inventory` returns entries keyed only by
`hostSessionId` and a non-unique `workspace`, with no coordinator `sessionId`, `paneId` or
`tabId` to join to. That is the same absence seen from the other end: the join was meant to
run through the store's session row, and the store's row does not carry the helper linkage
in production.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `grep -rn "\.CreateSession(" --include=*.go . | grep -v _test` — every hit is inside
   `internal/content` and every one is a test file.
2. Open a helper-hosted session in a real run; the row is written by `ensureLedgerContext`
   with `{"ensure":"agent-capture"}`.
3. Reconcile. `carryOver` finds no generation, so no inventory may judge the session, and
   the verdict is `unknown` — permanently, for every session.

## Fix

The production path that opens a helper-hosted session must record the session with its
host, account and generation — the binding, not a marker. Either `CreateSession` gains a
production caller at that seam, or `ensureLedgerContext`'s insert learns the binding and
`CreateSession` retires. One owner per behaviour (AD-8): do not end with two writers that
set different halves of the same row.

Do NOT satisfy this by having reconciliation infer the binding from anything. Inferring
host or generation from a session id is what the ordering in nocx-k6p18.15 exists to
prevent — asking a helper about another generation's id space turns truthful absence into
deletion.

## Acceptance Criteria

A helper-hosted session opened through the shipped path has its host, account and
generation in `sessions.payload`, asserted by a test that drives the PRODUCTION open path
rather than calling CreateSession itself. `deadcode -tags gtk3 -whylive` on whichever
writer survives shows a path from main, and the retired one is gone rather than left
unreachable. Reconciliation of a real session reaches a verdict other than unknown.
close_reason:
The binding is written where it is learned, and CreateSession has a production caller for the first time.

THE DEFECT. `sessions` had two writers and only one ran in production. ensureLedgerContext (ledger_agent_sqlite.go:137) is reachable from a recorded entry and inserts a synthetic row with the payload {"ensure":"agent-capture"}. CreateSession (ledger_sqlite.go:39) is the writer that sets {generation, host, account} — the binding nocx-k6p18.15 built its whole reconciliation chain on — and EVERY caller was a test. internal/content/ledger.go:24 said so in the file itself, under "WHAT IS STILL TEST-REACHABLE ONLY".

So production rows existed carrying no binding. carryOver read an empty generation, reconcile.go says "empty means no inventory may judge it", and every session was `unknown` FOREVER. The adapter, the DTO, the sessions.inventory RPC, its schema, the generated renderer type, and the ordering that asks only the helper owning the id space were all correct, tested, and reading something nothing wrote. Their tests passed because they called CreateSession themselves — the nocx-rtg0 shape exactly: a reachable READ path hiding an unreachable WRITE path in one package.

THE DECISION, which was the real content of the task. CreateSession stays and gains its caller in handleOpen, recording the helper-authoritative {sessionID, host, account, generation} BEFORE the open ack. ensureLedgerContext keeps its synthetic rows and is not made a second binding writer. One owner per behaviour (AD-8): two writers setting different halves of one row are two answers to "what does this session belong to" that agree until they do not.

Nothing is inferred. The triple arrives synchronously from helperRegistry.OpenHosted (nocx-45zyd) — deriving host or generation from a session id would be the thing nocx-k6p18.15's ordering exists to prevent, turning a truthful "I do not hold it" into a deletion.

VERIFIED BY THE COORDINATOR, not on report:

  deadcode -tags gtk3 -whylive '…/internal/content.sqliteContent.CreateSession' ./cmd/nocx-server
    cmd/nocx-server.main -> run -> … -> openHandlers.handleOpen
      -> internal/content.sqliteContent.CreateSession

  the binding is never written        -> TestShippedHelperOpenPersistsBindingForReconciliation
                                         AND TestShippedHelperOpenRefusesUnpersistedBinding
  a failed write no longer refuses    -> TestShippedHelperOpenRefusesUnpersistedBinding

Tree byte-identical after each revert. go test -race on transport (3 packages, 249s) and content (232s): ok.

THE TEST THAT COULD NOT BE FAKED, and it is why the acceptance was worded as it was. The success regression drives the real WebSocket open path, persists to real SQLite, REOPENS the database, decodes sessions.payload, and puts the result through the REAL reconciler, which reaches VerdictLive rather than unknown. A test that called CreateSession itself would have proved nothing — that is precisely how the defect survived nocx-k6p18.15's review, including mine.

AND THE FAILURE PATH HAS ITS OWN TEST, which AGENTS.md calls the highest-yield check there is: a binding write that fails refuses the open and closes the helper session, rather than acknowledging a session no inventory may later judge. Its red before the fix: "helper open succeeded after its durable binding write failed".

title: The epic's own end-to-end check: one run watches the whole assistant sentence
description:
nocx-hp8p2 was created WITHOUT the end-to-end check its own acceptance field
demands. Today the sentence is covered in four pieces, each in a different file
with a different fixture: e2e/agent-ask.spec.ts (mark, ask, the payload carrying
the item), e2e/agent-turn.spec.ts (a tool announced and run inside a turn),
e2e/agent-refusal-stop.spec.ts (Stop preserving streamed prose), and the
stopped-header assertions spread across several files.

Four green pieces do not prove one journey. Nothing today establishes that the
SAME marked block reaches the model, that the tool the model then calls is the
one announced, and that stopping THAT turn seats THAT answer with a stopped
header. AGENTS.md testing rule 2 is explicit that this is the only check that
can report a missing feature.

This bead is the one spec file that watches one person do the whole sentence in
one run, against the shipped backend (cmd/nocx-server, headless), with a
scripted fake model endpoint. One file, one test: a second test would mean the
sentence has been split again, which is the thing this bead exists to stop.
acceptance_criteria:
One e2e spec, one test, one run, six assertions each able to fail on its own and
each carrying a message naming which promise broke:

1. A block is marked — the mark is visible on THAT block (data-granted) and the
   grant chip counts it.
2. The ask carries that item — asserted on the REAL request body reaching the
   fake endpoint: it names the marked block's announced id and its command, and
   a DIFFERENT block on screen is ABSENT from it.
3. The assistant announces a tool and runs it — the announcement is in the pane
   (the tool child names the tool and its arguments), and the answer text is
   DERIVED from the tool's real return, not from a fixed string a script could
   produce with no tool at all.
4. The person stops it — through the real gesture (the turn's own overflow menu
   Stop), never a client call.
5. The answer is seated in scrollback — it survives as a top-level block, after
   the blocks that preceded it, still holding its children in seat order.
6. Its header says stopped — the ask kind's cancelled vocabulary, on the turn's
   OWN header chip, and not the exit chip of the shell command block nested
   inside it.

No waitForTimeout, no sleeps, no duration-based waits. Verified by running the
spec at least three times per browser in the e2e container, and by breaking the
product or the script deliberately for each of the six and watching that
assertion go red alone.
close_reason: Shipped in 58c04f04, merged to main in eac1aae3 (PR #165). e2e/agent-whole-sentence.spec.ts walks the whole sentence in one run — mark a block, ask about it, the ask carries that item and not the other block on screen, a tool is announced and run with the answer derived from its real result, the person stops it through the real gesture, the answer seats in scrollback and its header says stopped. Plus e2e/ask-gesture.ts, the shared gesture module. Green in both browsers on CI 33509461352, and 5/5 per browser locally before that. Each of the six promises was watched going red alone, on its own message, and the breaks reverted — falsification, not assertion.

title: The output-budget run-lease test races its own accounting: a fixed burst can finish before ledger.bind opens the budget
description:
ci-backend went red on PR #164 four times out of four, always the same test,
always pinned at the same second:

  --- FAIL: TestRunLease_OutputBudgetBoundsAndTheBlockNamesIt (30.44s)  job 99626354670  (with-secret-service)
  --- FAIL: TestRunLease_OutputBudgetBoundsAndTheBlockNamesIt (30.58s)  job 99626354708  (no-secret-service)
  --- FAIL: TestRunLease_OutputBudgetBoundsAndTheBlockNamesIt (30.77s)  job 99643444327  (no-secret-service)
  --- FAIL: TestRunLease_OutputBudgetBoundsAndTheBlockNamesIt (31.04s)  job 99654588092  (no-secret-service)
      ws_run_lease_test.go:1002: socket closed before agent.runState arrived

It also failed once in with-secret-service, so the keyring correlation the first
reading suggested is not real.

## The cause

The command was one BURST and then a wait:

  sh -c 'echo $$ > PID; dd if=/dev/zero bs=256 count=8 2>/dev/null; sleep 100'

Budget accounting does not open until ledger.bind, which submitLeaseCommand
sends AFTER waiting for the shell to echo the command. The 2 KiB is written by
the child as soon as the shell reaches it — i.e. potentially before that RPC
lands. Bytes written before accounting opens are not counted, `sleep 100` then
produces nothing, and the 512-byte budget never fires. The run therefore has
only the 60-second WALL CLOCK left, and the test's 30-second wait expires first.

Whether the burst won that race was decided by how fast the machine was: it lost
on a developer host and in the emulated container, and won on the GitHub runner
every single time.

## Why the error message named something else entirely

The failure does not say "the run never reached completed". It says "socket
closed", and that is a second mechanism sitting on top of the first.

readLoop (ws.go:2620) sets SetReadDeadline(now + heartbeatReadWindow) around
every inbound frame, and heartbeatReadWindow is DefaultHeartbeatReadWindow =
30s (heartbeat.go:14). The window is refreshed only by frames the CLIENT sends.
socketTap sends nothing at all after ledger.bind, and waitForRunState's own
deadline is also 30 seconds — so the server's window always expires first, the
socket dies, and the test reports the corpse instead of the cause. That is why
all four durations cluster at 30.4-31.0s: it is a deadline, not load variance.
Filed separately.

## Steps to Reproduce

Insert `time.Sleep(2 * time.Second)` before the ledger.bind call in
submitLeaseCommand (ws_run_lease_test.go:296) — which is exactly what a loaded
runner supplies for free — then:

  go test -race -run TestRunLease_OutputBudgetBoundsAndTheBlockNamesIt -count=1 ./internal/transport/

Observed, byte-for-byte the runner's failure:

  --- FAIL: TestRunLease_OutputBudgetBoundsAndTheBlockNamesIt (31.25s)
      ws_run_lease_test.go:1003: socket closed before agent.runState arrived

and the server log alongside it shows the run being cancelled by the dead socket
rather than bounded: `agent ask: the stream ended run=1 elapsed=30.04s ...
outcome=failed`, `run: context canceled`. Without the delay the test passes on
the host in 2.8s, which is why it looked environmental.

## The fix

Output that KEEPS COMING cannot lose the race, whenever accounting opens:

  sh -c 'echo $$ > PID; while :; do dd if=/dev/zero bs=256 count=2 2>/dev/null; sleep 0.1; done'

512 bytes per 100ms crosses the 512-byte budget within a fifth of a second of
accounting opening, and is slow enough that a run which somehow is NOT bounded
floods nothing.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The test passes with a deliberate multi-second delay injected before
  ledger.bind — the machine's speed must stop being able to decide the outcome.
  Verified: PASS at 4.7s with a 2s delay, PASS at 12.7s with a 10s delay, where
  the old command FAILED at 31.25s under the same 2s delay.
- It still asserts what it was there to assert: the budget fires, the block
  names it, the ledger records TermOutputBudget, and the child is dead.
- ci-backend is green in both keyring variants.
close_reason: Fixed in 3056116d: the command streams 512 bytes per 100ms until killed, so the budget fires whenever accounting opens. Verified against an injected pre-bind delay — old command FAIL at 31.25s with 2s, new one PASS at 4.7s (2s) and 12.7s (10s); full internal/transport package green locally at 271s. CI's ci-backend is the remaining confirmation.

title: The run-lease tests match a wrapped PTY echo against an unwrapped literal, so they fail by terminal geometry
description:
`ci-backend` went red on PR #164 — a frontend-only branch with zero Go changes
and `internal/transport` byte-identical to main. The failure is in
`ws_run_lease_test.go`, which reached main through PR #160 (nocx-o6qtx) and has
never been run by CI: main's last CI run is 2026-08-30 on d2a9b779, before that
merge, and main is now on a7632941 with no run at all. PR #164 was the first CI
to compile it.

## The cause

`tapDataFor` (`ws_run_lease_test.go:150`) waits for the shell to echo the
submitted command by searching the RAW PTY byte stream for the command as a
literal substring. The session is opened at 80 columns
(`ws_acceptance_test.go:34`) and the command is built from `t.TempDir()`, into
which Go interpolates the TEST NAME:

    sh -c 'echo $$ > /tmp/TestRunLease_WallClockTerminalizesAndTheLedgerNamesIt932954368/003/child.pid; exec sleep 100'

That is 115 characters, and the prompt in front of it (`ubuntu@bccf61ffd179:~$`)
is another ~22 columns. The echo does not fit in 80, the terminal wraps, and the
wrap puts a CR and a repeated byte into the stream. The arithmetic lands exactly
on the observed bytes: the wrap falls at offset 58 of the command, where the
text reads `And`, and what arrives is `TerminalizesAn\rnd`.

The rule is consistent across all five failures — the last byte before the CR is
re-emitted after it:

    An\rnd   -> And          (WallClock)
    A\rAnd   -> And          (Inactivity)
    Fo\ror   -> For          (EscalationReachesTerm, EscalationReachesKill)
    Th\rhe   -> The          (OutputBudget)
    nul\rll  -> null         (OutputBudget, /dev/null)
    10\r00   -> 100          (EscalationReachesKill, sleep 100)

So the literal is not in the stream, `tapDataFor` spends its 10s and fails.

## Why it looks like a different bug in every environment

Where the wrap lands depends on the prompt width (the container's hostname is in
it) and on the TMPDIR path length (the test name and a random number are in it).
Same code, three faces:

  host, `go test ./internal/transport/`      PASSES, 260.7s
  CI container, `scripts/ci-linux.sh`        5 TestRunLease_* FAIL at ~10.5s each
  GitHub runner, ci-backend                  the echo matched; a later wait
                                             failed — "socket closed before
                                             agent.runState arrived", 30.58s

This is the shape AGENTS.md forbids outright: a test may not depend on its
environment, and one that needs a particular terminal geometry to pass is broken
everywhere else too, only not caught yet. It also wasted an investigation on
nocx-2h08, the CLOSED starvation bug, whose signature (a 30s timeout under a
different test name each run) this imitates.

## Steps to Reproduce

    ./scripts/ci-linux.sh -- ./internal/transport/

Five `TestRunLease_*` fail with "the session's output never contained ..." and a
`got` string carrying `\r` inside the expected text. The same package run on the
host passes, which is the point.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `./scripts/ci-linux.sh -- ./internal/transport/` passes, and passes again with
  a deliberately long test name or a deliberately long TMPDIR — the geometry
  must stop being able to decide the outcome.
- The wait still asserts what it was there to assert: that the shell has echoed
  the submitted command before the bind RPC opens accounting. It is not weakened
  into a sleep or into matching a shorter prefix that could match something else.
- CI's `ci-backend` is green in both keyring variants.
- The 30.58s "socket closed before agent.runState arrived" seen on the runner is
  either explained by this same cause or filed separately with its own evidence.
  It is NOT assumed to be fixed by this.
close_reason: Merged to main in a1fbb5d0 (PR #164). The PTY wrap is undone by unwrap() with its own case table, and the last criterion — the runner's 'socket closed before agent.runState arrived' — was explained rather than assumed: it was a separate defect, filed and fixed as nocx-qmtr2, with nocx-a96sf carrying the misleading message it hid behind. ci-backend green in both keyring variants.

title: SweepStale deletes a long-running session's recording for being long-running
description:
Found by an adversarial review, 2026-08-31, and confirmed by the coordinator by reading the
code: pendingSession.sinceMs is populated from `SELECT id, started_at FROM sessions`
(internal/content/reconcile_sqlite.go carryOver), and SweepStale compares that against
time.Now() minus the retention age.

The binding design says the opposite in as many words: the retention age is on THE MARK —
the time since this restart could not reach the host.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start a command that runs for eight days.
2. Replace the coordinator. During the replacement the host is briefly unreachable, so the
   session is unreconciled for one second.
3. SweepStale runs with the 7-day default, compares started_at against now-7d, and DELETES
   the recording and the sessions row immediately.

It is exactly inverted: the longer a session has been usefully running, the faster it is
swept. And long-running sessions surviving a coordinator replacement is the entire promise
this design exists to keep.

## The second half

After deleting, the code removes the session from the in-memory pending set while LEAVING
ITS ENTRY OPEN. The third state is derived solely from that pending set, so the block then
renders as RUNNING — with its recording gone — until the next application restart. A user
sees a command presented as running that nothing can any longer report on.

## Fix

Measure from the mark. The pending set already exists and is created at Open; give the
pending record the time the mark was made rather than the session's start. Then decide the
entry's fate in the same operation as the sweep, so no path leaves an open entry with no
pending record behind it.
acceptance_criteria: The retention age is measured from the moment the session became unreconciled, not from when it started. An eight-day-old session unreachable for one second survives. And a swept session leaves no entry that renders as running: the third state survives the sweep, or the entry is closed by it.
notes:
Two phrases in the closing reason were eaten by the shell (backticks inside a double-quoted
argument were executed). They were: the diff command "git diff feat/relay-pty-owner..HEAD",
and the identifier "sink Sink" which is still threaded through five call sites after the
merge.
close_reason:
Committed as 08359d09 on omp/k6p18-17-sweep by an omp worker through herdr; merged as 2c231a93. Verified on the merged tree: build rc=0, ./internal/content/ ok 20.4s, ./internal/helper/session/ ok 5.1s.

THE FIX: carryOver now TAKES the mark time as a parameter instead of reading started_at out of the sessions table, so pendingSession.sinceMs is when this incarnation became unable to reach the host — which is what the binding design said all along and what the code did not do.

THE TEST IS THE ONE THAT WAS WRONG BEFORE, written with the exact durations from the defect: TestRetentionMeasuresFromCoordinatorReplacement uses an eight-day-old session, one second of unreachability and the seven-day bound, and asserts it SURVIVES. Its comment states the rule in one line — the mark is when this incarnation became unable to reach the host, not when the remote command started. The clock is INJECTED (retentionClock), so nothing sleeps and nothing depends on a duration.

The paired positive is present and separate: TestRetentionSweepsSessionPastTheMarkAgeAndClosesEntry proves the bound still BINDS, which matters because dropDeadSessions was the only thing bounding session recordings and they are deliberately outside the budget sweep. And its name carries the second half of this bead: the sweep now CLOSES the entry rather than dropping the pending record and leaving an open entry behind — which was the user-visible half, where a block rendered as running with its recording already destroyed until the next restart.

A MERGE HAZARD WORTH RECORDING, because it nearly cost the previous task: this branch was cut before nocx-k6p18.16 landed, so  showed the entire write-lease change as DELETIONS — lease_serialization_test.go and multi_connection_test.go as -71 each, session.go rewritten. That is an artifact of diffing against a base that moved, not a revert. Merging rather than taking the branch's version is what preserved it; confirmed after the merge by checking the file exists and  is still threaded through five call sites.

title: The write lease is not bound to the connection that acquired it
description:
Found by an adversarial review of the composed level 1, 2026-08-31, and CONFIRMED against
the code by the coordinator rather than taken on report. It defeats D8's "exactly one write
capability", which is the guarantee the lease epoch exists to provide.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Coordinator A attaches and obtains subscriber S at epoch E.
2. Coordinator B connects concurrently — which D12 permits and nocx-k6p18.4 asserts is
   SERVED rather than refused.
3. B sends a session-data frame carrying S and E.
4. The helper applies it to the PTY.

B does not even have to guess the values: the inventory PUBLISHES the current subscriber and
epoch (internal/helper/session/session.go around line 243).

## Why it happens

internal/helper/host/host.go's sessionData decodes the frame and calls plane.SessionData(f)
with the frame ALONE — no connection identity travels with it. hostSession.write then
accepts on subscriber and epoch only. Verified by reading both.

D12 does not repair this. Same-UID trust says B is ALLOWED TO REQUEST the capability; it
does not make two simultaneous writers consistent with "exactly one".

## Three defects, one shape

1. NOT CONNECTION-BOUND, as above. Fixable WITHOUT touching the frozen frame ABI: pass the
   connection identity from Host.sessionData into the service and require the current writer
   attachment to belong to that connection. `ack` and `detach` need the same binding — today
   an old connection can acknowledge the REPLACEMENT's subscriber, and detach searches
   globally by attachment without checking the caller.

2. NOT LINEARIZED. write snapshots holder and epoch under the mutex, RELEASES the mutex, and
   only then calls proc.Write. So: an old frame reads epoch 1 and passes validation; the old
   attachment disconnects; the replacement receives epoch 2; the epoch-1 frame writes to the
   PTY. That is precisely the late write the epoch claims to prevent, and the code comment
   above write claims it is prevented.

3. REUSED SUBSCRIBER IDENTITY CORRUPTS. A second attach for the same subscriber replaces its
   pump but leaves the old attachment record behind. A later detach of the old attachment
   deletes whichever subscriber currently occupies that ID — including the replacement.

## Why P0

Two coordinators attached at once is not an edge case here: it is a designed property of
level 1, asserted by a passing test. The write capability is the only thing standing between
that and two processes typing into one shell.
acceptance_criteria: A frame carrying another connection's subscriber and epoch is REFUSED. Validation, lease transition and the PTY write share one serialization boundary, so a frame validated at epoch N cannot land after epoch N+1 was granted. ack and detach are equally connection-bound. A second attach for a subscriber that already exists does not leave an old attachment record that a later detach can use to delete the replacement.
close_reason:
The lease is connection-bound, and unlike when this bead was first reported green, every property now has a gate that has been SEEN to fire.

The fix: Host.sessionData carries the connection into the service; hostSession.write requires the current writer attachment to belong to that connection, holds s.mu from validation through the return of proc.Write, and ack/detach carry the same binding. A second attach for one subscriber now deletes the old attachment record instead of leaving it to be detached later.

The verification is why this stayed open. Four mutations, each re-introducing one defect behaviourally inside the CURRENT code — not a revert to the old API, which is what the first round did and which fails at compile time, proving nothing:

1. drop `attachment.sink != sink` in write  -> TestAWriteFrameCannotUseAnotherConnectionsAttachment: `PTY received "wrong\nright\n", want only the legitimate holder's write`
2. release s.mu before proc.Write           -> TestWriteSerializesProcessWriteWithLeaseTransition: the probe took the mutex during Write
3. drop `sub.sink != sink` in ack           -> TestAckAndDetachAreBoundToTheAttachmentConnection: `old connection acknowledged the replacement's subscriber`
4. keep the stale attachment record         -> same test: `replacement connection lost its subscriber after stale detach`

Mutation 4 is the finding. On its first run it did not go red — it hung to the ten-minute suite timeout, because the test observed the defect only as an ABSENCE of bytes at the PTY, which a lost subscriber never produces. A gate that expresses a violation as silence is a timeout wearing a test's name. It now asks the replacement to acknowledge, which fails immediately and says what happened, and reads the reader's bytes separately.

TestOutputPumpDoesNotTakeSessionMutex is new and closes the other end of the interval: write holds s.mu across proc.Write, so a pump contending on it would deadlock a blocked PTY write before it could drain. pump's comment asserted this; nothing checked it.

Production tree byte-identical after each revert (`git diff --exit-code HEAD` over host.go, service.go x2, session.go). Merged into feat/relay-pty-owner; `go test -race ./internal/helper/...` green on the merged tree, all seven packages.

title: A 30-second tool deadline preempts the run lease and orphans the command
description:
## What happens

The assistant runs a command that takes longer than 30 seconds. The run fails with 'the
assistant's session.run call did not finish: run: context deadline exceeded' — and the
command keeps executing, with nobody reading it.

Measured on 2026-08-31 from the owner's stand (backend.log, run=121):

    09:46:52.063  agent ask: streaming  run=121  question=66
    09:47:22.084  the run failed  sentence="...did not finish: run: context deadline exceeded"
    09:47:22.084  the stream ended  run=121 elapsed=30.021s toolCallsExecuted=1 outcome=failed

30.021s. The command was 'du -sh /* 2>/dev/null | sort -hr | head -n 10' on a 246 G disk.
In the panel the run showed failed at 35.4s while the command's own chip went on
ticking at 40s with a live working dot — the run died, the execution did not.

## The cause, and it is a fix applied one layer too low

internal/agenttools/registry.go gives EVERY tool row a flat Deadline of 30 * time.Second,
session.run included (:298). internal/assistant/kernel.go:1191 wraps the execution in it:

    runCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, decl.Deadline)

The run lease is the mechanism actually designed to bound a command:
internal/transport/run_lease.go:87 — WallClock 10 minutes, Inactivity 2 minutes, plus an
output budget. Thirty seconds always fires first, so the lease's bounds are unreachable
for session.run. It can never terminalize anything.

That is exactly the gap somebody already closed one layer down. ws_run.go:251 sets the
BROKER timeout to zero and says why:

    // The lease is the ONLY bound. A broker timeout that could fire
    // before the lease — ... — would terminalize the run without killing
    // the execution: the exact gap this bead closes.
    kind.Timeout = 0

The tool deadline does precisely that, from above, where that fix cannot see it.

## Why the command survives

run_lease.go:200-212. supervise() calls escalate() — the INT → TERM → KILL ladder — ONLY
when the lease itself fired (firedReason != ""). When the parent context dies from the
tool deadline instead, fn(ctx) returns the context error, firedReason is empty, escalate
is never called, and the function returns an error over a command still running in the
pty. The orphan is not a race; it is the structure.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Ask the assistant something that needs a command taking longer than 30s —
   'du -sh /*' on a large disk, a build, a long find.
2. Approve the call.
3. At 30s the run fails with 'context deadline exceeded'.
4. Watch the command's chip: it keeps running and keeps producing output, with no run
   left to read it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A command that runs longer than 30s and finishes before the lease's wall clock returns
  its output to the model and the run completes. A test watches a command outlive 30s.
- When a bound DOES end a command, the execution is killed, not abandoned: the ladder in
  escalate() runs on every path that terminalizes a run, and a test asserts no process
  survives its run.
- The bound that ended it is named in the block (the runLeaseSentence vocabulary already
  exists: wall-clock, inactivity, output budget) — never the generic 'context deadline
  exceeded', which names a mechanism rather than a reason.
- The relationship between the tool deadline and the lease is stated in code where both
  are visible, so the next reader cannot reintroduce a third bound above them.

## Deliberately open for the implementer

Whether session.run's row should carry a much larger deadline, or no deadline at all
(deferring wholly to the lease, as the broker already does). The second matches
ws_run.go's reasoning and validToolDeadline currently requires a finite duration
(agenttools/safety.go:65) — so that choice changes a validation rule and needs saying out
loud rather than assuming.
close_reason: Duplicate of nocx-tz0rt, which was filed 2026-08-30 for the same defect. Its evidence is merged into that bead's notes rather than kept here.

title: A path prefix defeats the command disqualifier: /bin/bash -c hides its nested command
description:
Found by worktree-calm-cloud-b209-b8 reviewing nocx-4h0m7.3 on branch w2-effects
(commit d226fb49), measured with a probe rather than read off the source. Confirmed
at the source by claude-panel2.

## Mechanism

internal/assistant/cmdeffect.go:812 disqualifyingWords compares words[0] LITERALLY
against bare program names (sudo, env, xargs, sh, bash, find, ...). "/bin/bash"
matches none of them. Then isExecutablePath (:388) returns true for anything starting
with /, ./ or ../ and appendResourceReport RETURNS at :163 with ResourceExecute —
before the program switch and before any further reading of the operands.

## Steps to Reproduce

Drive these six commands through appendResourceReport on branch w2-effects and compare
the pairs. The peer's measured output:

  rm -rf /home/me/x            disq=false unres=0 [{/home/me/x delete}]     ceil(Delegate)=mutate-destructive
  /bin/rm -rf /home/me/x       disq=false unres=0 [{/bin/rm execute}]       ceil(Delegate)=delegate
  bash -c 'rm -rf /home/me/x'  disq=TRUE  unres=2 []                        ceil(Delegate)=delegate
  /bin/bash -c 'rm -rf ...'    disq=FALSE unres=0 [{/bin/bash execute}]     ceil(Delegate)=delegate
  curl https://x.example       disq=false unres=0 [{https://... network}]   ceil(Delegate)=cross-boundary
  /usr/bin/curl https://...    disq=false unres=0 [{/usr/bin/curl execute}] ceil(Delegate)=delegate

Each pair is the same command; only the path prefix differs.

## Two consequences

(1) A path prefix moves a command to a DIFFERENT EFFECT ROW. Inert today only because
session.run declares mutate-destructive and delegate is not below it. It goes LIVE the
moment nocx-tyhel makes session.run declare its Delegate class, which is the next bead
by this bead's own dependency edge. Under a policy that permits delegate and asks on
mutate-destructive, typing "/bin/" is the evasion.

(2) The serious one: the disqualifier is DEFEATED, not bypassed. The invariant
"Disqualified implies non-empty Unresolved" is not VIOLATED, it is made VACUOUS —
Disqualified is false when it should be true, so finalizeInvocation's guard never
fires, and Effect() then trusts a command whose nested string nothing ever read. That
is exactly the net ADR-0053 leans on when it says an unresolved parse takes the worst
member. The defect is the argument FOR that clause and shows it is load-bearing rather
than decorative.

## The fix, which the repo has already decided once

content/floor.go:113 normalises with strings.ToLower(filepath.Base(word)) for precisely
this reason. Normalise the same way before the switch AND before the disqualifier
checks, and let isExecutablePath yield Execute only when the base name is not a program
the switch already knows. Do NOT add a second normalisation rule beside the floor's —
one owner per behaviour (AD-8).

## Not a defect, do not chase it

The floor is unaffected. forbiddenInvocation reads inv.Commands, not inv.Resources, and
session.run's ResolveResources is resourceSession, so the territorial half never
consumed command path operands. Checked by the peer before flagging.

## Also in the same round

TestPolicy_DistinguishesReadPermitFromExecuteAskOnOnePath on w2-effects is deliberately
red and must become t.Skip naming nocx-tyhel, so main never carries a red test.
nocx-tyhel unskips it.
acceptance_criteria: A path-prefixed program is disqualified exactly when its bare name would be: /bin/bash -c 'rm -rf X' produces Disqualified=true and a non-empty Unresolved, matching bash -c 'rm -rf X'. The same holds for every name disqualifyingWords lists (sudo, env, xargs, watch, setsid, ionice, flock, nohup, timeout, tee, sh, find). A table test drives the bare and path-prefixed form of each through ONE assertion so the two can never diverge again. Normalisation reuses the floor's filepath.Base rule rather than restating it. TestPolicy_DistinguishesReadPermitFromExecuteAskOnOnePath is skipped naming nocx-tyhel.

single helper whose correctness depends on which list the caller consults is MORE
dangerous than two, because nothing at the call site says which kind it is. Once ToLower

Recorded here so nobody helpfully merges them back later.

restate it' when NO EXPORTED HELPER EXISTED. 'Reuse' had no referent, so the worker did
the only thing available and restated it. A brief cannot instruct its way past a missing
thing; the instruction must name something that exists, or it is a wish.

title: The assistant panel is usable: every step of one conversation does what it appears to do
description:
The batch the owner filed from a single sitting with the product on 2026-08-30, 16:52:19 to 17:06:33 — twenty-one beads, each a thing he watched go wrong on his own screen. They were filed as separate symptoms and worked as separate symptoms; this epic is the deliverable they add up to, created at his request on 2026-08-31 so the batch has one handle and one finish line.

WHAT A PERSON CAN DO THAT THEY CANNOT TODAY

Hold one working conversation with the assistant about what is on the screen: mark a block or freeze a full-screen program, ask about it, watch the assistant act, stop it if it goes wrong, and read the answer — with every step doing what it appears to do, and any step that cannot do its job saying so.

Today almost every step of that sentence has a way of silently doing nothing. A marked block reaches the model as nothing. A frozen screen is painted over rather than beside. A stop is reported to the model as the command hanging. A question comes back offered as a command to run. A dump that would explain any of it is a 200px box over a megabyte.

WHY IT IS ONE EPIC AND NOT TWENTY-ONE BUGS

Each bead is defensible alone and none of them is the product. What the owner reported was not twenty-one defects, it was that the panel could not be used — and the reason a fix list does not converge on that is that the list has no finish line. This has one.

STRUCTURE, AND WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE TO THE BACKLOG

Sixteen of the twenty-one already belong to epics with their own DONE WHEN — nocx-7l4ex, nocx-vnirv, nocx-gxr9w, nocx-0mvpy, nocx-25k9, nocx-ms7v, nocx-takqr, nocx-uvac6. They were NOT reparented: taking a child out of an epic strands that epic short of its own criterion, and owning an epic means seeing it to that criterion. They are attached here with 'tracks' edges instead, which is what that edge is for. The five that had no parent — nocx-tsqfx, nocx-n5q44, nocx-be495, nocx-iqywv, nocx-p5rjv — are children outright.

Every one of the twenty-one also carries the label assistant-sweep-0830, so the batch is one query regardless of edge type:

  bd list --label assistant-sweep-0830 --status all

STATE AT CREATION (2026-08-31)

  11 fixed in code on branch fix/assistant-panel-wave1, open in the tracker only
     because that branch has not merged: gxr9w.8, gxr9w.9, vnirv.3, vnirv.5,
     uvac6.12, 7l4ex.14, 7l4ex.15, 7l4ex.17, 7l4ex.18, be495
   1 closed: 25k9.25
   1 in progress: 0mvpy.9
   8 remaining: gxr9w.10, tsqfx, takqr.9, vnirv.4, n5q44, 7l4ex.16, ms7v.10,
     iqywv, p5rjv

DELIBERATELY OUT

  - nocx-7l4ex.19 and .20, the split view. Filed later the same evening (19:21)
    as new BEHAVIOUR the owner asked for, not as a defect in what exists. They
    belong to nocx-7l4ex.
  - The snippets batch (16:58-16:59), a different feature that shares only a
    timestamp.
  - nocx-4lxxj and nocx-tyhel — the assistant not calling tools at all, and
    ADR-0053 behind it. Discovered the next day from a separate report, and
    structural rather than panel-level. They gate whether this epic's end-to-end
    check can pass, and that is an edge, not membership.

## Success Criteria

See the acceptance field.
acceptance_criteria: One automated end-to-end check watches a person do the whole sentence in one run against the shipped backend (cmd/nocx-server, headless): mark a block, ask about it, see the ask carry that item, watch the assistant announce and run a tool, stop it, and read a seated answer whose header says stopped — asserting at each step that the thing which appears to have happened has happened. Every one of the twenty-one beads is closed or explicitly reclassified with a reason. No step of that sentence can fail silently: where a step cannot do its job the product says so in the pane, not only in a log, and a test asserts the sentence a person is shown.

title: A tool declares the set of classes it can reach, and a withheld tool says so (ADR-0053)
description:
Implements ADR-0053, accepted 2026-08-31 with the owner. Read the ADR first — docs/decisions/0053-a-tool-declares-the-classes-it-can-reach.md. It is binding, including its rejected alternative.

THE SHAPE, in one line: agenttools.Declaration.Effect stops being one position on the lattice and becomes the SET of classes the tool can resolve to.

  files.read     -> {Observe}
  notes.create   -> {MutateReversible}
  session.run    -> {Observe, MutateReversible, MutateDestructive, Delegate, CrossBoundary}

Fifteen of the sixteen declarations are singletons and change only syntactically. Only session.run is genuinely plural, because it is a door rather than an action: lsblk and rm -rf are not two severities of one act.

WHY, IN THE OWNER'S WORDS (2026-08-31): 'session.run cannot be classified at all without its arguments.' The registry already recorded that distinction and then ignored it — CommandArg is set on session.run's declaration ALONE, out of sixteen.

THREE PIECES OF WORK.

1. THE DECLARATION AND THE OFFER FILTER. Registry.ForGrant stops asking 'is the declared class permitted?' and asks 'is ANY member of this tool's set not refused?'. If one is, offer it and let execution decide. If none is, the tool is useless under this policy and is dropped.

2. THE WITHHELD TOOL SAYS SO. This is product-visible and is NOT optional — it is half the reason the ADR exists. When a tool is dropped because every class it can reach is refused, the person is told, naming the tool and the rows that refused it. A tool withheld in silence is the defect nocx-4lxxj is about: the assistant plans a command in its visible reasoning, asks the person to run it, and the turn reports completed and green.

3. EXECUTION SELECTS FROM THE SET. commandEffect already parses the invocation; it now selects one member. lsblk -> Observe, ./deploy.sh -> Delegate, rm -rf -> MutateDestructive. An unresolved parse takes the WORST member, so not knowing still tightens. TestCommandEffect_DisqualifiedAlwaysHasUnresolvedCause guards that over 13 forms and must stay green and unweakened.

DO NOT ADD EffectUnknown. The owner proposed it and rejected it with me; the ADR records the full reasoning because it is the obvious move and will be proposed again. Short form: an effect class is a row in the policy matrix and therefore a question put to a person; an Unknown row set to allow is a universal bypass that favours exactly the commands the parser could not understand; and it would still produce one answer for the whole tool. Not-knowing is already modelled correctly one level down as content.ResourceUnknown and ResourceReport.Unresolved.

FILES: internal/agenttools/registry.go (declarations, ForGrant, LiveEffects), internal/content/effectpolicy.go (PermittedEffects), internal/assistant/cmdeffect.go and internal/content/resources.go (selection), plus wherever the withheld-tool explanation surfaces.

SEQUENCING: internal/agenttools/registry.go is held by the nocx-cmj11/nocx-klqjo worker. Do not dispatch until it releases. This bead also unblocks nocx-4h0m7.3, whose acceptance test TestPolicy_DistinguishesReadPermitFromExecuteAskOnOnePath is deliberately red on branch w2-effects and cannot go green until this lands — Delegate is not below MutateDestructive but beside it, so no derivation can reach it while a single declared point exists.

## Success Criteria

See the acceptance field.
acceptance_criteria: A declaration carries a set; the fifteen singleton tools behave exactly as before and a test asserts that for each. A policy that refuses mutate-destructive still offers session.run and still permits lsblk, while rm -rf is refused at execution — one test, both halves, failing today. When every class a tool can reach is refused, the tool is dropped AND the person is told, naming the tool and the refusing rows; a test drives that and asserts the message, not only the absence. commandEffect selects a member per invocation: lsblk to Observe, ./deploy.sh to Delegate, rm -rf to MutateDestructive. An unresolved parse takes the worst member, and TestCommandEffect_DisqualifiedAlwaysHasUnresolvedCause is still green and unmodified. No new row appears in the policy matrix and no stored setting migrates. nocx-4h0m7.3's TestPolicy_DistinguishesReadPermitFromExecuteAskOnOnePath goes green without being edited.
close_reason: Closed

title: session.run dies of its own 30s deadline after an approval round-trip, and the run fails instead of the command
description:
Found 2026-08-30 in the backend log, on the branch fix/assistant-panel-wave1.

Two runs, the same shape, minutes apart:

  run=70  streaming 14.92s -> outcome=suspended (approval raised)
          resumed 4s later
          34.25s later -> outcome=failed, calls=1
          'the assistant's session.run call did not finish: run: context deadline exceeded'
          [NodeRunError] failed to stream tool call: agent tool 'session.run' failed
          callPath: runAskStream < resumeRun < handleApprove < TrySubmit

  run=74  same sentence, same callPath, same tool.

session.run declares Deadline: 30 * time.Second (internal/agenttools/registry.go:293-306).
The failure arrives through handleApprove -> resumeRun, i.e. AFTER a human answered
the approval prompt.

WHAT MUST BE ESTABLISHED FIRST, because two different defects fit this evidence and
they need opposite fixes:

  A. The deadline is anchored at the ORIGINAL tool-call start and keeps running while
     the run is SUSPENDED waiting for a person. Then any approval a human does not
     answer within the remaining budget kills the run, and the slower the person the
     likelier it is. That is a clock that counts a human's reading time against a
     command's execution budget.
  B. The deadline is anchored at RESUME and the command genuinely ran longer than 30s.
     Then the defect is smaller but still real: a 30s ceiling on an interactive shell
     command is short, and the failure is reported as the ASSISTANT failing rather
     than as the command being cut off.

In run=70 the human answered in about 4 seconds and the resumed segment still ran
34.25s, which does not cleanly separate A from B. Measure it; do not guess. The
instrumentation to add either way is the anchor point and the remaining budget at
resume.

THE REPORTING IS WRONG IN BOTH CASES. The person is told 'the assistant's session.run
call did not finish', which describes the assistant as having failed. What happened is
that a deadline this product chose expired. A command that is cut off by our own
ceiling is not the same event as a model error, and a person cannot act on the
sentence they are given.

RELATED: nocx-j4hlr (the run lease's output budget counts the command's ECHO and
terminalizes before the command exists) is the same family — a budget measured against
the wrong interval. Read it before deciding the anchor.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Set the agent policy so an effect is 'Ask every time' (the default; anything not set is asked).
2. Ask the assistant something it answers by running a shell command.
3. The run suspends and the approval prompt appears. Approve it.
4. If the command's execution crosses the tool's 30s deadline, the run FAILS with
   'the assistant's session.run call did not finish: run: context deadline exceeded'
   rather than returning the command's own result or a truthful timeout.

A command cut off by our own ceiling is reported as that, naming the ceiling, and is distinguishable in the UI from a model or transport failure; a test asserts the sentence. Whether 30s is the right ceiling for an interactive command is decided explicitly and the reason recorded.

not counting the person's reading time.

Measured on the owner's stand, backend.log, run=121:

    09:46:50.051  the stream ended  elapsed=3.365s  outcome=suspended  suspensionTool=session.run

And it is a fix already applied one layer down, missed one layer up. ws_run.go:251 sets
the BROKER timeout to zero and says exactly why:

    // before the lease — ... — would terminalize the run without killing
    // the execution: the exact gap this bead closes.
    kind.Timeout = 0

The tool deadline does that very thing from above, where that fix cannot see it.

SECOND, and this is the part with teeth: THE COMMAND IS LEFT RUNNING. run_lease.go:200-212
calls escalate() — the INT -> TERM -> KILL ladder — only when the LEASE fired
(firedReason != ""). When the parent context dies from the tool deadline instead,
fn(ctx) returns the context error, firedReason is empty, escalate never runs, and
supervise returns an error over a command still executing in the pty. The owner watched
this: the run showed failed at 35.4 s while the command's own chip went on ticking at
40 s with a live working dot. The orphan is not a race, it is the structure.

This makes the reporting defect this bead already names worse than 'the sentence is
wrong'. The person is told the assistant's call did not finish, while the command it
started is still running, still writing, and no longer attached to anything that will
read it.

So the acceptance criteria above stand, and one is added: when a bound ends a command,
the execution is killed rather than abandoned — escalate() runs on every path that
terminalizes a run, and a test asserts no process survives its run.

or none at all, deferring wholly to the lease as the broker already does. The second
matches ws_run.go's reasoning, but validToolDeadline (agenttools/safety.go:65) currently

out loud, not assumed.

── 2026-08-31, WHY IT IS 30 SECONDS ──────────────────────────────────────────

Nobody chose 30 s for session.run. It is uniform filler that a required field forced:
all SIXTEEN rows in internal/agenttools/registry.go carry exactly 30 * time.Second, with
no exception — notes.create and 'run an arbitrary program in a shell' are given the same
budget.

The sequence, and it is the whole explanation:

  2026-08-25  d3078f14  the run lease is built (WallClock 10m, Inactivity 2m, output
              budget) and, in the SAME commit, the broker timeout is deliberately zeroed:
              'The lease is the ONLY bound. A broker timeout that could fire before the
              lease … would terminalize the run without killing the execution: the exact
              gap this bead closes.' The trap was seen and closed — from below.

  2026-08-28  e7483014  OutputTrust, ResultBound, Deadline and Cancellation become
              REQUIRED declaration fields. The commit's reasoning is entirely about
              output trust and truncation: 'a truncated result that looks complete is
              worse than an error'; 'a permissive default … makes "somebody forgot"
              indistinguishable from "somebody decided this output is trustworthy"'.
              Deadline rode along in that batch, and because the field is required every
              row had to carry SOME number. One number was given to all of them.

So three days after the bound below the lease was removed on purpose, an identical bound
was reinstated above it by accident — twenty times tighter, which is why the lease has
never fired since.

And the rule that is right for OutputTrust forecloses the right answer here. For
session.run the correct declaration is NO deadline, deferring wholly to the lease exactly
as the broker already does. That cannot be said: validToolDeadline (agenttools/safety.go:65)
requires > 0 and its comment calls the finiteness intentional. 'We did not forget, we
decided not to bound it here' is unrepresentable in this table.

Which turns that commit's own argument against it: a required field was meant to make
'forgot' distinguishable from 'decided'. For Deadline it did the opposite — sixteen
identical numbers are indistinguishable from sixteen decisions, and the one row where
duration is genuinely unbounded got the same number as a note edit.

This is the answer to the criterion 'whether 30 s is the right ceiling for an interactive
command is decided explicitly and the reason recorded': there is no prior decision to
overturn, so the implementer is making it for the first time, not revising one.
