THIS IS THE SECOND INSTANCE OF THE SAME DEFECT IN THE SAME TYPE. nocx-o3amz
was `WaitErr`, and the forward it added carries the warning: "Anything else
optional a pty grows needs the same forward, for the same reason."

Consequences beyond the report: the agent's run lease escalation
(`internal/transport/run_lease.go`) is a no-op on every enhanced local session
too — it reads the same error as "nothing to cancel" and terminalizes the run
without a kill.

Proven by `TestLocalEnhancedSession_SignalReachesTheForegroundExecution`
(`internal/app`), which drives the production composition root and fails on the
unfixed tree with `SignalForeground(0) over a running foreground job = pty: no
foreground process to signal`.

## Expected

A signal addressed to an integrated local session reaches the execution's
process group, exactly as it does on a non-enhanced one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `lifecyclePTY` forwards `SignalForeground` and `ForegroundProcessGroup`.
- A test through the production factory watches a signal reach a real
  foreground job on an ENHANCED session and end it.
- The e2e Stop journey passes without needing the protected-group fallback.
close_reason: Fixed in 0a7121ab. lifecyclePTY now forwards SignalForeground and ForegroundProcessGroup; TestLocalEnhancedSession_SignalReachesTheForegroundExecution drives the production composition root and fails on the unfixed tree with 'SignalForeground(0) over a running foreground job = pty: no foreground process to signal'. CI run 33248486551 green on all eight jobs, including both ci-e2e, which is the journey that was red before.

title: The coordinator's connection WaitGroup is added to while Close is already waiting
description:
Found by CI on PR #132 (run 33243823170): FAIL internal/coordinator on
ci-linux (both keyring variants) and on ci-mac, at
TestSystemPeerCredentialsReportsThisUser, "race detected during execution of
test".

Server.accept called s.conns.Add(1) per accepted connection with no ordering
against Server.Close's s.conns.Wait(). A WaitGroup whose counter goes from
zero to one while another goroutine is already inside Wait is a documented
misuse, and the detector reports it as a write in the test's Cleanup closure
(_ = s.Close()) against a read from the goroutine Start launched at
server.go:203.

Start already holds s.mu for its whole body and Close takes the same lock to
set closed, so the ordering the WaitGroup needs was one lock away and simply
not taken.

## Steps to Reproduce

go test -race -count=1 ./internal/coordinator/ on a runner where an accept
lands close enough to the test's cleanup. Reproduced on CI's ubuntu-24.04 and
macos-latest; did not reproduce in 3 runs on the NixOS dev host.

## Acceptance Criteria

Every Add happens under the same mutex that sets closed, and an Add arriving
after Close has begun is refused rather than raced — the connection is
dropped instead of served. The accept goroutine itself is counted, so Close
waits for it too.
close_reason: Fixed in 22fb8743, merged in fad33a64. trackConn adds under the mutex that sets closed and refuses once closing; the accept goroutine is counted too. Regression test TestTrackConnRefusesOnceTheServerIsClosing. Both ci-linux variants and ci-mac green on 8ad6e36d.

title: A resize racing a close touches the pty's file descriptor while it is being destroyed
description:
Found by CI on PR #132 (run 33243823170), reported under two different test
names in two different jobs, and both are one defect:

  ci-backend (with-secret-service), macOS: TestRunLease_ShortCommandRunsUntouched
  ci-mac:                                  TestBannerClickReachesTheRendererAsSessionFocus

Both race reports are identical in shape. LocalPty.Resize calls pty.Setsize,
which calls os.File.Fd() and READS the descriptor, while the read pump's
os.File.Read is inside the deferred destroy() that WRITES it once Close has
dropped the last reference:

  Write  internal/poll.(*FD).destroy  <- LocalPty.Read    <- realSession.readPump
  Read   os.(*File).Fd                <- pty.Setsize      <- LocalPty.Resize
                                      <- realSession.Resize <- sessionLane.apply

internal/pty/pty_local.go:258 (Resize) held no lock at all, while Close took
lp.mu and then closed the file. So the two reached the same descriptor with
nothing ordering them.

A resize arriving while a session closes is ORDINARY, not exotic: the lane
that carries it runs off the read loop by design (ADR-0026), so a client's
last resize and the tab's close are two goroutines on purpose. nocx-44349
fixed the nil dereference on this same path; this is the fd-level race left
underneath it.

## Steps to Reproduce

go test -race -tags gtk3 ./internal/transport/ ./internal/app/ on a machine
loaded enough to interleave a resize with a session close. It reproduced on
CI's macos-latest and ubuntu runners and not on the NixOS dev host.

## Acceptance Criteria

Resize takes the same lock Close does and refuses a closed pty rather than
touching its descriptor. A test closes a LocalPty and then resizes it, and
asserts the refusal names os.ErrClosed rather than the call reaching Setsize.
close_reason: Fixed in 22fb8743, merged to main in fad33a64. Resize takes lp.mu and refuses a closed pty with os.ErrClosed; regression test TestLocalPty_ResizeAfterCloseIsRefused. ci-backend and ci-mac green on 8ad6e36d.

title: The stop ladder signals one captured process group, not whatever is in front at each rung
description:
Found reviewing PR #121 (nocx-uvac6.10). `agent.cancel` can send SIGTERM and
SIGKILL to a command the PERSON started, which is the exact thing that PR's
headline promises it never does.

## The chain

1. `runLease.cancelExecution` (internal/transport/run_lease.go) checks `done`
   once, releases `mu`, and then calls `escalate()`.
2. `stopForeground` (internal/transport/foreground_signal.go) re-reads the
   foreground group at EVERY rung: `sess.SignalForeground(sig)` goes to
   TIOCGPGRP each time, never to a recorded pgid.
3. `cooperatedForeground` polls every 50ms for up to SignalGrace (1s) and
   reports "cooperated" only when there is NO foreground group at all.

So: Escape stops the turn, SIGINT reaches the assistant's command, it exits,
the person starts their next command inside the same one-second grace, the
poll sees *a* foreground group and concludes the execution did not cooperate —
SIGTERM, then SIGKILL, onto the person's command.

The lease's own comment claims the opposite: "A completed/disarmed lease is
inert, so a late turn cancellation can never signal a command the person
started afterwards". That is the invariant stated as a MOMENT (the `done`
check) rather than as an interval, which AGENTS.md rule 3 names directly.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Ask the assistant something that makes it run a host command through its
   `run` tool, so a runLease is attached to the turn.
2. While that command is running, press Escape to stop the turn.
3. The assistant's command takes the SIGINT and exits.
4. Within one second (the default SignalGrace) start a command of your own in
   the same pane.

Observed: the escalation continues against whatever is now in the foreground,
so the command started in step 4 receives SIGTERM and then SIGKILL.
Expected: the ladder addresses the group it started against and nothing else;
the command started in step 4 receives no signal at all.

## Why the tests do not catch it

- `TestRunLease_CancelExecutionAfterDisarmSignalsNothing` is the sequential
  case: cancel strictly after supervise returned. Not the interleaving.
- `TestAgentRunControl_CancelSignalsOnlyRegisteredAssistantLease` gives the
  "user-started" command a DIFFERENT fakeLeaseSession that is never attached
  to any lease. Its model is "the wrong session"; the hazard is "the right
  session, a later moment".

## The existing answer

`internal/pty` already has `ForegroundProcessGroup()` — the kernel's answer via
TIOCGPGRP. The ladder should name the group once and signal THAT group for
every rung, including the existence poll. This is not new authority: it is the
ladder keeping the addressee it started with.

The hazard is latent for the two pre-existing callers too — the lease's timeout
and the running block's Stop — so the fix belongs in the ladder, not in
agent.cancel.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `stopForeground` reads the foreground job's process group ONCE and signals
  that exact group for INT, TERM, KILL and the existence poll.
- A test in which the assistant's command exits after SIGINT and a DIFFERENT
  process group becomes foreground within the grace window asserts that the
  later group receives no signal. It fails before the fix.
- The interrupt intent (one SIGINT, no escalation) keeps addressing whatever is
  in the foreground now — that is what Ctrl+C means and it is unchanged.
- A prompt (foreground group is the shell's own) is still `nothing-running`,
  and a session with no local process group is still `unsupported`.
- `go test -race ./internal/transport/... ./internal/pty/... ./internal/session/...` passes.
close_reason: stopForeground now names the foreground JOB's process group once (internal/pty.ForegroundJob, built on the existing ForegroundProcessGroup) and signals THAT group for INT, TERM, KILL and the existence poll; SignalForeground stays the one-shot form an interrupt needs and is now its composition rather than a second implementation. cancelExecution re-reads `done` after the withdrawal, so the lease's inertness is an interval rather than a moment. Three tests failed before and pass after: successor-takes-the-foreground-mid-grace, escalation stays on one group, cancel racing completion signals nothing. go test ./internal/transport ./internal/pty ./internal/session green on the merged tree; pre-commit static gates green. The whole-package -race timeout on this workstation is the pre-existing nocx-2h08 starvation — reproduced on the pristine branch under a different test name. Commit 6bea2bd2, pushed to PR #121.

title: The vault unlock overlay covers the app during e2e, and eighteen specs cannot click anything
description:
Found by the coordinator running the full e2e suite in the container on the merged tree, then PROVING it is ours: the same ten spec files on a detached worktree at 64244ad4 (before our first line) are 32 passed, 0 failed. So these are regressions, not old redness.

18 of 19 failures are one cause, verbatim from the log:

  <div class="ui-prompt-overlay" data-placement="top-sheet"> ... from <div> subtree intercepts pointer events

The buttons resolve and are reported visible, enabled and stable — they simply cannot be clicked, because a prompt overlay is up over the whole app. The clusters follow the vault exactly: vault-sealed-probe (Lock now), snippets (a secret that cannot be resolved), secret-panel-position, agent-ask / agent-policy / agent-refusal-stop (endpoint credentials), connections-settings and quick-connect (SSH profile secrets).

The suspect is nocx-qhg3q: sealing on last-client-detach. Something makes the vault sealed when the suite does not expect it, ADR-0032 correctly has the vault raise its own unlock, and the renderer correctly shows the prompt — so the prompt is right and the SEAL is wrong. Verify that before fixing it: if the seal is correct and the prompt is what should not be modal, that is a different fix.

DO NOT fix this by making the tests dismiss the prompt. That would hide a product defect behind a test change.

## Steps to Reproduce

./e2e/run-in-container.sh on feat/nocx-server at 4ec7963e. PW_PROJECTS=chromium and the ten spec files reproduce it in about two minutes. The same command on a worktree at 64244ad4 passes.
acceptance_criteria: The ten spec files pass in the container, and no ui-prompt-overlay is up in a run that never sealed the vault deliberately. State as an interval with both ends when the vault is sealed and when it is not, and assert the interval rather than the moment.
close_reason:
Merged into feat/nocx-server as 8efb1e99, with the design amended in c652a2b2.

The defect was a definition, not a mechanism: D9 said the vault seals 'when the last client detaches' and never said what a detach IS. A reload and a reconnect both pass through zero clients, so reading the count instantaneously sealed the vault on a page refresh — and ADR-0032 then correctly raised the unlock prompt, which covered the whole app and made eighteen specs unable to click anything. The prompt was right; the seal was wrong. That is what the brief asked the worker to check rather than assume, and it held.

The fix is a departure window (DefaultDetachWindow, ten seconds, internal/vault/presence.go): the count must STAY at zero before the person is believed to have left.

The worker proved the fix is real by the reverse operation, which is what makes this evidence rather than a claim: it set DefaultDetachWindow to zero, re-ran vault-sealed-probe and connections-settings, and got back 2 failures and three ui-prompt-overlay interceptions; restored, ten spec files in the container are 33 passed, 0 failed, with ZERO occurrences of ui-prompt-overlay anywhere in the run.

Also run: go test -race on internal/vault, transport (98s), deadcode unchanged at 85 all baselined.

It flagged that the design doc had fallen behind the code and left it to me rather than editing a document it did not own. Amended in c652a2b2 — D9 now names the window and says why the instantaneous read was wrong.

title: sessionLane.apply dereferences a nil session and panics the backend, under ci-linux
description:
Found by the coordinator running scripts/ci-linux.sh on the merged tree — CI's own image, which is where it reproduces. The host-side run of the same package passed, and so did the FIRST keyring variant inside ci-linux (263s ok); the SECOND variant panicked. So it is ordering- or timing-dependent, not deterministic.

  panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
  [signal SIGSEGV code=0x1 addr=0xa8]
  internal/transport.(*sessionLane).apply(0xc0000d0240, {0x0, 0x0}, 0xc00087a1f0)
      /src/internal/transport/ws_session_ops.go:197
  internal/transport.(*sessionLane).worker(0xc0000d0240)
      /src/internal/transport/ws_session_ops.go:188
  created by internal/transport.(*sessionLane).enqueue.func1

Note the second argument: {0x0, 0x0} is a NIL INTERFACE. apply's own comment says 'The session reference is read under mu at claim time, so admitClose may nil it out from under a running apply without a race; the local copy keeps the session alive until the resize returns.' That reasoning is half right and the half that is missing is the defect: copying under the mutex removes the DATA RACE, but it does not stop the copied value from already BEING nil when admitClose ran before the copy. sess.Resize on a nil interface then panics, and it panics on a goroutine nobody recovers, so it takes the backend down rather than failing one resize.

Arrived with nocx-eidfb.2 (the active-client resize path). This is a crash in a shipped path, hence P0.

## Steps to Reproduce

./scripts/ci-linux.sh on feat/nocx-server at 62d38687. The first keyring variant passes; the second panics in internal/transport. Not reproducible on the host outside the container, which is why the per-branch gate could not have caught it.
acceptance_criteria: A resize claimed for a session that closes between the claim and the apply does not panic: it is dropped, or it fails that one resize, and the backend survives. Asserted by a test that FORCES the ordering — close between claim and apply — rather than hoping to observe it; a test that only passes because the race did not happen is not a test of this. scripts/ci-linux.sh is green on both keyring variants.
close_reason:
Merged into feat/nocx-server as 4ec7963e. THE DIAGNOSIS IN MY BRIEF WAS WRONG AND THE WORKER CORRECTED IT — worth recording, because the wrong one is the plausible one. I said admitClose nilled the session before the copy. The real cause: a TOMBSTONE LANE REACHED THE MAP OPEN — a lane holding no session that still accepts work — and the worker goroutine that enqueue started then dereferenced nil. The fix is newClosedLane: a tombstone is born closed rather than closed a moment after it is published.

Invariant 4 is now written in the file with both ends named, which is what the brief asked and what the original code lacked: from the moment the worker claims an op out of the pending slot until that op is settled, the lane holds either a usable session or the decision not to use one, never the absence of both. The open half is the constructor's, the closing half is apply's explicit nil branch, and the claim reads session and closed under one mu hold so the pair cannot be torn.

Four regression tests, and they force the ordering rather than hoping to observe it: TestResizeClaimedForALaneWithNoSessionIsAbandoned, TestCloseLaneNeverPublishesAnOpenLane, TestCloseBetweenClaimAndApplyKeepsTheClaimedSession, TestCloseLaneRacingAResizeNeverKillsTheBackend. Run by the coordinator with -race -count=3: ok. A recover on the lane worker was added as defence in depth and logs the panic with its stack, so a future bug in an applied op degrades one resize instead of the process.

Also added: a log line naming the session when a resize is abandoned. A dropped resize has no JSON-RPC request waiting on it, so without that line it is a degrade nobody can see.

ci-linux is NOT green on both variants on this machine, and none of the remaining reds are this bug: across four full runs the panic never returned and transport was green in 6 of 8 variant-runs, with a different test failing each time — one of them (internal/coordinator TestSystemPeerCredentialsReportsThisUser) also fires on a clean-tree baseline. CI remains the source of truth for the rest.

Discovered while proving the fix, in a package the diff never touched, and now filed as nocx-n5j79: LocalPty.Resize reaches the pty file with no lp.mu and no closed check while Close closes it under lp.mu, so a resize during teardown races the descriptor. Pre-existing and structural; nocx-eidfb.2 made it easier to hit by putting resizes on a lane goroutine, but did not create it.

title: Wire serverbin and the coordinator probe into the launcher, or 22 functions stay unreachable
description:
Created by the coordinator's own task split, not by a worker: nocx-ln6ht added internal/update/serverbin and the CoordinatorProbe seam whose only caller is main.go, which nocx-c4wek owned. Both are merged and neither is called. deadcode reports 22 new unreachable functions (20 in serverbin, 2 in the in-process probe); the ratchet is not in pre-commit so commits pass, but ci-mac and ci-linux are red until this lands. AGENTS.md names this exact failure at nocx-z7s6 — a task that adds a Go package lands with the wiring that makes it reachable, and the gate is the hook, not the brief.

1. Inject a CoordinatorProbe into the updater at the update.NewUpdater call in main.go. The launcher already holds the discovery Hello, which carries the coordinator's build — that is the fact pair.go wants. update.NewInProcessCoordinatorProbe exists for a build whose backend is still the window's own process.
2. Call serverbin.Ensure and serverbin.Prune and spawn from the path Ensure returns, instead of the current serverBinaryPath beside the executable. That path is right for the macOS bundle and wrong for an AppImage, which unmounts its FUSE directory when the process exits — the daemon would lose its own executable at exactly the moment it must survive.
3. cmd/nocx-server has no --version, so the release smoke checks cannot assert the coordinator's version independently of the app's. Both link from one LDFLAGS in one step today, so they cannot differ; add the flag if it is cheap. Note that A1.0a deliberately gave that binary no flag parsing at all so a token could not arrive by argv — a valueless --version is fine, a flag taking a value deserves a second thought.
acceptance_criteria: node .githooks/check-deadcode.mjs reports no new unreachable functions against the pre-merge baseline. An update cannot be certified by a window talking to a coordinator of a different build — asserted by a test that drives the sequence, not by reading. On Linux the launcher spawns from the versioned path serverbin.Ensure returned, asserted on the path actually executed.
close_reason:
Merged into feat/nocx-server. deadcode verified by the coordinator, not from the report: all 22 of this task's entries are gone (20 in internal/update/serverbin, 2 in the in-process probe), and none of them were baselined away. The launcher now resolves through serverbin.Ensure and spawns from the path it returns — asserted on the $0 the executed process recorded, so the test proves the path that RAN rather than a file that exists.

TestReportHealthy_MixedPair_CannotCertify drives the real sequence — signed manifest, Check, Apply, restart as a new Updater at 0.2.0, ReportHealthy through a probe attached to a 0.1.0 launch — and the journal is still on disk afterwards. Paired with matching-pair, same-version-different-commit and before-any-coordinator cases.

The worker DELETED NewInProcessCoordinatorProbe rather than call it, and was right to: with the launcher always talking to a real coordinator it has no honest caller, and using it would have certified exactly the mixed pair pair.go exists to refuse. It also added version.Requested rather than copy an argv scan into a second package main; internal/version was outside its stated ownership and it flagged that itself.

Verified by reading only, and CI has to prove: that an AppImage's FUSE mount dies with the launching process, that the macOS bundle ships nocx-server beside nocx, and the darwin branch of Resolve (exercised by passing GOOS darwin, never against a real .app).

title: A host that once got ~/.nocx/launch can never be given a newer one
description:
A host that once received `~/.nocx/launch` keeps that carrier forever, so a host
first connected before the bootstrap rework (31fbbe30, 2026-08-21) still execs a
carrier from the old protocol while nocx sends it the new frames.

Three mechanisms compose into it:

- `publisher.go` `ensureLaunch` wrote the carrier only when ABSENT ("launch
  carrier present, not rewritten").
- `buildManifest` EXCLUDES `launchName`, so the carrier's hash is recorded
  nowhere and no check could notice it was stale.
- `stage1.go` asks only `[ -x "$HOME/.nocx/launch" ]` before exec'ing it —
  existence, never identity.

And nothing converged it: publish skips entirely when the manifest version is
already >= ours (`checkInstalled`), and `Uninstall` walks `m.Files`, which the
carrier is not in — so "remove the footprint" left it too.

Measured on the owner's machine: `~/.nocx/launch` dated Aug 6 beside a manifest
saying version 12, while the app ships version 43; the carrier itself changed on
Aug 5, twice on Aug 8 and again on Aug 21. The comment called it "a stable
carrier over a changing bundle" — the bundle changed, and so did the carrier.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Connect to a host with nocx from before 2026-08-21, so `~/.nocx/launch` is
   written by that build.
2. Update nocx past 31fbbe30 and connect to the same host again.
3. The bundle republishes (or is skipped as already-installed) and the session
   comes up "Not integrated".

Owner's log, nocx.log 2026-08-28T17:32:45.302: "bootstrap stream ended before a
terminal outcome" error="ssh: bootstrap line exceeds the bound", one second
after that host was published v43 with published=true — the generation files
were fresh, the carrier was not. Same host, same error at 15:57:54.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A host carrying a stale carrier converges on the next connection with nobody
  deleting a file by hand.
- A test publishes a bundle, plants a different carrier, publishes again and
  asserts the file on disk is the shipped one — on the already-installed SKIP
  path, which is the path that could never reach it.
- The replacement does not truncate a carrier another session is executing: an
  open handle goes on reading the bytes it started with.

title: A1.2a — native dialogs, notifications and window focus become client-host requests
description:
Design .internal/specs/2026-08-28-the-nocx-server-design.md D3, section 2's ADR-0026 row. main.go's ServiceStartup injects file dialogs, URL opening, notifications, the updater and window focus into the backend before starting it, and file drops mint tickets straight into the backend's source store. With the backend detached these become CLIENT-HOST capabilities: the coordinator routes such a request to an attached client and answers honestly that no UI host is attached when there is none.

ADR-0026 already binds request contexts, disconnect cancellation, native-dialog admission, shutdown draining and multi-client first-consumer behaviour. 'Route it to an attached client' is not enough — WHICH client owns a given ask is already answered there, and that answer is reused rather than re-invented. AD-3 keeps the shell thin: this gives it a job, so read the result against that rule.
acceptance_criteria: Every native-host capability reached through the coordinator works with a client attached, and returns a typed 'no UI host attached' — never a hang and never a silent success — with none attached. Which client serves an ask follows ADR-0026's existing rule rather than a new one. A client that disconnects mid-ask cancels it the way ADR-0026 already specifies.
close_reason:
Merged into feat/nocx-server. The regression is gone: deadcode on the merged epic branch reports 85 unreachable, ALL baselined, exit 0 — none of the 15 functions that the launcher rewrite had orphaned. Verified by the coordinator on the merged tree, not from the report.

The capabilities did not come back as they were, which was the point: they are client-host requests now. internal/app/clienthost is the new seam; ws_clienthost.go routes an ask to an attached client and answers ErrNoUIHost when there is none — one shared sentinel with a per-capability wrapping (ErrNoDialogHost, ErrNoURLHost and so on), so a caller can tell WHICH capability had no host without matching on strings. All three new wire shapes carry additionalProperties:false and an explicit required, and host.request has its OverTheWireConformsToContract test off the real socket.

Run by the coordinator on the worker's tree: go test over transport (103s), notify, wailsadapter and clienthost — all ok.

The worker baselined before blaming: five failures in internal/app are pre-existing and environmental (fork/exec /bin/bash on a host that has no /bin/bash, plus one needing a live sshd), confirmed identical on a detached worktree at unmodified HEAD.

Worth keeping: its first commit carried a stray NUL byte inside a sentinel string in frontend/src/client-host.ts, which made git treat the file as binary. It replaced the sentinel with a typed outcome, rescanned every file in the commit for control characters, and amended.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
RAISED TO P0 — this is now a live regression on the epic branch, not only a refactor.

Merging nocx-c4wek rewrote main.go and dropped the native-host injection entirely, silently: the worker did not report the removal and I merged without running deadcode. Confirmed by diffing the pre-merge main.go, which had all of it (SetDialogService at :242, SetUrlOpener at :255, wailsadapter.New at :289, SetAttentionHost at :322, resolveNotificationPermission at :365). The current main.go has none.

deadcode now reports 15 functions unreachable that were reachable before:
  internal/app/app.go — App.SetDialogService, App.SetUrlOpener, App.SetAttentionHost, App.FocusSession, App.Log, App.Slog
  internal/notify/wailsadapter — 9, including New, Host.Permission, Host.RequestAuthorization, Host.Refresh, Host.handleResponse, Permission.String

So in the product as it stands: no native file dialogs, no URL opening, no notifications, no window focus. That is exactly this task's scope — these become client-host requests routed to an attached client, with an honest 'no UI host attached' when there is none, under ADR-0026, which already binds native-dialog admission, disconnect cancellation and multi-client first-consumer behaviour.

ACCEPTANCE GAINS A HARD LINE: deadcode reports none of those 15 as unreachable when this lands. Restoring them as they were is not the answer either — the point is that they move to the client-host boundary, not that the old injection comes back.

title: DECISION D6 — lossless with the work stopping, or continuing work with a possible gap; amend AD-10 either way
description:
Design .internal/specs/2026-08-28-the-nocx-server-design.md D6. The OWNER decides; this bead blocks the spill work and nothing else.

AD-10 (architecture.md:188) says: bounded credit per session; when credit is exhausted throttle the source; never drop, never grow unbounded; BYTES ARE LOSSLESS AND ORDERED. A bounded spill that discards its oldest content is not lossless, so there is no third answer and an amendment is required either way.

D6-a — lossless, the work stops at the bound. The spill extends the credit; at the bound the source throttles exactly as AD-10 says. A detached session survives up to N bytes and then waits for you. AD-10 gains one sentence: the credit may be backed by disk when no client is attached.

D6-b — the work always continues, the middle of the log may be lost. At the bound the spill discards its oldest bytes and the reclaim reports an explicit gap. AD-10 is amended to permit exactly one lossy case and to require the loss be stated in the product.

Context the decision needs: nocx is lossless TODAY. The existing reset fires when a client asks for an offset it had already acked and the ring has since trimmed; unacked bytes are never discarded. D6-b would be the first place nocx loses a byte.

Also open and deliberately unset: the per-session bound. There is no defensible number in this repository — the only rate-like figure is the illustrative 256 KiB/s at ring.go:20, at which 8 MiB is about half a minute. Measure build output, TUI repaint volume, absence duration and concurrent live sessions first.
acceptance_criteria: The owner has chosen D6-a or D6-b; docs/architecture.md carries the amended AD-10 in the same commit as the choice; and the per-session bound is either a measured number with its measurement recorded, or explicitly deferred to a named follow-up.
close_reason: Superseded by nocx-22k1c. The decision it posed — lossless-and-stop versus continue-with-a-gap — was posed against a spill file that will not be built. The retention policy for recorded output already shipped with nocx-2f0f.5 (four knobs and an eviction path), so the sink's bound is already answered. What remains of the question is narrower and belongs to nocx-22k1c: what the 256 KiB ring does when the recorder is unavailable or slower than the source, given AD-10 requires losslessness and throttling at the bound.

title: A beads clone that falls far behind cannot catch up, and every failed attempt makes the next one slower
description:
This bead's original description said the git-protocol Dolt remote could not be
reached and that `bd dolt pull` never completes. Both claims were too broad, and
the rewrite below is what a day of measurement actually established.

`bd dolt pull` works. Measured 2026-08-28 against the same remote, on a store
in sync with it: **5 seconds**, no leftover process. `bd dolt push` 5 seconds,
`dolt fetch` 2 seconds. Nothing about the remote or the protocol is unusable.

What does not work is catching up from a large divergence. The pull path reads
the carrier one object at a time, forking a fresh `git cat-file blob <sha>` per
read at 20-40 per second and re-reading the same multi-megabyte blobs. The cost
therefore scales with the size of the delta, not with the size of the change
being fetched. On the morning's store -- 881 issues and ~55 commits behind --
it made no measurable progress in eight minutes and was still going when killed.
On an ordinary delta the same code path finishes before you notice it. So the
defect is not "pull is broken"; it is "pull cannot be used to recover a clone
that has fallen far enough behind", which is exactly when it is needed.

**And failure is self-amplifying, which is the part that turned a slow morning
into a lost day.** `.dolt/git-remote-cache` never prunes or dedupes. Every
aborted pull, fetch or clone leaves another full pack behind: one 218MB pack at
09:00 became nine packs and 1.9GB by evening, all near-identical. Every object
read then searches nine archives instead of one, so operations that had been
fast degrade too -- `bd dolt push` went from 3 seconds to over 300, which is
what made the situation look like total breakage rather than a slow recovery.
Each retry makes the next retry worse.

The recovery is one command, and it is not a re-clone:

```
cd .beads/embeddeddolt/<db>/.dolt/git-remote-cache/*/repo.git
git repack -ad          # 1.9GB and 9 packs -> 214MB and 1
```

After that, `bd dolt pull` returned in 5 seconds and everything else with it.
Two full re-clones and a JSONL round-trip were spent before this was found;
neither was necessary.

For a clone too far behind for pull to recover, the standalone `dolt` CLI does
work, because its git-remote adapter takes the bulk path -- one
`git fetch --no-tags --refmap= origin +refs/dolt/data` -- rather than the
per-object loop:

```
cd .beads/embeddeddolt/<db>
dolt fetch && dolt merge origin/main --no-edit
cd - && bd dolt push
```

That reconciled 11 local commits against 55 remote ones with no conflicts, 80
rows added and none deleted. Note the version gap it rests on: the standalone
CLI here is 2.3.1 while beads 1.2.2 embeds `dolthub/dolt/go v0.40.5-0.20260605`.
Note also that the beads docs pin Dolt **2.2.0** and warn that 2.3.x breaks
"the rollback behind `bd dolt pull`" in a few percent of databases; that is a
separate defect from this one -- its symptom is `context canceled` from
`CALL DOLT_RESET('--hard')`, which we never saw -- but this machine is on the
wrong version either way.

Three things worth reporting upstream, in order of how much they cost:

1. The cache never dedupes, so every failed sync permanently costs ~210MB and
   slows every subsequent operation. Failure compounds instead of being inert.
2. The pull read path forks a process per object and does not scale with delta
   size, while clone and `dolt fetch` do the bulk fetch correctly.
3. `bd dolt pull` ignores SIGTERM. `timeout` without `--kill-after` reports 124
   and returns while the process keeps running, holding the embedded store's
   exclusive lock; every worktree on the machine then blocks on `bd ready`,
   `bd create` and `bd export` until somebody finds the pid by hand. Four
   sessions were found queued behind one such orphan, the longest at 85 minutes.
   Contained here by `timeout -k 5` in .githooks/beads-hook.sh, but the ignored
   signal is upstream's.

## Steps to Reproduce

Degradation from repeated failure, which is the reportable part:

1. `ls .beads/embeddeddolt/<db>/.dolt/git-remote-cache/*/repo.git/objects/pack/*.pack | wc -l` -> 1 on a healthy store.
2. Interrupt a `bd dolt pull` or `dolt fetch` several times.
3. Count the packs again: one more per attempt, ~210MB each, none deduped.
4. Time `bd dolt push`: seconds at one pack, minutes at nine.
5. `git repack -ad` in that bare repo restores both the size and the timings.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A clone that has fallen far behind can be brought current without a re-clone,
  and the documented route for it is written down where a reader will find it.
- Repeated failed syncs do not permanently degrade the store: the cache is
  bounded, or bd prunes it.
- A pull interrupted by a timeout leaves no process holding the store lock.
- The upstream report is filed with the measurements above.
- This machine runs the Dolt version the beads docs pin, not 2.3.1.

comments.author: shady
comments.text: Workaround found, and it narrows the defect: a fresh clone of the same remote works. `bd init --remote git+https://github.com/shady2k/nocx.git` completed twice today, pulling ~218MB at 0.6-0.8 MB/s via a single bulk `git fetch --no-tags --refmap= origin +refs/dolt/data:...`, with steady measurable progress throughout. Only pull takes the per-object path that forks `git cat-file blob` ~20/sec and never finishes. So the fix is likely to make pull fetch the way clone does, rather than anything about the remote or the store size. Until then, the recovery route for a diverged clone is: clone into a scratch dir named after the database, swap in .beads/embeddeddolt, `bd import` whatever is local-only, push. That is what nocx-akfl6 did.

title: the local Dolt store is missing 881 issues the tracked JSONL still has, and 284 of them are live
description:
The backlog database in /Users/shady/Documents/repos/nocx/.beads/embeddeddolt
holds 1701 issues. The tracked export .beads/issues.jsonl holds 2579. 881 ids are
in the JSONL and not in Dolt; 3 are in Dolt and not in the JSONL (nocx-61bh7,
nocx-h889z, nocx-s3m67 — today's local work).

Of the 881 missing: 239 open, 42 in_progress, 3 blocked, 597 closed. So ~284 live
issues do not appear in `bd ready`, `bd list` or `bd query` on this machine, and
have not been appearing.

A successful `bd dolt pull` does NOT bring them back, so the shared remote's
refs/dolt/data does not have them either. The JSONL is not stale: its size has
tracked the day's work normally (2569 → 2571 → 2576 → 2579 across commits on
2026-08-27 and 2026-08-28), so the export is current and the Dolt store is what
lost the records.

The only reason the loss has not reached git is bd's own guard: every write
prints "auto-export skipped: … contains 881 JSONL-only issue record(s) …;
refusing to overwrite". That guard is doing its job and is the only thing
standing between this and 881 issues disappearing from the repository. Nothing
should be done that bypasses it.

`bd init --from-jsonl` is the documented remedy, but it must not be run blind:
the 3 Dolt-only issues have to survive it, and other agent sessions on this
machine share the same store and were pulling and writing to it while this was
measured.

## Steps to Reproduce

Measured 2026-08-28:

1. jq -r 'select(._type=="issue") | .id' .beads/issues.jsonl | sort -u  → 2579
2. bd list --status all --limit 100000 --json | jq -r '.[].id' | sort -u → 1701
3. comm -23 of the two → 881 ids only in the JSONL
4. bd dolt pull succeeds and changes neither number.
5. Any bd write prints the auto-export refusal.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `bd list --status all` and .beads/issues.jsonl name the same set of issues,
  with the 3 Dolt-only ids among them.
- `bd ready` offers the live work that was invisible (the 239 open + 42
  in_progress).
- The shared remote carries the restored history, so a second clone reproduces
  it rather than diverging again.
- How the store came to lose 881 records is written down, because a repair that
  does not name the cause is a repair that will be needed again.
close_reason: Store rebuilt as a clone of the remote plus the 11 local-only issues: 2605 in the database and in .beads/issues.jsonl, identical sets, nothing lost from the remote (2594), the previous export (2590), the original tracked set (2579) or the 881. The 284 live issues are back in bd ready, and 15 more arrived that this machine had never seen. bd dolt push succeeded, so the remote carries it and a second clone reproduces it. Three of the four criteria are met; the fourth -- writing down how the store lost the records -- is deliberately dropped by the owner's decision not to investigate. The old store is kept at .beads/embeddeddolt.old, so the evidence still exists if that is ever revisited. The blocks edge on nocx-v48vl was removed rather than forced: publishing no longer depends on pull, because the clone route reaches the remote without it.

comments.author: shady
comments.text: Correction to this bead's own premise, measured 2026-08-28: the shared remote was never missing the 881. A fresh clone holds 2594 issues and lacks none of the 881, none of the 2579 the export tracked, and none of the twelve records the local store had moved on. The inference here -- 'a successful bd dolt pull does NOT bring them back, so the remote does not have them either' -- rested on a pull that never completed; it makes no progress and exits without reporting failure, so its silence described itself, not the remote. The damage was local-only, which is why the repair became a clone rather than a rebuild from JSONL. The remote was also 15 issues AHEAD, including six epics and two in progress that no clone here had ever seen -- a JSONL rebuild could never have recovered those.

title: Escape cannot dismiss the summon when focus sits in the terminal's own hidden textarea
description:
## What happens

2026-08-27. `top` running, the owner summoned the assistant, asked, the turn
reached `completed` — and Escape does not dismiss the summon. There is no other
key or control that does. The pane stays summoned over a running program.

The owner reported earlier in the same session that Escape DID work. Both
reports are true, and the difference is where the focus was. That is the
signature of this defect, not a contradiction between the reports.

## The chain, read from the code

1. **The editor hides itself when the question is submitted.**
   `terminal-content.ts:1545-1550`, `onTurnAccepted`:
   `if (this._summoned && this._summonedAnswer !== null) this.editor?.hide()`
   — deliberate, so the overlay belongs to the answer.

2. **So the second Escape branch never runs.** `:2469` is guarded by
   `this.editor?.isVisible`, which is now false.

3. **The first branch runs and bails on focus.** `:2447-2454`:

       if (e.key === 'Escape' && this._summoned && this._summonedAnswer !== null) {
         const active = document.activeElement
         if (active && isTextEntry(active) && !this.editor?.rootContains(active)) return
         ...

4. **`isTextEntry` is true for xterm's hidden helper textarea.** `:222-227`
   returns true for any `TEXTAREA`. The live grid parks focus there — that is
   how the terminal receives keys — and `rootContains` is false because the
   editor is hidden and contains nothing.

So Escape returns early, no branch owns the dismissal, and the summon has no
exit.

## The asymmetry is already written down one branch below

The `:2469` branch learned this exact lesson and says so:

    "A click on the live grid parks focus in xterm's hidden textarea — the
     terminal's own surface, not somebody else's field: while the editor is up
     the grid is read-only dead space, so the rescue runs here too"

The `:2447` branch — the one that owns dismissing the summon — never got that
carve-out. One of the two branches knows that xterm's textarea is not
"somebody else's text control" and the other does not.

## Confirm before editing

Read as a suspect chain, not a diagnosis. Reproduce and confirm which guard
returns: `isTextEntry(active)`, `hasOpenOverlays()`, or the
`.cmd-overflow-menu` check. All three bail silently and any of them produces
the same symptom.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `top` in a pane.
2. Ctrl/Cmd+Enter, ask anything, let the turn complete.
3. Click on the live grid (or simply leave focus where the terminal put it).
4. Press Escape.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Escape dismisses the summon regardless of where the focus sits, INCLUDING
  xterm's hidden textarea, and the person is back in the program.
- It still does not steal Escape from a real text control that is somebody
  else's, from an open overlay, or from the block action menu. Each is
  asserted, because the risk is a fix that takes the key from a legitimate
  owner.
- The two Escape branches stop disagreeing about what xterm's textarea is.
  Whichever way that is resolved, the answer is written once and both read it —
  the same rule the rest of this file follows for "who owns this input".
- Asserted from the state a person is in — a real summon, focus where the
  terminal parks it, a real Escape — never by calling `dismissSummonedEditor`
  directly. A test that calls the method cannot report that the key never
  reached it.
- The `nocx-7l4ex.5` end-to-end check covers "Escape returns the keys", so this
  case belongs in it rather than in a spec of its own.
acceptance_criteria: See the description's Acceptance Criteria section.
close_reason: Merged as 9c46ff66 + 27594b79. Root cause confirmed by reproduction, not from the suspect chain: isTextEntry(active) returned with document.activeElement an HTMLTextAreaElement inside xterm's live grid. The predicate now takes the terminal surface as a parameter and both Escape chains read it; grep shows one declaration at terminal-content.ts:231. Asserted from a real summon with focus where the terminal parks it and a real Escape.

title: Asking over a full-screen program leaves the answer unreadable: nothing is visible and nothing scrolls
description:
## What the owner did, and what happened

2026-08-27. `top` running in the pane. Pressed Ctrl/Cmd+Enter to ask the
assistant — the summon this epic exists for. Then:

- the answer's text was not visible;
- nothing scrolled.

## What is NOT part of this, established while triaging

Two things the owner reported first and then corrected or that turned out to be
deliberate. They are written down so nobody re-opens them:

- **Escape works.** The owner's first report said it did not; the second says
  it does. The summoned editor closes and the program comes back.
- **The target switch to Run is refused ON PURPOSE, and it says so.**
  `terminal-content.ts:4156-4169` refuses `shell` while the editor is summoned,
  and its own comment states the reason: "the summoned editor's only legal
  target is the assistant, so there is no state from which Enter could reach
  the pty. Said out loud rather than swallowed — a deliberate gesture that does
  nothing in silence reads as a broken control."

  So "cannot switch to Run" is the design. What the refusal does not say is how
  to LEAVE — a person reads why a command cannot start, not that Escape is the
  door. That is filed separately; it is not this bead.

## The defect that remains

The answer was not readable and the pane did not scroll, over a frozen
full-screen program.

`nocx-7l4ex` built this journey in four children, all closed: the overlay
exists over a running command and over a full-screen program (.1), the screen
freezes while the box is open and the program is never told (.2),
`session.read` in that turn reads the pinned frame (.3), and the answer lives
in the overlay and then takes its seat in the scrollback (.4).

Each proved its own half in unit tests. **The epic's own sentence has never
been watched end to end — that is `nocx-7l4ex.5`, still open.** This bead is
the defect; `.5` is the check that would have caught it. Whoever takes either
should look at both, and the honest order is probably to write `.5` first and
let it fail.

## Do not assume which half is wrong

Two candidates, and the bead must establish which before editing:

1. The answer never took its seat (.4's path), so there is nothing to see.
2. The answer is there, but the frozen frame is still pinned over the viewport,
   so nothing scrolls because what is on screen is not the scrollback (.2's
   freeze, `frame/display.ts` — the "Screen frozen while you ask" marker was
   visible in the owner's screenshots the whole time).

A screenshot the owner sent afterwards shows the answer block present and
complete beneath the `top` block, which points at 2 rather than 1 — but a
screenshot after the fact is not evidence about what the pane did at the time.
Reproduce.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `top` in a pane.
2. Press Ctrl/Cmd+Enter and ask something about the screen.
3. Try to read the answer and scroll.

## Acceptance Criteria

- After asking over a full-screen program, the answer is READABLE: it is on
  screen, and the scrollback scrolls.
- The program was not resized, redrawn or interrupted by any of it — a program
  that repaints on SIGWINCH does not repaint.
- Output the program wrote during the freeze is on screen after the thaw, and
  the program can be quit normally afterwards.
- Watched end to end in a real browser against a real backend, waiting on
  observable state and never on a duration. This is the same check
  `nocx-7l4ex.5` specifies; if that bead is done first, this one is its failing
  case rather than a second spec.
acceptance_criteria: See the description's Acceptance Criteria section.
close_reason: Merged as da251df9, 430b80f4 and e9cbfb0a — three rounds, and each found a different cause, none of them the two the bead named. (1) The answer WAS seated; reparenting it out of the overlay extends the scrollback after the command-end settle has measured, so the tail stayed below the fold. (2) That fix was a no-op on the merged tree because the deferred anchor took 'the last .cmd-block in the DOM' and the newly seated answer IS that block — top went 1219 back to 1135, tail 27px below the viewport. The frozen BlockRecord is now threaded through all six freeze paths, which also closes the same latent assumption in nocx-4ff.39. (3) Chromium then passed and WebKit did not: WebKit applies the reparented node's layout after the task that reads the scroll height. A one-shot ResizeObserver — the first observable point at which the seated node owns its final box — then the same scrollToBottomIfFollowing. Conditioned on what the DOM reports, never on the engine. Verified both engines and five repeats of each; the full suite is 440 passed.

title: The '@' picker answers a sealed vault with nothing at all
description:
Typing `@` in any API workbench value field renders no panel. Reproduced by the
owner on a dev stand whose vault was sealed (nocx-dev; backend restarted 21:20,
no unseal after it).

The trigger is NOT at fault: `findTrigger('@', 1)` in
`frontend/src/ui/secret-picker-field.ts` returns `{from:0,to:1,filter:''}`. A
bare `@` is recognised.

The failure is downstream, in `SecretPicker.open()`
(`frontend/src/ui/secret-picker.ts`), and it is INVISIBLE by construction:

    } catch {
      this.close()
    }

Any rejection from `source.status()` closes the panel with no row, no toast and
no log line. A sealed vault is supposed to render the "Unlock the vault to use
its secrets" offer instead — the owner's decision that the panel OFFERS rather
than traps. The owner sees neither the offer nor a prompt, so `status()`
rejected and the catch ate it.

Why the suite stayed green: NO test ever types a bare `@`. Every e2e fills
`@` plus the name in one `fill()` — a single input event carrying the whole
string — and the unit tests drive `onInput` directly. The moment a person
actually lives — "I typed @ and I am waiting for the panel" — is asserted
nowhere.

This makes the `@` door unreachable in practice, which is the owner's point: a
person unlocks the vault only when asked, and this path never asks.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the app on a dev stand whose vault is SEALED (a backend restart seals
   it; `~/.local/share/nocx-dev/nocx.log` shows "vault sealed" with no later
   "vault unsealed").
2. Open the API workbench, open any request, go to the Headers tab.
3. Click into an empty header VALUE field.
4. Type a single `@`.

Expected: the secret picker opens showing the "Unlock the vault to use its
secrets" offer row.
Actual: nothing renders at all. No panel, no row, no toast, no log line.
acceptance_criteria:
DONE WHEN a person with a SEALED vault types a bare '@' in a header value and sees the unlock offer row, and a person with an UNINITIALIZED vault sees the setup offer row — asserted by a check that types '@' as a keystroke, not as part of a filled string.

Also true when it is done:

- The catch in SecretPicker.open() no longer swallows. Whatever it caught reaches a log line AND the panel, as a row a person can read. A silent degrade the UI contradicts is how a feature that does not exist survives a release.
- The actual cause of the rejection is NAMED in this bead before the fix lands. 'It throws somewhere' is not a diagnosis.
- One test types a bare '@' and asserts the panel appears, for each of the three vault states.
- The existing e2e specs that fill '@name' in one call keep working; they are not the fix.
notes:
CAUSE FOUND, 2026-08-27, by the e2e suite on the merged wA-integration tree.

The panel is not missing. It is rendered ABOVE THE TOP OF THE WINDOW.

.ui-floating-panel is 'position: absolute; bottom: 100%' — written for the
terminal, where prompt-vault.ts mounts it into editor.root, which is
position: relative, so 'bottom: 100%' means 'just above the prompt'.

secret-picker-field.ts:150 mounts the SAME panel into document.body. The body
is static, so the containing block is the initial containing block: bottom:
100% puts the panel's BOTTOM edge at y=0 and the whole panel above it,
off-screen. applyGeometry only ever sets width and left, never top.

So every plain-input door — the API workbench's URL, header, parameter, body
and Auth fields, the connections editor, the endpoints page — has always
opened its panel out of sight. That is the owner's silence, and it is why the
sealed-vault theory never reproduced: the sealed path was fine, the panel was
simply not where anyone could see it.

WHY THE SUITE STAYED GREEN: every existing test drove the panel with the
KEYBOARD (type '@name', press Enter), and unit tests run in jsdom where
visibility is not geometric. nocx-3o0ed.4's specs are the first to CLICK a
row, and 10 of them failed across two browsers with the same words —
'element is visible, enabled and stable' plus 'element is outside of the
viewport', with scrolling into view changing nothing.

The refused-state work already committed (a7d45e6f) stands and is not undone
by this: silence on a refused read was a second defect on the same path.
close_reason: Cause was geometry, not the vault. The panel is position:absolute bottom:100%, written for the terminal's relative editor root; mounted on document.body its containing block is the ICB, so it rendered entirely above the top of the window — every plain-input door had always opened it out of sight. Fixed by a typed viewport-anchoring variance on FloatingPanel (ad0ff2e2), a pointer-events declaration for the relocated panel (8c133301), and a hover guard so the list stops rebuilding under the cursor (85c754bd). Every suite had stayed green because every test drove the panel by keyboard and jsdom lays nothing out. Full e2e now 421 passed; the one remaining failure is an unrelated webkit flake, filed. Two further defects found and filed rather than folded in: row activation on mousedown, and the dialog's light-dismiss having no exemption for a relocated panel (nocx-le5ic).

title: An operation-stance credential read inside a capability admission holds the vault gate, so the unlock it raises cannot be answered
description:
PR 108 (nocx-k41yv) routes credential reads through the vault's EnsureUnsealed.
Two of those reads happen INSIDE a capability admission that holds the vault
gate: capability.secretService.GetSecret (secrets.saveKeyPassphrase) and
resolveVaultSecret (vault.resolveLine). The prompt is raised from inside the
gate; the vault.unseal the renderer must call to answer it needs the same gate
(capacity 1, 1 s wait) and is refused -32004 control-saturated. unlockResolved
is only sent after unseal succeeds, so the operation is stranded and the vault
cannot be unlocked at all.

This contradicts the PR's own ADR-0032 amendment ("no control read loop or
capability admission blocks on unlock") and its design spec section 2.3. The
invariant has no test; both new e2e specs exercise agent.ask, the one path that
holds no domain gate.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Vault initialised and then sealed (auto-seal on idle is the ordinary way in).
2. A private key is already stored; the key-passphrase prompt is open.
3. Press Save, i.e. call secrets.saveKeyPassphrase over the wire.
4. The backend raises vault.unlockRequest with reason "load the secret".
5. Enter the passphrase in the dialog: vault.unseal answers after ~1.0 s with
   {"code":-32004,"message":"Control plane busy",
    "data":{"reason":"control-saturated","scope":"vault"}}.
6. The dialog cannot be satisfied; the save stays blocked until it is cancelled.

On main step 3 answers -32001/vault-sealed immediately and the renderer's
replay completes the save.
acceptance_criteria: vault.unseal over the wire succeeds while a credential-reading operation waits for the unlock, asserted by a transport test; internal/capability holds no credential.Resolver, asserted by an architecture test; credential.Unsealer is a named interface wired at the composition root with no structural type assertion; the design spec's architecture-test claim is either met or withdrawn
close_reason: Fixed in d4818e78 on the PR-108 branch. The wait is lifted above every capability admission: internal/capability holds no credential.Resolver (asserted by material_boundary_test.go), SecretService lost GetSecret and ResolveLine became PlanLine + a pure SubstituteLine, and both handlers resolve material between two short operations. credential.Unsealer replaced the two anonymous EnsureUnsealed assertions, wired explicitly in app.go and via WithVaultUnsealer. Two transport tests carry it: the raised unlock can be answered and the operation continues, and a dismissed one answers as the cancellation. Pre-commit gate green. Remaining: nocx-0dvf2 (lane permits held across the wait).

title: Reconcile and review PR 108 against current main
description: Merge current origin/main into PR #108, preserve explicit vault unlock intent and the ADR-0011 secret boundary, resolve conflicts semantically, review the effective PR delta, fix findings, validate request and run paths, and push the PR branch. GitHub PR merge is explicitly out of scope. Discovered while updating nocx-k41yv.
acceptance_criteria: PR #108 contains current origin/main with no unresolved conflicts; main behavior and ADR-0011/ADR-0032 invariants survive; review findings are fixed with observable tests; targeted validation is green; the updated commit is pushed to the PR head branch without merging the PR.

title: [bug] Five API e2e specs assert doors the workbench deliberately moved
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

`./e2e/run-in-container.sh`, or CI run 32849934578 at 58a1b1aa. Five specs fail
identically in chromium AND webkit — reproducible, not flake:

    api-folder-variable.spec.ts:127  region 'Folder variables' not found
    api-move.spec.ts:99              menu gained 'Close request'
    api-secret-in-path.spec.ts:99    response body no longer the compact bytes
    api-tree.spec.ts:193             #api-save-request not found
    api-tree.spec.ts:327             menu gained 'Close request'

Six of the other CI jobs are green at the same SHA, including ci-mac.

## Root cause

Each is a spec left behind by a DELIBERATE product change on this branch. The
unit suite was updated for all five; the e2e specs were not, so nothing caught
them until the containerized run.

- `39ceab54` put the folder's variables editor behind a `Tabs` section, and the
  page opens on Contents. The region exists but is not rendered until the
  Variables tab is picked.
- `ff2c2a1d` removed the folder page's Save button — folder variables autosave,
  and a "Saved" status replaced the button.
- `0ca67708` removed `#api-save-request`; saving a request stopped being a
  gesture (nocx-2aunx).
- `8a54e106` added 'Close request' to a request row's menu (nocx-8aczn.10). Both
  menu specs assert the label list with `toEqual`, so an ADDED act fails them.
- `ca0fa90b` lays the response body out for reading and keeps Raw as the bytes,
  so the pretty-printed view carries a line-number gutter and indentation.

## Acceptance Criteria

- All five specs pass in `./e2e/run-in-container.sh` for both projects.
- Each keeps its ORIGINAL intent: the folder-variable spec still proves a folder
  variable is saved and inherited by a request that sends; the secret-in-path
  spec still proves the token reaches the server and appears nowhere on screen —
  the security assertions are not weakened to make the body assertion pass.
- No spec is deleted or skipped to reach green.
close_reason: All five specs pass in the container, both projects (7 passed chromium, 7 passed webkit). Each kept its intent: the folder spec still proves a folder variable is saved and inherited by a request that sends; the secret-in-path spec's security assertions were untouched and only the body comparison moved to .cm-content with the layout's whitespace removed. Nothing was skipped or deleted. Found on the way: the folder spec's 'region' locator had never matched anything — EditableRowList draws a labelled <table>, whose role is table, and only once it has rows.

title: A person who approves one harmless command must not be granting every destructive one
description:
Reported by the owner 2026-08-24 with two screenshots: they asked how much disk space was free, the assistant proposed `df -h`, they pressed "Allow always", and the Agent policy page now reads "Make changes that cannot be undone — Allowed". They approved one read-only command and granted every destructive operation, permanently.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Ask the assistant a read-only question about the machine ("сколько у меня свободного места?").
2. It proposes `run` with `df -h`. The approval window says "This call can make changes that cannot be undone".
3. Press **Allow always**.
4. Open Settings → Agent policy.

Observed: "Make changes that cannot be undone — **Allowed**". Every destructive call from now on runs without asking.
Expected: approving one harmless command grants, at most, harmless commands.

## What is true in the code

**1. The effect is a property of the TOOL, not of the CALL.** `internal/agenttools/registry.go:149` declares `run` with `Effect: content.EffectMutateDestructive`, unconditionally. Nothing refines it per command — grepping `EffectMutateDestructive` finds the declaration, the lattice member list and the validator, and no derivation from the proposed command. So `df -h`, `ls` and `rm -rf /` are one effect class. The approval window then describes the TOOL truthfully while telling the person something false about the CALL, which means the sentence that should make somebody careful is the sentence that trains them to ignore it.

**2. "Always" is a rule over the effect class.** `applyStandingAnswer` (`internal/transport/ws_agent.go`) calls `globalPolicy.Policy().SetRowDecision(effect, permit)` — one row of the global matrix, for the effect the BACKEND classified the proposal under. That half is deliberate and right: ADR-0028 decision 4 forbids a rule over a tool NAME, because a rule over a name is bypassed by a different spelling of the same call. Combined with (1) it means the FIRST "always" a person ever presses grants everything.

The window does say so — "An answer of always is a standing answer for make changes that cannot be undone, which you can change on the Agent policy page" — in the third paragraph, which is exactly the prose the owner separately reported as unreadable and which `nocx-0mvpy.2` has now cut into rows. Legibility helps and does not fix this: the person would still be reading a TRUE sentence about a MISCLASSIFIED call.

## Where the fix probably is — not decided here

The effect must be derived from the canonical invocation rather than from the row that declares the tool. `nocx-d6gn4.3` ("One effect kernel: both carriers become the same canonical invocation before policy") is the neighbouring work and this bead should be read with it.

The classifier cannot help: `nocx-kpy23` lets it RAISE permit to ask and never lower, and it is consulted only where the policy already says permit.

**Do not fix this by letting the renderer or the model name the effect.** ADR-0028 decision 4 puts that with the backend and nowhere else.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A read-only command proposed through `run` — `df -h`, `ls`, `cat` — is not presented to the person as a call that can make changes that cannot be undone.
- Pressing "Allow always" on such a call does not leave the global policy with "Make changes that cannot be undone — Allowed".
- Whatever the person grants, the window states the BLAST RADIUS of the answer in the same place they read the call, not only in a paragraph below it, and a test asserts that sentence by name.
- One automated check watches a person approve a harmless command and then finds that a destructive one still asks.
- ADR-0028 decision 4 and the classifier's direction of travel both still hold afterwards, or are changed deliberately with the ADR amended in the same commit.
notes:
OWNER DECISIONS 2026-08-24, after a design discussion. Two things settled, one still open.

SETTLED 1 — run keeps ONE command string. Splitting it into argv was considered and rejected by the owner: run exists to go through the same submit path a person uses, which is what makes pipelines, redirections, globs and && work. The assistant produced 'du -h --max-depth=2 -x / 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -20' in the reported session; argv cannot express it. A parsed representation may sit BESIDE the verbatim string for the approval window and the policy — never instead of it.

SETTLED 2 — anything we do not understand is dangerous. The effect of a compound command is the JOIN of its parts over the existing content.Effect lattice, worst wins:
  du -h | sort -rh | head -20  ->  observe
  ls && rm -rf /tmp/x          ->  destructive
  cat f > /etc/passwd          ->  destructive (the redirect is a write)
and every construct we cannot resolve keeps the declared worst case. Lowering is therefore permitted ONLY for a closed allowlist of programs known to read, and ONLY when the command contains none of: a program in a variable position (, ); a carrier of somebody else's program (sudo, env, xargs, sh -c, find -exec, git -c core.pager); command substitution (, backticks, process substitution); any redirection to a file; backgrounding; tee.

Note the asymmetry and record it deliberately: the classifier (nocx-kpy23) may only RAISE suspicion and never lower it. This parse does the opposite — it may lower from run's declared worst case. That is the whole point of it and it is why the disqualifying list above is a hard gate rather than heuristics.

THE HOLE THAT PARSING CANNOT CLOSE, and it must be written into whatever ADR comes out of this: an ALIAS OR SHELL FUNCTION LIES. 'ls' may be a function in the person's rc files, resolved by THEIR shell, which nocx does not read. Our parse is not the shell's.

Why that hole is nevertheless bounded, and the argument the fix rests on: a lowered call becomes 'observe', and the default policy for Read and inspect is 'Ask every time'. So a misclassified alias still asks, and the person still reads the command TEXT before answering. What they lose is not the question — it is only the blanket grant. The win is precisely that 'Allow always' on df -h stops writing 'make changes that cannot be undone: Allowed'.

STILL OPEN, and the coordinator's own reading is that this may be the better lever: the blast radius of 'always' itself. Today one click writes a row of the global matrix for the whole effect class. Narrowing what a standing yes covers needs no shell parsing at all. The two are not exclusive; whoever takes this bead should say which one they are doing and why, and an ADR is the right home for the answer.

RESEARCH 2026-08-25, owner asked how other harnesses solve this. Two were
read: Claude Code's permission docs and the pi-permission-system package.
Both converge, and both AGREE WITH SETTLED 2 above rather than with the
argHash alternative that was considered and dropped.

Claude Code keys a rule on the COMMAND, never on the tool or an effect class:
the table's "Yes, and don't ask again" behaviour for Bash is "Permanently per
repository and command", written as Bash(npm run test *). Four rules make a
command pattern safe, and each one matches a clause of SETTLED 2:

  - A compound command is split and the rule must match EVERY subcommand.
    The separators are named: && || ; | |& & and newline. Bash(safe-cmd *)
    does not permit `safe-cmd && other-cmd`.
  - Approving a compound command saves a SEPARATE rule per subcommand (up to
    5), never one rule for the whole string.
  - Exec wrappers cannot be prefix-approved at all: watch, setsid, ionice,
    flock, and find with -exec or -delete always prompt. Only an exact-match
    rule for the full string approves those.
  - A rule may not match the tool's primary content field: Bash(command:rm *)
    is IGNORED with a startup warning, precisely because a compound command
    would bypass it.
  - Word boundary: Bash(ls *) matches `ls -la` and not `lsof`.

pi-permission-system reaches the same place from a different direction: rules
over tool names, bash wildcard patterns ("git *: ask", "rm -rf *: deny") and
path patterns; four layers with MOST-RESTRICTIVE-WINS; unparseable commands
resolve to `ask` (fail-closed); and the approval offers only `once` and `for
session` — there is no `always` in the window at all.

THE PRINCIPLE THAT NAMES OUR DEFECT EXACTLY, from the Claude Code docs:
"Claude Code offers those options only when the prompt CAN SHOW YOU
EVERYTHING THEY WOULD ALLOW, so a rule you save from a prompt covers only
what its option named."

Our window showed `df -h` and saved "every irreversible change". That is the
inversion of this rule, and it is the whole bug in one sentence.

DISPOSITION OF ADR-0028 DECISION 4. It forbids a rule over a tool NAME
because a different spelling bypasses it. The objection is correct and both
references ANSWER it rather than ignore it — subcommand splitting, word
boundaries, wrapper disqualification, and refusing rules over the primary
content field are exactly the conditions under which a command rule is sound.
So §4 is not overturned; it gains the conditions. Amend it in the same commit
as the code, per the acceptance criteria.

ALSO MISSING AND WORTH RECORDING: we have no project/repository level at all
— only "this session" and "global". Both references have a middle level and
in both it carries most of the load. Claude Code writes a prompt-saved rule
to .claude/settings.local.json at the REPOSITORY root, so its default radius
is a project, not a machine.

OWNER DECISION 2026-08-25: do it the way the references do — SETTLED 2's
parse plus "the window may only save what it showed", with ADR-0028 §4
amended in the same commit. The argHash-only variant was rejected as nearly
useless: df -h would be permitted while df -h / asked again, training the
person to press always on every variant.
close_reason: all five criteria met and merged into feat/ai-assistant. df -h classifies as observe so the window describes the CALL not the tool; allow always on it leaves the destructive row at ask; each answer control states its own radius, always naming effect + every session + no expiry; one run proves the read half by escalating a destructive proposal after the harmless always; ADR-0028 decision 4 amended with the soundness conditions rather than deleted, and the classifier's raise-only direction is untouched. Gates run once on the merged tree before anything reaches main.

title: agent.cancel: the method, the teardown, and the run's own word for stopped
description:
agent.cancel exists only as a name in comments: internal/transport/ws_assistant.go:10, internal/content/ledger.go:824, and the generated agent.ask contract ('a later agent.cancel/agent.approve/agent.status addresses the run by this id'). Registered methods are exactly agent.captureFrame, agent.ask, agent.approve (ws_agent.go:2062-2070).

A command's Stop is a different mechanism and is NOT the model for this: terminal-content.ts:1282 signalActiveCommand('stop') puts a signal into the PTY. A turn has no PTY; it has a live provider stream, possibly a suspended approval, and an open ledger run.
acceptance_criteria:
- agent.cancel is a registered method with a contract in contracts/, validated params, and the three tests contracts/README requires (generated types match the schema, the Go DTO conforms, and the real result off the real socket conforms).
- Cancelling a streaming run terminalizes it within one second with a state that says A PERSON STOPPED IT — its own word, not 'failed' — and the prose already received is kept.
- The model stream and any in-flight tool call are torn down; no delta, no tool result and no approval question arrives after the cancel is answered.
- Cancelling a run that is already terminal, or a run id that never existed, is answered honestly and cancels nothing.
- A cancelled run's ledger record is complete on the next start: state the invariant with BOTH ends (what is true from before the cancel is written until the run's terminal row references it) and test the partial failures.
- The ask/approve paths still behave exactly as their existing tests say.
close_reason: merged at e7cb7f7e; gate green including go test -race in container

title: A refusal reaches the model as the call's result, and the turn answers
description:
internal/transport/ws_agent.go:1363-1376 — on !p.Approved: applyStandingAnswer, ClearRetained, then terminalize(RunFailed, TermAgentDeclined, 'the run was declined'). internal/assistant/policy.go:395-401 — policyRefuse returns PolicyRefusedError through tripLatch, same end.

Both contradict internal/assistant/systemprompt.go, 'What you can do': 'A refusal is an answer: say what you could not do and what you would need, and never route around it…'. The approved design agrees — .internal/specs/2026-08-21-what-the-model-is-told-design.md §2 has 'refused by policy' as a factual line a turn contributes to the conversation.

Boundaries: ADR-0028 (eino runs the loop, the grant is ours) — the refusal must be produced by our middleware and travel as the call's result, not as a framework error rendered into prose. AD-8: 'what happened to this call' has one owner. Do not weaken the gate: this changes only what happens AFTER a decision to refuse, never the decision.
acceptance_criteria:
- A policy decision of refuse produces a TOOL RESULT the model receives, naming the tool and why it was refused in our words, and the run continues. The turn reaches a terminal state of its own accord, with prose.
- A person's Deny does the same: the run resumes with the refusal as that call's result rather than terminalizing.
- 'Deny always' and 'deny in this session' additionally tell the model the refusal is standing, so it does not re-propose the same call in the same turn. A test watches a model that retries be told the second time that it is standing.
- The refusal text is OURS (nocx-avogl.3), never eino's, and never leaks policy internals the person did not choose to show.
- A run still terminalizes on real breakage — a dead stream, a malformed model output, the ask cap — and the tests that hold those lines still pass.
- For every external call this path makes, there is a test where that call fails.
close_reason: merged into feat/ai-assistant; pre-commit gate green including go test -race in container

title: A refusal is an answer, and a turn can be stopped
description:
Two defects the owner found on 2026-08-24, both in how a run ends.

REFUSAL KILLS THE TURN. handleApprove (internal/transport/ws_agent.go:1363-1376): on !p.Approved it calls terminalize(... RunFailed, TermAgentDeclined, 'the run was declined'). The model is never told; the turn is simply dead. A policy refusal without a question ends the same way — policy.go:395-401 returns PolicyRefusedError and tripLatch takes the run down.

This contradicts what we already tell the model. internal/assistant/systemprompt.go, section 'What you can do': 'Some calls run straight away, some are put to the person for approval first, and some are refused. A refusal is an answer: say what you could not do and what you would need, and never route around it with another tool or a different spelling of the same call.' We promise the model a refusal is an answer and then deny it the chance to give one. The approved design says the same in the conversation's vocabulary — .internal/specs/2026-08-21-what-the-model-is-told-design.md §2 lists 'refused by policy' as one of the factual lines a turn contributes.

NO WAY TO STOP. agent.cancel exists ONLY as a name in comments — ws_assistant.go:10, content/ledger.go:824, and the generated agent.ask contract ('a later agent.cancel/agent.approve/agent.status addresses the run by this id'). The registered methods are exactly three: agent.captureFrame, agent.ask, agent.approve (ws_agent.go:2062-2070). A command has Stop through a different mechanism entirely — running.stop() → signalActiveCommand('stop') (terminal-content.ts:1282), a signal into the PTY — which a turn has no equivalent of.

Boundaries this epic crosses and what they already decided: ADR-0028 (eino runs the loop, the grant is ours) — the refusal result must be produced by OUR middleware, not by letting the framework surface its own error text; nocx-avogl.3 already established that a refused or failed run says what happened in our words.
acceptance_criteria:
REFUSAL. A person sets a policy that refuses `run`, then asks the assistant to do something that needs it. The assistant is told, as the call's result, that the call was refused and by what — the policy's standing decision, or the person's denial of this exact call — and it ANSWERS in words: what it could not do and what it would need. The turn reaches 'completed', not a dead header. The same holds for a person pressing Deny on the approval window, and a 'deny always' additionally tells the model not to propose it again in this turn.

STOP. A person asks a question and presses Stop while it is thinking. The run terminalizes as stopped-by-the-person — its own word, not 'failed' — within one second, the model stream and any in-flight tool are torn down, whatever prose had arrived is kept, and the next question works normally. Both watched end to end by one automated check.

## Deliberately out
- Resuming a stopped run. Stop ends it; asking again is a new question.
- Changing what the policy DECIDES. This epic changes only what happens to the turn after it has decided.

title: A drip of bells can evict a real unread notification from the feed
description:
MEASURED by the worker that wired `bell` (nocx-n3nfg part 2), against the real
code and the real VT parser, not argued:

The catalogue default-deny keeps bells out of every SINK -- `bell` has no
DefaultChannels, Router.Resolve returns an empty route set, no banner, no toast,
no sound. That half is safe.

The FEED is a different path and is unconditional. Ingress.Admit records into
the feed FIRST and submits for delivery SECOND, deliberately, so a suppressed
event is still remembered. So every accepted notify.bell becomes a feed
occurrence whatever the channels say.

Numbers, from internal/app/app.go:514-516 and internal/notify/feed.go:

- CollapseWindow is 30s; collapseKeyOf is {Backend, SessionID, Kind, Level} and
  reads no title or body. A CONTINUOUS run of bells collapses into ONE row
  reading "Bell xN" -- collapsibleLocked scans backwards past intervening
  events, so this holds for as long as the run lasts. This is the common case
  and it is fine.
- The bad case is bells MORE than 30s apart: each starts a fresh row. One bell
  every 31s is ~116 rows/hour against MaxOccurrences = 200.
- victimLocked evicts the oldest READ occurrence, and when everything is unread
  it evicts index 0 -- the oldest unread, which may be a genuine notification.
