2. The rewrite now had to be gated on _shellIntegrated. The new line is
POSIX/bash/zsh syntax where the inline one parsed anywhere, and pty_local.go
honours $SHELL, so a fish or csh tab would have taken 'then' as a command and
never run the ssh. Both happy-path tests had never fired a marker, so both were
asserting the rewrite in an unintegrated tab — the state the feature is not for.

Left open deliberately: nocx-eeyf (discovered-from). bash's readline is in raw
mode, so MAX_CANON is not obviously what truncated the owner's session, and a
35 KB single write into a real interactive bash arrived complete in the harness.
Whatever loses bytes on the renderer's side of the paste is shared by every
large paste. This fix is below every candidate threshold either way.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
REOPENED 2026-08-04. The rewrite ships a command line the tty cannot carry, and the owner's screenshot is the payload being truncated and its tail executed as garbage.

MEASURED, not reasoned:

- StartCommand(ShellAuto, ...) returns 34856 bytes. The three embedded scripts are 17470 (bash) + 3260 (zsh) + 2686 (posix) = 23416 raw, and `printf %b` octal-escaping inflates that to ~34.8 KB.
- A real Linux pty in canonical mode was driven directly (pty.fork + cat, echo on): 4095 bytes on one line survive intact; 8000 already lose data; 34856 come back as 27873. The canonical line buffer is 4096 bytes (N_TTY_BUF_SIZE); getconf MAX_CANON reports 255.

So the line is cut mid-script and the shell executes the fragments — which is exactly what the screenshot shows: script text with its comments printed to the terminal, \0012 escapes intact, ending at `> "$d/env" ... exec "${SHELL:-/bin/sh}" -l;`.

This is a CHANNEL CAPACITY problem, not a quoting one. The managed path does not have it because it hands the command to sshd over the SSH protocol, where no line discipline is involved. A typed ssh has only the tty.

A second, independent defect in the same construction: the dispatcher is `sh -c '<disp>' "$0" '<bash>' '<zsh>' '<posix>'` and `$0` is expanded by whichever shell parses the line. On the managed path that is the far shell, which is the point — it is how the far side names itself. Typed locally, the LOCAL shell expands it first, so the far side is told it is whatever the local shell is called. The dispatcher would pick the wrong arm even if the payload fitted.

## The way out, and why it is still safe

The safe half of nocx-pu4.6 stands: we act at the LOCAL prompt, inside our own integrated shell, BEFORE ssh runs — so nothing is ever typed into a password prompt. What has to change is delivery: a single line cannot carry 34 KB, but many lines can, and typing many lines at OUR OWN prompt is not the hazard that typing into an unknown foreground process was.

Shapes worth measuring before choosing:
1. A here-doc at the local prompt assembling the payload into a shell variable, then `ssh -t host "$payload"`. Each line stays under the limit.
2. A wire-minified copy of the scripts (they are heavily commented ON PURPOSE — the comments are the documentation, and they are most of the 23 KB). Measure nocx.posix minified; it may fit a single line on its own.
3. Choosing ONE tier rather than shipping all three, which needs the far shell's identity — and $0 cannot give it to us here.

Do not fix by escaping. Measure the resulting byte count against the 4096 limit and put THAT number in the test.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
MEASURED 2026-08-05, before touching code — the reopening comment names two defects; only the first is real.

Defect 1 (channel capacity) CONFIRMED. StartCommand(ShellAuto) is 35243 bytes on this
tree; the whole rewritten line is 35286. Single tiers: bash 23572, zsh 7259, posix 4218 —
so even the smallest tier alone does not fit a 4096-byte canonical line. Minifying the
scripts cannot close a 8.6x gap, and shipping one tier needs the far shell's identity we
do not have. The payload must leave the tty.

Defect 2 ($0 expanded by the LOCAL shell) REFUTED. The reopening reasoned it from the
dispatcher's shape; the shipped construction does not have it. ws_shell_launcher.go:112
wraps the WHOLE launcher in shellQuote before the renderer appends it, so the local shell
sees "$0" inside a single-quoted word and never expands it. Measured: the real 35243-byte
launcher was built, quoted, spliced into 'ssh -t user@host <quoted>', and run under both
bash 5.3 and /bin/sh with ssh replaced by an argv printer. argv[3] came back 35243 bytes,
byte-identical to the launcher, with the literal "$0" intact, on both shells. There is no
$0 fix to make; do not encode one as an acceptance criterion.

FIX: keep the payload off the tty. The backend stages the launcher into a private 0600
file and returns its PATH; the renderer types a short line that lets the LOCAL shell read
the file and hand the bytes to ssh through argv (bounded by ARG_MAX, not MAX_CANON):

  if [ -s 'P' ]; then ssh -t <flags> <dest> "$(cat 'P')"; else <the line the user typed>; fi

Command-substitution output is not re-scanned for expansion, so "$0" still reaches the far
login shell unexpanded — verified on bash and sh. The [ -s ] guard is the fail-open: a
missing or empty file runs exactly what the user typed, never 'ssh host ""'.

Rejected: an env var carrier (NOCX_REMOTE_LAUNCHER on the local pty). It taxes every child
exec with 35 KB, is visible in /proc/pid/environ, can be unset by the user's rc, and — the
decisive one — is chosen at spawn, so a nested shell or a pre-existing tmux server hands a
later tab a stale session id. A backend-chosen path in the line is correct by construction.
Consulted codex on the carrier choice; it independently reached the same conclusion and
caught the defect-2 error.

title: The launcher is built and nobody can reach it from main()
description:
internal/shellintegration/launcher.go builds the start command and internal/ssh consumes a RemoteLauncher interface, but nothing at the composition root connects them: grep for RemoteLauncher in internal/app and internal/transport returns nothing. cfg.RemoteLauncher is set on ssh.ConnectConfig, which transport/ws.go:982 builds, so the wiring runs app.go -> transport -> ConnectConfig.

Two things make this its own task rather than a line in another one.

The types are mirrored, not shared: internal/ssh declares its own ShellKind/RefusalReason/LaunchOptions following the RemoteInstaller precedent of declaring the interface at the consumer, so shellintegration's concrete launcher does NOT satisfy ssh.RemoteLauncher directly. An adapter at the composition root is the intended fix — that is where wiring belongs — and it keeps ReasonRemoteCommand in the ssh layer where it is discovered, rather than pushing an ssh_config concern into the launcher's vocabulary.

And this is exactly AGENTS.md check 5. nocx-rtg0 shipped an entire encrypted store whose write path had no caller and reported 'deadcode empty' because the read path was reachable. A launcher with no caller is the same shape.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. grep -rn RemoteLauncher internal/app internal/transport — no hits.
2. Open an SSH session; the launcher is never consulted.
acceptance_criteria: deadcode -filter 'nocx/internal/shellintegration' reports NewRemoteLauncher reachable from main(); an SSH session opened through the real transport receives the launcher's start command; and the refusal reason travels from the ssh layer to a JSON-RPC result declared by a contracts/ schema, so the product can say why it degraded rather than only the log.
close_reason: Launcher wired from the composition root through transport.WithRemoteLauncher into ssh.ConnectConfig via an adapter in internal/app; refusal reason travels over the open result with contracts/open.schema.json and a generated renderer type. deadcode -filter 'nocx/internal/shellintegration' is empty. Proof is a full-stack test driving a real WSServer and ssh client against an in-process SSH server, written red first. Merged. Follow-up nocx-axpz on the adapter's panic.

title: A recorded command is deleted by the retention sweep the moment it is written
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Set History → "Keep history for" to 30 days (history.retentionDays=30).
2. Run any command in the terminal.
3. Press Up, or open the recall overlay.

Observed: "0 results — this session only — no history yet". The store is
open (content.db exists, its WAL is being written) and history.record IS
sent; querying the database directly returns zero rows.

Reproduced against a copy of the owner's real config directory on a stand at
127.0.0.1:5181; a probe reading content.db with the same derived key returns
hasRows=false after a successful record.

## Root Cause

The frontend stamps startedAt/endedAt with performance.now() — milliseconds
since page load. Observed on the wire:

  {"method":"history.record","params":{"command":"echo repro-alpha",
   "status":"success","startedAt":755,"endedAt":757,"trusted":true}}

internal/content reads ended_at as Unix epoch milliseconds, and doAdd runs
the age sweep in the SAME writer turn as the INSERT:

  DELETE FROM command_history WHERE ended_at IS NOT NULL AND ended_at < cutoff

so with retentionDays > 0 every row is deleted microseconds after it is
inserted: 757 ms after the epoch is January 1970, far below any cutoff.
history.record returns its ack, the renderer is told nothing, and the
overlay reports "this session only".

Why the acceptance e2e is green: history.retentionDays defaults to 0 and the
sweep only runs when days > 0. The e2e builds a fresh XDG profile, so it
never exercises the value a user who touched the setting actually has.

## Fixes wanted

1. The ledger's timestamps are wall-clock facts, not durations. Stamp them
   epoch ms (Date.now()); command-ledger.ts currently documents "Never call
   Date.now()" and that comment is the defect. recall.ts passes
   performance.now() into relativeTime at line 567 and must move to the same
   clock, or every row renders as 56 years old.
2. The store must not silently delete a row it just wrote. Validate at the
   history.record boundary that a non-null startedAt/endedAt is a plausible
   epoch (reject below 2020-01-01) with -32602, so a wrong clock surfaces as
   an error instead of a vanishing row.
3. The acceptance e2e must run with history.retentionDays non-zero — the
   setting that hid this. A check that only ever sees defaults cannot report
   a feature that breaks the moment a user configures it.
acceptance_criteria: With history.retentionDays=30, run a command, restart the backend, press Up: the command is there and the panel does not say 'this session only'. A history.record carrying a performance.now()-shaped timestamp is rejected with -32602 rather than accepted and swept.
close_reason: Ledger and recall panel moved to wall-clock epoch ms; history.record rejects a pre-2020 timestamp with -32602; the acceptance e2e now seeds history.retentionDays=30. Verified on a copy of the owner's real profile: the recall panel shows the command with no 'this session only' badge, and a separate process reading content.db with the derived key finds the row on disk.

title: The history key never touches the vault: OS keystore, else derived from the machine
description:
Owner's decision, 2026-08-02, after considering and rejecting both a passphrase prompt and degrading the feature: 'Наша цель - защитить файлы от чтения напрямую. Пароль не должен быть в vault.'

So the threat model is stated and narrow: a copy of the file must not be readable as it stands. Not a live attacker, not a process running as this user — that boundary is not defensible on a desktop anyway, and ~/.bash_history has never pretended otherwise. Encryption defeats the DETACHED copy: a backup, a synced folder, an exported file, a pulled disk.

Derivation: key = HKDF-SHA256(ikm = salt || machine-id || uid, info = 'nocx-contentdb-v1'). Sources for the machine id: /etc/machine-id on Linux, IOPlatformUUID on macOS, MachineGuid on Windows. The machine id is NOT a secret — /etc/machine-id is mode 444 — so the random salt is the ingredient that carries the protection and its file permissions are the control.

Consequence that must be handled rather than hidden: a key derived from the machine id does not survive migration to another machine, so a restored backup opens on the old laptop and not the new one. Whatever the product says about history must say that. And the existing ErrKeyLost rule matters more here, not less: if the salt is gone and content.db exists, the key is unrecoverable and MUST NOT be re-minted — a new key would strand the database while the UI claimed history worked.
acceptance_criteria: The content key resolves in one declared order and the vault appears in neither branch: the OS keystore where there is one (Keychain / Secret Service / Credential Manager), else a key DERIVED at startup from a random salt file plus the machine id. No passphrase is ever requested for history, on any platform. On a host with no OS keystore the app opens content.db at startup and records everything, output included. The salt lives in the CONFIG dir, 0600, never in the data dir beside content.db, so a copy of the database carries nothing that opens it. Proven by a test that starts the composition root with no OS keystore available AND a sealed vault, and asserts the store is NOT the stub — the seal must be irrelevant to it.
close_reason: Landed in 5583655; acceptance verified in a browser against a real backend — command recorded, backend restarted, command back with source=store

title: Nothing ever records a command: the store is wired for reading only
description:
ContentDB.Add exists, is tested, and has no caller outside tests. The composition root hands the store to the transport, which reads it for history.query; the write half of the epic (rtg0.2 schema, rtg0.3 ledger.* over the wire, rtg0.4 outbox, rtg0.5 EntryDriver) was never built, so the History settings section governs a feature that never runs.

Why it was not caught: the acceptance criterion was 'deadcode reports no unreachable exported symbol', and deadcode was empty because Query IS reachable. A reachable read path hid an unreachable write path. The metric answered 'is this package reachable' when the question was 'does a command get recorded'.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run several commands.
2. ls ~/.local/share/nocx — there is no content.db.
3. grep for a caller of ContentDB.Add outside _test files — there is none.
acceptance_criteria: Running a command in a tab writes a row to content.db; after a restart the recall panel answers that command with source=store, not source=session. Proven by a test that goes through the seam a user reaches — run, restart, recall — not by calling ContentDB.Add directly.
close_reason: Landed in 5583655; acceptance verified in a browser against a real backend — command recorded, backend restarted, command back with source=store

title: A sealed vault should raise the unlock prompt, not fail the call
description:
Pressing Test with the vault sealed answers 'Test failed: probe config: vault is sealed'. The unlock prompt is wired at individual SAVE sites (ensureBeforeSave, saveSecretWithVault), so every other path that happens to need a secret reports the internal state as an error instead.

Needing the vault is a property of the call, not of the call site: the seam is the dispatcher, where a vault-sealed reason can raise the prompt and replay the call after unlock. Doing it per call site guarantees the next new method reintroduces the bug.
acceptance_criteria: Any RPC that fails because the vault is sealed raises the unlock prompt and, once unlocked, completes the original call; the user never reads 'vault is sealed'. Proven for a read path (connections.test) as well as a save path, and for a cancel, which must fail the original call cleanly rather than hang.
close_reason: A sealed vault now raises the unlock prompt for every control method: a Responder wrapper installed by connMethods normalizes any sealed failure to one canonical shape, and the renderer's dispatcher owns the replay. The backend cannot own it — a synchronous re-run re-acquires an admission the first attempt still holds (measured 'Control plane busy' on three methods), and a bounded lane refuses the re-submission; ADR-0032 carries the reasoning. agent.status's credentialResolvable boolean became a five-state credential enum so a sealed vault and a deleted secret get different sentences. Merged as d5f0ef9f.

title: There is no way to accept a host key, so a new host can never be reached
description: hostKeyCallback is built from known_hosts and nothing in the repo ever writes to it: grep finds no AddKnownHost, no WriteKnownHost, no trust path. A host absent from the file therefore fails forever, and the only thing offered is a toast reporting the fingerprint. Depends on the outcome split so that trusting a NEW key and overwriting a CHANGED one cannot be the same button.
acceptance_criteria: From a failed test or connect, the user can read the offered fingerprint and accept it; accepting writes ~/.ssh/known_hosts and the next test succeeds. A key that CHANGED requires a distinct, stronger confirmation that names both fingerprints and is not the default action. Rejecting leaves known_hosts untouched.
close_reason: connections.trustHostKey writes known_hosts; a changed key REPLACES the old line (hashed entries included) rather than appending beside it, so the rejected key stops being trusted. 077a9f5

title: A host key that is merely unknown is reported as changed
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Test a connection to a host that is not in ~/.ssh/known_hosts.

Expected: nocx says it has never seen this host before.
Actual: the toast reads 'Host key changed: unknown host key for 192.168.0.57:22 …' — the label and the detail contradict each other.

## Why P0

The two cases mean opposite things. First contact is routine; a key that has changed is the signature of a man in the middle. Spending the alarming words on the routine case is how a real warning gets ignored — ClassifyProbeError maps ErrUnknownHostKey and ErrHostKeyMismatch to one outcome (host-key-problem) and the renderer labels that outcome 'Host key changed'.
acceptance_criteria: An unknown host key and a changed host key are distinguishable on the wire and in what the user reads; the words 'host key changed' appear only when the stored key and the offered key differ.
close_reason: host-key-unknown and host-key-changed are separate outcomes carrying the offered and stored fingerprints; the alarming words are spent only on a changed key. 077a9f5

title: Typing in the connection and group editors loses the caret after one character
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Settings → Connections → + New connection, get to the full form.
2. Click into Host and type two characters.

Expected: both characters land.
Actual: the first lands, document.activeElement becomes BODY, the second goes nowhere. Same in the group editor's User field.

## Cause

Not the UI kit. A render helper called from a JSX position that reads its draft signal synchronously becomes one computation over the whole form, so every keystroke rebuilds the DOM and replaces the input being typed into: renderProfileForm took the profile by value, and renderConnectionDefaults opened with const auth = gv('auth').
acceptance_criteria: Focus stays in the field across keystrokes in the connection editor (Name, Host, Port) and in the group editor (User), asserted from the state a user starts in; a browser check confirms document.activeElement is still the field after two characters.
close_reason: renderProfileForm and renderConnectionDefaults take accessors; verified in a browser (activeElement stays on the field) and by two behavior tests. 3cb94e3

title: Silent OS-keychain setup is unreachable: osKeyAvailable reports vault state, not machine capability
description:
Document.HasOSKey is set inside Setup (internal/vault/vault.go:202) and means "this
vault HAS an OS-held key". Snapshot marshals it as json:"osKeyAvailable"
(vault.go:1165) and the transport forwards it as OSKeyAvailable (ws_vault.go:144).
The renderer reads status.osKeyAvailable at frontend/src/vault.tsx:136 and :248 to
decide whether silent setup is POSSIBLE — a machine capability, not a vault state.

On an uninitialized vault HasOSKey is false by construction, so the silent-setup
branch can never run. Every user is asked to invent a master passphrase even when the
OS keychain is present and working, which makes the system provider — one of the two
providers, and the reason ADR-0011's SecretStore capability exists — unreachable from
the UI.

The two facts need separate names: capability (a ready+writable system entry in the
provider snapshot, or an explicit field) and state (the existing document flag).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Have a working Secret Service:
   nix-shell -p gnome-keyring dbus --run 'dbus-run-session -- bash -c "
     eval \$(echo -n nocx-ci | gnome-keyring-daemon --daemonize --login)
     echo -n nocx-ci | gnome-keyring-daemon --unlock
     NOCX_WS_PORT=19876 PW_PROJECTS=chromium npx playwright test e2e/vault.spec.ts -g \"silent vault setup\"
   "'
2. Start with no vault configured, create a connection and set a password.
3. Observed: the "Set Up Vault" dialog appears asking for a master passphrase.
   Expected: nothing appears; the vault is set up against the OS keychain.

The backend is not at fault — under the same session it logs
`vault system-provider availability probe ready=true reason=""`.

## Acceptance Criteria

With a working Secret Service, saving a password on a fresh profile sets the vault up
silently: no Set Up Vault dialog, no passphrase prompt, and the secret lands in the
system provider. e2e/vault.spec.ts case 3 passes unmodified under the recipe above.
With no Secret Service the passphrase dialog still appears and case 1 keeps passing.
close_reason: Fixed in c729fa9: Snapshot derives osKeyCapable (machine capability) from the provider list, separate from osKeyAvailable (vault state); the two silent-setup call sites read the capability, the three unseal/display sites keep the state. Verified independently by e2e case 3 under a real Secret Service, and case 1 still passes without one.

title: Vault errors from legacy handlers carry no reason, so the UI cannot recognise them
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

Found by e2e/vault.spec.ts, which is the first thing in this epic to drive the app the way a user does.

With no vault configured, set a password on a new connection and click Create Connection. Expected: the setup dialog. Actual: a dismissible toast reading 'Could not save the password: store secret: vault is not initialized'.

## Root cause

The save does not go through a vault.* method. It goes through credentials.savePassword, whose handler predates the vault: internal/transport/ws.go:1652 does fmt.Errorf('store secret: %w', err), wrapping ErrVaultUninitialized into a plain string. grep confirms no handler outside ws_vault.go attaches a reason code at all.

So the renderer receives a JSON-RPC error with a message and no data. frontend/src/vault.tsx's saveSecretWithVault can only recognise a vault error by RpcError.data.reason, finds none, rethrows, and connections.tsx:1082 turns it into a toast.

The wiring is fine — main.tsx:139 passes the controller, settings.tsx:321 forwards it, and connections.tsx calls saveSecretWithVault when it is present. Nothing is missing on that path. The error simply does not look like a vault error by the time it arrives.

## Why the previous bead missed it

nocx-25k9.3 was accepted on: tsc clean, eslint clean, 1073 frontend tests green, and a grep proving vault.tsx is now imported. All true, and none of it exercised the real error path — the unit tests fed the controller an error that already carried a reason, because that is the error the test author had in mind. The e2e is what found it, on its first run, exactly as intended.
acceptance_criteria: Saving a password with no vault configured opens the setup dialog rather than showing a toast, and the e2e cases 1 and 2 in e2e/vault.spec.ts pass unchanged — the assertions are the specification and must not be weakened. Every handler that can surface a vault error attaches the reason code, not only the vault.* ones, and a test covers at least credentials.savePassword, credentials.saveKeyPassphrase and settings.secretSet.
close_reason: Fixed: every SecretStore-touching handler renders errors through rpcErrorFor, preserving code and data.reason. Proven red-then-green by internal/transport/ws_vault_reason_test.go (real *vault.Vault, not a stub) and by e2e/vault.spec.ts cases 1 and 2, which now pass end to end.

title: Vault core: the journal is cleared on success, Setup deadlocks, and Unseal races Seal
description:
Found by adversarial review (codex) after the coordinator had already accepted the work on build, vet, lint, 18 tests and a clean go test -race. Every one of these passed all of that — which is the point: the tests exercised the happy path and asserted the implementation rather than the property.

## Steps to Reproduce

Two were verified directly by the coordinator:

1. vault.go Setup takes v.mu at :166 and returns WITHOUT unlocking at four sites — :182 (OS key Put failure), :189 (wrap passphrase), :195 (recovery code), :209 (save document). Any of them deadlocks every subsequent State/Setup/Seal/secret operation.

2. vault.go Create writes PhasePrepared, calls Put, and on SUCCESS calls clearJournalEntryLocked. PhaseSecretWritten is never written anywhere — grep finds it only in a doc comment at :415 that claims otherwise. So a crash between Create returning and the caller saving metadata leaves a provider orphan with no journal record. That is precisely the gap ADR-0011 §4's journal exists to close.

## The rest, from the review

3. Unseal installs rootKey then releases the mutex before unlocking providers (:293-310) without capturing a generation. Seal can interleave, leaving the file provider holding keys while the Vault reports sealed — or Unseal returning success when the end state is sealed.
4. Get (:504-534) and Exists (:619-643) never re-check the generation after the provider returns, so a read that began before a seal completes after it and is accepted.
5. Setup saves the document and installs rootKey before file provider Unlock/NewDataKey (:208-245). If NewDataKey fails the document says initialized, Setup refuses to retry, and normal Unseal never creates the data key — a persistently bricked vault.
6. Silent setup writes the OS-held key before saving the document; if the save fails the OS store keeps a root key for an instance no document knows about, with no compensating delete.
7. Concurrent Setup calls are not serialized: both pass the uninitialized check because the mutex is released at :136.
8. Delete captures gen, releases the mutex, then journals and delegates without re-checking lifecycle (:548-579) — deletion can land after seal, and rejecting the result does not undo it.
9. Exists maps EVERY provider error to (false, nil) at :637-642, so denied, timeout, locked and corrupt all read as 'not configured'. Only ErrSecretNotFound may mean false.
10. journal.go:104-106 retains PhasePrepared/PhaseSecretWritten entries with a non-empty target but does not append them to blocked, so New logs nothing. Unknown phases fall through likewise.

## Test-quality defects, same review

11. vault_concurrent_external_test.go:77-89 reads all 50 secrets back through the SAME live provider instance, which serves from its in-memory map. A saveBlob that persisted only the last write would leave it green. It must seal, construct fresh instances over the same directory, unseal and read back — with DISTINCT values, since identical ones cannot detect id/value cross-association.
12. vault_test.go:142-150 checks only exact attribute equality, so plaintext embedded in an error or a message slips through — and Vault does log provider errors.
acceptance_criteria: All ten confirmed defects below are fixed with a regression test each that fails against the current implementation. go test -race ./internal/vault/... stays green and golangci-lint clean. Two test-quality defects are also fixed: the concurrency test proves durability by reading back through a FRESH provider over the same directory, and the no-plaintext log test asserts on rendered output rather than exact attribute equality.
close_reason:
All twelve fixed, each with a named regression test, verified here rather than taken on report. Setup no longer returns holding the mutex — every error path now unlocks first, and TestSetup_MutexNotHeldOnError proves it with a timed State() call. Create advances the entry to PhaseSecretWritten and explicitly does not clear it (vault.go:603-607); AttachTarget and CommitMetadata are the two steps that finish the protocol, and the task rewiring the call sites must use them. Exists maps only ErrSecretNotFound to false. Unseal captures a generation and re-locks on conflict; Get, Exists and Delete re-check it. Setup initialises providers before committing the document, serialises concurrent callers behind an initializing flag, and rolls back the OS-held key. Reconcile now reports retained and unknown entries instead of dropping them silently. Both weak tests are rebuilt: the concurrency test reconstructs the Vault over the same directory with distinct values, and the log test asserts on rendered output.

Three things the worker reported against itself, which is the behaviour I asked for: it ran a prohibited gofmt -w (harmless, the tree was quiet); the defect-8 test checks the initial state rather than the pre-journal re-check timing, which is inherently racy and it said so; and the OS-key rollback swallowed its own Delete errors with _ =. That last one was a real gap against the brief, which asked for cleanup failures to be reported distinctly, and I closed it: the three sites now route through reportOrphanedOSKey, which logs the identifier at WARN. That matters more here than the usual best-effort case — go-keyring has no enumeration, so a stranded root key can never be found by a later sweep (nocx-dm0), and this function is the only moment its id is known.

title: export.import accepts renderer-forged secret references
description:
internal/transport/ws_export.go:143 unmarshals the whole ConfigExport and passes it on. ConfigExport.Credentials is []profile.Credential (export/config.go:12) including SecretID, PassphraseSecretID and Versions[].PasswordSecretID. Neither import path strips them: ImportConfiguration calls CreateCredential(c) verbatim (export/import.go:70-77), and AtomicImport only runs c.Validate() (service.go:267), which checks id/name/username. connection/resolver.go:250 later resolves the secret by that reference at connect time.

The intent to forbid this already exists one method over: ws.go:1371-1375 rejects a renderer-supplied secretId on credentials.create. Compounding it, export.configExport returns credentials with SecretID intact (export/config.go:51-60) while credentials.list strips them (ws.go:1354-1363) - so the renderer is handed the identifiers it needs.

ADR-0011 makes secrets backend-owned. This is the one path where the renderer names one.

## Steps to Reproduce

Send export.import with a credentials entry whose passwordSecretId is another credential's keychain reference, plus a profile that uses that credential and points at a host the caller controls. Connect the profile. The backend resolves the victim secret and spends it against the attacker's host.

## Acceptance Criteria

Both import paths refuse or strip renderer-supplied secret references, matching what credentials.create already does. export.configExport stops emitting SecretID, matching what credentials.list already does. A test sends an import carrying a foreign secret reference and asserts the stored credential does not carry it.
close_reason: Landed in 207aaab; round trip verified in a real browser

title: Audited input-validation defects on the control plane
description:
## Success Criteria

See acceptance.

## Provenance

Found by a read of every JSON-RPC handler in internal/transport on 2026-07-29, prompted by a user asking what library validates input. Answer: none — go.mod carries no validation dependency and every check is a hand-written if. The findings below are what that costs today, each with the file:line the audit read.
acceptance_criteria: Each defect listed as a child is either fixed with a test that fails without the fix, or closed with a written reason it is not a defect. DONE WHEN: every child is closed. OUT OF SCOPE: the dispatch mechanism itself (nocx-98rn) — these are the holes it exists to make unreachable, and they are worth closing whether or not it lands first.
close_reason: All review findings are corrected: ack follows current subscriber ownership, stored hosts fail at the connection sink, Unicode slug semantics are preserved, and obsolete NeedsReview state is deleted cleanly.

title: The control plane cannot dispatch an unvalidated call
description:
## Success Criteria

See acceptance. The mechanism, not the individual fixes — the audited defects are children of nocx-VALIDATION-BUGS and land against whatever this establishes.

## Why

Validation today is 44 hand-written switch cases in internal/transport/ws.go:609-670. Some are careful (profiles.patch has a real allowlist at ws_effective.go:113; credentials.create refuses a renderer-supplied secretId at ws.go:1371). Others do nothing at all (profiles.create at ws.go:1194 goes straight from json.Unmarshal to the store). Nothing tells the two apart, and nothing stops the next method from being the second kind.

The ask is a Fastify-style guarantee: no route without a schema. Go can do better than a runtime middleware — a generic registration constrained on an interface makes the omission a compile error.
acceptance_criteria: Every JSON-RPC method reaches its handler only through ONE registry, keyed on exact method names, whose registration signature requires a params type implementing Validate() error — so a method with no validation fails to COMPILE rather than at review. The same Registration carries the execution class the executor needs: Ingress disposition, Lane, Conflicts, Handler (defined by nocx-sfv6.3; this bead adds the validated params type to that record, it does not declare a second one). One decoder for all params, with DisallowUnknownFields. One read limit on the socket. A duplicate registration is refused at startup rather than silently shadowed. A test walks the registry and fails if any dispatched method name is not registered through it. DONE WHEN: internal/transport contains no switch over product method names, no handler there calls json.Unmarshal on req.Params directly, adding a method to an existing module requires no edit under internal/transport, and a test proves a method cannot be added without a validator. OUT OF SCOPE: validating the binary data plane (AD-1 frames), and the renderer's own form validation.
notes:
2026-08-08: collides with nocx-sfv6 (control-plane executor: lanes, admission, declared conflicts) and nocx-yscw. All three rewrite transport dispatch and all three describe a registration record. One record: Name, params type with Validate() error, Ingress disposition, Lane, Conflicts, Handler. First to land defines it; the rest add fields. Do not build a second registry beside this one.
2026-08-08: nocx-yscw folded in as a child — it and this bead described the same registry from two sides (exact-name dispatch vs compile-time validation), which is the two-owners-for-one-concept defect AGENTS.md names. Sequencing settled: blocked by nocx-sfv6, because yscw's description already records the owner-reviewed reasoning — the executor and its execution classes come first, or the same 86 lines get written twice. So this epic extends a Registration record that already exists rather than inventing one.
2026-08-08, round 2: the registry stores the injected Submission, NOT an ingress enum. Ingress handlers are accepted through a separate constructor/type that cannot receive domain capabilities, so no general handler can be wired to immediate execution. And the registry must move handlers into constructed types with narrow fields — registering method values such as s.handleVaultSetup keeps every handler reachable to every field of WSServer and leaves the ambient-locator defect intact.

title: Editing a connection creates a duplicate instead of updating it
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Settings -> Connections, create a connection named `web`, host `10.0.0.1`. Save.
2. Select it, change the host to `10.0.0.2`, save.
3. The list holds two connections. The original still points at `10.0.0.1`, and any session
   opened from it still goes there.

## Cause

`saveProfile` in `frontend/src/connections.tsx` always calls `createProfile`. It mints the id
in the renderer via `newProfileID` when `profile.id` is empty, and `ProfileClient.updateProfile`
is called from nowhere in the surface.

This is the same defect as `nocx-0w2f.6`, which wave 5 fixed for credentials — the update path
existed on the client and no caller took it. Nothing generalised the fix to profiles, and no
gate could have caught it: an uncalled public method of an exported class is indistinguishable
from a legitimate public API (`nocx-nc4i`).

## Also in scope

Renderer-minted ids. `credentials.create` already ignores the renderer id and mints its own
(`internal/transport/ws.go`); profiles should be no different, and the renderer should stop
inventing them.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Editing an existing connection updates that record. The list count does not change.
- Creating one uses the id the backend returns.
- The renderer mints no profile ids.
- Frontend tests covering both directions: an edit that mutates in place, and a create whose
  returned id is what subsequent calls use.
close_reason: saveProfile branches: existing profiles with host/name changes go through profiles.update, options-only changes through profiles.patch, and nothing the user typed is discarded silently. The renderer no longer mints profile ids and no longer keeps a private copy of the patchable-path list. The first attempt silently dropped host/name edits and showed a success toast for a partial write; rejected and reworked.

title: Editing a credential creates a duplicate instead of updating it
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Settings → Connections → "Saved credentials".
2. Create a credential named `prod-db`, user `deploy`, auth `password`. Save it.
3. Select it in the list to edit, change the username to `ops`, and save.
4. The list now holds two credentials. `prod-db` (`deploy`) is unchanged and a second
   `prod-db` (`ops`) sits beside it. Every connection referencing the first one still
   authenticates as `deploy`.

## Symptom

Editing a saved credential creates a second one. The original keeps its old values, the
list grows a near-duplicate, and every connection pointing at the original still resolves
to the pre-edit identity — so a corrected password appears to have been saved and changes
nothing.

## Cause

`saveCred` (`frontend/src/connections.tsx:716-733`) always calls `createCredential`.
`isNew` is computed at `:708` and never used to branch. `ProfileClient.updateCredential`
exists (`frontend/src/profiles.ts:234`) and is called from nowhere in the app.

The backend cannot save the caller from this: `credentials.create` deliberately mints its
own id and ignores the renderer's (`internal/transport/ws.go:1170-1173`, "The renderer's id
is ignored, not honoured"). With a fresh uuid there is no collision, so the create succeeds
and a duplicate lands.

Wave 1 (`nocx-ec2u`) built create/update parity in the backend. This call site never got it.

## Two more defects in the same fifteen lines

- `:721` `savePassword(credential.id, …)` passes the locally minted id — the one the backend
  just ignored — so the secret is stored under a key no credential has. The real id comes
  back in the discarded return value of `createCredential` at `:719`.
- `:712` mints `cred:<name>:<Date.now()>` from the first keystroke of the name. Nothing
  should mint ids in the renderer; the backend owns them.
- `:206-207` the form still validates `host` ("Bind to Host") and `port` — fields
  `internal/profile/credential.go` no longer has. The user is made to fill a required field
  whose value is discarded.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Editing an existing credential calls `credentials.update` and mutates that record. The
  list count does not change.
- Creating one uses the id the backend returns, for the record and for its secret.
- The renderer mints no credential ids.
- `host` and `port` are gone from the credential form and from its validation, and from the
  `Credential` type in `frontend/src/profiles.ts:79-86`.
- Frontend tests covering both directions: an edit that updates in place, and a create whose
  password is retrievable afterwards under the returned id.

## Note

Fixing this in isolation would be wasted work — wave 5 (`nocx-0w2f.1`) extracts this form
into one shared component. The fix lands as part of that extraction, not before it.
close_reason: Editing now calls credentials.update; the create path uses the backend-returned id for savePassword; the renderer mints no ids; host/port are gone from the credential type, form and validation. Covered in both directions by frontend tests.

title: Production updater has no compiled-in manifest verification keyring
description:
main.go constructs update.UpdaterConfig with Keyring:nil and the repository has no ldflags-backed keyring variable or generated key source. VerifyManifest rejects an empty keyring, so every non-dev production update check fails before version comparison. The comment that release CI populates it cannot affect a literal nil field.

## Steps to Reproduce

Build a non-dev release and call CheckForUpdate against a correctly signed newer manifest. Verification returns keyring is empty.
acceptance_criteria: Release builds contain the intended rotatable ed25519 public-key set; a release smoke test proves a valid signed manifest passes through the production composition root, while an unknown signer and an empty keyring fail closed.
close_reason:
Fixed by 6be1cac and 7eeb546, and now demonstrated end to end. main.go:123 calls update.ReleaseKeyring() and passes the result to the updater; internal/update/keyring.go carries the maintainer's key as a compiled-in constant with the rotation policy stated. The comment that claimed 'populated by release pipeline via ldflags' — describing an arrangement nothing built and nothing could — is gone.

What was still missing until today was proof rather than code: the step that checks the shipped keyring can verify what CI signs lived in the tag-gated publish job and had never executed (nocx-94kl). It ran in dry run 31246707047 and passed, so the keyring is not merely present, it is the mate of the signing secret. A degraded keyring also fails in the right direction: main.go logs and VerifyManifest refuses every manifest, costing the update check and never the terminal.

title: The .ui-settings wrapper breaks the height chain, so Settings cannot scroll
description:
`settings.tsx:654` wraps `<Page>` in `<div class="ui-settings">`, and there is no bare
`.ui-settings {}` rule anywhere — `settings.css` defines only descendant selectors
under it.

That plain block sits between `.surface-host` (flex column, `min-height: 0`) and
`.ui-page` (`flex: 1 1 auto`, `min-height: 0`) and breaks the chain. `.ui-page`'s flex
properties now address a *block* parent, so they do nothing and it takes content
height; `.ui-page__scroll` therefore never receives a bounded block size and its
`overflow-y: auto` never engages. The content runs past the viewport and `.pane`'s
`overflow: hidden` clips it.

This is exactly the failure `base.css` §6.1 warns about in its own comment: "a single
missing `min-height: 0` in the chain causes the scroll container to never receive a
bounded block size."

Why the gate missed it: `ui/scroll-ownership.test.tsx` renders `Page` directly,
without the `.ui-settings` wrapper, and states in its own header that jsdom computes
no layout. It verifies which elements *may* scroll, never that one *does*. The
invariant it checks is real; the composition it checks is not the one that ships.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the app at roughly 700px window height.
2. Open Settings and scroll the right-hand pane to the bottom.

Expected: the pane scrolls to the last export card. Actual: it does not scroll at all;
the content is cut mid-row at the window edge.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Settings scrolls to its last row in a 700px-tall window.
- The regression test exercises the real composition — `.surface-host` >
  `.ui-settings` > `.ui-page` — and runs where layout is actually computed, not in
  jsdom.
close_reason: Fixed in ed3a997; check-css-integrity.mjs now gates the class

title: 21 kit.css selectors escape the dot, so no kit control is styled
description:
21 selectors in `styles/components/kit.css` write the scope class with an escaped
dot: `\.kit-scope input`, `select\.kit-scope`, `button\.kit-scope:disabled`, and so on.

An escaped dot is a *literal character in an identifier*, not a class delimiter. So
`\.kit-scope` parses as a **type selector** for an element named `.kit-scope` — valid
CSS, no parse error, no console warning, and it matches nothing that can exist in HTML.

Every kit rule for inputs, selects, checkboxes, placeholders and disabled states is
therefore dead, and those controls render as unstyled native macOS chrome. The
correctly-written class selectors in the same file (`.ui-btn-primary`, `.ui-field`)
do apply, which is why the file looks half-working rather than absent.

Affected lines: 6, 67-68, 85-86, 91-92, 99-103, 116-117, 121-122, 127-131.

Production consumers of the scope are few — `settings.tsx:658`, `settings.tsx:720`,
`ui/dialog.tsx:152,156` — so the blast radius is Settings and the dialog.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the app, open Settings.
2. Look at the search field, the "Modified" checkbox, and the Tab placement / Theme
   selects.

Expected: kit controls (`--control-height-md`, token border, custom caret). Actual:
native macOS controls — white checkbox, blue system caret, system focus ring.

Static equivalent: `grep -c -F '\.' frontend/src/styles/components/kit.css` → 21,
and zero in every other stylesheet.

## Acceptance Criteria

- No selector under `frontend/src/styles` carries an escaped dot.
- Kit controls on a `.kit-scope` surface are styled by the kit.
- A gate rejects the pattern so it cannot come back — this class of typo is invisible
  to the CSS parser, so a linter is the only thing that can see it.
close_reason: Fixed in ed3a997; check-css-integrity.mjs now gates the class

title: light.css is never imported, so the theme switch is inert
description:
`style.css` imports `themes/tokyo-night.css` and never `themes/light.css`. Switching
Theme to Light sets `data-theme="light"` on `documentElement`
(`theme-bootstrap.ts:118`) and nothing else happens: no loaded rule matches
`[data-theme='light']`.

Second defect in the same place, and it is why the one-line fix is wrong. Both theme
files select `:root, [data-theme='<id>']`. The bare `:root` makes a theme
unconditional, so simply adding the missing `@import` would let whichever file loads
last win on `:root` and break the other theme. The theme files have to be
attribute-scoped, with exactly one of them additionally serving as the `:root`
default.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the app, open Settings → Interface → Theme.
2. Select "Light".

Expected: the UI repaints light. Actual: the dropdown shows Light and marks the
setting Customized; every colour stays Tokyo Night. Selecting Tokyo Night again is
equally inert — it was never not applied.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Selecting Light repaints the UI and selecting Tokyo Night repaints it back, in the
  running app.
- A test asserts each theme file's rules are reachable only through its own
  `data-theme` value, plus exactly one documented `:root` default — so adding a third
  theme cannot silently override the other two.
close_reason: Fixed in ed3a997; check-css-integrity.mjs now gates the class

title: Font family tokens are used in 18 places and declared nowhere
description:
`cc92306` deleted the `--nocx-mono` and `--nocx-ui` declarations from `style.css`
and renamed all 18 usages to `--font-family-mono` / `--font-family-ui`, but never
declared the new names. Both theme files carry the section header comment
"Font families (§2.4) — ADR §2.4 mandates these per theme file" with nothing under it.

An undefined custom property makes `font-family` invalid at computed-value time, so
the declaration is dropped and the element inherits — at `#app`/`body` that is the UA
default, serif. Every surface in the app renders in Times.

Original values, from `cc92306^:frontend/src/style.css`:

    --nocx-ui: ui-sans-serif, -apple-system, 'SF Pro Text', system-ui, sans-serif;
    --nocx-mono: ui-monospace, 'SF Mono', Menlo, Monaco, 'Apple Color Emoji',
                 'Apple Symbols', monospace;

Per ADR-0013 §2.4 these belong in each theme file, not in `tokens.css`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the app (`wails dev`).
2. Look at any surface — the terminal blocks, the tab titles, Settings.

Expected: the mono family. Actual: the UA serif fallback (Times) everywhere.

Static equivalent: `grep -rn -- '--font-family-mono:' frontend/src` returns nothing,
while `grep -rn 'var(--font-family-mono)' frontend/src` returns 17 hits.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `--font-family-mono` and `--font-family-ui` resolve to a non-empty value under
  both themes.
- A test asserts every `var(--token)` referenced by the stylesheet has a declaration
  somewhere in the loaded cascade, so the next rename cannot land half-done.
close_reason: Fixed in ed3a997; check-css-integrity.mjs now gates the class

title: [epic] The merged stylesheet does not reach the app
acceptance_criteria: In a running app (wails dev or the packaged build): (1) no surface renders in the UA serif fallback — every text node resolves to the mono or UI family token; (2) selecting Light in Settings repaints the UI, and selecting Tokyo Night repaints it back; (3) no native-chrome form control survives on a kit-scoped surface — every input, select and checkbox is the kit control; (4) the Settings body scrolls to its last row at 700px window height; (5) every CSS file under frontend/src/styles is reachable from the stylesheet entry, proven by a gate that fails when one is not. Out of scope: new visual design, the empty activity-bar top zone (that is nocx-708q), and the vertical-strip tab-rendering defect if it turns out not to be CSS.
notes: Backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh: all six children are closed and the epic has not moved since 2026-08-04, but it is LEFT in_progress for the owner rather than closed, because two of its five acceptance clauses have no check that could fail. Covered: clause 2 by e2e/theme-switch.spec.ts (which asserts a resolved token VALUE off the running bundle, not just the data-theme attribute); clause 4 by e2e/settings-scroll.spec.ts, though WebKit-only and at 520px rather than the criterion's 700px; clause 5 by frontend/lint-fixtures/check-css-integrity.mjs, whose unreachable rule is itself gated by a negative fixture (101 css files under styles/, 101 imports in style.css). Uncovered: clause 1 (no surface in the UA serif fallback) has no rendering-level check at all — nothing asserts a computed font-family anywhere in e2e; and clause 3 (no native-chrome control on a kit-scoped surface) has no enumerating check, and is explicitly owned by the still-open epic nocx-pp3y. Decide whether to close on pp3y's edge or write the two missing checks.

title: ADR-0012: Grant check на every open (target + jump hosts)
description: open{profileId} никогда не расширяет trust. Backend loads saved profile + credential metadata + grant + secret references как authorization snapshot. Resolves current effective endpoint, requires grant for same credential+profile+canonical host+effective port. Verifies known_hosts. Missing/stale/mismatching grant fails closed с credential-not-authorized error. Применяется независимо к target и каждому jump host. Проверяется перед new dial И перед pooled channel open. Pool security identity includes canonical endpoint + credential ID + auth revision + jump-route identity.

title: ADR-0012: TrustedEndpoints модель + grant workflow
description: Заменить Credential.Host/Port на []CredentialTrustedEndpoint{ProfileID, Host, Port uint16}. Сохранение connection = единственный автоматический grant: атомарный upsert profile+grant через backend connection service. Изменение host/port/credential пересоздаёт грант. Удаление profile удаляет грант. Idempotent save. Интерфейс в backend connection/profile service, не assembly из renderer calls.

title: ADR-0012: Credential-Scoped Trusted Endpoints
description: Implement ADR-0012: replace Credential.Host/Port binding with TrustedEndpoints (profile-sourced grants). Backend-owned, atomic profile+grant save, grant check on every open, remove Bind to Host from credential UI. Migration from legacy Host/Port fields.

title: Creating a new tab leaves the first tab unable to accept input
description:
Opening a second tab silently kills input in the first one. The user's existing
work becomes unusable the moment they open a new tab — the highest-severity
symptom of the set.

Screenshot 2026-07-26: tab 1 (`Users/shady`) has run `ls` successfully and shows
a fresh prompt block with a cursor, but after tab 2 was created it no longer
accepts keystrokes.

Suspected area: input ownership / InputTarget registry per ADR-0004 — creating a
tab appears to move the active input target without the previous tab keeping or
regaining its own. Sibling bug: switching back to a tab needs a click into the
editor first.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the app. Type in tab 1 — works.
2. Click `+` to create a second tab.
3. Switch back to tab 1 and type.

Observed: tab 1 does not accept the typed characters.
Expected: tab 1 accepts input exactly as it did before tab 2 existed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- With N tabs open, every tab accepts keyboard input when it is the active tab,
  regardless of creation order or how many tabs were opened after it.
- Creating a tab does not mutate any other tab's input state.
- A test opens two tabs, returns to the first, and asserts a typed character
  reaches that tab's input target.
close_reason:
Fixed and merged to main as 8f15a54 (fix commit e349e9d).

Root cause: _globalKeydown is registered on document by EVERY TerminalContent and was guarded only by !target.isConnected. Inactive panes use visibility:hidden rather than display:none, so a hidden tab's guard passed. Its handler saw document.activeElement outside its own containers and called focus() on its own editor, stealing the keystroke from the active tab. The guard now also requires the pane to carry the active class.

VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY by the coordinator, not accepted from the worker's report: with the fix e2e/multi-tab-input.spec.ts passes 2/2; with the one-line guard reverted the cross-tab test fails. The test asserts observable behaviour — a typed OSC 0 command changes tab 1's title — and carries a negative control that tab 2's title must NOT change, which is what makes it a focus-theft test rather than a smoke test.

Full gate green on the merged tree: gofumpt, golangci-lint, go test -race, root prettier and eslint, tsc, vitest 26 files / 539 tests, and the full e2e suite 20/20.

TWO THINGS DELIBERATELY LEFT OPEN rather than quietly folded in:
- nocx-ifgp — the new spec flakes under full-suite load, roughly one failure in three suite runs, while passing 3/3 in isolation. Measured, not suspected. Filed rather than ignored, because reporting this as simply green would repeat the nocx-d3q failure where a suite passed while the feature was broken.
- The guard reads target.classList.contains('active') — behaviour keyed on a CSS class. Tab.setActive already holds an authoritative _active boolean one line above where it toggles that class, so the fix re-derives ownership from presentation. It also crosses the nocx-njrx migration boundary: tabs.ts sets the class and WILL be rewritten in Solid, terminal-content.ts reads it and stays imperative under AD-6. ADR-0012 says state crosses that boundary through explicit methods, not DOM inspection. Accepted anyway because TabContent has no activation hook to use — only mount, viewportChanged, focus, dispose — so the proper fix means widening that seam, which is too much to block a P0 on. Follow-up needed.

nocx-4ff.29 is NOT fixed by this and stays open; the new test clicks into the editor after the tab switch precisely to isolate the two.

title: Switching tab placement back to Horizontal does not restore the tab strip
description:
Switching Tab placement back to Horizontal does not restore the tab strip. The
only recovery is restarting the app.

Distinct from the sibling bug where vertical renders empty: this one is the
return path. Even if vertical rendered correctly, a placement change must be
reversible without a restart. Same root area — see nocx-ycet.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Set Interface > Tab placement = Vertical (tabs disappear — sibling bug).
2. Set it back to Horizontal.

Observed 2026-07-26 on main: the setting reads `Horizontal` / `Default` again,
but the UI does not change — the top bar stays collapsed to a bare `+` and no
tabs return.

Expected: the horizontal tab bar returns with every open tab listed and the
active one marked.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Vertical -> Horizontal restores the horizontal bar with all open tabs, no
  restart.
- Round-tripping placement N times leaves exactly one strip in the DOM (no
  orphaned strip elements accumulating).
- Tab identity and active selection survive both directions.
close_reason: Fixed by the same commit as nocx-98z6 (c28bd4d). The V→H swap carried .tabstrip-vertical (width:240px) into the horizontal strip, narrowing it and hiding tabs. The replaceStrip fix resets all container classes and ARIA attributes before re-mounting, so both directions work. Test covers V→H specifically: starts with VerticalTabStrip, replaces with HorizontalTabStrip, asserts .tabstrip-vertical gone and .tabbar present, tab count preserved.

title: Vertical tab placement renders an empty strip — no tabs at all
description:
Setting Tab placement to Vertical leaves the user with no tab list at all.

nocx-d3q closed as complete with e2e green across both placements, so this is
either a regression landed after that epic or a gap the headless e2e harness
(cmd/devharness) does not see — the failing path is likely the live swap
through `tm.replaceStrip` (frontend/src/main.ts:157-178) rather than a cold
start already in vertical mode. Confirm which before fixing: a cold start in
vertical mode is a different bug from a live swap into it.

Underlying cause is filed as the epic nocx-ycet — the strip is replaced at the
composition root while tab state lives inside TabManager, so the two disagree.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the app with one or more tabs open (horizontal, the default).
2. Open Settings (Cmd+, or the gear in the activity bar).
3. Interface > Tab placement > Vertical.

Observed 2026-07-26 on main: the top bar collapses to a bare `+` button and no
tab is listed anywhere — neither along the top nor down the left edge. The open
tab still exists (its content renders in the pane) but is unreachable.

Expected: the tabs move to a vertical strip down the left edge, per the epic's
Warp-style spec — per-row icon, title, subtitle, status indicator, `+` in the
panel header.

## Acceptance Criteria

- With N tabs open, switching to Vertical lists all N in the vertical strip,
  the active one marked active.
- Starting the app cold with placement already Vertical lists them too.
- Clicking a row in the vertical strip switches to that tab.
- An e2e test covers the live swap (not only cold start in each mode), because
  that is the case the current suite missed.
close_reason:
Root cause: TabManager.replaceStrip cleared innerHTML but left the old strip's className and ARIA attributes on the container. After H→V swap, .tabbar (height:38px; overflow:hidden) clipped vertical tabs to invisible. After V→H swap, .tabstrip-vertical (width:240px) narrowed the horizontal strip.

Fix: reset className, role, aria-label, aria-orientation before re-mounting the new strip in replaceStrip (frontend/src/tabs.ts:414-423). Tests cover both H→V and V→H directions and assert tab-count preservation.

Committed c28bd4d on shady2k/fix-nocx-98z6-vertical-tabs, pushed to origin.
