title: The skill's card: what it carries, any file readable, and the switch
description:
Where the review actually happens, and the reason the parent epic can allow scripts at all.

Opening a skill on the Settings page shows what it is made of: every file it carries, any of them readable in place, with the scan's findings marked where they sit. The switch that puts it in play lives here, beside what it is a decision about — not on the install's success screen, where it would be two clicks in one flow and a reflex within a week.

The viewer exists: FileReadout (nocx-872jc.2), which draws a file or the true sentence about why its bytes are not here. The wire exists: skills.file (nocx-872jc.1) reads one file of one skill, any provenance. What is missing is the LISTING — skills.list answers with skills, not with their files — and the card that holds it.

The file list was deliberately cut from nocx-872jc.2 because a skill was exactly one file and the list would have been empty on every row the product could produce. Its sibling child gives it something to show, which is why this one waits for it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A person opens an installed skill and sees every file it carries, and opens any of them without leaving the page.
- The scan's findings are marked on the file and the line they matched, not summarised elsewhere.
- The switch that enables the skill is on this card, and turning it on records the digest.
- A skill that is off because its bytes changed says so, and says it differently from one nobody has turned on yet.
- Nothing is compulsory: no forced scroll, no "I have verified this is safe" checkbox. The card offers a look; it does not extract a signature.
- A skill of one file still shows one file rather than a list control with one row in it.
close_reason:
932be44a. The row's button is Open; the card holds where the skill lives and where its bytes came from, its file list, the switch, and the FileReadout. skills.files is new — one skill in, its paths out — with contracts (additionalProperties false, explicit required), the generated type, an over-the-wire test and its consumer in the same commit; not a field on skills.list, which would pay a directory walk per skill on every refresh (the list refreshes after every toggle, delete, approve and install) to fill an array one open card reads. The walk was not written twice: backup.go's inline WalkDir was extracted and shared, so 'what is this skill made of' has one owner and backup and the card cannot disagree about symlinks. Capped at 256 with 'truncated' on the wire, because a hand-moved directory has no bound and a card showing 256 of 300 would assert a manifest it had not read.

ENABLING STILL DOES NOT RECORD THE DIGEST, and the argument is now in SetEnabled: in the ordinary case there is nothing to record, since install wrote it over exactly the bytes the card shows. The only state where re-recording changes anything is 'changed' — which is where silent adoption is worst, turning the cheapest control in the product into the one that admits a stranger's edit, reached by somebody flipping the switch because the skill stopped working. Approve adopts bytes, is drawn only when there are bytes to adopt, and the card carries it beside them. Pinned by TestTurningTheSwitchDoesNotAdoptChangedBytes.

The two kinds of off never substitute for each other and each says its own sentence: off-and-unchanged is a warning naming that a skill from outside arrives off so the look happens before it can act; changed is a danger saying the assistant is not offered it WHATEVER THE SWITCH SAYS, with Re-approve as its single action. Both can appear at once.

The card reads the skill live out of the list rather than capturing it, so its switch and the row's are one control over one state. The file list is drawn only when there is more than one file. Nothing compulsory: no forced scroll, no signature.

Worker's kit reasoning, checked: Tabs was rejected (fixed 9.5rem rail that references/troubleshooting.md overflows; panels position-keyed with content captured once) and Select was rejected (does not SHOW every file, which is the criterion); RecordRow with onActivate gives a visible list, keyboard operation and a selected marker with no new component and no new CSS.

go test skill + backup + transport ok; vet, gofumpt, contracts:check, tsc clean; frontend lint with the ratchet at 149 all-baselined; 101 vitest across five specs; the epic's happy path re-run in the container and green, now opening the card, reading the file there and enabling from the card.

title: An installed skill arrives inert, and its effective state is computed
description:
discover.go:157 sets enabled := true unless the document says otherwise, so a skill is live the moment it lands. Under the parent epic an installed skill arrives inert instead, and stops being in play the moment its bytes change.

Two decisions from the parent, restated because a child must not quietly do otherwise:

DISABLED APPLIES TO THE INSTALLED ROOT AND TO NOTHING ELSE. A managed skill is one the assistant wrote because the person asked; an authored one the person wrote. Both are inside the boundary, and making somebody confirm what they just did is ceremony.

THE EFFECTIVE STATE IS COMPUTED, NEVER WRITTEN. Enabling records the digest (recordApprovalDigest already exists); discovery reports whether the bytes still match (hashSkillDirectory already does); what the assistant is offered is (enabled AND NOT changed). Writing enabled=false on noticing a change would make listing the skills a WRITE and would race the person who just turned one on. This is what AGENTS.md says about a bead's blocked state: computed, never stored.

It follows that restoring a file byte-for-byte brings the skill back by itself. That is right — the same bytes carry the same review — and it is a consequence to state in the code rather than discover.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A newly installed skill is not offered to the assistant until a person turns it on, asserted through the run's skill index rather than through a field.
- An authored or managed skill is unaffected, asserted by its own case.
- Changing any byte under an enabled installed skill takes it out of the index, and the row says why; restoring the bytes puts it back.
- Nothing writes to the document during discovery, asserted by a read-only document that would fail a write.
- The wire shape says enough for the page to distinguish "off because nobody turned it on" from "off because it changed", and that distinction is asserted over the socket.
close_reason:
d6e2509b. An installed skill arrives inert; managed and authored are unaffected. Provenance.inertOnArrival() is the one owner of that default and it is the ROOT, so a skill dropped in with mv arrives inert for the same reason a fetched one does. The effective state is Skill.Offered() — a method, enabled AND NOT changed — never a field and never written: a third value beside its own inputs can disagree with them, and writing it on noticing a change would make listing the skills a WRITE and race the person who just flipped the switch. Index() still asks the whole conjunction although discovery has already dropped the switched-off ones, so a change to what discovery excludes cannot silently become a change to what reaches the prompt.

The document records DEPARTURES from a root-decided default: 'disabled' for roots that arrive on, 'enabled' for roots that arrive off. Two sets because they answer to two defaults, and the root settles which applies before either is read, so a name in both cannot make the document mean two things. Schema 2 -> 3; migrateToSources generalised to restampTo(version) because the old rung hardcoded Current and would have made the 1->2 step claim 3. Existing v2 installed skills all become inert, no shim: nobody has looked at those bytes on the page.

FOUND AND FIXED, and the design was self-defeating without it: locate() gained offToo, so the assistant reaches only what is switched on while the PERSON may read anything. Otherwise every freshly installed skill would have been unopenable in Settings — the exact surface where §8 says the person examines it before turning it on. Read was already refusing any disabled skill while the row offered Read on every one.

nocx-hzsxl folded in: the row, execute.go's tool note and the Status doc comments all say 'changed since it was installed'. The wire enum keeps 'approved' deliberately — it names the state a person put the skill in, not the fact the row states.

No wire shape change, so no new generated type and no dead export; the two kinds of off are already distinguishable (enabled:false/status:approved vs enabled:true/status:changed) and TestSkillsList_OverTheWireTellsTheTwoKindsOfOffApart pins it off the real socket through the shipped install and setEnabled handlers. New tests in internal/skill/inert_test.go include one asserting discovery NEVER writes the document, with a write-counting store.

Also caught by the worker: moving Index() off Discover left Discover reachable only from tests — deadcode -whylive said 'dead code' — so Index goes back through Discover. Ratchet clean.

THE EPIC'S HAPPY PATH WAS RED and is now green: e2e/skill-install-url.spec.ts needed the enable step, and its locator was wrong because .ui-record-row__state hangs off the actions region and is a SIBLING of .ui-record-row, never a descendant — which record-row.css says where the cell is declared. Fixed and run in the container, 1 passed. go test skill/assistant/transport ok, vet, gofumpt, golangci-lint, contracts:check, frontend lint at 149 baselined, tsc all clean.

title: The bundle travels whole: a skill's own referenced files come with it
description:
Today internal/skill writes exactly one file per skill: Create, Update and Install all funnel through prepareSkill and produce a single SKILL.md. A skill's body that links references/typescript.md therefore installs with a dangling link, which is how the AgentMail skill — the one this whole epic started from — arrives half-installed.

The bundle now travels whole, and the rules are the ones the spec already wrote down (§5), taken from hermes's UrlSource and tightened in one place:

- the document names its own dependencies; the repository is never enumerated
- relative paths only, and ONE HOP: links in SKILL.md, never links found inside a support file
- allowlisted directories only, and scripts/ is now among them (see the parent epic for why that is defensible)
- the same effective origin across every redirect, not merely on the first request
- traversal refused, count and total size bounded, UTF-8 only for anything that can reach a reader
- pinned to one commit where the source can be pinned
- a referenced file that 404s FAILS the install rather than being skipped. hermes skips, and skipping is precisely how an installed skill stops matching the one that was shown.

Operational lessons from hermes worth taking whole, both bought by incidents:

- refuse a binary by its NUL byte rather than trying to parse it. Feeding machine code to their scanner "tokenizes machine code into bogus NUL-bearing paths and crashes the scanner" (their comment cites the bug number).
- bound the read AT THE SOURCE. Their cat of a 166 MB ELF "pinned the gateway's tool thread on a superlinear shlex scan for 30+ minutes"; they read with head -c on the far side.

The digest already hashes the whole skill directory (hashSkillDirectory, discover.go), so change detection needs nothing new — but it now has more than one file to be about, and that is the point of the parent epic's last criterion.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A skill whose body links support files installs with them, and the links resolve.
- Every rule above is asserted by its own test, including the one-hop bound and the same-origin check ACROSS a redirect.
- A missing referenced file fails the install, and the failure names the file.
- Nothing is written outside the skill's own directory under the installed root, driven by a traversal attempt and a symlink.
- The whole directory is what the digest covers, asserted by changing a support file and watching the status move.
close_reason:
b32ba7f4. A skill's referenced files now travel with it: one hop (links in SKILL.md, never links inside a support file, asserted by the URL never being REQUESTED), allowlist references/ and scripts/ with the argument for the exclusions in the code, same origin across every redirect, traversal refused rather than sanitised (5 shapes including backslash, percent-encoded and NTFS ADS), bounded in count, per file and in aggregate, UTF-8 only, binary refused by its NUL byte, and no execute bit (bash runs a non-executable script; the bit is a capability the delivery does not need). A 404 FAILS the install and the refusal names the file. 13 behavioural tests plus TestSkillsInstall_TheBundleTravelsOverTheWire off the real socket; the epic's happy path re-run in the container, 1 passed.

Preview and Install fetch through ONE function, and the digest joining them is now over the BUNDLE rather than the document — otherwise the install could write support files nobody had compared against anything and 'install writes what preview showed' would be a claim, not a property. skills.preview gained files[] so the person is not asked to approve a list they cannot see; contract, generated type and consumer (MarkerList in the install dialog) landed together, ratchet unmoved at 149.

PARTIAL FAILURE, which the brief asked for and which drove the design: the write interval now opens on the first byte of the bundle, not on the record. Install snapshots the directory first and restores it exactly. Fresh install that fails part-way leaves NO skill; an update that fails leaves the version approved before; an undo that itself fails leaves the skill 'changed' — listed, never offered, Approve beside it — and the test asserts discovery's own status rather than asserting it on discovery's behalf.

TWO DEFECTS THE BUNDLE WOULD OTHERWISE HAVE INTRODUCED, both found and fixed by the worker: an update now prunes what the new bundle does not name, because hashSkillDirectory hashes the DIRECTORY and a leftover would sit inside the recorded digest, so the skill would read approved while holding a file nobody was shown; and Remove takes the whole bundle, pruning BEFORE SKILL.md, because a prune failing after would leave an undiscoverable skill with a live digest and its files on disk — a state nothing in the product names.

The same-origin rule went into internal/httppolicy as an opt-in per request, not into internal/skill, because CheckRedirect is the only place that sees every hop — a caller is handed the last one. hermes compares hosts on the FIRST request, which passes a chain that leaves on hop two; a test drives exactly that two-hop chain.

FLAGGED FOR THE OWNER and left in: SameOriginOnly is applied to the SKILL.md fetch as well, so a vanity host that 302s to another origin is refused at preview. The argument is in preview.go — the manifest resolves against the named address, the recorded source is that address and an update re-fetches it, and that address is what the person read — and the remedy is one paste of the address it forwards to. It is one field to reverse.

Left open deliberately: Scan still reads only the body, so a bundled scripts/setup.sh gets no findings in the install dialog. Adding them needs a path on Finding and another contract change, and spec §8 assigns 'findings marked in place' to epic nocx-872jc's viewer. Needs its own bead there.

title: A skill arrives inert, and the person turns it on after looking at it
description:
The owner's decision, recorded in .internal/specs/2026-09-04-skills-under-the-same-policy-design.md §8.

This is what makes carrying executable text defensible, and nothing weaker would. The objection to scripts/ was never that a script is dangerous — a skill's body can tell the assistant to write one and run it, so a ban buys no incapability. It was VISIBILITY: the body is read at install, while a bundled script would first be seen when the assistant reached it, possibly weeks later. A review that happens after the bytes are on disk and before the skill can act closes exactly that gap.

Not copied from hermes, and the difference matters. hermes allows scripts/ too and pays at a different counter: tools/skills_guard.py scans every download BEFORE installation and blocks on any finding for a community source, where "trusted" is a hardcoded list of two organisations. Our scan is deliberately advisory and never refuses, so taking "scripts are allowed" from that design without taking "any finding blocks" would take its permissive half alone. What we trade in instead is the person's own look — which is why the look has to be real: on the page, later, with the files in front of them.

THREE THINGS THAT ARE DECISIONS, not implementation, and children must not quietly do otherwise:

1. Disabled applies to the installed root and to nothing else. A managed skill is one the assistant wrote because the person asked; an authored one the person wrote. Both are inside the boundary, and making somebody confirm what they just did is ceremony. The roots already tell them apart.

2. The effective state is COMPUTED, never written. Enabling records the digest; discovery reports whether the bytes still match; what the assistant is offered is (enabled AND NOT changed). Writing enabled=false on noticing a change makes listing the skills a WRITE and races the person who just turned one on. This is what AGENTS.md says about a bead's blocked state: computed, never stored. It follows that restoring a file byte-for-byte brings the skill back by itself, which is right — the same bytes carry the same review.

3. The audit is a button, not a page load. It is a model call, which is money, and internal/profile/role.go already refuses to spend that silently.

The file list returns here. It was cut from nocx-872jc.2 because a skill was exactly one file and a list would have been empty on every row the product could produce; with bundles there is something to list.
acceptance_criteria: A person asks the assistant for a skill; it lands on disk WHOLE — references and scripts and all — and does nothing. Opening it in Settings shows what it is made of, any file of it readable, with an audit available on request. The person turns it on there, and only then does the assistant see it. Changing any of its bytes on disk takes it back out of play without anybody being asked. One e2e check watches the whole of that on the shipped backend against a local fixture server: install a multi-file skill, assert the assistant is not offered it, open its card and read a file from each of references/ and scripts/, enable it, assert the assistant is now offered it, rewrite one byte of a support file, and assert it is out of play again and says why. Deliberately out: an automatic audit on opening the card, any forced reading before enabling, and a blocking scan — the scan stays advisory.
close_reason: All four children closed: .1 the bundle travels whole (b32ba7f4), .2 an installed skill arrives inert with a computed effective state (d6e2509b), .3 the card where the person looks (932be44a), .4 the audit they ask for (b49e9be4). A skill from outside now lands whole — references and scripts — and does nothing; the person opens its card, reads any file, can ask a model for a reading that certifies nothing, and turns it on themselves; changing any byte takes it back out of play whatever the switch says. The epic's happy path (e2e/skill-install-url.spec.ts) drives install, card, read, enable and answer, and is green in the container.

title: The wave record is durable, and the spec that governs it decided it should not be
description:
The spawn-and-register design §2 ("Whether a journal is needed at all") decided
this and the decision was not followed:

  "Across a backend restart there is no deferred cleanup either, because the
   2026-08-15 D5 makes stage-1 workers die with the backend. A RECORD THAT
   OUTLIVED THEM WOULD DESCRIBE NOTHING."
  "Decision: no journal."

The orchestration design §10 open question 7 ("Does the record survive a BACKEND
restart?") was, and is, OPEN — nothing decided for durability anywhere.

What pulled the other way was one sentence in the same section — "But the record
IS durable while the process is not" — a premise the paragraph above it had just
refuted, reasoning by analogy with `executions`, whose rows are durable because
they are HISTORY. It became `.internal/plans/2026-09-03-the-wave-record.md` §2
("internal/content owns the DURABLE ROWS"), which no bead and no spec asked for,
and shipped as six tables and two schema rungs in 62ffce63 and 20691d93.

The rows buy nothing. The daemon that owns the PTYs exits when its last session
exits (generation-daemon design D2), so the record's lifetime and the
participants' lifetime coincide by construction; a record that survived a restart
would describe processes that are gone, which is why Registrar.Sweep terminalizes
every open participant as `interrupted` and deliberately adopts none. Durability
buys a memorial, and costs a schema, two rungs and a second place for the record
to disagree with itself.

And the same section already wrote what happens when the helper repeals D5:
a participant "becomes a session-class record with a carry-over set", and sessions
are "CARRIED OVER IN MEMORY, judged later by reconcileSessions, never judged by
Open". No branch leads to a store.

History — what a wave did, read tomorrow — is content and belongs in the ledger,
written deliberately. It is NOT this bead: nothing here replaces the rows with a
history write.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `waves`, `wave_participants`, `wave_delegations`, `wave_delegation_effects`,
  `wave_messages` and `wave_cursors` are gone from schemaV1 along with
  `wave_participants_open`; rungs 16->17 and 17->18 are gone; `schemaVersion` is
  16, matching origin/main.
- `ContentDB` no longer has `Waves()`; `internal/content/wave_sqlite.go`,
  `wave_stub.go` and `wave_test.go` are deleted, and the five ContentDB test
  fakes no longer stub it.
- `wave.Store` keeps its interface and gains one in-memory implementation inside
  `internal/wave`, wired at `internal/app/app.go` in place of
  `contentDB.Waves()`. Every assertion the deleted store tests made about
  behaviour (a terminal state is never overwritten; `MarkLive` only from
  `prepared`; `HeldBy` joins through the wave, not the delegation; a mailbox read
  consumes nothing and cursors are per-reader) has a test against the new
  implementation, and those tests are written BEFORE it.
- `Registrar.Sweep` and its call at startup are deleted: an in-memory record
  starts empty, so there is nothing to sweep, and the carry-over set that
  replaces it belongs to the helper epic and is not built here.
- `internal/app/wave_test.go` and `internal/app/wave_model_test.go` still pass
  unchanged in what they assert about the product.
- `go build -tags gtk3 ./... && go test -tags gtk3 ./internal/wave/... ./internal/content/... ./internal/app/...` is green.

## Notes

Any dev content.db opened by this branch is at schema 18 and a build at 16 will
refuse it as newer. Greenfield, unmerged, unpushed: delete the dev database
rather than write a down-migration.
close_reason:
The wave record is in memory. Commits ae34ce68 (the removal and MemoryStore) and
31adedab (drop AllNonTerminal, amend the two documents); 4e57e672 is a red test
found on the way, see below.

Evidence a stranger can check: `git diff origin/main -- internal/content/sqlite.go
internal/content/schema_migrate.go` is EMPTY. The six tables, the two indexes, both
rungs and both migrate functions are gone, schemaVersion is 16, and the 15->16
digest is main's own rather than a recomputed one. `grep -rn AllNonTerminal
--include=*.go .` returns nothing.

CRITERIA, one by one:
1-2. Tables, rungs, schemaVersion 16, Waves() and the three internal/content/wave_*
files gone; five ContentDB fakes cleaned. Proven by the empty diff against main.
3. wave.Store keeps its interface; internal/wave/memory.go (395 lines) implements it
and is wired at app.go as wave.NewMemoryStore(). Every behavioural assertion of the
deleted internal/content/wave_test.go lives in internal/wave/memory_test.go (618
lines, 80 --- PASS under -race): terminal state never overwritten, MarkLive only
from prepared, HeldBy joins through the wave so a takeover cannot hide a worker,
read-consumes-nothing with per-reader cursors. Two were dropped deliberately and
named: the stub's refusal (the stub is gone; an in-memory record cannot fail to
open, and wave.ErrRecordUnavailable went with it) and the uint64->INTEGER narrowing
(no such boundary in memory). Added because a map does not give them free: a reader
cannot rewrite the record through what it was handed; 32 goroutines under -race; a
second Ensure does not move a wave to another coordinator.
4. Registrar.Sweep and its startup call deleted. AllNonTerminal deleted with it - it
had no production caller left, which is the shape the deadcode ratchet cannot see
(RTA calls a method behind a live interface reflection-reachable; this is
ContentDB.Add's shape). Its assertions moved to NonTerminal and gained one the
record-wide read could not state: an open participant in wave-2 must not appear in
wave-1's answer.
5. internal/app/wave_test.go and wave_model_test.go assert exactly what they did; the
harness now tracks its own wave ids instead of asking the record for all of them.
6. go build -tags gtk3 ./... ok; go test -tags gtk3 -race -count=1 ./internal/wave/...
./internal/content/... ./internal/app/... all ok (content 193s, app 171s).

NOT VERIFIED: the TDD ordering the criteria asked for cannot be read back from the
committed history, only the worker's account of it.

ALSO FOUND, not caused here: TestRunGrantFor_OffersPathToolsAndKeepsSessionScope in
internal/transport/ws_readscreen_test.go had been red since 20691d93 (nocx-dkawo.11
added wave.say to the coordinator's grant and left the expectation at two names);
6db4b205 then added wave.wait and wave.close to an already-failing test. The product
is right and the expectation was stale - fixed in 4e57e672. It rode two commits
unnoticed because a worker runs the tests for the packages it changed, and this one
lives in a package neither commit touched.

Two documents amended so the mistake is not re-derived: the plan's "internal/content
owns the DURABLE ROWS" bullet is struck through and answered, and the spawn design
S2 carries a dated amendment naming the sentence that misled ("But the record IS
durable while the process is not") without touching its decision.

Nothing pushed; no PR.

title: A draft refuses a session that never found a working method
description:
First child of nocx-rb8ka, and it lands on the path that already exists rather than beside it.

DraftSkill (internal/assistant/skilldraft.go) turns a transcript into name/description/body through the summarizing role, today when a PERSON asks the assistant to remember something. The epic's automatic trigger comes later; the capture rules come first, because a trigger without them writes the wrong skills faster.

Applying them to the manual path is a real deliverable on its own: a person who asks to remember a session where nothing worked should be told there is no working method here to record, not handed a skill made of failed attempts. Same rules, live consumer, no dead code.

hermes bought this list with pain (agent/background_review.py). Each line carries its own reason and the reasons belong in our prompt too:

  - environment-dependent failures — a missing binary, 'command not found', unconfigured credentials. The person can fix these; they are not durable rules.
  - negative claims about tools ('X is broken') — hermes: they 'harden into refusals the agent cites against itself for months after the actual problem was fixed'.
  - transient errors that resolved — if retrying worked, the lesson is the retry pattern, not the original failure.
  - one-off task narratives — 'summarize today's market' is not a class of work.
  - UNRESOLVED FAILURES, which is what this child is named for: a session that ended without a working method must not be written up as a recommended approach, because that presents an untested sequence of failures as validated guidance.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A transcript that reached a working method still drafts, and the draft names that method.
- A transcript that ended without one draws a refusal in the person's words, and no draft at all.
- Each rule above is asserted by its own case over a transcript that exhibits it — the negative-claim rule in particular, because it is the one whose damage arrives months later.
- The refusal is an ANSWER, not an error: the person asked a reasonable thing and gets a sentence, not a failure.
- Where the judgement lives is decided explicitly — the drafting prompt, a check over the transcript before it, or both — and the reasoning is in the code.
close_reason:
1cc76182. All five hermes capture rules now reach the summarizing model with the reason each exists, and the refusal is a reply shape rather than an absence: {"nothing_to_capture":"…"} is read BEFORE the three draft fields, so a model hedging with both has still said the draft is unsafe. Carried by skillNotCapturableError; kernel.go tells it from a drafting failure by errors.As, returns it to the person as a modelNocxMessage and logs at info — a verdict is not a breakage. The reason clause is model prose reaching a person unquoted, so it is whitespace-collapsed and capped at 300 runes.

THE DECISION, and it corrects the brief: the brief invited a structural Go pre-check over the transcript (is there a successful outcome at all?). The worker wrote it down and rejected it, with the reason in the code — the only structural signal available is 'did the assistant ever produce prose', which is ANTI-CORRELATED with the rule it would police, because a session that tries five things and fails at all five is full of assistant prose. Such a check would refuse only transcripts that cannot reach production anyway, while binding DraftSkill's contract to ComposeDraftInput's line prefixes. So the model judges and Go owns the protocol.

WHAT THE TESTS PROVE, stated exactly because it matters here. Plumbing: TestDraftSkillRefusesWhatMustNotBeCaptured (five subtests, one transcript per rule, stubbed model) pins that a refusal never becomes a draft, never becomes a generic error, and carries the reason; TestDraftSkillDraftsTheMethodThatWorked pins the success path still drafts; TestSkillCreateRefusalReachesThePersonAsAnAnswer drives the real HTTP path through the fake OpenAI server and asserts Invoke returns no error, the text is the refusal a person reads, and the ledger opened zero execution attempts. Proxy for judgement: TestSkillDraftPromptCarriesEveryCaptureRuleAndItsReason asserts the prompt names each rule and the negative-claim rule's own reason ('months after'). NOTHING here proves the model's judgement — only a live summarizer over those transcripts would, and that is an evaluation harness rather than a unit test. Worth its own bead if the epic wants that evidence.

go test/vet/gofumpt clean on internal/assistant. No new exports without a live caller; frontend/src/systemprompt.json needs no regeneration (systempromptgen marshals SettingsSystemPrompt, which never referenced the drafting prompt).

title: The approval window shows the script a command names
description:
Third child of nocx-872jc, and the one the epic is really for.

The approval window shows a proposed command verbatim and the shell's reading of its variables, and nothing about the FILE the command runs. Approving 'bash deploy.sh' while the meaning lives in deploy.sh is approving a name, not an act.

Uses the viewer the sibling child built. What is new here is the question of WHICH file a command names and how its contents reach the window — the command is parsed already (internal/content owns the Invocation and its ResourceReport), so ask that owner rather than parsing a command line a second time.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When a proposed command names a file the backend can read, the whole of that file is in the question, beside the command and labelled as what it is rather than as what runs.
- The command itself is still what is sent, byte for byte. The file is a reading, exactly as the variable expansion beside it is a reading (nocx-4h0m7.5 decided this shape once already; follow it).
- A command that names no file, or names one that cannot be read, draws no empty affordance and says nothing false.
- Which file a command names comes from the existing parse, not a second derivation of it.
- Nothing here is compulsory: no forced scroll, no checkbox.
notes:
2026-09-04, coordinator: THE EARLIER BLOCKER ON THIS BEAD WAS WRONG AND IS
WITHDRAWN. It said the parse never produces execute or source, so this
child's criterion ("which file a command names comes from the existing
parse") could not be met without first loosening effect classification from
Unknown to Delegate. That was written from memory rather than from the file.

Measured instead, against parseCanonicalInvocation on this branch:

  "bash deploy.sh"        -> [{deploy.sh execute}]        Unresolved []
  "sh ./setup.sh"         -> [{./setup.sh execute}]       Unresolved []
  "./run.sh"              -> [{./run.sh execute}]         Unresolved []
  "source env.sh"         -> [{env.sh source}]            Unresolved []
  "bash /tmp/x/deploy.sh" -> [{/tmp/x/deploy.sh execute}] Unresolved []

internal/assistant/cmdeffect.go:290 is the bash/sh case, :289 the source
case, :320 the executable-path default. They landed 2026-08-31 in d226fb49
(nocx-4h0m7.3), an ancestor of this branch four days before the blocker was
filed. nocx-o37n7 is closed as not a defect and the dependency edge removed.

So the criterion holds as written: ask internal/content's Invocation for the
resources whose verb is execute or source, and read THAT file. Do not parse a
command line a second time.
close_reason:
7961cc34. Which file comes from the existing parse: ScriptReadingsFor asks the Invocation's
ResourceReport for entries whose verb is execute or source, deduped, in parse order — no second
tokenizing. Reading goes through filesProviderFor, the same provider files.read is served through,
so a remote script is read over the session's own SFTP lease; a provider per reading, closed after.
The wire field is `scripts`, modelled on `expansion` and absent (never []) when the parse named no
file; entries are {path, verb, text, refusal, maxBytes, reason} with refusal reusing skills.file's
vocabulary plus `unreadable`, which is this notification's own because a notification has nowhere to
put an error. Drawn through FileReadout — the same viewer skills.file uses, which is the epic's
point. Decided and defended in the commit body: one bounded deadline rather than an async follow-up
(a question that mutates under the reader is worse than one that appears a beat later); a relative
path with no cwd is refused rather than guessed; an over-budget file shows nothing rather than its
head; not bound to the Approval record, because a reading is advisory. Wiring proved by
deadcode -whylive: main -> escalate -> bindApprovalScripts -> ScriptReadingsFor -> WSServer.ReadScript.

NOT PROVED, from the worker and checked by me:
- The remote arm has never run. Every ReadScript test is against the local provider; SFTP
  acquisition, its cost inside the deadline and its error mapping are untested. This is the
  largest gap and it is worth its own bead if the remote path matters before release.
- No single test runs kernel -> transport -> socket in one process. The worker called the
  ApprovalRequest.Scripts -> notification assignment uncovered; that is too modest —
  TestAgentApprovalRequested_ScriptsOverTheWireConformsToContract drives real ScriptReadingsFor
  through the real server and asserts the bytes off the real socket, which crosses that line. What
  is genuinely untested is the assistant-side production of AskParams.Scripts reaching transport in
  one process.
- Nothing measures the deadline under a genuinely slow read; it is tested by handing the source
  context.DeadlineExceeded, deliberately, since a duration-dependent test is broken on a fast
  machine too. "The question is never delayed" is an argument from the code's shape.
- No e2e watched a person read a script.
- Invalid UTF-8 with no NUL reaches the person as text with replacement characters rather than as
  not-text — the provider's own answer, deliberately not second-guessed, and it differs from
  skills.file's utf8.Valid test.

title: The Skills page opens a skill's SKILL.md in a read-only viewer
description:
Second child of nocx-872jc. The kit's read-only file viewer lands HERE, with its first consumer, because a kit component with no caller is a new dead-exports violation and fails the pre-commit ratchet (frontend/knip.json lists no test files as entry points).

The row discloses what the skill holds and any file opens read-only, with the scan's findings marked in place. Uses the wire from the sibling child; invents no second read path.

Read frontend/src/ui/README.md before adding to the kit, and add the component to its table.

## Acceptance Criteria

- From the Skills page a person opens any file of any discovered skill and reads it, without leaving the page and without editing anything.
- The three refusals are drawn, not thrown: not text, too large, gone. A viewer that goes blank lies about what is there.
- The viewer is a kit component with a stable identity class, placed and never repainted by the surface, and it is the SAME component the approval prompt will use.
- A skill of one file does not grow an empty file list.
- Findings from the scan are marked on the line they matched, in the file where it sits.
acceptance_criteria: From the Skills page a person opens a skill's SKILL.md and reads it, for any provenance including builtin, without leaving the page and without editing anything. The three refusals are DRAWN, not thrown: not text, larger than the read budget, gone. The viewer is a kit component with a stable identity class that the surface places and never repaints, and it is the same component the approval prompt will use. Deliberately out: a file LIST — see the note below.
notes:
2026-09-04, coordinator: SCOPE NARROWED, and the reason is worth having.

The original criterion said 'lists a skill's files'. There is no listing method on the wire — skills.list answers with skills, not with their files — and, more to the point, there is nothing to list yet: internal/skill writes exactly ONE file per skill (write.go Create/Update, install.go), and support files only arrive with nocx-ojfuc. A file list today would be a control that is empty on every row the product can produce, which is the 'a skill of one file does not grow an empty file list' criterion taken to its conclusion.

So this child is the viewer and one file. A listing method and the list become their own child when bundles give them something to show.
close_reason:
56799e74. Every Skills row has Read; the bytes come back through skills.file, builtin included (its file is inside the binary and has no path a file provider could open). FileReadout is a new kit component (ui-file-readout, data-state text|not-text|too-large|unreadable) composing FactList, CodeBlock and StatusCard and painting nothing — its stylesheet is four layout declarations. It is a component rather than three lines in the surface because the CHOICE between those parts and the sentences that go with it need one owner: nocx-872jc.3 draws the same file, and a surface composing it itself would be the second author of 'this file is not text'. It knows nothing about skills, and its outcome union is its own four-way answer rather than a second spelling of the wire's refusal field, so maxBytes exists only where it means something.

src/file-viewer/ was checked and cannot be reused: it is a workspace TAB (reading would leave the page) reading files.read against a live binding, which a builtin's bytes do not have. Argument recorded in the component header.

The three refusals are drawn, never thrown, in two tones: not-text and too-large describe a file that IS there, so warning — the tone the scan findings already use for evidence rather than failure — with the budget named from the number off the wire so no second copy exists; unreadable is the request with no subject, so danger, carrying the backend's sentence verbatim. An empty file draws an empty block rather than nothing, so a blank reader and a refused one cannot look alike.

Two smaller decisions in the code: Read is not disabled by busy(), which marks a row whose STATE is mid-change and has no bearing on reading; and the ask carries the skill in every member with a generation counter, because opening one skill, closing it and opening another puts two reads against one panel and the slower would win by arriving last.

91 tests across file-readout, skills-section, skills-store, settings and skills-client; ui/README.md has its row; lint clean with the dead-exports ratchet at 149 all-baselined and no other ratchet moved; tsc clean on both projects.

title: skills.file: the person's read path for one file of a skill
description:
First child of nocx-872jc, and the one the other two wait on.

skills.read exists as an AGENT tool (internal/skill/read.go Read(name, path), reached through internal/assistant/execute.go). The renderer has nothing: the Skills row prints a path and there is no way to read a file from the interface. This child supplies the wire and nothing else.

The store already answers the question. What is missing is a JSON-RPC method beside the other skills methods in internal/transport, its schema in contracts/, and the generated renderer type.

Read internal/transport/ws_skill_handlers.go and contracts/skills.list.schema.json first and follow their shape rather than inventing one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A method that answers with one file of one discovered skill: its path, its bytes as text, and enough for a viewer to refuse honestly — see below.
- It answers for ANY provenance, builtin included: reading is not writing and the person may read what the assistant reads.
- Containment is the store's existing answer, not a second one. A path escaping the skill's own directory is refused by the same check the agent tool goes through; a test drives ../ and a symlink at it.
- The three refusals a viewer must be able to state are answers and not errors where that is honest: the file is not text, the file is larger than the read budget, the file is gone. Decide which are errors and which are results, and say why in the code.
- Declared in contracts/ with additionalProperties false and an explicit required, the renderer type generated and committed, the Go side validated, and an OverTheWire test that validates the real payload off the real socket.
- Deliberately out: writing, listing (that is .2's question), and any renderer consumer.
close_reason:
b8afcc6f. skills.file answers {name, path, provenance, text, refusal, maxBytes} for one file of one discovered skill, any provenance including builtin, with the client method SkillsClient.file() reaching it. Contracts skills.file.schema.json and skills.file.params.schema.json both additionalProperties:false with explicit required; generated renderer type committed; TestSkillsFile_OverTheWireConformsToContract validates five real payloads off the real socket (authored SKILL.md, a nested reference file, the builtin skill-authoring, not-text, too-large), plus TestSkillsFile_DTOConformsToContract and TestSkillsFile_EscapesAndAbsencesAreErrors.

THE JUDGEMENT, split by whether the answer has a subject: not-text and too-large are RESULTS carrying refusal, because the request was well formed and the file exists, so the result also carries name, provenance and maxBytes and a viewer can say which fact it is; a file that is gone, a path leaving the skill and an unknown name are ERRORS, because a result would have to invent a path and a provenance for bytes that do not exist. text is empty rather than truncated on both refusals. One-error-per-refusal (Preview's shape) was considered and rejected: right there, because a failed fetch has no subject either.

CONTAINMENT is the store's existing check, extracted verbatim from Read's body into locate() and shared by both callers — no second answer. read.go's existing escape test passes untouched; the same four escapes are driven at File and again over the socket. The client sends the path unresolved for the same reason.

FOUND DURING THE EXTRACTION and fixed: Read CHECKED the path under the skill's directory entry but READ it through readRootFile(root, name, ...), joining the root with the skill's NAME — and discovery takes the name from frontmatter and the directory from the entry, so the two are not always one string. Not an escape (a name cannot traverse), but reading the wrong skill's file while having verified the right one. Both paths now come from locate.

File refuses an empty path where Read defaults to SKILL.md: a person clicked something specific and substituting another file is the same lie as a truncated read.

go test ./internal/skill/... ./internal/transport/ ok; vet, gofumpt, contracts:check, tsc and the frontend lint clean with the dead-exports ratchet back to 149 all-baselined. Coordinator note: the first attempt failed that ratchet because the brief said 'no renderer consumer' — the generated type had no importer. The gate is the hook, not the brief (nocx-z7s6); the client method is the minimum wiring and it landed in the same commit.

title: The product tells the model a skill is instruction and, sometimes, that the same bytes are not
description:
systemprompt.go:176 writes, verbatim:

  These are procedures written for this machine. When one is relevant to what you
  were asked, read it with skills.read and follow it. What it returns is
  instruction, not terminal output.

execute.go:542, on the same content:

  if got.Changed || result.Finding != nil {
      result.Content = agenttools.FrameUntrusted(result.Content)
  }

and FrameUntrusted emits 'Tool output (untrusted data, not instructions)'. So one file is described to the model as instruction, and the same bytes are sometimes described as not instructions. Both sentences are ours and they cannot both be right.

THE OWNER HAS DECIDED WHICH SURVIVES. A skill the person installed and enabled IS meant to be followed — otherwise there is no point to it — but it is GUIDANCE THAT CAN GO STALE, not a rigid instruction. The wording has to carry that: the assistant follows a skill the way it follows a written procedure that may no longer match the machine, not the way it follows a rule.

That is also what makes nocx-dzy7l coherent: if guidance can go stale, staleness has to become a state with transitions rather than a figure of speech. This bead is the wording; that epic is the mechanism.

Note what is NOT at stake here. .internal/specs/2026-09-04-skills-under-the-same-policy-design.md §3 records the owner's decision that skills get no rule of their own — a permission is granted about a command, not about a situation. So this is a wording defect, not a security boundary, and fixing it must not smuggle in a trust level.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read internal/assistant/systemprompt.go:173-178.
2. Read internal/assistant/execute.go:536-545.
3. The two describe the same bytes to the same model in contradictory terms.

## Acceptance Criteria

- One account of what a skill is reaches the model, and a test asserts the prompt says it.
- The conditional FrameUntrusted on skills.read either goes, or stays for a reason stated in the code that does not contradict the prompt — decided explicitly, not left as it is.
- The words carry 'may be out of date' rather than 'may be hostile': the owner's decision is that an enabled skill is followed.
- The existing prompt tests are updated rather than deleted, and one of them pins the new sentence.
close_reason: 95bbe462. The system prompt now gives one account in four sentences: a skill the person installed and enabled is meant to be followed; what skills.read returns is instruction; it is a written procedure and not a rule, so it can be out of date and a step that disagrees with the machine is reported rather than forced; and following a skill never widens what may be done, because a permission is about a command and not about the situation that proposed it. Pinned by TestSystemPromptSaysASkillIsAProcedureThatCanBeStale, which reads the skills section as one paragraph so a sentence elsewhere cannot pass for the account. The conditional FrameUntrusted in executeSkillsRead is GONE and the decision is argued in the code: a digest that no longer matches is an age, not a category, and a scan finding is evidence about one line, not a verdict on the file — so both are now stated in prose above the content instead. A second softer marker was refused for the reason FrameUntrusted's own comment gives. The two framing tests were rewritten rather than deleted. Worth knowing: skills.read was already OutputTrustTrusted in the registry, so the registry and the prompt had agreed all along and the conditional frame was the only thing out of step. go test/vet/gofmt clean on internal/assistant and internal/agenttools; frontend/src/systemprompt.json byte-identical, no regeneration needed.

title: A person installs a skill by asking for it
description:
From .internal/specs/2026-09-04-skills-under-the-same-policy-design.md §5, which reverses the earlier spec's refusal.

2026-09-03-installing-a-skill-by-url-design.md §2 refused an agent-callable installer because a model proposing an install would be 'laundering untrusted bytes into an instruction through a door the person holds open'. The owner's decision that skills get no rule of their own removes that reason: installing writes a file, and what the file can cause is whatever policy permits, the same as for any other text the assistant reads.

ADR-0053 does not block this and was checked rather than recalled: it does not forbid doors, it requires a door to declare a SET of effect classes with the decision moved to execution, and its own consequences name 'a package manager wrapper' as exactly the future case its mechanism already covers.

WHAT THIS DELETES from the previous plan is most of the work: the HTML parser, the candidate extractor, the origin-transition display, the GitHub adapter, ref-to-commit resolution, registry adapters. The assistant already searches, reads a page, follows it to a repository and lists a directory. Settings keeps the list, the enable switch, deletion and change detection — none of which a conversation replaces — and loses the paste box.

WHAT MUST HOLD:
  - the tool declares itself a door with its class set (ADR-0053's mechanism, no new one);
  - the approval names the RESOLVED source, the name, the description, the digest and the files that will land;
  - the description is prominent, because it is the one part of a skill that lives in the system prompt afterwards — and it is capped, which is nocx-l4lz9 and a blocker for this epic;
  - what is recorded is WHAT resolved (repository, path, commit, digest), not HOW, because an agent's route is not repeatable and the result still has to be auditable.

Support files, when fetched: relative paths only, one hop (links in SKILL.md, not links inside support files), same effective origin across every redirect, traversal refused, bounded count and size, UTF-8 only, pinned to one commit, and a missing referenced file FAILS the install rather than being skipped — skipping is how an installed skill stops matching the one that was shown. references/ text only to start.

Determinism was never the thing that mattered: it buys reproducibility, not authenticity, since a compromised page links mechanically to a hostile repository just as well. Our digest is TOFU — good change detection after the first install, no evidence at it.
acceptance_criteria: A person pastes into the conversation the page they actually have — https://www.agentmail.to/docs/integrations/skills, an HTML docs page — says install the agentmail skill from it, and gets it, without ever constructing a raw URL. One e2e check watches the whole path on the shipped backend against a local fixture server: the assistant resolves the page to a repository and a file, proposes the install, the approval names the RESOLVED source and every file that will land, approving writes the bundle under the installed root, and the row afterwards records repository, path, commit and digest. Deliberately out: registries and their slugs, /.well-known/ discovery, arbitrary ZIP URLs, and a person-driven paste box — the Settings ask is removed by this epic, not kept beside it.
close_reason: 7e7acb2d is the epic's happy path: e2e/skill-install-by-asking.spec.ts, green in the container. A person names a docs PAGE in the conversation, the assistant resolves it to a document, the approval names what RESOLVED with every file's bytes readable, approving writes the bundle, and the skill lands OFF. Children: .1 (39b4f18c) skills.install as a door with one url param, preview inside the call after the policy decision and before the question; .2 (f70f52ba) the install block on agent.approvalRequested, drawn through the viewer nocx-872jc built, bytes in the question rather than fetched per file so 'what was shown' stays a property and not a claim; .3 (9f9d41e6) the resolved URL stored whole and the SERVED-bundle digest recorded, which closed a real hole where the first Approve after an edit erased the only trace of what the address gave; .4 (47cb6b0b) the Settings paste box, its dialog and the skills.preview/skills.install JSON-RPC methods deleted, which is what makes this a deletion rather than a second surface; .5 the check. Deliberately out and stayed out: registries and their slugs, /.well-known/ discovery, arbitrary ZIP URLs, and a person-driven paste box. Blocked the close and was fixed on the way: nocx-ck02x, whose fix (42b6e4cc) is merged into feat/agent-ploicy and not into main, so this branch lacked it and the install question — the tallest nocx asks — put all six answers past the bottom of a 900px window with nothing to scroll. Cherry-picked as fcb55793 rather than running the spec at a viewport chosen to hide it. Still open from this epic's work: nocx-ykjai (ForGrant offers on ANY class while this row needs BOTH), nocx-aesm2 (one preview slot, two callers). NOT PROVED: the model's judgement — every model in these checks is scripted, and the spec's header says so.

title: The assistant records what it learned, and only when it worked
acceptance_criteria: A person drives a task where the assistant's first approach fails and a later one succeeds, is never asked to save anything, and finds afterwards that a managed skill carries the working method — and the next run of the same task does not repeat the failed approach. One e2e check watches both halves on the shipped backend: a run that reaches a working method writes a managed skill naming that method, and a run that ends WITHOUT one writes nothing at all. Deliberately out: writing anywhere but the managed root; capturing user preferences into memory rather than into the skill; and any foreground pause — the review never blocks the conversation.

title: A person can read every byte they are being asked about
description:
From .internal/specs/2026-09-04-skills-carry-no-authority-design.md §7a, and it depends on none of that document's five open questions — it is worth building whichever way they are answered.

The frame says nobody is asked to certify bytes. It does not say the bytes should be hard to find, and today they are: skills.read is an AGENT tool, the Skills row prints a path, and there is no way to read a skill's files from the interface at all. Meanwhile the approval window shows a proposed command verbatim and the shell's reading of its variables, and nothing about the FILE the command runs. Approving 'bash deploy.sh' while the meaning lives in deploy.sh is approving a name, not an act.

Three places, ONE capability, and that is the point of the epic. Building them separately is how one surface ends up disagreeing with another about what a skill contains:

1. Settings: an installed skill's file list, any file open read-only, findings marked in place.
2. Approval: the whole of a script a proposed command names.
3. Install: the same viewer over the bundle about to land — available, never compulsory.

They share one component and one refusal shape: a file too large, not text, or gone. The refusal is part of the deliverable, not an afterthought — a viewer that goes blank on a 40 MiB file is a surface that lies about what is there.

Sequence its children so the front stays around three, and land the shared viewer before any of the three call sites.
acceptance_criteria: A person opens an installed skill in Settings and reads any file it holds, read-only, with the scan's findings marked in place; and when the assistant proposes a command that names a readable script, the approval window shows the whole of that script beside the command. One e2e check watches both: install-or-discover a skill with more than one file, open each from the Skills page, then drive a proposal of a command naming a script in the workspace and assert the script's text is in the approval window. Deliberately out: editing a skill from the interface, and any forced-reading affordance — no compulsory scroll and no 'I have verified this is safe' checkbox.
close_reason: a219d68f is the epic's happy path: e2e/read-every-byte.spec.ts, one check in one browser context, both halves in the criterion's order — a two-file skill discovered, its card listing both, each opening read-only with its own bytes compared by textContent (not toHaveText, which normalises whitespace: 'the whole file' is a claim about bytes), the scan's finding marked inside that file's own pre and asserted against line N of that same pre, SKILL.md's zero marks making 'in place' mean that file; then a session.run proposal naming a script, the window carrying the script byte-identical to disk, the approve button ungated by any checkbox and approving as the first interaction with the window, and the command that ran compared byte-for-byte with what the window stated. Green on chromium and webkit in CI's image; two negative controls run and reverted. Children: nocx-872jc.1 (viewer), .2 (card opens SKILL.md), .3 (7961cc34, the script a command names), .4 (74c4540a, a finding names its file). Deliberately out and stayed out: editing a skill from the interface, and any forced-reading affordance. The epic also turned up nocx-69sew, a P1 the check could see and neither suite could — fixed in bcba9918.

title: An installed skill's description enters the system prompt uncapped
description:
sanitizeDescription (internal/skill/write.go:496) strips control and format characters and trims. It caps nothing. There is no length limit on a description anywhere in internal/skill — I grepped for one.

systemprompt.go:173-178 writes every skill's name and description into the SYSTEM prompt, and ws_agent.go:776 fills that index from everything in the run's grant. So an installed skill puts prose of arbitrary length into the most trusted region of the context, under our own sentence vouching for it: 'These are procedures written for this machine.'

This is not hypothetical length. The live AgentMail skill's description is 449 characters. Nothing stops 4490, or 44900 up to the 64 KiB file ceiling.

Worth doing on its own, whatever else is decided: .internal/specs/2026-09-04-skills-carry-no-authority-design.md §5 records three possible answers to the wider index problem and this cap is worth having under all three. It is also what bounds the damage if the assistant is ever the one acquiring skills (§7).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Author or install a skill whose frontmatter description is a paragraph.
2. It is discovered, and the whole paragraph is written into the system prompt index, unbounded and unquoted.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A description longer than the cap is refused at the write, with a refusal naming the limit — not silently truncated, because a truncated description is a claim the author did not make.
- The cap is one number, declared once, beside the file ceiling it belongs with.
- Discovery of an ALREADY-WRITTEN over-long description is decided explicitly and asserted either way: refuse the skill, or clamp at read with the clamping visible.
- A test pins the boundary on both sides, and the paired 'and on a normal machine it succeeds' case for an ordinary description.
close_reason: 8a31e4be. maxDescriptionRunes = 2048 in internal/skill/write.go beside maxSkillFileBytes, one comparison (descriptionOverCap) and one refusal sentence (checkDescriptionLength) so the words a person reads and the line discovery logs cannot drift. Enforced at the write through prepareSkill (Create, Update and Install all funnel there), at documentPreview so a preview never offers a button the install can only refuse, and at discovery over bytes no write of ours saw. MEASURED, not picked: across 140 SKILL.md files on this machine the median description is ~200 characters, p95 ~530, longest genuine 1506, AgentMail's 449 — so 512 and 1024 each refuse skills Anthropic ships today and were rejected; 2048 refuses nothing published while cutting one skill's worst case from ~16000 tokens to ~500. Runes not bytes, because a byte cap gives a Cyrillic author half and a Japanese author a third of the same prose. Over-long is REFUSED, never shortened, at all three points — a truncated description is a claim its author did not make. The read path refuses and warns with both numbers. Beyond the brief and necessary: MaxFrontmatterBytes is now DERIVED from the cap (4*runes+512) instead of chosen beside it, because a rune cap next to a byte-counted 4096 parse budget meant a 2048-character Cyrillic description would be written, accepted and then dropped as malformed — this bug through the other door. Six tests in internal/skill/description_test.go, including the paired 'and an ordinary description succeeds' cases and a Cyrillic-at-the-cap round trip. go test, vet, gofumpt, golangci-lint and go build -tags gtk3 all clean. Residual filed separately: a skill refused at discovery leaves the list with only a log line.
