title: A restored ssh pane finds its profile by string-matching an endpoint, not by an id
description:
A restored ssh pane finds its profile by STRING-MATCHING the endpoint it was
stored with against a string the profile store rebuilds. The pane row has no
column for a profile id, so identity is reconstructed from a derived key:

  frontend/src/panes.ts reopenSSH()
    const profileId = overlay?.identity === endpoint ? overlay.profileId : ''

`endpoint` is written by panes.ts endpointOf(); `overlay.identity` is written
by quick-connect-assembly.ts profileIdentity(). Two constructions of one
string, in two files, that must agree byte for byte or the pane silently
reopens as an unauthenticated direct-host dial (openSSHSessionByHost, which
reads a key only from `ssh -G` / ~/.ssh/config).

nocx-xhm9e was one instance: the palette never passed the port, so every
palette pane stored `:22`. That is fixed. THREE MORE ARE LIVE TODAY, all the
same shape:

1. IPv6. profileIdentity() calls joinHostPort(), which brackets a bare IPv6
   host (`e2e@[::1]:2222`); endpointOf() does not (`e2e@::1:2222`). A profile
   on a bare IPv6 address can never be matched back. Asserted in opposite
   directions by two green tests today — quick-connect-assembly.test.ts "the
   identity normalizes the port to 22 and brackets a bare IPv6 host", and
   panes.ts endpointOf's own construction.

2. Two profiles on one host. resolveSshProfileOverlay() answers null unless
   EXACTLY ONE profile matches the host (and the typed user). Two saved
   connections to the same machine on different ports with different keys —
   a normal thing to have — means both of their panes restore unauthenticated,
   with correct endpoints, because the resolver refuses to choose.

3. Editing or re-creating a profile. Changing a saved connection's port
   silently unbinds every open pane that came from it. Deleting it and saving
   the same address again silently REBINDS those panes to a different profile
   id, with different auth, and nothing says so.

WHAT THE ENDPOINT IS AND IS NOT. Storing it is right: a pane applies at a
destination, that fact is true whether or not a profile exists, and a pane
opened on a bare host or an ssh-config alias has nothing else to reconnect
through. What is wrong is using it as the KEY for "which saved connection was
this opened from" — a derived key standing in for an identity, which is exactly
the pattern AGENTS.md's "look for the existing answer" section describes: two
derivations of one concept that agree everywhere anyone looked.

THE CHANGE. Give the pane row a nullable `profileId` column alongside
`endpoint`. newSSHPane already HAS the profile id at open time and throws it
away; reopenSSH reads it back instead of re-deriving it. The endpoint stays,
unchanged, as where the pane applies — it is what a pane with no profile
reconnects through, and what the "could not reconnect" toast names. A row whose
profileId names a profile that has since been deleted falls back to the
endpoint, which is the current behaviour and the right one.

This crosses the layout schema and the transport contract (internal/layout, the
pane row DTO in contracts/, and the renderer's generated types), so it was not
folded into the P1 fix.

## Steps to Reproduce

Any of the three below; the second is the cheapest.

1. IPv6. Save an ssh profile on host `::1` with a port and a keyPath. Open it
   from the quick-connect palette; it connects. Restart the coordinator. The
   tab comes back on "nothing to authenticate": the row stored
   `user@::1:2222` and the profile's identity is `user@[::1]:2222`.

2. Two profiles, one host. Save two ssh profiles both on host `127.0.0.1`,
   on different ports, each with its own keyPath. Open either from the
   palette; it connects. Restart. resolveSshProfileOverlay sees two
   candidates for that host, answers null, and the tab reopens as a
   direct-host dial with no key.

3. Edit after opening. Open a profile from the palette, then change that
   profile's port in Settings. Restart. The stored endpoint no longer equals
   the profile's identity and the tab reopens unauthenticated, with nothing
   on screen saying the pane has come unbound from its connection.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A pane row carries the id of the profile it was opened from, and reopenSSH
  reads it rather than re-deriving one from the endpoint string.
- A saved connection on a bare IPv6 address reopens through its profile after
  a restart.
- Two saved connections to the same host on different ports both reopen
  through their own profile after a restart.
- Deleting the profile a stored pane names reopens that pane through its
  endpoint — the present fallback — and never silently through a different
  profile that happens to share the address.
- endpointOf() and profileIdentity() are no longer required to agree, or there
  is one construction of that string with one owner.

title: Quick connect stores an ssh pane's endpoint on port 22, so a restored tab can never match its own profile
description:
A pane opened from the Ctrl+Shift+P palette records where it applies as
`user@host:22` regardless of the profile's real port, so on restore it can never
be matched back to the profile it came from and reopens as an unauthenticated
direct-host dial.

THE CHAIN, all first-hand:

  frontend/src/quick-connect-assembly.ts  profileRows() maps a saved profile to
    {id, label, detail, host, user} — HostProfileRow HAS NO PORT FIELD.
  frontend/src/quick-connect.tsx:317      run: () => void this.newSSHPane(p.id, p.host, p.user)
    — three arguments; the ctor's type (:303) has no port parameter either.
  frontend/src/panes.ts newSSHPane()      calls mintPane('ssh', endpointOf(host, user, port))
    with port === undefined.
  frontend/src/panes.ts endpointOf()      `${user}@${host}:${port ?? 22}` — the
    default lands, and `:22` is what is persisted in the pane row.

On restore, panes.ts reopenSSH() re-derives the profile from that string alone,
because the chain has no column for a profile id (its own comment says so):

    const profileId = overlay?.identity === endpoint ? overlay.profileId : ''

and quick-connect-assembly.ts profileIdentity() builds the other side of that
comparison from the PROFILE's port. For any profile not on 22 the two strings
differ, profileId is '', and internal/transport/ws_session_handlers.go takes the
direct-host branch — which reads a key only from `ssh -G`/~/.ssh/config and never
consults the profile store. The tab comes back saying:

    Terminal failed to start: ssh connect: nothing to authenticate
    e2e@127.0.0.1 with: no key, no password and no reachable agent

The first connection is unaffected: newSSHPane is given the profile id and the
open resolves the profile, port and key correctly. Only the STORED ENDPOINT is
wrong, so the defect is invisible until a restart.

Settings -> Connect does pass the port (frontend/src/main.tsx), and so do the
alias and ad-hoc providers. The palette is the one caller that does not.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create an SSH profile on a port other than 22, with a keyPath.
2. Open it from the Ctrl+Shift+P quick-connect palette. It connects fine.
3. Restart nocx-server on the same profile directory.
4. The tab is restored and reads "Terminal failed to start: ssh connect: nothing
   to authenticate ... no key, no password and no reachable agent". The backend
   log shows "SSH open via direct host" rather than "SSH open via profile".

Observed on branch omp/k6p18-9-e2e-c while running
e2e/remote-coordinator-reclaim.spec.ts, whose fixture sshd binds an ephemeral
port. Reproducible without any helper involvement.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A pane opened from the quick-connect palette stores an endpoint carrying the
  profile's actual port.
- After a coordinator restart, that tab reopens through the PROFILE branch — the
  backend logs "SSH open via profile" and the connection authenticates with the
  profile's key.
- A regression test covers a profile on a non-22 port across a backend restart;
  today no e2e spec restarts the backend with a remote session at all.
close_reason:
Closed 2026-09-02, verified by the coordinator. Commits c508d8eb and 087a6776,
fast-forwarded onto feat/relay-pty-owner. Sent back once.

THE FIX. HostProfileRow carries port; profileRows reads it from the profile,
treating 0 as unset -- the same reading profileIdentity makes, and the two
strings must agree or the restore match cannot hold. The provider's opener type
gained port. The port was actually dropped at the COMPOSITION ROOT, in
main.tsx's lambda `(id, host, user) => tm.newSSHPane(id, host, user)`, which
spelled three of four arguments; it is now tm.newSSHPane.bind(tm), so there is no
second parameter list for the next optional argument to go missing from.

WHY IT WAS SENT BACK. The first round's test wired the provider itself, with a
correct opener. So it proved the provider threads a port when handed a good one
-- never in doubt -- and could not report the shipped composition root handing it
a bad one, which is the only place the bug ever lived. I proved it: restoring the
arity-losing lambda in main.tsx left all 30 tests GREEN. AGENTS.md rule 1 in its
exact form.

Two things made that worse than a coverage hole. TypeScript assigns a
3-parameter function to a 4-parameter type by design, so the type-checker could
not catch it either; and `bind` is a structural improvement, not a guard --
nothing stopped the next person writing a lambda there.

WHAT REPLACED IT, and it is better than what I asked for. The arity loss is now a
TYPE ERROR. A CallableWith<F, N> conditional intersects the opener type with a
branded object unless N is in Parameters<F>['length']. That length is a UNION
over the optional tail, so bind's `2|3|4|5` satisfies `4 extends`, while a
three-argument lambda's `3` does not. The naive direction --
Parameters<F>['length'] extends Parameters<Target>['length'] -- does NOT work; it
rejects the good bind too. That is worth keeping written down.

My own mutation, the same one that was green before: the lambda restored at
main.tsx:1326 now fails to COMPILE, with a message that names the defect in
English --
  error TS2345: Argument of type '(id, host, user) => Pane' is not assignable to
  ... & { readonly [ARITY]: "this opener drops one of the destination arguments" }
Reverted; tree byte-identical; both tsc programs and 114 frontend tests green on
the merged tree.

AND THE GUARD IS ITSELF PINNED, which is the part I did not think to ask for. A
type-level guard can stop guarding with nothing going red, so quick-connect.test
.tsx carries three @ts-expect-error openers beside one accepted four-argument
one; neutering CallableWith turns all three into TS2578 unused-directive errors.
tsconfig.test.json is in pre-commit and in CI's frontend job, so the pin is gated.

The two sibling openers (alias, ad-hoc) MUST stay lambdas -- the root supplies an
empty profile id -- so they are the one shape bind cannot substitute, and they
are guarded the same way.

A PREMISE OF MINE WAS WRONG and the worker corrected it: I said "main.test.ts
exists, so some seam into main.tsx already does". It does not. main.test.ts never
imports main.tsx -- it rebuilds a comparable arrangement. main.tsx is one
main(): void invoked at module scope, 1670 lines, with no seam at all. Filed as
nocx-7hrti rather than opened inside a bugfix.

STILL NOT COVERED, stated rather than left silent: argument ORDER (four
compatible types in the wrong order type-check fine); rest-parameter openers
(`length: number`, so `4 extends number` holds vacuously -- which is why the ~40
existing vi.fn() call sites still compile); and every non-arity wiring mistake at
the composition root, unreachable by anything but e2e until nocx-7hrti.

DISCOVERED AND FILED, not folded in: nocx-yrgxc (P1) -- the endpoint string is
used as the IDENTITY for "which saved connection was this opened from", and it is
a derived key assembled by two constructions in two files that must agree byte
for byte. I verified its strongest claim myself: endpointOf (panes.ts:3312) is
`${host}:${port ?? 22}` with no bracketing, while profileIdentity
(quick-connect-assembly.ts:201) goes through joinHostPort, which brackets. A
profile on ::1 yields `::1:22` against `[::1]:22` and can never match. Live today,
independent of the port.

title: A command reaching its bound asks the model whether to keep waiting, and the person owns both ceilings in Settings
description:
The owner ran `df` through the assistant. It produced no output for over two
minutes — a stuck mount does exactly that — and the lease killed it. The command
was healthy and the silence was normal.

The bound is INACTIVITY, not wall clock (`internal/transport/run_lease.go:101`):
`WallClock: 10m`, `Inactivity: 2m`, `OutputBudget: 4 MiB`. So a command dies for
two minutes of SILENCE while a chatty eight-minute build survives. Two minutes
of silence is less than `npm ci` on a cold cache, a cold build, a migration, or
`df` on an unreachable mount. The model is told "the command was terminalized
for inactivity: it produced no output for too long"
(`internal/assistant/requester.go:172`) and nothing in that sentence says a
longer bound exists, so the model cannot act on it.

## What the owner decided (2026-09-02)

Three parts, and the first is what makes the other two safe.

**1. A bound reached ASKS THE MODEL instead of killing.** "No output for N, the
command is still running — keep waiting, or stop?" The model has the command and
the task in front of it and is the party that can judge whether this silence is
expected; the person is not woken for it. This is ADR-0020 decision 2's
"renewable" clause finally built — and note it is deliberately NOT decision 3's
`awaiting-takeover`, where the HUMAN takes over an interactive program. Same
lease, different answerer, for a different reason: an interactive program needs a
person because it wants input, while a quiet program needs only a judgement about
whether to keep waiting.

**2. The model may set the bound for its own call**, below the person's value.
It asks; it never widens.

**3. The person owns the ceiling, in Settings, and both bounds go there —
default 10 minutes each.** The wall-clock bound and the quiet bound become two
`MustRegisterNumber(NumberSpec{...})` declarations in `internal/settings`, so the
generated screen renders them like every other number, with a unit and a range.
`DefaultRunLeaseConfig`'s own comment already predicted this: "a future settings
surface flip one bound in one place".

## A consequence of 10/10 worth stating rather than discovering

The quiet timer resets on output; the wall clock does not. So with both ceilings
at ten minutes the quiet bound can never fire BEFORE the wall clock — a command
silent from the start reaches both at the same moment, and a command that prints
at minute 9 is killed by the wall clock at ten before its extended quiet bound
matters. At these values the quiet bound is effectively subsumed.

That is not wrong and is not a reason to pick different numbers: it fixes the
reported case exactly (`df` quiet for three minutes now runs), and the quiet
bound becomes load-bearing again the moment somebody raises the wall clock above
it, which is precisely what the setting is for. It is written down here so the
next reader does not conclude the quiet bound is dead code.

## Design note for whoever takes this

Both the inactivity and output bounds are armed only with an authenticated
lifecycle attempt (`RunLeaseConfig.needsShellIntegration`), so on a session
without shell integration there is no quiet bound at all and neither the defect
nor the fix is observable. Any test that means to see this must have integration
up.

Where the question reaches the model is the decision to make deliberately.
Today the model learns everything through tool results, and the cheapest shape
that does not invent a mid-run channel is to end the attempt with a result that
says the command is STILL RUNNING and offers the continuation — rather than a
new backend-to-model push. Whichever is chosen, say why in the code, and the
answer must not be able to outlive the ceiling: renewals stop at the person's
number, or the ceiling is not one.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Ask the assistant to run `df` on a machine with an unreachable network mount
   (or `sleep 150`, the same shape with no mount required).
2. Nothing is printed for two minutes.
3. The run is terminalized for inactivity, and the model is told only that the
   command produced no output for too long. Nothing offers a way to run it
   anyway.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `sleep 150` completes and returns its exit status, with shell integration up.
  This is the reported case; it is the first assertion because it is the one a
  person can see.
- At the quiet bound the command is NOT killed: the model is asked, answers
  "keep waiting", and the command runs to completion — one test watches all
  three steps.
- The model answering "stop" terminalizes the command, and the run reports the
  stop as the reason rather than as a timeout.
- Renewal cannot outlive the ceiling: with the person's wall-clock setting at N,
  a model that answers "keep waiting" every time still ends at N, asserted.
- Both bounds appear in Settings as declared numbers with a unit and a range,
  default 10 minutes each, and changing one changes what the next run is bound
  by — asserted end to end, not on the settings store.
- A call asking for a bound BELOW the person's setting gets what it asked for;
  a call asking for more is clamped to the setting and the tool result SAYS it
  was clamped and to what. Both ends asserted; a silent clamp is not acceptable.
- With no bound asked for, a run is bound by exactly the person's setting: one
  test asserts the unstated path is unchanged.
- The sentence the model receives names the bound that fired, its value, and the
  continuation available — asserted on the string, not on the reason code.
notes: 2026-09-02, owner: the escalation ladder is exactly two rungs — the lease asks the MODEL, and the model may then ask the PERSON at its own discretion ('спрашиваем модель. А модель может спросить человека, если нужно'). Consequence for the implementation: build NO person-facing path from the lease. No new approval kind, no notification, no surface. The model already reaches the person through the turn or through an ordinary proposed call, and a second route from the lease to a human would be a second owner for 'how a person is asked about a run' (AD-8) — waking somebody for the question the model was handed precisely so they would not be woken. This also settles why ADR-0020 decision 3's awaiting-takeover is a different mechanism and not a near-duplicate: there the PROGRAM demands a human because it wants input; here a judgement is requested of the model and whoever it consults afterwards travels the path that already exists. Neither the model nor the person it consults can push a run past the ceiling in Settings.
close_reason: c527dd92. The quiet bound parks instead of killing: the model is asked and answers with the new session.wait tool (continue re-attaches to the SAME execution, stop ends it). Both time bounds are now Settings numbers, 10 minutes each; a call may ask for a shorter quiet bound and is told when it is clamped; the wall timer is armed once so renewals cannot outlive the person's ceiling. No new termination reason and no CHECK-set change. Verified: internal/settings, agenttools, assistant, content, filesystem and transport all green (go test -count=1), golangci-lint clean tree-wide, contracts:check current, and deadcode -whylive shows NewRunWatcher, RunWatcher.Allows, WSServer.RequestRunWait and executeRunWait all with real call paths. internal/app and internal/shellintegration fail here — verified IDENTICAL on origin/main in a scratch worktree, so environmental, not this change (AGENTS.md's known local-vs-CI list). Two findings on the way: a continuation naming a run that is no longer waiting used to fail the whole turn and is now an answer (ErrRunNotWaiting), and session.wait declares observe alone with the argument written into the declaration. NOT covered: the e2e suite and CI.

title: An approval question can ask the live shell, because the shell can speak while idle
description:
nocx-4h0m7.5 built everything the expansion facts need — the syntactic
classifier, the one-query-per-approval shape, the display form beside the
verbatim string, the re-read fence, the wire contract and the surface — and then
could not ask. In the shipped product every expansion therefore reports the
`unasked` state, which is honest and product-visible, and is not the feature.

**The constraint is measured and already written down here**
(`internal/shellintegration/scripts/nocx.bash:1687-1692`, nocx-z9s9.16):

> "It has to be a prompt, and that is a constraint rather than a preference: a
> shell idle in readline runs no traps at all. Measured on bash 5.2 and 5.3, a
> SIGUSR1 raised while the user is sitting at a prompt does not run its handler
> until the next command is submitted, and SIGWINCH does not flush it either —
> so there is no way for the shell to speak on its own."

An approval question is asked at exactly that moment: the lane is idle in
readline. The kernel's only backend-originated request today,
`refresh_request`, is answered at the NEXT prompt boundary for this reason
(`internal/lifecycle/transport.go:5-8`; `internal/shellintegration/channel_exec_test.go:798`
asserts the next-prompt delivery). Waiting for the next prompt is useless here —
the next prompt is the command we are deciding about.

So this is a per-shell-tier capability, not a bug in nocx-4h0m7.5:

- **zsh can.** `zle -F <fd> handler` runs a handler while the line editor is
  idle, so a zsh session can answer while sitting at a prompt.
- **bash cannot**, on the measurement above, and the honest outcome there is
  the named `unasked` state that already exists — never a silent guess.

That asymmetry is the decision this bead owes: a capability the tiers answer
differently, with the refusal named per tier rather than a fallback that
pretends.

Shape suggested by the worker that hit it: a kernel-originated request kind
beside `refresh_request`; a `Port.Send` path with a correlation slot like
`Domain.refreshRequest`; a zsh tier via `zle -F`; a named refusal for bash. The
shell-side JSON escaping already exists (`__nocx_lc_json_escape`,
`nocx.bash:79`).

Until this lands, nocx-4h0m7.5's criteria 2 and 4 are exercised only through the
fake source in tests, and criterion 1 (the command is byte-identical) holds
unconditionally because nothing is ever substituted.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A zsh session with our integration answers an expansion query while sitting
  idle at a prompt, with no command submitted in between; asserted end to end,
  not on the transport.
- The approval window for a command containing `$HOME` in that session shows the
  value beside the verbatim command, and the verbatim command is still what
  runs — asserted byte for byte in the same test.
- A bash session reports the named `unasked` state with the tier's own reason,
  and the surface says so in words that cannot be read as "we asked and it was
  safe".
- A shell that does not answer within the bound leaves the question unblocked:
  the person is still asked, with `unasked` shown. One test holds the shell
  silent and asserts the approval still arrives.
- The tier capability is stated where tiers are owned, not only in a Go comment.

title: A command operand that is not an absolute path is unbounded: the new resource layer skips exactly what it cannot see
description:
nocx-cs8h2.1 gave a shell command its first path check ever: the resources the
parser named must lie inside the selected row's scopes
(`EffectPolicy.namedResourcesWithinRow`). It is lexical and absolute-only, by
construction — `namedResourceScope` returns false for anything that is not an
absolute path, and the loop then SKIPS that resource as unbounded.

So under `Observe: {permit, scopes: [path /home/dev/project]}`:

- `cat src/app.ts` — relative, skipped, PERMITTED.
- `cat ../../../etc/passwd` — relative, skipped, PERMITTED.
- `cat /home/dev/project/../../../etc/passwd` — absolute, prefix-matches, PERMITTED.

The shell then resolves all three and reads the file. Unlike `files.read` there
is no capability behind this to catch it: the runner submits the text to a
terminal (internal/agenttools/runner.go), so for commands the policy layer IS
the enforcement, and it is a `strings.HasPrefix`.

`pathScopeContains` says so about itself already
(internal/content/resource_scope.go:43-47): "NEVER a filesystem authorization
check: callers authorizing a filesystem read must use the provider-backed
capability in internal/filesystem/scoped.go". For a command there is no such
caller to defer to.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. On the Agent policy page set "Read and inspect" to permit, scoped to one
   directory — say `/home/dev/project`.
2. Ask the assistant to run `cat ../../../etc/passwd`, or
   `cat /home/dev/project/../../../etc/passwd`.
3. No question is asked. The command runs and the file is read, from outside the
   only directory the row names.

Two reasons this is worth its own bead rather than a footnote on cs8h2.1. First,
a check that quietly passes what it cannot see is worse than no check, because
the next reader believes the row means something. Second, cs8h2.3 adds a greedy
trailing token to the pattern language, and its whole safety argument is that the
resource layer bounds what the shape layer widens — that argument is only as good
as this.

The run has no cwd to normalize against: `RunContext`
(internal/agenttools/registry.go:59-72) carries none. Inventing one is worse than
asking. So the honest answer is likely "an operand that cannot be resolved to a
canonical absolute path is `ask`, never silently unbounded" — but that is a
decision to take deliberately, and if it is taken it belongs in the ADR-0020
amendment that owns path containment, not only in a Go comment.

Related: nocx-cd6vp (the same lexical/canonical split, on the file-tool side, and
the capability there is broken too); nocx-esh2j (the floor's path roots never see
a command's paths at all, because `session.run` resolves only a session
resource).

## Acceptance Criteria

- With `Observe: {permit, scopes: [path /home/dev/project]}`,
  `DecisionForInvocation` for `cat /home/dev/project/../../../etc/passwd` is not
  `permit`.
- Same row, `cat src/app.ts` and `cat ../../etc/passwd` are not `permit`.
- Same row, `cat /home/dev/project/src/app.ts` IS `permit` — the paired success
  case, so the tightening is not just a blanket refusal.
- A row scoped to a directory does not permit `cat` of a path that RESOLVES
  outside it, asserted with a real symlink on disk, using the same relation
  `filesystem.contained` uses.
- Whichever answer is taken for an unresolvable operand, it is written where
  path containment is owned — the ADR-0020 amendment — and not only in a
  comment.

title: The ack round-trip runs on the client's only reader goroutine's critical path, and wedges it
description:
Found 2026-09-02 by an adversarial second reading of feat/relay-pty-owner.

internal/helper/client/sessions.go:290 acks SYNCHRONOUSLY via
a.client.Call(context.Background(), ...), which blocks until the response frame is
delivered -- by Client.onFrame, i.e. by the single connection read loop. That same
read loop is what calls deliver / deliverLifecycle, which block on
a.data / a.lifecycleData (cap 64) when full, escaping only via <-a.done.

## Steps to Reproduce

PTY variant: the read loop fills a.data to 64 entries; the consumer pops one and
blocks in Call awaiting the ack response; the read loop then blocks in deliver on
the 65th payload. Neither can proceed -- nothing else drains a.data, and nothing
else can deliver the ack response.

Observed: the whole client wedges. Every session on that helper, plus any
in-flight Call (resize, detach, inventory). Expected: an ack cannot block the
reader that must deliver its answer.

Reachability: the helper's credit limit (internal/helper/session/session.go:170,
64 KiB) bounds BYTES, not frames, and window.read returns as little as one byte,
so an interactive echo storm or a program flushing per byte produces thousands of
tiny frames inside the 64 KiB allowance. Over ssh with a 50 ms RTT this is not
exotic.

Lifecycle variant, easier to hit: lifecycleData (cap 64) has NO drainer between
Client.Attach -- which starts the helper's serveLifecycle immediately -- and
StartLifecycle(), which transport calls only AFTER the open ack
(internal/transport/ws_session_handlers.go:675), after the ledger write,
getOrCreateRx and discovery. A slow SQLite ledger write plus a chatty handshake
fills the buffer and wedges the read loop before the bridge ever starts.
acceptance_criteria:
A client test with a fake conn emits 100 one-byte session frames and one ack
response, with a consumer that reads one frame, and asserts it does not hang.
A second test covers the lifecycle variant: attach, do not call StartLifecycle,
push more than 64 lifecycle frames, assert the read loop still serves an ordinary
Call. Both fail before the fix.
close_reason: Closed 2026-09-02, verified by the coordinator. Commit 045817c1, merged as aa20a020. Each carrier's queue is a slice behind a mutex whose push cannot block, so the read loop's progress never depends on a consumer. The bound is not a buffer size but the helper's credit limit — only bytes that have been READ are acked, so an undrained carrier stalls its producer after one credit window. That is AD-10 applied at the source instead of at a channel in the middle of the connection's only reader; a bigger buffer would have moved the deadlock rather than removed it. Acks stay synchronous on the consumer's own goroutine deliberately: with a read loop that cannot block, waiting for an ack is latency, not deadlock. Fell out on the way and is worth as much as the fix: the partial-read remainder used to be pushed back by a goroutine and could land BEHIND a later payload — bytes to a terminal out of order. unpop puts it at the front.

title: The shell's last output is dropped: finish() races the buffered data channel in AttachedSession.Read
description:
Found 2026-09-02 by an adversarial second reading of feat/relay-pty-owner.

internal/helper/client/client.go:284-285 does recordExit then finish(), closing
a.done the instant the exit notification arrives. But AttachedSession.Read
(sessions.go:274-303) selects on a.data and a.done with no priority:

    select {
    case data := <-a.data:   // still holds the shell's last bytes
    case <-a.done:
        return 0, io.EOF     // Go picks uniformly when both are ready
    }

The same race is on the delivery side: deliver (sessions.go:230-236) selects on
`a.data <- payload` against `<-a.done`, so frames arriving after the exit
notification are dropped even when the buffer has room.

This is the defect the HELPER side documents having fixed and refuses to repeat.
hostSession.watchExit (internal/helper/session/session.go:233-248): "the process
ending and the OUTPUT ending are two events and the second is later... losing the
last thing the shell ever printed, which is the single most valuable line in the
session." The helper carefully leaves the window to be closed by the pump alone;
the coordinator client then closes done on the process event anyway. Two halves,
each right about its own half.

## Steps to Reproduce

Run `echo goodbye; exit` in a helper-hosted tab.

The helper's pump writes "goodbye\r\n" to the window, serve sends it as a
TypeSessionData frame, and watchExit then fires the exit notification. Both are
handled by the SAME client read-loop goroutine, in order, so by the time the
session pump calls Read, a.data holds "goodbye\r\n" AND a.done is closed.

Observed: about half the time Read returns io.EOF and the line is lost. With k
chunks still buffered, the chance of draining them all is 2^-k. Expected: every
buffered byte is read before EOF.
acceptance_criteria:
A client test queues N payloads, then delivers an exit notification, then asserts
all N are read before EOF -- run under -count=100 so an unbiased select cannot
pass by luck. The fix shape is either that the exit notification records the
status and lets EOF come from the STREAM ending, or that Read drains a.data
non-blockingly before honouring a.done; whichever is taken, say in the code why.
close_reason: Closed 2026-09-02, verified by the coordinator. Commit 8313b910, merged as aa20a020. take() drains the queue before honouring done, in one place for both carriers, plus a room-first push on delivery. The alternative shape — EOF arriving from the stream ending — is not buildable from this side: the wire has no end-of-stream marker, the helper's per-subscriber pump simply returns, so a coordinator waiting for one would hold the tab open forever. The closing event is therefore STATED rather than received: the queue is empty AND the session has ended. Mutations: an unbiased select again loses everything after the first chunk; removing the room-first push drops from the middle.

title: The epic's happy path, watched end to end
description:
The epic's happy path, watched end to end by one automated check, through the seam
a person actually reaches (testing rule 2, and rule 1: the dialog is driven, not
the classifier).

## Acceptance Criteria

- One e2e spec: the assistant proposes `df -h /home/dev`; the prompt shows the
  option menu; the person chooses "any path" and answers "always"; a later
  `df -h /tmp` runs with no question at all; a later `df -h > /etc/hosts` asks
  again. All three observed through the UI.
- A second spec drives the unrecognised-program path from .7: the prompt says what
  could not be determined, the person names a class, and the next call still asks —
  as that class.
- The saved answers are visible on the Agent policy page with the class they were
  approved at (the page itself is nocx-takqr.3 — this asserts what it must show,
  and is the join between the two epics).

title: A program the parser does not understand: the person names the class, and naming it permits nothing
description:
For a program the parser does not understand, the person is never asked what it
is — the ceiling answers for them. `session.run` declares a set,
`ResourceReport.Effect` returns the worst member whenever `Unresolved` is
non-empty, so `fd`, `jq` and `htop` are asked about forever as the worst thing
their carrier could do.

The allowlist in `cmdeffect.go` cannot be completed and MUST NOT be delegated to
the person: its entries carry flag-level disqualifiers (`sort -o` writes,
`uniq -w` writes) that nobody approving a dialog can be expected to know. So the
person is not asked to complete the allowlist. They are asked the one question
they can answer — what is this program — and their answer does NOT permit
anything: it only names the class the next call is judged at, and that call still
goes through the matrix.

The dialog therefore says what the parser could not determine (the `Unresolved`
reasons are retained for exactly this), offers the classes, and saving one is a
classification, not a permission.

Related and unresolved: nocx-fx4z3 asks whether an unresolved parse should take a
RANKED worst member at all — `WorstEffect`'s total order ranks delegate above
`rm -rf`, which the lattice was written to refuse. This child must not re-decide
that; if fx4z3 lands first, take its answer.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Saving a class for an unrecognised program does not permit it: the next call of
  that program still asks, and the question now names the person's class instead
  of the ceiling. One test drives both calls and asserts the class on the second.
- The question for an unrecognised program states what could not be determined,
  from the `Unresolved` reason, rather than only naming a class.
- A classification never widens: a class saved as `observe` for a program whose
  invocation derives a write does not lower that invocation's class.
- The classification is over the program word, never over a tool name
  (ADR-0028 decision 4), and is stored where the policy page can show it.

title: The offer crosses the wire as options, and the dialog has no text input to type a pattern into
description:
`agent.approvalRequested` carries `standing: {available, rule, reason}` — one rule,
or a reason there is none — and the renderer draws three widths (once / in this
session / always) over that single rule. The menu from .4 has nowhere to land.

`standing` becomes the offer: the options the backend generated, each with its id,
its label and the rule text a person reads. `agent.approve` gains the chosen
option's id, and refuses an id that was not in the offer — the width (once /
session / always) stays exactly what it is, orthogonal to which option was chosen.
The dialog renders the options as a choice; it has no text input, and cannot
acquire one, because there is no wire field a typed pattern could travel in.

Both contracts move together with their generated renderer types
(`npm run contracts:check`), and the over-the-wire conformance test is the one
that matters — a payload the test built proves nothing about what the server
sends.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `contracts/agent.approvalRequested.schema.json` and
  `contracts/agent.approve.schema.json` carry the option list and the chosen id,
  both with `additionalProperties: false` and explicit `required`.
- An `agent.approve` naming an option id that was not in the offer is refused, and
  the run does not resume; asserted over the real socket.
- `…_OverTheWireConformsToContract` covers a notification whose offer has several
  options and one whose offer is empty with a reason.
- The renderer has no free-text control anywhere in the approval prompt; asserted
  by a test that queries the prompt for input elements and finds none.
- Choosing an option and answering "always" saves that option's rule, with its
  class, and one test watches the saved policy afterwards.

title: Widening is a menu generated from the parse, never a typed pattern
description:
A person is offered exactly one reusable answer — "allow always", saved as the
exact token list they were shown. Widening has no expression at all, and free text
in a dialog under time pressure is exactly the over-matching that
`LiteralInvocationRule`'s refusal of `*` was written to prevent.

Widening becomes a MENU GENERATED FROM THE PARSE. From one canonical `Invocation`,
produce the set of rules a person may be offered, each with the label saying what
it covers: the exact line (today's answer); "any path" for each resource operand
the parse identified; "any arguments" using the trailing token from .3. Authoring
a pattern by hand belongs on the policy page, where the whole rule set is visible
at once — never here.

Owner: `internal/content/rules.go`, beside `StandingRule`, which becomes one member
of the set it returns. The generator reads only the parse — it never re-tokenizes
the command, and it never names a program.

## Acceptance Criteria

- For `df -h /home/dev` the menu contains the exact line, "any path" and "any
  arguments", each carrying the rule it would save and a label naming what it
  covers; asserted field by field.
- Every option in the menu is a rule that `validateInvocationRules` accepts and
  that carries the approved class from .2.
- For an invocation with no resource operand, no "any path" option is offered —
  the menu never contains an option derived from nothing.
- For a disqualified, unresolved, compound or unparsed invocation the menu is
  empty and carries the reason `StandingRule` already produces.
- The generator has no path that accepts a caller-supplied pattern string.

title: A pattern can say 'and whatever follows', once, at the end of a subcommand
description:
`InvocationRule.Matches` requires the same number of subcommands and the same
number of tokens in each, and `*` matches only within one token. So "any df,
whatever the flags" is not expressible at all, even by an operator: `["df","*"]`
matches a df with exactly one token. Rules accumulate one per exact command line
— `df -h /home` and `df -h /home/dev` are two separate rules.

Add a trailing token meaning "and whatever follows", valid only as the LAST token
of a subcommand. The bound that makes it safe is not arity any more: .1 keeps the
resources a command names inside the matrix rows and the fence, and .2 stops the
rule matching once the shape derives another class. Both must be green first.

The parser is deliberately NOT changed. Redirections stay where they are, inline
in the token list, and keep setting `Disqualified` plus an `Unresolved` entry for
a real file target — so a redirecting invocation still cannot match any rule at
all. Splitting `>` out as its own subcommand (the arity answer) was considered and
rejected: `>` is not a program, its operand is a resource of the left command, and
putting it in a position every consumer reads as "program" costs `Label()` and the
floor's word scan for a bound the resource layer already provides.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A rule `df ...` approved at `observe` permits `df`, `df -h` and `df -h /tmp`,
  asserted as three cases in one test.
- The same rule does NOT permit `df -h > /etc/hosts`, and the test states which
  layer refused it — the resource check of .1 — rather than asserting only the
  outcome.
- The trailing token is refused anywhere but last in a subcommand, by
  `validateInvocationRules`, with the position in the message.
- `LiteralInvocationRule` still refuses a person's literal command containing the
  token: it is produced by the menu, never typed.
- `Label()` renders it in a form a person can read back, asserted on a rule with
  and without it.

title: A rule carries the class it was approved at, and stops matching when the shape derives another
description:
A saved rule records the command shape and the decision, and nothing about what
the command was understood to BE when the person answered. So a rule stays true
forever, even after the same shape starts deriving a different class.

The epic's answer: a rule carries the CLASS it was approved at, and matches only
while derivation still produces that class. `df` approved as observe stops
matching the moment an invocation of that shape derives a write. This is what
makes "any arguments" safe without knowing anything about the program — the
person's answer is a checkable fact ("this is a read"), not an authority
decision, and it stops being honoured the moment it stops being true.

`InvocationRule` gains the effect it was approved at. `Matches` needs the derived
class, which `DecisionForInvocation` already receives as its `e Effect` argument.
`LiteralInvocationRule` and `StandingRule` record it from the classified
proposal; `applyStandingAnswer` (internal/transport/ws_agent.go) already holds it
— the same value the wire sends as `effect`.

Greenfield: no migration and no compatibility fallback. `ParseEffectPolicy` is
strict, so a stored rule without the field stops parsing, and an unparseable
policy is already an ask-everything policy — the fail-safe direction.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A rule saved from `df -h /home` approved at `observe` does not match an
  invocation of the same shape that derives `mutate-reversible`; one test drives
  both through `DecisionForInvocation` and asserts permit then ask.
- A rule with no class does not match anything, asserted directly.
- A policy document whose rule omits the class fails `ParseEffectPolicy` with
  `ErrPolicySyntax`, and the store's caller treats it as ask-everything.
- The class a rule carries is the one the gate classified, not one re-derived at
  save time: asserted by a test where the two would differ.

title: A matching rule stops short-circuiting the matrix: the resources a command names still face their effect's row and the fence
description:
`EffectPolicy.DecisionForInvocation` treats a matching rule as an exception to the
whole matrix: a rule that matches turns an `ask` row into `permit` and returns.
Nothing afterwards checks the resources the invocation named against that row's
`Scopes`, or against the run fence. The rule short-circuits the layer that owns
resources.

That is what makes every widening of the command shape dangerous, and it is why
`InvocationRule.Matches` had to be nailed to a fixed number of subcommands and a
fixed number of tokens in each: with the resource layer bypassed, the token count
was the only thing standing between "any argument" and "any file".

The two dimensions are already built and are already separate. `ResourceReport`
carries a verb per named resource; `EffectRow.Scopes` is the per-effect resource
selector; `RunFence` is the outer bound. A rule should answer only "what shape is
this command line", after which the matrix decides over the resources as it
already does — which is what the epic's own sentence says: not "permit this line",
but "this is a read", after which the matrix decides.

The comparison that settled the shape: @gotgenes/pi-permission-system composes
four layers most-restrictive-wins — `path` (cross-cutting), `external_directory`
(the boundary), per-tool patterns, and `bash` command patterns — so its greedy
`git *` is safe because the redirect target is checked on `path_write` regardless
of what the command pattern allowed. We have the same two dimensions; only the
composition is missing.

Scope: `internal/content/effectpolicy.go` and whatever consumes `RowScopes`. No
change to the pattern language here (that is .3) and none to the parser.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A permitting rule whose invocation names a resource outside the matched row's
  `Scopes` does NOT permit: the call asks (or is refused, per the row), and one
  test asserts exactly that with a permit rule and a row scoped to one directory.
- A permitting rule whose invocation names a resource outside the run fence does
  not permit, asserted with every row set to permit and a one-directory fence.
- Refusal stays final and most-restrictive-wins among matching rules is unchanged:
  the existing rule tests stay green without edit.
- The composition order is stated once, in a comment on `DecisionForInvocation`,
  naming ADR-0020 §7 and where each layer's owner is.
close_reason: 3e7cd218. DecisionForInvocation composes the resource layer after the shape layer; a permit whose invocation names a resource outside the selected row's scopes falls back to ask. Fence needs no second check — WithRunScopes folds it into every row. Red verified by removing the gate (3 of 4 new tests fail); green: go test ./internal/content/ and ./internal/transport/ both ok. Hole found and filed: nocx-cs8h2.9 (non-absolute operands are skipped), which now blocks cs8h2.3.

title: The lie-down sheet is a transition played as a loop
description:
Watched by the owner on 2026-09-02: the lying animation is strange, it repeats several times.

`laying.png` is not a cycle. It is a transition, and the frames say so: 0-5 are stand -> crouch -> sit -> sit up, 6-7 are lying down. Declared `loop('laying.png', 8)` in pack.ts, so the cat lies down, snaps back onto its feet and lies down again for as long as the occupation lasts.

Non-loop modes already play through and clamp on the last frame, so the immediate fix is one word. The better fix uses what the artist actually drew: this is the ONLY transition in the pack, and reversed it is a get-up. Lie down = frames 0->7, hold, stand up = 7->0. That gives the pet an entry and an exit from the one posture it spends the most time in.

## Success Criteria

- The cat lies down once and stays lying for the whole occupation.
- Leaving the lying posture plays the sheet backwards rather than cutting to a standing frame.
- A test names the frame ranges, so a repacked sheet fails loudly rather than looping again.
close_reason: Landed as d5ab77f0. Verified on the live stand: grooming 15.5s (was 0.5s), sitting 21.2s, lying 23.8s, stretching 1.5s; the get-up phase observed as idle/lie|none -> idle/lie|getup -> idle/none with the pet stationary.

title: Cornered at the wall, the pet blinks instead of facing what scared it
description:
Watched by the owner on 2026-09-02: with the cat in a corner and the cursor next to it, it keeps trying to run and cannot, and the result is a blinking. It also walks into the wall, which looks wrong on its own.

One cause. The pointer response picks a direction without asking whether that direction leads anywhere: step 3 sets `dir = threat` every frame, the walk drives into the boundary, `past` fires, and `corneredByPointer` takes the animal off the end. On the FLOOR there is nothing below, so `fall` lands it in the same spot on the same frame with a fresh `land` phase -- the squash -- and the whole cycle repeats about five times a second. That is the blink.

A cornered cat does not moonwalk into a wall. It stops, turns to face what it does not like, and watches it. The fleeing branch needs to know the difference between "away" and "nowhere", and stepping off an edge needs a place to land.

## Success Criteria

- Pinned into a corner by the pointer, the pet stops, faces the pointer and holds -- it does not run on the spot, and its position does not oscillate.
- No `land` phase is ever entered twice within a second without a real fall between them.
- Stepping off an edge is not offered when the ground underfoot is the floor.
- Climbing back up is unaffected: the jump remains the way out of a corner, and a test watches a cornered pet leave by jumping.
close_reason: Landed as fb2a9901. Measured on the live stand: teleport gone (was dy=3117 to y=-3589 on an output burst, now no jump on scroll, 41px on a burst, 66px on a 700px window resize); the sprite never leaves the pane (was 31px outside, now 0); cornered by a fast cursor, zero land phases and zero distinct positions over four seconds.

title: An occupation lasts as long as the occupation, not one clip cycle
description:
Watched by the owner on 2026-09-02: every action changes far too fast. A cat washes itself for tens of seconds; ours washes for HALF A SECOND, because `licking1.png` is five frames at 10 fps and `chosenHold` gives a `once` clip a behaviour lifetime equal to one cycle of the clip.

That came out of nocx-ds0ki, which is right about the thing it was written for -- a REACTION clip must not be cut mid-cycle -- and wrong as a general rule. Clip length and behaviour length are two different quantities. The clip is how long one wash takes; the occupation is how long the cat feels like washing.

The model that holds both: an occupation runs for its own hold, the clip repeats WHOLE cycles inside it, and the occupation does not end until the cycle in progress has finished. Nothing is ever cut mid-cycle, and nothing is ever a single half-second flicker either.

## Success Criteria

- Grooming, seen by a person, lasts several seconds and repeats the wash rather than playing it once.
- No clip is ever cut mid-cycle -- the existing nocx-ds0ki assertions stay green.
- A one-shot REACTION (meow, scratch) still plays exactly once and is still protected from interruption.
- The menu's holds are re-read against what the drawings actually take, and a comment states which number is a drawing's length and which is a decision.
close_reason: Landed as d5ab77f0. Verified on the live stand: grooming 15.5s (was 0.5s), sitting 21.2s, lying 23.8s, stretching 1.5s; the get-up phase observed as idle/lie|none -> idle/lie|getup -> idle/none with the pet stationary.

title: Choosing an OSC 52 clipboard action clears every terminal pane
description:
Solid render disposer owns #panes and removes every pane after a banner choice

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Open two terminal panes/tabs.
2. Trigger the OSC 52 clipboard permission banner.
3. Choose Allow clipboard writes, Don't show again, or Dismiss.
4. Observe that the banner closes but terminal panes lose their contents.

## Expected Behavior
The banner choice removes only the banner and preserves both existing terminal panes.
acceptance_criteria: allow, suppress and dismiss remove only the banner; two existing terminal panes remain interactive in Chromium and WebKit
notes:
Confirmed cause: ClipboardBannerImpl rendered Solid directly into #panes; the Solid disposer cleared #panes descendants, including terminal panes. Fix mounts into an isolated .clipboard-banner-host appended under #panes and disposes the Solid root before removing only that host.

Verification:
- frontend: npx vitest run src/banner.characterization.test.ts — red before fix (3 failures, pane.isConnected false), green after fix (14 passed).

title: Glyph corruption on macOS: atlas page merge leaves stale texture coords with no follow-up frame
description:
Symptom, reported from the shipped macOS app with a screenshot: the viewport
renders correct cell backgrounds over garbage glyph SHAPES -- fragments of
other characters, only some cells affected while neighbouring runs render
perfectly. Buffer and parser are intact; only the atlas lookup is wrong.
Resizing the window repairs it completely. macOS only, intermittent, not
reproducible on demand.

## Root cause

Confirmed by reading the locked sources (@xterm/xterm 5.5.0,
@xterm/addon-webgl 0.18.0; frontend/package-lock.json), independently by two
readers.

The WebGL renderer draws quads carrying texture coordinates into a shared
glyph atlas. When the atlas reaches maxAtlasPages -- set per GL context to
min(32, MAX_TEXTURE_IMAGE_UNITS), which on macOS/Metal is 16 --
TextureAtlas._createNewPage() merges four pages and MUTATES the cached glyph
records in place:

    g.texturePage = mergedPageIndex
    g.texturePosition.x += xOffset
    g.texturePosition.y += yOffset
    ...
    this._requestClearModel = true

_deletePage then decrements texturePage on every glyph of the pages that
shifted. Cells already in the renderer's model keep the coordinates they had,
which now point somewhere else on a rearranged page -- garbage shapes.

The recovery is purely temporal and that is the defect. WebglRenderer.renderRows
reads the flag ONLY at the top of a frame:

    if (this._glyphRenderer.value.beginFrame()) { clearModel(true); updateModel(0, rows-1) }
    else { updateModel(start, end) }

The merge happens LATER IN THAT SAME FRAME, inside _updateModel while
rasterising a newly encountered glyph -- beginFrame() has already returned
false. Setting _requestClearModel does not call refreshRows, does not request
an animation frame, and does not mark anything dirty. It only says "rebuild
fully IF another frame happens".

So the corruption is a one-frame state that persists indefinitely when the
output that filled the atlas was the last output. Any later render heals it
(and _requestClearModel is never reset in this version, so every subsequent
render is a full-viewport one). A resize supplies exactly that missing frame,
which is why resizing "fixes" it.

Why macOS only: isLinuxWebKit() installs a FORCED_REFRESH_MS pump
(frontend/src/renderers/xterm.ts:426) that re-marks every row, so Linux always
has a next frame. macOS has no pump.

Why heavily coloured output triggers it: the atlas cache is keyed by
character + fg + bg + extended attributes, so diffs, syntax-highlighted logs
and truecolor multiply the key space and fill the pages.

Aggravating factor: CharAtlasCache holds ONE module-global cache and hands the
same TextureAtlas to every terminal whose font, cell size, DPR, options and
colours match -- which is every nocx tab. So a merge triggered by tab B's
rendering moves coordinates out from under tab A's model. Each tab has its own
canvas and GL context; only the atlas and its glyph records are shared.

## Refuted hypotheses (do not spend time here)

- DPR change. xterm handles it itself: CoreBrowserService re-arms its own
  resolution query, RenderService.onDprChange -> handleDevicePixelRatioChange
  -> renderer.handleDevicePixelRatioChange (reacquires the atlas) followed by
  an unconditional refreshRows(0, rowCount-1). The refresh conditional in
  nocx's fitViewport (frontend/src/renderers/xterm.ts:590, inside
  `if (cols !== t.cols || rows !== t.rows)`) is therefore NOT a stale-atlas
  gap: if xterm saw the DPR change it also repainted; if it did not see it, it
  did not rebuild the atlas either.
- WebGL context recovery. Renderer replacement is a full-refresh operation
  inside xterm: WebglAddon.activate calls RenderService.setRenderer, which ends
  in _fullRefresh(). Disposing the addon installs the built-in renderer through
  the same path, as does the CanvasAddon fallback. And native restoration
  within the addon's 3 s grace period does removeTerminalFromCache +
  _initializeWebGLState + _requestRedrawViewport.

Remaining alternative if the fix below does not close the report: a
WKWebView/Metal texture-upload fault. No nocx code path evidences it; treat it
as the fallback only after atlas telemetry shows no page addition near a
failure.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Field, macOS, shipped app: run a session producing heavily coloured output
   (large git diff, syntax-highlighted logs, truecolor TUI) until the atlas
   passes 16 pages, and let the output STOP. Garbage glyphs remain on screen;
   resizing the window clears them.
2. Deterministic, renderer unit test: drive the atlas past maxAtlasPages (or
   fire the addon's onAddTextureAtlasCanvas event directly), with no further
   terminal output, and assert a full viewport refresh is scheduled afterwards.
   Today none is.

## Acceptance criteria

- When the active WebGL atlas adds or merges a page, a full viewport refresh is
  scheduled AFTER the current render, even if no further terminal output
  arrives. This is the one criterion tied to the demonstrated defect.
- Proposed minimal fix: subscribe to WebglAddon.onAddTextureAtlasCanvas before
  loading the addon and request a full terminal refresh when it fires.
  RenderService already coalesces refresh requests and page additions are rare,
  so the cost is bounded.
- The fix must survive the shared-atlas case: a merge caused by another tab's
  rendering must repaint THIS tab too (each terminal owns its own addon, so
  each gets the event -- assert it for a second renderer).
- Out of scope: a periodic refresh pump on macOS. It hides the defect and costs
  a full redraw per tick -- the reason the Linux pump is guarded.
- Out of scope for now: upgrading xterm. The scheduling window is an upstream
  defect (the merge should request its own redraw); an upgrade is worth it only
  after verifying a newer addon actually closes it.

nocx-q18 covered the same corruption class on the resize and tab-close triggers
and is closed; this is a different trigger.
notes:
Implemented on branch worktree/lucky-stone-19f4, commit 17680359. XtermRenderer now subscribes to the accelerated addon's onAddTextureAtlasCanvas in attachWebGL (so context-loss recovery re-arms it) and schedules one coalesced full-viewport repaint on the NEXT animation frame via _scheduleRepaintAfterFrame. The addon is constructed through an injected factory (XtermRendererOptions.createWebglAddon) typed as AcceleratedAddon -- that path had no test at all while built inline. The four sites that spelled out 'mark every row dirty' now go through one _repaintViewport. Canvas fallback deliberately NOT wired: it reads coords at draw time into a retained canvas and has no model to go stale.

Five tests in frontend/src/renderers/xterm.test.ts ('XtermRenderer atlas invalidation'): repaint happens on the next frame and not synchronously; several page changes coalesce to one; the seam re-arms on the addon installed after a context loss; every renderer repaints (the atlas is shared across tabs, so a module-global scheduler would repaint only the last-mounted one); a scheduled repaint is dropped on dispose. Each was watched failing first -- the last two by temporarily reverting the guard they cover.

Verified: frontend typecheck, eslint, dead-exports/two-owners/row-grammar ratchets, prettier, and the full frontend suite 5894 passed. NOT run (integrator's job per AGENTS.md): make ci-full, the containerized jobs, e2e.

Not merged. Upstream report filed as nocx-a8r90.
close_reason: Merged to main in PR #174 (commit 17680359, merge 7c8940da). XtermRenderer subscribes to the accelerated addon's onAddTextureAtlasCanvas in attachWebGL, so context-loss recovery re-arms it, and schedules one coalesced full-viewport repaint on the next animation frame — supplying the frame xterm's atlas page merge assumes will happen but never schedules. Five tests, each watched failing first. Upstream report tracked separately as nocx-a8r90.

title: A sealed vault left on the shared stand breaks every later spec that assumes there is none
description:
Specs that assume the shared stand has no vault fail whenever one was created
earlier in the same run. Diagnosed on nocx-6wgcw with the stand's own log and
the failing DOM; this bead is the fix for the specs.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the suite so that a vault-creating spec is scheduled before
   e2e/snippets.spec.ts.
2. Wait for internal/vault/presence.go to auto-seal it — ten seconds after the
   last client page goes away.
3. e2e/snippets.spec.ts:355 fires a snippet holding {{secret:e2e-absent}}.
4. Observed: the product opens `dialog "Unlock the vault…"`, the refusal toast
   never appears, and the assertion fails with "element(s) not found".
5. Expected: the spec establishes its own vault precondition and does not
   depend on what ran before it.

Evidence, CI run 33621032607 (ci-e2e (webkit), PR #172):

    10:48:47  msg="vault initialized" state=unsealed defaultProvider=file
    10:54:59  msg="vault sealed" generation=1
    10:54:59  msg="vault sealed: the last client left and did not come back" window=10s
    10:56:34  snippets.spec.ts:355 fails

## The product is not wrong

With no vault, a {{secret:…}} reference cannot resolve and the fire refuses.
With a SEALED vault it asks the person to unlock. Both are correct. The spec
carries the false premise, in its own words: "This stand has no vault set up,
so the reference cannot resolve."

## The blast radius, and why the failing set looked random

The unlock prompt is a native <dialog>, so it makes the rest of the document
inert. A spec that runs behind it fails on an element that exists but is
"hidden" — which is the shape of connections-settings.spec.ts:72 and
ssh-reconnect.spec.ts:289 — while the spec that owns the missing assertion
reports "element(s) not found". Which specs are hit depends only on what is
scheduled in the seal window, which is why no two runs agree.

## Out of scope

api-run-lifecycle.spec.ts:114 failed in the same run with no unlock dialog in
its DOM; it timed out on getByRole('menuitem', { name: 'Open folder…' }).
Different cause, stays on nocx-6wgcw.
acceptance_criteria: e2e/snippets.spec.ts:355 passes with a vault present and sealed on the stand, and with no vault at all, without weakening what it asserts: an unresolved secret still refuses the whole fire and still writes nothing. Demonstrated by running it after a vault-creating spec in the same stand, not only alone.
close_reason: Merged to main as 66c04356 (PR #173). All eight CI jobs green on the first attempt, ci-e2e (webkit) included — no rerun needed. Watched failing first: the shared stand was driven to vault.setup then vault.seal through the control-plane helper, the unmodified spec then failed exactly as CI did (4 passed, 1 failed, 'element(s) not found' waiting for the refusal toast, editor hidden behind the unlock dialog), and the same sealed stand with the fix passed all 5.

title: A clip finishes what it started
description:
`hold` is a timer and the clip is a loop modulo its frame count, so the two disagree: an answer is cut off mid-cycle, a two-frame clip and a thirteen-frame clip get the same time on screen, and a cycle starts again a moment before it is replaced.

Give a clip a mode -- `loop`, `once`, `hold-last` -- and end a one-shot action at its last frame rather than at a duration. The meow, the stretch, the scratch and the wash finish; idle, walk, run and lie cycle; sleep holds its pose.

Idle should also not run ten frames forever: play the cycle, hold a still frame for 0.4-2.0s, play it again.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A reaction is never replaced before its clip's last frame, whatever the value of reactionHold.
- A clip declared `once` is never seen mid-cycle at the moment another activity begins.
- `reactionHold` stops being a number the reaction depends on.
close_reason: Clips declare loop/once/hold; only a once clip's lifetime comes from the drawing, through the single owner chosenHold, which react, attend and the menu all use. Idle holds its final frame 0.8s between cycles. Committed a07896cd.

title: Anticipation before a jump, recovery after a landing
description:
The animal changes direction, leaves the ground and lands with no transition at all, which is the single loudest tell that a machine is choosing states.

Add a motion phase distinct from locomotion and activity -- anticipate-jump, air-up, air-down, land, turn -- carried alongside them, driving a transform the pack does not have to draw:

- before a jump: 120-180ms, horizontal motion stopped, scaleX 1.04 / scaleY 0.94
- take-off: release the squash over 70-100ms
- landing: 150-220ms scaled by impact speed, squash then a small rebound
- turning at an edge: 80-140ms pause, and the sprite flips in the MIDDLE of it -- an instant scaleX(-1) is what reads as an automaton

This needs the transform split across two elements: a world layer carrying position and facing, an expressive layer carrying rotation and squash. They fight in one transform.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every jump, landing and turn passes through its phase, asserted on the state rather than on a screenshot.
- transform-origin stays at the feet: a squash never lifts the animal off the ledge it is standing on.
- No phase is longer than 220ms.
close_reason: MotionPhase as a fourth axis: anticipate 150ms, takeoff 85ms, turn 110ms flipping at the midpoint, land 150-220ms scaled by impact. Transform split into .pet-world (translate + facing) and .pet-sprite (squash), origin kept at the feet. Ground resolved before the phase, so a scrolling block carries the pet and a deleted one drops it at once. Committed 7f559ddc.

title: The helper links the coordinator's ssh client, and D3's size argument is stale by 2x
description:
The helper links the COORDINATOR's ssh client. `go list -deps ./cmd/nocx-helper`
contains `golang.org/x/crypto/ssh`, `ssh/agent`, `ssh/knownhosts` and
`github.com/pkg/sftp` — a full outbound SSH client, an agent client, a known_hosts
parser and an SFTP stack, inside the binary that RUNS ON the far side of an ssh
connection somebody else already made.

It arrives the same way nocx-k6p18.19's embed did, through a package the helper
genuinely needs dragging in one it does not:

  cmd/nocx-helper -> internal/helper/session -> internal/shellintegration
                  -> internal/ssh  (the coordinator's client)

internal/shellintegration bundles the LOCAL bundle the helper runs from memory
(nocx-k6p18.8) together with the REMOTE install path (install_remote.go), which needs
internal/ssh's SFTP adapter. The helper needs the first and never the second: it is
already on the host.

WHY THIS IS NOT COSMETIC. D3 licenses the helper to exist as a survival component on
the strength of one measurement — "~2.8 MiB against ~40 MiB". The helper measures
5.35 MiB stripped today (nocx-k6p18.19's ceiling test), so the number the design rests
on is off by nearly 2x and nobody noticed, because until nocx-k6p18.19 there was no
check behind it. A survival component deployed to machines we do not own should not
carry an ssh client, an agent client and a known_hosts parser it cannot use: every one
of those is attack surface on the far side, and D3's argument is what is supposed to
keep them out.

## Steps to Reproduce

  go list -deps ./cmd/nocx-helper | grep -E 'x/crypto/ssh|pkg/sftp'

  golang.org/x/crypto/ssh/internal/bcrypt_pbkdf
  golang.org/x/crypto/ssh
  golang.org/x/crypto/ssh/agent
  golang.org/x/crypto/ssh/knownhosts
  github.com/pkg/sftp
  github.com/pkg/sftp/internal/encoding/ssh/filexfer

The size it costs is the ceiling test's own measurement, nocx-k6p18.19:
decompressed darwin/amd64 = 5618624 bytes.

## Acceptance Criteria

cmd/nocx-helper's dependency graph contains no ssh client, agent, known_hosts or sftp
package, asserted by a TEST in the same shape as nocx-k6p18.19's graph assertion —
this is the second package to reach across the same seam, so the check belongs beside
the first rather than being written a second way.

The helper's measured size after the split is recorded, and D3's "~2.8 MiB" is either
met again or AMENDED in the design to the number that is now true. A design argument
carrying a stale measurement is worse than one carrying none: it reads as evidence.
close_reason:
Fixed and merged as d337ff61. Route B: shellintegration no longer imports internal/ssh or x/crypto/ssh at all — the FS and a narrow RemoteCommandRunner seam are injected, and the SSH/SFTP adapter lives in the composition root (internal/app/shellintegration_remote.go). EnsureInstalledRemote left the ShellIntegration interface with it. Route A (a separate package) was rejected in the code with its reason: it would have needed launchBundle exported or the Bundle owner duplicated, and would have put the publisher tests across an import-cycle boundary.

Verified independently of the worker's report. go list -deps ./cmd/nocx-helper contains zero of x/crypto/ssh, ssh/agent, ssh/knownhosts, pkg/sftp, internal/ssh; internal/app still contains all seven. Size measured by building darwin/amd64 in both trees myself: 5,618,624 -> 4,212,352 bytes, 1,406,272 saved, 25.0%. The ceiling test moved 8 MiB -> 5 MiB, 24.5% headroom. Both mutations were shown red by name, and the graph assertion was EXTENDED in the existing dependency_test.go over a shared helperDependencyDirs walk rather than written a second way.

D3's '~2.8 MiB against ~40 MiB' is still not met and this is deliberate, not outstanding work. The helper measures 4.21 MiB and carries no library it should not: no go-git (git on the host is done through processes), no ssh client any more. The 2.8 figure predates the helper owning PTY spawning, the shell-integration bundle, the git host service and the session inventory — scope D3 itself grants it. The number is stale because the job grew as designed. It is NOT amended in the level-1 design spec, which is a design document and gets superseding records rather than edits; the current-state record is the ceiling test, which now carries the measured number behind a check instead of a comment.

title: Text on its own is acknowledged, not saved: the model answers 'Noted.' and no note exists
description:
2026-09-01, home/dev pane, google/gemma-4-26b-a4b. The person pasted an article
(Debian 11 LTS end of life) with no question, which the system prompt defines as
an instruction to keep it. The model reasoned its way to the right conclusion and
then did nothing:

    However, I'll check if there are any instructions in the persona about
    how to handle a note. "Text on its own means remember this as a note."
    I will respond that I've noted the information.

    Noted.

No note was created. The text is gone.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open an ask in any pane.
2. Paste several paragraphs of prose. No question, no link, no marks.
3. Send.

Expected: a note exists afterwards, holding that text.
Observed: the answer is "Noted." and notes.search finds nothing.

## Not an authority problem — the tool was offered

Checked rather than assumed:

- notes.create declares EffectMutateReversible over ResourceContent and has a
  Narrow constructor, so ForGrant does not drop it (registry.go:432, :671).
- runGrantFor's fence includes {ResourceContent, "content"}
  (ws_readscreen.go:260), and an unstated policy row decides ASK, not refuse
  (effectpolicy.go:74), so PermittedEffects keeps MutateReversible.
- Lazy presentation would have hidden it behind search, but AskParams.Presentation
  is never assigned outside tests — the transport does not set it
  (ws_agent.go:1246), so p.Presentation is nil, lazy is off, and every eligible
  tool is visible.
- The same session called fetch.url ten minutes earlier, so the policy is wired.

## The defect is the prompt line

systemprompt.go:153-157:

    A link on its own means go there and tell the person what is on it.
    Text on its own means remember this as a note.

The link half works because "go there" has no reading that is not a tool call.
The text half has an obvious non-tool reading, and "remember" is the word that
invites it — the model read it as an instruction about its own attitude to the
input, acknowledged, and stopped. Its thinking shows the tool never entered
consideration at all.

Every other intent line in this prompt names its tool. The attached-content
block says "Use session.read with each item's id below; for a row mark, pass its
listed start and count". This one names nothing, and it sits under "What a
person's input means", a heading about interpretation, textually separated from
"What you can do", which is where tools are discussed. A small local model has
no reason to cross that gap.

## Fix and its check

Name the tool and make the act external, the way the session.read line does.
Whatever the wording, the check is behavioural, not a string assertion: an ask
carrying text and no question ends with a notes.create call and a note that
exists afterwards.

systemprompt_test.go:40 and frontend/src/settings.test.ts:1760 both assert the
current sentence verbatim and will need updating. Note WHY this stayed invisible:
two tests pinned the exact prose, so they proved the sentence was present and
never that it worked — testing rule 1, a test asserting what the code says rather
than what a user can do.

Watch the failure this could introduce in the other direction: pasted text that
IS a question, or text pasted as context for the sentence next to it, must not
turn into a note. That is the paired "and on a normal input it does not fire".
acceptance_criteria: An ask whose input is text with no question ends with a notes.create call, and the note is readable by notes.search afterwards. An ask whose input is text that asks something is answered and creates no note. Neither assertion is a check on the prompt's wording.

title: The end-to-end check: a person reads a feed, and reads past the bound
description:
The epic's DONE WHEN, as one automated check that watches a user do it (AGENTS.md testing rule 2). cmd/nocx-server runs the shipped coordinator headless, so there is no harness excuse.

Two asks against a stub server, not the live habr — a test that depends on a third party's uptime is not a check:
1. A feed served as text/xml with a windows-1251 declaration. The answer names an item from it. This is the exact shape of the 2026-09-01 screenshot that opened the epic.
2. A document larger than the tool's bound where the fact asked about appears only in the tail. The answer names it, and the transcript shows a second fetch.url call carrying start, not a second HTTP request.

Watch the tool calls, not just the final text — an answer that happens to be right without the second window has not proven anything.
acceptance_criteria: Both asks pass through cmd/nocx-server end to end. The second one asserts a second fetch.url call with a start param and exactly one HTTP request to the stub.
close_reason:
internal/transport/ws_agent_fetch_e2e_test.go, two asks over the real WebSocket against the real WSServer with the REAL apifetch client wired via WithAgentFetcher (apifetch.New with a direct route) — not the canned-document stub the contract test uses, so charset decoding, XML declaration, feed rendering, snapshot and window are exercised together.

1. A feed served as text/xml with no header charset and a windows-1251 XML declaration: the answer delta and the tool result both contain the decoded Cyrillic title, the result contains no raw <rss>, and exactly one HTTP request reaches the stub.
2. A document larger than the bound with the fact only in the tail: two fetch.url calls, the first with no start or revision, the second carrying both; first result truncated with window.end equal to the second call's start; one revision across both; the marker present in the second result and absent from the first; exactly one HTTP request.

VERIFIED FALSIFIABLE by the coordinator, because an acceptance test that cannot fail proves nothing. Two mutations of production code, each reverted: making a continuation re-fetch -> 'feed HTTP requests = 2, want exactly one snapshot fetch'; removing the XML-declaration lookup -> the result came back as mojibake ('# Íîâîñòè'). Both were caught by the assertion that should catch them.

DEVIATION, approved and recorded: the bead's acceptance said 'through cmd/nocx-server'. The harness drives the same shipped WSServer over a real WebSocket and this repo already treats it as authoritative for over-the-wire claims, so requiring a second process would duplicate a proof the harness gives. Commit 25afa859.

NOTE: the worker's pane died before it reported. The commit and a clean worktree survived it, and everything above was verified by the coordinator directly rather than taken from a report.

title: Window two comes from the same document as window one
description:
A file and a terminal ledger do not change between two reads; a web page does. If a continuation re-fetches, window two of a news feed can come from a document window one never saw, and the model stitches two different pages into one answer without any signal that it happened.

files.read already answers this shape with revision — an opaque token binding a later call to the exact bytes observed. Fetch needs the same guarantee for a different reason. Cache the decoded body for the run, keyed by the FINAL url after redirects, and serve continuations from the cache.

URLScope.Allows (internal/agenttools/registry.go:47) matches the URL string exactly, so a continuation naming the same URL is already inside the grant. No grant work is needed and none should be invented.

Bounds, both ends (AGENTS.md rule 3): state when an entry is created and when it dies — the run ending is the closing event, and a cache with no stated end is a leak. Say what happens when a continuation names a URL the cache no longer holds: refetch and say so, or refuse by name. Do not let it silently look like a clean continuation.
acceptance_criteria: Two windows of one document are served from one fetch — the second call performs no HTTP request, proven by a transport that counts. A continuation whose cache entry is gone is reported as such rather than silently re-fetched. The cache is empty once the run ends.
notes:
DESIGN DECIDED 2026-09-01 after a codex review; this CORRECTS the description above.

Both a snapshot and a token, not one or the other. Do NOT key the cache by final URL
as the description says — that was wrong twice over: a redirect makes the final URL
something URLScope.Allows would refuse, and a URL is not an identity for a document
that changes. Key the decoded snapshot under an opaque REVISION, scoped to the run,
bound to the exact authorized request URL. The final URL is retained as metadata.

A continuation echoes the revision and MUST be served from the snapshot with no
second GET.

Accepted failure, stated deliberately: staleness. Later windows may describe a page
older than the live web. That is much safer than silently stitching two different
