- A body containing an instruction-override pattern produces a `Finding` naming the pattern and the line.
- `skills.read` on a skill whose bytes produce a finding returns the content wrapped by `agenttools.FrameUntrusted` and a result field naming the skill and the pattern — never silently, and never an error that hides the skill.
- A builtin skill is not scanned.
- The scan is bounded: at most 64 KiB is examined, and the pattern table uses bounded filler (`(?:\w+\s+){0,8}`) so an adversarial near-miss cannot cause runaway backtracking.

title: Task 0: ForGrant matches the content family, not just the kind
description:
Plan: `.internal/plans/2026-09-01-assistant-skills.md` — Task 0. Read that task in full before starting; it carries the code for every step.

A pre-existing defect this design would otherwise inherit and rely on. `ForGrant` builds its coverage set from scope KINDS alone, so **any** `ResourceContent` scope covers **every** content tool: a grant naming only `note/x` offers `snippets.list` today, and would offer `skills.read` tomorrow. Two claims in the spec are false until this is fixed — that the prompt lists skills only when the run can read them, and that the global switch removes the tools.

**Files:**

- Modify: `internal/agenttools/registry.go:104-176` — `Declaration.ScopeFamily string`.
- Modify: `internal/agenttools/registry.go:594-628` — `ForGrant` containment check.
- Modify: `internal/agenttools/registry.go:542-579` — `validateDeclaration` requires `ScopeFamily` on a row whose `ResourceKinds` include `ResourceContent`.
- Modify: the `notes.*` and `snippets.*` rows — `ScopeFamily: "note"` / `"snippet"`.
- Test: `internal/agenttools/registry_test.go`

- A grant whose only content scope is `note/x` offers `notes.*` and does **not** offer `snippets.*` — the pre-existing leak, closed and asserted.
- A grant holding the `content` root offers every content tool, unchanged.
- A declaration with `ResourceKinds` containing `ResourceContent` and no `ScopeFamily` fails assembly, so a future content tool cannot forget it.

title: Skills for the built-in assistant
description:
A person tells the assistant once how something is done here, and it does it that
way in every later question, pane and restart.

Spec: `.internal/specs/2026-08-31-assistant-skills-design.md`
Plan: `.internal/plans/2026-09-01-assistant-skills.md`

Skills are `SKILL.md` directories under three roots (builtin embedded, authored
`<ConfigDir>/skills`, managed `<ConfigDir>/managed-skills`), discovered per ask,
indexed into `SystemPromptFacts`, read through a `skills.read` agent tool and
written through `skills.{create,update,delete}` whose managed root is baked into
the narrowed capability. Trust is earned in four layers, not granted by location:
structural provenance, an untainted drafting input, a static scan at both
boundaries, and the classifier plus the person's approval at the write.

## Success Criteria

- In pane A the person asks the assistant to remember a procedure; the approval
  shows the name, description and body; they approve.
- A new ask in pane B lists the skill in its index, calls `skills.read`, and the
  answer reflects the skill's content.
- One Playwright spec watches that end to end against the fake endpoint, with no
  `waitForTimeout` anywhere.
- Settings has a Skills page listing name, description, provenance and path, with
  per-skill enable/disable and delete, built from `frontend/src/ui` only.
- A corrupt `skills.json` fails closed: nothing is discovered and the page shows
  the failure with its path.
- Skills survive a backup and restore with their enabled state.
close_reason:
Merged to main as ae75b059 (PR #168), all eight CI jobs green including ci-mac and both e2e projects.

A person can teach the assistant a procedure in their own words, approve it once, and have every later ask in any pane find it and use it: the summarizing role drafts the skill, the approval prompt shows name, description and body before anything is written, and a new ask in another pane lists it in its index, calls skills.read and answers from its content. Settings has the Skills page with provenance, path, enable/disable and delete; a corrupt skills.json fails closed and says so with its path; skills survive backup and restore with their enabled state.

The rule worth remembering: every skills mutation asks the person whatever their standing policy decision, because a person who allowed reversible mutations has not thereby allowed the assistant to rewrite its own instructions (isSkillMutationTool, guarded by TestASkillsWriteNeverAutoPermits and TestASkillsDeleteNeverAutoPermits). The run grant carries content families rather than the content root, so a tool is offered only when its family is inside the grant.

Three defects the gate found and this epic fixed: the Summarizing card's fallback line names the answering role, which made a Playwright filter on the whole card's text match two cards and skip seven serial tests in both browsers; syscall.Stat_t.Nlink is uint64 on Linux and uint16 on Darwin, which broke ci-mac's typecheck and cascaded into eight errors across four packages; and the first fix for that grew a per-OS file, which ci-os-split correctly refused because the package would have silently left ci-mac's coverage.

Deliberately out: the classifier role is assignable but unused, skill drafting has no editor beyond the approval prompt, and skills are not shared between machines.

title: 'The host session exists' is not 'the command is running', and the store conflates them
description:
Found by an adversarial review of the composed level 1, 2026-08-31.

internal/content/reconcile.go's VerdictLive says the open entry stays open "because the
command is still running". The helper's inventory does not say that and cannot: it
deliberately RETAINS a session after its process exits, so its exit status can be delivered
(internal/helper/session/session.go says so at the top), and a session is equally live while
its shell sits at a prompt with the command long finished.

So the two facts are not equivalent, and the store is treating one as the other.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. The inventory reports the host session — truthfully.
2. Reconciliation applies `live` and clears the pending marker.
3. The block renders as running.
4. Snapshot recovery has not happened yet, or fails because the shell exited.

The product has then confidently displayed a lifecycle verdict that inventory never
supplied. That is the same class as the third state existing at all: showing a confident
answer nobody reached.

## Fix

Two facts, not one. Either D7's recovery must complete BEFORE the lifecycle-unreconciled
state is cleared, or the store carries 'host session exists' and 'open attempt recovered'
separately and the running presentation keys on the second.

Inventory can preserve rows. It cannot adjudicate a block.

Bound to nocx-k6p18.6, which is building the recovery, and to nocx-k6p18.15, which is
building the inventory — whichever lands second inherits the ordering.
acceptance_criteria: Two distinct facts are represented: the host session exists, and the open attempt has been recovered. A block renders as running only on the second. Inventory alone never clears the lifecycle-unreconciled state.
notes: Verification: content reconciliation changes are included in commit 540a1f09; backend content and transport tests passed in the prescribed race run, while app tests hit the environment's missing /bin/bash. Frontend full verification passed.
close_reason: Closed

title: The coordinator never asks a helper what sessions it holds
description:
Named INDEPENDENTLY by two workers on 2026-08-31, which is why it is a bead rather than a
note. nocx-k6p18.5 reported 'no production sessionInventory — an adapter over client.Client
plus proto.OpSessions'; nocx-k6p18.13's worker blocked on the same seam from the other end
and refused to build a renderer-only fallback, correctly, because that would have shown a
stale launch.cwd as a current observation.

VERIFIED BY THE COORDINATOR, not taken on the workers' word: the only mention of OpSessions
outside internal/helper is a COMMENT in internal/app/session_reconcile.go:35 saying it will
be used once a coordinator records the generation. Nothing calls it. There are zero readers
of the helper's SessionEntry.Observed outside internal/helper — every other .Observed* hit
in the tree is ObservedAt or ObservedCount, unrelated concepts.

WHAT IS MISSING IS A CHAIN, not a function. internal/helper/client.Client.Call exists and
sends helper operations over an established connection, and nocx-k6p18.4 built the carrier
under it — the Unix socket and the bridge. What does not exist: anything that INVOKES
Call for the sessions op, a coordinator-owned DTO for proto.SessionEntry, an RPC
registration, its contract schema, or a mounted surface at the end.

WHY IT IS P1 DESPITE BEING PLUMBING. It is the single piece that turns two finished
mechanisms from shape into behaviour:

  - Reconciliation (nocx-k6p18.5) runs today with NO inventories, so every verdict is
    unknown/noInventory and only the retention age does any work. The live and absent paths
    are unit-provable and production-unreachable.
  - The observation reader (nocx-k6p18.13) has nothing to read.

Both were built correctly and deliberately ahead of this, because the ABI had to be frozen
before a generation ships. This is the piece that was always going to come after.

sessions.live is NOT this and must not be pressed into service: its contract deliberately
excludes cwd and observation, and it describes coordinator-owned sessions rather than what
a helper holds.

TWO THINGS THIS MUST NOT DO. It must not ask a helper about an id space that helper does
not own — Owns exists precisely because a truthful 'I do not hold that' about somebody
else's id would be turned into a DELETION by the absent path. And it must record WHICH
GENERATION a stored session belongs to, or there is nothing to match an inventory against.
acceptance_criteria: A coordinator-side adapter calls the helper's sessions op over an established helper connection, maps proto.SessionEntry into a coordinator-owned DTO, and exposes it through an RPC with its JSON Schema in contracts/. Reconciliation gets a real inventory that Owns a generation's id space, so verdicts stop being universally unknown. Asserted end to end: a session spawned on a helper is reported by the coordinator with its hostSessionId, its generation and its observation.
close_reason:
Committed as 481c8a92 plus 029b0339 on omp/k6p18-15-inventory by an omp worker through herdr; merged as 6c439f32. 22 files.

THE WHOLE CHAIN LANDED: an adapter over client.Call (internal/helper/client/sessions.go), a coordinator-owned DTO rather than the proto type leaked upward, an RPC (internal/transport/ws_helper_sessions.go) with its schema in contracts/ and a generated renderer type, and the durable binding recorded beside the session.

THE SAFETY PROPERTY IS ORDERING, AND THE CODE SAYS SO: an inventory is queried only after a pending session's persisted generation, host and account have SELECTED it. Asking a helper about another generation's id space would turn its truthful absence into a deletion, and the absent path is the one that destroys work. Owns() is checked last, after the target has already narrowed the field.

THE HOST LOCATOR WAS THE CORRECTION THAT MATTERED. The bead first said 'record which generation a stored session belongs to'. That is insufficient: a generation is a CONTENT-ADDRESSED BINARY and the same one exists on many hosts, so generation+session does not say where to ask. The durable binding is host/account plus generation plus session, persisted beside the row and exposed through PendingSession — and the frozen HostSessionID ABI was not touched, correctly.

FIRST-WINS IS GONE, on a second round. The loop originally broke on the first inventory that claimed an id. It now counts matches: zero is unknown/noInventory, more than one is unknown/CauseAmbiguousInventory with a detail, and only exactly one is judged. The comment names why — multiple owners mean a duplicate registration, and choosing one would make a broken ownership map silently first-wins. A condition that can only arise from a bug is the one that must be loud.

THE OVER-THE-WIRE TEST DRIVES THE REAL SOCKET, verified by reading it rather than by report: it calls jsonrpcCall against a live connection and validates envelope.Result — what came back off the wire — against the schema. A test validating a payload it built itself proves the struct is well-formed, not that the server sends it, which is how vault.status once shipped a field nobody could read.

-whylive contrast present and real: main -> control dispatch -> hostSessionInventoryHandlers.handle -> helperSessionInventories.Sessions, against sqliteContent.AddEdge reporting 'reachable only through reflection'.

THREE MERGE-ONLY DEFECTS were resolved by the coordinator; see 6c439f32 for the reasoning. In short: this branch carried the old Since semantics that the retention fix had just corrected, in both prose and code; and CreateSession bound json.Marshal's []byte into sessions.payload, which is TEXT on a STRICT table, failing every test that creates a session.

AND ONE DEFECT THAT WAS NOT THE MERGE'S, recorded because the cause is mine: TestSessionWithoutGenerationRemainsUnowned asserted a property of the carry-over set WITHOUT restarting the store, so it could never have passed — carryOver runs at Open over a previous incarnation's rows. Its own sibling two functions above does restart. It had never been run, because the brief that produced it named internal/app, internal/helper and internal/transport and not internal/content, the package it edits. That is a gap in the brief, not in the work.

Verified on the merged tree: build clean, internal/content ok 20.0s, internal/transport ok 96.7s, the full static gate including contracts:check and both tsc projects. internal/app shows the five environmental failures AGENTS.md records for this machine, confirmed by cause rather than assumed.

WHAT THIS UNBLOCKS: reconciliation's live and absent verdicts stop being unreachable, and nocx-k6p18.13 — the observation reader — now has something to read.

title: Expanding one folder re-lists the whole expanded tree, because the watch set is replaced not diffed
description:
Found in review of the cadence epic, and it is the cheapest large win in it —
because unlike the poll, this cost lands on a FOREGROUND gesture.

`filesBaseline` (`internal/transport/ws_files.go`) lists EVERY path in the new
watch set, synchronously, inside `files.watch`, before the response. And
`files.watch` REPLACES the set rather than adding to it, so the client resends
the whole set on every change to it.

`pushWatchSet` (`frontend/src/files/files-store.ts`) is called after a
directory's first successful listing, when a loaded directory expands or
collapses, on reconnect, and after refresh.

So expanding ONE directory re-lists the ENTIRE expanded tree. With a deep tree
that is N full enumerations — each an lstat per entry plus a sha256 — charged
to a click, and the cost grows with every folder the person has open.

The same shape exists provider-side: `Binding.swapWatches`
(`internal/filesystem/binding.go:305`) establishes a FRESH watch for every
path before closing the old set — "every path is established first; if any
fails, the partial set is closed and the existing set is untouched". That
atomicity is right, but it is bought by rebuilding watches that did not
change, and at 512 paths it briefly needs nearly twice the resources. Today
that is free because both providers refuse to watch at all; it stops being
free exactly when fsnotify lands (nocx-9stiv), which is why this belongs
before it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Files and expand several directories, each with a few hundred entries.
2. Expand one more directory.
3. Every previously expanded directory is fully re-enumerated inside that one
   `files.watch` call, before the response — an lstat per entry per directory,
   charged to the click.

## The fix

Diff the set rather than rebuilding it, on both sides:

- retain the rev baseline for a path already watched — it is still valid;
- baseline ONLY the additions;
- close only the removals;
- a failure while establishing an addition leaves the existing set intact,
  which is the property `swapWatches` already promises and would keep.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Expanding one directory in a tree with N already-expanded directories costs
  ONE baseline listing, not N. Asserted by counting `List` calls against a
  fake handle, not by inspection.
- Collapsing a directory closes one watch and re-baselines nothing.
- The atomicity `swapWatches` documents is preserved: a failing addition
  leaves the previous set live and unchanged, with a test for it.
- Retained baselines are genuinely still valid — a change to a retained path
  during the swap is still announced, not folded into a baseline nobody saw.
  This is the same "safe direction" rule `filesBaseline` already states.
- Reconnect still re-baselines everything; that is a different event and it
  keeps its current behaviour.
notes:
Committed as b35bd921. Both sides of the watch set now diff.

THE DEFECT WAS TWO THINGS AND THE SECOND WAS NOT IN THE ORIGINAL REPORT.
Re-baselining an already-watched path overwrote the poll loop's comparison
point with the current rev, so a change that landed after the last tick and
before the next files.watch was folded into a baseline nobody saw and was
NEVER announced. Expanding one folder could silently swallow a pending change
in another. The red test hung the full 30s timeout waiting for a files.changed
that never came — so this was a lost signal, not only a cost.

The cost half is as filed: every resend re-enumerated every already-watched
directory (readdir + lstat per entry + sort + sha256, since both providers
enumerate the whole directory before slicing), charged to a click, growing
with the number of folders open.

Transport: filesBaseline takes the watcher's existing rev map and skips those
paths. Installation builds the next map from the LIVE map for retained paths,
not from the pre-listing snapshot — the poll loop keeps updating it while
additions are listed, and writing the snapshot back would re-announce a change
already delivered. A path neither retained nor added (the loop dropped it as
vanished) becomes the empty-string marker so the first successful listing
announces. A retained empty marker is kept rather than retried, since
re-listing would establish a silent baseline where the contract promises an
announcement.

Provider: swapWatches diffs. Preparation rather than an observable change
today (both providers still refuse to watch), and a PREREQUISITE for
nocx-9stiv: rebuilding at the 512-path ceiling briefly holds nearly twice the
watch resources, exactly when a descriptor limit is hit.

THE TRAP DIFFING INTRODUCES, now pinned by a test: the new set shares watch
objects with the live one, so a refused addition may close only what that call
established. Closing the whole new set would turn a refused addition into a
silent loss of every existing watch.

Two existing tests asserted the rebuild and were CHANGED, not deleted —
recorded so nobody reads it as a weakened suite. TestWatchSwapIsAtomicAndReplaces
checked that a "partially established /c" was closed; under diffing there is
no second /c, so it now asserts a failed swap establishes nothing at all.
TestWatchModeAggregation watched /x twice with the stub mode changed between,
measuring re-establishment rather than aggregation; it uses a second path.

go test -race green on internal/filesystem/... and the whole of
internal/transport (255s), plus all pre-commit static gates. Not run on this
branch by design: make ci-full, the containerized jobs and e2e.

title: Brainstorming: skills for the built-in nocx assistant
description:
Design session: what a "skill" is for `internal/assistant`, where it is stored,
how it reaches the model, and how it stays distinct from personal instructions
(settings) and snippets (`internal/snippet`).

## Acceptance Criteria
- A design doc exists at `.internal/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-assistant-skills-design.md`
- The design names what a user can do that they could not before
- The design states how a skill relates to ADR-0020 (grant per run), ADR-0045
  (declared calls) and ADR-0053 (tool classes), and why it is not a second
  answer to snippets or personal instructions

title: DECISION — the derived-diagnostics freeze window is closing, and start time and ppid are free
description:
Raised by nocx-k6p18.10, 2026-08-31, about its own change, and it is time-sensitive rather
than important.

Adding Observation.Unavailable was legal ONLY because nothing is deployed.
additionalProperties:false — which is what makes the contract exact rather than theatre —
means the next such field is a BREAK, not an addition. Generations are content-addressed
and immutable and live for months; after the first publish this stops being a decision.

Two fields are already free from the kinfo_proc call the darwin inspector now makes, and
procfs has both trivially: START TIME and PPID. Free means measured: no new syscall, no new
dependency, no new parse. If either is ever wanted, adding it now costs nothing and adding
it later costs a protocol break.

So the question is not 'shall we add these two' but 'what is the whole set', asked once,
while it is still askable. D3's rule bounds it: DERIVED diagnostics only — facts about a
process whose source is the OS. No human-authored name, ever; that stays the local server's
and later the host ledger's. One owner ever.

Related to nocx-k6p18.11, which is the same clock on a different field: proto.Version has
not been bumped, and both decisions expire at the same moment — the first published
generation.
acceptance_criteria: The set of derived diagnostics the helper reports is decided and frozen deliberately, before any generation is published. Every field wanted for the foreseeable product is in it, or the code says why the cost of adding one later was accepted.
notes:
DECIDED 2026-09-02 (coordinator). The frozen set is the four fields already on
Observation plus THREE, and nothing else:

  startTime  ADD  the process's start time
  ppid       ADD  the parent pid
  state      ADD  the kernel's process state (R/S/D/Z/T)

WHY THESE THREE AND NOT MORE

startTime is not a nicety, it is the pid-reuse guard. A pid alone cannot say
whether the process answering today is the one we launched; (pid, startTime) can,
and D3's own list already names start time. Without it every liveness answer the
inventory gives is true only until the host recycles a pid, and nothing in the
product could ever notice.

ppid and state are the two questions a person asks next when a session looks
wrong -- who owns this, and is it running, sleeping, stopped or a zombie. A
stopped shell and a live one are indistinguishable today.

COST, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED

darwin: genuinely free. inspect_darwin.go already calls
unix.SysctlKinfoProc("kern.proc.pid", pid) for comm and for the liveness check;
kinfo_proc carries P_starttime, Eproc.Ppid and P_stat in that same answer. No new
syscall, no new dependency, no new parse.

linux: one new read. inspect_linux.go reads comm and argv today and does NOT read
/proc/<pid>/stat, so this adds that file -- fields 3 (state), 4 (ppid) and 22
(starttime). No new dependency, and it is the same read every ps does. "Free" in
the bead's title is therefore true on darwin and cheap-but-not-free on linux; that
correction is the reason to record the measurement rather than the slogan.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY OUT

Anything whose source is not the OS. No human-authored name, no title, no label,
no last-command, no product state -- D3 gives those to the local server and later
to the host ledger, one owner ever. Also out: rusage/CPU/memory, which are a
sampling problem rather than a fact and would put a rate on a wire that has no
clock; and the tty path, which the launch record already holds and which does not
change.

WHY IT IS A FREEZE AND NOT A PREFERENCE

additionalProperties:false plus an explicit required list is what makes the
contract exact rather than theatre. Generations are content-addressed, immutable,
and two are resident at once with one lingering as long as it holds a session --
months. So the next field after the first publish is a protocol BREAK and a
proto.Version bump (nocx-k6p18.11), not an addition. This window closes at the
first published generation, and it closes for good.

Every added field is optional on the wire and carries the same Diagnostic
"unavailable" treatment as cwd: an OS that cannot answer one says so by name,
never by omission, so a reader can never fall back to the launch record and
present a stale value as a current observation.

NEXT: implementation task, not yet filed. Blocked behind nocx-k6p18.9 only
because one worker at a time.
close_reason:
Closed 2026-09-02 after independent verification by the coordinator, not on the
worker's report.

The frozen set is startTime, ppid, state, as decided in this bead's notes.
Commit dd382338.

WHAT I VERIFIED MYSELF, rather than accepting:

- /proc/<pid>/stat is parsed from strings.LastIndexByte(line, ')'), which is the
  only correct way: field 2 is the unescaped command name, so a process named
  `evil) X 1` puts a state letter and a parent pid inside it and a whitespace
  split reads them silently because they parse.
- The reader is genuinely wired, which deadcode could never have told us here
  (AD-8, RTA cannot see a dead method behind a live interface): panes.ts:3165
  calls processObservationFor, and overview-model.ts:386 calls cardProcess.
- The pid-reuse guard is protected by a test rather than only by a comment.
  panes.test.ts feeds startedAt = 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z and observed.startTime =
  2026-09-01T03:00:00Z -- three hours apart on purpose -- and asserts the
  rendered instant is the OBSERVED one. A reader that silently fell back to the
  helper's spawn record would leave the guard nothing to compare against, and
  that test is what stops it.
- My own mutation, not one of the worker's ten: `if status.Ppid > 0` relaxed to
  `>= 0`, so a zero parent is emitted as a value instead of named unavailable.
  Three named tests go red:
    TestProcfsNamesWhatItCouldNotRead: Unavailable = [cwd argv startTime state],
      want it to name "ppid"
    TestAProcessStatusReadThatFailedNamesAllThreeRatherThanLeavingThemZero: same
    TestEachFactOfTheTripleIsJudgedOnItsOwn/the_kernel_gave_no_parent
  Reverted; tree byte-identical; ./internal/helper/... green.

DECISIONS TAKEN ON THE WORKER'S OPEN QUESTION

`idle` stays OUT of the vocabulary. Linux `I` is an idle KERNEL THREAD; darwin
SIDL is a process BEING CREATED BY FORK. They share a word and are not the same
fact, so one `idle` member would be two facts wearing one name -- the exact
defect this field set exists to avoid. Neither is a state a login shell the
helper spawned is meaningfully observed in. Both report state as unavailable,
which is the honest answer.

The wire carries an RFC 3339 instant on both platforms rather than ticks plus a
boot id, because darwin has no counter to send -- p_starttime is already an
absolute timeval -- so the counter form would have put a darwin instant beside a
linux pair in one field. Linux pays one extra read of /proc/stat's btime, taken
ONCE per source: btime is wall clock less uptime, so re-deriving it per row would
make a constant wobble, and a start time that wobbles cannot be compared against
a recorded one.

proto.Version deliberately not bumped, and the commit body says so. Nothing is
published, so this is part of what version 2 turns out to be rather than a change
to it -- the same argument version.go already makes for nocx-k6p18.1 and .3. That
argument expires at the first published generation, together with this window.

NOT VERIFIED: the darwin path is compile-verified only (GOOS=darwin go build and
go vet). It has never executed on this Linux host. Field types were checked
against x/sys@v0.47.0's ztypes_darwin_{amd64,arm64}.go and are identical on both
arches. CI's macOS backend job is the first real execution.

title: The Files poll cadence is chosen with a reason, not left at a guessed 500ms
description:
`defaultFilesPollInterval = 500ms` (`internal/transport/ws_files.go:231`) is
the only cadence in the project chosen without a written reason, and it is
ten times faster than either panel that came after it — Git and Ports both
use `POLL_INTERVAL_MS = 5000` on the frontend, and the Ports backend samples
a remote host every 10s.

It is also the most expensive tick of the three: see the parent epic for what
one `List` actually does.

Fixed-versus-adaptive is the open question and this bead decides it in
writing. The tension is real: a person's own file operations should feel
instant, while a panel left open on a quiet directory should cost nothing.
An adaptive cadence — short right after a change, backing off while nothing
moves, reset by a change or a user action — serves both, at the cost of a
state machine that has to be right. A single slower interval is duller and
simpler. Pick one and say why, next to the constant, in the form
`internal/discovery/schedule.go:13-43` uses.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The interval (or the adaptive schedule) is stated with its reason in a
  comment next to the constant, referencing the cadences the other panels
  already use rather than inventing a third number in isolation.
- A change to a watched directory is still surfaced promptly enough that a
  person doing their own file operations does not perceive a lag.
- An idle panel left open costs materially less than it does today, and that
  is asserted by a test counting `List` calls over a fixed span, not by
  inspection.
- Whatever is chosen, a user action (expand, refresh, show-more) resets the
  schedule to its responsive end.
- Blocked on the visibility gate landing first: measuring an idle cadence is
  meaningless while a hidden panel polls at all.
notes:
REVISED after adversarial review (codex, 2026-08-31).

TWO CORRECTIONS, one of them structural.

1. DROP time.Ticker. filesPollLoop arms a ticker (ws_files.go:1041), so a tick
that outlasts its interval leaves a pending tick and the next scan starts
immediately — that IS the 100% duty cycle, and no interval fixes it. Arm the
timer AFTER the work finishes instead. This is a correctness fix, not a
tuning one, and it belongs here.

2. A concrete ladder to argue against, reusing values the repo already states
(Ports 1s settle/debounce + 10s periodic, Git 5s):
   visible            -> immediate
   ok, unchanged      -> 1s, 1s, 2s, 5s, 10s
   change detected    -> reset to 1s
   user mutation/hint -> immediate, coalesced, then 1s
   failure            -> 10s, 20s, 40s, cap 60s
   remote             -> +/-10% jitter
The hot phase is short because the tree is visible; the tail is long because
an idle panel must cost nothing.

Also: a completed terminal command is a legitimate HINT here, the way
schedule.go:20 uses it for Ports. D5 rejected command-end as the SOLE refresh
source, not as a supplementary hint — worth using, and worth saying so.
close_reason:
Landed as cb8f2429.

WHAT SHIPPED. The 500 ms cadence now has a written reason next to the constant,
in schedule.go's form, calibrated against the cadences the repo already states
(Ports 1s settle/debounce and 10s periodic, Git 5s) rather than a third number.
On top of it, a watcher-local adaptive ladder expressed as MULTIPLES of the one
base interval, so filesPollInterval stays the only knob tests turn and every
existing test that sets it to 20ms or to an hour keeps working untouched:
idle 2x, 2x, 4x, 10x, 20x; failure 20x, 40x, 80x, capped at 120x, separate so an
unreachable host is not re-probed at the idle cadence. A remote binding gets
+/-10% jitter; a local one gets none, which also keeps the ladder exact in test.

THE STRUCTURAL HALF, which was the point. time.Ticker is gone. A tick that
outlasted its interval left a PENDING tick, so the next scan began the instant
the previous one returned — a 100% duty cycle no interval could fix, reachable at
maxWatchPaths 512 x entryCap 10_000. The timer is armed after filesPollTick
returns.

A DECISION WORTH RECORDING, because it reverses the bead's own note. The note's
ladder says "user mutation/hint -> immediate". files.list and files.watch are
NOT that, and wiring them to an immediate scan (the first attempt did) is
quadratic: expanding a tree issues both per folder, so n folders cost 2n full
scans over a watch set that is itself growing. The first has just listed the path
it cares about; the second already took a synchronous baseline for every path it
ADDED (nocx-8hdia.5). Both now reset the rung without spending a listing. Only an
upload — a real mutation — spends an immediate scan.

TESTING. The ladder's arithmetic is pinned by a test with no server, no goroutine
and no clock. The first attempt asserted it with time.Sleep(145ms) and a band of
2-4 listings, which is exactly the timing dependence AGENTS.md forbids: on a
loaded box it reads 1 and goes red for a reason unrelated to the code. The
integration tests assert the WIRING instead, on observable state with generous
deadlines: a real file written into a watched directory resets the rung through
the real files.changed chain; a real provider failure walks the failure ladder and
recovers to the idle one; and a listing made deliberately slower than its interval
does not have the next scan waiting for it. The one remaining duration is the
strict half of that last assertion — an absence inside a window SHORTER than the
wait, so a slow machine can only make it more certain.

PROCESS. Pre-commit caught three gosec findings the worker's own runs did not:
G404 twice on the jitter generator and G115 on uint64(time.Now().UnixNano()).
G404 is answered by //nolint:gosec with a specific reason (scheduling jitter
grants no access and alters no path) in the house form; G115 was not silenced but
restructured away. go vet clean; TestFiles|TestUpload|TestWatch green (9.7s);
TestFilesPoll green under -race.

NOT RUN, deliberately, per AGENTS.md: make ci-full, the containerized jobs and
e2e belong to whoever integrates, on the merged tree.

title: The Files poll pauses when nobody is looking, the way Ports already does
description:
The Files poll is BACKEND-driven, so unlike Git and Ports the frontend cannot
stop it by going away. `filesPollLoop` ticks on a bare `time.Ticker` and asks
nothing about whether anyone is looking.

Design section 5.5 already requires this: polling is "paused while `visible()`
is false, and one immediate poll when the panel becomes visible".

Ports already has the whole pattern and it should be copied rather than
reinvented: a `ports.visible` method (`ws_ports.go:181`) drives
`Scheduler.SetVisible` (`internal/discovery/schedule.go:232`), so the SAMPLER
stops — not merely the reading of its results. The frontend half exists too:
`ports.tsx` sends the flag on every visibility transition, and a collapsed
sidebar counts as hidden.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A `files.visible` method, its params schema in `contracts/`, its validation
  and its OpenRPC entry, shaped after `ports.visible`.
- `filesPollLoop` observes the flag: while not visible it issues no listing
  at all — not a cheaper one, none.
- Becoming visible issues one immediate poll before resuming the interval, so
  nobody waits an interval to see the truth.
- The frontend sends the flag on the same transitions Ports does, including
  the collapsed sidebar and a switch to another sidebar view.
- A Go test asserts zero `List` calls against a fake handle across several
  intervals while hidden, and exactly one immediately on becoming visible.
- Not in scope: the interval itself and the per-tick bound (sibling beads).
close_reason:
Committed as af7b8e35. files.visible pauses the backend digest poll; a
hidden->visible edge polls once immediately.

DECISION WORTH RE-READING BEFORE CHANGING IT: handleVisible does NOT go
through h.op.Run, unlike every other binding method. That path composes the
filesystem gate (capacity 1, queue 8, 1s wait) against listings bounded at
10s local / 30s SFTP, so a visibility signal behind it is refusable by
exactly the contention it exists to reduce — the busier the backend, the
likelier "I am hidden" never lands and the poll goes on running.
Authorisation is the same D15 property asked of the transport's own record
(this connection owns the binding's session), not a second answer to it: the
watcher's comment already records that the authorisation happened once, in
files.watch, which acquired the handle the loop still holds.

FOUND WHILE WRITING THE TEST, and the effect alone could not have covered
it: collapsing the sidebar leaves the panel MOUNTED with visible() false,
but putting another sidebar view in front UNMOUNTS it — disposing the effect
before it can say anything, so the backend kept polling for a panel that no
longer existed. The store outlives the panel (the filter and tree survive a
swap), so the last word is an onCleanup in the panel.

The becoming-visible poll is an EDGE, not a value, with its own test: a
repeated "visible: true" must not poll, or the panel gains a second cadence
no interval governs.

NOT covered, filed as nocx-8hdia.6: hiding the WINDOW stops nothing in any of
the three panels. Ports has the same gap, so this is not a Files regression —
the sidebar has no opinion about the window and nobody composes
document.hidden.

Red proved before green by removing the gate: "hidden panel issued 10
listings over 10 intervals, want 0" and a timeout on the becoming-visible
poll.

Verification: go test -race ./internal/transport (308s, exit 0, no races);
frontend suite 5775 tests / 303 files; all pre-commit static gates.

TWO PROCESS NOTES. The params-contract gate refused the method until it had
probes, which is the gate working — both boolean values are given, since a
set that only ever says true would accept a schema that had made the field a
constant. And twice I reported "transport green" after reading the exit code
of a `tail` in a pipeline rather than of `go test`; the second reading, with
the status captured explicitly, showed that contract test failing. Capture
the status, never the pipe's.

title: Nothing polls a host for a panel nobody is looking at
description:
Found while investigating why the Files filter cannot see past a folder's
first page (nocx-708q.8). The filter turned out to be the small defect; this
is the large one underneath it.

## What a person gets

nocx stops costing them a laptop fan and a remote host round trips for panels
nobody is looking at. Open the Files panel on a home directory, switch to
another view, and the machine goes quiet.

## What is happening now

`filesPollLoop` (`internal/transport/ws_files.go`) ticks every
`defaultFilesPollInterval = 500ms`, and `filesPollTick` walks EVERY watched
path sequentially calling `h.List(path, Page{Offset: 0, Limit: 1})`.

`Limit: 1` is not a small request. Both providers enumerate the whole
directory before slicing, so each of those calls does, in
`local.Provider.List` (`internal/filesystem/local/local.go:177`):
EvalSymlinks, `os.ReadDir`, `de.Info()` — an lstat PER ENTRY (`local.go:292`)
— plus Readlink and Stat per symlink, the `entryWireCost` byte loop,
`sortEntries`, and `ComputeRev`, a sha256 over the name, size, mtime, mode,
kind, link kind and link target of every entry (`internal/filesystem/
rev.go:29`). Then it returns `entries[0:1]` and the rest is discarded.

For a 261-entry directory that is ~261 lstats, two sorts and a sha256, twice
a second, forever, while the panel is open. The ceilings make the worst case
absurd: `maxWatchPaths` 512 x `entryCap` 10_000 = 5.12M lstats per tick — a
tick that cannot finish in 500ms, so it degenerates into a continuous stat
storm at 100% duty.

There is no visibility gate, no backoff, and no bound on the work in one tick.

## It contradicts the panel's own design

`.internal/specs/2026-08-06-file-manager-design.md` D5: "Refresh comes from
the filesystem: fsnotify locally, polling over SFTP". Section 5.5 adds that
polling is "paused while `visible()` is false, and one immediate poll when
the panel becomes visible", and that "there is a ceiling on watched
directories and on outstanding re-lists".

None of the three is implemented. The poll loop is the acknowledged interim —
`ws_files.go:26` says so — and it is being used for the local provider, where
the design did not put it at all. Replacing it with fsnotify is a separate
epic; this one is the cadence discipline that is missing whatever the change
signal turns out to be, and that SFTP needs permanently.

## The other two panels, for calibration

Ports is the model and its doctrine is already written down in
`internal/discovery/schedule.go`: "background polls become bugs exactly here,
so each timer exists for a stated reason", and "a background tab running `ss`
on a loop against a production host is a defect, not a feature". It has a
settle delay, a prompt debounce, a 10s periodic sample, one in flight, a user
pause, AND a backend `ports.visible` RPC driving `Scheduler.SetVisible`
(`schedule.go:232`) — so the sampler stops, not just the reading of it.

Git took half of it: 5s, frontend-driven, a visibility gate (D13), one in
flight never queued, suppressed during a mutation — but no backoff, while
every poll runs a real `hnd.Status(ctx)` traversal (`ws_git.go:722`).

Files took none of it and runs ten times more often than either, on the most
expensive tick of the three.

## Deliberately out

- Implementing fsnotify (its own epic). This epic must leave the SFTP poll
  correct and cheap, because that one never goes away.
- A global throttler keyed by host (its own epic). A throttler bounds the
  damage; cadence is what removes the work. Doing only the throttler would
  build a busy-loop that produces refusals.
- Changing what the panels DISPLAY.

## Success Criteria

- With the Files panel not visible — sidebar collapsed, another view
  selected, window hidden — the backend issues NO filesystem listing on its
  behalf. Asserted against the poll loop, not inferred from the frontend.
- Becoming visible again produces one immediate refresh, so nobody waits an
  interval to see the truth.
- The Files poll interval is a number with a written reason next to it, in
  the shape `discovery/schedule.go` already uses, and it backs off while
  nothing is changing.
- One poll tick is bounded regardless of how large the watched tree is: a
  ceiling on paths per tick, round-robin, so 512 watched directories cannot
  produce a tick that outlasts its own interval.
- The Git poll backs off when nothing is changing, and a user action resets it.
- An automated check watches a person do it: open the panel on a directory,
  collapse the sidebar, and observe that listings stop; re-open, and observe
  exactly one immediate listing.

title: The Files filter searches only the first page of a folder, and the empty state says otherwise
description:
Owner, reproducing on a home directory of 261 entries: `/home/dev/log.txt`
is not found by the Files filter until "Show next 211" is clicked by hand.
After clicking, the same query finds it.

The panel's empty state says "Only the folders you have opened are searched."
That sentence is FALSE: only the first PAGE of an opened folder is searched.

## Cause

`FILES_PAGE_SIZE = 50` (`files-store.ts:94`), and `narrowFilesRows` is a pure
function over the rows the tree already produced. Typing never issues a
request — deliberately, per the module comment, so the filter cannot churn
the watch set or race the reveal walk. The consequence is that anything past
offset 50 is invisible to it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Files on a directory with more than 50 entries (261 in the report),
   so the tree shows "Show next 211".
2. Type a string matching only an entry beyond the first page — `log` against
   `/home/dev/log.txt`.
3. "No files match". Click "Show next 211", type the same string: it is found.

## Why the fix is a wide re-list and not a wire-level filter

Measured, not assumed. Both providers enumerate the ENTIRE directory before
slicing — `local.Provider.List` (`internal/filesystem/local/local.go:177`)
does EvalSymlinks, ReadDir, an lstat per entry, the sizeCap byte loop,
sortEntries and ComputeRev over every entry, and only then returns
`entries[lo:hi]`. `sftp.Provider.List` is the same shape. Pagination is a
wire/render bound, not an enumeration bound. `refreshLimit`'s own comment
(`files-store.ts:618`) already says so: a wider limit "buys wire bytes and
merged rows, never round trips".

Three consequences decide the design:

1. Client-side auto-paging is the worst option — 6 full re-enumerations of a
   261-entry directory instead of 1.
2. A `nameFilter` parameter on `files.list` costs a round trip per DISTINCT
   QUERY (every keystroke is a new result set), through a filesystem gate of
   capacity 1 with an 8-deep queue and a 1-second wait timeout
   (`ws.go:1527`, `DefaultDomainMaxQueue`, `DefaultDomainConflictWaitTimeout`)
   against list timeouts of 10s local / 30s remote. And the WebSocket is
   127.0.0.1 (`ws.go:1615`), so what it saves is loopback bytes while it
   pays remote round trips per character. Bad trade. Deferred to its own
   bead as an optimisation, to be taken on measurement.
3. Fetching the directory ONCE when the filter activates costs the same N
   listings as (2) does per keystroke, and then zero for the rest of the
   session, because the fetch does not depend on what was typed. The payload
   is bounded by the caps the backend already enforces on every call:
   `sizeCap` 8 MiB is computed over the COMPLETE listing, `entryCap` is
   10_000 local / 5_000 remote. A directory that lists at all has already
   been measured and accepted whole.

## The shape

While the filter is active, one wide `files.list` per EXPANDED and TRUNCATED
directory (`hasMore === true`). A fully loaded directory needs no request —
today's client-side filter is already correct for it.

Results land in a DISPOSABLE PROJECTION, never merged into the tree. That is
what keeps the module's existing invariant literally true: clearing the
filter restores exactly the view the person had, because nothing was touched.

## Acceptance Criteria

- With a directory expanded and truncated, a filter matching only an entry
  beyond the first page FINDS it, without the person clicking "Show next".
- The projection never reaches `applyListing` and never writes `children`,
  `rev`, `busy`, `canonical`, `total`, `hasMore`, `nextOffset` or
  `appliedGeneration` on a `DirListing`. Asserted, not merely intended.
- Requests are issued one at a time, next on the previous response, and are
  deferred entirely while a reveal walk or a header refresh is in flight —
  the filesystem gate is capacity 1 and a queued request expires after 1s.
- Activation is debounced; subsequent keystrokes issue NO request at all.
- The projection is dropped on clear, on `rescope`, and on a binding change,
  and is invalidated when the directory's `rev` moves.
- Row identity is by path: an entry already present in `dir.children` reuses
  its `FilesNode`. A projected-only DIRECTORY that is clicked goes through
  `revealPath`, never by appending a node to `children` — that would make
  `nextOffset` a lie.
- The "Show next N" row says which state it is in: searching, N more
  matches, or a refusal. "No files match" appears only after every eligible
  directory has answered.
- The empty-state sentence stops lying — opened folders really are searched,
  and unopened ones are named as not searched.
- One automated check watches a person do it: expand a directory of more
  than 50 entries, type a name that exists only past the first page, and see
  the row appear.
close_reason:
Landed as df6557d7. This is the defect the owner originally reported, in full:
log.txt on a 261-entry home directory is now found by typing, without clicking
"Show next 211".

THE DESIGN, and why it is not the obvious one. Both providers enumerate the
ENTIRE directory before slicing, so pagination is a wire/render bound, not an
enumeration bound. Auto-paging on the client would have cost six full
enumerations instead of one. A nameFilter on the wire would have cost a round
trip per DISTINCT QUERY — every keystroke is a new result set — through a
filesystem gate of capacity 1 whose queue expires after 1s, and the socket is
127.0.0.1, so it saves loopback bytes while paying remote round trips per
character (deferred as nocx-708q.9). Fetching each expanded-and-truncated
directory ONCE on activation costs the same listings that would cost PER
KEYSTROKE, then nothing for the session, because the fetch does not depend on
what was typed.

DISPOSABLE PROJECTION, never merged. That is what keeps "clearing the filter
restores exactly the view the person had" literally true. Criterion 2 is
asserted by SNAPSHOTTING the DirListing's own fields before and after and
comparing — not by spying on applyListing, which would pass if the write were
later inlined. That distinction was worth insisting on; it is the assertion a
future refactor would otherwise break silently.

ONE WALKER, after a send-back. The first version had rows() and
buildFilterRows() as two recursions over one tree with two copies of emitNode
and two copies of the structural-row decision. They MUST agree: rows() is what
the reveal walk and the watch-set reconciliation reason about, filterRows() is
what the person sees, so a divergence surfaces as a row on screen that is not in
the watch set. Now one walkRows parameterised by where children come from and
which structural row closes the directory.

A PAGINATION ROW NOW RETIRES once a projection has answered for its directory,
because it really has been searched completely. The bead named three states for
that row and the code answers with two; that is correct rather than an omission,
and files-filter.ts now says why — the third state is vacuous once the whole
directory is in hand.

THE EMPTY STATE STOPPED LYING, twice over. Its sentence is now "Opened folders
are searched completely. Unopened folders are not searched." And "No files
match" waits until every eligible directory has answered — but settles AT ONCE
when there is nothing to search, which was a send-back: the first version made
the common case (a fully loaded tree, nothing matching) show neither rows nor
the empty state for the whole 150ms debounce.

WHAT THE SEND-BACK WAS MOSTLY ABOUT: three tests for nine acceptance criteria,
four of which say "asserted, not merely intended" in so many words. Now 136
tests green across the three files, covering the projection's isolation, that
later keystrokes issue NO request, invalidation on clear/rescope/binding/rev,
serialization behind a reveal, and the panel-level check that watches a person
find a file past the first page.

VERIFIED: 136 tests, eslint, tsc, prettier, and the full pre-commit static gate.
NOT RUN, deliberately: make ci-full, the containerized jobs and e2e belong to
whoever integrates, on the merged tree.

title: The filter hides the 'Show next N' row that would explain why nothing matched
description:
Owner, reproducing on a large home directory: type a name into the Files
filter and the panel answers "No files match" with an EMPTY tree — no rows at
all, not even the folders that are open.

The "Show next 211" row under the open directory is what would explain the
empty result, and it is the row that disappears.

## Cause

`narrowFilesRows` (`frontend/src/files/files-filter.ts`) keeps a structural
row — 'more', 'loading', 'state' — only when its owning directory was
emitted, and a directory is emitted only when it matched or a LOADED
descendant matched:

    const owner = row.depth === 0 ? null : chain[row.depth - 1]
    if (owner === null || owner.emitted) out.push(row)

So when nothing loaded matches, the owner is not emitted and its "Show next
N" goes with it. The module's own comment claims the opposite — that
structural rows "are retained rather than filtered away" precisely so that
"a 'Show next 47' under a folder that is on screen says there are 47 entries
this filter has not seen". The implementation delivers that only in the case
where it is not needed.

This is separable from the larger defect that the filter cannot see past the
first page at all (its sibling bead): even once that is fixed, a refused or
in-flight search still needs its row on screen.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Files on a directory with more than 50 entries, so "Show next N"
   appears.
2. Type a string matching only an entry beyond the first page.
3. The panel says "No files match" and shows nothing — the "Show next N"
   that would explain it is gone.

## Acceptance Criteria

- With a filter active and no match among loaded rows, a structural row
  ('more', 'loading', 'state') is emitted together with its ancestor chain,
  so the person can see WHERE the unsearched entries are and reach them.
- A structural row still never drags in a folder that is not otherwise on
  screen for any other reason — ancestors appear because the structural row
  needs them, in tree order, exactly as a match's ancestors do.
- The root's own structural rows keep working as they do now.
- The module comment stops claiming a property the code does not have.
- A test asserts the empty-match case specifically: rows for an expanded,
  truncated directory with zero matching entries produce the 'more' row and
  its ancestors, not an empty array.
close_reason:
Committed as 99ad35a5. A structural row ('more', 'loading', 'state') now flushes
its ancestor chain and is emitted, exactly as a match does.

ONE DELIBERATE RULE WAS REVERSED, and it is worth naming rather than burying:
the previous behaviour — asserted by a test whose comment defended it — was
'a structural row must not drag a folder into view'. That is right about
entries and wrong about listings. A structural row is not an entry with a
name; it is a statement that this directory holds entries the filter has NOT
SEEN, which is as good a reason to show the folder as a descendant that
matched. The old rule delivered the honesty the rows exist for in every case
EXCEPT the one that needed it: when nothing matched, the folder left the
screen and took its 'Show next 211' with it.

Rejected alternative, recorded: flush only when the result would otherwise be
empty. It hides the same fact in the non-empty case — two matches found with
three folders unsearched is a different answer from two matches found.

The rule stays single: a row is shown when it matches, when something below
it matches, or when something below it was never searched. A fully listed
folder holding nothing matching still stays out, which is what keeps this
from collapsing into 'show everything'. Root structural rows unaffected (at
depth 0 the chain is empty).

17/17 in files-filter.test.ts, 330/330 across frontend/src/files, all
pre-commit static gates green. Not run on this branch by design: make
ci-full, the containerized jobs and e2e — those belong to whoever integrates.

title: Nothing catches a schemaV1 edit that forgets its rung
description:
Found by nocx-lmb6v.5, 2026-08-31. It is the last unguarded edge of the migration epic and
it is the one a person will actually hit.

validateLadder's contiguity check catches a ladder that does not END at schemaVersion.
Nothing catches the other direction: editing schemaV1 and forgetting to bump. The comment
on schemaVersion asks for it BY EYE, which is the mechanism this epic exists to replace.

nocx-lmb6v.7 built the parity test, which catches a step's frozen DDL drifting from
schemaV1 — a divergence between two populations that both exist. This is the case where
there is no rung at all, so there are no two populations to compare yet, and the parity
test is silent: a fresh install gets the new shape, an upgrade never runs anything, and
the two differ with nothing to compare because the ladder was never told.

The exposure just grew: nocx-lmb6v.5 moved the api_run tables INTO schemaV1, so this gap
now covers them too.

Adjacent to nocx-lmb6v.8 (validateLadder calls an empty ladder well-formed) but not the
same thing — that one is a wrong answer about a degenerate input, this one is a missing
question.

## Fix

Something mechanical: a checked-in digest of schemaV1 that must change in the same commit
as schemaVersion, or a test that derives the expected fresh shape from the ladder's
endpoint. The digest is cruder and would actually work.
acceptance_criteria: A change to schemaV1 without a corresponding new rung fails a gate rather than being caught by eye. The gate names what to do — add a rung — rather than only reporting a mismatch.
close_reason:
Committed as a323bb3e on omp/lmb6v-12-rung, by an omp worker through herdr. Merged; go test ./internal/content/ ok 23.3s.

THE DESIGN IS BETTER THAN THE BRIEF ASKED FOR, and the worker argued for it rather than just doing it. The brief offered a standalone digest of schemaV1 beside schemaVersion as the crude option that would work. The worker pinned the digest ON THE FINAL LADDER RUNG instead, with the reason in the code: a standalone digest could be updated while the ladder stayed still, so it would gate the edit without requiring the rung that actually carries existing files to the new shape. Pinning it to the rung makes the two inseparable.

migrationStep gains schemaDigest; the final rung {15->16} carries the sha256 of schemaV1; validateLadder checks it before the walk. validateLadderForSchema is parameterised solely so the paired positive can be written — production always calls validateLadder with the compiled-in constants.

FALSIFIED BY THE COORDINATOR, not accepted on report. I added an index to schemaV1 without touching schemaVersion or the ladder and ran the gate:

  schema_parity_test.go:98: schemaV1 changed without a migration rung: add a new
  rung and update its schema digest (schema version 16); got 45cfff56..., want 4688f8fc...

The message NAMES WHAT TO DO rather than only reporting a mismatch, which was the requirement — a gate that says only 'these differ' gets suppressed by the next person in a hurry. Reverted afterwards and confirmed production code byte-identical.

THE PAIRED POSITIVE IS GENUINELY PAIRED: TestAChangedSchemaPassesWhenANewFinalRungCarriesIt appends a rung carrying the digest of a CHANGED schema and requires validateLadderForSchema to accept it. So the gate cannot be satisfied by 'only the current shape', which is the failure mode that would have made it a test nobody trusts.

This closes the last unguarded edge of the migration protocol. The contiguity check already caught a ladder not ending at schemaVersion; the parity test caught a rung's frozen DDL drifting from schemaV1; this catches the case with no rung at all, where the parity test is silent by construction because there are not yet two populations to compare.

One nit left alone rather than churned: TestTheFinalMigrationRungPinsSchemaV1 calls t.Helper() at the top of a test function, where it does nothing. Harmless.

title: A migrated database and a fresh one are never asserted to have the same schema
description:
Found by nocx-lmb6v.2 while testing the ladder from its criteria, 2026-08-31. It is the
defect the whole epic exists to prevent, and nothing currently catches it.

After the walk, schemaV1 runs with every statement IF NOT EXISTS — so it CANNOT fix up a
table a step already rebuilt. The 14->15 step's grant_scopes DDL duplicates schemaV1's by
hand today, and the step's own comment says the two must be allowed to diverge the moment
16 exists. That divergence is correct and intended.

What is missing is the check that they agree AT THE SAME VERSION. So a future edit to
schemaV1 that is not mirrored into the frozen step DDL gives UPGRADED users a permanently
different table shape from FRESH installs — silently, with every test green, and the two
populations then diverge forever with no event to notice.

This is the highest-value single test in the epic: it is the one that catches the class of
mistake the ladder makes easy, rather than the ones it makes obvious.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Edit schemaV1's definition of a table that a migration step also rebuilds.
2. Do not mirror the edit into the step's frozen DDL.
3. Fresh install: the new shape. Upgrade: the old one. Every test passes.

## Fix

Compare normalised sqlite_master between a fresh database and a migrated one at the same
version. The fiddly part, and the reason this is a bead rather than a two-line addition:
the step's ALTER TABLE ... RENAME leaves the stored DDL quoted (CREATE TABLE
"grant_scopes"), so it needs normalising rather than a text compare.
acceptance_criteria: One test compares a normalised sqlite_master between a freshly created database and one migrated up to the same version, and fails if they differ. Normalised, not text-compared: a step's ALTER TABLE ... RENAME leaves the stored DDL quoted, so a naive comparison fails on cosmetics and would be deleted by the next person.
close_reason:
Committed as 9753d9c2 on worktree-agent-adf35adb907e35a2f. One new file, 572 lines, ZERO existing files touched — production code byte-identical against the merge base.

THE COMPARISON IS STRUCTURED FIRST, NORMALISED DDL SECOND, and the fallback is required rather than a nicety: no pragma reports a CHECK, STRICT or WITHOUT ROWID, and a CHECK is exactly what the 14->15 edge changes. PRAGMA table_xinfo / index_list / index_xinfo / foreign_key_list give facts that need no text handling and name the difference by column; everything in sqlite_master is included, sqlite_autoindex_* rows too, so a rebuild that loses a PRIMARY KEY shows up as a missing object.

WHAT IS NORMALISED AWAY, each a way two CREATE statements differ while the databases do not: identifier quoting (the reason this bead exists — CREATE TABLE \"grant_scopes\" after the RENAME), IF NOT EXISTS, whitespace and SQL comments outside string literals, case outside string literals, and the order of sqlite_master rows.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY KEPT, and this is where the value lives: THE CONTENTS OF STRING LITERALS, INCLUDING CASE AND SPACING — the scanner tracks quotes for this reason and no other, because the enum values inside the CHECK are what the edge exists to widen, and a normaliser that folded them would pass while the two populations genuinely differed. Also kept: column names, types, order, nullability, defaults, PK membership and position; the set of objects present including internal constraint indexes; index uniqueness, partiality, column order, direction and collation; foreign keys with both column lists and their ON UPDATE / ON DELETE; CHECK, STRICT and WITHOUT ROWID.

FALSIFIED FOUR WAYS, each mutation of the frozen step DDL run and then reverted. Added column -> RED, naming the column and the DDL. CHECK narrowed by one kind -> RED on the ddl fact ONLY, with the pragmas silent — and the test asserts that silence, so the file's claim about why the DDL fallback exists is checked rather than argued in prose. Dropped PRIMARY KEY -> RED across nine facts including the constraint index going absent. And the one that matters most: COSMETICS ONLY — the same DDL reformatted onto different lines, identifiers double-quoted, keywords recased, an inline comment added and IF NOT EXISTS inserted -> GREEN. That is what stops this being a test the next person deletes, after which the real check would be gone.

The headline error names the mechanism and points at the right fix: a new rung, never an edit to an old step's frozen DDL.

go test ./internal/content/... ok 19.9s; -race ok 207.3s; golangci-lint clean; the full pre-commit gate passed.

title: Two version counters answer 'what shape is this file in'
description:
Noted by nocx-lmb6v.1, 2026-08-31, as a deliberate refactor rather than a side effect.

migrateAPIRuns keeps its own api_run_schema.version beside user_version. Its
justification was that bumping user_version used to rebuild the whole ledger, so the API
runs needed a counter of their own to avoid being destroyed by somebody else's change.

That reason EXPIRED with the rebuild. There is now a ladder, and folding the API-run
tables into it is possible. Two counters for one question is the duplicate-owner shape:
they agree everywhere anyone looks, and the day they disagree, nothing says which is
right.

Related to nocx-lmb6v.3, which is the same question asked from the other side — one
integer governing three subsystems. Answer them together or the answers will conflict.
acceptance_criteria: One counter, or a stated reason in the code why two are correct. If the API-run tables join the ladder, their migration is an ordinary rung with the same crash-safety interval as every other.
notes:
RAISED TO P1 ON 2026-08-31 BY A FINDING FROM nocx-lmb6v.7, which turns this from a tidy-up into a hole in the epic's own promise.

Open's schema sequence is THREE steps, not two: the ladder walk, schemaV1, and then migrateAPIRuns (internal/content/api_run_sqlite.go:34). That third step creates the api_run* tables and versions them through its OWN api_run_schema table — outside user_version, outside schemaLadder, and OUTSIDE EVERY REFUSAL THE LADDER MAKES.

Two consequences, and the second is the serious one. schemaVersion does not describe the whole file: a database can be stamped 15 with api-run tables at any version of their own. And the migration protocol this epic exists to establish — one explicit ordered step per edge, crash-safe, stamped only after the edge commits, refuse a newer file without modifying a byte — is SILENTLY NOT IN FORCE for roughly a quarter of the tables. nocx-7qunp's newer-schema refusal does not cover them either.

So the answer is almost certainly to fold the api-run tables into the ladder rather than to justify two counters. Its original justification — that a user_version bump used to rebuild the ledger, so the api runs needed a counter of their own to survive somebody else's change — expired with the rebuild.

Answer this together with nocx-lmb6v.3, which is the same question from the other side.
close_reason:
Committed as 6035c0cf on worktree-agent-a8bab05bbe754e3b2. Both beads answered together, because they are one question from opposite sides and separate answers would have conflicted.

THE GRANULARITY DECISION: ONE COUNTER, FOR ONE FILE. Written into schema_migrate.go with the argument, not just the conclusion. (1) The unit of the decision IS the file: Open is handed a path and must answer open / migrate / refuse once, for the whole of it, before it hands anything out — a version finer than the thing being versioned has nowhere to put the extra resolution. (2) A per-subsystem version needs a per-subsystem REFUSAL and nothing can express one: if the layout were ahead and the ledger were not, the only honest answer is still to refuse the file, because ContentDB is a single interface carrying all three repositories and 'open the ledger half' is a store reporting itself healthy while a third of it is missing. A refusal that has to be total is a version that may as well be single. (3) nocx-lmb6v.3's cost is real, small, and falls on the right person: a layout-only bump adds a rung that is a no-op for the other two, and 'an older binary refuses over a bump that touched nothing it owns' is not a cost but the CORRECT answer — that binary cannot know the new shape is compatible with its own reads. (4) Three counters would be three ladders over one set of tables, needing a walk ordered across them the moment a foreign key crosses a boundary, which grant_scopes -> authority_grants shows is ordinary.

So nocx-lmb6v.3 is answered by SAYING SO IN THE CODE and changing nothing, and nocx-lmb6v.5 by folding the api-run tables into the ladder. schemaVersion 15 -> 16; migrateAPIRuns and apiRunSchemaVersion deleted; the four api_run CREATEs and two indexes moved into schemaV1 unchanged; rung 15->16 drops api_run_schema.

A REAL DEFECT WAS FOUND AND IT IS THE BEST PART. refuseAPIRunTablesFromANewerBuild is called BEFORE the walk, and the test names why: before the fix, a file whose api-run tables were ahead of this build WALKED 14->15 AND COMMITTED THE STAMP, THEN REFUSED — a refusal that has already rewritten what it refuses. The check cannot live inside the retiring rung either, because a step refusing in its own transaction still refuses only after every rung below it has committed. It is the retirement's precondition: dropping a counter whose value this build cannot understand would erase the evidence. It is inert from 16 on, when no file carries the table.

The fixture for that test is a released 14 database plus the two-counter era's own api-run DDL with api_run_schema.version = 2 — representable PRECISELY BECAUSE the two counters were independent, which is the defect being closed. Asserted against migrateSchema, where byte identity is real, and again through Open, where the file still answers 14.

PARITY WAS CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED, and the check found a hole: schema_v14.sql has no api-run tables at all, so after the fold both sides of the existing comparison get them from schemaV1 and it could not catch a divergence in them EVEN IN PRINCIPLE. A new test compares a fresh database against one upgraded from a two-counter-era file, whose api-run tables schemaV1's IF NOT EXISTS cannot repair — that is the population that matters.

Five inline one-rung ladders in the existing suite became theLadderWithThisEdgeSwapped(...), because validateLadder refuses a chain not ending at schemaVersion and a literal goes stale on every new rung.

go test ./internal/content/ ok 32.7s; -race ok 250.3s; golangci-lint clean; deadcode -whylive shows both new functions reachable from main via Open -> migrateSchema. Red before the fix in order: the two refusal tests, TestOneVersionCounterAnswersWhatShapeTheFileIsIn, and the two-counter-era retention test — with the parity test green throughout as the paired positive. Re-verified on the merged tree: build clean, ./internal/content/ ok 20.9s alongside nocx-lmb6v.10's engine-posture test.

title: A displaced client loses the session; nothing in the product can watch one it does not own
description:
Found while implementing nocx-eidfb.3, 2026-08-31, and it is why that bead could not
finish the epic's first acceptance line.

The line reads "two clients attach to one session; both show the same content". Today
the loser of a session is DISPLACED, not demoted: contracts/session.displaced.schema.json
is "another client has claimed a session this client was holding", and a displaced client
drops the session entirely. The helper ABI freeze (nocx-k6p18.1, D8) is where independent
per-subscriber read cursors are being decided; until something can hold a session it does
not own, there is no second client to render at the session's grid.

So nocx-eidfb.3 built the machinery and deliberately did not build a wire notification to
drive it, because that notification would have had NO REACHABLE CONSUMER — which on this
codebase is not a style objection but the deadcode ratchet and AGENTS.md's rule 5.
renderAtSessionGrid is public and takes the size from whoever knows it, so this bead can
supply a caller without changing its shape.

WHAT THIS NEEDS FIRST: nocx-afgkj.1, the controller decision. An observer role and
"the last attach silently takes the session" are two answers to one question, and
displacement is the implicit answer taken to its conclusion. Deciding the lease decides
what a non-owner is allowed to be.

THE GENERAL MECHANISM, as nocx-eidfb.3 left it described: publish "the session's size
changed" from the lane's applied-resize seam, and pin the client's grid until the backend
confirms that client's own report. nocx-eidfb.2 explicitly deferred "telling a client the
session's size" to this work.
acceptance_criteria: Two clients are attached to one session at different window sizes at the same time, and both show identical terminal content — the epic's first line, meant literally. The one that does not own the size renders at the session's grid and pads or scrolls; the machinery for that already exists (TerminalContent.renderAtSessionGrid) and needs a caller that can hold a session it does not own.

title: Unresolved commands now rank as delegation, because the worst member of a set is chosen by a total order the lattice says it does not have
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Ask the assistant to run a command whose program is not in the command resource allowlist — anything the parser cannot resolve.
2. Watch the approval prompt: the class is 'delegate', not 'mutate-destructive'.
3. Under a policy that permits destructive mutation and asks about delegation, the call now asks where it previously did not.

## What changed and why it is not obviously right

nocx-tyhel (ADR-0053) made Declaration.Effect a SET and made an unresolved parse take the worst member, which is correct in principle: not knowing should tighten. session.run's set is {observe, mutate-reversible, mutate-destructive, delegate, cross-boundary}, and content.effectOrder ranks delegate 6 — above cross-boundary 5, disclose 4, privilege-change 3 and mutate-destructive 2. So every command the parser cannot resolve is now a DELEGATION, where before the migration it kept session.run's single declared mutate-destructive.

That is a silent widening of what a person is asked about, and it was a side effect of adding delegate to a set rather than a decision anybody took.

## The specific reason to doubt the ranking

The code the migration replaced said, in two places, that this ordering does not exist:

  'Mixed verbs remain declared because this lattice has no implicit total ordering for combining unlike effects.'

  'effectBelowCeiling states the only safe lowering relations. Observe is already the historical lowering for a read-only report; every other relation is named instead of inferred from the effect strings order.'

effectBelowCeiling existed precisely to avoid inferring a relation from rank. WorstEffect reintroduces exactly that inference, over the same unlike effects, and effectOrder is a total order written as a switch. Delegation is not a more severe kind of mutation; it is a different kind of act. Ranking it above rm -rf asserts a comparison the lattice was written to refuse.

## What was already paid for this

The e2e went red on the merged tree — three specs, both browsers — because 'echo hi' was outside the allowlist and therefore unresolved and therefore a delegation, and the turn suspended on an approval the run never gave. That instance was fixed by classifying echo as observe (2a84e9b0). The class of commands behind it was not: every unrecognised program still resolves the same way.

## Acceptance Criteria

- It is decided and written down whether an unresolved parse takes a RANKED worst member or a named one, and if ranked, why a total order over unlike effects is admissible here when effectBelowCeiling said it was not.
- If the ranking stays, effectOrder carries a comment saying it is a deliberate severity order and what the person is being asked to accept at each step.
- If it does not, the selection for an unresolved parse names its answer explicitly rather than inferring it, the way effectBelowCeiling did.
- A test states what an unresolved command resolves to, so a future set change cannot move it silently.
- The allowlist gap is separately visible: a test or a comment records that membership of the resource allowlist is what decides resolved-vs-unresolved, so adding a set member cannot again change the class of every command outside it.

title: The connection overlay is a loading screen, not a card: an opaque ground and a mark that says it is working
description:
The owner watched two frames of the shipped overlay and rejected both (2026-08-31).

FRAME ONE — a card holding one static logo and nothing else. The overlay is
held visible by `minimumVisibleMs: 1000` after the socket is already `online`;
in `online` `sentence()` returns '' and the Spinner is hidden, so what is left
is a 480px bordered card containing a motionless icon. An empty box for a
second.

FRAME TWO — `waiting`, and the countdown is the headline. "Retrying in 6
seconds" is set 16px/600 as the largest thing on screen, so the biggest text a
person reads is a ticking number while WHAT IS WRONG is said nowhere. The
`Stack gap="loose"` puts the same distance between mark, text and Retry, so
there is no grouping and the button floats.

Under both: the ground is not opaque. `dialog.nocx-dialog::backdrop` is
`--color-scrim` (rgba(0,0,0,.5)) in every theme, and the panel draws card
chrome. The 2026-08-30 spec §8 already says "the opaque overlay covers it
regardless" — the implementation departed from a decision that was made.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `make dev-web` and open the client. The startup overlay is visible for its
   one-second minimum: a bordered card with a static logo and no sentence —
   the socket is already `online`, so there is nothing left to render.
2. Stop the backend and let the dispatcher back off. The overlay shows
   "Retrying in N seconds" as its headline, a Retry button under it at the same
   distance the icon sits above it, and the terminal visible through a
   half-transparent scrim behind the card.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The overlay renders on an opaque ground: no card chrome, and nothing behind
  it is visible in any theme. Asserted against the stylesheet, not by eye.
- No state of the overlay ever renders an empty sentence. While it is visible,
  `online` is not displayed — the last non-`online` state is held. A test
  drives it to `online` inside the minimum-visible window and asserts a
  sentence is still shown.
- The mark's ring animates in `connecting` and is still in `waiting` and
  `blocked`, and stops entirely under `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- `waiting` and `blocked` render the same three-level structure: a headline
  saying what is true, a dimmed line saying what happens next, and Retry. The
  countdown is not the headline.
- A cold start's first frame is `connecting` — it does not offer Retry for an
  attempt nobody has made.
- `dialog.tsx` and the overlay share ONE modal-host implementation: there is
  exactly one `showModal()` call site and one `pushOverlay` call site in
  `ui/`, asserted by grep in a test.

## Agreed design (owner, 2026-08-31)

1. Mechanism. `ui/overlay/modal-host.ts` is extracted FROM `dialog.tsx`: the
   `<dialog>` lifecycle, showModal/close, push/popOverlay, the
   --wails-draggable guard, focus return, the `element` the toast host renders
   into, and the Escape veto. `Dialog` = host + card chrome + height animation
   + focusInitial. `ConnectionOverlay` = host + full-bleed ground. Two siblings
   on one mechanism — NOT a `presentation="fullscreen"` variant of Dialog,
   which would be a mode in which none of Dialog's own props mean anything,
   and NOT a second showModal call site, which is the second implementation of
   one concept AGENTS.md forbids.
2. Ground. Opaque --color-bg over the whole window. No card, no border, no
   radius.
3. Mark. The 96px icon with a 128px ring around it. The ring turns only in
   `connecting`.
4. Text, three levels instead of one sentence:
     connecting  Connecting to nocx…            —                     —
     waiting     Cannot reach the nocx backend  Next attempt in 6 s   Retry
     blocked     <message>                      <remedy>              Retry
   This extends spec §8's "the app logo, one sentence, and Retry" and makes
