   `waiting` and `blocked` one structure rather than two.
5. Rhythm. Mark and text are one tight group; Retry is separated. No new
   Button size — Button is sm|md and air is what the button needed.
6. `main.tsx` seeds `{kind:'connecting'}`.
7. The overlay leaves by fading, with the reduced-motion switch.
notes:
Landed as d8cc5c8e (the overlay itself) plus a follow-up for four defects the
owner found by running it, three of which the first commit's tests could not
have caught because they are about motion and about the dispatcher, not about
the rendered shape.

MEASURED, not reasoned about — a browser driven with Playwright against a vite
stand with a dead backend port:

1. The icon twitched. `waiting` put the mark at y=267 and `connecting` at
   y=295: `connecting` has no detail text and no Retry, the group is centred,
   so it rose and fell 28px on every attempt. Fixed by rendering the action row
   in every state with the control `visibility: hidden` where it cannot act —
   which reserves the exact height with no number to keep in step and takes the
   button out of the tab order and the a11y tree.

2. The countdown did not run — it counted UP in jumps: 1, 2, 3, 6 seconds. The
   dispatcher publishes a wait ONCE when it schedules the attempt, and the
   number it publishes is the NEW backoff. Fixed by keeping a deadline in the
   component and deriving the remaining time from the clock, ticked four times
   a second (the published wait carries up to 50% jitter, so it is never a
   whole number of seconds and a 1s tick would sit out of phase).

3. The headline strobed between "Connecting to nocx…" and "Cannot reach the
   nocx backend" for as long as the backend stayed down, because every attempt
   in the outage is a `connecting` state lasting a few hundred ms. After the
   first failure the condition now stays put and the detail says
   "Reconnecting…"; the ring is what says an attempt is in flight.

4. "I brought the backend back up and it does not reconnect" — two causes.
   (a) PRODUCT: `_attemptConnection` set `blocked` on a discovery failure and
       returned WITHOUT scheduling anything, and `_onVisibilityChange` only
       retries out of `waiting`. So `blocked` never tried again — and
       `no-server` ("the backend could not be reached") was in it, which is the
       textbook case a bare repeat fixes. Transient kinds (`no-server`,
       `not-ready`) now schedule a retry and carry their sentence on the
       `waiting` state, so a stopped coordinator does not read the same as an
       unreachable port. `token-refused` stays terminal on purpose.
   (b) DEV STAND: `vite.dev-view.config.ts` baked the per-launch token into the
       HTML at config load, so a restarted backend's new token never reached an
       open page; the backend answered 401 before the upgrade and the browser
       WebSocket API does not expose the HTTP status, so the client could not
       tell that from a closed port and retried against it forever. The shim
       now serves the endpoint from a middleware that reads process.env per
       request. Verified: one open page, no reload, resolved 9999/TOKEN-A
       before the stand restart and 7777/TOKEN-B after it.

EXPONENTIAL BACKOFF was already there and is unchanged — dispatcher.ts, 250ms
doubling to a 5s cap with up to 50% jitter. The owner reported it missing
because the frozen counter hid it; with the countdown running it is visible as
each cycle starting from a larger number.
close_reason: Merged to main in a1fbb5d0 (PR #164). The overlay is an opaque full-bleed loading screen with a ring that animates only while a connection is actually being attempted; countdown, jitter-aware backoff display, reconnect and the lost-session copy all landed with it. CI green on all eight jobs at 3056116d.

title: The epic's happy path is watched end to end: quit nocx mid-build on a remote host, reopen, and the build is still running
description:
AGENTS.md rule 2: every epic that is not a chore proves its happy path, and the check
is written when the epic is created rather than at the end — by the end you know what
the code does, and that is the knowledge that makes you write the test the
implementation passes.

The sentence: on a remote host where the helper is installed, a build survives you
quitting nocx and updating it, and when you come back it is still running, its blocks
are there, and what you missed is named rather than silently absent.

Three conditions, each of which the check is worthless without:
  1. The client must go away ENTIRELY — a fresh coordinator, not a reconnect.
  2. The command must out-produce the helper's window while detached, or the gap path
     was never exercised.
  3. Liveness is proved by counting per-second markers across the detached window, not
     by a pane having rendered.

deadcode and coverage are FLOORS, never criteria — neither can report a feature that
is missing. And on this codebase deadcode cannot even report a dead METHOD behind a
live interface, which is most of it (AD-8). This check is the only thing that reports
the feature is wired.
acceptance_criteria: ONE automated check, through the seam a person actually reaches, under conditions without which it proves nothing: start a long command on a REMOTE helper host through the product; the command emits a marker per second; kill the coordinator entirely; bring a FRESH coordinator up; reattach to the same session by its hostSessionId; count the markers spanning the detached window afterwards — that is what proves the process RAN rather than that a pane rendered. The command must have produced more than the helper's window while detached, so the gap path is exercised and the gap is REPORTED in the product. Its exit status, when it finishes, is the real one and not 'unknown'. Run through cmd/nocx-server headless — the SHIPPED coordinator, not a harness beside it.
notes:
2026-09-02: the omp worker in /home/dev/.herdr/worktrees/nocx/omp-k6p18-9-e2e-c
died when the machine filled its root filesystem (246G at 100%, 941M free). Its
work survived: e2e/remote-coordinator-reclaim.spec.ts, uncommitted, 20037 bytes.
It had also modified e2e/run-in-container.sh to pass a PW_MIN_FREE_GB nothing
reads -- an out-of-scope reaction to the disk, reverted by the coordinator.

WHAT IT FOUND BEFORE IT DIED, and it is worth more than the spec: the spec
reached the product and hung on command submission. The cause is nocx-k6p18.24 --
AttachedSession.Write puts the session frame on the wire with no outer envelope,
so a helper-hosted tab renders output and accepts no input. An adversarial second
reading of the branch found the same defect independently, from the other end.
That is the acceptance test doing its job before it was even green.

Now blocked on nocx-k6p18.24 and nocx-k6p18.25. Resume the spec after both land.

2026-09-02: the spec is written, committed (009308f1 on omp/k6p18-9-e2e-c) and
RED, and what it is red about is the deliverable. It reaches the coordinator
replacement with everything before it passing: helper installed through the
git-panel consent path, session helper-hosted with a hostSessionId, a .cmd-block
in the pane, the detach observed server-side, and the build overrunning the
helper's 4 MiB window while nothing records. Then sessions.live answers [] on
the fresh coordinator for 120 s while the build is provably still advancing its
marker file on the host. Filed nocx-k6p18.30 (P0, no coordinator path re-adopts
a live helper-hosted session across a restart) and nocx-xhm9e (P1, the palette
stores an ssh pane's endpoint on port 22 whatever the profile says, so the
fallback dial has no key). Both now block this bead.

Three defects in the inherited draft were fixed, not papered over: the filler
was released while the OLD coordinator was still running, so no hostWindow hole
could exist; the exit chip was asserted on a block, but a clean shell exit
closes its own tab, so the status is read from the notification centre instead;
and the gap assertion counted holes rather than naming the reason, which is now
asserted as hostWindow both in session.output and in the recovery card.

Falsification: removing the lifecycle socketpair from spawn_local.go turns the
run red in 22 s, at promptReady rather than at the block assertion (no lifecycle
channel means no command editor, so it dies one step earlier). The ExitOutcome
and gap-reason mutations sit behind the reclaim and CANNOT be reached until
nocx-k6p18.30 is fixed — they are unverified, not verified.
close_reason:
Closed 2026-09-02. The epic's happy path is watched end to end, and it passes.
Spec e2e/remote-coordinator-reclaim.spec.ts, commits c5d7bf77 and eada72cf,
merged as 91c3c116.

FOUR GREEN RUNS, spec unmodified, no .only and no skips. Every run:
windowBytes=4194304 detachedBytes=4259937 markersAtDetach=1
markersBeforeReturn=6, gaps=[{1797..98304 hostWindow},{131072..4046848 cap}].
The detached window overran the host's own 4 MiB bound by 65 kB, five markers
advanced with no coordinator alive at all, and the build kept advancing through
the reclaim.

All three conditions the bead demanded hold. The client goes away ENTIRELY --
the browser context is closed AND the backend restarted, so this is a fresh
coordinator and not a reconnect. The command out-produces the helper's window
while detached, so the gap path is genuinely exercised. And liveness is proved by
counting per-second markers the REMOTE PROCESS wrote to its own file across the
detached window, not by a pane having rendered: a rendered pane cannot make a
remote process advance a file.

WHAT THIS CHECK FOUND, none of it by reading code:

  nocx-k6p18.24 (P0) AttachedSession.Write put the session frame on the wire
                     with no outer envelope, so a helper-hosted tab rendered
                     output and accepted no input.
  nocx-k6p18.30 (P0) NOTHING in the coordinator re-adopted a live helper-hosted
                     session across a restart. The epic's central promise had
                     never been built; .5, .15 and 1u0am are all about judgement
                     and none claims to re-adopt anything.
  nocx-k6p18.31 (P0) the lifecycle capability is minted by the dead process's
                     kernel, so a re-adopted pane went markerless: every restored
                     block built, in the DOM, and display:none, with no editor.

That is the case for rule 2 in one bead. `deadcode` could not have reported any
of the three, and on this codebase it cannot even report a dead METHOD behind a
live interface (AD-8), which is most of it.

FALSIFIED IN ALL FOUR DIRECTIONS, against the committed spec:

  lifecycle socketpair not built -> red at harness.ts:39, promptReady, the pane
    never shows a command editor. One step earlier than aimed; recorded as it
    lands rather than engineered around.
  ExitOutcome's ExitCode branch deleted -> red at spec.ts:763, the tab never
    closes, because a loss-classified status does not close it.
  host-window hole recorded as `unrecorded` -> red at spec.ts:724 on the
    reason's own clause.
  LifecycleOffset moved from the window's head to its BASE -> red at spec.ts:691,
    twice on independent runs. The mechanism is worth more than the FAIL line:
    the DOM snapshot shows the pane back in inner-fullscreen-mode over
    live-unstructured, byte-for-byte the pre-.31 collapse. Replaying the
    authenticated stretch does not merely re-deliver commands that already ran --
    it stops the adopted domain reaching prompt_ready at all. The security defect
    and a total functional collapse are the same event, and that also retroactively
    justifies toBeVisible over toBeAttached on that line: the weaker form passes
    in BOTH broken states it exists to catch.

ONE ASSERTION WAS CHANGED and it was right. `not.toContainText('size limit')` was
UNSATISFIABLE BY A CORRECT PRODUCT: this scenario honestly produces two holes with
two owners -- hostWindow for the ~96 kB the host's window took while nothing
existed to receive them, and cap for the ~3.9 MB the fresh coordinator's own
retention then evicted -- and the recovery card emits one clause per owner. The
negative would have failed the product for telling the truth. Replaced with the
strictly stronger positive: the reason must appear as its OWN clause, which is
exactly what the third mutation destroys.

NOT VERIFIED: chromium only, in the Linux container at 4 CPUs -- not WebKit and
not macOS. Mutation 1 was measured before the .31 merge; the other three after,
on the committed spec.

title: Blocks on a helper host with no rc-file script, and AD-5 is amended in the document rather than routed around
description:
The half of the epic title that is not about survival: "the helper is the INTEGRATION,
not a script". Because the helper spawns the shell and owns its PTY, integration needs
no rc-file editing and no SFTP delivery.

THREE LEVELS, NOT TWO, and the owner's decision is that the script level STAYS:
  Level 0  the script substrate (AD-5 Tier A). OSC 7/133 through shell hooks, zero
           remote install, no consent, works on any host you can reach. It is the
           answer wherever nothing may be installed.
  Level 1  the helper. Installed BY CONSENT. THIS EPIC.
  Level 2  the server on the host (nocx-6ojko, nocx-afgkj).

So this bead REPLACES script-based integration for hosts that opt in; it does not
retire it. Both paths must be exercised.

AMENDS AD-5, NARROWLY. architecture.md:139 says Tier B augments and never replaces the
remote shell. A helper that spawns the shell DOES replace the substrate for that host.
What AD-5's stated purpose protects — "Prevents: coupling MVP features to a
remote-install requirement" — is preserved intact, because Tier A remains the substrate
everywhere the helper is not installed. The amendment lands in docs/architecture.md; it
is NOT routed around. Change the AD deliberately, the way an AD gets changed.

OUT OF SCOPE, deliberately: the git panel (nocx-457v) and the file tree and listening
ports (nocx-m7k90) are their own epics and build ON this seam. This bead delivers the
seam and blocks; it does not build those panels.

Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-31-level-1-the-helper-owns-the-host-design.md (sections 2, 3; D3).
acceptance_criteria: On a host where the helper is installed, blocks, cwd and exit status work with NO rc-file edit and NO SFTP script delivery — asserted by removing the script path from the host entirely and watching a block open, bind and close. On a host where the helper is NOT installed, the script substrate still works exactly as it does today, unchanged. docs/architecture.md's AD-5 carries the amendment: Tier A remains the substrate everywhere the helper is not installed, and a helper that spawns the shell does replace it for that host.
close_reason:
The helper is the INTEGRATION, not a script. On a host where the helper is installed, blocks, cwd and exit status work with nothing written to the host at all: the integration bundle reaches the shell over an inherited descriptor — no rc-file edit, no SFTP delivery.

THE TEST IS THE POINT, and it is why the acceptance was worded as it was. It REMOVES $HOME/.nocx/integration and asserts the directory is absent both BEFORE and AFTER the spawn, then watches OSC 133 A/B and OSC 7 arrive, a `false` run produce C then D;1, and a `cd /tmp` update the reported cwd. A test where the script merely goes unused passes on a build that still depends on it; absence is what makes the claim falsifiable. Red before the fix: "timed out waiting for the helper's initial prompt: helper emitted no required marker bytes".

LEVEL 0 STAYS, and that is the owner's decision rather than an omission. On a host without the helper the substrate is unchanged: bash gets a transient --rcfile, zsh a transient ZDOTDIR, conventional shells bypass the in-memory path, and no existing shell script was touched. This bead REPLACES script-based integration for hosts that opt in; it does not retire it.

AD-5 IS AMENDED in docs/architecture.md rather than routed around. "Tier B augments, never replaces" was true of every host without a helper and false of one with it. Both halves are now stated: Tier A remains the substrate wherever the helper is not installed, and Tier B replaces delivery on a helper-installed host. AD-5's stated purpose — preventing MVP features from coupling to a remote-install requirement — survives intact, because that is exactly what Tier A remaining the substrate protects.

TWO ROUNDS, AND THE SECOND IS THE ONE WORTH RECORDING.

The worker flagged its own unverified ground: "aggregate verification remains explicitly unverified", with the race suite timing out and TestTheBinaryPlaneIsNotRewrappedInJSONRPCOnTheSocket stuck in endpoint teardown, after an earlier run died on `no space left on device`. The disk was a red herring — 63 GB free. The hang was real and it was in the change: internal/helper/endpoint took 3.6s before the commit and panicked at 60s after it. Measured by the coordinator on a tree without the merge, so it was not the machine.

The cause was a FOURTH one, and none of the three the coordinator's brief proposed. LocalSpawner treated every zero-argument executable as a shell. The AD-1 test deliberately launches `cat`; it was handed shell-only -i and ENV=/dev/fd/3, exited immediately and emitted nothing. The worker said so explicitly and named what that ruled out — bracketed-paste/readline mangling, fd inheritance, startup-output ordering — rather than quietly picking one. In-memory integration is now restricted to a classified bash or zsh, explicit-argv bypass unchanged.

AND THE SECOND DEFECT WAS THE TEST'S OWN SHAPE. await's only deadline was the test context's, which does not fire before the package timeout, so a violation arrived as a 60-second panic naming the whole package instead of an assertion naming the property — a timeout wearing a test's name, which is what cost the diagnosis. Awaits now carry a ten-second deadline. The byte-for-byte marker assertion is untouched: weakening it would remove the only check that AD-1 holds.

VERIFIED BY THE COORDINATOR, by mutation on the merged tree: restoring `if true` in place of the bash/zsh classification produced

  --- FAIL: TestTheBinaryPlaneIsNotRewrappedInJSONRPCOnTheSocket (10.01s)
      serve_test.go:403: timed out: the marker did not come back off the process

Ten seconds and a sentence, where the same defect previously gave sixty seconds and a stack. Tree byte-identical after the revert. endpoint 5.8s on the merged tree; go test -race ok on all seven helper packages and all three transport packages.

title: Three verbs: detach, close-session and uninstall, and closing a tab is the first of them
description:
D9. The three verbs, and level 2 may not reinterpret one of them.

  detach         drop this attachment. The process SURVIVES; it is in the inventory
                 and reattachable.
  close-session  deliberately end the helper-hosted session.
  uninstall      revoke machine consent and, after naming every live process and
                 asking, end everything.

Level 2's `close-tab` is NOT a fourth helper verb: it mutates a durable container on
the host, and whether it ALSO requests close-session is a separate explicit choice
made there. Helper uninstall must never silently define deletion of a level-2
content.db.

In level 1, closing a tab is `detach` plus losing the local tab. The process is not
lost — it is in the inventory. And "losing the tab" is weaker than it sounds:
DeleteTab (internal/content/layout.go:397) already marks the tab and its panes closed
and KEEPS EVERY ROW, precisely so an ordinary Cmd-W does not destroy block history.

KEEPS ADR-0034 and this is the part that breaks if it is forgotten: consent stays
keyed by machine identity, not by helper connection or daemon instance. A durable
session outlives the SSH channel, so "the channel is closed" stops meaning "no helper
is running" — consent inventory, stop and uninstall need a daemon-aware liveness
protocol, or the reversibility the helper design promises becomes FALSE.

Uninstall is whole or not at all (the execution-host draft's D14, unchanged).

Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-31-level-1-the-helper-owns-the-host-design.md (D9).
acceptance_criteria: detach drops the attachment; the process survives, stays in the inventory and is reattachable — asserted by reattaching to it. close-session deliberately ends the helper-hosted session. uninstall revokes machine consent and, AFTER naming every live process and asking, ends everything; it is whole or not at all, with no partial removal, and it never deletes a level-2 content.db. Closing a tab in level 1 is detach plus losing the local tab: the process is asserted still present in the inventory afterwards, and the tab's blocks are still in recall because DeleteTab keeps every row. Consent inventory, stop and uninstall work while the SSH channel is closed — 'the channel is closed' no longer means 'no helper is running' (ADR-0034: consent stays keyed by machine identity).
notes: CARRIED FROM nocx-k6p18.3, and the first is a live consequence rather than a nicety: AN EXITED SESSION IS NEVER REAPED FROM THE INVENTORY. It must stay to deliver its exit status, and nothing may remove it until close-session exists — which is this bead. So until you land, the inventory grows monotonically for the life of the helper. That is the shape of your work: close-session is what closes the interval nocx-k6p18.3 opened, and its invariant is stated there as 'in the inventory from the moment its PTY exists until close-session ends it'. Also owed here: signal. The helper already owns exit status and signals; the verbs are what a person reaches them through.
close_reason:
The three verbs, and closing a tab is the first of them.

detach drops this attachment and the process survives in the inventory, reattachable. close-session deliberately ends a helper-hosted session. uninstall names every live process, asks, then revokes machine consent and ends everything, whole or not at all, and never defines deletion of a level-2 content.db.

Closing a level-1 tab is now detach rather than close-session — the distinction the bead's title carries. Getting it wrong in the other direction would have made an ordinary Cmd-W kill a remote build. DeleteTab already keeps every row, so the tab's blocks stay in recall.

close-session also closes an interval nocx-k6p18.3 opened and could not close on its own: an exited session may never be reaped from the inventory, because it stays to deliver its exit status. Until this landed the inventory grew monotonically for the life of the helper.

ADR-0034 is handled rather than assumed: a durable session outlives the SSH channel, so "the channel is closed" no longer means "no helper is running", and inventory and uninstall redial the daemon after carrier loss. TestSessionInventorySurvivesCarrierLossUsesFreshDaemonHandshake.

THREE ROUNDS, AND WHAT EACH ONE COST IS THE RECORD WORTH KEEPING.

Round one delivered close-session, signal and uninstall, and its ENTIRE pre-fix evidence was compilation errors — `c.CloseSession undefined`, `RemoveMachine undefined`, `expected declaration, found FAIL`. A test that does not compile proves the symbol did not exist, which was never in doubt. The worker said so itself, plainly: "no trustworthy semantic pre-fix result was obtained for those two tests." That honesty is why it got a second round rather than a rejection. It also committed with --no-verify (frontend ESLint killed by memory pressure) and closed the bead itself.

Round two delivered the two acceptance clauses that had no evidence — tab-close as detach, and the closed-channel case — with behavioural reds this time (`ws_test.go:483: detach removed the session receiver`). But it did not answer the five mutations round one had been asked for.

SO THE COORDINATOR RAN THOSE FIVE, on the merged tree:

  close-session ends the PTY but leaves the inventory row   RED  TestCloseSessionEndsTheProcessAndRemovesItsInventoryRow
                                                                 + TestSessionLifecycleVerbsCrossTheHelperSocket
  close-session removes the row but never calls hs.stop()   RED  same test — it asserts BOTH halves
  signal to pgid 0 instead of hs.launch.Pgid                RED  TestSignalSendsTheRequestedSignalToTheOwnedProcessGroup
  uninstall proceeds when enumeration fails                 GREEN — NO GATE
  uninstall's compensating consent restore skipped          RED  TestFootprintHelperUninstall_ObservationFailureRestoresConsent

Tree byte-identical after each revert. Four of five gated.

Round three closed the fifth, and it was the one that mattered: the code CLAIMED the property four lines above the branch — "a daemon that cannot enumerate sessions refuses the operation rather than allowing uninstall to delete a live session's executable" — and nothing checked it. closeSessions reaches a remote daemon over a network; its failure path had no test. That is the rule AGENTS.md calls the highest-yield check we have. TestHelperCloseHelpersForRefusesWhenSessionsCannotBeEnumerated now fails with "uninstall continued after the daemon could not list its sessions, so a live session's executable was about to be deleted".

ONE ADJACENT CLAIM CHECKED AND NOT A DEFECT. The worker reported that CloseHelpersFor with an unknown non-empty fingerprint leaves r.closing[fp] set, because there are no victims and it never calls FinishHelpersFor. True about the function, and not a live defect: its only production caller is ws_shell_footprint.go:412, which holds `defer h.closer.FinishHelpersFor(params.Fingerprint)`. Worth writing down anyway, because the gate is SET in one file and RELEASED in another — an interval whose closing event lives outside the function that opens it is one refactor away from being a real leak.

title: The exit code still lands: a fresh lifecycle domain on reattach, and the outcome comes back from the bytes
description:
REWRITTEN 2026-08-31 after the original premise was found wrong. The wrong version is
recorded below so it is not re-derived.

WHAT THIS BEAD SAID, AND WHY IT WAS WRONG. It specified "authenticated snapshot recovery":
the helper retains the lifecycle rendezvous, epoch material and sequence state, and a
replacing coordinator sends a refresh_request and rebuilds its kernel from the shell's
authenticated active_attempt / last_completed / next_seq.

Two independent facts kill that, and both were already written down:

1. THE HELPER HAS NO LIFECYCLE INVOLVEMENT AND MUST NOT GAIN ANY. The lifecycle transport
   is coordinator-to-shell — nocx establishes it (locally a descriptor handed over at
   spawn, remotely a loopback port from the remote sshd) and the shell's bootstrap
   connects to it. internal/helper/session/ mentions lifecycle nowhere, correctly: D3 says
   the helper never owns blocks, the ledger or product policy. So "the helper retains the
   rendezvous" was asking for something the helper never had.

2. THE PROTOCOL ALREADY DECIDES THIS CASE, THE OTHER WAY. docs/lifecycle-protocol.md:424
   describes our exact situation in its own words — "The channel dies, the pty lives" —
   and :438 says the domain stays PERMANENTLY Lost, any future integration being a fresh
   one; :460's transition table "can never revive a DomainLost". Snapshot recovery was an
   attempt to revive a Lost domain, which is forbidden by the document the design cited.

AND THE PROBLEM IT WAS SOLVING LARGELY DOES NOT EXIST. Block boundaries and exit status
travel IN THE BYTES as OSC 133, and the backend never parses them (AD-6, ADR-0001) — the
FRONTEND derives them from VT state. The helper writes bytes to its window whether or not
a coordinator is attached. So a returning coordinator replays the window, its frontend
re-parses the same OSC 133, and the block boundaries and exit codes come back on their
own. The worked example this bead was built on — a writer queues two commands and detaches,
losing command one's completion — is simply false: that completion is in the bytes.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY OWED, and it is smaller:

  - On reattach, establish a FRESH lifecycle domain with a new epoch, which is what the
    protocol prescribes. Not a resumption.
  - An entry kept open across a coordinator replacement gets its real outcome from the
    replayed bytes, and is neither left open forever nor stamped `unknown` while its
    outcome is sitting in the window.
  - Where the outcome fell OUT of the window, it is genuinely unknown, and the gap D1
    already reports is the honest answer. Do not invent a second mechanism for it.

DELIBERATELY OUT, and both were considered and rejected on the evidence above: a durable
event journal on the host, and a bounded in-memory one. Neither is needed once the bytes
are understood to carry the block facts.

The one thing this shares with the old version: the helper still owns exit STATUS of the
shell process and reports it, and that is not the same fact as an attempt's completion.
nocx-k6p18.18 is where that distinction is being made.
acceptance_criteria: A command running when the coordinator is replaced has its real exit status shown on its block after the reattach — derived frontend-side from the replayed bytes, not stamped unknown and not left open. Reattaching establishes a fresh lifecycle domain with a new epoch; nothing attempts to revive a Lost one. An outcome that fell outside the helper's window is reported through the existing gap, with no second mechanism invented for it.
notes:
Verification: frontend tsc --noEmit passed; npm test passed (305 files/5810 tests and 4 files/48 tests). Focused stale-counter regression was red before the fix with: a fresh session must not abandon its pending command because an old domain ended: expected [ Array(2) ] to deeply equal [ 'abandon-pending' ]; it passed after resetting _ended. Backend go vet passed; go build and go test -race were blocked by missing GTK4/WebKit pkg-config and /bin/bash in pre-existing app tests.
Backend verification limitation exact: go test -race -count=1 ./internal/content/... ./internal/app/... ./internal/transport/... returned ok for internal/content and internal/transport but FAIL for internal/app; failing tests TestLocalEnhancedSessionIsWatchedForReplacement, TestClosingAnEnhancedSessionEndsItsWatch, and TestAPlatformThatCannotObserveStillOpensTheSession, each reporting NewPTY: fork/exec /bin/bash: no such file or directory. go build ./... separately failed because pkg-config could not find gtk4 and webkitgtk-6.0.
close_reason: Implemented fresh-domain replay outcome association with frontend OSC 133 C/D capture, durable restored-block settlement, causal descendant lookup, and lifecycle-state separation. Commit 2df9a82b. Focused frontend tests and typecheck pass; full frontend npm test remains blocked by pre-existing API workbench timeout failures reproduced on clean HEAD.

title: Open stops judging: a live session survives a coordinator replacement, and unknown never becomes absent
description:
internal/content/sqlite.go's Open runs two sweeps founded on a premise stated in the
code: "a session is server-authoritative (AD-7), lives inside one backend process and
CANNOT OUTLIVE IT". This epic's D1 repeals that premise. Left alone, a replacing
coordinator would delete the sessions row of a RUNNING session, delete its recording,
null the session_id of every entry naming it, and close its open entry as `unknown` —
declaring finished a command that is still running.

A WRONG ARGUMENT, recorded so it is not made again: that this needs only one UPDATE —
stop forcing phase='closed' and keep both deletes, because "the pipe died". The pipe
is the ATTACHMENT. The session and its output stream survived. Deleting the recording
because a READER went away throws out exactly what the promise exists to keep: a
coordinator that recorded thirty minutes of a build, updated, and returned after the
helper's window had rolled would have destroyed those thirty minutes, and "start a
fresh recording" avoids the discontinuity error only by discarding them.

THREE VERDICTS:
  live    the exact generation reports this host session -> keep everything: row,
          recording, provenance, and the OPEN ENTRY STAYS OPEN
  absent  the exact reachable generation was asked and says it does not exist ->
          exactly what Open used to do, for that session alone, in ONE transaction
  unknown nobody could be asked -> change nothing; reconcile on a later attempt

`unknown` MAY NEVER COLLAPSE INTO `absent`. absent requires an ANSWER, never an error.
Liveness is a fact obtained, not an inference from a failure.

ORDERING, and codex retracted its own first answer here: Open CANNOT ASK, because
asking needs a carrier, the carrier may need the vault, and the vault needs the store.
So Open opens and judges nothing; carriers come up; inventory runs; each session is
reconciled. A pending set in memory is sufficient — a durable stamp is optional and
buys only the ability to display cause and age.

ONE BOUND IS OWED HERE and it is not optional: dropDeadSessions was the ONLY bound on
session recordings, which are deliberately outside the budget sweep because their unit
is not artifacts.byte_len. The absent path restores it for the ordinary case; the
unknown case needs a retention age, or a host that never comes back accumulates
recordings forever. Removing the bound without replacing it is not an acceptable
intermediate state.

pane_id is UNTOUCHED IN EVERY BRANCH. It is the anchor; a block whose session is gone
is still a command that ran, in the pane it ran in.

Needs a real inventory to ask (the helper's session service), or every verdict is
`unknown` and nothing is proved.

Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-31-content-store-restart-reconciliation-design.md (whole);
.internal/specs/2026-08-31-level-1-the-helper-owns-the-host-design.md (D5).
acceptance_criteria: With a session running on a reachable generation, a fresh coordinator's Open deletes no sessions row, deletes no recording, nulls no session_id and closes no entry — asserted against the real Open, which deletes all four today. Its open entry stays open. An absent session is reconciled exactly as Open used to sweep it, for that session alone, in ONE transaction: a reader never sees the entry closed while the execution is not, or the reverse. pane_id survives every branch. A refused connection, a timeout, a sealed vault and an unreachable host EACH leave the session unreconciled — asserted per failure mode, not once — and none produces absent. Reconciliation is idempotent and resumable: killed at each step in turn, the next pass completes it and no row is half-judged. One connection throughout (ADR-0043). An unreconciled recording past its retention age is removed, and doing so deletes neither its entry nor its anchor. The product shows a third state: an unreconciled entry renders as neither running nor finished, with its cause.
close_reason:
Committed as c93c2b17, merged as fe7adc24. 36 files, +2306/-198.

THE INVARIANT IS STRUCTURAL, NOT TESTED, which is better than the bead asked for: causeFor's return type is UnreconciledCause, so NO BRANCH CAN RETURN A VERDICT AT ALL. 'A failure never produces absent' is enforced by the type system rather than by remembering to assert it.

Open stops judging: dropDeadSessions DELETED; closeOpenEntries became closeUnanchoredEntries, narrowed to entries that never reached closed AND NAME NO SESSION — a pipe whose provenance had already ended, which nothing could ever report live. An entry that names a session is not judged at Open at all. The carried-over set is read once at Open from sessions union session_output and held in memory, exact without needing a durable stamp.

PER-FAILURE-MODE EVIDENCE, eight cases run separately rather than one loop: ECONNREFUSED, a refusal reported only as prose, a net.Error timeout, context.DeadlineExceeded, ErrVaultSealed, ErrNoUnlockClient, an unreachable host, and an unclassifiable error. Each asserts verdict != absent, verdict == unknown, the exact cause, and a carried detail. TWO PAIRED POSITIVES stop the negative from being satisfiable by 'always unknown': an inventory that answers yields BOTH live and absent, and an inventory never judges an id space it does not own.

THE REPLACEMENT BOUND EXISTS AND BINDS, which the bead said was not optional: SweepStale(age) takes a recording and its sessions row from a session still unreconciled after the age, WITHOUT judging it absent — the entry and its pane_id stay, and the next Open closes the now session-less entry. Default 7 days. Tested at both ends: nothing taken at 1h, taken at age 0, and a recording outlives the coordinator until a host says otherwise.

ONE DECISION BEYOND THE SPEC, and it is right: an ASK closes at Open whatever its session, because the assistant that answers it lives in THIS process. SubmitAgentAsk is the one production writer of entries.session_id, so without that clause a restart left every unfinished question open forever. Same for executions carrying a state — that is this process's work.

THE THIRD STATE REACHES A PERSON through the whole chain: ledger.query carries the cause per row, restore-client maps it to an 'unreconciled' block status that outranks the status column, blocks.ts paints NO OUTCOME CHIP IN EITHER DIRECTION, and the pane mounts a kit StatusCard saying the commands are neither running nor finished and why. Sentences keyed on the closed enum in one module. 16 vitest cases including one per cause and a stylesheet gate proving the surface repaints nothing.

HONEST LIMIT, and it is in app.go's own comment: reconcileSessions runs today with NO inventories, so every verdict is unknown/noInventory and the age bound is what does the work. Nothing yet records which generation a stored session belongs to, so no inventory owns any stored id space — and asking the nearest helper anyway would take a truthful 'I do not hold that' about somebody else's id and turn it into a DELETION. That is exactly why Owns exists, and it is the right call.

Re-verified on the merged tree after resolving a merge-only conflict with the api-run fold: build rc=0, content ok, transport ok 94.3s, contracts:check clean.

title: One shape locally and remotely: a private Unix socket, and 'nocx-helper bridge' carries it over ssh
description:
D11, which is the requirement the owner set at the start of the turn: the helper runs
on every machine, INCLUDING YOURS. Locally the coordinator connects to its endpoint
directly; remotely through the bridge. There is no second mechanism, no "local special
case", and no code path that exists only for one of them.

Section 5, the carrier. SSH is a TRANSPORT for reaching the helper, not the terminal
protocol — the same relationship internal/apisend/ssh_dialer.go already has with HTTP.
AD-1 is therefore untouched: the binary plane is not re-wrapped in JSON-RPC, it is the
same plane on a different socket.

The authoritative endpoint is a private Unix socket in a 0700 directory, mode 0600.
NOT a loopback TCP port: a port on 127.0.0.1 is reachable by any user of that machine,
and the whole authorization model is the Unix account (D12), so a loopback listener
would annul it. This is the boundary.

Remotely, NOTHING IS FORWARDED. `nocx-helper bridge <generation>` is stateless and
disposable. direct-streamlocal@openssh.com is an optional carrier improvement and
never the boundary — this corrects a claim made during the design turn that it was a
security prerequisite.

The ssh carrier needs no authentication of its own, because reaching that socket
already required becoming the account. A non-ssh carrier must supply one; that is the
carrier's problem, not the protocol's.

Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-31-level-1-the-helper-owns-the-host-design.md (D11, section 5);
generation and bridge mechanics: .internal/specs/2026-08-31-the-generation-daemon-lifecycle-design.md (D6).
acceptance_criteria: The coordinator reaches the helper through the same endpoint locally and remotely — one code path, with no branch that exists only for the local case. The endpoint is a Unix socket mode 0600 in a 0700 directory; there is no loopback TCP listener anywhere in the path. 'nocx-helper bridge <generation>' runs over the pty-less exec lane, connects to the endpoint on the far side and copies bytes, holding no session, no window and no lock. The ordinary nocx WebSocket rides inside unchanged: the binary plane is asserted NOT to be re-wrapped in JSON-RPC. No port forwarding is configured and none is required.
close_reason:
Committed as e49c8e48, merged as 6617230c.

THE BOUNDARY, and there is one of it: internal/helper/endpoint holds Listen/Dial/Serve/Bridge/Ensure/Path/Dir — a socket mode 0600 in a 0700 directory under the account's home, named <proto.Version>-<generation[:16]>.sock, with the same-UID check per D12. THE STDIO-SERVING MODE IS GONE, so there is no second mechanism left to pick — which is stronger than the bead asked for, since it removes the local special case rather than merely not adding one.

NO LOCAL SPECIAL CASE, proved through the shipped code: TestOneShapeLocallyAndRemotely BUILDS the real cmd/nocx-helper, starts one serve, then drives the shipped client.Dial TWICE — once over a socket, once over a pipe-pair exec lane running the real 'nocx-helper bridge <gen>' — and finds the session one opened THROUGH THE OTHER, same durable handle, neither displacing the other. And one level down, connectOver(t, io.ReadWriteCloser) is the shape of every test in the file: not one of them says which carrier it got.

NO TCP LISTENER, proved by walking the AST of every non-test file in endpoint, host, session, client, proto and cmd/nocx-helper. Two rules: any net.Listen* must name "unix" literally, and no file may contain a tcp/udp/ip* network literal at all, which catches a ListenConfig held in a variable. VERIFIED FALSIFIABLE — a planted net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0") fired both rules.

AD-1 PROVED RATHER THAN ASSERTED: a run containing a double quote, a backslash, ESC and the bytes 0xfe 0xff is sent through cat under the PTY and found BYTE-FOR-BYTE in the raw wire capture. JSON would have escaped the first three and cannot carry the last two at all.

THE REAL VALUE WAS THREE DEFECTS THE SECOND CONNECTION EXPOSED, invisible while stdin/stdout made one connection the only possibility, and one of them presented as a HANG rather than a failure. (1) A subscriber's pump wrote to whichever connection bound LAST — a reader attached by coordinator A had its bytes delivered down B's socket; the connection is now a property of the request, stamped by host.WithConnection and read out of the context. (2) A release that no longer held the sink slot did NOTHING, so a coordinator dying after its replacement connected kept the write capability forever and no later coordinator could take it; sinks is a set now, and releasing drops only that connection's subscribers and clears the writer only if the holder attached there. (3) Exit notifications went to one connection; an exit is a fact about a SESSION, not an attachment, so now to every bound one. Plus: Serve must close live connections on shutdown, because a handler blocked in a socket read cannot be reached by a context. Each has its own test.

FAILURE PATHS, enumerated rather than sampled: a loose directory is REPAIRED to 0700 by helper and coordinator alike, since a directory loosened under a live endpoint is as reachable as one always loose; a foreign-owned directory is REFUSED and never repaired. A stale socket is probed by dialling, unlinked and rebound; dialling one is ErrNoEndpoint, never a verdict. A live socket is ErrAlreadyServing and never stolen, and the loser of the bind race gets the same answer confirmed by DIALLING rather than read off an errno. A bridge with no far-side endpoint exits 43 leaving no socket, which the client maps to its own sentence. A helper that dies before serving ends the wait on the CHILD'S EXIT, not a duration. An ssh channel dying mid-copy leaves session, window and process alive and a new bridge reattaches to a still-growing window. Two coordinators at once are BOTH SERVED — asserted, not refused, per D12.

The accept loop really was two lines, as nocx-k6p18.3 predicted. Everything above is what the second connection exposed.

All internal/helper packages ok including the new endpoint; -race clean; golangci-lint clean; deadcode 82 all baselined 0 NEW; cross-compiles for linux/arm64, darwin/arm64 and darwin/amd64 with CGO_ENABLED=0. Merged with one merge-only fix — see 6617230c — where this branch's serve_test.go called session.NewProcFS, a constructor nocx-k6p18.10 had deleted in parallel.

title: The helper spawns the shell and owns its PTY, and serves the inventory of what it holds
description:
The core of level 1. The session service the remote-helper design reserved and
deliberately did not build (its D15) — internal/helper/host/host.go:85 still panics
on the name.

D3 — what the helper OWNS: the PTY and process group, the OS-specific operations,
the bounded output window, the session inventory, exit status, signals, and the
enforcement of one writer.

D3 — what it must NEVER own: blocks, the ledger, content.db, UI state, product policy,
or a human-authored name. Fat infrastructure, thin product: ~2.8 MiB against ~40 MiB,
and a survival component that must stay compatible across generations has no business
carrying SQLCipher and a vault.

ON NAMES specifically, settled against an earlier proposal and against codex's first
recommendation: the helper may report DERIVED diagnostics — cwd, argv, foreground
process, start time — because those are facts about a process and the OS is their
source. It may NOT persist a name a person typed. In level 1 a friendly alias is a
local projection owned by the local server. One owner ever.

D10 — there is no router and no registry beside the helper: it holds the PTYs, so it
is the only thing that can answer. /proc and proc_pidinfo are EVIDENCE, not authority:
argv is mutable, a process can be replaced, and the semantics differ per OS. Launch
metadata is recorded explicitly by the helper when it spawns; OS inspection is a
fallback and a cross-check, never the canonical identity.

D1's bound, stated rather than discovered: output produced while no coordinator was
attached is kept only up to the helper's WINDOW. Beyond that it is gone and the gap
is reported. This is nocx-8mllr's lossy-continue decision, and it is what makes the
promise implementable without a disk on the host.

Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-31-level-1-the-helper-owns-the-host-design.md (D1, D3, D10).
acceptance_criteria: The reserved 'session' service in internal/helper/host/host.go — which panics on the name today — is implemented and reachable from main() (prove it with deadcode -whylive on the spawn method, not deadcode -filter). The helper spawns the shell, owns its PTY and process group, and keeps a bounded output window. An inventory call returns every live host session with its hostSessionId, generation, start time, and the derived diagnostics of D3. Killing and restarting the coordinator leaves the session in the inventory and reattachable, and the process is proved to have RUN across the gap by a per-second marker counted afterwards, not by a pane having rendered.
notes:
CARRIED FROM nocx-k6p18.1 so it is not lost between beads — three things that bead deliberately left to this one:

1. THE INVENTORY AND SPAWN ENVELOPES ARE NOT YET FROZEN, and D15's opaque WorkspaceID reservation belongs in 'sessions' and 'spawn'. nocx-k6p18.1 froze the attach/ack/detach/reset half and stopped, because freezing sessions/spawn without their semantics would have been worse. The reservation is recorded in internal/helper/proto/abi.go's doc comment and contracts/helper/README.md. THIS IS THE LAST MOMENT: nothing is deployed yet, so it is still free; once a generation is published it is not.

2. THE ENCODE HALF of the session-frame codec lands here, with its producer. Only the decode half landed in .1 because only it had a caller. Literal-byte golden vectors are already committed to check the encoder against.

3. host.Register REFUSES any op whose params carry a free-form []string (D3). So 'spawn' cannot take argv in that shape — know it before designing the op, not after.

Also: proto.Version was NOT bumped in .1, on the argument that nothing is deployed and bumping would refuse every dev helper for no gain. If a generation is ever published before this bead lands, that decision needs revisiting.
close_reason:
Committed as 7173f98b on worktree-agent-a258cd80e00d6d1f0. The reservation in internal/helper/host is cashed in: the helper is now the shell's PARENT — it spawns it, owns its PTY and process group, keeps a bounded output window, serves the inventory, and enforces exactly one writer. That is what makes it the integration rather than a script: nothing goes into an rc file and nothing is delivered by SFTP, because the process is ours.

THE ABI HALF nocx-k6p18.1 LEFT OPEN IS NOW FROZEN WITH IT, and this was the last moment it could be: spawn, sessions and resize, their schemas in contracts/helper, and D15's opaque WorkspaceID in all three places it was owed. Two decisions are ENFORCED rather than documented. Launch is the AUTHORITY and OS inspection is EVIDENCE, in two fields that can never be one — argv is mutable by the process itself, a process can be replaced by exec, and macOS has no /proc at all, so merging them would report a lie with the authority of a launch record. And there is no name anywhere: additionalProperties:false is what stops a later generation becoming a second owner of one.

AD-10 IS AMENDED IN docs/architecture.md, and that was a DEBT, not scope creep: the closed decision bead nocx-8mllr is titled 'amend AD-10 either way'. AD-10 said never drop, never grow unbounded, throttle the source; a helper-hosted window is deliberately lossy, so the code would have violated the AD without it. The amendment is narrow — exactly one lossy case, only on a host the helper owns, the coordinator's own replay ring unchanged and still throttling — and it states why: on a host the coordinator can be replaced, and throttling then means a three-hour build STOPS BECAUSE NOBODY IS WATCHING. The loss is stated in the product, never only logged.

THE DECISION RULE nocx-k6p18.1 REFUSED TO WRITE landed as proto.ResumeAt, and internal/transport's outputRing.snapshot now takes its VERDICT from there rather than keeping a second derivation of one predicate; ring_resume_rule_test.go asserts the two agree across the boundary. What the ring still keeps is only WHERE a reset restarts, and that is a fact about two buffers rather than a divergence: the ring is lossless and throttles its source, so an offset below its base is a stale cursor and 'resync at now' is honest; the helper's window is capacity-reclaimed, so an offset below ITS base names bytes nobody ever held, and the honest answer is the oldest surviving byte plus an explicit gap. Both reasons are in the code.

TWO REAL DEFECTS, found by tests that HUNG rather than failed, and both the same mistake — copying a lossless-ring rule into a lossy window. The exit watcher closed the window when the PROCESS ended, racing the pump's write of bytes still in the PTY buffer, so a reader attaching after an exit could find the window closed and empty and conclude the stream was over — losing the last line the shell printed. The window has one closer now, the pump, at the fd's end. And the credit floor took the window's base, which in a capacity-reclaimed window rises as fast as a non-acking reader falls behind, so credit never bound and the reset path was unreachable by construction. Limits now REFUSES a floor at or below the credit allowance, because a window that looks configured and is not is worse than either setting.

THE RATCHET WAS FIXED, NOT BASELINED. It reported three new dead functions; WithShell became a constructor argument main passes, mustBase was deleted, and allocated became a real production observation — the resident-bytes log line when a session exits, which is the cost D8 says must be named because it is spent on someone else's machine.

-whylive CONTRAST, as AGENTS.md requires rather than deadcode -filter:
  WIRED  main -> Host.frame -> Host.request -> Service.Call -> Service.spawn
  WIRED  ...same chain... -> Service.spawn -> hostSession.pump
  DEAD   vault.newRecoveryCode                -> 'is dead code'
  DEAD   Service.WindowBytesInUse             -> 'reachable only through reflection'

INVARIANTS AS INTERVALS: a session is in the inventory FROM the moment its PTY exists UNTIL close-session ends it — the coordinator dying, the connection being replaced and the PROCESS ITSELF EXITING are all inside it. From Bind until its release, frames go to that sink and nowhere else. base <= written from construction until close.

FAILURE PATHS: fork succeeded / PTY did not (no entry, no window, no budget consumed, next spawn works); budget refused before the fork, asserted on the process count; id minting failed after a live PTY (closed, not leaked); session in inventory but process gone (entry survives with exit status, a reader still drains the last bytes); wire dies mid-stream (attachment dropped, session and process survive); stale lease epoch and non-holder writes rejected; ack ahead and behind refused; an inspector that cannot answer reports null.

ACCEPTANCE proved end to end over the real frame protocol with a real shell under a real PTY: a coordinator spawns a per-second marker loop, is killed, and its replacement finds the session in the inventory under the same durable handle, reattaches at the offset the dead one stopped at, and COUNTS the markers in the range that existed before it attached — consecutive, and starting where the first coordinator left off.

go test ./internal/helper/... ./internal/pty/... ok; -race ok; -count=3 -race on session ok; ./internal/transport/ ok 95.4s (full suite, since ring.go changed); the other host.Register callers in internal/git ok; deadcode ratchet 82 unreachable, all baselined, 0 NEW.

title: Skip: a recording resumes across a hole nobody recorded, and the hole is not called a cap
description:
Self-contained in internal/content; nothing in this epic blocks it.

Append refuses any discontinuity today (session_output_sqlite.go:141), and
session_output.go:70 calls a gap "a caller defect and not a fact about the stream".
That is right while a recorder cannot be absent. D1 of this epic makes a recorder
absent, so it stops being right.

The clause that matters most is the last one: the recording must be APPENDABLE after
a skip. ws_session_record.go:106 stops recording permanently once it loses its place,
so without it one missed second costs the whole session.

The reason is a SECOND VALUE, not `cap`. Telling a user the cap dropped bytes nobody
ever had is a false statement in the product, and Truncation already carries a reason
precisely so it can be exact.

session_output.go's sentence is amended rather than contradicted: a gap is a caller
defect WHEN THE CALLER HAD THE BYTES, and a fact about the stream when nobody did.

Produced already measures the hole — "including what was dropped ... what makes a hole
measurable rather than invisible" — so nothing parallel is invented.

Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-31-level-1-the-helper-owns-the-host-design.md (D6);
also .internal/specs/2026-08-31-content-store-restart-reconciliation-design.md (D5).
acceptance_criteria: SessionOutputRepository.Skip(sessionID, resumeAt, reason) advances the produced cursor across a range that was never offered, records the gap in the same Gap shape the cap uses, and SUBSEQUENT APPENDS SUCCEED. The gap's reason distinguishes never-ingested from cap-evicted, and the product's wording differs between them. Produced has advanced past the range. A recording that loses its place no longer stops recording permanently.
notes: FOUND WHILE DOING nocx-fz4qa, 2026-08-31, and it is half of this bead's job already sitting in the code: internal/transport/ws_session_record.go:464 sessionOutputGapReason returns `cap` for ANY hole with no recorded reason, and its comment says so deliberately. So the backend's fallback GUESSES the retention bound for every unexplained hole, while the renderer already carries unknown reasons through verbatim. The moment Skip introduces a second legitimate reason, that fallback starts confidently naming the cap for bytes the cap never touched — which is the exact false statement this bead's acceptance forbids. Fix the fallback here, in the same change; it is not a separate bead.
close_reason:
Committed as c7323074 on worktree-agent-accf0b4a4a1ce4638, merged as 7a3eda56. TDD: both test files were red on 'Skip undefined' before any implementation.

APPENDABLE-AFTER-A-SKIP is proved twice, at two seams. Against the real SQLite store: append 4096, Skip to 9000, then four appends at 9000+ all succeed, and Read comes back Produced==11048 with two runs and one gap [4096,9000) reasoned unrecorded. And against the SHIPPED recordSessionOutput loop over a ring whose base is already past the cursor: exactly one skip to the ring's oldest byte, and the bytes after the hole are recorded at the post-hole offset — the branch that used to return and stop recording forever.

THE TWO REASONS: cap (ingested, then evicted — the knob that dropped them would have kept them) and unrecorded (nobody was there; the cap never touched them). The renderer had already coined 'unrecorded' for the same fact it derives on its side, and the word was kept EQUAL on purpose rather than minting a second one — one fact arrived at from two directions is not two owners, and both files now say so.

sessionOutputGapReason no longer guesses. It answered 'cap' for any hole with no recorded reason; it now answers 'unknown'. Checked at merge rather than assumed: recovery-notice.tsx, which landed from another branch the same day and knew nothing about this one, already carries an unrecognised reason verbatim into 'X missing as "..."' — so the new value reaches a person as itself instead of being swallowed, and the acceptance clause about the product's wording differing holds across all three.

The contract description for session.output's gaps now names both reasons and forbids assuming the cap; the generated frontend type was regenerated, not hand-edited.

go test ./internal/content/... ok; ./internal/transport/ ok 117.3s; ipc suite 88 passed; contracts:check OK; deadcode -whylive traces main -> handleOpen -> pumpToRing -> recordSessionOutput -> sqliteContent.Skip.

STATED LIMIT, and it is the epic's structure rather than a shortfall: Skip's only production caller today is the defensive needsReset branch. The coordinator-replacement path D6 is actually about belongs to nocx-k6p18.5 and .6, and until nocx-k6p18.5 lands, sqlite.go's startup DELETE FROM session_output means no recording survives a restart at all — so Skip's cross-restart value is real but not yet reachable. 'Skip is wired' must not be read as 'the epic's hole is handled'.

title: The helper ABI is frozen: two identities, subscriber-addressed reads, and exactly one write capability
description:
FIRST, and the reason is that this cannot be changed afterwards. A generation is
content-addressed and immutable, two coexist at once, and one lingers for as long as
it holds a session — months. A generation whose ABI assumes a single unnamed client
can never later serve two observers correctly, and an opaque identifier can never
later become authorization.

D2 — the three identities, and the correction that produced them. Before it, "the
session" meant the coordinator-owned PTY channel, so its death was the session's
death. That is now false, and conflating the two is exactly what makes a replacing
coordinator delete live work.

  hostSessionId   the PTY and its process group, minted by the helper, qualified by
                  the generation that minted it. SURVIVES coordinator replacement.
  attachmentId    one coordinator<->helper connection and its lease. Disposable, and
                  it appears NOWHERE in the ledger.
  streamOffset    the monotonic output coordinate of a hostSessionId. Survives
                  attachments; a new reader does not restart it.

A new attachment is a new READER of the same stream, never a new stream.

D8 — what must be frozen now even though level 2's product rules about who may type
are not decided here: subscriber identity on attach/data/write, independent 64-bit
read cursors per subscriber, `fresh` as an explicit flag, gap and reset semantics,
and one write capability carrying a lease epoch.

D12 — same-UID trust, decided by the owner and frozen: any nocx running under that
Unix account may connect. No session capability is reserved. If independent same-UID
servers must ever be isolated, the capability is owed NOW, not later.

D2 also: the helper's identity is not the pane's. The ledger holds a BINDING from
pane to hostSessionId; one host session may be projected into several panes, which is
what level 2 needs and what level 1 must not foreclose.

REUSE, do not mint: AD-9's ring, offsets, acks, replay and reset are implemented in
the transport today (ring.go, ws.go:64, ipc.ts:403) while internal/helper/proto only
RESERVES seq/ack. A second notion of resumability here is the delay-fused regression
AGENTS.md names.

Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-31-level-1-the-helper-owns-the-host-design.md (D2, D8, D12).
acceptance_criteria: internal/helper/proto carries hostSessionId (qualified by generation), attachmentId and streamOffset as distinct types, and no call conflates them. An attach names its subscriber and carries 'fresh' as an explicit flag, never inferred. Each subscriber has its own independent 64-bit read cursor. Exactly one write capability exists and it carries a lease epoch. Gap and reset semantics are specified and tested. Every result shape has its JSON Schema in contracts/, the renderer's types are generated from it, and an over-the-wire conformance test validates the real payload off the real socket.
close_reason:
Committed as 4ee242fb on worktree-agent-a2cdbb7a862a3cb6e. 17 files, +1699/-3.

FROZEN, and the type system enforces it rather than a comment asking nicely: HostSessionID is a STRUCT {generation, session}, so there is no way to spell a session without the generation that minted it. AttachmentID, SubscriberID, StreamOffset (uint64) and LeaseEpoch are defined types, and a test asserts each carries the package's own PkgPath/Name — converting any of them to an alias fails the suite. AckParams is keyed by subscriber+session and NEVER by attachment, which is the cursor outliving the connection made structural. AttachParams' fresh and requestWrite are required and never omitempty, so false and absent are different bytes. WriteGrant carries granted, epoch (from 1; 0 = no grant) and holder, so a refusal names who holds it.

RESUMABILITY WAS EXTENDED, NOT MINTED — verified by reading. Resume is contracts/attach.schema.json's resumed/reset/from verbatim, ack is contracts/ack.params.schema.json's {…, offset}, and the DATA FRAME CARRIES NO OFFSET, for the reason internal/transport/frame.go states for its own: the subscriber counts received payload bytes. A test asserts SessionFrame has no StreamOffset field so this cannot be quietly undone. The gap reuses content.Gap's {start,end,reason}.

AD-1 INTACT, verified: TypeSessionData carries a fixed 40-byte binary header (session[16] | subscriber[16] | leaseEpoch:uint64BE) then raw bytes — PTY bytes are not wrapped in JSON. The layout is pinned by literal-byte golden vectors rather than the encoder's own output, and contracts/helper/ deliberately has no schema for it.

THE DECISION RULE IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT and that is the right call: 'is the offset still in the window, and where does the reader restart' is outputRing.snapshot, which moves into the helper with the window itself in nocx-k6p18.3. Writing it here would have been the second owner. Gap/reset semantics are specified in the SCHEMA (oneOf plus not-required) and tested by an accept/refuse matrix — reset without gap, resume with gap, both flags, neither, reset omitted, negative offset, a gap blamed on cap, a gap with no reason: all refused.

NOTHING LANDED DEAD AND NO --no-verify. Only the DECODE half of the codec landed, because only it has a caller; both ends handle TypeSessionData and drop it logged with the connection intact, so a peer of another generation costs one dropped write rather than a decoder resyncing byte-by-byte through a live PTY stream. Proven with the tool AGENTS.md names: deadcode -whylive on DecodeSessionFrame traces main -> Host.Serve -> Host.sessionData -> DecodeSessionFrame, and the ratchet is identical to the pre-change baseline.

ONE DEVIATION FROM THE BRIEF, and it is justified in contracts/helper/README.md: the schemas are in contracts/helper/ rather than contracts/, following the contracts/files/ precedent. Mechanically, gen-openrpc.mjs turns every top-level *.params.schema.json into an OpenRPC method and the manifest test would then demand a JSON-RPC registration that must not exist. Conceptually the renderer never speaks this wire, so no renderer type is generated — the generated-type rule exists to stop a second hand-written type drifting, and here both ends are one Go package.

60 tests pass across proto/host/client, -race clean on all five helper packages, contracts:check unchanged, the OpenRPC manifest gate undisturbed, build/gofumpt/golangci-lint/prettier clean.

HONEST LIMIT, stated at the top of the over-the-wire test: it drives the real Host and real Client over a real socket and validates the payload that comes off it, but not the session service, because there is none — proto.ServiceSession is reserved and Register still panics on it. That case is owed by nocx-k6p18.3, and the schemas do not change when it lands, which is the whole claim of a frozen ABI.

title: Released old-schema fixtures migrate forward, and one is killed mid-migration
description:
The test half of nocx-lmb6v, and it is a SEPARATE bead on purpose.

AGENTS.md rule 4: do not let the author of the code be the only author of its tests,
and reserve the expensive form for code where a defect is costly. A migration that
silently drops rows is the costliest defect this repo can ship once content.db stops
being disposable — it destroys the only copy of work a user cannot reproduce. So the
tests here are written FROM THE ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA by someone who did not write the
ladder, not by reading the ladder.

The fixtures must be REAL databases written by released schema versions. A fixture
synthesised by the current code from the current schema tests the migration against
the migration's own idea of the past, which is precisely the model that is wrong when
it is wrong.

The fault injection is the point of the exercise, not a bonus: enumerate the partial
failures — the edge's writes are half done, user_version is not yet stamped, the
process dies — and assert what is true on disk and how the next start recovers.

Depends on the ladder existing.
acceptance_criteria: The suite carries real databases written by released schema versions, not fixtures synthesised from the current schema. Each is migrated forward to current and its rows are asserted present and correct afterwards. At least one run injects a failure in the middle of an edge and asserts the old database is byte-intact and the next start completes or refuses. Every 'returns an error when...' has a paired 'and on an ordinary database it succeeds'.
notes:
CARRIED FROM nocx-lmb6v.1, and the first item is a case its author could not reach:

1. NO CRASH TEST KILLS A REAL PROCESS MID-EDGE. nocx-lmb6v.1 ends the span by returned error and by rollback, which is the mechanism. A genuine SIGKILL between the stamp and the COMMIT, exercised AGAINST A HOT -wal, is reachable only from a subprocess test — and the WAL matters: a live content.db is a ~4 KB main file plus megabytes of hot -wal (measured in nocx-7qunp), so 'the old database is intact' has to mean it in the presence of one. This is in your scope.

2. THE FAULT-INJECTION SEAM IS ALREADY CLEAN AND YOU SHOULD USE IT AS IS: apply is a field on migrationStep and migrateSchema takes the ladder as a parameter, so you hand it a ladder whose step runs the real DDL and then returns an error. No build tag, no hook, no test-only export. If you find yourself adding one, something has gone wrong.

3. THE FLOOR IS DERIVED, NOT DECLARED: schemaLadder[0].from. A database below it is refused, never rebuilt. Test that boundary too.
close_reason:
Committed as ab79023f on worktree-agent-a08bd8f6dd0737689. Three new files, +1371, and ZERO modifications to any existing file — the fault-injection seam nocx-lmb6v.1 left was sufficient exactly as designed: no build tag, no hook, no test-only export.

FIXTURE PROVENANCE WAS VERIFIED, NOT TRUSTED. testdata/schema_v14.sql was diffed against the schemaV1 constant at a2fa7e3e, the last mainline commit with schemaVersion = 14: byte-identical, diff produced no output. The second side of the boundary was added — testdata/schema_v13.sql, lifted verbatim from 1ccad4de — because 13 is schemaLadder[0].from - 1, the newest database this build must refuse, and it is a genuinely different shape: its entries has NO source column and a different kind CHECK while every table NAME is familiar. That is precisely the file the old unknown-table gate could never catch, since the gate compared names. Neither fixture was produced by current code.

THE SIGKILL TEST, and it observes rather than waits. The test binary re-execs itself; the child switches to WAL with wal_autocheckpoint=0 and commits ~4.5 MB first, so at kill time the file is a 204 KB database beside a 6.2 MB hot -wal holding committed frames that must survive and uncommitted ones that must not. The injected step runs the real edge's DDL, writes the real stamp on applyStep's own transaction — the one window where the forbidden file exists — prints one line to stdout and parks in a read on a pipe the parent never writes. Two observables, no duration anywhere: the parent blocks on that stdout line so the kill cannot land early, and requires ProcessState.Signaled() so it cannot land late, since a child that exited cleanly fails the test.

EVERY NEW ASSERTION WAS MUTATED BEFORE BEING TRUSTED, each mutant turning exactly one test red at exactly the right line, then reverted with production code confirmed byte-identical: child commits before the kill -> "user_version = 15 after the kill, want 14"; foreignKeysIntact returns nil -> "a step that left a dangling foreign key committed"; the edge's INSERT...SELECT drops path rows -> "read 1 rows, want 2" — which is the silently-drops-rows defect this bead exists to catch.

FINDING, and it is why this bead was separated: foreignKeysIntact had ZERO test coverage. Foreign keys are suspended for the entire walk and that one check is the sole compensating control, yet mutating it to always return nil left the whole pre-existing suite green. Now covered, with the paired positive.

A QUALIFIER THE CRITERIA DID NOT GIVE, measured rather than argued: byte-identity after an injected mid-edge failure HOLDS on the direct migrateSchema path, which sets no journal_mode, and does NOT hold through Open, which runs WAL and checkpoints on close. Both are true at different seams. The strong form is pinned where it is true and rows-only through Open. Recorded because if someone later writes an acceptance test demanding byte identity THROUGH Open it will be unsatisfiable, and the temptation will be to "fix" the store.

The worker also caught one of its own: the floor test originally t.Skipf'd when the first rung moves off 14 — a boundary test that disables itself exactly when the boundary moves. It now fails loudly, naming the fixture to add and warning against generating one from the current schema, verified by hiding the fixture.

go test ./internal/content/... ok 19.176s; -race ok 199.920s; gofumpt and golangci-lint clean.

title: The migration ladder: one explicit ordered step per schema edge, and the rebuild path is gone
description:
The core of nocx-lmb6v. Today internal/content/sqlite.go's resetIfSchemaChanged
drops and rebuilds on any version difference, and says so in its own comment. That
is correct while content.db is local and disposable. It stops being correct the
moment a remote server owns tabs, names and blocks that are the only copy.

THE PROTOCOL, settled 2026-08-31 and not open for reinterpretation:

  onDisk == current  -> open
  onDisk <  current  -> one explicit ordered migration per edge (14->15), each in
                        one crash-safe operation, user_version updated only after
                        that edge commits
  onDisk >  current  -> REFUSE, without modifying a byte

The refusal half is nocx-7qunp and lands first — this bead takes the ladder.

Crash-safety is the part that is easy to get subtly wrong and expensive to get
wrong: the invariant has two ends. Not "the step writes user_version" (a moment)
but "from before the step's first write until user_version names the new edge,
either the whole edge is applied or none of it is" (a span). Name the closing
event or you do not have the invariant.

DELIBERATELY OUT: a minMigratableSchema floor — while the chain is complete there
is nothing to declare, and it is owed only if old steps are ever retired. Also out:
the server-to-server wire compatibility floor, which must NOT be encoded in
user_version because a peer never opens the remote database; that belongs to the
connection epic.

Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-31-level-2-the-server-on-the-host-design.md (D1, D2).
acceptance_criteria: A database at N-1 opened by a binary at N is migrated by an explicit ordered step and its rows are still there afterwards. user_version is stamped only after that edge commits, in the same crash-safe operation. A migration killed midway leaves the old database intact and the next start either completes it or refuses — never a half-migrated file. resetIfSchemaChanged no longer contains a path that drops tables for a version difference.
close_reason:
Committed as 85baa36b on worktree-agent-a3bfecbdaa61cacb5, cut over origin/feat/relay-pty-owner so nocx-7qunp is under it. 10 files, +1278/-652. resetIfSchemaChanged and rebuildDropOrder are DELETED; Open now walks a ladder.

THE INVARIANT, written as an interval with both ends named. OPENS when a step's first statement executes inside its transaction. CLOSES when that transaction's COMMIT returns. Across the span the file still answers user_version = step.from and holds exactly the rows of from; the COMMIT is the single event that makes it answer to with the rows of to. Anything else ending the span — failed statement, cancelled context, crash, kill — ends it by rollback, restoring the opening state, and the next start re-enters the same span at the same from. That is WHY the stamp is inside the step's transaction: a stamp that commits separately is a moment, and the moment is the window where a half-migrated file exists.

The stamp's transactionality was NOT taken on trust. TestAVersionStampRollsBackWithItsOwnTransaction asserts it against this driver and the adiantum VFS — visible to the writer inside the tx, gone after rollback. Without that test a crash between stamp and commit produces the one forbidden file while every other test stays green.

THE FAULT-INJECTION SEAM IS CLEAN, which was an explicit requirement because nocx-lmb6v.2 is written by someone else: apply is a FIELD and the ladder is a PARAMETER, so a test hands migrateSchema a ladder whose step runs the real edge's DDL and then returns an error. No build tag, no hook, no exported test-only entry point.

THE FIRST RUNG IS REAL: 14->15, the grant_scopes.resource_kind CHECK widening. SQLite cannot ALTER a CHECK, so it is a table rebuild — the hardest migration shape, not the easiest. An engine with no edge is a dead half.

The chain starting at 14 is NOT a minMigratable declaration, which the bead put out of scope: below 14 the file was explicitly disposable, and two branches shipped the number 15 for two different shapes before merging, so pre-14 does not name one shape. A database below the first rung is REFUSED, never rebuilt, and the floor is schemaLadder[0].from — derived, never written down.

FKs are suspended for the walk per SQLite's documented table-rebuild procedure, with PRAGMA foreign_key_check inside every step's transaction as the compensating assertion. A step writes only what CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cannot, since schemaV1 runs right after the walk; the trap that a step's DDL is frozen at the version it produces and must never be edited to follow schemaV1 is stated in the code.

Four rebuild tests were deleted and schema_reset_test.go names each promise and where it went; two of their fixtures are kept and now assert the OPPOSITE — a nested entry tree, and a user's tabs, come through the version change.

go test ./internal/content/... ok 20.368s; -race on the schema set all PASS; golangci-lint and gofumpt clean; deadcode ratchet 82 unreachable, all baselined, no new violation.

title: DECISION — is the controller an explicit lease, or does the last attach silently take it?
description:
Must be settled BEFORE nocx-afgkj is implemented, and it is the owner's call.

The two designs do not disagree about the OBSERVER. nocx-eidfb.3 says an inactive
client renders at the session's effective size and never reflows to its own window;
the level-2 design's D7 says observers never resize. Those are the same sentence,
and no work is blocked on them.

They disagree about how a client BECOMES the controller.

  IMPLICIT (shipped, nocx-eidfb.2): the client that attached last becomes active and
  the channel resizes to it; announceDisplacement tells the loser afterwards.

  EXPLICIT LEASE (level-2 design D7): a lease with epochs, taken and released, so a
  second machine cannot silently reflow a window somebody is typing into.

  LEASE WITH DEFAULT ACQUISITION (the likely answer, and it is not free): attaching
  takes the lease when nobody holds it or the holder is idle, and asks otherwise.

Implicit is cheaper and already built. Explicit is what the durable-tab promise is
worth: once tabs live on the host, "attached last" stops being a proxy for "the person
is here" — a laptop waking from sleep and reconnecting would displace the desktop the
user is actually sitting at, mid-keystroke.

Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-31-level-2-the-server-on-the-host-design.md (D7).
acceptance_criteria: One of the three options is chosen by the owner, written into the level-2 design's D7 and into nocx-eidfb's description, so the two stop reading as a contradiction. If the lease is chosen, its acquisition, release, epoch and refusal are specified before nocx-afgkj's first line of code.

title: The mixed e2e run is unstable: 12 failures on main against 1 in webkit-only
description:
The mixed containerised run (chromium + webkit sharing one stand) is unstable
on `main` and fails specs that are green in every single-project configuration.

Measured 2026-08-31, same image, same machine, `origin/main` at ac06a437:

| configuration | result |
|---|---|
| mixed, both browsers | 460 passed, **12 failed** |
| webkit-only | 234 passed, **1 failed** (`api-run-lifecycle`) |
| the same specs run alone | green |

A different set fails each time, and the sets barely overlap. The twelve in the
mixed run: api-secret-in-path, prompt-vault, sidebar-resize (two),
tabby-import, vault-sealed-probe, workspaces (chromium); about, activity-bell,
connections-settings, secret-panel-position, snippets (webkit).
