  e2e/agent-ask.spec.ts:855, "cancelling an ask unlock stops its durable run" —
  that is Cancel on the vault unlock overlay, not Stop pressed on a turn that is
  thinking.

So the epic's own sentence is unwatched, which is the shape AGENTS.md rule 2 was
bought by, and the same gap nocx-7l4ex.5 records for its epic. The epic does not
close before this is green.
acceptance_criteria:
One automated check in e2e/ drives BOTH halves of nocx-uvac6's DONE WHEN, in a
real browser against a real backend:

REFUSAL. A policy refuses run (or the person presses Deny on the approval
window). The assistant is told the call was refused and by what, and it ANSWERS
IN WORDS — the answer body says what it could not do and what it would need —
and the turn's header reaches 'completed', not a dead header. A 'deny always'
additionally leaves the model not proposing it again in that turn.

STOP. A person asks a question and presses Stop while the turn is thinking. The
turn's header shows the person's own word for stopped — never 'failed' — the
prose that had already arrived is still on screen, and the NEXT question is
answered normally afterwards.

It waits on observable state — a DOM state, a frame, a record — never on a
duration (AGENTS.md).

It runs in e2e/run-in-container.sh, i.e. in CI's own e2e job, and is not marked
skip.
close_reason: Merged into feat/ai-assistant as f1468d2b: e2e/agent-refusal-stop.spec.ts, three journeys, green in the container on the merged tree (3 passed). Deny once and Deny always both derive the rendered answer from the real role:tool result, so a dropped refusal cannot pass; Deny always asserts the standing 'from now on / Do not propose it again.' sentence refusalResult composes from the DeclineKind. Stop is held with holdAfter rather than slept: the fake reaches streaming, the partial prose is on screen, the real overflow-menu Stop leaves it under a stopped header, and the next question completes. The epic's FOURTH route — a standing Never rather than a gesture — could not be written: the effect is dropped from the grant before any tool is declared, so there is no call and no refusal result. That is nocx-uvac6.8, which now blocks the epic.

title: The secret panel promises "esc to dismiss" and has no dismiss listeners at all
description:
The secret panel prints "esc to dismiss" in its own footer and cannot do it. Clicking outside does nothing either — there is no outside-dismiss path at all, in any state.

`FloatingPanel` owns both. `floating-panel.ts:560` opens with

```
if (!this.callbacks.onDismiss || this.dismissListenersAttached) return
document.addEventListener('keydown', this.onDocumentKeydown, true)
document.addEventListener('pointerdown', this.onDocumentPointerdown, true)
```

so a panel constructed WITHOUT an `onDismiss` callback silently installs neither listener. `secret-picker.ts:219` constructs its panel with `onHover` and `onPick` and no `onDismiss`, so the secret variant is exactly that panel.

What is left is the field's own key handler — `secret-picker-field.ts:321` down to `secret-picker.ts:352` — which sees Escape only while the FIELD has keyboard focus. So the promise holds for one state and no other, and the outside click has no owner anywhere.

The mechanism is not missing; it is unused. `floating-panel.test.ts:258` and `:265` already assert `onDismiss('escape')` and `onDismiss('outside')` against the same class. This is the existing answer not being asked.

Reported by the owner from the running app, with the panel on screen and its own "esc to dismiss" hint visible in the shot.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a request in the API workbench and put the caret in a header value.
2. Type '@' so the secret panel opens over the field.
3. Click anywhere outside the panel — it stays.
4. Press Escape with focus anywhere but the field — it stays, while its footer goes on saying "esc to dismiss".

## Acceptance Criteria

- Escape dismisses the panel whatever holds focus, and a pointerdown outside it dismisses it too.
- Both go through `FloatingPanel`'s existing `onDismiss` seam; no second dismiss mechanism is written beside it.
- The field's own Escape keeps working and does not fire the close twice.
- A check drives it from a state where the field does NOT hold focus, because focus is what the current path silently depends on.
close_reason: FloatingPanel installs its document keydown and pointerdown listeners only when given an onDismiss, and SecretPicker built its panel without one — so the footer's 'esc to dismiss' held only while the field itself had focus, and the outside click had no owner at all. The existing seam is used rather than a second dismissal written beside it; the field's own Escape routes into the same reset. The panel's listener is on document in the capture phase and stops the event there, so Escape cannot fire twice and the dialog underneath does not close. Two Playwright checks drive it from a state where the field does not hold focus.

title: The proposed name collides with the one already in the vault, so the second secret from a request cannot be accepted
description:
`nocx-3o0ed.7` made the lock propose a name instead of asking for one. The proposal is derived from the site and the request's host, so storing a SECOND secret from the same request proposes the name the first one already took, and the ask refuses it:

```
- textbox "Name" [invalid]
- alert: A secret named "127.0.0.1 token" is already in the vault
```

The epic's DONE WHEN is "accept a proposed name". It holds exactly once per host. The second time — a header token and an Auth token on the same request, which is an ordinary thing to have — the person is handed a name they cannot accept and must invent one after all, which is the detour the epic exists to remove, returned by a different door.

`secret-name-proposal.ts` derives from site and host alone; it is not told what the vault already holds, so it cannot avoid a collision. The vault knows, and the ask that reports the clash knows, so the fact exists on the path — it is simply not consulted before the name is proposed.

Found by the epic's own e2e walk (`api-secret-in-any-field.spec.ts:335`), which stores a header secret and then an Auth secret against one server. The header journey passes; the Auth one stops on the alert.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. A request against any host, with the vault unsealed.
2. Store a header value through its lock; accept the proposed name (e.g. `example.com token`).
3. Store the Auth tab's token through its lock.
4. The ask proposes `example.com token` again, marks Name invalid, and refuses to save.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Storing a second secret from the same request proposes a name that is free, so it can be accepted without editing.
- The first proposal for a host is unchanged — disambiguation appears only when it is needed, so an ordinary single secret does not gain a numeral.
- A unit test on the seam that decides the name covers both: the free name and the taken one.
- The epic's e2e walk stores both secrets and accepts both proposals without typing a name.
close_reason: Deriving the name from site and host proposed a taken name the second time a request stored a secret. proposeSecret is given what the vault holds and picks the first free variant; both doors (api-pane and request-form) pass it, so the defect cannot move from one to the other. The ask keeps its own recovery for the two cases the proposal cannot see — a name typed by hand, and one created between proposal and save — and both call one exported numbering rule rather than a copy each. The e2e walk names both proposals it accepts.

title: Focusing a field moves the row around it: the lock's reserve is taken on focus, and an auto table re-lays out
description:
The lock is the field's own affordance, and pressing into the field must not move the surface around it. Today it does: focusing a header value widens its column, narrows the name column beside it, and shifts the remove button — the row visibly re-lays out under the pointer that is about to aim at something in it.

`ui/text-field.tsx:377` sets `data-action` only while the field has focus:

```
data-trailing={props.trailing !== undefined ? 'true' : 'false'}
data-action={props.trailingAction && focused() ? 'true' : undefined}
```

The asymmetry is the tell. `data-trailing` reserves its room unconditionally; `data-action` reserves it only on focus, and `text-field.css:36` turns that into `padding-right: 40px` on the input. The button itself is absolutely positioned (`.ui-text-field__trailing`) and costs no layout, so the 32px of padding is the whole of the movement.

In a flex column that padding is invisible. In a table it is not: `row-list.css:50` gives `.ui-row-list__table` `width: 100%` and `border-collapse: collapse` and no `table-layout`, so the columns are auto — content-driven. Raising one cell's min-content width by 32px redistributes every column in the row.

Reported by the owner from the running app, with before/after screenshots of the Authorization row.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. API workbench, a request, the Headers tab, with at least one header row.
2. Note where the name column ends, where the value field starts, and where the remove button sits.
3. Click into the header VALUE field so its lock appears.
4. The value field widens, the name field narrows, and the remove button moves right. Clicking away puts them back.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Focusing a field that has a trailing action changes NO box on the surface around it: the field's own border box, its neighbours' and the row's are the same focused and unfocused, to the pixel.
- The reserved room still exists when the action is visible — text never runs under the lock.
- Asserted by a check that measures the boxes before and after focus rather than by eye, on the header table where the columns can move.
- One owner for the reserve. Whatever fixes this fixes every surface that places a field with a trailing action, not the header table alone.
close_reason: data-action was set from focus while its sibling data-trailing was set from existence, so 32px of padding appeared and vanished on focus; in an auto-layout table that redistributed the whole row. The reserve now follows the affordance's existence and only the button's visibility follows focus, which fixes every surface placing a field with a trailing action rather than the header table alone. A Playwright check measures the field, its neighbour and the row before and after focus and asserts all three unchanged.

title: the composer reclaims a scrollback selection, and the Mark offer dies with it
description:
Select output in the scrollback while the CodeMirror composer has focus and
the selection is taken away about 50 ms later: CM6 restores the DOM selection
into its own document whenever it holds focus and the selection is anchored
outside it. `TerminalContent.onSelectionChange` then sees a collapsed
selection, hides the mark affordance, and the "Mark block" offer vanishes
before anyone can press it.

Measured, in the e2e container, by polling the live DOM from the page after
the affordance appears:

    0: wd=block  selCollapsed=false anchor=SPAN.term-line   active=DIV.cm-content
    1: wd=none   selCollapsed=true  anchor=DIV.cm-line      active=DIV.cm-content

One frame the anchor is a terminal row; the next it is a CM line and the
wrapper is display:none. Nothing called hide() by decision — the guard at the
top of onSelectionChange took the `selection.isCollapsed` branch, which is
correct behaviour on a selection somebody else moved.

This is AGENTS.md's "two surfaces may never own the same input": the document
selection is claimed by the scrollback (which offers a grant over it) and by
the composer (which restores its own), and the composer wins by evaluation
order. The loser goes on advertising an offer it can no longer deliver.

A real mouse drag mostly hides this — mousedown in the scrollback moves focus
off CM first, so CM does not reclaim. It is reachable whenever a selection is
made WITHOUT taking focus from the composer.

## Steps to Reproduce

`e2e/agent-ask.spec.ts`'s `pointAt` makes the selection with a DOM Range and a
dispatched `selectionchange` — deliberately, "a synthetic drag across rows is
a geometry test in disguise" — and by doing so it also skips the focus
transfer a real drag performs. It therefore races CM's reclaim on every call,
and only wins because it clicks within a few milliseconds.

    PW_PROJECTS=chromium ./e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/agent-ask.spec.ts

  - origin/main (0aa521e6): 8 passed. Insert a 2-second poll between
    `toBeVisible` and `click` in pointAt and `point at a finished block` fails
    the same way — main wins the race, it does not avoid it.
  - feat/orchestration merged (59b8e413): `custom headers ride the completion
    AND the connection check (nocx-lyyk)` fails 3 runs out of 3, with
    `element is not visible` on the click. The merged tree loses the race
    where each parent won it; both parents are green unmodified.

So the merge did not introduce the mechanism — it changed the timing enough to
make an existing race lose every time.

## What is NOT the cause (ruled out by measurement)

  - Not a lost CSS import: `mark-affordance.css` and every neighbour import
    survive the merge's style.css resolution.
  - Not two affordances or a stale one: exactly one `.mark-affordance`, parent
    BODY, in-document.
  - Not geometry: at show() the button measured 66x22 at (424,747) in a
    1280x900 viewport, display block, visibility visible, opacity 1.
  - Not a focus bounce firing late: the last focusin landed on cm-content
    ~100 ms BEFORE the affordance was shown, not after.
acceptance_criteria:
- A person can select output rows while the composer holds focus and the Mark
  offer stays up until they act on it. One owner for the document selection:
  either the composer does not restore a selection anchored outside its root,
  or the scrollback takes focus when it claims one — decided in the code, not
  by evaluation order.
- An automated check watches that: make the selection without moving focus,
  wait a beat that is longer than the reclaim window, and the offer is still
  pressable.
- `pointAt` in e2e/agent-ask.spec.ts no longer depends on clicking faster than
  the reclaim.
- `PW_PROJECTS=chromium ./e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/agent-ask.spec.ts` is
  green on the merged feat/orchestration tree.
close_reason: fixed on feat/orchestration: the scrollback takes the focus when it claims a selection and re-asserts the range the blur may empty (1b8bd331, 877f3af4); e2e agent-ask 8/8 on both chromium and webkit

title: The lock door opens Create secret with an empty name — the proposal is computed and thrown away
description:
The epic's DONE WHEN is "focus the field, press the one affordance it shows, ACCEPT A PROPOSED NAME". The lock door proposes nothing.

`secret-picker.ts:430` passes the panel's FILTER as the name: `requestCreate(typed, row.value)`, where `typed = s.filter` — the word a person typed after '@'. The lock door has no '@' and no filter, so `typed` is the empty string.

`api-pane.tsx:454` then computes `proposeSecret({site:{at:'field'}, url})` and reads ONLY `proposal.kind`: `openSecretCreateAsk({ name, kind: proposal.kind, value })` passes the EMPTY argument, never `proposal.name`. So the proposal is computed on every store and thrown away — a dead half inside a live path: `proposeSecret` is genuinely reachable, and the half of it that matters is not read.

`proposeSecret` itself is fine — `secret-name-proposal.ts:48-61` can never return an empty name; the worst case is 'token'.

Found by the merged e2e gate, which is the only place it was ever visible: `#secret-create-name` resolved 14 times as the empty string against `toHaveValue(/.+/)` (`api-secret-in-any-field.spec.ts:277`), in chromium and webkit alike. No unit test could see it — each side is correct alone.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the API workbench on a request and go to Headers.
2. Type a token into a header value and leave it focused.
3. Press the field's lock and take the `Store "…" in the vault…` row.
4. The Create secret ask opens with the value filled in and the NAME EMPTY.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Storing from a field's own lock opens the create ask with a NON-EMPTY proposed name, so a person accepts it rather than inventing one.
- Asserted by the epic's e2e spec on the header journey — the value field, not only Auth.
- A unit test covers the seam that decides the name, including that the '@' door still proposes the typed word rather than the derived one.
close_reason: The lock door opened the create ask with an empty name because SecretPicker passed its filter — the word typed after '@' — and the lock has none, while createSecretInPlace computed proposeSecret and read only its kind. 'value' tells the two doors apart and now decides: a store door with nothing typed takes the shared proposal, the '@' door still offers the typed word. Asserted by unit tests on both doors and by the epic's e2e walk.

title: The per-commit gate runs no containerized tests: static checks only
description:
The pre-commit hook launched two containers on every commit — go test -race in .githooks/images/go-tests and vitest in a node image — and they were 72 percent of its wall time by its own comment. On a machine running several agent workers that is not merely slow: on 2026-08-27 three concurrent hooks put this host at 232 MB free RAM with swap at 5965 of 5980 MB, a gate child was OOM-killed, and the hook reported it as a lint failure (nocx-y6d9j). Two workers answered by committing with --no-verify.

The owner's decision: a commit is gated by STATIC checks only. Formatting, linting, type-checking, the ratchets, the wire contracts and the beads export stay; the two test runners come out, and with them the docker requirement and the containerized-tests helper whose only caller they were.

What this deliberately gives up, said plainly rather than discovered later: a commit can now be made whose tests do not pass. The suites keep their teeth at three addresses that already exist — CI on every pull request, 'make ci-full' which the integrator runs once on the merged tree, and 'make test' on demand. What it buys is a gate that finishes in seconds, needs no daemon, and cannot be starved into lying about which check failed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- git commit runs no docker container and requires no docker binary: asserted by committing with the docker daemon stopped.
- Every static gate the hook had is still enforced on the same commit: gofumpt, golangci-lint, the control-goroutine ratchet, prettier, both eslint territories, the frontend and e2e typechecks, the fixture gate, contracts:check, check-site, and the beads export last.
- No unreachable helper is left behind: the containerized test harness and its image go with the callers, and every comment that pointed at them says where tests live now.
- README and AGENTS.md state what the per-commit gate covers and what it does not, so nobody reads a green commit as a green suite.
close_reason: Done in 30a41667. The hook sources no containerized-tests.sh, requires no docker binary, starts no container, and prints 'All static checks passed' with 'any test at all' first in its NOT-covered list. Proved by the commit itself: gofumpt, golangci-lint, the goroutine ratchet, prettier, both eslint territories, the fixture gate, contracts:check, both typechecks and the beads export all ran and passed with no docker involved. The harness and its image are deleted rather than left unreachable, and the three comments plus README, AGENTS.md and architecture.md now say where the tests live.

title: A pre-commit gate that DIED is reported as a gate that FAILED, and two agents answered it with --no-verify
description:
host_gate in .githooks/pre-commit reports one word for two different events: the gate ran and found violations, and the gate never got to run. Measured on 2026-08-27 with three workers on one machine:

- 'eslint (frontend)' printed its npm banner, then nothing at all, then 'FAIL: eslint (frontend)'. Zero diagnostics. Twice, in two different worktrees, at 219s and 376s.
- The same command in the same worktree, run alone minutes later: exit 0, every ratchet violation baselined. The clean base of the branch, alone: exit 0.

WHAT KILLED IT, corrected later the same day. The first reading was memory: swap was at 5965 of 5980 MB with 232 MB free, and an OOM-killed child exits non-zero printing nothing. That was measured but it was not the whole answer, and probably not the answer at all. Hours later the ROOT FILESYSTEM turned out to be full — 197 GB with 388 KB free, 100% — and a process that cannot write its temp files dies exactly the same way: non-zero, silent. The disk had been filling all day (docker held 43 GB, ~100 stale worktrees another 28 GB), so it was already at or near full during both failures. An OOM kill and an ENOSPC death are indistinguishable from this hook's output, which is itself the point of this bead.

The cost is not the flake, it is what the flake teaches. Both workers concluded the gate was broken infrastructure and committed with --no-verify — the one thing AGENTS.md forbids outright — and one of them went further and began terminating processes it believed were the contention. A gate that cannot say 'I did not run' trains agents to bypass it, and a bypassed hook is a backlog that looks green. A coordinator reading the same output misdiagnosed it too, and told a worker the wrong cause.

Related: nocx-0p9jo (npm ci --silent swallowing its own errors) is the same family — a gate whose failure output is not the failure.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Fill the filesystem the toolchain writes temp files to, or put the machine under memory pressure so a node process can be OOM-killed. Either produces the same shape.
2. Commit a staged frontend change so the hook runs 'eslint (frontend)'.
3. Observed: 'FAIL: eslint (frontend)' with no diagnostic above it, then 'Fix the issues above and try again'. There are no issues above.
4. Re-run 'cd frontend && npm run lint' alone once there is room: exit 0.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A gate that exits without producing output is reported as something OTHER than a violation: the hook says the gate did not complete, names the step, and says so in words an agent will not read as 'your code is wrong'.
- A gate killed by a signal is distinguished from a gate that exited non-zero on its own. Asserted by killing a gate child during a hook run and reading what the hook says.
- The hook checks the two conditions that produce this shape and names them when it sees them: free space on the filesystem it is about to write to, and whether the last failure left a kill signal. A number in the failure line beats an agent's guess.
- The hook's own advice line stops telling the reader to 'fix the issues above' when there are no issues above.

title: app: TestBannerClickReachesTheRendererAsSessionFocus races the subscriber install
description:
The test opens a session over the real socket, and the moment `open` answers
it calls a.FocusSession(sid), then waits 30 s for session.focus.

But handleOpen installs the subscriber AFTER it writes the open result, and
deliberately so (ws_session_handlers.go:572-580):

    _ = respond(r, resp)
    // Every session-scoped notification must follow the open result (AD-7).
    // Install the subscriber only now: lifecycle can authenticate during the
    // dial above, and publishing it to this shared WebSocket before the
    // renderer knows sessionId lets an existing tab claim the fact.
    rx.setSubscriber(wconn, state)

WSServer.FocusSession drops the notification when there is no subscriber yet —
`s.log.Debug("session.focus dropped: no subscriber")` — and the drop is at
Debug, so the run says nothing and the test sits out its 30 s deadline. The
window is between respond() and setSubscriber(); on a loaded machine it is
wide enough to lose.

The product is not implicated: the ordering it violates is one the product
documents and wants. The test is waiting on a duration instead of on an
observable state change, which is what AGENTS.md forbids.

Fix: wait for something that proves the subscriber is installed before
clicking. The replay that follows setSubscriber emits session-scoped
notifications for this session — read until one arrives, then call
FocusSession. Do not sleep.

Branch-new: added on feat/orchestration by bbcc4c21 (nocx-jiwq.1, nocx-c6ef,
nocx-3mniv). Not on origin/main.

## Steps to Reproduce

Intermittent, and only in a FULL-package run — `-count=30` on the test alone,
with -race, is green.

Seen twice on 2026-08-27 against the merged feat/orchestration tree
(59b8e413), in two independent environments:

  - host `make ci` (go test -race -tags gtk3 ./...)
  - `scripts/ci-linux.sh` — the real backend-linux job, ubuntu-24.04 container

both reporting:

    --- FAIL: TestBannerClickReachesTheRendererAsSessionFocus (30.1s)
        app_notify_focus_test.go:62: a banner click never reached the renderer
        as session.focus: read tcp ... i/o timeout

A third full-package host run of ./internal/app/ was green, which is the flake.
acceptance_criteria:
- The test waits on an observable fact that the subscriber is installed before
  calling FocusSession — a session-scoped notification read off the socket,
  never a sleep and never a bare deadline.
- 30 consecutive full-package runs of ./internal/app/ under -race are green.
- Deliberately out: handleOpen's ordering. respond-then-setSubscriber is
  AD-7's requirement and does not move.
close_reason: fixed on feat/orchestration: the test waits for a session-scoped notification proving the subscriber is installed before clicking (168153ff); 11 full-package runs clean

title: A program parked on an approval wakes to a cancelled context and the run reports a lost connection
description:
The first live program that asked for anything died on the person's YES. Measured
2026-08-27 09:42 on the dev stand, HEAD 4b8149d1, carrier=program, policy
ask-every-time.

The model wrote the right program on the first try (the new tool description
works — no loop, one chained program):

    result = run(command="for f in *; do ... done | sort -rn", sessionId="6bf441...")
    answer(result["text"])

09:42:44.724  agent program: running        run=349
09:42:44.728  agent program: stopped        run=349 error="agent run suspended for approval: run prog-1"
   ... the person is asked, and answers YES 8.5 s later ...
09:42:53.199  agent program: running        run=349            (the resume: eino restores the
                                                                checkpoint and re-enters the tool)
09:42:53.204  agent program effect failed   tool=run call=prog-1 error="context canceled"
09:42:53.204  agent program: stopped        run=349 error="program failed: ... Error in run: context canceled"
09:42:53.204  agent ask: the run failed     run=349 reason=transport-gone
              sentence="the connection was lost while the answer was streaming"

The connection was fine. `transport-gone` is classifyAskFailure mapping
context.Canceled, and the sentence it produces is a lie about what happened.

## What is established

The bare "context canceled" can only come from `invokeParking`'s own selects
(internal/assistant/starlarkcarrier.go:319,324) — every other error on that path
is wrapped (RequestRun wraps "run: %w", the kernel wraps ToolFailedError). So the
parked goroutine was released and found `runCtx` cancelled.

`runCtx` is `context.WithCancel(context.WithoutCancel(ctx))`, created in
`parkedRuns.drive` (internal/assistant/parkedrun.go:102), so no ask's death can
cancel it. Only `p.cancel()` can: drive's three branches, or `parkedRuns.discard`
via `client.Discard`.

And it was cancelled AT the resume, not before: a goroutine parked in select #2
would have woken the moment ctx died, so an earlier cancellation would have
logged "effect failed" at that earlier moment, not at 53.204.

Who called it is NOT yet established. A probe is in the tree, uncommitted: a
caller stack logged from `client.Discard`, and `ctx.Err()` logged at
`programCarrier.Invoke` entry.

## Why no suite saw it

Every transport approval test drives a SCRIPTED engine (scriptedApprovalClient),
which parks nothing. Every engine-level parked-program test drives Ask directly
with an uncancelled context. Nothing exercised the real engine, the real approval
wire and the real broker together — which is exactly where it broke.

Two tests now do, and both PASS, so neither reproduces it yet:
  internal/transport/ws_agent_program_approval_test.go
    TestAgentAsk_AProgramThatStopsForAnApprovalFinishesAfterIt
  internal/assistant/carrier_test.go
    TestAsk_AParkedProgramSurvivesTheDeathOfTheAskThatParkedIt
Stable at -count=20 -race, and with a 10 s delay before the approval.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Settings: carrier = program; policy = ask every time (the shipped matrix).
2. Ask a question whose answer needs one command: "which text file here is the
   biggest".
3. The program proposes `run`; the prompt appears; answer YES.
4. The run fails with "the connection was lost while the answer was streaming"
   and the command never runs.

Reproduces on the dev stand with a live model; does NOT reproduce in either test
above.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The live path: with carrier=program and ask-every-time, one approved effect
  reaches the renderer and the program finishes — asserted by a test that fails
  before the fix.
- The cause is NAMED, not worked around: whoever cancels the parked context is
  identified, and if it is a Discard, the caller is fixed rather than the parked
  run being made harder to cancel.
- A cancelled continuation never reports itself as a lost connection: whatever
  sentence a killed program produces says the program was ended, not that the
  socket went away.
notes:
=== ROOT CAUSE FOUND, 2026-08-27, and it was the instrumentation that found it ===

The second live run (run 352, 10:37) with the new logging says it in two lines:

  effect failed    trace=run-352 request=1/agent.ask#197      <- the parked program
  program: stopped trace=run-352 request=1/agent.approve#202  <- the drive resuming it

Nobody cancelled the parked context: the "the parked program was ended" line
that every p.cancel() now writes never appeared. The program was released and
then called THE KERNEL OF THE ASK THAT PARKED IT — the request tag on the
effect's own failure line is agent.ask#197, while the drive around it is
agent.approve#202.

That kernel's ask-scoped seams die with that ask. The one that bites is
onCall (kernel.go step 5b, "the call becomes visible"): the transport's sink
seals the open prose block through `h.op.Run(ctx, ...)` with the PARKING
ask's context, which was cancelled when that ask returned. SealProse comes
back with a bare context.Canceled, onCall returns it, the kernel returns it
unwrapped, the program dies — and context.Canceled is exactly what
classifyAskFailure maps to transport-gone, "the connection was lost while the
answer was streaming".

Which is why it needed a live model to reproduce: a scripted model that goes
straight to the tool call opens no prose block, so there is nothing to seal
and the dead context is never touched. The transport test passed against the
broken build until the fake model was given a sentence to say first.

THE FIX. Only the program's LOCALS have to survive an approval; its kernel
must not. parkedRun now carries a rebind, drive hands the resuming drive's
kernel to the carrier before releasing the parked effect, and invokeParking
re-reads the kernel for the retry instead of using the one it was entered
with. Both composing carriers (starlark, graph) got a mutex-guarded
setKernel/kernelNow.

AND THE INSTRUMENTATION IS THE OTHER HALF, kept:
  - log adapter builds its own record with the caller's PC, AddSource on in
    app.go -> every line in the product names module:function:line;
  - log.WithTraceID / WithRequestID + WithContext -> trace=run-352 on the ask,
    the approval and the resume; request=<conn>/<method>#<id> per frame. The
    reader half existed and had no producer: every record said traceID="".
  - cancelling a parked program carries a named cause (WithCancelCause), the
    program reports context.Cause, and the transport says which cause ended
    the run instead of blaming the socket.
close_reason: Fixed and asserted: the parked program is rebound to the drive that resumes it (a red-first test at the transport reproduces the live sentence), every cancellation carries a named cause, every log record names its module and its exchange, and a tool now declares what it returns with the kernel holding the executor to it.

title: content: a cancelled ctx abandons a write the writer goroutine is still running
description:
`sqliteContent.run` (internal/content/sqlite.go:139) waits for the writer's
answer in a select that also has `<-ctx.Done()` and `<-s.stop`. Once the
request has been ACCEPTED onto s.writeCh, taking either of those branches
abandons a mutation that the writer goroutine is still executing.

Two consequences, and the second is the worse one.

1. A data race on every caller that assigns into a variable it returns.
   `out = ProseBlock{...}` at ledger_agent_sqlite.go:871 runs on the writer
   goroutine; `return out, err` at :874 runs on the caller's, with nothing
   between them once run() has returned early.

2. A COMMITTED transaction reported to the caller as a cancel. The writer runs
   fn to completion including tx.Commit(); the caller has already returned
   ctx.Err(). The ledger has the row, the transport believes it does not.

The `process` doc already states the invariant this violates: "A request that
reached process is owed an answer, whatever happens next: a caller waiting for
its outcome must never hang, and a committed outcome must never be replaced by
a proxy error." The first select (before the send) is correct and stays — a
request not yet accepted is genuinely abandonable.

PRE-EXISTING ON main, not a merge defect: both the code and the test are on
origin/main; `run`'s shape dates to c981fa63 (nocx-rtg0.19). Filed standalone
because it arrived from nowhere.

## Steps to Reproduce

Caught by `go test -race -tags gtk3 ./...` on the merged feat/orchestration
tree (59b8e413), 2026-08-27, under load. It does NOT reproduce with
`-count=20` on that test alone — the window needs the cancellation to land
between the send and fn's return.

    WARNING: DATA RACE
    Write at 0x00c000d9a160 by goroutine 7338:
      content.(*sqliteContent).OpenProse.func1()  ledger_agent_sqlite.go:871
      ... content.(*sqliteContent).process() / writer()
    Previous read at 0x00c000d9a160 by goroutine 7361:
      content.(*sqliteContent).OpenProse()        ledger_agent_sqlite.go:874
      capability.(*agentService).OpenProse()
      transport.agentHandlers.runAskStream.func2.2()
    --- FAIL: TestAgentAsk_TheTurnIsAnchoredToTheSessionsPane (0.48s)
        testing.go:1712: race detected during execution of test

The surrounding log lines are `reason=transport-gone ... error="context
canceled"` — that is the cancellation taking the branch. Deterministic repro
is the first half of the fix: inject a fn that blocks until the test cancels
the ctx, then commits.
acceptance_criteria:
- A test drives one run() call whose ctx is cancelled after the request is
  accepted and before fn returns, and asserts that run() does not return until
  the writer has answered — and that a fn which commits reports success, not
  ctx.Err().
- `go test -race` over internal/content and internal/transport is clean with
  that test in place.
- Deliberately out: the first select. A request still queued may be abandoned.
close_reason: fixed on feat/orchestration: run waits for the writer's answer once a request is accepted (758969b1); regression test TestRunWaitsForAnAcceptedWriteAfterCancel

title: A press on a row's edge dismisses the whole dialog behind the panel
description:
ui/dialog.tsx:325 implements light-dismiss by comparing the mousedown coordinates against
.nocx-dialog__panel's box, with explicit exemptions for .ui-toast-host and
.ui-prompt-overlay — both added for surfaces that re-home themselves into the dialog to
escape the top layer.

nocx-vzdna made the secret panel do exactly that, and it has no exemption. It is appended
to the <dialog>, not to .nocx-dialog__panel, and being anchored to its field's left edge
with a 480px minimum width it overhangs the dialog panel by roughly its own padding. A
press on the right-hand end of a row therefore lands OUTSIDE the panel's box and dismisses
the whole connection editor — the person loses the form they were filling in, having
aimed at a row that was plainly in front of them.

The row centre is safe, which is why the e2e run and its helper never trip it. A user's
click is not aimed at the centre.

Found by the worker on nocx-vzdna while removing that bead's diagnostics. Not fixed there,
deliberately: it is a third mechanism, and moving it in the same pass would have left
neither verified.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the connection editor (a modal .nocx-dialog) and focus its password value field.
2. Press the lock so the secret panel opens anchored to that field.
3. Press on the far right of any row, past the dialog panel's edge.
4. The dialog light-dismisses. The row never acts and the form is gone.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A mousedown anywhere inside a .ui-floating-panel does not light-dismiss the dialog,
  by the same exemption shape the two existing ones use.
- A test presses on the overhanging part of a row and asserts the dialog is still open
  AND the row acted.
- Light-dismiss still works for a press on genuinely empty backdrop, asserted, so the
  exemption cannot be widened into disabling the feature.
close_reason: A press on the part of the panel hanging past the dialog dismissed the whole form. The exemption is the third instance of the shape .ui-toast-host and .ui-prompt-overlay already are. Proving it turned up a second, independent defect: SecretPicker.pick refused every state but 'list', so the single offer row a person with no vault sees was reachable by Enter and by nothing else — those states now route into the same activate the keyboard uses. Measured, not derived: the overhang comes from the field's horizontal offset, not the dialog's width — #profile-auth-password sits at x=510 and its 480px panel runs to 990 against a dialog ending at 960. Green in both browsers in the full suite.

title: The epic's own sentence, watched end to end: ask inside htop and get it back untouched
description:
Filed by the coordinator on 2026-08-26 while integrating nocx-7l4ex.2, not by
anyone who found a bug.

This epic states a sentence a person can say — "a person inside htop presses the
chord, gets a box, asks what this process is, reads the answer without the
program being resized, redrawn or interrupted, and quits htop normally
afterwards" — and has no child that watches them do it. Its four built children
each prove their own half in unit tests: the overlay exists (.1), the display
freezes (.2), session.read returns the pinned frame (.3), the answer takes its
seat (.4). Every unit correct and the user's task unproven is precisely the
shape AGENTS.md rule 2 was bought by.

The check should have been written when the epic was created; it was not, so it
is a child now, and the epic does not close before it is green.

Blocked by the children whose seams it drives.
acceptance_criteria:
- One automated check drives the WHOLE sentence in a real browser against a real backend: a full-screen program is running, the chord opens the box, a question is typed and sent, the answer appears in the overlay, Escape returns the keys, and the program is quit normally afterwards.
- Within that same run it asserts the three facts the unit tests can only assert separately: the program is never redrawn by a resize (a program that repaints on SIGWINCH does not repaint), the screen is visibly frozen while the box is up and live after it closes, and output written during the freeze is on screen after the thaw.
- It runs in e2e/run-in-container.sh, i.e. in CI's own e2e job, and is not marked skip.
- It waits on observable state — a frame, a DOM state, a record — never on a duration (AGENTS.md).
close_reason: Merged as 3b9d2fb4. e2e/ask-about-full-screen-program.spec.ts drives the whole sentence in a real browser against a real backend, on the ALTERNATE buffer with a pty of its own: it records SIGWINCH so a resize cannot hide, freezes, asks, and thaws. Two things make it evidence rather than decoration — the answer is DERIVED from the model request, so it can only name the pinned frame's marker if that frame actually reached the model; and a second marker is written only after the pin, so the answer must refuse it and the live grid must show it after Escape. Every wait is on a DOM state, a provider state, an OSC signal or a file, never on a duration. It was written first and run red, and it located the P0 nocx-7l4ex.6.

title: A minted rule inherits the person's own '*', so approving `rm *` once permits `rm /etc` forever
description:
Found in review of the nocx-takqr.1 change before it landed; the code is staged
in the `work/rules` worktree.

`internal/transport/ws_agent.go:1594` mints a standing answer from the parsed
invocation verbatim:

    rule := content.InvocationRule{Pattern: invocation.Commands, Decision: d}

`internal/content/rules.go` then matches each pattern token with
`tokenPatternMatches`, in which `*` matches any run of characters within the
token. The doc comment above `InvocationRule` reasons about `*` as an
OPERATOR-authored affordance and calls the bound "deliberately narrow ... safe
because over-matching is the failure mode these rules remove". It does not
consider that the pattern can be minted from what a PERSON typed.

## Steps to Reproduce

Approve, as a standing session answer, a command whose token is literally a
pattern — the shell never expanded it because this is the typed line, not the
executed one:

    rm *

The rule saved is `[["rm","*"]]` with decision permit. Every later `rm <one
token>` matches it, including `rm /etc`.

Bounded by, and only by, the base row: `DecisionForInvocation` returns early
when the matrix row is `refuse`, so the exposure is exactly the rows whose base
is `ask` — which is the row a person is most likely to have been asked about
and said yes to.

Narrower cases are just as wrong and less visible: `git push *`, `curl *`,
`kubectl delete *`.

The epic's sentence is "a yes covers only what you were shown". A yes shown as
`rm *` covered one command line; the rule it wrote covers a family.
acceptance_criteria:
- A test that is RED before the fix: a rule minted from an invocation whose token is literally `*` does not match a different token afterwards.
- The mint path treats a person's tokens as literal. Whatever mechanism is chosen (escape at mint, refuse to mint a standing answer for a token carrying a pattern character, or a literal-token rule kind distinct from the operator-authored pattern kind), a pattern character typed by the PERSON never becomes a wildcard in the rule saved on their behalf.
- Operator-authored patterns in the config keep their `*`; this narrows only what nocx mints from a person's yes.
- The refusal path, if that is the mechanism chosen, tells the person the yes applied to this call and was not saved, and why — a silent non-save is the failure mode of the whole epic.
- internal/content and internal/assistant stay green.
close_reason: Minting goes through content.LiteralInvocationRule, which refuses a token carrying a pattern character; operator-authored patterns in the config keep theirs. The refusal is not silent — it returns on the existing warning channel, names the token the person typed and says a standing answer is saved exactly as shown. Red first: the test approving rm * on both scopes observed the warning, then that rm /etc still asks and neither the session overlay nor the global store holds a rule. Found in review before it landed, so the hole was never on a branch anyone could merge.

title: TestSessionSignal_InterruptReachesTheRunningCommand exhausts its whole 20s window under container load, on a clean tree
description:
`session.signal` answers `delivered`, the second command is ECHOED by the tty,
and its OUTPUT never comes. The shell did not get the terminal back.

    --- FAIL: TestSessionSignal_InterruptReachesTheRunningCommand (20.04s)
        ws_signal_test.go:124: the session's output never contained "INTERRUPTED-OK";
                               got "printf %s%s INTERRUPTED -OK\r\n"

## Steps to Reproduce

From any worktree root, on a LOADED machine (this is the whole trick — it passes
on an idle one):

    docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/src:ro" -w /src golang:1.26-bookworm \
      sh -c "go test -race -tags gtk3 -run 'TestSessionSignal' -count=3 ./internal/transport/"

## It is not a change, it is load

Measured 2026-08-26 by alternating the same command between a CLEAN checkout of
163c0d48 and a branch that touches no signal code:

    clean  run1  FAIL  (20.04s)   loadavg ~15
    staged run1  FAIL  (20.03s)   loadavg ~20
    clean  run2  PASS  (9.2s)     load fallen

A clean tree fails it. Two earlier readings that each looked decisive were one
run against one run, which is how this was twice mis-attributed to whatever
branch happened to be under the microscope (see memory
`a-test-that-fails-under-load-and-passes`).

## The lead worth pulling first

The failure is NEVER MARGINAL. The first wait in the same test —
FOREGROUND-READY, proving the child owns the pty foreground group — is satisfied
in well under a second in the very same run. The second wait then consumes its
ENTIRE 20 seconds, to two decimal places, every time. A slow machine produces
late arrivals; this produces none at all.

That is the signature of a lost event, not of a starved one. Candidates, in the
order they are cheap to disprove:
- the SIGINT reached a process group that was no longer the foreground one by
  the time `pty.SignalForeground` read TIOCGPGRP;
- the second `submitCommand` wrote its line into the tty input queue while the
  job was still foreground (it was echoed, so it was written), and the shell
  discarded that queue when it reclaimed the terminal;
- the data-plane tap dropped the frame carrying the output.

The third is testable by reading what the pty produced independently of the tap.

Family: nocx-8b47, nocx-mgevc, nocx-qqhsm are the same shape in other packages;
nocx-2h08 named a starved shared resource in this very package and recorded its
own disproof condition. This is a DIFFERENT shape from nocx-2h08: one scoped
test, a content assertion rather than a 30s timeout, and no moving test name.
acceptance_criteria:
- The failure is explained: named as either a lost event in the product (SIGINT delivered to a group that is no longer the foreground one, or the shell's reclaim racing the next submitted line) or a wait in the test that is not on an observable state change. Not "raised the deadline".
- The test passes 5 consecutive container runs of the repro command WHILE the machine is under load comparable to the one that produced this report (loadavg >= 15), measured and stated.
- No marker is relaxed, no window lengthened, no sleep added. The two-piece markers stay two-piece.
- If the cause is in the product, the fix is in the product and a test that fails without it is written first.
notes:
Full A/B, 2026-08-26, alternating arms, identical command shape, one Docker daemon:

  clean  163c0d48      FAIL 20.04s | PASS 9.2s | FAIL 20.07s | FAIL 20.06s   -> 3/4 FAIL
  branch work/rules    FAIL 20.03s | FAIL 20.11s | PASS 7.7s | PASS 7.6s     -> 2/4 FAIL

The CLEAN tree fails MORE often than the branch that was accused of breaking it.
loadavg over the window ran 11 -> 101 (other agents' gates on the same box) and the
failures track the load, not the tree.

Every failure is 20.03-20.11s, i.e. the whole window; every pass is under 10s for the
entire package. There is no middle.
close_reason: explained and fixed on feat/orchestration: the readiness marker was printed by the INTERMEDIATE shell before it forked the target, so a SIGINT arriving in that window reached a group whose only member was dash — which catches SIGINT and drops it, then forks sleep 300 and waits forever. kill(2) succeeded and session.signal honestly answered delivered. All three filed candidates were disproved by measurement first (foreground group correct and stable via TIOCGPGRP at three points; no input-queue flush across 238 runs; reproduced against LocalPty.Read with no codec, socket or tap). The job is now tail -f over a file whose content is the marker, which closes the window by construction: the marker cannot reach the data plane until the process bash put in the foreground has exec'd, and it carries tail's own default SIGINT disposition. No product change — one SIGINT is what Ctrl+C does, and stop has its escalation ladder. Five repro runs green at loadavg 23.8-41.8; A/B at loadavg 49, 120 iterations each: old shape 2 fails, new shape 0.

title: T5 One check watches a person do it from a header and from Auth
description: The epic's DONE WHEN, watched end to end on the real backend and a real vault set up through the product's own pages.
acceptance_criteria:
- One Playwright spec: paste a token into a header value ALREADY holding 'Bearer <token>', select the token, store it through the field's own affordance, accept the proposed name, send, and assert the server received the real value.
- The same spec does the Auth tab, where the whole field is the credential and nothing is selected.
- NEITHER journey retypes the value and neither passes through Settings, and the spec asserts the absence rather than merely not doing it.
- The request file is read off disk: only secrow: handles, and for the header row the 'Bearer ' prefix survives as text beside the reference.
- Green in both browsers in CI before the epic closes.
close_reason: One Playwright spec watches both journeys end to end: a header value already holding 'Bearer ' takes a pasted token selected with real keys, stored through the field's own lock with the proposed name accepted; the Auth tab stores its whole field with nothing selected. Neither retypes the value — the create ask must arrive already holding it, asserted — and neither passes through Settings, guarded by a mutation observer. The request file is read off disk: only opaque secrow: handles, and 'Bearer ' survives as text beside the reference. Green in both browsers in the containerised suite.

title: T3 An explicit ask may raise the unlock; the passive one still offers
description:
The 'offers, never traps' rule was earned by a PASSIVE trigger: a person who typed '@' did not ask for a modal. A click on the lock is an explicit request, and answering it with a prompt is what was asked for. The owner's words: a person unlocks the vault only when asked, and today nothing asks.

This lands on top of nocx-vzdna, which is what makes the passive path answer at all.
acceptance_criteria:
- Vault SEALED plus a click on the lock: the unlock prompt is raised directly, and on success the panel opens with the list. On cancel or refusal nothing is lost — the typed value stays exactly where it was.
- Vault SEALED plus a bare '@': the offer row, unchanged. The two doors differ, and the difference is stated in the picker's source with the reason.
- Vault UNINITIALIZED: the setup offer, from both doors. Raising a setup wizard off a click is a decision this task does NOT take without asking.
- The lock is visible while the vault is sealed. A door that hides when it is needed is the defect this task exists to remove.
notes: OPEN QUESTION ANSWERED (owner, 2026-08-26): an UNINITIALIZED vault is OFFERED setup from the explicit click too, not only from the passive '@'. Same reasoning as unlock: the click is a request, and answering a request with silence is the defect. So the click may raise the setup surface; the passive '@' keeps its offer row.
close_reason: SecretPickerDoor passive|explicit: the lock raises requestUnseal/requestSetup and lands on the list; '@' keeps its offer rows, no assertion weakened. Cancel closes without re-offering and leaves the value untouched; session counter invalidates a late prompt. Landed 445cdc5a.

title: T2 The panel answers according to what the field holds
description: The lock opens the SAME panel '@' opens (frontend/src/ui/secret-picker.ts). What changes is what the panel offers, and the only inputs are: is the field empty, and is part of it selected. Never what the value looks like.
acceptance_criteria:
- Empty field: the existing secrets, narrowable by typing.
- Filled field: a create-from-this-value row ABOVE the same list, so the person can also replace what they typed with a secret they already have.
- Part of the value selected: a create-from-the-selection row, and it stores ONLY the selection and replaces only that span. 'Bearer <token>' keeps 'Bearer ' as text — asserted on the resulting field value.
- The row names what will be stored, truncated, so a person can tell the whole value from a selection before acting.
- No part of the value decides what is offered. A test proves a value that looks nothing like a credential gets the same rows.
- ONE panel: '@' and the lock reach the same code. No second picker, no third chooser.
close_reason: One panel: the lock opens the same SecretPicker '@' opens; store offer orthogonal to purpose, listRows() one row vocabulary, requestCreate(name, value?). Empty field narrows by typing, filled field closes on keystroke (both deliberate). 120 tests over the four files, 401 with neighbours. Landed 6bd8c3ea, merged to wA-integration.

title: T1 The value field grows one vault affordance, and the kit owns it
description:
The single owner of 'this value can live in the vault'. Every later task places THIS; none of them builds a second one.

It is a trailing action inside the field, rendered only while the field has focus. Read frontend/src/ui/README.md and list frontend/src/ui/ before choosing: a surface may PLACE a kit component and may never REPAINT it, and this is a variance TextField is missing rather than a new component beside it.
acceptance_criteria:
- A typed trailing-action variance on the kit's text field, used by SecretTextField and by the Auth tab alike. One module, one CSS file if it needs one, a stable identity class, a row in the kit README.
- Visible ONLY while the field is focused. The table at rest carries no extra chrome — asserted on a rendered table of several rows.
- Visible when the field is EMPTY and when it is filled, and when the vault is SEALED. Its meaning changes; its presence does not.
- Clicking it does not lose focus or the caret: a mousedown that blurs the field before the click lands is the defect this must not have. Asserted.
- It never inspects the value. Its presence is a function of focus alone.
close_reason: Trailing-action variance on the kit TextField, focus-only presence, selection reported to the caller; SecretTextField places it. 96 frontend tests green. Landed b015bb64.

title: The vault's door belongs to the field, not to the Auth tab
description:
`nocx-7mfwb` made a secret creatable from where a person stands, and the owner
found the door on his own screen within the hour: the Auth tab shows "Token"
twice, wears a mode switch nobody asked for, and every OTHER field — header,
parameter, URL, body — has no door at all except `@`, which is broken
(`nocx-vzdna`) and which carries only a NAME, never the value already typed.

So a person looking at `Authorization: Bearer t.Yixxxx` must copy the token,
clear the field, type `@`, create, and paste the value back into the dialog.
That is the detour `nocx-7mfwb` set out to remove, made shorter rather than
removed.

The cause is that the vault's door was attached to a TAB (Auth) instead of to
the thing that actually holds a credential — the value field. Three surfaces
then grew their own vocabulary for one question: `SecretSource`'s segmented
control, the `@` picker, and a bare `Store` button bolted beside a text box.

The design, decided with the owner on 2026-08-26:

ONE affordance, on the field, appearing only while that field is focused. The
table at rest is clean; the lock cannot be missed, because a token cannot be
typed into a field nobody focused. It opens THE SAME panel `@` opens — not a
second picker — and the panel adapts to what the field holds:

  empty            -> choose an existing secret
  filled           -> create from this value, OR replace it with an existing one
  part selected    -> create from the selection only

The selection rung is what makes `Bearer t.Yixxxx` work without guessing where
the scheme prefix ends: guessing is the credential detection `nocx-0khco`
ruled out, and a selection is the person saying it themselves.

And the "offers, never traps" rule is kept where it was earned and dropped
where it was not: `@` is a PASSIVE keystroke and still offers a row; the lock
is an EXPLICIT click and may raise the unlock prompt directly, because that is
what was asked for. The owner's words: a person unlocks the vault only when
asked, and today nothing asks.
acceptance_criteria:
DONE WHEN a person holding a token in ANY request value field — a header, a query parameter, the URL, the body, or the Auth tab — can put it in the vault without leaving the request and without retyping it: focus the field, press the one affordance it shows, accept a proposed name, and find the field holding a reference chip while the request file on disk holds only a secrow: handle. One Playwright spec watches a header value and the Auth tab do it, and neither journey retypes the value or passes through Settings.

Also true when it is done:

- ONE control answers 'where does this value come from' everywhere. SecretSource's segmented control is gone, and with it the duplicated 'Token' label; the connections editor, the endpoints page and the Auth tab place the same field.
- The affordance opens THE SAME panel '@' opens. No second picker, no third chooser.
- The panel adapts to the field: empty offers the existing secrets; filled offers create-from-this-value beside them; a selection offers create-from-the-selection.
- A selection stores ONLY the selection and replaces only that span, so 'Bearer <token>' keeps its prefix as text. No part of the value is ever inspected to decide what to offer.
- The lock is visible when the vault is SEALED, and clicking it raises the unlock prompt. Typing '@' keeps the passive offer row instead.
- No content sniffing anywhere: non-empty is the whole condition, exactly as nocx-0khco and nocx-7mfwb already ruled.

Deliberately out: detecting a pasted credential and offering to store it; ranking or hiding rows by kind; the terminal prompt's handoff to Settings, which is legitimate because there is no form there.
close_reason: A person holding a token in any request value field can put it in the vault without leaving the request and without retyping it. Six children closed, three of them product defects the epic's own walk uncovered: the lock proposed no name, the proposal collided with a taken one, and the offer row could not be reached by mouse. Full containerised suite: 428 passed, 1 failed — agent-ask, a known flake filed as nocx-quqbz and unrelated. Go jobs remain red locally on a tree that changes zero Go files; filed separately.

title: The carrier seam: one effect kernel behind an interface, and today's loop becomes one carrier
acceptance_criteria: The policy kernel — schema validation, classification, policy decision, scope check, approval escalation, ledger attempt, capability narrowing, execution, egress screening — is reachable as a carrier-neutral call, not only as an eino middleware. The eino path becomes a thin adapter over it and every existing assistant test passes unchanged. A second carrier can reach the kernel without importing eino. Asserted: the same effect, proposed through either carrier, produces the same policy decision and the same ledger shape.
close_reason: Landed with the experiment merge (0da79e69, merged as fe976555 into feat/ai-assistant): the effect kernel stopped being an eino middleware and became something any carrier can reach — internal/assistant/kernel.go behind an interface, with einoadapter.go as the eino-facing shim. The seam survived nocx-d6gn4.14's deletion of both composing carriers, which is the check that it was a seam and not a switch.

title: The graph carrier: a declarative effect DAG with CEL expressions, shown whole before it runs
acceptance_criteria: A question needing two dependent steps is answered in one model turn with the method set to graph. The approval shows the WHOLE validated plan and its maximum envelope before anything runs, then the resolved effect at each gate plus the remaining budget. Nodes: let, if, bounded foreach, effect, format, error handling; CEL only inside pure expressions; cycles rejected structurally; every collection carries a declared bound, including host-returned ones. Same ledger shape as the other carriers: one action entry per effect, each joined to its turn. Asserted end to end through the real backend.
notes: SUPERSEDED, 2026-08-27, WITHOUT a measurement of its own — and that is recorded rather than dressed up. The owner's call: a declared tool call is faster, and another day of correcting our own defects before this carrier could be measured fairly is not worth what it could return. What we saw live was the model looping fifteen rounds and concluding the tool was broken, and the cause was OURS: a step's arguments are CEL expressions, the compile failure hands back CEL's column number instead of the fix, and the one example in the description writes its args as {...} — omitting the exact thing that breaks. Removal is nocx-d6gn4.14; the measurement that decided the program carrier is in nocx-d6gn4.8.
close_reason: Shipped on feat/tool-experiment (d0765060), merged as fe976555, and removed by nocx-d6gn4.14 (b68e280b). Removed WITHOUT a measurement of its own, deliberately and on cost — nocx-d6gn4.14 records that this is not evidence the plan carrier is bad, only that we had not finished telling it what it was: its one example omitted the CEL string-literal rule that breaks it, and its compile failure returned CEL's column error rather than the fix.

title: The sleep sweep traded 78 failure diagnostics for the word 'timeout'
description:
The nocx-td6d4.2-.6 sweep converted 138 duration-based waits to testwait waits. 78 of those
call sites had a t.Fatalf carrying state — the accepted kernel events, the shell output so
far, the bootstrap stages that did arrive, the goroutine counts before and after — and the
conversion replaced it with "timed out waiting for <description>".

That trade was not deliberate. It happened because internal/testwait had no way to attach
state to a failure, so the only shape available to a worker converting a hand-rolled loop was
to drop the message. The gap in the helper is now closed: WaitForDetail and
WaitForTimeoutDetail take a func() string evaluated only on failure. One call site,
internal/proc/group_test.go's waitGone, is already restored — it was the only one the `unused`
linter could see, because its diagnostic lived in a named helper (procField) that the
conversion orphaned. The other 77 inlined their state into the Fatalf, so nothing flagged
them.

## Why this matters more here than it would elsewhere

The packages that lost the most are the ones that cannot be verified outside a container on a
Linux workstation: shellintegration 22, transport 14, app 11, ssh 9, and then vault 4, pty 4,
git/local 4, transport/control 4, discovery 2, transport/outbound 2, proc 1, lifecyclepub 1.
For those, the failure message IS the evidence — there is no local rerun to fall back on.

This was measured, not supposed. On 2026-08-26 a red container gate reported:

    agent_enrol_shell_test.go:51: kernel never accepted "complete";
      accepted=[{1 hello …} {2 prompt_ready …} {3 start …}]
      output="\x1b]636;H;…"

and that list of accepted events plus the raw shell output is what distinguished a starved
machine from a real defect. The same failure today would read "timed out waiting for the
kernel to accept complete" and would not be judgeable at all. Given that telling starvation
from a defect is the daily work on this machine, the sweep has made the gate harder to read
in exactly the packages where reading it is hardest.

## Steps to Reproduce

    git log -p <the nocx-td6d4.2-.6 commit> -- internal/ \
      | grep '^-' | grep -E 't\.(Fatalf|Errorf)\(.*%[dsvq]'

78 lines. Each is a diagnostic that no longer exists.

## Acceptance Criteria

Every wait whose removed failure message carried state has that state back, through
WaitForDetail or WaitForTimeoutDetail, evaluated lazily so it costs nothing on the passing
path. The grep above, run against the restoring commit's parent, finds nothing that is still
missing. No new bare `t.Fatalf("timed out …")` is introduced where the pre-sweep code said
more than that.

Deliberately out: inventing diagnostics for waits that never had one. This restores what was
removed; it does not audit the suite for messages it never had.
close_reason: 78 deleted diagnostics audited against the restoring commits; 83 Detail closures now stand in those files and every sampled one carries the same state. The only deleted messages still absent are ones that carried none: 'pty start: %v' (a setup error, not a wait) and two generic 'timed out waiting for %s' forms that testwait prints from the description. Landed as 77ffdcee, 39c52646, 5c04e7ef, 022b6ad0, 348fc3d1, 3d0b8ada.

title: The assistant can change a file, and an edit written against a stale read is refused rather than applied
description:
## Where this came from

The owner, 2026-08-26, driving the real assistant: "нам явно не достает
инструмента file.edit". Today the registry declares five tools and the only one
that can WRITE anything is `run` — so every edit the assistant makes is a shell
command it composed itself (`echo ... > file`, sed, a heredoc). That is the worst
of both: the most destructive effect class for the most ordinary task, an
approval that describes a shell command rather than a change, and a ledger entry
that says a command ran rather than that a file was edited.

## Take the SNAPSHOT TAG from omp, not the patch language

`~/repos/oh-my-pi`, `docs/tools/edit.md` and `packages/hashline/`. Its edit tool
has an elaborate line-anchored patch language — blocks resolved with tree-sitter,
cut/paste registers, a Lark grammar for constrained decoding. That is a large
system and most of it is NOT what we need first.

The load-bearing idea is one line of it: **every section must copy a four-hex
snapshot tag from the latest `read` result, and hashline rejects an untagged or
stale anchored edit at application time.** That is optimistic concurrency for a
model-authored edit — the edit declares WHICH VERSION of the file it was written
against, and the host refuses it if the world moved.

AND THAT IS ALREADY OUR OPEN QUESTION. nocx-d6gn4.1 asks every effect to
revalidate the world it assumed immediately before it runs, and the third review
round said the bead was underdefined precisely because a check followed by an
effect is another race — what closes it is a STABLE IDENTITY TOKEN the executor
can bind ATOMICALLY to the effect. A file's snapshot tag is exactly that token,
for exactly one effect class. This epic is where that idea gets built for real
rather than argued about, and nocx-d6gn4.1 should generalise from what is learned
here instead of the other way round.

## Deliberately out, for now

- The full hashline language: blocks, registers, MV, REM, the Lark grammar.
  Start with the smallest contract that can express a real edit and be refused
  when stale.
- Constrained decoding. It is a nocx-d6gn4.6 question and it is not settled.
- Creating files and whole-file overwrite, unless the smallest useful contract
  turns out to need them — say which and why.
- AST-aware anchors.
acceptance_criteria:
## What a person can do that they could not before

Ask the assistant to change a file — "rename this function", "add the missing
error case" — and have it edit the file directly instead of composing a shell
one-liner with sed or a heredoc, which is what it does today because `run` is the
only way it can write anything at all.

## Success Criteria

- An edit lands on a real file through a declared tool, end to end through the
  real backend, and the ledger records it as its own effect rather than as a
  shell command. Asserted.
- AN EDIT WRITTEN AGAINST A STALE READ IS REFUSED. The model must carry a token
  from the read it based the edit on, and application fails if the file changed
  underneath it. Asserted by a test that edits, mutates the file behind the
  assistant's back, and applies: the apply must fail and say so, and the file
  must be untouched.
- The refusal is a tool result the model can act on, not a run failure.
- The effect class is right: an edit is a mutation, and the approval names the
  FILE and shows what will change, not just the tool.
- What is deliberately out is stated in the bead.
notes:
## 2026-08-28 — what a donor review established, before any code

Three findings that change how this is built. All verified in ~/repos/oh-my-pi
in this session, not taken on trust.

1. HASHLINE AS SHIPPED WOULD VIOLATE THIS EPIC'S OWN CRITERION. packages/
hashline/src/patcher.ts:739 — on a tag mismatch, head/tail-only inserts are
applied anyway with a warning ('position-stable'), and anchored edits go to
recovery.tryRecover, which remaps anchors onto unchanged live lines. So omp
recovers from a stale read rather than refusing it. Take the tag; do not take
the recovery. Any byte changed -> refuse, and no normalisation of trailing
whitespace, BOM or line endings when TESTING staleness.

2. THE 4-HEX TAG IS TOO WEAK FOR STRICT CAS. Sixteen bits; omp already carries
collision-handling logic for it. Use an opaque run-local snapshot id backed by
the exact stored bytes, or a >=128-bit digest of exact bytes plus canonical
file identity.

3. MULTI-SECTION IS NOT ATOMIC IN THE DONOR, whatever its README says.
patcher.ts:266, verbatim: 'Commits are non-atomic: when a later write fails,
the sections before it are already on disk.' The preflight is of PREPARATION
only. So: ONE FILE PER CALL. Sections with [PATH#TAG], named registers, MV and
REM are dropped — they are what produces that non-atomicity, and they break
'one call, one resource', which the grant scope check depends on.

## The shape

    { path, revision, patch }

path stays a top-level argument so the policy can scope it; revision binds the
call to the exact read. Ops in v1, and no more: PUT N.=M: / PUT <N: / PUT >N: /
CUT N.=M.

SEEN-LINES: only lines actually DISPLAYED under that revision may be addressed.
Editing lines the model has not seen is the off-by-memory mistake that mangles
files.

## files.read is a precondition and is not ready

internal/assistant/execute.go:26 — filesReadWindowBytes = 64<<10, a fixed
first-64KiB window; the schema takes only 'path', with no range arguments. And
contracts/tools/files.read.schema.json describes window.start as 'First line of
the window returned, IN BYTES' — the contract mixes line and byte vocabulary,
which is its own small bug. read and edit land together: stable-read detection,
canonical file identity, strong revision, line-window addressing, numbered
output, seen-line recording, explicit UTF-8 and line-ending policy.

## A second row, and two that are deferred with a reason

files.create (create-if-absent) earns a row: the shell cannot do it safely.

files.move and files.delete are DEFERRED, and the reason matters because it
decides whether they ever arrive. Not 'run already does mv and rm' — that
argument would equally condemn files.read (cat) and git.status (git status),
and run's own description says to reach for it when no narrower tool will do.
The real distinction is SCOPE: run is session-scoped and its approval shows an
opaque shell program, while files.delete(path, revision) is path-scoped and
means 'delete exactly the canonical object whose bytes I observed' — quoting,
expansion, aliases, symlinks and helper programs stay shell semantics the
policy cannot see. They arrive once multi-resource extraction exists
(nocx-6m7wh). If they would only be os.Remove and os.Rename with prettier JSON,
they should not be built at all.
close_reason: A person can ask the assistant to change a file and it edits directly instead of composing a shell one-liner; an edit written against a stale read is refused with the file untouched, proven end to end by TestAsk_StaleEditIsRefusedAsToolResult.

title: The answer lives in the overlay, then takes its seat in the scrollback
description:
The answer appears where the question was asked, and lands in the right place afterwards.

While the program runs the overlay holds the answer as well as the question. It is a VIEW:
the durable record is the ledger entry it always was (ADR-0039, a turn is one entry). When
the command ends and the pane returns to the ordinary flow, the turn takes its seat in the
scrollback AFTER the command's own block — and if the answer is still streaming at that
moment it goes on streaming in that seat.

It must be drawn by `answer-body.ts`, the same function the live block and the restore
already draw through. A second prose renderer beside it is the defect two epics
(nocx-pp3y, nocx-v0ai) were spent unwinding, and it is what this criterion exists to
forbid.

## Acceptance Criteria

• The answer streams into the overlay and is readable there while the program runs.
• When the command ends, the turn is in the scrollback after that command's block — never
above the rows it was painting. Asserted on the order of the children.
• A turn still streaming when the command ends continues in its seat with no gap and no
duplicate.
• The prose is produced by answer-body.ts: asserted, not asserted by inspection.
• The ledger entry is the same one either way — nothing about where it was drawn reaches
the record.
close_reason: Done in 9982d5fa (merged 72d8fef7). The turn is ONE DOM node throughout: openAnswer parents it into the pane overlay while the program paints, and when the command reaches a terminal state the same node is reparented directly after that command's block — reparenting rather than rebuilding is what keeps a still-streaming AnswerBody and the entry identity intact. Asserted on the ORDER OF THE CHILDREN (indexOf(command) < indexOf(answer)), never on geometry, because jsdom does not lay out; on the same [data-answer-body] node before and after the move with its text concatenated, which is the no-gap-no-duplicate criterion; and on [data-md] to show answer-body.ts drew the prose rather than a second renderer. dataset.entryId is unchanged by the move, so nothing about where it was drawn reaches the record (ADR-0039). Review found one defect on the way in and it was the reachable one: hiding the editor when the turn is accepted also removed the Escape that ended the freeze, so a person asking inside htop was left with a frozen screen and no exit until the program died. The worker proved it with a red test, then routed Escape through the document handler that already owns keys the editor's own listener cannot see — not a second Escape owner — and the answer goes on streaming over the live screen. 233 tests green on the merged tree (terminal-content + agent-ask).

title: session.read in that turn reads the pinned frame
description:
`session.read` in the turn asked over a frozen screen returns the PINNED frame, not the live
buffer. That is what makes the person and the model discuss the same thing, which is the
entire reason the question is asked at that moment.

It also removes the starvation half of nocx-2ryxf.3 for this path: reading a snapshot cannot
wait on the capture fence that a repainting TUI never lets settle
(frontend/src/frame/capture-identity.ts awaitSettled). It does NOT close that bead — a live
read taken any other way still goes through the fence, and if `unsettledWrites` can leak the
pane wedges silently. Read it before starting.

## Acceptance Criteria

• A `session.read` of the current screen inside such a turn returns the pinned frame, and a
second call in the same turn returns the SAME frame.
• A read in a turn with no overlay open still reads the live screen — the pin is scoped to
the turn that pinned it and does not leak into the next question.
• The read answers while a TUI is repainting, in a bound a person would wait for: the `top`
case is the assertion, not an illustration.
• The renderer's honest `failed` outcome still exists for a frame that cannot be produced.
close_reason: Done in 8c5e41d4 (merged 8480ef1b). captureLiveFrame serves a whole-screen read from the turn's pinned frame; the frame captured at the summon binds to the generated askId at the submit seam, so the DISPLAY freeze still ends with the overlay while the READ pin ends when that run reaches a terminal state — the two lifetimes were one until review found the Escape-mid-answer path. Seven tests, each on a criterion: two reads in one turn return the same frame; a turn with no overlay reads live; a repainting top answers without waiting on the capture fence; region reads stay live; the renderer's failed outcome survives; the pin holds through Escape until the turn ends; and an unsettled turn's pin is cleared by the next question even when that question has no summon — the leak-into-the-next-question path review found second. Hook green with no bypass.

title: The screen freezes while the box is open, and the program is never told
description:
The screen freezes when the box opens, and thaws when it closes.

At the summon the renderer pins the current frame — the existing CapturedFrame /
mintLiveFrame machinery, not a new one — and the pane shows that frame while the overlay is
up. Bytes keep arriving and keep being parsed: the pty is untouched, nothing accumulates,
and no flow control is invented. Holding the PARSE was considered and rejected — it would
put backpressure on the pty.

The freeze must be VISIBLE. A person whose `top` stopped updating with nothing saying why
reads it as the program having hung, and that is worse than not freezing at all.

## Acceptance Criteria

• The display holds one frame from the summon until the overlay closes, and is live again
afterwards — asserted on what the pane shows, not on a flag.
• The program keeps writing throughout and none of its output is lost: what it wrote during
the freeze is on screen after the thaw.
• The pty was never paused and the program was never signalled.
• The frozen state is visible and says what it is, in the kit's vocabulary.
• Nothing is frozen when no overlay is open.
close_reason: The display pins the frame the renderer produced at the summon and thaws when the overlay closes; the parse is never held, so the pty keeps its pace and the program is never signalled. Asserted on what the pane shows, not on a flag: the pinned view is in the DOM, bytes fired during the freeze reach renderer.write and are on the live grid after the thaw, disposal removes marker, frame and the temporary containing-block style. The frozen state says what it is in the kit's Badge. Landed in f97fc466, merged in 39f36456. Not covered here and deliberately: the whole-sentence e2e, which is now nocx-7l4ex.5 and blocks the epic.

title: The overlay exists over a running command and over a full-screen program
