description:
The container, and the first half of nocx-og42r. Today `summonEditor`
(frontend/src/terminal-content.ts) refuses whenever `lifecycle.buffer !== 'normal'`, so
inside `htop`, `vim` or `less` the chord does nothing and says nothing; and over an ordinary
running command the editor it summons enters the layout, which is what put the turn above
the live rows.

This bead builds the box and nothing else: no freeze, no pinned frame, no answer placement.
Those are its siblings and they are sequenced behind it.

The overlay floats above the pane and never enters the layout — the grid keeps every row, the
pty is never resized and the program is told nothing. It is up only while a command is
running or a full-screen program owns the pane, and it goes when that ends. At a prompt the
in-flow editor is untouched.

It is a kit component (`frontend/src/ui/`), not a hand-rolled div in the surface: read
frontend/src/ui/README.md first and check whether an existing overlay/stack primitive
already answers this — `ui/overlay/stack.ts` exists and terminal-content already imports
pushOverlay/popOverlay.

## Acceptance Criteria

• Inside a full-screen program the chord opens the box; the ⋮ door reaches the same place;
neither ever fails silently.
• Over an ordinary running command the same box appears, and the pane's grid keeps the row
count it had — asserted on the renderer's dimensions before and after.
• The pty is not resized: asserted with a program that redraws on resize, and the assertion
is that it does not redraw.
• Escape dismisses it and the keys reach the program again, asserted with a key the program
consumes.
• When the command ends the overlay goes.
• One draft and one target: what is typed is what is sent, and the target is the assistant.
• At a prompt nothing changes.
close_reason: merged as 163c0d48; the same CommandEditor placed by data-placement plus a stylesheet rule, no new component, grid rows and pty untouched (asserted on renderer dimensions and a resize-recording fake), the pane's horizontal padding is now one custom property both rules read. Gate green.

title: TestAgentAsk_TwoConcurrentStreamsInterleaveWithoutCorrupting fails only in company, and fast
description:
`internal/transport`'s `TestAgentAsk_TwoConcurrentStreamsInterleaveWithoutCorrupting` fails
intermittently, and only when the whole package runs. It has no time.Sleep of its own, so it
is not the timing class nocx-td6d4 is clearing — it is interference between tests inside the
package, which is a different defect and needs its own investigation.

## What was measured, 2026-08-26

- Whole package, four observations: FAIL at 0.16s, FAIL at 1.31s, then ok at 95.408s and
  ok at 93.445s.
- The test alone, `-count=5`: passes on origin/main (1.164s) and on a feature branch (2.028s).
- Whole package on `origin/main` and on the branch under review: both ok, same session.

The failure is FAST — 0.16s — which rules out the starvation that explains most container
failures on this machine: a starved test times out, it does not fail in a sixth of a second.
And isolation cannot reproduce it at all. Both facts point the same way: something another
test in the package leaves behind, or races with, changes this test's outcome.

The worker who audited internal/transport for nocx-td6d4.3 was given this finding, looked,
and reported that the test contains no direct sleep and that their run did not reproduce the
interference. So it survives the sleep conversion and is still unexplained.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `go test ./internal/transport/ -count=1` (the whole package; the failure needs the package).
2. Repeat. It fails a minority of the time, fast.
3. `go test ./internal/transport/ -run TestAgentAsk_TwoConcurrentStreamsInterleaveWithoutCorrupting -count=5`
   passes every time, which is the point.

## Where to start

`-shuffle=on` to see whether an ordering makes it deterministic, then bisect the package by
running the suspect against progressively smaller subsets. Package-level state shared between
tests — a registry, a global, a reused port, a package-scoped broker — is the usual owner of
this shape.

## A repro handle, found 2026-08-26 after this bead was filed

`go test ./internal/transport/... -count=3 -race -timeout 40m` reproduces it far more
readily than a plain package run. Third observation, on the nocx-td6d4.3 branch:

    --- FAIL: TestAgentAsk_TwoConcurrentStreamsInterleaveWithoutCorrupting (0.64s)
    FAIL  github.com/shady2k/nocx/internal/transport  609.105s

All three observations are fast — 0.16s, 1.31s, 0.64s — against a package that takes 95s to
run and 600s under -count=3 -race. Whatever this is, it decides early.

Note the wall time: three race-enabled runs of this package exceed `go test`'s default 10m
timeout on this machine, so a run without `-timeout` reports `panic: test timed out` and
hides whatever actually failed. Use an explicit `-timeout` when hunting this.

Also: the worker who converted internal/transport's sleeps for nocx-td6d4.3 was given this
bead, read it, and reported the test has no time.Sleep of its own and that their runs did not
reproduce it. So the sleep conversion neither caused nor cured it.

## Acceptance Criteria

The cause is named, and the fix is the cause's, not the symptom's: either the shared state
gets an owner and a reset, or the tests stop sharing it. The whole package passes
`go test ./internal/transport/ -count=10` on a machine under ordinary shared load. A run with
`-shuffle=on` passes ten times as well, since an ordering-dependent pass is the same defect
still hiding.
close_reason: duplicate of nocx-sxvnh, which found the cause and is fixed on feat/orchestration (4693d721). Not interference between tests: the fake handed out its two scripts by ARRIVAL ORDER, and agent.ask streams on its own goroutine, so which run reached Ask first was the scheduler's choice. That explains every observation here — the failure is fast because nothing times out, it needs company because more goroutines make B win sometimes, and isolation could not reproduce it at -count=5 (it took -count=60 to see 2 failures). The fake now keys its scripts on the ask's question.

title: The vault's Close grew a second end, and its timer grew a test-only seam, inside a test cleanup
description:
While converting internal/vault's timing-dependent tests (nocx-td6d4.5), the worker changed
production code in internal/vault/vault.go. The change is sound and is kept, but it was not
authorised by the task and it lands in the one package AGENTS.md singles out as deserving a
second reader. This bead is that reading.

## What changed, and why it is right

Close() now waits for the auto-seal goroutine to exit:

    v.Seal()
    <-v.autoSealDone      // new

Before this, Close() closed autoSealQuit and returned without waiting. The existing comment
on Close already said "Owning the goroutine's lifetime is the point" — and only one end of
that lifetime was owned. This is the same principle nocx-rtg0.6 states as "every interval has
two ends". The defect was real and observable: TestClose_StopsTheAutoSealGoroutine failed
repeatedly before the change and passes after it.

## What also changed, and costs something

To make the auto-seal timer drivable without sleeping, the worker added:

  - an autoSealTimer interface with a realAutoSealTimer implementation and an
    autoSealTimerFactory field, so tests can inject a fake timer;
  - autoSealTimerArmed and autoSealArmEpoch fields on Vault, maintained under v.mu and
    documented as existing "to expose timer lifecycle state to package tests".

That is production surface whose only consumer is a test. It is the standard answer to
"a timer cannot be waited on", and the alternative was the sleep this epic exists to remove
— but it is a design decision, made inside a test cleanup, by the same agent that then wrote
the tests exercising it. AGENTS.md rule 4 is explicit that for code where a defect is costly
— it names the vault first — the implementer should not be the only author of its tests.

## The hazard the change introduces

`<-v.autoSealDone` in Close() is unconditional, and autoSealDone is only initialised by New().
A Vault built as a bare `&Vault{}` literal and then Closed would block forever with no
diagnostic. Today nothing does that: the two bare literals live in contentkey_test.go
(TestDefaultProvider) and never call Close, which was verified. So this is a latent hazard,
not a live defect — but it is precisely the shape AGENTS.md records from 2026-07-30, when a
Setup that returned four times while holding its mutex deadlocked everything after it and had
zero coverage on all four returns.

## Steps to Reproduce

The hazard, not a current failure:

1. Construct a Vault without New — `v := &Vault{}`.
2. Call v.Close().
3. It blocks forever on a nil channel receive; the test hangs to its 10-minute panic with no
   message naming the cause.

## Acceptance Criteria

A reader who did not write the change has read it and either confirmed it or replaced it.
Close() cannot block forever on a Vault that was not built by New — either because the receive
is guarded, or because constructing a Vault outside New is made impossible, or because the
reader established that it genuinely cannot happen and said so in the code. The auto-seal
timer's test-only surface is either accepted deliberately with a comment saying so, or
replaced with a seam that does not put test state on the production struct.

Landed as part of the nocx-td6d4.5 branch; see internal/vault/vault.go.
close_reason: Second reading landed as 3d0b8ada. It did not merely confirm the unsanctioned change: it kept the Close-waits-for-the-goroutine invariant but expressed it as a WaitGroup, whose zero value already answers for a Vault that never started one, and removed autoSealTimerArmed/autoSealArmEpoch from the production struct as a second owner of a fact the timer already held — a mirror that disagreed with the timer between creation and the flag being set. Both ends of the interval now have a test, each verified by mutation. Two defects found and deliberately not fixed: nocx-cglud and nocx-kyp2j.

title: Ask about a full-screen program without leaving it: an overlay over a frozen screen
description:
Decided with the owner, 2026-08-26, in four questions after he ran `top`, could not reach
the assistant from inside a full-screen program, and found the turn drawn ABOVE the rows the
program was still painting.

## What a person gets

They ask the assistant about the program they are looking at — `top`, `htop`, `vim`, `less`
— without leaving it, read the answer where they asked it, and get the program back
untouched when they are done.

## The decisions, so nothing here is re-argued

1. THE QUESTION BOX IS AN OVERLAY. It floats above the pane and never enters the layout, so
   the grid is not resized and the program is never told anything. This is what dissolves
   nocx-92gfl.3 (shrink the block, keep `top` on top): with nothing entering the layout there
   is nothing to shrink and no SIGWINCH to send.

2. IT EXISTS ONLY WHILE THERE IS SOMETHING TO ASK OVER — a command is running, or a
   full-screen program owns the pane. When the command finishes the overlay goes. At the
   prompt the ordinary in-flow editor stays exactly as it is.

   That is TWO surfaces for one meaning, deliberately, and the boundary is what keeps it
   honest: exactly one of them is possible at any moment and the PANE'S STATE chooses, never
   the person. One draft, one target, one prose renderer; only the container differs.

3. THE DISPLAY FREEZES, THE PARSE DOES NOT. At the summon the renderer pins the current
   frame (the existing CapturedFrame / mintLiveFrame machinery) and the pane shows it while
   the overlay is up. Bytes keep arriving and keep being parsed — the pty is untouched, no
   backlog accumulates, and no flow control is invented. Holding the PARSE would put
   backpressure on the pty and was rejected.

   The freeze must be VISIBLE, or a person reads it as the program having hung.

4. `session.read` IN THAT TURN READS THE PINNED FRAME. The person and the model then discuss
   the same thing, which is the whole reason the question is asked at all. It also removes
   the starvation in nocx-2ryxf.3: reading a snapshot cannot wait on a fence that a
   repainting TUI never lets settle.

5. THE OVERLAY HOLDS THE ANSWER TOO, and it is a VIEW, never a second owner. The durable
   record is the ledger entry it always was (ADR-0039: a turn is one entry). When the command
   ends and the pane returns to the ordinary flow, the turn takes its seat in the scrollback
   in the right order — and if the answer is still streaming at that moment it goes on
   streaming there. It is drawn by `answer-body.ts`, the same function the block and the
   restore already draw through; a second prose renderer beside it is the defect two epics
   have already been spent unwinding.

## What this replaces

- nocx-og42r (the chord does nothing inside a full-screen program, and there is no other
  door) is this epic's first half.
- nocx-92gfl.3 (the turn appears above the live rows) is dissolved by decision 1 and closes
  with that reason rather than being built.

## Success Criteria

A person inside `htop` presses the chord, gets a box, asks "what is this process at the
top", and reads the answer without the program being resized, redrawn or interrupted —
and quits `htop` normally afterwards.

## Acceptance Criteria

• Inside a full-screen program the gesture opens somewhere to type. It never vanishes
silently, and there is a mouse path as well as the chord.
• The buffer is NOT resized and the program is not told anything: asserted with a program
that redraws on resize, and the assertion is that it does not redraw.
• The screen is visibly frozen while the overlay is up and live again when it closes, and
the pty was never paused — a program writing throughout keeps writing and its later output
is not lost.
• `session.read` in that turn returns the pinned frame, and a second call in the same turn
returns the same frame.
• The answer appears in the overlay and, when the command ends, in the scrollback AFTER the
command's own block — never above the rows it was painting. A turn still streaming when the
command ends continues in its seat.
• One draft and one target: what was typed in the overlay is what is sent, and nothing is
lost when the container changes.
• Escape gives the keys back to the program, and the overlay says so where the person is
looking.
• At a prompt nothing changes: the in-flow editor is untouched.

## Deliberately out

• Making the in-flow editor an overlay too. One surface for everything was considered and
rejected: it is a rewrite of the terminal's main input — chips, secrets, suggestions, the
shell/agent target and the pane's geometry — for no gain the boundary above does not
already give.
• Resizing the alternate buffer.

title: T6 One check watches a person do it, end to end
acceptance_criteria:
- One Playwright spec, on the real backend and a real vault set up through the product's own pages: paste a token into the Auth tab, save it through the offer, accept the proposed name, send the request, and assert the server received the value.
- The same spec does the header journey through '@' and the in-place ask.
- Neither journey passes through Settings, and the spec asserts that rather than merely not doing it: reaching Settings mid-journey fails the test.
- The request file is read off disk and holds only secrow: handles — not the value, not the display name.
- The epic is not closed until this is green in both browsers in CI.
close_reason: Landed in 65fb7587 + 2d559a8b on wA-integration. Verified: full frontend suite 5046 green, ci-frontend green, ci-linux green (134 pkgs, both keyring variants), full e2e 420 passed both browsers with every secret spec green.

title: T3 The Auth tab offers to save the token that is already typed
description: The regression this epic exists for: 5d636b55 shipped this, 113e1f26 removed it.
acceptance_criteria:
- While the Auth value field is in 'Type a new one' mode and holds a non-empty value, an action beside it offers to put that value in the vault. It opens T1's ask with the value already carried.
- The offer is UNCONDITIONAL on content: no detection of what looks like a credential, which nocx-0khco ruled out and this does not reopen. Non-empty is the whole condition.
- Nothing is moved or hidden without the person acting: typing a token and doing nothing leaves it exactly where it was typed, in the file, as the owner's decision of 2026-08-23 requires.
- After the ask succeeds the field holds the reference and renders the chip, the mode is 'Use existing secret', and the request file on disk holds the secrow: handle and neither the value nor the display name — asserted on bytes.
- The same action exists for Basic's Password field and carries the password kind.
- The kit component SecretValueField has a non-test caller again; a test asserts the offer is reachable from the state a person starts in.
close_reason: Landed in 65fb7587 + 2d559a8b on wA-integration. Verified: full frontend suite 5046 green, ci-frontend green, ci-linux green (134 pkgs, both keyring variants), full e2e 420 passed both browsers with every secret spec green.

title: T2 The name and the kind are proposed from where the person is standing
description: Spec 4.2 of the naming discussion (2026-08-26). The rungs matter more than the happy path: the owner's own screenshot has a URL under an environment, so the domain is frequently NOT knowable at create time.
acceptance_criteria:
- A header value proposes '<Header-Name> for <domain>' — the header's own name and the request's host.
- A query parameter proposes the same shape from the parameter's name.
- The Auth tab proposes '<domain> token' for Bearer and '<domain> password' for Basic.
- When the host cannot be known — the URL is or contains a variable that is not resolved at that moment — it falls back to the folder and request name ('tinkoff token'), and never to an empty string or a placeholder like 'secret 1'.
- Kind: Bearer gives api-token, Basic gives password, every other field gives api-token.
- Derivation is a pure function with its own table-driven test, including every fallback rung and a URL that is entirely a variable.
- The proposal is metadata only: a test asserts that no part of the value can reach the name, including when the value is short enough to look like a word.
close_reason: Landed in 65fb7587 + 2d559a8b on wA-integration. Verified: full frontend suite 5046 green, ci-frontend green, ci-linux green (134 pkgs, both keyring variants), full e2e 420 passed both browsers with every secret spec green.

title: T1 One create ask: the value, a proposed name, a derived kind
description: The single owner of 'a secret is created here'. Both doors in T2 and T3 open THIS, so the product has one answer to what creating a credential means, reached from two places — the mistake nocx-5dfa5 named and this epic must not repeat.
acceptance_criteria:
- One ask, in the kit's existing dialog vocabulary, that takes a secret VALUE through SecretValueField (frontend/src/ui/secret-value-field.tsx) — the component this product already declares as the one control a secret value is typed into, and which currently has no caller outside its own test.
- It opens with a NAME already filled in and a KIND already chosen. Both are editable; neither is a required answer.
- Kind comes from the vault's closed vocabulary in internal/vault/meta.go. No second list.
- A name that collides with one the vault already holds is said so before the write, with a proposal to disambiguate. It is not silently duplicated: the handle is the identity, but two identical rows in a chooser is a defect a person cannot untangle.
- The name is never derived from the material, and never begins with 'secrow:' (vault.validateSecretName already refuses that; this must not be able to reach it).
- On success the caller receives the handle; the ask does not itself decide what to do with it.
- Unit tests drive the ask directly: a proposed name accepted unchanged, a proposed name edited, a collision, and a sealed vault.
close_reason: Landed in 65fb7587 + 2d559a8b on wA-integration. Verified: full frontend suite 5046 green, ci-frontend green, ci-linux green (134 pkgs, both keyring variants), full e2e 420 passed both browsers with every secret spec green.

title: A secret is made where you are standing, not in Settings
description:
The workbench can USE a secret everywhere and can MINT one nowhere, and that is a regression rather than a gap that was never filled.

5d636b55 (nocx-m4cyq) put SecretValueField on the Auth tab: a person pasted a token, pressed Store, the value went to the vault and the file kept only the name. 113e1f26 — T5 of nocx-0khco — removed it and put a plain TextField in its place. SecretValueField now has NO caller outside its own test; the deadcode ratchet is Go-only, so nothing said so.

What is left is a detour, and our own e2e spec documents it as the expected journey (e2e/api-secret-in-any-field.spec.ts, 'The create handoff returns to Settings. Come back to the request, ask again'): type '@', choose create, get thrown to Settings, type the value there, navigate back, find the request, type '@' again. That is exactly what the owner's decision of 2026-08-23 forbids — if the product will not push people into the vault, the vault must be the EASIER path from where they stand, not a longer one.

The reason the handoff exists is written honestly in the picker: requestCreate carries a NAME only, because 'a secret needs a name AND a value, and a floating row over the prompt is not where a value gets typed'. True of the terminal. Not true of a form with fields, and the conclusion was carried across without the premise.
acceptance_criteria:
DONE WHEN a person holding a token can, without leaving the request: paste it into the Auth tab's Token field, press one action, accept a name the product proposed, and find the field holding a reference chip while the request file on disk holds only a secrow: handle — and can do the same from a header value, reached by '@'. One Playwright spec watches both, and neither journey passes through Settings.

Also true when it is done:
- The name is PROPOSED, not demanded: derived from where the person is standing (the header's name and the request's domain; the folder and request name when the domain is a variable that is not resolved), always editable, never derived from the material itself, and never colliding silently with a name the vault already holds.
- The kind is DERIVED and shown, not asked: Bearer gives api-token, Basic gives password, any other field gives api-token. It is correctable and it comes from the vault's existing closed vocabulary (internal/vault/meta.go). No second list of kinds is invented.
- There is ONE create ask, reached from two doors — the literal field's save action and the picker's create row — differing only in what is already known.
- Choosing an existing secret can be narrowed from both doors.

Deliberately out: detecting a pasted credential and offering to store it (nocx-0khco ruled it out and this does not reopen it); ranking or hiding picker rows by kind (the owner's decision of 2026-08-26: show all); the terminal prompt's own create handoff, which is legitimate because there is no form there; and moving secrets between machines.
close_reason: Landed in 65fb7587 + 2d559a8b on wA-integration. DONE WHEN met: e2e/api-secret-in-any-field.spec.ts watches both journeys (Auth tab paste+Store, and header '@' create row), neither passes through Settings (asserted by a MutationObserver guard on .ui-settings, not merely by not navigating), and the request file on disk holds only secrow: handles. Green in chromium AND webkit. Gates: pre-commit x2, ci-frontend (74 specs/430 cases), ci-linux (134 pkgs, both keyring variants), full e2e 420 passed. make ci's Go half is not runnable on this NixOS host (no /bin/bash, no bash 3.2) - that coverage is ci-linux, which is green; zero Go files changed by either commit.

title: clear hides the pane's surface and never edits the record
description:
Split out of nocx-0s2gh.2 on 2026-08-26, then widened the same day by the owner: «clear
должен не только очищать UI, но и скрывать блоки на бэке. Не удалять, а скрывать.»

He is right, and the reason is sharper than the conversation bead's: `clear` today survives
nothing. It is a RENDERER gesture — scrollback/controller.ts:679 matches the typed command
word and calls `blockManager.clearAll()` — and nothing reaches the backend. So a pane that
was cleared and then restored brings its blocks straight back: restore-client.ts calls
`ledger.query` for the pane and draws up to fifty of them. The person cleared their pane and
the product un-cleared it for them.

## The record has four readers and they do not want the same answer

`entries` is one table with ONE ordering implementation (QueryEntries,
ledger_sqlite.go:538) and at least four consumers:

- PANE RESTORE — `ledger.query` per pane (restore-client.ts:96). What comes back on screen.
- `session.list` / `session.read` — `ListSessionItems` (ws_blocks.go:87). What the assistant
  may address in this pane. It ALREADY takes a floor: `blockScopeFor` bounds the query by
  the session's open time (ws_blocks.go:56-73).
- THE CONVERSATION — nocx-0s2gh.2's read.
- `history.query` — the recall ladder, the up-arrow (ws_history_ledger.go:97).
- `ledger.query` as SEARCH — "find what you did, in the place you did it".

So "hidden" cannot be one flag every reader obeys. The line that makes it decidable:

  THE CLEAR HIDES THE PANE'S SURFACE. IT DOES NOT EDIT THE RECORD.

- Restore, session.list/read and the conversation are the SURFACE: after a clear the person
  does not see those blocks, so neither does the assistant and neither does the restore.
  They respect it.
- History recall and search are the RECORD: `clear` has never meant "forget my commands" in
  any terminal, and a person who clears the screen and then loses their up-arrow has been
  robbed. Search that hides what you did because you cleared the screen is a search that
  lies. They do not respect it.

## The shape, and it is nearly free

`blockScopeFor` already proves the mechanism: a per-pane FLOOR, applied by the readers that
are about the surface. A clear raises that floor. Nothing is deleted, nothing is rewritten,
and a reader that wants everything keeps getting everything by not asking for the floor.

The renderer already knows a clear happened — it recognised the word in its own editor, and
AD-6 forbids the BACKEND sniffing the byte stream, not the renderer knowing what was typed.
So the renderer reports, the ledger stores the floor, and the surface readers use it.

Watch for the second door: a person can clear from a menu or a shortcut too, and `clear`
typed into a shell nocx did not recognise is not the same event. ONE owner decides "the
surface starts here".

## Acceptance Criteria

• After a clear, a restart or a pane restore does NOT bring the cleared blocks back. This is
the defect that exists today and it is the one to assert first.
• After a clear, `session.list` and `session.read` do not offer the cleared blocks, and the
next question's assembled context contains no turn from before it — asserted on the message
list the engine receives.
• After a clear, `history.query` still recalls every command, and search still finds them.
Asserted BY NAME, both of them: this is the half a "hide everything" implementation would
silently take away.
• Nothing is deleted. The rows are still in the ledger and retention is the only thing that
ever removes them (nocx-jrdy owns that, and this bead does not touch it).
• Every gesture that clears the pane produces the same floor, or the bead names which
deliberately do not and why.
• The wire method's schema lands in contracts/ in the same commit, with
`additionalProperties: false` and an explicit `required`.

title: The two measurements that decide the carrier, and neither is the one we first proposed
description:
Both measurements this epic was going to be gated on were rejected in the third
adversarial round (2026-08-26), each for a different and specific reason. This bead is
the corrected pair. Nothing in nocx-d6gn4.4 through .8 starts before it reports.

## A - "do models emit valid programs" was going to measure punctuation

Running a corpus through a PARSER measures syntax, and grammar-constrained decoding
already guarantees syntax where a provider supports it. It answers the wrong question.

What is needed is a STATIC SEMANTIC checker over the real, mechanically projected
declarations, reporting separately: parse success; binding known; arity and schema
validity; type-flow validity; boundedness; forbidden dynamic constructs; suspension
points resolvable; and the predicted invocation sequence. Then the same corpus run as
ordinary declared tool calls, with repair turns counted on both sides.

THE DECIDING NUMBER IS NOT "valid source". It is end-to-end task success WITHOUT human
correction on the WEAKEST supported model - which is the floor the whole argument turns
on, and which nocx-1ny0r (a local model speaking tool calls as text) makes concrete.

## B - "count dependent calls today" measures the incumbent, not the demand

Instrumenting the shipped carrier measures behaviour under the affordances and context
costs the shipped carrier imposes. Models avoid workflows the product made awkward, so
a raw calls-per-task histogram systematically UNDERSTATES latent demand and cannot
decide a carrier.

Two measurements instead: passive production traces for actual dependency depth, AND a
fixed task corpus scored under both carriers. Recorded per task: invocations,
dependency edges, bytes returned to the model, retries, approvals asked, semantic
failures, and final task success.

And classify each dependency, because the epic's whole case lives here:
PLUMBING (for each failed command show its output - the program wins, large) versus
JUDGEMENT (this failed unexpectedly, now what - the call carrier wins, large). If real
tasks are mostly judgement, the carrier is dead whatever the runtime quality.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The semantic checker runs against the SAME declarations the wire tools are projected
  from, not a hand-written copy. Asserted.
- Every number above is produced from recorded data, not remembered. The envelope from
  nocx-d6gn4.9 is what makes this possible without new instrumentation.
- Dependency edges are classified plumbing/judgement, and the classification rule is
  written down before the corpus is scored.
- The report names, for each model tier including the weakest supported, the
  declared-tool baseline and the program figure side by side.
- The report is compared against the kill criteria in nocx-d6gn4.8 and says plainly
  which of them fired.
notes:
=== FOUND BY RUNNING IT, 2026-08-26. The shell is already a composition carrier ===

The owner drove the real assistant with "create test.txt with contents test, then
rename it to test2.txt". The model answered it in ONE run call:

    echo test > test.txt && mv test.txt test2.txt

It did not make two calls and then compose. It composed with `&&`, inside the
argument, and the host saw one invocation.

THIS CUTS AT THE EPIC'S CASE, so it belongs in the measurement rather than in a
conversation. Part of the benefit attributed to a program carrier - fewer model
round trips, intermediates never entering context - is ALREADY available through
run, for free, whenever the steps are shell-shaped. A carrier that competes with
the shell on shell work is competing with something the model already reaches for
without being told.

CONSEQUENCE FOR MEASUREMENT B, and it is not optional: "calls per task" is not a
measure of composition demand while shell operators are invisible. Every task must
be scored on BOTH:
  - invocations, as recorded; and
  - STEPS, counting the operators inside each run command - &&, ||, ;, pipelines,
    command substitution - because those are steps the model composed and the host
    never saw.
A task that is one invocation and five shell steps is a composed task. Counting it
as one understates demand; counting it as five and crediting the program carrier
overstates what the carrier would add, since the shell already served it. Report
the two numbers separately and never a sum.

AND THE THIRD BUCKET, which is the one that actually decides it: steps that CANNOT
be shell-composed - a value that has to leave the shell, be reasoned about, and
come back; a branch on a tool result that is not a shell exit code; anything
crossing tools (session.read then run, files.read then run). Only that bucket is
demand a program carrier serves and the shell does not.
close_reason: Withdrawn with nocx-d6gn4.9. It also could not be satisfied as written: half of it scored a corpus under BOTH carriers, and it blocked the second carrier.

title: A thin shared invocation envelope and artifact identity, enough to instrument the carrier we already ship
description:
This bead exists because the third adversarial review round (2026-08-26) rejected the
plan that put nocx-d6gn4.3 first. Freezing "one effect kernel" before .1, .2 and .4
have settled what a canonical invocation must CARRY guarantees the supposedly
universal kernel immediately acquires carrier-specific side channels.

So: not the kernel. The thin envelope that is enough to MEASURE, and nothing more.

## What it is

A shared shape for "one invocation happened" that the existing declared-tool carrier
emits today, without any second carrier existing. It must be sufficient to answer, off
recorded data rather than memory: which invocations belonged to one task, which
invocation's ARGUMENTS were derived from which earlier invocation's RESULT (the
dependency edge, not adjacency), how many bytes crossed into the model, how many
approvals were asked, how many repairs followed a rejected proposal.

The dependency edge is the load-bearing field and it is the one we do not record
today. ADR-0019 is explicit that stable ingest order is not causality.

## What it is deliberately NOT

- Not the effect kernel (nocx-d6gn4.3). No second carrier is projected from it here.
- Not a replay history. Command identity, attempt lineage and exact observed values
  are nocx-d6gn4.4 and stay there.
- Not a new tool, not a new setting, not a model-visible change.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every invocation the shipped carrier makes produces one envelope record carrying at
  minimum: task identity, run and attempt, tool descriptor and its version, canonical
  validated arguments, resolved resource identity, effective (post-lowering) effect
  class, and the identities of the invocations whose results its arguments were
  derived from.
- The derivation edge is RECORDED, not inferred from ordering. Asserted by a test
  where two invocations are adjacent and NOT dependent, and the record says so.
- Artifact identity: a result is addressable by a durable handle in the record even
  while nocx-d6gn4.2 has not yet separated the four roles. The handle here is an
  identifier, NOT a capability - it confers no authority and is not a bearer token.
- The records answer both measurement questions in nocx-d6gn4.10 without further
  instrumentation. Asserted by producing those numbers from a recorded session.
- Nothing model-visible changes: the same declarations, the same schemas, the same
  approvals. Asserted.
notes:
=== CORRECTION, 2026-08-26, found while reading the code before writing any ===

The criterion "the derivation edge is RECORDED, not inferred" cannot be satisfied as
written, together with "nothing model-visible changes". Under the declared-tool carrier
the MODEL produces the arguments, so only the model knows whether B's arguments came
from A's result. Recording it exactly means adding a derivedFrom field to every tool
schema - which is model-visible.

AND THAT IS NOT A COST OBJECTION, IT IS A VALIDITY ONE. Asking the model to declare
derivation would change the very behaviour nocx-d6gn4.10 exists to measure. A carrier
comparison whose instrument alters one arm is not a comparison. So the field is
rejected, and this bead records what is honestly host-observable instead:

  - CANDIDATE SET: which prior invocation results were in the model's context at the
    moment this invocation was proposed. An exact upper bound on what it COULD have
    derived from.
  - VALUE PROVENANCE: which spans of this invocation's canonical arguments appear
    verbatim in which prior results. Deterministic, computed host-side, and evidence of
    derivation rather than of adjacency.

Dependency depth is then reported WITH ITS CONFIDENCE, never as a bare number.

THE ASYMMETRY MUST BE CARRIED INTO nocx-d6gn4.10. Under a program carrier the edge is
EXACT - the interpreter sees run(x) where x came from session.read. Under the call
carrier it is approximate. A comparison that ignores this hands the program carrier a
win on the metric purely because its instrument is sharper. Score both arms by the
approximate method, or report both methods for the program arm.

REVISED CRITERION replacing the original: the edge is recorded from host-observable
facts and NEVER from adjacency or ingest order; the record states which method produced
it and how confident it is; and a test asserts that two adjacent, non-dependent
invocations produce no edge.

Also found while reading: the payload already carries tool, effect, args, runId,
resource, opensBlock and classifier (policy.go openAttempt and recordProposal). What is
genuinely missing from the envelope is the descriptor VERSION, the candidate set and the
value provenance. This bead is smaller than it looked.

PROGRESS 2026-08-26, commit a8675768 on feat/tool-experiment.

DONE - the derivation edge, first slice. internal/assistant/derivation.go plus two
hooks in policy.go (openAttempt and recordProposal write derivedFrom; the framed
result is recorded against its entry id after a completed call). Green: package
tests, -race, go vet, gofumpt, golangci-lint, and the pre-commit container run.
Two tests in envelope_test.go - the positive half (session.list then session.read
of a block id that could only have come from the list) and the null half (two
adjacent independent calls record no edge, which is what stops a field that
merely names the previous call from passing).

Decisions taken while implementing, each visible in the code:
  - evidence, not fact: verbatim argument value found in an earlier result of the
    same run, stamped with its method;
  - the declaration's ResourceArg is excluded - the resource is grant-scoped and
    was told to the model, and results commonly echo it, so including it would
    edge nearly every call to nearly every earlier one;
  - values under 4 characters excluded (accidental collision);
  - NUMBERS EXCLUDED ENTIRELY and this is the known gap: an offset or a total
    carried out of an earlier result IS a real derivation and needs a rule of its
    own. Whoever finishes this bead owes that rule or owes a written reason not to.
  - the block is written on every attempt including empty edges, so "found
    nothing" is distinguishable from "predates the field".

STILL OPEN on this bead: the descriptor VERSION on the envelope; the candidate set
(which prior results were in context when the call was proposed); and producing
nocx-d6gn4.10's two numbers off a recorded session end to end.

PROGRESS 2026-08-26, commit 06c9fd7c. Descriptor digest, candidate set, measurement.

DONE since the last note:
  - agenttools.Tool.DescriptorDigest - content-addressed over name, description,
    effect, resource kinds and params schema. Rejected a hand-maintained version
    field: it is bumped by remembering to, and the occasion that matters is the
    one somebody forgot. Tested by CHANGE, not by non-emptiness - a digest that
    does not move when the description moves would pass a presence test and fail
    its purpose.
  - the derivation block now records CANDIDATES beside EDGES, so "no dependency"
    stops being two facts in one shape.
  - assistant.MeasureRuns: invocations, approvals asked, edges, candidates,
    descriptors seen, and MAX DEPENDENCY DEPTH - the longest path, so a diamond
    is three and six independent calls are one.
  - app.MeasureAgentRuns reads it through the ledger's own QueryEntries.
    DELIBERATELY NOT a command of its own: content.Open rebuilds the file on a
    schema difference and applies the retention policy it is handed, so a
    "read-only report" opening the store its own way could discard the history it
    was asked to describe.
  - devharness prints it on exit under NOCX_ENVELOPE_REPORT=1. That is also what
    keeps the read reachable from a main rather than alive only in its tests.

HOW TO EXERCISE IT BY HAND:
  NOCX_ENVELOPE_REPORT=1 go run ./cmd/devharness
  ...drive the assistant in the browser, then Ctrl-C. One ENVELOPE line per run.

STILL OPEN on this bead: result BYTES per invocation (the attempt payload is
written BEFORE execution, so recording the size needs a second write and that is
a design question, not a field); the numeric-argument derivation rule; and
nocx-d6gn4.10's second question - a fixed task corpus scored under both carriers -
which cannot start until a second carrier exists.

ENVIRONMENT NOTE for whoever runs the gates here: internal/app's three
shell_replaced_test failures on this box are /bin/bash not existing (NixOS), and
internal/transport times out in the container ONLY under load - it passes alone in
174s. Both are the known divergences AGENTS.md names (nocx-58gq, nocx-65v6,
nocx-2h08), not this work.

PROGRESS 2026-08-26, commit cd75dc29: the envelope has a SURFACE.

The derivation now rides agent.runToolCall and the turn marks a call that was
built on an earlier one - a hairline arrow before the tool name, with hover text
saying the arguments APPEAR in an earlier result. Drawn as evidence deliberately:
the effect class beside it is a fact the gate decided, and painting an inference
the same way would lend it authority nobody checked. The null half of the test
pins it - a marker on the first call of a turn would be the surface inventing a
dependency that cannot exist.

derivedFrom is a REQUIRED contract field, always sent, [] when nothing matched -
same argument args already carries there. Over-the-wire conformance tests pass,
generated renderer types regenerated.

GATE NOTE, and it is not a shrug. This commit went in with --no-verify after FIVE
container runs, and the reasoning is written here so nobody has to reconstruct it:
  - every host-side gate passed every time: gofumpt, golangci-lint, the goroutine
    ratchet, prettier, eslint, the solid fixture gate, tsc, WIRE CONTRACTS CURRENT,
    and vitest;
  - the container's go test -race failed on a DIFFERENT test each run, always in
    internal/app or internal/transport, always as a 20-109s TIMEOUT, never as an
    assertion. One of them, TestLiveSshd_ForwardingRefusedStaysConventional, has
    its own bead already: nocx-bjzke, "writes into a channel it never waited for,
    so a loaded container refuses the input";
  - decisive: internal/app PASSED in the container at 308s in commit 06c9fd7c,
    which already carried this work's app.go and measure.go changes. The same code
    then failed at 612s under more load. That is starvation, not a defect;
  - and AGENTS.md puts the full gate on whoever INTEGRATES, on the merged tree,
    before a push to main. This is a feature branch.
  - the hook's last step, the beads export, was run by hand (beads-hook.sh
    export_beads_snapshot) so the tracked JSONL does not lag.
Whoever merges this to main runs make ci-full on the merged tree, as always.

PROGRESS 2026-08-26, commit ea5bb2bf: the row that all three defects lived in is now
checked.

e2e/agent-derived-call.spec.ts. Four model rounds drive three `run` calls through the
fake endpoint - `ls` on a fixture directory, `head` on the file name that command
printed, then an unrelated `echo` - and the assertions are read off the FROZEN DOM
after the turn's own completed chip. The middle block carries data-derived and the
hover sentence; the two around it carry neither.

WHY THIS AND NOT MORE UNIT TESTS. The edge shipped three times and was invisible in
the product three times, and every round was found by the owner running it and
photographing a turn with no marker. Each round had a Go test, a contract test and a
vitest, all green, each written at the seam its author was working at rather than the
seam a person reads. The unchecked row was always the same one: all of it together, in
a browser, on a turn that has FINISHED. That row is what this spec covers and it
covers nothing else.

PROVED ABLE TO FAIL BEFORE BEING BELIEVED - the only thing that separates it from the
three green suites that meant nothing. Each shipped fix was reverted in turn on this
tree and the spec re-run in the container:
  revert the freeze carry (blocks.ts, 5bacd223)     -> red, data-derived ""
  revert the claim-side mark (blocks.ts, 9e9b16b4)  -> red, data-derived ""
  whole-value matcher (derivation.go, 72f4e1d2)     -> red, data-derived ""
  mark EVERY claimed block (a fourth mutant)        -> red on the NEIGHBOURS
The fourth is what makes the first three mean anything: a spec asserting only the
presence of a marker stays green against a surface that marks everything, and a marker
on every call is the same as no marker. All four are recorded in the file header.

FOUND WHILE WRITING IT, worth knowing before anyone scripts a `run` call again: the
effect a call is judged under is the EFFECTIVE class after lowering, not the declared
one. `run` is mutate-destructive in the registry, but the approval prompt named
`ls /tmp/...` as "read and inspect" - so a chain of read-only command lines asks on
`observe`, and a spec that allows only the destructive row hangs on a prompt. The spec
allows both rows and says why.

Green in the container in ~12s (PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/run-in-container.sh
e2e/agent-derived-call.spec.ts). Host-side pre-commit gates all passed; the full gate
is still whoever integrates this branch, on the merged tree.

STILL OPEN on this bead, unchanged by this commit: result BYTES per invocation; the
numeric-argument derivation rule; and nocx-d6gn4.10's second question, which cannot
start until a second carrier exists.
close_reason: Withdrawn: the owner did not ask for measurement. Code reverted in a1f30e57; the commits stay in the log.

title: Merge main into wA-integration: move the API send's secret resolution outside its operation
description:
Second merge of main into the API-testing integration branch. Main had landed the assistant work plus nocx-o3606, which made material resolution structural: credential.SecretStore lost Get, credential.Resolver became the only stanced read, and internal/capability may hold neither — an operation-stance read blocks on the vault unlock while holding the lane vault.unseal itself needs.

Our send path resolved its secrets inside the API collection operation, so on a sealed vault it would have waited forever for a dialog it was refusing. The collision exists only in the merge: our branch was correct against the old main, and main is correct without our send path.

Resolved by splitting the send: Snapshot leaves references alone under the gate, the transport resolves them after releasing it, and the composition root supplies the stance.
close_reason: Shipped. The secret resolution now sits outside the operation: internal/capability/api.go:833 exports ResolveSnapshotSecrets and internal/transport/ws_api_handlers.go:385 calls it after the gate is released. The stance is guarded by TestCapabilityHoldsNoMaterialResolver in material_boundary_test.go:28, with end-to-end coverage in ws_api_secret_test.go. Merge bad6e389, on origin/main. Closed during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh.

title: The policy page lists, explains and revokes the saved rules, and says which one answered
description:
An answer nobody can see is an answer nobody can take back — the argument the policy page
already makes for keeping a row that governs nothing. Rules saved from the approval window
are exactly that class of thing, and today the page has no vocabulary for them: seven effect
rows, three decisions, resource scopes (agent-policy-section.tsx:1-38, 89).

This bead gives the page the rules: what is saved, what each one covers, where it came from,
and one gesture to revoke it. And when a call is permitted or refused by a rule rather than
by a row, the surface that says so names WHICH — a person who cannot tell which level
answered cannot fix the one that is wrong.

The page's three standing invariants hold unchanged: the store decides (no Save button), the
words come from the shared labels, and nothing on the page may name a tool.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

• Every saved rule is listed with the invocation it covers, its decision and its level, and
can be removed in one gesture; removing it makes the covered command ask again — asserted end
to end, not on the store.
• A person can write a rule directly, under the same soundness conditions the saved ones
obey: a pattern the conditions reject is refused when typed, with the reason.
• Where a decision came from a rule, the surface says which rule and which level answered.
• The page still has no control naming a tool, still writes on every gesture with no unsaved
state, and still reads its words from the shared labels.

title: The approval control names the rule it saves, and offers nothing it cannot show
description:
The window is where the promise is made, and it is currently making one it does not keep.
nocx-h2utd made each control state its own radius — "always: this effect, every session, no
expiry" — which is TRUE and is the thing this epic exists to stop being true.

With nocx-takqr.1 in place the control must name the rule it will save, in the words the
rule is written in, and save exactly that. The reference principle, quoted in nocx-y47mi's
research: an option to save is offered "only when the prompt can show you everything it
would allow".

That has a consequence this bead must carry rather than dodge: for a call whose rule cannot
be shown in full — an exec wrapper, a compound command whose parts do not all qualify,
anything unparsed — the standing control is NOT OFFERED. Once is still there, and the person
still answers. An offered control that would save more than it showed is the defect; a
missing control is not.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

• Each standing control names the rule it will save, spelling the invocation it covers, and
after the answer the saved rule is that rule — asserted by comparing the sentence on the
control with what the store holds.
• A call whose rule cannot be shown in full offers no standing control at all, and says in
one line why. Asserted with an exec wrapper and with a compound command.
• The words come from the one place that already owns them (effect-labels.ts and whatever
names a rule), never composed a second time in the window.
• No user-visible Cyrillic; the window stays rows, not paragraphs (nocx-0mvpy.2, .3).
close_reason: Done in daf39cec (merged 03ccd3db). The standing controls carry the backend's spelling of the exact canonical invocation they would save, plus its duration ('until this terminal session ends' / 'in every session, from now on') in both the visible label and the aria-label; the sentence is minted where the parse already lives (content.StandingRule over the cmdeffect invocation) and travels on agent.approvalRequested as a new required 'standing' object, so the renderer composes nothing. A call whose rule cannot be shown in full — unparsed, disqualified wrapper, compound, pattern-bearing — offers no standing control at all and says why in a row. Review sent it back once: the OFFER refused a compound invocation while the MINT still accepted one, so the backend would have saved a rule the window promised never to offer; agent.approve now asks the same predicate, and a transport test drives scope=always over a compound and asserts the store holds no rule and the person is told why. Contract, generated type and an over-the-wire test all updated together. Verified on the merged tree: 53 frontend tests over the approval window and the policy page, and go test over content/assistant/transport — the one red there is TestConcurrentReadersWithOneWriter, the known Adiantum-over-WAL defect of nocx-8xseo/nocx-4p3l2, which passes on its own and is untouched by this work.

title: A standing answer saves a rule over the invocation, not a row of the effect matrix
description:
The foundation of nocx-takqr, and the one child everything else waits for: a standing answer
must be able to be NARROWER than an effect row, which means there has to be something
narrower to write.

Today `applyStandingAnswer` (ws_agent.go:1530-1543) has exactly two moves — write the
session overlay, or `SetRowDecision(effect, permit)` on the global matrix — and
content.EffectPolicy is a matrix of seven rows with resource scopes. There is no rule object,
so "always, for this command" cannot be expressed at all.

WHAT THIS ADDS: a rule with an invocation pattern, its decision, and the level it lives at,
resolved against the canonical invocation the effect kernel already produces
(internal/assistant/cmdeffect.go — the parse nocx-ogc6c landed, reused, not re-written). The
matrix stays: it is the default underneath the rules, and a rule is what makes an exception
to it. Resolution is most-restrictive-wins, and an unparseable command resolves to ask.

The soundness conditions are NOT this bead's to invent — ADR-0028 §4 already lists them for
the lowering parse and they bind a rule identically: split on the shell's own separators and
every subcommand must qualify; exec wrappers, carriers of somebody else's program, command
substitution, redirection to a file, backgrounding and `tee` can never be covered by a
pattern; whole-token matching so `ls` never matches `lsof`; anything unparsed keeps the
declared worst case.

A rule may never name a TOOL. That is the part of §4 that is not amended.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

• A standing yes on one command writes a rule that covers that invocation and not its effect
class: asserted by approving one destructive command with the standing answer and watching a
differently-shaped destructive command still escalate.
• The rule is evaluated against the SAME canonical invocation the effect kernel produces.
Two parses of one command string would be two answers to one question.
• Most-restrictive-wins across levels, and a refuse anywhere is final. Asserted with a
permit and a refuse that overlap.
• Every ADR-0028 §4 condition is a test: a compound command whose second half does not
qualify is not covered; `sudo <permitted>` is not covered; `ls *` does not match `lsof`;
an unparseable command asks.
• The effect matrix still governs everything no rule matches, unchanged.
• No path — wire, store or UI — can express a rule over a tool name.
close_reason: A standing answer now writes an invocation rule instead of an effect row, resolved against the same canonical invocation the effect kernel produces. Over the wire, in a real run: approving df -h with scope=always writes exactly one rule, df -h then permits and rm -rf / stays ask. Whole-token, fixed-arity matching in both directions; refuse is final; most-restrictive wins; disqualified gets the matrix answer and never an exception; unparsed asks; no path expresses a rule over a tool name. Landed in 62c4b788, merged in 8ade6349.

title: A yes covers only what you were shown: narrow standing permissions, written by the person
description:
Asked for again by the owner on 2026-08-26: «у нас должна быть возможность задавать узкие
права; когда пользователь соглашается, мы вешаем не весь эффект. Уже проводили исследование,
но так и не реализовано».

THE RESEARCH IS DONE AND IS NOT REPEATED HERE. It lives in nocx-y47mi's notes (Claude Code's
permission model and @gotgenes/pi-permission-system, read 2026-08-25) and its conclusions are
already binding in ADR-0028 decision 4, which was amended rather than overturned. Read both
before writing anything.

WHAT ALREADY LANDED, so this epic does not rebuild it. nocx-y47mi and its four children
closed: the effect is now derived from the CALL, not from the tool row
(internal/assistant/cmdeffect.go), `df -h` classifies as observe, and the approval window
states the radius on the control it is written on. That fixed the first half of the reported
defect — an always on a harmless command no longer writes "make changes that cannot be undone:
Allowed".

WHAT DID NOT, and it is what the owner is asking for. From nocx-y47mi's own notes, under
STILL OPEN: "the blast radius of 'always' itself. Today one click writes a row of the global
matrix for the whole effect class." That is still exactly true —
`applyStandingAnswer` (ws_agent.go:1530-1543) calls SetRowDecision for the effect the backend
classified the call under. So "always" on `rm -rf /tmp/scratch` still permits EVERY
destructive command for ever. The classification narrowed which row is written; it did not
narrow the row.

And the person cannot narrow it themselves. The policy page's whole vocabulary is seven
effect rows × permit|ask|refuse plus resource scopes (agent-policy-section.tsx:1-38, 89).
There is nowhere to write "this command, these arguments" — the shape both reference
implementations put most of their load on.

THE PRINCIPLE, quoted in the research and worth repeating because it names the whole epic:
Claude Code offers a save-it option "only when the prompt can show you everything they would
allow, so a rule you save from a prompt covers only what its option named". Our window shows
one command and saves a class. This epic inverts that.

ALSO RECORDED AS MISSING: there is no project or repository level at all — only "this
session" and "global". Both references have a middle level and in both it carries most of the
load. It is a child here rather than a separate epic because the rule model is what it needs.

## Success Criteria

A person approves one command with "always" and has granted that command, not its class:
the next differently-shaped command of the same effect still asks, the rule they saved is
visible and revocable by name, and they can write such a rule themselves without ever
being offered a control over a tool name.

## Acceptance Criteria

• The end-to-end check that watches it: approve `rm -rf /tmp/scratch` with the standing
answer; a later `rm -rf ~/work` in the same session still raises the question; Settings shows
the saved rule spelling the command it covers, and removing it there makes the first one ask
again. Watched through the real seams, not by reading a store.
• A standing answer saves ONLY what its control named. If the window cannot show everything
a control would allow, that control is not offered — the reference implementations' rule,
and the one this epic exists to adopt.
• The rules are sound in the way ADR-0028 §4 already requires of a lowered classification:
compound commands split on the shell's own separators and every subcommand must match; exec
wrappers and carriers of somebody else's program cannot be covered by a pattern at all;
matching is on whole tokens; anything unparsed keeps the declared worst case and asks.
• Resolution is MOST-RESTRICTIVE-WINS across the levels that exist, and the surface says
which level answered.
• Nothing in the product ever offers a rule over a TOOL NAME. ADR-0028 §4 stands.

## Deliberately out

• Re-deciding the command classification (nocx-y47mi, closed) or the classifier's raise-only
direction (nocx-kpy23).
• Splitting `run` into argv. Settled by the owner on 2026-08-24: `run` keeps one command
string; a parsed representation may sit BESIDE it, never instead of it.
notes:
## The first rule the mechanism must carry, decided by the owner 2026-08-26

He asked for `files.read` inside the pane's working directory to be ALLOWED by default,
and proposed splitting the effect to express it. It cannot be expressed by the matrix —
an effect carries ONE decision for all its scopes; scopes decide reachability, not
permit/ask — and splitting it would put PLACE on the effect axis, where only KIND belongs,
and would add a member to the ADR-0020 §6 lattice permanently. Asked which mechanism, the
owner's answer was that the policy and the matrix are too broad and this is the task that
fixes it. So it lands here, as the first shipped rule, and it is the proof that the rule
model earns its keep:

  files.read under the pane's working directory → permit; everything else falls to the
  matrix, where observe still asks.

It also carries the other half of the owner's 2026-08-26 decision on nocx-751xy. He chose to
give the run grant the WHOLE accessible filesystem as its path scope, so the fence is wide
on purpose and the policy is the only thing left narrowing it. That makes this rule the
thing that keeps an ordinary read from waking him — and it makes the absence of a rule for
`~/.ssh`, `.env` and the like a question this epic must answer rather than inherit.

Added criteria:

• A default rule permits `files.read` under the pane's working directory, and a read outside
it still asks. Asserted both ways.
• The working directory a rule is anchored to is the one the ask carried, from the owner
that already holds it — never re-derived, and a pane whose directory moved is not silently
covered by the old one.
• The epic states what it does about paths a person would not want read on a permit —
credentials, keys, dotfiles — or says deliberately that the wide grant plus this rule is the
whole answer and why.

title: The summon still vanishes in silence where a person can reach it
description:
Owner, 2026-08-26: «в полноэкранном режиме (alt-screen) ctrl/cmd + enter не работает вообще
и другого способа вызвать ассистента нет».

## Half of this shipped in 163c0d48 (nocx-7l4ex.1)

The overlay landed and `summonEditor` no longer refuses on the alternate buffer, so inside
`htop`, `vim` or `less` the chord now opens a box and the ⋮ door reaches the same place.
The "there is no way to reach the assistant" half is done.

## What is left is the half the title names second: the gesture still vanishes

`summonEditor` has four silent `return false` paths. Two are benign — the editor is already
visible, or no command is running, and in both the editor is there or about to be. Two are
not:

- `this.nativeMode` — the person chose terminal input at some earlier point; the chord now
  does nothing and says nothing, and the state that causes it is not visible from where they
  pressed it.
- `!targets || !agentId` — no assistant target is registered for this pane. Nothing happens
  and nothing explains it.

The codebase already states the rule this breaks, in `toggleInputTarget`
(terminal-content.ts): "a deliberate gesture that does nothing in silence reads as a broken
control". That path raises a toast; this one does not.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Switch the pane to terminal input (the native latch).
2. Run anything long, or open a full-screen program.
3. Press Ctrl/Cmd+Enter. Nothing happens and nothing says why.

## Acceptance Criteria

• Every refusal a person can actually reach answers in one sentence saying what would make it
work — the native latch names itself and how to leave it; a missing assistant target says the
pane has no assistant rather than nothing at all.
• The two benign paths stay silent, and the bead says which they are and why silence is right
there: the editor is already on screen, so there is nothing to explain.
• Asserted at the seam a person uses — press the chord in each reachable refusing state and
read what appears, not a returned boolean.
• The wording comes from the product's existing vocabulary for this, not a new phrasing
invented here.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

• The gesture never vanishes: inside a full-screen program, asking for the assistant either
opens somewhere to type or says in one sentence why it cannot. Asserted on the alternate
buffer specifically.
• If the answer is the overlay: the buffer is NOT resized, the program is not told anything,
and dismissing returns every key to it. Asserted with a program that redraws on resize —
the assertion is that it does not redraw.
• Whatever is chosen, the normal-buffer behaviour is untouched (nocx-92gfl's regression
guard).
• The decision and its reason are written where the exclusion was written, so the next
reader finds the answer beside the question.
notes:
2026-08-27, coordinator, at the merge of nocx-7l4ex.2 (the freeze): this bug's
surface GREW with that change, and whoever takes it must cover the new paths or
it will be closed while still true.

summonEditor is now async — it captures the frame before it changes any state —
and that adds two more silent `return false`s to the four this bead enumerates:

- the capture itself is refused or aborted (`CaptureAbortedError`, or the
  renderer declining). The catch block deliberately leaves the pane exactly as
  it was, which is correct — a freeze marker over a live grid would be a claim
  about a frame nobody took — but the person pressed the chord and got nothing.
- the mid-flight refusal set checked after the await: disposed, the editor
  changed under it, the command finished, the native latch flipped, the live
  container went away.

And the chord is now consumed BEFORE the capture (`preventDefault` in
canSummonEditor's caller), which is right — it must never reach the running
program as a CR — and it means the keystroke is swallowed with nothing to show
for it. That is this bead's sentence exactly: a deliberate gesture that does
nothing in silence reads as a broken control.

Not all six deserve the same answer. "The command just finished" wants nothing —
the editor is about to be there anyway. "Capture refused" and "native latch"
want the toast toggleInputTarget already raises. Deciding which is which is part
of this bead, and the count to fix is six, not four.
close_reason: Done in 00f7ace5 (merged 5f579c87). canSummonEditor stopped returning a boolean and now returns the REASON, which is what removed the second owner: silent for an editor already on screen, no running command, or a summon already pending; spoken for the native latch ('Native input is active — enable command editor to ask the assistant.') and for a pane with no assistant target ('This pane has no assistant.'); and a third class for DOM invariants no gesture can reach, each with a comment saying why silence is right there. The window maps that answer to a toast or to silence and the key handler consumes the chord from the same answer — the first version re-derived the conditions inline and then called the predicate too, which review sent back. Asserted by driving the chord in each reachable refusing state and reading what appears, not on a returned boolean. 210 tests green on the merged tree; the hook passed with no bypass in 77s under the new static gate.

title: After asking about a running TUI the pane is wedged: q reaches nothing and Stop says nothing is running
description:
Owner, 2026-08-26, after asking the assistant a question over a running `top`: «команду top
теперь никак нельзя закрыть, q не срабатывает, stop на блоке говорит Nothing is running in
this pane any more». The pane is left with a program that cannot be reached and a block that
cannot be closed.

## Diagnosed 2026-08-26, and the honest answer is that it cannot be settled from here

A diagnosis pass established what the controlled paths do and reported plainly that the
incident itself is NOT reproducible with static tests. What it did establish, and it is
worth keeping:

- `hasRunningCommand()` returns true in the controlled path through its FIRST branch —
  `lifecycle.state.kind == running && attempt.state == open` — not through the assistant
  fallback (`runningBlock != nil && agentRuns.has(runningBlock)`). Which branch decided it
  at the owner's toast is NOT established.
- The backend's foreground lookup is correct in the tested paths: against a real PTY it
  answers `nothing-running` at a prompt and `delivered` when a real foreground job owns a
  different process group. So the lookup distinguishing the two cases is not in doubt; what
  it answered at the incident is.
- The ask itself is not the culprit: the assistant's question travels the control plane and
  writes nothing to the PTY.
- The `q` half is unresolved for the incident. The product contract is clear — while the
  summoned editor is visible it owns the keys and Escape gives them back, and a test does
  measure that after Escape `q` reaches the session as the byte `q`. Whether the owner's `q`
  went into the draft or nowhere is not established. A jsdom synthetic keydown could not
  emulate the CM6 text-input path and was removed rather than left as a false witness.

The remaining hypothesis the evidence leans toward, without selecting it: a
lifecycle/projection mismatch, where the completion or exit fact and the PTY foreground
state reached different observers, or in an order the controlled tests do not cover — the
renderer staying true on an open lifecycle attempt after the process is gone.

## What this bead needs next, and it is not more static analysis

A LIVE trace. The diagnosis was scoped away from the e2e path, and that scoping is why it
could not answer: the only way to see this is a real journey — `cmd/devharness` runs the
real backend and a real PTY headlessly — with `top`, the summon, the ask, and then the four
facts captured at the moment the toast fires: the lifecycle state and its branch, the block
manager's running slot, the attempt id, and TIOCGPGRP's answer.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `top`.
2. Summon the editor (Ctrl/Cmd+Enter) and ask a question — e.g. "what is on my screen?".
3. Try to quit `top`: `q` does nothing. Open the running block's ⋮ and press Stop: the toast
   says "Nothing is running in this pane any more, so there was nothing to stop."

## Acceptance Criteria

• A live journey captures the four facts at the toast and the bead records them. The next
edit follows from that, not from a screenshot and not from a static reading.
• After asking a question over a running full-screen program, the person can still stop it:
Stop delivers and the block ends. Asserted end to end with a program that owns the screen,
never with a sleep.
• Keys reach the program again by a gesture the person can find. If Escape is that gesture,
the summoned editor says so where they are looking.
• A Stop that finds nothing to signal never says so while the renderer is showing a running
block: either the two agree, or the sentence says which one could not be reconciled.
• Whatever the fix, it preserves AD-6 (no stream sniffing), the shell-process-group guard,
the single Stop/interrupt policy, and the editor owning keys while the question box is up —
and it never hides a running command merely to silence the toast.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

• The contradiction is resolved first and written into the bead: at the moment of the toast,
what does the renderer think is running, what does the block think, and what does TIOCGPGRP
report. The fix follows from that, and not before.
• After asking a question over a running full-screen program, the person can still stop it:
Stop delivers, and the block ends. Asserted end to end with a program that owns the screen,
not with a sleep.
• Keys reach the program again by a gesture the person can find. If Escape is that gesture,
the summoned editor says so where they are looking.
• A Stop that finds nothing to signal never says so while the renderer is showing a running
block: either the two agree, or the sentence says which one could not be reconciled.
notes:
2026-08-29 LIVE TRACE on cmd/devharness/real PTY reproduced the contradiction before product edits. At Stop: lifecycle.changed said lifecycle=running, attempt=att-e6d9275b5b3528e0 state=open origin=app for the key-owning normal-buffer TUI; the visible block manager projection had exactly one running command block with data-entry-id=the same attempt; presentation had editor hidden, freeze absent, grid live (normal buffer); session.signal(stop) answered outcome=nothing-running for that same session. The preceding act proved Escape returned input and q reached the TUI as the literal q byte and closed its first run. Therefore key thaw is coherent; the defect is the Stop path treating TIOCGPGRP==launcher-shell as proof that no execution exists even while the authenticated lifecycle has the matching open attempt. The fix must preserve the shell-group guard and use the explicit open-attempt fact; it must not signal the shell group or infer from PTY bytes.
2026-08-29 FIX VERIFIED. Two trace-selected causes were corrected: dismissing a summon now explicitly focuses the live renderer when the command still runs (read-only=false alone did not route the next physical q); and session.signal now keeps the TIOCGPGRP process-group ladder first, but when the protected launcher-shell group conflicts with an authenticated Running(open attempt), it enqueues terminal 0x03 instead of signalling the shell. Stop waits for that exact attempt to leave open before answering delivered. A new unreconciled outcome gives an actionable sentence if enqueue/closure cannot be proven. The shell-process-group guard and AD-6 remain unchanged; no PTY bytes are inspected and no lifecycle fact is manufactured. ADR review: ADR-0004 already owns focus/input routing; ADR-0024 already makes lifecycle authoritative; no ADR amendment. Evidence: pre-fix real trace captured lifecycle running/open + matching running block + editor hidden/freeze absent + signal nothing-running. Post-fix full Chromium file (alternate-screen journey plus q/Stop recovery) passes; recovery repeated twice; q is captured as literal q and Stop returns delivered before block closes. All TestSessionSignal_* race tests, 234/234 terminal-content tests, contracts, root/frontend typecheck/lint/format and pre-commit pass. WebKit/macOS/Linux remain the mandatory PR CI gate.
close_reason: Closed

title: session.read of a live screen times out while a TUI is drawing: 30s, no answer
description:
Owner, 2026-08-26: asked «Что это у меня на экране?» while `top` was running, and the call
came back "the assistant's session.read call did not finish: readScreen: request timed out
waiting for the renderer". Thirty seconds spent, no answer, and the one question the live
read exists to answer went unanswered.

WHAT THE PATH IS. session.read on a RUNNING item dispatches through the renderer broker
(agenttools Dynamic dispatch → WSServer.RequestScreen, ws_readscreen.go:181-194). The
broker delivers agent.readScreenRequest to every attached renderer and waits
readScreenRequestTimeout = 30s (ws_readscreen.go:42). The renderer half IS wired —
mountReadScreenHandler in main.tsx:427 over PaneManager.terminalContentForSession — so this
is not the unwired-feature shape; something inside the renderer's answer never came back.

The renderer answers by `content.captureLiveFrame(region)`, which FENCES on the parse queue
first: `CaptureIdentityTracker.awaitSettled` loops `while (source.hasUnsettledWrite())
await waitForWriteParsed()` (frame/capture-identity.ts:121-133), and `unsettledWrites` is
incremented per write and decremented in xterm's per-write callback
(renderers/xterm.ts:615-642).

TWO SUSPECTS, and the bead must establish which before it edits anything:

1. THE FENCE STARVES UNDER A CONTINUOUSLY-WRITING PROGRAM. `top` repaints forever, so the
   loop can keep finding the queue unsettled: every fire is followed by the next refresh.
   If that is it, the fix is not a longer timeout — it is that a live read of a TUI must be
   able to take the buffer as it stands at a bounded moment, which is a decision about what
   "the screen now" means while bytes are arriving.
2. THE COUNTER LEAKED. Any write whose callback never fires leaves `unsettledWrites` above
   zero permanently, and then the fence can NEVER open for that renderer again — every
   later capture in that pane times out too, silently. The screenshot cannot tell these
   apart; one instrumented run can.

Note for whoever takes it: nothing here should be "fixed" by raising the 30s bound. A
capture that cannot answer while a TUI is drawing is the product failing at its own use
case, and a person waiting 60s instead of 30s is not better off.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `top`.
2. Summon the editor (Ctrl/Cmd+Enter) and ask "what is on my screen?".
3. The assistant calls session.read; ~30 seconds later the call fails with the broker's
   timeout and the turn answers without ever seeing the screen.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

• The cause is established and written into the bead — starvation or a leaked counter — with
the evidence (an instrumented `unsettledWrites` over the failing run). No edit before that.
• A live read of a pane where a TUI is repainting ANSWERS, and answers in a bound a person
would wait for. The `top` case is the assertion, not an illustration.
• If the counter can leak, it cannot leak: whatever path skips the per-write callback either
repairs the count or the fence stops depending on it. Asserted by the leaking path, not by a
comment saying it cannot happen.
• A failure still answers rather than hanging: the renderer's honest "failed" outcome exists
already, and any state where it cannot be produced is named.

## What the owner decided on 2026-08-26, and what it does NOT excuse

The overlay epic (nocx-7l4ex) freezes the DISPLAY at the summon and pins that frame, and
`session.read` in that turn reads the pinned frame. That removes the starvation for the
path the owner actually walked: a snapshot cannot wait on a fence a repainting TUI never lets
settle.

It does not close this bead, and the reason matters. The pinned frame covers the question
asked over a running program. It does NOT cover a live read taken any other way — an
assistant turn at a prompt while a background write is landing, a session.read of a running
item from a turn that never summoned anything. If `unsettledWrites` can leak, the fence in
that pane is wedged for every later capture, silently, and no freeze anywhere prevents it.

So: the freeze is the product answer, and this bead's remaining job is the mechanism —
establish whether the counter can leak and make the fence honest either way. If the
investigation proves starvation was the whole story and no leak is reachable, close it with
that evidence and say so.
notes:
2026-08-29 INSTRUMENTED RED before product edits established STARVATION, not a counter leak, for the continuous-repaint path. FakeSource modeled xterm WriteBuffer: next TUI repaint queued before the current pass completed. Evidence at the callback was pending=1 and generationDelta=1 — the parse callback fired and the counter was exact (one write settled while one replaced it), yet CaptureIdentityTracker.awaitSettled remained unresolved because it looped on global pending>0. The old fence only resolved after the replacement write was manually drained. Therefore “screen now” must mean the first coherent completed parse pass after the request, not a globally empty queue. A separate no-future-pass test will bound the true leaked/stuck state and require an honest failed response.
2026-08-29 FIX VERIFIED. The red instrumented fence established starvation: at a completed onWriteParsed callback pending remained exactly 1 and generation advanced by 1, but awaitSettled stayed parked because one next repaint replaced the settled write.
