No counter leak was required. The fence now treats the first completed parse pass after a request as the coherent “screen now” boundary; the per-write count only distinguishes immediate capture from waiting for that boundary. A claimed pending write with no parse/disposal rejects CaptureUnsettledError after a renderer-local 1s bound, its waiter is removed, and readScreen answers failed instead of reaching the 30s broker timeout. Disposal rejects even at pending=0. ADR review: AD-6/ADR-0029 ownership and frame comparability do not change; no ADR amendment. Evidence: 118 focused frame/read-screen/xterm tests passed, including exact starvation, fake-timer no-boundary, throw-counter repair and disposal; continuous background TUI-like Chromium E2E kept repainting through session.read and the renderer frame/model answer contained the live marker; root/frontend typecheck, lint, format and pre-commit pass. WebKit/macOS/Linux remain mandatory PR CI gates.
close_reason: Closed

title: There is no mouse path to the question box over a running command: the ⋮ item marks instead of summoning
description:
The owner, 2026-08-26: «хочу задать вопрос по блоку, редактор можно вызвать только через
ctrl/cmd + enter, нет возможности это сделать с помощью мыши».

This is an UNMET CRITERION of this bead, not a new idea. nocx-92gfl says it twice — in the
decision ("the running block's ⋮ menu gains 'Ask about this command', doing exactly what the
chord does … without it the gesture is invisible") and in the acceptance criteria. The
comment on `summonEditor` (terminal-content.ts:3843-3846) states it as fact: "Two gestures
land here and nowhere else: ⌘/Ctrl+Enter from the grid, and 'ask about this block' on the
block's ⋮ menu … a second DOOR, never a second implementation." The comment is wrong.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED. The menu item exists (scrollback/blocks.ts:1029-1040) and is
labelled "Ask about this block" — but it is wired to `toggleGrant`
(terminal-content.ts:4269), which only adds the block to the marked list. It never summons.
So on a running command the item marks a block for a question the person has no way to type,
and the person sees nothing happen.

TWO MEANINGS, ONE LABEL, which is the thing AGENTS.md forbids: the summon bead named the
item "Ask about this command", the marks epic (nocx-wcswn / nocx-5u3oz) took the same words
for "mark this block", and whichever loses goes on advertising something it cannot deliver.

RECOMMENDED ANSWER (owner asked «как лучше сделать?»): fold them, do not add a second item.
"Ask about this block" should mean what it says end to end — mark the block AND make sure
there is a box to ask in: summon the editor when a command is running, point the target at
the assistant, focus it. On a finished block the editor is already up and the summon is a
no-op, so one item behaves the same way in both states and there is still one door per
meaning. "Unmark" stays exactly as it is.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `top`. The editor hides.
2. With the mouse only, try to ask the assistant about it. The running block's ⋮ menu offers
   "Ask about this block"; clicking it marks the block and nothing else appears.
3. The only way to get a box to type in is Ctrl/Cmd+Enter.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

• A person with a mouse can reach the question box over a running command, from the running
block's ⋮ menu, and the item's words say so.
• Whatever the item is called, ONE meaning: no two controls in the product claim "ask about
this block" with different effects. If the mark and the summon are folded into one item,
the fold is asserted — the click marks and the editor is up and focused.
• The stale comment on `summonEditor` is corrected in the same change: it currently states a
door that does not exist.
• Asserted through the seam a person uses: open the menu on a running block, click, and the
editor is visible with the assistant as the target.

title: The summoned editor wears 'Enable command editor': the summon never re-derives the capability axes
description:
Seen by the owner on 2026-08-26 and asked as a question — «что такое enable command
editor?» — which is the report: the chip is on screen, in the chrome of the editor it
offers to enable, while that editor is visible and focused.

CAUSE, exact. `_presentation` is derived as `editor.isVisible ? 'editor' : 'terminal'`
(terminal-content.ts:3556) and is only recomputed inside `_updateCapability`.
`summonEditor` (terminal-content.ts:3859-3877) shows the editor through
`_syncLifecycleOwnership` and focuses it, and never calls `_updateCapability`. So the axis
still says `terminal`, `deriveActions` takes its first branch — integrated shell + terminal
presentation → offer to switch back — and the chip renders (capability.ts:106-110).

It is also the anti-pattern capability.ts says it exists to prevent. The chip's click runs
`_restoreEditor`: clears the native latch and re-syncs. While a command is running
`shouldShowEditor` is false and only `_summoned` is holding the editor up, so the click
changes nothing a person can see — a control that is offered, pressed, and does nothing.

The label is the second half of the report. "Enable command editor" is the vocabulary of
the input-presentation machinery, not of the thing a person is looking at, and it is the
only text in that row that is not about the question being asked.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `top`. The editor hides.
2. Press Ctrl/Cmd+Enter. The editor is summoned in ask mode.
3. The chip row reads "Enable command editor" beside the cwd, the machine and the model.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

• The capability axes are re-derived when the summon shows or hides the editor: one owner,
and it is `_updateCapability`, called from wherever visibility changes rather than from the
summon alone.
• With the editor on screen, no action offering to enable the editor is derivable. Asserted
on `deriveActions` input AND on the rendered chip, because the defect was that the input was
stale, not that the derivation was wrong.
• No recovery action is ever offered whose click cannot change what the person sees. If the
click would be a no-op in the current state, the action is not in the set.
close_reason: merged into feat/ai-assistant as 3508d953, full pre-commit gate green (containerised go test -race and vitest, contracts, tsc, linters, prettier)

title: A finished turn can show the raw dump: what was sent and what came back
description:
Asked for by the owner on 2026-08-26, in the middle of debugging an answer that contradicted
a command he had watched run: «хочу видеть полный системный промпт и что конкретно мы
передаём модели». Then, on where it lives: «давай дадим возможность посмотреть полный дамп
что было отправлено и получено в сыром виде через три точечки на блоке, типа show dump,
copy dump или download dump».

So it is BOTH directions, RAW, reached from the turn's own ⋮ menu.

This epic already gave him the standing prompt WITH PLACEHOLDERS (nocx-0mvpy.1, Settings →
Instructions). That is the right thing for "what does nocx tell the assistant, in general".
It is not the thing that answers "what did THIS turn send and what came back", and the
difference is where every defect filed on 2026-08-26 lives: the resolved facts, the
assembled conversation, the tools array, and what the provider actually streamed back.

What is sent today, for the record — dumped by driving the real engine against the fake
OpenAI server, which is currently the only way anyone can see it:

  messages[0] system    the resolved SystemPrompt: session id, cwd, local/ssh + OS,
                        the marked items as `- id: …; command: …; state: …; start; count`,
                        the person's own paragraph last when they wrote one
  messages[1] user      the previous turn's question, verbatim
  messages[2] assistant the previous turn's PROSE only — no tool calls, no results
                        (nocx-0s2gh.4)
  messages[3] user      this question
  tools                 session.list, session.read, run  (files.read and git.status are
                        absent; nocx-751xy)
  model, stream: true, stream_options.include_usage

The response side is worth more than the request side for one open epic: nocx-1ny0r is about
a local model that speaks tool calls as TEXT, and diagnosing that needs the bytes the
provider sent, not eino's parse of them.

RECOMMENDED SHAPE, for the owner's "что лучше не знаю" — one door, not three:

  ⋮ → Show dump  opens a read-only panel with two sections, Request and Response, each raw,
                 each with the kit's copy affordance. Copy is a control INSIDE the panel
                 rather than a second menu item, because a menu item that silently fills the
                 clipboard with 30 kB gives no way to check what was taken; and Download is
                 deliberately out of the first pass — it needs a save dialog, a path and a
                 filename convention, and every debugging use the owner named is served by
                 copying into a chat window.

WHAT THIS MUST NOT BE: a second assembler that re-renders the payload on demand.
Re-rendering answers "what would we send now", which is a different question and drifts
silently. What is shown is what the run really sent and really received.

TWO DECISIONS THE BEAD MUST MAKE, and neither is made here:

1. WHERE THE BYTES LIVE, and whether they are always kept. A dump per turn is roughly the
   size of the turn's whole context, so it is not free. The recommendation is: recorded like
   any other artifact, under the retention budget that already exists (internal/content), so
   it ages out with everything else and no new storage owner appears — and NOT behind a
   setting the person has to have switched on before the bug they wanted to report happened.
2. WHAT RAW MEANS on the response side. The honest answer is the SSE frames as received,
   because a parsed-and-reassembled response cannot show a model that emitted a tool call in
   the wrong shape — which is exactly nocx-1ny0r's failure. A cap on the recorded size is
   part of this decision, not an afterthought.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

• From a finished turn's ⋮ menu, a person opens the dump and reads BOTH directions: the
request in full — the system prompt with its facts RESOLVED, every message in order with its
role, and the tools the model was offered — and the response as the provider actually sent
it.
• It is what the run SENT and RECEIVED, recorded at the time — not re-assembled when the
panel opens. A turn answered before a settings change still shows the text that turn used.
• Both sections can be copied, from a control in the panel, and what lands in the clipboard
is what is on screen.
• The API key never appears, and neither does any header value the vault resolved. Asserted
by name, with a key set, because this is the one thing in the payload that must never be
shown.
• A resumed run (an approval was answered) shows every drive, or says plainly which one it
shows. Silence about which drive it is would make the panel a second thing to debug.
• A turn that failed before the provider answered still has a dump: the request is there and
the response section says what happened instead. The failing case is the one somebody most
wants to read.
• Watched end to end by one automated check: ask a question with a block marked, open the
dump, and the marked item's id is in the request text on screen.

## Deliberately out

• Download to a file. Copy serves every use named, and a save path is its own decision
(revisit when somebody actually needs to attach one).
• Editing the payload, replaying it, or sending a hand-edited one.
• A live view while the turn streams. This is for reading afterwards.
close_reason: Merged as 500f66c8 + merge commit. Recorded at the HTTP boundary into two turn-owned ledger artifacts (request/response, one pair per provider drive), read back by agent.dump; the panel does not reassemble. Key absence asserted by name in e2e/agent-dump.spec.ts against a real-looking key; headers never enter the capture. Three follow-ups filed: kit conformance of dump-panel, storage/retention impact of always-on capture, and the response record lost when the turn's context is cancelled.

title: files.read and git.status are never offered: the only grant the product mints carries no path scope
description:
Found while dumping the real request body for an ordinary ask (2026-08-26). The tools array
the model is offered in a default install is exactly session.list, session.read and run.
files.read and git.status are assembled into the registry, described for the model, shipped
in the binary — and never declared to anybody.

WHY. Registry.ForGrant (agenttools/registry.go:271-298) keeps a tool only when every one of
its Resources kinds is covered by a scope in the grant. files.read and git.status take
content.ResourcePath. The only run grant the product ever mints is
WSServer.runGrantFor (ws_readscreen.go:238-250):

    g := p.AsGrant([]content.GrantScope{{Kind: content.ResourceSession, ID: sessionID}})

one session scope, and nothing else. `grep -rn 'GrantScope{' --include=*.go internal cmd |
grep -v _test` finds no other construction site, and ResourcePath appears nowhere in
internal/transport or internal/app. The rows of the policy matrix can carry operator scopes
(the agent policy page offers a `path` kind), so a person who types a path scope by hand
does get the two tools — but out of the box nobody has one, and nothing tells them that a
whole class of tool is switched off by its absence.

WHAT IT COSTS. The model has no cheap, observe-effect way to look at a file. To read one it
must reach for `run`, which is mutate-destructive, which the policy asks about — so reading
a file wakes the person with a destructive-effect approval, and the narrow tool that exists
precisely to avoid that is not on the list. This is visible in the owner's 2026-08-26
session: every look at the filesystem went through `run ls`/`run find`.

This is the shape AGENTS.md warns about: deadcode cannot report it (both tools are
constructed, described and covered by tests), and a suite that builds its own grant with a
path scope — internal/assistant/tools_test.go does exactly that — proves the projection
works without ever asking what the product actually mints.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Default install, no path scope typed into the agent policy page. Ask the assistant
   anything in a pane.
2. Look at the tools array in the outgoing request (or add a path scope and look again):
   session.list, session.read, run. No files.read, no git.status.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

• Decide, and write down where the decision lives, what the default run grant scopes: a
person who has typed no scopes either gets the path tools or is told why they are absent.
Silence is what this bead is against.
• If they are to be offered, the scope the grant carries is named from an owner that knows
it (the pane's cwd is the obvious candidate) and never guessed in the transport.
• Asserted against WHAT THE PRODUCT MINTS, not against a grant a test built: one check
drives runGrantFor's output through Registry.ForGrant and names the tools that come out.
The existing tools_test.go fixtures cannot fail this way.
• If the answer is that path tools stay off by default, git.status and files.read stop
being described to a model that can never be offered them, or the registry says why they
are kept.
notes:
## Decided by the owner, 2026-08-26

Asked which path the run grant should carry, he chose the WHOLE accessible filesystem: the
scope stops being a fence and the policy matrix is the only thing narrowing what a read may
touch.

Two consequences to carry, not to argue with:

1. ADR-0028 DECISION 4 IS AMENDED IN THE SAME COMMIT. Its mechanism survives — the
   middleware still resolves the grant into a scoped capability and the tool still holds
   only that — but "the dispatcher narrows" now narrows to everything for paths, and the
   ADR must say so deliberately rather than being routed around. AGENTS.md: if an AD is
   wrong, change it, do not walk past it.

2. THE DEFAULT MUST NOT BECOME A SILENT PERMIT. With observe at "ask every time" nothing
   opens up today, and the egress gate still screens a result that carries vault-known
   material before it leaves for the provider. But a person who later sets observe to permit
   has granted every file on the machine, `~/.ssh/id_rsa` included. The narrow-rule epic
   (nocx-takqr) carries the answer — `files.read` under the pane's cwd permitted, everything
   else asking — and this bead's own job is only to make the tools reachable.

So the criterion "decide what the default run grant scopes" is answered: the whole
filesystem, with the ADR amended and the narrowing moved to the policy.
close_reason: merged as 41e4d978; the run grant carries the whole accessible filesystem as its path scope, ADR-0028 decision 4 amended in the same commit, and ForGrant now omits a declaration with no capability constructor so git.status is not offered as a tool that can only fail (follow-up nocx-5nzrk). Asserted against what the product mints, not a fixture grant. Gate green.

title: The assistant denies the command it just ran: a turn's tool calls never reach the next turn
description:
Observed by the owner, 2026-08-26, and it is the worst shape this defect has: the
assistant told the person it had lied to them.

Turn 1, "Удали файл SiYuan-20250828105651.zip": the model called `run ls -la …; find …`,
then `run rm -f … && echo удалено`, the block printed `удалено`, and the prose said
"Файл `SiYuan-20250828105651.zip` удалён." The file was really deleted.

Turn 2, "А это что?": the model's own reasoning reads "I claimed to have deleted it, but
did I actually? … I never actually ran a delete command! That was a hallucination", and
the answer to the person was "Честно говоря: я не удалял файл — я пообещал это сделать, но
на самом деле никогда не выполнял команду удаления." Every word of that is false, and the
person now believes the file is still there.

CAUSE, read out of the code and confirmed by dumping the real request body off the wire
(a throwaway test through the real engine against the fake OpenAI server): the next turn is
handed the previous turn's QUESTION and PROSE and nothing else. ws_agent.go:999-1006 maps
one content.PriorTurn to two Messages; priorAnswerMessage (ws_agent.go:2120) returns
p.Prose.Text. assistant.Message has only Role and Content, and engine.go:302-312 maps it to
schema.UserMessage / schema.AssistantMessage / schema.SystemMessage — there is no tool_calls
field and no tool-role message anywhere on the path. So the assistant message the model
reads is prose with no evidence under it, and a model asked to reconcile "I said I deleted
it" with "I see no delete call" concludes, correctly given what it was shown, that it made
the claim up.

The dumped body for exactly this turn carried four messages — system, user, assistant, user
— and a tools array of session.list, session.read, run. No trace of either `run` call.

THE FIX IS nocx-0s2gh.2, which already specifies it: "for a turn that used tools ONE short
factual line and never the output — what was called, how it ended, how big the result was".
This bead is not a second assembler. It exists to carry the evidence and to name the
regression check that bead's criterion should be asserted by, because "a follow-up cannot
mean what it says" undersells what actually happens: the assistant contradicts a command
the person watched it run.

Note also that only ONE prior turn is carried at all (PriorTurn is singular), so by the
third question the first is gone entirely. Same bead, same fix.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. In a pane with an answering endpoint configured, ask the assistant to run something that
   changes the machine — "Удали файл X" — and approve the calls. The command runs; the
   answer says it ran.
2. Ask a second question in the same pane that refers back to it — "А это что?", "ты правда
   удалил?".
3. Read the model's reasoning and answer: it has no record of the calls and denies them.

Same defect, cheaper to see: dump the outgoing request for turn 2 (drive
assistant.Client.Ask against the fake OpenAI server in internal/assistant and print
f.body()). The messages are system, user, assistant, user; no tool_calls, no tool role.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

• Two turns in one pane, the first of which ran a tool: the second turn's request carries a
factual line naming that call and how it ended, derived from the ledger and never written
by the answering model.
• The regression check is the owner's own case, asserted on the outgoing request rather
than on an assembler's return value: turn 1 runs a command, turn 2 asks about it, and the
messages the engine sends contain the account of the call.
• A model that is asked "did you delete it" after a turn that deleted it does not deny it.
Watched end to end through the real seam (the fake OpenAI records the request), because the
failure is invisible to every unit that does not look at the message list.
close_reason: merged as 6409fc64; the regression is asserted on the message list the engine receives: after a turn that ran a destructive command, the next turn's context carries the evidence that it ran

title: Wails v3 makes Linux PTY interaction stall and slows OpenCode
description:
Owner report against an up-to-date main build on Linux after the Wails v3 migration:

1. OpenCode became noticeably slow after submitting a request.
2. Commands that require interactive input hang; concrete example: `npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web` while installing DeepSeek Harness.

These observations are ground truth. Diagnose the regression at the Wails v3 / WebView / WebSocket / PTY boundary rather than re-running them merely to confirm the report. Preserve AD-1: PTY bytes remain binary WebSocket frames, and preserve AD-6: the backend does not sniff the stream.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Build and run current main on Linux with the Wails v3 desktop shell.
2. In a terminal tab, start OpenCode and submit a request; observe the post-submit slowdown.
3. In a terminal tab, run `npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web` and proceed to the interactive installation input.
4. Observe that the command stops advancing while waiting for interactive input.

The current working checkout is on fix/remote-host-integration, so compare it with current origin/main before measuring or editing.
acceptance_criteria:
- The first regressed boundary after Wails v3 is identified with measured evidence against current main.
- OpenCode request/response interaction no longer suffers the introduced latency on Linux.
- A real interactive command that reads from the PTY accepts input and advances instead of hanging; exercise `npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web` when safely available, otherwise an equivalent real PTY program that switches between output and stdin.
- PTY bytes remain lossless, ordered binary frames with bounded per-session backpressure; no JSON or WebView-specific ownership is introduced.
- A regression test protects the observable failure at its owning seam, and Linux behavioral verification passes.
notes:
Root cause and proof, 2026-08-26:

- `TerminalContent` called `log.debug` for every received PTY output chunk.
- The generated v3 `Log` binding uses `Call.ByName`; Wails v3 beta.9's default runtime transport implements every call as an HTTP POST/fetch. The fire-and-forget calls had no bound, so PTY output created a fetch/promise/log-write queue in WebKitGTK's event loop.
- RED proof: 32 real session data callbacks rendered 32 chunks and invoked `log.debug` exactly 32 times. After deleting the side effect, all 32 still rendered and no debug binding call occurred.
- Focused `terminal-content.test.ts`: 189/189 passed. Frontend typecheck and scoped eslint passed. Production frontend build passed. Linux Wails v3 build passed with the required CGO_ENABLED=1 and gtk3 tag.
- Real Wails v3/WebKitGTK smoke in an isolated HOME: `seq 1 2000` followed by shell `read` accepted `interactive-ok` and printed `GOT:interactive-ok`; backend logs contained zero `session data received` entries.
- `npm audit` remains red on 4 high and 1 moderate transitive advisories, all matching the already-open security bead nocx-l3pk; no dependency or lockfile belongs in this fix.
Published branch fix/nocx-svxik. PTY fix commit: 42e14529. The branch also carries the already-closed Vitest budget fix nocx-jzlsf as 16475255 because its 5s default blocked the mandatory hook with a different timed-out test on each run; with that single-owner budget, the final pre-commit hook passed.
Owner retest after Wails v3 build, 2026-08-26: the change did not help; OpenCode still behaves badly and remains strongly delayed. The per-chunk Wails logging removal is retained as a valid hot-path cleanup, but its causal hypothesis is rejected. Reopened for real OpenCode debug tracing across WebKit, PTY and provider timelines.
OpenCode debug analysis after owner retest, 2026-08-26:

The OpenCode response-delay symptom is outside nocx. A minimal `opencode run` from /home/avlokhturo/git took 107.65s in an ordinary process with no Wails/PTY. `--pure` cut it to 28.71s. In the real nocx Wails v3 window, `opencode --pure --log-level DEBUG` rendered normally, accepted every typed character, began the session loop 0.55s after creation, streamed the provider answer, and painted OK in 7.7s.

The non-pure config loads three plugins sequentially: global Tokenscope, project-local .opencode/plugins/entire.ts, and global Hindsight. The OpenCode log repeatedly shows session created/event connected followed by 70-120.7s with no loop. entire.ts explains that interval structurally: session.created awaits `entire hooks opencode session-start`, and the first user message calls `Bun.spawnSync(... turn-start)`; neither has a timeout and both suppress stderr. `--pure` removes the interval.

Other measured costs are secondary: mcp-atlassian times out after 8-10s; Hindsight is unauthenticated while autoRecall/autoRetain are enabled and emits failed API calls, but the logged failures return in ~0.2s; project-copy refresh was 2-6s in controlled runs, with one historical 121s outlier on the 15GB repository root.

Conclusion: keep the per-chunk Wails logging removal as a valid hot-path cleanup, but it was not causal for OpenCode. The OpenCode slowness belongs to the external plugin/MCP chain. nocx-svxik remains open only for the separately reported generic interactive-input stall (`npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web`), which this OpenCode analysis did not reproduce or close.
Owner-approved OpenCode environment cleanup, 2026-08-27: removed the global Hindsight and Tokenscope entries from ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json after removing the project-local Entire integration. No provider/MCP/credential fields were read or changed; package caches were left intact. `opencode debug info` now reports `plugins: none` in /home/avlokhturo/git. The already-running PID 3635286 still has its old plugins in memory until a normal restart.

Clean non-pure verification returned OK in 14.95s. Logs contain no plugin initialisation or recall errors; session-created-to-loop is 1.106s (formerly 70-120.7s), project-copy is 1.118s, and the main provider stream begins 7.459s after session creation. Rollback: restore the global plugin array for Hindsight/Tokenscope and run `entire agent add opencode` for Entire.

title: internal/ssh and internal/app: 36 sleeps audited, and the assertions moved onto observables
description:
20 calls in internal/ssh and 16 in internal/app, taken together because the live-sshd tests straddle them.

nocx-bjzke is the worked example and is a child of this epic in its own right: TestLiveSshd_ForwardingRefusedStaysConventional sleeps 500ms to prove no domain is minted, then uses that same sleep as an unstated bound on channel bootstrap and writes into a channel that is still bootstrapping. Fix it first — it is currently red in the container and is one of the three tests blocking the feat/orchestration merge.

Also here: nocx-1wwm (TestLiveSshd_SSHChildAssembly_ChildEstablishesOverComposedLine waits out 30s after the child domain is granted — a test paying a full timeout for an event that already happened).

## Acceptance Criteria

No assertion in internal/ssh or internal/app depends on a duration having elapsed. nocx-bjzke and nocx-1wwm are closed. TestLiveSshd_ForwardingRefusedStaysConventional passes in the pre-commit container under ordinary shared load.
close_reason: 36 sleeps, 33 converted, 3 kept as pacing in ssh/pool_test.go. nocx-bjzke fixed and closed with it: the test now waits for the native prompt — the observable that bootstrap released input — and asserts no domain was minted at that point, which is a stronger claim than the 500ms sleep ever made. internal/ssh verified green under -count=3 -race; internal/app cannot run on this host (no /bin/bash) and was verified in 9a736ee8's container gate. Two environment blockers reported and not worked around: the missing /bin/bash, and the ssh fixture's far-side PATH lacking zsh (captured output: '/bin/sh: line 1: exec: zsh: not found').

title: internal/transport: 45 sleeps audited, and the assertions moved onto observables
description:
45 time.Sleep calls. This is the package that has produced the most gate roulette: TestBroadcastFeedChangedSurvivesARefusingClient and TestSessionSignal_InterruptReachesTheRunningCommand both timed out at 30s and 20s in today's runs and both pass natively in under two seconds.

Standing symptoms: nocx-2bvy (transport tests flake at their 5s bound under container load), nocx-8b47 (two over-the-wire contract tests and a descriptor test flake by timeout on Linux CI), and nocx-2h08, closed, which fixed three tests that discarded the frame they later waited for — read that one first, it is the worked example of what this conversion looks like here.

## Acceptance Criteria

No assertion in internal/transport depends on a duration having elapsed. Every surviving time.Sleep is pacing inside a state-waiting loop or carries a comment naming the observable it stands in for. TestBroadcastFeedChangedSurvivesARefusingClient and TestSessionSignal_InterruptReachesTheRunningCommand pass in the pre-commit container under ordinary shared load.
close_reason: 43 sleeps found in this base (the epic said 45; that count came from a branch carrying more), 36 converted, 2 kept as pacing in ws_ctx_ownership_test.go, 5 kept as unreachable-observable with reasons: ring_test.go has no signal for waiter parking, run_lease_test.go's 50ms bound IS the behaviour under test, ws_rate_limit_test.go has no injectable clock. No conversion required a production change, which the brief demanded be reported rather than done. Verified: internal/transport/... green under -count=3 -race, and in 9a736ee8's container gate. TestAgentAsk_TwoConcurrentStreamsInterleaveWithoutCorrupting was investigated and has no sleep of its own — it is nocx-quqbz, filed separately with a repro handle.

title: internal/shellintegration: 46 sleeps audited, and the assertions moved onto observables
description:
46 time.Sleep calls, the largest concentration in the repo, in the package whose tests drive real shells. Audit every call site: convert the ones an assertion rests on to a wait on the observable they stand in for, and leave the ones that are genuine pacing inside a loop that already waits on state — with a comment saying so.

Standing symptoms in or near this package: nocx-yjen (TestBashInterruptAnnouncesNoPhantomCommand intermittently never sees the prompt after the interrupt), nocx-x8ol (TestOneLaneSeveralDomainsNoCurrentDomain fails under low parallelism). Read them before starting; one or both may simply close.

## Acceptance Criteria

No assertion in internal/shellintegration depends on a duration having elapsed. Every surviving time.Sleep is pacing inside a state-waiting loop or carries a comment naming the observable it stands in for and why none is reachable. The package passes in the pre-commit container while the machine is under ordinary shared load.
close_reason: 46 sleeps audited, 44 converted to testwait waits, 2 kept as pacing with comments, 0 kept as unreachable-observable — the cleanest result in the wave. Also restored a lost exit\n write in the no-transport fail-open test. The worker could not run the package natively: this host has no GNU Bash 3.2 and no dash (nocx-wxgf covers that), so nocx-yjen and nocx-x8ol were left unclassified rather than guessed at. Verified where it can be verified: the container Go run in 9a736ee8's gate, green.

title: One way to wait, and it is findable
description:
"Wait until a condition holds" exists nine times under five names: waitFor in internal/lifecycleremote:129, internal/uistate:780, internal/apisend:536, internal/transport (ws_files_test.go:107) and internal/proc:56, each with its own signature — some take a timeout, some do not, some take a description — plus waitForOutput, waitForCount, waitForEither and waitForFile in shellintegration, pty and git.

That is the cause, not a tidiness complaint. When the idiom is spelled differently in every package and findable in none, time.Sleep is the cheaper move at every call site, and it will go on being cheaper after every conversion in this epic unless this lands first.

Give it one owner: a small shared test helper package, the way internal/storage/storagetest and internal/vault/vaulttest already are. It waits on a predicate, names what it is waiting for in the failure, and has one timeout policy. Convert the nine existing spellings to it and delete them, so the next package has nothing to copy from but the right thing.

## Acceptance Criteria

One exported waiting helper, in one package, used by every suite that previously had its own. No package-local waitFor/waitForOutput/waitForCount/waitForEither remains. A grep for 'func waitFor' outside the helper package returns nothing.
close_reason: internal/testwait owns 'wait until a condition holds'. WaitFor takes the predicate plus a description, so a timeout names the missing state instead of a line number; the timeout is a default rather than a per-call-site parameter, which was the specific cost that made transport's spelling push callers toward time.Sleep. WaitForTimeout keeps an explicit ceiling for genuinely slow fixtures and carries 121 of the converted calls, so the 15s PTY waits and 20s zsh verdict waits kept exactly the ceilings they had. 91 call sites converted, 11 helper declarations deleted across lifecycleremote, uistate, apisend, transport, proc, discovery, lifecyclechannel, shellintegration, pty. Landed as 13ac6a3f on branch w-waitfor with the full pre-commit gate green, container Go run included - which is the only place internal/shellintegration and internal/app can run on this host at all, since it has no /bin/bash and no dash. Coordinator fixed three things the worker's report missed or got wrong: four transport files and one shellintegration file left un-gofmt'd (all clean at origin/main, so introduced), and a missing t.Helper() in the inner waitFor that would have reported every timeout against wait.go instead of the caller.

title: A merge is not a lottery: no test rests on a duration
description:
A merge into main is currently decided by how busy the machine is. Every failure this
session was reproduced as environment-dependent and none was a product defect, but that
was four gate runs and roughly two hours to establish, and the answer would have been the
same on any of them: a test asserted that something had happened because a fixed number of
milliseconds had passed.

## What this crosses, and what those documents already decided

AGENTS.md settled the rule in 2026-08-11, when the per-runner CPU caps came off: "a test
may not depend on timing. Wait on an observable state change — a frame, a record, a DOM
state — never on a duration. A spec that needs a slow machine to pass is broken on a fast
one too; it has only not been caught yet." The caps had been keeping timing-dependent
specs reproducible, which is what kept them alive. Taking the caps off made the rule
binding and left the existing violations in place. This epic is that debt.

It is also AD-8 stated as a habit. "Wait until a condition holds" is already implemented
nine times under five names — waitFor in internal/lifecycleremote, internal/uistate,
internal/apisend, internal/transport and internal/proc, each with a different signature,
plus waitForOutput, waitForCount, waitForEither and waitForFile elsewhere. When the idiom
is that hard to find, writing time.Sleep is the cheaper move at every single call site,
which is why counting the sleeps measures a symptom and not the cause. One owner for the
behaviour comes first; the conversions follow it.

## The surface

200 time.Sleep calls in Go tests: internal/shellintegration 46, internal/transport 45,
internal/ssh 20, internal/vault 16, internal/app 16, internal/discovery 15, internal/git 11,
internal/pty 7, internal/filesystem 5, internal/content 4, and 9 across the rest. An unknown
fraction are legitimate pacing inside a loop that does wait on state — the 2ms between a
child process's writes, for instance. The audit is per call site and the count is a floor
on the work, not a description of it.

## Why the front is deliberately wide

Once the shared idiom exists, the package conversions do not collide: different files,
different suites. The children after the first are parallel on purpose, so a wave of
workers can take one package each. This is the one place where "sequence the children so
the front is ~3" is the wrong shape — that rule serves one person's queue, and this epic
is meant to be worked by several at once.

## What it does not contain

The Playwright suite's own timing (a separate stand, a separate set of rules). The
NOCX_CI_CPUS and NOCX_E2E_CPUS capping knobs, which stay what AGENTS.md says they are — a
bisecting tool for a suspected concurrency defect, never the gate. And any change to what
the gate runs or when it runs it.

## Standing symptoms this explains

nocx-2h08 (closed — three transport tests discarded the frame they later waited for),
nocx-2bvy, nocx-x8ol, nocx-8b47 (in flight), nocx-j41jx, nocx-1wwm, nocx-yjen (open) and
nocx-bjzke (filed today). Each is a real bug in its own right and each stays where it is;
they are listed because the epic is done when this list stops growing, not when it is
empty.

## What the first wave learned, 2026-08-26

The sweep ran as one worker on the shared idiom, then five in parallel on disjoint packages.
180 call sites audited, 147 converted, landed as 13ac6a3f and 9a736ee8. Four things came out
of it that the next round should not have to rediscover.

**A sleep that stands in for an ABSENCE is not convertible, and that is not a cop-out.**
25 of the 33 kept sleeps assert that something did NOT happen — a retry that did not fire
early, a malformed candidate rejected with no event, a rate-limiter window not yet expired,
a lease whose configured 50ms bound IS the behaviour under test. You cannot wait for a thing
not to happen; the elapsed time is the observation. Ten are in discovery's negative-cadence
tests, four in filesystem's deliberate latency injections, five in transport. They are
commented in place so the next reader does not "finish the job" by converting them into
assertions that assert nothing.

**A brief must name the CONDITION, never the command.** Four separate misses, all the same
shape, all mine: the brief said `gofmt` where the gate runs `gofumpt` (four of five branches
came back unformatted, every case introduced, every case invisible to the worker who had
truthfully run what was asked); it listed `-count=3` and `-race` on separate lines, so all
five ran them separately and nobody ran the combination; it never mentioned golangci-lint,
which is in the gate; and it gave the first worker a FILE LIST rather than "the tree
compiles", so it stopped at the list with six packages broken. The second brief said "go vet
must exit 0" and that was enough. Say what must be true, not what to type.

**Counting sleeps measures a symptom.** The real cause was that "wait until" had eleven
spellings under five names and was findable from none of them, which made `time.Sleep` the
cheaper move at every call site. That is why nocx-td6d4.1 had to land first and why the wave
was blocked on it: five workers starting from the old state would have written five more
spellings.

**A helper that cannot carry a diagnostic will silently eat them.** 78 of the 138 conversions
dropped a t.Fatalf carrying state, because testwait had no shape for it. Only one was caught,
and only because its diagnostic lived in a named function that the conversion orphaned and
`unused` flagged. See nocx-td6d4.8. The helper now has WaitForDetail; the restoration is
still owed.

**Worktree counts differ from this epic's.** The wave was cut from origin/main, which carries
neither internal/git's test files nor the internal/content conversion from nocx-796iq. Every
worker reported a different total than the brief stated, and every one of them was right.

## Success Criteria

A merge staging Go files across every package passes the pre-commit container gate three
consecutive times on a machine under ordinary shared load — the condition under which four
runs out of four failed today, each on a different test. No Go test asserts that an event
occurred because a duration elapsed: every remaining time.Sleep is either pacing inside a
loop that waits on state, or carries a comment naming the observable it stands in for and
why none is reachable.

Falsified if a package is declared converted while a sleep still gates an assertion in it,
or if a sixth spelling of "wait until" is added rather than the shared one being used.
notes:
## Two sightings on 2026-08-26, both under a machine another session had saturated

Recorded as evidence rather than as a diagnosis: in both cases the failure appeared only
while the box was oversubscribed (load average 33-65 on 6 cores, ~2 GB of 11 free) and
neither reproduced on a quiet machine.

1. `frontend/src/api/api-workbench.test.tsx` — "dragging the OPEN request leaves it open"
   and its neighbours failed inside the CONTAINERIZED vitest of a pre-commit run whose
   staged change touched no frontend source at all (a Go change plus a contract, a generated
   type and a lint baseline). The failing line is
   `await vi.waitFor(() => expect(runCards()).toHaveLength(1))` — a wait on a duration, which
   is what this epic exists to remove. Same run, an earlier attempt, died differently:
   `ERR_IPC_CHANNEL_CLOSED` from tinypool, i.e. a worker process killed rather than a test
   failing.

2. `internal/content` failed once, in company with `internal/assistant`, in a plain host run.
   It then passed four times: three plain runs and one `-race` run of 49s. The failing test's
   name was lost (the coordinator's own command truncated the output), so this sighting is a
   report of the SHAPE and not an accusation of a named test.

What both have in common is what the epic already says: a spec that needs a fast machine to
pass is broken on a slow one, and the only reason it looks green is that nobody has run it
under load yet. The container gate is where this surfaces, because it competes with whatever
else the developer is running.

Also seen the same day and already filed separately: nocx-quqbz
(`TestAgentAsk_TwoConcurrentStreamsInterleaveWithoutCorrupting` fails only in company).
2026-08-29, coordinator, drive-by observation: TestWSServer_AttachWithStaleOffsetReturnsReset (internal/transport) failed once on a baseline run and passed on the next full run of the same tree, same commit, no edits between. Reported by a worker recording its baseline, not chased. One data point, not a diagnosis — recorded here because this epic is where a test that passes or fails by luck belongs, and because the next person to see it red should know it has been seen before rather than assume their change caused it.

title: TestLiveSshd_ForwardingRefusedStaysConventional writes into a channel it never waited for, so a loaded container refuses the input
description:
internal/app/live_sshd_test.go:938. The test sleeps 500ms to establish that a refused
tcpip-forward mints no domain, then writes into the ssh channel to show the terminal is
still an ordinary usable shell. The write is refused:

    live_sshd_test.go:950: write echo: ssh channel is bootstrapping: input refused

The 500ms was never a bound on bootstrap — it is there to give minting a chance to happen
so the test can prove it does not. That it also happened to outlast bootstrap was
incidental, and on a loaded container it does not. The failure is fast (0.83s, 0.99s), not
a timeout, which is why it reads as a defect and is not one.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Merge anything into feat/orchestration, or otherwise stage Go files across packages, so
   pre-commit runs the whole Go suite in its container.
2. Run it while the machine is busy — other agents' gates, a Rust build, foreign go test
   processes.
3. internal/app fails with "write echo: ssh channel is bootstrapping: input refused",
   in under a second.
4. Natively on an idle host the same test passes.

## The fix

Wait on the channel leaving bootstrap — an observable state — before writing, and keep the
minting assertion on its own footing rather than on the same sleep. AGENTS.md: a test may
not depend on timing; a spec that needs a slow machine to pass is broken on a fast one too,
it has only not been caught yet.

## Wider context

This is the same class as nocx-796iq, which was fixed the same day. Counting is not
diagnosis, but the surface is large: 200 time.Sleep calls across Go tests, concentrated in
internal/shellintegration (46), internal/transport (45), internal/ssh (20), internal/vault
(16) and internal/app (16). Some are legitimate pacing inside a wait loop; an unknown
fraction are assertions resting on a duration. Related: nocx-2h08 (one starved resource in
internal/transport reporting a 30s timeout under a different test name in every
environment) and nocx-2bvy (transport tests flake at their 5s bound under container load).

## Acceptance Criteria

TestLiveSshd_ForwardingRefusedStaysConventional does not write into the channel until the
channel reports it is past bootstrap, and the no-domain-minted assertion no longer depends
on a sleep having outlasted anything. The test passes inside the pre-commit container on a
loaded machine, which is where it currently fails, and still passes on an idle host.
close_reason: Fixed in 9a736ee8 as part of nocx-td6d4.4. The 500ms sleep is gone; the test waits for NATIVE_PROMPT> — the observable that channel bootstrap has released input — then asserts no domain was minted, then writes. Both halves now stand on their own footing, and the minting assertion is stronger than before: it holds at the moment the shell reached its prompt rather than after an arbitrary interval.

title: Report the Adiantum-over-WAL concurrency defect to ncruces/go-sqlite3
description:
nocx-4p3l2 is contained in nocx by maxOpenConns=1 (ADR-0042), but the defect is the library's and reproduces with no nocx code on v0.35.2 and v0.35.3.

WHAT TO SEND. A standalone program: driver.Open with vfs=adiantum, PRAGMA hexkey, journal_mode=WAL, SetMaxOpenConns(16); one goroutine doing 2000 INSERTs while 16 goroutines each run 300 SELECTs; repeat in rounds against one growing database. Readers fail with 'database disk image is malformed' in roughly 3 rounds in 16, and in 10 of 12 once the table has tens of thousands of rows. The same program is clean with the VFS removed, clean with journal_mode=TRUNCATE, and clean at SetMaxOpenConns(1).

THE MECHANISM to state: vfs/adiantum/hbsh.go enciphers 4096-byte blocks; a WAL frame is 24+page_size, so frames never align to them and appending one does a read-modify-write of the block holding the tail of the previous, already-committed frame. SQLite's WAL locking guarantees a reader's FRAMES do not change, not that the surrounding bytes hold still, and a wide-block cipher turns a torn read of those bytes into a garbled plaintext block.

A SECOND, SEPARATE DEFECT found in the same read: hbsh.go's ReadAt returns (n, err) when the underlying ReadAt gives m != blockSize, so an implementation that returns a short read with err == nil produces a silent short read; the WriteAt path has the mirror of it, and vfs.go's vfsWrite does not check n == iAmt. An os.File will not do this, so it does not explain the failure above — but vfs.File is an interface and is not entitled to assume every implementation preserves ReaderAt semantics.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An issue is filed upstream with the reproducer, the mechanism and the version tested, and its URL is recorded on this bead.
- The short-read/short-write observation is included, clearly marked as a separate defect from the race.
- If upstream fixes it, nocx-jsvvv (restore reader concurrency) is unblocked and references the release that carries the fix.

title: Stop on the turn stops the turn and leaves its command running
description:
Owner, 2026-08-26, with a screenshot: the turn block reads `stopped` and carries 2m 40s,
while the tool command nested inside it — `find / -type f -name 'SiYuan-…zip'` — is still
going, its own row showing 2m 5s and a live dot.

A turn is the parent node and its command is a child (ADR-0040: a block is a node in an
ordered tree). Stopping the parent must reach the children it caused, or "stopped" is a
label the product applies to itself while the machine keeps working — the exact shape
AGENTS.md calls a soft degrade the UI contradicts.

Related but not the same as nocx-uvac6.4, which is Stop on the COMMAND block reporting
nothing to stop. Both may share a cause; establish that rather than assuming it, and if
they do, say so in both.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Ask the assistant something that makes it run a long command; approve it.
2. Press Stop on the TURN block (the parent, whose header is the question).
3. The turn is marked stopped. The command row underneath keeps running to completion.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Stopping a turn ends the tool calls and commands that turn caused, and the turn is not
  marked stopped until they are actually stopped.
- A child that cannot be stopped (a remote host nocx cannot signal) leaves the turn
  saying so, rather than claiming a stop that did not happen.
- Asserted end to end: a real assistant run with a live command, stopped from the parent,
  with the child observed to end.
close_reason: agent.cancel signals the connection-owned foreground stop before cancelling the assistant context and terminalizes on its outcome, so a stopped turn takes the command it caused. foregroundUnsupported is now its own outcome so an un-signalable session cannot be reported as a stop. Real-socket test observes the renderer-submitted command's child exit. The visible-warning half is nocx-uvac6.6. Commit 4b868730.

title: Stop on a command the assistant is running says there was nothing to stop
description:
Owner, 2026-08-26, with a screenshot: the assistant proposed `find / -type f -name
'SiYuan-…zip' 2>/dev/null`, it was approved, the block is visibly running with its
progress dots — and Stop raises the toast "Nothing is running in this pane any more, so
there was nothing to stop." The command keeps running.

What is known so far, from reading rather than guessing:

- The renderer sends nothing unless it believes a command is running:
  `signalActiveCommand` (terminal-content.ts:3957) returns early on
  `!hasRunningCommand()`. So the toast means the WIRE answered, and answered
  `nothing-running` — the renderer's own check passed.
- The backend decides that from the pty's foreground process group via TIOCGPGRP
  (`internal/transport/foreground_signal.go`): `foregroundNothingRunning` is returned when
  the foreground group is the shell's own.
- `internal/agenttools/runner.go:17` says how a run is performed is the renderer's
  business — "the renderer submits it into the pane's own composer" — which should make
  an assistant command an ordinary foreground command with an ordinary process group.

So one of those three is not true for an assistant-submitted run, and which one is the
whole bead. Establish it before editing: whether the command reaches the pty at all,
whether it reaches a DIFFERENT session than the one Stop signals, and what TIOCGPGRP
actually reports while it runs.

Note nocx-uvac6's own sentence: "a Stop that quietly did nothing is worse than one that
failed". This one is louder than that and still wrong.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Ask the assistant to do something that makes it run a long command (`find /` will do).
2. Approve it; the block runs.
3. Press Stop on the running block's ⋮ menu. The toast says there was nothing to stop,
   and the command carries on.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Stop on a running assistant command reaches that command and ends it.
- The refusal sentence is reachable only when nothing is genuinely running — asserted by
  a test that drives a real assistant run and stops it, not by constructing the outcome.
- Ctrl+C from the pane does the same thing as Stop on that block; one owner, both
  gestures (the seam terminal-content.ts already documents).
close_reason: The pane's liveness predicate now also asks the agent-run waiter it already holds, closing the window between block creation and the lifecycle acknowledgement where Stop believed nothing ran. Real mounted assistant-command test asserts Stop is available and goes through the one signal path. Commit 4b868730.

title: TestTwoProcessesShareDatabase kills its children on a stopwatch, so the container gate is red and the host is green
description:
internal/content/sqlite_internal_test.go:348. The test starts a writer child and a
checkpointer child against one database, sleeps 800ms, SIGKILLs both, reopens and
asserts count(*) > 0. On a container the two re-execs plus opening an encrypted SQLite
store do not reliably reach their first commit inside 800ms, so the reopen finds zero
rows and the test fails as "no rows survived two processes writing to one database".

Reproducibly red in the pre-commit container (3/3 runs, 1.10s each, identical message)
and green natively on the host (1.04s) — the signature AGENTS.md names: a test that
depends on a duration is broken on the fast machine too, it has just not been caught
there.

It blocks integration rather than a feature. pre-commit scopes its Go run by what is
staged, so an ordinary commit touching a few files never reaches internal/content, while
a merge — which stages Go files across many packages — always does. That is why this
surfaces only when somebody merges, and why merging main into feat/orchestration stopped
on it.

Not a product defect and not introduced by a merge: internal/content is untouched both by
feat/orchestration and by the seven vault commits main brought in.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Stage a change that touches Go files in several packages (any merge of main will do).
2. Let the pre-commit hook run, or invoke its Go leg directly: ./scripts/ci-linux.sh
3. internal/content fails with
   sqlite_internal_test.go:390: no rows survived two processes writing to one database
4. Run the same test natively on the host — go test ./internal/content/ -run
   TestTwoProcessesShareDatabase -count=1 — and it passes.

## The fix this package already contains

newChildReporting (sqlite_internal_test.go:301) hands the caller the child's stdout
precisely so a parent can wait until the child has DONE something; its doc comment cites
the AGENTS.md timing rule by name. retention_crash_internal_test.go:152 consumes it
correctly — the evictor child writes one ack byte per completed pass, the parent
io.ReadFull's exactly N of them and only then kills.

So extend that pattern rather than inventing a second one: have childWriter and
childCheckpointer each emit an ack byte per iteration, take both children through
newChildReporting, read the acks, then SIGKILL. No sleeps remain and the assertion
becomes true on any machine.

## Acceptance Criteria

TestTwoProcessesShareDatabase contains no time.Sleep in its body; both children are
started through newChildReporting and are killed only after their acknowledgements have
been read. The test passes inside ./scripts/ci-linux.sh, which is where it currently
fails, and still passes on the host.
close_reason: Both children now acknowledge each committed unit of work (a byte per row, a byte per WAL truncation) and the test reads those acknowledgements instead of sleeping: eight rows and three truncations before the checkpointer is killed, eight more rows before the writer is. No time.Sleep remains in the test body. newChild had no callers left and is gone, its doc folded into newChildReporting, which also now reaps its child via t.Cleanup so an early t.Fatalf cannot leave one spinning on a shared machine. Proven where it failed: 'ok github.com/shady2k/nocx/internal/content 62.301s' inside the pre-commit container, which had been red 3 runs of 3 at 1.10s. Landed as 74203e6e.

title: internal/content: a reader saw 'database disk image is malformed' once, under a full ./... run
description:
TestConcurrentReadersWithOneWriter (internal/content/sqlite_test.go:359) failed once in the backend-linux no-Secret-Service variant with

    reader: sqlite3: database disk image is malformed

The test runs one writer inserting 1000 entries while four readers each run 100 QueryEntries against the same store. A malformed-image error is not a timeout and not a lock contention message — SQLite is saying it read a page it could not parse. Whatever the cause, this is the store this product keeps a person's command history in, and the symptom deserves an answer rather than a re-run.

MEASURED 2026-08-26, on the wA-integration merge commit 8cc137ca, in .githooks/images/ci-linux on every core:

- ./scripts/ci-linux.sh, full ./... — no-keyring variant RED on this one test; the with-keyring variant of the SAME script run green in the same invocation.
- ./scripts/ci-linux.sh --no-keyring -- ./internal/content/... three times — green (41.3s, 42.7s, 41.0s).
- ./scripts/ci-linux.sh again, full ./..., both variants — GREEN (content 45.5s and 55.7s).

So it reproduces only under the I/O contention of the whole package set running at once, roughly one run in two.

NOT A MERGE DEFECT, and this is checked rather than assumed: internal/content on the merge commit is byte-identical to origin/main (git diff --quiet origin/main HEAD -- internal/content/ is clean). The merge brought main's ledger-tree work into the branch and changed nothing in it. This bead belongs to main.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. ./scripts/ci-linux.sh --no-keyring   (the whole ./... package set, uncapped cores, on a loaded machine)
2. Repeat. Roughly one run in two, TestConcurrentReadersWithOneWriter fails with 'reader: sqlite3: database disk image is malformed'.
3. The same test with only ./internal/content/... passes every time.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The cause is named: either the store's connection setup is wrong for concurrent readers under load (journal mode, shared cache, pool size, the busy handler) and is fixed, or the corruption is shown to be the container filesystem's and the test is made to say so instead of failing as if the store were at fault.
- If it is the store: a test that fails on the defect before the fix and passes after, and it does not need a loaded machine to do it.
- 20 consecutive full-./... no-keyring runs are green.
- Whatever the answer, ContentDB's promise about concurrent readers is written down where the next person reads it — right now the only statement of it is this test's name.
close_reason:
Root cause found and contained. The adiantum VFS enciphers whole 4096-byte blocks; a WAL frame is 24+page_size, so appending one rewrites the block holding the tail of the previous, already-committed frame, which a reader on another connection is entitled to be reading — and a wide-block cipher turns a torn read of those bytes into a garbled plaintext block. Isolated on the raw ncruces driver with no nocx code (encrypted+WAL fails, plaintext+WAL does not, encrypted+rollback-journal does not, encrypted+WAL at one connection does not); present on v0.35.2 and v0.35.3. Transient: no rows lost, integrity_check ok afterwards.

Fixed by maxOpenConns=1 (0d3c90de) with ADR-0042. A rollback journal was chosen first and reversed on measurement: 3.89 ms/commit against WAL's 0.03, on a store whose AppendChunk commits once per streamed assistant delta. Two latent cursor-held-across-pool-read deadlocks (executionsFor, artifactsFor) had to be repaired for one connection to be viable; codex found the first, and the package hung 3m54s in Entry before the fix. Guarded by TestThePoolIsOneConnection (deterministic gate) plus TestConcurrentReadersWithOneWriter (net, red 5 of 8 at sixteen connections; 65192a4f trimmed it after it put the package at 400s against a 600s CI timeout). Full gate green: ci-linux both variants, ci-frontend 4957 tests, e2e 417 passed, deadcode ratchet 0 new.

Follow-ups: nocx-8xseo (upstream report, including the separate silent short-read in hbsh.go ReadAt), nocx-amst3 (Backup holds the only connection; ADR-0018's multi-process claim now unproven).

title: Merge main into wA-integration before the API-testing PR
description: wA-integration carries two closed epics (nocx-0khco, and the workbench work under nocx-6hg2w) and had not moved since main released v0.3.0. Main gained the assistant ledger work (ADR-0039, ADR-0040), agenttools, and a fix to the api-testing e2e spec that this branch deletes. This is the merge, its conflict resolutions, and the full gate on the merged tree.
close_reason: Merged origin/main (90e45c02) into wA-integration as 8cc137ca. Four conflicts resolved (ADR renumbered 0039->0041, api-testing.spec.ts deletion upheld, kit README table, app.go imports) plus one defect that existed only in the merge (duplicate onKeyDown on ui/text-field.tsx, now composed). Gate on the merged tree: ci-linux both variants green, ci-frontend green, e2e 417 passed / 9 skipped both browsers, deadcode ratchet 85 baselined and 0 new. Host-side backend job cannot run on this NixOS machine (no /bin/dash, no /bin/bash) — CI's ci-mac is the source of truth for it. One flake filed as nocx-4p3l2, one test-budget bug as nocx-jzlsf.

title: A sealed vault refuses the ask before the command runs, and raises the unlock
description:
The product half of nocx-1mf3v, and the owner's report of 2026-08-26: "для локальной
модели для ответа нужен vault, запрос не появляется" — the ask needs the vault and no
unlock is ever raised.

The egress gate screens the RESULT, so by the time it fails closed the command has
already run. Failing closed is correct (design §7.1: nothing may leave when the gate
cannot see); a fail-closed gate placed AFTER the effect is a design fact that must be
visible in the product. A sealed vault is not an exotic state — it is the state after
every restart and after any timed re-seal.

The readiness ladder (nocx-rikz5) already owns one sentence per unready state and one
repair page, and already refuses an ask with no answering role assigned. A sealed vault
belongs on that ladder. ADR-0032 says the vault raises its own unlock; the ask path
does not reach it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Restart nocx so the vault is sealed; configure a local model endpoint whose key is a
   vault secret.
2. Ask the assistant anything that needs the endpoint.
3. No unlock sheet appears. The turn spends a command and fails.

## Acceptance Criteria

- With the vault sealed, asking raises the unlock sheet instead of spending a command.
- Unlocking from that sheet lets the same ask proceed without retyping the question.
- Declining leaves a sentence that says the vault is sealed and how to unlock it later.
- An e2e check watches a person ask with a sealed vault, unlock, and get their answer.
design:
Coordinator investigation, 2026-08-26 — read this before designing anything.

nocx-k41yv (P0, closed 2026-08-23, commit ca472bee) already fixed the CREDENTIAL half of
exactly this shape. Its finding is the one that matters here: ADR-0032's seam covers ONE
shape of traffic — a failure travelling out as the error on a control REQUEST, which
sealedNormalizer rewrites and the renderer's dispatcher acts on by raising the unlock. A
failure that travels as a run-state NOTIFICATION escapes the seam by construction. k41yv
resolved it by moving the credential resolution BEFORE the run is created, so a sealed
vault is a failure of the agent.ask REQUEST and reaches the person as the unlock prompt.

The egress gate cannot use that answer, and this is why this bead is not a duplicate. Its
screening happens mid-run, after a tool has already executed:

  policy.go WrapInvokableToolCall → KnownMaterial.FindKnown
    → transport/known_material.go:44 vaultKnownMaterial.FindKnown
      → vault.BuildInventory → inventory.go:141: `case StateSealed: return nil, ErrVaultSealed`

BuildInventory returns the sentinel directly. It never reaches UnlockRequester, so no
prompt is raised, and by then the command has run and its result is discarded.

And the method written for precisely this case has no caller: `Vault.EnsureUnsealed`
(vault/unlock.go:87) raises ONE prompt for every waiter and blocks until answered.
app.go:1248 says so in as many words — "NOT YET LIVE FOR USERS: EnsureUnsealed has no
production consumer until nocx-k41yv routes the sealed secret-access paths through it" —
and that comment is still true after k41yv, because k41yv took the move-it-earlier route
instead. Confirmed by grep: the only occurrence outside internal/vault is that comment.

So the shape of the answer is probably: the egress gate declares its stance (k41yv's own
vocabulary — a USER-INITIATED OPERATION may raise, a READ THAT REPORTS A FACT may not),
and a screening call for a live ask raises through EnsureUnsealed, waits, and continues
with the result intact rather than discarding it. That makes EnsureUnsealed live and
retires the app.go note. Decide it deliberately; k41yv's last criterion — amend ADR-0032
to cover runs and streams, saying whether wait-and-continue or re-drive was chosen and
why — was written for this and should be honoured here.

Do NOT re-decide k41yv's credential path. It shipped and has tests.
close_reason: The egress gate declares an Operation stance and resolves through the shared credential.Resolver, so a sealed vault raises the unlock, the run waits, and screening continues with the result intact. One resolver serves connection and egress. ADR-0032 records wait-and-continue over re-drive. Admission established by reading handleAsk (holds op.Run only around SubmitAsk, releases before the stream task). Real-socket test observes the unlock, answers vault.unseal, and reads the streamed answer. Commit d36cb646.

title: The withheld-result error has no type, so it lands on 'the details are in nocx's log'
description:
The Go half of nocx-1mf3v. internal/assistant/policy.go:528 returns a plain
fmt.Errorf("agent tool %q: egress screening failed — the result was withheld: %w").
classifyAskFailure (internal/transport/ws_agent.go:1767) matches by TYPE, deliberately
and by its own doc comment, so an untyped error cannot be reached by any arm and lands
on UnexplainedFailureSentence — "the model failed to answer. The details are in nocx's
log." — naming a log a desktop user cannot open.

The cause is nameable and the repair is one click: the vault is sealed.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Leave the vault sealed (the state after every restart).
2. Ask the assistant something that makes it call a tool.
3. The command runs, its output appears, and the turn ends with the log sentence.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The screening failure is a typed error carrying which gate withheld the result and why.
- classifyAskFailure has an arm reaching it by type, whose sentence names the cause and
  the repair in the person's words, with no framework text.
- A sealed vault specifically produces a sentence that says the vault is sealed and where
  to unlock it.
- A test drives the real path — screening fails, the error crosses classifyAskFailure —
  rather than constructing the typed error in the test and asserting the arm.
close_reason: EgressScreeningError carries the tool, the gate and the wrapped cause; classifyAskFailure gains a typed arm after the tool-failure arm; a sealed vault is recognised by vault's own sentinel and gets its own sentence. Test drives a real agent.ask over the socket through the policy middleware and reads the sentence off runState. Commit ab1cc64c, full gate green.

title: A selection offers to be marked again: the affordance comes back, and the selection stops marking itself
description:
Owner decision 2026-08-26, asked directly: the floating control that `attach-affordance.tsx`
used to be should come back, as the explicit step between selecting and marking.

Today a selection marks its block the instant `selectionchange` fires
(terminal-content.ts:533 → grantBlockFromSelection → ensureGrant). Selecting output to
read it, or to copy it, therefore also marks it, and nothing was confirmed. nocx-a7mw7.1
had exactly this thesis — "a selection offers to be attached, and never attaches itself" —
and the affordance was deleted in f7a31ba2 as the leftover of a surface nocx-wcswn had
replaced. What was left behind was the offer, not the styling.

Reinstating it must not recreate the defect AGENTS.md names under "Two surfaces may never
own the same input": the affordance and the block's ⋮ mark item must be two doors to ONE
derivation (ask-entry.ts), not two implementations of "what did this selection mean".
nocx-5u3oz.16 settled that derivation on 2026-08-26 — a selection covering a block's whole
output is a whole-block mark, a genuine subset is a row window — and the affordance
confirms whatever it yields rather than deciding again.

Sequencing: this touches terminal-content.ts and the grant surface, so it lands after
nocx-5u3oz.18/.21.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Selecting output does NOT mark anything. A control appears near the selection offering
  to; marking happens only when it is used.
- The control names what will be marked — the block, or N lines — from ask-entry.ts's
  derivation, with no second derivation anywhere.
- Dismissing the selection dismisses the offer; nothing is left marked by accident.
- The ⋮ menu item and the affordance produce identical grants for the same block.
- A unit test asserts a selection alone leaves `current` empty, and an e2e check watches a
  person select, confirm, and ask — the epic's happy path.
close_reason: The floating Mark control is back: a selection offers, the button confirms, and grantBlockFromSelection stays the one derivation both doors use — asserted by a test that compares the menu's grant with the button's. e2e pointAt now presses the offer. Commit add95edd.

title: A block from an earlier session cannot be marked: its menu has no mark item at all
description:
Owner review 2026-08-26. On a restored block — the scrollback of a session that was
reopened — the ⋮ menu offers Copy command / Copy output / Copy all / wrap, and no way to
mark it for a question. The gesture is gone too, so the earlier session's work simply
cannot be brought into an ask.

The menu builds the item under `if (running?.toggleGrant)`
(frontend/src/scrollback/blocks.ts:1031), and `running` is the live-block controller
terminal-content.ts hands in at line 1309. A restored block has no such controller, so
the item is absent — by omission, not by decision. Marking is attention, not liveness
(see nocx-5u3oz.15), and a restored block carries a durable ledger entry id, which is
exactly what a mark identity is.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a session with restored scrollback (blocks from an earlier run).
2. Open a restored block's ⋮ menu: there is no "ask about this block".
3. Select its output: the chip's count does not move.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A restored block's menu offers the mark item, and marking it makes the chip count it.
- A selection inside a restored block marks it, exactly as in a live one.
- The mark identity is the block's durable entry id, never a renderer-local counter.
- An ask that names a restored block reaches the model with that block readable.
close_reason: restored blocks get the same runningActions object the live path uses, threaded through restoredBlock/restoredTurn and every caused-child path; mark identity is the durable entry id. Commit 87271fb3.

title: The marks popover cannot be closed without clearing the marks
description:
Owner review 2026-08-26. Once the popover is open there is no way out that keeps the
marks: Escape does nothing, a click outside does nothing, and the only control that
closes it — "Dismiss all" — throws away every mark on the way. Looking at what you
marked therefore costs you the marks, which is the opposite of what the surface is for.

`GrantController` mounts a `FloatingPanel` and never registers a dismissal path; the
panel is hidden only from inside its own row handlers (frontend/src/grant.ts).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Mark a block, flip to Ask, click the chip — the popover lists the mark.
2. Press Escape: nothing. Click the terminal behind it: nothing.
3. The only way to close it is "Dismiss all", which also unmarks everything.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Escape closes the popover and every mark survives.
- A pointer press outside the popover closes it and every mark survives.
- "Dismiss all" keeps its current meaning (clear the marks) and is not the only way out.
- Unit tests assert all three.
close_reason: Escape and an outside pointer press close the popover with the marks intact, via an optional onDismiss + dismissBoundary on the kit FloatingPanel; the three other consumers pass no callback and are unchanged. Commit 8bfb14d9.

title: A selection covering a block's whole output marks rows, not the block
description:
One gesture — a drag across every output row of a finished block — now yields a row
window rather than a whole-block mark, because `selectedWindow` (frontend/src/ask-entry.ts)
returns a window whenever any `.term-line` intersects the range. The block loses
`data-granted`; the chip's popover and `session.read` carry a line range instead of the block.

The owner's decision (2026-08-26): a selection that covers ALL of a block's output rows
IS the block. A person who drags across the whole output made one movement and meant the
block; "select everything" and "select the block" must not be different things behind the
same gesture. A window stays a window only when it is a genuine subset.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run a command that prints output; wait for the block to finish.
2. Drag a selection from the first output row to the last.
3. Look at the block: `.cmd-block[data-granted]` is absent; every `.term-line` carries
   `data-granted` instead.

Automated: `e2e/agent-ask.spec.ts:322`, both browsers, reproduces on clean state.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `grantBlockFromSelection` returns a grant with no `start`/`count` when the range
  intersects every `.term-line` in the block.
- A genuine subset of rows still yields `{start, count}` — the existing row-window test
  stays green.
- `e2e/agent-ask.spec.ts` passes unchanged (no edit to `pointAt` or `expectGranted`).
close_reason: selectedWindow collapses a full-coverage selection to a whole-block grant; ask-entry unit test added, frontend suite 4940 green, agent-ask.spec.ts 6/6 green in the container

title: [bug] The e2e stand's disposable HOME is not disposed, so a spec is green or red by what an earlier run left behind
description:
Measured 2026-08-26 while gating an epic, and it cost about an hour of
coordinator time before the method error was caught.

THE SAME COMMIT, in two worktrees, in the same container image:

  ed448299 in a fresh worktree                -> PASSES
  ed448299 in the worktree used all session   -> FAILS 3 of 3
  the same worktree after `rm -rf .e2e test-results` -> PASSES in 1.6s

So `e2e/run-in-container.sh` is not hermetic with respect to the checkout it
runs in. `.e2e/home` is the disposable HOME the suite gives the backend —
AGENTS.md calls that boundary the thing that keeps a run off your settings,
your vault and your rc files — but it PERSISTS between runs, and what an
earlier run left in it changes a later run's result.

WHAT IT COSTS, measured on this one gate:

- A full 41-minute run reported 14 failures. Re-run from a clean state, 12 of
  them were green. Only one was real.
- Those 12 were spread across shell-mode, ports-row-width, snippets (x3),
  activity, api-import, api-secret-in-path and nocxify-journey — i.e. it does
  not look like flakiness in one area, it looks like a broad regression, which
  is the most expensive false signal a gate can produce.
- It defeats bisecting entirely. Changing the commit means changing the
  worktree, which changes the state, so every bisect step measures the
  directory rather than the commit. This coordinator bisected to a four-line
  commit that removes two non-null assertions and an unused test binding —
  a change that cannot affect an SSH session — and only then noticed the
  result contradicted causality.

It also silently invalidates the guidance in AGENTS.md that the container is
where you iterate before confirming in CI: iterating there is exactly what
pollutes it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. In a worktree, run `./e2e/run-in-container.sh` for any spec set. Let it
   finish.
2. Run `./scripts/ci-frontend.sh` in the same worktree, or simply run the
   suite again a few times.
3. Run `./e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/shell-mode.spec.ts` — it fails, with
   `.nocx-editor-input` resolved but `hidden`.
4. `rm -rf .e2e test-results` and run the identical command — it passes.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A run starts from a HOME that carries nothing from any earlier run. Either
  the directory is recreated per run, or the run refuses to start on a dirty
  one and says so — a silent reuse is what this bead is about.
- The same commit produces the same result in a fresh worktree and in one that
  has been used all day. Asserted by a check, not by convention.
- Whatever the fix, `git status --ignored` after a run does not leave state
  that the next run reads.
- Name in the fix which of `.e2e`, `test-results` and the shared node_modules
  volume actually carried the difference — this bead proves .e2e/test-results
  together are enough to flip it and does NOT isolate which.

## Deliberately out

- The one REAL failure found underneath this, agent-ask.spec.ts:322, which is
  a genuine consequence of the mark-granularity change and belongs to
  nocx-5u3oz.

title: Three SSH e2e journeys are red on feat/orchestration, and were before the main merge
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

From feat/orchestration:

    PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/git-panel.spec.ts e2e/git-remote.spec.ts e2e/nocxify-journey.spec.ts

## What happens

Three fail, chromium and webkit alike:

  e2e/git-panel.spec.ts:701   on an SSH tab with no consent the consent offer is present
  e2e/git-remote.spec.ts:248  a commit from the panel, on a remote host, through its own pre-commit hook
  e2e/nocxify-journey.spec.ts:341  a hand-typed ssh: frozen local block, remote blocks, ...

The visible symptom of the first is that [data-testid="git-consent-required"] never appears. The element IS in git-panel.tsx (line 602, under state() === 'consentRequired'); the state is never reached, so the panel draws without the offer and the spec waits out its 30s.
