title: End to end: the stand is remembered across a restart, and a pinned folder overrides it
description:
The epic's success criterion. Everything under it will have unit tests; nothing will have
watched a person do it, and AGENTS.md rule 2 is explicit that on an interface-first
codebase that is the only check that can report the feature missing.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A Playwright spec: pick an environment for a collection, restart the backend, reopen,
  and the picker shows it without being touched — then send and assert the server saw the
  value that environment carries.
- The same spec, or its sibling, pins a folder to a second environment and shows that a
  request inside it sends under the folder's pin while a request outside it sends under
  the collection's stand. Asserted from what the two servers received, not from the
  picker.
- It runs in the container the way CI runs it, and it passes there.

title: A folder or a request can be pinned to a stand, and the picker says which level answered
description:
With the collection's stand remembered (nocx-6hyke.1), the second half: a `tinkoff/`
folder that always goes to the tinkoff stand while the rest of the collection goes
wherever it is currently pointed.

## The chain, and the one rule that keeps it single-owner

A send's environment is answered nearest-first: the request's own pin, then the nearest
folder's pin, then its parents', then the collection's stand. Same shape as the variable
chain (nocx-x3cax), and a person is owed the same sentence for both.

THE PICKER EDITS WHATEVER LEVEL CURRENTLY ANSWERS. It shows the EFFECTIVE environment for
what is open and names where it came from — "the collection's stand", "pinned on this
request", "pinned on folder tinkoff". Changing it changes that same level: unpinned, it
moves the collection's stand, which keeps switching stands one click for the ordinary
case; pinned, it re-pins. Pinning and clearing a pin are separate, explicit gestures, so
a pin can never be created by a person who thought they were switching stands.

That rule is what stops this being two surfaces owning one input — the defect this repo
keeps meeting. The chain is the owner; the picker is its view and its writer.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A folder can be pinned from the folder page, and a request from the request surface.
- A request inside a pinned folder, with no pin of its own, sends under the folder's pin —
  proven by what the send actually carried, not by what the picker displays.
- The nearest pin wins: a request's own pin beats its folder's, and a nearer folder beats
  a further one.
- The picker never shows an environment that is not the one a send would use, and always
  says which level answered.
- Clearing a pin is reachable and returns that level to what it inherits.
- Pins live in uistate beside the stand, keyed by collection path plus the request or
  folder relPath. Nothing is written into the collection.

title: The stand a collection is pointed at survives a restart
description:
`environmentFor(handle)` in api-store.ts is the single owner of "which environment does a
send from this collection go out under", and its backing is `chosenEnvironments`, a Map
keyed by the open HANDLE and held in memory. So the choice dies with the window, and the
handle is not even a stable name for the collection — it is minted per open.

## What to build

- The uistate document (ADR-0033, `internal/uistate`) grows an `api` section holding, per
  collection PATH, the environment relPath it is currently pointed at. The path, never
  the handle: the handle is per-open and means nothing after a restart.
- `environmentFor` keeps being the one answer. It reads the stored stand for the open
  collection's path, and falls back to what it already falls back to — the only
  environment when there is exactly one, otherwise none.
- `setEnvironment` writes through the same uistate client the shell uses. That client
  holds the whole renderer half and merges, because `uistate.set` replaces the document:
  two writers that do not go through it will silently drop each other's fields.
- Nothing about this is written into the collection. §8's rule is the reason and it is
  not negotiable: a collection arriving in a pull request must not choose what a reader's
  request sends.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Pick an environment, restart the backend, reopen the collection: the picker shows the
  same environment and a send goes out under it. One automated check watches that.
- A collection whose stored stand names an environment that no longer exists falls back to
  the ordinary rule rather than sending under nothing silently.
- The wire is a party: the uistate schema grows the section, the renderer type is
  generated from it, and the Go DTO conforms.
- A second writer to uistate (the sidebar width) does not lose the stand, and the stand
  does not lose the sidebar width. There is a test for that, because `uistate.set`
  replaces the document.

title: The prompt names the marked blocks, and nothing is inlined
description:
Parent: nocx-5u3oz. The last half. The frontend sends grants and the backend ignores them; the identity epic made the ids real, so nothing else blocks this.

agent-ask.ts sends attachedContent: an array of {itemId, command, state}. itemId is now the lifecycle attempt id, which is also the ledger row id, which session.read accepts. ws_agent.go accepts References []agentRefWire under the key references and knows nothing of attachedContent - and decodeParams (ws_git.go:64) is a plain json.Unmarshal, so the unknown field is silently ignored. The ask succeeds carrying zero references and the model is told nothing was attached.

SystemPromptFacts.AttachedContent (systemprompt.go:51) is a bool today. It becomes the list: the item id spelled exactly as session.read requires it, the command, and running or exited. The argument is already written in that same file about SessionID - a model that was never told the id must invent one, and an invented one is refused terminally.

Nothing is inlined. The frame text loop in ws_agent.go around line 1034 goes, and with it agent.captureFrame on the ask path. Whether captureFrame survives for another caller is a question to answer in a comment, not to leave open - and the deadcode ratchet will ask it anyway.

## Acceptance Criteria

- agent.ask accepts the grant list and refuses a malformed one rather than ignoring it. A field the wire sends and the handler drops is how this defect happened once already.
- The system prompt names each marked block by the id session.read accepts, with its command and whether it is running. A question with nothing marked says nothing about attachments, exactly as the bool did.
- No block text is inlined into the ask. Asserted by a test that submits a question with two marked blocks and checks the outgoing engine request carries no output text.
- A marked block that no longer exists - the person cleared the scrollback between marking and asking - is handled deliberately. Say what the model is told and assert it.
- The ask path no longer calls agent.captureFrame. If captureFrame survives for another caller, name that caller in a comment; if it does not, delete it.
- End to end over the real socket: a question naming two marked blocks arrives with both ids, and session.read returns each of them.
close_reason: merged; strict decode of the grant list, prompt names each item by the id session.read accepts, nothing inlined, injection guard restored and asserted by name, captureFrame deleted

title: A byte after a bootstrap frame reached the shell — intermittently, and it ran
description:
`TestStage1_AByteAfterACompleteFrameNeverBecomesShellInput` failed inside the
containerized backend-linux job. It is not a flaky assertion: the captured pty output
shows the command ACTUALLY RAN.

    LAUNCH_TEMP_GONE
    LAUNCH_DONE
    $ TRAILING_BYTE_RAN
    $ echo AFTER_TRAILER

The next line is the terminal echo of the test's own following input (`echo
AFTER_TRAILER`), which is what an echoed input line looks like. `$ TRAILING_BYTE_RAN`
has no `echo ` in front of it, so it is the OUTPUT of the trailing command, not an echo
of it. The property the test guards — the stage-1 reader consumes exactly the declared
frame length and the bytes after it never reach the user's shell — did not hold in that
run.

## What was measured, on 2026-08-25

Container, `./scripts/ci-linux.sh`, both keyring variants each time.

- Whole package at feat/api-testing tip (94722016): 3 runs. The "no Secret Service"
  variant FAILED in 2 of them; the Secret Service variant passed every time.
- Whole package at e42f158b (the branch before this session's commits): passed.
- The single test with `-run` and `-count=10`, both trees, both variants: 40 iterations,
  ZERO failures.

So it does not reproduce in isolation and needs the rest of the package running. That
points at interference between tests — leftover pty state or a process from an earlier
test in the same binary — rather than at anything the frame reader does on its own.

NOT ATTRIBUTED TO THIS SESSION'S WORK. Nothing in the seven commits touches
internal/shellintegration, the stage-1 loader or internal/pty, and no mechanism connects
them. The baseline comparison is weaker than it looks, though: one whole-package run
there against three here, so "it does not happen at baseline" is not established.

## Why it is P1 rather than a test chore

This is the boundary between the bootstrap protocol and the user's shell. A byte the
loader over-reads becomes a command somebody's shell executes, and the trailing bytes in
a real session are whatever the person typed while the shell was starting. A property
that holds most of the time is what the test exists to catch.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `./scripts/ci-linux.sh -- ./internal/shellintegration/...`
2. Repeat. The "no Secret Service" variant is where it appeared, roughly two runs in
   three at the time of writing.
3. When it fails, read the dumped pty output for `$ TRAILING_BYTE_RAN` with no `echo `
   before it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The interleaving that lets a post-frame byte reach the shell is named, not
  worked around by ordering tests differently or by draining the tty in the test.
- Whatever the cause, the reader's guarantee is stated as an interval with both ends —
  from before the frame is read until the shell is exec'd, no byte beyond the declared
  length is readable by anything downstream.
- The whole package passes 20 consecutive containerized runs in both keyring variants.
- If the cause turns out to be a test leaking a process or a pty into its neighbours,
  that leak is closed at its source and the test that leaked is named here.
notes:
DECISIVE, measured after filing: the tested code is IDENTICAL at both commits. internal/shellintegration's whole nocx dependency set is itself plus internal/log, and neither changed between e42f158b and 94722016 (go list -deps + git diff per package, both empty). So the test binary is built from the same source in the baseline runs and the failing ones, and this session's commits cannot be the cause — the description's caveat about a weak baseline is resolved.

What differs is the MACHINE. The three tip runs happened while make ci-full, container image builds and three worker agents were live; the three baseline runs happened on a quiet machine. For a race that is the expected signature, and it makes the defect worse rather than better: load makes the interleaving likelier, and a developer's machine under load is the ordinary case.

Final tally: whole package, both keyring variants — tip 3 runs, the no-Secret-Service variant failed in 2; baseline 3 runs, 6 variant-runs, all green. The single test with -count=10 in both trees and both variants: 40 iterations, zero failures. It needs the rest of the package running.

SEEN ON GITHUB'S OWN RUNNER, 2026-08-25 — which the evidence above did not yet
cover. Every occurrence recorded so far was on a developer machine under load,
and the reading was "load makes the interleaving likelier". This one had no
such machine behind it:

  CI run 32874289674, ci-backend (with-secret-service), feat/ai-assistant at
  bbe9a27f, ubuntu runner:
    --- FAIL: TestStage1_AByteAfterACompleteFrameNeverBecomesShellInput (0.04s)
        stage1_exec_test.go:525: a byte after a complete frame became shell input

The same job's OTHER variant (no-secret-service) passed in the same run, and
BOTH variants passed in the immediately preceding run 32872132780 — whose tree
differs from this one only by the removal of dead readScreen code in
internal/assistant and internal/agenttools, neither of which
internal/shellintegration depends on. So the "identical tested code, different
outcome" finding above holds on the runner too.

What this adds: the race does not need a busy workstation. A hosted runner
running the same package concurrently is enough, which makes this a
CI-flakiness source as well as a local one — and it means a red ci-backend on
any branch should be read against this bead before it is attributed to the
branch.

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

THE INTERLEAVING IS NAMED, 2026-08-25 (measured while fixing nocx-1druc; NOT
fixed — the fix is a design decision, see the end).

NOTHING IN THE BOOTSTRAP DISCARDS THE BYTES AFTER A FRAME. The loader reads
its frame with `dd bs=1 count=$L`, stage-1 reads frame 2 the same way, and
`dd bs=1` consumes exactly the declared length — that half is correct and was
never in doubt. What neither of them does is DROP WHAT IS LEFT: the trailing
bytes stay in the terminal's input queue, unread and (because the queue was
filled while the loader had `stty raw -echo`) unechoed, all the way to the
exec.

Measured directly rather than inferred. A launch carrier that reports its own
pending stdin instead of becoming a shell —

    P=$(dd bs=1 count=64 iflag=nonblock 2>/dev/null)
    printf 'LAUNCH_PENDING=[%s]\n' "$P"

— prints, on a PASSING run of the test:

    LAUNCH_PENDING=[echo TRAILING_BYTE_RAN]

So on the runs where the test is GREEN, the trailer is still sitting on the
terminal when the launch carrier starts. The loader's guarantee ends at its
own `dd`; everything after that is somebody else's.

WHAT MAKES IT PASS IS THEREFORE THE SHELL, NOT THE READER. Whether those
pending bytes become a command is decided by whatever the launch carrier
execs and what that shell does with typeahead as it prepares the terminal.
That is the race: identical tested code, different outcome, no mechanism in
our own source between them — exactly the "same binary, different result"
finding above, now with a mechanism.

Two probes bound the claim. On a bare pty (no bootstrap): the trailer written
in the same write as the frame is ALWAYS readable afterwards, whether the
line discipline is switched back to canonical immediately or after a settle,
and `/bin/sh -i`, `/bin/sh` and a plain read all get it — so the kernel is
not eating it and `n_tty_set_termios`'s canon change is not eating it either
(that was the first hypothesis and it is WRONG). In the real bootstrap the
same bytes are pending at LAUNCH and usually never run.

WHAT THE FIX IS, AND WHY IT IS NOT MADE HERE. The property the test asserts
can only be enforced by the reader: stage-1 must DISCARD the terminal's input
queue between its last frame byte and the exec (`stty min 0 time 0` plus a
draining read, or a real tcflush). That is a deliberate decision about
typeahead and it contradicts, in tone at least, carrier.go's own account of
the ordering defect it fixed — where a shell that "SWALLOWED THE USER'S NEXT
TYPED LINE" is written down as the failure. Dropping typeahead protects the
frame boundary and costs a person the line they typed during bootstrap; the
owner picks. Until then this is a known intermittent red on ci-backend, on
code no branch is changing.

title: The block carries the attempt id, not a renderer counter
description:
Parent: nocx-a240p. The frontend half. Base branch is w-grantchip, NOT feat/ai-assistant - that branch already rewrote these files for the grant surfaces and is waiting on exactly this task.

Today blocks.ts sets data-block-id from this._nextId++, a renderer-local counter meaning the third block I drew. It is not the ledger id and not the attempt id, so a grant naming it names something no backend tool accepts.

The attempt id is server-assigned at submit before the pty write (internal/lifecycle/kernel.go:409), and the submitAttempt contract already says the published running fact carries the same id and the block projection binds on it. So the renderer ALREADY receives the identity it needs; it mints a second one beside it.

After this task the block carries the attempt id, and the grant names it. The sibling backend task makes that same id the ledger row id, so session.read accepts it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A command block carries the lifecycle attempt id as its identity, and a grant raised from that block names it.
- The renderer counter is gone, or is demonstrably internal and never crosses a seam. If it survives for list keying, prove by test that nothing outside the renderer reads it.
- The identity survives the running to frozen replacement - the visual freeze replaces the element, and the id must not change with it.
- A block created by a path that has no attempt - a restored block, an answer block - keeps working. Say what identity each carries and why. Restored and answer blocks already carry data-entry-id; reconcile the two rather than adding a third.
- The test exercises the real submit path to a real block, not a constructed element with the attribute set by hand.
close_reason: merged; block carries the attempt id, identity survives the freeze, one data-entry-id attribute for all block kinds

title: A shell command's ledger row opens at submit, under the attempt id
description:
Parent: nocx-a240p. The map (nocx-vh07j notes) established the shape; this is the backend half.

Today a human command reaches the ledger only through RecordCompleted (internal/content/ledger_command.go:101), which mints its own entryID and inserts phase=closed with NO open interval. So a running command has no row, nothing can address it, and when a row finally appears it carries a third identity nobody else knows.

The generic Submit (internal/content/ledger_sqlite.go:119) already inserts open/pending AND already takes the id from its caller. The open to bound to closed transitions already exist and work - StartExecution and FinishExecution. The machinery is all there; the human command path simply does not use it.

After this task: lifecycle.submitAttempt opens the entry with the ATTEMPT id (att- plus hex, minted in internal/lifecycle/kernel.go:409 before the pty write), and the existing transitions carry it to closed. One name from submit to read.

HARD CONSTRAINT - masking. The single owner of masking durable command text is ws_history_record.go:194 (masking.MaskWithSegments). Opening the row at submit must not route text into the store around that owner. Note that the submit-time text is the app-owned reference-intact line, not the resolved line that reaches the pty (ADR-0024 decision 5 privacy rule), so vault references are already safe - but a secret the person pasted inline is not, and that is exactly what MaskWithSegments catches. Whatever persists command text masks it, through ONE function.

Costs the map already priced, do not rediscover them:
- retention.go:618 never evicts a unit whose owning entry is open, so an abandoned command pins its output. Bounded by sqlite.go:322, which closes every non-closed row as unknown at startup.
- ws_ledger.go:464 drops a backward phase event by rank. Opening earlier moves WITH that protocol; it was inserting closed early that would have broken it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A shell command has a ledger entry from submit, in phase open, whose id is the lifecycle attempt id.
- The existing StartExecution and FinishExecution transitions carry that row to closed. No second phase machine is written.
- ListSessionItems reports that row as running while it runs, and session.read addresses it by the attempt id, asserted.
- Durable command text is masked by the one existing owner. A test pastes an inline secret at submit and asserts the stored text is masked, on the SUBMIT path.
- RecordCompleted no longer mints a second identity for this path. If it survives for another caller, say which and why in a comment.
- Every partial failure is enumerated: the row opens and the pty write fails; the row opens and the process is killed; the store is unavailable at submit. State what is true on disk and how the next start recovers.
- ADR-0019 says what the store judges by the store must own. Submit already accepts a caller id, so the precedent exists - record the reasoning deliberately rather than leaving it implied.
close_reason: merged; row opens at submit under the attempt id, existing transitions close it, one command one row, store-unavailable still runs the command

title: End to end: a folder variable sends, with no environment and no request variable
description:
The epic's success criterion, and the only check that can report the feature missing
rather than confirming that what was written does what it was written to do (AGENTS.md
rule 2). Everything under it is unit-tested; nothing has watched a person do it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A Playwright spec drives the product: open a collection, open a folder, add a variable
  on the folder page, save, open a request inside that folder whose URL references it,
  send, and assert the server saw the substituted value.
- NO environment is selected and the request has no variable of its own. That is the case
  the folder scope exists for, and a spec that leaves either in place proves nothing about
  inheritance.
- The request's Variables tab shows the folder's row as the winner, naming the folder.
- It runs in the container the way CI runs it, and it passes there.
close_reason: Committed as a9192097. e2e/api-folder-variable.spec.ts drives the product end to end: import, open the folder, type a variable, save through the page, open a request inside whose URL is {{folderValue}}, send with NO environment selected and no request-owned variable of that name, and assert the spec's own server received the substituted path. Then the Variables tab shows the inherited row naming the folder with its scope cell reading 'folder'. Green in the container, the way CI runs it: PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/run-in-container.sh, 1 passed.

title: Map the identity: every writer into entries, and how attempt, execution and entry ids relate
description:
Parent: nocx-a240p. The epic cannot be sequenced until the write paths into entries are known, and the epic body itself flags the unknown: it says a running command must be addressable, and if that means the ledger opens a row at submit rather than at completion, then what else reads phase has to be checked.

This is a READ-ONLY investigation that produces a map, not a change. It exists because the alternative is designing the identity change from a guess about who writes what.

What is already established and does not need re-deriving:

- blocks.ts sets data-block-id from this._nextId++ (a renderer counter).
- lifecycle.submitAttempt returns a server-assigned id at submit, before the pty write, and its contract says the block projection binds on it.
- ledger_command.go mints a separate entryID with mintID() and inserts phase=closed hardcoded.
- ws_blocks.go ListSessionItems reads entries by pane and reports running when phase is not closed, so SOME writer produces non-closed rows.
- history-client.ts says only a COMPLETED attempt persists through history.record.

The last two cannot both be the whole story, and that gap is the point of this task.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every writer into the entries table is named, with its file and function, and what phase each one writes.
- Where non-closed entry rows come from is answered concretely - which path, on what event.
- The relationship between the attempt id, the executions table and the entry id is stated: which of them reference each other, and which are minted independently.
- Whether an attempt id is available and stable at the moment a block is created in the renderer is answered yes or no, with the code path.
- What reads entries.phase is enumerated, so the cost of opening a row earlier is known rather than guessed.
- The map names which ADRs constrain each part - ADR-0019 for the record, ADR-0024 for the attempt - and quotes the sentence that binds.
- The output is a written map in the bead notes, not a code change. No file in the repository is modified.
notes:
# Block identity map

## 1. Every writer of `entries`, including test-only writers

### Production writers

- `internal/content/ledger_sqlite.go:119-214` — `sqliteContent.Submit` is the generic entry writer. It assigns `phase=open,status=pending` for every non-`text` entry and `phase=closed,status=success` for `text` (`internal/content/ledger_sqlite.go:191-210`), then inserts once. This is the normal open-entry path for shell/agent/action kinds.
- `internal/content/ledger_command.go:101-216` — `sqliteContent.RecordCompleted` is the completed shell-history writer. It mints a backend `entryID`, inserts directly with `phase='closed'` and the supplied terminal status, and inserts one completed execution in the same transaction (`internal/content/ledger_command.go:184-208`). It does not create an open row first.
- `internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:191-294` — `sqliteContent.CaptureFrame` writes a frame entry directly as `phase='closed',status='success'` and a completed capture execution (`internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:280-294`).
- `internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:426-513` — `sqliteContent.SubmitAgentAsk` writes the question/turn directly as `phase='open',status='pending'` (`internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:497-504`), then creates its pending execution in the same transaction (`internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:506-513`).
- `internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:625-704` — `FinishAgentRun` does not insert an entry; it closes the existing ask entry and pairs `phase='closed'` with `success` for `RunCompleted`, otherwise `failure` (`internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:659-694`).
- `internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:772-858` — `OpenProse` mints and inserts a child `text` entry directly as `phase='closed',status='success'`, with empty intent and no execution (`internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:843-858`).
- `internal/content/ledger_sqlite.go:733-827` — `StartExecution` does not insert `entries`; it transitions the existing entry to `phase='bound'` (`internal/content/ledger_sqlite.go:819-825`).
- `internal/content/ledger_sqlite.go:863-905` — `FinishExecution` does not insert `entries`; it transitions the existing entry to `phase='closed'` and writes the final status/facts in the same transaction (`internal/content/ledger_sqlite.go:887-898`).
- `internal/content/sqlite.go:322-325` — startup recovery is another phase writer, not an insert: every non-closed entry is changed to `phase='closed'`; asks receive `interrupted`, all other kinds receive `unknown`.
- `internal/content/ledger_sqlite.go:711-716` and `internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:705-716` delete entries, but are not writers of new phase values. They matter because deletion is the only end of row existence after a phase interval.

### Test-only/raw writers

- `internal/content/ledger_test.go:49-60` defines `rawLedger`, the direct encrypted-SQL fixture writer. Its callers insert `entries` at `internal/content/ledger_test.go:181-184,1375-1396,1446-1468`; these deliberately exercise malformed/edge schema values and are not product paths.
- `internal/content/ledger_tree_test.go:144-181` defines and uses `textRow`, a raw `INSERT INTO entries` generator specifically to test schema CHECKs that typed callers cannot express.
- `internal/content/schema_reset_test.go:265-274` creates an old-schema fixture and directly inserts one closed entry before setting `user_version=1`; this is migration/reset-test setup only.
- Other tests call the production writers (`Submit`, `RecordCompleted`, `SubmitAgentAsk`, `CaptureFrame`, etc.); they are not additional SQL writers.

## 2. Where each identity is minted, and which identity is authoritative

There are three independent identities:

1. **Renderer block identity.** `frontend/src/scrollback/blocks.ts:1887-1918` mints `const id = this._nextId++` when `BlockManager.startBlock` creates the visible block. This is renderer-local and is the block projection's DOM/model identity. It is not the ledger `entries.id` and not the lifecycle attempt id.
2. **Lifecycle execution-attempt identity.** `internal/lifecycle/kernel.go:385-411` synchronously creates an app-originated `ExecutionAttempt` before PTY bytes, using `k.newAttemptID()` (`internal/lifecycle/kernel.go:409-410`); the helper mints `att-` plus random hex (`internal/lifecycle/kernel.go:1071-1073`). The wire contract says the id is server-assigned and that the published running fact carries the same id for the block projection (`contracts/lifecycle.submitAttempt.schema.json:5,10-12`; generated mirror `frontend/src/generated/lifecycle.submitAttempt.ts:13,16-19`). This is the authority for command-attempt ownership and attachment, not the block id.
3. **Ledger entry identity.** Generic `Submit` receives its caller-supplied id (`internal/content/ledger_sqlite.go:119-124`) and uses it as the row/idempotency identity. `RecordCompleted` mints a separate backend `entryID` (`internal/content/ledger_command.go:135-136`; inserted at `:184-190`). `CaptureFrame` and `OpenProse` also mint their own store ids (`internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:272-274,843`). `SubmitAgentAsk` receives the ask id and uses it as the question row id (`internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:497-502`). The ledger row id is the durable history identity used by recall, capture rewrite and provenance (`internal/content/ledger_command.go:99-101`), not an attempt or renderer block id.

The app-owned command text is separate again: the attempt contract explicitly says the attempt id is not renderer-correlated directly; the published running fact binds the block (`contracts/lifecycle.submitAttempt.schema.json:10-12`), while the app-owned command text remains reference-intact (`contracts/lifecycle.submitAttempt.schema.json:23-25`).

## 3. Every production reader of `entries.phase`

### SQL/typed readers that affect product behavior

- `internal/content/ledger_sqlite.go:300-335` (`Entry`) scans `e.phase` into `LedgerEntry.Phase`; `internal/content/ledger_sqlite.go:409-435` (`entryPage`) scans it for list/query summaries. These are the canonical recall reads. `internal/transport/ws_ledger_query.go:553-556` serializes that typed phase to `history.query` results.
- `internal/transport/ws_blocks.go:69-116` (`ListSessionItems`) reads each row's phase. At `:106-110`, only `closed` rows become `exited`, get an exit code, and have body text loaded; otherwise the item stays running. `internal/transport/ws_blocks.go:127-148` (`ReadSessionItem`) returns `running` and no body whenever `entry.Phase != closed` (`:144-148`).
- `internal/transport/ws_ledger.go:429-480` reads the current row phase during event application. `ledgerPhaseRank` defines open < bound < closed (`internal/transport/ws_ledger.go:179-187`); `:464-480` drops a backward phase event and replays an equal-phase event. This is the phase state machine's production reader.
- `internal/content/retention.go:618-642` excludes any unit whose owning entry is not closed; for a `text` child it checks the parent/run phase (`:637-640`). An open/bound owner therefore cannot be evicted.
- `internal/content/sqlite.go:322-327` reads `WHERE phase != 'closed'` as startup recovery and closes those rows. This is both a reader and a recovery transition.
- Schema-level phase consumers also constrain behavior: `internal/content/sqlite.go:815` requires closed/success for text rows, and `internal/content/sqlite.go:968` indexes all non-closed rows. These are database constraints/access support, not alternate semantic owners.

### Test-only typed readers/assertions

The phase assertions are verification, not product readers: `internal/content/ledger_agent_test.go:169-171,414-416,475-476,736-747`; `internal/content/ledger_command_test.go:67-68`; `internal/content/ledger_test.go:616-626,777-778,983-984`; `internal/content/ledger_tree_test.go:207-209`; `internal/transport/ws_agent_ask_test.go:284-318`; `internal/transport/ws_agent_locates_itself_test.go:283-285`; `internal/transport/ws_ledger_test.go:141-188,235-236,536-540,656-701,993-1034`; and `internal/transport/ws_run_thread_test.go:373-480,561-631,751-779`.

No frontend production code reads the backend `entries.phase` vocabulary directly; the renderer's own `phase` signals in unrelated stores are not ledger readers. The frontend receives lifecycle state from the attempt facts, while history results expose the backend phase through the transport query.

## 4. Phase assignment at every writer and its paired status

- **Generic `Submit`:** non-text entries are inserted `open/pending`; `text` entries are inserted `closed/success` (`internal/content/ledger_sqlite.go:191-210`). The open row is the durable intent before execution; text is already printed prose and has no run.
- **Completed shell `RecordCompleted`:** inserts `closed` with the supplied non-pending terminal status (`internal/content/ledger_command.go:105-116,184-190`). It also writes a completed execution in the same transaction (`:199-208`), so this path has no persisted open interval.
- **Frame capture:** inserts `closed/success` and a completed capture execution (`internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:280-294`). A frame is a fact complete at ingest, not a running command.
- **Agent ask:** inserts the question/turn `open/pending` (`internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:497-504`); the pending execution is created immediately after it in the same transaction (`:506-513`).
- **Execution start/bind:** `StartExecution` changes the entry to `bound` and leaves its pending status unchanged (`internal/content/ledger_sqlite.go:819-825`). The phase means a live execution is attached; status is not yet an outcome.
- **Execution finish/close:** `FinishExecution` changes the entry to `closed` and stores the supplied terminal status (`internal/content/ledger_sqlite.go:887-895`), while mapping an agent execution's termination to its terminal run state in the same transaction (`:830-838`).
- **Agent run finish/close:** `FinishAgentRun` maps `RunCompleted` to `EntrySuccess`, every other terminal run state to `EntryFailure`, then writes `closed` (`internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:659-694`).
- **Prose child:** `OpenProse` inserts `closed/success` with empty intent, parent and position set; it has no execution (`internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:843-858`).
- **Startup recovery:** `sqlite.Open` changes every non-closed entry to `closed`; ask rows become `interrupted`, other rows become `unknown` (`internal/content/sqlite.go:322-327`). This is the named recovery close for a missing completion, not a successful outcome.

The typed lifecycle model documents the intended interval as `open` until execution is confirmed, `bound` while it runs, and `closed` once its outcome is known; the store records/sweeps rather than inventing driver events (`internal/content/ledger.go:110-119`).

## 5. What an earlier `open` row would change in each reader

- **Recall (`Entry`, `ListEntries`, `QueryEntries`, wire query):** it would surface `phase=open` and whatever status/facts the row carried (`internal/content/ledger_sqlite.go:300-335,409-435`; `internal/transport/ws_ledger_query.go:553-556`). This is a visible state difference, but those readers do not independently convert it to a lifecycle state.
- **Session block list/read:** it would be treated as running, not exited. `ListSessionItems` would omit exit code and body loading (`internal/transport/ws_blocks.go:106-116`), and `ReadSessionItem` would return running without body (`:144-148`). A formerly open row is therefore not equivalent to a historical completed block.
- **Ledger event application:** an earlier open row is the expected starting state: bind is rank-forward and applies, close is rank-forward and applies; a repeated open is replay; a late lower-phase event is dropped (`internal/transport/ws_ledger.go:464-480`). Starting from closed would instead make open/bind late events non-authoritative, so inserting closed too early breaks the driver protocol.
- **Retention:** an earlier open row excludes the entry/body unit from eviction until the owner closes (`internal/content/retention.go:618-640`). This protects in-flight output from being deleted under a running command.
- **Startup recovery:** an earlier open row is selected by `WHERE phase != 'closed'` and is closed as `unknown` (or `interrupted` for asks) on the next open (`internal/content/sqlite.go:322-327`). A row inserted closed would be treated as already terminal and would not receive that honest recovery outcome.
- **Schema/prose interpretation:** an open `text` row would be refused by the text CHECK; prose is required to be closed/success (`internal/content/sqlite.go:815`). For non-text entries, open is legal and is the state from which execution binds.

## 6. Binding ADR constraints

- **Ledger/record identity — ADR-0019.** The ADR states: “**what the store judges by, the store must own**” (`docs/decisions/0019-one-authoritative-ledger-disposable-projections.md:30-33`). It also binds one authoritative ledger: human and agent commands are both `entries`, with authorship in a column, not a second transcript (`:37-41`). Therefore the durable entry id and its phase belong to the content store; the renderer block id is only a disposable projection identity.
- **Phase/execution split — ADR-0020.** Its consequences state verbatim: “**`phase = open | bound | closed` stays small and stays on the entry; approvals, retries, takeover, cancellation and timeouts live on the execution**” (`docs/decisions/0020-the-agent-gets-a-lane-authority-is-granted-per-run.md:149-152`). The same decision ships the lane/lease, `executions` table and a grant recorded on every run (`:119-124`). Thus a phase change cannot be replaced by an execution state or approval status.
- **Attempt identity and ordering — ADR-0024.** The lifecycle decision states: “Editor submit synchronously creates an `ExecutionAttempt` — attempt id, app-owned command text, domain, cwd and host at submit, start time — **before** the bytes that could cause the shell's own start event are written to the pty” (`docs/decisions/0024-authenticated-shell-integration-channel.md:313-319`). Its interval contract is: “**An attempt is open from submit or authenticated start until an authenticated same-domain completion. Channel loss, session exit, tab close, native-mode escape or a confirmed environment change may abandon it as `unknown`. Nothing may mark it successful, and nothing may assign it an exit code it did not report.**” (`:345-351`). Therefore the server attempt id is the authority for lifecycle attachment and completion; it is not interchangeable with the ledger entry id or renderer block id.
- **Boundary:** ADR-0024 also says the lifecycle is taken off the anonymous PTY byte stream (`docs/decisions/0024-authenticated-shell-integration-channel.md:64-68`), so no phase/attempt identity may be inferred from raw output or OSC marker writers. The authenticated lifecycle fact and the store's explicit entry transitions are the only authoritative paths.
close_reason: map delivered; recorded in notes

title: One block, one identity: the id the renderer shows is the id the ledger keeps and the tools accept
description:
A command block has three identities today and no two of them are the same
thing, which is why the assistant cannot name a block the person pointed at.

1. The renderer's counter. `blocks.ts` sets `data-block-id` from `this._nextId++`
   — "the third block I drew". Local to the pane, meaningless outside it, and
   different after a restart.
2. The attempt id. `lifecycle.submitAttempt` returns a SERVER-ASSIGNED id at
   editor submit, before the bytes reach the pty. Its own contract says "the
   published running fact carries the same id and the block projection binds on
   it" — so a real, durable, server-owned identity already exists at the moment
   the block is born.
3. The ledger entry id. `ledger_command.go` mints a THIRD one with `mintID()` at
   record time and inserts the row with `phase = 'closed'` hardcoded. It is
   unrelated to (2) and does not exist until the command has finished.

`session.list` returns (3) and `session.read` addresses (3). The renderer holds
(1). Nothing connects them, and (2) — the one identity that is server-owned and
present from the start — is used for the lifecycle binding and then dropped.

This never mattered while the assistant received block TEXT pasted into the
prompt: identity never crossed the boundary. It matters now that a question
names the blocks it may read instead of carrying a copy of them.

## What a user can do that they could not before

Mark a command block — running or finished — ask a question about it, and have
the answer be about THAT block, because the id the prompt names is the id the
reading tool accepts.

## Success Criteria

The end-to-end check that closes this epic: a person runs a command, marks its
block while it is STILL RUNNING, asks a question, and the model reads that
block through session.read using the id it was given in the prompt — no
guessing, no session.list search, no id invented by either side. Watched end to
end.

Stops being false exactly once: today the renderer cannot name the block in a
vocabulary the tool accepts, and for a running command no ledger row exists to
name at all.

## Deliberately out

- The attachment surfaces themselves — chip, popover, mark, menu. They are
  built and waiting on branch `w-grantchip` (nocx-wcswn), and they land after
  this.
- Narrowing session.read to the marked blocks (nocx-hnh7r). Identity first;
  scoping is a separate argument.
- Any change to what the ledger RECORDS. This is about the name of a row, not
  its contents.

## Constraints

- ADR-0019 owns the record and ADR-0024 owns the attempt. Whichever gives way,
  it is amended deliberately in the same commit, never routed around.
- AD-7: session-id is server-authoritative. The same reasoning applies to a
  block's id — the renderer must not mint the identity that crosses the wire.
- A running command must be addressable. If that means the ledger opens a row
  at submit instead of at completion, say so and check what else reads phase.
close_reason: All four children merged into feat/ai-assistant, and the success criterion is watched rather than inferred: TestLifecycleLedger_RunningBlockReadKeepsAttemptIDThroughCompletion takes the id out of the prompt the model was given, reads the still-running block through session.read with it, then reads the finished output and exit code through the same id after completion. The renderer counter no longer crosses any seam; the ledger row opens at submit under the attempt id and the existing transitions close it; one command makes one row.

title: Prove the read half: after an always on a harmless command, a destructive one still asks
description:
Parent: nocx-y47mi. Its fourth acceptance criterion reads: one automated check watches a person approve a harmless command and then finds that a DESTRUCTIVE one still asks.

What exists after nocx-em9az is one inference short of that. TestAgentApprove_ScopeAlways_RealRunClassificationWritesTheObserveRow (internal/transport/ws_agent_approval_scope_test.go:488) approves df -h with scope always and asserts the stored destructive ROW is still ask. That proves the standing WRITE went to the right row. It does not prove the policy READ then escalates a destructive call - and the read path is the half the person actually experiences.

The difference matters because they can fail independently: a defect that widens the read (a lookup falling back to permit, a grant minted before the write) leaves the row correct and the behaviour wrong, and every existing assertion stays green.

## Acceptance Criteria

- In ONE run: the model proposes df -h, the person answers allow always, the run resumes, the model then proposes a destructive command, and the second proposal ESCALATES rather than executing. Asserted on the escalation reaching the wire, not on the policy document.
- The second proposal is a real destructive command through the same run tool, not a different tool chosen to make the assertion easy.
- The test name says which half it holds, so it is not mistaken for the row-writing test beside it.
close_reason: merged; one run, df -h allowed always, destructive proposal through the same tool escalates on the wire; falsifiability shown with a temporary read-widening overlay

title: The address bar does not know the folder scope exists
description:
`variableAnswer` in api-store.ts derives, in the renderer, which scope answers a
`{{name}}` in the address field: the request's own draft rows, then the environment's
plain values, then its secret names, then nothing. It predates folder variables and
knows only three scopes.

Since nocx-x3cax.1 a fourth scope resolves ahead of the environment. A name answered
ONLY by a folder therefore paints as unbound in the address, and the menu behind the
chip says "nothing answers it: neither this request nor <environment>" and offers to add
it to one of those two — about a name that resolves perfectly well and will send. The
surface advertises what it can no longer deliver, which is what AD-8's "one owner per
behaviour" exists to prevent.

The answer already exists now: `api.request.scope` returns the whole chain, in order,
with the winner first, computed by the same Go code the send uses. The chip must read
that instead of deriving a second, shorter chain beside it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Put `baseUrl` in a folder's variables. Leave it out of the request and out of the
   environment.
2. Open a request in that folder whose URL is `{{baseUrl}}/ping`.
3. The chip paints unbound, and clicking it offers to define a variable that is defined.
   The send resolves it correctly, so the surface and the send disagree.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `variableAnswer` reads the scope the backend answered; it derives no precedence of its
  own.
- A name answered by a folder paints as bound, names the folder it came from, and the
  menu offers the folder as a place to edit rather than pretending nothing answers.
- A name nothing answers still says so, and `unknown` still covers the window before the
  scope has been read — a name painted unbound while the answer is in flight is how a
  person learns to ignore the colour.
- A test drives the seam: a request whose only answer is a folder's shows a bound chip
  naming that folder.
close_reason: Committed as 65b4f94b with .3. variableAnswer now reads the backend scope's winning row instead of deriving a three-scope chain in the renderer, so a name answered only by a folder paints bound, names its folder, and the menu offers that folder instead of offering to define what is defined. unknown keeps its window: nothing paints unbound while the answer is in flight.

title: The approval window states the blast radius on the control, not in a paragraph below it
description:
Parent: nocx-y47mi. Its first two acceptance criteria are met by nocx-em9az (merged a4e91bd9). This is the THIRD, which is still false.

The criterion: whatever the person grants, the window states the BLAST RADIUS of the answer in the same place they read the call, not only in a paragraph below it, and a test asserts that sentence by name.

The principle comes from the 2026-08-25 research in the parent bead. Claude Code offers a standing option only when the prompt CAN SHOW YOU EVERYTHING IT WOULD ALLOW, so a rule saved from a prompt covers only what its option named. Our window showed df -h and saved every irreversible change. Even now that the classification is right, the window still says the standing part in a paragraph below the call rather than on the control the person is about to press.

The wire already carries what is needed: the approvalRequested notification names the effect the gate chose. This is wording and placement on the control, not a new backend fact.

The three scopes are once, session and always (ws_agent.go). Each has a different radius and the window must say which, next to the button, in the products own words.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Each answer control states what accepting it covers, adjacent to that control - not only in prose below the call.
- A test asserts each sentence by name, so a later edit that quietly widens one is caught.
- The sentence for always names the effect class the row will be written for, using the same vocabulary the Agent policy page shows, so the two surfaces cannot drift. effect-labels.ts is the existing owner of that vocabulary - extend it rather than inventing a second set of words.
- The window still reads as one thing, not three warnings. If a scope is not offered, no sentence is shown for it.
close_reason: merged into feat/ai-assistant; coverage is a Button secondary-line variant, each sentence asserted by name, always names effect + every session + no expiry

title: Three ADR numbers each name two decisions, and 278 citations pick one by coin flip
description:
docs/decisions/ has three number collisions, and unlike nocx-zlboz (PR 91, resolved once
already) these are not a chain about to be rebased — they are live in the tree now, and two
of the three pairs are BOTH accepted, so neither supersedes the other:

  0029-a-keystroke-is-bound-to-what-makes-it-meaningful.md   Proposed
  0029-a-program-may-ask-never-choose.md                     Accepted
  0033-auto-is-the-name-for-not-yet-answered.md              Accepted
  0033-ui-state-is-a-document-not-a-setting.md               Accepted
  0035-appimage-carries-webkits-helper-processes.md          accepted
  0035-the-channel-we-own-is-the-carrier.md                  accepted (2026-08-20)

MEASURED 2026-08-25, and the first count in this bead was low. There are 278 citations of the
bare numbers outside their own ADR files: 153 for 0029, 74 for 0033, 51 for 0035, across Go,
TypeScript, e2e specs and .internal/ designs.

The harm is not hypothetical and not confined to docs. BOTH ADR-0029s are cited from production
code, in different packages, meaning different documents:

  internal/notify/*, internal/transport/ws_notify*, frontend/src/notify-client.ts,
  terminal-content.ts:1854 ('a program asked nocx to present a message'), :2602 ('a program
  printed BEL')                        -> 'A program may ask; it never chooses'

  internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go:353 ('the capture identity, ADR-0029's comparison
  vocabulary'), ledger.go:564 ('generation inequality is a trigger, never a verdict'),
  ledger_agent_test.go:9 ('the identity vocabulary')
                                       -> 'A proposed keystroke is bound to what makes it
                                          meaningful, not to the frame'

A reader of ledger.go:564 who globs docs/decisions/0029-* gets two files and no way to tell
which was meant. The same split exists at 0033 (uistate.ts, sidebar*, panes-layout, and
active-tab-restore mean 'UI state is a document'; capability.ts, connections.tsx and
generated/open.ts mean 'auto is the name for not yet answered') and at 0035 (internal/
shellintegration and internal/app/childdomain mean 'The channel we own is the carrier').

WHICH ONE KEEPS THE NUMBER IS THE DECISION, and 'the earlier file keeps it' is the wrong rule
here. In all three pairs the LATER file is the heavily cited one, because it is the recent
feature work with fresh code around it:

  0029  keystroke (2026-08-13, Proposed)   vs  a-program-may-ask (2026-08-14, Accepted)
  0033  auto (2026-08-15, Accepted)        vs  ui-state (2026-08-18, Accepted)
  0035  appimage (2026-08-20, accepted)    vs  channel-carrier (2026-08-21, accepted)

Renumbering by date would move the majority of all 278 citations. Renumbering by citation
weight keeps the code still and moves the quieter document, but hands a fresh number to a
decision whose old number is already published in commit messages and in .internal/ specs.
This is the owner's call, per pair, and it is why this bead is not a mechanical fix.

nocx-zlboz ('PR 91: the sandbox ADR chain collides with main's ADR-0035') is the same hazard
resolved once before, which is the argument for the third success criterion: this recurs
whenever two branches mint an ADR in parallel, so the fix that lasts is a check, not a
renumber.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. ls docs/decisions/ | grep -E '^(0029|0033|0035)'
2. Two files appear for each number.
3. grep -rn 'ADR-0035' --include=*.go --include=*.ts --include=*.md docs internal frontend/src
   and try to resolve any hit without opening both files.

## Expected

One number, one decision. A citation resolves to exactly one document.

## Actual

Three numbers name two decisions each. Renumbering is the obvious fix and is NOT free: the
191 citations move with it, and an ADR number that has already been published in commit
messages and specs cannot be silently reused. Deciding which of each pair keeps its number,
and whether the loser gets a fresh number or a superseding note, is the work.

## Acceptance Criteria

Each number under docs/decisions/ names exactly one decision.
Every citation outside docs/decisions/ resolves to the document its author meant, checked
rather than assumed for the three colliding numbers.
A check fails if two files ever claim one number again, so this cannot recur silently.
close_reason: Closed by the owner's call, and correctly. I filed this bead myself, mid-task, off the back of a detail I hit while rewriting a spec — nobody asked for it and nothing was blocked by it. The measurement stands and is left in the description so the next person does not redo it: three numbers name two documents each, 278 bare citations, and both ADR-0029s are live in Go at once. What the measurement does NOT support is the work the bead proposed. Renumbering moves 278 citations, burns numbers already published in commit messages, and does not prevent recurrence — nocx-zlboz resolved this same collision once and it came back three times. The observable harm is two instances of confusion, one of them caught in review. Cost exceeds benefit; the repo's own citation form in binding documents already carries the path, which is unambiguous.

title: An endpoint with no key cannot answer, though the probe already dials one without a credential
description:
Reported by the owner 2026-08-25: an endpoint demands a token, but a local model does not have one.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Settings, Endpoints, add an endpoint pointing at a local server (Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp). Leave the key empty - ValidateEndpoint (internal/profile/endpoint.go:249) does not require one, and the form validation (frontend/src/endpoints-section.tsx:533) checks name, baseUrl, models and headers only, so it saves.
2. Press Test on the row. It SUCCEEDS.
3. Ask the assistant anything through that endpoint.

Observed: the ask is refused with "the endpoints credential is missing". Expected: the same thing the probe just did - dial without an Authorization header.

## What is true in the code

1. The probe path ALREADY knows local models exist. The comment on endpointProbeParams (internal/transport/ws_assistant.go, the credential resolution rule) says it in as many words: rule 3 is "Else (no key, no id, or a saved endpoint with no credential) the probe runs without one - the local-model case."

2. The ask path does not. resolveEndpointMaterial (internal/transport/ws_agent.go:816) resolves endpoint.CredentialRef unconditionally and returns errors.New("the endpoints credential is missing") both when Resolve fails and when the secret is empty. There is no branch for an endpoint that never had one.

So there are TWO derivations of "does this endpoint need a credential" and they disagree. Test says yes it works; the ask says it is unusable. That is the defect shape AGENTS.md spends a section on, and here the two surfaces are one function apart.

3. The readiness enum carries the same assumption. credentialStateFor (ws_assistant.go:242) returns credNone when ref is empty, and credentialLine (frontend/src/agent-status-line.ts) renders none as tone warning, "The endpoint has no key yet". The word "yet" presumes a key is coming. For a local endpoint none is not a rung of a ladder, it is the finished state.

## The fork the fix has to settle

Simply allowing an empty credential everywhere costs the person who FORGOT a key on a remote endpoint: they would get a 401 from the provider instead of the sentence that names the problem. The probe already accepts that trade; the ask and the status line do not. Whether nocx should GUESS from the base URL being loopback, or carry an explicit "this endpoint needs no key" fact on the record, is an owner decision - a fact with no owner is absent here rather than guessed, which is this codebases stated stance.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An endpoint saved with no credential answers a question, with no Authorization header sent, asserted end to end through the real transport.
- Exactly ONE derivation of "does this endpoint need a credential" exists, and the probe path and the ask path both read it. A test proves they cannot disagree.
- A remote endpoint whose key is missing or deleted still gets its own sentence naming that, not a bare provider 401.
- The status line says nothing alarming about an endpoint that legitimately has no key.
notes:
OWNER DECISION 2026-08-25: an EXPLICIT fact on the endpoint record — a checkbox
in the form saying this endpoint needs no key — not a guess from the base URL,
and not a blanket "empty means no auth".

The reason is the stance this codebase already states in systemprompt.go about
the far host's OS: a fact with no owner is ABSENT rather than guessed, because a
guess is worse than silence. A loopback heuristic gets both ends wrong — a local
server that DOES want a key, and a remote one that does not — and it decides
something the person already knows and can simply say.

What follows from it:

- The endpoint record carries the fact. profile.Endpoint gains it,
  ValidateEndpoint learns the pairing rule, and it crosses the wire, so the DTO
  needs its contracts/ schema and the renderer type is REGENERATED, never
  hand-edited (AGENTS.md testing rule 5).

- ONE derivation reads it, and both the probe path and the ask path consult that
  one. Today endpointProbeParams rule 3 and resolveEndpointMaterial are two
  answers to one question; afterwards they must be one, with a test that proves
  they cannot disagree.

- credNone splits in two. An endpoint declaring it needs no key is not a warning
  at all and credentialLine says nothing about it; an endpoint that expects a key
  and lacks one keeps the existing sentence. The word "yet" belongs only to the
  second.

- Pairing rule to settle in the code: an endpoint that declares it needs no key
  must not also carry a CredentialRef. Decide whether that is refused at
  validation or the declaration simply wins, and say which in a comment.

SEQUENCING: this collides with both wave-2 workers — wsurf owns all of frontend/
and wwire owns ws_agent.go — so it is wave 3.
close_reason: merged; explicit NoKey fact on the record, NeedsCredential is the one derivation read by the status, both probe paths and the ask, contradiction refused, credential enum split with not-required silent in the status line

title: A request remembers which stand it goes to, and a folder can pin one
description:
Owner's request of 2026-08-25, alongside two complaints that turn out to be one
question: the environment picked beside Send is forgotten, and in Postman a person
ends up forking a whole collection per stand.

WHAT A USER CAN DO THAT THEY CANNOT NOW: open a request they used yesterday and send
it at the same stand without picking one again; and keep ONE collection whose
`tinkoff/` folder always goes to the tinkoff stand while the rest of it goes wherever
the collection is currently pointed.

THE SHAPE IS THE ONE ALREADY BEING BUILT FOR VARIABLES (nocx-x3cax): a chain, nearest
first. The environment a send goes out under is answered by the request's own pin, then
the nearest folder's pin, then the collection's current selection. One mechanism, two
things travelling through it, and the same sentence explains both to a person.

IT IS LOCAL STATE AND NEVER THE COLLECTION FILE, and this is the load-bearing decision.
substitute.go states the rule the whole product is built on: a collection arriving in a
pull request must not choose what a reader's request sends. A pinned environment written
into a shared file is exactly that, with production on the other end of it. So the pin
lives where uistate lives, keyed by collection path plus the request or folder relPath,
and a colleague who pulls the collection inherits none of it.

ONE OWNER FOR THE SELECTION. The picker beside Send shows the EFFECTIVE environment and
says where it came from — pinned here, inherited from folder X, or the collection's
current one. Changing the picker writes the pin at the level the person is standing on.
The chain is the owner; the picker is its view and its writer. Two surfaces both
claiming to decide which environment is used is this repo's recurring defect, and the
loser goes on advertising what it can no longer deliver.

## Success Criteria

- A person picks an environment for a request, restarts the app, opens that request,
  and the picker shows the same environment without being touched. One automated check
  watches exactly that.
- A folder can be pinned to an environment from the folder page, and a request inside it
  with no pin of its own sends under it.
- The picker always names the effective environment AND where it came from, so a person
  can never be sending at a stand the surface does not show.
- Nothing about a pin is written into the collection: a fresh clone of the same
  collection on another machine inherits no selection.
- Clearing a pin is reachable and returns the request to what it inherits.

## Deliberately out

- Auth that varies by stand beyond the credential's value. The auth KIND is in the
  request file today, so a stand that authenticates differently in kind still cannot be
  expressed. That is a real residual gap and it is its own decision (folder-level auth
  defaults, or the environment answering the auth kind); this epic does not settle it.
- Any per-stand override of a request's body, headers or method. That is a fork, and a
  fork is a second request.

title: The request's Variables tab shows the whole scope it sends under
description:
The tab lists only the request's OWN rows, so for almost every request it is
empty and says "No variables of this request's own" — a panel about a scope
nobody uses, next to two scopes that decide what actually goes out. The owner
opened it expecting to see what the request resolves against and found nothing.

The request's own rows STAY. They are the top of the chain and they answer the
case the code already names: `id` in `/users/{{id}}` belongs to the request
because two requests want different ones, while `baseUrl` belongs to the
environment because every request under it wants the same one. What changes is
that the tab also shows what the request INHERITS, and from where.

THE ORDER IS ANSWERED ONCE, BY THE BACKEND. apicoll owns resolution
(RequestLookup + Environment.Lookup + the vault binding, chained in
capability/api.go Snapshot). The renderer must not re-derive precedence from
three lists — that is this repo's most recurrent defect, two owners of one
input, and it would drift the day a fourth scope arrives.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A new JSON-RPC method answers the effective scope for one request under one
  environment: every name the request can resolve, its value, which scope
  answered (request / folder / environment / vault binding), and for a folder
  the folder's own path.
- A name answered by more than one scope appears ONCE as the winner, and the
  losing rows are visible as overridden with their scope named — that is the
  question the tab exists to answer.
- A vault-bound name crosses with NO value, marked as bound in the vault. The
  environment file's plain values already cross (the environment editor reads
  them); a secret does not, and this method is not the hole it starts doing so
  through.
- The wire is a party: a JSON Schema in contracts/ with additionalProperties
  false and an explicit required, the renderer type generated from it, the Go
  DTO conforming, and one test validating the real result off the real socket.
- The tab renders the request's own editable rows first, then the inherited
  rows read-only with their source. Its empty state is only reachable when
  there is genuinely nothing in any scope.
- A test drives the seam a person reaches: open a request under an environment
  and a folder that both carry variables, open Variables, and read the whole
  chain with each row's source.
close_reason: Committed as 65b4f94b. api.request.scope answers the whole chain in resolution order, computed by the same Go a send uses; the renderer derives no precedence. Takes the editor's DRAFT rows (required, not optional — one path only), so an unsaved row overrides inherited ones and a draft row shadowing an environment secret is reported per row rather than failing the call. Answers ordered by a revision counter plus target/environment identity. Design decided against a renderer-side recompute after a codex consult.

title: The attachment surfaces become one grant: a chip, a popover, a whole-block mark, one menu item
description:
Parent: nocx-5u3oz. The owner-approved design is in the notes of nocx-5u3oz.9 and is the specification for this task - read it there, it is not repeated here.

This is the FRONTEND half only. The prompt naming the marked block ids, and dropping the inlined frame text, is a sibling task; ws_agent.go is owned by nocx-em9az right now and must not be touched here. That is why the chip says otmecheno dlya voprosa rather than naming a read scope - see nocx-hnh7r for why that wording is a constraint and not a preference.

What changes: the bare-text counter becomes an ordinary chip, LAST in chromeLeft after the provider and model chips; clicking it opens a popover listing the marked blocks with a per-row dismiss and a reveal; the block mark covers the whole block rather than rows; the block menu collapses to one item.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The chrome row carries an ordinary .nocx-chip for the grant, last in chromeLeft after modelEndpointChip and modelChip, before the clock. No bare text and no bare multiplication sign anywhere in that row.
- The chip has two states as a typed data attribute on ONE component: default when nothing was marked, chosen when something was. No fork of the chip component and no repainting it from the surface.
- Clicking the chip opens a popover listing each marked block by its command, with a dismiss per row and a dismiss all; clicking a row scrolls to that block and flashes its mark. Built from the existing ui/floating-panel and ui/context-menu.
- A marked block is marked WHOLE - a left rail plus a faint tint from existing tokens, not per term-line, and it must not look like a selection.
- The block menu offers ONE item for this, reading unmark on an already-marked block, and identical on a running and a finished block. Attach output and Ask about this command as separate items are gone.
- The floating Attach button, referenceChipLabel and its coordinates, the fingerprint dedupe, per-row data-attached, rowStart/rowEnd on attachOutput, and .nocx-editor-reference-count are all deleted. A grep test asserts none of them remains.
- Marking still does not move the input target, with the chip on screen.
close_reason: merged with the identity halves; chip, popover, whole-block mark, one menu item, old surfaces deleted

title: The approval window classifies the call, not the tool
description:
Parent: nocx-y47mi. The kernel landed as nocx-ogc6c (CommandEffect in internal/assistant/cmdeffect.go); nothing calls it yet. This task makes the policy ask it.

Today the effect a proposal is classified under comes from the tool row: registry.go declares run as EffectMutateDestructive unconditionally. So the approval window describes the TOOL truthfully while telling the person something false about the CALL, and applyStandingAnswer (ws_agent.go) writes the global matrix row for that same wrong class.

After this task the effect of a run proposal is CommandEffect(command, declaredEffect): df -h classifies as observe and lands under Read and inspect; rm -rf / keeps the declared worst case. Everything downstream follows for free, because the window and the standing write both already read the backend classification.

ADR-0028 decision 4 must be amended in the SAME commit. It forbids a rule over a tool NAME because a different spelling bypasses it. That objection is correct and is answered rather than ignored: the kernel splits on the shell separators, requires every subcommand to be an allowlisted read, disqualifies carriers and wrappers and substitutions and redirections, and enforces word boundaries. Record those as the conditions under which per-call classification is sound. The 2026-08-25 research in the parent bead notes has the two reference implementations that do the same thing.

Do NOT let the renderer or the model name the effect. ADR-0028 decision 4 puts that with the backend and nowhere else.

The classifier (nocx-kpy23) may only RAISE permit to ask and never lower, and is consulted only where the policy already says permit. This parse does the opposite - it lowers from the declared worst case. Note the asymmetry deliberately where the code does it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A read-only command proposed through run - df -h, ls, cat - is not presented to the person as a call that can make changes that cannot be undone.
- Pressing Allow always on such a call does not leave the global policy with Make changes that cannot be undone Allowed. Asserted end to end from the approve params to the stored policy document.
- rm -rf / and ls AND rm -rf /tmp/x still classify as destructive after the change, asserted.
- Exactly one place converts a proposal to an effect. Two derivations of it is the defect AGENTS.md names.
- ADR-0028 decision 4 is amended in the same commit, naming the conditions rather than deleting the rule.
close_reason: merged into feat/ai-assistant as a4e91bd9; CommandArg on the declaration, classifyCall at the policy gate, ADR-0028 decision 4 amended with the soundness conditions

title: The effect of a run call is derived from its command, not from the tool row
description:
Parent: nocx-y47mi. This is SETTLED 2 of that bead, and the 2026-08-25 research confirmed both Claude Code and pi-permission-system do exactly this.

Today internal/agenttools/registry.go:149 declares run with Effect: content.EffectMutateDestructive unconditionally, so df -h and rm -rf / are one effect class. This task adds the pure kernel that derives the effect of a CALL from its command string. Wiring it into the policy is a separate task.

The kernel: split the command on the separators && || ; | |& & and newline; classify each subcommand; JOIN worst-wins over content.Effect. Lowering below the declared worst case is permitted ONLY for a closed allowlist of programs known to read, and ONLY when the whole command contains no disqualifier.

Disqualifiers (fail closed - any of these keeps the declared worst case): a program in a variable position ($VAR, ${...}); a carrier of somebody elses program (sudo, env, xargs, sh -c, bash -c, find -exec, find -delete, git -c core.pager); an exec wrapper (watch, setsid, ionice, flock, nohup, timeout); command substitution ($( ), backticks, process substitution); ANY redirection to a file (> or >>); backgrounding; tee.

Word boundary matters: a rule or allowlist entry for ls must match "ls -la" and must NOT match "lsof".

ADR-0028 decision 4 is not overturned by this: it forbids a rule over a tool NAME because a different spelling bypasses it, and the disqualifier list plus subcommand splitting are precisely the conditions that answer that objection. Amending the ADR belongs to the wiring task, not this one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A pure function maps a command string to a content.Effect, with no dependency on the tool registry, settings, or runtime.
- du -h | sort -rh | head -20 resolves to observe; ls && rm -rf /tmp/x resolves to destructive; cat f > /etc/passwd resolves to destructive.
- Every disqualifier above has a test proving it keeps the destructive worst case even when the program is on the read allowlist.
- An unparseable or unrecognised command resolves to the destructive worst case, asserted.
- "ls" is lowered and "lsof" is not, asserted.
- The read allowlist is one table in one place, and the test names every entry.
close_reason: merged into feat/ai-assistant as 96680e14; kernel only, wiring is its own task

title: The block menu offers Stop and Ask on a finished block: isActive is never supplied, and liveness is derived twice
description:
blocks.ts:1048 gates "Ask about this command" + "Stop" on `running.isActive?.() ?? true`. The only production supplier of runningActions — terminal-content.ts:1313 — passes ask, stop and attachOutput, and NEVER isActive. So the optional chain falls through to the `?? true` default and both items render on every block, finished or not.

Meanwhile "Attach output" two lines up gates on `!blockEl.classList.contains("cmd-block-running")` — a SECOND derivation of the same predicate, from a different source. That is why one menu carries Attach output, Ask about this command and Stop together: each branch believed the block was in its own state.

Stop is the sharp end: on a finished block it calls signalActiveCommand("stop"), which signals whatever is running NOW — a different command from the one whose menu was opened.

blocks.test.ts:2118 passes `isActive: () => true` explicitly, so the suite is green on a value no production path supplies (AGENTS.md testing rule 1).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run a command and let it finish.
2. Open that finished block’s ⋮ menu.
3. The menu shows Attach output AND Ask about this command AND Stop.
4. Start a second, long-running command; press Stop in the FIRST block’s menu — the second command is signalled.

## Acceptance Criteria

- One owner decides whether a block is still running; both the Attach-output branch and the Ask/Stop branch read it.
- A finished block offers no Stop and no "Ask about this command"; a running block offers no "Attach output".
- The test exercises the production wiring rather than supplying isActive itself.
close_reason: merged into feat/ai-assistant as 91f677fb; isActive is required and block-specific, both branches read one derivation, production wiring asserted in terminal-content.test.ts

title: An environment can carry the CA a server was issued under, and then it verifies
description:
Owner, 2026-08-25, with evidence: a send to sandbox-invest-public-api.tbank.ru
shows a chain issued by "Russian Trusted Sub CA, The Ministry of Digital
Development and Communications". That is not a self-signed certificate — it is
an ordinary CA that is not in this machine's trust store. The only way through
today is to turn verification OFF entirely (the environment's "Accept
self-signed certificates"), and the run then carries the yellow "unverified
TLS — certificate signed by unknown authority" badge, correctly.

Turning verification off to reach a host whose CA you actually have is the
product stating a rule at somebody instead of applying it for them. Give the
environment the root, and the same send comes back VERIFIED.

WHERE, and why: beside `insecureTls` on the environment's Route
(internal/apicoll/collection.go). That field's own comment settles the scope
argument — it is per environment so a person turns it on for dev and cannot
thereby turn it on for production, it is in the FILE so a colleague reviewing
the collection sees it in the diff, and every run says which trust it went out
under. A CA is public; it belongs in git. This is the same question with the
same answer.

WHAT IS OUT: a CLIENT certificate for mTLS. Its private key is a credential,
and a credential belongs in the vault, never in a collection file that goes
into a pull request (ADR-0011, design §8). That is a different task and the
owner has not asked for it.

THE SEAM ALREADY EXISTS AND HAS NO CALLER. `apisend.Client.tlsConfig` is a
field whose comment says "Go's default trust is the only trust" and that only
the tests set it — `trustOf` already reads `c.tlsConfig.RootCAs` when deciding
what a chain means. So the pool is consulted; nothing ever fills it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An environment can name a CA in PEM. The same send that came back
  `unchecked-untrusted` comes back `verified`, and the panel shows no warning
  badge — asserted on the run's trust state, not on a pixel.
- The pool is PER ENVIRONMENT, like insecureTls, and reaches the transport
  through `apisend.Key` — a transport trusting an extra root and one that does
  not are never the same transport, which is the rule tlsFor already states
  for verification itself.
- A PEM that parses to nothing is refused when it is SAVED, in the backend's
  own sentence, rendered where the person typed it. A root nobody can parse
  that silently degrades to system trust is the silent degrade this repo
  forbids: the environment would claim a trust it does not have.
- The extra root ADDS to system trust rather than replacing it, or replaces it
  deliberately and says so in the UI. Decide, and write down which and why.
- With the CA present and `insecureTls` also on, the run still says it went out
  unverified — the setting wins and the record does not flatter it.
- The wire is a party: the field is in the environment's schema in contracts/
  with additionalProperties false and explicit required, the renderer type is
  generated, and one test validates the real result off the real socket.
- Failure paths: an unreadable PEM, a PEM of the wrong kind, an empty pool, and
  the paired success on an ordinary machine.
notes: Backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh: moved from in_progress (untouched since 2026-08-24) back to open — NOT STARTED, no commit and no tree mention. The seam the bead describes is still exactly the caller-less seam: internal/apisend/client.go:61 tlsConfig is set only from tests, sender.go:1153 reads opts.Roots = c.tlsConfig.RootCAs, apisend.Key has no CA field, and apicoll Route (collection.go:168) has InsecureTLS with no PEM sibling. No caPem or RootCAs anywhere in contracts/ or frontend/src/.

title: The folder page edits them, and says which scope answered
description:
## Acceptance Criteria

- The folder page (frontend/src/api/folder-view.tsx) edits the folder's

  tab uses, never a second table for one concept.
- A request's variables panel says which scope answered a name: its own, the
