Folder page table matches the request tab's row grammar. Two review rounds: the row grammar/note class/refusal routing, then a real regression — the first fix suppressed the generic refusal card on the folder page, which would have made a refused delete silent, so folder-variable refusals now stay out of store.error() entirely.

title: A folder carries variables on disk, and a send resolves them
description:
## Acceptance Criteria

- A folder file inside a collection carries a `variables` list of the SAME
  shape a request's does — name, value, enabled — because the model grows by
  one more list of the same thing rather than by a new idea.
- api.collections.list says which folders have one, so the tree and the folder
  page need no extra round trip to know.
- The resolution order, asserted at every pair: the request's own variable
  wins over the folder's, and the folder's wins over the environment's
  PLAIN value. Nested folders: the NEAREST folder up the path answers first.
- A folder variable shadowing a name the environment declares SECRET is
  refused with the same sentence a request variable is refused with. The
  argument in substitute.go — a collection arriving in a pull request must not
  choose what a reader's request sends — applies unchanged to a file in the
  same git repository.
- A folder with no variables file behaves exactly as today, and opening a
  collection writes nothing into it.
- The wire is a party: a JSON Schema in contracts/ with additionalProperties
  false and an explicit required, the renderer type generated from it, the Go
  DTO conforming, and the real result off the real socket conforming.
close_reason: Committed as 247fa5a8 on feat/api-testing: .variables.json per folder, inherited nearest-first into RequestLookup, secret-shadow refusal answered again for the new scope, variableFolders on list/open/create/createFolder with schema, generated type and DTO+over-the-wire conformance. The renderer half (four adoption doors + fixtures) was finished by the coordinator; six contract fixtures were emitting variableFolders as null and are now [].

title: End to end: send it, restart, read it, fire it again
description:
## Acceptance Criteria

- The epic`s DONE WHEN, as one automated check through the seam a person
  reaches: send a request against the check`s own server, restart the backend,
  see the run with its answer, press repeat, and the server receives the

- The check`s own server asserts what arrived, both times.
- Nothing waits on a duration.

title: Any run can be repeated, including one whose file has since changed
description:
## Acceptance Criteria

- One control puts that exact request back in the form and sends it. The
  record IS the request as sent, so this works when the file was edited after
  the run, and when it was deleted.
- A repeated run says what it is: the list shows which exchange it was
  repeated from, so a person reading the list is not told two stories about
  one request.
- A secret in the repeated request resolves through the vault at send time,
  never from the record — the record holds a reference, and re-sending must
  not turn a reference back into bytes from the store.

title: The runs a person sees come off disk
description:
## Acceptance Criteria

- A JSON-RPC method reads a request`s runs, declared as a JSON Schema in
  contracts/ with additionalProperties false and an explicit required; the
  renderer`s type is GENERATED from it and committed.
- Three checks, and the third is the point: contracts:check, the Go DTO
  conforms, and the REAL result off the REAL socket conforms.
- The store`s `runs` signal stops being the owner of what happened: the panel
  reads the backend. A run that is in flight is still the renderer`s until it
  settles.
- Restarting nocx and opening a request shows its exchanges, with their

title: The send path records what it sent, in the same commit that can read it
description:
## Acceptance Criteria

- api.request.send`s completion path writes the run. THIS IS THE WHOLE POINT
  OF THE TASK: nocx-rtg0 shipped an encrypted store, a key lifecycle, a
  budget, a retention policy, five settings controls and a query method whose
  WRITE path had no caller, and `deadcode is empty` could not see it, because
  RTA marks every method reached through an interface as reachable.
- The evidence is `deadcode -tags gtk3 -whylive <the record method> ./...`
  printing a path from main, contrasted against a method that is genuinely
  unwired. The contrast is what makes it evidence.
- A send that FAILS is recorded too — a run is what happened, not what
  succeeded.
- A stopped send records that it was stopped.
- The write failing does not fail the send: the person got their answer, and a
  store that could not keep it says so where the surface can render it, never
  only in a log.
notes:
MEASURED 2026-08-25, on feat/api-testing at 182d50e8, before that branch merges.

The store from nocx-kpl58.1 is on the branch and is NOT wired. deadcode cannot
report it — APIRunRepository is an interface, and RTA marks every method reached
through one as reflection-reachable — so the ratchet is green with the write path
dead. This is the ContentDB.Add shape AGENTS.md names.

The contrast, run as AGENTS.md prescribes:

  deadcode -tags gtk3 -whylive '.../internal/content.sqliteContent.Ledger' ./...
    -> static@L1193 --> transport.NewWSServer
       ... --> capability.newAgentService
       dynamic@L0061 --> content.sqliteContent.Ledger          # WIRED

  deadcode -tags gtk3 -whylive '.../internal/content.sqliteContent.Begin' ./...
    -> "reachable only through reflection"                     # NOT WIRED

Said a second way: grep for 'APIRuns()' outside internal/content finds five hits
and all five are test fakes returning nil.

So this task is the one that makes the feature exist, and until it lands nothing
a person does records a run. The PR body for #105 says so rather than implying
runs persist.

title: The store keeps one API exchange, under an identity that survives a restart
description:
## Acceptance Criteria

- A new typed repository on ContentDB beside Ledger() and Layout(), with its
  own tables and migration. NOT the ledger: consulted 2026-08-24, and the
  deciding fact is that the ledger`s `environments` model identifies an
  execution LOCATION (host, cwd, versioned observations pinned per execution)
  and cannot honestly say "collection X, request file Y, API environment Z".
- The identity a run is stored under is DURABLE. `ApiRun.handle` is minted per
  session and means nothing after a restart; the collection`s path and the
  request`s relPath are what a row carries.
- Request and response bodies go in artifacts + ordered chunks, never a large
  body column. `artifacts.execution_id` currently requires a LEDGER execution
  and LedgerRepository is declared that table`s sole writer — resolve that
  without creating two writers for one table, and say in the code which way
  and why.
- Retention: completed exchanges evict oldest-first under the existing budget,
  chunks cascading in the same transaction. A pending run is not a candidate.
- No credential is ever written. Asserted on the BYTES of the database, the
  way the vault`s tests already do it.
- Every external call has a test where it fails, and the partial failures are
  enumerated: what is true on disk when step 3 of 5 fails, and how the next
  start recovers.
close_reason: Shipped. internal/content/api_run.go and api_run_sqlite.go add the typed repository with a migration in schema_migrate.go and a ladder test; durable identity across restart, retention and the credential-bytes guarantee are asserted in api_run_test.go by TestAPIRunRoundTripSurvivesRestartAndKeepsDurableIdentity, TestAPIRunRetentionEvictsOldestCompletedButNeverPending and TestAPIRunBackupContainsOwnTables. Commits e43c156c and fc01a88e. Closed during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh.

title: A folder carries variables, and the requests inside it inherit them
description:
Owner's request of 2026-08-24, from the folder page: a folder should be able
to hold variables.

WHAT IT ADDS: a third scope in a chain that already has two. `substitute.go`
owns the order today — a request's own variables win over the environment's
plain values, and a request variable shadowing a name the environment
declares secret is REFUSED (ErrSecretShadowed, and the reason is written
there: a collection arriving in a pull request must not choose what a
reader's request sends). A folder's variables sit between those two, and
every rule that guards the request scope has to be answered again for this
one — including the shadowing refusal, which is the whole reason this is an
epic and not a field.

WHERE THEY LIVE: a file in the folder, listed by api.collections.list the
way `folders` already is, read and written by their own methods with their
own schema in contracts/. Bruno's `folder.bru` is the same shape one product
over. Not decided yet: the file's name and whether a folder file grows other
folder-level facts later (Postman puts auth and scripts there).

WHERE THEY ARE EDITED: the folder page (nocx-8aczn.8), which exists and is
the surface a person is already on when they are thinking about a folder.

## Success Criteria

- A person opens a folder, adds a variable, and a request inside that folder
  sends with it resolved — without an environment and without a variable of
  its own. One automated check watches exactly that, end to end.
- The order is asserted at every pair: a request's own variable wins over the
  folder's, and the folder's wins over the environment's plain value.
- A folder variable shadowing a name the environment declares SECRET is
  refused with the same sentence the request scope is refused with — the
  argument in substitute.go applies unchanged to a file in the same git
  repository.
- A folder with no variables file behaves exactly as it does today; nothing
  is written into a collection by opening it.
- The wire is a party: the folder file's shape is a JSON Schema in
  contracts/, the renderer's type is generated from it, and one test
  validates the real result off the real socket.

## Deliberately out

- Folder-level auth, scripts and tests (Postman has them; nothing has asked).
- Nesting rules beyond "the nearest folder up the path answers first".
close_reason:
All five children closed. A person can put a variable on a folder and every request inside it inherits it — request's own row, then nearest folder, then parents, then the environment's plain value, then the vault binding — and the Variables tab shows that whole chain with the winner marked and the loser rows named. The happy path is watched end to end by e2e/api-folder-variable.spec.ts, green in the container.

Six commits: 247fa5a8 (disk + resolution + variableFolders on four schemas), 50038587 (folder page edits them), 65b4f94b (api.request.scope + the tab + the address bar), a9192097 (e2e), 94722016 (the OS-split gate this exposed).

Two defects were caught in review that would otherwise have shipped: a suppression that would have made a refused delete silent while the folder page was open, and a second implementation of precedence in the renderer that was blind to the secret-shadowing refusal for unsaved rows. Both are recorded on .2 and .3.

Out of scope and still open: nocx-6hyke (a request remembers which stand it goes to), which reuses this chain's shape for the environment binding.

title: A selection offers to be attached, and never attaches itself
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-21-attaching-context-to-a-question-design.md §'The gesture' 1 and 4, approved 2026-08-21. Re-confirmed by the owner 2026-08-24 from a screenshot where a double-click raised 'block · row 16'.

Today: terminal-content.ts:2878 listens on document selectionchange → raiseChipFromSelection (:4123-4144), which freezes any qualifying selection into a chip. The predicate is already written and correct — chipFromSelection (ask-entry.ts:57) returns the block and row span or null — so what changes is who calls it and when.

The button is the kit's Button (variant primary, size sm) inside a surface-owned fixed wrapper: the surface PLACES, the kit paints. Read frontend/src/ui/README.md. Its viewport clamp is the same geometry problem as the block ⋮ menu (nocx-vnirv.2) and the kit's ui/context-menu.tsx:100-118 — use one implementation, do not write a third.
acceptance_criteria:
- A selection inside a finished block's output raises NO chip. Copying output attaches nothing; typing a command and pressing Enter afterwards runs it in the shell, with the affordance on screen.
- While such a selection exists, one Attach button floats near the end of it: never covering the selection, anchored below the last client rect, flipped above when there is no room, clamped to the viewport, and following the scrollback while the selection is alive.
- It disappears when the selection collapses, when it stops satisfying chipFromSelection (two blocks, a running block, the editor), and once pressed.
- Pressing it raises exactly ONE chip — including for a drag across three rows, simulated as the three intermediate selections a real drag fires.
- Attaching a region already attached is a no-op, not a second chip.
- Attaching does not move the input target and does not touch the selection (nocx-4wtlh's rule, now asserted with the affordance on screen).
- Every chip in the product is minted by ONE function, attachRegion(blockEl, rowStart, rowEnd); a test names it as the single seam.

title: The approval window states its facts as rows

- The lead is one sentence. The two explanatory paragraphs (what approving covers; how once/session/always differ) are cut to what cannot be a row and no longer occupy half the window.

title: Settings shows nocx's own instructions, with placeholders and nothing resolved
description:
internal/assistant/systemprompt.go:78 SystemPrompt(facts) is a pure function, exposed by nothing: no RPC, no surface. The Instructions page's own description (internal/settings/settings.go:846) says 'where they contradict NOCX'S OWN INSTRUCTIONS yours win' — a page pointing at a text nobody can read.

Owner's decision, 2026-08-24: placeholders, nothing resolved, 'мы это уже обсуждали'. That choice removes the need for an RPC over live pane facts — the text is static. Whether it crosses the wire at all, or is generated into the frontend from the Go owner, is the implementer's call; what is NOT allowed is a second hand-maintained copy of the prompt text.

Read frontend/src/ui/README.md before adding any control. Read-only prose in a settings section is very likely an existing kit component.
acceptance_criteria:
- Settings → Instructions shows nocx's standing system prompt in full, above the person's own field, read-only.
- Every per-pane fact appears as a PLACEHOLDER and is never resolved: the session id, the cwd, the local-or-ssh line. The page reads identically whatever tab is focused, and nothing on it depends on a live session.
- The person's own paragraph is visibly in the place the prompt says it is: last, under its heading.
- The shown text and internal/assistant/systemprompt.go cannot drift: a test fails if the prompt gains a section the page does not show. Do not fork the text into a second string.
- Long text does not push the person's own field off the screen — say how it is contained and test it.

title: A tool call's outcome and duration reach the renderer, and its row shows them
description:
frontend/src/scrollback/blocks.ts:265-280 — kind 'tool': outputClass null, statusChips null, headerRight { chips: [], terminal: () => null }; style.css:945-971 paints it as a margin note. The comment gives the reason and it is correct as of today: the renderer is never sent the outcome. So the wire comes first and the rendering second.

Owner, 2026-08-24: tool calls should read as blocks, the way a command does. What is NOT decided here is whether the call's result body is shown — that is deliberately out of the epic.
acceptance_criteria:
- The wire carries, for each announced tool call, how it ended and how long it took; the schema in contracts/ says so with additionalProperties:false and an explicit required, and the three contract checks pass.
- A tool call's row in the turn shows the duration and the outcome in the same vocabulary a command's block uses, and a failed call is visibly distinct from one that succeeded.
- A call still in flight shows the working indicator of nocx-vnirv.1 and nothing that claims an outcome it does not have.
- A RESTORED turn shows the same figures as the live one did — the store's own values, never a second derivation (the defect nocx-hoeq3 records).
- ADR-0037 is amended in the same commit, deliberately, where it says a tool call is 'a header and nothing else' and that a chip would be a second owner of an outcome this surface never receives.

title: session.read and session.list: one tool reads what is in a session, addressed or live
description:
internal/agenttools/registry.go:136-180. readScreen: 'reach for this for a command that is still RUNNING… a command that has already finished has left it'. blocks.read: 'Read a window of one FINISHED command's output'. The model is asked to decide on a fact it does not have. Measured cost from the owner's session: one question produced readScreen → blocks.list → blocks.read.

Execution site is the work: blocks.read is Executes:InGo (the ledger), readScreen is Executes:InRenderer (the broker), because a live command's output lives in xterm — AD-6. Executes is a property of the Declaration ROW today, so a tool whose execution site depends on the block's state is a change to that model. Read internal/agenttools/registry.go:105-124 and .internal/specs/2026-08-16-agent-tools-design.md before designing it.

OPEN QUESTION FOR THE OWNER — a full-screen program on the alternate buffer (vim, htop) owns the screen and is NOT a block, so it has no id to address. Either readScreen survives with its description narrowed to exactly that case, or we decide the case is out of scope. Do not guess.
acceptance_criteria:
- One tool takes a block id and returns a window of that block's output plus the block's STATE — running, or exited with its code. The model never chooses a tool by whether the command has finished.
- It works for a block that is still running (the output is in the renderer) and for one that has finished (the output is in the ledger), and the person cannot tell from the outside which path served it.
- AD-6 is not crossed: the backend does not sniff the byte stream, and the live half is answered by the renderer through the broker, exactly as readScreen is today.
- The tool descriptions in the registry no longer instruct the model to pick by finished-vs-running.
- For every external call the new path makes, there is a test where that call fails — including the renderer being gone mid-call.
- The design question in the notes is ANSWERED IN THE BEAD by the owner before implementation starts.
notes:
OWNER DECISION 2026-08-24, in two parts.

PART 1 — the word 'block' leaves the tool names, and readScreen disappears as a NAME rather than as a capability.

- session.list — what can be addressed in this session right now. Empty in an unstructured pane, which is an honest answer and not an error.
- session.read — with an id, that item; WITHOUT an id, what is on the screen now.

So a finished command's output, a running command's output, the alternate buffer of a full-screen program, and a pane that has no blocks at all are ONE tool, and the model never chooses by a fact it does not have (whether the command has finished). The optional id is the whole mechanism: readScreen turns out to be session.read with no argument.

PART 2 — the namespace is the RESOURCE KIND the call addresses, not the product.

Rejected: nocx.read / nocx.list. Every tool in the product is nocx's, so that prefix partitions nothing; the real distinction would move into the suffix (nocx.listTabs, nocx.connect) and the prefix becomes a junk drawer — the same defect readScreen has.

Chosen: the closed content.ResourceKind set already in internal/content/ledger.go:242-250 (environment, session, path, credential, destination, tool). It is the axis the grant is scoped along (Declaration.Resources, Declaration.ResourceArg) and the axis a refusal already names. So the tool's name and its authority say one word: the Agent policy page shows rows over resources, the model sees the same nouns, the refusal names the same thing. Tabs and ssh connections arrive as new ResourceKinds — which they must anyway, for the policy to scope them — and their tool names follow rather than being invented.

Known limit, stated rather than glossed: this does not cover the whole registry. git.status is named by domain and addresses a path. The rule governs the axis the model actually chooses along; it is not a universal law.

WHY THE FULL-SCREEN CASE FOLDS IN (checked in code): a full-screen program IS a block — vim is submitted as a command, its running block exists, and enterFullscreen (frontend/src/scrollback/controller.ts:513) changes only the LAYOUT, not the block. Reading a running block already routes to the renderer, which reads the alternate buffer's viewport (frontend/src/terminal-content.ts:945-951).

CAVEAT THE ANSWER MUST STATE: the alternate buffer has no scrollback (frontend/src/scrollback/controller.ts:207). What comes back is the CURRENT SCREEN, not accumulated output, and the result must say so rather than let the model read it as a window into history.

THE UNSTRUCTURED PANE is the case the no-id form serves: a pane with no shell integration has no blocks at all. Every pane starts that way (frontend/src/terminal-content.ts:2212 — 'a conventional terminal, no ownership') and a host where integration cannot be installed stays that way (epic nocx-pu4).
close_reason: merged into feat/ai-assistant; gate green

title: Stop is on the live turn, in the place a command's Stop already is
description: The ⋮ on a turn block is built by the same buildOverflowMenu, but the running branch (scrollback/blocks.ts:1005-1031, 'if (running)') is only ever supplied for command blocks — a turn passes no RunningBlockActions. Depends on agent.cancel existing.
acceptance_criteria:
- While a turn is live, its ⋮ carries Stop, and it is gone the moment the turn settles.
- Pressing it calls agent.cancel for that run and nothing else; the turn's header then shows the stopped word, and the working indicator is removed.
- The item is built through the SAME menu path a running command's Stop uses — one vocabulary for 'stop the thing this block is doing', not a second control.
- A test starts from the state a person is in (a live turn on screen), activates the item, and asserts the client method was reached.
close_reason: Landed in c1889f5e/a1897360, on feat/ai-assistant; agent-ask.test.ts:283 asserts the live-turn Stop reaches agent.cancel with the minted run id. Bead was left in_progress by the merging session.

title: The ⋮ menu never leaves the viewport
description:
buildOverflowMenu (frontend/src/scrollback/blocks.ts:1038-1042) sets position:fixed, top = btnRect.bottom + 2, right = innerWidth - btnRect.right — no clamp, no flip. .cmd-overflow-menu (style.css:1175-1183) has no max-height and no overflow. A running block is at the bottom of the scrollback by construction, so 'Ask about this command' and 'Stop' — the two items that exist ONLY while it runs — are off-screen in practice, which is what the owner hit.

The kit already owns this: ui/context-menu.tsx:100-118 clamps both axes with EDGE_MARGIN_PX and explains itself. The block menu is imperative DOM and the kit's is Solid, so the component cannot be imported as-is — extract the geometry, do not copy it. AGENTS.md, 'Look for the existing answer before you write a second one'.
acceptance_criteria:
- With the ⋮ button close enough to the bottom edge that the menu cannot fit below it, every item is fully inside the viewport after opening. Same for the right edge.
- A menu taller than the viewport is still fully reachable — say how (scroll within the menu) and test it.
- The clamp is ONE implementation shared with ui/context-menu.tsx, not a second one; a test names the shared seam.
- Opening the menu never scrolls the page or moves the block underneath it.
close_reason: merged into feat/ai-assistant at d96bd10c; pre-commit gate green (contracts, both typecheckers, vitest in container)

title: One owner for 'working, nothing written yet' — on a turn and on a command
description:
Today: the turn's dots (scrollback/blocks.ts:2176-2183) are a stand-in for an EMPTY body, removed by stopTyping (:2217) at the first tool call (:2303), first reasoning chunk (:2367) or first delta (:2375), and never restored — so a turn inside a 28-second tool shows nothing where its answer will go. A running command has no indicator in its body at all: createRunningBlock (:1275-1321) builds no body element, because a running command's body IS the live xterm region, a sibling of the blocks in .scrollback-inner.

Owner, 2026-08-24: 'вообще поведение должно быть одинаковое'.
acceptance_criteria:
- The indicator stands in the place the output will be written from the moment work starts until the first byte of that output arrives, on BOTH kinds of block. Specifically for a turn: it returns while a tool call is in flight and no prose is being written, and it is gone the moment a delta lands.
- It is ONE piece of markup with one owner; a test asserts that the turn's and the command's indicator are the same class, not two that look alike.
- It is removed by failure and by cancellation as well as by output — no dots left typing an answer that will never arrive.
- The running command's indicator does not change the height the live region occupies (style.css:975-979: the live region and the frozen body it becomes must be the same height, or the pane jumps at the swap). State in the code how that is held.
- prefers-reduced-motion still opts out of the animation and keeps the report.
close_reason: merged into feat/ai-assistant at d96bd10c; pre-commit gate green (contracts, both typecheckers, vitest in container)

title: Inline code inside bold or emphasis renders as code
description: inlineHtml (frontend/src/ui/answer-markdown.ts:84-101) takes the first alternation match and escapes its whole contents as text. Measured: '**`.herdr`** (14G)' matches as ONE bold token, so the backticks print. The comment at :63-72 explains — correctly — why code must win the alternation; what is missing is the other direction, that the CONTENTS of a bold or emphasis span are markup and must go through the inline pass again.
acceptance_criteria:
- `**`repos`** (8.7G)` renders 'repos' as a .ui-md-code chip inside a .ui-md-strong, with no literal backtick anywhere.
- The reverse never happens: the contents of a code span are never re-scanned, so ```**not bold**``` inside backticks keeps its asterisks. A test holds both directions.
- Nesting is bounded and cannot recurse without end on adversarial input.
- Every byte still goes through escapeHtml; no new element carries an attribute the model can influence.
close_reason: merged into feat/ai-assistant at d96bd10c; pre-commit gate green (contracts, both typecheckers, vitest in container)

title: Every list marker sits inside the block — bullets and numbers alike
description:
Cause, measured on the owner's screenshot: styles/components/answer-markdown.css:45-48 builds the hanging indent from padding-left plus text-indent:-1.2em. text-indent is an INHERITED property and .ui-md-marker (:65-69) is display:inline-block — a block container — so the -1.2em applies AGAIN to the marker's own first line. The glyph moves a further 1.2em left, out of .cmd-children's padding, and is clipped by its border-left (style.css:923-925). Both markerHtml call sites are affected: the bullet (answer-markdown.ts:139) and the ordered number (:132).

The one-line patch is .ui-md-marker { text-indent: 0 }. Prefer rebuilding the hanging indent WITHOUT text-indent (the property inherits and will bite the next thing placed in a list row); if you keep text-indent, say in the CSS why, beside the reset.
acceptance_criteria:
- A rendered list item's marker is fully inside the block: no part of the glyph is left of .cmd-children's content box, at depth 0 and at depths 1-3, for a bullet and for an ordered number.
- The marker and its item text are adjacent — the gap between them is the marker column's width, not the block's padding.
- Wrapped continuation lines of a list item still align under the item's text, which is what the hanging indent was for.
- A test asserts the geometry, not the declaration: it must fail on the current CSS.
close_reason: merged into feat/ai-assistant at d96bd10c; pre-commit gate green (contracts, both typecheckers, vitest in container)

title: You can read what the assistant was told, and what it is asking for
description:
Two asks from the owner on 2026-08-24; the first was asked for before and never filed.

THE PROMPT IS INVISIBLE. internal/assistant/systemprompt.go:78 SystemPrompt(facts) is a pure function and is never exposed: no RPC returns it, no surface shows it. Meanwhile the Instructions page's own description (internal/settings/settings.go:846) tells the person 'They come last, so where they contradict NOCX'S OWN INSTRUCTIONS yours win' — the page refers to a text the person has nowhere to read. Shown with placeholders (owner's decision, 2026-08-24), it needs no RPC at all: the text is static and the pane-specific lines are the placeholders themselves.

THE APPROVAL WINDOW IS A PARAGRAPH. frontend/src/agent-approval-prompt.tsx:390-400 buries the machine and the tab inside the lead sentence ('on this machine, in the tab home/dev'), the effect gets its own prose line, and two more paragraphs explain what approving covers and how once/session/always differ — they occupy half the window and are read last, though the decision is made from the top. Only cwd and the parsed arguments are rows today (:260-289), through the kit's FactList (:404). The mechanism is already there and already right; what is missing is that three facts are not using it.
acceptance_criteria:
THE STANDING INSTRUCTIONS. A person opens Settings → Instructions and reads nocx's own system prompt, in full, above their own field. It is shown with PLACEHOLDERS — the session id, the cwd, the machine — never resolved against any pane, so the text is the same whatever tab is focused and nothing on the page depends on a live session. It is read-only, and their own paragraph is visibly where the prompt says it goes: last.

THE APPROVAL WINDOW. A person is asked to approve a call and can answer without reading a paragraph: the machine, the tab, the cwd, the call's arguments and what the call can do are each their own row, in that order, and the prose is a single lead sentence plus what genuinely cannot be a row. Watched end to end by one automated check.

## Deliberately out
- Editing nocx's own prompt. It is shown to be read, not changed; the person's field is the only writable half.
- Redesigning what the approval window ASKS. The six answers stay exactly as they are.

title: A tool call accounts for itself: one block-reading tool, and every call says how it went
description:
Two findings from the owner on 2026-08-24, joined because both change what a tool call reports.

TWO TOOLS FOR ONE QUESTION. internal/agenttools/registry.go:136-180 declares readScreen ('reach for this for a command that is still RUNNING … a command that has already finished has left it') beside blocks.read ('Read a window of one FINISHED command's output'). The split hands the model a choice it cannot make: it does not know whether the command has finished, and that is exactly the fact it is being asked to decide on. Measured cost, from the owner's screenshot: 'удали вот этот pdf' produced readScreen → blocks.list → blocks.read, three calls, to find what one block already held.

The state of execution is a FACT OF THE BLOCK and belongs in the answer, not in the choice of tool.

What makes this real work rather than a description edit: blocks.read executes InGo from the ledger, readScreen executes InRenderer through the broker, because a live command's output is in xterm and not in the ledger — AD-6 puts render state in the frontend and forbids the backend sniffing the stream. Executes is currently a property of the registry ROW (Declaration.Executes), so one tool whose execution site depends on the block's state is a change to that model.

A TOOL CALL IS A HEADER AND NOTHING ELSE. scrollback/blocks.ts:265-280: kind 'tool' has outputClass null, statusChips null, headerRight { chips: [], terminal: () => null }, and style.css:945-971 paints it as a margin note. The comment states the reason — 'the call's result has an owner already (the ledger's attempt)' and 'a chip here would be a second, later-arriving owner of an outcome this surface never receives'. That is the point: the renderer is NOT SENT the outcome. So this is a wire change first (the outcome and the duration must reach the renderer), and a rendering change second. ADR-0037 must be amended in the same commit that changes it, deliberately — not routed around.
acceptance_criteria:
ONE TOOL. A person asks about a command that is still running and about one that finished, in the same session. The assistant reads both through the SAME tool, addressing each block by id, and the answer tells it which state the block is in — running, or exited with a code. No question forces the model to choose a tool by whether the command has finished.

EVERY CALL ACCOUNTS FOR ITSELF. In a turn that made several calls, each call's row shows how long it took and how it ended, in the same vocabulary a command's block uses, and a call that failed is visibly distinct from one that succeeded. Watched end to end by one automated check.

## Deliberately out
- Rendering a tool call's full result as block output. What the row gains is the OUTCOME and the duration; whether the result body is shown is a separate decision, deliberately not taken here.
- Removing readScreen's remaining job (a full-screen program on the alternate buffer owns the screen and is not a block at all) unless the owner decides that case is out of scope — see the design question in the child bead.

title: A block that is working says so, wherever the work is
description:
Two defects the owner found on 2026-08-24.

THE INDICATOR. The turn's typing dots (scrollback/blocks.ts:2176-2183) are a one-shot stand-in for an EMPTY answer body: stopTyping (:2217) removes them at the first thing the turn draws — first tool call (:2303), first reasoning chunk (:2367), first delta (via stopWaiting) — and nothing ever puts them back. So a turn that spends 28 seconds inside a tool shows nothing at all where its answer will be written; only the header chip and pulse report. A running COMMAND has no dots at all: createRunningBlock (:1275-1321) builds no body, because the body of a running command is the live xterm region, which is a sibling of the blocks in .scrollback-inner.

The constraint that makes this non-trivial and must be honoured: style.css:975-979 requires the live region and the frozen body it becomes to occupy the SAME height, 'or the pane moves at the moment one replaces the other'.

THE MENU. buildOverflowMenu positions fixed at btnRect.bottom + 2 with no viewport clamp and no flip (scrollback/blocks.ts:1038-1042); .cmd-overflow-menu (style.css:1175) has neither max-height nor overflow. A running block sits at the bottom of the scrollback by construction, so 'Ask about this command' and 'Stop' — the two items that only exist while it runs — are off-screen almost always. The kit already owns this: ui/context-menu.tsx:100-118 clamps on both axes with EDGE_MARGIN_PX. Two implementations of one concept; the second one is wrong.
acceptance_criteria:
One indicator, one owner, both kinds of block. A person asks a question whose turn calls a tool that takes seconds: from the moment the question is sent until the moment the answer's first word lands, the place the answer will be written shows the working indicator — including the whole time the tool is running. They run a command that prints nothing for seconds: the same indicator stands where its output will appear, and it is the SAME markup, not a second one that looks similar. Neither indicator survives the first byte, and neither survives a failure. Watched end to end by one automated check.

Separately: the bottom-most block on screen has its ⋮ menu opened and every item is fully visible inside the viewport, with no scrolling and no clipping.

## Deliberately out
- Progress, percentages or a spinner per tool call. This is 'something is happening here', nothing more.

title: The assistant's answer reads like a document, not like a stream
description:
Three defects found by the owner on 2026-08-24, all in the answer renderer, all visible in one screenshot.

The renderer paints ONE COMPLETED LINE at a time (frontend/src/ui/answer-markdown.ts:8-27) because the answer body is a stack of .term-line rows that selection, copy and the reference chips all stand on. That contract is right and this epic keeps it; what it does not keep is the three costs that turned out not to be inherent:

1. The hanging indent for list markers is padding-left + negative text-indent (styles/components/answer-markdown.css:45-48). text-indent is INHERITED and .ui-md-marker is an inline-block — a block container — so the -1.2em applies a second time, inside the marker's own box. The glyph lands left of .cmd-children's padding and is clipped by its border-left (style.css:923-925). Bullets and ordered numbers both.
2. inlineHtml (answer-markdown.ts:84-101) does not recurse: the alternation takes the whole **...** token and escapes its contents as text, so **`repos`** prints literal backticks while `repos` on its own renders as a chip. Two spellings of one concept in one answer.
3. Fenced code is on the deliberately-unrendered list because it spans lines. A minimal multi-line accumulator is enough for it alone, and the kit's CodeBlock has no copy button for anyone.
acceptance_criteria:
A person asks a question whose answer contains a bulleted list, a numbered list, a word in bold with inline code inside it, and a fenced code block. Every list marker — bullet or number — sits in its own column INSIDE the block and never crosses its left rail. The code inside the bold renders as a code chip, not as literal backticks. The fenced block renders as ONE formatted unit with a copy button that puts exactly its text (no fences) on the clipboard. Watched end to end by one automated check.

## Deliberately out
- Tables, setext headings, nested block quotes, horizontal rules, images, task lists — the other things answer-markdown.ts names as deliberately unrendered. Only the fenced code block graduates here.
- Links becoming anchors: answer-markdown.ts refuses that on purpose (the model chooses the target) and this epic does not reopen it.

title: The header's plus makes the request beside the one you are in, not at the root
description:
Reported by the owner: with a request open inside a folder, the header's New
request (#api-new-request) writes to the collection ROOT. The crumb trail
directly above the control says `acme-api > users > create`, so the button
contradicts the line it sits in.

The precedent is `duplicateRequest`, which already lands the copy "BESIDE THE
ORIGINAL" using `directoryOf(relPath)`. The header's plus is the only door
that ignores where the person is; the folder row's menu already passes its
own path.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a collection with a request inside a folder (`users/create.json`).
2. Click that request, so the header reads `acme-api > users > create`.
3. Press the plus in the header.
4. The new request appears at the collection root, not under `users/`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- With `users/create.json` open, pressing New request calls `writeRequest`
  with `users/untitled-request.json`.
- With nothing in the form, it still writes to the collection root.
- With the workbench pointed at a DIFFERENT collection from the open
  request, it writes to that collection's root — the open request's folder
  belongs to another tree.
close_reason: The header's plus reads an omitted folder as 'here': newRequest(dir?) falls back to the open request's folder inside the ACTIVE collection. Watched at the seam a person presses (api-workbench.test.tsx) and at the store, including the cross-collection guard. 446 api tests green, pre-commit gate green. 7165856b

title: The shell JSON decoder drops a character: 2>&1 becomes 2>1 and writes a file named 1
description:
Found by a worker fixing the e2e container residue (nocx-qkid5) on 2026-08-24, while accounting for every file a run leaves behind. It is not a container defect — it happens on every real machine.

internal/shellintegration/scripts/nocx.bash:517-521 converts \uXXXX to octal so one printf %b pass decodes it with everything else:

    printf -v oct '%03o' "$((16#$hex))"
    s="${s//\\u$hex/\\$oct}"

For & (\u0026) that yields the three-digit form \046. But bash's %b reads \0nnn — a backslash, a ZERO, then up to three octal digits. Given \046 it takes the 0 as the marker, then 46, then EATS THE NEXT CHARACTER as the third octal digit. So \0461 is one character, not two, and the 1 is gone.

Measured at the shell:

    printf '%b' '2>\0461'    ->  2>1      (the & and the 1 collapse into one byte)
    printf '%b' '2>\00461'   ->  2>&1     (the four-digit form is correct)

The observable consequence: the far shell's bootstrap loader ships 2>&1 and receives 2>1, so its stderr is redirected to a FILE NAMED 1 in whatever directory the loader runs from. A 0-byte file named '1' had been sitting untracked in this worktree for the whole session and was dismissed as a shell typo by a human and by an agent; it was the product writing it.

Two reasons this is P1 rather than tidy-up. Any \uXXXX followed by a digit silently loses a character in an rcfile the product executes — the corruption is arbitrary, not limited to this one sequence. And a redirection that was meant to discard stderr instead creates a file in the user's working directory, which is a write nobody asked for, on every host the shell integration reaches.

The fix is the leading zero (\\0%03o), but the test is the point: the pass has never had one that puts a digit after an escape.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. printf '%b' '2>\0461'  ->  '2>1'
2. Start a shell-integration bootstrap on any host and look for a 0-byte file named '1' in the loader's cwd.
acceptance_criteria:
- The \uXXXX pass emits a form printf %b cannot over-consume. Reproduced at the shell: printf '%b' '2>\\0461' gives '2>1'; printf '%b' '2>\\00461' gives '2>&1'.
- A test decodes a JSON string containing \u0026 followed by a digit and asserts the exact result. It must FAIL before the fix.
- The same test covers the neighbours: any \uXXXX whose octal is followed by a digit, and one whose octal is followed by a non-digit (which works today and must keep working).
- No file named '1' appears in the cwd after a shell-integration bootstrap on a normal machine.

title: A backend from an older build refuses a newer frontend, and says how to fix it
description:
A backend that outlives its window also outlives an upgrade: yesterday's daemon serving today's frontend is the ordinary case, not the edge one.

AD-1 allocated a version byte and the control plane is JSON-RPC, so the skew is expressible. What is missing is the policy. Refusing is honest and cheap; a live handoff is what herdr does (it carries handoff.rs and exports live PTYs to a replacement server) and is a great deal more work.

Whatever is chosen, the failure must be legible: a user who upgraded and cannot connect needs to be told to restart the backend, not shown a connection error.

Related and not the same: nocx-1p1h4, 'A worker survives the network, and an upgrade never strands one'.
acceptance_criteria:
A frontend meeting a backend of an incompatible version is told so, in the product, with the action that fixes it.
A compatible pair connects with no prompt.
The refusal is distinguishable from a transient connection failure, so the client does not retry a mismatch forever.

title: nocx finds a running backend at startup, or starts one
description:
herdr's ordering: the server comes up first, the UI attaches to it. For nocx this is the frontend's Backend seam from phase A of this epic, pointed at a backend that happens to be on this machine but not in this process.

Needs: a socket path, named sessions so more than one can exist, and a handshake that establishes this is our backend and not somebody else's. Starting one when none is running, and not starting two when the user opens two windows.
acceptance_criteria:
Launching nocx with no backend running starts one and attaches.
Launching a second window attaches to the same backend rather than starting a second.
A stale socket from a crashed backend does not prevent a new one from starting.

title: The backend does not exit when the window closes
description:
Most of this is already true and that is the point. Session lifetime is already detached from connection lifetime — internal/transport/ws_git.go:24 says bindings 'are bounded by the session, not the WebSocket, so a reconnect' keeps them, and ring.go:35 keeps the replay ring 'stored connection-independently so the ring survives a disconnect'. A dropped client does not kill a PTY today.

What kills it is the process exiting, because the backend is in-process with the Wails shell. So this task is 'do not exit', not 'rewrite ownership of processes' — and cmd/devharness already proves the headless target runs the real backend with no wails, no GTK and no display.

The consequence to settle rather than inherit: the 2026-08-15 design's D5 says stage-1 workers die with the backend. That decision made sense while the backend was tied to a window and does not survive this task.
acceptance_criteria:
Closing the window leaves running processes running, and reopening finds them.
A long-running command started before the window closed is still producing output afterwards, and that output is recorded.
D5 of the workspaces design is revisited explicitly and the new answer is written down.

title: The client that attached last becomes active, and the channel resizes to it
description:
herdr's rule, and the reason attaching from a second machine feels right rather than cramped: on connect the newcomer becomes the foreground client (src/server/headless.rs:3027) and the shared runtime is resized to it immediately. The active client therefore always fits exactly, because it is the one that defined the size.

This is deliberately NOT tmux's smallest-common-size. Choosing the minimum makes every client wrong except the smallest; choosing the active one makes the client you are looking at right, always.
acceptance_criteria:
Attaching from a second client resizes the session to that client, and a program running in the pane reflows.
Returning to the first client resizes back.
Detaching every client leaves the session at its last size or the default, and does not kill it.
close_reason:
Merged into feat/nocx-server as 6d62d718. The client that attached last is active and the shared channel follows it — herdr's answer, not tmux's: the runtime size is shared, the layout stays each client's own.

Six tests, and the names are the criteria: TestActiveClient_TheClientThatAttachedLastOwnsTheChannelSize; _TheDisplacedClientIsStillToldItLostTheSession (asserted on this path, not assumed from the earlier task's test); _TheForegroundSizeHoldsUntilTheLastClientDetaches, which is the interval with both ends named; _AnAttachThatMeasuredNothingLeavesTheSizeAlone; _OpenStillCreatesTheChannelAtItsFinalSize, so AD-1's letter is re-checked rather than assumed to survive; and _TheChannelRefusesTheResize_TheClaimStillSucceeds.

Run by the coordinator: transport 151s and session, both ok.

Two judgements the worker made and explained rather than hid. It did NOT add effectiveSize to the attach result, because the resize is admitted on the lane and applied asynchronously, so an ack could only carry a size the channel had not taken yet — which would break the session's own rule that it never reports a grid its channel never took. Telling a client the session's size is nocx-eidfb.3's job. And the only contract change is the open schema's DESCRIPTION — no result shape moved, hence no new schema and no new over-the-wire test, which is the right call rather than a skipped one.

Stated honestly and worth carrying: two behaviours are verified only by reading — that monitorExit removes an exited session from connState and tombstones its lane before teardown could ask for a resize, and that announceDisplacement removing the session from the loser's connState is what stops a displaced connection's teardown firing a spurious return-to-default. Both are covered indirectly by the passing suite; neither has a test naming it. Recorded on nocx-eidfb.3 rather than lost.

title: effectiveSize is a session property, owned by the backend
description:
Move the decision, not the measurement. The client still measures itself — only a webview knows its font metrics and pane geometry — but open stops SETTING the channel size and starts REPORTING the client's window size. The backend decides.

With no client attached the session holds a named default rather than having no size, which is what a backend outliving its window needs (nocx-if6).

AD-1's letter survives: the channel is still created at its final size and never spawned-then-resized. What changes is who chose that size.
acceptance_criteria:
A session created with no client attached has the default size and a working channel.
A client attaching reports its geometry and the backend, not the client, sets the channel size.
The contract in contracts/ is updated in the same commit and the generated renderer types match it.
close_reason:
Merged into feat/nocx-server as 488ea004. The decision moved without the measurement moving: the client still measures itself and reports its geometry, and the backend sets the channel size. A session with no client attached holds a named default rather than having no size — which is the state a coordinator outliving its window produces, and the reason this epic blocks A1.4.

AD-1's letter is ASSERTED, not merely intended, and that is the part I checked hardest: TestOpen_ChannelIsCreatedAtItsFinalSize_AndNeverResized and TestOpen_NoClientAttached_ChannelIsNotSpawnedThenResized. Eight tests in internal/session/size_test.go cover no-client, client-reports, unusable-report-falls-back, remote channel, and resize.

The wire: contracts/open.schema.json carries additionalProperties:false with a full explicit required list including effectiveSize, TestOpen_OverTheWireConformsToContract validates the real result off the real socket, and there is a NEGATIVE schema test asserting a 0x0 effectiveSize is rejected — 'a session always has a size, and minimum:1 is what has to enforce it'. That is the kind of assertion a schema is for.

Run by the coordinator: go test ./internal/session/... ok. Worker's own scoped run: transport 131s ok, deadcode 85 all baselined unchanged, contracts:check and tsc clean, full pre-commit green on its commit.

Boundaries held exactly against a concurrent worker in the same package: it touched ws_session_handlers.go, ws_session_ops.go and the session contract, and left ring.go, ws.go, ws_ledger_capture.go, internal/content and internal/settings alone.

Out of scope by design and still open: choosing an active client among several (nocx-eidfb.2) and rendering at the session size rather than the window size (nocx-eidfb.3).

title: A client asks for output older than the replay ring and gets it
description:
The ring is 256 KB, about ten screens (internal/transport/ring.go:14), and is deliberately not scrollback. Today that is the whole of what a reattaching client can recover, so a client that joins an hour into a run sees ten screens of it.

The client asks by offset — it already speaks that coordinate system for AD-9 acks — and renders what comes back with its own VT, at the session's size. So the same bytes plus the same size give the same screen, which is what makes two clients agree without a grid on the backend.

Block boundaries are not re-derived here: they are already the backend's, from the lifecycle channel.
acceptance_criteria:
A client attaching an hour into a session recovers output from before the ring window.
Two clients attached to the same session render the same content.
A request for an offset that has been dropped by the retention bound answers with what remains and says what is missing, rather than silently returning less.
