That is also why the author saw green and why the second subtest passed while the first failed: once an earlier fixture holds fds 4 and 5, the next socketpair lands higher and the stray write goes into a socket nobody is reading.

The product is not implicated: internal/lifecyclechannel sets close-on-exec on both ends (socketpair_other.go, nocx-1w69) and internal/pty's own fixture does the same dance. Only the shellintegration test fixtures skipped it.

## Steps to Reproduce

go test ./internal/shellintegration/ -run TestBootstrapProgress_AClosedDescriptorCostsNoTerminal -count=1 — whichever subtest starts the first shell of the process fails after 10 s with 'handshake never completed; accepted=[hello]'; the next one passes.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The package's fixtures mint the pair with close-on-exec on both ends, so the shell inherits fd 3 and nothing else of the harness.
- TestBootstrapProgress_AClosedDescriptorCostsNoTerminal asserts its premise — the shell reports fd 4 closed — rather than assuming it, and fails naming the leak instead of timing out on the handshake.
- go test ./internal/shellintegration/ is green with -count=2 and with -shuffle=on, and the closed-descriptor test passes as the first shell in a fresh process.
close_reason: Shipped. internal/shellintegration/channel_exec_test.go:1279 lifecycleSocketpair now takes syscall.ForkLock.RLock() and CloseOnExec on both descriptors, and all thirteen fixtures in the package go through it. The premise is asserted by TestBootstrapProgress_AClosedDescriptorCostsNoTerminal in launcher_bootstrap_progress_test.go:406. Merge a30a68d4. Closed during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh.

title: a Go test that starts the app installs shell integration into the developer's real home
description:
## Summary

App.Start calls os.UserHomeDir() and ShellIntegration.EnsureInstalled(home) (internal/app/app.go:1337). storagetest.Isolate moves the profile directories and deliberately does NOT move HOME, so every test that starts the composition root after a plain Isolate — TestStartShutdown, the capture and history acceptance rounds, the launcher rounds — writes ~/.nocx and the rc-file hooks into the home directory of whoever runs the suite. That is the same class as nocx-ti8w: a run of the Go suite editing the developer's real per-user state.

The reason IsolateWithHome is opt-in is written in its own doc comment, and nocx-o4hg has just removed it: a fake HOME left macOS 'security' with no login keychain, so every system-provider call waited out its 5-second bound and vault.setup went from 132 ms to 5.1 s. Tests no longer reach the system provider at all — app.New builds it over an absent keyring unless the test opts in — so moving HOME costs nothing on that axis any more, and Isolate can become what its name says.

Worth measuring rather than assuming: the shells those tests spawn will then read an empty home rather than the developer's rc files, which is the OTHER half of nocx-58gq and may change which tests pass locally.

## Steps to Reproduce

Note the mtime of ~/.nocx, run go test ./internal/app/ -run TestStartShutdown, look again. On a machine that has never installed nocx, the directory appears.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A full go test ./... leaves ~/.nocx, ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc and ~/.config/nocx* untouched on the machine that ran it, asserted rather than eyeballed.
- storagetest.Isolate moves HOME by default, or the tests that start the app say why they need the real one.
- The 5-second keychain bound that justified the split is gone from the reasoning, not merely from the comment.

title: the e2e harness declares the keystore stance only for the specs that are about it
description:
## Summary

e2e/harness.ts sets NOCX_NO_SYSTEM_KEYSTORE=1 only inside the withoutSecretService branch (harness.ts:331). Every other spec launches devharness without it, so app.New takes the production stance and probes the real system provider: a keyring.Set + Get under service 'nocx' per backend start, which on macOS is a login-keychain dialog for whoever is running the suite. e2e/stand.ts already sets it unconditionally (stand.ts:163), so the two launchers disagree about the same premise.

nocx-o4hg inverted the default for GO tests — app.New now refuses to build from a test binary that has not declared a stance. That refusal cannot reach devharness, which is an ordinary binary, not a test one: the declaration has to come from whoever launches it, and only one of the two launchers makes it.

The container path (e2e/run-in-container.sh) has no keychain to reach, which is why AGENTS.md documents it as the local path. This is about the macOS host path, which still exists and still runs.

## Steps to Reproduce

On macOS: PW_PROJECTS=chromium npx playwright test e2e/sidebar.spec.ts (any spec that is not about the passphrase path). A keychain dialog appears per backend start.

## Acceptance Criteria

- e2e/harness.ts declares the keystore stance on every start, not only for the specs whose subject it is; a spec that needs the real store says so by name.
- A macOS host run of the suite produces no keychain dialog.
- The two launchers (harness.ts, stand.ts) take the premise from one place rather than each setting the variable itself.
close_reason: The two launchers now take the keystore premise from one place, and it is not a variable either of them sets. cmd/devharness is deleted with the cutover (nocx-gpyxp): e2e/stand.ts and e2e/harness.ts both start cmd/nocx-server, and a build without -tags nocx_login_session declares no login session, so it takes the file provider and never calls the OS keystore at all (design D10, internal/app/keystore_build_headless.go). VaultBackend's withoutSecretService flag is gone with the reason for it, so a spec cannot forget it; the one spec whose subject IS the OS key asks for readStand().serverLoginSession by name. A macOS host run therefore raises no keychain dialog on any path, because there is no path left that probes.

title: Backup & Restore ships without the ADR that decides it
description:
PR #61 replaces ADR-0011 section 7's four export/backup modes (configuration export, portable encrypted, same-machine backup, import) with one structured Backup & Restore capability, and deletes internal/export. The ADR that decided this and the user guide that explains it were written in 7c7e15e8 (docs/decisions/0015-structured-backup-and-restore.md, docs/backup-and-restore.md) and LOST when the branch was refreshed onto main — 0015 had meanwhile been taken by 'ssh -G as the ssh config oracle'.

So the branch as it stands supersedes a binding decision silently: ADR-0011 section 7 still reads 'Export and backup are several products, not one button' and lists four modes the branch removes.

The recovered draft has also drifted from what the branch now does and cannot be restored verbatim:
- The configMu/configErr gate it describes does not exist. Backup runs through the existing configGate Admission from ADR-0026 (capability.NewBackupOperation composes configGate then lane), which is the correct outcome and the ADR must say so.
- There is no 'poisoned until restart' recovery mode. app.New calls backupService.Recover() and returns an error if it fails — the app does not start.
- The group-defaults safe subset is eleven fields, not ten: portDiscovery was added.
- Create saves through a native dialog (backup.saveToFile, zenity/osascript, argv-bound since 85ab69e9) and falls back to a browser download only when that is unavailable.

## Acceptance Criteria

docs/decisions/0027-structured-backup-and-restore.md exists, describes the gate and recovery the branch actually implements, and lists the eleven group-default fields. ADR-0011 section 7 carries a superseded block pointing at it. docs/backup-and-restore.md exists and matches the shipped save path and recovery behaviour. No claim in either document is contradicted by the code on the branch.
close_reason:
ADR-0027 and docs/backup-and-restore.md written against the code on the branch rather than the recovered draft, ADR-0011 section 7 marked superseded, and the ADR-0018 references in internal/backup and the Backup & Restore surface retargeted. Pushed to PR #61 as a96c93fc.

Four claims in the recovered draft were wrong and are corrected rather than restored: the configMu/configErr gate does not exist (the refresh replaced it with the ADR-0026 configGate admission, which the ADR now states as the decision it is); there is no poison-until-restart mode (app.New refuses to start when Recover fails); the group-defaults subset is ten fields but not the ten listed — host and canBeJumpServer are not defaultable at all, desiredMode and portDiscovery are; and create saves through a native dialog before it ever downloads.

Checking those claims found a defect the docs would otherwise have had to describe. backup.saveToFile returns null for a cancelled dialog and rejects when no dialog exists; the surface treated both as 'not saved' and downloaded, so cancelling handed the user the plaintext file they had just declined. Fixed in 4bf624ec with the component's first unit tests (12), cancel first as a red test. The create summary also only appeared on the download path, so a user who saved was never told a credential binding had been dropped; both paths carry it now.

Verified: vitest 143 files / 2538 tests green, tsc and eslint clean on both changed files, prettier clean at frontend and repo root, go build and internal/backup green, gofumpt clean.

title: the not-integrated card is 10 seconds late, because the handshake bound is the only detector
description:
The user opens a tab, sees a working terminal, and ten seconds later a card
appears over it. The delay is HelloTimeout: today the only way we learn the
shell will not answer is that it did not.

But the wrapper that took the shell is OUR OWN CHILD PROCESS, and becomes one
within milliseconds. Measured on the installed build launched from Dock:

  23608  /Applications/nocx.app/Contents/MacOS/nocx
  +- 23678  zsh (kiro-cli-term)
     +- 23688  /bin/zsh --login

Observing a process we started (kqueue EVFILT_PROC / NOTE_EXEC on macOS) is
not stream sniffing and does not touch AD-6: the backend watches a process it
owns, never the bytes it produces. Pairs with the bootstrap progress facts,
which report the same event from inside the shell.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Install a shell wrapper that execs from the user's rc (Kiro CLI, Amazon Q).
2. Launch the packaged app from Dock, so no terminal environment is inherited.
3. Observed: a working terminal for ten seconds, then a card over it.
acceptance_criteria: A takeover is reported in well under a second, and the card does not appear after the user has already started reading the terminal.
close_reason: A takeover is detected by internal/procwatch (kqueue NOTE_EXEC on the process nocx forked) and reported immediately: the acceptance test in internal/transport sets the handshake bound to an hour, so only the observation can have produced the notification. Wired at the composition root and proven reachable there. Closed with --force: the DEPENDS ON edge is the parent bug nocx-viil, which stays open for its other children.

title: the not-integrated card overlays the terminal instead of taking space above it
description:
Measured on the installed build: the card floats over the terminal and covers
the first prompt line. The owner's decision was a persistent tab mark plus a
card, and a card that hides the thing it is describing is worse than the toast
it replaced. It must occupy layout space above the terminal and push it down.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a local tab whose shell cannot integrate.
2. Wait for the card. Observed: it floats over the terminal and hides the
   prompt line underneath.
acceptance_criteria: The card never covers terminal output; the terminal is laid out below it.
close_reason: The card is the pane's first child in the flow (mountIntegrationNotice insertBefore) with flex: 0 0 auto; the stylesheet declares no position and no z-index, so it cannot lift out of the flow. The pane is a flex column and .scrollback-layout is flex 1 1 auto, so the terminal is laid out below it; the reflow goes through scheduleLiveResize on mount and on dismissal, the same path the editor appearing/disappearing takes (the pane's own box never changes, so the viewport observer does not fire for this). DOM order carries the placement rather than a CSS order, so reading order and visual order stay one thing. Proved by terminal-content.test.ts 'takes space above the terminal instead of covering it' and notice.test.tsx 'declares no rule that could lift it out of the flow'.

title: the zsh tier shadows the user's ~/.zprofile, so a macOS tab can start without the PATH their login shell would have
description:
The zsh tier points ZDOTDIR at a transient directory, which is structural — zsh has no --rcfile. The consequence is that zsh looks for ~/.zshenv, ~/.zprofile and ~/.zlogin THERE, so only the user's ~/.zshrc is replayed (the deviation zshRcfileTemplate declares). /etc/zshenv, /etc/zprofile, /etc/zshrc and /etc/zlogin still run, because those are absolute paths.

Measured on the owner's Mac, 2026-08-12: ~/.zprofile carries the Homebrew shellenv eval, the Python 3.11 PATH entry, OrbStack's init and ~/.local/bin. Homebrew's own documented install instructions put that eval in ~/.zprofile, so this is the common macOS layout, not one user's. This machine happened to re-add /opt/homebrew/bin from ~/.zshrc as well, which hid most of it; a user who followed only the Homebrew instructions would open a nocx tab with no brew on PATH at all.

It affects the REMOTE zsh tier identically — same template, same declared deviation (nocx-xs1d) — so this is one decision for both, not a local patch. Replaying ~/.zprofile is not free: it must run at the zprofile PHASE to be equivalent (before ~/.zshrc, with the login-shell semantics the user's file expects), and a file that execs or exits changes what the rest of the bootstrap means.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. On macOS with a zsh login shell, put a PATH entry in ~/.zprofile only (the Homebrew shellenv eval is the canonical case) and nothing equivalent in ~/.zshrc.
2. Open a local tab in nocx.
3. The entry is missing from PATH; the same shell started by Terminal.app has it.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A local zsh session on a machine whose PATH additions live in ~/.zprofile has those entries on PATH, proven by a real zsh on a real pty with a fixture ~/.zprofile.
- The remote zsh tier does the same thing, or the difference between them is stated in zshRcfileTemplate's declared equivalence set.
- A ~/.zprofile that execs or exits still leaves the session usable (the fail-open direction the tier already promises).
close_reason: Closed

title: the remote lifecycle adapter never says which path lost its channel, so a degraded ssh session stays silent
description:
nocx-dvql gave internal/lifecyclechannel a LossCause and a LossReporter, and wired the composition root so a local session's handshake timeout and channel loss reach session.integrationChanged. internal/lifecycleremote/adapter.go has the identical shape — one lose() reached from the hello timer, the pump's end of stream, the Done watcher and Close — and it reports nothing and logs nothing at the loss point, exactly as the local one did before this bead.

Consequence in the product: a remote session that integrates and then loses its channel never publishes lost/channel-lost. It keeps whatever status it last had (integrated), so the tab carries no mark and the user watches blocks stop appearing with no explanation. A remote handshake that expires is the same silence the local one had.

Scope: mirror the local change — a cause on lose(), the log line naming it, a LossReporter option, and the composition root routing it to WSServer.NoteIntegrationLoss. The vocabulary must have ONE owner: internal/lifecyclechannel.LossCause is it today, so either lifecycleremote imports that type or it moves to a package both can hold. Do not spell a second set of strings.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open an ssh session to a host where integration establishes (blocks appear).
2. Drop the ssh connection, or kill the far shell's lifecycle helper.
3. Observed: the tab keeps its integrated presentation and no session.integrationChanged arrives. Nothing in the product or the log says which path lost the channel.

## Acceptance Criteria

A test drives a remote adapter through each of its loss paths and asserts the session's published status is lost/channel-lost after establishment and conventional/handshake-timeout before it. The spelling-conformance test in internal/app/integration_status_test.go covers the remote adapter's causes too.

title: nocx offers to apply the startup-file fix, with a backup and a diff the user approves first
description: The community workaround for a third-party wrapper that execs away our shell is to guard its block with a condition on NOCX_SHELL_INTEGRATION; measured working on this machine. Offering to apply it is a real convenience and a real risk: we would be editing configuration we do not own, and a block another vendor also rewrites on update. Therefore: never silent, always a preview of the exact diff, always a backup, never on a file we did not parse cleanly, and never as a default action. See upstream kirodotdev/Kiro#7169, open since 2026-04-05 with no maintainer response, where the same workaround is what users converged on.
acceptance_criteria: The user sees the exact diff before anything is written, a backup exists afterwards, and a file we could not parse is refused rather than edited.

title: A trivial command's block stays running for 15s on a cold start, and the receipt that arrives meanwhile is dropped for good
description:
e2e/prompt-vault.spec.ts:96 fails on webkit by waiting out its 15s budget for .ui-block-receipt. It is not the spec being impatient.

MEASURED from the Playwright trace of a failing run — the three snapshots that contain a command block:

  t=11.1s  cmd-block            (an earlier block)
  t=15.4s  cmd-block-running    <- sk-proj-... starts
  t=30.4s  cmd-block            <- it finally freezes

Fifteen seconds for an echo, while a healthy run of the WHOLE test takes 8s. The assertion's 15s expired at the same instant the block froze. The page snapshot shows the command and its echoed output present, so the command itself ran; what took fifteen seconds was the completion reaching the block.

Correlates with a COLD start, not with repetition: 10 repeats of the spec in the container, and the only failure was run 1 at 22.5s — runs 2-10 took 7.7-9.7s. CI hit it once in five runs of the suite (31577505729), on webkit only; chromium passed the same commit in 8.4s.

Second defect, and it is what makes the first one permanent. attachRecordedAck refuses a block that still carries cmd-block-running and returns — silently, with no retry and nothing in the UI or the log. Its comment justifies the silence with 'the capture died with them on the backend anyway', which holds for a cleared scrollback and a disposed tab and does NOT hold for a block that has merely not frozen yet. So a history.record ack landing inside that window loses its receipt for good.

For a user that reads: run a command containing a key, the backend captures it, and no receipt ever appears — nothing offers to save it and nothing says why.

## Steps to Reproduce

PW_PROJECTS=webkit e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/prompt-vault.spec.ts --repeat-each=10

The cold first run is the one that fails; a warm container usually will not reproduce it. Read the trace's snapshot timestamps rather than the Playwright output — the failure message names the receipt, and the receipt is the symptom.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A completed command's block freezes within a bound that does not depend on whether the run is cold, stated as a measured worst case rather than a hope.
- An ack that arrives before its block has frozen is not lost: it is applied when the freeze lands, or refused where the user can see it. No path drops a receipt in silence.
- 10 consecutive cold container runs of e2e/prompt-vault.spec.ts on webkit are green, stated as a measured count.
close_reason: Fixed by 12a6582: attachRecordedAck reads block.status (the logical freeze) instead of the cmd-block-running class (the visual one), and parks an ack that arrives before the visual boundary in a new one-shot, afterVisualFreeze, which _freezeVisual runs when it replaces the element. Measured: the unit test fails without the change and passes with it; 2546 frontend tests green; the spec green 12/12 across three COLD container invocations on webkit, the cold run being the one that failed; ci-e2e green in CI three times since, including both release runs.

title: TestLiveSshd_SSHChildAssembly_ChildEstablishesOverComposedLine waits out 30s after the child domain is granted
description:
internal/app, one failure in three full containerized runs at 30e4e65. The log shows the test reaching its subject — 'child domain granted env=ssh host=127.0.0.1 lane=lane-ssh-child-assembly domain=dom-65a6b8ad851a292f epoch=2 opts=[] bootstrapBytes=82363' — and then nothing for thirty seconds, after which the listener transport ends with a live domain and the test reports its bound.

So the grant happens and whatever the test waits for afterwards does not arrive. It fails by sitting out a fixed budget rather than by asserting anything, which is the same shape as nocx-8b47 and tells you nothing about WHICH step stalled.

Found while verifying the fix for nocx-8b47 under the condition that flake needed (three full scripts/ci-linux.sh --no-keyring runs). Runs 1 and 2 green, run 3 red here. Unrelated to that fix — internal/app was not touched.

Note for the CI split (nocx-qvtu): internal/app is portable, so this lives in the ci-backend job and is in the release gate.

## Steps to Reproduce

./scripts/ci-linux.sh --no-keyring

Repeat; observed once in three at 30e4e65 on 2026-08-12. Not reproduced in CI, which has been green across the same period.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The wait names what it was waiting for when it gives up — which frame, fact or state, not just the elapsed time.
- 10 consecutive containerized runs of ./internal/app/... are green, stated as a measured count.
- If the stall is real rather than slow, the defect it exposes is filed and linked; a widened bound alone does not close this.
notes:
SEEN AGAIN 2026-08-18, in the CONTAINERIZED ci-linux job on feat/workspaces, and the surrounding facts make it a clean data point rather than an anecdote.

The merge it failed under changed NOT ONE LINE OF GO — git diff --stat over '*.go' between the branch point and the merge is empty — and an immediate re-run of the same script on the same commit was green with zero failures. So a regression was arithmetically impossible and the flake reproduced roughly one run in two.

The failure is verbatim this bead's signature: 'timed out after 30s waiting for child domain Established via its own hello', with the log showing 'child domain granted ... bootstrapBytes=92411' immediately before. So the grant lands and the hello does not, which is the shape the title already names.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE NOW THAN WHEN IT WAS FILED: this is the containerized runner, which AGENTS.md holds to be byte-for-byte CI's in software. A flake here is a flake on the runner, not a developer-machine artefact — and it costs a coordinator a ten-minute re-run to tell innocent from guilty, which is exactly the indistinguishability the gate exists to remove.

title: make ci-full is weaker than the CI gate: ci-linux was narrowed to the OS packages and ci-backend was never added
description:
9527464 redefined ci-linux to mean the OS-SPECIFIC packages only:

  ci-linux:   ./scripts/ci-linux.sh -- $(OS_PKGS)          # 8 packages
  ci-backend: ./scripts/ci-linux.sh --no-keyring -- <the rest>

but left the composite untouched:

  ci-full: ci ci-linux ci-frontend ci-e2e

So ci-backend is in NO composite target, and make ci-full now runs the portable Go suite on Linux not at all — only the 8 OS packages, in both keyring variants. CI's backend-linux job runs go test ./... in both variants. make ci-full is therefore strictly weaker than the gate it claims to be, and the gap is invisible: every target it invokes is green.

Same defect class as nocx-cn86 and nocx-1e7x, which is what ci-full was created to close — a local gate reporting green for a job it does not run. It went unnoticed because the surviving NAME is the same: ci-linux meant 'the backend-linux job' before the commit and means '8 packages' after it, so the composite kept reading as correct.

make ci-os-split is also in no composite, so the drift check that keeps the partition honest never runs unless somebody types it.

Measured 2026-08-12: the release-blockers branch was verified by invoking the JOBS directly (scripts/ci-linux.sh with no arguments = ./...), not the make wrappers, so that branch's green is real. A developer following the Makefile would have run less.

## Steps to Reproduce

  make -n ci-full | grep ci-linux.sh

Reports one invocation, narrowed to the eight OS packages. Then:

  grep -n 'ci-full:' Makefile

shows ci-backend is not among its prerequisites, while CI's backend-linux job runs go test -race -count=1 ./... in both keyring variants.

## Acceptance Criteria

- ci-full runs a set of targets whose union is every CI job, with no job covered only by a target outside it.
- ci-os-split runs as part of the composite, so the partition cannot drift silently.
- Each target's echo says which CI job it IS, so a name that changes meaning cannot keep reading as correct.
close_reason: ci-full now runs ci-os-split, ci, ci-backend, ci-linux, ci-frontend, ci-e2e — the union is every ci.yml job, with ci-backend + ci-linux partitioning ./... exactly (41 portable + 9 OS = 50, no overlap, none dropped). ci-backend lost its --no-keyring so both variants cross the whole partition, matching what backend-linux does. Each target's banner names the CI job it is. Wiring in ci-os-split made it fail on the first run: it could not tell //go:build linux from //go:build release, flagging internal/log while internal/storage sat in OS_PKG_DIRS with the same shape; it now derives from GOOS tokens, checks both directions, and carries OS_EXEMPT with a stated reason per entry. Negative-tested both ways. Commit 72e99ad.

title: ci.yml still has the old four jobs while the Makefile has the five, and the deferral lives only in a commit body
description:
9527464 (nocx-yx4x) added the five local targets — ci-backend, ci-linux, ci-mac, ci-frontend, ci-e2e — and deliberately did NOT split .github/workflows/ci.yml, whose jobs are still backend / backend-linux / frontend / e2e. Its reason, verbatim: 'Splitting the workflow in release week risks the release itself for no gain — the local targets are what a developer runs, and the workflow can follow once the branch is green.'

The branch is now green: all four jobs run locally at 2803cef (make ci exit 0; scripts/ci-linux.sh both variants green; scripts/ci-frontend.sh exit 0; e2e 274 passed / 8 skipped). So the condition the deferral named has been met.

Filed because the deferral existed only in a commit body. Nothing surfaces that, and the owner asked why the job names had not changed — which is the failure AGENTS.md names: a reported blocker becomes a bead in the same minute or it evaporates between rounds.

What the split has to preserve: ci-backend and ci-linux partition ./... exactly (OS_PKG_DIRS in the Makefile, with make ci-os-split as the drift check), so a red run says whether portable or platform behaviour broke. The keyring matrix rides with the Linux job, not with the OS split. ci-mac has no CI counterpart today — macos-latest currently runs the whole suite as backend — so the split has to decide whether the runner keeps doing that or narrows to the OS packages.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every job name in ci.yml has a make target of the same name, and every one of those targets is the command that job runs.
- The union of the Go jobs still covers ./... with nothing dropped and nothing run twice, checked by make ci-os-split rather than by eye.
- AGENTS.md's runner table names the five, and no document still lists four.
close_reason: Shipped, for the half this bead actually owns. .github/workflows/ci.yml is now split into five jobs — ci-mac:104, ci-backend:203, ci-linux:308, ci-frontend:398, ci-e2e:493 — each with a same-named make target, which was this bead's first and second criteria. Verified by grep during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh. Its third criterion, that AGENTS.md's runner table names the five and no document still lists four, is NOT met — AGENTS.md:480 still says the four names below are the whole of ci.yml and :485 still calls the Linux job backend-linux — but that is the entire scope of the open nocx-li6w, which was discovered from this bead. Left there rather than duplicated here.

title: internal/ssh: the test server logs through *testing.T after its test has finished, so -race fails the package
description:
backend-linux is red on a race the assertions never see: no test reports --- FAIL, and the package fails purely on two DATA RACE reports from the race detector.

The read side is testSSHServer.serveConn calling s.t.Logf (ssh_real_test.go:236) from the accept goroutine; the write side is tRunner marking the test done. Seen under TestConnect_HostKeyMismatch_Rejected, and the ordering is inherent to what that test does: the client rejects the host key and drops the connection, the test asserts and returns, the deferred srv.close() closes the LISTENER only — and gossh.NewServerConn on the already-accepted connection then returns its error and logs into a *testing.T whose test is over.

Four call sites are reachable from server goroutines and none is joined before the test ends: 236 (handshake), 265 (accept session channel), 272 (accept direct-tcpip), 390 (direct-tcpip dial). close() closes the listener and the shell channel and waits for nothing.

Not a flake in the usual sense — it needs only a connection whose handshake outlives its test, which is that test's whole subject. It went unseen because -race must be on AND the timing must land, and it costs the whole package when it does.

## Steps to Reproduce

scripts/ci-linux.sh --no-keyring -- ./internal/ssh/...

Observed 2026-08-12 on shady2k/release-blockers at 8e279e8: variant 'no Secret Service' FAILED with two race reports, variant 'with Secret Service' green at the same commit.

## Acceptance Criteria

- No server goroutine touches *testing.T after its test has returned; the mechanism that guarantees it is named in a comment, not left to timing.
- 10 consecutive containerized runs of ./internal/ssh/... under -race are green, stated as a measured count.
- The diagnostics the four Logf calls carry are still emitted when the test is live — the fix does not buy silence.
close_reason: Fixed by 2803cef: the four server-goroutine t.Logf calls go through logf, which holds a mutex and checks a flag close() sets under the same mutex as its last act, so the interval is closed at both ends. Measured since: no race report in internal/ssh across 2 full local scripts/ci-linux.sh runs and 6 CI runs of ci-backend/backend-linux (2803cef, 72e99ad, dry run 4e21183, 12a6582, and both release runs). Short of the bead's 10-run bar by count, closed on the strength of the mechanism: the race needed a t.Logf after tRunner completed, and no such call can now occur.

title: The nocxify journey never paints the block for the remote session's exit, and is the last red spec
description:
e2e/nocxify-journey.spec.ts is the only red spec left in the suite (272 pass,
2 fail — the same spec on chromium and webkit, identically). It fails at
step 3, line 484:

    Locator: locator('.pane.active').locator('.cmd-block')
             .filter({ hasText: 'Connection to 127.0.0.1 closed' })
    Expected: visible ... Error: element(s) not found

So the journey gets FURTHER than either previous report of it. Step 2 passes:
the hand-typed ssh connects, the remote host's commands become blocks, and the
location chip reads `e2e@127.0.0.1` — the child domain establishes and remote
execution works. What fails is the block painted when the user types `exit`
and the remote session ends.

This supersedes both earlier readings, which were taken at older commits:
CI run 31478263946 (at 968fd52, five commits behind) failed much earlier, on
`e2e-sshd: saw 0/1 CONN= lines in 30000ms`; nocx-ak2d describes it reaching
step 4 and failing on installed-facts.json. Neither is the current failure.

TWO blockers, and they are separable:

  1. THIS ONE — the exit block never appears. Unknown cause; the remote
     session demonstrably worked up to that point.
  2. nocx-ak2d — the installed-fact assertion at line ~497, which the journey
     reaches only after (1) is fixed. That bead escalates a design question to
     the owner and is not blocked on this one.

Both engines fail identically, so this is deterministic, not a flake.

Starting points: the backend log inside the disposable home
(.e2e/home/.local/share/nocx-dev/nocx.log) covering the journey's window, and
the trace at test-results/nocxify-journey-*/trace.zip. The spec's own comments
at step 3 note that a previous version raced the prompt's return by using raw
page.keyboard.type instead of submitInEditor — worth confirming the current
`exit` submission is not in that shape.

## Steps to Reproduce

  PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/nocxify-journey.spec.ts

## Acceptance Criteria

- The exit block appears and freezes with no exit code, on both engines.
- The cause is named, not worked around by relaxing the locator.
- The spec passes end to end once nocx-ak2d is also resolved.
close_reason: Fixed. This was a spec locating the exit block by a farewell line that races it, not a product defect — as this bead's own comment recorded when it narrowed the reproduction: run alone the journey passes step 3, so the exit block is not deterministically broken and fails only with the rest of the suite ahead of it. Two commits resolved it, both ancestors of HEAD: 22833307 and 4d97e1c8, 'the exit block is found by the command typed, not by the farewell that races it (nocx-8tf6)'. Verified during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh: the old filter on 'Connection to 127.0.0.1 closed' is absent from e2e/nocxify-journey.spec.ts, replaced at :522 by a filter on the typed command with .last(). NOT a duplicate of nocx-z5k9 and not its missing reproduction: that bead is the PARENT's ssh block never settling over a real network (running dot, climbing timer, no exit code), while this was an element never appearing in the container — different block, different symptom, different cause. nocx-z5k9 stays open, still unreproduced.

comments.author: shady
comments.text:
REPRODUCTION NARROWED. Run ALONE the journey passes step 3 — the exit block appears — and fails at line 498, installed-facts.json (nocx-ak2d), in 5.7s:

  PW_PROJECTS=chromium NOCX_LOG_LEVEL=debug e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/nocxify-journey.spec.ts

In the full suite it fails at step 3 in 35.8s, on both engines. So the exit
block is NOT deterministically broken: it fails only with the rest of the
suite ahead of it, which points at load or at state left by earlier specs
rather than at the paint itself.

That demotes this below nocx-ak2d, which fails identically either way and is
the assertion the journey actually cannot get past. Fix the writer first, then
re-run the FULL suite to see whether this survives at all — it may be a
symptom of the run, not of the product.

title: TestBashInterruptAnnouncesNoPhantomCommand intermittently never sees the prompt after the interrupt
description:
TestBashInterruptAnnouncesNoPhantomCommand times out waiting for the prompt
that follows the interrupt:

    interrupt_pty_test.go:77: timed out waiting for OSC 133 A after the
    interrupt (want 2, have 1)

Seen once in scripts/ci-linux.sh (both keyring variants run; it failed in one),
and NOT in the immediately preceding run of the same tree, so it is
intermittent rather than a regression. The package around it is heavy — real
bash on a real pty, many times over — and the container is linux/amd64
emulated on an arm64 host.

The test is already carefully anchored: it waits for OSC 133 B before typing
(readline must own the terminal), and waits for the partial line to be echoed
before sending \x03, both with reasons in comments. So the obvious races are
already closed and the remaining one is not obvious.

Worth checking first, in order:
  - does the interrupt reach readline at all, or is it consumed while the
    shell is still inside __nocx_prompt_command?
  - is the 15s bound being hit because nothing arrives, or because the A
    marker arrives without the count changing (a counting bug rather than a
    delivery one)?
  - does it reproduce with NOCX_CI_CPUS=4, which is the runner's shape?

Do NOT fix by raising the bound. Per the 2026-08-11 decision recorded in
AGENTS.md, a test waits on an observable state change and never on a duration;
if the observable here is genuinely absent, the product is what to look at.

## Steps to Reproduce

  ./scripts/ci-linux.sh -- -run TestBashInterruptAnnouncesNoPhantomCommand ./internal/shellintegration/

Repeat: it does not fail every run.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The cause is named — which of the three above, or a fourth.
- Green over 5 consecutive container runs.
- No deadline was extended to achieve it.
notes:
FIRED ON MERGED MAIN, 2026-08-16, ./scripts/ci-linux.sh in the container:

  --- FAIL: TestBashInterruptAnnouncesNoPhantomCommand (16.57s)
      interrupt_pty_test.go:77: timed out waiting for OSC 133 A after the interrupt (want 2, have 1)
      accepted=[{1 hello ...} {2 prompt_ready ...}]

The immediately following run at the SAME commit passed this test and failed a different one in another package (nocx-2h08). Two consecutive containerized runs, two different intermittents, no overlap — recorded because it is the evidence that a merge is not deterministically red when one of these fires.

COST, stated because it is now the dominant one in the integration cycle: three red gates today were all explained by these two beads, and each costs the integrator an extra four-minute containerized run to distinguish 'known flake' from 'my merge'. Both beads have been open since 2026-08-11.
NOT OUR BUG, established with a control that removes nocx entirely, 2026-08-16.

PLAIN INTERACTIVE BASH — no integration, no hooks, no PROMPT_COMMAND, no DEBUG trap — absorbs a ^C at its own readline prompt without aborting the line or reprompting. Measured: 1 hang in 120 rounds. That control is the whole finding: whatever this is, it happens with nocx absent.

WHAT THE WIRE SHOWS AT THE HANG: readline echoes the signal char, runs its signal cleanup and re-preps the terminal — ^C, ESC[?2004l, CR, ESC[?2004h — and then nothing, ever. No newline, no PROMPT_COMMAND, no OSC 133 A, no prompt_ready. /proc/<pid>/syscall is pselect6, wchan is poll_schedule_timeout, and the pty Lflag stays at readline's 0x8a31. The line is still in readline's buffer: a later Enter runs it MINUS ITS FIRST CHARACTER (bash: cho: command not found).

THE OBVIOUS FIX WAS MEASURED AND REJECTED. Driving readline to a Ctrl-L clear-screen redraw before sending the interrupt — which proves it owns the terminal, has drained its read-ahead and is sitting at the next key — left the rate UNCHANGED at 3 hangs in 600 rounds. So 'make readline provably idle first' is not the answer, and nobody should spend a second round discovering that.

SO THE ANSWER TO THIS BEAD'S QUESTION IS A FOURTH OPTION: bash occasionally swallows an interrupt at its own prompt. There is no product observable to add, because the shell is bash and this test's subject is what nocx ANNOUNCES AROUND an interrupt, never whether readline takes every one.

THE FIX, and why it is not a retry-until-green loop: the test sends the same ^C the frontend sends and, if no prompt cycle follows, sends it again — inside the SAME 15s bound, no deadline extended. Its assertions count deltas from before the FIRST interrupt, so N interrupts are as strong a case as one: none of them may emit a C marker, a start or a complete. A retry is logged when it happens.

600/600 green afterwards at --cpus=1 with three competing containers, and the retry fired 4 times — bash swallowed a real interrupt in four of those runs and the test survived every one. That is the same rate that used to be a red gate.

NOT CHASED, deliberately: why readline's interrupt_state never reaches throw_to_top_level, and why exactly one character disappears from the line buffer. Upstream, reproducible without nocx, and it did not gate the fix.

UNTESTED: macOS. The interrupt path there is bash 3.2 on a Darwin pty and was not exercised.

title: The local runners throttle themselves to keep timing-dependent tests reproducible, and cannot reproduce the runner anyway
description:
The local runners throttled themselves to the runner's 4 vCPU so that
timing-dependent tests would keep failing locally the way they fail on CI.
That preserved the tests instead of fixing them, and it could not deliver
what it promised anyway: the images are --platform=linux/amd64 and a
developer's Mac is arm64, so the containers run EMULATED. Capping an emulated
run to four cores does not reproduce the runner — it produces a third machine
whose timings match neither.

nocx-2h08 is the case that settled it: one 30-second timeout in
internal/transport reporting under a different test name in every environment,
including a commit that was green on the runner and red locally. Removing the
cap changed nothing about it, because it was never a capacity problem.

So the caps come off by default and the rule that replaces them is stronger:
a test may not depend on timing. Wait on an observable state change — a frame,
a record, a DOM state — never on a duration. NOCX_CI_CPUS and NOCX_E2E_CPUS
still cap on demand for bisecting a suspected concurrency defect; that is a
debugging tool, not the gate.

Also in scope, because the five job names were asked for in the same breath:
make targets become ci-backend / ci-linux / ci-mac / ci-frontend / ci-e2e.
ci-backend and ci-linux partition ./... exactly — nothing dropped, nothing run
twice — so a red run says whether portable behaviour broke or platform
behaviour did, which one job answering for both could never say. ci-mac is the
only gate with no container (macos-latest is the target OS and Docker on a Mac
runs Linux), is excluded from `make ci`, and refuses to start unless the
profile directory, HOME and TMPDIR all point into a disposable root.

## Steps to Reproduce

  grep -n 'NOCX_CI_CPUS\|NOCX_E2E_CPUS' scripts/ci-linux.sh e2e/run-in-container.sh

Before: both defaulted to 4. e2e/run-in-container.sh additionally had
`[ "$cpus" != "0" ] && cpu_flag=(...)` under `set -e`, so the documented
opt-out would have exited the script silently before docker ever ran.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Neither local runner caps CPU by default; both still cap on request.
- The five targets exist and `make ci` is the four containerized ones.
- ci-backend and ci-linux together cover exactly ./..., checked mechanically
  rather than by a hand-kept list.
- ci-mac cannot run against the developer's own profile, home or temp root.
close_reason: Closed

title: A notification with no successor rides the droppable queue: the transport has three delivery classes and models two
description:
Every notification goes out through TryNotify, which enqueues on the
REFRESHABLE outbound queue — the one whose overflow policy is to drop the
frame, mark the connection stalled and let the renderer resync
(outbound.go:239, and the overflow doc at outbound.go:310).

That policy is correct for what the name promises: PTY output and lifecycle
facts that a later fact supersedes, or that a reattach replays. It is wrong
for the ones that have no successor and no replay:

  the lost lifecycle fact of a DEAD session — nothing follows it, and a dead
  session cannot reattach, so "the projection re-syncs on the next attach"
  describes an attach that will never happen;

  git.changed(reason=sessionClosed) — documented in the frontend as the only
  session-close writer of binding liveness (frontend/src/main.tsx:367), so a
  dropped one leaves the UI showing bindings for a session that is gone.

Responses already have the honest policy: a response that cannot be queued is
NEVER silently dropped — the connection closes and the renderer's
disconnect/reconnect surface rejects the pending promise, "a result, an
error, or a closed connection, never silence" (outbound.go:282). Terminal
notifications need the same contract and do not have it.

So there are three delivery classes and the code models two: reserved
(responses), refreshable (data), and terminal (a fact with no successor).
Today the third is filed under the second.

Found while diagnosing nocx-2h08 and deliberately left out of its scope: that
bead is the teardown ordering race, this is the queue class, and they are
separable. Fixing the ordering makes the drop rarer without making it
impossible — saturation is a different door to the same silence.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A notification the transport promises to deliver either reaches the
  outbound queue or fails loudly; it is never dropped to make room.
- The classes are named in the code, and the choice of class is made at the
  call site rather than inherited from TryNotify being the only verb.
- A test drives a saturated connection and asserts a terminal fact is not
  among the frames dropped.

## Steps to Reproduce

By reading: outbound.go:239 (TryNotify enqueues refreshable), outbound.go:310
(overflow drops the frame), outbound.go:282 (responses never dropped), and
the two callers named above.

Not reproducible from the UI today without forcing saturation, which is the
point: the failure appears only under load, on the path that has no second
chance. A test that floods the refreshable queue and then publishes a dead
session's lost fact demonstrates it.

title: TestLifecycleRecoverAck_CompositeFlow asserts the reverse of the transport's write priority: a response is drained ahead of a notification
description:
TestLifecycleRecoverAck_CompositeFlow stopped reading at the recoverAck
response and then asserted that it had already seen the lane's native
lifecycle.changed. That assumes the notification reaches the socket before
the response.

The transport guarantees the OPPOSITE. outbound.Conn holds notifications and
JSON-RPC responses in two separate channels:

    queue     chan Frame // refreshable: PTY output, notifications
    respQueue chan Frame // reserved: JSON-RPC responses (never dropped)

and its pump drains respQueue ahead of the refreshable queue deliberately —
"a response, the other half of a promise, is never stuck behind a burst of
data the caller is not waiting on". The test's comment claimed the order was
safe because RecoverLane publishes before the response is written, which is
true of the calling order and irrelevant to the wire.

So the test encoded the reverse of the documented design and passed by luck
wherever the notification happened to be written before the response was even
enqueued: this developer's Mac (1.6s, green) and the ubuntu runner
(backend-linux (false), green). It failed EVERY time in scripts/ci-linux.sh,
whose image is linux/amd64 emulated on an arm64 host — the skew there is
consistent enough to lose the toss every run, which is why a nondeterministic
assumption presented as a deterministic failure.

FIX: one read loop that ends only when BOTH the response and the lane's
native fact have been seen, in either order, bounded by a whole-loop deadline
rather than a per-read one. Any other lifecycle.changed is recorded for the
failure message and read past, so the loop cannot settle for the first
notification to arrive. The post-loop assertion is gone: the loop condition
is the assertion.

Sibling of nocx-2h08 (the 30s timeout class in the same package) and found
in the same container run, but a different defect: this one is an ordering
assumption, that one is a starved resource.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The test passes on macOS, on the runner, and in the emulated container.
- It asserts nothing about the order of a notification and a response.
- Its wait is bounded by an observable pair of messages, not a duration.

## Steps to Reproduce

  ./scripts/ci-linux.sh --no-keyring -- -run TestLifecycleRecoverAck ./internal/transport/

Fails every run before the fix ("post-ack fact = <nil>, want native"), and
passes on macOS and on the runner at the same commit — which is the tell.
close_reason: Closed

title: An interrupt before the shell's first prompt kills the session's integration, silently
description:
SIGINT is not a keystroke, and that asymmetry is the whole defect.

Ordinary keys typed at a freshly-opened tab queue in the tty input buffer and
readline reads them when it gets there — which is why a spec can submit a command
the instant the editor is focused and have it run. \x03 does not queue: the line
discipline turns it into SIGINT the moment it arrives, and it lands on whatever
the shell is doing right then. If the shell is still sourcing its rc — which at
4 vCPU it often is — the interrupt hits the integration's install.

The session never recovers. Measured in the container with NOCX_LOG_LEVEL=debug:
the domain is established and acknowledged, and then the shell sends NOTHING for
the next twenty seconds. Not a rejected frame, not a prompt_ready, nothing. A
neighbouring healthy session in the same run keeps talking.

The user-visible consequence is nocx-viil's shape: the editor keeps focus and
keeps accepting text, the app still believes the domain is live, and every
command the user submits from then on goes nowhere. Nothing in the product says
so.

Found while closing nocx-xplc, whose e2e symptom this was. That spec now
establishes a real prompt before interrupting (a completed block for a real
command), which is the correct premise for a test named 'Ctrl-C AT A PROMPT' —
and it leaves this, which is the case the test was never about.

## Steps to Reproduce

Open a tab and send \x03 before the shell has reached its first prompt — on a
4-vCPU machine, simply pressing Ctrl-C as soon as the editor takes focus. The
session goes quiet for good.

Before nocx-xplc's spec fix this reproduced as e2e/enhanced-input.spec.ts:34 on
both engines at NOCX_E2E_CPUS=4.
acceptance_criteria:
- An interrupt arriving before the first prompt either leaves the shell able to reach a prompt afterwards, or the session is reported as degraded rather than staying silently dead (nocx-viil is the reporting half).
- One automated check drives that order deliberately — interrupt first, prompt second — rather than reaching it by racing.
- The check runs on both bash 3.2 and the container's bash.

title: Ctrl-C at a prompt announces nocx's own line to the kernel as the user's command
description:
extdebug makes the DEBUG trap fire inside functions, and `__nocx_prompt_command`'s
first line — `local __nocx_exit=$?` — satisfies NEITHER of the wrapper's two
suppressions: its text does not start with `__nocx_`, and __nocx_in_prompt_command
was set four lines further down. So there is exactly one unguarded command at the
top of every prompt cycle.

It is normally harmless because the C-marker latch (__nocx_preexec_done) has
already been disarmed by the user's real command. After an INTERRUPT it has not:
no user command ran, and __nocx_precmd armed the latch at the previous prompt.

So Ctrl-C at a prompt emits an OSC 133 C to the renderer and sends the kernel a
`start` naming the command `local __nocx_exit=$?`, followed by a `complete`
carrying SIGINT's status (130 on bash 5, 1 on bash 3.2). A phantom attempt, for a
command the app never submitted, on every interrupt.

Found while investigating nocx-xplc, in the same code, and it is NOT established
to be its cause: in an isolated pty harness the shell still returns to a prompt
and the next command still runs, on both shells — which is not the xplc symptom
(shell-side silence). What it does mean is that the kernel's attempt bookkeeping
disagrees with the renderer's after every Ctrl-C, and xplc's next step should be
run against a kernel that ANSWERS the phantom rather than one that ignores it.

## Steps to Reproduce

Drive a real interactive bash on a pty with an authenticated lifecycle channel
(a kernel that accepts the hello is enough), reach the first prompt, send \x03,
and read the frames. Before the fix:

    start    attempt=s-<dom>-0  command='local __nocx_exit=$?'
    complete exit_code=130
    prompt_ready

Reproduced identically on macOS /bin/bash 3.2.57 and the container's bash 5.x.
acceptance_criteria:
- Ctrl-C at an authenticated prompt sends no `start` and no `complete` — only `prompt_ready`.
- No OSC 133 C is emitted for an interrupt at an empty prompt.
- A real command after the interrupt still gets its own start/complete with the correct exit code.
- Guarded by a test that drives a real interactive bash on a pty.

title: Three of four CI jobs have a local runner; make ci claims to be all of them
description:
`make ci` runs the host-side gates only — the macOS `backend` job plus frontend/'s
gates on the developer's node — and ci.yml's header described it as mirroring
"this same set of checks so green is identical locally and in CI". It covered one
job of four.

What had no local runner at all:

  frontend on the runner's node    CI pins node 24; this host is node 22
  the repo-root gates              tsc/eslint/prettier over e2e/, hooks, config
  e2e/check-coverage.mjs           the receipt that no spec file is uncollected
  go test -tags release ./internal/storage/...

The root row is the expensive one: `eslint .` and `prettier --check .` at the
repo root ran ONLY in the pre-commit hook, where they were dying on EACCES
against the e2e container's root-owned output. A crashing gate reports nothing,
so nothing was reported and 19 lint errors and 15 unformatted files accumulated
behind it (nocx-z9s9.8). CI grew steps for them; nothing local did.

Same shape as nocx-cn86, which closed the backend-linux half. This is the rest.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `make ci` — green.
2. Compare its output against the four jobs in .github/workflows/ci.yml: it runs
   one of them, plus part of a second on the wrong node version.
3. `node --version` on the host vs `node-version: '24'` in ci.yml.
acceptance_criteria:
- One command (`make ci-full`) runs every job in ci.yml, each in the environment that job runs in.
- The frontend job has a container runner on the runner's node version, covering frontend/ AND the repo root.
- Anything CI runs that no local command runs is named, in the Makefile, as not covered — rather than being silently absent.
- The e2e image's architecture choice is stated in the Dockerfile as a decision, so a reader can tell it from an omission.
close_reason: Shipped. Makefile:272 defines ci-full as ci-os-split ci ci-mac ci-backend ci-linux ci-frontend ci-e2e; scripts/ci-frontend.sh gives the frontend job its node-24 container over frontend/ and the repo root; Makefile:230 states what make ci does not cover. Commit ce7b79d9. Closed during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh.

title: Ctrl-C at an enhanced prompt traps input: the shell stops answering and no later command runs
description:
e2e/enhanced-input.spec.ts:34 ('Ctrl-C at a prompt does not trap input') fails
on BOTH engines in the container at the runner's 4 vCPU, and the spec is
reporting exactly what it is named for.

WHAT IS MEASURED (not inferred):
  - The frontend does its part. Instrumented run: 'cancel' fires with a live
    session (so \\x03 is sent), and the subsequent submit fires with
    lifecycle = prompt_ready — a live domain, not a conventional session.
  - The shell then answers nothing at all. Five 'session data received'
    events for the whole test, where a healthy neighbouring test in the same
    file has fifteen. No ^C echo, no new prompt, no output.
  - It is not a race. The submit was put under a retry that re-types and
    re-submits for 20 seconds; not one attempt lands.

NOT A REGRESSION OF shady2k/release-blockers. Verified by swapping
internal/shellintegration/scripts/nocx.bash and scripts.go for origin/main's
(v28) and re-running the spec in the container: it fails identically there.
So it predates this branch's shellintegration work and belongs on its own.

NOT YET ESTABLISHED, and deliberately not claimed: which side stops. The
backend log carries establishment-acknowledgement refusals during the run
(rule=e-publisher 'no establishment is pending acknowledgement', and
rule=c-lane-registered elsewhere), but those counts are consistent with
benign duplicate acks — successes are not logged, so a refusal cannot be
told from a second ack of an already-flushed generation. Deciding that needs
the success side logged too, or a PTY-level capture showing whether the
bytes reach the shell.

Related shape: nocx-viil (a session that fell back to conventional never
says so). If the domain is live but the shell is not at a prompt, the
product currently has no way to say so either.

## Steps to Reproduce

  PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/enhanced-input.spec.ts --grep Ctrl-C

## Acceptance Criteria

- The side that stops is named with evidence: either the \\x03 does not reach
  the pty, or it does and the shell does not return to a prompt.
- e2e/enhanced-input.spec.ts:34 passes on both engines in the container at
  NOCX_E2E_CPUS=4, without the spec asserting a DOM event the product does
  not promise.
notes:
Logs added, and they answer the open question — in the other direction from
what this bead suspected.

Run with NOCX_LOG_LEVEL=debug, chromium, the Ctrl-C spec alone:
  refusals:    0     acks ok:     2
  write fails: 0     frame drops: 0
  sessions:    2     channels:    2

So the whole path from renderer to pty is clean: the establishment was
ACKNOWLEDGED (not refused), the domain is live, and every input write to the
pty returned without error and without a short write. The earlier suspicion
of rule=e-publisher is dead — and it is dead because successes are now
logged beside refusals, which is exactly the ambiguity this bead said had to
be resolved before anything could be claimed.

WHAT IS LEFT, stated narrowly: the shell receives \\x03 and does not come
back to a prompt. No OSC 133 A follows the interrupt, so nothing after it
can land — which is why a 20s retry of the submit changes nothing. The
defect is shell-side, in what happens after SIGINT at a SUPPRESSED prompt.

Confirmed not a regression of this branch: reproduced with origin/main's
v28 nocx.bash swapped in.

THE INSTRUMENTATION IS THE REUSABLE PART, and it was missing at three
levels:
  - NOCX_LOG_LEVEL did not exist. Both slog handlers in internal/app/app.go
    were pinned to LevelInfo, so EVERY Debug line in this codebase was
    unreachable without editing source and rebuilding. That is why debugging
    a live session meant console.log in the renderer.
  - lifecycle.establishAck logged only refusals, and refusals alone are
    unreadable (see above).
  - internal/session's write loop discarded the pty write result whenever
    res == nil — which is the TRANSPORT's path, i.e. every keystroke a user
    types. An error there had one reader and it was thrown away, so 'the
    keystroke never reached the pty' and 'it did' looked identical in every
    log this product keeps.

Next step for whoever takes this: drive a real pty in the container, source
the script, send \\x03 at a suppressed prompt, and observe whether
PROMPT_COMMAND runs at all afterwards. internal/shellintegration already has
pty harnesses (inband_pty_test.go, launcher_publish_pty_test.go).

comments.author: shady
comments.text:
v34 (nocx-678o) is NOT the cause. Measured, not inferred.

Found and fixed a real defect in the same code: Ctrl-C at a prompt announced
nocx's own line — `local __nocx_exit=$?` — to the kernel as the user's command
(start + complete carrying SIGINT's status) and emitted an OSC 133 C for it. The
DEBUG trap fires inside functions under extdebug, and that line satisfied neither
of the wrapper's two suppressions. Reproduced on bash 3.2 and 5.x; fixed in v34;
guarded by TestBashInterruptAnnouncesNoPhantomCommand.

It is not this bug. With v34 in the tree, the container run at NOCX_E2E_CPUS=4 is
UNCHANGED: enhanced-input:34 and nocxify-journey:338 still fail on both engines,
4 failed / 4 passed. So the phantom attempt was never what trapped the input.

WHAT THIS BUYS THE NEXT SESSION — a reproduction that costs 1 second instead of a
Playwright run. internal/shellintegration/interrupt_pty_test.go drives a real
interactive bash on a real pty against channel_exec_test.go's fakeKernel and
watches BOTH sides of the interrupt (the pty stream and the lifecycle frames).
Point it at the remaining symptom and iterate there, not in the browser.

Two cautions it cost me to learn:
- The handshake is not readline. prompt_ready is sent from inside
  __nocx_prompt_command, BEFORE bash displays the prompt; the B marker is the
  first byte meaning readline owns the terminal. Typing on the handshake alone
  races it and produces a failure that reads exactly like this bug.
- In that isolated harness the shell RECOVERS from the interrupt (fresh A,
  prompt_ready, next command runs) both before and after v34. So whatever stops
  the shell in the product is not reproduced by script + pty + a passive kernel
  alone. The next variable to add is a kernel that ANSWERS — the real one
  validates sequences and can desynchronize the domain, and this fixture does
  neither.

comments.author: shady
comments.text:
CAUSE FOUND, and it is the spec's premise rather than the shell.

SIGINT is not a keystroke. Ordinary keys typed at a fresh tab queue in the tty
input buffer and readline reads them when it gets there — which is exactly why
the two neighbouring tests in the same file submit immediately and pass. \x03
does not queue: the line discipline turns it into SIGINT the instant it arrives,
and it lands on whatever the shell is doing right then. promptReady() is a DOM
statement (the editor is visible and focused) and says nothing about the shell,
which at 4 vCPU is often still sourcing its rc.

MEASURED, with NOCX_LOG_LEVEL=debug in the container. The failing test's session
is established and acknowledged and then sends NOTHING for twenty seconds — no
prompt_ready, not even a rejected frame — while sessions in the same run belonging
to the passing tests keep talking. That is the 'shell answers nothing at all'
this bead recorded, and the reason a 20s retry lands nothing.

THE FIX. enhanced-input.spec.ts:34 now establishes the prompt it is named for:
it submits a real command and waits for its completed block before interrupting.
Same lesson as completion's commandSnapshotReady — a premise that is not free is
established, not assumed.

RESULT: 6 passed, both engines, in the container at NOCX_E2E_CPUS=4. The Ctrl-C
test goes from a 20.8s timeout to 1.7s green.

The product behaviour underneath is NOT closed and is filed as nocx-c509: an
interrupt before the first prompt kills the session's integration and nothing
says so. This bead was about the spec reporting a trapped input; that one is
about the case the spec was never testing.

title: [bug] two over-the-wire contract tests and a descriptor test flake by timeout on Linux CI
description:
Two contract tests in internal/transport fail intermittently on Linux, each by
sitting out a 30-second timeout rather than by asserting anything:

    TestConnectionsPasswordRequest_OverTheWireConformsToContract  (30.04s)
    TestGitChanged_OverTheWireConformsToContract                  (30.04s)

Seen on main's CI run 31414181750 (backend-linux, no Secret Service) and in the
local pre-commit container on 2026-08-11, where the SAME tree passed the run
before and after. So it is a flake, not a regression, and it is currently
costing a commit attempt each time it lands.

These are the "over the real socket" halves of the contract checks — the ones
AGENTS.md calls the point of the whole exercise, because they prove the server
SENDS what the schema says rather than that a struct can be built. A flaky one
is worse than a missing one: it trains everybody to retry.

A 30s wall with nothing else reported means the test waited for a payload that
never came, and the wait is its only failure mode. Whatever it waits for should
be waited for with a bound that reports WHAT was missing — the assertion should
name the frame it wanted, not the clock.

Related but distinct: TestChildDescriptorReachesSpawnedProcess in
internal/lifecyclechannel flakes the same way on the same runners with a 2s
budget under -race on 4 vCPU (adapter_test.go:73). Same family — a fixed
deadline standing in for an event — and worth fixing together.

## Steps to Reproduce

Not deterministic. Observed by running the containerized suite repeatedly:

    sh -c '. ./.githooks/containerized-tests.sh; go_test_containerized' .githooks/pre-commit

## Acceptance Criteria

- 20 consecutive containerized runs of ./internal/transport/... and
  ./internal/lifecyclechannel/... are green, stated as a measured count.
- No test in either package fails by timeout alone: each wait names the event
  it was waiting for in its failure message.
- Where a fixed deadline stands in for an event, either the event is awaited
  directly or the deadline's basis is stated in a comment.
notes:
Third instance, same family, on shady2k/release-blockers CI run 31478263946:

  TestLifecycleChanged_DeadSessionGetsNoRecoveryClaim (30.02s)
  ws_lifecycle_test.go:990: waiting for lifecycle.changed notification:
  read tcp 127.0.0.1:42908->127.0.0.1:41515: i/o timeout

Failed in backend-linux (with-keyring) ONLY; the no-keyring variant of the
same commit passed. That asymmetry is the evidence: dbus-run-session plus
gnome-keyring is the slower of the two arms, and this test races there.

Line 990 is the SECOND readNotification — the 'lost' fact. The test does
registry.Close(sid) and then pub.TransportLost("T") deliberately back to
back ('the strictest race'), so the lost fact has to be routed through a
connection whose session is being torn down. 30s with nothing else reported
means the fact was never delivered, not that it was slow: the subscriber
teardown wins the race under load.

Same shape as the two contract tests already in this bead — a fixed
deadline standing in for an event — so it belongs here rather than in a new
bead. Reproduce locally with scripts/ci-linux.sh --keyring.
Fourth instance, and this one is reproducible on demand rather than flaky-
by-luck: TestInBand_AuthenticatedChannelFromStreamedCapability
(internal/shellintegration) fails in a FULL scripts/ci-linux.sh run and
passes when the same package is run alone.

Measured 2026-08-11, four runs, both trees:

  run                      baseline tree   with local changes
  targeted (2 packages)    ok              ok
  full (all packages)      FAIL            FAIL (3 of 3)

So it is load-dependent, not tree-dependent — the full run puts every
package on the same 4 vCPU. The failure message is 'streamed capability not
held in the shell variable', and the echoed command line in the output has
DOUBLED characters throughout ('reead', '___nocx_ib_line', 'NOCX_IB__SRC',
'nocx-ib-ccomplete'), which is a pty echo race in the fixture rather than a
defect in the dispatcher being tested.

Same family as the rest of this bead: a fixed deadline (or an unsynchronised
pty read) standing in for an event. Worth fixing together with them —
whatever the fixture waits for should be waited for by name.

TestTunnelConnDoneRevokesDomainUnknownsAttempt (internal/lifecycleremote)
appeared once in the same full run and did not recur in three later ones;
recording it here as a sighting, not a reproducer.

Method note, because it cost four runs to be sure: 'the output looks like an
echo race' was the right guess and was not evidence. In the same session and
the same package, a change that looked equally safe HAD introduced a real
regression (see nocx-cbtc), and only a baseline-vs-changed comparison at the
same load told the two apart. A targeted run proves nothing about a full
one.
Four of this family fixed, one attempt reverted. All were the same error —
the test waited for the wrong event — and none was fixed by raising a budget.

FIXED (each verified by repeat runs, and three got faster):
  TestInBand_AuthenticatedChannelFromStreamedCapability
      Waited for the substring 'IB_CAP_SET=', which a pty puts in the buffer
      as the ECHO of the command being typed. The wait was satisfied by the
      echo, so the assertion read a buffer whose answer had not arrived. The
      marker is assembled by printf now, so it exists only in the output.
  TestTunnelConnDoneRevokesDomainUnknownsAttempt
      Waited for DomainEstablished, then called SubmitAttempt, which needs
      the domain PAST ACCEPT. The kernel sets acceptPending in the same step
      that takes the lane to PromptReady and clears it only on delivery, so
      the submit landed inside that window and failed instantly with
      'domain not past accept'. acceptPending is unexported here, so the
      wait is on the operation itself — submit until the kernel stops
      refusing; a refusal creates no attempt, so retrying leaves none behind.
  TestOrderedSubmission_RefusesWhenFull
      Submitted  tasks and expected the next to be refused. That
      does not fill the queue: the worker starts on the first submit and
      dequeues at once, so a slot is free. Now the worker is occupied first
      (a task that signals it is running and blocks), and only then is the
      queue filled — occupancy is fully determined from that point.
  TestConnectionsPasswordRequest_OverTheWireConformsToContract
      Broadcast to a connection the server had not registered yet.
      broadcastAsk returns ErrPasswordNoClientConnected on an empty conn set
      and the goroutine swallowed it, so nothing was written and the read
      sat out 30s. waitForConns is the EXISTING answer —
      password_requester_test.go calls it before every ask; the contract
      tests never did.

REVERTED, and the attempt is worth recording as a warning:
  TestLifecycleChanged_DeadSessionGetsNoRecoveryClaim
      This one asserts behaviour in a TRANSIENT window — the session dead
      while its rx and lane registration still exist — which production
      closes as fast as it can (monitorExit → closeSession removes the rx,
      then unregisters the lanes). I tried to construct the window: wait for
      the teardown, then put the subscriber and the lane back. It made the
      test fail 10 times out of 10 rather than occasionally, so my model of
      the delivery path is wrong somewhere and I reverted rather than leave
      a deterministic failure in place. The original is flaky-under-load;
      that is strictly better than what I wrote.

      Whoever takes it: the question to settle FIRST is whether the product
      should deliver that fact at all. After teardown PublishLifecycle finds
      no rx and drops it, so the strip path this test guards may only be
      reachable in a window no user ever occupies — in which case the honest
      fix is to test the strip at its own seam rather than over the wire.

Still unfixed and seen once each in full Linux runs:
  TestConnect_LifecycleRemoteCommand_CloserClosed (0.01s)
  TestWSServer_OpenPasswordAsk_DoesNotBlockTheReadLoop (30.03s)
  TestGitChanged_OverTheWireConformsToContract (30.03s, likely the two
      closeSession callers racing — the explicit-close path captures no
      subscriber once monitorExit已 removed the rx)

Method: a targeted package run proves nothing here. Every one of these
passes alone and fails inside a full ./... run at 4 vCPU, which is what
scripts/ci-linux.sh reproduces.
Corrections to the note above, which the shell mangled on the way in:
  - "Submitted capacity tasks" — the word was eaten by backtick expansion.
  - "once monitorExit已 removed the rx" — a stray character; read "once
    monitorExit has removed the rx".
Nothing else in it changed meaning.
close_reason: Shipped. The timeouts were replaced by state waits rather than longer bounds: internal/transport/ws_contract_test.go:2519 waits with waitForConns(t, ws, 1) before the ask, and its comment names this bead; internal/lifecyclechannel/adapter_test.go now closes after the frame lands. Commits 65354c71, 2803ceff, 30e4e656. Not verified here: the twenty-consecutive-green-runs receipt is recorded nowhere in the repo. Closed during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh.

comments.author: shady
comments.text:
Both remaining tests reproduced LOCALLY for the first time, in one run of
`NOCX_CI_CPUS=4 scripts/ci-linux.sh` (2026-08-11, this branch):

  no Secret Service    TestGitChanged_OverTheWireConformsToContract (30.04s)
                       ws_contract_test.go:3389: waiting for git.changed
                       notification: read tcp ...: i/o timeout
  with Secret Service  TestChildDescriptorReachesSpawnedProcess (2.04s)
                       lifecyclechannel/adapter_test.go:429: timed out waiting
                       for domain established by the spawned process

That is this bead's own title — 'two over-the-wire contract tests and a
descriptor test' — with the third one (connections password) already fixed in
this branch by the waitForConns guard. The two that remain are the two above.

Note which variant each landed in: they are load-sensitive, not variant-specific.
The same run's CI counterpart (31478263946) was red on a THIRD test —
TestLifecycleChanged_DeadSessionGetsNoRecoveryClaim, keyring variant — which
passed here. So the set is not stable; the shape is.

The reproduction is the news. Until now no local command exercised this job at
the runner's capacity, so these were only ever observed after a push.

title: Stabilize parallel shell syntax highlighting test
description:
## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run `npm test -- --run` in `frontend/` on the refreshed current-main branch.
2. Observe `src/editor.test.ts` fail in the shell syntax highlighting case: `tok-command` is absent, while `npm test -- --run src/editor.test.ts` passes in isolation.

The failure is unrelated to Backup & Restore; it appeared while validating the latest main refresh and is intermittent/order-dependent under the full Vitest run.
acceptance_criteria: The complete frontend Vitest suite passes repeatedly, including the shell syntax highlighting assertions when run with all test files.
close_reason: Warm the lazy Shiki shell grammar before publishing readiness; full canonical container Vitest passed 146 files / 2680 tests including the previously flaky shell token assertions.

title: [bug] internal/pty hangs and internal/git/local fails on a macOS workstation while both are green on the runner
description:
Two packages are green on the macOS CI runner and broken on a macOS
workstation. One of them does not fail — it HANGS, and takes the whole `go
test ./...` run with it after the 10-minute timeout, which is the part that
matters: a developer running the suite locally waits ten minutes to be told
nothing useful.

    internal/pty       TestLocalPty_ExtraFilesReachTheShell  hangs (CI: 1.120s)
    internal/git/local TestResolveShellEnvSucceedsOnAnOrdinaryMachine  fails (CI: 10.646s)

Both verified pre-existing: they behave identically with the nocx-sw4p changes
stashed. Both verified green on the runner in CI run 31418267046, so CI is not
lying and neither is the workstation — they are running different things.

The shared suspicion, not yet confirmed: both reach the DEVELOPER'S real shell
environment rather than an isolated one. TestLocalPty_ExtraFilesReachTheShell
spawns a real login shell through NewLocal with a default Config, and its own
read loop is deadline-bounded at 3s — so the hang is upstream of the assertion,
in spawning or closing, not in waiting for the proof. A fresh CI runner has a
default rc; a developer's does not, and this developer's machine runs the
product whose shell integration the rc files carry.

That makes it the same family as nocx-ti8w (an e2e run wrote the developer's
real settings) and nocx-65v6 (the child-environment probe observes nothing on a
workstation). Worth treating as one question — which tests reach the real
environment, and why any of them may — rather than three fixes.

Not a release blocker on its own: CI is the gate and CI is green on both. It IS
a blocker on anybody running the suite locally, which is every pre-push check.

## Steps to Reproduce

On a macOS workstation:

    go test -count=1 -timeout 90s ./internal/pty/        # panics on timeout
    go test -count=1 ./internal/git/local/               # one failure

## Acceptance Criteria

- Both pass on a macOS workstation and on the runner.
- Whatever the tests need from the environment they construct themselves, or
  they state the requirement and skip-with-a-reason rather than hang.
- No test in these packages can block indefinitely: every wait is bounded, and
  the bound is shorter than the package timeout so the failure names itself.
notes: Backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh: moved from in_progress (untouched since 2026-08-11) back to open, and LEFT OPEN deliberately for the owner rather than closed. Fix commits exist and cite this bead: 9c0f6950 makes internal/pty/extra_files_test.go set unix.SetNonblock before os.NewFile (the read deadline was a no-op on a blocking socket) and pins the shell to /bin/sh, and internal/git/local/shellenv.go:202 switched to env -0 rather than export -p because zsh omitted the array-tied PATH. But this bead's acceptance is an OBSERVATION ON A macOS WORKSTATION, which cannot be made from this Linux host — so it is not closed on the commit alone. One macOS run settles it. Note that AGENTS.md still lists this bead as a known-open local-vs-CI divergence; that passage stays correct meanwhile because its other bead, nocx-65v6, is genuinely still open.

title: [bug] the pre-commit container image cannot build on Apple Silicon, so the gate's only test run never starts
description:
The pre-commit hook's container image cannot build on an Apple Silicon Mac, so
`go test -race (container)` — the gate's only test run — fails before executing
a single test:

    FROM bash:3.2 AS bash32
    RUN ... cp -L /usr/local/bin/bash /lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1 ...
    ERROR: process "..." did not complete successfully: exit code 1

musl names its loader for the architecture. `bash:3.2` resolves to arm64 on
Apple Silicon and ships /lib/ld-musl-aarch64.so.1; the Dockerfile asked for
ld-musl-x86_64.so.1, which is not there. Three places carried the same
assumption:

    .githooks/images/go-tests/Dockerfile:47,56
    .githooks/images/ci-linux/Dockerfile:30,63   (plus an amd64 Go tarball, :53)
    scripts/install-bash32.sh:46,51,57

Two DIFFERENT fixes, because the two images want opposite things:

  - go-tests just needs a Linux box to run our tests in, so it is now
    architecture-agnostic: the loader is discovered by glob and staged under a
    fixed name. Nothing links it by soname — it is only ever exec'd.
  - ci-linux exists to BE the runner, and already fetched a linux-amd64 Go, so
    it is now pinned with --platform=linux/amd64. Emulated and slow on arm64 is
    correct here: a job that reproduces CI beats a fast one that does not.

Arrived with the bash32 work in nocx-cn86. Not caught there because it was
