So when the shell restores its visible native prompt and writes ESC]1337;NOCX_RECOVERY;<hex>, nothing matches it, `_ackRecovery` never runs, `this._recovery` is never cleared, and the session stays in the "restoration pending" interval forever: no editor offered, and the backend never sees the acknowledgement it is waiting for.

This is the shape AGENTS.md names twice (nocx-rtg0, the vault): a function with tests and no production caller. `parseRecoveryFence` has five assertions in xterm.test.ts covering its parsing, all green, and nothing calls it. Note that `deadcode` does not cover TypeScript, and the frontend suite passes, so nothing in the gates reports it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Establish an enhanced session.
2. Kill the lifecycle channel while the pty stays alive (the AC3 case: the adapter dies, the session channel does not).
3. The shell notices its failed send at the next prompt boundary, clears the active latch, restores a visible native prompt and writes ESC]1337;NOCX_RECOVERY;<nonce>.
4. Observed: nothing acknowledges. `_ackRecovery` is never called; `this._recovery` stays set; the lane never goes Lost -> Native.
5. Expected: the renderer matches the nonce it was given in the lost fact and acknowledges, and the lane falls Lost -> Native.
acceptance_criteria: The OSC 1337 handler dispatches BOTH NOCX_FENCE and NOCX_RECOVERY payloads, and a test drives a real recovery nonce through the renderer's OSC path — not through parseRecoveryFence directly — and observes the acknowledgement reach the client. One handler owns OSC 1337; two surfaces never own one input.
close_reason: The single OSC 1337 handler now dispatches NOCX_RECOVERY to recoverySubs alongside NOCX_FENCE; one handler still owns the ident (AD-8). Test drives real OSC bytes through the parser rather than calling parseRecoveryFence directly, which is what hid it. Committed 3fb6980a.

title: Local lifecycle bootstrap never delivers lane/capability — the local channel is test-reachable only
description:
Found by the nocx-u7uh.15 worker while wiring the recovery nonce; verified independently by the coordinator.

The LOCAL enhanced path creates a lifecycle channel and hands the shell fd 3, but never tells the shell how to address it. localPTYFactory.NewPTY (internal/app/app.go:808-833) passes only ShellIntegration.ActivationEnv — NOCX_SHELL_INTEGRATION, NOCX_PROMPT_MODE and a freshly minted NOCX_SESSION_ID (shellintegration.go:195-209) — plus the descriptor via pty.WithExtraFiles. It never sets NOCX_LIFECYCLE_LANE / DOMAIN / EPOCH / FD, and it never uses internal/shellintegration/launcher.go, which already builds exactly that rcfile with the @CAP@ substitution for the remote tier (launcher.go:117-124).

internal/pty/pty_local.go:160 spawns exec.Command(shell, "-i") and ignores cfg.Command/cfg.Args entirely, so there is no per-session rcfile to carry the capability.

Consequence: __nocx_lc_init in nocx.bash bails on the missing NOCX_LIFECYCLE_* and the empty capability, leaves __nocx_lc_active=0, and every local enhanced session in production is a conventional terminal. Fail-closed, so it is SAFE — and it means the local half of ADR-0024 has no production caller. The REMOTE path is fully wired via the launcher rcfile; the in-band path reads the capability over the tty.

This is the nocx-rtg0 shape exactly: a reachable read path (the adapter, the kernel, the lane registry) hiding an unreachable write path in the same feature. deadcode would not report it, because the packages are genuinely reachable from the remote tier.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start a LOCAL enhanced session in production wiring (not a test): cmd/devharness or the app, with cfg.Enhanced true and a non-nil lifecycle kernel.
2. In the resulting shell, inspect the integration state: `echo "$NOCX_LIFECYCLE_LANE / $NOCX_LIFECYCLE_DOMAIN / $NOCX_LIFECYCLE_EPOCH / $NOCX_LIFECYCLE_FD"`.
3. Observed: all four are empty. `__nocx_lc_active` is 0, no hello is ever sent, the kernel's hello timeout expires and the domain is abandoned.
4. Expected: the shell has its addressing tuple and its capability, `__nocx_lc_init` completes the handshake, and the domain reaches Established.

Contrast: the same check on a REMOTE enhanced session shows the tuple populated, because the remote tier goes through launcher.go.

## Decided mechanism

Reuse internal/shellintegration/launcher.go for the local tier rather than writing a second bootstrap — it is the existing owner of "how a shell learns its addressing and its capability" (AGENTS.md, "look for the existing answer before you write a second one"). That requires pty_local.go to honour cfg.Command/cfg.Args so bash can be started with --rcfile. The capability travels in the rcfile, never in an env var (ADR-0024 decision 2).

Blocks the epic's POSITIVE and NESTED criteria, which go green in nocx-u7uh.11, and the local half of nocx-u7uh.15's AC3 pre-provisioned recovery nonce.
acceptance_criteria: A local enhanced session reaches an Established domain against the real kernel in PRODUCTION wiring, not only in tests: assert __nocx_lc_init completes, the domain is live, and prompt suppression follows ACCEPT. pty_local honours cfg.Command/cfg.Args. The capability never appears in any environment variable — assert that over the child's actual environment. A local session whose bootstrap fails still falls back to a visible conventional terminal (the current safe behaviour must not regress).
close_reason: Local bootstrap now goes through shellintegration/launcher; pty_local honours cfg.Command/Args; capability travels in the rcfile and never the environment, asserted against the child's actual environ. Proven through production wiring. Committed dc7de406.

title: The editor's submit has no seam that opens an attempt
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

Submit a command through the editor in an authenticated session. No attempt is opened by the app; only a shell-originated start creates one, so the app-owned command text and its secret references never reach the attempt.

## Root cause

The projections bead (nocx-u7uh.7) wired every consumer to the kernel and then reported, unprompted, that there is no renderer-visible SubmitAttempt seam. The kernel has SubmitAttempt and its attach rule is tested on the Go side; the renderer has no way to call it.

ADR-0024 decision 5 requires the app to open the attempt synchronously BEFORE the pty write, precisely so the later authenticated start attaches rather than opening a second top-level attempt. Without the seam, an editor-submitted command is indistinguishable from a hand-typed one, and the privacy rule that keeps vault-resolved text out of history has nothing to attach to.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: Submitting a command through the DOM editor synchronously opens an ExecutionAttempt BEFORE the bytes are written to the pty, and a test asserts that ordering rather than assuming it. The shell's authenticated start then attaches to it and does not replace its id, command text, cwd, host or secret representation.
close_reason: landed in 5cf536b4: lifecycle.submitAttempt, ordering asserted not assumed

title: Make stream-derived authority architecturally impossible
description:
The recurrence-prevention child, and the reason the epic can claim the CLASS is closed rather than the instance. A validator module plus review discipline decays; these do not.

Ranked by durability per unit of effort: enforced dependency direction first, then the single publication port, then the shared conformance suite, then deterministic corpus seeds, then fuzzing, and static grep only as a backstop for what eslint cannot express (as ValidatedLifecycleEvent, raw constructors, registerOscHandler outside renderer-owned files).

The authority inventory is the guard that import rules cannot provide: it stops a future contributor writing `if (looksLikePrompt)` in a new feature that never imports the old type. Duplicated inference under a new name is exactly how this defect arrived the first time.

Blocks the early severance on purpose: delete the old source only once the single legitimate one exists, or the deletion gets replaced by another ad hoc source mid-build. Also blocks epic closure.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: Assertions: an enforced dependency direction — lifecycle modules cannot import renderer marker types or xterm parser modules, renderer modules cannot import lifecycle reducers, attempts, ledger persistence, input ownership or the domain registry — expressed as eslint no-restricted-imports in the pattern frontend/eslint.config.js:828 already uses, NOT as a grep; a negative lint fixture proves every restriction actually fires, so the rule cannot be weakened while CI stays green; exactly one LifecycleSource implementation in production, backed by authenticated backend publication, with no renderer implementing it; an authority inventory test enumerating every operation that requires authority (show editor, persist history, complete attempt, assign exit status, freeze a block, activate an environment, enable ssh rewriting, enable rerun) and proving each takes a domain or attempt capability rather than a boolean; a shared adversarial conformance suite that takes an assembled session harness and replays bare/tagged OSC, passports, private lookalikes, malformed and oversized sequences, OSC 7, mode changes, alt-buffer transitions, the hostile cycle both mid-command and at a suppressed prompt, and a replayed fence with no event — snapshotting every security-sensitive projection before and after.
close_reason: landed and verified by the coordinator

title: Local descriptor transport
description:
Adapter only. Capability delivery and the shell hooks are nocx-u7uh.3; the domain model is nocx-u7uh.2.

Open and to be closed here: descriptor discovery without exporting a secret, socket type (SOCK_SEQPACKET preserves message boundaries where supported), direction, and shutdown ownership. The shell is started by exec.Command(shell, "-i") + pty.StartWithSize at internal/pty/pty_local.go:160.

Measured and load-bearing: bash {var} redirection is NOT close-on-exec — a child still sees the descriptor. The capability is what makes that survivable, which is why it is not this bead.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: Assertions: the local shell receives a lifecycle descriptor at spawn through exec.Cmd.ExtraFiles and reaches an accepted domain; killing the shell closes the domain and abandons the open attempt as unknown; the adapter registers ONE lane and can carry several domains on it; the transport exposes envelopes and loss notifications and has no currentDomain(); a shell that execs another shell is handled deliberately and the behaviour is stated.
close_reason: landed in 455c2ee with the kernel and codec; close did not take on the first attempt

title: Domain loss and reconnect policy
description:
Split out of the old .9: desynchronisation and loss have different triggers and different dependencies. This one needs both transports and the publication boundary.

ADR-0024 decision 8: in one LOCAL transition revoke ownership, expose the terminal, mark attempts unknown. Restoring the user prompt is a protocol action, promised only when the shell is still reachable — the atomic-restoration promise is impossible over a dead connection and must not be written as though it were.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: Assertions: SSH transport loss (TunnelConn.Done) revokes every domain bound to it, abandons attempts as unknown, and a new session gets a fresh epoch — never a resumed one; frontend/backend reconnect either resumes the existing domains or reports ambiguity and revokes, and the two paths do not share a code path with SSH loss; a lifecycle-channel-only failure while the pty still lives restores a visible prompt and that restoration is ACKNOWLEDGED before the session is treated as a usable conventional terminal; a dead connection produces a disconnected terminal and no restoration claim.
close_reason: AC1-AC4 landed in dc7de406. SSH loss revokes every bound domain with a fresh epoch; reconnect resume/ambiguity-revoke is a separate code path from SSH loss; channel-only failure while the pty lives restores a visible prompt acknowledged via a composite ACK (shell-emitted one-shot recovery fence matched by the renderer, never a grid inspection, plus applied conventional presentation) before the session is treated as conventional; a dead connection makes no restoration claim. Ack RPC is narrow: session+generation only, pending-and-alive only, Lost->Native only, idempotent, dies with the session.

title: Authenticated framing and the published lifecycle fact
description:
Split out of the old protocol child. Domain cardinality is decided first (nocx-u7uh.2) — writing framing before the domain model is correct is how a singleton assumption gets baked into the wire.

contracts/ carries the PUBLISHED DTO, not the channel framing: contracts/README scopes that directory to JSON-RPC result shapes, and the lifecycle channel is neither JSON-RPC nor necessarily JSON. Expanding that scope would be a deliberate change to the README, not a side effect.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: Assertions: the authenticator choice (bearer field or MAC) is made and justified in one place; frames are length-delimited with a bounded maximum; duplicate or decreasing sequences are rejected and sequence state mutates only AFTER authentication; a reconnect never resets the counter inside an epoch; scan and resynchronisation budgets are explicit numbers; the published backend-to-frontend DTO has a contracts/ schema with additionalProperties:false and explicit required, a DTOConformsToContract test and an OverTheWireConformsToContract test.
close_reason: landed and verified by the coordinator

title: Ingress decodes the envelope only: a huge control frame must not spend the read loop's CPU before admission sees it
description:
The read loop calls `ReadMessage` and then validates and unmarshals the WHOLE
JSON object before dispatch (ws.go:981, ws.go:995). A single large text frame
therefore spends unbounded memory and CPU on the ingress goroutine — before any
executor, admission or conflict rule can see it.

This is the same class the epic exists to remove, reachable by a route none of
the other children close. Worse, nocx-98rn makes it easier to overlook: once
every method has a validated params type, the parse looks like the safe part.

* A read limit on the WebSocket.
* A strict size limit on the control envelope.
* Ingress decodes the JSON-RPC ENVELOPE only. Full typed parameter decoding and
  `Validate()` run after ordinary admission, on the worker.
* Immediate resolver methods, which by design run on the ingress goroutine, get
  small method-specific parameter limits — they are the one class that cannot
  defer its decode.
acceptance_criteria: A control frame far above the envelope limit is refused without being fully parsed, and input to another session on the same connection is unaffected while it arrives — over the real socket. Typed parameter decoding and Validate() run on the worker, not the read loop; a test asserts the read loop never sees a decoded params struct for an ordinary method. Resolver params have their own bounded limit.
notes:
RISK OF REAL FUNCTIONAL LOSS — the limit must be per method, not one global number. Verified 2026-08-08: internal/transport sets no SetReadLimit at all today, so a control frame is currently unbounded. Several methods legitimately carry a whole document: export.importPortable takes Payload string, a base64 blob of an entire encrypted backup (ws_export.go:173); export.import takes Data json.RawMessage (ws_export.go:145); profiles.importTabby / tabbyPreview / tabbyExecute take Config string, a whole Tabby YAML (ws.go:2504, ws.go:2612).

A single conservative envelope limit would refuse a real restore — turning a freeze bug fix into 'you can no longer import your backup'. The envelope limit bounds the ENVELOPE (jsonrpc, id, method) which is always small; the params budget is declared per registration alongside its validator, so a document-carrying method declares a large one and a resolver declares a tiny one. Size the document limits against a real exported backup and a real Tabby config before choosing numbers, and add a test that restores a large genuine backup end to end so the limit cannot be tightened later without something going red.
close_reason:
Landed as e27910a. SetReadLimit(16 MiB), envelope-only decode through a stdlib json.Decoder capped at 4 KiB, per-method params budget on len(data) before any full decode (1 KiB resolvers / 64 KiB default / 8 MiB documents), tiers measured against a real 123,025-byte backup and a 2,661-byte Tabby config.

First attempt was REJECTED and redone. It hand-rolled a ~250-line JSON scanner, and a codex review found it was not merely a second parser but a wrong one: invalid escapes, raw control characters, mismatched containers, invalid literals and trailing garbage after params were all accepted, so a transport action could run for input that is not valid JSON-RPC. The serious one was duplicate members — the scanner took the first, encoding/json takes the last, so a frame could claim the 8 MiB document budget under one method name and dispatch to an ingress-critical handler under another.

Two things the revision taught that are worth keeping: Decoder.Token() alone does NOT bound allocation, because it materialises each token and a 16 MiB string is one token — the io.LimitReader in front is what makes it safe (measured: 14.5 KiB heap growth on exactly that frame). And InputOffset does not report a read truncated by a limit, so envelopeReader records cap exhaustion itself to tell 'method never appeared' from 'syntax error inside the envelope'.

Duplicate envelope members are refused, and req.Method is compared against the method the budget was chosen from, so the two passes can never read one frame differently. Also corrected from the brief: profiles.tabbyExecute carries a planToken, not a document, so it keeps the default budget.

title: Marker-only prompt is gated on a live domain, not on a spawn flag
description:
ADR-0024 decision 9. Suppressing the user only native cue while accepting readiness from an anonymous source is the phishing primitive in the threat model, and the two must never be separable.

This also closes the failure ADR-0006 §5 exists to prevent — a shell with no usable prompt — by making readiness a handshake rather than a spawn-time flag.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: Prompt suppression happens only after ACCEPT. Assertions: a shell that connects but never completes the handshake keeps its visible native prompt; a Desynchronized domain is not live and the prompt becomes visible again; a session with no transport at all never suppresses; there is no window in which the prompt is suppressed and no editor is available.
notes: 'No window' is unfalsifiable without fault injection. Acceptance needs a fault injected at EACH handshake boundary — connect but never HELLO, HELLO but never ACCEPT, ACCEPT but publication path stalled — each asserting the native prompt stayed visible.
close_reason: ACCEPT is downstream of an acknowledged publication (lifecycle.establishAck), keyed by domain/epoch, subscriber-bound, with an establishment timeout that rolls the domain back. All four criteria asserted, including fault injection at each handshake boundary — which found two real shell defects: 'read -t N -N 0' never waits, and 'exec 200<>... 2>/dev/null' nulled the shell's stderr so every restored prompt was invisible.

title: Migrate environments to authenticated domains, then delete the passport machinery
description:
The migration half of the old demolition child, and the risk that the plan review named as most likely to sink the epic: deleting the environment machinery before its authenticated successor exists would look excellent against omp and be architecturally wrong — nested ssh/sudo/docker losing domain identity, parent restoration back to frontend stack guessing.

So this lands LAST and proves parity. The severance half went early as nocx-u7uh.1.

The epic positive acceptance spec lives here, because this is where it goes green.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: Behavioural parity, not merely absence of old imports. Assertions: ssh, sudo and su each establish an authenticated child domain and restore the parent through an authenticated activation; docker exec is EXPLICITLY conventional-only (owner decision 2026-08-09, matching the epic's 'Deliberately out': neither an inherited descriptor nor a loopback port crosses the container boundary, so it is Tier B work) and the fallback is visible in the product rather than only in a log; cwd, host, title and completion scope follow the ACTIVE domain only; the epic's POSITIVE and NESTED criteria pass here; the conventional-fallback criterion still passes; OSC 636 passport machinery is deleted rather than left inert; deadcode over the touched packages is empty; the forbidden-import gates pass; DECIDE whether our scripts still EMIT OSC 133 C/D for third-party interop. The per-epoch capability NEVER enters a child's environment.
close_reason: Nested environments establish authenticated child domains: domain_request/domain_grant over the authenticated channel, kernel the sole minter, capability never in the child's environment (preserved descriptor for sudo/su, rewritten command line per ADR-0022 for ssh). sudo/su proven end to end on a real pty including the stillborn-child interval; the descriptor handoff is stated with both ends. Passport machinery deleted on both sides; OSC 133 C/D kept with reasoning at the site. docker exec is conventional-only by owner decision. Two named gaps carried as nocx-u7uh.28 (zsh tier) and nocx-u7uh.29 (ssh proven in pieces, not as an assembly); the epic stays open until .28 lands.

title: Desynchronization and the authenticated snapshot
description:
The argued-out core of ADR-0024 decision 7. Revoking on any gap would hand every ordinary program a one-write kill switch for enhanced mode — reported as flaky, not as secure. Bounded resynchronisation is safe because unauthenticated bytes can never be published.

Framing recovery is NOT state recovery, and that is the part that is easy to get wrong. Only a snapshot answering our own refresh request restores authority.

Loss and reconnect are a DIFFERENT trigger with different dependencies and live in nocx-u7uh.15.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: A child writing garbage into the inherited descriptor does NOT kill enhanced mode. Assertions: the domain enters Desynchronized (ownership revoked, input raw, terminal visible, ordinary events quarantined) and recovers after a snapshot; a Complete whose Start was lost attaches to nothing; a PromptReady whose Complete was lost does not restore ownership over the open attempt; an unresolved attempt reconciles as unknown and never as success; corruption while the prompt is suppressed restores a VISIBLE prompt immediately rather than waiting for the next one; scanning is bounded in bytes and time; a recovery budget exhausted by repeated corruption revokes the domain.
close_reason: landed in 92bae754: snapshot reconciles the open attempt, bash answers the refresh

title: The render fence: freeze the block where the output actually ended
description:
The lifecycle channel and the pty are independent streams. SSH preserves order within a channel, not across them, so an authenticated completion can arrive BEFORE the command last output bytes, and freezing the block on the event alone truncates real output.

Logical completion comes from the authenticated event. The visual freeze waits for that event AND a matching fence written to the pty after the output — the carve-out in ADR-0024 decision 1.

This is a rendering mechanism whose worst failure is cosmetic. It must never grow into a second authority: a fence alone carries none.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: A fixture whose last output bytes are delayed past its authenticated completion produces a block containing ALL of its output. Assertions: a fence with no authenticated event behind it changes nothing; an authenticated completion with no fence completes the attempt logically and defers the visual boundary rather than truncating; the fence nonce is unpredictable per completion.
notes: Stays separate — a clean orthogonal seam between logical completion and render ordering. Add to acceptance: history completion does NOT wait for the fence, while visual serialization does; the two happening at different times is the point and must be asserted, not incidental.
close_reason: landed in 5cf536b4: logical freeze on the event, visual boundary on the fence, asserted as two moments

title: Projections consume the kernel
description:
The projection half of the old .7. The model lives in .6; this rewires everyone who used to read markers.

The command-text rule is a privacy rule, not only an authority rule. For an attached app attempt the shell text is ignored outright — the wire line may carry vault-resolved secrets while the app text carries references, and terminal-content.ts:988 already keeps those distinct. Authenticated origin does not make a line the user typed a password into safe to store.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: Assertions: the ledger, the block manager, history, the environment/location/title UI, typed-ssh rewriting and the input router all read the kernel and hold no lifecycle state of their own; every operation requiring authority takes an ActiveDomain or a CompletedAttempt rather than a boolean; ledger.onMarker no longer exists; adding a new projection that infers lifecycle from bytes fails the guards from nocx-u7uh.16. DECIDE HERE: whether a shell-originated attempt persists its command text at all — getting it wrong writes hand-typed passwords to disk.
close_reason: landed in fa812fda: projections read the kernel; shell-originated text never persists

title: The lifecycle kernel: one authoritative model
description:
Merged from the old .6 and the model half of .7. They were never two machines: prompt readiness, running attempts, app-pending attachment, shell-originated starts, domain activation, desynchronisation and loss are one state space, and landing a state machine without the attempt rules only to rewrite it a bead later is the wrong seam.

One authoritative model, disposable projections — the same shape ADR-0019 already chose for the ledger.

Axes: Lifecycle (Native | PromptReady(domain) | Running(attempt) | Desynchronized(domain) | Lost) and Buffer (Normal | Alternate). Deletes the laundering rule at input-state.ts:100 rather than patching its condition.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: One reducer owns lifecycle, domain and attempt state, with exhaustive transition tests. Assertions: PromptReady(domain) is unconstructible without an authenticated event for a live domain; B,A,B from the byte stream reaches no state at all; the buffer is a SEPARATE axis, so entering and leaving the alternate buffer while the domain is revoked underneath cannot restore ownership; an app attempt is created synchronously BEFORE the pty write and a test asserts that ordering rather than assuming it; an authenticated Start attaches without replacing id, command text, cwd, host or secret representation; a Start with nothing pending creates a shell-originated attempt; a Start while one runs never opens a second top-level attempt; only an authenticated same-domain Complete supplies an exit status; abandonment yields unknown and never a code; the trusted boolean does not exist.
notes: BLOCKED-ON-LANDING detail for whoever takes this: frontend/src/generated/lifecycle.changed.ts is generated and sitting UNCOMMITTED in the coordinator's tree. It cannot land alone — the dead-exports ratchet rejects a generated type nothing imports, and contracts:check rejects a schema whose type is absent. So .6 must land the type together with its first consumer. The schema and the whole Go half are already committed in 3a1674a.
close_reason: landed in bd32495: two-axis kernel, domain stack, input-state.ts deleted

title: The publication boundary: authentication terminates in the backend
description:
Location was unstated in ADR-0024 and it matters. The backend already owns ExtraFiles, TunnelConn, the capabilities and the candidate connections; shipping raw frames or secrets to the renderer would widen the trusted computing base for nothing and make a second frontend harder.

This does not weaken AD-6. The backend parsing its OWN protocol on its OWN socket is not sniffing the pty; AD-1 amendment already permits typed facts crossing the control plane.

Corpus seeds: captured omp bytes, the full hostile cycle, sequences split across chunks, interleaved valid-looking private messages, malformed lengths, a valid fence with no lifecycle event, old-domain events, duplicate/decreasing/gapped sequences, OSC embedded in filenames and log lines. A fuzz target CI never runs past compilation is worth less than deterministic seeds that always run.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: Assertions: raw channel framing and domain authentication happen in Go, adjacent to the transports; NO capability and NO raw lifecycle frame ever crosses the control plane; only schema-checked published facts cross, with their contract in contracts/ and an OverTheWire conformance test; the frontend reducer validates legal application transitions and can construct no authority of its own; the raw frame parser is fuzzed with a committed corpus that runs in ordinary CI; the protocol machine is model-tested.
close_reason: landed in 3a1674a; the generated renderer type waits for its consumer in .6

title: Remote transport, on the TunnelConn seam that already exists
description:
Do NOT build a transport. internal/ssh/ssh_tunnel.go:23 already defines TunnelConn: Listen(addr) does the remote -R over the pooled connection AD-5 multiplexes, Done()/LostErr() are a declared connection-loss contract, and its doc comment already classifies server refusal (AllowTcpForwarding off, bind outside PermitListen) as a refusal rather than a dial failure, and records that a hostname bind is resolved by the server and cannot be verified locally.

The remote hook connects with bash network redirection: exec {fd}<>/dev/tcp/127.0.0.1/<port>. Verified working end to end. Port and capability are substituted into the script text.

Refusal is detectable synchronously but NOT distinguishable — do not promise a diagnostic that names AllowTcpForwarding.

Scope: bash first. zsh needs zmodload zsh/net/tcp and is its own adapter. POSIX sh, fish, PowerShell get nothing here and that is the accepted loss in the epic.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: An ssh session to a bash host reaches an accepted domain with nothing installed on the remote host. Assertions: the bind is the literal 127.0.0.1 and never a hostname; a host with AllowTcpForwarding no falls back to a conventional terminal with a visible prompt and no error dialog; an unauthenticated connection to the forwarded port can neither revoke nor preempt the live domain; TunnelConn.Done firing revokes the domain and abandons the open attempt as unknown.
notes: Now an ADAPTER over the protocol kernel, not a transport design. Registers one lane, may carry several domains on it, exposes envelopes and loss notifications, and never exposes currentDomain(). Add to acceptance: candidate-connection limits and rate limiting on the forwarded port, since any local user on the remote host can open it.
close_reason: landed in bd32495: remote transport on the existing TunnelConn seam, bash only, no live-sshd run

title: Shell adapter and bootstrap security
description:
Transport-independent on purpose: capability exposure is identical on the local and the remote path, so it is not decided inside either adapter. The local mktemp script (inband.go:113) is the hard case — 0600 plus unlink does NOT protect it from the same user, because sourcing runs the whole file before the unlink.

The shell adapters translate hooks into protocol messages. They do not know about transports, ports or descriptors beyond the handle they are given.

If the capability genuinely cannot be kept out of a named file, say so in the bead and amend ADR-0024 decision 10 rather than letting the mode bits flatter the boundary.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: Assertions: the per-epoch capability appears in NO environment — checked against env AND /proc/<pid>/environ of the shell AND of a child; a child writing a well-formed event without the capability produces no accepted event; HELLO/ACCEPT completes before any prompt suppression; bash and zsh adapters each reach an accepted domain; the capability is kept out of every named file, or the ADR boundary is amended to exclude same-user bootstrap inspection and the amendment is committed in the same change.
close_reason: landed in 6cba76f: bash/zsh hooks on the authenticated channel, capability out of env and out of every named file

title: Sever every stream-derived authority edge
description:
The owner merges only finished functionality, so this can go early — but it is HALF of the old demolition child, and the halves are different acts. Severing an authority edge only ever removes power from bytes. Replacing the environment machinery is migration of a working feature and must wait for its authenticated successor; that is nocx-u7uh.11.

Deliberately unavailable from here until migration lands: DOM editor ownership, marker-only suppression, authoritative blocks, ledger and history recording, lifecycle-derived exit status, authenticated environment activation, integration-sensitive typed-ssh rewriting, rerun authority. Acceptable ONLY because nothing merges until the epic is whole.

Note OSC 636 passports are also pty bytes. Parsing may remain as inert observation during migration, but it cannot activate, suspend or restore a domain from here on.

Blocked by the guards child on purpose: delete the old source only once the single legitimate source exists as an interface, or the deletion gets replaced by another ad hoc one mid-build.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: No byte sequence reaches authority. Assertions: OSC 133 A/B/C/D, tagged variants, OSC 636 passports and private OSC/DCS lookalikes cannot mutate lifecycle state, domain state, attempts, keyboard routing, blocks, history, rewriting or rerun authority; OSC 133 A/B affect ONLY renderer-owned prompt partitioning and OSC 7 only its existing validated location projections; every session is visibly conventional (native input, visible prompt, one continuous grid, no blocks, no ledger); raw local and ssh interaction including nested ssh/sudo/su/docker stays usable as a plain terminal; the environment, location, title and completion projections survive behind named interfaces, neither deleted nor duplicated; no dormant compatibility path remains — disconnected reducers and anonymous entry points are deleted; gates green.
close_reason: landed in 6cba76f: every stream-derived authority edge cut, adversarial corpus armed

title: The protocol kernel: domains, lanes, attempts, transitions
acceptance_criteria: A protocol document plus a PURE MODEL test that runs this scenario before any transport exists: establish transport T; authenticate domain A on lane L; start and complete attempt A1; suspend A and authenticate child domain B over the SAME transport; reject an A completion while B is active; start and complete B1; close B; restore A only through authenticated activation; reject stale B events; disconnect T and lose every domain bound to it; reconnect through a new transport and require fresh epochs; run the same model with two lanes multiplexed through one fake relay-like transport. If the protocol cannot express this, STOP — do not let a transport implementation choose the domain model by accident.
close_reason: landed and verified by the coordinator

title: A program's output can no longer drive your terminal
description:
## What a user can do that they could not before

Run a program that prints prompt markers — `omp`, any agent TUI, `cat` of a file
full of escape sequences, a remote host's MOTD — and have it stay visible, keep
the keyboard, and be unable to summon nocx's editor, forge a block's exit code,
or write a record into the command history.

Today all of that is reachable from bytes. `omp` printing its own
`ESC]133;B` + `ESC]133;A` makes the live region collapse to zero height while the
program still runs and still takes keys, and the sequence `B, A, B` from any
source reaches `owned: true`, which shows nocx's own editor while a foreign
program is the foreground process reading stdin.

## The decision this implements

[ADR-0024](../docs/decisions/0024-authenticated-shell-integration-channel.md) —
the lifecycle leaves the byte stream. PTY output is render-only; the shell
reports its lifecycle over a transport that is not the terminal, authenticated
per epoch; the lifecycle becomes attempt-based; ownership becomes a state that
can only be given rather than a flag that can be laundered.

It supersedes ADR-0004 §1, ADR-0006 §4 and the lifecycle half of AD-5, and
amends AD-1 and AD-6. Read it before touching any child.

## Deliberately out

- **Tier B and the relay.** POSIX `sh` remotes, hosts with `AllowTcpForwarding
  no`, and `docker exec` shells lose enhanced input and become conventional
  terminals. That is a named, accepted loss, not a defect to route around with an
  in-band tier. `su`/`sudo` keep blocks — same machine, inherited descriptor, new
  capability through the existing environment machinery.
- **The wire format.** Bearer field versus MAC, framing details, descriptor
  numbers: the ADR fixes the property, not the mechanism.
- **Persistence policy for shell-originated command text.** A separate decision;
  authentication does not make a hand-typed password safe to store.

## Success Criteria

See `--acceptance`. The check is written FIRST and stays red until the last
child lands; the owner has said intermediate results do not matter, so children
are sequenced for correctness rather than for shippable increments.
acceptance_criteria:
FOUR criteria, and the first alone is deliberately insufficient — a terminal with enhanced mode deleted would satisfy it.
(1) HOSTILE: a devharness fixture writes omp's captured bytes (ESC]133;B BEL ESC]133;A BEL) mid-command, and the full hostile cycle (C, D;0, A, B, B) plus OSC 636 passports and private-OSC lookalikes. Nothing moves: lifecycle state, active domain, keyboard route, attempt state, block state, history calls, environment stack, rewrite and rerun authority are byte-identical before and after.
(2) POSITIVE: in an authenticated session the user submits a command; the authenticated Start attaches to the app attempt; ALL output stays visible; Complete plus fence freezes the complete block; the exit status persists exactly once; PromptReady returns the editor; the next submitted command reaches the shell.
(3) CONVENTIONAL: a session with no transport is visibly plain — native input, visible prompt, one continuous grid, no blocks, no ledger, no history, no integration-sensitive rewriting.
(4) NESTED: sudo/su/ssh inside a session each get their own authenticated domain; an attempt cannot complete across domains; closing the child restores the parent only through an authenticated activation, and stale child events after restoration are rejected.
close_reason: A program's output can no longer drive your terminal. All four criteria have automated checks: HOSTILE (stream-adversary conformance with ASSERT_AUTHORITY, every sensitive projection byte-identical), POSITIVE (the whole cycle through the real seam, exit status persisted exactly once), CONVENTIONAL (fail-open and no-transport tests), NESTED (bash and zsh sudo/su child domains on a real pty, ssh as a live assembly against a real sshd, plus the renderer half). Lifecycle authority left the byte stream: authenticated channel per epoch, ACCEPT downstream of an acknowledged publication, ownership given rather than laundered, passport machinery deleted. docker exec is conventional-only by owner decision. Six real product defects were found by the fault-injection and assembly proofs that no green test had seen.

title: The ADR, and the real-socket suite that pins each invariant at both ends
description:
The ADR in docs/decisions/. It exists because the control plane has always had
an implicit FIFO and this epic removes it; a guarantee that disappears without a
document is one the next person reinstates by accident.

It must state: the scope (control-plane execution only, AD-1 framing and AD-6
byte ownership untouched); the readLoop invariant with both ends; the closed
ingress-critical set and the most work a member may do; the resolver invariant
(a resolution reaches its waiter before any potentially blocking write); the two
lanes and why native user-waits are isolated; the three bounds; the saturation
schema, retry semantics and mandatory renderer visibility; that there is NO
response-completion FIFO; the conflict and atomicity guarantee including
cross-connection operations; the explicit rejection of namespace FIFO and why;
the three context owners; disconnect behaviour for queued, running and dialog
work; that two connections have no transport ordering relationship but do share
domain conflict enforcement; that outbound serialization is bounded separately
from admission; the observability set; the migration rule for nocx-yscw; and the
shutdown invariant.

Also that late resolver replies get "unknown request id" and cannot affect a
later ask — asks broadcast to every connection (unlock_requester.go:87) and
first-consumer-wins is deliberate, but it is written nowhere.

## The trap in the acceptance test

The epic's own claim is that the renderer never depends on ordering. If the
acceptance test sends a mutation and a read together, it canonises FIFO by
accident and proves nothing. It must await the mutation response before sending
the read.

And because a static audit of the renderer can be incomplete — there is no
`no-floating-promises` rule in frontend/eslint.config.js holding it — one test
forces the failure directly: send mutation A, send conflicting mutation B
without awaiting A, hold A at an injected dependency, let B reach the
coordinator, release A, and assert the documented outcome. Serialized arrival
order or an explicit conflict rejection — never accidental last-finisher-wins.
That is the regression test for the audit being wrong.
acceptance_criteria: The ADR is committed in docs/decisions/ and states every item in the description. Enforcement, not prose: an external-package fixture proves a handler cannot obtain wsConn or a domain service it was not given, and a lint rule forbids 'go' statements in control-handler packages (Go cannot remove the keyword, so this is the available structural check and it runs in the gate). A mutation awaited then read observes the mutation, the two never sent together. Reverse-completion of two conflicting mutations gives the documented result, not last-finisher-wins. With every ordinary and native-dialog permit occupied AND the outbound writer blocked, a resolver still signals its waiter. Shutdown closes admission first and returns only once admitted work cancelled or restored its invariant, including against a non-cooperative fake.
close_reason: Landed as ddbf69a3. ADR-0024 with all 17 items grounded in the code, plus three enforcement pieces because prose is not a gate: an external-package boundary proof, a baselined ratchet forbidding new 'go' statements in control-handler packages, and a NonblockingAdmission type distinction that makes wiring a waiting admission into a submission a COMPILE error. Worker reported one brief-vs-code discrepancy rather than transcribing it: the four observability signals are uninstrumented; the ADR states the gap and it is filed as a follow-up.

title: resize and close are per-session serialized work: the renderer never awaits them and resize blocks on a dead SSH link
description:
Found while checking the epic's ordering claim, and it is the counterexample to
it.

`resize` and `close` are the only control methods the renderer sends without
awaiting — `ipc.ts:467-484`, both explicit `void ... .catch(() => {})`. (The one
true notification is `ack`, ipc.ts:360.) So `resize` carries a last-write-wins
semantics that only holds if the two calls are applied in order: drag a window,
release it, and an out-of-order pair leaves the PTY at the wrong size for good.

And `resize` is not safely inline either: `handleResize` calls
`sess.Resize(context.Background(), ...)` (ws.go:1509), which for SSH is a
`window-change` channel request over the network. On a dead link it blocks —
precisely the `deadChannel` the data plane already pins in
ws_input_stall_test.go.

Ordering-sensitive AND blocking, so neither inline nor the shared lane is
correct. Both are `session:<id>` conflict work: serialized per session, parallel
across sessions, off the readLoop.

`close` racing `resize` on the same session is the same edge from the other
side — `state.has` (ws.go:764) guards the map lookup, not the interval from
check to use.
acceptance_criteria: A resize on a session whose SSH channel is dead does not delay input to another session, and does not delay that session's own close — the close preempts it and completes. Rapid resizes coalesce to the last dimensions, asserted at the PTY rather than at the response. After close admission begins, a later resize for that session cannot reach it.
notes:
2026-08-08, round 2 — a defect in my own proposal. Strict per-session FIFO recreates head-of-line blocking inside the tab: if a dead resize owns the session lane and close queues behind it, the one operation that could tear down the dead channel cannot run.

Required semantics: resizes for one session are coalesced to the latest dimensions (preferred) or ordered; close is TERMINAL — it cancels queued and in-flight resize work and preempts further session operations; after close admission begins no later resize may reach the session; and close may never wait behind anything that needs the session closed to unblock.
close_reason: Landed as 28f789f. Per-session resize lane with latest-wins coalescing, off the read loop on a cancellable per-session context (context.Background at the sess.Resize call site is gone). close is terminal: it admits the gate, drops the pending resize, cancels the lane context and never waits for the worker, so it cannot queue behind the dead resize it exists to cancel — the head-of-line trap review caught before it was built. Five tests over the real socket, four red on the old code, dimensions asserted at the PTY rather than at a response the renderer never reads.

title: Context ownership: request-scoped work takes the connection context, session-owned lifetimes keep theirs and say why
description:
There are 59 `context.Background()` calls in non-test `internal/transport` code.
Cancellation stops at the transport boundary. Today that is invisible because
the readLoop blocks anyway; once handlers detach, every one of them outlives its
connection.

The mechanical sweep is wrong and would break AD-9. `pumpToRing` (ws.go:1410)
uses Background deliberately so a session survives disconnect for replay. The
audit sorts every call into one of three owners and records the closing event
for each:

* **request-scoped** — the connection context from ws.go:942, which is already
  independent of the unreliable hijacked-request cancellation and ends when
  `handleSession` returns. Admission waits, probes, ssh-config resolution,
  file/git work, unlock/password waits.
* **server/session-owned** — outlives the connection on purpose. Keeps
  Background, gains a comment naming the owner and the closing event.
* **domain-owned commit interval** — child .2 owns it. No
  `context.WithoutCancel` in transport to paper over a broken transactional
  boundary.

`ws_probe.go:164` runs the 30s probe on Background and is request-scoped.

`dialog.openFile` on disconnect: cancel and dismiss the OS dialog where the
native API allows it. Where it does not, the result is discarded, no response is
sent to the dead socket, and the native capability stays marked busy until the
adapter actually returns — otherwise a reconnect opens a second dialog over the
first. The limitation belongs in the platform adapter contract, tested with a
cancel-aware fake.
acceptance_criteria: Disconnect cancels a running connections.test probe and frees its admission slot for the next connection. A session opened before a disconnect still replays on reattach (AD-9 unbroken). Every remaining context.Background() in non-test transport code carries a comment naming its owner and closing event. Disconnect during a dialog sends no response to the dead socket and leaves the native capability busy until the adapter returns.
notes: 2026-08-08, round 2: context propagation does not make a dependency cancellable if the implementation ignores context. Safety comes from the operation occupying a bounded resource, not from the ctx. Shutdown tests must use non-cooperative fakes, and shutdown needs a documented maximum wait plus a forced-abandonment policy outside commit intervals.
close_reason:
Landed as 89c4e3d. 61 non-test context.Background sites audited: 52 moved to the connection context, 9 retained as server/session/domain-owned with a comment naming owner and closing event, enforced by a structural test that fails on an uncommented survivor. AD-9 protected by a test that a session opened before a disconnect still replays on reattach — the check that catches a mechanical sweep.

connections.test and dialog.openFile had to move off the read loop for any of it to be observable (nothing to cancel concurrently while a 30s probe runs inline). Both go through the control seam under capacity-1 admissions. Dialog limitation is honest: where the native API cannot dismiss, the result is discarded, no response reaches the dead socket, and the capability stays busy until the adapter returns so a reconnect cannot open a second dialog over the first — tested with cancel-aware AND non-cooperative fakes. Stop cancels, waits a documented 5s, then abandons; tested against a prober that ignores cancellation.

Side effect worth tracking: 10 baseline entries became reachable (semaphore, bounded submission, saturationErrorFor). Outstanding against the 104 target: composite.*, ImmediateSubmission.TrySubmit, saturatedNotificationParamsFor, and the 139 capability entries.

title: handleControlFrame makes one unconditional submission call, with no ingress fork
description:
Where the epic's user-visible change actually happens: `handleControlFrame`
(ws.go:995) stops calling handlers and starts admitting work.

The readLoop invariant, with both ends: from before `ReadMessage` returns until
the next `ReadMessage` begins, control handling performs only bounded parse,
validation, ingress-critical resolution, and a non-blocking admission attempt.

The ingress-critical set is closed and validated at construction, because a
handler that wrongly claims it recreates this bug: binary-frame routing, `ack`
while it stays bounded bookkeeping, `vault.unlockResolved`,
`connections.passwordResolved`. Nothing else. `open` already documents the
deadlock that forces this (ws.go:1029-1039) — a resolver that queued behind a
saturated pool could never arrive, because the loop that would read it is the
loop waiting.

Everything else is admitted. Rejected admission answers immediately; it never
waits.
acceptance_criteria: Over the real socket: a keystroke reaches a live session while connections.test is blocked mid-probe on another session of the same connection, and again while dialog.openFile is outstanding. While the ordinary lane is saturated, vault.unlockResolved still completes its pending unlock and the blocked originating RPC resumes; same for connections.passwordResolved. Responses may complete out of request order and still correlate to the right promises.
notes:
See the collision note on nocx-sfv6.3. If nocx-98rn lands first, this bead wires admission into an existing registry rather than into the 86-case switch, and the diff here shrinks accordingly. If it lands second, 98rn constrains the record this bead introduces. Either way the switch is replaced exactly once.
HARD OBLIGATION carried from nocx-sfv6.3 (936d319): twelve internal/transport/control entries were added BY HAND to .githooks/deadcode-baseline.json, because the contract has no consumer until this bead wires it and the baseline updater refuses growth on purpose. Removing all twelve is an acceptance criterion of THIS bead — nocx-sfv6 cannot close while they remain. The repo shipped an unreachable ContentDB behind a green gate once (nocx-rtg0); this is the tripwire so it cannot be quiet a second time.
SECOND OBLIGATION carried in: the over-the-wire conformance test for the saturation error (…_OverTheWireConformsToContract) belongs to THIS bead. nocx-sfv6.8 builds the schema, the generated renderer types, the Go DTO and the central renderer mapping, but a real saturation off a real socket needs the executor wired into handleControlFrame, which is this bead. The repo's wire rule is explicit that validating a payload the test itself built proves the struct is well-formed, not that the server sends it — so .8 was told NOT to fake it, and the missing third check is deliberate, not an oversight.
close_reason: Landed as 168061ca. One unconditional registration.Submission.TrySubmit, no branch on method names; ingress-critical is a wired ImmediateSubmission validated at construction. All four obligations closed: deadcode 95, dead-exports notification entry gone, real over-the-wire contract test, rate limiter. Rejected on the first pass: the permit outlived the response, so a sequential client hit a still-held capacity-1 gate and was told 'Control plane busy'. Fixed by scoping refusal to execution saturation and making domain conflicts wait, bounded.

title: The executor contract: internal/transport/control, injected admission and one submission path, never a method name
description:
The scheduling contract, in `internal/transport/control`. It lives under
transport because architecture.md:85 assigns control-plane backpressure to
transport; it holds no WebSocket types, so it stays testable without a socket.

The executor schedules declared work and never learns a method name. That is
AD-8 read literally: alternative scheduling behaviour is a different `Executor`
injected at the composition root, never a mode field or a type test. It is also
what lets nocx-yscw's exact-name registry consume this without rework — the
registry supplies handler, lane and conflict declaration; the executor
dispatches none of it.

    type Lane string
    const (
        LaneWork     Lane = "work"
        LaneUserWait Lane = "user-wait"
    )

    type Access uint8
    const (
        Read Access = iota
        Write
    )

    type Conflict struct {
        Domain string
        Key    string // empty means the whole domain
        Access Access
    }

    type Work struct {
        Lane      Lane
        Conflicts []Conflict
        Run       func(context.Context)
    }

    type Rejection struct {
        Reason     string
        Scope      string
        RetryAfter time.Duration
    }

    type Executor interface {
        TrySubmit(ctx context.Context, work Work) *Rejection
    }

`TrySubmit` is non-blocking by contract: the readLoop must never wait for
capacity. A goroutine per admitted request is fine once admission tokens bound
the live count — the bound is on admitted operations, not on goroutine creation.

Two lanes, not three. Pure-CPU and bounded-IO both draw on one finite budget and
splitting them needs a measurement nobody has taken. `dialog.openFile`
(ws.go:1104) is different in kind: it holds capacity while waiting for a person,
possibly forever, so it gets its own lane at capacity 1 per native capability.

Three separate bounds, because each fails differently: ordinary process-wide
active work, ordinary per-connection active-plus-queued, and per-capability
user-wait. A process-wide bound alone lets one renderer take every slot; a
per-connection bound alone lets many connections exhaust the process. The
numbers are composition-root defaults, not architecture. Queues stay tight —
a long queue converts overload into stale mutations whose user intent has moved
on.

The constructor rejects duplicate registrations and invalid combinations such as
ingress-critical paired with the user-wait lane.
acceptance_criteria: No Lane enum and no ingress enum anywhere: admission is an injected resource (Admission.TryAcquire returning a Permit or a Rejection) and dispatch is one unconditional registration.Submission.TrySubmit call. A third admission resource is added by wiring, with no edit inside the executor — asserted by a test that injects one. Conflict admission is acquired BEFORE a scarce execution permit, or waiting conflict work sits in a separately bounded queue: a test fills every ordinary worker with conflicting requests and proves unrelated work still runs. The package exposes Responder and the ingress AskResolver capability and imports no websocket type.
notes: COLLISION, must be resolved before this is built. Three beads now describe one registration record for transport dispatch: nocx-98rn (P0 epic — a registry whose registration signature requires a params type implementing Validate() error, so an unvalidated method fails to COMPILE; replaces the validation switch at ws.go:609-670), nocx-yscw (registry keyed on exact method names, replacing the 86-case dispatch switch), and this bead (registration supplying handler + lane + conflict declaration). That is one concept with three owners, which AGENTS.md names as the defect regardless of which wins by evaluation order. There must be ONE Registration record: Name, params type with Validate() error, Ingress disposition, Lane, Conflicts, Handler. Whichever bead lands first defines it; the others extend it by adding fields, never by declaring a second registry. The executor still never learns a method name — that stays true whichever way the sequencing goes.
close_reason:
Landed as 936d319. Contract only — internal/transport/control with injected Admission/Permit, Submission with ImmediateSubmission and a bounded admission-backed implementation, and NewComposite fixing conflict-before-execution acquire order. No Lane enum and no mode field: the AD-8 proof is a third Admission defined in the test file and consumed unchanged. 11 tests green under -race, full pre-commit gate green including the container go test -race and vitest.

Coordinator review found and fixed one real defect the worker's own tests missed: Permit.Release was not idempotent, so a double release took a token belonging to another holder and a semaphore of 2 admitted 3. Proven with a failing test first, then fixed with sync.Once on both permit types, and the Permit interface now states idempotence as part of the contract for implementations supplied from outside. The release-on-panic test was also rewritten — it spawned a helper subprocess and read back a marker file, which cost three gosec suppressions; calling the runner directly from an internal test and recovering there proves the same interval.

title: Typed domain operations that own access and exclusion together; handlers stop being methods on WSServer
description:
"The stores are mutex-guarded, so this is not a data race" is true and beside
the point. A mutex protects memory, not an invariant spanning two lock
acquisitions or two stores.

Concurrent execution is permitted only where declared conflict sets do not
overlap. Grain is a property of the declaration, not of the mechanism: an empty
`Conflict.Key` means the whole domain, so a method whose conflict set is not yet
confidently known declares its domain wholesale and is serialized. That is how
this ships correct on day one and gets refined later without touching the
coordinator.

Initial domains: `config` (profiles + groups + settings + configuration import),
`vault-lifecycle` (setup, reset, seal/unseal, provider change),
`vault-secret:<id>`, `session:<id>`, `git-binding:<id>`,
`filesystem-binding:<id>`.

Reads need a policy too — "reads run freely" is not automatically safe. A read
overlapping a conflicting mutation either participates in the read/write guard
or comes from a store giving a coherent versioned snapshot. Say which, per
domain.

Named hazards to cover, each of which survives mutex guarding:

* `groups.apply` is atomic only inside the group store (ws_groups.go:518); a
  profile update can add or remove a group reference after group validation.
* Vault rename/delete/replace racing inventory or profile-binding work, so
  validation passes against a secret that is gone before persistence.
* Read-modify-write handlers each individually locked but losing updates when
  the lock is released between load and save.
* Notifications ordered differently from commits — `vault.setup` broadcasts
  `vaultChanged` before writing its own response (ws_vault.go:260).
* `close` removing a session while `resize` or a git/file binding has already
  passed `state.has`: connState guards its map (ws.go:764), not the whole
  check-use interval.
acceptance_criteria: Every handler is constructed with exactly the typed domain operations it needs and cannot obtain a store nobody gave it — proved from an external test package, not by inspection. No handler is a method on *WSServer. A domain service does not escape its operation callback. Operations acquire all permits in one canonical order, and a test drives two operations whose resource sets overlap in opposite request orders without deadlock. Conflicting mutations from ONE socket and from TWO sockets get identical protection; non-conflicting long operations genuinely overlap.
notes:
2026-08-08, round 2 — MECHANISM CHANGED. 'Conflicts []Conflict' as registration data is rejected, and the objection that killed it is that a declaration is a claim nothing verifies: a handler declaring 'config' can still reach ambient s.vaultLifecycle. WSServer is a service locator, and vault inventory already reaches profiles, groups and lifecycle directly (ws_vault.go:448-467).

My proposed fix — a claim vending stores, claim.Config() / claim.Secret(id) — was refuted on six counts, all correct: it is a runtime lookup not a compile-time guarantee; a nil-handle panic is not enforcement; incremental capability acquisition lets handlers deadlock by ordering; a store handle can escape the claim closure and outlive the permit; raw stores still permit non-atomic multi-step work; and a generic claim is a smaller service locator with the same smell.

Adopted instead: typed, scoped domain-operation capabilities that own access and exclusion together — ConfigOperation, VaultLifecycleOperation, RestoreOperation, each Run(ctx, func(ctx, Service) error). The service lives inside the callback so it cannot safely escape; the implementation acquires every permit it needs in one canonical order. Dynamically keyed domains stay typed via SessionOperations.ForSession(id) / SecretOperations.ForSecret(id), which return an error for an unknown id and never nil. A handler is constructed with exactly the operation it needs and cannot reach a store nobody gave it.

So this bead is now: construct the typed operation capabilities and migrate handlers off ambient WSServer. Conservative domain-wide locking lives INSIDE the initial operation implementations, which is where the grain can later be refined without touching a handler.
close_reason:
Landed as 168061ca. One unconditional registration.Submission.TrySubmit with no branch on method names; ingress-critical is a wired ImmediateSubmission, not an if, and the set is closed and validated at construction. 100 methods on typed capabilities; the only three WSServer methods left are the HTTP upgrade, the control-frame dispatcher and the binary router. All four obligations closed: deadcode baseline 95, dead-exports notification entry gone, real over-the-wire contract test, rate limiter with unit and wire tests. Eight acceptance tests over the real socket, including both headline ones.

REJECTED ON THE FIRST PASS, and the reason matters. The containerised gate failed a different set of ordinary single-client tests each run with -32004 scope config. Cause read from the code: runAndRelease releases its permit in a defer AFTER task.Run, while the handler enqueues its response INSIDE task.Run — so the response reaches the client, and the client's next request arrives, while the permit is still held. With capacity-1 gates refusing instantly, a perfectly sequential client was told the control plane was busy. Microseconds on a fast host, wide open under container load; a green host run was not evidence against it.

Fix restores what the design review asked for and the first implementation lost: refusal is for EXECUTION saturation (the ordinary lane, which the read loop calls and which must never wait), while a DOMAIN CONFLICT is a serialisation point — a queue of length two — so its gate waits, bounded by both a wait timeout and a queue depth. The waiting admission is reachable only through capability.Gate, always inside the task goroutine.

title: Close the cross-store commit boundary: export.import and vault.setup own their atomicity before anything runs concurrently
description:
This exists today, before any concurrency, and it is why it comes first:
`export.importPortable` commits configuration at ws_export.go:200 and then
restores private content at ws_export.go:205. A failure between the two leaves
profiles/groups/settings at the new generation and content at the old one. Two
concurrent `vault.setup` calls can both observe "uninitialized", both mint key
material, and race to publish metadata (ws_vault.go:241, ws_vault.go:253).

Detaching handlers multiplies both. A race laid over a leaky commit cannot be
tested to a conclusion, so the commit boundary is closed before the executor
lands.

The rule the domain owns, not the transport: cancellation is accepted before the
operation crosses its commit point; once commit starts the domain service owns
completion or rollback and returns only after its invariant is restored. The
transport must not be the thing deciding which half of an import is safe to
abandon.

Also here, because it is the same interface being touched: the runtime type
assertion on `ApplyGroups` (ws_groups.go:552) is an AD-8 violation — variation
belongs in the interface, not a type test inside an implementation.
acceptance_criteria: A failure injected between the config commit and the content restore leaves all stores at one generation, never split — asserted on disk, not in a log. Two concurrent vault.setup calls yield exactly one initialized vault, a deterministic loser, and no orphan key or metadata. ApplyGroups is reached through the interface, with no type assertion.
notes:
2026-08-08, round 2: the deliverable is a domain-level RestoreOperation that OWNS the profiles/groups/settings/content transaction, not locks placed around the transport handlers. A handler must not receive four raw stores and be trusted to sequence them. Same for vault setup: the lifecycle owns initialisation, so 'both saw uninitialized' is not expressible rather than merely serialized.
SCOPE EXPANDED 2026-08-08, worker question answered (option A). The acceptance criteria could not be met inside internal/export + internal/vault, because the stores lack the primitives: ProfileService offers only SaveProfile, SaveGroup, AtomicImport (a MERGE, no wholesale replace) and ClearReviewFlag — no snapshot, no delete — and ContentDB restores row-by-row on autocommit with no bulk transaction. Verified against internal/profile/service.go:53-240 before answering.

Two additive primitives are therefore in scope: ProfileService.Snapshot() / AtomicReplace() in internal/profile, and ContentDB.RestorePrivate(ctx, convs, history) as ONE sqlite transaction in internal/content. AtomicImport keeps its merge semantics and signature untouched — other callers depend on it. The restore operation itself stays in internal/export, and the transport call sites stay a few lines.

The alternative offered was config-rollback-only with the content-partial limitation written into a comment. Refused: that ships the split-generation defect this bead exists to close and records it in prose, which is the 'soft degrade visible only in a log' pattern AGENTS.md forbids.

Open risk carried forward: the worker reports conversations are stubbed in ContentDB. If any part of the restore remains non-atomic after the primitives land, the worker must name it in worker_done rather than round up to full atomicity — and it becomes a follow-up bead here, not a comment.
close_reason:
Landed as a4e134d. RestoreImport in internal/export owns the whole profiles+groups+settings+content transaction; the transport hands over a payload and gets one outcome. Commit point named (the profiles+groups file write in AtomicImport), interval documented with both ends, closing event is the error return. Two additive primitives: ProfileService.Snapshot/AtomicReplace and ContentDB.RestorePrivate as one sqlite transaction; AtomicImport's merge semantics untouched.

The brief's vault.setup claim was WRONG and the worker said so: Setup already takes the document lock and marks itself initializing, so a concurrent call fails before minting. It was documented rather than re-engineered, including the real limit (in-memory, per-instance; two Vault instances over one store are out of scope). vault.changed moved after the setup response.

Coordinator review added one fix: the rollback re-applied settings only when the captured snapshot was non-empty while the import applied them whenever the export carried any, so on a fresh machine — which is what restoring a backup onto a new install looks like — settings would have been applied and left standing while profiles rolled back. Now decided by what was applied. Regression test proven red first.

title: Exclusive outbound authority: only the pump touches the socket, enforced by a package boundary
description:
`wconn.writeJSON` takes `wsConn.mu` and holds it for up to `wsWriteDeadline`
= 10s (internal/transport/ws.go:744-755). The comment above the constant already
records why: without the deadline a stuck renderer made WriteMessage block
forever while holding the mutex, and any control response then stalled the
readLoop (nocx-o2le). The deadline bounded it at ten seconds; it did not remove
it.

So a resolver handler that answers inline is not non-blocking, and the whole
ingress-critical class the epic depends on is unachievable until the response
write stops being synchronous.

Two things change:

* A bounded per-connection outbound queue owns every control-plane write. One
  writer goroutine drains it; `wsConn.mu` stops being contended by handlers.
  The bound is separate from executor admission — a blocked socket and a
  saturated worker pool are different failures and must be countable
  separately.
* `handleUnlockResolved` (unlock_requester.go:167) and `handlePasswordResolved`
  (password_requester.go:89) end their critical interval when the waiter is
  signalled, not when the acknowledgement is written. `pendingAsk.ch` is already
  buffered with capacity 1 (unlock_requester.go:47), so the send can be
  non-blocking.

The interval to state, both ends: from the moment a valid resolution is parsed
until the waiting `RequestUnlock`/`RequestConnectionPassword` observes it, no
lock held by a socket write is acquired.
acceptance_criteria: A test holds the outbound writer blocked and proves vault.unlockResolved still releases its waiter. The queue's bound is reached in a test and the overflow policy is asserted, not inferred. No handler calls writeJSON directly.
notes:
2026-08-08, measured: 506 direct writeJSON/writeMessage call sites in non-test internal/transport code. Every one of them is a place where a handler can block on the socket for up to wsWriteDeadline (10s). This is why the outbound queue is a type-level change, not a convention: the count is the argument that discipline will not hold it.

Second instance of the same class, found alongside: broadcastAsk (unlock_requester.go:108-110) writes to every connection SERIALLY in a loop, each write bounded only by the 10s deadline — so an ask to N connections can take N*10s, inside RequestUnlock, which handlers call. Two more loops of the same shape: ws_vault.go:881 and ws.go:3121. Once writes are enqueued rather than performed, all three become N bounded enqueues and the failure disappears rather than being documented.
2026-08-08, round 2 — scope widens from 'a bounded queue' to EXCLUSIVE OUTBOUND AUTHORITY, and the enforcement is a package boundary, not a naming convention. Unexporting writeJSON is not enough: anything in package transport can still reach wconn.conn.WriteMessage. Socket ownership and the outbound pump move into a narrower subpackage, and handler implementations live outside the package owning wsConn.

Handlers get only: TryResult / TryError / TryNotify, all non-blocking by contract. A Respond that may block is just writeJSON behind an interface.

Broadcasts go through the same capability, or a handler that cannot stall the read loop can still stall behind a slow renderer while broadcasting (unlock_requester.go:108, ws_vault.go:881, ws.go:3121). Same for synchronous notification callbacks: WithSettingsRegistry installs a notifier that calls broadcastSettingsChanged directly (ws.go:471), so a domain callback inherits socket congestion. Every notification enters the bounded outbound system.

Queues and pumps are PER CONNECTION, with a process-wide cap only as an extra bound — one global queue lets one renderer delay another.

Terminal policy when the outbound queue is full, because a queued 'busy' response cannot be delivered either: mark the connection outbound-stalled, try one reserved control-overload slot, and if even that fails, close the socket and let the renderer's existing reconnect surface make it visible.
close_reason:
Landed as 3df9242. internal/transport/outbound owns the socket; one pump per connection drains a bounded queue (256 frames, 32 MiB process budget); handlers hold a Responder that only enqueues. 513 direct write call sites -> 0. Broadcasts and the settings domain notifier enqueue, so an ask to N connections no longer costs N x the 10s deadline. Terminal policy: stalled -> reserved outbound.stalled slot -> close, with sessions surviving by AD-9.

Coordinator review found a nil-pointer panic the worker's green suite missed, and it is the interesting one: gitSessionClosed took its subscriber as the Responder INTERFACE, while both callers get it from rx.getSubscriber(), which returns a nil *wsConn when nobody is attached. A nil pointer in an interface is not equal to nil, so 'wconn == nil' kept looking correct while passing, and TryNotify dereferenced a nil receiver on a goroutine — a backend-killing panic that only fires when a subscriber happens to be absent. Parameter reverted to the concrete type so 'absent' stays expressible; regression test added.

Worker disclosed an ast-grep pattern that deleted 86 function bodies across 25 files mid-migration, recovered by splicing from HEAD. Independently verified by diffing the function-name set of every touched file against HEAD: the only four that disappear are the intended ones (writeJSON, writeMessage, and the filesChangedMessage/gitChangedMessage/newVaultError envelope helpers).

title: [epic] A long control method no longer freezes input: capability-restricted handlers behind injected admission
description:
Today `handleControlFrame` (internal/transport/ws.go:995) runs ~86 JSON-RPC
methods synchronously on the readLoop (ws.go:971) — the one goroutine that also
feeds every session's input on that WebSocket. `connections.test` (a 30s SSH
probe), `dialog.openFile` (waits on a person, unbounded), `sshConfig.aliases`
(`ssh -G`, 10s per pattern) and the vault methods on a cold keychain each freeze
every tab on the connection while they run.

The data plane was already fixed — per-session write queues, pinned by
`ws_input_stall_test.go`. This epic is the control plane.

## What a user can do that they could not before

Press Test on a host that never answers, or open a file dialog, and keep typing
in another tab. The keystroke reaches the PTY while the probe is still running.

## Design source

Grew out of the bug nocx-u687 after a design consultation (2026-08-08) that read
the code rather than the conversation. Two of the six decisions recorded on
nocx-u687 turned out to be wrong and one had to be narrowed; the corrections are
carried in the children, and the ADR (child .9) is where they land.

The headline corrections:

* "Ingress-critical runs inline and strictly non-blocking" is not achievable as
  written: resolvers answer through `wconn.writeJSON`, which holds `wsConn.mu`
  for up to `wsWriteDeadline` = 10s (ws.go:744-755). The comment above that
  constant already names this as the nocx-o2le freeze. The ingress-critical
  interval must END AT THE CHANNEL SIGNAL, not at the response write — which
  requires a bounded outbound queue that does not exist yet (child .1).
* "No ordering at all" is too broad. It says nothing about two connections
  (`s.conns` is a set), and the renderer-awaits-everything audit is not
  structurally held — there is no `no-floating-promises` rule in
  frontend/eslint.config.js. The contract becomes "no transport FIFO, plus
  declared domain conflict sets" (children .3, .4).
* `resize` and `close` are fire-and-forget from the renderer
  (frontend/src/ipc.ts:467-484) AND `handleResize` blocks on a dead SSH channel
  (`sess.Resize(context.Background(), ...)`, ws.go:1509) — the exact deadChannel
  scenario the data plane already pins. They are simultaneously
  ordering-sensitive and blocking, so neither inline nor a shared pool is right
  (child .6).
* The 59 `context.Background()` calls must NOT be replaced mechanically:
  `pumpToRing` (ws.go:1410) uses it deliberately so a session survives
  disconnect for AD-9 replay (child .7).
* `export.importPortable` commits config (ws_export.go:200) then restores
  private content (ws_export.go:205) — a cross-store partial commit that exists
  TODAY, before any concurrency. It is closed first (child .2), because
  concurrency on top of a leaky commit is a race we cannot test our way out of.

## Boundaries this crosses, and what they already decide

* **AD-1** — one WebSocket, binary data plane + JSON-RPC control plane. Nothing
  here moves bytes into JSON; the split is preserved verbatim.
* **AD-8** — interface-first + DI, variation via the interface, never a fork
  inside an implementation. This is why the executor schedules declared work and
  never learns a method name: alternative scheduling is a different `Executor`
  injected at the composition root, not a mode field. It is also why
  `ws_groups.go:552`'s runtime type assertion on `ApplyGroups` is in scope — it
  is the same violation in the code being touched.
* **AD-9** — replay ring outlives the connection. Session-owned contexts stay
  session-owned (child .7).
