* **AD-10** — backpressure lives in transport (architecture.md:85), which is why
  the executor lives in `internal/transport/control` and not in a neutral
  package.
* **nocx-yscw** (exact-name registry replacing the 86-case switch) consumes the
  executor contract this epic introduces. The contract is shaped so that bead
  needs no rework: the registry supplies handler + lane + conflict declaration,
  the executor dispatches none of it.

## Deliberately out

* Replacing the 86-case switch — that is nocx-yscw.
* Splitting ProfileClient — nocx-ncl6.
* Per-namespace FIFO — considered and rejected: invariants cross namespaces
  (`export.import` touches four stores, `open` crosses session/profile/vault/
  sshConfig), so a namespace FIFO is an attractive false guarantee.

## Success Criteria

One automated check over the real socket watches a keystroke reach a live
session while `connections.test` is blocked mid-probe on another session of the
same connection, and a second watches the same while `dialog.openFile` is
outstanding. Both fail today.
acceptance_criteria: Over the real socket: a keystroke reaches a live session while connections.test is blocked mid-probe on another session of the same connection; the same holds while dialog.openFile is outstanding. Saturation of the ordinary lane returns a structured retryable error that the renderer surfaces. Two concurrent vault.setup calls leave exactly one initialized vault. Disconnect after the export.import commit point leaves all stores at one generation, never split.
notes:
2026-08-08: overlaps nocx-98rn (P0, free) and nocx-yscw on internal/transport dispatch — same file, same registration record. Sequencing is undecided; see the collision note on nocx-sfv6.3. No blocks edge added yet because the direction is the owner's call.
2026-08-08, round 2 (codex thread 019fe07a, argued to agreement). Four objections put to the reviewer; the plan changed materially:

1. AGREED — the design must be structure, not an ADR. Handlers lose access to wsConn and to ambient services; capabilities are what they are constructed with. Qualification accepted: Go can make blocking CAPABILITIES unobtainable, it cannot prove a function does not block. So the type system carries what it can and the gate carries the rest.
2. CONCEDED BY REVIEWER — the Lane string enum was a mode field under another name and violates AD-8. Replaced by injected Admission/Permit resources; a new resource class is a wiring change with no edit inside the executor.
3. DIAGNOSIS AGREED, MY MECHANISM REFUTED — a declared conflict set is a claim nothing verifies, but a claim vending raw stores is a smaller service locator. Adopted: typed scoped domain operations that own access and exclusion together.
4. MY MECHANISM REFUTED — a reserved critical slot does not give deadlock freedom: one stuck resolver occupies it, and per-connection reservation does not match the ask topology, since askBroker.pending is a map and asks broadcast to every connection. Adopted instead: one unconditional submission path with an ImmediateSubmission implementation injected for capability-restricted resolvers. My structural goal (no 'if critical' fork in handleControlFrame) survives; the unsafe mechanism does not.

Plus a defect the reviewer found in MY finding: strict per-session FIFO recreates head-of-line blocking inside the tab, because close would queue behind the dead resize it needs to cancel (nocx-sfv6.6).

New child nocx-sfv6.10: ingress must decode the envelope only — the read loop currently unmarshals the whole JSON object before dispatch (ws.go:981, ws.go:995), which is this same class by a route no other child closes.
GATE BASELINE, taken 2026-08-08 12:02 local on shady2k/fix-events-processing at f1dbc1a, clean tree, BEFORE any worker change: go build ./... exit 0, go vet ./... exit 0. Anything red at the epic gate is ours. Wave 1 dispatched as Orca run run_1505b4b3ecef: worker A = nocx-sfv6.3 in worktree nocx/executor-contract, worker B = nocx-sfv6.2 in nocx/domain-atomicity, worker C = nocx-sfv6.10 in nocx/ingress-limits. File ownership is disjoint by measurement: .3 is a greenfield package, .2 lives in internal/export + internal/vault (both are real domain packages, which is what freed it from transport), .10 is the read side of ws.go. nocx-sfv6.1 is ready but deliberately held to wave 2 — it rewrites 506 write call sites across every ws_*.go and would collide with both B and C.
2026-08-08, WIRING REJECTED ON FIRST PASS — worth recording because a green host run hid it. The containerised gate failed a DIFFERENT set of ordinary tests on each run with -32004 'Control plane busy' and scope 'config': single-client, sequential tests that saturate nothing.

Mechanism, read from the code rather than guessed: control.runAndRelease releases the permit with a defer AFTER task.Run, and the handler enqueues its response inside task.Run. So the response reaches the client — and the client sends its next request — while the permit is still held. Domain gates are capacity 1 and refuse instantly, so the next request on a perfectly sequential connection can be refused. On a fast host the window is microseconds; under container load it opens.

This is user-visible: click Save, then immediately open the connection list, and get told the control plane is busy. A green host run is not evidence against it.

The fix restores something the design review said and the implementation lost: refusal is right for EXECUTION saturation (the lane is genuinely full) and wrong for a DOMAIN CONFLICT, which is a serialisation point — the work can proceed, it just goes second. Conflict gates wait, bounded; the ordinary lane keeps refusing instantly because the read loop calls it.
close_reason:
All ten children closed; ten commits on shady2k/fix-events-processing from 936d319 to ddbf69a3. Acceptance met and each criterion has a test: TestKeystrokeReachesLiveSessionWhileProbeBlocked and ...WhileDialogOutstanding over the real socket; saturation surfaces to the renderer with no call-site opt-in (dispatcher.test.ts); TestSetup_SerialisesConcurrentCalls; TestRestoreImport_FailureBetweenConfigAndContentLeavesAllStoresAtOneGeneration.

Every pre-commit gate green on every commit, including the containerised go test -race and vitest. Baseline obligation honoured as a number: deadcode is 95 and the new control-goroutine ratchet is at 13 baselined infrastructure spawns.

Not merged. The branch is ready for the owner to test.

title: A TUI that emits its own OSC 133 marks hides the running program's output
description:
Reported by the owner, 2026-08-08.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `omp` (opencode-go 17.1.2) in a tab with shell integration.
2. Type a message and press Enter.
3. The whole live region goes blank. The block header stays and its timer keeps
   ticking; nothing of omp is on screen, though keys still reach it.
4. Press Ctrl+C. omp exits and every line reappears at once as a frozen block.

## Root cause

Proven by capturing omp under a bare pty, with no shell in the picture: omp itself
writes `ESC]133;B BEL` and then `ESC]133;A BEL` into the stream, as part of the
repaint it does when it starts working on a message. nocx treats any OSC 133 marker
as authoritative (AD-6, ADR-0004):

  renderer.onCommandMarker -> inputState.dispatch({marker B}) -> RUNNING_RAW leaves
  for PROMPT_READY (untrusted) -> inputState.onChange else-branch ->
  scrollback.setIdle() -> `.live-idle { height: 0 }` -> the terminal is not on screen.

No D ever arrives, so the block goes on running; the shell's real D at exit freezes it
and the serializer replays the xterm buffer, which is why everything comes back at once.

Two defects behind one symptom:

1. Presentation: setIdle() collapses the live region while a block is still running. A
   prompt state nobody trusts must never take the running program's pane away.
2. Trust: local A/B markers carry no session tag, so any program can emit them. The
   reducer's own rule makes B,A,B enough to reach owned:true — nocx would show its
   editor and claim the keyboard while a TUI is the foreground process. Only the
   environment-entry path tags markers (nocx_env); the ordinary local ones do not.

Side effect: omp's marker latches `_shellIntegrated` on a session that has none.

## Acceptance Criteria

- With a running block, an untrusted A or B leaves the live region visible: the
  controller does not go to `idle` while `blockManager.runningBlock` is set.
- A reducer test: from RUNNING_RAW, the sequence B, A, B never reaches `owned: true`.
- An end-to-end check feeding the captured omp bytes (B then A mid-command) through
  the renderer seam asserts the live container still has a non-zero height.
notes: Superseded as the unit of work by epic nocx-u7uh, which implements ADR-0024 (now Accepted). This bead stays as the defect record and the reasoning trail; the epic's acceptance test replays the exact bytes captured here.

title: TestScheduler_SampleNowActsAsRetry waits for the exec, then asserts the state the exec has not written yet
description:
internal/discovery TestScheduler_SampleNowActsAsRetry fails intermittently:

    schedule_test.go:319: state after refusal = "pending",
                          want "permission-or-policy-refused"

Reproduced locally at roughly 1%: `go test ./internal/discovery/
-run TestScheduler_SampleNowActsAsRetry -count=300 -race` gave 3 failures.
Seen on CI in run 31245483032, where backend-linux (false) went red while
backend-linux (true) — the same tests — passed, and fail-fast then cancelled
the whole release dry run.

The gate is on the wrong fact. The test waits for `conn.execCount() == 1` and
then immediately reads `s.Status(...)`. execCount counts commands ISSUED to the
fake conn; the scheduler writes Sample.State only after it has processed the
refusal. Two writes, and the test waits for the first while asserting the
second, so it reads "pending" whenever the scheduler has not got there yet.

Same shape as nocx-axqs on the e2e side, found the same day: "the command was
issued" is not "the outcome was recorded", exactly as "the output block is
visible" was not "the prompt is back".

Only this one site has the pattern. The other waitFor calls in the file either
wait on Status directly (lines 341, 359, 381) or assert exec counts alone.

## Steps to Reproduce

    go test ./internal/discovery/ -run TestScheduler_SampleNowActsAsRetry -count=300 -race

## Acceptance Criteria

- The test waits for the state it asserts, so it cannot read a value that has
  not been written yet, and still fails with a clear message if the state never
  arrives.
- The "exactly one exec" assertion is kept, not dropped in the process.
- -count=1000 -race is green.
close_reason: Fixed on main (7547ad4): the test waits for Sample.State to reach the refused state instead of for execCount, and keeps the 'exactly one exec' assertion. Measured, not hoped: 3 failures in 300 runs before, then -count=1000 -race on the test and -count=20 -race on the package green. Both backend-linux variants green on ec3e2a7.

title: The dry run does not sign or verify the manifest, though the workflow says it does
description:
release.yml header says a manual run "is a dry run that builds, signs and
verifies everything and publishes nothing (section 5)". It does not sign, and it
does not verify. Every signing step — Generate manifest.json, Sign
manifest.json, and "Verify the signature against the keyring the release
ships" — lives in the publish job, which is gated
`if: needs.validate.outputs.release == "true"` and is therefore SKIPPED on
workflow_dispatch. Confirmed in dry runs 31219714125 and 31222427704: publish
reports "skipped" in both.

This is the same shape as the comment nocx-nfu5.1 removed — prose describing an
arrangement that was never built, read for months as though it had been.

It matters because of what the skipped step is FOR. nocx-1d54 exists to
foreclose exactly one failure: CI signing with a seed whose public half is not
in the artefact"s compiled-in keyring, which nobody notices until a user cannot
update. The check that forecloses it is `manifest-sign -verify` against that
keyring — and it runs only on a real tag. So the pairing of
RELEASE_SIGNING_KEY with internal/update/keyring.go has never been executed,
and the first execution will be the release itself.

It fails safe rather than shipping something broken: verify runs before
`gh release create`, so a mismatch fails the job and publishes nothing. The
cost is a full pipeline and a tag that produced no release, on the one input
that cannot simply be retried in place.

The design constraint to respect: the signing key must stay out of any job that
runs build tooling (section 5). publish runs none — it only downloads artefacts —
so signing and verifying there on a dry run does not weaken that. Only
`gh release create` needs the tag.

## Steps to Reproduce

Trigger release.yml via workflow_dispatch and look at the publish job: skipped,
including the verify step, while the header says otherwise.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A dry run generates, signs and verifies manifest.json, and creates no
  release. The gate moves from the whole job to the publishing step alone.
- The signing key stays out of every job that runs build tooling.
- A dry run whose RELEASE_SIGNING_KEY does not match the compiled-in keyring
  FAILS, and a test or a deliberate one-off proves that, rather than a green
  run being taken as evidence the pair matches.
- The header describes what the file does.
close_reason: Fixed on main (ec3e2a7): the job split into sign (always runs, no write permission, no build tooling) and publish (tag-gated, holds contents: write, uploads only). PROVEN by run 31246707047, where 'Verify the signature against the keyring the release ships' reports success for the first time in the project's history — so RELEASE_SIGNING_KEY's public half IS in the compiled keyring, which nocx-1d54 could previously only assume. The manifest travels between the jobs as an artefact, so the verified bytes are the uploaded bytes. The file header is now true.

title: The AppImage step writes a desktop file with no icon, so appimagetool refuses to package
description:
The AppImage output plugin refuses to package:

  Icon entry not found in desktop file
  (null){.png,.svg,.xpm} defined in desktop file but not found
  ERROR: Failed to run plugin: appimage (exit code: 1)

Two causes, one step. The inline .desktop file the workflow writes has no
Icon= key, and appimagetool treats that as fatal, not cosmetic. And linuxdeploy
was invoked with only --appdir, so the .desktop dropped into AppDir/ by hand
was never INSTALLED — it warned "Could not find desktop file in AppDir, cannot
create links for AppRun, desktop file and icon in AppDir root" in the same run.

Found immediately after nocx-xy9z unblocked the compile, in dry run
31222427704: the webkit tag let the build through to the packaging step, which
had never executed before. Each fix reveals the next never-run step, which is
what a pipeline that has never completed looks like.

build/appicon.png has been tracked since nocx-azxe.4, which exists so a clean
CI checkout carries the project icon rather than Wails" default. Nothing on the
Linux path ever referenced it, so even a successful AppImage would have shipped
with no icon at all — the same defect nocx-azxe.4 fixed for macOS, still open on
Linux.

## Steps to Reproduce

Run release.yml (workflow_dispatch) and watch build-linux fail in "Package
AppImage" after the compile and the GTK bundling both succeed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The AppImage is produced and reports its version through
  --appimage-extract-and-run.
- It carries build/appicon.png, not nothing and not a placeholder.
- The desktop file is installed by linuxdeploy rather than placed by hand, so
  the AppDir root links are created.
close_reason: Fixed on main across a3175ab (Icon=nocx, --desktop-file/--icon-file) and 0c3bdb9 (512x512 derived from the 1024 master, which hicolor refuses). Proven by run 31246707047: 'Deploying icon to AppDir root: AppDir/usr/share/icons/hicolor/512x512/apps/nocx.png', desktop file installed to usr/share/applications, AppImage built and it RUNS — 'nocx 0.0.0 (commit ...)' via --appimage-extract-and-run. The icon is derived, not committed, so build/appicon.png stays the single master.

title: The Linux release build never told Wails to use webkit2gtk-4.1, so build-linux has never succeeded
description:
release.yml build-linux installs libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev and then runs
`wails build -tags release`. Wails v2 resolves its cgo pkg-config against
webkit2gtk-4.0 unless the `webkit2_41` build tag is set, so the compile fails:

  Package webkit2gtk-4.0 was not found in the pkg-config search path.
  Package "webkit2gtk-4.0", required by "virtual:world", not found

The Linux half of the release has therefore never built. It was invisible
because nothing ever ran the pipeline to completion: build-linux sits behind
the full ci.yml gate, and while CI was red on main the job was never reached.
The first dry run that got past the gate (run 31219714125) failed here — which
is the whole point of nocx-2785 doing a dry run before a tag.

4.1 is the decided target, not an accident of the runner image: ADR-0007 and
the README support envelope both name libwebkit2gtk-4.1, and the apt line
already installs it. The repository also already knew the answer — several
briefs and reports under .internal/ record `wails dev -tags webkit2_41` as
required on a 4.1 box. It had simply never reached the workflow.

## Steps to Reproduce

Run release.yml (workflow_dispatch is a dry run) and watch the build-linux job
fail at "Compiling application" after the CI gate and the macOS build pass.

## Acceptance Criteria

- build-linux compiles and packages the AppImage, and the AppImage reports its
  version through --appimage-extract-and-run.
- The tag states the decision in the workflow rather than being implied by the
  apt line.

## Also noticed, not fixed here

Makefile `build` runs `wails build -tags release` with no OS branch, so
`make build` on a Linux dev box fails the same way. Out of the release path,
so it is not bundled into this fix — but the primary dev machine is Linux.
close_reason: Fixed on main (aa2d325): -tags release,webkit2_41. Proven by dry run 31246707047 on ec3e2a7 — build-linux compiles and the GTK plugin bundles libwebkit2gtk-4.1.so.0.

title: A throwing actions.submit strands the editor: commit() hides and clears before it
description:
CommandEditor.commit() is the atomic handoff (ADR-0004 section 2): clear, hide,
THEN call actions.submit. The order is deliberate and correct for the happy
path — the committed command is painted once by the shell rather than echoed
twice.

What it has no answer for is a submit that throws. The editor is already
cleared and hidden when actions.submit runs, so any exception from there
escapes onKeydown as an unhandled page error and leaves the editor hidden with
the draft gone. Nothing shows it again: the pane keeps no prompt for the rest
of the session, and the only visible trace is a console error the user never
looks at.

nocx-axqs was one instance of this (an empty draft reaching CommandLedger.open)
and is fixed at its own source. The ordering hazard is what made a refused
command into a dead pane rather than a no-op, and it is still there for every
other reason actions.submit could throw — a ledger invariant, a renderer that
has gone away mid-submit, a hook that faults.

Note the asymmetry already in the file: the beforeSubmit planner path is
explicitly fail-open ("a throwing planner keeps the draft"), because it runs
BEFORE the handoff. The submit call has the same failure mode and no such
protection, only because it runs after.

## Steps to Reproduce

Make actions.submit throw (frontend/src/editor.test.ts already has a
throwing-submit case for the clear half) and observe that the editor stays
hidden with no path back.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A throwing actions.submit leaves the pane with a usable prompt: either the
  handoff is undone (draft and visibility restored) or the failure is surfaced
  and the editor is shown again. Decide which and say why in the code.
- The user sees the failure in the product, not only in a console error — a
  silent degrade the UI contradicts is the failure mode AGENTS.md names.
- A test asserts the recovered state, not merely that the throw was caught.

title: The SSH spec leaves a profile on the shared stand and quick-connect fails
description:
e2e/git-panel.spec.ts's SSH spec created an ssh profile through profiles.create
and never removed it. e2e/stand.ts owns ONE backend and ONE home for the whole
run, so that profile outlived the spec, and quick-connect.spec.ts asserts the
picker says "No matches" on a stand with no profiles. It found a row instead.

Reproduced locally by running the two files in sequence — red without the
teardown, green with it — which is what a shard does.

It appeared now, and not before, because sharding splits by FILE: this branch
added spec files, the split changed, and the two landed on one runner. The
dependency was always there; the file list is what exposed it.

## Steps to Reproduce

    PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/git-panel.spec.ts e2e/quick-connect.spec.ts

## Acceptance Criteria

- The spec removes the profile it creates, best-effort, without replacing a real
  test failure with a teardown failure.
- The two files pass in sequence.
- Worth considering separately, not here: quick-connect asserting global
  emptiness makes every other spec's state its business. That is a second bead
  if it bites again.
close_reason: Fixed: the SSH spec deletes the profile it creates, best-effort inside the existing finally so a teardown failure can never replace the real test failure. Verified both directions locally by running git-panel.spec.ts and quick-connect.spec.ts in sequence, which is what a shard does: red without the teardown with CI's exact error, 25/25 green with it.

title: Two git tests compare an unresolved temp path against git's resolved one (macOS)
description:
CI's backend job runs on macOS. Two tests compare a path they chose against the
path git reports, and on macOS those are different strings: /var is a symlink to
/private/var, t.TempDir() hands back the unresolved form, and `git rev-parse
--show-toplevel` resolves it.

    Toplevel = "/private/var/folders/.../001", want "/var/folders/.../001"

Green in the Linux container, red on the platform the app ships on — the exact
disagreement AGENTS.md says to expect between the container and CI, and the
reason CI is the source of truth.

## Steps to Reproduce

Run internal/git/local's TestOpenResolvesRealRepository or
internal/transport's TestGitOpen_RealGitRoundTrip on macOS.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Both tests pass on macOS and on Linux.
- The fix canonicalises the fixture's path rather than loosening the assertion:
  the path a test calls "the repository" should be the same string git calls it,
  so no future assertion has to be lenient about a difference that is not its
  subject.
close_reason: Fixed by canonicalising the fixture paths rather than loosening the assertions: internal/git/local's newGitRepo now returns filepath.EvalSymlinks(t.TempDir()) through a named helper, and the transport round-trip resolves its own. The path a test calls 'the repository' is now the same string git calls it, so no future assertion has to be lenient about it. Both pass on Linux; the macOS-only difference is what CI's backend job checks.

title: the remote launcher sat 2KB under a cap it can never raise, and nothing watched the margin
description:
## Summary

Measured 2026-08-07 on a clean tree: the ShellAuto bootstrap command is 112,676
bytes against maxFullLauncherLen of 114,688 — 98.2% full, 2 KB of headroom for
THREE scripts. The comment on the constant still said the form was '~97 KiB
today', which had quietly stopped being true.

The intended 15 KiB margin was eaten a few hundred bytes at a time and nothing
failed, because TestAutoCommand_UnderCap asks whether the command FITS. It fit,
right up until a 2 KB script edit (nocx-z9s9.16) made every remote launch refuse
at once — 8 tests, all reporting 'ShellAuto launcher refused'. Adding a line of
shell had become impossible and no one could have known.

The ceiling is not ours: the whole remote command travels as ONE argv word, so
Linux MAX_ARG_STRLEN (128 KiB) is the binding bound and cannot be raised.

## Fix

Cap raised to 120 KiB, and TestFullLauncherStaysUnderArgLimit now asserts the
margin against MAX_ARG_STRLEN rather than the ceiling — erosion is the failure
mode, and only a test watching the gap can report it in time. Raising the number
again is not available next time: see nocx-z9s9.17 for the payload itself.

Also fixed here: the two sh-publish tests spelled their generations as the
literals '11' and '12', which were 'one behind' and 'current' when written. The
bump made '12' one BEHIND the installed version, so the no-downgrade test was
publishing an older generation where it meant to publish a newer one. Now derived
from `version` so the RELATION is what is asserted.

## Steps to Reproduce

Before the fix, with any script edit larger than ~850 bytes applied:

  go test ./internal/shellintegration/ -run TestAutoCommand_UnderCap
  # ShellAuto launcher refused

To see the margin directly:

  go test ./internal/shellintegration/ -run TestFullLauncherStaysUnderArgLimit -v
acceptance_criteria: A test asserts the MARGIN between the ShellAuto command and MAX_ARG_STRLEN, not merely that it fits, and fails while there is still room to act. maxFullLauncherLen respects the kernel bound with that margin intact.
close_reason: Cap raised to 120 KiB and, more importantly, the margin against MAX_ARG_STRLEN is now asserted instead of the ceiling, so erosion reports itself while there is still room to act. The two sh-publish tests now derive their generations from version rather than from literals with a shelf life.

title: a fresh tab never gets its command snapshot when compgen misses the first prompt
description:
## Summary

The shell emits the OSC 636 command snapshot ONLY from a prompt
(nocx.bash:148). The first prompt grants a 250ms grace; if `compgen -c | sort -u`
misses it, emission waits for the NEXT prompt. A freshly opened tab where the user
has typed nothing has no next prompt, so the snapshot never arrives.

What a user sees: open a tab, press Tab before running anything, and completion
says 'Command names are still loading — press Tab again in a moment' for the life
of that tab. Pressing Tab cannot help — Tab re-runs the frontend providers and
never reaches the shell. The UI makes a promise the shell has no way left to keep.

Three e2e tests are exposed; two were green only by winning the race:
  completion.spec.ts:139 (no-match)   — failed on CI run 31196136604
  completion.spec.ts:73  (ghost text) — reproduced locally at NOCX_E2E_CPUS=1.5
  completion.spec.ts:37  (real command)

NOTE: nocx-z9s9.6 was closed against a different cause (a shared-history prefix).
That fix was real but did not touch this; the instrumentation quoted there
('snapshot accepted at 800ms while the panel still said still loading') is
inconsistent with the code, since each Tab re-reads store.status synchronously.

## Fix

The source-time job signals the shell (SIGUSR1) after the atomic mv; a chained
trap emits the payload. bash defers a trap until the running foreground command
finishes, so the handler runs BETWEEN commands — the same 'sole writer to the tty'
invariant a prompt provided, obtained directly rather than by waiting for the user
to press Enter. The trap is installed before the job starts: SIGUSR1's default
disposition is TERMINATE.

## Steps to Reproduce

  go test ./internal/shellintegration/ -run TestBashSnapshotArrivesWithoutASecondPrompt
  PW_PROJECTS=webkit NOCX_E2E_CPUS=1.5 e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/completion.spec.ts
acceptance_criteria: The snapshot pipeline completes well inside the first prompt's grace on representative hardware (measured: ~41ms against a 250ms bound in the e2e container at a 1.5-CPU cap, down from ~104ms), and the encoder's escaping is pinned byte-for-byte by a test that fails when the fast path lets a separator through. The completion panel no longer tells the user to do something that cannot work. NOT claimed: guaranteed delivery on a fresh tab — bash cannot do it, see the comment below.
close_reason: Fixed as far as bash allows, and the limit is documented rather than papered over. The encoder fast path takes the snapshot pipeline from ~104ms to ~41ms against a 250ms grace, and the panel no longer tells users to press Tab again when that cannot help. NOT closed as 'guaranteed on a fresh tab': measurement showed a shell idle in readline runs no traps at all, so the grace is the only automatic delivery point that exists. The residual risk under heavy load and the bind -x design that would remove it are recorded in the comments and in nocx-z9s9.19.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
REFUTED, and the refutation is the main finding here.

The first fix attempted — and the one two independent readings agreed on — was to have the source-time job raise SIGUSR1 when the snapshot file is ready, and emit from a trap, on the premise that 'bash defers a trap until the running foreground command finishes, so the handler runs between commands'.

The premise is false. Measured directly on a real pty, twice:
  bash 5.3.15 (host)      -> trap does NOT run while bash is idle in readline
  bash 5.2.21 (container) -> identical
A handler for a signal raised while the user sits at a prompt does not run until the next command is submitted. SIGWINCH does not flush it either. So the trap fires only at a moment PROMPT_COMMAND would already have covered, and the change delivered nothing. Reverted.

Worth recording: the e2e suite went green with that change in place, and it was luck. In the pre-fix run at the same CPU cap, chromium's ghost-text test passed while webkit's failed — the failure is intermittent, so one green run was never evidence. A mechanism has to be tested as a mechanism.

CONSEQUENCE: there is no way for a bash shell to emit anything on its own while idle. The first prompt's grace is the ONLY automatic delivery point. Delivery on a fresh tab therefore cannot be guaranteed in-shell, and this bead no longer claims it.

WHAT WAS DONE INSTEAD, after measuring where the time actually goes:
  compgen -c | sort -u        17ms
  __nocx_snapshot_build      ~85ms   <- the whole cost, a per-character bash
                                        loop with printf -v, ~7000 iterations
  total                     ~104ms   against a 250ms grace
A fast path for names needing no escaping takes the total to ~41ms, a 6x margin
instead of 2.4x. That shrinks the tail rather than removing it.

Also: the panel said 'press Tab again in a moment', which given the above was
advice that could not work. It now says the snapshot arrives after the next
command, which is true.

REMAINING RISK, deliberately not closed: under heavy load (the suite has
observed arrivals past 20s with ~200 PTYs behind it) the job can still miss the
grace, and that tab has no command names until the user runs something. If that
proves unacceptable, the designed-but-unbuilt answer is a user-triggered
readiness request: bind a reserved readline sequence via 'bind -x', and have the
renderer send it on Tab when the snapshot is pending, so the shell emits
synchronously from inside readline while it owns the terminal. That crosses the
input boundary (ADR-0004) and needs a design amendment, not a bugfix.

title: activity-bell has activity.spec's race, and a wait-loop stops the alt screen registering
description:
## Summary

Two things, and the second is why the first is still open.

1. `activity-bell.spec.ts` carries activity.spec's defect verbatim, including the
   comment: `sleep 3` between entering the alt screen and ringing the bell is
   described as "a genuine ordering constraint that cannot be expressed as a
   Playwright condition", and it is a race whose clock starts at Enter rather
   than when the second tab exists. It failed on CI run 31196136604 (chromium,
   first test of the run) exactly as activity.spec did on the run before.

2. The fix that worked for activity.spec — block the shell on a file the test
   creates after asserting the tab backgrounded — CANNOT be applied here as
   written, and the reason looks like a product defect. Measured in the
   container, chromium, three runs each:

       printf '\033[?1049h'; sleep 3; printf '\a'; cat
         -> .xterm-live-container is `live-fullscreen`   (passes)

       printf '\033[?1049h'; while [ ! -e GATE ]; do sleep 0.1; done; printf '\a'; cat
         -> .xterm-live-container is `live-idle`         (fails at 1.5s and at 5s)

   Same escape, emitted first in both. The difference is what the shell does
   AFTERWARDS: a wait that forks `sleep` ten times a second instead of one long
   sleep. `enterFullscreen()` runs off `renderer.onBufferChange('alternate')`
   (terminal-content.ts:1542), so either that event never fires or something
   returns the buffer to normal. A full-screen program that spawns short-lived
   children is an ordinary thing — if this reproduces outside the test, the
   fullscreen layout is lost for a class of real programs.

   Not yet distinguished, and the two possibilities need different owners:
   a renderer/buffer-tracking defect, or something specific to how a compound
   `while` command is submitted through the editor.

The spec is left in its original racing form rather than made worse: the loop
version fails every run, the sleep version fails occasionally on CI.

## Steps to Reproduce

    PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/run-in-container.sh activity-bell     # passes
    # then swap the sleep for the wait-loop above and re-run       # live-idle
acceptance_criteria: The bell provably rings after the tab is backgrounded, without a timed sleep, and activity-bell.spec.ts passes on a cold CI container. The alt-screen finding below is either explained as correct behaviour or filed as a product bug in its own right.
close_reason: Both halves resolved. The bell's ordering is now a file gate created only after the tab is asserted backgrounded, not a sleep racing the tab open. And the alt-screen finding in this bead is explained rather than left open: the wait-loop version failed every run because the spec never waited for the prompt before typing, so the leading printf of the alt-screen sequence was typed into nothing — the loop is just the longer line and lost the same race more often. Nothing is wrong with a compound while command; no renderer defect exists to file.

title: activity.spec races a sleep against opening a tab, and calls it an ordering constraint
description:
## Summary

`a background tab lights the activity indicator on normal-buffer output` failed
on CI run 31193916276, chromium only, while webkit passed and both pass locally:

    Error: expect(locator).toBeAttached() failed
    Error: element(s) not found          (11.3s: ~1s of work, then a 10s budget)

The test submits `sleep 3; echo PROBE-OUTPUT` in tab 1, opens tab 2 so tab 1
backgrounds, then waits up to 10s for the indicator. The 3 seconds is the whole
ordering guarantee, and the clock starts at Enter, not at the moment the second
tab exists. On a cold 2-core runner — first spec of the run, vite still
compiling the new tab's modules on demand — opening tab 2 can take longer than
that, `echo` fires while tab 1 is STILL in the foreground, and the indicator has
no reason to light at any point afterwards. The 10s then expires on an event
that already happened.

The comment in the file asserts the opposite: "The shell `sleep 3` is a genuine
ordering constraint (output must arrive after backgrounding, not before), not a
test synchronization issue." It is a race, and it is one whichever way the
timing happens to fall.

## Steps to Reproduce

    gh run view 31193916276 --log-failed        # chromium, first project, test 2
acceptance_criteria: The output the test observes provably arrives after the tab is backgrounded, by construction rather than by out-waiting a sleep. activity.spec.ts:10 passes on both browsers on a cold CI container as well as locally.
close_reason: The three-second sleep was a race the clock started at Enter, and the first fix (a file gate) landed the output inside the 400ms resize-echo suppression that opening a tab triggers. Output now repeats for ten seconds, so the observation does not depend on any single instant.

title: the journey's second connection produces no third entered block
description:
## Summary

Newly REACHABLE, not newly broken: until nocx-z9s9.12 the journey died at
`waitConn(1)` and nothing after it had ever run in the container. With the
fixture fixed the spec gets through the first connection, the remote blocks, the
exit and into the second connection, and then:

    Locator:  locator('.pane.active').locator('.cmd-block.cmd-block-entered')
    Expected: 3
    Received: 2
    (nocxify-journey.spec.ts:556, 64 polls over 30s, stable at 2)

Step 4 of the journey is the one under test — the SECOND connection must send the
compact `"$HOME/.nocx/launch"` line rather than the argv-borne bootstrap
launcher, on the strength of the installed fact the first connection recorded.
Two entered blocks exist and stay at two, so the second connection either does
not enter an environment or does not paint one.

Ruled out by measurement: the CONN= signal's timing. Firing it on the "none"
probe (a whole round trip earlier) and on the first real method both produce
exactly this failure, so the password is not being typed too early.

## Steps to Reproduce

    PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/run-in-container.sh nocxify-journey
acceptance_criteria: nocxify-journey.spec.ts reaches its end on both browsers: the second connection over the compact ~/.nocx/launch line paints an entered block carrying the banner and the password prompt, exactly as the first does. If the product is right and the spec's count is wrong, that is established and written down rather than the count being lowered.
close_reason: The fixture inherited SHELL instead of setting it, so the installed launcher carrier took the POSIX fallback and reported tier=minimal. sessionEnv now publishes the shell the fixture execs; the journey passes on both browsers.

title: the e2e sshd fixture writes a key OpenSSH cannot load, and its readiness signal hides it
description:
## Summary

`nocxify-journey.spec.ts` fails on both browsers, locally and on CI, with

    e2e-sshd: saw 0/1 CONN= lines in 30000ms: ADDR=…|USERKEY=…|READY

Two defects, and the second is what turns the first into a 30-second timeout
that names the wrong thing.

1. `writeUserKey` marshals the ed25519 user key as PKCS#8 (`-----BEGIN PRIVATE
   KEY-----`). OpenSSH reads ed25519 private keys only in the OpenSSH format.
   Reproduced by hand in the container:

       Load key "/tmp/nocx-e2e-sshd-*/id_e2e": invalid format

   Having no key it can load, the client sends no publickey userauth request at
   all. Nothing on the Go side could catch this: `ssh.ParsePrivateKey` accepts
   both encodings, so every assertion this repo makes about the file passed.

2. `CONN=` was emitted only from `PublicKeyCallback`. So the signal meant "a
   client offered a public key", not "a client arrived" — and a client that
   cannot offer one connects, authenticates by password and runs a full session
   while the fixture stays silent. The waiting spec then reports a missing
   signal instead of the unloadable key.

The connection was reaching the server the whole time: key exchange completed
and the banner was delivered, verified with `ssh -v` against a hand-started
fixture in the container.

## Steps to Reproduce

    PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/run-in-container.sh nocxify-journey
acceptance_criteria: cmd/e2e-sshd writes the user key in the OpenSSH encoding, so the OpenSSH client can offer it. CONN= is emitted for a client's first userauth attempt by any method, so a client that offers no key is still observed. Both are covered by Go tests, and nocxify-journey.spec.ts passes on both browsers.
close_reason: Key written in the OpenSSH encoding; CONN= fires on the first real userauth method from one place. Covered by Go tests.

title: e2e aims mouse gestures at pixel constants instead of at the element
description:
## Summary

Seven gestures in the suite find their target by arithmetic on a pixel constant
rather than by asking for the element.

`command-editor.spec.ts:63` is the one that is red: `page.mouse.dblclick(box.x +
120, ...)`. 120px from the left edge of the input is a claim about the terminal
FONT, not about the product. In the Linux container that point lands on the space
between two words, so the selection comes back as " " and the test fails; on the
macOS runner the same constant lands inside a word and it passes. The test as
written asserts "a word begins 120 pixels in", which nothing in the product
promises.

Six more aim at `box.y + box.height - 30` on the pane, and every one carries a
comment saying what it actually means — "near the bottom of the pane, where the
editor lives":

    e2e/clipboard.spec.ts:118
    e2e/click-focus.spec.ts:50
    e2e/focus-after-tab-switch.spec.ts:110
    e2e/multi-tab-input.spec.ts:39
    e2e/tabs.spec.ts:163
    e2e/tabs.spec.ts:215

These are green today. They are the same defect at a wider margin: 30px is a guess
about how tall the editor is, and the editor's height follows the font. Each file
already holds the locator the comment is describing.

## Steps to Reproduce

    PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/command-editor.spec.ts

  Expected value: " "
  Received array: ["echo", "hello", "world", "foobar"]
acceptance_criteria: No e2e mouse gesture names a pixel constant to find a target. Where a gesture is inherently positional (a double-click inside text), the coordinate is derived from the target's own geometry at run time. command-editor.spec.ts:57 passes on a host whose terminal font differs from the author's.
close_reason: No live pixel constant is left in e2e/ — grep for 'box.x + 120' and 'box.height - 30' finds only historical comments in command-editor.spec.ts and harness.ts explaining what was removed. clickIntoEditor() in the harness replaced the six 'box.height - 30' gestures with the editor's own locator, and the double-click derives its coordinate from the target at run time. command-editor.spec.ts is green in the Linux container, which is the host whose font differs from the author's — the case the bead named.

title: a run does not record which shell it drove, and nothing pins it
description:
## Summary

`internal/pty/pty_local.go:114` reads `os.Getenv("SHELL")` and falls back through
a candidate list to `/bin/bash`. `e2e/home-isolation.ts` does not restrict or set
it, so the shell a run drives is whatever the host exported — bash in the e2e
container, something else on a macOS runner — and nothing anywhere records which.

That is not cosmetic. `nocx.bash` emits the OSC 636 command snapshot; `nocx.zsh`
emits only the readiness passport (grep 636: 9 hits vs 3). So the shell decides
whether tab completion ever learns a command name, and today the shell is an
accident of the host.

Cost measured on 2026-08-07: reading a CI failure required downloading the trace
artifacts and inferring the shell from which dotfiles appeared in the file tree,
and the inference was still not conclusive.

## Steps to Reproduce

    grep -n 'Getenv("SHELL")' internal/pty/pty_local.go
    grep -n SHELL e2e/home-isolation.ts e2e/stand.ts     # no hit
    grep -ci shell test-results/stand/backend.log        # the run never says
acceptance_criteria: The backend logs the shell it resolved for a local PTY, so a run's account answers 'which shell did this test' without inference. The e2e stand pins SHELL rather than inheriting it, so the suite drives the same shell on every host. A Go test covers the resolved-shell log line.
close_reason: All three criteria met. internal/pty/pty_local.go:158 logs 'local pty shell resolved' with the shell and its source (SHELL / detected / fallback); resolveShell is covered by table tests in pty_local_test.go with an assertion on the log line itself. The stand strips SHELL rather than pinning a path — deliberately, and better than the criterion as written: there is no one path (/bin/bash is absent on NixOS), so what is made identical across hosts is the backend's POLICY, which it already owns.

title: e2e in CI runs the same Linux container a developer runs
acceptance_criteria: The e2e job in ci.yml runs e2e/run-in-container.sh on ubuntu-latest, so the command a developer runs and the command CI runs resolve to the same image, the same shells and the same browser builds. A developer's green run is a statement about that job. Deliberately out: WKWebView, which e2e never covered on either runner, and the macOS Go jobs, which keep Darwin PTY, Darwin paths and both macOS shells.
close_reason: Done: ci.yml's e2e job runs e2e/run-in-container.sh on ubuntu-latest and nothing else — no setup-go, no setup-node, no playwright install — so a developer's command and CI's resolve to the same image, shells and browser builds. 1bb80cb added the CPU cap for reproducing the runner's capacity. Confirmed by run 31206530320.

title: The degraded-environment warning can never be withdrawn (regression from nocx-6pz0)
description:
The owner restarted the backend after nocx-6pz0. Opening is fast now, and the
degraded-environment warning is STILL on screen.

It is not the shell. Measured on the machine running the backend, twice:

    $SHELL -i -c 'export -p'                        31 ms
    newEnvCache("", 5s, 256K).resolve(Background)   state=resolved, 22 ms, 84 vars

The defect is that envState is a ONE-SHOT value that can never be corrected.

- contracts/git.open.schema.json is the ONLY result carrying envState/envReason.
- git-store.ts sets them from the git.open response (lines 583 and 620) and from
  nowhere else. git.status does not carry them, so the 5-second poll cannot
  refresh them.
- Before nocx-6pz0, Open WAITED for the resolution, so whatever it reported was
  final and one-shot was correct.
- After nocx-6pz0, Open takes the settled-so-far answer and never waits — by
  design, that is the whole fix. envCache.known() returns `degraded` while the
  background attempt is still in flight, and a failed attempt is remembered for
  a 30s cooldown and then retried.

So a single open landing in the pre-settle window, or during one failed attempt,
pins `degraded` for the lifetime of the binding. The background resolution then
succeeds, the commit path acquires a perfectly good environment, and the panel
goes on warning about a degradation that no longer exists — the exact inversion
of D6's purpose, which is to make a real degradation visible.

The warning the owner sees says "context deadline exceeded", which means his
backend did have at least one attempt time out; the cooldown would have retried
it and very likely succeeded. He cannot tell, because the panel cannot change
its mind.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start the backend and open the Git panel quickly enough that git.open lands
   before the background environment resolution settles (or while an attempt is
   failing).
2. Wait for the resolution to succeed.
3. The panel still shows "Hooks will run in a degraded environment".

## Acceptance Criteria

- A test that fails without the fix: open with the resolution unsettled, let it
  settle to resolved, and the panel stops warning — WITHOUT re-opening the
  repository.
- The value reaches the renderer on a channel that repeats. The status poll is
  the obvious one and it is already epoch-scoped (D17); a second notification is
  a second owner and needs an argument.
- The interval stated with both ends (AGENTS.md rule 3): the warning appears
  when the environment is known-degraded and disappears when it becomes
  resolved — not "is set at open".
- Paired assertion: on a machine where the resolution succeeds immediately, no
  warning is ever shown, including in the first frames after open.
- D6's guarantee is unchanged: a genuinely degraded environment still warns
  before the first commit.
close_reason: The environment fact now rides the git.status poll (Repo.EnvState reads envCache.known, never resolves): the degraded warning appears when the environment is known-degraded and is withdrawn by the poll that carries resolved, without re-opening. Contract change is git.status only; envState required so the over-the-wire test catches a server that never sends it. Store interval test proven to fail against the pre-fix code; D6 unchanged (commit still waits). Commit b593827, full pre-commit gate green.

title: Hosting links do nothing in a browser: openUrl is Wails-only
description:
The owner clicked an open-on-hosting link in the Git panel at 127.0.0.1:5180
and nothing opened.

The cause is not a defect in nocx-hc0m's work: shell.openUrl is backed by
wailsUrlOpener over runtime.BrowserOpenURL, wired in main.go's WailsApp.startup.
`make dev-web` has no Wails runtime at all, so the transport reports -32601 and
the panel toasts, exactly as designed. In a packaged build the link works.

But "works only in the packaged app" is not good enough for a link. A browser
can open a URL perfectly well on its own — window.open — and the whole dev-web
path is a browser.

The owner asked whether we need global state for "where our app is running".
We already have it and it must not be duplicated (AD-8): frontend/src/platform.ts
resolves Platform = darwin | linux | windows | web, where `web` means precisely
"a plain browser, no Wails runtime", from the runtime's own Environment() with a
user-agent fallback. It is resolved at startup and already stamped on
document.documentElement as data-platform.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. make dev-web, open 127.0.0.1:5180.
2. Open the Git panel on a repository with a GitHub remote.
3. Click the open-on-hosting link beside the upstream, or on a commit row.

Observed: a toast saying the capability is unavailable; no browser tab opens.
Expected: the page opens in a new browser tab.

## Acceptance Criteria

- In a plain browser the link opens a new tab; in the packaged app it still goes
  through shell.openUrl to the system browser.
- The decision between the two paths is SYNCHRONOUS inside the click handler.
  A window.open called after an await has lost the user gesture and popup
  blockers eat it — this is the defect that will not show up in a test that
  stubs the seam, so it needs the real path exercised.
- The web path opens with noopener/noreferrer; a tab opened from the panel must
  not get a handle back on the app's window.
- Platform detection is platform.ts's, extended if it needs extending. A second
  "are we native" predicate anywhere in the tree is the defect, not the fix.
- The capability is general, not the Git panel's private seam: it is the same
  class of thing as frontend/src/clipboard.ts (a platform capability behind one
  owner), and any surface that later needs a link uses it without rewiring.
- Paired assertion: for every "refuses when…", a "and on an ordinary GitHub
  remote in each of the two environments it opens".
close_reason: Shipped in bd136b7. open-url.ts is a platform capability like clipboard.ts: on web the click opens the tab synchronously (window.open with noopener,noreferrer, no await before it); native still routes through shell.openUrl with the backend's scheme validation untouched. platform.ts owns two facts — the stamped chrome platform and the runtime currentPlatform() — so a macOS browser keeps its traffic-light chrome but opens in-renderer. Unit tests cover both environments, blocked popups, refused/throw-transport paths, and the synchronous-gesture regression; e2e asserts the seam via a window.open stub (no real tabs) plus the blocked-popup toast. Full gates green: gofumpt/golangci/go test -race, prettier/eslint/tsc (both configs)/2466 vitest, 16/16 chromium e2e in the container.

title: shell-mode may be asserting the absence of an offer the product owes
description:
## Summary

Needs the owner. I changed e2e/shell-mode.spec.ts to assert the editor chrome offers NOTHING after an SSH connection, on the reasoning that `script` is the default destination mode and integration therefore succeeds. The spec passes. The backend log says integration did NOT succeed:

    WARN ssh: could not determine remote home for shell integration
         error="shellintegration: get remote home: Process exited with status 255"

By capability.ts, a session that is authorized (policy != raw) and NOT integrated derives shellState `unsupported`, which yields the action "Integrate this shell". The chip is empty instead. So one of these is true and I cannot tell which without a decision:

1. the product should be offering the integration and is not — in which case my assertion is green over a real defect, which is the exact failure AGENTS.md names; or
2. something else legitimately suppresses the offer (an eligibility gate, ALT_SCREEN, a refusal classification), and the assertion is right for a reason I have not established.

Do not leave it as it stands. Either the spec goes back to asserting the offer and the product is fixed, or the suppression is understood and written down.

Context: the fixture (cmd/e2e-sshd) cannot answer the remote-home probe, which is why integration fails there. That may itself be the thing to fix — a fixture that cannot be integrated cannot stage the epic.

## Steps to Reproduce

    npx playwright test e2e/shell-mode.spec.ts
    # green; then read test-results/stand/backend.log for the WARN above

## Acceptance Criteria

- It is established, from the code, whether an un-integrated authorized SSH session should offer "Integrate this shell".
- shell-mode asserts that answer, and the answer is what the product does.
close_reason:
Established from the code and the backend log: the assertion is right, and the reason is legitimate. Not a green test over a defect.

The session IS integrated. The log shows 'shell.launcherCommand mode decided ... mode=bootstrap reason=no-installed-fact' — integration is delivered by the argv-borne bootstrap carrier, which needs neither the remote home nor SFTP. The two WARNs belong to the INSTALLED delivery route only ('could not determine remote home', 'publish failed: sftp subsystem request failed'): cmd/e2e-sshd offers no SFTP subsystem, so publishing into a remote ~/.nocx cannot work there, and the launcher correctly falls back. A later line in the same log reads mode=installed reason=installed-fact, so that route is exercised too, by the nocxify journey which installs first.

So shellState is 'integrated' and presentation is 'editor', which deriveActions (capability.ts:93) treats as the healthy state and returns no actions for. The chip is empty because there is nothing to recover, not because an owed offer is suppressed.

The bead's possibility 1 is also ruled out for the general case: an unintegrated authorized session does derive 'Integrate this shell' (capability.ts:99), and integrateShell() carries an explicit markerlessPath beside the trusted-prompt path (terminal-content.ts:2338) written for exactly the shell that can never satisfy PROMPT_READY && trusted && owned. The capability is reachable when it is genuinely needed; it is reached from the palette and the chord, since a markerless session shows no command editor for a chip to live in.

title: an SSH connection stops local Tab-completion from ever loading
description:
## Summary

`e2e/completion.spec.ts` → "no candidates: Tab opens a row that says nothing matched — never silence" keeps showing "Command names are still loading" for 45+ seconds, in any run that also opened an SSH session. Deterministic; which browser project loses moves between runs, so it is a race, not an engine property.

**It is a frontend defect, and the search space is now small.** Instrumented and measured, not inferred:

    [webkit] SNAPDIAG accepted-hello    t=578
    [webkit] SNAPDIAG accepted-snapshot store=1 t=800 names=1529
    [webkit] TESTLIFE ms=46163

The snapshot is ACCEPTED at 800ms and the store is ready. The command provider never reports `snapshot-pending` again after that — instrumenting providers.ts:128 showed it firing repeatedly before acceptance and NOT ONCE after. The panel still says "still loading" for the next 45 seconds.

So the stale text survives in the rendered panel. Not in the shell, not in the store, not in the provider.

Ruled out by measurement:
- the shell — the payload arrives, 1529 names, under a second;
- CommandSnapshotStore — one instance (logged its id), hello and snapshot both accepted;
- commandProvider — never takes the `unavailable` branch after acceptance;
- `bestReason` staleness across queries — controller.ts:547 clears it at the top of every runQuery, and `open()` (Tab) calls runQuery(true).

Where it must be: the controller settle/render path, or the dropdown DOM, between "this query produced no candidates and no reason" and what the panel displays. Start at trackEmptyReason / settleIfDone / render, and at what the dropdown does when a reason goes from present to absent.

What a user sees: press Tab in the first second of a new tab, and completion tells you "still loading" for the life of that tab, though the data arrived immediately.

## Hypotheses DISPROVEN — do not spend time on these again

1. The store anchors its nonce on the first hello and discards later ones, `reset()` having no production caller. Refuted: the sibling test passes on a fresh store, and every test gets one.
2. The snapshot is emitted only from a prompt and this test never produces one. Refuted: added a real command + Enter; no change.
3. One prompt is not enough. Refuted: made the poll produce a prompt per iteration — dozens over 46s; no change.
4. The EXIT trap group-kill (`kill -- -$PID`) reaps a neighbour session job. Refuted: removed the group form; no change.
5. The shell never produces the .snap file. Refuted by the acceptance log above.

The dead `reset()` is real and separate — filed on its own.

## Steps to Reproduce

    npx playwright test e2e/shell-mode.spec.ts e2e/completion.spec.ts

## Acceptance Criteria

- Pressing Tab before the snapshot arrives, then again after, shows the real answer — the panel reflects the state that exists now, not the one it first saw.
- completion.spec.ts passes wherever it runs in the suite, on both browsers.
close_reason: Not still-loading and not a render race: the test's own Enter recorded its fixed prefix in the shared history, so the SECOND browser project typed a prefix its history already held and the panel correctly offered the history row. Prefix now carries a per-invocation nonce, the way the sibling test in the same file already did.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
Correction from 2026-08-07, recorded because the close reason here sent the next reader the wrong way.

The history-nonce fix closed with this bead was real and is kept. But it was not the whole cause, and the symptom this bead is named for — 'still loading' for 45+ seconds — survived it: CI run 31196136604 failed on CHROMIUM, the FIRST project, whose history could not yet contain the prefix. The shared-history explanation cannot account for that.

The remaining cause is in the shell, not the frontend: nocx.bash emitted the OSC 636 snapshot only from a prompt, so a compgen that missed the first prompt's 250ms grace waited for a next prompt that a fresh tab never has. Filed and fixed as nocx-z9s9.16.

The instrumentation quoted in this description ('snapshot ACCEPTED at 800ms ... the panel still says still loading for the next 45 seconds') is inconsistent with the code as written: each Tab calls runQuery(true), which clears bestReason and re-reads store.status synchronously (controller.ts:547, providers.ts:126). A ready store cannot yield snapshot-pending on the next iteration. Most likely it observed a different store instance — they are per renderer/tab — rather than a stale render path. The 'search space' this bead narrowed to the controller/dropdown render path was therefore pointed at the wrong file; nobody should spend time there on this evidence.

title: Staged, Unstaged and Commits should collapse
description:
The owner asked for it: with 17 unstaged files the Commits section is below the fold and the commit form is unreachable without scrolling past everything. orca collapses each of its sections and remembers the state.

The kit's Section has no collapsible variant — this is a kit change (a variant, never a fork or a hand-rolled disclosure inside the surface), and TreeRow already establishes this repo's disclosure vocabulary: a native button part with aria-expanded, Enter/Space operable.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A user collapses Staged, Unstaged or Commits from the panel and the section's rows disappear while its heading and count stay; expanding restores them.
- The state survives leaving the Git view and coming back — the panel unmounts and the store outlives it (design 5.5), so the state belongs where the store lives, not in the component.
- The disclosure is a real button with aria-expanded, reachable and operable from the keyboard, and the heading is still a heading.
- It is a variant of the kit's Section with a row in frontend/src/ui/README.md — not a second titled-group component and not a disclosure hand-rolled in git.css.
close_reason:
Delivered and merged. Section gained a controlled collapsible variant with a native disclosure button carrying aria-expanded, Enter/Space operable; the git store owns the collapse state, so it survives leaving the view and coming back. 12/12 in the container including the keyboard specs.

Found and fixed on the way, outside the brief and correctly: the terminal's typing rescue was eating Space from focused controls, so the disclosure could not be operated by keyboard at all. I narrowed the worker's selector on acceptance — it matched a bare [tabindex], which also catches tabindex=-1 (the tab strip's roving items, inactive CollectionRows) and would have stood the rescue down exactly when a user clicked a tab and typed. The repo already spells this [tabindex]:not([tabindex='-1']) in three places (AD-8).

title: The sidebar is 240px, fixed, and the CSS says it is resizable
description:
The owner asked for a resizable sidebar after watching file names clip in the Git panel. Three findings behind that ask:

1. `#sidebar { width: 240px }` in frontend/src/style.css is the real width, hard-coded, with no drag handle anywhere in the app.
2. `--sidebar-width: 240px` exists in tokens.css and NOTHING reads it — a second declaration of the same number that cannot drift into view because it is dead.
3. base.css:318 tells the reader 'The sidebar is narrow and user-resizable, so "it fits on my machine" is not a width the kit may assume.' The reasoning it supports is sound; the fact it asserts is false today.

Why it matters more than any further tightening: at 240px the Git panel spends its width on a status letter, a type glyph, the counts and a stage control, and whatever is left goes to the file name. Every micro-optimisation buys ~15px. A drag handle buys as much as the user wants.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A user drags the edge between the sidebar and the panes and the sidebar resizes; the file names in the Git panel get longer as they do.
- The chosen width survives a restart (settings, like every other persisted preference — find the existing owner rather than adding a second store).
- A minimum below which it will not go, and a maximum, both stated as numbers with a reason.
- The dead `--sidebar-width` token is either the single source of the width or gone. Not both declarations.
- base.css:318's comment becomes true, or says something else.
close_reason: Closed

title: A broken e2e spec passes every pre-commit gate
description:
While merging two workers' branches I resolved a conflict in
e2e/git-panel.spec.ts badly and left a test function unterminated. The commit
passed EVERY gate in .githooks/pre-commit — gofumpt, golangci-lint, deadcode,
prettier, eslint, tsc, go test -race in the container, vitest in the
container. Playwright then refused the file outright: "SyntaxError: Unexpected
token (601:0)".

Two separate holes, both of the same shape — a checker that exists and is
never invoked:

1. prettier ran as `cd frontend && npm run format:check`, so it only ever saw
   frontend/. The hook's own comment claimed it "covers markdown and config the
   scoping misses", which `cd frontend` made false. The repository root has its
   own .prettierrc.json and .prettierignore and a `format:check` script, and
   nothing ran them.

2. The root tsconfig.json covers e2e/**/*.ts and playwright.config.ts. It
   EXISTS because two specs once shipped as compile errors and ran anyway — its
   own comment names nocx-azxe.2 and the run-time message that named nothing.
   The hook never invoked it; it only ran `cd frontend && npm run typecheck`.

So the e2e suite — the only place several properties of this product are
asserted at all, including the one that caught the Git panel's broken row —
was TypeScript that no gate compiled.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Break the syntax of any file under e2e/ (delete a closing brace).
2. git commit.

Observed: every gate reports OK and the commit lands.
Expected: the gate that already knows how to compile that file runs.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A staged e2e/ change runs the root `npm run typecheck`; verified by breaking
  a spec and watching the hook fail with the TS error, then repairing it.
- prettier runs from the repository root, so e2e/, docs and root config are
  formatted-checked; the root run includes frontend/ as a subdirectory, so this
  is a widening rather than a second checker.
- The scoping keeps its property: a commit touching no e2e/ pays nothing.
close_reason:
Fixed in 493541f. A staged e2e/ change now runs the root npm run typecheck (whose tsconfig already covered e2e/**/*.ts and was invoked by nothing) and a prettier pass over e2e/ and playwright.config.ts. Verified both directions on the actual broken file: the new gate reports TS1005, the old frontend-scoped pair reports success.

Deliberately narrowed: running the root prettier over everything reports 17 pre-existing unformatted files outside frontend/ — reformatting them inside this commit would have buried the gate change in whitespace. nocx-pvjj carries that.

title: The degraded-environment warning outlives its cause: check a backend restart first
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-07, on the machine running the backend:

    time $SHELL -i -c 'export -p' >/dev/null
    real 0m0.031s      ($SHELL = bash)

So the premise of this bead is WRONG. The probe does not hang and is not slow;
31 ms is nowhere near the 5 s envTimeout. The 'context deadline exceeded' the
owner saw cannot have come from that deadline.

The likely explanation, and the one to check first: the owner was looking at a
frontend that vite had hot-reloaded against a Go backend still running from
before nocx-6pz0. That older code resolved the environment synchronously inside
Open and passed it the REQUEST's context, whose deadline is shorter than the
probe's own — which is exactly how the message arrives faster than 5 s. The fix
moved the resolution to a background context.Background() at factory
construction, so a restarted backend should not produce it at all.

Next step is a restart of the backend process, not a code change. If the warning
survives a restart, the cause is something else again and this bead needs
re-opening with that evidence.
close_reason:
Premise disproven by measurement, and the real defect is filed separately.

This bead assumed the environment probe hangs on the owner's machine. It does not: $SHELL -i -c 'export -p' is 31 ms there, and calling the resolver directly returns state=resolved in 22 ms with 84 variables.

The warning the owner kept seeing has a different cause — envState is delivered only by git.open and can never be updated afterwards, so one unlucky open pins it forever. That is the regression nocx-6pz0 introduced by making Open stop waiting, and it now has its own bead with the evidence.

title: connections-settings stops at + New connection, which now opens quick-connect
description:
## Summary

`e2e/connections-settings.spec.ts` failed on both browsers at line 42, waiting 20s for `.cm-form` after clicking "+ New connection". Working through it in the container (35s per iteration) found FOUR stale assumptions, not one — the spec describes a surface that has been rebuilt around it:

1. **"+ New connection" no longer opens the form.** `startNewProfile` (connections.tsx:1400) sets `quickConnectOpen` — a Dialog with `#quick-connect-input` and a "Next" button. Creation starts from one field, and `.cm-form` appears only after quick-connect parses what was typed.
2. **The User field is behind a tab.** `#profile-auth-user` lives in the form Tabs "Authentication" panel, and the kit Tabs renders only the active panel.
3. **`.cm-form-actions` is dead CSS.** It survives in styles/surfaces/connections.css:269 with no markup behind it. The editor is a Dialog and its actions are its footer; the primary button is named "Create Connection", not "Create".
4. **There is no Connect button in the form at all.** Saving runs `closeDialog()`, so the form going away IS the save landing; connecting happens from the list row (`[aria-label="Connect to <name>"]`, the control connection-password.spec.ts already drives).

Four fixed. The spec now walks the whole route and reaches its LAST assertion.

## Where it stands

Still red, one line from the end. `nocx: connect from Settings {"profileId":"ssh:custom:test-ssh:..."}` fires, and no third tab appears:

    expect(page.locator(".nocx-tab-title")).toHaveCount(tabsBeforeConnect + 1)

The profile points at localhost:22 and nothing is listening there, in the container or on a CI runner. So the open question is a product one and should not be guessed: **does a refused SSH connect still open a tab that shows the failure, or is the tab only created once the session establishes?** If the former, the assertion is right and something else is wrong; if the latter, the spec needs the `cmd/e2e-sshd` fixture connection-password.spec.ts uses rather than a dead port.

Answer that first, then finish the last line.

## Steps to Reproduce

    PW_PROJECTS=webkit e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/connections-settings.spec.ts   # 35s

## Acceptance Criteria

- The spec walks the real route: quick-connect dialog, Authentication tab, "Create Connection" in the dialog footer, Connect from the row.
- What a refused connect does to the tab strip is established from the product, not assumed, and the final assertion states that.
- The spec passes on both browsers.
close_reason: Fixed on this branch across 3a8dafb (the spec walks the route the surface actually has — creation now starts from quick-connect, not the .cm-form that no longer opens) and b677037. connections-settings.spec.ts is green on both browsers.

title: the host-key spec seeds its profile at a path only Linux reads
description:
## Summary

`e2e/connection-password.spec.ts` fails on both browsers in the `e2e-headless` CI job (macOS): after a complete vault setup the Connections page never shows the profile, and the click on `[aria-label="Connect to Host Key Proof"]` burns the full 60s timeout.

Two answers to one question, in one file:

- `seedProfile` (line 56) asks `documentDir(isolatedHome)` — the harness helper, which returns `Library/Application Support/nocx-dev` on darwin and `.config/nocx-dev` elsewhere (e2e/harness.ts:175).
- `seedPublicKeyProfile` (line 84) spells `join(isolatedHome, ".config", "nocx-dev")` by hand.

On Linux the two agree, so the container run of the whole headless set passes — 10 passed, 1.2 min. On macOS the hand-spelled one writes a profiles.json the app never reads, which is why the FIRST test in the file passes on CI and the second does not. This is the shape AGENTS.md names: a second derivation that agrees everywhere anyone looks and disagrees exactly where it matters.

It is the only hardcoded document path left in e2e/ — the earlier "the profile store lives at a different path on macOS" pass introduced `documentDir` and converted `seedProfile`, and missed this one.

Established from the run 31164732414 headless trace (the action log ends at "waiting for locator([aria-label=Connect to Host Key Proof])" with vault setup fully green) plus a container run that passes; no CI re-run was spent on it.

## Steps to Reproduce

CI, `e2e-headless` job on macOS: 2 failed (chromium + webkit), both `open-time host key consent`.

Locally the bug is invisible — `PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/connection-password.spec.ts` passes, because Linux is the platform where the two spellings agree.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `seedPublicKeyProfile` resolves its directory through `documentDir`, so there is one answer to "where do documents live".
- The `e2e-headless` job is green on macOS.
close_reason: Fixed on this branch: 282f48c seeds the profile where the app actually reads, and 5337f6c did the same sweep for the other three specs that were guessing at backend paths. connection-password.spec.ts is green on both browsers in the container, locally and on CI run 31206530320.

title: The Git panel has no filter box, which the design promised
description:
The design's kit table (§5.4) lists 'Filter box → SearchField' among the components the panel composes. The delivered panel has none: grep for SearchField in frontend/src/git/git-panel.tsx returns nothing.

termic — one of the two products the owner supplied as the reference — puts a filter above its UNSTAGED/STAGED lists, and it is the control that makes a 761-row list usable at all. The D9 cap and the filter answer different halves of the same problem: the cap stops the panel drowning, the filter lets a user find one file in what survives.

This is not a design gap like the commit list. It is a line of the design that was not built, and the epic closed without anyone noticing — the acceptance criterion watched one file through the happy path, and one file needs no filter.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the Git panel on a repository with hundreds of changed files.
2. Try to find one file.

Observed: no filter control exists; the only option is scrolling.
Expected: a SearchField filtering both lists, as the design's kit table says.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An e2e in e2e/git-panel.spec.ts: with several changed files, typing part of a path into the filter leaves only the matching rows in both lists, and clearing it restores them.
- The control is the kit's SearchField, placed and never repainted (ADR-0014).
- Filtering is renderer-side over the status the store already holds — it must NOT issue a scoped request per keystroke, and must not disturb the poll or the epoch discipline (D17).
close_reason:
Delivered and merged (a0f902a). Typing part of a path narrows both lists; clearing restores them. The design's own kit table promised this and the panel never had it.

Renderer-side over the status the store already holds — no request per keystroke, so the epoch discipline (D17) and the visibility gate (D13) are untouched. One predicate in one file with its own tests: case-insensitive substring over the repository-relative path, trimmed, literal characters, deliberately not fuzzy — the reasoning is in git-filter.ts, including why substring is what lets the section counts honestly describe what is on screen. Section headings count the rows visible under the filter, and a filter that matches nothing renders an empty state rather than a blank panel.

title: files.spec waits for an Expand button the reveal has already consumed
description:
## Summary

Five specs in e2e/files.spec.ts fail on both browsers — 10 of the ~27 e2e failures, the largest single group. All die in the same helper, `openFilesAtFixture`, on

    await fixtureRow.getByRole("button", { name: `Expand ${fixtureBasename}` }).click()

with the full 60s per-test timeout, so this group alone costs ~10 minutes of every e2e run.

Read from the trace artifact of run 31164732414 (shard-2, webkit), no re-run needed. At the moment of the timeout the fixture row is:

    data-disclosure="expanded"  data-selected="true"
    aria-label="Collapse nocx-files-e2e-aBpTMp"

and its children `bigdir` and `notes.md` are already rendered rows. The reveal EXPANDS its target, so a button labelled `Expand <fixture>` never exists — only `Collapse <fixture>`.

The product is right and the test is stale. `finishReveal` (frontend/src/files/files-store.ts) sets `node.expanded = true` and lists the first page. Three comments in `descend` a few lines above say the opposite — "The target: select it. Its own children are NOT listed — selecting is not expanding" and "select it without listing or expanding it". The helper was written from those comments rather than from the code, which is how a test can be green-by-construction about behaviour that does not exist.

Fix both ends: the helper asserts what the reveal actually leaves behind (target expanded, children visible) instead of clicking a control that is not there, and the stale comments in `descend` stop contradicting the function they call.

## Steps to Reproduce

    gh run download 31164732414 -D traces
    # traces/playwright-traces-shard-2/files-*/error-context.md — five of them,
    # each "waiting for locator(...).getByRole(button, { name: Expand ... })"

Or on CI: any e2e run on main; files.spec contributes 5 failures per browser.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `openFilesAtFixture` no longer clicks a disclosure button; it asserts the fixture row is `data-disclosure="expanded"` and selected, and that `bigdir` and `notes.md` are visible rows.
- The five specs that use the helper pass on both browsers.
- The comments in `descend` describe what `finishReveal` does.
close_reason: Confirmed on macOS CI, run 31167919744: the five Expand-button timeouts are gone from both browsers. files.spec went from 11 failures to 3, and the three that remain are different defects the timeout had been hiding (nocx-z9s9.5).

title: The branch's commits, in the panel
description:
Reported by the owner against orca, which devotes the lower half of its source-control panel to COMMITS with a lane graph and ref badges. nocx shows none of the history.

Not listed as out of scope in the design's section 4 — it was never considered.

The shape to respect: a new Repo operation (the seam is operation-shaped, D16 — the relay implements the same method over the socket), its own contract under contracts/, and a read-only list. git log with a NUL-delimited format, bounded, with the same Completeness discriminator the other bounded reads use.
acceptance_criteria:
An e2e watches a user open the Git panel and read the subject of the commit they just made, at the top of a Commits list, without leaving the panel.

Deliberately out: the branch GRAPH (orca draws lanes and merge topology), commit selection, and opening a commit's diff — each its own bead.
close_reason:
Delivered and merged. A Commits section lists the branch's recent commits — subject, short hash, relative time, ref badges — read on open, on refresh and after a commit, never on the 5s poll (D13), epoch-scoped (D17), bounded with the D9 completeness discriminator.
