title: connection-password seeds the profile at the Linux path, so it never ran on macOS
description:
## Summary

seedProfile in e2e/connection-password.spec.ts wrote the profile document to <isolatedHome>/.config/nocx-dev/profiles.json, with a comment asserting that createHomeIsolation strips the XDG variables so the config dir resolves there. True on Linux, false on macOS: internal/storage/paths.go sends darwin to <home>/Library/Application Support/<app> through os.UserHomeDir() and never consults XDG.

So on any Mac the spec wrote the profile where nothing read it. The Connections page stayed empty and the [aria-label="Connect to Password Proof"] button it waits for never appeared. Green in the bash container, red on every Mac including the CI runner.

Second time this repo has paid for that directory being derived twice — e2e/harness.ts's DisposableRoot comment records the first, where the vault specs believed they were isolated and were writing the developer's real Application Support directory.

Fixed by giving the resolution one owner: harness.ts exports documentDir(isolatedHome), which reproduces the platform split once, and the spec calls it.

## Steps to Reproduce

Before the fix, on macOS:
  PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/headless-run.sh e2e/connection-password.spec.ts
  -> fails at :181, element not found, on both chromium and webkit.
In the container (Linux, bash) the same spec passes.

## Acceptance Criteria

- No spec derives a document directory from a literal.
- connection-password passes on macOS and in the container.
close_reason: Closed

title: seven e2e specs fail on both browsers for reasons unrelated to the backend mix-up
description:
## Summary

Separating these from nocx-w4vy so its fix is not credited with them. In run 31116081576 these fail on chromium AND webkit, and none of them starts a devharness backend:

- completion.spec.ts:139 — 'no candidates: Tab opens a row that says nothing matched'. Expected 'No matches', received 'still-loading', after 20s. The completion panel never leaves its loading state.
- completion.spec.ts:217 — erasing the line closes the panel entirely
- connections-settings.spec.ts:15 — walks from Settings gear to a created SSH tab
- nocxify-journey.spec.ts:319 — the hand-typed ssh journey
- activity.spec.ts:10 — background tab lights the activity indicator (webkit shard 2)
- proof-matrix.spec.ts:787 and :810 — focus placement after page switch (webkit only; AGENTS.md notes layout/focus specs differ by engine, so these two may be a separate story)

'still-loading' is a product-shaped symptom, not a harness one: something the panel waits on never resolves under `wails dev`. Worth checking before assuming these are test bugs.

## Steps to Reproduce

Run 31116081576, jobs e2e (1) and e2e (2). Traces are uploaded as playwright-traces-shard-1 and -2.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Each of the seven has a named cause and is either fixed or split out into its own bead with that cause recorded.
- The completion 'still-loading' case in particular is resolved as product or test, with the evidence stated.
notes:
Triaged 2026-08-06. The completion pair is diagnosed and split out as nocx-qduc: nocx.zsh implements no OSC 636 command snapshot at all, so on macOS (zsh) the dropdown never learns a command name. Reproduced on a macOS host and green in the bash container, both directions.

Still unattributed in this bead: connections-settings.spec.ts:15, nocxify-journey.spec.ts:319, activity.spec.ts:10, proof-matrix.spec.ts:787 and :810. shell-mode.spec.ts:118 stays here too — it reads the port through whichever bindings exist rather than injecting, so it is NOT part of nocx-w4vy and was never fixed by it.

Worth checking whether connections-settings and nocxify-journey share the zsh cause: both drive a real shell, and nocxify-journey is about shell integration end to end.
CI evidence from run 31120617127 shard 2 (the first run since nocx-w4vy landed). 7 failed, 81 passed. None of the seven devharness specs appears — the exclusion works and the remaining set is exactly this bead. Three distinct error shapes, so this is at least three bugs, not one:

1. shell-mode.spec.ts:118 [chromium] — .nocx-editor-recovery is PRESENT but hidden, and it flickers. The call log shows the chip resolving 4x empty and hidden, then once with text 'Enable command editor', then 38x hidden again over 20s. So the recovery chip is being rendered and un-rendered, not merely late. This is the only chromium failure in the shard and the most product-shaped of the three.

2. completion.spec.ts:139 and :217 [webkit] — 'still-loading' again, the nocx-qduc shape.

3. connections-settings.spec.ts:15 [webkit] — .cm-form never attaches within 20s. Unrelated to either of the above.

proof-matrix 787/810 (focus placement) remain the two AGENTS.md flags as engine-sensitive; they are the likeliest of the set to be a genuine WebKit-vs-WKWebView difference rather than a defect.

Also visible in the same job log and probably relevant to shell-mode and nocxify-journey: WARN 'ssh: could not determine remote home for shell integration ... get remote home: Process exited with status 255'.

title: .e2e home is never reset, so one spec's writes become the next spec's preconditions
description:
## Summary

The suite gives every spec in a shard ONE backend and ONE home (`.e2e`, a fixed path under the repo). Specs run sequentially in one worker, so what one writes is the next one preconditions — and across browser projects too, since the root survives chromium → webkit and later invocations.

It stopped being theoretical on 2026-08-07. `connections-settings.spec.ts` is the only spec that writes a stored connection; while it was broken it died before its Create and leaked nothing. The moment it was repaired (nocx-z9s9.4), two `quick-connect.spec.ts` specs it never touches went red, because the picker asserts it is empty. Contained with UI cleanup at both ends of connections-settings; that is a tourniquet and says so in the code.

## What this has to decide

Reviewed with codex; the correction that matters most is first.

1. **Resetting the home is only safe while the owning backend is STOPPED.** The backend caches documents, holds SQLite files open and keeps profile state in memory, and can rewrite stale state later. Deleting files underneath a live process leaves exactly the state that answers the next spec. The unit is `fresh home → start backend → run → stop backend → keep or discard home`, never `start → run → delete underneath → run`.
2. **Name the isolation scope.** Per test, per spec file, or per stateful group — "per run" does not buy order-independence *within* a run, which is the failure above.
3. **Fresh roots instead of one fixed active path.** e.g. `.e2e/runs/<run-id>/<project>/<test>/`, discarded on success, preserved (or symlinked as `last-failure`) on failure. The current fixed path was chosen for post-mortem inspectability; a retention policy gives that without giving up isolation.
4. **Two receipts, or it will regress.** An order-independence one — polluter → observer and observer alone agree — and a cross-project one, so chromium state cannot become webkits precondition.
5. **Decide the mechanism for stateful specs**: a dedicated devharness backend per spec, or a devharness-only reset facility that goes through application services. Not a production JSON-RPC method — that ships to users.

## Also worth fixing, separately

`quick-connect.spec.ts:11` asserts GLOBAL emptiness ("no saved hosts at all"). That is only valid if a fixture guarantees a pristine store; today it is inherited from whether every preceding teardown happened to work. Either give it that fixture, or have it filter on a token nothing can match and assert "No matches" without claiming the whole store is empty. Left alone for now deliberately: the spec subject IS the empty-state experience, and narrowing the assertion would quietly change what it proves.

Only one writer today is an accident, not a design. Settings specs already write persistent settings and happen to tolerate each other. `workers: 1` makes the collisions deterministic, not absent — raising PW_WORKERS will expose the full size of this.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The isolation scope is stated and enforced by the harness, not by each spec remembering.
- An order-independence receipt exists and runs: polluter-then-observer and observer-alone agree.
- A cross-project receipt exists: chromium state cannot be webkits precondition.
- The UI cleanup in connections-settings.spec.ts can be deleted, and is.
notes:
Measured on current main predecessor 5e8784db / CI run 32508439589 (2026-08-21), after the browser matrix split: each project collects 184 tests and still runs one worker. Chromium: 9.9m job, 475s test phase, 444s reported test bodies; WebKit: 9.6m job, 469s test phase, 438s reported test bodies. Reported test bodies are 93% of the test phase and the test phase is 81-82% of the whole e2e step. Median over 15 recent runs: Chromium 10.52m, WebKit 11.62m. Per-test median is 1.9-2.0s; top 20 tests are only 36% of the body time, so this is a serial long tail, not one pathological spec. There are no Playwright retries. The 2026-08-15 project split already cut 314 tests / 22.0m in one worker to about 8.5m wall then; the remaining wall-clock lever is the isolation this bead owns, after which PW_WORKERS can safely exceed 1. Job-level sharding is technically isolated already, but run 32482238866 had a 17.2m hosted-runner queue delay for one WebKit leg, so multiplying matrix jobs trades test time for queue risk.
Expanded runner-queue check on 2026-08-22: 40 non-skipped PR CI runs after the browser split, 80 e2e jobs. Three independent PR runs had an e2e leg start more than 10 minutes after the immediately eligible sibling jobs: PR #91 / run 32250758273 — WebKit +23.03m (and backend with-secret-service +11.63m); PR #103 / run 32482238866 — WebKit +17.22m while all other seven jobs started at +0.05m; PR #94 / run 32348597549 — WebKit and both backend legs all started at +14.53–14.55m while five siblings started at +0.05m. Thus 3/40 runs (7.5%) and 3/80 e2e jobs (3.75%) hit a >10m start delay. ci-e2e has no needs, concurrency, or environment gate; both projects are the same strategy.matrix on ubuntu-latest. The delayed WebKit log begins only when Hosted Compute Agent / Worker ID / Azure Region appears, 17m after the workflow was created. This confirms job-level GitHub scheduler/runner allocation wait and rules out WebKit/e2e execution as the delay. Public Actions API does not expose a reliable queued_at or reason (job.created_at can be later than started_at), so hosted capacity versus account/org concurrency cannot be distinguished without GitHub administrative data. This strengthens the warning against multiplying matrix jobs before measuring queue behavior.

title: local gates trust frontend/node_modules exists, never that it matches the lockfile
description:
## Summary

AGENTS.md and ci.yml both claim the pre-commit hook and `make ci` mirror CI so that "green is identical locally and in CI". They do not, in one specific way: both check only that frontend/node_modules is a DIRECTORY (.githooks/pre-commit and Makefile:104), then run eslint/tsc/vitest against whatever is in it. CI runs npm ci, which deletes node_modules and installs the lockfile exactly.

So a developer's tree can carry packages the lockfile does not install, and every type-aware lint rule, every tsc program and every test resolves against them. nocx-r717 is exactly that: @types/node present locally, absent after npm ci, 112 lint errors visible only in CI. The class is general — any drifted or extra package hides a break the same way.

Second contributor, smaller: the frontend job's step order runs npm run lint before the root npm ci, so during lint there is no root node_modules to walk up into, while locally there always is. Any check that depends on what a PARENT directory installed will read differently in the two places.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. cd frontend && npm install --no-save some-package-not-in-the-lockfile, or simply keep a node_modules from before a dependency was dropped.
2. Write code that only type-checks because that package is present.
3. make ci and the pre-commit hook are green — they only test -d frontend/node_modules.
4. Push. CI runs npm ci and fails. Observed as run 31115207733.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The pre-commit hook and `make ci` fail, with the fix in the message, when frontend/node_modules does not match frontend/package-lock.json — cheaply enough to run on every commit (npm ls --package-lock-only style check or equivalent), not by reinstalling.
- Same for the repo-root install that the e2e typecheck uses.
- A tree with an undeclared package present is caught locally rather than in CI.

title: The connection editor draws the password action twice
description:
## Summary

AuthenticationEditor renders `passwordAction` in two places at once when the method is Password: AuthMethodEditor shows it (authentication-editor.tsx:81), and the editor shows the same element again under its own "Type a new one / Use existing secret" choice (:161). A user picking Password saw two identical "Set Password" buttons under two "Password" labels.

Two surfaces owning one control is the defect AGENTS.md names, whichever one wins by evaluation order. Here the newer one is right: it is the only surface that can also offer a row the vault already holds, and the other is what it replaced.

## Steps to Reproduce

Open a connection editor, Authentication tab, method = Password. Two "Set Password"
buttons appear. In e2e this surfaced as `strict mode violation: getByRole("button",
{ name: /Set Password/i }) resolved to 2 elements` across vault.spec and
vault-settings.spec, both browsers.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The password action appears exactly once, under the password-source choice.
- Picking "Use existing secret" removes it — the user is choosing a stored row.
- The public key action is likewise drawn once.
- A unit test on the component asserts the counts; no e2e spec needs `.first()`.
close_reason: Fixed by 7243622 — AuthenticationEditor drew passwordAction twice for the Password method; it is one control, drawn once. Not gate-covered (UI), so verified by reading the commit rather than by a green suite.

title: A superseded files.open leaks its backend binding
description: A `files.open` response that arrives after its context went stale is dropped(frontend/src/files/files-store.ts:561, `if (!openCurrent(ctx)) return`). Thebackend has already created the binding by then, and nothing closes it — soevery superseded open leaks one binding, with its provider and, on SFTP, itssubsystem lease, until the session dies.Found by codex during the cwd-following review.## Steps to Reproduce1. Switch tabs fast enough that a second files.open is issued before the   first resolves (or trigger any rescope race).2. The first response is discarded; its bindingId is never passed to   files.close. Backend binding count grows.## Acceptance Criteria- A stale open result is explicitly closed rather than discarded.- A test issues two opens back to back and asserts the superseded binding was  closed.

title: A session dying destroys its file bindings silently; the viewer never learns
description: `filesSessionClosed` (internal/transport/ws_files.go:920) tears down everybinding of a dying session, and tells nobody. The frontend liveness registry(frontend/src/main.tsx:283) flips only on frontend-issued open/close, so aftera terminal exits, a file-viewer tab still believes its binding is live andwill issue reads against a bindingId the backend has destroyed.Found by codex during the cwd-following review, not by a test.## Steps to Reproduce1. Open a file in the viewer from a terminal tab.2. Close/exit that terminal tab (its session dies; the backend destroys the   binding).3. In the viewer, trigger a reload. The call goes out against a dead binding   and the viewer had no way to know beforehand.## Acceptance Criteria- The backend announces binding destruction (a `files.closed` notification or  equivalent) whenever it destroys a binding the client did not close.- The viewer marks itself unavailable on that notification and issues no  further reads.- A test kills the session and asserts the viewer stopped calling.
notes: MECHANISM (found while designing the git panel, 2026-08-06): both session-teardown paths remove the session receiver BEFORE they clean up bindings - monitorExit calls removeRx at ws.go:1701 and filesSessionClosed only at :1711, and the explicit-close path does the same at :1745/:1747. So a notifier that resolves 'who is subscribed to this session' at emit time finds nobody, which is why the viewer never learns. monitorExit already has the answer: it CAPTURES the subscriber at ws.go:1696, before removal, and uses that capture for its own exit notification at :1717. Fix: pass the captured subscriber into the binding teardown as a parameter, and capture it the same way on the explicit-close path, which captures nothing today. Emit-time resolution stays the rule for a LIVE session (that is what survives an AD-9 reconnect); the capture is only for the teardown moment. Shared with nocx-yx9m, which needs the same fix for git.changed - whichever lands first should do it for both.

title: File tree: no type icons, and leaf rows do not align with directory rows
description: The file tree has no type icons and its leaf rows do not line up with itsdirectory rows. Both reference products (~/repos/termic, ~/repos/orca) show anicon per entry; nocx shows a chevron on expandable rows and nothing at all onfiles, so a file name starts where a directory chevron starts and the columnis ragged.## Steps to Reproduce1. `make dev-web`, open the Files panel on a local tab at $HOME.2. Directory rows carry a chevron and are indented; `.bashrc`, `.gitconfig`   and every other file start flush at the panel edge, a chevron-width to the   left of the directory names above them.3. No entry carries an icon of any kind.## Acceptance Criteria- Every row carries a type icon: folder (closed/open, following the  disclosure), file, symlink, and the unreadable state.- A leaf row reserves the disclosure width, so names form ONE column  regardless of expandability. Asserted in a kit test, not by eye.- The icon is derived inside TreeRow from data it already has (kind,  linkKind, cyclic, expanded). No new prop that takes a glyph, a colour or a  class, and no mapping table in the surface.- Icons live in frontend/src/ui/icons/ as siblings of the existing ones, in  the same stroke vocabulary. No new npm dependency.- ui/README.md TreeRow row updated with the new variance.
close_reason: Type icons + leading-slot alignment landed in bb6fec0

title: Files header: a permanent Polling warning, and actions that overflow the panel
description:
The Files panel header shows a permanent "Polling" warning badge, and the header
actions overflow the panel and get clipped.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. `make dev-web`, open the Files panel on a local tab.
2. The header reads `FILES  ~ (INFERRED)  <refresh>  POLLIN…` — the badge is
   permanently lit and clipped by the panel edge.

Cause 1: no provider implements Live watching yet, so `Watch` always returns
`ErrWatchUnavailable`; ws_files.go turned that error into a `degradedReason`,
which is exactly the condition the §5.5 badge lights on. A build-time "not yet
written" is not a runtime degrade, and a warning that is on for every user on
every local binding forever warns about nothing.

Cause 2: `.ui-sidebar-view__actions` had no `min-width: 0`, so a flex items"
floor is its content and the row pushes past the panel edge instead of
shrinking. The Files path also inherited the header"s uppercase, which is wrong
for content on a case-sensitive filesystem.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `files.watch` returns `mode: "polling"` with NO `degradedReason` while
  `ErrWatchUnavailable` is the reason for polling; the badge stays dark.
- The badge still lights for a provider-reported reason on a local binding.
- The header fits at the sidebar"s default width: the path ellipsises, Refresh
  stays fully on screen.
- The path is not uppercased.
- e2e waits on the established watch mode, not on the badge.

title: build/appicon.png is gitignored, so every release ships the default Wails icon
description:
## Summary

.gitignore had `/build/*` with only `!/build/darwin/` excepted, so build/appicon.png was never committed. `wails build` on a clean CI checkout does not find it and generates its own default, which means no release has ever carried the projects icon — the file existed only on the maintainers machine.

## Steps to Reproduce

`git check-ignore -v build/appicon.png` matched `/build/*`; `git ls-files build/` listed
only the two darwin plists. release.yml runs `wails build` on a fresh checkout.

## Acceptance Criteria

- build/appicon.png is tracked by git.
- A release build produced from a clean checkout carries it.
close_reason: Fixed by fb4067d. Verified directly, not inferred: git ls-files lists build/appicon.png, and run 31246707047 deploys it into the AppImage at hicolor/512x512/apps/nocx.png. Note the Linux half was still missing until nocx-zvd7 — the icon was tracked but nothing on that path referenced it.

title: The e2e home boundary does not cover the login keychain
description:
## Summary

`app.New` probed the system vault provider on every backend start, and the
comment there said what it is: "a probe is a real keychain write".
`e2e/home-isolation.ts` redirects `$HOME` and names the three things that
covers — `~/.config/nocx-dev`, `~/.nocx` plus rc files, `~/.ssh/config`. The
login keychain is a fourth CLASS: `$HOME` moves directories, and a per-user OS
SERVICE is not a directory.

## The recorded cause was wrong, and this is the correction

This bead used to say: "wails dev rebuilds and re-signs the binary each run, so
macOS re-asks for access every time." **That cannot be the mechanism.**
zalando/go-keyring v0.2.8 shells out to `/usr/bin/security` on darwin
(`keyring_darwin.go`, used by Get and Set), so the process the keychain sees is
Apple's own signed binary. Our signature never enters a keychain ACL, and
re-signing therefore cannot produce a prompt.

What was measured on macOS instead (design session, 2026-08-28):

- `$HOME` **does** move the login keychain — `security` resolves it under
  `$HOME/Library/Keychains`.
- A **read** under a `$HOME` with no keychain fails **silently**.
- A **write** under a `$HOME` with no keychain raises "Keychain not found" — a
  modal, and one nobody can dismiss on a headless host.

`system.Provider.Probe` opens with a write of a fresh random entry. So the
dialog the owner watched every two seconds was the disposable `$HOME` having no
login keychain in it, once per backend start. Not a signature; not something
re-signing or notarising would have changed.

The general rule survives its wrong explanation: `$HOME` isolation covers
DIRECTORIES and cannot cover a per-user OS service — the keychain, the Secret
Service, a launchd agent, D-Bus.

## Steps to Reproduce (as it was)

On macOS, run the suite with a redirected `$HOME`. "Keychain not found" dialogs
appear repeatedly for the duration of the run, one per backend start.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A local e2e run touches no real keychain. Either the boundary covers the
  keystore the way it covers `$HOME`, or the documented local path runs
  somewhere that has no keychain to reach.
- The boundary documents the keystore explicitly, so the next reader does not
  have to rediscover that `$HOME` does not move it.

## How it was closed out

"Probe, then fall back" cannot be the mechanism, because the probe IS the
failure — it has no fall-back path, it deadlocks in front of a person who is
not there. So the stance is DECLARED, never discovered (the nocx-server design,
D10):

- `app.New` refuses to build from a test binary that has not said whether it
  may reach the OS keystore (`internal/app/keystore.go`).
- A backend binary takes the stance from its BUILD:
  `internal/app/keystore_build_headless.go` is the default and excludes the
  keystore; `-tags nocx_login_session` declares a login session and is the only
  thing that lets the probe run.
- `cmd/devharness` — the last environment-variable override — is deleted with
  the cutover (`nocx-gpyxp`), so the e2e suite drives `cmd/nocx-server` built
  without the tag and has nothing to remember to switch off. That is what
  closes `nocx-nhhr`.

AGENTS.md carried the same wrong re-signing claim and is corrected in the same
commit.

comments.author: shady
comments.text:
Wider than the title says, and the title should follow. This is not an e2e-only defect: ANY host-side Go run touches the developer's real keychain, which is what 'make ci' is. Measured 2026-08-12: 261 test call sites construct the composition root, 5 of them pass WithoutSystemKeystore/WithKeystoreProbe. The other 256 each perform a real keyring.Set — internal/vault/system/system.go:143 writes 'probe-'+id under service 'nocx' with a fresh random hex account, which is why every dialog names a different id. The owner watched these dialogs continuously while three agents ran gates.

The seam already exists and is documented as test-only (app.go:200 WithoutSystemKeystore, app.go:206 WithKeystoreProbe). It is opt-in, and that is the defect: reaching a per-user OS service should be a decision a test states, not the default it inherits.

Why containerising is not the answer here: on Linux this class already runs in a container with no D-Bus (that IS the --no-keyring variant), so the user's instinct is right and implemented. macOS is the one job that cannot be containerised, because macos-latest is the target OS; moving it would delete coverage of bash 3.2, WKWebView and the Darwin PTY. So the fix is to invert the default, not to move the job.

Shape: one test constructor applying WithoutSystemKeystore unless the caller opts in; explicit opt-in plus a reason on the few tests that genuinely need the real store; and a check that fails when the app is constructed around the constructor, or this decays inside a month.

The general rule worth recording: $HOME isolation covers DIRECTORIES and cannot cover per-user OS services — keychain, Secret Service, launchd agents, D-Bus. e2e/home-isolation.ts names three things it moves; this is a fourth class and it does not move.

comments.author: shady
comments.text:
CORRECTION to the previous comment: the '261 call sites / 256 unguarded' figure is WRONG and should not be planned against. It came from a grep for '= New(' that matched every package's constructor — lifecycle.New, pty.New, shellintegration.New and the rest.

Measured properly: the app constructor is built 17 times across internal/app's tests, 5 of those already pass WithoutSystemKeystore/WithKeystoreProbe. So 12 sites to change, all in ONE package. This is an hour of work, not a sweeping refactor, and it does not have to wait for unrelated branches to land.

Everything else in the previous comment stands: the probe is a real keyring.Set (internal/vault/system/system.go:143), the seam exists and is opt-in, Linux is already containerised and macOS cannot be.

Why it accreted, which is the part worth fixing beyond the 12 edits: app.New takes options and is cheap to call, so nothing ever forced a shared test constructor — even though the repo already has the pattern in internal/storage/storagetest and internal/vault/vaulttest. And the cost is invisible where it is paid: on CI nobody sees a keychain dialog, the probe simply reports availability and the test continues. It surfaces only on a developer's Mac, as a modal that looks like it belongs to the OS rather than to the suite. So the fix needs a check that FAILS when the app is constructed outside the helper; without it the 12 sites become 20 again within a month.

comments.author: shady
comments.text:
Landed on the branch for this bead (not yet merged): the app constructor's keystore stance is now declared rather than inherited.

app.New refuses to build from a test binary that has not said whether it may reach the OS keystore — resolveKeystoreStance keyed on testing.Testing(), the same shape and the same reason as storage.NewAppPaths' refusal about profile directories. Production is untouched: off go test an undeclared stance still means 'build the real provider and probe it once', which is what tells a user's machine whether it has a store.

The measured 12 unguarded sites were 14 by the time the branch opened, all in internal/app, all now through one helper (newTestApp in a _test.go file, not a package: every caller is in package app, so an apptest package importing app would be an import cycle). It applies WithoutSystemKeystore plus a log path under the test's own temp dir; the caller's options come after, so any of them can be overridden.

How many tests genuinely needed the real store: NONE. Every one of the 19 construction sites is happy with an absent keyring, including the five that used to pass WithKeystoreProbe to fake the answer. WithKeystoreProbe is deleted — it was a second, weaker answer to 'does this host have a keystore' (it skipped the startup probe but left a live real keyring underneath, so any later vault call still reached the login keychain), and with the stance declared it would have been shadowed at every call site. WithRealSystemKeystore(reason) is the declared exception in its place: unused today, required to state why, logged at startup so a dialog during a run leads back to the test that asked, and baselined in the deadcode ratchet exactly like WithLogFilePath above it.

Two things this does NOT cover, both filed:
- nocx-nhhr: e2e/harness.ts sets NOCX_NO_SYSTEM_KEYSTORE only for the specs that are ABOUT the passphrase path. devharness is an ordinary binary, so the testing.Testing() refusal cannot reach it; the declaration has to come from the launcher, and stand.ts makes it while harness.ts mostly does not.
- nocx-an6d: App.Start installs shell integration into os.UserHomeDir(), and storagetest.Isolate does not move HOME. The reason it does not — a fake HOME costs 5 seconds per keychain call on macOS — is exactly what this change removes.

Also note for whoever holds AGENTS.md: 'every host-side Go run writes to the developer's login keychain (nocx-o4hg)' in the gate section stops being true once this merges.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
Cause established 2026-08-28, on the owner's Mac, by four security(1) commands.

The recorded cause is wrong. "wails dev re-signs the binary each run, so macOS re-asks" cannot be it: we never link Security.framework and never call SecKeychain*. internal/vault/system/system.go:54-62 calls zalando/go-keyring, and keyring_darwin.go execs /usr/bin/security for Get, Set and Delete alike. Our code signature never enters a keychain ACL — the keychain client is always /usr/bin/security, Apple-signed and identical whoever spawns it.

This description's other claim is also wrong, and inverted: \$HOME DOES move the login keychain. security resolves it under \$HOME/Library/Keychains, so the e2e redirect does isolate the keystore — into a directory that has no login keychain at all.

Measured:
  security add-generic-password -U -s nocx-acl-t3 -a t -w hello   # lands in /Users/<user>/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db
  HOME=\$(mktemp -d) security find-generic-password -s nocx-acl-t3 -a t -w
      -> "item could not be found", silently, NO dialog
  HOME=\$(mktemp -d) security add-generic-password -U -s nocx-acl-t4 -a t -w hello
      -> DIALOG: "Связка ключей не найдена / Для хранения «t» не найдена связка ключей" [Отменить | Вернуть по умолчанию]

So: reads under a redirected HOME are silent, WRITES raise a modal. internal/vault/system/system.go:139-146 Probe writes a fresh random entry on every backend start, and the suite restarts the backend per spec — one modal every couple of seconds, exactly as observed.

The fix is therefore in the e2e boundary, not in internal/vault: the wails dev path must declare its keystore stance the way a Go test now must (app.go:842 already constructs system.New(system.WithKeyring(system.AbsentKeyring{}))), or provision a keychain inside the redirected HOME. That is nocx-nhhr's shape.

Also correct AGENTS.md, which carries both wrong claims in the 'Git authority' section.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text: Related, and probably the larger half of this bug's cause: nocx-pq26e. Vault.Snapshot calls Provider.Status on every vault.status RPC, and system.Provider.Status is a bare 'return p.Probe(ctx)' whose first operation is a keychain WRITE. So the dialogs were not only one per backend start — they were one per status query too, which is a great many more during an e2e run.

title: CI never builds devharness, so nine e2e specs fail on every shard
description:
## Summary

Nine specs start their own backend through cmd/devharness instead of driving `wails dev`, so they can restart it mid-test. e2e/harness.ts:177 refuses to construct a VaultBackend without the binary. Nothing in ci.yml builds it — only scripts/dev-web.sh does, for the local headless path — so each of those specs fails outright with "devharness binary not found": 9 files x 2 browsers, in every shard. It was invisible while the whole e2e job hit its 20-minute cap without reporting (nocx-qth1); sharding made it report.

## Steps to Reproduce

Run 31095239709, any e2e shard: `Error: devharness binary not found: /tmp/nocx-devharness`
from connection-password, history-persistence, prompt-vault, recall-search,
tabby-import, vault-settings, vault (x2). home-boundary-live skips instead, because
it is the one spec that guards with test.skip.

## Acceptance Criteria

- ci.yml builds /tmp/nocx-devharness plus the -vault and -srch aliases before
  `playwright test`.
- No shard reports "devharness binary not found".
close_reason: Fix is on main and the gate that would catch a regression is green on ec3e2a7 (run 31246707047: backend, backend-linux x2, frontend, e2e all pass). Fixed by 5698c15 (CI builds the devharness) and 69d23f5.

title: The bash launcher delivers its rcfile through a pipe, and a loaded machine reads it short
description:
## Summary

launcher_bash.go:122 ships the rcfile as `exec bash --rcfile <(printf %b "...") -i`. That is a PIPE, and the payload is ~21KB / 458 lines (the whole embedded nocx.bash). Under load the reader outpaces the writer and bash stops at a short read, so the rcfile is truncated mid-construct and shell integration silently does not install. The failing test is the symptom; the defect is that a user on a loaded machine gets no integration and no error.

## Steps to Reproduce

On the macOS CI runner, `go test -race ./internal/shellintegration/` fails
TestFullLauncher_ForeignRoot_RefusedAndStillIntegrated with the session output:

    USER_RC_RAN
    bash: /dev/fd/63: line 415: syntax error: unexpected end of file

Does not reproduce on an unloaded Mac (5x with -race, and 4-way parallel, all green),
which is the point: it is scheduling, not syntax.

## Evidence that no commit caused this

nocx-0ije was closed by reverting script v12 (35f5e56) on the theory that v12 broke
this test. But internal/shellintegration is BYTE-IDENTICAL between the green run
31085068686 (1c7a3b9) and the red revert run 31092113036 (35f5e56) —
`git diff 1c7a3b9 35f5e56 -- internal/shellintegration/` is empty — and both ran
runner image macos-26-arm64 20260728.0273.1. The test then stayed red across four
consecutive runs and had never failed before dcb6512. So it is load-sensitive, v12
is exonerated, and the revert was made on a false premise.

## Fix

Deliver the rcfile as a file, not a stream. launcher_zsh.go already answers exactly
this question — mktemp, write, self-remove via an EXIT trap — and the bash tier
forked a second answer to it. One owner.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The rcfile reaches bash whole regardless of reader/writer scheduling.
- TestFullLauncher_ForeignRoot_RefusedAndStillIntegrated is green on the macOS runner.
- The bash and zsh tiers share one rc-delivery mechanism rather than two.
- A test drives a payload large enough to exceed one pipe read and asserts the last
  line of the rcfile executed.
close_reason: Fix is on main and the gate that would catch a regression is green on ec3e2a7 (run 31246707047: backend, backend-linux x2, frontend, e2e all pass). Fixed by a2fdd13 (an rcfile is a file, not a pipe read short) and 27ccccf, which sizes the payload from the two limits that bound it.

title: The e2e suite is green on main and can gate a release
description:
Run 31092113036 is the first run in which the suite reported at all rather than being cancelled at its cap: 163 passed, 44 failed across three shards. Two causes were removed to get there and are already fixed on release/v0.1.0 — the single-worker cap (sharding) and Playwright's 5-second default expect timeout, which alone accounted for roughly half the failures because a page.goto under wails dev is a full reload and the tab legitimately takes longer than five seconds to appear on a shared macOS runner.

What remains is NOT one root cause, which is why it is an epic rather than a bug. Shard 1's eight are eight different assertions: toBeVisible, toBeFocused, toContainText x3, toBeAttached, an Object.is equality, and an e2e-sshd that saw 0 of 1 expected CONN= lines in 30s. The next step is to group the 44 by cause and file a child per group — not to fix them one at a time from the top of the list.

Context worth keeping: the suite had not been green on main since 2026-07-26, when it was 40 tests. It is now 200. Nobody has seen this suite pass at its current size, so some of the 44 have probably never passed rather than having regressed.
acceptance_criteria: A CI run on main reports the e2e job green across all three shards, and release.yml can therefore gate a tag on it. Deliberately out: making the suite faster, and adding coverage — this epic only makes the existing 200 specs tell the truth.
close_reason:
Criterion met on both halves, verified on main rather than inferred from a branch.

CI run 31209553077 on main (merge commit 212df9e): e2e green — 229 passed, 7 skipped, 0 failed — alongside backend, backend-linux (both variants) and frontend. The 'three shards' the criterion names no longer exist: nocx-z9s9.8 replaced them with one Linux container job that is the same image and command a developer runs, so 'the e2e job is green' is the reading that survives. And release.yml calls ci.yml through workflow_call with every downstream job needing it (release.yml:34, :80, :180), so a tag cannot exist without a green run on that exact commit — which is the gate this epic existed to build.

nocx-z9s9.5 stays open under it and is the honest asterisk: two files.spec defects that are real, macOS-only, and — since e2e moved to the Linux container — run by no CI job anywhere. They are unobserved, not fixed. They cannot make the e2e job on main red, which is what this epic gated, so they do not hold it open; but a green suite must not be read as having settled them.

title: A dead jump-host SSH session blocks every tab's input (readLoop stuck on sess.Write)
description:
When an SSH session through a jump host silently dies (NAT/firewall drops the TCP connection without RST), the backend readLoop blocks forever on sess.Write because gossh stdin.Write has no deadline. Since handleDataFrame runs synchronously on the single readLoop goroutine, one dead session freezes input for ALL sessions on that WebSocket connection — the user types ls in an SSH tab, nothing happens, the execution timer ticks, and other tabs also stop responding. After ~2 minutes the user sends Ctrl-C (exit 130).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Connect to a remote host through a jump server (profile with jumpHost set).
2. Leave the connection idle long enough for the NAT/firewall to silently drop the TCP session (or kill the jump host's sshd process).
3. Type `ls` in the SSH tab. The command appears to hang — the execution timer starts ticking.
4. Switch to another tab (local or another SSH). It is also frozen.
5. After ~2 minutes, Ctrl-C gives exit 130.

Root cause: handleDataFrame (ws.go:1544) calls sess.Write(frame.Payload) synchronously on readLoop. For a dead SSH channel, stdin.Write blocks indefinitely (no write deadline, no context). The readLoop cannot process frames for any other session.

Secondary: no keepalive is configured by default (KeepaliveInterval=0), so a dead connection is never detected and the channel never errors out.
acceptance_criteria: handleDataFrame dispatches sess.Write off the readLoop (or with a bounded timeout), so one dead session never blocks input to other sessions. A dead SSH channel is detected within a reasonable timeout, not left blocking forever.
notes: Reopened 2026-08-06: closed while the work was still only on PR #64, which is not merged. #64 was split into per-concern branches; this bead's work lives on one of them and is not on main yet.
close_reason: The write-queue fix is on main: bounded per-session queue, FIFO, no close race, and the tab is told when input is dropped. The control-frame handlers that also block the readLoop are carved out to nocx-u687 — that part of #64 was not taken.

title: TestBashSnapshot* emit no OSC 636 snapshot on either CI runner
description:
Reverted on release/v0.1.0 after the fix caused a worse regression. Keep the diagnosis, which is sound and was verified:

THE PRODUCT DEFECT IS REAL. The first prompt's wait for the source-time snapshot counts ITERATIONS and calls them milliseconds - ten passes of sleep 0.025 adding 25 to a counter (internal/shellintegration/scripts/nocx.bash, __nocx_prompt_command). sleep is not a builtin, so every pass forks and execs; under load the fork dominates and CI measured a first prompt held for 1.161s against a bound the script documents as 250 ms. The user's prompt is what pays.

THE ATTEMPTED FIX AND WHY IT WAS BACKED OUT. Script v12 polled an EPOCHREALTIME deadline on bash 5 and spent the budget in one sleep on bash 3.2. It passed everywhere available locally - including real bash 3.2 in the bash:3.2 container, where the script sources and emits markers correctly - and it broke TestBashLauncher_EmitsMarkersAndRunsUserRc and TestFullLauncher_ForeignRoot_RefusedAndStillIntegrated on the macOS runner, which were green before. Those tests drive the REAL launcher path, so the suspicion is the product's shell integration on macOS bash 3.2, not the tests. Cause never found; no macOS host was available to reproduce on.

WHAT IS KNOWN ABOUT THE REGRESSION. The failing sessions show bash-3.2 default prompt, no USER_RC_RAN, empty sentinel - the launcher rcfile never executed at all, and bash printed no syntax error. The launcher inlines the whole script into a SINGLE LINE passed to /bin/sh -c: 85186 bytes at v11, 89936 at v12 (measured). A size threshold is the obvious hypothesis and is unverified. An attempt to reproduce in a container was INVALID and proved nothing: it ran without a PTY, so bash was not interactive and never read the rcfile under either version - v11 and v12 looked identical for that reason alone.

NEXT STEP. Reproduce on a macOS host with bash 3.2 as /bin/sh, on a PTY, comparing the two commands byte for byte. If it is the length, the fix is not a smaller patch to the wait - it is that a 90KB single-line command is already at a limit nobody measured, which is a separate and more important bead.

Reverting restores the three snapshot test failures on CI (TestBashSnapshotEmitsHelloThenSnapshot, TestBashSnapshotFirstPromptBoundedWait, TestBashSnapshotArrivesBeforeFirstPrompt). That is the deliberate trade: three known red tests beat shipping a possibly-broken shell integration to every macOS bash user.
acceptance_criteria: The cause is named, and the three tests pass on both CI runners without weakening what they assert.
close_reason: Fix is on main and the gate that would catch a regression is green on ec3e2a7 (run 31246707047: backend, backend-linux x2, frontend, e2e all pass). Fixed by a2fdd13 and dcb6512 — waits bounded by the thing waited for.

title: A dry run of release.yml builds, verifies and packages both platforms
description: workflow_dispatch on release.yml is the dry run by design: no tag, version 0.0.0, publish job skipped. It is the last thing that can catch a packaging or signing fault while it is still free. Both artefacts must appear: the macOS universal .dmg and .zip with both Mach-O slices and matching plist versions, and the linux AppImage that reports its version through --appimage-extract-and-run.
acceptance_criteria: A workflow_dispatch run of release.yml is green through build and build-linux, both artefacts are uploaded, and the publish job is correctly skipped.
close_reason: Done. Dry run 31246707047 on release/v0.1.0 (ec3e2a7) is green end to end: ci gate, build-macos, build-linux, sign, and publish correctly skipped. Both artefacts uploaded (linux-amd64 87MB, macos-universal 42MB) and the AppImage reports its version through --appimage-extract-and-run. It earned its keep: this dry run found four defects that would otherwise have been found by a tag — nocx-xy9z, nocx-zvd7 (twice), nocx-s8df and nocx-94kl.

title: Tag v0.1.0 and publish the release
description: The last step, and the only one that is not reversible from inside the repo: a published GitHub release with downloadable artefacts. Requires green CI on the tagged commit, the signing secret set, and a green dry run first. The tag must be a stable vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH on a commit reachable from main, which is what release.yml validate enforces.
acceptance_criteria: github.com/shady2k/nocx/releases shows v0.1.0 carrying the .dmg, the .zip, the AppImage, manifest.json and manifest.json.sig, and the README install instructions work against it as written.
close_reason: v0.1.0 published by run 31584091964 at 2026-08-12T10:00:11Z, carrying all five artefacts: the .dmg, the .zip, the AppImage, manifest.json and manifest.json.sig. Verified after publication that the manifest's asserted URLs resolve (HTTP 200) and both sha256 values match the bytes GitHub serves — the one check no dry run could make, since those URLs do not exist until the release does. NOT verified here, and left to the owner: installing and launching the app on real hardware.

title: backend-linux has no zsh, so five shellintegration tests fail rather than skip
description: ci.yml installs dash on the macOS backend job (brew install dash) because the launcher tests fail rather than skip when their shell is absent - nocx-gd84. The backend-linux job never got the same treatment and ubuntu-latest ships no zsh, so TestLaunchCarrier_GoodManifest_ZshExecsIntegratedShell, TestZshFullLauncher_PublishesAndPassportNamesGeneration, TestZshLauncher_TransientDirFlow, TestZshLauncher_CleanupAfterEarlyExit and TestZshLauncher_CleanupAfterSyntaxError all fail on main. The tests are right to fail loudly; the job is what is under-provisioned.
acceptance_criteria: The backend-linux job installs the shells the suite requires and the five zsh launcher tests pass there.
close_reason: backend-linux is green in both matrix variants on run 31095239709. Two provisioning gaps, not one: ubuntu-latest ships no zsh, and once installed its completion directories are group-writable so compinit stopped at an interactive prompt a test PTY never answers. Both fixed in ci.yml; the compinit fix then exposed a real product defect in the zsh launcher's transient-dir cleanup, filed and fixed separately.

title: The renderer decides in silence: no way to tell why a ghost was refused or which surface ate a key
description:
Two symptoms in one session — arrows not moving the dropdown selection, and Right not accepting the ghost — could not be diagnosed because the renderer records nothing about its own decisions. The backend got a log for exactly this reason (nocx-j4rm); the frontend writes only ad-hoc console lines, and the owner has confirmed the console is an acceptable destination.

A real asymmetry found while looking: canAcceptGhost requires ghostBox.queryDoc === this.queryDoc and the render path does not, so a ghost can be drawn that Right silently refuses — the drift the comment above ghostDecorations says must never happen again.

## Steps to Reproduce
Type ssh so a ghost appears and press Right; when it does not take, nothing anywhere says which condition refused.

## Acceptance Criteria
The render guard and the accept guard are one function, so a ghost that cannot be accepted is never drawn; every refusal names the failing condition; the key arbiter names the surface it gave a key to; all through the existing log module with a stable, filterable prefix, and nothing per-keystroke when the level is off.
close_reason: Landed as 84171e4: ghostAcceptable() is the single predicate both the draw and accept paths call, and nocx:decide tracing (window.nocxDebug) names the refusing condition, the surface a key was granted to, and the passport/entry decisions

title: A key that lives in the vault cannot reach a hand-typed ssh — serve it through an agent
description:
The saved connection for root@192.168.0.57 holds keySecret and keyPassphraseSecret, not keyPath: the key material is in nocx's vault per ADR-0017. So the profile overlay (nocx-pv3h) contributes -p but has nothing to put after -i, and a typed ssh to a key-based saved connection still asks for a password.

OpenSSH cannot read a key from our vault, and writing it to a temp file puts private key material on disk. The standard mechanism is an agent: nocx holds the decrypted key in an agent it controls, and the typed ssh gets SSH_AUTH_SOCK pointing at it. The passphrase is already ours, so nothing is asked twice.

Sits beside nocx-jee1 (askpass): both give a child process an environment through which nocx serves a secret without exposing it.

## Acceptance Criteria
A typed ssh resolving to a saved connection whose key is a vault secret authenticates with that key and asks for nothing, with no private key material written to disk at any point. The agent's lifetime is bounded and stated; a locked vault raises the unlock prompt rather than failing silently; and a profile that has a keyPath instead keeps using -i as it does today. Assert against cmd/e2e-sshd with a key-only host that the session authenticates and that no file outside the agent ever holds the key.

title: The completion dropdown advertises arrows that recall takes first
description:
The arbiter chain in terminal-content.ts is recall, then the vault picker, then completion, then the editor. A bare ArrowUp reaches recall first, whose gesture is 'up at the top of a single-line draft opens recall' — and opening recall dismisses the completion dropdown. So with the dropdown open and its footer advertising arrows to navigate, the arrows do something else entirely.

Same class as nocx-fijh and nocx-v03i, now between a different pair of surfaces: two surfaces over one input, and the loser keeps advertising what it cannot deliver (AGENTS.md, 'Look for the existing answer before you write a second one').

## Steps to Reproduce
Type 'ssh' so the dropdown opens with hosts and history, then press ArrowUp or ArrowDown: the selection does not move.

## Acceptance Criteria
While the completion dropdown is open it owns the arrows, because that is what its footer says; recall's bare-arrow gesture applies only when no dropdown is open, and the explicit recall shortcut still opens it from anywhere. The rule is stated in the arbiter rather than implied by call order, and a test drives ArrowUp and ArrowDown from the state the user is in — dropdown open under ssh — and asserts the selection moved and recall did not open.
notes:
Ownership rule landed as b181004, but the reported symptom was NOT reproduced in tests — arrows moved the selection before and after. Keep open until the live app is checked.
Backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh: moved from in_progress (untouched since 2026-08-05) back to open. The rule shipped — frontend/src/suggest/controller.ts:537 ownsArrows() with the arbiter consuming it at terminal-content.ts:5293, commit b1810047 — but this bead's OWN gate is unmet: the commit body says the reported symptom was not reproduced and that it pins the rule without proving it was the user's bug, and the bead note says to keep it open until the live app is checked. No evidence of that live check was found. Note also that the two tests covering the rule (terminal-content.test.ts:902, suggest/controller.test.ts:986) are tagged nocx-mlm7, not this bead.

title: A password a command asks for should be asked in nocx's dialog, through askpass — never guessed from the stream
description:
Owner request: when sudo (or ssh) asks for a password, show nocx's own prompt — the vault surface — and when the right secret is stored, let the user confirm instead of typing it.

The mechanism must be askpass, not detection. ADR-0004 rejects inferring 'a process is reading stdin' from the byte stream as unknowable, and AD-6 keeps the backend out of the stream entirely. sudo -A with SUDO_ASKPASS, and ssh with SSH_ASKPASS plus SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE=force, make the program itself call a helper we provide — no heuristics, no matching on the word Password.

The remote case is now reachable because the epic installs a bundle: the askpass helper can live beside ~/.nocx/launch and talk back over the channel that already exists.

What this deliberately does NOT cover: programs that read the tty directly and know nothing about askpass (su, mysql -p, passwd). Those stay an ordinary terminal, and nothing tries to guess for them.

## Acceptance Criteria
An askpass helper is delivered locally and, on an installed host, remotely; a command run through nocx that asks for a password raises nocx's prompt naming which password it wants (nocx-s8jn) and which command asked. A stored secret turns the prompt into a confirmation rather than a typing box, and the secret key distinguishes a host login password from a sudo password for the same account — using one where the other belongs is a defect, not a convenience. Declining or cancelling leaves the command to fail on its own terms. No code path matches text in the terminal stream to decide any of this, and a test asserts that removing the askpass environment leaves behaviour exactly as it is today.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
Merged with nocx-5175 on 2026-08-10 by owner decision: one mechanism, one owner. nocx-5175 was filed separately for the hand-typed ssh case; it is closed into this bead, which keeps sudo and ssh together because they are the same seam (SUDO_ASKPASS / SSH_ASKPASS + SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE=force) and a second helper would drift from the first.

What 5175 adds that this description did not carry:

- The local hand-typed ssh is reachable because nocx already composes the argv for a nested ssh (ADR-0022), so it can set the askpass variables without touching the user's environment permanently.
- The destination is known BEFORE the connection: host and user ride the domain_request (ADR-0025), so the secret lookup can happen up front and the dialog can offer a match rather than asking blind. This is the same lookup the profile path already does.
- SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE is OpenSSH 8.4+. Older clients ignore it and read the tty; that path must stay exactly as it is today.
- Open for the brief: where the LOCAL helper lives and how it authenticates back to the backend. It runs on the local machine as the user, so the lifecycle channel is not automatically the right carrier — unlike the remote case, where the helper can sit beside ~/.nocx/launch.
- A no-match must fall back to the client's own tty prompt. A broken helper must never make a host unreachable.

Acceptance criteria of 5175, folded in: typing 'ssh host' for a destination with a stored secret logs in through the vault dialog without the user typing anything; with no stored secret the user gets nocx's prompt and may choose to remember the answer; with the helper unavailable or refused the client prompts on the tty exactly as today; nothing anywhere matches the word 'password' in the output stream.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
Deferred by the owner on 2026-08-10, in favour of nocx-fk32.

The owner's ruling, verbatim in substance: 'Мы не знаем что там будет на экране' — nocx cannot know when a password is being asked, so the surface must be always available rather than offered at an inferred moment. The askpass seam would have removed that inference for ssh and sudo specifically, but the owner chose the simpler, more general answer first: a picker that inserts a saved secret into whatever is in front, which also covers every program askpass can never reach (su, mysql -p, passwd).

The reasoning that made the askpass half expensive, recorded so it is not re-derived:

1. sudo has no equivalent of SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE=force. It calls the helper only when invoked as 'sudo -A', so nocx would have to rewrite a line the user typed — a different authorisation question from composing its own ssh child line, and against ADR-0025's reasoning that the composer refuses options it does not model. sudoers policy (askpass, NOPASSWD, the timestamp cache) changes the behaviour visibly on top.
2. The secret CLASS differs: a sudo password for user@host is not the login password for the same account, and the bead itself calls confusing them a defect. Today's naming is user@host (ADR-0016/0017) and has no second dimension; adding one touches the Secrets page.
3. The remote half is deferred architecture, not an afternoon. The helper must run on the far host, the bundle publisher ships shell scripts rather than per-OS binaries, and the channel back is the shell's own per-domain capability — reusing it widens what that capability authorises, minting a second class is a protocol decision. architecture.md and AD-2 hold the Tier-B remote helper deferred; this is it.

Nothing here says askpass is wrong. It says the general surface comes first, and this bead should be re-read against what nocx-fk32 actually leaves wanting.

title: sudo su is not recognised as entering an environment, so the chips keep naming the shell you left
description:
environment-commands.ts recognises 'su' as a first token and 'sudo -i'/'sudo -s', but not 'sudo su' — the most common way to become root — nor 'sudo -u user -i', 'sudo bash', 'sudo -H su -'. So the entry is not tracked: the block chips keep naming the previous shell and cwd, the shell-integrated latch is not cleared (nocx goes on believing the marker contract holds while the new shell emits nothing), and on exit the environment stack has nothing to pop.

This is separate from nocx-eepi, which is about INTEGRATING such shells. This one is about noticing them, which is what keeps the product from lying about where you are.

## Steps to Reproduce
In an integrated shell run 'sudo su': the root prompt appears natively, and the block header still shows the previous user@host and cwd.

## Acceptance Criteria
The entry table recognises the common shapes of becoming another user — sudo su, sudo -u <user> (with or without a following shell), sudo <shell>, su - — and each marks the environment with an honest label. The shell-integrated latch is cleared on entry as it is for ssh, so no marker contract is assumed for a shell that never announced itself. What the table cannot classify confidently stays unrecognised rather than guessed, and a test names each accepted shape and one refused.

title: A hand-typed ssh ignores the saved connection it matches
description:
The completion dropdown offers saved connections as host rows, the user accepts one, and the line then runs as if nocx knew nothing about that host: no key, no port, no jump host. Saving a connection buys nothing on the path where nocx itself suggested it.

Warp behaves the same way we do in the parts that matter — same tab, plain OpenSSH, and it prompts for a password too — so the transport is NOT the thing to change (ADR-0022 and the OpenSSH-semantics argument stand). What is missing is that the profile's settings never reach the line we already rewrite.

## Acceptance Criteria
When a submitted simple interactive ssh resolves to a saved profile by the same identity the installed fact and the footprint surface use, the rewritten line carries that profile's connection settings: keyPath as -i, port as -p, user, and jumpHost as -J resolved through the profile it names. Anything the user typed explicitly WINS over the profile — a typed -p or -i is never overridden, and a typed flag we do not understand still refuses the rewrite entirely. A profile whose auth is an interactive password changes nothing about the prompt, and the product does not pretend otherwise: OpenSSH takes no password non-interactively and nocx will not feed one into a tty. Tests assert the argv OpenSSH receives, through the fake-ssh recorder that already exists.
close_reason: Landed as 60ee732: profile user/port/key/jump overlay the typed ssh line, typed flags win, matching by spelled host, wired into submit with the sync path preserved when no profile client exists

title: ssh history is capped at five rows to protect paths that no longer appear there
description:
providers.ts caps history at MAX_HISTORY_IN_ARGUMENT_POSITION (5) whenever position is argument and the session is local, and the comment states the reason: the path provider always answers there, so history is a sidebar that must not bury the paths. Since nocx-r35s, ssh argument position produces no path candidates at all, so the cap now squeezes history in the one place where it is the most useful thing on offer — a user's previous 'ssh user@host' lines.

## Steps to Reproduce
With more than five distinct ssh lines in history, type 'ssh ' in a local integrated tab: only five history rows appear, though nothing else is competing for the space.

## Acceptance Criteria
The sidebar cap applies only where the filesystem provider actually answers — gated on the same NO_FS_CANDIDATES table that decides that — so ssh argument position gets the full provider cap. A test asserts more than five ssh history rows survive in ssh argument position, and that the cap still holds for a command where paths do answer.
close_reason: Landed as f74cb83: the sidebar cap is gated on NO_FS_CANDIDATES, so ssh keeps the full 20 history rows and cd/ls keep 5; TDD, red at 5 before the gate

title: Arrows and Tab do nothing in the completion dropdown when the ssh hint list is also open
description:
editor.ts owns ArrowDown/ArrowUp/Enter/Escape whenever _hintItems is non-empty, and the completion dropdown has its own navigation. In ssh argument position both surfaces are live, so the keys are consumed by the hint list and the dropdown never sees them — while its own footer advertises them.

## Steps to Reproduce
Type 'ssh ' in a local integrated tab so the dropdown opens with its footer visible, then press ArrowDown, ArrowUp or Tab: the dropdown selection does not move.

## Acceptance Criteria
Exactly one surface owns those keys at any moment, decided deliberately rather than by which check runs first, and the footer never advertises a key the surface will not receive. A test drives the keys from the state a user is in (dropdown open under ssh) and asserts the selection moves.
close_reason: Landed as 2d0e0e4: the completion dropdown owns the keys and the alias hint list no longer opens under ssh, so the footer is true by construction; 193 tests green including a seam test driving ArrowDown through editor+arbiter

title: ssh offers directories from the local filesystem, ranked above the host it should offer
description:
fsProvider.applicable returns true for every argument position, and the DIRECTORIES_ONLY table can only narrow cd/pushd/rmdir to directories — nothing excludes paths under ssh. So 'ssh ' offers Downloads/, go/, orca/, repos/ ABOVE root@192.168.0.57, which is the one candidate kind that makes sense there. fd68cd2 (nocx-n9i6) promised 'ssh offers hosts, not shell history and file paths'.

## Steps to Reproduce
In a local integrated tab type 'ssh ' and look at the dropdown: directory rows labelled 'Directory path' appear, ranked above the host row.

## Acceptance Criteria
In ssh argument position the filesystem provider does not run at all (a path is not a destination), hosts and ssh history are what the dropdown offers, and a test asserts no candidate of kind path is produced for that position. The exclusion is a table that grows by addition, like DIRECTORIES_ONLY, not an if buried in a provider.
close_reason: Landed as 2d0e0e4: NO_FS_CANDIDATES table beside DIRECTORIES_ONLY gates fsProvider on commandWord, so ssh produces zero path candidates

title: P11 End to end: a hand-typed ssh becomes blocks on the far host
description: Package P11 of .internal/specs/2026-08-05-nocxify-delivery-modes-design.md (section 10). Read that spec first — it is committed on this branch.
acceptance_criteria: One e2e run against cmd/e2e-sshd: first connection shows the long bootstrap line and remote blocks from the first remote prompt; the second sends the compact launch line; auth failure stays raw with the real exit status; exit returns the local editor; remote rc files are byte-identical afterwards.
close_reason: Landed as 5cd8227: e2e/nocxify-journey.spec.ts proves all seven criteria against a real sshd, twice, ~6s each; three red runs found a passwd-home ssh_config resolution, a canvas-vs-DOM observability error, and a CR overwriting the fixture banner

title: P9 The ssh block is local and ends at entry; only a local D pops the environment
description: Package P9 of .internal/specs/2026-08-05-nocxify-delivery-modes-design.md (section 10). Read that spec first — it is committed on this branch.
acceptance_criteria: Every row of section 6.1 holds: entry only on expected passport then tagged A then B; the ssh block carries the local cwd and host; a remote D closes a remote command and does not pop; a local D pops and completes the transition record; POSIX orphan D, tmux markers and nested ssh (raw at depth>0) change nothing; Ctrl-D with no running remote block still restores the parent environment.

title: A large paste into the editor may be truncated on the way to the pty
description:
Discovered while fixing nocx-pu4.6 (2026-08-05), and NOT closed by it.

nocx-pu4.6 was reopened because a 35 KB rewritten line came back truncated at
27873 bytes and the shell executed the fragments. The reopening attributed it to
the canonical line buffer (N_TTY_BUF_SIZE, 4096). That ceiling is real and I
re-measured it independently — pty + cat, echo on: 4095 bytes survive intact,
4096 loses one byte, 8000 returns 12095 of 16000 echoed+catted, 35243 returns
39338 of 70486.

But the local shell in nocx is NOT a canonical-mode reader. It is bash at a
readline prompt, and readline puts the tty in RAW mode, where MAX_CANON does not
apply. Measured in internal/shellintegration/stage_pty_test.go's harness: a
single 35243-byte write to the pty master, into a real interactive bash, arrived
COMPLETE — argv reached the child byte-identical. So the harness could not
reproduce the owner's truncation through that seam.

Which means the mechanism that truncated the product is still unidentified. The
candidates the harness does not exercise are all on the renderer's side of the
paste, and they are shared by EVERY paste, not just the ssh rewrite:

  - xterm.js paste() chunking or an input-buffer cap in the renderer;
  - the websocket data frame path (frontend/src/ipc.ts) splitting or dropping;
  - a short write to the pty master in the backend that is not looped.

Why this matters on its own: the editor invites multi-line composition and
people paste long commands and heredocs into it. If a large paste silently loses
its tail, the shell runs a fragment — the same failure the screenshot showed,
reachable without ssh being involved at all.

nocx-pu4.6 is not blocked on this. Its fix removed the payload from the tty
entirely (145-273 bytes now cross it), so it is below every candidate threshold
regardless of which one is real. This bead is the unanswered question, filed so
it does not evaporate between rounds.

## Steps to Reproduce

Measure, do not reason. Drive the REAL product path, not a Go pty harness:

1. Start the backend headless (cmd/devharness) and open a local integrated tab.
2. Paste a single-line payload of a known size into the command editor and
   submit it — a line that ECHOES its own byte count, e.g.
   `x=<N bytes of a repeated character>; printf '%s\\n' ${#x}`.
3. Repeat at 4 KB, 8 KB, 32 KB and 128 KB.
4. Compare the count the shell prints against the count that was pasted, and
   record the first size at which they differ.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The size at which the product's paste path first loses bytes is MEASURED and
  the number is written down, or it is shown that no loss occurs up to 128 KB.
- If a layer loses bytes, it is fixed, and a test asserts the measured threshold
  rather than a reasoned one.
- If nothing is lost, this bead closes stating that — and the reopening comment
  on nocx-pu4.6 gets a correction, because the mechanism it named would then not
  be the one that fired.

title: A host you reached by hand offers to become a connection, on its own block
description:
Owner, 2026-08-04: 'А почему мы не предлагаем создать соединение? Может сделать также, как и для vault мы сейчас предлагаем сохранить секрет'.

Yes — and the pattern is already built and already documented, so this is a second caller for it rather than a new invention. frontend/src/ui/block-receipt.ts states the contract in its own header: attached to the FROZEN BLOCK of the command that occasioned it, never floated over the prompt; not modal, does not steal focus or a keystroke; one primary action whose label names its scope; it does not expire, living on its block until answered or until a real destruction event takes it; several blocks can carry an unanswered receipt at once, 'because deciding about a key is rarely the next thing anyone does'. Its own comment names the reference: the way Bitwarden offers to save a password after the form is submitted.

Every one of those properties is what this offer needs, and one of them is load-bearing here in a way it was not for secrets: an offer on a BLOCK cannot land in the password window, which is what killed the dialog in nocx-atyf.3.

## Why this is the more valuable offer

nocx-pu4.6 makes a hand-typed ssh integrate, which gives blocks. It cannot give what only a MANAGED connection has: a connection nocx dials itself, and therefore a second exec channel — port discovery (internal/ssh.DiscoveryConn), forwards, remote completion (nocx-w7h.15). A child ssh process has no control channel and never will. So 'save this as a connection' is the step that unlocks the rest of the product for a host the user found by hand.

## Shape

The receipt component takes vault-shaped captures today. Either it grows a second content kind, or the kit gains a sibling that shares its behaviour contract — decide deliberately and record which, per ui/README.md: the kit grows by variants, never by near-duplicates.

Dismissal must persist across sessions (a per-destination note in settings), not just for the tab: an offer that returns on every ssh to the same box is the nag this design exists to avoid.
acceptance_criteria: After a hand-typed `ssh user@host` to a destination that is not already a saved profile, that command's block carries an offer to save it as a connection, with an editable pre-filled name. Accepting creates the profile and the next connection to that host is managed — ports, forwards and silent launcher integration. Dismissing is remembered for that destination so it is never offered again. The offer never floats over the prompt, never steals focus or a keystroke, never expires on a timer, and several blocks may carry an unanswered one at once. A destination that IS already a profile gets no offer — one test proves the absence.
close_reason: Closed

title: Use terminal input for this session: discoverable without knowing our vocabulary
description:
Codex: palette-only assumes the user knows both that the mode exists and what vocabulary to search for. The context menu is the discoverability layer that assumption skips.

Also: do not label it 'Use native input'. 'Native' is ambiguous here — native to what? Name the thing the user gets: terminal input. And scope it in the label, because a session escape hatch and a product default are different decisions and the label is where users learn which one they are making.
acceptance_criteria: The escape hatch is reachable from the tab/terminal context menu AND the command palette, labelled 'Use terminal input for this session'. Switching is immediate and reversible; the way back reads 'Use nocx command editor' and is offered from the same two places. The choice is session-scoped and does not persist globally unless the user changes a Settings preference — one test proves a new session is unaffected.
close_reason: Terminal/editor input switching from the context menu and the palette, session-scoped.

title: A running command looks running on the POSIX tier — app-owned start, shell-owned end
description:
nocx.posix emits A, B and D with a real exit status plus OSC 7, verified against dash 0.5.12 and busybox ash 1.37.0. C (command started) is unreachable through portable prompt hooks and is deliberately not faked, so a block currently appears already finished — the user never sees that something is running.

Codex challenged the premise, and it is right: nocx knows when its OWN editor submitted the command, and D supplies the authoritative completion and exit status. App-owned start, shell-owned end. That fabricates nothing and sniffs nothing, and the distinction stays explicit in the internal model.

Presenting a completed-looking block while the command may still be running is materially false state, not minor polish.
acceptance_criteria: On dash and busybox ash, a command submitted through the editor is shown as RUNNING from submit until D arrives, and finished with the real exit status afterwards. No OSC 133 C is fabricated, no byte stream is read, and the internal model still records that C was never received. If a case exists where submit cannot mark the start, the limitation is disclosed ONCE contextually at the first affected block, dismissible — never per command and never as a permanent warning.
close_reason: App-owned block start: a command looks running from submit until D, so the POSIX tier stops showing already-finished blocks. No OSC 133 C fabricated.

title: A hand-typed transition offers integration once, and the answer is remembered per destination
description:
The owner proposed silent in-band injection everywhere. Codex disagreed and we accepted the disagreement.

'Leaves no file' is too narrow a definition of harmless. Behind `ssh host` there may be a restricted shell, an appliance CLI, a production console, a bastion workflow, a forced command or an audited environment; the real destination can differ from the command text because of ssh config, proxies and server-side policy; the wrapper line lands in audit logs and shell history; and the bootstrap changes the live shell process — prompt, environment, hooks, input mode — even changing no file.

Decisive: ADR-0004's scope note, written 2026-08-04, states that the authorisation for in-band delivery IS the explicit user gesture. Silent injection reverses an accepted trust decision. If we want it, we change the ADR deliberately — we do not quietly redefine 'user initiated' to mean 'the user typed ssh once'.

Remembering per DESTINATION (profile / resolved host), not globally by raw hostname text, is what makes 'integration everywhere' true without asking twice. A global 'automatically integrate shells reached from the command editor' setting is legitimate as an informed opt-in, not as the default.
acceptance_criteria: A profile-launched session integrates silently with nothing on screen announcing it. After a simple hand-typed interactive transition the user is offered it ONCE, in context; accepting is remembered for that DESTINATION so later transitions there are silent. It is never offered or attempted for a remote command, a redirection, a pipeline, non-interactive ssh, or an alt-screen state — anything nocx cannot classify confidently. ADR-0004's scope note is extended in the same commit to state what authorises in-band delivery and why remembered consent counts. The wording is 'Use nocx command editor' / 'Enable command blocks for this shell' — never 'install'.
close_reason: A hand-typed ssh transition offers integration once and the answer is remembered per destination. One ssh parser for the product: environment-commands.ts delegates to ssh-transition.ts (merge resolution 15cbda5).

title: Retire the capability rail: recovery actions live in the editor's own chip row
description:
The owner's five complaints about what nocx-4t37.2 shipped, all correct: the rail permanently eats a row of terminal output for a status label; the editor already has a chip row answering the same question, so this is a second vocabulary in a second place; the FloatingPanel popover renders as a full-width banner that pushes the pane down; on a tab with no editor it floats bottom-left over the terminal; and the action it offered was refused by the gate with a toast.

Codex: do not use 'Native input', 'Enhanced input' and 'Command blocks' as three peer modes — they expose our internal taxonomy and make the user decode the difference. The meaningful distinction is binary: nocx can present its editor here, or this is currently a conventional terminal. Name the recovery action, not the state.

THE INVARIANT, and it alone kills the worst defect: every visible action is executable from the state in which it is shown. If prerequisites are absent the action is OMITTED. Clicking an offered action never produces a prerequisite-rejection message.

A tab warning mark is for an UNEXPECTED loss of integration only, never for a deliberate terminal-mode choice.
acceptance_criteria: The nocx-capability-rail element and the 'capability' FloatingPanel variant are gone. In the healthy state nothing on screen mentions integration — one test asserts the absence. In an exception state a single control appears in the editor's existing chip row beside the host and cwd chips, its label names the RECOVERY ACTION ('Enable command editor', 'Retry integration', 'Restore command editor'), and clicking performs it directly with no popover. The words 'Native input', 'Enhanced input' and 'Command blocks' appear nowhere in the UI. On a tab with no editor chrome there is NO floating chip — the action is in the tab context menu and the palette instead.
close_reason: Rail, popover and floating chip gone; recovery actions in the editor chrome row, the chip IS the action. Healthy state shows nothing and a test asserts the absence.

title: Three axes, not one capability: delivery, observed shell state, input presentation
description:
Codex, 2026-08-04, on why the rejected rail's offer and gate disagreed: we collapsed three independent axes into one 'capability'.

- Delivery: launcher / in-band bootstrap / Tier B relay.
- Observed shell state: eligible, integrating, integrated, lost, unsupported, failed.
- Input presentation: nocx editor / conventional terminal.

A shell can emit useful markers while the user has deliberately selected terminal input. A shell can be ELIGIBLE for integration without nocx being AUTHORISED to inject it. One axis cannot say either thing.
