Second, separate authorisation from technical trust. A trusted top-level prompt answers 'is it technically safe for nocx to own input'. It does not answer 'has the user authorised nocx to submit a bootstrap command'. The rejected UI mixed them: it offered an authorised-looking action whose technical eligibility was denied later.
acceptance_criteria: The model carries three independent values, and one test shows a combination the old single axis could not express — a shell emitting markers while the user deliberately sits in terminal input. The action set is derived only AFTER both authorisation and technical eligibility are resolved, and one test asserts an action is absent (not disabled-then-rejected) when its prerequisites are false.
close_reason: Three axes: delivery, observed shell state, input presentation. Action set derived only after authorisation AND technical eligibility.

title: [epic] Integration just happens, and the UI speaks only when it must
description:
The capability rail shipped in nocx-4t37.2 and the owner rejected it on sight, with five correct complaints: it permanently eats a row of terminal output for a status label; the editor ALREADY has a chip row saying where you are, so the capability chip is a second vocabulary for one question in a second place; its popover renders as a full-width banner that pushes the pane down; on a tab with no editor it floats bottom-left over the terminal; and clicking 'Integrate this shell' produced the toast 'only available from a trusted prompt' — an offered action the gate refused.

Consulted codex 2026-08-04. Its diagnosis of the root cause: we collapsed THREE independent axes into one 'capability' — the delivery path (launcher / in-band / relay), the observed shell state (eligible, integrating, integrated, lost, unsupported, failed), and the input presentation (nocx editor / conventional terminal). A shell can emit markers while the user deliberately sits in terminal input; a shell can be eligible while nocx is not authorised to write into it. One axis cannot describe that, which is exactly how the offer and the gate came to disagree.

Its second finding, and the more valuable one: we do not need OSC 133 C. nocx knows when its OWN editor submitted the command, and D carries the authoritative end and exit status. App-owned start, shell-owned end — no faked marker, no stream sniffing. The 'blocks appear already finished on POSIX' limitation is induced, not inherent.

Its disagreement with the owner and with me, which we accepted: silent in-band injection after every hand-typed ssh is wrong even though it leaves no trace. Behind `ssh host` there may be a restricted shell, an appliance CLI, a production console, a forced command or an audited environment; the real destination can differ from the command text because of ssh config and proxies; the wrapper line lands in audit logs and history; and the bootstrap changes the live shell process. Decisive: ADR-0004's scope note (written 2026-08-04) states that the authorisation for in-band delivery IS the explicit user gesture. Injecting silently reverses an accepted decision without changing the document.
acceptance_criteria:
A user connects from a saved profile and gets command blocks with nothing on screen announcing it. A user who types `ssh host` into the editor is asked ONCE, and after answering yes that destination is silent forever. A user on busybox sees a running command look like it is running. A user who wants a plain terminal finds the way there without knowing our vocabulary, and finds the way back. And every action the UI offers can be taken from the state it is offered in — clicking one never produces a prerequisite-rejection message.

One end-to-end check watches the whole arc against a real bash on a real PTY (cmd/e2e-sshd): connect, blocks appear with no announcement, switch to terminal input, switch back.

Deliberately out: the Tier B relay itself (nocx-if6 phase B) — only the shape of its consent card is decided here.
close_reason: All five children merged (15cbda5). The rail is gone, the vocabulary is gone, the offer is once-per-destination, the POSIX tier shows a running command as running, and the escape hatch is discoverable. Merge resolution unified two ssh parsers into one.

title: A forward you started from the palette is invisible once its tab is gone
description:
Owner, 2026-08-04: 'если мы форварднули порт, где посмотреть что именно мы форварднули и убрать их?'

The answer today is 'the Ports panel', and it is only PART of an answer. The panel's target comes from the active tab: TabManager.portsTargetId() returns activeTerminalContent()?.portsTargetId, and every call is ports.status(profileId) / ports.sample(profileId) scoped to it. The Forwarded section (copy / open / stop) and the Stopped section are also behind Show when={!isLocal()}.

So a forward is visible exactly while a tab for its host is the active tab. nocx-4t37.1 then shipped 'Forward a port' in the palette, which opens a forward with scope palette:<profileId> and needs no tab at all — tunnel.open resolves the profile and dials its own connection. Start one that way and there is no surface in the product that lists it or stops it. The same holds for a forward whose tab was closed while the forward kept running.

A forward is a process-lifetime resource holding a local port. A resource the user can create and cannot find is worse than one they cannot create.

Design note before building: this is an argument for one place that answers 'what have I forwarded, anywhere' rather than for widening the per-tab panel. Whether that is a target selector on the existing panel or a distinct surface is the deliverable's first decision — make it deliberately and record it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the palette (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P), run 'Forward a port', pick a saved server and a port.
2. Make sure no tab for that server is the active tab (close it, or never open one).
3. Open the Ports panel. The forward is not listed, and there is no way to stop it.
acceptance_criteria: Every running forward is reachable and stoppable from somewhere that does not depend on a tab being open — including one started from the palette with no tab for that host, and one whose tab was closed while it kept running. It names its host, its bind, its destination and its direction. Proven with a forward started from the palette when no tab for that host exists at all.

title: The ports panel shows the local machine's ports while the pane is on a remote host
description:
Owner, 2026-08-04, screenshot: a local tab sitting at pi@raspberrypi's prompt after a hand-typed ssh, and the Ports panel listing 0.0.0.0:22, 127.0.0.53:53, orca-ide, devharness — the BACKEND machine's listeners, under a tab titled pi@raspberrypi, with nothing saying whose they are.

The panel picks its target from the SESSION KIND (a local session resolves to LOCAL_TARGET_ID), which is a tab-lifetime fact.

Know the honest limit before designing: remote discovery runs over internal/ssh.DiscoveryConn, which needs a MANAGED connection from a profile — a second exec channel on a connection we own. A hand-typed ssh is a child process of the local shell; there is no control channel to it, so that host's ports cannot be enumerated at all, integrated or not. The fix is not 'show the remote ports here'. The fix is that the panel stops lying.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. In a local tab, submit `ssh user@host`.
2. Open the Ports panel.
3. It lists the backend machine's listeners, presented under the remote host's tab title.
acceptance_criteria: The panel never presents one machine's listeners as another's: it names whose ports it is showing. Where the pane's current environment cannot be enumerated, it says that and why, and names what would change it. Proven with a local tab that has entered a remote shell by hand.
close_reason: The panel names its subject as a kit Badge (ebee5ef), and the target now follows the environment (d127640): inside a shell reached by hand it goes null and the panel names the host it cannot see plus what would change it, instead of showing this machine's listeners under that tab. Enumerating a hand-typed remote stays impossible by construction — no managed connection, no second exec channel — and the panel says so.

title: The pane tracks the environment it is in, not the one the tab started in
description:
The structural core the other three children read.

Today `_shellIntegrated` (frontend/src/terminal-content.ts) is a fact about the tab's lifetime: set true the first time markers arrive and never cleared. Inside a nested shell it is still true, so deriveCapability reports 'enhanced-input' — 'the shell speaks our protocol, nocx just does not own the prompt right now' — when nocx has NO evidence whatsoever about the shell now on stdin.

What we may know without breaking AD-6: we submitted the line ourselves (ADR-0004 §2 hands it to the PTY atomically at submit), and no D has arrived, so the thing we launched has not returned. Neither is inspection of the byte stream.

Recognise: ssh, docker exec, podman exec, kubectl exec, su, sudo -i/-s, nix-shell, tmux, screen. Conservative by design — a missed offer is invisible and cheap; a wrong one is noise on every `sleep 5`.
acceptance_criteria: A submitted command that enters a new environment clears the pane's marker-arrived fact for the duration; the D that ends it restores what was true before. The recognised set lives in ONE named place with a comment that it grows by addition, and the default for an unknown command is 'not an environment change'. input-state.ts is unchanged — one test asserts the machine's transitions are identical.
close_reason: Closed

title: The tab title and the location chip name where you actually are
description:
Owner, 2026-08-04, screenshot: `exit` from a hand-typed ssh, 'Connection to 192.168.0.93 closed.', a fresh local prompt — and the tab still reads `pi@raspberrypi: ~`.

The title is whatever the last OSC 2 set, and the remote shell set it on the way in. Nothing resets it on the way out, because nothing knows there was a way out. Depends on the environment fact from the core child.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. In a local tab, submit `ssh user@host`.
2. Land at the remote prompt — the tab adopts the remote title.
3. Type `exit`. The prompt is local again; the tab title is not.
acceptance_criteria: Leaving an environment restores the title the pane had before entering it, within one prompt. Entering one adopts the new environment's title. No title outlives the environment that set it.
close_reason: The tab title, the location chip and the cwd chip all follow the environment now: entering adopts the destination we parsed from the line we submitted, the D that ends the command restores what was there before. The cwd goes BLANK inside a nested environment rather than keeping a local path that is now false — we know the host, not the directory. Merged d127640.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
Widened by the owner 2026-08-04: 'мы же должны добавлять бейдж, когда мы через ssh общаемся, чтобы было видно?'

Yes, and the mechanism already exists — it just never fires here. editor.ts builds `locationChip` (`nocx-chip nocx-chip-muted nocx-editor-location`) and hides it until setLocation receives a value, so a MANAGED ssh session grows the chip and a local tab correctly grows none. A shell reached by a hand-typed `ssh` is a local session, so the chip stays hidden and the pane looks like home while the prompt is on the Pi.

We can fill it honestly without integration and without sniffing: we submitted the line, so we know the destination. The cwd we do NOT know until OSC 7 arrives, and the chip must not invent one — a host with no cwd is the truthful shape here.

So this bead now covers both surfaces that name a place: the TAB TITLE (restore what it was on the way out; adopt on the way in) and the LOCATION CHIP (name the environment we entered, for as long as we are inside it). Both read nocx-695k.1's environment fact, which has landed.

Also: nocx-695k.3 shipped the honest half — the ports panel now names its subject as a chip, so nothing implies the rows belong to the tab's title. The rest of .3 (follow the environment, and say when the environment cannot be enumerated at all) still needs the environment fact plumbed to the panel's target.

title: [epic] The pane says where you are, and it is right
description:
Three reports from the owner on 2026-08-04, one root cause.

1. Typing `ssh pi@192.168.0.93` in a local tab: no offer to integrate, no blocks, nothing (nocx-pu4.4).
2. The Ports panel goes on listing the BACKEND machine's listeners — 0.0.0.0:22, orca-ide, devharness — under a tab titled pi@raspberrypi, with no statement of whose they are.
3. After `exit`, the tab is still titled `pi@raspberrypi: ~` while the pane is back on the local machine.

Every surface that names a place reads a fact about the TAB'S LIFETIME — the session kind, the sticky integrated flag, a title the remote shell set once — when the thing it must describe is the ENVIRONMENT CURRENTLY ON STDIN. terminal-content.ts's own `_mountRail` states the false premise out loud: 'a local shell's capability is static (always our own, always integrated)'.

Two facts are ours without touching the byte stream (AD-6): we submitted the line (ADR-0004 §2 hands it over atomically at submit, so the renderer knows what it sent), and the input-state machine knows no D has arrived. That is the seam.
acceptance_criteria:
In a local tab the user submits `ssh <host>`, and the tab title, the ports panel and the capability chip all agree the pane is on that host. The user types `exit`, and all three go back to the local machine within one prompt. Where nocx cannot see a place (a hand-typed ssh has no managed connection, so no DiscoveryConn), it says so and names what would change it — it never presents one machine's facts as another's. One end-to-end check watches exactly that round trip against a real bash on a real PTY (cmd/e2e-sshd).

Deliberately out: enumerating a hand-typed remote host's ports (there is no control channel to a child ssh process), and environments entered by typing raw into xterm in native mode (we did not submit the line and genuinely do not know).
close_reason: The pane says where you are: environment fact (695k.1), tab title + location chip + cwd (695k.2), ports panel subject and target (695k.3). Merged 3f91a08 and earlier.

title: Complete remote paths over the connection we already hold
description:
Path completion stops at the network boundary: `fs.complete` reads the backend's
own filesystem, so `fsProvider` is gated to local sessions and a remote tab gets
nothing.

The mechanism that was missing now exists. `internal/ssh.DiscoveryConn` is an
owned pooled lease that runs a bounded command on a second exec channel without
touching the user's shell — built for port discovery and not specific to it.
Remote completion is the same shape: a bounded listing of one directory,
answered from the host the user is actually on.

Design notes worth carrying from discovery: the probe must not assume a tool
(`ls` dialects differ; the shell's own globbing may be the better oracle), the
output needs framing that rejects a banner-polluted response whole rather than
half-parsing it, and the result must be capped.

`fs.complete` gains a target the way `ports.*` did, rather than a second method.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `cd /` on an SSH tab lists the remote root, asserted against a real SSH server.
- A local tab's behaviour is byte-identical to today.
- A host where the listing cannot be obtained says so, and never falls back to
  local paths.
- One directory listing is bounded in both rows and bytes.
close_reason: Duplicate of nocx-w7h.15, which was filed 2026-08-02 and is the better design: it answers remote paths through the shell's own completion machinery rather than a listing we reimplement, and the same mechanism also answers subcommands, dynamic completers and the user's own completions. Its acceptance criteria already name remote-filesystem completion over SSH verbatim. Filed without checking — AGENTS.md check 1.

title: Path completion is off on a remote host, and the product says 'No matches' instead of why
description:
Owner, 2026-08-04, with a screenshot of `cd /` on an SSH tab answering
"No matches".

Two separate things, and the first is not a defect.

**Path completion is deliberately off on a remote session.** `fsProvider`'s
applicability opens with `if (!ctx.isLocal) return false`
(`frontend/src/suggest/providers.ts:298`), and `fs.complete` in the transport is
`completeLocalPath` — the backend's own filesystem. The gate exists so a local
path can never masquerade as a remote one
(`terminal-content.ts:406`, design §8.5), and it is right: silently offering the
developer's `/etc` while the user is on someone else's server would be worse
than offering nothing.

**What is a defect is the sentence.** `EmptyReason` exists precisely so zero
candidates is a state the product explains rather than a silence — and here the
truth is not "nothing matched", it is "path completion does not work on a remote
host yet". The user read the generic message and concluded the feature was
broken, which is the correct conclusion from what we told them.

Remote path completion itself is `nocx-w7h.x` — the seam now exists (an owned
pooled lease and a second exec channel, `internal/ssh.DiscoveryConn`), so it no
longer needs a new mechanism.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open an SSH tab.
2. Type `cd /` and ask for completion.
3. "No matches" — with no indication that paths are a local-only capability.

## Acceptance Criteria

- On a remote session the empty state names the reason rather than claiming
  nothing matched.
- The local-path gate is unchanged: a local path must never be offered for a
  remote cwd.

title: A draft that crossed hosts should say so before Enter
description:
Review, 2026-08-04, and the one idea that falls out of something only nocx has:
trustworthy remote environment identity bound to the pending command.

The context rail becomes part of the editor rather than ambient chrome — the
draft is visually bound to where it will run:

```
deploy@production · /srv/api · Enhanced input
──────────────────────────────────────────────
$ systemctl restart api
```

If the environment changes while the draft survives — tab switch, nested shell,
markers lost — updating the label is not enough. The draft is marked as having
crossed context:

```
Draft began on staging:/srv/api
Enter would now run on production:/srv/api       [Review]
```

`nocx-3779` already renders the location and already degrades it to "context
unknown" on trust loss; this is that chip growing a memory of where the draft
started.

ADR-0004 is untouched: Enter is never blocked categorically and nothing is
auto-submitted. A lightweight acknowledgement is the whole feature.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A draft carries the environment it was begun in.
- Changing environment with a non-empty draft surfaces the crossing, naming both
  sides.
- Acknowledging clears it; the draft is preserved byte-for-byte throughout.
- Nothing is blocked and nothing is auto-submitted (ADR-0004 fail-open).

title: A service is a consequence of a command, not an entry in an inventory
description:
Review, 2026-08-04: the novel move in the ports panel is not better discovery —
it is connecting a listening service to the command interval during which it
appeared. Other products show ports as infrastructure inventory; nocx can show
them as consequences of work, because it has trusted command boundaries on a
remote host with no server footprint.

The sentence is already in the spec (§9, D6) as an incidental future offer. It
should be the primary interaction:

```
npm run dev                                      running
● :3000  vite  · appeared during this command   [Forward]
```

after forwarding:

```
● localhost:49172 → host:3000                    [Open] [Copy] [Stop]
```

and when the command exits:

```
○ localhost:49172 · command ended · forward still active
```

That last state carries the weight: do not silently stop the tunnel and do not
let it keep looking healthy. D6 still holds — the ledger labels, it never claims
causation. "Appeared while X was running" is true; "opened by X" is not.

The sidebar becomes the aggregate ledger, and selection is bidirectional:
picking a port scrolls to and emphasises its block; picking a block's service
reveals it in the panel.

First version needs only a trusted command interval, the honest wording,
one-click forward, and the receipt updating when either side stops. No process
ancestry, no traffic counters, no protocol detection.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A listener that appears during a trusted command interval is attached to that
  command's block, with wording that never claims causation.
- Forwarding from the block is one action, and the receipt follows the tunnel
  and the command independently.
- A forward outliving its command says so rather than disappearing or looking
  healthy.
- Selecting a panel row reveals its block, and vice versa.

title: An offer appears where the capability is relevant, and remembers being refused
description:
The primitive both offers need: one dismissible, in-context offer attached to a
tab, shown at the moment it becomes relevant and never again once refused.

Two first users:

- **Integrate this shell.** The tab is at a prompt and no markers have arrived,
  so integration is available and absent. Warp does exactly this when you enter
  a server without warpify.
- **Save this as a connection.** A host was reached by a hand-typed `ssh` and is
  neither a saved profile nor an alias.

The gate does not move: accepting an offer still runs the existing
`shell.integrate` path with its trusted A→B prompt window, because consent
changes authorisation, not the identity of the foreground process. The offer is
about discovery, not permission.

Do not infer any of this by sniffing the byte stream (AD-6). The absence of
markers is already known to the input-state machine.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A user who has never read the docs is offered integration on an unintegrated
  shell and gets blocks after accepting — end to end, one automated check.
- Refusing hides it and it does not return for that host in that session.
- The offer never appears on a shell that is already integrated.
- The component lives in `ui/` with its CSS file, identity class, test and
  README row — it has two callers on day one.
close_reason: Capability statement above the pending command (native input / command blocks / enhanced input), the markerless integration gate split into two named authorisations with the scope note in ADR-0004 §1, and profile.ShellIntegrationMode finally enforced — it had shipped with no behavioral consumer. Happy path watched end to end against a real bash on a real PTY behind an in-process sshd. Merged 6311746.

title: One palette, prefix-scoped: commands are not hosts
description:
`Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P` opens quick connect, which carries "Local shell", "New
connection" and (until now) "Integrate this shell" and "Ports" beside SSH hosts
and aliases. It is neither a host picker nor a command palette.

One surface, two modes, the model people already have from VS Code: a `>`
prefix means commands, no prefix means hosts. One implementation, one chord to
remember, and the mode is visible in the input rather than in the user's head.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P` opens the palette in command mode with `>` present;
  clearing the prefix returns to hosts in the same surface.
- Every action currently in `ActionsQuickConnectProvider` is a command, not a
  host row, and none of them appear when the query has no prefix.
- An ad-hoc `user@host` still connects from host mode, and a saved profile
  still outranks an alias.
- A test asserts a user can reach a command from the state they start in.
close_reason: Palette rebuilt to the Raycast model: one field, mixed typed rows, drill-in for target-needing commands (Forward a port: server -> port -> tunnel.open). Caret keeps the plain server list. Merged 86eeb39, 1886/1886 frontend green.

title: You are offered what you did not know to ask for
description:
Owner, 2026-08-04: *"зачем нам ручная интеграция? Вот warp когда входишь на
сервер без warpify предлагает на него его поставить... В quick connect оно
зачем? Это странно."*

Two problems that look separate and share one cause: we put a capability where
only someone who already knew about it would look.

**A palette serves what you know you want. An offer serves what you do not know
exists.** "Integrate this shell" is the second kind — nobody searches a palette
for a feature they have never heard of — so it belongs at the moment it becomes
relevant, not in a list. The same is true of saving a host you just reached by
hand.

And the palette itself: `Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P` currently opens **quick connect**,
which grew action items until it was neither a host picker nor a command
palette. That is the strangeness the owner names.

## Success Criteria

- A user lands on an unintegrated shell and is offered integration in context,
  without having read anything.
- The offer is refusable and the refusal is remembered.
- Commands and hosts stop sharing one undifferentiated list.
- The integration gate is unchanged: consent changes authorisation, not the
  identity of the foreground process.

Out: rewriting the `ssh` command before it runs; auto-integrating without
consent; anything that infers state by sniffing the byte stream (AD-6).
acceptance_criteria:
A user who has never read the docs lands on an unintegrated shell, is offered
integration in context, accepts, and gets blocks — proven end to end by one
automated check. And a command they know they want is found in one palette,
which no longer mixes commands with hosts.

title: Typing ssh by hand gets you a plain shell, and nothing offers to fix it
description:
Owner, 2026-08-04, with a screenshot of `ssh pi@192.168.0.93` in a local tab:
no blocks, no markers, no prompt of any kind.

`shell.integrate` (nocx-ynsx) is exactly the cure and it is **manual** — the
palette item and Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+I. A user who does not know it exists gets a
plain terminal and no reason to think anything is available. The capability
shipped; the moment where a person would use it did not.

The gate must not weaken: consent changes authorisation, not the identity of
the foreground process, so integration still happens only inside a trusted A→B
prompt window. But the OFFER can be made where the offer is obviously right —
a tab that is at a prompt, is not integrated, and got there through a command
the user typed.

Do not infer this by sniffing the byte stream (AD-6). The absence of markers is
already known to the input-state machine without reading anything.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. In a local tab, type `ssh user@host`.
2. Land at the remote prompt. No blocks, no cwd, no hint that integration
   exists.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A user who has never read the docs discovers integration from the product.
- The offer is refusable and the refusal sticks for that session at least.
- The trusted-window gate is unchanged; nothing auto-types into a shell that
  might not be a shell.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text: Retargeted 2026-08-04: this is symptom 1 of nocx-695k ('The pane says where you are, and it is right'), whose core child nocx-695k.1 makes the environment a first-class fact. The offer cannot be built correctly without it — today integrateShell() refuses this case from BOTH named authorisations (integrated path needs PROMPT_READY, we are RUNNING_RAW; markerless path needs !_shellIntegrated, which the local shell set true). Also note the bead's line 'integration still happens only inside a trusted A→B prompt window' predates nocx-4t37.2 and is superseded by the two-named-authorisations ruling recorded in ADR-0004 §1.

title: The panel never asks for the local target, so local ports still do not show
description:
The backend answers `ports.*` for the literal target `"local"` (nocx-wzc4.8:
`discovery.LocalTargetID`, native per-OS module, same result shape, `forwards`
always empty). The panel still maps a tab without a profile to `profileId ===
null` and renders "No active connection", so nothing reaches the user.

Worker A's handoff shape, verbatim: a local tab calls `ports.status`/`sample`/
`pause`/`visible` with `profileId: "local"`; `host` is the machine's hostname;
`probe` is `linux-procfs` / `darwin-lsof` / `windows-getextendedtcptable`;
permission-denied evidence arrives identically to remote and must render
identically — it is a fact about privilege, not an error on the user's own
machine.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a local tab and the Ports view.
2. "No active connection", while the backend would answer for `"local"`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A local tab shows this machine's listeners, asserted through the panel.
- A local row offers copy-address and **no** Forward — there is nothing to
  forward from the machine you are on.
- A tab that is neither local nor an SSH profile (Settings) still shows the
  no-connection state.
- Switching local ↔ SSH re-scopes in both directions.
close_reason: Merged: the panel's scope is the ports target, not the profile id (a distinction profileId could not express — local shell vs alias tab want opposite answers). Local rows offer copy and refuse Forward structurally; Forwarded/Stopped hidden on a local scope.

title: The ports panel is unreadable in a sidebar: no loading state, wrapped rows, controls that should not be there
description:
Owner, 2026-08-04, with screenshots. Three separate defects in one surface.

**No loading state.** Ports appear seconds after opening — the settle delay plus
a round trip — and until then the panel is blank, which reads as broken.

**The rows do not fit.** The address is the row's primary key and is truncated to
`127.0....`, while the process chip takes most of the width and wraps to three
lines, making rows three times taller than they need to be. The panel was
designed against a tab's width and now lives in a narrow sidebar.

**Retry and Pause are permanent body controls.** Retry belongs inside a failure
state, where it already exists; a second copy in the toolbar is a second
vocabulary. Pause is a real need — do not poll a production host — but it belongs
in the view's header actions, which `SidebarViewDescriptor` already provides.
"last sample" is muted micro-text, not a Badge chip.

Owner also asks whether sampling is heavy enough to need a manual control at all.
Answer with a measurement, not an opinion.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the Ports view on an SSH tab. Blank for several seconds.
2. Once populated, read the addresses. You cannot.

## Acceptance Criteria

- First open shows a loading state; later refreshes update in place without
  blanking the list.
- The full address is readable at the sidebar's default width; the process is
  secondary and truncates before the address does.
- Retry appears only in a failure state. Pause is a header action. The sample
  time is muted micro-text.
- The report states the measured cost of one sample.
close_reason: Merged e970209: loading state gated on absence of data (refresh updates in place), address holds flex 1 1 0 while chip and destination ellipsize first via a new Badge truncate variance, icon actions, toolbar Retry removed, Pause moved to the view header behind one shared controller. Measured one sample at ~12ms (0.35 exec open + 11.5 probe + 0.03 parse), 0.24% duty cycle at 5s — the cadence runs without asking.

title: Ports shows nothing for a local tab, and the local machine listens too
description:
Owner, 2026-08-04: "почему для локального шелл мы не показываем порты? Давай
показывать."

A local tab renders "No active connection". The local machine listens on ports
like any other, and the probe ladder that finds them is not SSH-specific — only
the transport is.

`discovery.Connector` returns `ssh.DiscoveryConn`, so the package depends on the
transport it happens to use first. The exec seam belongs in `internal/discovery`
as its own interface, with `ssh.DiscoveryConn` satisfying it and a local
implementation running the same ladder through `exec.CommandContext`.

Forwarding is the part that genuinely differs: there is nothing to forward from
the machine you are on. A local row offers what is useful locally instead.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a local tab.
2. Open the Ports view.
3. "No active connection", while `ss -H -lntp` on the same machine lists
   plenty.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A local tab lists the machine's listening ports through the same ladder and
  the same five result states.
- No Forward action on a local row; whatever replaces it is useful rather than
  disabled chrome.
- Switching between a local tab and an SSH tab re-scopes correctly in both
  directions.
- The discovery package no longer names an SSH type in its own seam.
close_reason: Merged 5cb9017: internal/nativeports (per-OS build-tagged, contentkey pattern) behind a new discovery.Provider seam; /proc/net/tcp + inode walk on Linux, GetExtendedTcpTable via iphlpapi on Windows without cgo, lsof on darwin as a stated fallback with libproc as the named upgrade. Local target is the literal 'local'. Cross-compiles for every target so the nocx-if6 relay ships it unchanged.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text: This work is upstream of nocx-if6 phase B (the remote relay). The provider seam must be shaped so a relay provider drops in beside local-native and remote-command; the native module should be compilable for the far side unchanged. Do not let the seam name the transport.

title: Ports is a view, not a palette action and not a tab
description:
Owner's call, 2026-08-04: "Зачем мы это в quick connect добавили? У нас же есть
прекрасная activity bar."

Two things are wrong with how the panel is reached, and they are separable.

**It is in the command palette.** Quick connect is for one-shot verbs — "new
tab", "integrate this shell". Ports is a surface you keep open and glance at
while you work. Putting it in the palette makes the palette a menu.

**It opens as a tab**, which replaces the terminal. Watching a port appear is
something you do *while* typing the command that opens it; a tab makes the two
mutually exclusive. The reference the owner gave for this feature — Orca's PORTS
panel — sits beside the terminal for exactly that reason.

The sidebar already supports this and its views zone is empty: `mountSidebar`
takes `SidebarViewDescriptor` (id, title, icon, view, actions, order) and
`main.tsx` passes `[]` with a comment reserving it for `nocx-708q`. Ports is a
smaller first view than the file tree and proves the same seam.

The view must follow the active tab, not capture a profile at open time —
switching SSH tabs must re-scope it, and a local tab must not show a stale host's
ports.

Keep `Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+O` as reveal-or-focus for the view. "Integrate this shell"
stays in the palette: it is a verb, and it belongs there.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the palette. "Ports" is an item there.
2. Activate it. The panel takes over as a tab and the terminal is gone.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Ports is a sidebar view with an activity-bar icon; the palette item is gone.
- The view re-scopes when the active tab changes, and shows nothing meaningful
  on a local tab.
- Sampling still pauses when the view is not visible — collapsing the sidebar
  counts as not visible.
- A test asserts a user can open it from the activity bar and see the ports of
  the tab they are looking at.
close_reason: Merged b26bb62: Ports is the sidebar's first real view (PlugIcon), palette item and tab surface deleted, view follows the active tab via a new onActiveTabChange funnel, collapse counts as not visible, Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+O reveals and focuses. SidebarViewDescriptor grew reactive view props and revealView; guarding revealView found setActiveView orphaning the panel on unknown ids.

title: shell.integrate hangs on a busybox host — the tier the minimal path exists for
description:
With busybox on PATH, `TestInBandBootstrap_Real*` (bash, zsh, dash — all four)
time out after 15s. The transcript shows the wrapper reaching
`\033]1337;NOCX_IB_READY` and then nothing: the payload is consumed and the
integration markers never arrive.

The applets the wrapper depends on are `stty`, `mktemp`, `sed`, `grep` and
`printf`, and busybox's differ from GNU coreutils'. Most likely candidates are
`sed -n '/^NOCX_IB_EOF$/q;p'` and the `stty -g` string round trip.

This is not a test-environment artifact. Integrating a shell you reached by hand
is exactly what you do after `ssh`-ing into an Alpine container, and the POSIX
minimal tier was built and measured against busybox ash precisely because those
hosts matter.

## Steps to Reproduce

```
nix shell nixpkgs#busybox --command go test ./internal/shellintegration/... \
  -count=1 -run TestInBandBootstrap_Real
```

Without busybox on PATH the same tests pass.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The in-band pty tests pass with busybox providing the utilities, and the run
  asserts which applet was the cause rather than working around it blindly.
- A case exists for the wrapper on a host where an applet is genuinely missing:
  fail-open to a usable shell, never a hang.
close_reason: Merged a83800a: busybox sed's 1024-byte lookahead reader stalls on a pty (staged file stopped at 24576 of 24622 bytes); staging is now a POSIX while-read loop on builtins only. Paired fail-open test with mktemp genuinely absent.

title: The panel never shows the bind caveat, so a -R forward looks verified
description:
`Tunnel.Caveat()` exists, crosses the wire as `caveat` on every forward record,
and `frontend/src/ports.tsx` does not mention it. A remote forward whose bind
address sshd silently replaced (GatewayPorts) renders identically to one that
bound exactly what was asked — which is the failure the field was added for: the
user builds a URL that only works on the server.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a remote forward with a non-loopback bind address.
2. The row shows the requested address with no caution.
3. `grep -n caveat frontend/src/ports.tsx` finds nothing.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A forward carrying a non-empty caveat renders it as a caution on the row.
- The wording says the bind address is not verified; it never says the forward
  failed, because it did not.
- A forward with an empty caveat renders no extra chrome.
close_reason: Merged: caveat rendered on forwarded rows through the kit's MarkerList note tone, backend wording verbatim, no chrome when empty, omitted on stopped rows.

title: Stored forwards are never replayed: connectfwd.Replay has no caller
description:
`internal/connectfwd.Replay` opens a profile's stored forwards and is
unreachable: `deadcode` names it directly. The profile carries the list, the
editor saves it, and connecting opens nothing — the whole point of storing them.

The seam is the transport's open handler, beside where discovery comes up; the
worker who built the engine did not own `internal/transport`.

This is the `nocx-rtg0` shape: a store, a policy and five controls around a
write path with no caller.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Save two forwards on a connection profile.
2. Connect.
3. Nothing is forwarded. `deadcode -filter 'nocx/internal/connectfwd' ./...`
   reports `unreachable func: Replay`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `deadcode -filter 'nocx/internal/connectfwd' ./...` is empty.
- Connecting with two stored forwards opens both, asserted through the transport
  against a real SSH server rather than by calling Replay directly.
- A busy local port reports against its row and leaves the session usable.
close_reason: Merged bb2e533: Replay runs from the open handler after the ack; forwards registered connection-owned so closing the opening tab does not stop them; failed rows stay visible in ports.status. deadcode on internal/connectfwd empty.

title: A pinned shell cannot be set: the composition root never calls WithShell
description:
`internal/ssh` honours a pinned shell (`WithShell`, beating auto-detection), and
nothing calls it. The profile field that would carry the pin is not read at the
composition root, so a user who knows their host runs zsh has no way to say so —
detection is the only path, and where detection is wrong the user cannot
override it.

Handed off by `nocx-6rj0`, whose worker did not own `internal/app/app.go`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Set the shell on a connection profile.
2. Connect.
3. The dispatcher auto-detects regardless; `grep -rn "WithShell(" --include=*.go .`
   finds only the option and its tests.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A profile with a pinned shell reaches `WithShell`, asserted through the app
  rather than through `internal/ssh` alone.
- An unpinned profile still sends `ShellAuto`.
close_reason: Merged bb2e533: sshOptionsFromConfig was dropping cfg.Shell, so a transport-side pin died in the registry. WithShell now has a production caller at internal/session/session.go:368; unknown pins are warn-dropped in the open handler.

title: The ports panel exists and nothing can open it
description:
`frontend/src/ports.tsx` has no importer outside its own test: `PortsContent` is
never registered with the surface registry and no palette item or keybinding
opens it. The panel was built while `main.tsx` was held by the shell-integration
worker, so the registration was deferred — and a deferral that lives only in a
report is the failure `AGENTS.md` rule 2 names.

The worker left the exact call shape in
`.internal/reports/nocx-wzc4.2-ports-panel.md`: `createPortsPanelServices`,
`PortsContent`, `registry.register` with surfaceType `nocx.ports`, opened via
`tm.openTab`. `setVisible` already reports visibility, so the hidden-tab pause
works once it is mounted.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open an SSH tab.
2. Look for any way to open the ports panel — palette, keybinding, menu.
3. There is none; `grep -rn "PortsContent" frontend/src` finds only the module
   and its own test.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A user with an SSH tab open can reach the ports panel from the state they
  start in, and a test asserts that path rather than mounting the component.
- `grep` for the module finds an importer outside its test.
- Opening the panel starts sampling; switching away pauses it.
close_reason: Merged 87c0c0f: ports-surface.ts registers nocx.ports, palette item plus Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+O through one openPorts(), profileId resolved from the active tab at open time, reachability asserted from a real TabManager.

title: The ports panel: what is listening, what is forwarded, and what stopped
description:
`internal/discovery` has no caller outside its own tests — the write half of the
feature is unreachable. Wire it at the composition root with the cadence timers
(settle sample, prompt debounce, hidden-tab pause), add the RPC and its
contract, and build the panel.

Spec: `.internal/specs/2026-08-03-port-forwarding-design.md` sections 5, 6, 8.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `deadcode -filter 'nocx/internal/discovery' ./...` is empty.
- The panel shows Detected / Forwarded / Stopped, and forwarding a detected port
  is one action from the row.
- Three-valued process evidence renders as a fact about privilege
  ("run as root to see owners"), never as an unexplained blank.
- `available-limited` and `permission-or-policy-refused` are distinguishable in
  the UI; a host with no probe at all says so instead of showing an empty list.
- Discovery does not run while the tab is hidden, and does not run twice
  concurrently.
- An over-the-wire conformance test for the new result shape.
close_reason: Merged e1f42d8: discovery wired at the composition root with the four cadence rules, ports.status/sample/pause/visible with schemas and over-the-wire conformance, Detected/Forwarded/Stopped panel. deadcode on internal/discovery empty. Reachability from the UI is nocx-wzc4.4 — main.tsx was held by another worker.

title: Remote (-R) and dynamic (-D) forwarding, behind the strategy the model already has
description:
The Tunnel model carries all three directions but only DirectionLocal has a
strategy. `-R` needs `Client.Listen` plus the sshd policy facts
(AllowTcpForwarding, PermitListen, GatewayPorts) surfaced as reasons a user can
act on rather than a bare failure. `-D` needs a SOCKS5 server whose CONNECT
opens a `direct-tcpip` channel per request.

Spec: `.internal/specs/2026-08-03-port-forwarding-design.md` sections 7.2, 7.3.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A remote forward opened against the in-process test server carries bytes from
  a remote-side dial back to a local listener.
- sshd refusing the listen (AllowTcpForwarding no) stops the tunnel with a
  reason naming the policy, not "failed".
- `-R` with port 0 reports the port sshd actually allocated.
- A SOCKS5 client through `-D` reaches a target, and one refused CONNECT leaves
  the proxy serving.
- SOCKS5 rejects unsupported auth methods and unsupported commands (BIND, UDP)
  with the correct reply codes rather than closing.
- Connection loss stops all three directions the same way.
close_reason: Merged b7418e0: -R and -D behind the strategy interface, shared forwardLifecycle, proven against real in-process SSH servers (remote-side dial carries bytes, real SOCKS5 client reaches a target, port 0 reports the allocated port, refused listen surfaces the policy wording). Caveat field carries the unverifiable GatewayPorts bind.

title: CI: make shellintegration snapshot tests deterministic
description:
## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run `go test -count=1 ./...` on the current main-integrated branch.
2. Observe `internal/shellintegration` failures in `TestBashSnapshotEmitsHelloThenSnapshot`, `TestBashSnapshotFirstPromptBoundedWait`, and `TestBashSnapshotArrivesBeforeFirstPrompt`.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Shell snapshot tests emit and parse their OSC 636 snapshot deterministically.
- `go test -count=1 ./...` passes without these failures.
notes: 2026-08-09: runShellProgEnv now forces LC_ALL=C and TestBashSnapshotFirstPromptBoundedWait passes. Full race gate remains blocked only because this environment has no dash executable; requireShell intentionally fails rather than silently substituting another shell. CI or a dash-equipped environment is still required.
close_reason: Shipped, and re-run to confirm. internal/shellintegration/scripts_exec_test.go:824 pins HOSTNAME and LC_ALL in runShellProgEnv and replaces the sleep with a bounded NOCX_SNAPSHOT_WAIT_MS wait. The three named tests were executed read-only during this sweep: go test -count=1 -run TestBashSnapshot... ./internal/shellintegration/ reported ok in 1.218s. The old blocker (no dash in the image) is provisioned by .githooks/images/ci-linux/Dockerfile:53, commit 1c7a3b9f. Closed during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh.

title: CI: restore jsdom localStorage for sidebar tests
description:
## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run `cd frontend && npm test` on the current main-integrated branch.
2. Observe all 12 cases in `src/sidebar.test.tsx` fail at `localStorage.clear()` because `localStorage` is undefined.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The Vitest environment supplies localStorage to sidebar tests.
- `cd frontend && npm test` reaches the sidebar suite without this environment failure.
close_reason: Vitest setup now supplies a scoped localStorage implementation; the full frontend suite passes: 136 files and 2464 tests.

title: The tunnel package is built and nothing at the composition root can reach it
description:
nocx-6nh6 built internal/tunnel — the domain model for all three directions plus the local strategy behind an AD-8 strategy interface — and internal/ssh grew a TunnelConn lease seam with its own pooled reference. The worker reported the remaining step itself: wiring tunnel.Connector at the composition root, where RealClient satisfies it without an adapter.

Until that lands the package is reachable from its own tests and from nowhere else. That is AGENTS.md check 5, and this epic has already paid for it once — nocx-ei04 was the same shape for the shell-integration launcher, and nocx-rtg0 before that shipped an encrypted store whose write path had no caller while deadcode reported empty.

The control plane also has to exist: opening and stopping a forward is a JSON-RPC method, so it needs a contracts/ schema with additionalProperties false and an explicit required, a generated renderer type, and a test that validates the real result off the real socket rather than one the test built (AGENTS.md rule 5).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. grep -rn 'internal/tunnel' internal/app internal/transport — no hits.
2. There is no way for a user to open a forward.

Discovered from nocx-6nh6.
acceptance_criteria: deadcode -filter 'nocx/internal/tunnel' reports the local strategy reachable from main(); a JSON-RPC method opens and stops a local forward through the real transport, declared by a contracts/ schema with an over-the-wire conformance test; and a forward survives the tab that shares its connection closing while its own tab's close stops it.
close_reason: Local forward wired from the composition root through transport.WithTunnelConnector; RealClient satisfies tunnel.Connector without an adapter. tunnel.open/tunnel.stop declared by contracts with over-the-wire conformance tests; actual bound port reported, not the requested one; tab-scoped teardown proven with two tabs. deadcode -filter nocx/internal/tunnel empty. Merged.

title: The SSH path always says bash, so the other two tiers can never happen
description:
internal/ssh/ssh_real.go passes ShellBash unconditionally, with a comment marking it a temporary default rather than a decision (landed that way in nocx-r52q, deliberately and on the record). The launcher now implements all three tiers — bash, zsh and the POSIX minimal tier (nocx-518d) — so two of the three are reachable from the launcher's own tests and from nowhere else.

Consequence today: a zsh host gets the bash launcher, and a busybox host gets a bash command that cannot exec. Fail-open catches it, so the session works — but it works as a plain terminal, and the minimal tier we just built and measured against real dash and busybox never runs.

The hard part is that the shell is genuinely unknown before connecting, and the obvious shortcuts are barred: AD-6 forbids sniffing the byte stream, and probing over a second exec channel is the discovery mechanism the port-forwarding spec is introducing — which may or may not be available (MaxSessions, ForceCommand, restricted shells). Candidate sources worth weighing: a field on the connection profile, ssh -G, and a one-shot exec probe with the port-discovery consent model.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Connect to a host whose login shell is zsh.
2. The bash launcher is used; the zsh launcher never runs.

Discovered from nocx-518d.
acceptance_criteria: The shell kind passed to the launcher is determined rather than assumed: a host whose shell is zsh gets the zsh launcher and a host with neither bash nor zsh gets the minimal tier, both asserted against a real sshd. Where the shell genuinely cannot be determined, the choice is stated in the product rather than silently defaulted, and the fallback still leaves a usable session.
close_reason: Merged 292c5f2: ShellAuto with a single-line POSIX dispatcher keyed on the login shell's argv[0]; verified against a docker sshd with bash, zsh, dash and tcsh users (4 auto tiers + 2 pin-beats-detection). Composition-root wiring is nocx-6rj0.1, the ADR is nocx-6rj0.2.

title: The remote's listening ports are discovered without touching the user's shell
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-03-port-forwarding-design.md sections 3, 3.1, 4 and 5.

Measured before specifying: ss -tlnp as non-root named 3 of 9 listeners on this machine — :53 and :5355 belong to another user and come back bare. That is exactly the owner's Orca screenshot with 4 of 6 rows unlabelled, and it is why process evidence is a three-valued fact rather than a string that might be empty.

The second channel is nearly free (internal/ssh/pool.go holds a ref-counted ConnPool; openShell already has a *gossh.Client at ssh_real.go:561) and buys three things: AD-6 compliance, because the result is backend-owned SSH metadata rather than the terminal byte stream parsed; it works WHILE a command runs, which is the common case and the moment the interactive shell physically cannot run anything; and it touches neither tty nor history.

It does NOT work anywhere SSH works, and the code must not pretend otherwise — MaxSessions 1 refuses the second channel, ForceCommand substitutes its own output, restricted shells permit a shell and forbid exec.

Cadence is in the spec and is rejected as written elsewhere: per-prompt sampling would write three sshd audit records per command.
acceptance_criteria: A discovery service opens a SECOND exec channel on the existing SSH connection, selects a probe once per connection from the ladder (ss, netstat, busybox netstat, lsof, sockstat), and returns typed results: available | available-limited | unavailable | failed-transiently | permission-or-policy-refused, with per-row process evidence known | permission-denied | unsupported. A successful empty result means no listeners; every other state renders as 'could not determine', never as 'no ports'. MaxSessions 1, a missing tool, and a ForceCommand host each produce their named state with the interactive session unaffected. Output without the version sentinel is rejected whole.
close_reason: internal/discovery + DiscoveryConn merged (84f2b08); probe ladder, sentinel framing, three-valued process evidence, owned pooled lease. 41 tests, -race green x3. Wiring to main() is the panel task's.

title: A tunnel is one model with three directions, and local forwarding works
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-03-port-forwarding-design.md sections 7 and 7.1.

The model is built for all three directions from day one even though only local ships here, because -R brings remote-listener policy (AllowTcpForwarding, PermitListen) and -D brings SOCKS semantics, and a direction flag threaded into one forwarding loop collapses under both. AD-8: a strategy behind an interface, never a switch inside an implementation.

The lifetime rules are the part that bites. AD-7 gives a tab one interactive channel while the connection is pooled and shared (internal/ssh/pool.go), so a forward must not hang off the shell's goroutine or borrow its pool reference — closing one tab would then kill another tab's tunnel. Each forward takes its own handle.

Explicitly NOT this task: discovery, the panel, the block offer, stored profile forwards, -R and -D implementations.
acceptance_criteria: A Tunnel domain type in the backend carries direction (local|remote|dynamic), requested and actual bind, destination, scope/owner, lifecycle state, error reason and discovery provenance, behind a strategy interface per direction (AD-8). The local strategy binds 127.0.0.1 by default, accepts port 0 and reports the ACTUAL bound port, fails synchronously and visibly on EADDRINUSE without pre-checking (no TOCTOU), gives each accepted connection its own direct-tcpip channel so one failed stream never kills the listener, holds its OWN pooled-connection handle, and on tab close tears down only its own forwards. Tests cover every one of those, including a busy port, port 0, a refused remote target, and connection loss moving the tunnel to stopped rather than silently rebinding.
close_reason: internal/tunnel: model for local/remote/dynamic with requested vs actual bind, scope, provenance, lifecycle and stop reason; local strategy behind an AD-8 interface. All five traps tested — bind-before-success, no TOCTOU, port 0 reports the real port, a refused stream leaves the listener alive, own pool lease proven by tab teardown. Also fixed a pre-existing race in openShell exposed by -race. Merged. Wiring is nocx-8gix.

title: There is no way to integrate a shell you entered by hand
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-03-nocxify-design.md sections 4.4 and 5.3.

The owner typed 'ssh somehost' into a local nocx tab and nothing integrated. Two paths were designed for that and neither exists yet:

- automatic rewriting of the command before it runs (section 5.3) — deliberately moved to epic nocx-eepi, because ssh, docker exec, sudo and su are four grammars and the transparency obligations are per-adapter;
- the EXPLICIT action (section 4.4) — never beaded. That is a decomposition oversight, not a decision: with adapters deferred, the explicit action is the only path a user has, and deferring both leaves the feature with no manual route either.

The mechanism is the in-band fallback, and section 4.4 fences it tightly: permitted only while nocx still holds a trusted A/B prompt from the CURRENT integrated shell — never after markers have already disappeared, because consent changes authorisation, not the identity of the foreground process. Inside that window: an input lease (submission paused, draft preserved byte-for-byte, Esc cancels), stty -g captured and restored exactly, never stty sane.

ADR-0004 rejects inferring who reads stdin from the byte stream. This does not do that: it acts inside a window nocx already owns, on explicit request.
acceptance_criteria: A command-palette entry and a keybinding integrate the shell currently at the prompt: with a trusted A/B prompt from the current integrated session, the user's draft is preserved byte-for-byte, input is paused, Esc cancels, and on success the tier and environment update. Every failure path leaves a usable terminal with a visible native prompt. It is never automatic and never remembered as automatic.
close_reason: Merged a9183a4: shell.integrate with the in-band bootstrap, the PROMPT_READY&&trusted&&owned gate, input lease with byte-for-byte draft restore, palette item and Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+I. stty raw -echo approved; ADR-0004 carries the scoping note. Verified on real bash/zsh/dash ptys.

title: No completion for ssh — the host list quick connect already has never reaches the prompt
description:
CandidateSource in frontend/src/suggest/candidate.ts:10 is 'command' | 'history' | 'path'. There is no host source, so 'ssh <TAB>' offers shell history and filesystem paths — the two things that are never the answer there.

The data is already assembled: quick-connect.tsx builds exactly this list from profileClient.listProfiles() and listSSHAliases(), deduplicates an alias already targeted by a saved profile, and surfaces an unavailable resolver rather than hiding it. Route that, do not rebuild it — two derivations of 'which hosts do I know' would drift.

The owner asked for precisely this: 'completion for the ssh command, showing what quick connect shows'.
acceptance_criteria: Typing 'ssh ' and asking for completion offers hosts — saved profiles and live ~/.ssh/config aliases, the same set quick connect shows and deduplicated the same way — as a distinct candidate source with its own badge, ranked above history in that argument position. It applies to ssh and its argument position only: 'ls ' must not offer hosts. A degraded ssh_config resolver surfaces the condition rather than silently offering an empty list.
close_reason: hostProvider routes quick-connect's profiles+aliases assembly read-only with its dedup and degraded-resolver handling, scoped to ssh's argument position, ranked above history. 1773 -> 1783 tests. Merged. Follow-up nocx-51t3 on extracting the assembly out of the Solid component.

title: Quick connect cannot connect to a host you just typed
description:
Quick connect already connects without saving: SSHAliasQuickConnectProvider takes newTabByHost(host, user, port) and opens a tab from a ~/.ssh/config alias with no profile written. What it cannot do is accept a host that exists in neither the profiles nor the config.

parseQuickConnect (frontend/src/profiles.ts:120) already parses user@host:port and the ssh:// scheme, including IPv6 in brackets — but its only caller is connections.tsx:1304, which uses it to PREFILL THE NEW-PROFILE FORM. So typing a connection string today means 'define a connection', never 'connect to it'. The parser for the feature exists and points at the wrong door.

The owner asked for it in one line: 'a quick connect without adding a connection'.

Ordering matters: a free-form entry must not outrank a real match, or a typo'd alias silently becomes an ad-hoc connection to a host of the same name.
acceptance_criteria: Typing user@host:port (or ssh://user@host:port, or a bare host) into the quick-connect picker offers a Connect entry that opens a session directly — no profile created, nothing persisted — reached by keyboard alone. An input that matches a saved profile or an ssh_config alias still prefers that entry over the free-form one. A malformed string reports why instead of silently connecting to a wrong host.
close_reason: Free-form Connect entry in quick connect: parses user@host:port / ssh:// / IPv6, opens via newTabByHost, persists nothing. Consulted only when no static item matched, so it can never outrank a profile or alias. Malformed input reports the accepted formats. 45/47 -> 47/47 tests. Merged as ce5d074.

title: The editor does not say which machine Enter will reach
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-03-nocxify-design.md section 8.2 — one of the five promises in nocx-pu4's acceptance, and the only one still unbuilt.

The finished block already carries it: scrollback/blocks.ts:157 renders a cmd-header-location chip from the string terminal-content.ts:862 feeds the block manager. The live prompt does not: editor.ts:253-259 builds the chrome row from cwdChip and timeChip only. So a user reads 'root@192.168.0.57' on every block they have already run, and sees only a folder icon on the one they are about to run — the single moment where the answer is irreversible.

The owner found this the first working day of SSH blocks and phrased it exactly: 'in the editor you cannot see at all which server the command will run on'.

THE HARD PART IS NOT THE CHIP, IT IS THE FAILURE EDGE. Section 8.2 is explicit: when markers stop arriving, the rail must say the context is unknown immediately. It must never keep rendering the last trusted host and cwd as though they were current — that is false precision, and false precision beside an irreversible action is exactly what invites running the right command on the wrong machine. nocx-uahp exists because of this.

Scope: the location chip and its honest unknown state. The full per-facet rail (profile, jump route, privilege, integration tier) waits for nocx-uahp's environment identity; do not invent a parallel model here.
acceptance_criteria: While composing, the prompt shows where the command will run: the same location chip a finished block carries (user@host, and the jump route when there is one), beside the cwd. When the session is local it shows nothing extra — a local prompt must not grow a chip that says 'localhost'. When markers stop and the shell's identity is no longer trusted, the chip says so rather than continuing to show the last known host. A test asserts the chip is present for an SSH session, absent for a local one, and turns to the unknown state when ownership is lost.
close_reason: The prompt now carries the block header's location chip, fed the same locationLine derivation routed to both consumers from one place. It tracks trust: on trust loss it renders 'context unknown' — shown rather than hidden, because an absent chip reads as local, and never the stale host. Local sessions still grow no chip. 1766 -> 1773 frontend tests. Merged as e8c1a7d. Layout itself remains unverified (jsdom computes none) — nocx-a44m.

title: The launcher adapter panics where the epic's own invariant forbids it
description:
internal/app/app.go's remoteLauncherAdapter panics twice: on a refusal reason it cannot map, and on a launcher that returns ok=true while naming a reason.

The reasoning behind it is sound and worth preserving. A decline that silently becomes ssh.ReasonNone renders in the product as 'integration succeeded', which is the invisible soft degrade AGENTS.md forbids; the author refused that and chose to fail loudly instead.

But loud here means a panic in the composition root of a terminal backend, and ADR-0004:60 makes fail-open an invariant of this very epic: no failure path may leave the user without a working terminal. A crash is the most extreme violation of that available. So the two correct instincts collide, and the collision is currently resolved in favour of the one the ADR rules against.

The middle path exists and neither instinct loses: a distinct reason value — 'unknown' — that is visible in the product, plus a loud log. That is not the silent ReasonNone fallback that was correctly rejected.

NOT URGENT: the switch is exhaustive over the three declared reasons, so the default arm is unreachable today. It becomes live the moment somebody adds a reason to one package and not the other — which is exactly what the tripwire was built to catch, and exactly when a user would lose their terminal to it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Add a fourth RefusalReason to internal/shellintegration and return it from the launcher.
2. Open an SSH session. The backend panics instead of degrading.

Discovered from nocx-ei04.
acceptance_criteria: An unmapped refusal reason, or a launcher that accepts while claiming one, degrades visibly instead of crashing: the session stays usable, the product shows a distinct reason rather than 'integration succeeded', and a test asserts the terminal survives both cases. Alternatively the panic is kept and ADR-0004's fail-open clause is amended to carve out programmer-error paths, deliberately and in writing.
close_reason: Both panics replaced with fail-open decline: unmapped reasons become a distinct ssh.ReasonUnknown, accept-with-reason declines carrying the claimed reason, both log loudly. Contract enum, generated type and conformance test moved together. Merged.

title: The zsh and dash launcher tests skip silently when those shells are absent
description:
Twelve launcher tests pass — but only three of them run on a bare NixOS dev box. TestBashLauncher_RunsUnderDash and all three TestZshLauncher_* skip when dash and zsh are not on PATH, and the zsh transient-ZDOTDIR path is the riskiest code in the epic: it creates a directory on somebody else's machine and must erase it before any user code runs.

Verified: 'nix shell nixpkgs#zsh nixpkgs#dash --command go test ./internal/shellintegration/...' turns all three zsh tests and the dash test from SKIP to PASS (10.6s). Without it the suite is green and the zsh launcher is untested.

AGENTS.md is explicit that a skipped test reporting success is the failure mode the testing rules exist to prevent — the same shape as nocx-rtg0's 'deadcode empty'. A green suite that silently omits the riskiest path is worse than a red one.

The fix is a choice, not obvious: fail rather than skip, or make the harness provide the shells. Whichever, the repo must name the command CI runs.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. go test ./internal/shellintegration/... -run Launcher -v
2. Observe SKIP on TestZshLauncher_TransientDirFlow, TestZshLauncher_CleanupAfterEarlyExit, TestZshLauncher_CleanupAfterSyntaxError, TestBashLauncher_RunsUnderDash — and an 'ok' summary.

Discovered from nocx-xs1d.
acceptance_criteria: A run of the shell-integration suite on a host without zsh or dash either exercises those launchers or FAILS loudly; it never reports success while skipping them. The repo states one command that runs the suite with the shells present, and CI uses it.
close_reason: Merged 0838fa3: four launcher tests fail loudly instead of skipping; pre-commit container gets a derived image with dash+zsh (27.6s apt-get per commit vs 0.29s warm image build, measured), macOS CI gets brew install dash.

title: The SSH path stops editing other people's rc files and starts asking the launcher
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-03-nocxify-design.md sections 4.2 and 7, plus section 1 defects 1 and 2.

Today internal/ssh/ssh_real.go:507 silently SFTPs into every remote home and appends a gate to ~/.bashrc, then starts '$SHELL -l' — a LOGIN shell, which reads ~/.bash_profile and never sources the gate that was just appended to ~/.bashrc. So we pay the full cost of mutating a stranger's server and get nothing. That path stops being the default here.

RemoteCommand resolution already landed (nocx-difd): HostConfig now carries it, and 'ssh -G' renders an unset directive either as an absent line or as the literal 'none' depending on version — both already collapse to the empty string, so the caller tests for non-empty.

Explicitly NOT this task: building the launcher itself.
acceptance_criteria: openShell no longer calls EnsureInstalledRemote on the default path; it asks the RemoteLauncher for a start command and falls back to a plain shell with a typed reason when the launcher declines. A destination whose ssh -G reports remotecommand != none gets NO launcher, runs its configured behaviour, and reports reason remote-command. Tests cover: launcher accepted, remote-command refusal, launcher error, and that a plain-shell fallback leaves a usable session in every one of them.
close_reason: openShell asks a launcher and no longer SFTPs into remote homes by default; RemoteCommand destinations get no launcher and report reason remote-command; every decline falls back to a usable plain shell with a typed reason reachable from the session. ssh 106->112 tests, session 22->26. Merged as 9b2877a. Integration seam (mirrored named types) closed by an adapter at the composition root — coordinator work, tracked in nocx-xs1d's merge.

title: The launcher: integration arrives as shell startup arguments, not as typing into a tty
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-03-nocxify-design.md sections 4.1-4.3. This is the mechanism the whole epic rests on.

Verified before specifying: 'bash --rcfile <(...)' is a bashism that dies with 'Syntax error: "(" unexpected' when the parsing shell is dash, and sshd hands a remote command to the user's LOGIN shell — so the launcher must invoke /bin/bash -c explicitly rather than rely on the remote login shell to parse process substitution.

zsh has no --rcfile equivalent; ZDOTDIR names a directory and cannot name a pipe, which is why the transient directory is structural rather than a shortcut, and why D1 in the spec says 'no PERSISTENT footprint' rather than 'no writes'.

Explicitly NOT this task: the ssh/session wiring that calls it, and the refusal matrix.
acceptance_criteria: A RemoteLauncher policy in internal/shellintegration builds, for a named far shell, the exact remote command string that starts an integrated interactive shell: bash via an explicit /bin/bash -c wrapping 'exec bash --rcfile <(printf %b ...) -i', zsh via a mode-700 transient ZDOTDIR whose generated .zshrc removes itself before any user code runs and restores the original ZDOTDIR unset-vs-set state. Tests drive real bash and real zsh, assert the integration is active (A/B markers arrive), assert the user's own rcfile still ran, assert the transient zsh directory is gone before the first user command and after each of success, syntax failure and early exit, and assert no path under $HOME is created or modified during the bash launch.
close_reason: RemoteLauncher built: bash via env -u BASH_ENV bash -c with --rcfile process substitution and no remote write, zsh via a mode-700 transient ZDOTDIR that erases itself before user code. 12 tests pass against real bash 5.3, zsh 5.9 and dash 0.5.13. Merged as eafc50c. Coordinator fixed a /bin/bash absolute path that broke NixOS and silently skipped five tests of the primary path. Follow-ups: nocx-ei04 (reachability), nocx-gd84 (silent skips), plus the rcfile-return limitation.

title: The POSIX sh script is embedded and reachable by nobody
description:
nocx-q6xj built scripts/nocx.posix, embedded it as posixScript in scripts.go, and stopped there — deliberately and with the reason reported, which is why this bead exists rather than a silent gap.

Three things block the wiring, and each is a decision rather than a typo:

1. TestScriptContent_ContainsMarkers asserts every script in the scripts map emits a C marker. nocx.posix structurally cannot — POSIX sh has no preexec hook — so adding it to the map turns a green suite red. The test encodes 'every script emits C' as an invariant, and that invariant is now false; it has to become per-script rather than be weakened for all.

2. The version const must be bumped, or existing installs keep their old script set and never receive the new file (nocx-6b3x is the bead that bought that lesson).

3. The gate line and the install path have to select the posix script for a shell that is neither bash nor zsh — which is the launcher's tier negotiation, so this task lands with or after the RemoteLauncher.

Until then posixScript is an embedded variable with no caller: the exact shape AGENTS.md rule 2 names — a reachable read path hiding an unreachable write path in the same package. golangci-lint does not flag it, which is precisely why it needs a bead and not a TODO.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. grep -n 'posixScript' internal/shellintegration/*.go — declared at scripts.go, referenced nowhere else.
2. The scripts map lists only shell-integration.zsh and shell-integration.bash, so no install path ever writes the posix script.

Discovered from nocx-q6xj.
acceptance_criteria: shell-integration.posix is in the scripts map and reaches a real session: the launcher selects it when the far shell answers as neither bash nor zsh, TestScriptContent_ContainsMarkers no longer demands a C marker from a script that structurally cannot emit one, the version const is bumped so existing installs are rewritten, and deadcode -filter 'nocx/internal/shellintegration' reports posixScript reachable from main().
close_reason: nocx.posix wired into the scripts map on both install paths, version 9->10, ShellUnknown becomes the minimal tier via a posix launcher following the zsh shape (transient dir that erases itself, explicit /bin/sh outer, fail-open without mktemp). Marker test is per-script and a bash script missing C still fails. deadcode empty; 54 PASS 0 SKIP under real zsh, dash and busybox. Merged. Follow-up nocx-6rj0: ssh still passes ShellBash unconditionally.

title: A connection decides its own shell integration: auto, ask or off
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-03-nocxify-design.md section 5.1.

The cascade's containers already exist — Group.Defaults at internal/profile/profile.go:263 and Profile.Options at :94 carry agentForward and the keepalive options the same way — but a new field does not come free: it must be threaded through the dense/stored/sparse option types, the allowlist, the conversion functions, the layer merge, the provenance map, the contract schema and the generated frontend types, and each of those is a place it can be silently dropped.

This is the field that answers 'when does nocxify happen' for a connection nocx opens, so nothing has to guess. It does not yet DO anything — the launcher that consumes it is a later task. Persisting and resolving it correctly is the whole of this one.
acceptance_criteria: shellIntegration (auto|ask|off) resolves through the existing cascade — hardcoded default, then global setting, then ancestor group defaults, then nearest group, then the profile — and is carried through the dense, stored and sparse option types, the allowlist, the conversion functions, the layer merge and the provenance map, with a JSON Schema in contracts/ and the generated frontend type regenerated. A table-driven test proves every precedence step including an explicit off.
close_reason: shellIntegration (auto|ask|off) threaded through all 21 agentForward sites plus the enum half; unrecognised stored values fall back to auto at resolution with provenance 'default', never a silent off. New contracts/profiles.effective.schema.json closes the fields map; merged as 2494415.

title: A POSIX sh integration script: blocks with exit status where bash and zsh are absent
description:
The third tier of the nocxify design (.internal/specs/2026-08-03-nocxify-design.md section 6). Verified reachable before being specified: 'docker run --rm -e PS1=... alpine:latest sh -c ...' shows busybox ash re-expanding PS1 per prompt with a correct $?, and dash on debian:stable-slim does the same.

Two constraints that fall out of that, and both are easy to get wrong: the PS1 assignment must be SINGLE-quoted or $? freezes at install time; and the exit status must be captured BEFORE any command substitution used to build the OSC 7 payload, which would otherwise clobber it.

C (command-started) is unreachable through portable prompt hooks, so it is not faked. A block appears already finished.

Warp cannot reach this tier at all — its bootstrap is 'read -r -d ""', a bashism (verified in its binary).
acceptance_criteria: internal/shellintegration/scripts/nocx.posix emits OSC 133 A, B and D (with the real exit status) plus OSC 7, entirely from PS1, under both dash and busybox ash; scripts.go embeds it; a script-exec test drives dash and asserts the marker sequence and the exit code for a succeeding and a failing command, and asserts that no C marker is claimed.
close_reason: nocx.posix emits A/B/D with a real exit status plus OSC 7 from a single-quoted PS1; C is deliberately absent and the test asserts the absence. Exercised against real dash 0.5.12 and busybox ash 1.37.0. Merged as 380bd0d. Wiring into the scripts map is nocx-518d, filed with its three blocking reasons.

title: ssh -G oracle discards RemoteCommand, so nocxify cannot know when its launcher would be refused
description:
ADR-0015 makes 'ssh -G' the resolution oracle, but HostConfig at internal/ssh/ssh_resolver.go:51 carries only HostName, User, Port and IdentityFile, and the parser switch at :284 recognises only those keys. 'remotecommand' is read and thrown away.

This matters for nocxify: when the user's ssh_config sets a RemoteCommand for a destination, OpenSSH refuses to also run a command-line remote command ('Cannot execute command-line and remote command'). Our startup launcher IS a command-line remote command, so integration is structurally impossible there and we must fall back to the configured behaviour and report 'integration: none, reason: remote-command' rather than break the connection. Warp does exactly this precheck — verified in its binary, which shells out to 'ssh -G' and greps 'remotecommand'.

RequestTTY belongs in the same change for the same reason.

Discovered during the nocxify design review (nocx-ht37).
acceptance_criteria: HostConfig carries RemoteCommand (and RequestTTY), populated from ssh -G; a resolver conformance test asserts a host with 'RemoteCommand ...' in ssh_config resolves with that value, and one without resolves to the 'none' ssh -G reports.
close_reason: ssh -G now surfaces RemoteCommand and RequestTTY; merged as c1e371f. OpenSSH 10.4 omits the remotecommand line for both an absent directive and a literal 'none' — measured — and other versions print 'remotecommand none'; both collapse to empty, which the oracle forces rather than the code choosing.

title: Remote shell-integration install writes VERSION before the gates, so a failed gate strands the host forever
description:
install_remote.go:52 writes VERSION right after the scripts and BEFORE the appendGateRemote loop at :57. install_remote.go:31 early-returns whenever the version matches.
