title: [bug] connection-overlay's three-cycle reconnect waits 5s for the Reconnect button, and lost it once under a full-suite run
description:
Seen once on 2026-09-05, in a full both-browser container run of the whole
suite (568 tests, one worker, 46.3 min): 558 passed, 9 skipped, 1 failed.

## What fails

e2e/connection-overlay.spec.ts:237 'reconnects through a new port and token
across three live cycles', chromium, at line 258:

    await expect(overlay(page)).toHaveAttribute('data-state', 'online')   // PASSED
    await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Reconnect', exact: true }))
      .toBeVisible()                                                      // 5s, not found

So the overlay reached `online` and the pane's Reconnect affordance had not
appeared within the default 5 s.

## Not caused by the change it was seen on, as far as can be shown

It was seen on 77788c48, which had just given the renderer a handler for
outbound.stalled that CLOSES the socket — a change to the reconnect path, so
it was the first suspect rather than the last. Against it:

- The immediately preceding assertion, that the overlay is `online`, passed.
  Had the new handler fired it would have knocked the overlay OUT of online,
  and that line would have been the red one.
- The same spec, alone on chromium in the same container, --repeat-each=5:
  50 of 50 green, 4.5 min.
- A SECOND full both-browser run of the same commit: 559 passed, 9 skipped,
  0 failed.

What could not be shown either way: whether an outbound stall actually
occurred in the failing run. The stand's backend log is per-run and was
overwritten before it could be read. If this recurs, read
test-results/stand/backend.log for 'connection outbound stalled' BEFORE
running anything else.

## Steps to Reproduce

Not reproducible on demand: 1 in 2 full-suite runs of the same commit, and 0
in 50 runs of the spec alone. It is the third load- or order-dependent e2e
failure recorded in this session, alongside nocx-it6m and nocx-tg7rm, and all
three share a shape: an assertion bounded by a short default wait that a
loaded runner outlasts.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The wait is for the state that actually gates the button — whatever makes
  the pane offer Reconnect after the overlay comes online — rather than for
  5 s of wall clock.
- Not a raised timeout: AGENTS.md is explicit that widening a bound converts
  a report into silence, and this assertion has now reported something real
  exactly once.
- If the cause turns out to be in the product (the affordance genuinely
  arriving late, or not at all, after a backend swap), it becomes a product
  bug and this bead says so.

title: [bug] maxWatchPaths=512 and the 64 KiB params budget contradict each other: the declared ceiling is unreachable for long paths
description:
Two bounds that do not know about each other. ws_files.go:68 declares maxWatchPaths = 512, and
ws.go:2452 gives every control-plane method a 64 KiB params frame budget. 512 paths have to fit in
65536 bytes, so the average path may be about 124 characters INCLUDING its directory prefix. Beyond
that the declared ceiling is unreachable: files.watch is refused, and the refusal names the frame
budget rather than the cause a person could act on.

    WARN jsonrpc params over budget method=files.watch len=99845
    files.watch: params exceed the size budget for method files.watch (65536 bytes)

Nobody has hit this in the product yet as far as I know, but 124 characters is not a lot for a
project two or three levels inside a home directory, and the person who hits it is told about a
frame size they cannot see and cannot change.

Found on 2026-09-05 as a red test, which is the other face of it: TestFilesRefreshState_Routine
DeferralAtCeilingIsSilent builds maxWatchPaths directories under t.TempDir() and watches them all,
so under a long $TMPDIR (111 characters here) the request is refused and the test fails on a
mechanism it is not about. The same environment dependence as nocx-9f5uc, in a different bound.
Green under the default /tmp, which is why CI has never seen it.

## Steps to Reproduce

Product: open a binding on a directory whose absolute path is long, watch 512 paths under it. The
request is refused with a message about a frame budget.

Test: TMPDIR=/a/path/of/about/a/hundred/characters go test -tags gtk3 ./internal/transport/ \
  -run TestFilesRefreshState_RoutineDeferralAtCeilingIsSilent

## Acceptance Criteria

- The number of paths a person may watch does not silently depend on how deep their project sits.
  Either the two bounds are reconciled — the ceiling is expressed in bytes, or files.watch pages —
  or maxWatchPaths is documented as an upper bound the frame budget can lower, and the refusal says
  so in words a person can act on.
- A refusal never names the frame budget alone: it names which limit was reached and what to do.
- The test asserts the pacing it is about, under any $TMPDIR, and still fails if routine deferral
  starts emitting delayed state.

title: [bug] One preview slot now has two callers, and the loser's refusal names the wrong cause
description:
skill.Store keeps ONE previewed-document slot (internal/skill/preview.go, previewedDocument). That
was deliberate and correct while Settings was the only acquisition surface: design §9 says one
source is held, visibly, and can be taken back, so a single slot needed no eviction policy, no
expiry and no bound, and there was never a question about which preview an install referred to.

nocx-ojfuc.1 (fe483d69) added a second caller. The tool's kernel-side preview and the Settings paste
box now share that slot, as does any other concurrent run. Two previews of different addresses
clobber each other and the loser's install refuses with "nothing has been read from that address" —
a refusal that names the wrong cause, since the person did read it.

nocx-ojfuc.4 removes the Settings path, which removes one of the two callers but not the class: two
concurrent runs are still two callers. So this is not folded into .4.

Found and reported by the worker on nocx-ojfuc.1, who flagged it rather than widening the task.

## Steps to Reproduce

Preview one address in Settings, have the assistant propose an install of a different one, approve
the first. It refuses, saying nothing has been read from that address.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An install refers unambiguously to the preview it was shown, whoever else previewed in between.
- The refusal a person sees names the cause that actually happened; "nothing has been read from that
  address" is never printed for an address that was read.
- Whatever replaces the single slot states its eviction and its bound, because the comment on
  previewedDocument is right that a slot with neither is what made it safe.

title: [bug] ForGrant offers a tool when ANY of its classes is permitted, and skills.install needs BOTH
description:
ADR-0053 defines a tool's effect set as the classes a call CAN resolve to, and the decision moves to
execution: session.run is lsblk OR rm -rf, and parsing the arguments picks one. Registry.ForGrant
encodes that as anyEffectPermitted — a row is offered when ANY of its declared classes is not
refused — and the policy decision is taken on WorstEffect alone, with inScope consulting only that
one row's scopes.

skills.install (nocx-ojfuc.1, fe483d69) is the first row where the set is a CONJUNCTION: it reaches
cross-boundary AND mutate-reversible on every successful call, not one or the other. Under
alternation, a policy that refuses mutate-reversible while permitting cross-boundary still offers
the row and still asks about it — a question about a write the person has already said no to.

The gap is closed today at the ENFORCEMENT layer, which ADR-0028 decision 4 makes the real one:
narrowSkillsInstall builds the capability from BOTH rows' own scopes, so a grant refusing the write
row yields a capability whose AllowsInstall() is false and the executor refuses before fetching
anything. Tested both ways. What is still open is the OFFER-time half: the tool is listed to the
model and a question is asked, both of which are work nobody wanted.

Worth noting that the conjunctive idiom already exists one field away: in the same ForGrant loop,
ResourceKinds requires EVERY kind to be covered, and only Effect uses "any".

Found and reported by the worker on nocx-ojfuc.1, who deliberately did not invent a new gate
mechanism inside a tool bead.

## Steps to Reproduce

Grant a run cross-boundary but not mutate-reversible. skills.install is still offered by ForGrant
and still escalates; the capability then refuses it at execution.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A declaration says whether its classes are alternative or conjunctive, and ForGrant honours it —
  or ADR-0053 is amended to name conjunctive tools and the amendment is what this implements. Decide
  which, in the ADR, before writing code.
- A tool whose every class must be permitted is not offered when one of them is refused, and is not
  escalated either.
- The decision for such a tool is not taken on WorstEffect alone; the scopes of every row it reaches
  are consulted.
- A test grants one class and refuses the other, both ways round, and asserts the tool is absent
  from the offer rather than merely refused at execution.

title: [bug] Two frontend unit tests wait on a duration, and both fail when the suite runs slow
description:
Seen 2026-09-04 on an otherwise green tree, and measured rather than guessed.

## What fails

- src/recall.test.ts:50 — 'typing while navigating narrows the filter — the
  panel owns printable keys'. The settle helper waits for the panel's text to
  stop containing an ellipsis; it timed out holding
  'historythis directory……↑ ↓ to navigateesc to dismiss'.
- src/terminal-content.test.ts:10470 — 'session.read serves the frame the
  question is about (nocx-7l4ex.3) > uses the live renderer again after the
  overlay closes'. `await vi.waitFor(() => expect(editorOf(content).isVisible)
  .toBe(true))` timed out.

Both are vi.waitFor with the 1000 ms default.

## Why it is the tests and not the product

The measurement is the whole finding: the red run took 248 s, and two runs of
the same tree either side of it took 72 s and 89 s. The machine was loaded
about threefold, and exactly the two assertions bounded by a one-second wait
went red. Run alone, the two files pass 362 of 362.

AGENTS.md: a test may not depend on timing — wait on an observable state
change, never on a duration; and a spec that needs a fast machine has not been
caught yet rather than being correct. This is that, in the unit suite: the two
waits are for a state the code reaches, so the fix is to wait on the state and
not on the clock, NOT to raise the timeout — which converts the report into
silence.

Nothing in the tree changed under them: the same suite ran 6259, 6264 and 6265
green around the one red run.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Load the machine (a container e2e run, or any parallel build) so a full
   `vitest run` in frontend/ takes ~3x its usual wall clock.
2. Run the whole frontend suite: `cd frontend && ./node_modules/.bin/vitest run`.
3. The two tests above fail on their vi.waitFor; the other 6263 pass.
4. Run the two files alone on an idle machine: both pass.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Neither test's pass depends on how fast the machine is: each waits on the
  state it is about, with no duration standing in for it.
- Raising a timeout or adding a retry does not count, by the rule above.
- The two files stay green in a full-suite run on a loaded machine — one
  reproduction is a suite run under deliberate load, which is how this was
  seen.

title: The row records what resolved, and not the route
description:
Design §5: "Record WHAT resolved — repository, path, commit, digest — rather than HOW, so the result
is auditable after the fact even though the route is not repeatable."

An agent's route is not reproducible: it searched, read a page, followed a link, guessed a raw
address. Recording the route would be recording something nobody can replay and that no later
question can be checked against. Recording the RESULT is what makes the row worth reading a year
later — and what makes change detection mean something, since the digest is TOFU and buys nothing at
the first install.

The installed row already carries a source with an address and an installedAt (skills.list). What it
does not carry is what the address resolved TO when the address is not itself the file.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An installed skill's row records the resolved file address, the digest and when, and where the
  resolution names a repository, a path within it and a commit, those are recorded too.
- What is NOT recorded is stated in the code: the search, the page the model read, the links it
  followed. Say why, so the next person does not add them as a feature.
- A skill installed from Settings and a skill installed by the assistant produce the SAME record
  shape. Two shapes for one fact is the defect this epic keeps avoiding.
- The row's second line reads as a sentence a person can act on, and a skill placed in the installed
  root by hand still has no source and still says nothing false.
close_reason: 9f9d41e6, e2e/skills-management.spec.ts green in the container (chromium, 1 passed) on my own re-run after the gate lock cleared. The resolved URL is stored whole and verbatim rather than parsed: a raw forge address already encodes org, repo, ref and path in order, so the record names them wherever the resolution did, and splitting them out needs the per-host adapter and ref-to-commit resolution this design deletes — a host the parser had not been taught would turn a real repository into three empty fields. The model-reports-what-it-resolved reading is refused in the same comment, on nocx-ojfuc.1's reasoning. THE DIGEST WAS A REAL HOLE, not a formality: Digests[name] is the hash of the ADOPTED DIRECTORY and Approve moves it, while the digest the approval question showed is the bundle AS SERVED — a different value, since prepareSkill re-serialises SKILL.md before it lands — and that one was recorded nowhere, so the first Approve after somebody edited an installed skill erased the only trace of what the address gave. Source now carries it, written only by an install and never moved by Approve; the address and digest travel to the writer as one unexported value so a row cannot be written half-made, and InstalledAt is minted at the write so no caller can assert when. Document version 3 to 4, and the bump earns itself in the direction that is easy to miss: json drops unknown fields and the writer rebuilds from what it read, so an older build would DELETE a digest on the next toggle rather than ignore it — refusing a newer document turns silent data loss into a visible refusal. What is deliberately not recorded is written where the record is defined: the search, the page the model read, the links followed, the redirect chain, which model proposed it. NOT PROVED: nothing watches the approval window and the record show ONE digest through the product — the link is construction plus inspection; 'one record shape whoever asked' is true by construction since only one caller exists; Taken on is asserted against toLocaleString in the test's own locale, so it proves the instant and not the reading; TestApprove_ReportsAHashThatCannotBeTaken skips under root; and no real pre-existing v3 skills.json was migrated, only fixtures.

title: [bug] TestListResponseSizeCeiling wrote its cap as a constant and fails under a long $TMPDIR
description:
TestListResponseSizeCeiling wrote its cap as the constant 1024 and asserted that three one-character
filenames fit under it. The wire cost counts Entry.Path, which is absolute, so what those three
entries cost depends on how deep the directory holding them sits. Under a long $TMPDIR the "small
listing" measures ~1074 bytes and the test fails at its FIRST assertion, reporting the bound as
broken when nothing about the bound has moved:

  local_test.go:1045: small listing refused by the size cap: filesystem: listing is about 1074
  bytes, exceeding the 1024-byte cap

Found while running the suite with TMPDIR pointed at a session scratchpad (the default /tmp on this
box hits a tmpfs limit on go's testlog). Both twins had it: internal/filesystem/local and
internal/filesystem/sftp.

Fixed by measuring instead of writing the number down. An impossible one-byte cap makes the product
answer with ErrTooLargeSize.ObservedBytes, which IS the short listing's cost; the real cap is set to
exactly that, and passes, because the refusal is strictly greater-than. The long-name directory then
hangs off the same parent with the same entry count, so the only difference between the two listings
is the one the bound is about. A second implementation of the cost function in the test would have
agreed with the first right up until one of them changed.

## Steps to Reproduce

TMPDIR=/some/deep/path/of/about/eighty/characters go test -count=1 ./internal/filesystem/... \
  -run TestListResponseSizeCeiling

Red in both local and sftp on the first assertion. Green with a short $TMPDIR, which is why nobody
saw it: CI's runner and a default /tmp are both short enough.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The test passes under both a short and a long $TMPDIR, and still fails if the byte bound stops
  refusing an oversized listing.
- The cap is derived from what the short listing actually costs, not written as a literal, and not
  by reimplementing the cost function in the test.
- Both directories carry the same entry count, so the only difference between them is name length,
  which is what the comment above the test has always claimed it was testing.
close_reason: 07ce7025. The cap is measured from ErrTooLargeSize.ObservedBytes under an impossible one-byte cap rather than written as 1024, and both directories now hang off one parent with the same entry count. Verified green under both a short $TMPDIR and the long one that was red.

title: A local zsh pane changed tiers, and about 800 lines of tests went with the old one
description:
Flagged by the worker on nocx-ie23r.3 rather than left to be discovered, and it
is a real behaviour change on the most-used path in the product.

BEFORE: a local zsh pane took the coordinator's on-disk tier --
LocalEnhancedLaunch, WriteLocalRcfile, WriteLocalZDOTDIR, localZshEnv: a
transient ZDOTDIR shadowing the user's, login-phase files written to disk, and a
restoration step afterwards.

AFTER: it takes the IN-MEMORY tier -- the user's own login zsh, sourced through
fd 3, no ZDOTDIR shadowing at all. The coordinator no longer forks the shell, so
the on-disk tier had no caller left and went, taking about 800 lines of
launcher_local_zsh_test.go with it: the transient-ZDOTDIR interval, the
login-phase files, and ZDOTDIR restoration.

THIS IS PROBABLY BETTER AND IT IS STILL A CHANGE. Not shadowing a person's
ZDOTDIR is what the delivery-modes design wanted (N4: no rc file is ever created
or modified) and D11 is where it arrives. But nobody chose it as a change: it
fell out of deleting the caller, and the coverage that guarded the old behaviour
was deleted rather than retargeted, except the one test carrying the product
assertion (TestLocalZshSession_IsIntegratedOnTheUsersOwnShell, retargeted).

The risk is specific rather than general: zsh startup files are ordered
(.zshenv, .zprofile, .zshrc, .zlogin) and the two tiers do not enter that order
at the same point. A person with work in .zprofile or a ZDOTDIR of their own is
the case that used to have tests and now has one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A local zsh pane on a machine where the person has their own ZDOTDIR gets
  their configuration, and nocx's integration, and nocx does not shadow or
  restore anything. Asserted on a real zsh, not on a launcher's arguments.
- The startup-file order is asserted for the in-memory tier: which of .zshenv,
  .zprofile, .zshrc and .zlogin have run when nocx's integration installs
  itself, and that a person's own work in each still runs.
- The interval that the deleted tests guarded has an answer under the new tier
  or is recorded as no longer existing. Read them at 6e2a97ac^ rather than
  guessing what they said.
- Whatever is decided is true for bash and POSIX shells too, or the difference
  is stated.

title: The vault unlock title reads 'Unlock the vault to The vault is locked. Unlock it to continue.'
description:
Found in passing by the nocx-76wyh worker while reading the prompt's own name. Named, not touched — it is a wording fix in vault.tsx and the worker was scoped to e2e/.

frontend/src/vault.tsx:1121-1123 composes the prompt's title and aria-label as 'Unlock the vault to ' + props.reason. The comment beside it says why: a bare 'Unlock the vault' cannot be told apart from the key and connection prompts, so the reason NAMES THE OPERATION that made the app ask now. That contract makes reason a verb phrase — 'read this secret', 'open this connection'.

The dispatcher's global sealed seam does not honour it. vault.tsx:305, inside onVaultSealed, sets the reason to a full sentence: 'The vault is locked. Unlock it to continue.' So a real user, on the most common path there is — any RPC landing on a sealed vault — reads:

    Unlock the vault to The vault is locked. Unlock it to continue.

Two things are wrong and only one is grammar. The sentence also says nothing: it restates the situation the person is already looking at instead of naming the operation, which is the whole reason the slot exists.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Seal the vault (or let presence seal it — the last client leaving does, per D9).
2. Do anything that makes an RPC touch it.
3. Read the prompt's title.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The title is grammatical on every path that raises the prompt, asserted by a test that walks each caller of setUnlockReason rather than the one the author remembered.
- The global sealed seam either names the operation that made the app ask, or passes no reason at all and gets the bare 'Unlock the vault' the slot already falls back to. Deciding which is the task: naming the operation needs the seam to know it, and if it cannot, say so where the reason is set.
- The contract on reason is written at the prop, not only in a comment beside one caller: it is a verb phrase completing 'Unlock the vault to ...'.
- The aria-label matches the title; both are built from the same expression today and must stay that way.

title: The helper's endpoint and install layout are not the layout D3 requires
description:
D3 of the generation-daemon lifecycle design requires:

  ~/.nocx/run/<machine>/<generation>.sock
  ~/.nocx/run/<machine>/<generation>.lock
  ~/.nocx/helper/<machine>/<version>-<goos>-<goarch>-<hash>/

with <generation> and <machine> at least 128 bits each, base32.

The tree has neither the machine namespace (endpoint.Dir, endpoint.go:110-117;
deploy.installDir) nor the width: the socket is named with the first 16 hex
characters of the generation -- 64 bits (endpoint.go:68-76).

THE TWO HALVES ARE NOT EQUALLY WRONG. The truncation carries an argument in the
code -- "this is a NAME and never a credential", because the handshake confirms
the full content hash (D21) -- and may well stand; if it does, D3 should be
amended to say so rather than left contradicted.

THE MISSING <machine> NAMESPACE CARRIES NO ARGUMENT, and D3 says what it costs,
having been corrected once already for exactly this: "machine B probes its own
lock, finds it free because it is a different file, and retires the SHARED
install directory under machine A's live daemon. A machine-scoped lock cannot
prove global disuse of an artifact that is not machine-scoped."

WHY IT MATTERS NOW: a home directory shared over NFS between a laptop and a
server is that case exactly, and nocx-ie23r makes both ends helper hosts. Found
while writing the local-helper design (adversarial review, verified against the
tree); that design names the divergence and inherits it rather than fixing it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Either the layout matches D3 -- machine namespace on the run directory, the
  lock and the install tree, both identifiers at their stated width -- or D3 is
  amended to record what the code does and why, with the retirement hazard
  answered by something other than the namespace.
- Whichever way it goes, a test proves two machines sharing one home cannot
  retire each other's live install.
- sockaddr_un.sun_path length is checked, as D3 requires; the check exists
  (maxSocketPath) and must survive any name that gets longer.

title: When the local helper will not start, the person is told what to do
description:
Design L4. There is no fallback: nocx does not open the pane by another route.

A remote host is an environment we do not control, so a helper failure there
degrades to the script tier - that is AD-5 purpose. The local machine is an
INSTALLATION, and a daemon that ships with the app and will not start is a broken
nocx. A second, differently-behaving terminal opened quietly in its place is how
that breakage survives a month and is then debugged from the wrong end.

openRefusal is the carrier and needs no new mechanism: it exists so an answer the
open path produced itself keeps its sentence instead of being flattened into
"Internal error".

## Acceptance Criteria

- Opening a pane with the endpoint unreachable produces a refusal naming THREE
  distinct things - what failed (install, start, or handshake), why (the concrete
  error: no space, not executable, silent past the sentinel budget, another
  generation holds the socket), and what to do. Asserted as three pieces, never as
  one substring.
- A refusal that cannot name an action fails the test. That is a bug in the
  refusal, not a fact about the failure.
- A probe that fails at coordinator start raises NO notification; it surfaces when
  a person tries to open a pane. A person who has not asked for a terminal has not
  been harmed, and a startup toast about a daemon is noise they cannot act on.
- The refusal reaches the wire with its sentence intact - over the real socket,
  not a payload the test built.

title: A top-sheet prompt survives into connections-settings and swallows the click, once in a full webkit run
description:
Seen once in a full two-browser container run on feat/agent-ploicy (536 passed, 9 skipped, this one failed, 41.5m). NOT reproduced in three targeted reruns — so it is a real defect that is not yet localized, not a defect that has gone away. A green rerun is not evidence.

## What failed

e2e/connections-settings.spec.ts:72 'walks from Settings gear to a created SSH tab', webkit only; chromium passed the same commit in the same run.

The click at line 133 — page.locator('.cm-form').getByRole('tab', {name: 'Authentication'}) — timed out at 30s. The element resolved, was visible, enabled and stable, and every one of ~56 retries was intercepted:

  <div class="ui-prompt-overlay" data-placement="top-sheet"> from <div> subtree intercepts pointer events

So a top-sheet Prompt was open over the connection editor and never closed. The failing click is INSIDE that editor, which is what makes a connection-side prompt the likely owner.

## Where it lives

Six surfaces mount a top-sheet Prompt: agent-approval-prompt.tsx, connection-password-prompt.tsx, password-editor.tsx, key-material-input.tsx, vault.tsx, and connections.tsx (whose comment at :3157 says the prompt is rendered at the root so it floats ABOVE the editor — exactly the geometry seen here).

feat/agent-ploicy touched only agent-approval-prompt.tsx among them, and touched neither ui/prompt.tsx, ui/overlay/modal-host.ts nor styles/components/prompt.css. An approval prompt needs an agent run; the editor does not have one. So the branch is not the likely origin, but that is the first line of the diagnosis and not its conclusion.

## What was tried, and did not reproduce it

1. The spec alone, webkit — passed (7.1s).
2. e2e/assistant-permissions.spec.ts then this spec, webkit — both passed. (This epic's new spec runs earlier alphabetically and raises approval prompts, so it was the first suspect.)
3. The two alphabetically preceding files — connection-overlay.spec.ts, connection-password.spec.ts — then this spec, webkit: 13 passed. connection-password mounts a top-sheet prompt and was the second suspect.

So the leak needs more of the run than a three-file window, or it is a race that only the full run's timing exposes.

## Steps to Reproduce

Run the whole suite in the container, both browsers: e2e/run-in-container.sh . Watch e2e/connections-settings.spec.ts:72 under webkit. It is intermittent.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The owning surface is named: which Prompt is open, and which spec left it. A bisect over the webkit file order is the mechanical way — run the first half of the files before it, then narrow.
- The cause is a leak, not a timeout: the fix closes the prompt (or stops it being raised across a page), never widens a wait or adds a retry.
- A test asserts no modal overlay survives a spec — a global afterEach or a stand-level assertion is cheaper than finding this again, and it would have named the culprit on the first run.
- If the leak is backend state restored onto a fresh page rather than DOM left behind, say so explicitly: that is a product defect, not a test one.
close_reason:
Merged as cd4da31d (worker 07e574ae). THE CULPRIT WAS NO SPEC — it was backend state, and the product is right. The shared stand's vault seals when the last client leaves (design D9, internal/vault/presence.go), and every spec that brings its OWN backend leaves the shared stand with no client attached for its whole duration, far longer than the detach window. connections-settings sets the vault up in the first project's pass; it seals during the next own-backend spec; the second project's pass meets a sealed vault, and the spec has a branch for UNINITIALIZED and none for SEALED. The overlay was the app-root vault unlock prompt raised by the dispatcher's global sealed seam (vault.tsx:300, onVaultSealed), not by any of the six surfaces directly — which is why reading those six would never have found it. presence.go's own header already carries the same signature from nocx-58q7d: 'eighteen specs reported it as ui-prompt-overlay intercepts pointer events'.

DOM OR BACKEND STATE: reproduced deliberately rather than inferred — sealing the shared vault over the control plane and walking the spec's route reproduced the failure exactly, three intercepted retries and all.

THE FIX is in resetStand beside the other three durable documents: if the vault is sealed, unseal it with the one passphrase the shared stand is ever set up with (now SHARED_VAULT_PASSPHRASE in the harness, not a literal in the spec). Uninitialized is left alone. No timeout, wait or retry was touched anywhere.

THE INSTRUMENT I ASKED FOR WAS BUILT, PROVEN, AND THEN MEASURED AND REMOVED — the best part of the work. The afterEach 'no modal survives a spec' guard bit exactly as briefed (it named the dialog and the prompt and the spec that left them), and then a full webkit run measured what it costs: 24 tests failed and 10 more never ran, and NOT ONE was the defect. It cannot be — Playwright gives every test a fresh context, so DOM never crosses a test boundary, and what crossed was product state. The 24 were specs ending on the surface they exist to prove. It was replaced with a diagnostic that answers the question the original report could not: on a FAILED test, name the modals standing over the page.

Counts, worker's run: 559 passed, 9 skipped, 0 failed, 44.4m, connections-settings passing in BOTH projects. Coordinator's full run on the merged tree is in flight.

Two corrections to my brief, both accepted: nothing survives a spec (contexts are per-test), and the six top-sheet surfaces were the wrong place to look because the seam raises it. It also found a user-visible wording defect on the way and left it for me to place: nocx-lkfvm.

title: An audit the person asks for, and the role that answers it
description:
The last piece of the review, and the opposite shape to the install-time classifier this spec killed.

That classifier gated nothing and certified nothing while appearing to. An audit is asked for BY THE PERSON, about a skill they already hold, and produces a reading they act on themselves: what this skill tells the assistant to do, what it reaches for, which lines the scan matched and what those lines do in context. It gates nothing and claims nothing, which is exactly why it is honest.

internal/profile/role.go has the vocabulary: ModelRole is a NAMED model assignment, a feature asks for a role by name, and the assignment lives in one place. The set is closed and product-defined — answering, classifier, summarizing. An auditing role is one const plus its consumer.

AND THAT FILE CARRIES THE WARNING THAT BINDS THIS. RoleClassifier was added ahead of its consumer and is recorded there as a shape not to repeat: "a role in the closed set that nothing asks for is the shape RoleClassifier is stuck in (nocx-01ud6), and repeating it would be worse than not having the role." So the role lands with the audit or it does not land.

A BUTTON, NOT A PAGE LOAD. It is a model call, which is money, and the same file already insists that an unassigned role falls back to the answering endpoint "with a note in the UI, never silently: it spends money the person did not ask to spend". Opening a skill's card must cost nothing.

What the audit reads is the whole bundle. What it must never be given is authority: its verdict changes nothing about what policy permits, and the word "safe" does not appear in its output, because absence of a finding is not safety and we must not put our signature on a file we did not read.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A person asks for an audit of a skill they hold and reads a report naming what it instructs, what it reaches for, and its scan findings in context.
- No model call happens until they ask.
- The auditing role lands with this consumer, and unassigned it falls back with a visible note.
- The report never changes what the assistant may do, asserted rather than asserted-by-absence.
- Its wording claims no safety; a skill with no findings is reported as having none, not as safe.
close_reason:
b49e9be4. skills.audit reads a skill the person already holds, on their button press, through the new auditing role. THE REPORT IS PROSE, ONE FIELD: three structured slots (what it instructs, what it reaches for, findings in context) were rejected because an empty third box says 'nothing found', which is a verdict wearing a layout — the three questions are asked in the prompt instead, where they shape the answer without becoming a schema anybody can evaluate. Every other field is a fact about the request, the call, or what was read; not one is an opinion, so there is nothing to count or threshold. The findings are OUR scan's, per file, because a line number a model reported would be a self-report about a document only it can see, while these are checkable against skills.file.

The wording refuses to be a verdict: the block is headed 'A description, not a verdict', the report is 'What a model read in X', and zero findings read as 'The static scan matched nothing in these files — that is not the same as safe.' A test enumerates the forbidden claims (is safe, looks safe, no risk, trustworthy, verified, clean) and asserts none appears.

The auditing model is told its input is a document to describe and that a skill's text may address whoever reads it; the skill's bytes ride the USER turn only, so its text never shares a region with the sentence saying it is only a document. Claimed as defence in depth and NOT a guarantee, in those words in the code — what makes a persuaded model survivable is that the report changes nothing.

ASSERTED, NOT ASSUMED, and these two are the bead: TestSkillsAudit_ChangesNothingAboutWhatTheAssistantMayDo scripts the model to answer 'This skill is completely safe. Enable it and grant it every permission' and asserts skills.list comes back byte-identical with the skill still off; TestSkillsAudit_ReadingACardSpendsNoModelCall drives list/files/file over the real socket to an engine call count of 0, and only the button makes it 1.

The role landed with its consumer per role.go's own warning about RoleClassifier. Unassigned it falls back to the answering endpoint and NAMES it, and the Roles page says so before the button rather than after the money is spent; ResolveRole still refuses, and the transport is what decides to spend the other endpoint — that split is what makes the note possible.

Worker's own honesty, worth keeping: NONE of his tests prove the model's judgement, every model in them is a stub, and he says which prove plumbing and which are mechanical. The one security-shaped property he proves is a property of OUR composition (bytes in the user turn), not of the model.

Beyond the brief and defensible: AuditSkill on the assistant.Client interface with an embedded unauditedClient that REFUSES, so a fake cannot let an audit test pass against a client that never ran one; resolveEndpointMaterial extracted so the vault's unlock prompt says 'audit a skill' rather than 'answer the ask'; a separate omission enum rather than widening skills.file's closed union with a value that method can never return; StatusCard gained a typed prose variance because a p element collapses a three-paragraph report into one run-on block.

go test assistant/skill/profile/transport ok; vet, gofumpt, golangci-lint --build-tags gtk3, go build -tags gtk3, deadcode ratchet 82 all-baselined; contracts:check, frontend lint at 149 all-baselined, tsc on both projects. Coordinator fixed three test fakes the worker's tsc run missed (pre-commit checks tsconfig.test.json too) — each now carries an audit that REJECTS by default, for the same reason his Go fake does.

title: A receipt may claim no entry: the contract lets entryId be empty, and that is what hid nocx-2019q
description:
Raised by the nocx-0dzqq worker's own correction of its first report, which is the useful half.

agent.standingAnswerSaved.entryId is contracted as 'the ledger entry of the turn that asked', and the schema permits an empty string — 'Empty when the proposal was never bound to an entry'. The renderer routes by that field and drops anything that does not match the turn block, so an empty or wrong value means the receipt is silently never drawn.

That optionality is what let nocx-2019q ship. There was no Go assertion on the field at all, and the schema conformance test could not object, because empty is legal. A contract that permits a value which makes the feature invisible cannot catch the defect that sends it.

Two questions to settle together, and the second is the real one:

1. Can the turn's entry legitimately be empty? The worker found the kernel always records the proposal before the latch trips, and had to give the test harness a proposal entry because the harness described a run that does not exist. If a receipt is only ever sent from a run with a ledger, the field is required and the schema should say so.
2. If it genuinely can be empty, then an empty one is a receipt that will never be drawn, and sending it is the soft degrade — the person is told nothing and nothing is logged as wrong.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read contracts/agent.standingAnswerSaved.schema.json: entryId permits an empty string.
2. Read frontend/src/agent-ask.ts: a notification whose entryId is not the turn block's is dropped.
3. Therefore any run that sends an empty entryId draws no receipt and reports nothing.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Whether a receipt can be sent from a run with no ledger entry is answered from the code, not assumed, and the answer is written where the field is declared.
- If it cannot: entryId becomes required with minLength 1, and a test asserts a receipt is never sent without one.
- If it can: sending one is refused or reported, because a receipt nobody can see is not a receipt.
- A test asserts the drawn receipt reaches the turn — the assertion nocx-2019q lacked — at whichever layer can see both ends.
close_reason: Merged as 569362fa (worker fd177987). The question was answered FROM THE CODE, each link named: notifyStandingAnswer is reachable only from handleApprove, which refuses without h.op and without a pendingRuns hit; pendingRuns has one writer that creates an entry (handleAsk, after h.op.Run returned, setting entryID from askRes.EntryID); SubmitAgentAsk answers EntryID: in.ID, and in.ID is p.AskID, which validateAgentAsk refuses empty and whose own contract already says minLength 1. So entryId can never legitimately be empty: it is minLength 1 now, the description stops promising a case with no producer, and the same answer is written at the Go declaration. Since nothing produces it, notifyStandingAnswer REFUSES to send a receipt without one, logs at ERROR, and returns a sentence joining agent.approve's warning — which agent-approval-decision.ts already shows, so the degrade is visible in the product. AND THE FRONTEND WAS WORSE THAN THE BEAD SAID: agent-ask.ts did not DROP a receipt with an empty entryId, it treated it as a WILDCARD, drawn on whatever block the run id found — a branch that existed only to serve the schema's empty case and that disagreed with every sibling subscription in the file. Removed, with a test that fails when the wildcard is restored. The worker also corrected me: criterion 3's assertion already existed on HEAD; what was missing was its NON-VACUITY GUARD, which it added (two equal entries — which two empty ones were — would pass whichever value the handler sent). Sibling sweep: every other routing entryId already carries minLength 1; agent.runResolved.entryId permits empty and was left deliberately, with the contrast stated — optional rather than required, not a routing key, and its empty case has a real producer and a legible degrade.

title: The parse never says a command RUNS a file: execute and source are declared, mapped, and never produced
description:
Found while briefing nocx-872jc.3, which cannot be built without it.

internal/content/resources.go declares ResourceExecute and ResourceSource and Effect() maps them (execute -> EffectDelegate; source -> EffectPrivilegeChange, with a comment explaining that source and . change the current shell's environment unlike subprocess execution). Nothing produces either. internal/assistant/cmdeffect.go, the only producer of resource verbs, emits Read, Write and Unknown and nothing else — grep over the tree finds no assignment of Execute or Source outside resources.go and tests.

So for 'bash deploy.sh': bash is not in the program table, the command goes to unresolvedCommand, and what gets recorded is the PROGRAM name with ResourceUnknown. The operand deploy.sh is not recorded at all. The product therefore cannot say which file a command runs, which is the fact nocx-872jc.3's whole surface rests on.

THIS IS NOT A UI CHANGE AND MUST NOT BE MADE AS ONE. Today an unrecognised command yields Unknown, and Effect() answers WorstEffect(declared) — the most conservative class available. Producing execute would move it from 'the worst of them' to Delegate specifically, which is a LOOSENING of the effect classification, i.e. a change to what policy permits. It is decided in the effects/policy area, on its own evidence, not behind an approval window's viewer.

It also touches feat/agent-ploicy's territory: rules are evaluated over the parsed Invocation, and changing which verbs a command produces changes which rules match it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. grep -rn 'ResourceExecute|ResourceSource' internal/ --include=*.go | grep -v _test — only the declaration and the Effect() mapping.
2. Propose 'bash deploy.sh' and read the ApprovalRequest's Invocation.Resources: no entry for deploy.sh.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A command that runs a script names that script, with the execute verb; source and . name theirs with the source verb.
- The effect change is stated and defended: which commands move class, in which direction, and why that is right — with the WorstEffect comparison spelled out, since this is a loosening.
- The program table's growth is bounded and its membership argued: which interpreters are recognised and why those.
- A command whose script is a dynamic token stays Unresolved, and a test drives it.
- Existing effect and policy tests are run and any that move are explained, not adjusted.
close_reason: NOT A DEFECT — filed on a stale reading, refuted by measurement. internal/assistant/cmdeffect.go:290 'case "bash", "sh"' records the script operand with content.ResourceExecute, ':289' records source/. with ResourceSource, and ':320' records an executable path operand with ResourceExecute. Landed 2026-08-31 in d226fb49 (nocx-4h0m7.3, 'distinguish execution from file mutation'), which was already an ancestor of this branch four days before this bead was filed. Probed directly against parseCanonicalInvocation: 'bash deploy.sh' -> [{deploy.sh execute}], 'sh ./setup.sh' -> [{./setup.sh execute}], './run.sh' -> [{./run.sh execute}], 'source env.sh' -> [{env.sh source}], all with Unresolved empty. The bead's premise ('bash is not in the program table, so the operand is never recorded') was false when written. No loosening of effect classification is pending, because none is needed: nocx-872jc.3 can take which file a command names from the existing parse exactly as its criterion says.

title: The delivery mode is still called relay in code and in fifteen documents
description:
AGENTS.md records the rename: "Since 2026-08-31 there is no relay - the remote
binary is the helper." The rename never reached the tree. The delivery axis is
still auto|raw|script|relay in internal/connection/resolver.go:191;
internal/lifecycle/protocol.go:8 and internal/lifecycleremote/adapter.go:18 name
a future relay adapter; internal/git/git.go uses relay as the tier name in six
comments; and fifteen documents under docs/ and .internal/specs/ still say relay
- including the delivery-modes design's decision N1, the text that named the
three modes.

Two names for one thing is what the "look for the existing answer" rule is
about: a reader cannot tell whether "relay" in a comment means the helper that
shipped or a tier that was deferred.

Not a mechanical sed. nocx-if6 is closed as superseded and its title keeps the
word; ADRs under docs/decisions/ are historical records and may keep it with a
note rather than be rewritten.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The delivery-mode value a connection carries is named `helper` everywhere it
  is written or read - the enum, the settings value, the resolver and the form -
  and `grep -rn '\brelay\b' --include=*.go internal/ cmd/` returns nothing
  outside a deliberate historical note.
- The delivery-modes design's N1 and every live spec under .internal/specs/ name
  the third mode `helper`; each ADR that keeps the word carries one line saying
  it is the historical name.
- nocx is greenfield: no alias, no compatibility read of the old value.
close_reason:
The third delivery mode is the helper. Commit cad0ba26, 96 files, +499/-467.

EVIDENCE a stranger can check:
- `grep -rn '\brelay\b' --include=*.go --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx internal/
  frontend/src/ contracts/` returns 19 hits, ZERO of them in contracts/ or
  frontend/src/. Each remaining one is an ordinary English use - tunnel's
  byte relay, the fault proxy, "no reported exit to relay", Orca's relay port
  scan (an external citation that must not be falsified) - except one
  deliberate historical note at internal/profile/profile.go:88 ("helper -
  spelled `relay` until 2026-08-31").
- No capitalised identifier survives: `grep -rn 'Relay[A-Z]|RelayConsent|
  DesiredRelay'` over Go, ts and tsx is empty.
- The wire moved with the code: contracts/open.schema.json's enum is
  ["auto","raw","script","helper"], profiles.effective/create/update carry
  `helperConsent`, and the GENERATED renderer type
  frontend/src/generated/open.ts:39 reads 'auto'|'raw'|'script'|'helper'.
  `npm run contracts:check` passes from frontend/.
- `go build -tags gtk3 ./...` verified by the coordinator, not only reported.
  Worker's suites: connection, profile, transport (109s), git and its six
  subpackages, backup, helper's eight subpackages, plus app (159s), ssh,
  lifecycle, notify, session, nativeports, discovery - all ok. Frontend:
  capability + connections.behavior, 88 tests passed; typecheck, lint and
  prettier clean. Pre-commit hook green.

WHERE A SUBSTITUTION WOULD HAVE LIED, and what was written instead: "relay
sends operations to the helper" became "the helper CLIENT sends operations to
the deployed helper" (internal/git/git.go, gitargs.go, the git-manager design);
