title: A skill refused at discovery vanishes from the list with only a log line
description:
Named as a residual by nocx-l4lz9 (8a31e4be) and true of the whole loop, not just the new refusal.

discoverDetailed refuses a skill and continues, logging: missing description, invalid name, invalid frontmatter, and now description too long. The Settings list simply does not contain it. A person who put a SKILL.md on disk and cannot find it in the product has nothing to read but a slog line they will never see.

AGENTS.md: 'A soft degrade must be visible in the product, not only in a log. A silent degrade the UI contradicts is how a feature that does not exist survives a release.'

The fix is a third thing a row can be. skills.list today reports a skill and its status; a directory that IS a skill-shaped thing and was refused needs to appear and say why, rather than being absent. That is contracts/skills.list.schema.json, the generated frontend type, internal/transport, and the Skills page.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Put a SKILL.md under a skill root whose frontmatter has no description, or a description over the cap.
2. Open Settings -> Assistant -> Skills. The directory is not there and nothing says why.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A skill-shaped directory that discovery refused appears in the list, named, with the reason in the person's words and the number where there is one.
- It is visibly not a usable skill: it cannot be enabled and the assistant is never offered it.
- The wire shape is declared in contracts/ and asserted by an over-the-wire test, not only by a DTO test.
- Every existing refusal in the loop reaches it, not just the newest one.

title: Forgetting a ROW answer still says nothing about the work already running
description:
Left in place and marked in the code at the call site by the nocx-r4fh8 worker, who scoped that bead to the one-rule seam as the brief said.

nocx-r4fh8 gave a RULE revocation a time: it says how many live runs decide differently without the answer, and offers apply-to-future against also-stop. A ROW answer — one of the seven effect rows moved off its default — still writes through policy.set, which carries no timing at all. So forgetting a row-level answer has exactly the defect that bead fixed for rules: the person takes an action specifically to stop something, and a run started thirty seconds ago goes on doing it, silently.

The predicate does not transfer as it stands: content.ChangedByRuleWrite is rule-shaped — it builds representative invocations per SELECTOR. A row write needs a whole-policy comparison, which is a different question and probably a different function beside it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Answer a live effect row (say, Allow always for reading and inspecting).
2. Start an agent run that uses it and leave it in flight.
3. On Assistant permissions, take that answer back.
4. Nothing is said about the running work, and the run goes on under the old answer.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A row change or forget affecting live runs says how many and offers the same two answers, in the same words rules already use — one vocabulary, not two.
- The count is the precise reading, as for rules: only runs whose own grant would decide differently. If a whole-policy comparison cannot be made that precise, say so on screen rather than showing a number that cannot be defended.
- Choosing future-only leaves running work alone, asserted at both ends. It fails first.
- policy.set carries the timing, its schema changes in the same commit, and there is an over-the-wire test.
close_reason:
Merged as 4073b1bb (worker c3a34433). policy.set now takes the same runs enum, answers the same four fields under the same names, and the page raises the same block with the same two buttons — the vocabulary is reused, not respelled: policyRuleWriteRuns became policyWriteRuns because it is every policy write's answer, and RuleGesture became PolicyGesture with a row variant so a row travels the ONE path that knows how to ask. policy.set's result lost its {ok: true}, a constant dressed as a fact; applied says what it stood for and can be false.

THE DERIVATION IS NOT A COPY AND NOT A PROBE. A rule names a selector, so probes bound the question; a row names none — its subject is every invocation classifying as its effect. EvaluateInvocation's composition order gives the shape instead: for one effect the evaluator reads exactly the row's decision, the rules, the row's scopes and the fence, and a matrix write moves rows alone. So equal rows cannot answer any invocation under that effect apart, and different decisions answer apart about every command line no standing answer speaks about — never an empty set, because a selector is always bounded to one command word. Comparing rows IS comparing decisions, and BOTH directions are asserted against the evaluator itself rather than restated in production code.

The comparison is against the run's authority MINTED AGAIN from the document the write leaves behind, through the same runGrantFrom the real run crossed — split out of the existing mint, not a second one. A run's rows have the session overlay resolved in and the fence folded in, so comparing a minted row against a stored one would report every fence-narrowed run as changed by a write that moved nothing; TestPolicySet_AChangeTheMintErasesReachesNoRun is that case.

MY BRIEF'S PREMISE WAS WRONG and the worker disproved it: a run's own rules cannot narrow the count. A permit over df -h makes one command line decide the same either way and says nothing about the rest of the row, and since every selector is bounded to a command word the rules can never cover the whole effect. TestChangedByRowWrite_AStandingAnswerOverOneCommandDoesNotShieldTheRow asserts both halves.

It also caught that the count and the SENTENCE were answering different questions: the sentence was derived from the document, but the prompt's own seam had already moved the row, so the document moved nothing while a run started earlier was still under the old one. Red first, quoted: 'the stopped run's sentence = an answer this run was using was changed: the matrix was saved as it stood, want it to name the answer that was changed'. The moved rows now come from the same walk the count does.

PRECISION, STATED HONESTLY AND ON SCREEN: exact but not narrow. It counts out a run with no grant, one whose session overlay answers that effect, one whose fence already refused it, one minted after somebody made the same change, a write that states what the rows already say, and a change the mint erases. It cannot bound the question to a few command lines because a row has no such bound — a write that really moves a row really does reach every live run still stating the old one. Said in three places, including a caption shown only for a row. Mutation check: settleRuns 'mode != runsStop' to 'mode == runsAsk' made future-only stop runs too, and BOTH revoke suites failed at the liveness assertion that sits before the counts.

Merged tree green: transport 393s and content 312s under -race, contracts:check, tsc --noEmit, 6257 frontend tests.

title: A distinct termination reason for a revoked answer needs a schema rung
description:
Found by the nocx-r4fh8 worker, who changed course rather than smuggle it in. Correct call.

Stopping a run because its permission was revoked wants its own termination reason. The worker added TermAnswerRevoked and the stop silently produced runs with NO durable ending: executions.termination_reason carries a SQLite CHECK enumerating the same strings content declares, so FinishAgentRun failed, was logged, and the startup sweep would have repaired the run as interrupted. A soft degrade of exactly the shape AGENTS.md forbids — visible only in a log.

Widening it is a rung on the ladder in schema_migrate.go plus a rebuild of the executions table and pinning schema 16's shape. That is a deliverable of its own, not something to land beside a transport change.

So today the stop uses TermUserKilled and names the revoked answer in the RUN'S SENTENCE, which is what a person actually reads. Both content.TerminationReason and StopRunsForRevokedAnswer record what a distinct name would cost.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A test asserts a revoked-answer stop lands a durable execution row whose termination_reason is the new one. It fails first, on the CHECK.
- The rung is added the way the ladder's existing rungs are, with schema 16's shape pinned by a test.
- No run can reach a terminal state the CHECK rejects: a test enumerates content.TerminationReason and asserts every value is accepted by the table.
- The run's sentence still names the revoked answer — the reason is machine-readable metadata, not a replacement for the words a person reads.
close_reason: Merged as 9b64533a (worker 4b24d796). TermAnswerRevoked joins content.TerminationReason AND the CHECK, via rung 16->17 on the ladder. Red first, quoted: 'the database REFUSED the termination reason answer-revoked that Go declares: CHECK constraint failed'. Then, pointing the stop at it with the CHECK still narrow, the trap fired through the product path and proved WORSE than the comment recorded: the transport test failed with 'run revoked never reached cancelled (last state streaming)' and grepping the run for constraint|ERROR|WARN produced NOTHING — the harness discards the logger, so the only trace the comment promised does not exist there. terminalize logs a Warn and returns, so no agent.runState is sent either: a person watches an answer stream forever until a restart. THE TRAP IS NOW CLOSED BY A TEST that parses ledger.go with go/ast rather than keeping a list, so it cannot be forgotten; it has both ends (a CHECK widened without its constant fails too) and a paired non-vacuity test proving the CHECK still refuses an unknown value. Proven to bite: adding TermBogusProbe made it red, naming the value and printing both vocabularies side by side. AND IT FOUND A LIVE DEFECT NOT ITS OWN: validateOnDiskSchemaShapeFor digested stored DDL verbatim, but SQLite re-emits a table name quoted after ALTER TABLE RENAME — so a database this build had just successfully migrated was REFUSED on its next open. The 14->15 rung had already armed that for anyone upgrading from 14. The parity test's normaliser moved into production (schema_shape_normalise.go), digests recomputed, and TestAnUpgradedDatabaseOpensAgainAfterTheMigrationThatWroteIt added from 14 and from 16. It also found schemaShapeDigests[15] had NO DATABASE BEHIND IT — nothing ever built a file stamped 15, so a wrong pin would have refused every genuine 15 database silently; testdata/schema_v15.sql is now frozen from 6035c0cf~1. Third place named rather than widened: runStateForTermination would default the new reason to RunFailed, but is unreachable for it today.

title: A skill ages, and the person can see it age
description:
The prompt is being reworded from 'follow it, what it returns is instruction' to guidance that can go STALE (see .internal/specs/2026-09-04-skills-under-the-same-policy-design.md). Staleness then has to be a real state with real transitions, not a figure of speech.

hermes's tools/skill_usage.py is the reference and its design notes carry two decisions worth taking whole:

  - TELEMETRY GOES IN A SIDECAR, not in frontmatter. Counters in a SKILL.md would put operational data inside authored content and create conflict pressure on skills their author owns. We already have the document beside the roots (internal/skill/store_doc.go DocumentPath) and it is the obvious home.
  - The lifecycle is three states plus an orthogonal flag: active, stale (unused beyond a configured age), archived (moved aside), and pinned meaning opt out of automatic transitions entirely.

hermes also keeps a list of bundled skills the curator must NEVER archive, because they back advertised paths in the UI — a silently archived builtin turns a promised affordance into nothing. Our builtin root is the same case and needs the same refusal.

Counters are best-effort by design there: a broken sidecar logs at debug and never breaks the tool call that was bumping it. Take that too — a skill that cannot be used because its usage counter failed is worse than a counter that is wrong.

Note what this epic is NOT. It is not the curator: no consolidation of overlapping skills, no LLM judgement about what to keep, no mass prune. It is the visible fact of age and one deliberate action on it.
acceptance_criteria: A person opens the Skills page and can tell which skills are still earning their place: each row says when it was last used, and one unused past the configured threshold says so. Archiving takes it out of what the assistant is offered while leaving the bytes on disk and recoverable. One e2e check watches it on the shipped backend, with the clock the test controls: a skill used in a run has its last-used moment recorded; a skill past the threshold reads as stale on the page; archiving it removes it from the index a later run is offered and a restore brings it back. Deliberately out: automatic deletion of anything, and automatic archiving without the person's say-so in this first cut.

title: Stack and CollectionRow both own a row's padding, the Stack wins, and the test that guards it reads stylesheet text
description:
Found while measuring nocx-zrh5z in a real engine.

.ui-collection-row declares padding: var(--space-2) var(--space-6) and its comment calls that horizontal value the list's text gutter, 'asserted by test (collection-view.test.tsx), not by eye'. Inside a divided dense Stack it computes to 0px 0px, because .ui-stack[data-divided='true'][data-dense='true'] > * (specificity 0,3,0) sets padding: var(--space-2) 0 and outranks .ui-collection-row (0,1,0).

Two components own one property, the Stack wins, and nothing tells anyone. This is the AD-8 two-owners shape in CSS.

The guard cannot see it. collection-view.test.tsx:188 reads the STYLESHEET TEXT of the row's own rule and asserts it says var(--space-6). That assertion is true of the text and false of the page. A test that reads a declaration rather than a computed value cannot report an override, so it will stay green through exactly the defect it was written for.

DO NOT 'FIX' THIS BY RESTORING THE 24px. On the Skills page the accident is currently benign and load-bearing: the zero is what puts the row's text on the same left rail as the settings label above it (both at 258.39 measured). Restoring the row's own padding would push the list's text 24px right of the settings label and take the switch column 6px off the rail that nocx-zrh5z just aligned. Whichever way it is resolved, it is a decision about which component owns row padding, not an arithmetic correction.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Render a CollectionRow inside <Stack divided dense> — the Skills list is one.
2. getComputedStyle on .ui-collection-row: padding is 0px 0px, not the declared 8px 24px.
3. npx vitest run src/ui/collection-view.test.tsx passes anyway.

## Acceptance Criteria

- One component owns a collection row's padding, and the other stops declaring it.
- The guard asserts what a browser computes, not what a stylesheet says — which means it is an e2e assertion, since jsdom performs no layout.
- The Skills page's left rail and switch column are unchanged, asserted by the existing e2e/skills-switch-column.spec.ts and by a left-edge assertion added beside it.
- Every other CollectionRow surface is checked for a shift before this lands.

title: Change to Allowed on a hand-written Program rule offers an answer the store refuses
description:
Found by the nocx-fl0o3 worker, pre-existing from nocx-hvb3r. Not fixed there — correct call, it is a different gesture.

On the Assistant permissions page, Change to Allowed on a Program rule that carries no grantedUnder — a hand-written refusal, say — sends a permit. content.validateInvocationRules refuses it: a rule whose selector covers more than one command line may only NARROW, and the one form that may widen must carry the effect it was granted under. So the store rejects the write, the page raises the danger toast and re-reads.

Nothing unsafe happens: the backend decides and the asymmetry holds. What is wrong is that the page OFFERS an answer it cannot deliver. A person clicks Allowed, sees a red toast, and has learned nothing about why — least of all that widening a loose rule requires a reading of a command, which is exactly what + Allow a command… exists to provide.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Write a refusal for a program (+ Write a refusal), producing a Program rule with no grantedUnder.
2. Open Change on that answer.
3. Choose Allowed.
4. The write is refused, a danger toast appears, and the page re-reads unchanged.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Allowed is not offered for a rule the store would refuse to widen. It fails first.
- Where it is not offered, the page says why in the person's words and points at the gesture that can do it — a permit comes from a command that was read.
- A test drives the control and asserts the offer is absent, not merely that the write fails.
- No new vocabulary: reuse the sentences + Allow a command… already builds.
close_reason: Merged as 25379046 (worker 856ee15a). canBeAllowed decides from the WIRE and nothing else — validateInvocationRules turns on exactly two facts (hasFeature may never permit; program may permit only with a non-empty grantedUnder; exact is unconstrained), and both ride on Rule in contracts/policy.get.schema.json. No command is read, no word mapped to an effect, no question asked about a call. Rows are untouched. Red first: 'Allowed is offered for any rm command', driving Change on a hand-written {program: rm, decision: refuse}. Where the answer is withheld a Caption names + Allow a command... and quotes verbatim the sentence that panel already says about itself — both are module constants read by the button, the writer and the caption, so there is ONE spelling. Criterion 4 (rules that CAN be widened still offer it) passed from the start by design: it is the guard against over-fixing. WORTH KNOWING: policy-explain-is-not-reimplemented.test.ts flagged the predicate on a grantedUnder comparison, and the worker did NOT rephrase around it. It separated the two questions instead — the ratchet bans the EVALUATOR's guard (the effect a permit was granted under versus the effect a CALL classified as, which needs a classified call), while whether a rule CARRIES one is the WRITE GATE's question, answered by the document and never by a call. The pattern was narrowed to exclude a presence test, the distinction written down at the pattern, and a test added guarding the narrowing from both sides: the evaluator shape in four spellings still trips it, two presence spellings do not.

title: The Skills page's two switches sit on different vertical lines: a settings cell and a record row have different trailing gutters
description:
Reported by the owner with a screenshot, and it is NOT what nocx-xa0cq fixed. That bead was about several ROWS disagreeing with each other, which was real; this is the page-level 'Enable skills' toggle disagreeing with the row's toggle. On the owner's screen there is one row, so the earlier defect could not even show.

What the code says, unmeasured:

- The settings toggle is a MatrixCell: .ui-settings-matrix-cell is an inline-flex holding the Checkbox AND a ProvenanceBadge, with gap var(--space-2) (8px) and .ui-settings-provenance at a fixed width: 18px. So roughly 26px of reserved gutter sits to the RIGHT of that switch.
- The row toggle is .ui-record-row__state, the last element of .ui-collection-row__actions (margin-left: auto), inside .ui-collection-row whose own padding is var(--space-2) var(--space-6) — 24px on the right, and the skills list passes no density so it is not the dense 4px variant.

Two components, two trailing gutters, two container insets, and nothing makes their right edges agree. Which of the two should move is a design decision, not an arithmetic one: the settings gutter exists to hold the reset/provenance affordance and is load-bearing.

MEASURE BEFORE FIXING. The numbers above are read off CSS and do not account for the containing PageSection/Section widths, which differ. jsdom has no layout, so this has to be measured in a real engine.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Settings -> Assistant -> Skills.
2. The 'Enable skills' switch and the skill row's switch do not share a vertical line; the row's sits further right.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The two switches share one right-hand line, measured in a real engine rather than by eye.
- Whichever container moves, it moves in the kit or in one stated place — no surface repainting a kit component to line something up.
- The settings cell keeps its reset/provenance gutter; the fix may not delete an affordance to win alignment.
- Deliberately out: aligning switches across unrelated Settings pages.
close_reason: f57232f3. Measured in Chromium in the e2e container, not reasoned about: the two containers are identical (.ui-page-section and .ui-section both span 258.39 to 1204), and .ui-collection-row's own horizontal padding computes to 0 here, so neither lead in the bead was the cause. The whole 30px was the settings rail: .ui-settings-control-line's gap (--space-3, 12px) plus .ui-settings-provenance's 18px reset slot sit to the RIGHT of a settings switch, so a settings row ends its CONTROL 30px short of where it ends its CELL, while RecordRow's state cell hangs off the row's trailing edge, which is the page's content edge. Fix: the rail's two numbers are named once on .ui-settings and read by all three consumers, and .ui-settings .ui-record-row__state takes margin-right of their sum, so the correction is derived from the values that create the offset rather than being a constant that cancels them today. Placement, not paint (check-css-integrity's APPEARANCE_PROPERTIES covers background/border/color/font/box-shadow/padding, not margin), and the reset gutter is kept. Pinned by e2e/skills-switch-column.spec.ts, which compares the two switches WITH EACH OTHER within 1px and never against a pixel constant; red-first shown with the margin set to 0; green in chromium and webkit. jsdom cannot see this — getBoundingClientRect answers zero there and every arrangement passes. 102 unit tests across settings/skills-section/record-row/collection-view, lint and both tsconfigs clean, check-coverage 101 spec files.

title: The Skills list's switches do not form a column: a row-state control shares the right-aligned actions group with buttons of varying width
description:
Reported by the owner while reading the Skills page.

The enable switch sits FIRST inside the row's ActionGroup, and the buttons after it are conditional, so its horizontal position is decided by which buttons that particular row happens to have.

  .ui-collection-row__actions { margin-left: auto; flex: 0 0 auto; }
  .ui-action-group            { justify-content: flex-end; }

The group is pinned to the right edge and is exactly as wide as its contents, so the switch's x = right edge minus the width of whatever follows it. In skills-section.tsx:334-369 that is: nothing (builtin, unchanged), Delete (authored/installed, unchanged), or Re-approve + Delete (changed). Three row shapes, three positions, in one list a person scans downward.

The kit already owns this exact reasoning on the OTHER side of the row. RecordRow's `expandable={false}` exists so a leaf beside expanding rows reserves the disclosure's width — 'so titles still form one column'. Nothing does that on the right.

Note what reordering alone would cost, because it is the obvious cheap fix and it is a trade rather than a win: putting the switch last anchors it to the right edge and makes Delete the thing that moves instead. A destructive button that changes position between rows is worse than a ragged switch, so the fix has to give the row-state control its own place rather than swap which control is ragged.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Settings -> Assistant -> Skills with at least one builtin skill and one installed skill.
2. The switches do not line up; the builtin's sits further right than the installed one's.
3. Make one skill's bytes change on disk so its row gains Re-approve, and that row's switch moves further left again.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every row's switch has the same horizontal position, whichever optional buttons that row carries, asserted by a test rather than by eye.
- The switch stops being an item of the free-form actions slot: a row's state and a row's actions are two different kinds of thing and the geometry says so.
- No surface repaints a kit component to achieve it, and the change is stated once in the kit rather than per surface.
- Deliberately out: making the buttons themselves form columns.
close_reason:
9d5e81f0. RecordRow gains a state slot drawn as .ui-record-row__state, the last element of CollectionRow's action region, so the control's place is the row's right edge rather than the sum of the buttons preceding it. skills-section passes the enable switch through it. Three states, the disclosure's three: prop absent = no cell (a list with no row state holds no column open), anything passed including null = the cell is drawn reserving --control-width-switch, so a row with no switch stops its buttons where its neighbours' stop. Pinned by 3 cases in ui/record-row.test.tsx and 1 in skills-section.test.tsx covering all three row shapes (builtin/unchanged, installed/unchanged, changed), asserted structurally because jsdom has no layout and getBoundingClientRect returns zeros there. 45 passed across record-row/collection-view/skills-section; 113 passed across the seven other RecordRow surfaces; lint and both tsconfigs clean, no ratchet baseline grew.

CORRECTION TO THIS BEAD'S OWN REASONING, from the implementer and verified: the description claimed reordering the switch to last would make Delete the ragged control. That is wrong for today's shapes — Delete is last in both shapes that carry it, so it would sit at a constant offset; the control that would move is Re-approve, which appears in one shape only. Reordering would have fixed today's symptom. The durable argument, which is what the code comments carry, is the other one: actions is free-form by design, so nothing in it is anchored except by the accident of what a surface renders last, and the next conditional control silently takes that anchor away.

Side effect worth knowing: with the switch out of the group, an approved builtin row's ActionGroup was empty — a named role='group' around nothing. The surface now draws the group only when the row has an action for it.

title: The contract generator treats agent.approve's params schema as its result, so the renderer's approve type is wrong
description:
Found in passing by the nocx-2019q worker, who left it and said so in a comment in frontend/src/agent-approval-decision.ts. Correct call — it is a generator defect, not a receipt defect.

scripts/gen-openrpc.mjs treats <method>.schema.json as that method's RESULT. But contracts/agent.approve.schema.json holds the method's PARAMS. Four consequences, and the third is the one that bites:

1. The manifest points agent.approve's result at its params.
2. frontend/src/generated/agent.approve.ts is a 'result type' that is actually params — and it is what main.tsx and the approval prompt's ApprovalScope read.
3. agent.approve.params.schema.json exists too, as a second, weaker copy of the same shape. Two schemas own one thing, which is the defect whichever wins.
4. The REAL result, {state, warning}, has no schema at all — so the one field a person's failed save travels in is unvalidated on the wire.

The obvious fixes are both wrong on their own: hand-writing the renderer's scope union is a second spelling of a closed set, and simply renaming the file leaves the generator unable to emit params types at all, which is what tempted the mis-filing in the first place.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. cat contracts/agent.approve.schema.json — it describes params (runID, tool, scope, approved).
2. Read scripts/gen-openrpc.mjs: <method>.schema.json is registered as the result.
3. Read frontend/src/generated/agent.approve.ts and see main.tsx import it as if it typed the result.
4. Grep for a schema covering {state, warning}. There is none.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The generator can emit a params type as a params type, so a method's params and result each have exactly one schema and one generated type.
- agent.approve's result {state, warning} has a schema with additionalProperties:false and an explicit required, plus an _OverTheWireConformsToContract test off the real socket.
- ApprovalScope in the renderer is still generated from the contract, never hand-written.
- agent.approve.params.schema.json and agent.approve.schema.json stop being two copies of one shape.
- A check catches the next mis-filing: a schema whose content is params must not be registered as a result.

title: files.edit and files.create put the capability's raw sentence into a model-visible result
description:
Found in passing by the nocx-4yjwk.3 worker while fixing files.read. Named, not touched — correct call.

executeFilesEdit and executeFilesCreate swallow every editor error into a tool result shaped {"status":"refused","reason":err.Error()}. So the capability's own sentence — 'filesystem: path outside the grant's scope: /some/path' — reaches the model verbatim.

That is the rule nocx-avogl.3 exists to prevent: the refusal text is OURS, written per reason, never the framework's stringification. refusalResult (kernel.go) says so in its doc comment and says why — a refusal must carry no scope list, no effect lattice and no error internals. These two paths bypass it entirely, so they leak an absolute path and the shape of the grant into the conversation.

nocx-4yjwk.3 fixed the same class for files.read by classifying at the kernel seam (capabilityRefusal, errors.Is on filesystem.ErrOutOfScope) rather than per tool, precisely so the fault-or-answer decision is not spread across tools. These two are the tools it is still spread across.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Narrow the run's filesystem capability to a directory.
2. Have the agent call files.edit (or files.create) on a path outside it.
3. Read the tool result the model receives: reason carries 'filesystem: path outside the grant's scope: <absolute path>'.

Expected: our own refusal sentence, from refusalResult, naming no path internals.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A test asserts the model-visible result for an out-of-scope files.edit and files.create contains our sentence and NOT the capability's stringification. It fails first.
- Both go through the same kernel seam files.read now uses; the fault-or-answer decision is not re-decided per tool.
- No absolute path, scope list or effect name reaches the model in a refusal.
- The person still sees what happened — the refusal is visible in the product, not only in a log.
close_reason: Merged as fcbbb3c6 (worker branch nocx-4yjwk5-files-refusal, 309256d5). files.edit and files.create now recognise the capability refusal with the kernel's ONE predicate, capabilityRefusal(err), and return ('', err); step 6c of kernel.go classifies it and answers with refusalResult(RefusedOutOfScope). A second and third CALL SITE of the predicate, never a second predicate — minting our sentence inside each tool was rejected because it puts fault-or-answer back in every executor, which is the spread that made files.read and these two disagree in the first place. Red first, verbatim: files.edit answered reason='filesystem: path outside the grant's scope: <absolute path>' — the leak reproduced with the path twice. Ordinary editor errors are untouched and still answer as tool results; no contract change was needed. The test fence is a symlink inside the granted directory resolving outside it (a symlinked DIRECTORY for files.create, which canonicalizes the parent), and its premise is asserted rather than assumed: the lexical predicate must not already refuse, or the capability would not be the check under test. Two mutations: false in executeFilesEdit broke three tests, each printing the filesystem sentence; err != nil broke the ordinary-editor-failure test with 'hashline: invalid revision' become a run-ending fault. Two existing assertions that encoded the defect as an expectation were moved with the behaviour.

title: Two prompt answers race and one is lost: applyStandingAnswer read-modify-writes outside the store lock
description:
Left deliberately un-widened by the nocx-fliln worker, who named it rather than fixing it unasked. Correct call.

ws_agent.go applyStandingAnswer still does Policy().WithRule(rule) then SetPolicy(next) — a read-modify-write OUTSIDE the store's lock, which also rewrites the whole matrix. Task 8 stopped the PAGE from clobbering rules (policy.set now refuses a document carrying them), but prompt-vs-prompt is untouched.

The fix is a few lines — store.SetRule is now the one seam that mutates under the lock — but content.StandingRule mints the rule's id itself, so the store would have to accept a caller-minted id for a NEW rule. That is exactly what policy.setRule refuses on the wire (a renderer may replace a rule it can see and may not choose the identity of a new one). So it is a design call about who may mint, not a typo.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Two agent runs suspend for approval on different commands at the same time.
2. Both people answer 'always', so both call applyStandingAnswer concurrently.
3. Each reads the policy, appends its rule to the copy it read, and writes the whole document back.
4. The later write wins and the earlier rule is gone — the person who answered sees no rule and is asked again.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A test drives two concurrent standing answers through the prompt path and asserts both rules survive. It fails first.
- applyStandingAnswer mutates through the store's locked one-rule seam, not through Policy() + SetPolicy.
- Who may mint an id is answered explicitly in a comment at the seam: the wire refuses a caller-minted id for a new rule, and either the reason the in-process prompt may is written down, or StandingRule stops minting and the store does it.
- The matrix is not rewritten by a rule write.
close_reason: Fixed with nocx-2019q in the same commit (0b0b49a9), because getting the rule id back for Undo and closing the race are one change. applyStandingAnswer now mutates through the store's locked one-rule seam instead of Policy() + WithRule + SetPolicy. Red first: with the old read-modify-write restored under the new tests, 'round 1: stored rules = 3, want 4 — an answer was lost' (TestApplyStandingAnswer_TwoAtOnceBothSurvive). The minting question was settled the SECOND way and the reasoning is a comment at the seam: content.LiteralInvocationRule stops minting and the store does it, because an id is the DOCUMENT's name for a rule and a rule that has never been stored has no name yet; the old mint also named rules that are never stored at all (standingOffer builds one per question just to read its label), and it put a second mint in front of the store's so the id a caller held was not certainly the id the document wore — which is exactly what Undo's exactness rests on. Letting the in-process prompt mint would have needed a door into the store that adopts a caller's id plus a guard holding the wire away from it; this way SetRule's contract holds whole with no exception carved into it. Scope deliberately widened by the worker and accepted: the NON-command answer wrote a matrix row through the same read-modify-write and lost answers identically, so the store got a locked SetRowDecision twin and that path was routed through it — with its own red-first test, ARowAnswerAndARuleAnswerAtOnceBothSurvive. Leaving half a race fixed would have been worse. One existing assertion was overturned with its reasoning recorded: TestEveryRuleCarriesWhereItCameFrom no longer claims a rule is identified from creation.

title: A participant has a mailbox, and reading it takes nothing from anyone else
description:
Filed 2026-09-04 as a gap, not as taken work. §6 of the orchestration mechanism design lists six things the wave record holds; nocx-dkawo.2, .6, .7 and .3 built five of them. The MAILBOX is the sixth and nothing has built it, and the WAIT-FOR GRAPH (D12) is a seventh thing the same section names — filed separately if it is ever wanted.

What it is: a mailbox per participant whose READ CONSUMES NOTHING, with per-reader cursors. That is the direct answer to the 17-minute split-mail failure the design was written from — a second reader cannot take the first reader's mail because reading is not taking.

What it unblocks: three of §7.2's five coordinator calls have no implementation — say to a participant, report structurally to the coordinator, and check the inbox. Only spawn and holdings exist (nocx-dkawo.8). It is also what gives the routing table a word for 'a worker ASKS', which today has to be read as 'a worker declared failure' (internal/wave/registrar.go, succeeded()).

D7 and D8 bind: mail rides our own calls and is acknowledged explicitly, and the four acknowledgements — committed, fetched, in the model's context, acted upon — are never merged, with the cursor advancing on the second.
acceptance_criteria:
Two readers read the same mailbox; neither loses a message, and the cursor of one does not move because the other read.
A message committed but never fetched is reported as committed-not-fetched, and is not reported as delivered.
notes: 2026-09-04: the COORDINATOR's half of the carriers lands with this bead — wave.say (it writes) and mail riding wave.holdings (D7: mail rides our own calls). The WORKER's half — an explicit inbox check over the authenticated lifecycle channel — is blocked by nocx-dkawo.12, which is the same gap that stops a worker declaring: there is no launcher and so no tool surface a worker agent can call at all (§7.1, D5).
close_reason: The mailbox is built, durable, and the coordinator's half is wired end to end. internal/wave/mailbox.go + registrar.go Say/Inbox/Acknowledge/Undelivered; internal/content wave_messages + wave_cursors, schema 17→18 with rung migrateWaveMailbox17to18 and digest 17eebbf6. A READ TAKES NOTHING: messages are rows that stay, cursors move, one per (mailbox, reader). Two marks, not one: fetched_to advances on the fetch (D8's second acknowledgement, the only one the backend can witness as it happens) and acted_to only when the reader says so — without the second, 'read consumes nothing' prevents loss and not a retry spawning the same worker twice. D8's THIRD acknowledgement, 'present in the model's context', has no column and no word here, deliberately: nothing outside the model can witness it. Delivery is the RECIPIENT's own cursor and no other reader's. Mail is checked against MEMBERSHIP only, so wave.say carries observe rather than send-input — leaving a message reaches nobody's keyboard and must keep working while a human takeover has suspended control. Durable unlike the fact set of ADR-0056, and the distinction is argued in the plan: a fact is a claim about a live process a restart has already judged; a message is a thing that was said and keeps its value afterwards. Carriers: wave.say (new tool + contracts/tools/wave.say.schema.json) and mail riding wave.holdings with its cursor, acknowledged back on a later call — D7 and §7.2 as written. Evidence: internal/wave/mailbox_test.go asserts §11.10 (two readers, neither takes the other's mail, one's cursor does not move because the other read) and §11.11 (committed-not-fetched reported as itself), plus a second reader delivering nothing, an acknowledgement that cannot run ahead of the page handed over, and a fetch whose cursor write failed handing nothing over. internal/assistant asserts the coordinator's mailbox is fetched under its own SESSION, that a fetch acknowledges nothing by itself, and validates the real wave.holdings result against its contract with mail present. Three mutations turn the suite red: a cursor that never advances, an acknowledgement past what was fetched, and a missing membership check. deadcode -whylive traces Say, Inbox, Acknowledge, Undelivered, sqliteContent.Commit and executeWaveSay to main. -race green on wave, content, assistant, agenttools, app. NOT DONE and filed as nocx-dkawo.12: the worker cannot read its mail, because nothing in the product can send an agent_report either — the receiving half is complete and no sender exists, so every worker terminalizes as abandoned. docs/lifecycle-protocol.md §16 now says so. Commit 20691d93.

title: The per-fact deadline gets a measured value, and the escalated fraction is read off real waves
description:
Split out of nocx-dkawo.4 on 2026-09-04, because it cannot be done without traffic and the rest of that bead can.

nocx-dkawo.3 named both ends of the per-fact interval and left the NUMBER a stated default (waveFactDeadline, 5 minutes, internal/app/app.go). §10.8 of the orchestration design says a number wrong in either direction breaks the backstop — too short and a thinking coordinator is escalated past, too long and the person learns late — and that it probably differs by fact class, a crash not being a completion.

nocx-dkawo.4 shipped the instrument: wave.Stats counts routine, judgement, woken, escalated and dispatched facts, Registrar.Cost() reads it, and the backstop writes it on every escalation and when a wave settles. What is missing is DATA. This bead is the reading, not another mechanism.

§12 says the escalated fraction is the number the whole design is judged by: if most facts reach the human rather than the coordinator, the mechanism moved the work to a person and should say so out loud rather than be described as orchestration. That is a finding this bead may legitimately return.
acceptance_criteria:
The per-fact deadline is set from an observed distribution of how long a coordinator takes to fetch, and the choice names the observations.
The escalated fraction is read off real waves and written down, including the case where it is high enough to falsify the design.

title: internal/content/sqlite.go still says Layout() has no production caller, and nocx-isoph.2 is closed
description:
`internal/content/sqlite.go:1156` carries this on `Layout()`:

    // Layout returns the workspace -> tab -> pane repository (layout.go). No
    // production caller yet -- nocx-isoph.2 puts it on the wire -- and layout.go's
    // header is where that statement is kept current [...]

nocx-isoph.2 is closed and the wiring landed.

The comment names layout.go's header as where the claim is kept current, and that header IS
current -- it already describes ClearWindow as existing "for exactly one caller -- the
composition root's clean start". So the two contradict each other, and the stale one is the
one a reader meets first, on the accessor itself.

This matters more than an ordinary stale comment because of what the comment block is FOR:
AGENTS.md records that `deadcode` cannot tell a wired write path from an unwired one behind
an interface, so this by-hand list IS the check for this package. A by-hand wiring list that
has gone stale reports the opposite of the truth.

Found while measuring repowise (nocx-14sbw): asked whether the content write path was wired,
it answered "Layout() has no production caller yet" and cited this comment. It was repeating
the comment, not computing reachability -- but a person reading the accessor gets the same
wrong answer.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read `internal/content/sqlite.go:1156` -- the comment on `sqliteContent.Layout()` claims
   no production caller yet, pending nocx-isoph.2.
2. `bd show nocx-isoph.2` -- closed.
3. `grep -rn "\.Layout(" --include=*.go . | grep -v "^./internal/content/" | grep -v _test`
   -- production callers: `internal/app/app.go:284` (`db.Layout().ClearWindow(ctx)`),
   `internal/capability/layout.go:81`, `internal/capability/uistate.go:54`,
   `internal/transport/ws_uistate_handlers.go:39,57`,
   `internal/transport/ws_layout_handlers.go:997`.
4. Read `internal/content/layout.go`'s header -- it already names the composition root as
   ClearWindow's one caller, contradicting the accessor's comment.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The comment on `sqliteContent.Layout()` states the wiring as it is, naming a production
      caller the way the `SessionOutput()` comment below it already does
- [ ] The by-hand test-reachable-only lists in ledger.go and layout.go headers are re-checked
      against callers in the same pass, since the same staleness can hide in either
- [ ] Nothing else in internal/content still cites nocx-isoph.2 as pending

title: Task 10a: the prompt offers the widening answer it advertises, and the run's notices are drawn
description:
`agent.approve` accepts `scope: "expand"` and `agent.approvalRequested` advertises
`outOfScope.widening.available`, but no renderer sends it: `frontend/src/agent-approval-prompt.tsx`
offers only once / in this session / always (SCOPES at :200-207). A person cannot reach the
widening end to end. `agent.runState.notices` is the same shape — the bound on asking is on the
wire and nothing draws it, which is exactly the silent degrade the notice was added to prevent.

Found by the nocx-b453p worker on 2026-09-03, outside its owned files.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The prompt shows a fourth answer ONLY when `outOfScope.widening.available` is true, and shows
  `widening.reason` where it is false. The offer is read off the wire, never re-derived from the
  cause in the renderer.
- Activating it sends `agent.approve` with `approved: true, scope: "expand"`; the test drives the
  button rather than calling the client method.
- The answer's label names the resource that fell outside, in the same words the backend used.
- `agent.runState.notices` renders where a person reading the run will see it.
- An RPC error from a refused widening is shown, and the question stays answerable.
close_reason: Merged as 4d10db24 (worker branch nocx-4yjwk1-widening-prompt, c54b1cb1). The prompt now renders the fourth answer: a last, separate ActionGroup offering 'Allow and widen to <resource>', shown only when outOfScope.widening.available is true on the wire and never re-derived from cause; where the backend refuses the widening its reason is printed with the answers. approvalScopeCoverage was extended with the 'expand' case rather than a second sentence-builder. agent-ask.ts appends run.notices as their own scrollback line, separate from unarmedBounds. 83 tests green (vitest src/agent-approval-prompt.test.tsx src/agent-ask.test.ts), tsc --noEmit clean via pre-commit. Every assertion drives the button, not the callback.

title: Tool.Effect and Tool.Declaration.Effect can disagree silently, and a test that set the wrong one passed vacuously
description:
internal/agenttools.Tool carries Effect, and Tool.Declaration carries its own Effect. The kernel selects a policy row by Tool.Effect. A test that sets only Declaration.Effect therefore leaves Tool.Effect as "", which matches the empty row of an effect outside the lattice, and every assertion in it passes without consulting the row it names.

Found by the nocx-t6h2u worker: TestPolicyNarrowRowRefusesOutsideRunFence was passing vacuously for exactly this reason. It is fixed and renamed in that task. This bead is the trap, not the one test.

This is AGENTS.md testing rule 1 in its purest form — a green test that could not report the feature it was written for — and nothing in the toolchain reports it. deadcode, the linters and the type checker are all satisfied.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Build an agenttools.Tool literal in a test, setting Declaration.Effect and leaving Tool.Effect zero.
2. Give the policy a narrowed row for the effect the declaration names.
3. Assert the narrowed row governs. It passes, and the row was never consulted: the kernel read Tool.Effect, which is "".

## Acceptance Criteria

- Constructing a Tool whose Declaration.Effect disagrees with Tool.Effect is impossible, or is reported: a constructor that derives one from the other, or a check that fails the build or the test run.
- A test that the trap is closed: the shape that used to pass vacuously now fails.
- Any other test setting one and reading the other is found and fixed; grep for Declaration.Effect and for Tool{ literal construction.

title: The source URL never leaves the backend: skills.list cannot say where an installed skill came from
description:
Spec .internal/specs/2026-09-03-installing-a-skill-by-url-design.md §9 ends with "the
source URL available on the row". It is not, and the wire cannot deliver it.

nocx-qja4m.2 records the source in skills.json, so the fact exists on disk. But
contracts/skills.list.schema.json has no `source` field and the generated Skill carries
name, description, provenance, path, enabled and status. So the one question a person
asks about an installed skill — where did this come from — is answerable only by opening
the JSON by hand.

Found while building nocx-qja4m.6, which could not invent the field.

## Acceptance Criteria

- skills.list carries the source for an installed skill: the URL and when it was
  installed, absent for every other provenance.
- The row shows it. RecordRow's detail slot already holds the path; decide deliberately
  whether the URL joins it, replaces it, or needs another line, and say which in a
  comment — a record's parts are its argument.
- A skill whose source row is missing (installed by hand into the root) renders without
  it rather than showing an empty field.
- ..._OverTheWireConformsToContract covers the new field.
close_reason: 1293d209. skills.list carries an optional source {url, installedAt}, inline in the schema rather than a $def because a named definition becomes a second generated export nothing consumes — the dead-exports ratchet caught the $ref form as NEW: src/generated/skills.list.ts: Source. Attached only where provenance is installed AND the document has a row, as a pointer so nothing-recorded is distinguishable from an empty address; a directory moved into the root by hand lists with no source. The field is never a second way to ask provenance: a managed skill with a hand-written source row carries none, asserted on the wire. On the row the URL JOINS the path rather than replacing it — they answer different questions and both are load-bearing, and replacing would leave installed rows the only ones that cannot say which file Delete removes, giving one list two row grammars, which is what RecordRow exists to prevent; detail is already typed as one line or a few, so this is the shape it had. Nothing drawn when nothing recorded. The over-the-wire test stopped validating a fixture and now installs a skill through the shipped handlers (preview then install against an httptest endpoint) before asking skills.list — the difference between proving the struct is well-formed and proving the server sends it. One deliberate loose end stated rather than hidden: installedAt travels and nothing draws it, because when a skill was fetched is not evidence about its bytes. All gates green, 6196 frontend tests.

title: The ask knows every effect the call derived and cannot say so: DerivedEffects stops at the kernel
description:
nocx-jxq97 carried the derived effect set as far as ApprovalRequest.DerivedEffects (internal/assistant/kernel.go, json:"-"), populated in escalate and escalateClassifier. It stops there.

The point of carrying it is that a person is entitled to see the call both reached a host AND wrote a file, even though one row governs (ADR-0020 §7 unchanged). That needs the approval notification contract to carry the set, the generated TS to declare it, and the approval prompt to state it — all UI work the nocx-jxq97 brief deliberately excluded.

## Acceptance Criteria

- contracts/agent.approvalRequested.schema.json carries the derived effect set, with the generated type regenerated and committed.
- The approval prompt names every effect the call derived, in the product words from effect-labels.ts, and names the one that governs.
- An _OverTheWireConformsToContract test proves the real result off the real socket carries it.
- A single-candidate call says one thing and does not gain a list of one.

title: A write is always classified reversible, so overwriting /etc/passwd is a change that can be undone
description:
ResourceWrite maps unconditionally to EffectMutateReversible (internal/content/resources.go, the verb-to-effect switch). So sort -o /etc/passwd in classifies as "changes that can be undone". Overwriting /etc/passwd is not reversible, and neither is truncating any file that was not backed up.

Pre-existing: it was already true for every single-write command. nocx-jxq97 only made it visible on more of them, because a mixed command now takes the worst DERIVED candidate instead of falling to the declared worst.

Reported by the nocx-jxq97 worker rather than left.

The question is whether reversibility is a property of the VERB at all. Creating a file that did not exist is reversible by deleting it; overwriting one is not, and the parser cannot tell which without touching the filesystem, which classification must not do. So the honest answers are probably: a write to an existing path is destructive, decided at approval time where the resource is already named; or write stops claiming reversibility and the class means something else.

Blocks nothing today. It matters for the Assistant permissions page (nocx-4yjwk): a person who answers "changes that can be undone: allowed" is told they can undo what they allowed.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Classify sort -o /etc/passwd in.
2. The report carries /etc/passwd with verb ResourceWrite; the call classifies as mutate-reversible.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A command that overwrites an existing path does not claim to be reversible, or the class stops meaning reversible and the product words change with it.
- The decision is made once, in the verb-to-effect mapping, and not per command in the classifier.
- A test per outcome, and the product words on the page match whichever was chosen.

title: A row can bound curl but not ssh: a destination scope must parse as a URL, and an ssh host does not
description:
nocx-c88xr made a command network resource into a ResourceDestination scope, so a row can now bound curl. It cannot bound ssh, and the Task 3 worker reported it rather than leaving it.

A destination scope id is parsed as a whole URL by destinationContains — the one predicate both the policy path and the dialler reach — so its scheme must be http or https. An ssh destination (user@host) and the literal "kubectl cluster" are both recorded with verb ResourceNetwork (internal/assistant/cmdeffect.go:308-315) and neither parses as a URL. They are therefore inside no narrowed destination scope.

The direction is right: they ask instead of slipping through, and "*" still permits them. What a person cannot do is narrow "reach another host" to a specific ssh host, which is one of the more obvious things they would want to narrow it to.

The design (.internal/specs/2026-09-03-assistant-permissions-design.md §5.4) named an endpoint as {scheme, asciiHost, effectivePort, includeSubdomains} and only considered http and https. Extending it to a host without a URL scheme is a scope-vocabulary decision, not something to guess inside a predicate.

Blocks nothing today. It becomes visible the moment the page offers a place picker for "reach another host" (Task 11, nocx-hvb3r): the picker will be able to offer a web address and not the ssh host the person is actually reaching.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A person can narrow reaching another host to a named ssh destination, and a test asserts an ssh command to a different host is outside it.
- The form is decided once, in the scope vocabulary, and both the policy path and any dialler read the same predicate.
- "kubectl cluster" is decided explicitly: either it gets a form or it is documented as unbounded-except-by-*, with the reason.
- A test that a destination scope of one kind never contains a resource of the other.

title: The classifier's verdict reaches the renderer and is never shown — the same defect as the scan finding, one field over
description:
Found while fixing nocx-swn1m, which was the same defect one field over.

Spec .internal/specs/2026-08-31-assistant-skills-design.md §6 layer 4 says the person
approves the bytes "with the scan finding AND the classifier's verdict beside them". After
nocx-swn1m only the first half is true.

`ApprovalClassifier` is built in internal/assistant/kernel.go (approvalClassifier, ~863),
declared in contracts/agent.approvalRequested.schema.json and generated into
frontend/src/generated/agent.approvalRequested.ts:83-90 with `consulted`, `verdict`,
`model` and `reason`. Nothing in frontend/src reads it.

Note the ordering fact that makes this less urgent than its sibling but not less real:
§6 also records that layer 4 is inert until nocx-01ud6 wires ResolveClassifier, so the
field may be absent in practice today. The renderer would drop it either way, so the
defect is in the renderer and not in the timing.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Reach an approval for a skills write with a classifier verdict on the ask.
2. Nothing on the prompt names the verdict, whether the classifier was consulted at all,
   which model answered, or its reason.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The approval prompt renders the classifier when the ask carries one: whether it was
  consulted, its verdict, and its reason in the person's words.
- A classifier that was NOT consulted says so rather than rendering nothing — "the gate
  did not run" is a fact a person deciding needs, and an absent gate that looks like a
  clean one is the silent degrade AGENTS.md forbids.
- No empty slot when the field is absent entirely.
- Kit components only, and the tone does not overstate: a verdict is evidence beside the
  bytes, exactly as the scan finding is.
close_reason: Drawn in frontend/src/agent-approval-prompt.tsx as a StatusCard after the scan finding, from the classifier field the wire has carried since kernel.go:821. Four shapes: clear (neutral), suspect (warning), consulted-with-no-verdict (warning), and consulted:false which says the gate did not run and carries why. Tone is never danger; clear is neutral rather than ok. 11 tests in agent-approval-prompt.test.tsx, 64/64 green. Commits e14e70f5 and 72245e2d.

title: Measured trial: does repowise beat grep on our real questions?
description:
AGENTS.md "Code search" forbids reintroducing a code index, or any hook in front of a
file read, without measuring against the graphify baseline (removed 2026-08-01: five
queries, zero answers, 91 MB of committed output).

repowise (https://github.com/repowise-dev/repowise) is that class of tool: an AST
dependency graph across 19 languages, git-history hotspots, an auto-generated wiki, and
embeddings in LanceDB + SQLite, exposed to agents over MCP.

Protocol: install into a throwaway venv, index a scratch worktree (never the main tree),
ask five questions we actually ask, and compare each answer with what grep gives for the
same question. Keep it away from CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md -- `repowise init` generates
both, and ours are the operating contract.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Five real questions asked of both grep and repowise, answers recorded side by side
- [ ] Each repowise answer marked: same as grep, better than grep, or wrong/absent
- [ ] Index size on disk measured, and .gitignore consequences stated
- [ ] Verdict recorded on the bead: keep (with an ADR saying why the index came back) or
      drop (with the measurement, as graphify was dropped)
- [ ] The main worktree is unchanged -- no .mcp.json, CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md edits leak
notes:
Trial run 2026-09-03, repowise 0.48.0, keyless (--no-prose, no LLM key, no embedder key).
Indexed a detached worktree at main 4f8172c3; the main tree was never touched.

SETUP COST
- venv 1.0 GB (torch et al). NixOS needs LD_LIBRARY_PATH to gcc-lib -- greenlet's
  extension fails on libstdc++.so.6 otherwise, and the failure surfaces as a SQLAlchemy
  ValueError, not as a missing library.
- init: 3m35s, 3599 pages, .repowise/ = 369 MB (wiki.db 210 MB, duplication_cache 85 MB,
  parse_cache 37 MB, lancedb 14 MB, knowledge-graph.json 12 MB). graphify was 91 MB.
- It rewrote .mcp.json (reformatted our playwright entry, added its own server with an
  ABSOLUTE path to this checkout -- wrong on any other machine) and wrote .claude/CLAUDE.md
  (94 lines, marker-delimited). Root CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md were NOT touched: md5 unchanged.
- `repowise hook read-skeleton` / `read-reread` / `search-digest` are hooks in front of
  Claude Code's Read. Opt-in, not installed by init. That is the exact thing AGENTS.md
  forbids reintroducing.

FIVE QUESTIONS, repowise vs grep
1. Is the content write path wired, or test-only? grep: 0.02s, locates the package, needs
   `deadcode -whylive` for the real answer. repowise get_answer: WRONG -- cited
   internal/vault/system tests and frontend/src/secrets.test.tsx, nothing in internal/content.
   get_context on `sqlite.go::sqliteContent.Submit` did not resolve the symbol at all
   ("No symbol matched") and silently fell back to a file-level rollup of 200 same-package
   callers, which cannot answer reachability from main(). WORSE THAN GREP.
2. Where is "am I in an ssh context" decided (the two-derivations defect)? grep: 0.08s,
   found commandWord in suggest/providers.ts and isSshPlan in ssh-transition.ts.
   repowise: returned internal/ssh/ssh.go, lineage_test.go, pets/pet.ts. Missed both.
   WORSE THAN GREP.
3. Where is a session id minted? grep: 0.005s (2nd iteration) -> session.go:372 NewID.
   repowise: session.go, no line, no symbol. SAME AT BEST.
4. Who reads vault.status defaultProvider? grep: 0.08s, 15 hits including the contract
   tests that record why it matters. repowise: the vault package generally. WORSE.

   repowise search missed it; but get_why DID surface ADR-0001, its consequences, and the

WHY THE SEMANTIC LAYER LOST: keyless runs report embedder "mock" and

i.e. BM25 over generated wiki pages, competing with grep over the source. The README's

THE ONE THING GREP CANNOT DO: get_risk's git layer. internal/transport/ws.go, hotspot
0.959, 210 dependents, co-change partners with support counts -- and

ws.go 223 commits, terminal-content.ts 284, 50 shared; app.go 121 shared vs its reported

=== KEYED PASS, 2026-09-04 (openrouter provider + openrouter embedder) ===

Same five questions, with synthesis:

Keyed score: 2 correct, 1 partial, 1 honest miss, 1 confidently wrong from a stale comment.
That is a real improvement on keyless (which was 0 correct and confidently wrong twice),
and it is still not competitive with grep on latency, precision or trust: every one of the

It is graphify again -- better mannered with a key, and 385 MB plus a paid re-index per

WORKS, verified live: MCP server responds (2010ms), semantic search returns a real ranking,
and get_risk on frontend/src/terminal-content.ts gives 111 fixes in 6 months, bug_magnet
true, hotspot 0.9988 increasing, top_symbols mount:35 / TerminalContent:16, bus_factor 1 at

=== WORKTREES, 2026-09-04, and a correction to the paragraph above ===
Every agent here works in a worktree, so "installed in main" would have meant installed
nowhere. Three of the four blockers I listed turned out to be already solved by repowise;
only one was real, and it was the dangerous one.

- AUTO-SEEDING WORKS. `repowise init -y` in an unindexed linked worktree prints
  "[worktree] Linked worktree of /home/dev/repos/nocx detected; seeding its index" and
  finishes in 1m47s at $0 (nothing to regenerate at the same HEAD). My first measurement
  said "regenerated, 2m17s" and I read that as seeding not working -- it was a run where
  the base's index was not where the seeder looked. Conditions for the seed, from
  docs/scale/WORKTREES.md: linked worktree, no existing state.json, healthy base index,
  and the base's last synced commit is an ancestor of the worktree's HEAD.
- DISK IS NOT SHARED. The seed is a COPY re-pointed at the worktree: 359 MB each. 18 live
  worktrees would be 6.5 GB.
- AGENT HOOKS ALREADY FOLLOW THE PATH. In a fresh worktree, before anything was installed
  there, `repowise hook read-skeleton status` already said "on (<worktree path>)". They are
  registered once in ~/.claude/settings.json and resolve per repo. post-commit is the
  exception -- per worktree, and it stays uninstalled.
- THE ONE REAL DEFECT: the user-scope MCP entry in ~/.claude/settings.json had the base
  path baked into its args ("mcp", "/home/dev/repos/nocx"). In any worktree that server
  starts fine and answers about MAIN -- stale exactly on the files the agent is there to
  change, with no staleness signal, because index_behind compares against main's HEAD.
  `repowise mcp` with no PATH resolves the CWD repo, so the fix is to drop the path.
  Done: the user entry is now {"command": "repowise", "args": ["mcp", "--transport",
  "stdio"]}, and the duplicate project entry in .claude/settings.local.json was REMOVED so
  one surface owns the registration. Verified by driving the stdio server from two cwds:
  each resolved internal/settings/settings.go against its own index.
  The `command` was also changed from the venv binary to the ~/.local/bin wrapper -- the
  bare venv binary has no LD_LIBRARY_PATH and would have died on greenlet.

STILL MANUAL PER WORKTREE: `repowise init` (1m47s, 359 MB) and `repowise hook install`.
And the hazard: `.repowise/` and `.claude/CLAUDE.md` land as untracked `??` on any branch
whose .gitignore predates the entries added here, so a `git add -A` can commit a 359 MB
index and the OpenRouter key. That is an argument for landing the .gitignore change first.

title: A nested domain's grant carries the CHILD's capability on the parent's inherited descriptor
description:
Found while closing nocx-aqz7o, flagged rather than folded into it because it is a different question
with a different answer.

nocx-aqz7o removed the bearer from OUTBOUND lifecycle frames: the kernel is the only sender in that
direction, the shell already holds its own capability from bootstrap, and the accept-identity check it
was serving is answered exactly by dom + epoch, which are non-secret and already on every frame.

That does not close this one. A domain_grant for a LOCAL nested environment carries a bootstrap whose
payload is the CHILD shell's rcfile text, and capabilityLiteral puts the child's capability into that
text (internal/app/childdomain.go:189 -> shellintegration.LocalBashRcfile). That frame rides the same
socketpair whose child end was handed over with ExtraFiles, which clears FD_CLOEXEC, and whose number
is exported as NOCX_LIFECYCLE_FD.

So a descendant of the PARENT shell can passively read a frame carrying the capability of a CHILD
domain it was never given.

It is inherent to the shape of section 9 of the protocol — the parent has to receive something in
order to hand it to its child — so this is not a slip to delete, it is a design question. Candidate
directions, none evaluated: hand the child's rcfile over a descriptor of its own rather than through
a frame the parent's descendants can read; mint the child capability at spawn on the far side; or
state plainly in the ADR that a nested child's capability is exposed to the parent's descendants and
argue why that is acceptable.

Recorded in the kernel comment, docs/lifecycle-protocol.md and the ADR-0024 amendment so nobody reads
more into nocx-aqz7o's fix than it bought.

## Acceptance Criteria

Either a nested child's capability no longer travels on a descriptor the parent's descendants
inherit, with a test asserting it; or ADR-0024 says in as many words that it does, names the actor
that can read it, and argues why the model tolerates it. Not left implicit.

title: The grant ledger cannot say whether a destination grant included subdomains
description:
Task 2 (nocx-5nkm7) added GrantScope.IncludeSubdomains (internal/content/ledger.go), and the durable grant record does not carry it: grant_scopes persists kind and id as columns (internal/content/sqlite.go:823) and has no include_subdomains column.

No predicate reads it back today — a run grant is minted from the policy, not from the ledger — so nothing is mis-enforced. What is lost is the audit record: the ledger no longer says what was granted. "everything on github.com" and "github.com itself" are two different grants over one id, and the record cannot tell them apart.

Reported by the Task 2 worker rather than silently left.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Mint a run grant from a policy whose destination scope carries IncludeSubdomains.
2. Read the grant back out of grant_scopes: the row has kind and id and nothing that distinguishes it from the same host granted without subdomains.

## Acceptance Criteria

- grant_scopes carries the marker, and a grant written with it reads back with it.
- A test that the two grants over the same id are distinguishable in the ledger.
- Greenfield: the column is added, not migrated around.

title: ssh -S names a socket the command creates, and it is in no resource
description:
Task 1 (nocx-06nzj) recorded curl -o and sort -o as written paths and covered the option table. The worker reported one it did not close, because it is outside the files it owned and outside its acceptance criteria:

ssh -S names a control-socket path that ssh CREATES. It is in optionTakesNextValue for ssh (internal/assistant/cmdeffect.go:544-549), so its value is consumed as an option value and appears in no resource. Same shape as curl -o before nocx-3j47q: a file the command writes, invisible to the policy.

The sweep the spec asked for is therefore not finished. Finish it against the whole optionTakesNextValue table with the question asked per entry: does this option value name something the command CREATES or MODIFIES on disk.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Classify ssh -S /tmp/ctl -M user@host.
2. Read the resource report: /tmp/ctl is in no resource, under no verb.

## Acceptance Criteria

- ssh -S records its socket path as a written resource and carries the writes-option-named-path feature.
- Every remaining optionTakesNextValue entry is decided explicitly, with a test either way, and the decision is written next to the table so the next reader does not re-derive it.

title: Task 6: a widened rule carries where it came from and the reading it was saved under
description:
Plan task 6. Task 1 changes how commands are read, so a rule saved under the old reading may classify differently under the new one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A Program rule whose EvaluatorVersion differs from the current one does not apply and is reported as needing confirmation.
- An Exact rule is unaffected by a version change.
- Confirming a rule rewrites its version and nothing else.
- Every rule has a stable id from creation and two rules never share one.
close_reason: Merged as 6c05bc77 (worker branch nocx-1ebzd-provenance, 8b02a5a7). InvocationRule now carries ID/CreatedAt/Source/EvaluatorVersion; content.EvaluatorVersion=2 lives in content, not assistant (assistant imports content — a constant there could not be compared against); cmdeffect.go aliases it. A loose PERMIT saved under an older reading is inert until ConfirmRule, listed by RulesNeedingConfirmation; an Exact rule never goes stale. Duplicate ids refuse to parse; a document's rules are normalised (minted id, source=written) before the gate. contracts/policy.get.schema.json + generated type updated in the same commit. go test -count=1 -race ./internal/content/... ./internal/assistant/... green on the merged tree. Review found one defect, fixed by me as 6eff87c4 with a red-first test: the guard ignored the decision, so a stale loose REFUSE fell through to a permitting row — TestAStaleRefusalStillRefuses.

title: Task 9: the decision explains itself, in the order it was taken
description:
Plan task 9. DecisionForInvocation returns one Decision and short-circuits the refusing row before rules are read, so the trace cannot be reconstructed in the renderer.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The trace for a permitted call lists the rule that permitted it, the row consulted and the resource verdict, in that order.
- A shadowed rule appears with the step that short-circuited it, rather than implying it was consulted.
- The trace is not reconstructed in the renderer: a test greps frontend/src for the precedence words and finds none.
- policy.explain has a schema and an over-the-wire test.
close_reason: Merged as 0c0863b9 (worker branch nocx-8nktm-why-trace, f4edcbd2). Verdict gains Trace []TraceStep, recorded by the evaluator as it decides — 11 kinds declared with their meanings in the new internal/content/effecttrace.go, grouped by the layer order they are crossed in: unparsed/effect-row/row-refuses/disqualified, rule-matched/rule-stale/rule-other-effect, resource-inside/resource-outside-fence/resource-outside-row-scope/resource-not-reached. Every pair a person would confuse gets two KINDS rather than one kind plus prose — row-refuses vs disqualified, rule-stale vs rule-other-effect, and fence vs row-scope, the last because a surface picks a different affordance and not just a different sentence. Opt-in: EvaluateInvocation and DecisionForInvocation keep their signatures and build nothing; ExplainInvocation is the paired opposite. The recorder is a *evalTrace whose step tolerates a nil receiver, so traced and untraced are literally ONE code path and the precedence order has no second copy. policy.explain has params+result schemas and an over-the-wire test; deadcode -whylive confirms it reachable from main through handlePolicyExplain. The renderer is forbidden the precedence words by a real test that excludes src/generated (a transcript of the contract's own prose) and comment lines, and says why. Merged tree green: content, assistant, transport under -race; contracts:check, tsc --noEmit, 17 vitest tests, dead-export baseline shrunk by 1. One fence crossed and declared: Verdict became non-comparable, so two tests comparing whole verdicts with != needed reflect.DeepEqual, one of them in internal/assistant/kernel_test.go which this wave had fenced off — the worker changed it rather than hand over a package whose tests do not compile, and said so. No conflict arose: the fence worker did not touch that file.

title: Task 11: Assistant permissions answers questions instead of editing a matrix
description:
Plan task 11. Replaces frontend/src/agent-policy-section.tsx.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Two sections: answers given (every rule and every row off its default, as a sentence, with Why, Change, Forget) and questions not answered yet (live rows on ask, with Answer this now).
- Why renders the backend trace and nothing computed locally.
- Change offers the three answers and, for a row, a picker of places nocx names itself: no free-form field and no scope-kind select.
- Forget previews what it releases before it is taken, naming the calls whose outcome changes.
- A rule needing confirmation is shown as inert with Review and Forget.
- The words effect class, resource scope and refuse do not appear, and no control names a tool: a test per claim.
- Every control comes from frontend/src/ui/; the surface places kit components and never repaints them.
close_reason: Merged as 4f3496a6 (worker branch nocx-hvb3r-permissions-page, 57724f05), plus my own df3f8685 fixing the e2e helper. The page is rebuilt: frontend/src/assistant-permissions-section.tsx replaces agent-policy-section.tsx, two sections — what you have answered (every rule and every row off its default, as a sentence, with Why/Change/Forget) and not answered yet (live rows still on ask, with Answer this now). Why renders the backend trace only. THE WORDS: 'effect class' vanished — the page never names the category, only its member; 'resource scope' became PLACE, which works for a folder, an address and a session without a second noun; 'refuse' became Never. Two consequences the worker named: the evaluator's detail prose is not rendered at all, because it says 'the row refuses' verbatim and printing it would put the banned vocabulary on screen at the moment the page explains itself; and effectHeading became dead and was deleted. THE BRIEF WAS WRONG and the worker was right to cross the fence: a rule needing confirmation is NOT visible from evaluatorVersion on the wire — policy-explain-is-not-reimplemented.test.ts bans that identifier next to a comparison and bans needsConfirmation outright, correctly, because the predicate joins three facts to the reading running NOW. So awaitingReview joined policy.get, filled from content.RulesNeedingConfirmation off one store read, exactly the shape live already has. Two transport tests cover it.
