title: Hiding the WINDOW does not stop any panel's background work — only hiding the view does
description:
Three panels now gate background work on visibility, and all three mean the
same thing by it: this VIEW is in front and the sidebar is expanded
(SidebarViewProps.visible). None of them means "the window is on screen".

Minimise nocx, switch to another application, lock the screen — and Files
keeps polling, Git keeps running `git status` every five seconds, and Ports
keeps sampling a remote host over SSH every ten. The sidebar has no opinion
about the window, and nothing else supplies one: the dispatcher observes
`visibilitychange` only to accelerate reconnect (frontend/src/dispatcher.ts),
and exposes no app-visibility signal at all.

This is a laptop on battery in somebody's bag, and a production host being
sampled by a window nobody has looked at since yesterday. The Ports doctrine
already names the shape: "a background tab running `ss` on a loop against a
production host is a defect, not a feature"
(internal/discovery/schedule.go:24). A hidden WINDOW is a background tab.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the Files panel on a directory, or the Git panel on a repository, or
   the Ports panel against a remote profile.
2. Minimise the window, or switch to another application.
3. The backend goes on listing, running `git status`, and sampling the remote
   host at full cadence.

## The fix, and why it is one bead rather than three

ONE shared accessor — effective visibility = this view is in front AND the
document is not hidden — consumed by Files, Git and Ports alike. Three
panels each composing `document.hidden` privately is three chances to get
the listener teardown wrong and three answers to one question, which is the
second-implementation defect AGENTS.md names. The accessor belongs beside
the sidebar's own `visible`, since that is what it refines.

Deliberately NOT in scope: changing any panel's cadence, or what any of them
does when it becomes visible again — each already has that path
(files.visible polls once, ports nudges, git refreshes).

## Acceptance Criteria

- One accessor owns "is anyone actually looking", composed from the
  sidebar's per-view visibility and the document's, with its listener
  registered and torn down in one place.
- Files, Git and Ports all consume it; no panel reads `document.hidden`
  itself, asserted by grep in the same way other single-owner rules are.
- Hiding the WINDOW stops all three: no files.list from the poll loop, no
  git.status, no discovery sample. Asserted per panel, not by inspection.
- Showing the window again restores each panel's existing
  becoming-visible behaviour unchanged.
- A tab or window that was hidden when a panel first mounted starts in the
  hidden state rather than polling until the first transition.
close_reason:
Landed as fde83383.

ONE ACCESSOR, not three. frontend/src/app-visible.ts owns the document's
visibility: seeded from document.hidden AT CREATION, one listener, one teardown.
sidebar.tsx composes it into the visible accessor at the single producer all
three panels already read (const visible = () => !collapsed() && appVisible()),
so Files, Git and Ports were fixed WITHOUT ANY PANEL CHANGING. That is why this
was one bead rather than three: three panels each composing document.hidden
privately is three chances to get the teardown wrong and three answers to one
question.

FOURTH LISTENER, DELIBERATELY, and the module says why where the next person will
look: dispatcher.ts accelerates reconnect, wake-report.ts detects a wake,
terminal-links/armed.ts disarms a link. None owns whether panel work may run.

THE SINGLE-OWNER RULE IS ENFORCED, not merely intended. The source-ownership
harness in grant.test.ts that already pins the grant label now pins this too, on
comment-stripped source, excluding test-support and permitting only
app-visible.ts. A fourth panel that reaches for document.hidden itself fails a
test. The three existing listeners do not trip it because what is asserted is the
READ, not the subscription.

ASSERTED PER PANEL, three ways each: hiding the window stops the work, showing it
resumes through each panel's existing becoming-visible path (untouched —
files.visible still polls once, Ports still nudges, Git still refreshes), and a
window ALREADY hidden at mount starts hidden rather than polling until the first
transition. That last one is what the seeding buys and it would have been invisible
without it. app-visible.test.ts closes the interval at both ends: after destroy()
the signal stops moving, and a second destroy() is harmless.

SUPERVISION NOTE, worth keeping. The worker's advisor raised a blocker about
time.Sleep in TestFilesPoll_ArmsTimerAfterPoll — a test belonging to nocx-8hdia.2,
already committed and closed — and the worker abandoned this bead to go rewrite it,
adding an unrelated dirtyGeneration field to filesWatcher along the way. I reverted
internal/ to the committed state and ruled explicitly: an advisor note is an input
to judgement, not an instruction outranking the brief, and work outside the current
task is reported, not done. Recorded here because the failure mode is structural,
not this worker's: a review loop pointed at the whole tree will always find the
previous task.

THE SLEEP IS DELIBERATE. It is the strict half of an absence assertion and strict
in the SAFE direction: the window is SHORTER than the wait being asserted, and the
counter increments at the START of List, before any work. A slower machine can only
make the absence more certain, never less, so it cannot flake red. AGENTS.md forbids
a spec that NEEDS a slow machine to pass; this one needs nothing. Do not reopen it.

A FIXTURE WAS CHECKED RATHER THAN INVENTED. panes-fixtures.ts needed a diagnostics
mock once tests dispatch visibilitychange (the wake reporter reads it). Its shape was
verified against TerminalRenderer.diagnostics() — { bufferRows: number; accelerated:
boolean } — not written to satisfy the call. This repo lost a whole feature to a
fixture written from what the reader wanted (vault.status/defaultProvider).

VERIFIED: 156 tests green across the five touched files; eslint and tsc clean; the
full pre-commit static gate passed. make ci-full, the containerized jobs and e2e
belong to whoever integrates, on the merged tree.

title: ADR: who owns what we cost a host, and does it refuse or does it pace
description:
The first child of the epic, and the one everything else waits on: decide
whether "what we cost a host" is owned by a REFUSING admission (a token-bucket
`control.Admission`) or by a SCHEDULER that never over-issues, and record what
was rejected.

Read before deciding — this crosses two boundaries that already have owners:

- `internal/transport/control/control.go` — the Admission contract. Its doc
  states the extension rule ("a new kind of resource is added by constructing
  another Admission and wiring it, with zero edits in this package") and the
  composition order rule ("acquire the conflict admission BEFORE the scarce
  execution permit"). `Rejection` already carries `RetryAfter`. `Name()` is
  for metrics only and no implementation may branch on it.
- `internal/discovery/schedule.go:13-43` — the cadence doctrine, already
  written, with a timer-by-timer justification. If the answer is a scheduler,
  this is the thing being generalised rather than a new invention.
- AD-8 (interface-first, one owner per behaviour) and AD-1 (the data plane
  stays out of this).

The questions the ADR must answer, not restate:

1. Admission that refuses, scheduler that paces, or both at different layers?
2. What identifies the target host where admission is acquired — binding id,
   profile id, ssh pool key — and does that mapping already have an owner, or
   does this create a registry?
3. How does "this call is background" reach the admission point? Not by
   branching on `Name()`, and not by a boolean at every call site that can be
   passed wrong. Context value, a distinct Admission per class, separate
   submission queues, or something else — with the failure mode of each named.
4. Do local and remote share a mechanism, or only a vocabulary? Local cost is
   lstats and page cache; remote cost is round trips on one SSH connection
   that already has `fsLaneCap`.
5. What does the person see when we are throttling, and at what threshold?
6. What the numbers are and what they were derived from.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An ADR in `docs/decisions/` following the existing numbering and form.
- It names the ADs and the existing owners it touches BEFORE it says what to
  build — this is a boundary decision and the brief is where architecture is
  decided.
- Each of the six questions above is answered, and each rejected alternative
  says why it was rejected rather than being omitted.
- No code in this bead.

title: Observation has no reader, and the reader must honour 'unavailable' or the fix evaporates
description:
Found by nocx-k6p18.10, which grepped rather than assumed: outside internal/helper there
are ZERO readers of SessionEntry.Observed.

So the coordinator-side projection that turns a session's cwd into a tab label does not
exist yet, and 'a tab shows a stale directory' is currently a LATENT defect rather than a
live one. The wire is correct ahead of its first reader, which is the right order given the
ABI freeze — you cannot add the field after a generation ships.

THE RISK IS THE HANDOVER. nocx-k6p18.10 built three distinguishable states so a reader can
tell 'the shell is in /tmp' from 'we do not know where the shell is':

  observed: null                     nobody could be asked
  observed: {..., unavailable: []}   asked, everything answered
  observed: {..., unavailable: [cwd]} asked, unknowable — do NOT read launch.cwd as current

A reader that ignores `unavailable` and falls back to the launch value reproduces exactly
the defect nocx-k6p18.10 existed to prevent — a stale launch value presented as a current
observation — and it does so silently, because the launch value is always present and
always plausible.

On macOS today that is not an edge case: cwd is unavailable on every session, because it
cannot be obtained without cgo (see nocx-k6p18.10's closing note). So the first reader
written on Linux will look correct and be wrong on the platform we ship.
acceptance_criteria: The surface that shows a session's directory reads Observation, and renders 'unavailable' as not-known rather than falling back to the launch value. A test drives the unavailable case to that surface.
notes: BLOCKED AND RE-SCOPED, 2026-08-31. A worker took this and blocked without writing a line, correctly: there is no coordinator-side session.sessions path, no DTO, no RPC and no mounted surface, so there is nothing to attach a reader to. It explicitly refused to add a renderer-only fallback, because that would have displayed a stale launch.cwd as a current observation — the exact defect this bead exists to prevent. The missing chain is nocx-k6p18.15, which now blocks this. Verified by the coordinator: OpSessions has no caller outside internal/helper, only a comment in session_reconcile.go:35 anticipating one.
close_reason:
The overview says what it does not know about a directory. Three states render distinctly: no observation at all, an observed directory, and "unavailable" as not-known. It never reads launch.cwd.

SessionEntry.Observed had zero readers outside internal/helper, so "a tab shows a stale directory" was latent rather than live. The wire was correct ahead of its first reader, which is the right order under an ABI freeze.

THE JOIN IS CORRECT, AND ESTABLISHING THAT COST A WRONG TURN OF MINE. The coordinator's session id is looked up in a map keyed by HostSessionID.Session, which reads like a type confusion. I held the merge over it. The level-1 design answers it: AD-7 is amended so the execution host mints the session identity — "the server" becomes "that host's helper", one authority as AD-7 always required, only the holder changes. internal/app/helper_inventory.go:39 does the same join and had been merged days earlier. I had not read far enough before calling it a guess. The amendment is still missing from docs/architecture.md; nocx-45zyd carries it.

THE TEST COULD NOT HAVE SHOWN THE READER WAS RIGHT, and this is the part worth keeping. The unavailable case was driven with cwd OMITTED, so the assertion passed through the empty-value branch. Deleting `entry.observed.unavailable.includes('cwd')` entirely left all 152 tests green — found by mutation, not by reading.

The case the three-state shape exists for is the other one: the helper ASKED, could not answer, and a cwd value is present anyway. That is the only case where the unavailable check does any work, and it is exactly the defect nocx-k6p18.10 built three states to prevent — a stale value presented as a current observation, silently, because such a value is always plausible. On macOS cwd is unavailable on EVERY session, so a reader written and tested on Linux looks correct and is wrong on the platform we ship.

The coordinator added that case (879cf2df) rather than sending it back, because the worker's process had died and the production code was already correct — only the gate was missing. With the assertion in place the mutation fails by name: "the overview showed a cwd the helper reported as unavailable: expected { state: 'known', … } to deeply equal { state: 'unavailable' }". Production tree byte-identical after the revert.

The worker's own pre-fix red was behavioural and named its property: "expected { state: 'unobserved' } to deeply equal { state: 'known', cwd: '/observed' }".

WHAT IS TRUE TODAY: the reader is correct and its inventory is EMPTY, because no shipped path makes a session helper-hosted (nocx-45zyd). It becomes live when that lands; it is not dead code — the overview calls it on every open.

title: A local file change reaches the panel from the filesystem, not from a stat walk twice a second
description:
Design D5 says "Refresh comes from the filesystem: fsnotify locally, polling
over SFTP, both behind one provider-side watch capability". Section 5.5
elaborates: "Local — fsnotify (new dependency), one non-recursive watch per
expanded directory", watches re-established when a watched directory is
renamed, deleted or recreated, and a ceiling on watched directories so that
"expanding a large dependency tree must not exhaust inotify watches or
descriptors".

The scaffolding for it is already built and the implementation is a stub.

- `Watch(ctx context.Context, path string) (Watch, error)` is on the Provider
  and Handle contracts (`internal/filesystem/filesystem.go:60`), with
  `Watch{Events() <-chan struct{}; Mode() WatchMode; Close() error}` and the
  `WatchLive` / `WatchPolling` kinds (`filesystem.go:214-226`).
- The wire already carries the answer: `files.watch` returns `{mode,
  degradedReason}` and "degraded to polling" is contract-tested
  (`internal/transport/ws_contract_test.go:3309`).
- The UI for it is designed: a persistent "Polling" badge beside Refresh with
  the reason on hover, clearing the instant watching resumes (design 5.5).
- And both providers refuse: `return nil, &filesystem.ErrWatchUnavailable{}`
  (`internal/filesystem/local/local.go:433`, `internal/filesystem/sftp/
  sftp.go:551`). fsnotify is not a dependency in go.mod.

So everything except the watcher exists, and the transport-side digest poll
(`filesPollLoop`) stands in for it — for BOTH providers, including the local
one the design never intended to poll. `ws_files.go:26` records that as
interim: "until the watching wave lands".

## What a person gets

A file they change appears in the panel at once instead of within half a
second of a full directory re-enumeration, and a local directory tree stops
being stat-walked twice a second for as long as the panel is open.

## Why this is a separate epic from the cadence work

The cadence epic (nocx-8hdia) fixes the poll — visibility, interval, per-tick
bound — and that work is needed whatever the change signal is, because SFTP
polls forever. This epic removes the poll for the local provider entirely.
They touch the same loop, so this one waits.

## Deliberately out

- Any watching over SFTP. The design is explicit that the asymmetry is honest
  and that remote polling "is the designed mode and warns about nothing"; a
  remote helper binary that could push events is a later, consent-gated epic
  (`nocx-if6`), not this one.
- Recursive watches.

## Success Criteria

- `local.Provider.Watch` returns a live watch on a normal machine, and there
  is a test asserting that — not only tests for its failure paths. (For every
  "returns an error when..." there is a paired "and on an ordinary machine it
  succeeds".)
- A change to a watched local directory reaches the panel WITHOUT the digest
  poll running for that path.
- A watch that cannot be established degrades to polling, reports
  `mode: 'polling'` with a reason, and the panel SHOWS it — the badge the
  design specifies, not a `slog.Warn` behind a UI that claims to be live.
- A watched directory that is renamed, deleted or recreated re-establishes,
  with a test for each transition.
- The watch ceiling is enforced and its exhaustion is a visible degrade to
  polling, not a silent stop.
- SFTP is untouched and still polls, under the cadence epic's discipline.
- One automated check watches a person do it: touch a file in a watched local
  directory and see the row update, with the poll loop not running for it.
notes:
REVISED after adversarial review (codex, 2026-08-31). Four additions, one of
which means this epic is larger than 'implement local.Provider.Watch'.

1. NOTHING CONSUMES Watch.Events() TODAY. Binding keeps the watches
internally and Handle.Watch returns only WatchMode (binding.go:42, :422),
while the transport starts filesPollLoop for any non-empty path set. Land
fsnotify without changing that and you get live events nobody hears while the
expensive poll keeps running. Wiring the event consumer is part of this epic,
not a follow-up.

2. THE Watch INTERFACE HAS NO HEALTH SEAM. Events() <-chan struct{} is right
for data — invalidation, not a diff — but there is no error channel, no
terminal reason, no way to say 'the watch was lost and polling resumed', and
no re-establishment signal. Add one (Done()/Err() or a typed event) before
the implementation, because the degrade path is the one that has to be
visible.

3. ONE HUB, NOT ONE WATCHER PER PATH. A single fsnotify watcher per
provider/binding, with a coalesced capacity-one invalidation per path, so an
editor's rename burst cannot block the reader. On overflow: invalidate every
path, rebuild the set, and report degradation only if the rebuild fails.
Quick delete-and-recreate at the same pathname must re-add the kernel watch
even though the requested path set did not change.

4. maxWatchPaths = 512 IS NOT A SAFETY GUARANTEE. Linux inotify limits are
configurable and kqueue-style backends spend descriptors. Treat 512 as a
product ceiling, attempt the allocation, and degrade honestly.

AND: when provider watching lands, DELETE the transport poll loop. sftp's own
Watch owns remote polling; local Watch owns fsnotify. Running provider
watching beside the interim transport poll is not a migration step, it is a
defect — two owners for one change signal.

Depends additionally on nocx-8hdia.5: swapWatches rebuilds every watch on
every set change, which is free while providers refuse to watch and expensive
the moment they do not.

title: The Git poll backs off when nothing is changing
description:
The Git panel polls every `POLL_INTERVAL_MS = 5000` while the sidebar is
visible, and every poll runs a real `hnd.Status(ctx)` traversal
(`internal/transport/ws_git.go:722`) — on a large repository that is not free.

Git already has the rest of the discipline (D13 visibility gate, one in
flight, never queued, suppressed during a mutation). What it lacks is backoff:
a repository nobody is touching is walked twelve times a minute forever.

Ports, by contrast, has a settle delay and a prompt debounce because "a
completed command is a HINT that the listener set most likely changed"
(`internal/discovery/schedule.go:20`). Git has the same hint available and
does not use it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The poll backs off while the status is unchanged, and resets to its
  responsive interval on a change, on a mutation, and on any user action.
- A command completing in the pane is treated as a hint, debounced and
  coalesced, in the way Ports already treats it — or it is stated in the bead
  why that hint does not apply here.
- A test asserts the call count over a span of unchanged status, and the
  immediate reset after a mutation.
- Not in scope: changing what the panel displays, or the mutation gate.
close_reason:
Landed as a99c3ae9.

THE CADENCE: 5s responsive, backing off through 10s, 20s to a 50s idle tail;
reset to 5s by a status that differs, a mutation completing, a refresh, becoming
visible, and a rebind. setInterval is gone for a self-arming timeout, because the
rung changes per tick and an interval measured from the START of the previous
poll cannot express that.

THE TAIL IS THE PART THAT HAD TO BE DECIDED, and the first attempt got it by
inheritance. The worker copied [1,2,4,10,20] from the Files ladder committed an
hour earlier (nocx-8hdia.2) and wrote that it "reuses the repository's stated
ladder". But that ladder was calibrated against a 500ms base, tail 10s; against
Git's 5s base the same multipliers give a 100-SECOND tail on a repository
somebody is looking at. Same shape, a number nobody chose. That is the bead's own
warning inverted — not a third number invented in isolation, but a number arrived
at by multiplication nobody performed. 50s is argued instead: slower than Ports'
10s remote-sampling floor, because a LOCAL repository costs less to leave alone
than a remote host costs to probe, and short of a view stale enough to mislead.
The comment states the cadence in SECONDS, not the multipliers.

A GOOD CATCH NOBODY ASKED FOR: pollScheduleVersion. A poll carries the schedule
version it was issued under, so a reset landing while that read is in flight is
not undone by the response when it arrives. Without it, a mutation during a poll
would have been silently demoted back to the backed-off rung by the poll's own
completion.

UNCHANGED is decided by comparing the whole snapshot. That is honest only because
both sides come from one decode path over a contract with additionalProperties
false — key order is what the comparison actually rests on, so the comment says
so rather than claiming completeness, which was the easy half.

CRITERION 2 (the command-completed hint) is answered with the SECOND permitted
answer, and it is now in the SOURCE rather than in a summary: Ports gets that hint
backend-side in discovery.Scheduler; this store is frontend-side; the seam that
would carry it — renderer.onCommandMarker's C/D callback — is severed from
application state by ADR-0024, so wiring it is cross-surface plumbing, not a poll
change. The seam is named so the next person does not re-derive it.

TWO PIECES OF RECORDED REASONING WERE DELETED AND RESTORED. The first attempt
removed the comment explaining why there are three per-class epochs rather than
one, to make room for new variables, and rewrote the one saying what an absent
inline status means and what recovers from it. Neither had anything to do with
this bead. Both are back verbatim. Worth noting as a pattern: a worker inserting
state into a declaration block will overwrite the comment attached to it unless
told not to.

VERIFIED: 62 tests green in git-store.test.ts, eslint and tsc clean, full
pre-commit static gate passed (prettier caught one formatting miss the worker's
own eslint run did not). D13's visibility gate and D23's per-repository
coalescing are unchanged and still asserted; the D23 count moved 3 -> 2 as a
direct consequence of backoff, and its comment still names what it protects.

NOT RUN, deliberately: make ci-full, the containerized jobs and e2e belong to
whoever integrates, on the merged tree.

title: One poll tick is bounded regardless of how large the watched tree is
description:
`filesPollTick` (`internal/transport/ws_files.go`) walks every watched path
sequentially in one goroutine. The watch set is bounded at `maxWatchPaths =
512` and each directory at `entryCap` 10_000 (local) / 5_000 (remote), so one
tick can be 5.12M lstats. That tick cannot complete within any sane interval,
so the ticker simply fires again and the loop runs continuously.

Design section 5.5 already asks for this bound: "there is a ceiling on watched
directories and on outstanding re-lists".

A ceiling on paths per tick with round-robin makes a tick's cost a function of
the ceiling instead of the tree, and a large expanded tree degrades into
slower detection rather than into a stat storm — the honest direction.

## Acceptance Criteria

- One tick visits at most N paths; N is a named constant with its reason.
- Paths not visited this tick are visited on the next, round-robin, so no
  watched directory is starved indefinitely.
- A test with a watch set larger than N asserts the per-tick call count and
  that every path is eventually visited across successive ticks.
- The degradation is visible if it becomes severe rather than silent — a
  detection lag nobody can see is the soft degrade AGENTS.md forbids.
- Blocked on the cadence bead: the ceiling and the interval are one policy and
  choosing them apart produces two numbers that have to agree.
notes:
REVISED after adversarial review (codex, 2026-08-31).

'A ceiling of N paths per tick' is the wrong shape. ONE PATH PER DISPATCH is,
because a single SFTP path already carries a 30s bound — a tick of N paths can
be N x 30s whatever N is. Keep per-path DUE TIMES and round-robin among
equally-due paths; a dispatch handles one path and then re-arms.

Consequence to state honestly rather than hide: at 512 watched paths, exact
freshness, bounded load and full enumeration cannot all hold. When the
scheduler falls behind, prefer stale-but-responsive over continuous load, and
surface 'updates delayed' only once a DECLARED freshness threshold is actually
missed — not on every deferral. A routine scheduling delay is not a degraded
feature and must not produce a badge.

Foreground work never waits for a dispatch: expand lists immediately (it
already does), Refresh lists immediately, and a mutation whose destination
directory is known invalidates that directory directly.

--- SECOND CONSULTATION (codex, 2026-09-01), against the code as landed ---

WHERE THE LADDER LIVES: per PATH, not per watcher. A shared ladder with
per-path due times is internally inconsistent — one failing directory would
move every healthy one onto the failure ladder, and one noisy directory would
reset every quiet one to the responsive rung. Each path carries rev, idleStep,
failureStep, dueAt, last successful observation, and an identity/generation.
The WATCHER keeps exactly one timer (armed for the earliest dueAt, ties broken
round-robin), visibility, the stable path order and cursor, the remote jitter
source, the wake channel, the dirty set, handle lifecycle, and the AGGREGATE
freshness state. 512 path records is tens of KiB; one listing enumerates
thousands of entries. Memory is not the cost here. Do NOT create 512 timers or
goroutines.

'The panel is quiet' survives as a DERIVED aggregate (every path at its maximum
idle rung), but it stops being the scheduling authority.

THE VISIBLE DEGRADE NEEDS A NEW NOTIFICATION — there is no honest existing
carrier. files.changed means 'this directory is dirty, re-list it', not 'we
could not observe it' (contracts/files.changed.schema.json:5).
files.watch.degradedReason is provider ESTABLISHMENT mode and explicitly
excludes designed remote polling (contracts/files.watch.schema.json:10). A
files.watch RESPONSE cannot carry a transition that happens minutes later.
control.saturated is a different failure. So: a NOTIFICATION, not a callable —
files.refreshStateChanged { bindingId, state: 'ok' | 'delayed' }. Nothing else
crosses the wire: no paths, no queue depths, no ladder positions, no internal
errors. Binding-level state, emitted only on the threshold-crossing and
recovery EDGES, re-emitted on attach and on a reconnecting files.watch.

THE THRESHOLD: 60 seconds of VISIBLE, refresh-eligible time — grounded, not
invented. Routine idle polling caps at 10s and the failure ladder caps at 60s,
so ordinary round-robin deferral lights nothing while work that cannot complete
inside the whole failure envelope does. HIDDEN TIME MUST NOT COUNT, and a
hidden->visible edge gives the catch-up a fresh window; otherwise a panel
hidden for an hour warns before its first catch-up attempt.

THE SURFACE: reuse the sticky inline message and Retry that already exist for
stopped refresh (frontend/src/files/files-store.ts:263,
frontend/src/files/files-view.tsx:664). NOT the Polling badge — its shared
judgment deliberately hides routine and designed polling
(frontend/src/ui/watch-badge.tsx:54).

'WATCH ONLY WHAT IS VISIBLE' IS NOT CHEAPER AND IS NOT THIS BEAD. There is no
viewport model: visibleRows() means rows surviving expansion and filtering, not
rows intersecting the scroll viewport, and D10 explicitly rejects row
virtualization (files-view.tsx:500, :696). The watch set is the root plus every
successfully listed expanded directory, recursively, above or below the fold
(files-store.ts:45). Viewport watching would need scroll/intersection tracking
that does not exist, frequent files.watch replacement while scrolling,
synchronous baselines for newly visible paths, and a CHANGED correctness
promise — expanded offscreen directories going silently stale. That is a
different bead and probably an amendment to D10.

TWO DEFECTS IN WHAT LANDED, both to be fixed by this bead:

1. handleList's cadence reset is a defer registered BEFORE the List call
   (ws_files.go:773), so a FAILED list resets the ladder as though it had
   succeeded. Replace it with a path-specific successful observation carrying
   the returned listing.Rev.

2. ws_upload.go:1367 knows the exact destination directory, checks it is
   watched, and then asks for a PATHLESS immediate poll. Today that is merely
   wasteful (a full scan). Under per-path dispatch it becomes a LOSS: two
   uploads to different directories collapse in a capacity-one channel and one
   destination is forgotten. The durable fact belongs in the per-path entry;
   the channel only tells the scheduler to recompute.

ALSO: emitFilesChanged must stop resetting the whole watcher
(ws_files.go:1272) — notification delivery has no scheduling side effect.
handleWatch must stop resetting RETAINED paths (ws_files.go:1042); added paths
get fresh state from their synchronous baseline, retained paths keep theirs,
and replacement must preserve the whole per-path state object rather than
rebuilding map[string]string (ws_files.go:1020).

AND AN ABA CASE the current code cannot see: the post-list check only asks
whether the path STRING is still present (ws_files.go:1556). A path removed and
re-added while its old listing is in flight lets the stale result overwrite the
new baseline. Apply a result only if the map still holds the exact
entry/generation that dispatch selected.

HIDDEN->VISIBLE stops meaning 'one immediate FULL scan' (ws_files.go:1383) and
becomes: mark every current path due now, dispatch one immediately, continue
one path per dispatch until every path present at the visibility edge has been
attempted once, then resume ordinary due scheduling. Interruptible between
paths, which is the point.
close_reason:
Landed as 01eecc79. Design settled by a second codex consultation against the
code as landed (recorded in this bead's notes); the epic's remaining bead
nocx-8hdia.7 was split out of this one during it.

ONE PATH PER DISPATCH, and 'a ceiling of N paths per tick' is the wrong shape
for a stated reason: a single SFTP path already carries a 30s bound, so a tick
of N paths is N x 30s whatever N is. One path is the only unit whose cost is
bounded by something other than the size of the tree.

THE LADDER MOVED TO THE PATH. A shared ladder with per-path due times is
internally inconsistent — one failing directory would drag every healthy one
onto the failure ladder, one noisy directory would reset every quiet one to the
responsive rung: per-path in representation, watcher-coupled in behaviour. The
watcher still owns exactly ONE timer, armed for the earliest dueAt, ties broken
round-robin. 512 entries is tens of KiB while one listing enumerates thousands
of entries, so state was never the cost and 512 timers would have been the wrong
answer to the right question. 'The panel is quiet' survives as a DERIVED
aggregate and stops being the scheduling authority.

THE ABA CASE, which the old code could not see. A completed listing was applied
if the path STRING was still present, so a path removed and re-added while its
listing was in flight let the stale result overwrite the NEW baseline. A dispatch
now captures the entry POINTER plus a generation and applies only if that exact
entry is still installed.

THREE DEFECTS IN THE CADENCE BEAD, all fixed here, the first invisible until
codex read it: handleList's reset was a defer registered BEFORE the List call, so
a FAILED list reset the ladder as though it had succeeded. It is now a
path-specific observation carrying the returned rev — strictly better than a
reset, because the foreground call already produced the fact the poll would have
gone to fetch. emitFilesChanged no longer reschedules anything (delivering a
notification is not a scheduling decision). A watch-set replacement preserves a
retained path's whole state OBJECT rather than rebuilding map[string]string, so
only genuinely added paths start fresh.

THE UPLOAD BECAME TARGETED, and this one changes category rather than degree.
ws_upload.go always knew its destination and then asked for a PATHLESS immediate
poll. Under whole-set dispatch that was merely wasteful; under per-path dispatch
it would have been a LOSS — two uploads to different directories collapse in a
capacity-one channel and one destination is forgotten. The durable fact now lives
in the path's own entry; the channel only says 'recompute'.

BECOMING VISIBLE stops meaning one immediate FULL scan: every path is marked due
and the catch-up proceeds one path per dispatch until each has been attempted
once. Same work, interruptible between paths — which is the whole point.

THE HONEST STATEMENT is written where the cadence is chosen, not left to be
inferred: at the 512-path ceiling, exact freshness, bounded load and full
enumeration cannot all hold, and a scheduler that falls behind prefers
stale-but-responsive over continuous load. One send-back was about exactly this
paragraph — it had been glued into the files.* INGRESS const block directly above
maxFileNameRunes, so it documented a filename bound and the filename bound read
as its continuation. A policy nobody can find is not written down.

WHAT WAS RULED OUT AND WHY, so it is not re-litigated: 'watch only what is
visible' is not cheaper and is not this bead. There is no viewport model —
visibleRows() means rows surviving expansion and filtering, D10 rejects row
virtualization, and the watch set is the root plus every expanded directory
recursively, above or below the fold. Viewport watching needs scroll tracking
that does not exist, frequent files.watch replacement while scrolling, and a
CHANGED correctness promise (expanded offscreen directories going silently
stale). A different bead, and probably a D10 amendment.

VERIFIED: TestFilesPoll green with and without -race; the sibling suites
TestFiles|TestUpload|TestWatch green at 8.8s including the over-the-wire contract
test; go vet clean; golangci-lint clean; full pre-commit static gate passed
(gofumpt caught two files the worker's own runs did not).

NOT RUN, deliberately: make ci-full, the containerized jobs and e2e belong to
whoever integrates, on the merged tree.

title: The released schema-14 fixture is missing the api-run tables every real 14 database had
description:
Found by nocx-lmb6v.5, 2026-08-31, and it sharpens what nocx-lmb6v.10 closed.

nocx-lmb6v.10 made the fixture reproduce the ENGINE POSTURE a released build produced —
auto_vacuum and journal_mode set before the first table. That was right and it is done.

This is a second, larger gap in the same fixture, and nocx-lmb6v.10 did not cover it:
testdata/schema_v14.sql is schemaV1 at version 14 AND NOTHING ELSE. But a real released 14
build also ran migrateAPIRuns at startup, so every schema-14 database that ever existed in
the world carried api_run*, api_run_schema and its own counter. The fixture carries none of
them.

So the fixture is still not the file a released build wrote — it is the file schemaV1
alone would have written, which no build ever ran on its own.

nocx-lmb6v.5 already built the honest shape for its own refusal and parity tests
(testdata/api_runs_two_counter_era.sql), and its parity test uses it. The released
acceptance suite from nocx-lmb6v.2 still uses the thin one, so that suite — the one whose
whole point is real released fixtures — runs against a file no build produced.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read testdata/schema_v14.sql. There are no api_run tables.
2. Read what a 14-era Open did: migrateAPIRuns created them unconditionally.
3. The two disagree, and the acceptance suite believes the first.

## Fix

Fold the api-run fragment into aReleasedSchema14Database so the nocx-lmb6v.2 suite runs
against a file a build actually wrote. Prefer one fixture over two: a suite with an honest
fixture and a thin one beside it will drift, and the thin one will be the one somebody
copies.
acceptance_criteria: aReleasedSchema14Database produces a file with the shape a released 14 build actually wrote — api_run* and api_run_schema included — and the whole nocx-lmb6v.2 acceptance suite runs against it. One fixture, not two: the honest shape is the only shape.
close_reason:
aReleasedSchema14Database now produces the file a released 14 build actually wrote: the api-run DDL and its counter are folded in, because a real 14-era Open ran migrateAPIRuns unconditionally before stamping, so every schema-14 database that ever existed carried api_run*, api_run_schema and its own counter. The fixture carried none of them, which meant the nocx-lmb6v.2 acceptance suite — the suite whose entire point is real released fixtures — ran against a file no build ever produced.

One fixture, not two. The two-counter fixture now varies only in DATA, not in shape, so there is no thin copy left for somebody to reach for.

Red before the fix, and it names the property rather than a count: `released schema 14 fixture has no api_run_schema table — a real schema 14 build created every api-run table before stamping the file`.
