title: A markdown table is painted as its source, because the answer is a stack of lines
description:
The model answered with a markdown table and the user saw the pipes and the
dashes.

This is not an oversight: ui/answer-markdown.ts states in its header that a
table is deliberately not rendered, because the answer body is a stack of
.term-line rows — one per line — and the selection path, the copy path and the
chip path all read those rows. A grid is not a stack of rows.

So this is a DESIGN question before it is a fix, and the epic it sits in is the
one that says the answer should read like a document. Decide, and record the
decision as an ADR: either a table is gathered across completed lines into one
grid element the row model still understands (selection, copy, chips), or
tables stay unrendered and the model is told not to emit them.

Do not start editing answer-markdown.ts before that decision exists.

## Steps to Reproduce

Ask the assistant for a comparison it answers with a markdown table. The pipes
and the separator row are painted verbatim. Owner screenshot 2026-08-30.
acceptance_criteria: An ADR in docs/decisions/ records the decision and its reason; if the decision is to render, a table in a streamed answer appears as a grid and the selection, copy and reference-chip paths still work over it, proven by a test for each.
notes:
CONSULT (codex, 2026-08-30, read-only over the tree). The design question is
answered; what follows is the decision to write into the ADR, with the file
references the consult grounded it in.

THERE IS a row-preserving way, and no sibling-only CSS trick that leaves every
path untouched. Render the table as a BOUNDED ISLAND that keeps one .term-line
per SOURCE line: a wrapper element (a semantic <table> whose <tr> carry the
term-line class, or a display:grid wrapper with each row on subgrid), the
delimiter row kept as a HIDDEN .term-line at its own source ordinal. Both
shapes need a common formatting-context parent; display:table-row on bare
siblings makes anonymous table boxes and can neither scope one table nor give
it a scroll container.

That precedent already exists here: a code fence puts rows inside a nested
container (answer-body.ts:135, :199) including a hidden structural row
(style.css:1347). So the island is not a new idea in this renderer.

WHAT SURVIVES UNTOUCHED. Row-range selection and the reference chip keep
working, because they count .term-line DESCENDANTS in document order
(ask-entry.ts:22 -> agent-ask.ts:82 -> grant.ts:185), and the hidden delimiter
keeps the ordinals aligned with the source. The answer's explicit 'copy output'
also stays exact: it already reads the STORED answer, not the rows
(blocks.ts:947, :1004).

WHAT DOES NOT. Copy-on-select uses Selection.toString() (terminal-content.ts:
2917); once pipes become cells that returns browser-generated table text, and
the whitespace differs by engine. So this bead OWNS that decision: either a
source-aware copy handler for a table island, or deliberately copying the
rendered text — say which, in the ADR, with the reason.

REJECTED, and why. (a) One .term-line holding the whole table: it collapses N
source lines into one ordinal and every later start/count is then wrong — a
cell selection would reference the wrong window. (b) Leaving the source but
monospace-aligning it is the only option that costs no architecture (the answer
is already monospace, style.css:1189), and it is still source, not a table. (c)
Telling the model not to emit tables is policy, not rendering, and does nothing
for answers already stored — restored answers use the same renderer
(restored-block.ts:122).

STREAMING. Keep painting candidate lines as raw source until the run is
complete, then convert ONCE. The body deliberately holds only the trailing
partial line and commits each newline-terminated row at once (answer-body.ts:
100, :213), so table support adds a small completed-line buffer. Converting at
the delimiter instead is possible but table-layout:auto then re-measures on
every later row; fixed layout avoids the churn at the cost of column sizing.
One localized relayout at the end is the stable trade — and it is NOT the
document-wide relayout on every chunk that the current design exists to avoid.

Sequence for whoever takes this: ADR first (docs/decisions/), naming the copy
decision and what is given up — progressive rendering of an incomplete table —
then the implementation.
close_reason: Closed

title: An answer block ends in a band of empty rows that nothing is written into
description:
After the model's prose ends there is a tall empty region between the last
written row and the composer — with a short answer roughly a third of the pane
is blank. Nothing is painted there and it is not scrolled into: it is space the
block claims and never fills.

Find where the height comes from — the answer block's own min-height, rows
appended for a stream that ended, or the turn container reserving room for a
tool call that never arrived — and stop claiming it.

## Steps to Reproduce

Ask the assistant a question it answers in a few lines. Below the last line of
the answer, before the composer, a band of empty rows remains. Owner screenshot
2026-08-30.
acceptance_criteria: An answer whose prose is shorter than the pane leaves no unfilled band under it: the composer follows the last written row; a test asserts the block's height matches its written rows.
close_reason: Landed on the epic branch in b8829c33. Of the three suspects the bead named, it is the second, and narrower than 'empty rows': the open row after a newline is a legitimate placeholder while the stream runs, insert() preserved it once another element took the stream seat, and finish() could not trim it because that element had become the final sibling. The trim is at element boundaries only — a non-empty partial row survives mid-stream and a completed interior blank row survives, because deleting empty rows indiscriminately would eat a partial row and fail intermittently.

title: A bound that cannot fire says so: missing shell integration is visible, never a silently disabled bound
description:
Боунды лизы опираются на shell-интеграцию, чтобы знать, что исполнение началось. Там,
где интеграции нет, боунд сегодня оказывается молча выключенным — а Settings и блок
продолжают обещать, что вывод ограничен.

AGENTS.md называет эту форму прямо: «A soft degrade must be visible in the product, not
only in a log. A silent degrade the UI contradicts is how a feature that does not exist
survives a release.»

Значит: либо отказать в надзоре и сказать это, либо вернуть ЯВНО деградированный
результат. Никогда — тихо выключенный боунд.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Когда shell-интеграции нет, продукт говорит об этом человеку в блоке — не только в лог.
- Ни один боунд не заявлен активным, когда он не может сработать.
- Утверждается тестом, который поднимает сессию без shell-интеграции и читает, что видит
  человек.
- Названо в одном месте, какие боунды зависят от интеграции и какие нет.
notes:
2026-08-31: edges to .2 and .3 added on MEASURED file overlap, not sequencing.
.4 needs run_lease.go (shared with .3) and ws_run.go (shared with .2). Parallel
workers in those files would overwrite each other.

2026-08-31: .4 IS NO LONGER OPTIONAL — .3 CREATES THE EXACT DEFECT .4 EXISTS TO PREVENT.

Measured in lease-w2's commit 3d58a6b8 (branch lease-w2-accounting), reviewed and
accepted in substance. run_lease.go now gates BOTH onOutput and checkInactivity on
a new accountingStarted flag, which only onAttemptStart() sets:

  onOutput:         if !l.accountingStarted || ... { return }
  checkInactivity:  if !l.accountingStarted || ... { return }

onAttemptStart is reached from the AUTHENTICATED lifecycle start. Where there is no
shell integration, that start never arrives, accountingStarted stays false forever,
and the output budget and the inactivity bound are BOTH permanently inert — no log,
no error, no visible degrade. Settings and the block go on promising a bounded run.

That is verbatim the shape AGENTS.md names: 'A soft degrade must be visible in the
product, not only in a log. A silent degrade the UI contradicts is how a feature
that does not exist survives a release.'

This is the correct decomposition, NOT a defect in .3 — the flag is what makes the
accounting honest, and making the absence visible is .4's whole job. But it means
the epic MUST NOT close on .2+.3+.5 alone: between .3 landing and .4 landing, the
bounds are weaker than before .3, because previously they at least fired on
something. .4 is now a release gate for nocx-o6qtx, not a P2 nicety.

Note the wall clock is deliberately NOT gated this way — it still arms in supervise,
before authenticated start. That is correct and is .2's subject (a bound firing
before the command exists cancels the SUBMISSION). Do not 'fix' it into symmetry.
2026-08-31: ПРИНЯТО оркестратором. a86980a3 на lease-w3-visible; go test ./internal/transport -run 'Lease|ShellIntegration' — ok 9.4s.

Все четыре критерия закрыты: отказ виден человеку в блоке (не только лог), ни один
боунд не заявлен активным, тест поднимает сессию БЕЗ интеграции и читает видимый
текст, и needsShellIntegration() — единственное место, где сказано, какие боунды
зависят от интеграции (WallClock явно исключён и это прокомментировано).

ИЗМЕРЕННЫЙ РАДИУС ПОРАЖЕНИЯ, зафиксирован честно, а не спрятан.
defaultRunLease = {Inactivity: 2m, OutputBudget: 4MiB} — оба ненулевые, поэтому
needsShellIntegration() истинно ВСЕГДА на продовом дефолте. Следствие: ассистент
отказывается выполнять ЛЮБУЮ команду на любой сессии без shell-интеграции (ssh на
чужой хост, шелл, который мы не зацепили). Человек видит:
'shell integration is unavailable; inactivity and output bounds cannot be enforced,
so the command was not run'.

Почему это всё равно правильный ответ, а не перебор: без интеграции onAttemptStart
не вызывается никогда, поэтому inactTimer не взводится, а onOutput закрыт флагом.
Оба боунда МЕРТВЫ, а не просто неверно посчитаны. Бид запрещал именно тихо
выключенный боунд и разрешал ровно два ответа; это один из них.

Альтернатива (выполнять с ЯВНОЙ деградацией) требует новой видимой поверхности в
блоке и изменения контракта — это не входит в этот эпик. Заведено отдельным бидом.
2026-08-31 ПРИЁМКА ОТОЗВАНА. Измерение, а не мнение.

a86980a3 ЛОМАЕТ два существующих теста, которые проверяют ОБЫЧНЫЙ путь пользователя:
  TestRun_AuthorisedThreadReadsBackFromTheLedger
  TestRun_GrantedPathThreadReadsBackFromTheLedger  (internal/transport/ws_run_thread_test.go)

Бисект по одному коммиту:
  712217e9 (ДО .4)  — ok  0.559s
  lease-int (С .4)  — FAIL, обе по 10s таймауту
    'waiting for agent.runRequest notification: i/o timeout'

Механизм понятен и прямой: .4 возвращает отказ в RequestRun ДО доставки брокеру,
поэтому уведомление agent.runRequest не отправляется никогда, и тест ждёт его до

Собственная докстрока теста называет, что именно сломано: 'after one ORDINARY
exchange — a tool call proposed, AUTHORISED by a person, run, completed'. Это не
экзотическая настройка, это счастливый путь. Значит .4 в нынешнем виде — регрессия
продукта, а не только широкий радиус, о котором я писал выше.

ПОЧЕМУ ЭТО ПРОШЛО МИМО. И воркер, и я проверяли шаблоном -run 'Lease|ShellIntegration'.
Оба сломанных теста называются TestRun_*Thread*, под шаблон не попадают. Приёмка,

Требование бида при этом сохраняется полностью: тихо выключенного боунда нет —

2026-08-31 МАСШТАБ ПОЛОМКИ ИЗМЕРЕН ПОЛНЫМ ПАКЕТОМ. Их не два, их ОДИННАДЦАТЬ.

Три полных прогона go test ./internal/transport/ -count=1, без выборки по имени:

МОЯ ОШИБКА, зафиксирована чтобы не повторить. Я проверял выборкой

Атрибуция проверена: на w3-deadline в одиночку он ok за 0.628s, на слитом падает по

РЕШЕНИЕ ПО СЛОВАРЮ, принято с владельцем соседней части и проверено на диске.
Формулировку 'граница НЕ ДЕЙСТВУЕТ' кладём рядом с assistant.RunLeaseSentence
(requester.go:79), у ТОГО ЖЕ владельца — второй глагол, а не второй словарь.
Звать RunLeaseSentence или добавлять член в TerminationReason ЗАПРЕЩЕНО, и причина
не в сигнатуре: TerminationReason пишется на диск в

termination_reason = ?). Выдуманный член — это ложная терминализация в журнале
навсегда, ломающая отвечаемость журнала на вопрос 'какая граница завершила команду'.

Восьмым критерием добавлена страховка: тест, печатающий обе фразы для ОДНОЙ границы
рядом, чтобы поймать момент, когда поправят одну и забудут вторую.

ГЛАВНЫЙ КРИТЕРИЙ ПРИЁМКИ: go test ./internal/transport/ -count=1, ВЕСЬ пакет
зелёный, все 12 падений исчезают. Выборка по -run на этом эпике запрещена — она
дважды прятала поломку.
close_reason:
77e28ad8 на lease-w6-degrade. Отказ заменён явной деградацией: команда выполняется, agent.runState и зарезервированный ответ agent.cancel называют каждый недоступный боунд текстом, который читает человек; действуют только те боунды, которые могут сработать.

ГЛАВНЫЙ КРИТЕРИЙ ПРОВЕРЕН МНОЙ, а не принят с отчёта: go test ./internal/transport/ -count=1 — ok 105.7s, ВЕСЬ пакет. Все 12 падений, внесённых отказом, исчезли.

Формулировка легла рядом с assistant.RunLeaseSentence — второй глагол у того же владельца, не второй словарь. Отдельная функция, а не новый член TerminationReason, потому что перечисление пишется на диск (ledger_agent_sqlite.go:665) и выдуманный член был бы ложной терминализацией в журнале навсегда.

Восьмой критерий (защита от расхождения двух глаголов) закрыт тестом TestRunLeaseSentenceAndUnavailableSentenceNameTheSameBound.

Своё же подозрение о дублирующем пути через context снял проверкой: leaseDegradation лежит на askRunContext, а не на agentRunControl, askRunContext в контекст не кладётся, а шов реквестера принимает только (ctx, sessionID, command). Другого канала из runAskStream через ядро обратно в RequestRun нет — context-value здесь единственный путь, а не дубль.

title: The e2e container runner has no npm cache volume, and --silent hides why npm ci died
description:
Every `e2e/run-in-container.sh` run re-downloads the whole dependency tree:
the script mounts named volumes for node_modules, the Go build cache and the
Go module cache, but nothing for `/root/.npm`. On a slow or IPv6-only network
`npm ci` then dies with `ETIMEDOUT` and the run exits 146 having produced two
header lines and nothing else — because `container-entry.sh` runs it with
`--silent`, which swallows the diagnosis.

This is the same defect the module-cache volume was added for on 2026-08-18
("with no /root/go/pkg/mod the build re-downloads the whole module graph each
time and the suite dies in globalSetup when DNS blinks — three times, each one
indistinguishable at a glance from a real failure"). The npm half was never
done.

## Steps to Reproduce

On a host whose route to registry.npmjs.org is slow or IPv6-only:

1. `PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/<any>.spec.ts`
2. The run prints the two header lines and exits 146. No error text, no spec
   ever starts.
3. `docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work nocx-e2e:local npm ci` prints the
   real cause: `npm error code ETIMEDOUT ... network read ETIMEDOUT`.

Measured 2026-08-30: five consecutive runs exited 146 that way. The same
`npm ci` by hand with `--prefer-offline --no-audit --no-fund` succeeded in
5m11s, which is what identified the cause.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A named volume carries /root/.npm across runs, keyed the way the Go caches
  are (shared, not per-worktree: the npm cache is content-addressed).
- `npm ci` no longer hides its failure: a run that dies in install says why.
- A run on a cold cache still works; a run on a warm one does not need the
  registry for packages it already has.
close_reason: npm cache volume mounted (shared, content-addressed) and --silent dropped so an install failure says why. Verified: the same command that had failed five times ran both browsers to 6 passed once the cache was warm. 449ed02d

title: The publish job looks for release notes in a directory it never checked out, so every release ships the fallback text
description:
The publish job reads docs/release-notes/v${VERSION}.md and falls back to a
one-line caveat when the file is absent (.github/workflows/release.yml:560-567).
The job has no actions/checkout step — it downloads three artefacts and nothing
else (checkout appears at lines 46, 89, 316 and 424, i.e. validate, build-macos,
build-linux and sign, never publish). So the test is evaluated against an empty
working directory, the file can never be found, and every release publishes the
fallback text with a ::warning:: nobody reads.

docs/release-notes/v0.2.0.md and v0.3.0.md exist in the repository, written to
be published, and never were.

Found while planning the signing change (nocx-2s0zc) by reading the publish job
end to end.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read .github/workflows/release.yml publish job — no actions/checkout.
2. `[ -f docs/release-notes/v0.3.0.md ]` in that job is false by construction.
3. Look at the v0.3.0 release on GitHub: its body is the generic caveat, not
   the notes file that exists in the repository.

## Acceptance Criteria

A tagged release whose docs/release-notes/v<version>.md exists publishes THAT
file as the release body. Either the job checks out the single path it needs, or
the notes travel from a job that already has the source as an artefact — but
the fallback warning must be reachable only when the file genuinely does not
exist.
close_reason: validate stages the notes and reports whether this version has any; publish downloads that artefact, guarded on the same output, and reads notes/notes.md. No checkout added to publish — its GH_REPO comment's reasoning stands. Fallback kept and now reachable only when the file genuinely does not exist. Merged by the owner as PR #153.

title: files.trash: deleting is reversible when a person asked for it, and rm is never silently replaced
description:
A delete that goes to the trash is reversible, and a person answers a
reversible question differently — which is why the delete verb (nocx-4h0m7.3)
is worth having at all.

But the obvious implementation is a trap, and it is worth writing down why.
Swapping `rm` for a trash wrapper on PATH changes the contract of rm in ways
scripts notice: disk-full errors, cross-filesystem moves, mount points,
hardlinks, extended attributes, watcher events, and the atomicity of the name
disappearing. The worst variant is a wrapper that, when it cannot trash,
silently falls back to a real rm — which is a delete that lied about being
reversible.

So: an EXPLICIT `files.trash` tool, capability-scoped like the other file
tools, with its own row in the registry and its own contract. Not a PATH shim,
not an alias, and nothing that changes what `rm` means to anybody's script.

Then a delete the assistant proposes has two forms a person can be offered —
"move to trash" and "delete" — and the first is not a question in the same
weight class as the second.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `files.trash` exists as a declared tool with a narrowed capability, a params
  schema in contracts/ and a result contract, and is reachable from the
  composition root (a test names the seam, per AGENTS.md rule 2).
- It refuses rather than falling back when it cannot trash, and the refusal
  says why.
- `rm` is unchanged, everywhere, and nothing in the product aliases or shims
  it. Asserted by absence.
- The approval surface distinguishes trash from delete in the person's words.

title: internal/git/helper: TestLostMutationIsNeverARefusalOrSilentSuccess fails in TempDir cleanup, not on an assertion
description:
ci-backend (with-secret-service) went red on PR #147, run 33306174075, job
99243030392:

  --- FAIL: TestLostMutationIsNeverARefusalOrSilentSuccess (0.04s)
      testing.go:1464: TempDir RemoveAll cleanup: unlinkat
      /tmp/TestLostMutation.../002/.git/objects: directory not empty
  FAIL github.com/shady2k/nocx/internal/git/helper 2.680s

The test's own assertions PASSED. It fails in t.TempDir's cleanup, because
something — a peer git process the test started — is still writing into the
fixture repository when the temp directory is removed.

NOT the PR's doing: that branch changes zero files under internal/git/, and
ci-backend (no-secret-service) passed on the same commit, as did both
ci-linux variants.

This is the shape nocx-x2e53 already named and closed — "A helper test deletes
its fixture repo while the peer is still committing into it" — in the same
package, on a different test. So either the fix was scoped to one test where
the pattern is shared, or a sibling was written the same way afterwards. Start
by reading what x2e53 did and asking why this test was not covered by it.

## Steps to Reproduce

Not reliably; observed once. Run internal/git/helper under the ci-backend
(macOS) job. Both keyring variants run the same tests, and only one went red,
so it is load- or timing-dependent.

## Acceptance Criteria

• The test waits for the peer process to have finished with the fixture before the directory is removed — an observable, not a duration.
• Whatever nocx-x2e53 did for its test covers this one too, or the reason it cannot is written down where the next reader will find it.
• A test that passes its assertions can no longer fail in cleanup in this package.
close_reason: Root cause was not the test: host.frame dispatches every request on its own goroutine (D13) and Serve returned on EOF with handlers still running, so x2e53's wait on the peer's exit meant nothing it claimed. Serve now waits on an inflight WaitGroup, abandoning the cancellable half first so a dead transport cannot hang the helper. Guards: TestServeWaitsForItsHandlersBeforeReturning (red in 0.00s before), TestADeadTransportAbandonsWhatMayBeCancelled (hangs to timeout before). 7e0ac219

title: History shows empty rows
description:
The recall overlay lists rows with no command text in them. Reported from the
product; the mechanism is not yet established, so establishing it is the first
half of this bead.

The owner's guess is that it is the same family as nocx-3dteo (a read handing
back rows that are not what the surface thinks they are). Treat that as a lead,
NOT as a conclusion — nocx-3dteo is a media-type lookup on an ask entry and has
no obvious path into history.query.

Where to look first, in order:
- What history.query returns: contracts/history.query.schema.json defines a
  `historyEntry`; find whether a row with an empty command can be produced at
  all, and if so by which writer.
- Who WRITES history rows: frontend/src/history-client.ts recordCommand and the
  HistoryOutbox (:145), plus the backend handler. A command that never got its
  text — a submit that recorded before the line was read, an agent-submitted
  row, an interrupted attempt — would be an empty row with a real timestamp.
- Whether the empty rows are the SESSION fallback rather than the store: the
  contract's `source` field distinguishes `store` / `session` / `unavailable`,
  and the in-memory ledger is a different set of rows with different fields.

State which of these it is with evidence before changing anything. If it turns
out the rows are legitimately empty and the defect is that they are LISTED,
the fix is at the read; if they are being written empty, the fix is at the
writer and the existing rows are a separate question.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Use the terminal normally for a while, then open recall (Up on an empty
   line, or the recall overlay).
2. Rows appear with no command text.

Establish a minimal reproduction as part of the work — which command, or which
kind of submission, produces one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The mechanism is named with evidence: which writer produced the empty row, or
  which read returned it.
- A test reproduces an empty row through the seam that produces it, and fails
  before the fix.
- Recall lists no row a person cannot act on; if empty rows can legitimately
  exist in the store, the read excludes them and says so in the code.

title: The shell tool is named 'run' while every other tool is domain.verb — it should be session.run
description:
`internal/agenttools/registry.go:286` declares the shell tool as `run`. Every
other row in the table is `domain.verb`: files.read, files.edit, files.create,
session.list, session.read, notes.*, snippets.*, git.status. `run` is the only
bare verb, and it is not even domainless — it takes a sessionId and is bounded
by the grant's session scopes, so it belongs to the session family by the same
relation session.list and session.read do.

The rename was decided in a session and never landed: `session.run` appears
nowhere — not in the tree, not in `git log --all -S'session.run'`, not on any
branch, not in contracts, not in a bead.

Radius is small. The tool name reaches production Go in exactly one place
(registry.go:286) plus the schema's filename and `$id`
(contracts/tools/run.schema.json) and the row's `Params:` field. The frontend
never branches on it — `grep` for the name over frontend/src is empty. So:
registry row, contract file + `$id`, the generated type, and the tests naming
the tool.

Already-recorded ledger rows keep the name `run`. The project is greenfield and
takes no migrations; old rows carrying the old name is the accepted outcome.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Ask the assistant to list its tools.
2. It names files_read, files_edit, files_create, session_list, session_read —
   and `run`, the only name that is not domain.verb.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The declaration is `session.run`; the contract is
  contracts/tools/session.run.schema.json with a matching `$id`.
- `npm run contracts:check` is green and the generated type is regenerated,
  not hand-edited.
- `grep -rn '"run"' internal --include=*.go | grep -v _test` names no tool.
close_reason: Merged as d71263ab. The declaration, the contract and its $id, and 18 test files carry session.run; contracts:check green, go test on agenttools/assistant/transport green, tsc green. No production Go outside the registry named the tool and the renderer never branched on it. Schema title and prose freshened by the coordinator (SessionRunParams/SessionRunResult).

title: The scrollback scrollbar floats in a 10px gutter beside the activity bar
description:
The activity bar moved to the trailing edge of the window. `.pane` carries
`--pane-inline-padding: 10px` (styles/base.css), so `.scrollback-layout` — and
with it the scroller's stable gutter — is inset 10px from the pane's right
edge. The bar therefore has canvas on BOTH sides: it reads as a free-standing
stripe between the content and the rail rather than as the pane's edge
treatment, and the eye catches on it. Orca is the reference: its scrollbar is
flush against the panel it borders, which is why the same bar there is quiet.

Not a colour problem — tinting the thumb was considered and rejected: in
tokyo-night `--color-surface-raised` (#2b3049) and `--color-divider` (#2a2b3d)
are within a hair of each other, so the tint changes almost nothing while the
floating geometry stays.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the app with the activity bar on the trailing edge and the sidebar collapsed.
2. Open a pane with enough scrollback to overflow.
3. Look at the right edge: thumb, 10px of canvas, the rail's 1px divider.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `.scrollback-layout` cancels the pane's inline padding on its trailing side, so
  the scroller's gutter ends on the pane's border edge.
- The frozen scroller and the live xterm container keep the SAME trailing edge —
  they are siblings and only one of them carries the scrollbar, so pulling one
  without the other reopens the 10px grid overhang of nocx-vydj.
- `.scrollback-area` gains NO padding: `usableViewport` reads its `clientWidth`
  as the grid width (terminal-content.ts), and padding counts in `clientWidth`.
- The composer/editor row keeps its 10px breathing room.
- A test pins all three against the shipped stylesheet.
close_reason: The layout cancels the pane's trailing inset, so the scroller's gutter ends on the pane's border edge and the thumb is flush against the rail. Fixed on the layout, not the scroller: clientWidth is the grid width.

title: The notification-choice spec's badge assertion has a 5s budget for an unbounded event
description:
## Description

e2e/notification-centre-choice.spec.ts:139 asserts toHaveText("2") on the default 5s
timeout, immediately after a 30s wait for the badge to appear at all. The badge reaches
"2" only when the parked command COMMAND_FINISHED lands, which is a second real event with
no 5s bound. On a loaded runner the bell arrives, the badge reads "1", and the five seconds
run out before the completion does.

Seen on PR #139 CI (run 33278105442, ci-e2e chromium): 14 polls, all "1", while webkit
passed. PR #137, which added the spec, was green — a race the spec loses under load, not a
product defect.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run e2e/notification-centre-choice.spec.ts on chromium on a loaded machine, alongside
   the rest of the suite so the run takes ~16 minutes.
2. The badge assertion at line 139 fails with Received "1".

## Acceptance Criteria

- The assertion that the badge reads "2" waits on the completion event with a budget
  matched to it, the way the preceding assertion already does.
- The spec still waits on an observable state change and on no duration.
- ci-e2e (chromium) is green on a run where the whole suite is in flight.
close_reason: Fixed on fix/panes-lifecycle in fbc6efc5: one expect.poll over the conjunction (badge text + both row counts) on a 30s budget, carrying numbers so a timeout names which half is missing. Could not reproduce the split locally — three 1-CPU container passes and one default pass all went straight to '2' (22/307/311ms first observation, already '2'). Cause of CI's 5s gap not established; the conjunction form still goes red, with counts, if the completion is genuinely missing.

title: make dev-web: give the dev stand back a stable backend port, without giving the daemon one
description:
The coordinator cutover (57400e85, nocx-gpyxp) removed `NOCX_WS_PORT` along
with cmd/devharness, so `make dev-web` now binds a port the OS picks. The
`ssh -L` line the script prints is therefore stale after every restart, and
whoever is watching the stand over a forward re-makes it on each edit-restart
cycle. Before the cutover the port was 9880 and the forward was made once.

That churn was a side effect of the move, not a decision about the dev stand —
the commit's reasoning is about the shipped daemon (design §6: a token must not
reach argv, and a daemon that took its ADDRESS from the environment could be
told to bind off loopback), and the stand paid for it silently.

## Steps to Reproduce

    make dev-web        # note the port in the printed `ssh -L` line
    <Ctrl-C>
    make dev-web        # a different port; the forward made from the first is dead

## Acceptance Criteria

- Two consecutive `make dev-web` runs print the same `ssh -L` line, with 9880
  as the backend port, and `NOCX_WS_PORT` overrides it.
- A nocx-server built WITHOUT the dev tag ignores the variable entirely: with
  it set, the server binds somewhere else. Asserted by a Go test in the default
  build, not only by reading the code.
- Under either build the listener is on 127.0.0.1 — the host is never an input,
  which is the half of §6 that carries the weight.
- A tagged build that is asked for nothing behaves like a shipped one: two
  WSServers in one process do not collide.
- A set-but-unusable value stops the server rather than sliding to an OS-chosen
  port.

## Design

Two files behind `-tags nocx_dev_bind`, the shape D10 already uses for the
keystore stance: the shipped half has no code that reads the variable at all.
What is settable is a NUMBER, never an address — `127.0.0.1` stays a literal in
ws.go — so §6's actual objection is untouched. The tag carries no default port
of its own; the number belongs to scripts/dev-web.sh, which is the only thing
that sets it. The variable is `NOCX_DEV_WS_PORT` rather than the old
`NOCX_WS_PORT`, because e2e/preflight.ts refuses a run with that name set.
close_reason: Merged in PR #143 (8711ebf6). Stable 9880 for the stand under -tags nocx_dev_bind; the shipped build ignores the variable.

title: nocxify-journey:341 went red once in CI at the ssh password step
description:
`nocxify-journey.spec.ts:341` failed on run 33274742860 (PR #141, chromium) and
passed on a rerun of the same job at the same commit. It has not failed in CI in
the surrounding window -- the other red chromium jobs nearby were
`secret-panel-position:213` and `ask-about-full-screen-program:717`, both
different specs. `bd memories` records nocxify-journey:341 as known-red in the
LOCAL e2e container and green in CI, so this occurrence is not that.

Filed rather than shrugged off because a rerun that goes green is not evidence
of a flake -- it is evidence of nothing, and twice on this repo a "flake" turned
out to be a spec asserting a state the application never promised (nocx-b0k9a,
nocx-kxtsc).

Where to look first: the password is typed with a raw `page.keyboard.type` right
after `primary.waitConn(1, 30_000)`. `waitConn` is the sshd fixture's word that
the client's first userauth reached it -- a SERVER-side fact that says nothing
about which surface in the BROWSER owns the keyboard at that moment. The spec's
own comment at the second `exit` names this same hazard for a different site
("Raw page.keyboard.type does not wait, so it raced the prompt's return"). If
the keystrokes land in the editor instead of the pty, ssh gets no password,
`NumberOfPasswordPrompts=1` closes the connection, and no block ever reaches
`cmd-block-entered` -- which is exactly the observed shape.

Not yet established: whether that is the actual cause. It is a hypothesis with a
matching signature, not a diagnosis.

## Steps to Reproduce

Not reliably reproducible yet. Observed once:

1. CI run 33274742860, job 99159382783, `ci-e2e (chromium)`, commit d32f8297.
2. `e2e/nocxify-journey.spec.ts:341` -- `expect(locator).toHaveCount(1)` on
   `.pane.active .cmd-block.cmd-block-entered` received 0, 63 polls over the
   30 s timeout.
3. Rerunning that job alone at the same commit passed (job 99161860175).

## Acceptance Criteria

- The step that types the ssh password waits on an OBSERVABLE frontend state --
  that the pty owns the keyboard -- rather than on the sshd fixture's
  `waitConn`, or it is established and written down why waitConn is sufficient.
- If the cause turns out to be the product rather than the spec, the bead is
  reclassified and the product fix carries its own check.

title: toast-clears-activity-bar types a cd before the editor has the keyboard
description:
The spec waits for a non-empty tab title and then types `cd <repo>`. A non-empty
tab title says the pane exists; it says nothing about which element holds the
keyboard, so the keystrokes can land before the editor is focused and lose their
leading characters.

Same shape as nocx-b0k9a: a spec asserting a state the application never
promised. The established answer is `promptReady(page)` from ./harness, which the
four other specs that type a `cd` already use; this one was the only one not
calling it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/toast-clears-activity-bar.spec.ts`
2. Observed: `cd /tmp/nocx-test-e2e-dNwLvP` arrives at the shell as
   `t-e2e-dNwLvP`, the shell runs the remains as a command, the cwd never
   changes, and the wait on the tab title times out at 21.4 s against a title
   that still shows the home directory.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The spec waits on `promptReady(page)` rather than on a non-empty tab title
  before typing anything.
- `PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/toast-clears-activity-bar.spec.ts`
  is green, and passes in seconds rather than timing out.
close_reason: Fixed in #141: the spec now waits on promptReady(page) rather than a non-empty tab title. CI green on both browsers.

title: Two projections of vault.status disagree, and the unreachable one omits defaultProvider
description:
`vault.Snapshot` has a `MarshalJSON` method (internal/vault/vault.go) and
nothing in production calls it. Every wire path goes through
`vaultSnapToStatus` in internal/transport/ws_vault.go — `vault.status`'s
handler and the `vault.changed` fan-out both — and that function builds a
separate `vaultStatusResponse`.

So there are TWO projections of one shape, and they DISAGREE. `MarshalJSON`'s
alias struct omits `defaultProvider` entirely; the contract
(`contracts/vault.status.schema.json`) lists it as required, and
`vaultSnapToStatus` sends it as a nullable pointer specifically so the renderer
can tell "no store chosen yet" from "a store id I do not recognise".

This is the shape of the defect ADR/AGENTS.md records for `vault.status`'s
missing `defaultProvider` in the first place: one concept, two owners, agreeing
everywhere anyone looked. It has not bitten because the second owner is
unreachable — which is luck, not design, and the next person to marshal a
Snapshot directly gets the wrong payload with no test failing.

Found while removing the OS-held root key (nocx-hqklb.1); deliberately not
fixed there, because it predates that change and is not part of it.

## Steps to Reproduce

    grep -rn "vaultSnapToStatus\|MarshalJSON" internal/transport internal/vault --include=*.go | grep -v _test

`MarshalJSON` appears only at its definition. Then compare its alias struct's
fields against `vaultStatusResponse`'s and against the required list in
`contracts/vault.status.schema.json`.

## Acceptance Criteria

Either `Snapshot.MarshalJSON` is deleted — the transport DTO is the wire's
owner and one owner is the rule — or it becomes the single projection that
`vaultSnapToStatus` is built from, and is validated against
`contracts/vault.status.schema.json` by a test the way the transport DTO
already is.

Whichever, a test proves the choice: after the change, `grep` finds exactly one
place that decides what `vault.status` carries.

title: handleAck trims the ring on an ack from a connection that no longer holds the session
description:
`handleAck` (ws_session_handlers.go:1013) looks the session's ring up by id and
acks it. It never asks whether the connection the notification arrived on is
the session's SUBSCRIBER, so any connection that knows a session id can move
that session's ack cursor — and the ack cursor is what `trim` frees bytes
against (ring.go:`trim`, floor = `acked`).

The reachable path is a displacement. `handleAttach` installs the new
connection in the subscriber slot and tells the loser through
`session.displaced`, but the loser's SOCKET stays up and its read loop goes on
answering. An ack it had already queued — for bytes it genuinely received
before the take — lands after the new subscriber's pump has started at a lower
offset, and trims `base` past that pump's position. From there the ring cannot
serve the pump the bytes it is asking for.

Found while fixing nocx-5v9zf, which is the OTHER half: the pump discards the
`needsReset` this produces and busy-spins. That fix makes the pump stop and say
so instead of spinning, which is the right stance for a state that should be
unreachable — this bead is what makes it actually unreachable, so a live
subscriber's stream cannot be reclaimed underneath it by a connection that no
longer owns the session.

`getSubscriber` is the existing answer to "who owns this session" and the
comparison `ringToConn` already makes on every pass (ws.go:2949). Nothing new
has to decide it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a session on connection A and let it receive some output.
2. Attach the same session from connection B, which displaces A. B's pump
   starts at the offset B attached with.
3. Send `ack` for the bytes A received, on A's socket, which is still open.
4. The ring's `base` moves past B's pump position. B is sent nothing further.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An `ack` arriving on a connection that is not the session's current
  subscriber does not move the ring's cursor, and is logged at warn like the
  other two refusals in that handler.
- A test drives it directly: two connections, the second attaches and displaces
  the first, the first then acks — the ring's `oldest` is unmoved. It fails on
  today's handler.
- The subscriber's own ack still trims, so AD-9's flow control is unchanged —
  asserted by the existing ack tests staying green.
close_reason: 6a4f44d1: handleAck now asks the subscriber slot; a displaced connection's ack cannot trim under the live pump. PR #142.

title: A refused archive is shown as validation on the destination field, which it reshapes the ask to display
description:
An unreadable archive is an outcome of the call, and the ask says it in the
wrong place, in the wrong words.

## Where it is said

import-dialogs.tsx renders the refusal into the destination field's validation
slot (`TextField error={refusal()}`), and line 212 makes any refusal FORCE that
field open: `editing()` is true whenever `refusal() !== undefined`, so
"Imports into: /work/postman" collapses into the path field for no reason
except that the message needs somewhere to live. A ZIP that is not a Postman
export is therefore presented as a validation error about a path nobody has
complained about, and the dialog changes shape to present it.

The kit already owns this question (frontend/src/ui/README.md, §Toast): "What
belongs on the field instead is field validation … The outcome of the call the
box triggered is a Toast", and the pattern it replaced is named there too — a
status line living in the document flow. A local comment in this ask says
"that is where every refusal in this ask has always been said", which is the
habit, not the rule.

## In what words

The refusal travels as previewErr.Error() verbatim, so a person reads
`apiimport: read Postman archive: invalid Postman archive: zip: not a valid
zip file` or `apiimport: Postman archive has no archive.json manifest` — the
name of a Go package and the internals of archive/zip.

What is already right and must stay: the refusal arrives on the DROP, before a
destination is chosen and before the first write, and ImportPostmanArchive
preflights every document before writing any, so a refused archive cannot
leave half an import on disk.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Import collection… and drop a .zip that is not a Postman export (any
   zip file will do).
2. The destination sentence collapses into the path field, and under that
   field appears "apiimport: Postman archive has no archive.json manifest".

## Acceptance Criteria

- The outcome of the call — the archive cannot be read, the import was refused,
  the destination is occupied — is raised with showToast at level `danger`,
  which is sticky, and is visible from inside the modal.
- The destination field carries field validation only: empty, and "must not
  exist yet". A refusal no longer forces the field open, and the ask does not
  change shape to display a message.
- The paste box keeps its own inline refusal: "this is not a Postman export or
  a URL" is about what is in that box and is answered by editing it.
- Each refusal class reads as a sentence addressed to a person, naming what to
  do: not a ZIP; a ZIP that is not a Postman export (export the workspace, not
  the folder); a damaged export; an export over the 16 MB limit.
- A test asserts the toast for a refused archive and the absence of a field
  error, from the state a person starts in.
close_reason: Outcomes of the call are raised with showToast at danger (sticky) and no longer rendered into the destination field's validation slot; the coupling that forced that field open for a message is gone. The paste box keeps its own inline refusal. Unit tests assert the toast and the empty field slot for a refused archive, a refused import, a failed picker and a multi-file drop.

title: The keychain releases a vault secret only to a person, not to any process under their login
description:
ADR-0050 steps 3 and 4, which are the half that cannot be done from this
repo's Linux dev hosts and cannot be believed without two measurements
nobody has made.

WHAT THE ADR DECIDED.

3. nocx stops reaching the keychain through `/usr/bin/security`. The darwin
   provider calls Security.framework directly, under our own code identity,
   signed by a project certificate whose designated requirement is stable
   across releases.
4. The item requires user presence — Touch ID or the login password, via the
   item's access control. A signature alone does not close the hole: trust
   anchored to our binary means "any instance of our binary", and our binary
   is on disk, signed, and designed to open the user's vault. An attacker
   runs it against the user's profile and satisfies the requirement. Only a
   prompt aimed at the human survives that.

WHY THIS IS NOT READY TO START.

Two things must be MEASURED before step 4 is believed rather than assumed,
and both need a Mac:

- Does `/usr/bin/security` actually get refused against an item our own
  provider wrote? The whole design rests on it and it is not established.
- Does the designated requirement survive a rebuild AND an update? A
  self-signed code-signing certificate was measured to yield
  `designated => identifier X and certificate leaf = H"…"` — anchored to the
  certificate rather than to a cdhash, so it should survive a rebuild. That
  is a measurement of the requirement string, not of an install surviving an
  update.

Two build obstacles, both in `.github/workflows/release.yml` and both
verified by reading it on 2026-08-29:

- `release.yml:235` signs ad-hoc (`codesign --force --deep --sign -`).
  ADR-0003's ad-hoc signature anchors the requirement to the CODE HASH, so
  it changes on every build — the opposite of what step 3 needs.
- `release.yml:199-203` builds `cmd/nocx-server` with `CGO_ENABLED=0`, which
  makes a direct Security.framework provider impossible. The desktop binary
  next to it already builds with `CGO_ENABLED=1` and explicit `-arch` flags
  (lines 182-186) — that is the shape to copy.

And one release concern the ADR names explicitly: a certificate anchors the
requirement by its own hash, so RENEWING it changes the requirement and every
existing install stops recognising nocx. Issue it long, and treat its private
key as a release secret — whoever holds it can sign a binary the keychain
accepts as ours.

## Success Criteria

A person's vault secret cannot be read by another process under their own
login without them touching the sensor or typing their login password —
the case that today is one `security find-generic-password -w` away.

Proven by measurement on macOS, not by reading the workflow: against an item
this provider wrote, `security find-generic-password -s nocx -a <id> -w`
fails, and a read through nocx itself raises the presence prompt. Recorded
here with the command and its output, the way `nocx-e7bhr`'s comment records
the measurement that started this.

DELIBERATELY OUT: Linux. The Secret Service under a desktop AppImage and a
headless VPS are not the same case, and one build tag cannot be right for
both by accident (`nocx-xsd03` question 4). File it separately when someone
takes it.

title: Six import specs assert a dialog state the dialog never promised
description:
e2e/api-secret-in-any-field.spec.ts timed out on WebKit clicking 'Change where this goes', 30s, in the gate for the #127 reconciliation. It reads as a flake and is not one: the spec asserts a state the app never promised.

The pencil lives inside <Show when={!editing()}> in frontend/src/api/import-dialogs.tsx, and the dialog defines

    editing() = props.editingDest || refusal() !== undefined || (sourceLabel !== '' && !nameable())

so a source that proposes no usable name opens the destination field BY ITSELF, and the pencil is then correctly absent — there is nothing collapsed left to expand. Six specs clicked it unconditionally and then filled the field, which reads as one step and is two claims: that the field is closed, and that the person opens it. Only the second is the spec's business. When the ask settled into the open-field shape the click waited out the full timeout on a button that was never coming.

Same shape as AGENTS.md's rule that a test may not depend on timing: the spec waited for a state instead of waiting for the state change that produces it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run e2e/api-secret-in-any-field.spec.ts under WebKit in the container.
2. The spec opens the import ask, fills #api-import-paste, then clicks 'Change where this goes'.
3. Observed: 'Test timeout of 30000ms exceeded' on locator.click, because editing() is already true and the pencil is not rendered.
4. Expected: the spec reaches the destination field whichever shape the ask settled into.

## Acceptance Criteria

- One helper owns 'reach the import destination field'; no spec names the pencil button directly.
- The helper waits for the ask to settle into one of its two legitimate shapes and then guarantees the field, with no duration anywhere in it.
- All six previously-affected specs pass under container WebKit.
close_reason: Fixed in the commit that names it: openImportDestination in e2e/harness.ts owns 'reach the import destination field', all six specs go through it, and the pencil button is named in exactly one place. Verified under container WebKit — the eight affected specs pass, and api-secret-in-any-field settles in 4.2s where it used to time out at 30s.

title: groupGone reads any poll error as cooperation, EPERM included
description:
The stop ladder's existence poll treats EVERY error from the probe as proof the group is gone:

    // internal/transport/foreground_signal.go, groupGone
    if err := sess.SignalProcessGroup(pgid, 0); err != nil { return true }

Only ErrNoForeground means gone. SignalProcessGroup folds just ESRCH and pgid <= 0 into it; anything else is a wrapped kill(2) failure. An EPERM — a group the backend may not signal, which is what a sudo inside the execution produces — therefore reads as 'the command cooperated', and the ladder answers delivered having proved nothing. A person is told the execution is gone while it runs.

Should be errors.Is(err, pty.ErrNoForeground).

NOT a merge regression: the same line exists on both sides that met in 159e9fc8 — main's cooperatedForeground carried it identically before it was deleted, and nocx-uvac6.11's groupGone inherited it. It predates the stack.

Interacts with the tail rule restored on top of 159e9fc8: with that fix an EPERM group honestly reaches unreconciled when no rung lands, but an EPERM on the POLL after a delivered INT still claims delivered. Both have to be right for Stop to mean what it says.

Found by worktree-quiet-river reading 159e9fc8 line by line.

## Steps to Reproduce

No test on either side exercises an EPERM poll, which is why this survived two independent reworks of this path. To see it:

1. In a stopProcessGroup test, make the session double return a wrapped EPERM (not ErrNoForeground) from SignalProcessGroup(pgid, 0) while the group is still alive.
2. Deliver SIGINT successfully on the first rung.
3. Observed: groupGone returns true on the first probe, the ladder stops, and the outcome is foregroundDelivered.
4. Expected: the probe failure is not cooperation; the ladder escalates, and if nothing lands the outcome is foregroundUnreconciled.

## Acceptance Criteria

- groupGone returns true only for errors.Is(err, pty.ErrNoForeground); any other probe error is not cooperation.
- A test drives a poll that fails with EPERM after a delivered INT and asserts the outcome is not foregroundDelivered.
- The existing cooperation and escalation tests still assert what they asserted before.

title: The stop-ladder guard catches the defect but neither of its halves
description:
The reconciliation of nocx-uvac6.11 (#121) with nocx-7l4ex.10 (#128) landed two
independent halves of one fix:

- the ADDRESSEE: the ladder names the foreground job's process group once and
  signals THAT group at every rung (`foregroundJob` → `stopProcessGroup(pgid)`);
- the POLLER: the existence check asks whether THAT group is gone
  (`groupGone(pgid)`), not whether anything at all is in front.

`TestStopForeground_SignalsOnlyTheGroupItStartedAgainst` is the guard for the
defect they fix. Measured by mutation on the merged tree by the merge
coordinator, three runs:

1. revert the poller only → the test PASSES. The ladder still addresses the
   named group, so it cannot reach a successor; a broken poller costs at most
   one refused call against a dead group.
2. revert the addressee only → the test PASSES. The correct poller sees the
   named group is gone and returns before TERM/KILL are ever reached.
3. revert both — the exact pre-fix state → caught immediately:
   `a command the person started afterwards was signalled: [terminated killed]`.

So the guard catches the real defect and neither of its halves. The two halves
mask each other, and the test only fires when both are absent.

That matters beyond this merge. Both halves were found by two agents READING the
code, independently, and each found only their own. Had either relied on "the
suite is green", their half would have been dropped silently and the guard would
still have passed — leaving a tree one later edit away from signalling a command
the person started.

## Steps to Reproduce

On the merged tree, revert one half at a time and run
`go test -run TestStopForeground ./internal/transport/`; both single-half
mutations are green, the double mutation is red.

## Fix

Two cases, each holding the other half correct, using the signal recording the
`handoffSession` double already has (`got []signalledGroup`, `signalsTo(pgid)`):

- ADDRESSEE alone: the job IGNORES SIGINT and stays alive while a successor
  group takes the foreground. The correct poller then does not short-circuit, so
  the ladder escalates — and every rung must address the original pgid, with the
  successor receiving nothing. Reverting the addressee sends TERM/KILL to the
  successor.
- POLLER alone: the job takes SIGINT and exits, and a successor takes the
  foreground. The correct poller answers "gone" and the ladder stops at INT.
  Reverting the poller escalates against the dead group.

The second case needs one change to the double: record the ATTEMPT before the
liveness check, so a signal aimed at a dead group is visible as an attempt
rather than vanishing. Without it the only discriminator is the returned
outcome word, which is weaker evidence than the addressee list.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Reverting the addressee alone turns exactly one test red.
- Reverting the poller alone turns exactly one test red.
- Reverting both still turns the existing guard red.
- The double records attempted signals, not only delivered ones, and the
  existing tests still assert what they asserted before.
close_reason: Duplicate of nocx-yqwdi, which describes the same gap (the stop-ladder guard catches only the conjunction, so neither half is independently guarded) and carries the mutation table. The two concrete per-half scenarios and the handoffSession attempt-recording fix from this bead are copied into a comment on nocx-yqwdi, so nothing is lost. Filed in parallel because the coordinator asked two sessions the same question separately — the duplicate is the coordinator's, not either author's.

title: ringToConn discards needsReset, so a pump the ring trims past busy-spins and sends nothing
description:
`ringToConn` (ws.go:2941) discards the `needsReset` its own snapshot returns, so
a pump whose position the ring has trimmed past busy-spins for ever and the
subscriber is sent nothing more:

    data, _, _ = ring.snapshot(pos)          // needsReset thrown away
    if len(data) == 0 { … ring.waitForData(ctx, pos); continue }

`snapshot(pos)` with `pos < base` answers `nil, w, true` (ring.go:326). The
pump sees an empty slice, cannot tell that from "nothing new yet", and waits —
but `waitForData(ctx, pos)` returns IMMEDIATELY, because its predicate is
`written() <= pos` and `written` is far ahead of the position the ring no
longer holds. So it loops back into the same snapshot, at the same `pos`, at
full speed: no byte is ever queued, `pos` never advances, and the goroutine
occupies a core while doing it. On a 4-vCPU box that spin also slows down
everything it is competing with.

NOT TEST-ONLY. `acked` is one field per ring, shared by every connection that
has held the session, and `ack` trims on the strength of it. Any subscriber
whose pump is still behind when another connection acks far enough forward
lands in the same state. `creditFloor` (ring.go:388) already names this case —
"a client reattaching over reclaimed bytes is told to reset rather than sent
them" — but the pump has no path by which to tell it: it has the reset flag in
its hand at ws.go:2963 and drops it on the floor.

## How it surfaces

`internal/transport/ws_reclaim_test.go:706` reports `the session's output never
contained "past the trim"; got ""` after 30s when the whole tree runs at
--cpus=4, and passes at every core. The test drives exactly the sequence:
connB attaches at offset 0 while the ring holds "some output"; the test then
acks to `writtenLocked()`, which trims `base` past 0; then it emits "past the
trim". Whether connB's pump read its first snapshot BEFORE that trim is the
whole difference between green and red, and CPU starvation is what loses that
race. The wait is not the defect — the frame is genuinely absent, which is the
case `waits_test.go:45` says to come and investigate rather than adjust.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `./scripts/ci-linux.sh` on a machine with other work in flight (the script
   caps at 4 vCPU by default).
2. The no-Secret-Service variant fails `TestAttach_OverTheWireConformsToContract`
   after 30.08s.

Measured 2026-08-29 on the merged tree of worktree/brave-field-ac50: red in the
first variant of a full run, green in the second variant of the SAME run, and
green in both variants when `./scripts/ci-linux.sh -- ./internal/transport` runs
uncapped (207s / 206s).

## Superseded diagnosis, and why it is recorded

This was filed as "the test waits on a duration, so a loaded container fails
it", with an acceptance criterion of "no wall-clock budget standing in for the
observable state". That was wrong twice over. `tapDataFor` already waits on the
observable state — the needle in the session's output — and the deadline is
only its bound; every wait needs one, and removing it would have hung the run
to `go test`'s own panic while hiding a livelock in shipped code. It is left
written down because the misreading is the one AGENTS.md warns about in the
other direction (nocx-2h08): "a timeout on a loaded box" is the right reading
often enough to be worth checking, and here checking it is what found the bug.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `ringToConn` acts on `needsReset` instead of discarding it: a pump whose
  position the ring has trimmed past resyncs from `base` or ends, and in
  neither case spins.
- A unit test drives a trim past a live pump's position directly — no timing —
  and asserts the subscriber receives the bytes written after the trim, or is
  told to reset. It fails on today's `ringToConn`.
- `NOCX_CI_CPUS=1 ./scripts/ci-linux.sh -- ./internal/transport` is green.
close_reason: cb7bb3c0: ringToConn acts on needsReset and stops instead of spinning; the reclaim test acks after the delivery it acks for. PR #142.

title: The API secret spec cannot tell its second send's run from its first
description:
The second send asserts against `.api-run` .first(), and the run list is newest-first, so
when no new run appears .first() is the PREVIOUS run — already answered with a 200. Both
waits are then satisfied vacuously and a send that never started reads as success until
`server.headerValues()` at line 350, which reports one recorded request against two.

That is why the CI failure points at the server instead of at the click: the spec has no
assertion that a second run exists at all.

Severity: a flaky red job whose message names the wrong subject.
Confidence: high on the defect; the underlying flake was NOT reproduced.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. ci-e2e (webkit), job 99091977067: the spec fails at line 350 with one recorded header
   value against two expected, while every wait above it passed.
2. The list is prepended at api-store.ts:1642 ([{new}, ...prev]), so .first() is the newest
   run — and the previous run, already answered with 200, when no new one appeared.
3. Not reproducible on demand: PW_PROJECTS=webkit e2e/run-in-container.sh on this spec
   passes.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The second send waits for a NEW run to appear before asserting anything about it.
- A send that never starts fails at the send, not at the server assertion.
close_reason: Second send waits for a new run to appear; the new row is the subject. Webkit green in the container. Flake itself not reproduced. 131fd813

title: Two broker tests resolve a request before it is armed
description:
`TestBroker_FailedDeliveryIsNotARecipient` failed on CI's
`ci-backend (no-secret-service)` at **0.00s** with

    request_broker_test.go:1138: resolution by the delivered recipient refused: Unknown request id

while `ci-backend (with-secret-service)` — the same tests, the same commit —
passed. It is not the starved-resource signature nocx-2h08 closed: that one
reported 30-second timeouts under a different test name each run; this fails
instantly.

`Broker.Request` registers and arms in two steps:

    rid, ch, err := b.register(kind)   // b.pending[rid] = &pendingRequest{...}  — recipients is NIL
    payload, err := marshalWithRequestID(rid, params)
    recipients := b.conns()
    ... comparability loop ...
    b.arm(rid, recipients)             // p.recipients is filled HERE

`Broker.Pending()` reports `len(b.pending)`, so it goes to 1 at `register` —
several statements before the request can be resolved by anyone. `Resolve`
refuses a connection that is not in `p.recipients` with the deliberate
"Unknown request id".

Both tests whose deliver seam is a no-op wait on `Pending() == 1` and then
resolve immediately, so under CI scheduling the resolution can land inside that
window: `TestBroker_FailedDeliveryIsNotARecipient` (line 1118) and
`TestBroker_WrongResolveMethodIsRefused` (line 1176). The third site, line 725,
is safe — it reads the notification off a real socket first, which cannot
happen before `arm`.

The tests wait on the wrong observable: "registered" is not "resolvable".

## Steps to Reproduce

Rare on an idle machine — 300 local runs under `-race` are green; it needs the
full package under CI scheduling (the package takes ~315s there). Seen on CI run
33245784702, job `ci-backend (no-secret-service)`.

Deterministic proof of the window instead: `register()` inserts the pending
entry with a nil `recipients` map, and `Resolve` refuses any connection missing
from it. A resolution between those two points is refused whatever the load.

## Fix

One helper that waits for the request to be ARMED — registered AND carrying the
connection about to answer it — and returns its id. Both no-op-deliver tests use
it instead of scraping the map after `Pending() == 1`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Neither test resolves a request before it is armed: the wait is on the
  recipient set containing the answering connection, not on `Pending()`.
- The helper is the single place that wait is written.
- A deterministic test proves the window is real: a request registered but not
  yet armed refuses a resolution from a connection that will become a recipient.
- `go test -race -count=200 ./internal/transport/ -run TestBroker` is green.
close_reason: awaitArmedRequest is the one owner of the wait; both no-op-deliver tests use it, and TestBroker_RegisteredIsNotYetResolvable states the register→arm window deterministically. -race -count=200 -run TestBroker green; CI 8/8. PR #133, merged 7c298b5c.

title: attach-with-stale-offset flakes: it acks a ring offset before the ring has the bytes
description:
Found while running the transport suite on a loaded machine (load average 81 on
6 cores). Not caused by the change under test; it is a race the test does not
wait on.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Load the machine heavily, or run two `go test -race ./internal/transport`
   at once.
2. `go test -race -tags gtk3 -count=1 ./internal/transport`

Observed: `--- FAIL: TestWSServer_AttachWithStaleOffsetReturnsReset` —
`ws_test.go:1237: expected reset for stale offset`, with this in the log one
line earlier:

    WARN ack rejected error="ack offset 999999 exceeds written 0"

The test writes a data frame, then acks offset 999999 to trim the ring, closes,
reattaches at offset 0 and expects `reset`. Nothing waits for the frame to
reach the ring, so under load the ack arrives while `written` is still 0, is
rejected, the ring is never trimmed, and offset 0 is not stale after all. It
passes 5/5 in isolation.

Same run, and same cause: the package twice hit `go test`'s 10-minute wall
with only one test running and that test 1-5s old — the suite simply does not
finish in 600s on a saturated box. It took 370s when the machine was quieter.
That part is capacity, not a defect, and is noted here so the next person
reading a red transport run checks the load first.

## Expected

The ack is sent once the ring has the bytes, asserted on an observable state
rather than assumed — AGENTS.md: "a test may not depend on timing. Wait on an
observable state change ... never on a duration."

## Acceptance Criteria

- The test waits for the written offset to cover the frame before acking, and
  fails with what the ring had actually seen if it does not arrive.
- It passes under `NOCX_CI_CPUS=1` or an equivalent starved run.

title: Two derivations of `which pane holds this session`
description:
Found while designing the notification centre refinements (nocx-9wsb5), deliberately NOT fixed there.

findBySession matches on content.lineage() (panes.ts:2311); paneForSession requires content instanceof TerminalContent and reads content.sessionId() (panes.ts:2319). Two derivations of one question. They agree on the pane they pick today because TerminalContent is the only production implementer of the lineage capability, and both ultimately read `this.session?.sessionId` -- but pane-content.ts:197 declares lineage as an optional CAPABILITY on purpose, so any future PaneContent implementing it diverges them.

## They already disagree on the empty id

Not future tense, and this half was not in the original report. findBySession refuses `sessionId === ''` explicitly (panes.ts:2312). paneForSession has no such guard, and `TerminalContent.sessionId()` answers `''` for a pane whose session has not opened yet (terminal-content.ts:4082, `this.session?.sessionId ?? ''`) -- while `lineage()` answers null for the same pane. So `sessionDisplayName('')` and `sessionWhere('')` return the FIRST session-less terminal pane in the window, named and located as though it held the session, where findBySession would have returned undefined. That is the cost of the second derivation, already banked: the guard was written once and the other walk never got it.

The half the original report worried about is not live: sessionWhere's tab comes from sessionDisplayName and its machine and cwd from terminalContentForSession, and BOTH go through paneForSession, so they cannot name different panes today. It is a constraint on the FIX rather than a present defect -- unifying only one of the two callers is what would introduce it, which is why the refinements work read displayTitle off findBySession at the call site instead.

## Acceptance Criteria

- One lookup answers `which pane holds this session`; terminalContentForSession narrows ITS result rather than walking again.
- The empty session id is refused by that one lookup, so sessionDisplayName('') and sessionWhere('') answer null -- asserted, with a session-less terminal pane present in the window.
- sessionWhere's tab, machine and cwd all come from one pane -- asserted.
- The approval prompt's existing tests still describe the same product behaviour, or the change to it is deliberate and stated.
close_reason: c617c046: paneForSession is findBySession; the empty-id guard exists once. PR #142.

title: fsConn.run answers from the select case that woke it, not from the lease state
description:
The same defect nocx-4c5d7 fixed in the discovery lease, in its sibling:
`fsConn.run` answers from whichever case its slot-wait select woke on.

`fsConn` has three lifecycle signals and the struct comment states their
precedence — "Calls check dead, then closed, then done — sequentially, not in
one select: when several have fired, the lease's own state is the deterministic
answer". The ladder is written out three times (the pre-flight in `run`, the
post-`fn` check, and `classify`), and the slot wait immediately below the
pre-flight then races all three as cases of ONE select and returns whichever
fires.

The ordering is causal, not a preference: `poison()` closes the subsystem and
`Close()` releases the pooled reference that shuts the transport, so the later
signals fire AS CONSEQUENCES of the earlier one. A lease closed by its caller
could therefore report `ErrFSLost` — "the sftp connection went away" — about its
own close, and a poisoned lease could report `ErrFSClosed`.

Found by sweeping for the shape after nocx-4c5d7, not by a failing test: the
window is a call blocked on a full lane at the moment the lease ends, which the
suite does not currently drive.

## Steps to Reproduce

No failing test today — the lane must be saturated (fsLaneCap = 4 in-flight
calls) at the instant the lease dies for the select to see two ready cases. The
defect is read off the code: `internal/ssh/ssh_fsconn.go` `run()`, the select
after the pre-flight ladder, returns `ErrFSDead`/`ErrFSClosed`/`ErrFSLost` from
the woken case rather than from the lease's state.

## Fix

`stateErr()` becomes the one owner of the ladder (dead, then closed, then
done; nil while usable). The pre-flight, the slot wait's three lifecycle
branches and `classify` all read it. Waking on any channel is fine; deciding
the answer from which one woke you is not.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `stateErr()` is the only place the dead/closed/done ladder is written.
- A lease that is closed AND lost answers `ErrFSClosed`; one that is dead AND
  closed AND lost answers `ErrFSDead` — asserted deterministically for every
  combination, through both `stateErr` and `classify`.
- The paired positives hold: each signal alone answers its own error, and a
  usable lease answers none.
- `go test -race ./internal/ssh/` is green.
close_reason: stateErr() is the one owner of the dead/closed/done ladder; the pre-flight, the slot wait's lifecycle branches and classify all read it. TestFSConnStateErr_Precedence asserts every combination through stateErr and classify — restoring either old ordering is red in one run. -race ./internal/ssh/ green. PR #130.

title: a probe error is read as proof the execution cooperated, so Stop can report delivered on a live process
description:
Predates PR #128; found reviewing it.

## Steps to Reproduce

`cooperatedForeground` (`internal/transport/foreground_signal.go:134`) polls with
`sess.SignalForeground(0)` and treats ANY error as proof the execution ended:

    if err := sess.SignalForeground(0); err != nil { return true }

Only `pty.ErrNoForeground` proves that. An EPERM, or an ioctl failure reading
TIOCGPGRP, arriving after a successful SIGINT makes `stopForeground` return
`foregroundDelivered` while the process is still alive — the one thing the ladder
exists to prevent, and the same class of collapse as nocx-7l4ex.10 finding 1.

## Expected

Cooperation is proven by the guard's own answer, not by any error.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `cooperatedForeground` returns true only for the error that means the foreground
  group is gone; every other error keeps the ladder escalating.
- A test drives a probe failure that is not that error and asserts the ladder does not
  report delivered.
close_reason: Duplicate of nocx-iuzak: one wrong err != nil reading, in one file, with one fix. Both say that any error from the existence probe is taken as proof the process group is gone, so the Stop ladder answers delivered while the process is alive. nocx-iuzak survives on evidence — this bead addresses cooperatedForeground at foreground_signal.go:134, and that function no longer exists (grep finds it only in a test comment), whereas iuzak names the surviving instance groupGone, explains that cooperatedForeground carried it identically before deletion and that nocx-uvac6.11's groupGone inherited it, and adds the EPERM/sudo case, the ErrProtectedForeground interaction and a reproduction recipe. Verified still broken during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh: internal/transport/foreground_signal.go:360 still returns true on any error. NOTE FOR WHOEVER PICKS THIS UP: this bead carried the only assignee of the pair — reassign nocx-iuzak.

title: the Stop fallback's contract says more than the code does
description:
Review of PR #128 (nocx-92gfl.4). Four statements the fallback makes about itself are
wider than what it does.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. **"the shell process group is never signalled" is not literally true.** With ISIG on,
   writing 0x03 makes the line discipline send SIGINT to the whole foreground group —
   which in the shared-group case contains the launcher shell. What is true is that
   there is no direct `kill(2)` on that group and no TERM/KILL escalation.
   `contracts/session.signal.schema.json` and `foreground_signal.go`'s package comment
   both promise the wider thing.

2. **`interrupt` is no longer always "one SIGINT".** A program that has cleared ISIG
   receives 0x03 as an ordinary byte and no signal at all. The schema still describes
   every interrupt as one SIGINT.

3. **`delivered` on the fallback path means "the queue accepted the byte".**
   `EnqueueWrite` is fire-and-forget; the write can still fail at `session.go:850` after
   the answer has gone out.

4. **The `unreconciled` toast contradicts the backend.** `terminal-content.ts:4667`
   tells the person to "Try its own exit key or Ctrl+C" immediately after the backend
   enqueued exactly Ctrl+C and it did not work.

Also: `waitLifecycleAttemptEnd` treats "attempt gone", "completed" and "unknown"
alike, so a transport loss counts as the attempt ending; and the sentence the schema
used to carry — "There is one owner for how do you stop a process ... never two
policies" — was deleted rather than satisfied.

## Expected

One stop policy with two delivery mechanisms, the mechanism chosen from foreground
topology and authenticated attempt state; every outcome word means what the renderer
and the person will take it to mean.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The schema restores the single-owner statement in a form that is true of the code,
  and states the ISIG caveat rather than promising a SIGINT.
- The schema and the pty package comment say "no direct kill(2) on the protected group
  and no escalation into it", not "the shell group is never signalled".
- `stop`'s promise is stated as outcome-conditional: `delivered` means the exact
  attempt is no longer open when the response is sent.
- `EnqueueWrite`'s doc comment names both senders and says what ordering now means.
- The `unreconciled` toast does not recommend the gesture that just failed.
close_reason: Fixed in 21f451b4 (exhaustive switch with a never binding, unreconciled text no longer recommends the Ctrl+C the backend just sent) and 019159be (schema restores the single-owner statement in a true form, states the ISIG caveat and what delivered does not claim; EnqueueWrite's ordering comment; e2e fixture comments; design spec).

title: Two panels are compared on a per-repository commit hash
description:
`TestHelperMutationsMatchLocal` compares the helper's git panel against the
local implementation field by field, over two DIFFERENT repositories built from
identical fixtures. `git.Status.Head` is the repository's own commit hash, and a
commit hash embeds the committer timestamp at one-second granularity — so the
two initial commits agree only while both land inside the same second, and
diverge otherwise.

Both assertions in the test compared it:

- the `Stage` half used `reflect.DeepEqual` on the whole `git.Status`, with
  nothing excluded;
- the `Commit` half knew about this — "the two commits are made moments apart,
  so the head hashes may differ" — and excluded the OUTER `Head`, then compared
  `Status` through `reflect.DeepEqual`, which carries `Status.Head` straight
  back into the comparison.

Surfaced as a red `ci-backend (no-secret-service)` job on PR #128, whose diff
does not touch `internal/git`.

## Steps to Reproduce

    go test -run TestHelperMutationsMatchLocal -count=60 ./internal/git/helper/

About 4 failures in 60 on a 4-core Linux box, at both assertions:
`helper stage disagrees with local` (Head 8293821 vs b185abe) and
`helper commit disagrees with local` (Head d71a72c vs 1c6e477).

## Fix

One `sameStatus` helper compares every field except `Head`, and both call sites
use it. Each asserts separately that a head is PRESENT: what it is belongs to
the repository, that there is one belongs to the contract.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `go test -run TestHelperMutationsMatchLocal -count=200 ./internal/git/helper/`
  is green (it failed about 4 times in 60 before).
- Neither assertion compares `Head`, on either nesting level.
- Both assertions still require a head to be PRESENT on each side.
close_reason: sameStatus() compares every field except Head at both call sites; each asserts a head is present. The Commit half's exclusion had been defeated by Status.Head nested inside the DeepEqual. -count=200 green (was ~4 failures in 60). PR #130.

title: Two e2e specs wait on a duration and fail only under full-suite load
description:
Found by the coordinator comparing a full container run against isolated re-runs on feat/nocx-server.

e2e/connections-settings.spec.ts:71 and e2e/snippets.spec.ts:215 fail in a full suite run and pass in isolation — 4 passed in 23.6s when run alone, one failure each under the full 456-test run. Neither shows the ui-prompt-overlay interception that caused nocx-58q7d; their failures are plain waits that ran out:

  connections-settings: locator.click timeout waiting for the Authentication tab to be clickable
  snippets: toContainText('could not be resolved') timed out at 10000ms, element(s) not found

AGENTS.md is explicit that a test may not depend on timing — wait on an observable state change, never on a duration — and that a spec needing a slow machine is broken on a fast one too, it has just not been caught yet. Under a full suite these two are on a slow machine.

Note snippets:215 does NOT seal a vault: its premise is a stand with no vault set up at all, so the departure window from nocx-58q7d is not the cause.

Whether this predates the coordinator work is being measured with a full-suite baseline run at 64244ad4; update this bead with the answer.

## Steps to Reproduce

./e2e/run-in-container.sh on feat/nocx-server: these two fail. PW_PROJECTS=chromium ./e2e/run-in-container.sh on the same two spec files alone: both pass.
acceptance_criteria: Both specs wait on an observable state change rather than a duration, and pass inside a full suite run repeated enough times to have caught the old flake.
