The four are not four instances of "wait for the fact, do not assume the order". They are
four instances of something narrower, and naming it changes what the fix should be:

**A handler answers, and then releases something, and the test reads the second through
the first.** The reply is observable; the release is not. So the test uses the reply as a
proxy for a state change that has no observable of its own. Idle, the gap is microseconds
and the proxy holds. Loaded, it does not. `TestAPIRequestSend_ATokenAlreadyInFlightIsRefused`
failing at **0.00s** is that exactly — the test is not slow, it is EARLY.

So a retry helper fixes the symptom in all four and leaves the cause standing: the release
still has no observable, and the fifth test will proxy it through the reply again, because
there is nothing else to reach for. (Retrying is still the right thing to ship to unblock a
push, which is what af5f95fd did.)

**The question this bead should decide, then, is not "one helper or four fixes" but: should
the release be observable at all?** If the sender's gate published "the name is free" the
way the reply publishes "the request was answered", none of the four needs a retry and the
fifth cannot be written wrong. That is a small production seam rather than test
scaffolding, and this codebase already prefers that shape — a fact published, then waited
on — over polling.

**If the answer is no** — the release genuinely has no business being visible outside the
handler — then the helper is right, and its NAME is the part that matters. `retryUntil`
invites use wherever anything is slow. Something like `untilSettled(fact, wantWithin)` says
the test waits for a state to become true rather than hammering until it gets lucky, and a
reviewer can then see when it is being used to paper over a missing observable instead of
to tolerate scheduling.

### Two things the fix's own author added, and the first one is evidence

**The retry is not free, and what it costs argues the same way.** The helper does not poll
a predicate — each attempt is a real `api.request.send`, and the attempt that finally
succeeds starts an actual run the test then abandons. Harmless in this test, but it means
the wait is only cheap because the thing being waited on happens to be near-idempotent when
refused. A published release would be waited on for nothing at all. That is a second reason
the helper is the weaker answer, and it is exactly the detail that disappears if this bead
is remembered as "flaky under load".

**On the name, agreed, with a caveat worth keeping.** If `untilSettled(fact, wantWithin)`
is written, its docstring must say what the discussion said: that reaching for it is a
SIGNAL the fact has no observable of its own, and the first question is whether it should
have one. Otherwise the good name becomes the comfortable one — this repo has already paid
for a helper that was correct and then became the path of least resistance.

**Whose call this is.** Whether the release should be observable is a production seam, not
a test decision, so it is the owner's rather than something two sessions settle between
themselves. Both options and their reasoning are recorded above deliberately, and the bead
should not be closed by picking one silently.
notes: Backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh: its sibling nocx-0nelq was closed as fixed, and this bead's DEFECT half is fixed too — commit af5f95fd ('the token's release is waited for, not assumed to precede the reply') has internal/transport/ws_api_cancel_test.go:287 retrying to the far end of the interval instead of asking once, and the production-side release-before-settle landed as 39d223df under nocx-f9har. This bead was deliberately NOT closed, because its own text reserves a question that the fix did not answer: the fix went in under duress ('Fixed in passing because it blocked a push'), and whether the release should be OBSERVABLE at all — or whether untilSettled(fact, wantWithin) is the right answer — is called a production seam and explicitly the owner's, not something two sessions settle between themselves. FOR THE OWNER: the flake is gone; retitle this to that design question and drop it to a design or chore, or re-file it and close this. It should not sit as an open P-whatever bug for a defect that no longer exists.

title: T2 A folder chooses an environment for what it holds
description:
Variables already have the rung — a request's own win, the environment's are inherited (nocx-kprt4.2), and a folder carries variables (nocx-x3cax.5). The environment selection has no rung at all.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A folder can be given an environment; everything inside it inherits that unless it says otherwise.
- The resolution order is request, then folder, then collection, then the default — one function, the same one the picker and the send already share.
- The order is asserted at each rung, including a request overriding its folder and a folder overriding its collection.
- A folder with no choice changes nothing.

title: A stopped turn loses the response it was streaming, because the record is written on the cancelled context
description:
Found in review of 500f66c8, not reproduced.

wireTap records through the REQUEST's context: wireResponseBody.finish calls parent.record(b.ctx, ...) and ledgerWireRecorder.RecordWire passes that ctx straight into ledger.AppendArtifact/AppendChunk. On the ordinary path the stream reaches io.EOF while the run is alive and the record lands.

On a stopped turn it does not. Cancelling the run cancels the request context, the body is Closed, finish(true) runs, and the two ledger writes are made on a context that is already Done — so they fail, the error is discarded by design ('losing a diagnostic must never abort a valid response'), and the dump for that turn shows a request drive with no response drive beside it. A stopped turn is exactly the turn somebody wants the dump of.

The request half has the same exposure whenever the transport closes the body after cancellation.

Two candidate answers, and the choice is the work: detach the write onto a context with only the store's own deadline (context.WithoutCancel plus a bounded timeout), or record what was captured before cancellation through a path that does not carry the run's ctx at all. Whichever is chosen, a dump missing a direction must say so rather than render an empty section that looks like 'the provider sent nothing'.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Ask the assistant something that streams for a few seconds.
2. Stop the turn while it is still streaming.
3. Open the finished block's menu and choose Show dump.
4. Expected: the bytes the provider had sent up to the stop, marked truncated. Read from the code: a Request section and an empty Response section.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A test cancels the run's context mid-stream and asserts the partial response bytes captured before cancellation are still readable through agent.dump afterwards.
- The same test asserts the recorded response is marked truncated, so a partial capture is never presented as a complete one.
- The recorder still cannot abort or delay a model response: a store that errors or blocks is asserted not to propagate into RoundTrip.

title: Every turn now stores its whole provider exchange, and nothing has measured what that costs the content store
description:
Raised in review of 500f66c8, unmeasured.

Before it, the verbatim wire was OFF unless someone set NOCX_WIRE_LOG, and the removed comment said why in as many words: the body carries the person's question, whatever their tools read, and their own paragraph from settings, so it is 'not something to leave lying in a file because it might be handy'. The dump feature reverses that deliberately and correctly — a panel cannot show bytes nobody kept — but it reverses it for EVERY turn, unconditionally, with no switch.

The size is the part nobody has looked at. Each provider drive stores its whole request body, which is the system prompt plus the assembled conversation plus the tools array, and its whole response. An agentic turn with several tool loops is several drives, each up to 1 MiB per direction. The content store has a budget and a retention policy (nocx-rtg0) that were sized before any of this existed, so the open questions are whether dump artifacts can now evict a person's actual command history, and whether retention ages them out at all.

Measure first, then decide. The decision is likely one of: dump artifacts get their own retention age, or they count against a sub-budget, or the capture is bounded per turn rather than per drive.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A measurement, in the bead, of what one ordinary turn and one multi-tool-call turn add to the store, taken by driving the real engine against the fake provider.
- A stated answer to whether wire artifacts can evict non-wire content under the existing budget, backed by a test rather than by reading the policy.
- Whatever is decided is enforced by a test that fails if wire capture grows unbounded across turns.

title: The dump panel is a kit component that never joined the kit
description:
500f66c8 added frontend/src/ui/dump-panel.tsx and exported it from ui/index.ts, but it landed without the four things AGENTS.md requires of a genuinely new kit component: no CSS file in frontend/src/styles/components/, no stable identity class, no row in frontend/src/ui/README.md, and no unit test. Its markup is bare
/

/

/

with no classes at all, so it inherits whatever the dialog body gives it and no surface can address it. The e2e (e2e/agent-dump.spec.ts) reaches it by role=dialog and pre[aria-label], which is why nothing was red. Not a redesign: give the panel and its two drive sections identity classes, move the typography and rhythm into one styles/components file, add the README row, and add a vitest. Do not repaint CodeBlock, Dialog or Stack from the panel — if something is missing, it is a variant on the kit component. ## Acceptance Criteria - DumpPanel and its drive sections carry stable identity classes, and e2e/agent-dump.spec.ts still passes unchanged (it addresses roles and aria-labels, not classes). - One CSS file in frontend/src/styles/components/ owns the panel's typography and rhythm; the panel sets no background, border, colour, font or padding on a kit component it merely places. - frontend/src/ui/README.md has a row for it naming its identity class and variance. - A vitest mounts DumpPanel with one truncated drive and one whole one and asserts the truncation sentence appears only on the truncated one, and that the empty case renders the 'no recorded drive' fallback.
close_reason: Merged as 3722a7ef. Identities ui-dump-panel/__drive/__entry/__intro, styles/components/dump-panel.css, README row, and a vitest over the truncated, whole and empty cases. No shared kit component touched.

title: Resumption is correct in a worktree AND in a shared checkout, which are not the same problem
description:
§5 decided this and it is the one subtlety that is load-bearing. In a worktree row each tree has its own directory, so the agent's most-recent-CWD session IS that row's session and a --continue style flag is correct. In a SHARED MAIN CHECKOUT the same flag lassos unrelated sessions belonging to other tasks, so an explicitly minted UUID is required there.

So the record carries both shapes - resume-by-cwd args and mint/resume-by-id args - and which is used is decided by where the task lives, not by the agent's preference. An agent that supports neither simply does not resume, and the surface says so rather than pretending.

termic also has a third case worth naming: an agent that creates its session LAZILY (opencode) can be given no id at spawn, so the id is captured after the fact. Decide whether we support that case or declare it out; do not leave it to be discovered.
acceptance_criteria:
In a worktree, relaunching an agent resumes that worktree's own session. In a shared checkout, relaunching resumes the session this task minted and never another task's. An agent configured for neither does not resume, and the UI says so.

A test that two tasks in one shared checkout resume their own sessions and not each other's.

Falsified if a shared-checkout launch can pick up another task's session, or if the lazy-session case is neither supported nor written down as out.

title: Placeholders expand at spawn, and one with no value passes through rather than vanishing
description:
The 2026-08-15 spec §5 names the placeholders: {UUID}, {WORKSPACE_SLUG}, {WORKSPACE_NAME}, {WORKSPACE_ID}, {WORKSPACE_PATH}, {BRANCH}, {PORT}. termic expands them case-insensitively and passes an unknown one THROUGH unchanged, deliberately, so an odd argument shape is not silently mangled - copy that, and copy the reason with it.

The tokenizer matters as much as the expander: a free-form command string splits into argv honouring quotes, and placeholders are expanded AFTER the split, so a placeholder whose value contains a space stays one argument. Doing it the other way round turns a branch name with a space into two arguments and the failure appears far from its cause.
acceptance_criteria:
An argument list with placeholders expands correctly at spawn; a placeholder with no value reaches the process unchanged; a value containing spaces stays a single argv element.

A test for each placeholder, and a test for the unknown-placeholder and the spaces-in-value cases specifically.

Falsified if an unknown placeholder expands to empty, or if expansion happens before tokenization.

title: The agent is offered where agents are offered, and Settings is where it is edited
description:
A record nothing reads is not a feature (AGENTS.md check 5). An added agent has to appear in the places a person starts one, and the built-ins have to be editable in the same surface without becoming a second vocabulary.

Per frontend/src/ui/README.md: this is a Settings page built from kit components. A per-agent card, the enable toggle as Checkbox variant=switch, the environment lines round-tripping as KEY=VAL text. No hand-rolled control inside the surface.

Edits take effect without a restart - a person fixing a wrong argument should see the next launch use it, not the next session.
acceptance_criteria:
An agent added in Settings appears in every place a built-in agent is offered, launches, and its edits take effect on the next spawn without a restart. A built-in's command and arguments are editable and the built-in cannot be removed.

An automated check watches a person add an agent and launch it.

Falsified if the page builds a control the kit already has, or if an edit needs a restart to take effect.

title: The agent record: shipped defaults embedded, user edits on disk, and the record is what everything reads
description:
One record per agent, following termic's shape because it is the one that has been used: id, display name, command, args, icon, colour, builtin (editable, not removable), disabled, environment lines, and the resumption fields the next bead needs.

The property worth copying from termic is not the field list, it is WHERE THE TRUTH LIVES: its hard-coded values are used only before the registry loads, and the registry is source of truth in steady state. Ours goes further - shipped defaults are embedded in the binary and NOT written to disk, so an upgrade improves an agent nobody touched and never silently rewrites an edited one.

What does NOT come across is termic's `signals`, its regex-over-the-OSC-title detection. That is the weak provenance row in this repository and detection is the sibling epic (nocx-dhq4u).

`extends` in termic is informational only - a clone, not inheritance. Copy that honesty or leave the field out; a field named extends that does not inherit is a lie in the schema.
acceptance_criteria:
One record per agent, shipped defaults embedded and absent from disk, user edits persisted under the app directory. Every place that spawns an agent reads the record rather than a constant.

An upgrade improves an untouched agent and leaves an edited one alone. Removing a user's edits restores the shipped values.

Falsified if a shipped default appears on disk on first run, or if any spawn path still carries a hard-coded command.

title: nocx proposes the rule from the labelled frames
description:
An empty predicate editor is a cliff for everyone except the person who designed the grammar. The labelled frames already contain the answer: what separates "it is asking you" from "it is waiting for input" is a difference between two frames the person just produced.

So nocx derives a DRAFT - where the cursor sits in each label, what opens a row, what appeared and what vanished between labels - and shows it beside the frames it came from. The person edits it.

The proposal is a convenience and may be wrong; the three rules in the claude driver that contradicted what reasoning predicted are the evidence that a derived draft will sometimes miss. Trust does not come from the proposal - it comes from verification, which runs afterwards either way. This is why the proposal lands AFTER the verification gate rather than before it.
acceptance_criteria:
From a labelled set, nocx produces a draft rule shown beside the frames it was derived from, and the person can edit every part of it.

A test that a draft derived from the committed claude corpus classifies that corpus - and an honest report when it does not, rather than a draft presented as finished.

Falsified if the draft cannot be edited, or if accepting a draft skips verification.

title: Progress: the transcript stopped growing, and a spinner does not count as growth
description:
The owner's third state - "says it is working, but nothing has changed for a long time" - is the coordinator's real question: has my wave stalled? It is not a fifth value of the screen facet. It is a conjunction: working AND not moving. Forced into one enum, a stalled worker leaves working, and a coordinator asking who is working stops seeing the worker that most needs it.

And the naive predicate is wrong. "The frame did not change for N seconds" reports MOVING for a hung agent, because the spinner keeps spinning. The predicate is that the TRANSCRIPT stopped growing - and which region is transcript rather than chrome is something only the rule knows. So progress is a second question asked of the SAME rule, not an independent timer bolted beside it.

N is per-agent with a default, and it is a setting because the right value for an agent that thinks for two minutes is not the right value for one that answers in seconds.
acceptance_criteria:
A third facet, progress: moving | stalled, stored beside liveness and screen rather than replacing either. A pane can be working and stalled at once, and a listing of working panes still contains it.

A test that an agent with a live spinner and a frozen transcript reports stalled, and one that a growing transcript reports moving however still the chrome is.

Falsified if progress is expressed as a value of the screen facet, or if the predicate is frame equality rather than transcript growth.

title: An agent you run is described once: its command, its arguments and its environment, and nocx launches it that way
description:
nocx can enrol an agent launched in a pane (nocx-szb40.5) but has no data about
HOW to launch one. There is no per-agent record of the command, its arguments,
its environment or how it resumes, so a wave cannot start a worker without the
person typing the whole line, and an agent the person prefers cannot be offered
anywhere.

Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-27-agent-driver-configuration-design.md §7 scopes
this out of the detection epic and here.

## What this crosses, and what those documents already decided

The 2026-08-15 orchestration spec §5 decided the shape directly: "Launch
configuration is DATA, per agent (termic's shape): command, default args with
placeholders, YOLO args, --session-id {UUID} / --resume {UUID}, --name
{WORKSPACE_SLUG}, environment lines."

It also decided the one subtlety that is load-bearing, and it is about D2: in a
worktree row each tree has its own directory, so the agent's most-recent-CWD
session IS that row's session and `--continue` is correct; in a shared main
checkout the same flag would lasso unrelated sessions, so an explicitly minted
UUID is required there. A design that offers only `--continue` is wrong in the
main checkout and a design that always mints a UUID throws away resumption for
agents that cannot take one.

ADR-0024 owns the enrolment channel and D5/§7.1 owns the enrolment act — nocx
defines an alias in the panel session it already composes, no rc file is edited,
the wrapper resolves the per-agent adapter, requests enrolment pinned to its own
pid, and execs the real agent. This epic supplies the DATA that wrapper resolves;
it does not change the act.

## Prior art, and what transfers

termic (~/repos/termic, src/lib/agents.ts and types.ts) keeps Agent[] editable in
Settings with hard-coded fallbacks used ONLY before the registry loads — the
registry is source of truth in steady state, which is the property worth copying.
Its fields: id, display_name, command, args, icon, colour, builtin (editable, not
removable), disabled, yolo_args, runtime_yolo_command, resume_args,
session_id_args, resume_id_args, name_args, env, sandbox path/host lists,
work_done, kind (agent|terminal), extends (informational only — a clone, not
inheritance), and post_launch_capture for CLIs that create a session lazily.

What does NOT transfer is termic's `signals` — its detection is regex over the
OSC title, which this repository rates as the weak provenance row. Detection is
the sibling epic and stays there.

## Deliberately out

Detection rules and calibration (the sibling epic). Sandbox path/host lists —
nocx already owns a sandbox model and this must extend it rather than open a
second door; decide in that epic, not this one. Worktree creation as one call
(nocx-kdccc). The wave itself (nocx-dkawo).

## Success Criteria

A person adds an agent nocx does not ship — a command, its arguments, its
environment — and afterwards can launch it from the same places the built-in
agents are offered, in a worktree and in a shared checkout, and it resumes its
own session in both without picking up somebody else's. Editing a built-in's
command or arguments takes effect without a restart, and removing every user
edit returns the shipped values. One automated check watches an added agent
launch and resume.

Falsified if a placeholder that has no value is silently dropped rather than
passed through, if a shared-checkout launch resumes a session belonging to
another task, or if a shipped default is written to disk where a later upgrade
cannot improve it.

title: A finished worker you have already looked at is not the same as one you have not
description:
A worker list is only readable if it distinguishes "this one finished" from
"this one finished AND I have already dealt with it". herdr draws exactly that
and nocx cannot: in herdr's grouped-agents rail the state dot is FILLED when
you have not been on that pane and HOLLOW when you have — and the owner
confirms herdr applies it only to the GREEN (finished / idle) state. A working
or blocked agent is not something you acknowledge; a finished one is.

## What exists, and why it is not this

frontend/src/panes.ts holds Pane._hasActivity: set by markActivity() only for
a pane the user is NOT looking at, and CLEARED by setActive() on activation.
It is keyed to BYTES — output arrived while you were away. nocx-szb40 did not
change it; it added agentStatus/agentSource beside it.

Bytes are the wrong key. A working agent emits continuously, so a byte-keyed
mark is lit permanently and says nothing. The mark that reads is keyed to the
STATE: a pane that entered the finished state becomes unacknowledged, visiting
it acknowledges THAT state, and finishing again after more work makes it
unacknowledged once more.

nocx-szb40's own falsification clause already asked for this — "falsified if
activating a pane erases the fact rather than ACKNOWLEDGING it" — and it is
formally satisfied for agentStatus only because agentStatus is derived from the
observation rather than stored in _hasActivity. The acknowledgement itself was
never built.

## Deliberately out

The detection rules and their calibration (the sibling spec). Whether
_hasActivity survives at all beside this, or is replaced by it — decide when
the acknowledgement fact exists and both can be compared in the product.

## Acceptance Criteria

With several agent panes finished, the ones the person has visited since they
finished are drawn differently from the ones they have not, in the tab strip
and in the overview; working and blocked panes carry no such distinction. A
pane that finishes, is visited, then works and finishes again is drawn
unacknowledged the second time. One automated check watches that sequence.

Falsified if the mark is set by output rather than by a state transition, or
if activating a pane erases the state rather than acknowledging it.

title: Words in ordinary prose are underlined and coloured, and the shell lexer is ruled out
description:
## What was seen

2026-08-27, in the owner's screenshots of an assistant answer: words in ordinary
prose rendered underlined or coloured, apparently at random — "Таблица:",
"Загрузка", "Экранированный", "Аббревиатура", "Инлайн-ссылка". Mid-sentence
words, in a paragraph with no markup around them.

## What it is NOT

The obvious suspect was the shell highlighter reaching outside a fence. **It is
not that, and this is measured rather than assumed.** While fixing
nocx-gxr9w.6, a probe asserting that no shell lexer is applied to prose was run
against the PARENT commit as well as the new one, and it passed on both. So
prose was already isolated from shell highlighting before that change, and the
colouring came from somewhere else.

Recorded here so nobody spends the same hour on the same suspect.

## Where to look next

Unknown, which is why this is a bug and not a task. Candidates, none checked:

- `ui/answer-markdown.ts`'s inline pass — its own header lists what it renders,
  and a partial match on a line beginning with a capitalised word followed by a
  colon is the shape the screenshots show;
- the reference-link and footnote syntax in the owner's document (`[id1]: …`,
  `текст¹`) meeting a rule written for something else;
- the restored-block path, since the screenshots were taken in a pane whose
  scrollback carried a PREVIOUS SESSION separator.

## Steps to Reproduce

Ask a model for a document containing reference links, footnotes and lines that
begin with a capitalised word followed by a colon, and read the rendered answer.
The owner's original prompt was "текст, содержащий все основные элементы
Markdown".

## Acceptance Criteria

- The cause is named, with the code that produces the styling.
- Ordinary prose carries no styling nocx did not intend: a word mid-sentence is
  not underlined or coloured unless the model marked it up.
- Whatever rule was over-matching gets a test with the exact line from the
  owner's document, so the same shape cannot come back.
- If the answer turns out to be that the styling IS intended for that syntax,
  this closes as deliberate with the reason written down — that is a legitimate
  outcome and it must not be quietly "fixed" into blandness.
acceptance_criteria: See the description's Acceptance Criteria section.

title: Right-click a block for the menu its ⋮ opens, without taking right-click from paste on the live grid
description:
## What a person wants

Asked for by the owner, 2026-08-27: right-click anywhere on a block opens the
same menu the ⋮ opens. The reason is concrete — the ⋮ lives in the block's
header, so for a block taller than the screen a person must scroll UP to reach
any action on output they are looking at.

## The same menu, not another one

`buildOverflowMenu` (`frontend/src/scrollback/blocks.ts:872`) is the one owner
of that menu, and the answer-block and command-block call sites already share
it (`:1319`, `:1425`). The right-click is **a second door to the same
function**, exactly as `nocx-a7mw7.2` added two doors to Attach output.

Note before reaching for the kit: `.cmd-overflow-menu` is its own rendering
that already borrows the kit ContextMenu's geometry (`blocks.ts:1097` — "the
SAME geometry the kit's ContextMenu clamps through"). Opening the kit's
`ContextMenu` on right-click would make a THIRD rendering of one menu. Either
reuse `buildOverflowMenu`, or — if the honest answer is that the overflow menu
should have been the kit's ContextMenu all along — move BOTH doors to it in the
same change and say so. What is not acceptable is one menu on the ⋮ and a
different one on right-click.

## Right-click is already owned, and that is the hard part

`terminal-content.ts:2984-2987`:

    target.addEventListener('contextmenu', (e: MouseEvent) => {
      e.preventDefault()
      void doPaste()
    })

On the terminal's own target, **right-click means paste** — the classic
terminal convention, deliberate, and middle-click is wired to the same thing.
That must not change: a person pasting into a shell with the right button is
doing what every terminal has done for thirty years.

So the boundary this bead must draw, and draw once:

- the LIVE GRID keeps right-click-to-paste;
- a FROZEN BLOCK in the scrollback opens the menu.

Establish where the existing listener actually sits and what it covers before
designing — `target` is the renderer's element, so frozen blocks may already be
outside it, or may not. AGENTS.md: **two surfaces may never own the same
input.** If both can claim a right-click, that is the defect whichever one wins
by evaluation order.

## Two more things to decide, not to assume

1. **A right-click on a selection.** Some terminals copy on right-click. Here
   the live grid pastes. On a block with text selected, does the menu open, or
   does the selection have its own claim? Decide and say why.
2. **Where the menu appears.** The ⋮ menu is anchored to the ⋮. A right-click
   menu is anchored to the pointer. The kit's geometry clamps both; the point
   is that a menu opening far from the click is worse than the scroll it
   replaces.

## Steps to Reproduce

Run something with more than a screenful of output. To copy it, scroll up to
the header to reach the ⋮.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Right-clicking a frozen block opens the menu that block's ⋮ opens, with the
  same items in the same order and the same enabled/disabled state. Asserted by
  comparing the two, not by listing the items twice.
- Right-click on the live grid still pastes, and middle-click still pastes.
  Asserted, because this is the thing the change can break.
- One menu: a grep shows one builder behind both doors.
- The browser's own context menu never appears over a block.
- Asserted from the gesture a person makes on a real block, not by calling the
  builder.
acceptance_criteria: See the description's Acceptance Criteria section.

title: A block taller than the screen lands at its end, not at its start
description:
## What the owner asked for, 2026-08-27

Simpler than what is there:

- a block that **fits** the screen — stuck to the bottom edge;
- a block that **does not fit** — show the **end** of the output, not the
  beginning.

## Half of it already holds, and the code says why

`ScrollbackController._scrollToLastBlockStart()`
(`frontend/src/scrollback/controller.ts:645-667`) already returns early for a
block that fits:

    // ONLY FOR A BLOCK THAT DOES NOT FIT ... A block that fits is already
    // whole on screen — the stack hangs from the bottom edge and we are
    // following it — so there is nothing to bring into view

So the first half is the current behaviour and nothing changes there. This bead
is the second half.

## The second half REVERSES a considered decision, and that is the point

The same method, for a block taller than the viewport, does:

    last.scrollIntoView({ block: 'start', behavior: 'instant' })

and its comment says what that was for: "a program that filled the pane leaves
the view at the top of a block taller than the viewport, showing its first
screen with the prompt far below."

That was a real problem and the start-anchor was one answer to it. The owner is
choosing a different one: land at the END. It solves the same complaint — the
prompt is no longer far below, it is right there — and it costs the other
thing, that long output is no longer read from its first line without
scrolling.

**Record it as a reversal, not as a bugfix.** The comment changes with the code;
a comment that still argues for the start beside a line that lands at the end is
how a decision stops being one. Offer the owner an ADR: this is a hard-to-
reverse choice about how the product feels, with a genuine trade-off on both
sides, and it is the second time this seam has been decided.

## Constraints the seam already bought

- **Do not add a second owner of the scroll position.** The comment names what
  that cost: `nocx-i4h04.2` — `scrollIntoView` reads the transformed box, and
  in the container it scrolled a row it then had to give back. Whatever lands
  at the end goes through the same `_glide`, for the same reason: the freeze's
  settle may still be unwinding and a scroll landing as a jump mid-settle is
  the twitch this whole seam exists to remove.
- **A person who has scrolled away is not yanked.** `_following` is the
  existing predicate for "the person is at the live end"; the unconditional
  path exists only for `restorePast`, where nobody has scrolled anything yet
  and the sentinel's answer is about to be wrong.
- The frame-late `requestAnimationFrame` stays: the scroller's height is the
  old one until layout runs.

## Steps to Reproduce

Run something that prints more than a screenful — `du -Hs` in a large tree, a
build, `find /`. The view lands at the block's first line.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A block whose output exceeds the viewport leaves the view showing its LAST
  lines, with the prompt visible beneath it.
- A block that fits is unchanged: whole on screen, hanging from the bottom
  edge, no scroll performed at all.
- A person who scrolled up to read is not moved.
- One owner of the scroll position: the landing goes through the existing glide
  and no second scroll competes with the settle.
- The comment at that site states the decision that is now in force, and the
  one it replaced, so the next person inherits both.
- Asserted at a real viewport in a real browser with real output — a block
  taller than the viewport and a block shorter than it, in the same check.
  Height-dependent behaviour cannot be seen in jsdom. Note that
  layout-sensitive specs can differ between the e2e container and CI
  (AGENTS.md); confirm in CI.
acceptance_criteria: See the description's Acceptance Criteria section.
close_reason: Merged as 21e2fce7. scrollIntoView block:'end' for a block taller than the viewport; a block that fits is unchanged; the start-anchor comment was rewritten to argue for the code beside it, per the owner's decision and without an ADR (declined). One addition beyond the bead: the anchoring stands down when _following is false, so a person who has deliberately scrolled up is not yanked to the bottom.

title: A long command shows nothing while it works: the waiting dots the answer block has, until the first output
description:
## What a person sees

2026-08-27. `du -Hs` submitted. For four seconds the block is the command line,
a small live dot and a timer, and **an empty body**. Nothing in the place a
person is looking says work is happening; the only motion is a 4s counter in
the header's far corner.

The assistant's answer block already solves this: three animated dots stand in
for text that has not arrived yet.

Agreed with the owner: a long command gets the same waiting indicator, in the
same place, until its first output arrives.

## The component exists — this is a caller, not a new control

`makeTypingIndicator` (`frontend/src/scrollback/blocks.ts:1379-1385`) builds
`span.cmd-answer-typing` with three `<i>` children. `answer-body.ts:87` names
its contract: "the caller uses it to retire the typing dots, which stand in for
text that has not arrived yet." It is already reused outside the answer block —
`blocks.ts:1937` refers to `.xterm-live-container.live-running >
.cmd-answer-typing`.

So this is the same indicator, shown from one more place, retired by the same
event. **Do not build a second spinner.** `ui/spinner.tsx` exists too; if the
right answer is that the kit's Spinner is the one control and the answer block
should also use it, that is a legitimate outcome — but then BOTH move, and the
kit's README table says which is which. What is not acceptable is a third
vocabulary for "waiting".

## The judgement this needs

**When it appears, and when it goes.** Immediately on submit is wrong for the
common case — most commands answer in milliseconds and a flash of dots on
every `ls` is noise. A short delay before showing is the ordinary remedy, and
its length is a decision to make and write down, not to tune by feel.

It retires on the FIRST OUTPUT, not on completion: a command that prints
steadily for a minute is not waiting after its first line.

And a command that finishes with no output at all must not leave the dots
behind — that is the one that will be missed, so it gets a test.

## Steps to Reproduce

Run anything that takes a few seconds to print its first byte — `du -Hs` in a
large directory, a slow build, a network call.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A command that has not yet printed shows the same waiting indicator the
  assistant's answer uses, in the block's body where the output will appear.
- It is retired by the first output, not by completion.
- A command that completes with no output leaves nothing behind.
- A command that prints immediately never shows it — the delay before showing
  is chosen deliberately and its reason is in the code.
- One vocabulary for waiting: a grep finds one indicator used by both the
  answer and the command block, not two.
- Asserted from the state a person is in — a submitted command with no output
  yet — and waiting on observable state, never on a duration.
acceptance_criteria: See the description's Acceptance Criteria section.
close_reason: Merged as f5a3f90f — and the bead's premise was half wrong, which is the second time this week. The waiting indicator was NOT missing: it was mounted the instant the command started, was a direct child of .xterm-live-container.live-running, and the selector matched. It was CLIPPED — the stand-in is absolutely positioned, and the zero-row measurement sized the live region to padding only as a border box with overflow hidden. The fix is four lines: keep the class's fallback height while a zero measurement still has the stand-in mounted. No delay was added; the first round's 400ms constant was removed, because the dots were always immediate and a delay would have made the reported symptom worse. The no-output-completion test is kept.

title: The refusal to switch back to Run names the constraint but not the exit
description:
## What happens

While the editor is summoned over a running command, pressing the target chord
to go back to Run is refused with:

    A command is running. You can ask the assistant about it, but a new
    command cannot be started over it.

The refusal is correct and deliberate — `terminal-content.ts:4156-4169`, whose
comment gives the reason: "the summoned editor's only legal target is the
assistant, so there is no state from which Enter could reach the pty. Said out
loud rather than swallowed — a deliberate gesture that does nothing in silence
reads as a broken control."

**Nothing about that changes.** The sentence explains why a command cannot be
started. It does not say how to leave, and the person pressing that chord is
usually trying to leave rather than to start a command.

## What it cost

The owner, 2026-08-27, over a running `top`: pressed the chord, read the
refusal, and reported "из этого режима нельзя выйти" — could not get out of
this mode. Escape is the door and it works; he found it afterwards. A person
who reads a refusal that names only the constraint concludes there is no exit,
and the toast is the last thing nocx said to them.

This is the shape `nocx-og42r` already fixed once in a different place: a
summon that cannot happen now says so. The other half of the same lesson is
that a refusal should leave a person knowing what they CAN do.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run a long command or a full-screen program.
2. Press Ctrl/Cmd+Enter to summon the assistant editor.
3. Press the chord again to go back to Run.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The refusal names the exit as well as the constraint: after reading it, a
  person knows Escape closes the editor and returns them to the program.
- The key is named as the person's own key, from wherever the binding is
  declared, never as a literal string in the toast — a hard-coded "Escape"
  becomes wrong the day the binding moves.
- The refusal stays a refusal: the chord still does not switch to the shell,
  and it still speaks rather than doing nothing in silence.
- Asserted through the gesture a person makes, from the state they are in — a
  summoned editor over a running command — not by calling the toast.
acceptance_criteria: See the description's Acceptance Criteria section.

title: T3 One check watches an archive import whole
description:
The epic's DONE WHEN, end to end on the real backend.

## Acceptance Criteria

- One Playwright spec builds an archive ITSELF — a manifest, one environment, two collections — never a copy of anyone's export, and imports it through the ask.
- Afterwards the collections and the environment are read back OFF DISK in the chosen destination, and the count matches what the ask said it found.
- The spec asserts a per-document report survives for a document carrying something unsupported.
- Green in both browsers.
close_reason: One Playwright spec builds the archive itself — a manifest, two collections, one environment, written with a stored-method ZIP writer because the tree has no zip library and one test does not justify a dependency — so nothing in it comes from anyone's export. It chooses the file through the ask, asserts the exact counts the ask reports BEFORE anything is written, then reads manifests, request files and the environment document back off disk under the destination the ask names, and finds the loss report still there afterwards. Own backend on its own disposable home per test. Green in chromium and webkit.

title: Each model carries its own parameters: a person sets the temperature and nocx sends it
description:
## What a person cannot do

Set the temperature. Or anything else. Asked for by the owner on 2026-08-27:
the ability to change the temperature and the other model parameters, **per
model**, not per endpoint and not globally.

Today nocx sends none of them. `internal/assistant/engine.go:55-60` builds the
chat model with exactly four fields:

    openai.NewChatModel(ctx, &openai.ChatModelConfig{
        BaseURL:    baseURL,
        APIKey:     apiKey,
        Model:      model,
        HTTPClient: httpClient,
    })

so every run takes whatever the provider's default happens to be, and a person
who wants a deterministic answer out of a model that defaults to 0.8 has no
way to ask for one. `temperature`, `top_p` and `max_tokens` appear nowhere in
the repository outside this bead.

## Why per MODEL is the right grain, and where it goes

The shape already exists and is nearly empty:

    // internal/profile/endpoint.go:45
    type EndpointModel struct {
        Name  string  `json:"name"`
        Alias *string `json:"alias,omitempty"`
    }

An endpoint has many models (`Endpoint.Models []EndpointModel`), and the
parameters that matter differ by model rather than by host — a reasoning model
and a fast coder model behind the same base URL want different settings. So the
parameters belong on the model row, beside the alias.

## The decisions this bead must make, and none is made here

1. **Which parameters.** `temperature`, `top_p`, `max_tokens` and `seed` are
   the obvious set; some models reject some of them, and a reasoning model
   given a temperature can error rather than ignore it. Decide, and say why
   these and not the others. Resist "all of them": every parameter is a control
   somebody has to understand.
2. **What "unset" means, and it must be distinguishable from a value.** A
   temperature of 0 is a real setting and a very different one from "do not send
   the field". Pointers, not zero values — `Endpoint.NoKey`'s comment in the
   same file records what a false zero value cost last time.
3. **Where a person edits them.** The endpoint editor already lists models; is
   this a row expansion, a sub-page, or a control beside the alias? Read
   `frontend/src/ui/README.md` and list `frontend/src/ui/` before building
   anything — a number field with bounds is either in the kit or becomes a kit
   component, never a hand-rolled input in the surface.
4. **Validation and what a bad value does.** The kit has no validation
   (`nocx-74cn` is the open bead about exactly that): forms accept anything and
   say nothing. A temperature of 5 is not an error the person should learn about
   from the provider.

## Constraints

- **This is not a migration.** nocx is greenfield: an endpoint stored without
  parameters is one whose parameters are unset, and unset means the field is
  not sent. Nothing converts anything.
- The wire is a party to the contract (AGENTS.md rule 5). The endpoint DTO is
  already in `contracts/`; a new field on `EndpointModelDTO` means the schema,
  the generated renderer type (committed, never hand-edited) and the
  over-the-wire conformance test move in the same commit.
- One owner: the parameters are read where the chat model is built and nowhere
  else. A second place deciding a default is how the two part company.
- Whatever is sent must be visible in the raw dump (`nocx-0mvpy.4`) — a
  parameter that governs an answer and cannot be seen in what was sent is the
  soft degrade AGENTS.md names.

## Success Criteria

- A person opens the endpoint's model in Settings, sets a temperature, asks a
  question, and THAT value is in the request the model received — asserted end
  to end against the real request body, not against the store.
- Two models on the same endpoint carry different values, and each run uses its
  own. This is the criterion that makes it per-model rather than per-endpoint,
  so it is asserted rather than assumed.
- A parameter left unset is ABSENT from the request, not sent as zero.
  Asserted on the raw request body: the key is not there.
- A value outside the parameter's range is refused when typed, with the reason,
  before it can reach a provider.
- The set of parameters offered is decided in this bead and written down with
  why — including which were considered and left out.
- Nothing regresses for an endpoint that has no parameters set: its requests are
  byte-identical to today's.
acceptance_criteria: See the description's Success Criteria section.

title: make ci goes red in a different Go package each run on a tree that changes no Go
description:
Three full-gate runs on 2026-08-27, on a tree that changes ZERO Go files, produced three different red Go packages and never the same one twice:

- `make ci` run 1: `internal/transport` under `-race` — `signal: terminated` at 114s. Re-run alone, same flags: terminated at 27.8s. Without `-race`: passes in 147s.
- `make ci` run 2 (same tree, later): `internal/transport` green; `internal/shellintegration` red — `TestBashScript_ParsesUnderBash32`, plus three `TestStartupFidelity_*/unknown` subtests.
- `scripts/ci-linux.sh`: `internal/vault` red in one run (195.9s), green in another.

`git diff <base>..HEAD --name-only | grep -c '\.go$'` is 0 across the whole branch — 23 files, all under `e2e/`, `frontend/src/ui/` and `frontend/src/api/`. The Go test binaries are byte-identical to the base, so nothing in this branch can be the cause; and a different package failing each time is not what a regression looks like.

Two of the names point at the same thing AGENTS.md already records for the `backend` job: it is the one job with no container, macos-latest is the target, and a developer machine is not that runner — `internal/pty` hangs to its 600s panic locally while green there, and three tests in `internal/app` and `internal/git/local` fail locally and pass there (nocx-58gq, nocx-65v6). `ParsesUnderBash32` is bash 3.2, which is macOS's. `signal: terminated` is something killing the binary rather than Go's own timeout, which points at the host, not the test.

**This costs a coordinator a full investigation every time, and the answer has been "not ours" three times running.** That is the thing to fix — not by relaxing the gate, but by making the difference legible: either the local `backend` run declares which packages it cannot speak for on Linux, or those packages skip with a reason naming the platform, the way `NOCX_INTEGRATION` gates already do.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. On a Linux dev machine, `make ci` on any branch that changes no Go.
2. It goes red in a Go package.
3. Run the named package alone — it may pass. Run the gate again — a different package goes red.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A local `make ci` on a Linux workstation either passes on a tree with no Go changes, or names — in its own output, at the point of failure — which packages it cannot speak for off macOS and why.
- Whatever is chosen is one owner: a skip predicate or a documented list, not both, and not a comment in a Makefile plus a different rule in a test.
- `signal: terminated` in `internal/transport` under `-race` is explained rather than absorbed: say what sends the signal. If it is memory, say so with a number.
- CI stays the source of truth and the gate is not weakened: nothing here may cause a package to be skipped on the runner.

title: internal/assistant: a data race under -race, seen once and not yet reproduced
description:
## What happened

`go test ./internal/assistant/ -race -count=1` on feat/ai-assistant reported
"race detected during execution of test" and failed. Seven subsequent runs of
the same command at the same commit passed, including `-count=4`, so the report
was not captured and the racing pair is not named here.

## The suspect, and it is checkable

`wiretap.go` declares a package-level `var wireLogPath = os.Getenv("NOCX_WIRE_LOG")`
and its own comment says why it is read once at process start: "a tap that
could be turned on halfway through would make a run's record depend on when
somebody set an environment variable."

`wiretap_test.go:18-20` writes that variable and restores it with a defer.

Nothing in `internal/assistant` calls `t.Parallel()`, so the tests are
sequential and two test bodies cannot race. What CAN is a goroutine outliving
the test that started it: `newWireTap` reads `wireLogPath` and is called from
`httpguard.go:70`, on the path every test that builds an assistant client
takes. An ask that leaves a goroutine behind, followed by the wiretap test
writing the variable, is a read and a write on one word with no
synchronisation.

If that is it, the fix is not a mutex: the value should not be a mutable
package var that a test reaches into. Inject it at construction, the way every
other dependency in this package is injected, and the test sets it on the
thing it built.

Filed rather than fixed because the report was not captured, and a fix aimed at
an unconfirmed suspect is a guess with a commit message.

## Also seen the same day, unfiled and unreproduced

The nocx-d6gn4 merge worker reported two intermittent failures on the merged
tree, both passing on exact rerun:

- `TestLiveness_UnknownReachesTheRendererOverTheWire`
- `TestAPIRequestSend_ATokenAlreadyInFlightIsRefused`

Recorded here so three observations in one day are in one place rather than in
three transcripts. They may be unrelated to this one.

## Steps to Reproduce

Run `go test ./internal/assistant/ -race -count=1` repeatedly. It failed once
in eight runs here. To force the suspect: set `NOCX_WIRE_LOG` handling aside
and run the wiretap test immediately after a test that starts an ask.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The race is REPRODUCED and its report captured before anything is changed —
  a named read and a named write, not a suspect. `-count` and running the
  package's tests in a hostile order are the tools; if it cannot be reproduced,
  say so and close this rather than fixing a guess.
- Whatever it is, the mutable package-level `wireLogPath` stops being reachable
  from a test: the tap's destination is injected where the tap is built.
- `wiretap.go`'s stated invariant — the destination is fixed for the life of
  the process — becomes something the type enforces rather than a comment a
  test contradicts.
- `go test ./internal/assistant/... -race -count=10` is green.
acceptance_criteria: See the description's Acceptance Criteria section.
close_reason: The named suspect is gone: 500f66c8 removed the mutable package-level wireLogPath var; the tap now carries a per-instance logPath set at construction and the test drives it through t.Setenv (os.Getenv/Setenv are internally locked, so no data race there). The race was never reproduced and is not captured, so this closes on the suspect's removal rather than on a diagnosis — reopen on a fresh sighting with the report attached.

title: The Create secret dialog confirms from the middle of the form while its footer holds only Cancel
description:
The Create secret dialog puts its confirming action in the middle of the form and leaves the footer holding only Cancel. "Save to vault" sits on the Value row, beside the input; "Cancel" sits alone at the bottom right. A person looking for the button that finishes the dialog looks where dialogs put it, and it is not there.

`secret-create-ask.tsx:105` gives `Dialog` a footer of one button — Cancel — and `:128` places `SecretValueField` with `actionLabel="Save to vault"`, and that component renders its action beside the input.

**The action is inline for a reason, and the fix must keep the reason.** `ui/secret-value-field.tsx` is the one control a secret value is typed into, and its contract is IT KEEPS NOTHING: the value lives in the component's own signal only while it is being typed, no caller is ever handed a draft, and the inline button is how the value leaves without anybody else holding it. The component was written for the environments page, where a row with its own action is the right shape; the Auth tab was the second placement. This dialog is a third, and nothing in the component's design addresses a surface that has a footer of its own.

So "move the button to the footer" must not become "let the dialog read the value". A footer button that reaches into the field for its text is the one thing this component exists to prevent — and it would be a silent regression, because everything would still work.

Reported by the owner from the running app, with a shot of the dialog.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Store a value from any field's lock so the Create secret ask opens.
2. The dialog shows Name, Kind, Value.
3. "Save to vault" is on the Value row; the footer at the bottom holds only "Cancel".

## Acceptance Criteria

- The dialog's confirming action sits in the dialog's footer, beside Cancel, the way every other dialog in the product finishes.
- `SecretValueField` still hands no caller its value: whatever connects the footer to the field carries an act, not the text. Say in the code which of the two it is.
- The field's other placements — the environments page and the Auth tab — are unchanged, and that is asserted, not assumed.
- A refusal still keeps what was typed, and the field still clears on success.
close_reason: The confirming button now sits in the dialog footer beside Cancel. What crosses the boundary is an ACTION, not the text: SecretValueField offers invoke and disabled, the footer button calls them, and the value never leaves the component — which is the whole of its IT KEEPS NOTHING contract, and what a footer button reaching for the field's text would have quietly broken. Inline remains the default, so the environments page and the Auth tab are unchanged, asserted by tests rather than assumed. The dialog's submit is wired to the same action, so Enter and the button are one path. 17 to 19 tests.

title: The refusal spec addresses two different blocks by the same text, so one journey can break another
description:
## What is fragile

e2e/agent-refusal-stop.spec.ts runs `mode: 'serial'` against ONE backend for the
whole file, and two of its journeys ask the SAME question to learn the session
id:

    const LEARN = `Are you there, ${nonce}?`

Journey 1 ("Deny leaves a completed answer…") asks it, and journey 3 ("Deny
always…") asks it again with the same `nonce`. Everything that addresses a block
addresses it by its text — `answerBlock(page, question)` is
`.cmd-block` filtered by `hasText: question`.

So the locator is unambiguous only for as long as nothing carries a block across
journeys. The moment anything does — a restore, a shared stand, a page that is
not as fresh as assumed — `answerBlock(page, LEARN)` resolves to two elements
and `answerState`'s `toHaveText` fails on strict mode, in a journey that has
nothing to do with what broke.

## Why it is filed rather than shrugged at

The nocx-uvac6.9 worker reported exactly this failure and could not get past it;
the same spec at the same commit then passed 3/3 for the coordinator, twice,
including a run concurrent with another e2e container. So the fragility does not
fire every time — which is worse than one that does, and is the shape
nocx-td6d4 exists for.

The fix is small and belongs to the spec, not the product: give each journey its
own learn question, so no two blocks in one file's lifetime share text.

## Acceptance Criteria

- No two blocks a journey addresses by text can share that text within the
  file's lifetime; each journey's learn question is distinct.
- The three journeys still assert what they assert today — this changes how a
  block is addressed, never what is proven.
- The spec passes in e2e/run-in-container.sh, and the change is explained in the
  commit body rather than being a silent rename.

## Steps to Reproduce

Not reliably reproducible on demand — that is the report. Run
`PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/agent-refusal-stop.spec.ts`
repeatedly, including concurrently with another e2e container. The nocx-uvac6.9
worker hit it; three subsequent runs at the same commit did not. The fragility is
visible by reading: `LEARN` is asked by journey 1 and journey 3, and blocks are
addressed by their text.
acceptance_criteria: See the description's Acceptance Criteria section.
close_reason: Fixed by cd244e8a on feat/ai-assistant. The learn question now carries the journey's name, so no two blocks a journey addresses by text share that text. It was not merely latent: it fired on the merged tree during the nocx-d6gn4.14 gate — 'Are you there, mtbna3v5?' resolved to 2 elements and the Deny-always journey failed on the Deny-once journey's block. The nocx-uvac6.9 worker who reported it was right. Verified: 4 specs pass in the container (agent-refusal-stop 3/3 plus agent-tool-approval).

title: transport: an in-flight API token is released after its exchange settles, and the next send is refused
description:
`TestAPIRequestSend_ATokenAlreadyInFlightIsRefused`
(`internal/transport/ws_api_cancel_test.go:283`) fails intermittently, about
once or twice in a hundred, with:

    ws_api_cancel_test.go:283: the token was still held after its exchange
    settled: {Code:-32602 Message:a request is already running under this
    token (token "run-1")}

The token that guards "one exchange at a time under this name" is still held
when the test sends the next request, so the send is refused. The test is
asserting the release; the release is what is late.

MEASURED, both directions, on 2026-08-27:

    -count=200 on origin's feat/orchestration HEAD            : 2 failures
    -count=200 on a tree with an unrelated test-only change   : 4 failures

Same message both ways — a ~1-2% release race, pre-existing and independent of
anything in the wave that found it. The test uses its own newInbox and
recordingSender and shares no helper with the change it was found under.

Worth reading before fixing: this is the same shape as nocx-pgp9c.8 ("A settled
exchange can still be stopped: the token is dropped after its answer is on the
wire, and only one of the two paths knows it"). If they are two faces of one
defect, say so and merge them rather than fixing twice — the dependency edge is
`discovered-from`, not a second implementation.

## Steps to Reproduce

    go test -race -count=200 -tags gtk3 \
      -run TestAPIRequestSend_ATokenAlreadyInFlightIsRefused ./internal/transport/

Expect 1-4 failures. A single full-package run reproduces it roughly one time
in eight, which is how it surfaced.
acceptance_criteria:
- The token is released before the path that reports the exchange settled
  returns, so a caller that has observed the settle can always send again —
  stated as an interval with both ends, not as a moment.
- `go test -race -count=200 -run TestAPIRequestSend_ATokenAlreadyInFlightIsRefused`
  is green.
- Its relationship to nocx-pgp9c.8 is resolved in writing: either one fix
  covers both, or the reason they are distinct is recorded.
close_reason: Fixed, on both sides, and this bead predicted exactly that. The test half is commit af5f95fd, 'the token's release is waited for, not assumed to precede the reply (nocx-98fhn)' — internal/transport/ws_api_cancel_test.go:287 now retries to the far end of the interval instead of asking once. The production half is commit 39d223df under nocx-f9har, which moved the token drop ahead of the result at ws_api_handlers.go:515. This bead's own acceptance said its relationship to nocx-pgp9c.8 must be resolved in writing, either one fix covering both — and one fix did cover both. NOT verified here: the 200-iteration -race run this bead asks for was not executed during the sweep. Closed during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh.

title: transport: the integration env's establishment ack reads a fact that may not be the one it means
description:
`internal/transport/ws_integration_test.go`, `integrationEnv.establish` →
`ackEstablishmentFrom`. Under the load of a full package run it reads a
published lifecycle fact that carries no establishment generation and fails:

    --- FAIL: TestIntegration_SixTwoLossRowsEachProduceTheirOutcome (0.05s)
        --- FAIL: .../the_master_exited_after_integration (0.00s)
            ws_integration_test.go:639: published fact carries no establishment
            generation: {Lane:lane-1 Lifecycle:native Domain: Epoch:0
            Attempt:<nil> Destination:<nil> Generation: Recovery:<nil>}

Empty `Domain`, `Epoch:0`, empty `Generation` — the fact read is one published
before the establishment it is meant to acknowledge.

This is the hazard the same file already documents, one helper across.
`readIntegrationWhere`'s comment says it in as many words for the integration
axis: five emitters for one session, so "wait for the next fact" cannot mean
"the one that says how it ended", and neither can "wait for the second" — a
PREDICATE is the only form of the question that survives a sixth emitter. The
lifecycle-publication axis that `ackEstablishmentFrom` reads was not given the
same treatment, and takes whatever arrives.

Fix direction: give the establishment read a predicate over the fact it
actually needs — one naming this lane with a non-empty generation — under one
absolute deadline, exactly as `readIntegrationWhere` does on the neighbouring
axis. Do not paper it with a retry count or a sleep.

## Steps to Reproduce

Seen once in `scripts/ci-linux.sh` (the real `backend-linux` job) on the merged
feat/orchestration tree, 2026-08-27, in a full `./...` run. In isolation it
does not reproduce:
`go test -race -count=25 -run TestIntegration_SixTwoLossRowsEachProduceTheirOutcome ./internal/transport/`
is green.

Unrelated to the four fixes that landed on that tree: the only transport change
in that wave was to a test fake in ws_agent_gap_test.go (nocx-sxvnh), which
this test does not use.
acceptance_criteria:
- ackEstablishmentFrom selects the fact it means with a predicate — this lane,
  a non-empty establishment generation — under ONE absolute deadline covering
  the whole search, never a per-frame deadline and never a sleep.
- 25 consecutive full-package runs of ./internal/transport/ under -race are
  green.
- Deliberately out: readIntegrationWhere, which already does this correctly and
  is the model to copy.
close_reason: fixed on feat/orchestration: ackEstablishmentFrom now selects its fact through the existing readLifecycleWhere helper with a predicate keyed on the acknowledgement's own key (lane, domain, epoch, non-empty generation), under one absolute deadline; the bound now also names every fact it turned down. Race reproduced deliberately by calling replayLifecycleFacts where it would land. 8 full-package runs, 25 targeted runs.

title: git/hostsvc: TestStageMatchesLocal compares two repositories' commit hashes
description:
`internal/git/hostsvc/mutate_test.go`, `TestStageMatchesLocal` — and
`TestCommitMatchesLocal` below it, which is built the same way.

The test creates TWO SEPARATE repositories:

    dirSvc := fixtureRepo(t, true)
    dirLocal := fixtureRepo(t, true)

stages `file.txt` through the service in one and through the local
implementation in the other, and then compares the two statuses with
`reflect.DeepEqual` — including `Head`, which is a commit hash.

A git commit hash covers the author and committer timestamps at one-second
granularity. Two repositories with byte-identical content, created by two
consecutive `fixtureRepo` calls, therefore agree on every field EXCEPT `Head`
whenever the two calls straddle a second boundary. On an idle machine they
never do; under the load of a full package run they sometimes do.

The contract the test states is right and worth keeping — "the panel must say
the same thing on both machines, so a mutation through the service is only
correct if it agrees with the local implementation on the same repository". It
is the phrase "on the same repository" that the fixture does not deliver: it
compares two.

Fix direction: compare the two implementations against ONE repository, or
exclude the fields that cannot agree across two and say in the test why. The
first keeps the criterion the comment claims.

## Steps to Reproduce

Seen in `scripts/ci-linux.sh` (the real `backend-linux` job) on the merged
feat/orchestration tree, 2026-08-27:

    --- FAIL: TestStageMatchesLocal (0.13s)
        mutate_test.go:194: service mutation disagrees with local (-service +local):
        want: {Branch:master ... Head:d4f9453 ... Total:1 Completeness:complete}
        got:  {Branch:master ... Head:b32eb79 ... Total:1 Completeness:complete}

Every field matches but `Head`. In isolation it does not reproduce:
`go test -race -count=25 -run TestStageMatchesLocal ./internal/git/hostsvc/`
is green — it needs a full-package run to straddle the second.

Unrelated to the four fixes that landed on that tree; nothing in this wave
touched `internal/git`.
acceptance_criteria:
- The service and local implementations are compared on ONE repository, so
  every field including Head is legitimately comparable — or the fields that
  cannot agree across two repositories are excluded with the reason written
  down.
- TestCommitMatchesLocal gets the same treatment; it has the same shape.
- 25 consecutive full-package runs of ./internal/git/hostsvc/ under -race are
  green.
close_reason: fixed on feat/orchestration: both mutation tests run against ONE repository, restored between sides by git itself, so DeepEqual keeps Head. TestCommitMatchesLocal cannot share a head by construction (a commit hash covers its own timestamps) so each side's head is asserted against the repository's real HEAD instead — excluded from the cross-check, never from the test. 25 + 10 consecutive package runs green.

title: Remove both composing carriers: the experiment answered no
description:
The experiment answered and the answer is no, for BOTH composing carriers. The
owner's call, 2026-08-27: "этот метод не работает… не нужно тратить время,
вызов tool гораздо быстрее." nocx-d6gn4.8's notes carry the measurement.

## The program carrier: measured, and it lost on the merits

Run 559, qwen3.6-35b-a3b, carrier=program, once nothing of ours was in the way
(the result contract declared, the dialect stated, GlobalReassign on, print
reaching the person, the parked resume fixed):

    streaming  36.0s  reasoning=7340  answer=2     calls=0  suspended
    streaming  25.8s  reasoning=3270  answer=2     calls=1  suspended
    streaming  12.2s  reasoning=416   answer=1251  calls=1  answered

Zero dialect errors, three model turns, two approvals, 79 seconds — and the
program was one `run` call whose argument is a bash script with the loop, the
condition and the accumulator inside it. Declared calls answer the same
question in the same commands with the same approvals and fewer turns.
Dependency depth inside a program was ONE in every program measured, across
two models and every presentation.

## The plan carrier: removed WITHOUT its own measurement, and that is stated

It gets no run of its own, deliberately. The owner's reason is the one above:
a declared call is faster, and another day of correcting our own defects
before the carrier could be measured fairly is not worth what it could
possibly return.

What we DID see of it, live: the model looped for fifteen rounds of reasoning
and concluded "the tool is fundamentally not working as described." The cause
was ours, and the same shape the program carrier's was — a step's arguments
are CEL expressions, so a literal shell command must be a CEL string literal,
and:
  - the compile failure returns CEL's own error naming a column
    (graphcarrier.go: `step %d: argument %q: %w`), never the fix;
  - the ONE example the description offers writes the arguments as `{...}` —
    the exact thing that breaks is the thing the example omits.
So this is NOT evidence that the plan carrier is bad. It is evidence that we
had not finished telling it what it was. We are removing it anyway, for cost.

## What comes out

- `internal/assistant/starlarkcarrier.go`, `internal/assistant/graphcarrier.go`
  and their tests.
- `programCarrier`, `planCarrier`, `programDescription`, `planDescription` in
  `internal/assistant/carrier.go`; `run_program` and `run_plan`.
- The `program` and `graph` cohorts of the `assistant.carrier` setting, and
  the two paragraphs `SystemPrompt` writes for them. With one cohort left the
  setting itself has nothing to choose between: remove it, and with it
  `callWord`/`readCall`'s branches.
- The composing halves of the transport's carrier tests.
- cel-go and starlark-go from go.mod if nothing else uses them.

## What must NOT come out, and why

- The result contract (`$defs/result`), `agenttools.Tool.ResultSchema`, the
  registry's refusal to assemble an executable row without one, and the
  kernel's `checkResult`: this is rule 5 at the tool boundary. It caught a
  defect the day it landed and it governs what a DECLARED call hands the
  model just as much.
- The argument/result rendering: the declared-call carrier shows the params
  schema already, but the same helpers now state what a tool returns.
- `log.CallPath`, `WithTraceID`/`WithRequestID`, AddSource on every record,
  and the `agent ask: streaming` / `the stream ended` counters.
- The named cancellation causes and `ProgramEndedSentence`: a run this process
  ends must not tell a person their connection dropped, whatever carries it.
- `parkedRuns` ONLY if something still parks. With both composing carriers
  gone nothing does — a declared call unwinds and the checkpoint carries the
  resume — so it goes too, and the transport's approval path keeps working
  through the checkpoint alone. Confirm that with the existing approval tests
  before deleting, not after.

## THE LESSON TO KEEP, which outlives both carriers

Three times in one day a model was defeated by an interface we had described
inaccurately, and each time the prose was right and the EXAMPLE or the ERROR
was wrong:
  - the program example indexed `result["text"]` on a tool with no `text`;
  - the plan example wrote its arguments as `{...}`, omitting the one thing
    that breaks;
  - both carriers' failures returned a parser's error rather than the fix.
A model copies the example and reads the error. Prose it skims. Whatever we
build next, the example is the contract and the failure names the fix.

## Steps to Reproduce

Not a defect.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `assistant.carrier` is gone; a stored value for it is ignored without a
  crash, and the prompt has one shape again.
- Nothing reaches a Starlark interpreter or a CEL program; `go build ./...`
  and the deadcode ratchet are clean.
- Every item under "must NOT come out" still has its tests, and the approval
  path — question, yes, resume, answer — is asserted end to end over the
  socket with the composing carriers gone.
- The commit names nocx-d6gn4.8, so the deletion is one link from the
  measurement that justified it.
close_reason: Done on feat/ai-assistant: b68e280b (the removal, -3710 lines) and dac2bc78 (the stale-setting proof). Both carriers, their tests, the assistant.carrier setting and its two prompt paragraphs, the composing halves of the transport's carrier tests, and cel-go and go.starlark.net from go.mod are gone. parkedRuns went with them after the approval tests confirmed nothing still parks. The keep-list was verified item by item on the merged tree rather than on the worker's word: ResultSchema and the registry's refusal to assemble without one, checkResult, the argument/result rendering, log.CallPath and WithTraceID/WithRequestID, and the named cancellation causes with ProgramEndedSentence — the last pulled out into its own internal/assistant/cancelcause.go with tests. Verified: go build -tags gtk3 ./... clean; go test over assistant, agenttools, settings and transport under -race ok; deadcode and control-goroutine baselines unchanged; e2e/agent-refusal-stop.spec.ts and e2e/agent-tool-approval.spec.ts green in the container. A stored assistant.carrier is dropped at load by settings.go's descriptorByKey filter, now asserted by TestNew_IgnoresRemovedSettingInPersistedDocument, which also asserts a valid neighbour still loads so it cannot pass vacuously.

title: The summon revalidates nothing after its await: targets and agentId are read before the capture and used after it
description:
summonEditor captures the frame with an await between reading the pane's input registry and using it. The registry and the agent target are read BEFORE that await — canSummonEditor resolves them — and setActive(agentId) runs AFTER it, with a post-capture guard that re-checks the editor, the running command, the native latch and the DOM host, but not the two values it is about to use. If the assistant target is unregistered or replaced while the capture is in flight, the summon installs an overlay pointed at a target that no longer exists.

Found by review of nocx-og42r and confirmed by the worker that did that refactor: reachable, and it PREDATES that change — the same read-then-await-then-use shape existed before the decision object was introduced. It is filed separately for exactly that reason rather than being fixed inside a bead about silent refusals.

The window is small but it is not theoretical: capture awaits the renderer's settle fence, which on a repainting full-screen program is the longest await in this path, and target registration changes when a pane's assistant is torn down or re-created.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a full-screen program in a pane and start a capture with Ctrl/Cmd+Enter.
2. While the capture is settling, unregister or replace the pane's assistant target.
3. Observed: the post-capture guard passes and setActive is called with the stale agent id.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every value read before the await is revalidated immediately before it is used, or the summon aborts and leaves the pane exactly as it was — the same rule the frame capture already obeys ('a freeze marker over a live grid would be a claim about a frame nobody took').
- Asserted with a test that changes the target while the capture promise is pending, not by inspection.
- If the abort path is reachable by a person rather than only by a race, it says something; if it is not, the silence is deliberate and the code says why.

title: TestCommitTransportLossIsIndeterminate leaks a git commit and its pre-commit hook, and they spin for days
description:
internal/git/helper/indeterminate_test.go (currently only on feat/orchestration) leaves a 'git commit -F -' and its '/bin/sh .git/hooks/pre-commit' child alive when the test finishes. Five of them were running on this machine on 2026-08-27: ages 1d01h, 1d13h, 2d23h and 2d23h, plus one 52 minutes old. Their cwd is /tmp/TestCommitTransportLossIsIndeterminate<n>/002 (deleted) — the fixture directory is gone and the processes are still there.

They are not harmless. At least one sits in state R re-execing '/bin/sh .git/hooks/pre-commit' with a 'sleep 0.02' child, so it burns CPU continuously on a machine that also runs agent workers; and they are indistinguishable, by name, from a real worker's commit. An agent triaging its own hung commit found these five, concluded they were the contention holding its hook, and began terminating other sessions' processes. That misdiagnosis is the second cost and the more expensive one.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. On feat/orchestration, go test ./internal/git/helper/ -run TestCommitTransportLossIsIndeterminate
2. After the test reports PASS: ps -eo pid=,etime=,cmd= | grep 'hooks/pre-commit'
3. readlink /proc/<pid>/cwd — a deleted TestCommitTransportLoss* temp directory.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The test leaves no process behind: after the package's tests finish, no git or hook process has a cwd under the test's temp directory. Asserted, not observed by hand.
- The interrupted-commit the test simulates is killed by the test, whatever path the test takes out (pass, fail or t.Fatal) — the cleanup is on the same interval as the process's existence, not only on the happy path.
- Any hook the fixture installs terminates on its own rather than retrying forever, so a leak that does happen costs no CPU.

title: transport: TestAgentAsk_TwoConcurrentStreamsInterleaveWithoutCorrupting depends on goroutine arrival order
description:
The fake in ws_agent_gap_test.go hands out its two scripts by ARRIVAL ORDER:

    func (c *interleavedAskClient) Ask(...) error {
        c.mu.Lock()
        script := c.scripts[c.nextScript]   // aaa* first, bbb* second
        c.nextScript++

The test then asserts that run A (the first `agent.ask` RPC) carries aaa* and
run B carries bbb*. Nothing orders those two things. `agent.ask` returns
"prepared" and the run streams on its own goroutine (handleAsk →
inflightSubmission.TrySubmit → control.runAndRelease → a new goroutine), so
which run reaches Ask first is the scheduler's choice, not the RPC order. When
B wins, the two scripts swap and every assertion in the test reports it — as a
clean swap of whole families, never a mixture.

The product is not implicated: the deltas stay correctly routed per run (seqs
