title: The switch, its cohorts, and the rule that ends the experiment
description:
The owner's proposal, and it is also the answer to the strongest procedural objection
raised in review: with both carriers declared at once, "which one the model reaches
for" measures tool-description salience, model bias and prompt wording — not fitness.
A setting gives controlled cohorts instead.

## Where it lives is a decision, not an assumption

There is no "Experimental" section today. Registered sections are Instructions and
Answers (group `assistant`), Interface, Clipboard and History (`application`), and
Test (`developer`) — see `RegisterSectionGroup` in internal/settings/settings.go.
Either add a section or put the switch under `developer`, and say which and why.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A person switches the method through the UI and the next question is answered by
  the chosen carrier. Asserted end to end, both directions.
- Cohorts are at least `calls` and `program`; a router that chooses by task shape is
  a third and is explicitly optional.
- The decision rule is WRITTEN BEFORE the switch ships: what evidence removes the
  program carrier, what evidence restricts the call carrier, by when, and what
  happens on a tie. If we cannot say what would remove it, it is not an experiment.
- The metrics are recorded rather than remembered: task completion, syntax or type
  failures before the first effect, effects per successful task, model round trips,
  approval prompts, policy denials, stale-precondition refusals, replays, elapsed
  time, tokens, and success broken down by model capability tier.
- One metric is named and rejected in the bead so it does not come back: "which one
  the model picks when both are offered".
notes:
=== THE KILL CRITERIA, WRITTEN BEFORE THE SWITCH SHIPS, 2026-08-26 ===

The bead already demanded a decision rule. This is it, and it is recorded now so it
cannot be softened later by whoever is invested in the outcome.

KILL nocx-d6gn4.4 through .8 if ANY of these holds:
  - the WEAKEST supported models' semantic PROGRAM success is materially below their
    declared-tool task success after one repair turn;
  - typical successful tasks have dependency depth near one or two;
  - approval counts under the program carrier exceed a tolerable bound (name the
    bound before measuring, not after);
  - typed handles (nocx-d6gn4.2) already remove most repeated context transfer without
    reducing task success.

NOT SUFFICIENT EVIDENCE TO KEEP IT, and each of these will be offered:
  - syntactic success alone;
  - an impressive demo on a frontier model;
  - reduced token count without equal task completion.

METRIC EXPLICITLY REJECTED, so it does not come back: "which carrier the model picks
when both are offered". With both declared at once that measures tool-description
salience, ordering and model bias, not fitness. The switch exists precisely to replace
it with controlled cohorts.

SETTINGS PLACEMENT - verified 2026-08-26, not assumed. Registered groups are assistant,
vault, application, developer; registered sections are Instructions and Answers
(assistant), Interface, Clipboard and History (application), Test (developer). The
string "experimental" appears nowhere in the backend or the frontend. RECOMMENDATION:
a new Experimental SECTION inside the existing developer GROUP, not a new group - the
group already means "not for everyday use", while a top-level Experimental group is a
promise about a whole class of features we do not intend to make. The bead still has to
state the choice and its reason.

ADR TIMING - owner's decision, 2026-08-26. The ADR for this whole question is written
FROM THE RESULT, not before it. Do not open one while the experiment is running: an
ADR written from intention would record the argument we happen to find convincing
today, and the point of .10 is that we do not yet know which way it goes. Closing this
bead is what makes the ADR due - it records what the measurements decided about the
carrier, and, whichever way that went, why declared tools remain the authority floor.

THE SWITCH SHIPPED 2026-08-26 (commit 1a6c8e1f), and this is what it is.

WHERE IT LIVES, decided as the bead demanded rather than assumed: a new Experimental
SECTION inside the existing developer GROUP. The group already means "not for everyday
use", a top-level Experimental group would be a promise about a class of features we do
not intend to make, and Test is where the test binaries declare fixtures - a shipped
setting there would be indistinguishable from one. Key assistant.carrier, default calls,
options calls / program / graph. The option ids ARE assistant.CarrierKind's values, so a
run's recorded method and the control that chose it cannot drift.

THE SEAM IS AN INTERFACE, not a switch in Ask (AD-8). The variance is exactly two facts
- the tool set the model is offered, and what one invocation does - and both belong to
the carrier; a fourth carrier is a fourth implementation and no edit to Ask. What does
NOT vary is the effect kernel: one owner of validation, policy, the attempt record, the
narrowed capability, execution and egress screening, for all three. A carrier is another
way to compose work, never a way round the gate, and there is a test for that per
carrier.

READ PER ASK, not at connection time. A value captured when the socket opened would make
"switch the method and ask again" mean "switch, reconnect, and ask again", which is not
a switch anyone can use to compare two methods in one sitting.

AN UNKNOWN CARRIER IS AN ERROR naming the value, never a quiet fall back to the shipped
one - a run recorded as one method and executed as another makes every measurement here
unattributable. Bounded at both ends: the settings declaration refuses to store one, and
the engine refuses to drive one.

STILL OPEN on this bead, and it is the larger half: the METRICS. Criterion 4 lists what
must be recorded rather than remembered - completion, syntax/type failures before the
first effect, effects per successful task, model round trips, approval prompts, policy
denials, stale-precondition refusals, replays, elapsed time, tokens, success by model
capability tier. None of that is recorded yet. The cohorts exist; the instrument does
not. The kill criteria are already written above, before any of it, which is the part
that cannot be added later.
=== THE EXPERIMENT'S ANSWER, 2026-08-27: THE PROGRAM CARRIER DOES NOT PAY ===

The owner's call, on the run below: "этот метод не работает."

MEASURED THREE WAYS, and the first two turned out to be measuring us rather
than the carrier. That is why the third one counts.

1. FIRST-SHOT PROBE, off the live endpoint, no nocx in the loop: the same
   system prompt and run_program declaration the backend sends, lifted from
   the wire log, one question per request, and whatever `source` came back.
   Four cross-tool tasks (the value the chain needs is produced by nocx — an
   item id, an exit code, a line count — and lives nowhere a shell pipeline
   can reach), three samples each.

     declared calls                     12/12 a valid call
     program carrier, description as shipped   1/12
     program carrier, description made truthful 9/12, and 0/12 chained
     code as the assistant's own content        0/12 — the model wrote a
       <tool_call> XML envelope BY HAND when no tools were declared

   All of it on tiel-coder-35b-a3b, which LM Studio reports as
   trained_for_tool_use=false. That invalidates it as evidence about the
   carrier: the one model we had been measuring cannot use a tool-call
   protocol at all, and every "the model refuses the envelope" result was
   that. On qwen3.6-35b-a3b (tool-trained) the SAME shipped carrier gave
   12/12 real programs and 4/12 with two different tools.

2. WHAT THE FIRST TWO MEASUREMENTS ACTUALLY FOUND — our own defects, each
   fixed and each worth keeping whatever happens to the carrier:
     - the parked program resumed through the kernel of the ask that PARKED
       it, whose sink writes through a dead context, so every approval killed
       the run with "the connection was lost" (nocx-d6gn4.8.1);
     - a tool never declared what it RETURNS, so a program indexed the dict
       blind: a live model guessed "output", then "stdout", then answered
       with the whole dict, and the worked example taught result["text"] from
       session.list, which has no text;
     - the arguments were printed as "(...)", three literal dots;
     - GlobalReassign was off, so a top-level loop that reused a name failed:
       ten consecutive programs died on it in one live run;
     - print went to the model rather than the person, against 40 measured
       programs in which 40% printed for the reader and 20% said nothing at
       all;
     - the dialect named one difference from Python and left the rest to be
       guessed; a reasoning trace shows the model starting `import
       subprocess`, stopping itself, and asking whether it was writing a
       shell script.

3. THE RUN THAT DECIDES IT, once none of that was in the way — run 559,
   qwen3.6, carrier=program, "which text file here is biggest, show its first
   ten lines":

     streaming  36.0s  reasoning=7340  answer=2     calls=0  suspended
     streaming  25.8s  reasoning=3270  answer=2     calls=1  suspended
     streaming  12.2s  reasoning=416   answer=1251  calls=1  answered

   Zero dialect errors. Three model turns, two approvals, 79 seconds — and
   the program it wrote was one `run` call whose argument is a bash script:

     result = run(sessionId="…", command="""
     largest=""
     max_size=0
     for f in *; do …
     """)

   The loop, the condition and the accumulator are in the shell. The Starlark
   program is an envelope around one command.

THE VERDICT against the rule written before the switch shipped: criterion 2,
"typical successful tasks have dependency depth near one or two", is met — it
is ONE, in every program measured across both models and every arm, including
the runs that worked. Declared calls answer the same question in the same
number of commands with the same number of approvals and fewer turns. The
carrier costs a language between the model and the shell and buys nothing.

NOT CLAIMED, deliberately: that no model could use it (qwen composed a
two-tool chain and a loop of reads when the framing was out of the way), and
that a code-native presentation could not do better (the one arm that tested
it ran on the non-tool-trained model and is void). What IS claimed is what
the rule asks: on the models this product supports, for the work a terminal
actually does, the shell is already the composition language and the carrier
does not pay for itself.

WHAT SURVIVES: everything in (2). The result contract, the kernel's check on
it, the description built from the schemas, the named cancellation causes,
the source and trace on every log line, and the parked-run fix are about the
declared-call carrier and the ledger just as much, and several of them found
defects the day they landed.
close_reason: The experiment ran and answered. The switch shipped 2026-08-26 (1a6c8e1f) as an Experimental section inside the developer group, key assistant.carrier, cohorts calls/program/graph, the option ids being CarrierKind's own values so a run's recorded method and the control that chose it could not drift. The kill criteria were written BEFORE it shipped and are in this bead's notes; the measurement that met them is there too — run 559, qwen3.6-35b-a3b, carrier=program, with nothing of ours left in the way: three model turns, two approvals, 79 seconds, zero dialect errors, and the program was one run call whose argument is a bash script with the loop, the condition and the accumulator inside it. Dependency depth inside a program was ONE in every program measured, across two models and every presentation. Declared calls answer the same question in the same commands with the same approvals and fewer turns. The owner's call, 2026-08-27: the method does not work, a declared call is faster. Removal is nocx-d6gn4.14. Per this bead's own notes, closing it makes the ADR due — written FROM the result, recording what the measurement decided and why declared tools remain the authority floor.

title: What an approval can honestly say about a program whose end it cannot see
description:
Under data-dependent control flow the host only ever holds the CURRENT resolved
effect plus whatever the source statically bounds. It cannot show the future
arguments because they do not exist yet. So the honest sentence is not "approve this
program" but something closer to:

  This program is asking to <X>. Its source permits up to N further calls of classes
  A and B, within scopes S, and their arguments are not known yet.

That is worth having and it is materially weaker than it sounds when someone says
"the person approves the program". Say the weaker thing.

## Also

Prompt fatigue is a safety failure, not a UX complaint: ask forty times and a person
approves mechanically or widens the policy to something dangerous. The remedy is a
bounded envelope — program digest, resource families, budgets — and NOT a mutable
grant. ADR-0028 already has the mechanism: approval mints a new attempt carrying a
new immutable grant.

And the surface must distinguish claims a person will otherwise conflate:
well-formed, authorized, bounded, executed, successful, semantically correct. A
deterministic executor lends an unsafe plan an aura it has not earned.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The approval names the resolved current effect, and separately the enforceable
  bounds on what may still follow. Asserted that the bounds shown are the bounds
  enforced — not a summary written by the model.
- An envelope approval mints a new attempt with a new immutable grant. An effect
  outside the envelope interrupts and requires a new one. Asserted for both.
- Nothing in the surface claims a program is correct because it parsed.
notes:
=== THIRD ROUND + THE OWNER'S REBUTTAL, 2026-08-26: this bead's premise was too weak ===

THE OWNER IS RIGHT ABOUT ONE APPROVAL. Suspend at ARGUMENT RESOLUTION: the intrinsic
evaluates its arguments, emits an inert canonical invocation, suspends, and the window
shows fully-resolved concrete arguments exactly as it does today for a direct call.
Per-effect approval is therefore NOT degraded. The bead's original framing conceded
too much and is corrected here.

WHAT IS GENUINELY DIFFERENT IS THE RUN. The approval boundary becomes a TRANSACTION
BOUNDARY WITHOUT TRANSACTION SEMANTICS: the person is not approving a call, they are
deciding whether an already-partially-executed workflow may cross its next commit
point. Concrete arguments answer "what will execute". They do not answer "why now,
what has already happened, what remains, and what does denying this leave behind".
So the window must carry, at minimum: workflow identity, step ordinal, effects already
committed, the current resolved invocation, static bounds on the remainder, and the
consequence of denial.

TWO CLASSES, AND THE SPLIT IS DECIDABLE - this is the design move the bead was missing:
  - APPLICATIVE program: no effect's arguments derive from any effect's result.
    Statically decidable by taint analysis over the source. For these the WHOLE program
    can be shown exactly and approved once. "Approve the transaction" is a fact here,
    not a promise.
  - MONADIC program: it cannot. The honest artifact is a bounded envelope.
Classify before running and offer whole-program approval ONLY to the applicative class.

AND THE ENVELOPE IS A GRANT, NOT A WEAKER PROMPT. ADR-0028 already mints a new attempt
carrying a new IMMUTABLE grant on approval. Approving an envelope therefore means
minting a narrower run grant derived from the program's static bounds - after which
effects INSIDE it do not ask at all, which is how the system already behaves. No new
mechanism; a truthful sentence over the existing one. This is also the only answer to
prompt fatigue that is not a mutable grant.

PROMPT FATIGUE IS A SAFETY FAILURE, NOT A UX COST. Forty individually accurate
questions do not compose into forty informed decisions; they predict habituation,
indiscriminate "allow always", or abandonment halfway through a mutated workspace.
nocx-y47mi is the same shape and is closed. So the runtime needs an explicit approval
BUDGET and a PRE-EXECUTION response when a program's static upper bound exceeds it:
refuse, demand a narrower program, or ask for a bounded batch grant whose full scope
can honestly be shown. A counter that stops at effect 41 leaves 1-40 committed and is
not a remedy.

A SHARP CONSEQUENCE FOR run, verified in the code. CommandEffect (internal/assistant/
cmdeffect.go) is a PURE function of the command TEXT, which is how df -h is lowered to
observe while rm -rf is not. In a program the text may be COMPUTED. Therefore an
envelope over run() with a computed command argument CANNOT be lowered and must claim
the declared worst case; lowering is available only at argument resolution, inside the
run. Consequence worth stating to the model: literal commands buy a narrower envelope
and fewer questions.

DENIAL AT EFFECT 5 IS A TERMINAL WORKFLOW OUTCOME over a partially committed world,
not "the program stopped". On disk effects 1-4 remain unless compensations run - and a
compensation is another fallible effect needing its own authority. In the ledger all
four attempts and the denied proposal remain, causally ordered (ADR-0019 is explicit
that adjacency is not causality). In the UI the sentence is "stopped after four
effects; these changes remain", never "denied". Every program declares termination
semantics for denial, cancellation, executor crash, result-serialization failure and a
lost renderer connection. "No rollback is promised" is an acceptable answer. Leaving it
implicit is not.
close_reason: Moot. 'What an approval can honestly say about a program whose end it cannot see' has no subject after nocx-d6gn4.14: no program exists whose end an approval cannot see. Under declared calls an approval names one invocation, which is exactly what it can see. The question it framed — an APPLICATIVE plan can be shown whole, a MONADIC one cannot, because evaluation and execution interleave — is recorded in the epic's description as a finding. Its edge to nocx-d6gn4.5 was removed first: the budgets bead survives the carriers and no longer gates anything here.

title: The program carrier: Starlark effect intrinsics over process-lifetime replay
description:
The carrier itself. `go.starlark.net`: Python-shaped, hermetic, no `while`, recursion
disabled by default, iteration over finite collections only, step limits, and no I/O
except what the host hands it.

## The shape, chosen among three

CHOSEN — ordinary-looking effect intrinsics. `files.read(path)` LOOKS like it returns
a value; on first execution it emits an inert canonical invocation and suspends, and
on replay it returns the journaled value. Models write this well precisely because
the surface is conventional; all the machinery is host-side. Call it what it is: a
Temporal-style workflow runtime, not "Starlark returning data".

REJECTED — programs that explicitly return effect descriptions. Semantically clean,
ergonomically strange, and the moment a later step depends on a result the program
needs a hand-written state machine. Models will not emit it reliably.

REJECTED — placeholder values standing for future results. Comparisons, branches,
indexing and formatting all have to build expression nodes instead of computing, and
at that point it is a bespoke IR wearing Python syntax.

## Traps that come with the chosen shape

Code before an effect runs REPEATEDLY during replay, so local computation must have
no host-visible side effects and logging must not duplicate. Errors and limits must
distinguish replay from first execution. Source-level debugging will mislead unless
replay is hidden deliberately. A reader will assume a binding executes once.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Replay is process-lifetime only. Restart-surviving suspension is out of this epic.
- Suspension holds no native stack and no closures: the resumable state is the
  program plus its history.
- Asserted: the same program, replayed, reaches the same next unsatisfied effect.
- Asserted: a binding that would perform host work without producing a canonical
  invocation cannot.
- Measured, not assumed: how reliably real models emit valid programs against THIS
  language profile — hermetic, no ordinary imports, no Python library, no `while`,
  restricted recursion, capability-aware bindings. Python familiarity does not
  transfer for free, and a language that fails more often but diagnoses precisely may
  beat one that fails opaquely at execution.
notes: SUPERSEDED by the measurement, 2026-08-27. This bead built the program carrier; nocx-d6gn4.8's notes record what it was worth, and the answer is that it composes nothing the shell was not already composing — dependency depth ONE in every program measured. The removal is nocx-d6gn4.14. Nothing here is a defect: the carrier works, on a tool-trained model, end to end. It just does not pay.
close_reason: Shipped on feat/tool-experiment (394b4967 a program carries a result from one effect into the next inside one model turn; bc82adba a program stops for a person's answer and continues where it stopped), merged as fe976555, measured under nocx-d6gn4.8, and removed by nocx-d6gn4.14 (b68e280b). The measurement that ended it: dependency depth inside a program was ONE in every program measured, across two models and every presentation.

title: A run is bounded by what it costs the world, not by interpreter steps
description:
Starlark forbidding `while` and recursion sounds like boundedness and is not. Finite
iteration over a million returned paths is finite. A step limit bounds INTERPRETER
work; it says nothing about what the program spends outside itself.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A run carries explicit budgets, each enforced and each visible: number of effects,
  total result bytes, mutations, distinct resources touched, remote calls, process
  time, wall time, bytes egressed to the model provider.
- Exhausting a budget is a first-class terminal state with its own sentence, not an
  error that reads like a crash.
- The budgets are readable off the source before the run starts, so an approval can
  state them. Asserted.

title: A replay history is not the audit ledger: command identity and exact observed values
description:
The claim "we already have the journal" is false and this bead is the gap. `caused-by`
joins an action to the turn that caused it; it does not say WHICH DYNAMIC INVOCATION
in which replay a given record satisfies. Matching by tool name and arguments is
ambiguous the moment a loop reads the same path twice. Matching by ordinal is brittle:
inserting one diagnostic read near the top shifts every ordinal after it.

What replay needs is a deterministic command identity — program digest, lexical
callsite, activation path, loop iteration — or an event counter whose stability
becomes part of the language's semantics. That is a workflow-history protocol. It may
be STORED in the ledger; it is not the ledger.

## And determinism is only as good as the Go boundary

The Starlark core can be deterministic while host bindings leak: Go map iteration
order, filesystem enumeration order, clocks and deadlines, random identifiers,
environment, locale, process exit timing, concurrent result ordering, error strings
carrying paths or timings, modules loaded from mutable files, resolution of "the
current session". Each one is journaled, prohibited, or canonicalised — and the
discipline belongs to every binding and every conversion, permanently.

`doc(name)` is the sharp instance: it is pure only if the documentation is immutable
within the run's semantic version. A changing corpus lets a program take a different
branch without issuing a single effect.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A dynamic invocation has a stable identity that survives inserting an unrelated
  call earlier in the program. Asserted with exactly that edit.
- The determinism contract is written down per binding, and a binding that cannot
  meet it is either journaled or refused — not left to chance.
- `doc()` is pinned to a version or journaled. Asserted that a changed corpus cannot
  change a replayed decision.
- An incompatible runtime or library upgrade invalidates suspended executions rather
  than replaying them under changed semantics. Stated deliberately, because the other
  two options (pinning per execution, version markers in programs) are heavier and
  this is a local terminal.
notes:
=== THIRD ADVERSARIAL ROUND, 2026-08-26: the vocabulary IS the defect ===

RESUME versus RE-EXECUTION. Calling both of them "replay" will create the bug, so the
bead adopts two words and holds them apart:
  - RESUME reconstructs the SAME interrupted attempt. It may reuse a recorded
    observation, and it may reuse the approval that attempt already carried.
  - RE-EXECUTION is a NEW run. It must re-enter policy and mint FRESH authority even
    when the invocation bytes are byte-identical to a recorded one.
An approval answered in run 1 must never authorize an effect in run 2. Verified in the
code, not assumed: Approval binds RunID, Attempt, Tool, CallID and ArgHash and lives
for the process lifetime (internal/assistant/approvals.go). Reusing one across runs
contradicts both bindings that are already there.

REVALIDATION UNDER REPLAY moves here from nocx-d6gn4.1. Recorded precondition outcomes
(reconstructing run 1) and fresh precondition checks (before a new physical attempt)
are different things and need different fields. Conflate them and either replay stops
being deterministic, or a stale fact authorizes a new effect - which is worse, because
it is internally deterministic and externally wrong.

WHAT THE HISTORY MUST CARRY, as an event vocabulary of its own or as authoritative
artifacts linked into the ledger: invocation resolved, proposal recorded, attempt
opened, approval answered, effect started, result committed, continuation selected.
Without it a crash can leave a world mutation with NO deterministic fact saying
whether the interpreter may repeat it. Note also that today's checkpoints are opaque
in-memory framework bytes, deliberately not authoritative records (internal/assistant/
checkpoints.go) - they are not a starting point for this.
close_reason: Moot with the program carrier. Replay identity — command identity and exact observed values — existed because a Starlark program replayed over the process lifetime, so a re-executed step had to observe what it observed the first time. Nothing replays after nocx-d6gn4.14: a declared call unwinds and the checkpoint carries the resume. The INSIGHT it bought is kept where it cannot be lost — the epic's description records that our audit ledger is not a deterministic workflow history, and that being append-only is not what would make them interchangeable. Its edge to nocx-d6gn4.2 was removed first: that edge existed because replay identity needed the result artifact split, and it means nothing now.

title: The assistant composes multi-step work in one turn, and a setting switches the method so the two can be compared
description:
## Where this came from

The owner found https://github.com/1hachem/lisptc and asked whether its method
applies here. Its agent integration is the interesting line: "the agent has no
tools, its replies are lisp source evaluated straight into the REPL, and replies
are constrained to valid lisptc via grammar-based structured output."

Two adversarial review rounds with codex followed (2026-08-23). What survived is
narrower than where the discussion peaked, and the narrowing is the useful part.

## The invariant, stated without the language

The model proposes a bounded executable artifact; a deterministic executor owns
control flow, authority, state transitions and the production of an auditable
trace. Lisp is one carrier of that invariant and an expensive one. Note also that
this does not make the agent deterministic — it makes the ORCHESTRATION BETWEEN
nondeterministic decisions deterministic. The model, the shell, the filesystem,
clocks and the network stay exactly as nondeterministic as they were.

## What is NOT true, though we believed it for a while

**"We already have the journal."** We do not. An audit ledger is not a
deterministic workflow history: Temporal's history is built to reproduce the
executor's internal decisions, ours records product facts for provenance and
recall, and being append-only is not what makes them interchangeable. See the
child bead on replay identity.

**"Effects as data means approval sees the whole program."** Only for an
APPLICATIVE plan, where every effect is describable before any result is known.
The moment a step depends on an earlier result the shape is monadic, evaluation
and execution interleave, and the host can only ever see the current resolved
effect plus static bounds read off the source.

**"A generated program is a script the person can keep."** Attractive and
incomplete: its behaviour depends on standard-library version, capability
injection, the grant, session bindings and journal semantics, and "a person can
read it" is not "a person can predict it".

## The sentence to keep

Replay reconstructs computation. It does not preserve consent, freshness, or truth
about the world. Every effect revalidates its own preconditions immediately before
executing, or the executor becomes wonderfully reproducible exactly when it is
reproducing the wrong decision.
acceptance_criteria:
## What a person can do that they could not before

Ask the assistant something whose answer needs two DEPENDENT tool calls — "which
commands failed here, show me the output of the last one" — and get it answered in
ONE model turn instead of three, with the intermediate result never entering the
model's context. And, because this is an experiment and not a conviction, flip a
setting and get the same question answered the way it is answered today, so the two
can be measured against each other rather than argued about.

## Success Criteria

- A question requiring two dependent tool calls is answered in one model turn with
  the method set to `program`, and as it is today with the method set to `calls`.
  Same answer, same SHAPE of ledger record — one action entry per effect, each
  joined to its turn. Asserted end to end, through the real backend.
- The switch is a setting a person reaches through the UI, not a build tag. WHERE it
  lives is decided deliberately and stated: there is no "Experimental" section today
  (the sections are Instructions, Answers, Interface, Clipboard, History and Test,
  in the groups assistant / application / developer), so this epic either adds one
  or puts the switch under `developer`, and says which and why.
- BOTH carriers converge on ONE effect kernel before anything is decided: canonical
  invocation -> policy decision -> narrowed capability -> action entry in the ledger.
  The interpreter binding is a mechanical adapter over the same canonical tool
  descriptor and independently defines NO schema, effect, resource extraction,
  authorization, result serialization, error classification, ledger behaviour or
  egress behaviour. Asserted: the same effect, proposed through either carrier,
  produces the same policy decision and the same ledger shape.
- Every effect revalidates its current-world preconditions immediately before it
  executes, on both carriers.
- A written decision rule exists BEFORE the switch ships: what evidence removes the
  program carrier, what evidence restricts the call carrier, and by when. Cohorts are
  controlled (calls-only / program-only), because "which one the model reaches for"
  when both are declared measures tool-description salience, not fitness.

## Deliberately out

- **Suspension surviving a backend restart.** Replay is process-lifetime only here.
  Durable suspension pulls in program/runtime versioning, durable pending-approval
  state and precondition revalidation across time, and the prize it was sold on —
  approval surviving a restart — is something the product does not have today either
  (ADR-0028: "approval does not survive a restart, which is already what the recovery
  rule says").
- **CEL as the scope language.** Structural scopes first — exact session, exact host
  identity, path subtree after canonical resolution, repository identity, command
  template with typed holes, destination set, maximum cardinality. The matrix's
  virtue is that a person can inspect it without simulating a program; do not trade
  that away before the structural forms have been shown insufficient.
- **Saved, reusable, trusted programs.** A program is an artifact of its turn and
  replayable evidence. A parameterized automation object and a capability-bearing
  reusable workflow are two further things, each with its own trust and compatibility
  contract, and none of the three may silently graduate into the next.
- **Removing the direct tool carrier.** The user configures arbitrary
  OpenAI-compatible endpoints, including small local models that are far better at
  one JSON tool call than at writing correct code.
notes:
FILE OVERLAP, deliberately NOT encoded as a blocking edge (2026-08-23).

This epic and nocx-x8s2 both touch internal/transport/ws_agent.go, and x8s2's own
nocx-e4bn (contracts and param validation for agent.*) sits in the same file. An
epic-level blocks edge was added and then removed: what it actually encoded was
"phase-2 comes after mvp", which is PRIORITY, and AGENTS.md is explicit that 13 of
20 epic edges once encoded "not yet" rather than overlap and made the queue
unusable. The overlap is narrow and is a merge, not a corruption; the merge slot is
what exists for it.

Whoever takes nocx-d6gn4.3 (the effect kernel) should check whether nocx-e4bn has
landed or is in flight before editing ws_agent.go.

RELATED, and it must be READ rather than re-decided: nocx-x8s2.1 already rejected a
model-authored staleness predicate and a model re-confirmation at delivery, with
reasons. nocx-d6gn4.1 generalises that decision to every effect and does not get to
overturn it.

=== THIRD ADVERSARIAL ROUND, 2026-08-26. Two owner positions, one rejected outcome ===

OWNER POSITION 1 - approval. "Show the request once the variables resolve." SOUND for
one approval, and it corrects nocx-d6gn4.7, which had conceded too much. Per-effect
approval under the program carrier is identical to today. What differs is the RUN:
the approval boundary becomes a transaction boundary without transaction semantics.
Details and the applicative/monadic split now live in .7.

OWNER POSITION 2 - "lisptc has no tools; maybe we need only a REPL, one execute tool".
REJECTED AS A DIRECTION FOR NOW, and the reason is stronger than the observability
argument this epic already recorded. It is AUTHORITY. Registry.ForGrant returns exactly
the tools the grant permits and the comment in the code states the principle: "a tool
the grant forbids is absent from the set, because the strongest refusal is the one
never proposed" (internal/agenttools/registry.go). A single execute tool destroys that
refusal outright - the provider always sees one tool and the real capability selection
happens only AFTER source is parsed. Declaration filtering, malformed-call
classification, rate limiting, previews, eval labels and tool-specific failure handling
all move behind an interpreter-specific opaque boundary at the same time.
It is also the wrong first move for a second reason: replacing the wire surface
DESTROYS THE CONTROL GROUP the experiment needs. So "REPL only" is not a premise; it is
what cohort `program` MEANS, and the experiment is what decides it.

DECIDED ORDER, replacing "do .1/.2/.3 regardless":
  1. nocx-d6gn4.9 - the thin invocation envelope and artifact identity. NOT the kernel.
  2. nocx-d6gn4.10 - the two corrected measurements. Both originally proposed
     measurements were rejected: a parser measures punctuation, and instrumenting the
     shipped carrier measures the incumbent's affordances rather than latent demand.
  3. .2 proceeds independently, because typed handles have a direct non-Starlark
     benefit - and may well weaken this epic's own economic case. That is a finding,
     not a failure.
  4. .1 stays on the front: it is a defect TODAY, with no carrier and no replay. Its
     replay half moved to .4.
  5. .3 no longer goes first. Freezing "one effect kernel" before .1, .2 and .4 settle
     what a canonical invocation must carry guarantees the universal kernel acquires
     carrier-specific side channels. It now depends on all three.
  6. .6 is blocked by .10. The runtime is not built before the measurements report.

Front after this restructure: .1, .2, .9.

title: A drop target that is not a tab has no address
description:
Discovered writing .internal/specs/2026-08-23-import-collection-ask-design.md.

The import ask reads a document on the machine the backend runs on. It is not a
session gesture. But SourceTicketStore.Dropped resolves a drop through
data-session-id and EmitFilesDropped addresses the notification to the renderer
attached to THAT session — so the import dialog has to borrow a local terminal
tab’s identity to receive a drop at all, and draws no drop target when no local
session is open.

That is an addressing scheme standing in for the one this gesture wants. It is
not a line of code: EmitFilesDropped addresses by session deliberately —
broadcasting was the defect it replaced, and a broadcast local path is still a
leak even when it carries no ticket. What a non-session target should be
addressed BY is the open question (the connection the modal belongs to is the
obvious candidate; Wails has no connection identity at drop time, which is why
this is a design question).

## Acceptance Criteria

- A drop target that declares no session receives files.dropped, and only the
  renderer that owns that target does.
- The import dialog draws its drop target with no local session open, and a drop
  on it fills the source field.
- No path reaches a renderer that did not own the target that was dropped on —
  asserted with two attached connections.

title: A long block shows both ends and loads its middle on demand
acceptance_criteria:
A block with a thousand lines of output takes the height of thirty, without
lying about what it holds.

## Why now, and why it is not an assistant feature

nocx-9sqii draws the agent's command block between the turn's fragments, so a
`make build` that printed two thousand lines would stand between the question
and the answer. But a human's `make build` buries its neighbours by exactly the
same amount, and blocks do not collapse at all today. So this lands in the
scrollback's block layer and applies to both authors on one rule; the assistant
is only the first caller that made it urgent.

## The shape the owner chose

Not a collapse — both ENDS stay, the middle goes, the way GitHub elides a diff.
The reason is specific to command output: the head carries what the command
began doing (its banner, its column headings) and the tail carries the error,
the summary and whatever the exit status is about. The bulk is in between. A
fully collapsed block hides the thing that makes a terminal a terminal.

## What the ends cannot hide

The middle is not inert the way a diff's context is. One failing test out of
five hundred, one warning mid-build, lives exactly where the elision is. That
makes the search criterion below the load-bearing one, not a nicety.

And "load on demand" needs a source. A block's body is `application/vt` captured
by the renderer off the frozen buffer (internal/content/ledger.go:108,
frontend/src/restore-client.ts:144), so the middle exists only as far as the
block ever held it: nocx-4ff.26 (OPEN) says xterm's 10000-line scrollback cap
truncates before the freeze, and ADR-0019 §7 says retention evicts bodies. The
repo's rule for exactly this is already written, in the run tool's output window
— "never a silent truncation" (frontend/src/terminal-content.ts:3992): the
window states how much more the block holds rather than quietly ending. The band
inherits that rule.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A frozen block over the threshold draws its head and its tail with a band
  between them naming HOW MANY lines are hidden. Asserted, including that a
  block under the threshold is untouched.
- Find reaches the hidden rows, and a match inside the middle expands it.
  Asserted. Without this a long block becomes unsearchable, which is a worse
  defect than a tall one.
- Copy yields the WHOLE output and `blocks.read` serves the whole body: no
  surface hands out an elided body without saying so. Asserted for both paths.
- The band degrades in words, never in a spinner, and each cause is asserted
  separately: the middle was truncated before the freeze (nocx-4ff.26), and the
  middle was evicted by retention (ADR-0019 §7).
- Elision applies only AFTER the freeze. A running command's tail follows as it
  does today — asserted, because a view that re-elides mid-run would jump under
  the reader.
- The tail keeps more lines than the head, and the rule is stated once, in one
  place, rather than tuned per caller.
- Expansion is progressive — up, down, all — so opening a two-thousand-line
  middle is the person's explicit choice, not the price of one click.
- One rule, both authors: a human's block and the agent's elide identically.
  Asserted over both.

title: The Operations panel's name touches its first heading — nothing supplies the room under a filterless panel's header
description:
The shell's header carries no padding below it on purpose: whatever follows it
supplies that room, and for Files, Git, Notes and Ports that is the pinned filter
row (`.ui-sidebar-view__filter`, `var(--space-2)` all round).

Operations is the only panel with no `filter` slot, so the body follows the header
directly and NOTHING supplied it — the panel name and the first group heading sat
flush. That is what the owner reported as "the padding on the operations screen is
not enough".

A two-owners defect from 2026-08-22: the header's `padding-bottom` and
`.ops-group__heading:first-child`'s `margin-top` were both retired that evening,
each on the argument that the other carried the room. Between them the room went
to zero.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the sidebar and select the Operations view (an upload makes it non-empty).
2. Compare the space between "OPERATIONS" and the "FINISHED" heading below it with
   the space between any other panel's name and its filter box.

Measured off the owner's screenshot at 2x: header text bottom and the first group
heading's cap top are the same pixel. Every other panel has 8px there.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The room under the header is the SHELL's, and one owner supplies it:
  `.ui-sidebar-view__header` still declares `0` below, and
  `.ui-sidebar-view__header + .ui-sidebar-view__body` declares `padding-top`
  equal to `.ui-sidebar-view__filter`'s own top padding.
- A filtered panel is unchanged — the filter is then the adjacent sibling, so
  the rule does not match.
- Asserted in `panels-one-shape.test.ts` against the shipped stylesheet, so it
  holds for a panel nobody has written yet.
close_reason: Kit rule: .ui-sidebar-view__header + .ui-sidebar-view__body takes padding-top: var(--space-2), so a filterless panel gets the room the filter row supplies elsewhere. Asserted in panels-one-shape.test.ts (room below header is 0, room above body equals the filter's top padding). Commit 6d6a2ee2.

title: internal/shellintegration: TestStage1_AByteAfterACompleteFrameNeverBecomesShellInput fails intermittently on CI
description:
Seen 2026-08-22 on the CI run for feat/notifications (workflow_dispatch 32593712918), job ci-backend (with-secret-service). The SAME commit passed ci-backend (no-secret-service), ci-linux in both keyring variants, and ci-mac, and the branch touches nothing in internal/shellintegration.

The failure dumps LAUNCH_ALLARGV -- the test reads the machine's whole process table via `ps -eo args=` -- and the dump is full of defunct bash/zsh/loader processes from the shellintegration suite's own earlier cases, alongside a WARN from TestUninstallRemote_RemovesManifestOwnedFilesOverSFTP that its generation dir was 'directory not empty' at teardown. Both point the same way: the assertion reads global machine state that neighbouring tests in the same package are still tearing down, so it is load- and order-sensitive rather than wrong about the product.

Related: nocx-lc15n is the same shape in internal/content, and the memory 'a test that fails under load and passes in isolation will destroy a bisect' is why this gets filed rather than retried into silence.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. go test -race -tags gtk3 ./internal/shellintegration/ on a loaded runner.
2. Occasionally: TestStage1_AByteAfterACompleteFrameNeverBecomesShellInput fails, printing the full process table.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The assertion no longer reads process state that another test in the package can be mid-teardown of -- it either scopes what it reads to its own launch, or waits on an observable belonging to its own case.
- A test that reproduces the interference deliberately (the neighbouring case's teardown still in flight) fails before the fix and passes after.

title: Two transport tests fail only under concurrent container load: both wait on a duration, not on an observable
acceptance_criteria:
The test reports what actually happened — a refused remote forward — rather than expiring a timer, and it does not depend on how busy the machine is.

## What happened, 2026-08-22

The pre-commit hook's containerized `go test -race` went red on
`internal/app/TestLiveSshd_SSHChildAssembly_ChildEstablishesOverComposedLine`
while five other agents were working and other worktrees' hooks were running
containers on the same Docker daemon:

    --- FAIL: TestLiveSshd_SSHChildAssembly_ChildEstablishesOverComposedLine (30.14s)
        ssh_child_assembly_test.go:602: timed out after 30s waiting for child domain Established via its own hello

and the composed-line terminal it printed carried the cause one line above:

    Warning: remote port forwarding failed for listen port 42104

Baseline measured immediately, before blaming the change under commit (which
touched only e2e/ and internal/transport): the same test on the host passes in
0.41s, and it RUNS rather than skipping (`--- PASS` under -v). Retried on a
quiet machine, the identical commit's gate went green — so the failure is the
machine, not the tree.

## Why this is a bead and not a shrug

AGENTS.md, the caps section: a test may not depend on timing. `--cpu-shares` is
a weight and not an isolation boundary, so a hook firing while other worktrees
run containers is the ordinary state of this repo, not an exceptional one. And
the 30s wait is a DURATION, which is exactly what that rule forbids — the
symptom it produced ("timed out waiting for Established") names the wait rather
than the refusal that made the wait pointless.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start several containerized runs at once on one Docker daemon (another
   worktree's pre-commit hook is enough; five agents were live here).
2. Commit anything in a second worktree so .githooks/containerized-tests.sh
   runs `go test -race` for ./internal/app.
3. The test expires its 30s wait; the composed-line dump above it says the
   remote port forwarding failed.
4. Same test, same commit, on the host or on a quiet machine: passes in 0.41s.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The refused forward is observed and reported AS a refusal. `lifecycleremote.New`
  already returns ErrForwardingRefused synchronously (adapter.go:229-231) — the
  test should fail on that, immediately, saying the sshd refused the bind.
- The success path waits on an observable state change, never on a duration.
  WIDENING THE 30s IS NOT A FIX and is explicitly forbidden: it would hide
  whichever explanation is true.
- If the forward refusal is a fixture defect (the fixture's sshd, its
  GatewayPorts/AllowTcpForwarding, or a port the container cannot bind), name it
  and fix it there. A test that cannot get its forward is not a product failure
  and must not be reported as one.
- Asserted: the test passes on a loaded machine. Reproduce the load rather than
  waiting to be unlucky — NOCX_CI_CPUS is the debugging tool AGENTS.md keeps for
  exactly this.
notes:
A SECOND test of the same shape, same day (2026-08-22/23), same machine state:

    --- FAIL: TestAgentApprove_YesResumesTheRun (5.69s)
        ws_agent_approval_test.go:306: waiting for agent.runDelta notification:
        read tcp ...: i/o timeout
    FAIL github.com/shady2k/nocx/internal/transport  189.357s

Baseline, immediately: the same test on the host, -count=3, passes in 0.447s
total. The package takes ~70s on the host and took 189s in that container run,
with two other worktrees' hook containers live on the same daemon.

So this bead is not about one ssh test. Both failures are a WAIT ON A DURATION
expiring because the machine was busy — a socket read deadline in one case, a
30s helper wait in the other — and both are invisible on an idle machine. The
fix that generalises is the one AGENTS.md already states: wait on an
observable state change, never on a duration. Widening either deadline is
still forbidden.

Where to look: the notification-reading helper in internal/transport's tests
(readNotification's per-call timeout) is shared by many tests, so this will
keep surfacing under different names until that wait is the thing that
changes. nocx-8b47 records the same shape on Linux CI for three other tests
and is probably the same defect; check before fixing separately.

title: Show next counts unloaded directory entries while a filter is narrowing something else
description:
Owner: with a filter typed, the tree still offers 'Show next 64'. The button counts total minus loaded for the DIRECTORY and knows nothing about the filter, so the number describes neither what is shown nor what pressing it would add to the matches.

It cannot simply be hidden. The filter narrows rows already in the store and issues no request, so matches may well be sitting in the unloaded remainder — the button is currently the only way to reach them. What is wrong is what it SAYS, not that it is there.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a large directory, type a filter that matches a few rows.
2. Under the matches: Show next 64 — a count of unloaded directory entries, unrelated to the filter.

## Acceptance Criteria

- With a filter active the control says what it actually does: load more entries so the filter can search them, not 'show next N' of a list nobody is looking at.
- With no filter it reads as it does today.
- Pressing it under a filter keeps the filter and does not silently widen the view.
- The empty case is honest: a filter matching nothing in what is loaded, with more to load, is a different state from a filter matching nothing at all.

title: Copy output on an answer block returns the rendered text, not what the model wrote
acceptance_criteria:
Copying an answer gives back exactly the text the model produced — markdown markers and all —
because that is what a person pastes elsewhere.

## Why

nocx-swoje renders markdown in the answer (headings, bold, inline code), and the markers are
consumed by the rendering. Copy output scrapes the DOM, so a structured answer copies out as
the painted text with its structure lost. Fenced code was never affected — it round-trips
byte-exact — but prose does not.

The owner rejected hanging the markers back in a dimmed span as a half-measure: "Сделай сразу
как положено."

## The shape

The answer's text is already durable: SubmitAgentAsk writes a text/plain artifact for the
answer (internal/content/ledger_agent_sqlite.go), and the renderer knows the answer entry
(answerEntryId — it routes deltas by it). So copy reads the STORE, not the screen.

restore-client.ts already does this shape for a command body — ledger.get for the entry, then
ledger.artifact for the payload — but selects application/vt. An answer needs the text/plain
one. One helper, two media types; do not write a second fetch path.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Ask the assistant something it answers with a heading, a bullet list and bold text.
2. Copy output from the block menu; paste it anywhere.
3. The markers are gone: the structure cannot be reconstructed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Copy output on an ANSWER block returns the stored answer text byte for byte. Asserted against
  the artifact, not against the DOM.
- A command block's copy is unchanged — it copies what the terminal drew, which is right for it.
- An answer whose artifact is gone (retention, or the store unreachable) says so rather than
  silently copying the painted text: a copy that quietly differs from the record is worse than
  a refusal. Both ends asserted.
- Copy becomes asynchronous; the surface must not appear to have done nothing while it fetches.
close_reason: Shipped in 789d55f6 on feat/ai-assistant; unit tests + typecheck + pre-commit gates (incl. containerized go -race and vitest) green.

- Whatever is left cannot silently eat a frame another wait needs.

title: The Instructions page shows the system prompt, so a person can see what is sent
acceptance_criteria:
On Settings -> Instructions, a person can read the system prompt the assistant is sent — as a
TEMPLATE with placeholders, not with the values filled in. Read only: this is disclosure, not
an editor.

## Why

Owner, 2026-08-22: "давай на этой странице показывать системный промпт. Просто показывать,
чтобы человек знал что отправляется." And, on the shape: "мы просто показываем с
плейсхолдерами без самих значений."

It also settles half of nocx-5u3oz.8, whose third criterion is that the owner approves the
fact list and the approval is recorded — reading the prompt on the page is a better approval
than reviewing a list in a bead.

## The shape, decided by the owner

Placeholders, not values. The prompt is assembled from the facts of a PANE (session id, cwd,
environment, the person's own paragraph) and Settings has no pane — so the page shows the
prompt's TEXT with each fact standing as a named placeholder. Nobody has to have a pane open,
nothing per-machine is painted on a settings screen, and what the reader learns is the thing
they asked about: what is sent, and what is filled into it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The page shows the prompt as it is written, with every per-pane fact rendered as a named
  placeholder rather than its value. The placeholder names what will be substituted, in the
  product's own words.
- It comes from the ONE assembler a real ask uses. A test proves the page and the product
  cannot drift — the page may not hold a second copy of the prompt text (AGENTS.md: one owner).
  If the assembler has no shape that yields the template, give it one and use it from both.
- The person's own paragraph is shown as a placeholder too, positioned where it really lands
  (last), so the page demonstrates the precedence rule it already describes in prose above.
- Read only. The editable half of this page is the paragraph, which already exists and stays
  exactly as it is.
- Say in the report what the prompt contains that a person might not expect. This page is where
  anything careless about what we tell the model becomes visible.
close_reason: Shipped. frontend/src/settings.tsx:1546 renders the system prompt in a CodeBlock inside the Instructions section, sourced from the generated frontend/src/systemprompt.json; one owner is enforced by TestSettingsSystemPromptArtifactMatchesPrompt in internal/assistant/systemprompt_settings_test.go:10, and the artifact carries placeholders rather than live values. Renderer assertions at frontend/src/settings.test.ts:1795 and :1816. Closed during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh.

title: nocx-pu4.7's offer to save a host as a connection has not run since 2026-08-08
acceptance_criteria:
The feature either works or is deliberately gone — not shipped, wired out, and silently absent
for weeks.

## What was found

While reporting on nocx-0zb1m, the worker grepped the whole repo for _maybeOfferConnection and
found exactly ONE occurrence: its own definition at frontend/src/terminal-content.ts:4281.
`git log -S` puts the removal of all three `void this._maybeOfferConnection()` call sites at
6cba76fd (2026-08-08, "the shell speaks over a channel").

So the BlockReceipt offer — "you just ssh'd somewhere that is not a saved profile; save it?" —
has not run since that commit, and nothing catches it: the method is private, so the frontend's
dead-exports ratchet has no opinion, and `deadcode` is Go-side only. This is the frontend twin
of the blind spot AGENTS.md documents for Go interfaces.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `grep -rn "_maybeOfferConnection" frontend/src` — one hit, the definition.
2. ssh by hand to a host that is not a saved profile. No offer appears.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Decide deliberately, and record it: the feature is rewired and proven by a test that watches
  the offer appear, or it is deleted with its receipt copy and nocx-pu4.7 is reopened or closed
  as withdrawn. Not left as an unreachable private method.
- If rewired: the blocks read in it is correct as written (it looks at the LAST block to offer
  saving a destination just ssh'd to; offering a host from the previous session's last command
  would be wrong) — keep that property and assert it.
- Name what would have caught this and say whether it is worth building: the frontend has no
  equivalent of `deadcode -whylive` for a private method.

title: A restored block can be selected but the manager does not know it
acceptance_criteria:
Selecting a restored block behaves exactly as selecting a live one: Escape clears it, typing
over it forwards into the editor, and switching between a live and a restored block does not
confuse the manager.

## Cause

Measured by the nocx-0zb1m worker with a throwaway spec against the code as it stood; the same
root, one step further on. wireBlockSelection does the DOM half itself and uses its callback
only to TELL the manager. The restoredBlock(...) call site in terminal-content.ts passes
`() => {}`, so the two halves diverge:

- clicking a restored block adds .cmd-block-selected while manager.selectedBlockId stays null;
- deselectAll() cannot clear it — its guard is `_selectedBlockId !== null` — so Escape does
  nothing, and terminal-content.ts's rescue (Escape, and typing a character to deselect and
  forward into the editor) is gated on the same value;
- worse across the boundary: select a live block, click a restored one (the DOM moves, the
  manager does not), click the live one back — the manager sees its own id still stored, reads
  the click as a toggle-off and sets null while the class was just added. Selected on screen,
  nothing selected as far as the manager is concerned.

nocx-0zb1m fixed DOM ownership. This is the callback half: the wiring is baked into the element
by restoredBlock() before the manager ever sees it, so closing this means the MANAGER supplies
the select wiring.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a pane with restored blocks.
2. Click one. Press Escape — it stays selected.
3. Select a live block, click a restored one, click the live one again — the manager's idea of
   what is selected and the screen's disagree.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The manager supplies the select wiring for restored blocks as it does for live ones; the call
  site has no empty callback to pass.
- Asserted: Escape clears a restored selection, and the live/restored/live sequence leaves the
  manager and the DOM agreeing.
- One owner for "which block is selected" (AGENTS.md).

title: A tool call cannot be opened: its arguments and its result are unreachable
acceptance_criteria:
A person can open a tool call the assistant made and see what it was asked and what came back.

## Why it is not there

nocx-shxv0 deliberately shipped the line without either. The result was left off because it
already has an owner (the ledger attempt, and for the run tool the block the command opened)
and because a copy sent to the renderer would be a second egress path around the gate that
screens results for the provider. The arguments were left off because the raw blob is JSON,
not a sentence. actionEntryId is ON THE WIRE precisely so this can be built later: it is the
ledger handle, not a second copy of the bytes.

The owner asked for it: "Команды сейчас без параметров и без ответа, а их хочется видеть."

## Acceptance Criteria

- The call opens on demand and shows what it was called with, and what it returned, fetched
  THROUGH the ledger handle (actionEntryId) rather than pushed down the run's stream.
- The egress question is answered explicitly, in the code, before any result text is shown:
  the gate screens a tool result for the PROVIDER; showing it to the person who is already
  looking at their own terminal is a different question with a different answer, and this
  bead states which and why.
- Nothing is fetched until the person opens it. A run that nobody expands costs one line.
- Closed by default stays the default; the expansion is the person's gesture.
notes:
2026-08-23, narrowed by nocx-9sqii: for the `run` tool the block IS what this bead would have opened — the chronological turn draws it at the call's own position, so there is nothing left to fetch through actionEntryId for run. What survives here is every tool that opens no block: readScreen, blocks.list, blocks.read. The egress criterion is unchanged and still belongs to this bead.
--- NARROWED by nocx-9sqii, 2026-08-23 ---

This bead stands but its population shrank. For the `run` tool the BLOCK is now what
the line would have opened: a turn is drawn as fragments and the command's own
top-level block sits between them, carrying the command, its output, its exit status
and its duration. So `run` no longer needs an openable line, and giving it one would
be a second owner of the same facts.

What is left for this bead is the tools that open no block: `readScreen`,
`blocks.list`, `blocks.read`. Their line is the only record of the occurrence, so
"a tool call cannot be opened" is still true and still worth fixing — for those three.

title: clear leaves the previous session's blocks on screen: scrollbackInner has two owners
acceptance_criteria:
`clear` empties the scrollback — all of it, including blocks restored from a previous
session — and leaves no "Previous session" boundary behind for content that is gone.

## What happens

Owner, 2026-08-22: ran `clear` in a pane whose scrollback had been restored from the
previous session. The command ran (27ms, ok) and its own block appeared, but every restored
block above stayed on screen, with the "Previous session" boundary still labelling them.

## Cause

Two owners for the children of .scrollback-inner. Live blocks are created and tracked by
BlockManager, which is what clearAll() empties — it walks this._blocks and this._answerBlocks.
Restored blocks are inserted straight into the DOM by the controller
(scrollback/controller.ts restorePast: `for (const el of blocks) this.scrollbackInner.insertBefore(el, anchor)`),
and BlockManager never learns about them: nextRestoredId() hands out an id and stores nothing.
The boundary element the same method appends is likewise nobody's.

So maybeClear -> clearAll does exactly what it was written to do and cannot see half the
scrollback. AGENTS.md: two surfaces may never own the same input.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a pane with a restored scrollback (blocks under the "Previous session" boundary).
2. Run `clear`.
3. The restored blocks and the boundary are still there.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A test restores blocks, runs the clear path, and asserts .scrollback-inner holds neither a
  restored block nor the restore boundary afterwards. Failing before the fix.
- ONE owner afterwards: restored blocks are registered with the same manager that owns live
  ones rather than inserted past it. Do not fix this by teaching clearAll a second place to
  look — that keeps two owners and adds a third thing to keep in step.
- Restoration itself is unchanged and asserted: restored blocks still land above the live
  ones, the boundary still labels them, and the view still lands at the newest block.
- While you are there, report (do not necessarily fix) what else could not see restored
  blocks: block selection is wired with an empty onSelect callback at the restoredBlock call
  site in terminal-content.ts, and _maybeOfferConnection reads blockManager.blocks. Say in
  your report whether each is deliberate or a second face of this defect.
notes: Follow-ups from this bead: nocx-h8luh (restored-block selection: the manager does not know) and nocx-rxvl5 (_maybeOfferConnection dead since 6cba76fd).
close_reason: Landed in ec76e2bf. The restored blocks and their boundary now go in through BlockManager, which is what clearAll empties — the controller had been inserting them straight into .scrollback-inner, so clear could not see half the scrollback. Fixed by ownership rather than by teaching clearAll a second place to look. Restoration is unchanged and asserted (past above present, boundary between, view lands at the newest), and both ends are tested: a clear with no restored blocks, and a restore into an already-cleared pane. Two further findings were reported rather than folded in: nocx-x14ge (restored-block selection) and nocx-cbihy (_maybeOfferConnection has been dead since 2026-08-08).

title: The Files panel has no filter box, which its design promised — the same defect Git had
description:
Owner: the Files panel has no filter, unlike every other panel, so finding anything is awkward. Confirmed: no SearchField in files-view.tsx, while Ports, Git, Settings and quick-connect all have one.

SECOND OCCURRENCE OF ONE SHAPE. nocx-52by was 'The Git panel has no filter box, which the design promised' and is closed. The file-manager design (nocx-708q) likewise put in scope: a name filter with its Names/Contents segmented toggle, at least for Names. Twice now a panel has shipped without the filter its own design promised, and both times a person found it by using the product. A third time makes it a rule worth gating, the way context-menu icons now are.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the Files panel with a large home directory. There is no way to narrow it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A filter over names, using the kit's SearchField as the other panels do — not a hand-rolled input.
- It filters the tree without collapsing what the person expanded, and clearing it restores the view rather than resetting it.
- The Names/Contents toggle may ship with Contents disabled, as the design allows, but if it ships disabled the reason is visible rather than a dead control.
- Behaviour matches the other panels closely enough that nobody has to learn it twice.
close_reason: Merged as dd5ff9f6. The Files panel gets the filter its design promised and every other panel already had, built on the kit's SearchField after reading how Git's was built — the second occurrence of this shape, after nocx-52by did the same for Git. The Names/Contents toggle ships with Contents disabled and the SegmentedControl gained a typed variance for it: a single option may be disabled with a title saying why while the group stays live and arrows skip it — a disabled control that cannot say why is one that teaches people the panel is broken.

title: Each GitHub e2e browser leg repeats a 100-second cold bootstrap
description:
## Measured

CI run 32508439589 on 2026-08-21, current browser-matrix arrangement:

- Chromium e2e step: 585s. Fresh Docker image build 62s; npm ci + Go module download/build + stand readiness 47s; tests 475s.
- WebKit e2e step: 571s. Fresh Docker image build 60s; npm ci + Go module download/build + stand readiness 41s; tests 469s.

Both matrix legs independently build the same nocx-e2e:local image from mcr.microsoft.com/playwright, run root and frontend npm ci, download the Go module graph and build cmd/devharness. Named Docker volumes help local repeated runs but are empty on every GitHub-hosted runner. The browser split therefore duplicates about 100 seconds of cold bootstrap per leg.

This is not the dominant cause of the 10-12 minute wall clock: 81-82% is the serial Playwright phase tracked by nocx-8rda. It is an independent bounded saving of roughly 1-1.5 minutes per leg. Preserve the pinned-image invariant in ci.yml; do not replace it with unpinned ubuntu-latest provisioning.
acceptance_criteria:
- A fresh GitHub e2e run exposes separate timings for image/bootstrap/test work.
- Image plus dependency/bootstrap time is materially below the measured 100s per browser leg, with the before/after run IDs recorded.
- Chromium and WebKit still use the same pinned Playwright/Go/shell environment, and lockfile changes invalidate any dependency cache.
- e2e/run-in-container.sh remains the reproducible local command.

title: The notification feed groups what belongs together
description:
Spec: .internal/specs/2026-08-22-notification-centre-design.md, epic 2.

Depends on nocx-p0xhg: it consumes the OccurrenceID identity and the feed that
epic establishes, and it moves the same files.

## What a user can do that they could not before

Expand a collapsed row to see the individual occurrences inside it, and narrow
a busy feed to one host, one session or one kind.

## Blocked on a decision epic 1 did not need

Point-in-time events versus stateful ones. Alertmanager-style grouping assumes
firing/resolved with a duration; program.notify is an instant. nocx has a
stateful class too -- session disconnected/reconnected, port appeared/
disappeared, agent run started/finished. Epic 1 needs no answer because it
groups only consecutive runs inside a bounded window. This epic cannot start
without one, and that decision is its first task.

## Success Criteria

- A run of occurrences collapsed into one row expands to the individual
  occurrences, each keeping its own timestamp and unread mark. Watched end to
  end by one automated check driving the UI.
- Narrowing the feed to one host hides rows from every other host and the
  unread count reflects the narrowed view or is explicitly stated not to.

## Deliberately out

Persistence; per-channel routing settings (epic 3).
close_reason: All five children closed. The epic's DONE WHEN is e2e/notification-centre-grouping.spec.ts at commit fe37fb0b: a run collapses to one row carrying a count, expanding it lists the individual occurrences each with its own time, narrowing to one host hides the other's rows and states the narrowed count, and the bell's badge does not move while the list is narrowed. The four decisions the epic was blocked on are recorded in .internal/plans/2026-08-22-notification-centre-epic-2.md and committed at 8014737d.
