  naming the AGENTS.md paragraph it does not contradict.
- No `--cpus` and no `--memory` is added — the measurement says neither is
  warranted, and adding them would reintroduce the "third machine" AGENTS.md
  rejected.
- A run on an otherwise idle machine takes the same wall clock as before, within
  noise, and the number is recorded here before and after.
- The value chosen is justified against Docker's default weight of 1024 rather
  than picked round.
close_reason: Landed on main in 380e6ab5. Both docker run invocations in .githooks/containerized-tests.sh now carry --cpu-shares=512, with the measurement and the reasoning in the file: a relative weight and not a ceiling, so an idle-machine commit keeps today's timing profile and the AGENTS.md objection to --cpus does not apply. No --memory was added — the measurement showed the host never below 4.5 GiB free. ci-linux.sh and the e2e runner deliberately unchanged: they are run by an integrator who has chosen to spend the machine, while the hook is involuntary. Verified in the strongest way available — core.hooksPath is .githooks, so the hook sources its own worktree copy, and the commit that introduced the flag ran through the hook WITH the flag applied and passed every gate.

title: Auto-categorization by a second model, which may only escalate
description:
Owner, 2026-08-16: "нужно добавить возможность авто-категоризации другой моделью" — a second
model judges the effect and risk of a proposed tool call, which is the classification-confidence
dimension of ADR-0020 decision 6 delegated to a model.

TWO INVARIANTS, both derived from decisions already taken, both load-bearing:

1. THE CLASSIFIER MAY ONLY RAISE SUSPICION, NEVER LOWER IT. ADR-0029 rule 7 settled this shape
for keystrokes: the model's judgement is untrusted input, and the local mechanical gate is what
keeps that path advisory. A classifier that can move a call from ask to permit makes the model
the author of its own authority, and a program printing "this is safe" is then writing into our
control flow. One-directional is not caution here; it is the same decision applied to another
input.

2. THE CLASSIFIER IS AN EGRESS POINT. It sees the call arguments, and arguments carry secrets.
The gate of design §7.1 covers it exactly as it covers the answering model, or we have cut a
hole in the gate the size of the thing it was built for.

COST: a second model call per proposed tool call, in latency and money, on every step the agent
takes. The role layer (its own bead) is what lets that be a cheap model rather than the
answering one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A classifier verdict can escalate a call that policy would have permitted; it can NEVER permit
  a call that policy would have escalated or refused. Asserted by feeding a classifier that says
  "safe" to a call the policy escalates, and watching it still escalate.
- The classifier's input passes the egress gate, asserted with an argument carrying known vault
  material.
- A classifier that is unreachable, slow or unparseable escalates rather than permitting.
  Asserted for each.
- The verdict is recorded on the attempt, so "why was this asked" is answerable afterwards.
- Both ends: with the classifier configured and quiet, an ordinary permitted call still runs.
close_reason: Classifier shipped: composes as the maximum over permit<ask<refuse so it can only escalate; consulted only where policy permits, asserted with a classifier that fails the test on invocation; its input passes the egress gate, asserted with known vault material reaching zero requests; unreachable, timed out, unparseable and role-unassigned all escalate. Merged.

title: tunnelLedger.track can assign into a nil map, and it runs on the control plane
description:
Found by wv6-approval while running the transport suite for an unrelated slice, and
reproduced by it on the clean tree with its own changes stashed — so it is not that slice.

internal/transport/ws_tunnel.go, tunnelLedger.track: the inner owners map is guarded against
nil and created on demand, while the two maps behind the pointers are not. An assignment into
a nil map panics, and this one runs on the control plane.

The panic did not reproduce on every run here — the transport package on this host is also
subject to the nocx-2h08 timing-flake class, and a run immediately after the failing one was
green. That is a reason to fix the nil-map hazard on its merits rather than to wait for a
reliable reproduction: the guard is missing whether or not the schedule exposes it today.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. go test ./internal/transport/ -race -count=1
2. Sometimes: panic, assignment to entry in nil map, reached from tunnel.open via seamSpecs.
3. Read tunnelLedger.track and compare the guard on owners with the absence of one on the
   maps behind l.tunnels and l.owners themselves.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every map the ledger writes into is non-nil by construction, or the write refuses honestly.
  Asserted by a test that constructs the ledger the way production does and the way a zero
  value would.
- Both ends: the ordinary open/close path still records and releases the tunnel.
- A test names the construction path that produced the nil, so the next reader knows which
  caller was wrong rather than only that a guard was added.

title: A tab shows its directory while a program runs in it: the title has no source between OSC 0/2 and cwd
description:
A tab running herdr is labelled "Users/shady". The owner reported it 2026-08-16
with a screenshot: four tabs, three of them showing a directory while a program
is running in them.

WHAT IS TRUE TODAY, and it is not a propagation failure. The title is composed
in one place and has exactly two sources:

    terminal-content.ts:627   const title = this.programTitle || this.cwdTitle
    tabs.ts:187               const next = <what arrived> || descriptor.defaultTitle

and programTitle is fed ONLY by an OSC 0/2 escape sequence — a program
declaring its own window title (terminal-content.ts:2009 attributes it to the
active domain). herdr emits none, so cwd wins. Everything behaves as written;
what is written is incomplete.

THE MISSING SOURCE ALREADY EXISTS IN THE RENDERER. frontend/src/command-ledger.ts
holds `readonly command: string` per record and a status of 'running', and the
shell integration is what puts it there. So the name of the foreground command
is known at the moment the tab is showing a directory instead of it. The chain
should be:

    programTitle  ||  the running command  ||  cwd

The middle link is the whole fix, and it closes exactly the reported case: a
program that declares nothing is still named by what it is.

A SECOND DEFECT FOUND ON THE WAY, and it is a naming lie with a consequence.
Tab._programTitle does NOT hold the program title. terminal-content composes
`programTitle || cwdTitle` and pushes the RESULT, so the field usually holds a
cwd. And tabs.ts:184 runs updateAgentStatus(title) on that same value — the
agent-state classifier is parsing a string that is often a filesystem path. The
field wants renaming to what it is, and the classifier wants the real program
title, which only TerminalContent has.

CARE: the middle link must not fight the first. A TUI clears its title on the
way out with an empty OSC 0/2, which tabs.ts:181 already documents. The running
command must not resurrect a name the program just cleared, and a finished
command must not leave its name on the tab.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a tab and run a program that sets no window title — herdr, or any plain
   long-running command.
2. Observed: the tab is labelled with the working directory.
3. Expected: the tab is labelled with the running command.
4. Contrast: run a program that DOES emit OSC 0/2 (vim, ssh to a host with a
   title-setting prompt) and the tab is named correctly — which is what shows
   the propagation itself is sound.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A tab running a program that emits no OSC 0/2 is labelled with the running
  command, not the directory.
- A program that DOES emit OSC 0/2 still wins over the command name.
- A TUI clearing its title on exit does not fall back to the command that is
  itself exiting; the tab returns to cwd.
- Tab._programTitle is renamed to what it holds, and updateAgentStatus is fed
  the real program title rather than the composed one.
- The design in .internal/specs/2026-08-16-tabs-panes-and-blocks-design.md §4.5
  says the label flows pane -> tab; this is that rule for a single pane, and
  the multi-pane label is derived from the same per-pane answer.
close_reason: Shipped. frontend/src/terminal-content.ts:1572 resolves a tab title as programTitle then commandTitle then cwdTitle, fed by runningCommandTitle(); panes.ts:114 renames the composed field to _pushedTitle and a real _programTitle is set by updateProgramTitle. Tests: terminal-content.test.ts:6444 and panes.test.ts:2236, both naming the bead. Commit 47dff7a7. Closed during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh.

title: Move the desktop shell to Wails v3, which is the only thing multi-window needs
description:
Move the desktop shell from Wails v2.13.0 to v3. Decided by the owner
2026-08-16: we are going there anyway, v0.1.0 is tagged and out so nothing is
in flight, and v3 has left alpha for beta. The earlier framing as a spike is
withdrawn — a spike only pays when the decision is open, and it is not.

WHAT MULTI-WINDOW HAS TO DO WITH IT. It is the only capability that needs v3:
v2's runtime has no window-creation call at all, every function is Window*
operating on the one window. The window model agreed the same day makes a
window a VIEWPORT, not a container — it shows one workspace at a time and owns
no tabs — so multi-window changes no object and no table when it arrives. This
bead is the shell, not the feature.

THE CODE IS SMALL, measured rather than estimated. Exactly TWO Go files import
wailsapp/wails:

    main.go                                the composition root: options.App
    internal/notify/wailsadapter/host.go    an adapter, and named one

The runtime surface used is SendNotification with the Notification* types,
OpenFileDialog, and the window options. The frontend has four touch points —
clipboard.ts (ClipboardGetText/SetText), log.ts (Log), platform.ts
(Environment) — plus the generated wailsjs bindings.

It is that small because AD-1 already made the backend a WebSocket server:
Wails shows a window and supplies three OS conveniences, and everything else
crosses the socket rather than the binding.

THE RELEASE PIPELINE IS WHERE THE WORK ACTUALLY IS, and it is verified only by
running it:

    wails.json              config.v2 schema; v3 has a different project shape
    release.yml:105,212     go install .../wails/v2/cmd/wails@v2.13.0
    release.yml:115         patches the product version into wails.json
    release.yml:128         wails build -platform darwin/universal -tags release
    release.yml:228         wails build -platform linux/amd64 -tags release,webkit2_41
    Makefile:9              WAILS ?= wails

A macOS universal binary and a Linux build with the webkit2_41 tag are not
things a unit test can confirm. Budget the work here, not in the two Go files.

WHAT DOES NOT MOVE, and it is most of the gate. cmd/devharness does not import
Wails at all, so the headless path, the Playwright suite and all three
containerized CI jobs are untouched. Only the `backend` job and the release
workflow are in scope.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The app builds and runs on macOS and Linux from the release workflow, and the
  produced artifacts are launched once each by hand before the bead closes.
- The three OS conveniences still work and are exercised: a notification is
  raised and its click resolves, the file dialog opens and cancels cleanly, and
  clipboard get/set round-trips.
- internal/storage/appdir.go still resolves nocx-dev without `-tags release`
  and nocx with it — a dev stand must not acquire the shipped profile
  directory (nocx-ti8w).
- cmd/devharness, the e2e suite and the three containerized CI jobs pass
  unchanged, with no edit to any of them.
- Nothing new imports Wails: the count stays at two Go files, or the bead says
  why it grew.
notes: macOS VERIFICATION IS THE OWNER'S, agreed 2026-08-16. The worker is on Linux and cannot build a darwin/universal binary, so the macOS half of release.yml lands UNVERIFIED by construction and the worker has been told to say so rather than claim it works. The owner will run it. Do not close this bead on a green Linux build alone — the acceptance criterion 'the produced artifacts are launched once each by hand' needs both halves, and the macOS half is handed over, not skipped.
close_reason: Shipped. go.mod:16 requires github.com/wailsapp/wails/v3 v3.0.0-beta.9, wails.json is gone, and docs/architecture.md:127 records the move to v3 at commit 8004fd72 and marks the open question closed. Follow-ups 1c417568 and b9cfbe65 already landed on top. Closed during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh.

title: The WebSocket has no origin check and no connection auth, which is fine for a webview and not for a browser
description:
The owner raised opening nocx in an ordinary browser (2026-08-16). Most of the
path already exists: cmd/devharness runs the backend with no Wails and no
display, main.ts falls back to the WS port when GetWSPort is unavailable, and
the whole e2e suite rides that path. What does not exist is the security
control that makes it safe, and this bead is that control — not the feature.

WHAT IS TRUE TODAY, verified rather than assumed. internal/transport/ws.go
listens on 127.0.0.1:0 (loopback, random port) and performs NO authentication
and NO origin check: CheckOrigin appears nowhere, and every token in that file
belongs to the import-plan store, not to the connection. The security model is
entirely "only a local process can reach it, and the only local process that
does is our own webview".

WHY THAT MODEL BREAKS THE MOMENT A BROWSER IS ALLOWED. A WebSocket handshake
from a browser page is NOT subject to the same-origin policy the way XHR is:
any page the user visits can open ws://127.0.0.1:<port>. The random port is
obscurity, not a control — a page can scan it in under a second. Behind that
socket are shell spawning, filesystem access and the vault unlock flow, so the
consequence of a successful connection is a shell on the user machine, not a
data leak. nocx-52b is the same class already met once in this repo: "XSS in
the connections UI + no CSP = renderer takeover".

SHAPE, not prescribed: the connection must prove it was launched by us rather
than merely reaching us — an Origin allow-list plus a per-launch secret the
webview (or the browser tab we opened) carries and a foreign page cannot
guess. The token-in-URL form Jupyter uses is the familiar one. Both halves are
needed: an Origin check alone is forgeable by a non-browser client, and a
token alone leaks through URL history and referrers.

DELIBERATELY OUT: the browser feature itself, any remote (non-loopback) bind,
and multi-window. Wails v2 cannot open a second window at all — its runtime
has no window-creation call, every function is Window* operating on the one
window — so multi-window is a Wails v3 question and a separate decision.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A connection without a valid Origin AND a valid per-launch secret is refused
  before any RPC is dispatched, and the refusal is tested over the real socket.
- The secret is per launch, never persisted, and never appears in a log line.
- The Wails path still connects with no user-visible change.
- A test asserts a forged Origin alone does not admit, and that a leaked token
  presented from a foreign Origin does not admit either.
close_reason:
WRONG, and closed as invalid rather than left open. Both controls this bead asked for ALREADY EXIST and are enforced.

internal/transport/ws_auth.go carries:
  - OriginPolicy, with LoopbackOriginPolicy for development and PinnedOriginPolicy for production ('exactly the origins the shipped app…'), matching scheme and hostname while deliberately ignoring the port because it exists only under wails dev;
  - a per-launch connection token: tokenProtocolPrefix 'nocx.token.', tokenBytes = 32, WithTokenSource, Token().

And it is enforced at the handshake: ws.go:1008 sets s.upgrader.Subprotocols = []string{tokenProtocol(s.token)}, so gorilla completes the upgrade only for a client that requested the matching subprotocol. A page that does not know the token cannot connect. That is precisely the 'Origin allow-list plus a per-launch secret the webview carries and a foreign page cannot guess' this bead proposed as work to be done.

HOW I GOT IT WRONG, recorded because the shape recurs: I grepped ws.go alone for CheckOrigin/token/auth, saw only the import-plan token store, truncated the output with head -10 — which cut line 1008 — and read absence out of my own truncation. Then I stated it to the owner as a security gap. AGENTS.md names this exact failure: writing from what the search remembered instead of reading the file that owns the boundary. One file is not the boundary; ws_auth.go is, and its name says so.

Surfaced by the Wails v3 worker (nocx-mgbjx), which had to touch ws_auth.go for a real reason: the v3 webview sends origin wails://localhost where v2 sent wails://wails, so the allow-list must learn the new hostname or the app rejects its own window.

What remains true and is NOT this bead: opening nocx in an ordinary browser still needs a decision about which origins are pinned for that case, because a browser tab is not the app's webview. If that is wanted, it is a small addition to an existing policy, not the construction of one.

title: Step 7: transition to writing-plans
description:
## Acceptance Criteria

The implementation plan exists and the epic references this brainstorm via discovered-from.

title: The egress gate: every tool return is screened against secrets before it leaves for the provider (design §7.1)
description: readScreen's production grant flip is blocked on this (nocx-ljfwz): no workspace grant policy is safe to name until the egress gate AND the approval surface land — autonomous/ask-on-mutate would send screen content to the provider unscreened, ask-every-time would suspend runs with no approval UI to render them. The gate is design §7.1 (refuse and ask, one consent surface with destructive commands — §7.3), the recognizer is already factored (internal/secrets.Detect beside Mask), and the approval machinery exists (ApprovalStore, escalate, compose.StatefulInterrupt); what is missing is the screening step at §6.7's ingest and the finding-carrying ask + its renderer surface (nocx-x8s2 owns the surface).
acceptance_criteria: A tool result containing a value known to the vault suspends the run and names the finding on the surface (design §7.1: refuse and ask; vault comparison beats any pattern). A heuristic match (secrets.Detect) suspends the same way, and the surface distinguishes known-material from heuristic. Error paths are screened on the same path. Paired: a tool result with no finding is returned unchanged.
close_reason: Egress gate shipped and merged: every tool return path including errors is screened before it leaves; known vault material and heuristic matches suspend distinguishably; a sealed vault fails closed rather than degrading to patterns; a finding carries offsets and the vault's own name, never the material. internal/masking is the one owner both directions use.

title: internal/notify: one test is 82 of the package's 90 seconds, proving a transitive property quadratically
description:
TestNoninterference_ResolutionIndependentOfPresentation (internal/notify/policy_test.go:928)
is 81.84s of internal/notify total 90.1s. The other 39 tests in the package sum
to about 1.3s. Measured 2026-08-16, go test -race -count=1 -v, on
integration/wave-1-2.

WHAT IT COSTS, from the code rather than a guess:

  payloadValues() has 29 entries, TWO of them a mebibyte
    (strings.Repeat("x", 1<<20) and the same for "Б", which is 2 MiB of bytes)
  presentations = 3 x 29                        =      87
  pairs         = 87 x 87 + 2000 random         =   9 569
  x 4 kinds x 3 trusts                          = 114 828 iterations
  x 2 Raise calls each                          = 229 656 calls

Roughly an eighth of those pairs carry a multi-megabyte payload on one side or
both.

THE PROPERTY IS TRANSITIVE AND THE SWEEP IS QUADRATIC. What the test asserts is
that route resolution does not depend on presentation — an equivalence over
outcomes, checked with sameOutcome. Equality is transitive, so "every
presentation resolves the same as every other" is proved by "every presentation
resolves the same as ONE FIXED REFERENCE". That is 87 comparisons where the
current code does 7 569, for exactly the same property and exactly the same
corpus. Nothing about the coverage weakens.

Estimated after: 114 828 iterations -> about 25 000, and with the reference
outcome computed once per (kind, trust) instead of per pair, one Raise per
iteration instead of two. 82s -> single digits.

CARE REQUIRED, or the change trades time for a wrong answer. The router carries
coalescing and rate state across Raise calls on the same SessionID, so the
sequence and COUNT of calls is itself an input. Keep the shape the test has now
— raise the reference, raise the candidate, compare — rather than reusing one
reference outcome across a whole loop, unless the state is proved not to move.

The random hostile pairs stay: they are the part that is not covered by the
corpus, and comparing each random payload against the reference is the same
transitive argument.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The test compares each presentation against a fixed reference rather than
  against every other presentation, and says in a comment why that proves the
  same property.
- The corpus is unchanged — no payload is dropped to buy time, including the
  two oversized ones.
- The random-pair portion still exercises randomly generated hostile payloads.
- internal/notify total drops below 15s under go test -race -count=1, and the
  test still fails if route resolution is made to depend on title or body
  (demonstrate by making it depend, once, and recording the failure).

title: The test suite never parallelizes: zero t.Parallel() in 276 files, and the slowest package sets the gate
description:
Not one t.Parallel() call exists in the repository: 276 test files declare tests,
zero declare parallelism. Packages run concurrently with each other; inside a
package every test waits for the one before it.

That is the dominant term in the gate wall clock, because wall clock is set by
the SLOWEST PACKAGE, not by the sum. Measured 2026-08-16 in the ci-linux
container on integration/wave-1-2:

  internal/shellintegration  111.4s   232 tests, no dominant — top test 6.52s
  internal/notify             90.1s    40 tests, ONE is 81.84s (see nocx-<sibling>)
  internal/transport          82.7s   718 tests, no dominant — top 8.04s
  internal/app                67.9s

shellintegration is the critical path and it is the clearest case: 232 tests
summing to 111s with the largest at 6.5s means the package is a long tail of
tests that each spawn a real shell and wait on it. Waiting is not CPU. Six
cores sit idle while one test drives one bash.

WHAT THIS IS NOT. It is not redundant tests, and the fix is not deleting any.
Nothing found in this measurement suggests a test that does not earn its place.
The finding is shape, not surplus.

WHY IT IS NOT A BLANKET EDIT, and why this is a task rather than a one-liner.
t.Parallel() is only sound where tests are independent, and these are the least
independent tests in the repo: they spawn processes, bind ports, write temp
dirs, set environment, and internal/app reaches a keystore. A blanket addition
would convert a slow suite into a flaky one, which is a strictly worse trade —
AGENTS.md already carries two P0 beads (nocx-2h08, nocx-fv1dw) bought by tests
that were merely timing-sensitive.

So the work is per-package and evidence-led: audit what each test actually
shares, parallelize the leaves that share nothing, and leave the rest serial
with a comment saying why. shellintegration first — it is the critical path
and its cost is almost entirely waiting.

## Acceptance Criteria

- At least internal/shellintegration parallelizes the tests that provably share
  no process, port, directory or environment, with the ones left serial naming
  their reason in a comment.
- ./scripts/ci-linux.sh is green across both keyring variants on three
  consecutive invocations after the change — parallelism that buys flake is a
  regression, not a win.
- The wall clock of the slowest package is reported before and after in the
  bead, from the container, so the next person knows what it bought.

title: The author reaches the wire and not the store, so a restart forgets who ran it
description:
Found by wv3-iadtt in its own work and confirmed by an independent review of the same
diff. Reported rather than hidden, which is why this bead exists in the same round.

history.record now carries the author and the ack echoes it, but nothing durable keeps it:
the command_history row has no author column, and no entries row is written at all. So
after a restart an agent command is indistinguishable from a human one, and the wire
promises a fact the store does not hold.

The durable home is NOT a new column on command_history. ADR-0019 has one authoritative
ledger and entries.kind IN (shell,agent,action) already carries exactly this
(internal/content/sqlite.go:570); command_history is the interim store and says so. So this
is the entries write path, and it belongs with the agent-mode write path rather than with
the wire slice that surfaced it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An agent command survives a restart still attributed to the agent, asserted by writing,
  restarting and reading back — not by asserting the ack.
- The attribution is read from the ledger entry, never re-derived from what was running.
- Both ends: a human command survives a restart attributed to the human.
- No second author column is introduced beside entries.kind.
close_reason: The author is durable: the command-history repository reads and writes through entries — insert, list, lookup, query, redaction rewrite and retention sweep — so a restart keeps who ran a command, and the interim command_history table is left with no reader and no writer. Merged 69a594c5.

title: The remote footprint is buried at the bottom of the Connections page instead of being its own settings screen
description:
The remote footprint is a section at the bottom of the Connections page. It
belongs on a settings page of its own.

It is not about a connection. It answers "what has nocx written on other
machines, and how do I take it off" — a per-machine ledger of shell bundles
and helper installs, keyed by host identity, that no saved connection owns.
Reaching it means opening Connections and scrolling past the whole profile
list, which is also where a user goes to do something else entirely.

The page is also where the consent answers must become visible and revocable
(footprint-consent design §5.3: "the footprint screen lists what is installed
where and revokes the answer"), which nocx-j49sp needs and which would sit
badly as a third block under a list of saved connections.

The settings rail already has the shape for this: pages are registered in
settings.tsx with an id, a title and an optional groupId from the Go-declared
catalogue (nocx-dgsp), and Connections itself is a top-level ungrouped page.
FootprintSection already takes its own client and renders a PageSection, so
the move is a registration plus a deletion, not a rewrite.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Settings → Connections. Scroll past every saved connection and every group.
2. "Remote footprint" is the last section on the page, mixed in with the
   editing surface for saved connections.
3. There is no rail entry for it, so it cannot be reached or linked directly,
   and a user who has never scrolled the Connections page will not know it
   exists.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The remote footprint is its own page in the settings rail, reachable by one
  click from a cold start, with the rail row named for what it is.
- The Connections page no longer renders it, and no longer takes a footprint
  client it does not use.
- Deep-linking still works: the section keeps a stable page id, and the e2e
  that visits it selects it by page id rather than by scrolling Connections
  (AGENTS.md: a display rename must not break a spec).
- An automated check watches a person reach the page and see a listed
  footprint — the epic rule, since this is the surface's only entrance.
- Whatever the page is grouped under is a deliberate choice, not a default:
  either a rail group from the Go catalogue or explicitly top-level beside
  Connections.
notes: Backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh: moved from in_progress (untouched since 2026-08-15) back to open — NOT STARTED, no trace of the id in the tree or in git log. The footprint is still rendered inside the Connections page: frontend/src/connections.tsx:2776 mounts FootprintSection and settings.tsx:494 still passes footprintClient into ConnectionsView. The settings rail registers backup, connections, secrets, vault, endpoints, snippets, skills, roles, policy and about — there is no footprint page id, so no rail entry exists.

title: Notes in a backup: a section somebody writes
description: Spec §10, ADR-0027, and the snippets backup section (nocx-utbm) as the shape.
acceptance_criteria:
A library survives backup -> wipe -> restore with bodies and timestamps intact.
A backup written before notes existed restores without touching notes.
The preview reports a non-zero note count.
A failed note write rolls back with everything else in the same restore.
close_reason: Notes are a backup section written inside the same prepared/committed interval as connections and settings, so a failed write rolls the library back with everything else. A document without the section says nothing about notes (a pre-feature backup restores without touching them); merge adds what is missing and never lets an old copy overwrite a newer edit; a service with no notes store refuses a notes-carrying document before the journal is written. The preview reports the count, which is why two backup schemas changed — the over-the-wire contract test caught the mismatch.

title: The consent ask has no No: denied is a state the resolver honours and no surface can write
description:
The consent store models three answers — unknown, granted, denied — and the
resolver honours all three: a denied machine is refused, never asked again and
never upgraded. Nothing can produce the third one.

`internal/helper/consent` exposes Grant and no Deny. The only writer in the
product is ws_shell_footprint.go:210 (`h.consent.Grant(fp)`), reached from
shell.footprint.consent. The Git panel's consent card offers a single button,
Accept. So the honest state of the surface is: accept, or leave the question
open forever and be asked again on every visit.

That is not merely a missing button. The design's whole argument for asking at
the feature (D8) is that the ask is rare and answerable; an ask with no "no"
is a nag, and the store's own comment has said so since it was written — the
Denied constant carries "This bead has no writer for it (the ask surface is
nocx-1xxa's)". nocx-1xxa closed with the ask surface built and the decline
half not.

The footprint-consent design has more to say about the shape than a plain
button. §5.2's neighbourhood spells the decline as an offer with two exits —
decline and keep what is installed, or decline and remove it — and says it is
"never the default, but not hidden in settings either". Whoever takes this
should read that before drawing a second button.

Found while writing ADR-0034, which settles WHERE the answer lives (keyed by
host-key fingerprint, not on the profile) and deliberately does not touch what
the surface can say. Deleting profile.RelayConsent removed a control that
could spell "denied" — but it was a control that governed nothing, so this gap
predates it and is unchanged by it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open an SSH tab to a host with no stored answer, then open the Git panel in
   a repository.
2. The panel raises "Allow the nocx helper on this host?" with one button:
   Accept.
3. There is no way to answer no. Close the panel and the machine stays
   unanswered, so the same ask is raised the next time anyone opens the panel
   on that host.
4. `grep -rn "\.Grant(\|Deny(" --include=*.go internal/ | grep -v _test`
   returns exactly one writer, and it grants.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A user can decline the helper for a machine, and the decision sticks: the
  ask is not raised again for that host key, asserted end to end rather than
  at the store.
- The decline is reachable from the same place the ask is — the panel — not
  only from settings, and is not the default action.
- Declining leaves shell delivery untouched: the session keeps its blocks
  (§5.2, "declining a deployed binary must not also decline shell scripts —
  different risks"), asserted, since ADR-0033/nocx-7k8ma put the same rule on
  the accepting side.
- Whether declining also offers to remove an existing footprint is decided
  against the footprint-consent design §5.2 rather than invented, and the
  choice recorded.
- A denied machine can change its mind: the footprint screen is where the
  answer is revoked (§5.3), and a revoked answer makes the machine askable
  again.

title: Notes: write it down without leaving the terminal
description:
Spec: .internal/specs/2026-08-16-notes-design.md (2026-08-16).

A person presses one chord and is typing. What they type survives the app closing, is named without being asked, and is found later by a word they remember from inside it.

Storage is SQLite in its OWN encrypted file (notes.db, adiantum VFS + the existing content key), NOT the content database: internal/content rebuilds its file on a schema change and discards the rows, which is right for a log and robbery for authored text. FTS5 was measured available on 2026-08-16 (ext/fts5.Register over the wasm module already in go.mod), including a Cyrillic match and snippet() for result excerpts.

Surfaces: an activity-bar panel (find), a tab (write), ⌥⌘N (capture). Notes never become a third input target — ADR-0004 keeps the prompt answering 'shell or agent'.
acceptance_criteria:
Press ⌥⌘N in a terminal pane, type two lines, close the tab, restart the backend, find the note in the panel by a word from its SECOND line, open it, and the text is exactly what was typed — one automated end-to-end check watches this.
deadcode -filter 'nocx/internal/note' is empty AND note.NewService has a caller outside its own tests.
The store survives a schema change: a migration test writes v1, opens with v2, and every row is still there (the notes store never discards — spec §4.2).
notes.search finds a note by a word that appears only in its body, and the result carries an excerpt containing that word.
No title is ever stored: editing the first line changes the tab title, the list row and the search result, and the database has no title column.
A failing save keeps the text on screen and says why; the tab cannot close silently over it.
With the store unavailable the panel states the reason and offers no create.
A library survives backup -> wipe -> restore with bodies and timestamps intact.
DELIBERATELY OUT: sync/sharing, folders/tags/links, attaching a note to a session or directory or block (spec §11 says where that would attach later), a rendered markdown preview, a second editor implementation, and any secret detector (§9).
NOT TOUCHED: frontend/src/snippets/** appears in no commit of this epic.
close_reason: Every criterion holds. The e2e gate watches a person press ⌥⌘N, type two lines, close the tab, lose the renderer to a reload, and find the note again by a word from its SECOND line — the search index answered, not a filter over titles. deadcode -filter 'nocx/internal/note' is empty and note.NewService is called from app.go. A v1 file opened by this build keeps every row (the store migrates, never rebuilds — the rule that separates it from internal/content). No title column: the name is derived on the way out and the renderer never derives its own. A failing save keeps the text on screen with the reason and never reports success. With the store unavailable the panel states the reason and offers no create. A library survives backup -> wipe -> restore with bodies and timestamps intact, and the restore rolls back with everything else when the write fails. frontend/src/snippets/** appears in no commit of this epic.

title: The exit cause is proved in two halves and never end to end
description:
nocx-ictcq gave the exit notification a cause and proved it in two halves:

  - the CAPTURE seam — RealChannel.recordWait before close(done), and the same
    in LocalPty — is covered by the ssh package's real-server tests;
  - the CLASSIFICATION and the WIRE are covered by internal/transport's exit
    tests against a controllable fake.

Their COMPOSITION is proved transitively, not by one test. No test drives a real
sshd channel through session.Wait() into the transport's exit monitor and out
onto the wire. The transport package deliberately has no in-process server with a
shell handler — its tunnel server has none — and the real-server infrastructure
lives in the ssh package instead.

Reported by the wv1-ictcq worker when asked to name what it could not verify,
rather than left silent. Recorded so the gap is scheduled instead of remembered.

ONE MORE UNDRIVEN BRANCH, same shape: *gossh.ExitError — a remote shell that
exited on its own with a non-zero status — is not fed to the mapping directly,
because the type cannot be constructed in a test (its Waitmsg fields are
unexported). Its real path is exercised in the ssh suite; the mapping branch is
reached only there.

WHAT THIS IS NOT. AGENTS.md's rule 2 asks an epic to prove its happy path end to
end. This is that check for the exit-cause work, and it is filed as a task rather
than a blocker because the halves are genuinely covered — what is missing is the
seam between them, which is exactly where a defect would hide and exactly what
transitive proof cannot see.

## Acceptance Criteria

One automated check drives a REAL ssh channel to a real in-process sshd, ends the
remote side without an authoritative exit status, and observes the exit
notification arriving on the socket with cause=interrupted and no status — the
whole path, not two halves.

The paired case: the remote shell exits with a non-zero status and the same check
observes cause=exited carrying it. That is the *gossh.ExitError branch, reached
by the real server rather than by constructing the type.

Where the check lives is the implementer's call, but it states in a comment why
the transport package could not host it, so the next reader does not re-derive
the reason.

title: A session that cannot be reached reads as unknown, never as dead
description:
Design: §8 item 4 and D7.

WHAT LANDS: liveness as {liveness, livenessEpoch, observedAt} over
alive | dead | unknown | interrupted. A node is 'dead' ONLY on an
AUTHORITATIVE TERMINAL EVENT.

UNKNOWN IS THE POINT. A child on a host we cannot currently reach is neither
alive nor dead, and both of the other renderings lie. The epoch is what stops a
late observation from a previous incarnation reviving a current record.

REUSE, DO NOT INVENT. internal/content/ledger.go:336 already uses 'interrupted'
as an assistant-run state after a restart rather than asserting liveness. Same
principle; take the word rather than spelling a second set.

BUILDS ON nocx-ictcq, which gives the exit notification a CAUSE separating an
authoritative terminal event from a loss. Without that cause this projection has
nothing to distinguish dead from unknown, so that bead lands first.
acceptance_criteria: A session's liveness is {liveness, livenessEpoch, observedAt} on the record and the wire, against its contract. A test drives each transition and asserts a host that stopped responding yields unknown, not dead. A test asserts a late observation carrying an older epoch does NOT overwrite a current record. A test asserts dead is reached only from an authoritative terminal event, by driving a loss and finding it is not dead.
close_reason:
Merged into feat/workspaces at b531d046 (032bed72). Liveness is {liveness, livenessEpoch, observedAt} over alive | dead | unknown | interrupted.

The set splits in a way the bead did not name and that is the best decision in it: alive and unknown are ASSERTED, dead and interrupted are DERIVED from ExitOutcome by one writer and can be asserted by nobody. A terminal record is final. And the terminal state is derived lazily on read rather than by a per-session goroutine watching Done, which makes the invariant structural instead of remembered.

'unknown' has a real producer, which is what stops this being a vocabulary nobody reaches: the ssh keepalive's NON-FINAL probe failure. deadcode -whylive confirms the chain from main through startKeepalive to PublishLiveness. Observations are host-granular, because a keepalive failure is evidence about a machine and the connection is pooled (AD-4).

Two AD-8 calls worth keeping. The wire carries two of the four values, not four: exit's cause already IS the terminal half in the same words, and publishing both would be two answers on one socket — the shellIntegrationReason defect. And the renderer shows a toast rather than the tab warning mark, because that mark already has an owner and a second writer is the two-surfaces-one-input defect.

Not persisted, and correctly so: nothing persists a session at all yet. The remote helper will enter through the Observation seam, which is why Observe takes an epoch it did not mint.

title: Lineage grants nothing, and a parent's death never closes its children
description:
Design: §8 items 5 and 6, and D6.

Two PROHIBITIONS. They cost nothing to state now and are enforced from this
epic's first commit so that no later epic can implement 'lineage implies
control' as a temporary shortcut.

1. NO ADDRESSABILITY FOLLOWS FROM LINEAGE ALONE. Being someone's child is
   provenance. It is never permission to observe, drive or close. The reason is
   ADR-0020's: A creates B; B is taken over, re-credentialed and ssh'd into
   production; B is a descendant of A forever, so ancestry alone would leave A
   reading and driving a session whose operator and context changed.

2. A PARENT'S DEATH NEVER CLOSES ITS CHILDREN — not on process exit, not on a
   backend restart, not on a dropped link. Only an explicit human act may, and
   closing a tab with live descendants ASKS rather than decides. Three of the
   four ways to lose a parent are FAILURES, and a failure carries no information
   about whether the work is still wanted.

A prohibition with no test is a comment. Both get assertions.
acceptance_criteria: A test asserts that a session holding only a lineage edge to another cannot observe, send input to, or close it — the attempt is refused at the backend, not hidden in the renderer. A test kills a parent by each of process exit, backend restart and dropped link, and finds its children still alive each time. Closing a tab with live descendants raises a prompt that NAMES them, asserted rather than inspected.
close_reason:
Merged into feat/workspaces at ce67e7ac (b3b5f1e3). Both prohibitions are enforced and, more to the point, both are ASSERTED — the bead's own line was that a prohibition with no test is a comment.

Prohibition 1 costs no new production code, which is the right price: the single owner of 'may this caller address this session' is already connState.Owns, so the rule is held against that rather than against a new gate. The strongest test is the differential one — a child and a stranger root are refused by close and resize with the identical code AND message, so any implementation that reads the edge passes 'a stranger is refused' and fails here. The data-plane half asserts the refusal reached nothing: a frame carrying rm -rf / addressed to the child never reaches its channel, paired with a legitimate frame so the negative is not an empty channel.

Prohibition 2 covers all four ways to lose a parent, including the explicit human close the bead did not list, and runs a two-level chain because 'descendants' is the claim.

EVERY ASSERTION WAS MUTATION-TESTED — each run against a deliberate implementation of the violation it forbids, and each went red: a subtree-closing Reg.Close, a disconnect handler reaping the sessions its lost tabs opened, an ancestor check bolted onto close and onto resize and onto the data plane separately, and a renderer closePane that takes the subtree with its root. That is the only evidence a prohibition can have.

One honest limit, stated rather than papered over: 'backend restart' cannot be asserted literally because nothing survives a restart — there is no session store. What a restart LEAVES is assertable and was: the parent's incarnation permanently unresolvable, and that unresolvability is never a reason to end a child.

The acceptance clause this does not fully reach — nothing in the renderer originates a parent edge, so no tab has a descendant and the close prompt cannot fire in the product — is nocx-ebl4.1, filed before this worker reported it.

title: Every session carries its workspace, and the field is not nullable
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-15-workspaces-ux-design.md §5.2, which supersedes
the prior design's §8 item 3.

The prior design called this the weakest item in the epic and kept it on the
retrofit argument alone, as a NULLABLE field. Both changed. A tab is always in a
workspace (the default one never renders), and the later fence epic consults the
field IN THE BACKEND before addressing, spawning, observing or input — an
enrolled external agent reaches the backend over its own socket and never
touches the renderer, so a fence the backend cannot name is a UI convention.

WHAT LANDS: a non-null workspaceId on the session record and on every session
wire and restore shape. It CARRIES NO BEHAVIOUR here. No authority is read from
it in this epic.

DO NOT ADD A BACKEND TAB ID. AD-7 makes the session the identity the backend
owns; a tab can hold several sessions; the renderer already knows which tab a
session is in. Every backend-to-renderer address is a sessionId.
acceptance_criteria: Every session record and every session wire shape carries a non-null workspaceId, asserted over the wire against its contract. A test asserts a session cannot be created without one. NEGATIVE: a test asserts nothing in this epic reads authority, addressability or reachability from the field — grep-level is not enough, the assertion is that the dispatcher has no such input.
notes: AMENDED 2026-08-17 by .internal/specs/2026-08-16-tabs-panes-and-blocks-design.md §4.5. workspaceId MOVES FROM THE SESSION TO THE TAB. The invariant is unchanged — never null, one owner of the default, which internal/workspace.Default now holds — and the argument for keeping it in the backend survives whole, because the backend now owns the whole chain and resolves pane -> tab -> workspace itself. On the session it becomes derived. The field added to session.Config and Session on feat/workspaces is therefore an intermediate step, not the destination; nocx-isoph is where it moves.
close_reason:
Merged into feat/workspaces at 2cca92c4 (908b4ec3). The work had been finished, committed and pushed on feat/nocx-fraus-workspaceid and never integrated — it sat eighty commits behind while this bead read in_progress and the epic was reported as having one task left. Found only because the workspaces decomposition needed to know whether the field existed, and grep said it did not.

Every session carries a non-null workspaceId, immutable for its lifetime like Identity, defaulted by the registry — the single owner of that decision — to internal/workspace.Default. It carries no behaviour: nothing reads authority, addressability or reachability from it, and the fence that later consults membership is a separate epic.

Four merge conflicts, all one shape: the lineage work and this branch each added a field to the same struct, the same result DTO and the same contract's required list. Kept both — a session has an incarnation identity, a parent edge AND a workspace. One defect existed only in the merge, exactly the shape AGENTS.md names: a struct literal in ws_lineage_test.go predated workspaceId becoming required with minLength 1, so the DTO-conformance test failed against a schema neither branch had alone. Both branches were green.

Note for nocx-isoph.2: the design moves workspaceId from the session to the TAB, and on the session it becomes derived. The field landing here is the intermediate step §8's retrofit argument asks for, not the destination.

title: A tab knows which tab opened it, by an edge that cannot be forged or rewritten
description:
Design: §8 item 2, and D8.

WHAT LANDS: an immutable parent edge using the FULL identity from the first
child — (backendInstance, sessionId, sessionEpoch) — not a bare parentId.
orca validates repo, host, project AND both endpoint instance ids and strips
cycles before projecting (src/shared/resolved-worktree-lineage.ts), and it
needed all of them.

The edge answers PROVENANCE ONLY. It never confers the right to observe or
control — that is a separate revocable Delegation and it belongs to nocx-mp2vd.
Bounds are an open question in the design §11 item 6: cycles, self-parent,
depth, fan-out, and what a restored child referring to an absent parent means.
acceptance_criteria: A child session carries an immutable parent edge naming the full identity, asserted over the wire against its contract. A cycle, a self-parent and a parent naming a different backend instance are each refused by a test. A test asserts the edge cannot be rewritten after creation.
close_reason:
Merged into feat/workspaces at b531d046 (f57f1fe9). session.Ref carries the full identity (instanceId, sessionId, sessionEpoch) rather than a bare parentId; validateParent is the single owner of what may be admitted and runs before any spawn or dial; open takes an optional parent and the ack reads it back off the record as a nullable, required object.

The judgment calls the bead left open were all decided with an argument. An unresolvable parent is refused AT ADMISSION, because creation is the only moment the backend can witness 'A created B' and the edge is immutable afterwards — a well-formed claim naming nothing is a forged edge, and refusing makes the cycle and depth walks total. The interval closes at the CHILD's record, not the parent's, so a parent that exits leaves the edge untouched (D6 as a property of the record). Depth bounded at 64 and refused rather than truncated, since a truncated edge names a parent that is not the parent. Fan-out deliberately unbounded — today's only creator is a human opening a tab.

Filed from this work: nocx-ebl4.1. The record and the wire accept an edge and nothing in the renderer produces one, so every session today is a root. That was deliberate and the deferral is right — 'which tab opened this one' is a surface decision with three ambiguous cases, and guessing writes a wrong edge that is immutable by design. But it is filed, because 'the seam exists and nothing uses it' is the shape this repo has shipped before.

title: A session has an identity that survives a restart telling it from its successor
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-15-workspaces-lineage-and-orchestration-design.md §8 item 1.
FIRST child of nocx-ebl4; everything else in the epic keys on what this lands.

internal/session/session.go is memory-only and makes a session addressable by
inserting it into a map. A bare sessionId cannot tell a RESTORED record from a
CURRENT incarnation, and cannot prevent id reuse — so a late observation from a
previous incarnation can revive a record that is gone.

WHAT LANDS: sessionId plus a backend-instance identity and a session epoch,
on the record and on every session wire shape. Shape only — no store.

The argument for doing it now is nocx-if6 phase A's, reused unchanged:
retrofitting session identity after tabs, restore, the ledger and blocks all key
on a bare sessionId is a wide, unpleasant change, while adding it now is
mechanical.
acceptance_criteria: A session carries {sessionId, backendInstance, sessionEpoch} on the record and on the wire, with a contract in contracts/ per AGENTS.md rule 5 — including the ...OverTheWireConformsToContract test that validates the REAL result off the REAL socket, not a payload the test built. A test asserts that a record from a previous backend instance does not resolve to a current session of the same id.
notes: IMPLEMENTED on feat/nocx-3oupk-session-identity (66bebe6e), NOT on main. Identity is (backend instance, epoch) on the session record and on four backend-emitted, session-addressed wire shapes: open, exit, session.integrationChanged, lifecycle.changed. Request params that merely target a live session are unchanged, and inputStalled is deliberately out (un-contracted, connection-live, transient). The doc comment answers what the bead left open: two LIVE sessions can never share an id because the registry map collides, so the epoch's work is across TIME, not between live sessions — which is what makes the refusal total rather than probabilistic. The epoch follows internal/lifecycle's stated rule and the comment says why it is nevertheless not that epoch. The ledger keys Session on the bare id and gains this identity when a restore path lands rather than being given a second vocabulary now. Two tests read the identity off the real socket and match it against the registry. Coordinator caught nothing in the design; three round-trips were spent on gates the brief had named imprecisely (golangci-lint vs go vet, then the deadcode ratchet, which correctly rejected a wrapper that swallowed the entropy error the production path refuses).
close_reason: Landed on main in 06912fc4 (66bebe6e): a session names its incarnation — instanceId + sessionEpoch on the record and on the open ack, contract and conformance test included.

title: A notification that fails after acceptance tells nobody
description:
notify.raise answers immediately with {} — acceptance, not delivery. Under the
policy (internal/app/app.go:829) the event may be held in a debounce window and
delivered when it closes, or coalesced into a summary, so there is no synchronous
outcome to report. That shape is deliberate and correct: a program asking for a
notification must not block until a debounce window closes.

THE COST IT CREATES. Before the policy, a delivery failure reached the caller as
a JSON-RPC error — the handler maps Outcome.Err to -32603. After acceptance there
is no such path: a delivery that fails AFTER the RPC returned has nowhere to go.
notify.WithResultHandler exists for exactly this and its outcomes currently reach
no surface.

The notification design requires a refused delivery to be visible somewhere the
product can show. So this is not a missing nicety — it is the difference between
a notification pipeline that fails loudly and one that fails silently, and
AGENTS.md names the shape: a soft degrade must be visible in the product, not
only in a log.

SCOPE. Route WithResultHandler outcomes to a renderer-visible surface — the kit's
showToast at danger level is the existing answer; do not build a second one. The
router owns the destination (the renderer choosing one for itself is what the
notification design forbids), so the outcome travels as a fact and the renderer
renders it.

GATED ON nocx-sb3f. Every notification currently rides TryNotify on the
REFRESHABLE outbound queue, whose overflow policy is to DROP the frame. A failure
report delivered on a droppable queue can itself be dropped, which would make
this fix report its own success unreliably. sb3f is the bead that gives the
transport a delivery class for frames with no successor and no replay.

Recommended by the wv1-notify worker as the alternative to changing the wire
shape, and accepted by the coordinator 2026-08-15 on that basis. Filed as a bead
with a dependency edge rather than left as a promise, per AGENTS.md: a reported
blocker becomes a bead in the same minute or it evaporates between rounds.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Raise a notification through notify.raise so the policy accepts it into a
   debounce window.
2. Make the delivery fail after acceptance — an unavailable sink, or a dropped
   outbound frame.
3. Observed: the RPC already answered {}. Nothing in the product says the
   notification never arrived. The only trace is a result handler with no
   consumer.

## Acceptance Criteria

A delivery that fails after notify.raise has returned produces a user-visible
danger toast naming what failed, asserted by a test that fails the sink and finds
the toast — not a log line.

The destination is chosen by the router, not by the renderer, and a test asserts
the renderer raises nothing of its own accord.

No second toast component: the assertion names frontend/src/ui/toast.tsx.
close_reason: Closed
