Selected row: `--color-tab-active` = #1f2235.

Five, six and six steps out of 255 apart — and in the darker direction.

## Why darker-when-active is wrong here

That is the horizontal strip metaphor: the selected tab drops out of the strip
and merges into the terminal below it, and the shared edge is what sells it. A
vertical row has no edge to share, because the pane is beside the strip rather
than under it. So the metaphor buys nothing and spends the only cue available on
it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The selected row is distinguishable from an inactive one without looking for
  the indicator.
- The device is one the app already uses, not a new value chosen here.
- Applies to the vertical placement only; the horizontal strip keeps the
  merge-with-content treatment, which works because it has the edge for it.
close_reason: Accent tint mixed with the row's own fill, not with transparency. Measured, the two rows differed by five, six and six steps out of 255 and in the darker direction; the first fix made it darker still, because a translucent fill composites over the strip behind it at #0e0f15.

title: The vertical strip's activity indicator is a horizontal underline
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Switch the tab strip to vertical.
2. Make an inactive tab produce output.

Expected: a mark on that row, in the same visual language as the rest of the
vertical strip.
Actual: a 2px underline along the row bottom edge, inset 10px from each side —
the horizontal strip geometry unchanged. A row in a vertical strip has no
meaningful bottom edge, because the next row starts there, so it reads as a
divider between two tabs rather than as a mark on one of them.

## Second half: it shares the accent with the selection bar

Both were `--color-accent`. In the horizontal strip the two were told apart by
which edge they sat on, top versus bottom. That distinction does not survive the
vertical strip, where the selection indicator is a left-edge bar and the activity
mark should be one too.

## Acceptance Criteria

- In vertical placement the activity mark is a left-edge bar, not an underline.
- It is inset from top and bottom where the selection bar runs the full height,
  so the two differ in shape as well as colour.
- Its colour is the warning token, not the accent.
- It is not dimmed. The one mark whose job is to be noticed does not get an
  opacity below 1.
close_reason: A left-edge bar on the warning token, same height as the selection bar, undimmed. A horizontal underline has no edge to sit on in a vertical strip: the next row starts there, so it read as a divider between two tabs rather than a mark on one.

title: The connection row's SSH button is a protocol label pretending to be an action
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Settings -> Connections.
2. Look at any row in the list.

Expected: it is clear what kind of connection this is, and separately, what
clicking will do.
Actual: one control does both jobs and reads as neither. A button labelled `SSH`
sits at the right of every row; the word names the protocol, the button performs
quick-connect. It looks like a type tag that is somehow pressable.

## Second half: there is no type indicator at all

Every saved profile is SSH today, so nothing has had to say so. That stops being
true the moment a second kind of connection lands, and a list that never said
which was which is a list nobody can read.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The row action is an icon with an accessible name, not the protocol word.
- The protocol is shown as a quiet neutral badge on the row, not as an action.
- The badge stays quiet: it carries no information while SSH is the only kind,
  and must not look as though it does.
- The address ellipses before the badge does when the row is narrow.
close_reason: The row's two jobs are two controls now. Type is a quiet neutral Badge on the meta line, read off Base.type rather than hard-coded, so the first non-SSH profile labels itself instead of silently claiming to be SSH. The action is an IconButton with a Lucide plug glyph and an accessible name, revealed on hover or focus. Two things fell out of it: the neutral tone — the DEFAULT tone, the one you get by writing <Badge> — had no rule at all in badge.css and painted nothing, so it rendered as bare text with padding and read as a stray gap; and the meta line was at 2xs, 10.5px at the current base, which is the bottom of the scale and too small for the only copy of the address.

title: No About section: the app cannot say what version it is
description:
## What is missing

The settings rail has Clipboard, Interface, Export / Backup / Import and
Connections. Nothing says what build this is. A user filing a bug, or checking
whether an update landed, has nothing to read and nothing to quote.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An `About` item in the settings rail showing: version, build date, commit sha,
  the Go and Wails versions it was built with, and the platform.
- The values come from the binary, injected at link time (`-ldflags -X`), not
  from a constant somebody has to remember to bump. A dev build says so rather
  than lying about a version it does not have.
- A new read-only RPC serves them; the frontend does not guess any of it.
- A `Copy diagnostics` button that puts the whole block on the clipboard in one
  action, because the reason anyone opens this page is to paste it into a bug
  report.
- `make build` sets the ldflags, and a test asserts an unset version renders as
  something explicit rather than as an empty row.
close_reason: About page shipped: app icon, version, and commit/built/platform/Go/Wails, with Copy diagnostics. internal/version.Info composes link-time stamps with process facts; app.about is a new read-only RPC with a contract schema, generated renderer type, DTO and over-the-wire tests (the wire test fails if the handler ignores its injected descriptor). No field is ever empty — absence is the word 'unknown', owned once. make build/build-release stamp commit and date; VERSION stays unset so 'dev' keeps its updater meaning. e2e watches it end to end. Commit c2355fec.

title: No way to test an SSH connection without opening a tab
description:
## What is missing

The connection form has Save and nothing else. The only way to find out whether
a profile actually works is to save it, open a tab, and read whatever the shell
prints. That is a slow loop for the exact moment someone is least sure — while
they are typing the credentials in.

## Backend

There is no RPC for this. Measured against `internal/transport/ws.go`: the
method table has `profiles.*`, `groups.*`, `credentials.*`, `settings.*` and
`export.*` — no `ssh.test` and no probe of any kind. So this needs a new method
that dials, completes the handshake and authenticates, then closes without ever
opening a session.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A `Test` button beside Save in the connection form.
- It works on the **unsaved** form — testing before committing a profile is the
  whole point, so it sends the form state, not a profile id.
- Result is shown against the form: reachable / auth failed / host unresolved /
  timed out, with the server error text where there is one.
- A bounded timeout, so a black-holed host cannot hang the button forever, and a
  way to cancel while in flight.
- The button reports the connection outcome only. It never echoes a password, a
  passphrase or a key back to the frontend, in the result or in a log line.
- Go tests cover the four outcomes against the existing SSH test server.

## Depends on

Not blocked by the validation epic, but the two meet in the same button row —
Test on an invalid form should refuse rather than dial.

title: Scroll containers render the engine default scrollbar
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Settings -> Connections and select a saved profile so the form panel
   overflows.
2. Scroll the form panel.

Expected: a scrollbar that belongs to the app.
Actual: a wide, pale, opaque bar in the engine default treatment, which against
the dark theme reads as a piece of the browser sitting on top of the app. It also
appears without warning, because the panel only overflows once a profile is
selected — so it looks like a stray artefact rather than a scrollbar.

Measured: `grep -rn scrollbar frontend/src/styles` returned nothing. Not one of
the scroll containers was styled — `.cm-form-panel`, `.cm-list`,
`.ui-page__scroll`, `.ui-page__rail`, and the xterm viewport all fell back to the
engine.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Scrollbar thumb and track are drawn from theme tokens, so light and dark are
  correct from one declaration.
- The treatment is declared once at the base layer, not per surface.
- Exactly one mechanism is used. Chromium ignores the `::-webkit-scrollbar`
  pseudo-elements once `scrollbar-width`/`scrollbar-color` are set, so declaring
  both makes WKWebView and Chromium render different scrollbars from the same
  stylesheet.
close_reason: Scrollbar treatment added once at the base layer, thumb and track from theme tokens so light and dark follow without a second declaration. ::-webkit-scrollbar only — Chromium ignores the pseudo-elements once scrollbar-width/scrollbar-color are set, so declaring both would have given WKWebView and Chromium different scrollbars from one stylesheet.

title: The quick-connect action on a connection row is invisible until hover
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Settings -> Connections.
2. Move the pointer away from the list.

Expected: each row shows that it is connectable.
Actual: the row is two lines of text and nothing else. The "SSH" quick-connect
button (`.cm-item-actions`, `connections.tsx` `renderListItem`) is `opacity: 0`
until `.cm-item:hover`, so a list of fifteen identical rows offers no visible
affordance at all.

## Why hover-reveal is wrong here

Hover-reveal earns its keep when a row carries several actions and showing them
all would be noise. This row carries exactly one. Hiding it buys no quieting and
costs the only signal that a click does something.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The quick-connect button is visible on every connection row without hover.
- No `opacity` transition keyed off `.cm-item:hover` remains in connections.css.
close_reason: Fixed, then deliberately reverted — recorded because the reversal is the finding. Making the button permanent was the wrong answer to a real complaint: the row had nothing that said it was connectable. What was actually wrong is in nocx-fmoz — one control was doing two jobs, naming the protocol and performing an action. Once the row states its own type in a badge, the control no longer has to stay visible to explain the row, so hover-reveal came back. It came back with :focus-within beside :hover, which it never had: an opacity:0 element is still in the tab order, so a keyboard user was tabbing into a button they could not see.

title: The quick-connect palette: fixed size, a real New-connection action, a readable selection
description:
Reported by the owner in one pass. The palette resized as the filter narrowed the list; the
selected row was unreadable because `.item:hover` (class + pseudo-class) outranked
`.item--selected` on background while the label kept the dark text meant for the accent fill — and
`onMouseEnter` sets the selection, so that was every row under the pointer. "New connection" was a
saved profile with an empty host: opening it handed the backend an empty address and the tab came
up on "Terminal failed to start".

## Acceptance Criteria

- The palette keeps one size while filtering, and its empty state occupies the list area rather
  than hanging below it.
- The selected row is legible, including under the pointer.
- A New-connection entry opens Settings on the Connections page with a blank profile, and works
  whether or not Settings was already open.
- Profiles with no host are not offered; a separator appears only between two populated groups.

title: Settings rows: the reset affordance, the modified dot and the storage tag
description:
Three things on one row, each measured on the owner screen.

The reset button sat directly BELOW the control — which is where the pointer already is after
operating that control, so undoing the change just made was one slip away. The modified dot was
rendered only when modified, so its 6px box plus margin entered the flow and shoved the label
sideways the moment a value changed. The storage-class tag (Public/Private/Secret) printed one of
three words on every row with nothing in the product consulting `dataClass` — export eligibility is
decided by the control kind in `Registry.GetSnapshot`, not by the class.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The reset affordance is an icon at the right end of the row, level with the control, in a gutter
  the row reserves whether or not it is showing one.
- The label does not move when a row becomes modified, and its column lines up with the section
  heading above it.
- The storage-class tag is gone from the markup and its CSS with it.
- The rail is one gutter: the filter count and the section counts line up.

title: The vertical strip lists, filters and names its tabs
description:
The vertical placement shipped as a flat list of 38px rows with the strip actions stranded at the
bottom of the column, a horizontal accent bar claiming to be a left-edge one, and the strip itself
sitting left of the activity bar. Warp is the reference for ideas, not a design to copy: the owner
chose search, two-line rows and a left-aligned label, and kept our own left-edge indicator.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The strip sits between the activity bar and the panes.
- Its actions are one group in a header row with the filter field, at the top of the column.
- Typing in the filter hides non-matching rows without closing, deactivating or reordering tabs.
- A row shows the title and, when the title is a NAME rather than the directory, a dimmer second
  line with the cwd or host.
- The label is left-aligned in vertical and still centred in horizontal.
- The active row is marked by the 2px accent bar on its left edge.

title: One base type size, everything else relative to it
description:
Groundwork for the epic: the scale was declared in pixels (12/13/15/18/22) and `body` set
`font-size: var(--font-size-md)`, so the "base" governed nothing — every rule took an absolute
value and there was no single number a zoom control could move. Twenty declarations bypassed the
scale entirely, including a 10px/11px cluster that was one register written as two numbers, and
the terminal DOM at 14px against a canvas at 13.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `--font-size-base` and `--ui-scale` on `:root`, `html` computing `calc(base * scale)`, every
  other type size a rem ratio of it.
- No raw px font-size outside the two documented exceptions (the base anchor and the terminal).
- A lint rule rejects a px font-size TOKEN, with a negative fixture proving it fires.
- The terminal token and `renderers/font.ts::FONT_SIZE` cannot drift apart silently.

title: The activity indicator lights on the tab you just left
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run a command in tab 1 and let it print.
2. Switch to tab 2. Tab 1 shows the unread-activity indicator although nothing has happened
   in it since the switch.

## What is happening

`Tab.markActivity()` set the flag for output arriving in the ACTIVE tab, where nothing renders
it, and `setActive()` clears the flag on activation but not on deactivation — so it survived
the switch away. The neighbouring code already had the guard: `updateAgentStatus` checks
`!this._active`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Output arriving in the active tab does not set the unread flag.
- Output arriving in a background tab still does (the existing e2e case passes).

title: Button variants have no rule: two equal actions look different on one page
description:
`Button` offers `default`, `primary`, `danger` and `ghost`, and nothing says when to use which. Counted across the app: default 11, primary 6, danger 3, ghost 1.

On the Export page this is visible in one screen: "Export Configuration" is `default` and "Encrypt and Export" is `primary`, though both are the main action of their own section. The user reads that as two different kinds of button and asks where they came from — they are the same component, chosen differently.

What is missing is written guidance plus enough consistency for it to be believed: one primary per section (the action the section exists for), default for everything secondary, danger for destructive, ghost for a control that is a row rather than a button. Then sweep the call sites.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The rule is written down where a developer will meet it — the kit's README next to Button, and `button.tsx`'s own doc comment.
- Every existing call site matches the rule or carries a comment saying why it does not.
- Two sections of the same kind do not show two different button looks for the same kind of action.
close_reason: Variant rule written where a developer meets it — button.tsx's doc comment and ui/README.md. primary is the one action a section exists for, at most one per section; default for every other real action; danger for destructive; ghost for a control that reads as a row. Two clauses added during review that the first draft did not have: a control that reveals, expands or navigates is not a primary even when it is the only button in its section (which is why Show Backup Paths stayed default), and a button rendered once per row of a list is never primary, because emphasis is spent by repetition. Sweep: Export Configuration, Import and Decrypt and Import to primary; everything on Settings, Connections, Banner and Dialog already matched.

title: Font family and base size become settings
description:
Two independent choices, one mechanism: the UI font (`--font-family-ui`, `--font-size-base`) and the terminal font (`renderers/font.ts`: `FONT_FAMILY`, `FONT_SIZE`, `LINE_HEIGHT`). They are separate on purpose — a terminal wants a monospace at a size the user reads code at; the chrome does not.

The UI half is nearly free now that the scale is relative: one token to write. The terminal half is the work — the renderer must re-measure its cell after a font change and the PTY must be told the new grid, which is the resize path, not a repaint. Changing the family can also change cell width without changing the size, so the two cannot share a code path that assumes only the size moved.

Offer only fonts the host has. Enumerating them is platform work; a documented shortlist with a free-text fallback is an acceptable first cut, and should be named as such.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The UI font family and base size are settings; changing either repaints the chrome live, with no remount and no reload.
- The terminal font family and size are separate settings; changing either re-measures the cell, re-fits the grid and resizes the PTY.
- The relationship between `--font-size-terminal` and `FONT_SIZE` stays enforced (today's unit test) or is replaced by a stronger guarantee.
- A font the host does not have falls back visibly rather than silently rendering in the UA serif — the failure ADR-0013 was written after.

title: UI zoom from the keyboard, driven by --ui-scale
description:
`--ui-scale` exists on `:root` and multiplies `--font-size-base`; nothing writes it yet. Zoom is therefore: a persisted number, three key bindings, and clamping.

Specifics that decide the shape:

- **What zoom covers.** rem-based type scales with the root; the terminal does not (AD-6) and must keep its own size, or the grid and the canvas disagree. Say in the UI what zoom applies to, or the first bug report will be "zoom does not change my terminal".
- **The bindings.** Cmd/Ctrl `+`, `-`, `0` are the convention. They must not reach the PTY — the terminal takes single keystrokes, so this joins the app-hotkey layer, next to Cmd+T and Cmd+,.
- **Persistence.** A settings key, like every other preference, applied live through `SettingsObserver`.
- **Clamping.** Below about 0.8 the 2xs step stops being legible; above about 1.5 the shell chrome starts wrapping. Pick bounds and justify them by looking, not by arithmetic.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Cmd/Ctrl +, − and 0 change and reset the UI scale, and the change is visible without a restart.
- The value persists across a restart and is clamped to documented bounds.
- The terminal's own type does not change with UI zoom, and the UI says so where the user can read it.
- The bindings do not reach the PTY: a test asserts the keystroke does not appear in terminal input.

title: Type is user-adjustable: font, size and zoom
description:
The mechanism landed today and is unused: `tokens.css` declares `--font-size-base` and `--ui-scale` on `:root`, `html` computes `calc(base * scale)`, and every other type size is a rem ratio of it. So UI zoom is now one number, and a size setting is one number — which is exactly why this is worth doing now rather than as five scattered overrides.

The terminal is deliberately NOT on that scale: xterm rasterises from TypeScript (`renderers/font.ts`, `FONT_SIZE`) and does not react to the CSS root, so it needs its own lever and its own live-apply path (AD-6). A unit test already asserts `--font-size-terminal` equals `FONT_SIZE`; whatever ships must keep that true or replace the test with something stronger.

## Success Criteria
See acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: The user can change the UI font family and its base size, change the terminal's font family and size independently, and zoom the whole UI from the keyboard — each persisted across a restart and applied live, without a remount. DONE WHEN all three ship with tests and the type scale still reads zero px font-sizes outside the two documented exceptions. OUT OF SCOPE: per-surface font overrides, font ligature settings, and web-font loading — every font offered is one the host already has.

title: Dragging a tab works with groups — within one and across two
description:
Reordering by drag exists (`onReorder`, wired through TabStripBase). Once the list has groups, a drop is ambiguous: it can mean *move within this group*, *move to another group*, or *nothing, because the group is derived and cannot be assigned*.

That last case is the real question. If groups are derived from `descriptor.surfaceType`, dragging an SSH tab into the "Local" group is a request the model cannot honour — the tab's kind is a fact about its content, not a position. The options are: refuse the drop (and show that it is refused), let the group be an explicit override that the derivation only seeds, or keep drag strictly inside a group. Each is defensible; the task is to pick one and say why.

Also unresolved by the current implementation: the drop indicator. A flat list needs a line between two rows; a grouped list needs to distinguish "between these two rows" from "into this group, at the end".

## Acceptance Criteria

- Dragging a tab to a new position inside its own group reorders it there, and the order survives a strip swap (horizontal ↔ vertical).
- A drag that crosses a group boundary does exactly one documented thing, and a test asserts it — including the case where the answer is a refusal.
- The drop indicator distinguishes a position between rows from a drop onto a group.
- Dragging is unchanged in the horizontal strip.
notes:
READ BEFORE TAKING. Three beads now want to own one gesture, and AGENTS.md's rule is that two surfaces may never own the same input — whichever wins by evaluation order, the loser goes on advertising what it can no longer deliver.

This bead already names the ambiguity: a drop in a grouped strip can mean move-within-this-group, move-to-another-group, or nothing. Since it was written, two more meanings arrived:

  • nocx-isoph — dragging a tab between WORKSPACES, which is a membership change the backend owns, not a reorder.
  • nocx-8m2x6 — dragging a tab ONTO another so both are shown at once, which mints nothing and moves a pane reference.

So one drop handler has at least five meanings, and they are decided by what is under the cursor rather than by which bead was written first. This bead is where that is decided ONCE — a table of (what is dragged, what it is dropped on) to (what happens), covering all five, before any of the three implements its own arm.

Also note the design's hard refusal survives all of it: dragging between LINEAGE groups is refused, because lineage is provenance and a drag is a display act (2026-08-16 design §4.2). A drop table that quietly permits it is wrong however tidy it looks.

title: Tabs group under headings in the vertical strip
description:
Warp sections its tab list with a dim heading per group. We have the natural key already: `descriptor.surfaceType` tells a local terminal from an SSH session from a service surface such as Settings, so nothing new has to be stored to group by it.

The decisions this carries, and why it is not styling:

- **What groups by.** `surfaceType` is the obvious first cut; grouping SSH tabs by host is a second, and the two can disagree. Pick one and write down why.
- **Order.** Tabs are reorderable by drag today. A grouped list either constrains that to within a group or has to re-derive order after every move — the drag half is its own task, so this one must state which it assumes.
- **Filtering.** The strip filters tabs now; a heading whose group is empty after filtering must go with it, or the list reads as broken.
- **The keyboard.** Cmd+1..9 addresses tabs by position; grouping must not change what those keys select.

Groups exist only in the vertical strip. The horizontal one stays a flat row.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Tabs of different kinds render under separate labelled headings in the vertical strip, and the horizontal strip is unchanged.
- A heading disappears when the filter empties its group, and comes back when the filter is cleared.
- Cmd+1..9 selects the same tab it selected before grouping — asserted by a test, not by inspection.
- The grouping key is documented at the code that derives it, with the alternative that was rejected.
acceptance_criteria:
• Tabs of different kinds render under separate labelled headings in the vertical strip, and no grouping appears in the horizontal one.
• A heading disappears when the filter empties its group, and comes back when the filter is cleared.
• Grouping by kind does not renumber the keyboard: Cmd+1..9 selects the same tab after grouping as before it — asserted by a test, not by inspection.
• The test above asserts THAT PROPERTY and not a global numbering. It must not pin "Cmd+N is the Nth tab in the application" as an invariant, because nocx-isoph deliberately breaks that (see below).
• The grouping key is documented at the code that derives it, with the alternative that was rejected.

WHY THE KEYBOARD CRITERION IS PHRASED THIS WAY, 2026-08-16. .internal/specs/2026-08-15-workspaces-ux-design.md §4.3 makes Cmd+1..9 WORKSPACE-SCOPED, and names this bead as the one it overrides. But the override lands in nocx-isoph, which this epic BLOCKS — so at the moment this bead ships there are no workspaces and nothing to scope to.

So the original assertion is not wrong for this bead's own scope; it is wrong as a permanent invariant. Visual grouping by kind must not renumber anything — that is this bead's promise and it survives. Global numbering is not a promise anybody made, and isoph replaces it deliberately: a position inside a real container is MORE stable than a global one, because another workspace's tabs no longer shift your numbers.

The value of the original criterion was that it was asserted rather than inspected. That survives whole; only its scope is written down.
notes:
NOT ABSORBED BY WORKSPACES, checked 2026-08-17. This bead groups by descriptor.surfaceType — a local terminal, an ssh session, a service surface such as Settings. nocx-isoph groups by WORKSPACE, which is a real container the backend owns. Two different axes over one strip.

What they do share is the MECHANISM: a strip that can draw headings at all. Build it here as one owner with the axis as an input, not as a hard-coded surfaceType heading that nocx-isoph then forks. The 2026-08-16 design §9 makes this explicit for a third set — project, host, worktree and branch are 'ways of drawing the flat list, not objects' — so the axis count only grows.

Vocabulary: this bead says 'tab' throughout meaning the thing that holds a shell. Since nocx-ehkvy that is a PANE. Re-read it against the design's §3 before starting.

THE MECHANISM YOU NEED IS BUILT, 2026-08-18. nocx-isoph.5 shipped frontend/src/layout/strip-groups.ts — groupStrip(rows, axis) with the axis as an INPUT, exactly as the note above asked. Add a surfaceTypeAxis beside workspaceAxis rather than a second grouper.

Read how GroupAxis.heading is shaped before you write yours: it is handed ONE KEY and nothing else — not the set, not a count — so 'no heading unless there is more than one group' is not expressible in it. That is deliberate and it is what makes the default workspace's 'never renders' rule structural instead of a branch somebody can add back. Keep it.

Two more facts from that work. A heading-less group emits NO ELEMENT AT ALL — no wrapper, no empty caption — which is what lets tab-strip.test.tsx compare the default's rows byte-for-byte before and after another workspace exists. And a heading-less group's rows DO NOT MOVE: grouping gathers rows only under a heading, which is what keeps a view pane like Settings in its slot, a rule four e2e specs bought.

ONE OF YOUR CRITERIA NOW NEEDS EDITING. Cmd+1..9 became workspace-scoped (activateByIndex indexes the drawn rows), so this bead's 'Cmd+1..9 selects the same tab' assertion is no longer true as written. There is a comment at the code saying so.

title: The vertical tab strip becomes a grouped session list
description:
Warp's tab panel is the reference for ideas, not a design to copy. Search, two-line rows and left-aligned labels shipped separately; what is left are the four items below, each of which carries mechanics rather than styling — which is why they are not one change.

## Success Criteria
See acceptance. Each child lands with its own tests and leaves the CSS integrity gate at zero.
acceptance_criteria:
The vertical strip lists tabs in labelled groups; a tab can be dragged within its group and between groups; each row carries a glyph naming what kind of session it is; and the strip's width is draggable and survives a restart. DONE WHEN all four ship with tests and the strip still passes the kit gates.

OUT OF SCOPE: any GROUPING in the horizontal strip, the round avatar Warp draws for agent sessions, and tab search (shipped separately).

THE EXCLUSION WAS NARROWED 2026-08-16, from "any change to the horizontal strip". .internal/specs/2026-08-15-workspaces-ux-design.md §4.3 puts a workspace chip on the left of that strip, shows only the current workspace's tabs in it, gives the chip a switcher with attention counts and a "New workspace" action, and scopes the + to the current workspace. "The row is still flat" is not "the row is unchanged", and an adversarial review caught the first draft claiming this exclusion survived intact.

THE CHIP IS NOT THIS EPIC'S, and the design settles that rather than leaving it to taste: §9 names the chip inside epic B's acceptance criterion — "switches to the default workspace and back via the chip" — and a chip has nothing to name until workspaces exist. So the horizontal-strip work lands in nocx-isoph. What this epic genuinely keeps is the part the design does preserve: the TREE stays in the vertical strip, and no grouping appears in the horizontal one.
notes: READ THIS BEFORE TAKING IT. .internal/specs/2026-08-16-tabs-panes-and-blocks-design.md §11 flags this epic and its children explicitly: everywhere they say 'tab' meaning the thing that holds a shell, the model now says PANE, and 'tab' is the strip entry that groups panes. nocx-ehkvy is the rename that moves the word through the tree. Re-read the children against §3 and §4 before starting; a child written in the old vocabulary will build the wrong object.

title: dev-web's WS port collides with the e2e headless runbook
description:
## Description

`make dev-web` pins `NOCX_WS_PORT=9876`, which is the same port the headless e2e
path pins for devharness (`.internal/briefs/w6-devharness-verify.md`,
`.internal/reports/devharness-verify.md`). A look-and-see session and a test run
evict each other on the backend socket the same way they used to on 5173 — the
web port was moved to 5180 for exactly that reason and the WS port was left
behind.

`frontend/vite.dev-view.config.ts` is worse: its `NOCX_WEB_PORT` fallback is
`5173` outright, so running the config without the script lands straight on the
e2e/dev vite port.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start the headless e2e backend: `NOCX_WS_ADDR=127.0.0.1:9876 go run ./cmd/devharness`
2. In another shell: `make dev-web`
3. It refuses to start — `port 9876 (backend WS) is already in use`. Reverse the
   order and the e2e run is the one that loses.
4. Separately: `cd frontend && npx vite --config vite.dev-view.config.ts` with no
   env — vite binds 5173, the e2e/dev port.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `make dev-web` defaults to a WS/web pair no other consumer claims, and both
  sit below the Linux ephemeral range (32768-60999) so `wails dev`s
  `127.0.0.1:0` backend cannot land on them either.
- `vite.dev-view.config.ts` fallbacks match the script rather than 5173/9876.
- The Makefile and script comments name the full port map, not just 5173.
close_reason: dev-web now owns 5180/9880; both fallbacks in vite.dev-view.config.ts match the script. Verified live: backend 127.0.0.1:9880, vite 127.0.0.1:5180, shim reports GetWSPort()===9880, a pre-existing 5173 server untouched. Commit a637649 on fix/dev-web-ports-nocx-z069.

title: The type scale has no small end, and the DOM's terminal text is 1px larger than the terminal
description:
Rule 7 (T20, nocx-zhjx) ships with an exemption list because the remaining 18 px font-sizes are two decisions rather than 18 mistakes, and neither can be made by arithmetic.

**The small end of the scale.** The scale is 12/13/15/18/22 (--font-size-xs..xl). Eight declarations use 11px and four use 10px: the tab index pill, the tab bar and vertical strip, the command editor's chrome, a Button at data-size=sm, the settings error, the export backup details, the Badge, the settings badge and breadcrumb, and the update notice. That is a register the scale does not have — 'smaller than xs' — not a dozen slips. Collapsing them into 12px is a visual change in twelve places, and this epic has twice been bitten by CSS that was obviously equivalent and was not. Decide it on a running page: either add the missing step, or move each to the nearest token having looked at it.

**The terminal register is inconsistent with the terminal.** frontend/src/renderers/font.ts sets FONT_SIZE = 13, so xterm draws the live screen at 13px. The DOM that shows the same content — .cmd-output, .term-line, .cmd-header-text and .nocx-editor-input — is 14px. A command block therefore changes size depending on whether it is being drawn by the canvas or by the DOM, which is a defect independent of tokens. --font-size-sm is already 13px, so the fix may be a one-token substitution; it needs looking at, because the mono metrics differ from the UI font's at the same nominal size.

Not in scope: 16px on .ui-icon-button[data-size='sm'], which is a glyph box for a '×' rather than type. If it moves it should become an icon-size declaration, not a font-size token.
acceptance_criteria: Every px font-size outside the token layer is either replaced by a token or deliberately kept with the decision recorded; rule 7's exemption list shrinks to what survives that decision; the mono blocks and the xterm canvas agree on a size or the difference is deliberate and stated.
notes: shipped: added --font-size-2xs (0.75rem) for the small-end register (replaced all 10px/11px); converted scale from px to rem with --font-size-base: 15px and --ui-scale: 1 for zoom; added --font-size-terminal: 13px matching FONT_SIZE; fixed terminal DOM 14px → terminal token; converted icon-button sm from font-size: 16px to SVG sizing; added unit test + CSS integrity rule enforcing px tokens are relative (except base and terminal); emptied all 19 rule-7 exemptions

title: Focus placement after a page switch belongs to Page, not to settings.tsx
description:
Reported by the T19 worker (nocx-dli6) in a correction to its own worker_done — it named this gap rather than letting it pass, which is worth recording.

Spec §3.8 lists focus placement after a page change among Page's duties. It works today, and the proof matrix's two 'focus placement after page switch' cases pass — but the behaviour lives in settings.tsx's handleKeydown, which also owns slash-to-search and Escape-to-clear. So this is misplaced ownership rather than missing behaviour: any future Page gets the rail, the scroll mode and the header for free, and would have to reimplement focus placement.

Not blocking. The matrix covers the behaviour, so a move can be verified rather than guessed at.
acceptance_criteria: Page places focus after a page change; settings.tsx's handleKeydown owns only domain behaviour, and the proof matrix's Page-duties cases still pass
close_reason: Page owns focus placement after a page change, keyed on title; the surface keeps deep-link focus, which is domain behaviour

title: Commit messages must name their bead
description:
Requested by the owner 2026-07-28. Every commit message carries the bead id of the work it does, in a standardised format documented under Git authority in AGENTS.md.

Enforced by eye at review for now. If that stops working, the follow-up is a commit-msg hook rejecting a subject with no (nocx-...) — file it rather than letting the convention rot.
acceptance_criteria: AGENTS.md states the commit format including the bead id, and the rule is being followed on new commits
close_reason: Format documented under Git authority in AGENTS.md

title: make dev-web: the browser dev stand as one command
description:
Look-and-see loop in an ordinary browser over an SSH tunnel: cmd/devharness plus vite with the two Wails bindings shimmed, ports read off the backend's stdout instead of copied by hand.

Port 5180, kept off 5173 because the headless e2e path serves the frontend there (playwright.config.ts BASE_URL).

Preflight check on both ports: a leftover vite on [::1]:5173 and a fresh one on 127.0.0.1:5173 do not collide at bind time, so localhost (::1 first here) reached the un-shimmed page and the WS was refused for an empty token.
acceptance_criteria: `make dev-web` starts backend + frontend, prints the ssh -L line, and a browser at the printed URL reaches an app whose WebSocket connects; a busy port fails loudly naming the holder instead of serving an un-shimmed page.
close_reason: Landed: Makefile dev-web target + scripts/dev-web.sh + frontend/vite.dev-view.config.ts (made permanent). Port 5180 rather than 5173 because the headless e2e path serves the frontend on 5173 (playwright.config.ts BASE_URL) — sharing it means a test run and a look-and-see session evict each other, or one attaches to the other's server via PW_REUSE_SERVER and reports on a tree it never built. Preflight port check because vite strictPort does not cover it: a vite on [::1]:5173 and one on 127.0.0.1:5173 both bind fine and neither notices the other, and since localhost resolves ::1 first here the browser reached the un-shimmed page — the only symptom being a WebSocket refused for an empty token. Same reason the printed ssh -L line spells the remote side 127.0.0.1. Verified in headless chromium: WS open to /session, no close, renderer mounted 80x24.

title: IconButton owns the selected indicator the activity bar draws for it
description:
Split out of nocx-zeti. The rule-3 decision allows a parent to reference a kit identity
for PLACEMENT only, which resolves eleven of the twelve cases found while landing
IconButton (nocx-wqrq) and Toolbar (nocx-jdhy).

The twelfth is genuinely appearance: `.activity-bar .ui-icon-button[aria-selected='true']::before`
draws the active-view indicator bar. A pseudo-element that paints is not placement under
any reading, so the surface must stop owning it.

It belongs to IconButton as a variant — the primitive already takes a `selected` prop, so
the indicator is a presentation of a state it already knows about.

Blocks T20 (nocx-zhjx), where rule 3 is enabled: leaving this in place forces either a
rule with a hole in it or an exemption on its first day.
acceptance_criteria: No surface selector declares appearance on a kit identity; the activity bar's selected indicator is an IconButton variant and its ::before is gone from style.css
close_reason: railIndicator prop; ::before moved into icon-button.css with position:relative in the base; surface reduced to placement

title: deleteProfile swallows RPC failures silently
description:
`connections.tsx` catches and discards the error: `catch { // Silent fail }`. Deletion works today, so the defect is invisible — until the RPC fails, at which point the row stays on screen, no message appears, and the user has no way to tell whether anything happened.

A catch that exists only to silence is worse than no catch: the failure still occurs, and now nothing records it.
close_reason: Already fixed on main and not closed. The bead describes 'catch { // Silent fail }' in connections.tsx; no such code remains (grep over frontend/src finds neither 'Silent fail' nor an empty catch), and the sole caller, connections.tsx:333-349, logs and raises a danger toast: 'Could not delete "<name>": <message>'. Verified 2026-07-29 while scoping the connection-manager redesign (nocx-52cd).

title: The tab index pill and the activity dot express one state twice, and collide
description:
Seen on 2026-07-27. The index pill renders only on the active tab, and the activity dot overlaps the number where both are present.

This is a design question before it is a CSS fix, and the fix should not start until it is answered: decide what the number carries and what the dot carries. If the number is a keyboard-shortcut affordance it belongs on every tab; if the dot means unseen output it is meaningless on the tab you are looking at. Today they say overlapping things in the same 16 pixels.

title: T18: quick-connect, banners and update-notice
description: Spec §6.2. QuickConnectRow stays with quick-connect — a generic ListRow arrives only when a second consumer does. Done when no surface selector addresses a kit identity; enables rules 3 and 10.
close_reason: No appearance left in these surfaces to move; deleted the dead .clipboard-banner-* rules the earlier transactions left behind

title: T16: retire the documents describing the old contract
description: Spec §6.2. ui/README.md:106 and dialog.tsx:124,172 describe a scope that no longer exists. Rule 6 permits them; leaving them is how the next agent rebuilds what was just removed.
close_reason: README rewritten to identities; kit.css references and the redundant Toggle section removed; dialog.tsx cleaned by T15

title: T13: Toolbar — structural, class bounded to layout
description: Spec §3.6. Same contract as Field. Consider the start/end slot composition as the replacement for placement classes.
close_reason: border-bottom moved from the surface into toolbar.css; placement stays with the surface

title: T10: EmptyState owns its element
description: Spec §3.6. Already emits ui-empty-state; loses its class prop and gains its identity test.
close_reason: class prop removed, dead .cm-list-empty rule deleted, passthrough test replaced by an identity test

title: T12: Section — structural, class bounded to layout
description: Spec §3.6. Same contract as Field.
close_reason: Two hand-rolled section divs became Sections; heading treatment and row gap folded into section.css; identity order pinned

title: T11: Field — structural, class bounded to layout
description: Spec §3.6. class stays but may carry only layout and placement — never background, border, radius, color, font, padding, shadow, appearance or a drawing pseudo-element. Rule 11's traced-class tier enforces it.
close_reason: class prop removed outright — zero consumers; identity pinned for both orientations

title: T9: Badge owns its element
description: Spec §3.6. Gains a ui-badge base class; the variant classes become tone: neutral | info | warning | danger.
close_reason: ui-badge base + data-tone; badge.css collapsed to one base and three overrides

title: [epic] A catalogue of terminal palettes, not two themes
description:
nocx ships two themes. Users coming from Warp, iTerm or Tabby expect a catalogue,
and ADR-0013 already makes this cheap: `--terminal-*` (background, foreground,
cursor, selection, ANSI 0-15) lives in the theme file, and `theme-adapter.ts`
reads it out of computed style. A terminal palette is therefore a data row, not
a code change.

Two MIT-licensed sources are already on this machine and were read while
investigating this:

- `~/repos/orca/src/renderer/src/lib/terminal-themes/` — 9 files
  (classic, popular-dark, popular-dark-core, popular-dark-extended,
  popular-light, defaults) of xterm `ITheme` objects, exactly our
  `--terminal-*` shape. MIT, Copyright (c) 2026 Lovecast Inc.
- `~/repos/orca/src/main/warp-themes/` — a parser for Warp's own theme files,
  so a user's existing Warp themes could be imported rather than re-typed.

What neither source provides, and what must not be confused with this: a **UI**
palette. Orca's chrome is one shadcn light/dark pair; Tabby's is Bootstrap
variables over a single dark background. Our `--color-*` tokens — canvas,
chrome, surface, border, text — have no counterpart to copy, and the contrast
work in nocx-u7wq was done by measurement for that reason.

So the shape of this is: a terminal-palette catalogue, with each entry providing
`--terminal-*` only, paired with one of the two UI palettes (light or dark)
chosen by the entry's own background luminance. Attribution required — MIT
notice for whatever is lifted.

## Success Criteria

A user can choose from at least a dozen named terminal palettes in Settings, the
choice repaints open terminals in place without a restart, and each palette
declares whether it pairs with the light or the dark UI. Adding the next palette
is one data entry and no code. Third-party MIT notices are recorded.

Out of scope: importing Warp/iTerm theme files from disk (a follow-on), and any
change to the UI colour tokens.

title: Ten colour literals hide in var() fallbacks and inline styles
description: Found by nocx-xrrl.4, which is the first independent check of the token migration's claim. Both shapes are invisible to a grep over CSS files: var(--x, #hex) hides a literal inside a fallback, and a JSX style prop is not in a stylesheet at all. That is precisely why ADR-0013 section 4 asked for a grammar rather than a denylist, and the check earned its keep on day one.
acceptance_criteria: The colour-literals baseline is empty: the six var() fallbacks in overlay.css either drop their fallback or use a token, and the four inline style colours in connections.tsx move to CSS classes. nocx-xrrl cannot close while the baseline is non-empty.
close_reason: Closed by nocx-vxqj.9: the six var() fallbacks in overlay.css and the four inline style colours in connections.tsx are gone; the colour-literals baseline is empty.

title: Eight raw controls survive in already-migrated shell surfaces
description:
Found when the guard's baseline was regenerated. banner (3), sidebar (2), tab-strip (2) and update-notice (1) all went through the Solid migration this session and still use raw <button>. They are not sloppiness: a tab close button and an activity-bar icon button are chrome-sized, and the kit's Button carries padding and variants built for form actions. Adopting it would restyle the shell.

This is the same shape as the Field problem (nocx-vxqj.7): a kit component built for one kind of consumer does not fit another, and the surface keeps its own. Worth deciding once for both.
acceptance_criteria: The eight baselined violations in banner.tsx, sidebar.tsx, tab-strip.tsx and update-notice.tsx are resolved one of two ways, decided deliberately: the kit gains a chrome/icon button variant those surfaces adopt, or the rule documents an exempt category with a stated reason and the baseline entries move into it. Either way the baseline loses those eight.
notes: Reframed 2026-07-27 by the owner together with nocx-vxqj.7. The eight raw controls are not a category to exempt; they are eight consumers the kit does not yet serve. Add the component they need — a chrome/icon button — and use it in all eight. Precedent from the same day: the quick-connect caret was rejected by the guard, Button gained a tabIndex prop in one line, and the caret became a kit component. The gap was small. Target is a baseline of zero, which is the epic's own closing criterion.
close_reason: Closed by nocx-vxqj.9: the eight chrome controls became kit Buttons with a close variant, not an exempted category. The kit grew to serve them.

title: Field does not fit a two-column row, which is where it was needed
description:
Found by nocx-imkb.2. Field was built in kit wave 1 as the label+description+error+control wrapper every form row needs. Settings — the surface that motivated it — could not use it: Field stacks vertically and the settings rows are label on the left, control on the right, so adopting it would have restyled the screen, which ADR-0012 section 4 forbids inside a migration.

So the one component built for the one surface that needed it does not fit that surface. That is worth fixing properly rather than leaving Settings with a private row layout, because the next form-heavy surface will face the same choice.
acceptance_criteria: Either Field supports a horizontal layout so a settings row can use it, or the kit gains a second wrapper for two-column rows and the README says which to reach for when. Settings stops carrying its own row layout either way.
notes: Reframed 2026-07-27 by the owner, and the reframing is the answer: a kit is a set of components that get USED. A component nothing uses is itself the defect, not evidence of a missing category. So Field either gains what settings rows need, or is replaced by a component that fits them — and then that component is used everywhere it fits, not just there. No 'two categories' exemption.
close_reason: Closed by nocx-vxqj.9: Field gained an orientation prop and settings rows adopted it. The component built for that consumer now fits it.

title: Declare ui.theme in internal/settings and call reconcileThemeFromGo
description: nocx-xrrl.5 built the resolver and wired reconcileThemeFromGo but could not call it: the Go setting does not exist, and declaring it is a backend change outside that bead's ownership. ADR-0013 section 8.1 settles the authority question — Go is authoritative, the local record holds a bootstrap cache that colours the first frame and always loses to Go on reconcile.
acceptance_criteria: internal/settings declares ui.theme as a select, so it appears in the generated settings screen, survives reinstall and travels with export/import. main.tsx calls reconcileThemeFromGo when the settings snapshot arrives; the bootstrap cache is updated on every accepted change and never read as authority. Changing the setting restyles the shell and live terminals without remounting a terminal, proved by mount/dispose counters.
close_reason: ui.theme declared in internal/settings; reconcileThemeFromGo wired in the composition root per ADR-0013 8.1 — Go authoritative, local record a bootstrap cache that always loses on reconcile. Picker appears with zero settings.tsx edits. Light theme added and it is a new file and nothing else: no component or surface CSS needed touching, every UI and terminal token covered including ANSI 0-15. Theme switch repaints shell and live terminals with zero pane churn, both engines.

title: The scroll-ownership invariant is only checked in jsdom, which computes no layout
description:
nocx-imkb.1 delivered the invariant test and its author stated the limit plainly: jsdom applies CSS from injected style elements but does not compute layout, so there is no flex resolution, no min-height chain and no scrollbar creation. The test therefore proves no rule DECLARES an overflow we do not own — it cannot prove the chain works.

That distinction is exactly the one that let the Settings scroll bug ship: the defect was invisible in jsdom and inconsistent in Chromium, and only WebKit showed it. An invariant meant to stop the next surface improvising a height chain has to run where the chain actually resolves.
acceptance_criteria: The invariant from design spec section 6.2 is asserted in a real browser context, in WebKit: render a Page whose rail and content both overflow inside a container under 400px tall, walk every node reading getComputedStyle overflow, and assert only .ui-page__scroll and .ui-page__rail are auto or scroll — plus that the rail is NOT scrollable at or below the 640px narrow breakpoint. The jsdom test stays as a fast structural check; it is not removed.
close_reason: e2e/scroll-ownership.spec.ts asserts the invariant where layout resolves: node walk over computed overflow, the narrow breakpoint, and that content actually scrolls. Six tests pass in Chromium and WebKit. The jsdom test stays as a fast structural guard. Coordinator changed the spec to READ surface.css instead of duplicating it — and that immediately broke four of six, because .pane lives in style.css and had been dropped. It is now the single mirrored rule, documented, and goes away when nocx-xrrl.2 moves .pane into styles/.

title: Migrate the export section to Solid
description:
Surface migration, 519 lines with only a 47-line test — the largest surface with the thinnest existing coverage, which is why the characterization test matters more here than anywhere else.

METHOD: characterization test of observable behaviour first, green against the CURRENT implementation, then rewrite, same test green, then delete export-section.ts and its structural test in the same commit.

Keeps its current behaviour exactly. If you find a defect while characterizing it, report it and let the coordinator file it — do not fix it here.

COST BASIS (measured, nocx-njrx.6): the pilot migrated a 139-line imperative leaf into a 122-line Solid component plus a 146-line characterization test in about 28 minutes, roughly 5 of which was toolchain friction. That surface had no reactive state, no terminal contact and no store, so it is a FLOOR: plan this one at 1.5-3x the pilot and say in your report where the real time went.

## Acceptance Criteria

The export section renders from Solid components using the local kit; the characterization test was green against the old implementation and stays green; export-section.ts and export-section.test.ts are deleted in the commit that lands the replacement; e2e green in both browser projects.
notes:
SEQUENCING CORRECTION 2026-07-27 (coordinator), made before dispatch. This bead and the settings migration (nocx-eerg) were first planned as parallel. They are not parallel: settings-content.ts:109 calls renderExportSection(this.contentEl, this.profileClient) — an imperative 'render into this element' API — so the export section is a leaf INSIDE the settings surface, not a sibling of it.

Running them together would have forced one of two bad outcomes: a temporary renderExportSection adapter kept alive so settings keeps compiling (a shim, which this epic exists to remove and the owner has explicitly forbidden), or a Solid settings surface handing one of its own elements to an imperative renderer, which is the ownership failure the migration is for.

So export-section goes FIRST and owns the single call site in settings-content.ts, converting it to mount the Solid component. nocx-eerg now depends on this bead and its worker consumes <ExportSection/> directly.
close_reason:
export-section.ts (519 lines) is deleted; the surface is export-section.tsx plus export-utils.ts, with a 12-case behaviour suite. The pre-existing 47-line base64 round-trip test is kept and now points at export-utils — it tests a pure function, not a DOM shape, so it survives the rewrite by construction.

Two coordinator fixes on the worker's result, both real: ExportSection was not exported, which would have forced the settings migration (the next bead, and the reason this one ran first) to keep calling an imperative renderer; and render()'s disposer was discarded, so the Solid root outlived its container — closing the settings tab removed the DOM and left effects running on detached nodes. Now mountExportSection returns the disposer, SettingsContent calls it in dispose(), and it is documented as an island boundary that disappears when settings migrates rather than a shim that stays.

title: e2e multi-tab-input.spec.ts:13 is flaky in chromium — about one run in four
description:
Measured 2026-07-27 while gating the first SolidJS wave. Not caused by that wave: reproduced on a clean checkout of origin/main (0b43e4e) with the wave's code absent — 3 passes and 1 failure in 4 consecutive runs. On the wave branch the same spec passed once and failed once in two runs. Chromium only; webkit ran the full suite green.

Failure surface:

Error: expect(locator).not.toHaveText(expected) failed
Locator:  locator('.tab-title').first()
Expected: not "home/dev"
Received: ""

The observed title is empty, i.e. the assertion is racing the tab title being (re)populated rather than catching a wrong title. The spec is the nocx-4ff.28 regression guard — the one that pins 'the first tab still accepts input after a second tab is created' — so leaving it flaky costs the guard: a run that fails for timing reasons trains people to re-run rather than read it.

Do NOT fix this by adding Playwright retries. The flake work in nocx-rdkh made the waits condition-based on purpose, and blanket retries would hide the next real failure.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start the headless path: go run ./cmd/devharness, then vite in frontend/.
2. NOCX_WS_PORT=<port> NOCX_WS_TOKEN=<token> npx playwright test e2e/multi-tab-input.spec.ts --project=chromium --reporter=line
3. Repeat four times.

Observed: roughly one run in four fails at multi-tab-input.spec.ts:13 with the empty-title comparison above.
Expected: deterministic pass, like the other 19 specs.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The condition the test waits on is the one it actually depends on: the tab title having been populated at all before it is compared, rather than a poll that can observe the empty intermediate state.
- Ten consecutive chromium runs of this spec pass.
- No retries added to playwright.config.ts and no timeout inflation used as the fix.
notes:
Backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh: checked against nocx-iqrf and found DISTINCT, not duplicate — a related edge now records the pair. The two report mutually exclusive reproductions of the same spec: this bead fails it IN ISOLATION about one run in four (chromium, webkit green), while iqrf passes it 4/4 in isolation on both engines and fails it only inside the full suite. Fails-alone and passes-alone cannot be one behaviour.

BOTH ARE STALE AND NEED RE-MEASUREMENT BEFORE ANY FIX. Commit 2bfe9c34, 'a tab title that changes on its own is not evidence of a keystroke (nocx-cbtc)', rewrote e2e/multi-tab-input.spec.ts on 2026-08-11 and root-caused this bead's exact shape: a fresh tab's title starts as ~ and becomes its real cwd when OSC 7 arrives, after promptReady, so the snapshot caught the title mid-transition and the assertion failed on a change the tab made by itself with no keystroke involved. The locator constant is now .nocx-tab-title rather than .tab-title, the snapshot comparison this bead's text quotes was replaced, and a missing await was restored. No re-measurement is recorded on either bead since. This one may well close on one run.

title: A secret setting offers a Reset button but has no default to reset to
description:
Found while extracting the settings domain transitions (nocx-njrx.3), not fixed there because it is a behaviour question rather than an extraction one.

settings.ts renderProvenance() offers a Reset control for every setting whose key is in the overridden set, with no check that the declaration HAS a default. Declaration.default is optional and, per the comment at settings.ts:47 and ADR-0011 section 3, is ABSENT for control:'secret'. So a customized secret shows 'Customized' plus a Reset button, and what that button does is undefined by the contract — there is nothing to revert to.

Decide, then implement: what Reset means for a secret (delete the stored secret? no-op? not offered at all?) — note deleteSecret() already exists as a separate control, which is evidence the answer is 'not offered' — and whether the provenance LABEL should change too or only the button. Those are different: the codebase deliberately defines Customized as PROVENANCE (the key is in the overridden set), not as a value-vs-default comparison, because an override that equals the default still pins the value for export.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Settings and set a value for a setting declared with control:'secret'.
2. Look at its provenance cell.

Observed: the row shows 'Customized' and a Reset button, alongside the separate Clear control for the secret itself.
Expected: undecided — the declaration carries no default, so Reset has nothing to revert to. That is the question this bead exists to settle.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A secret declaration's row is decided deliberately: either it does not offer Reset at all, or Reset has a defined meaning that a test pins.
- The provenance label's meaning is stated explicitly and is not changed as a side effect of the button decision.
- canResetSetting() in settings-domain.ts grows the hasDefault input back at that point. It was deliberately dropped in nocx-njrx.3 because hardcoding it to true made the 'noDefault' denial branch unreachable in production while unit tests still covered it.
close_reason: INVALID — the premise is false and I should have read the call site before filing it. settings.ts:473 already guards: 'if (decl.control !== "secret" && decl.default !== undefined) controlCol.append(this.renderProvenance(decl))'. A secret declaration therefore renders no provenance badge and no Reset button at all, so the behaviour this bead describes cannot occur. Filed 2026-07-27 from reading renderProvenance() in isolation and reasoning about Declaration.default being optional, without checking who calls it. The nocx-njrx.3 worker found the guard and said so in its round-2 report. Note the guard also makes the dropped hasDefault parameter redundant for a better reason than the one given in the revision brief: the caller has already established it.

title: multi-tab-input:13 fails on the headless e2e path but passes under wails dev
description:
`multi-tab-input.spec.ts:13` ("first tab still accepts input after second tab is created")
fails on the headless devharness + vite path while passing on the `wails dev` path that CI
runs. It is green in CI — main run 30219766801 at e5a4ae2 passed all three jobs — so nothing
is broken for the gate today. What is broken is the cheap local signal.

## Measured

On `main` at e5a4ae2, headless path, full suite, three consecutive runs:

```
run 1: 1 failed [chromium] multi-tab-input.spec.ts:13 · 37 passed · 2 skipped
run 2: 1 failed [chromium] multi-tab-input.spec.ts:13 · 37 passed · 2 skipped
run 3: 1 failed [chromium] multi-tab-input.spec.ts:13 · 37 passed · 2 skipped
```

Run in isolation (`npx playwright test e2e/multi-tab-input.spec.ts`) the same spec passes
4/4 on both engines, so the failure is order- or state-dependent within the suite rather
than a property of the spec alone. Which engine loses also varies: on a branch carrying the
same code it surfaced under webkit instead, and two of three runs were fully green.

## Why it matters

This is the second instance of the same structural problem, and the first one cost a full
investigation (nocx-5zl4): the headless path and the `wails dev` path do not exercise the
same application, so "green locally" and "green in CI" are different claims. Here the
divergence points the other way — headless is redder than CI — which is the less dangerous
direction but still means a developer cannot trust a local full-suite run to be meaningful.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start `cmd/devharness` and `vite`; export `NOCX_WS_PORT`, `NOCX_WS_TOKEN`, `NOCX_BASE_URL`.
2. `npx playwright test` (whole suite, not the single spec).
3. `multi-tab-input.spec.ts:13` fails; the same spec passes when run alone.

## Acceptance Criteria

Either the spec passes on both e2e paths, or the reason it cannot is understood and written
down — and if it genuinely depends on the wails runtime, it says so and skips on the headless
path rather than failing there. A developer running the full suite locally gets a result they
can act on.
notes:
Backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh: checked against nocx-m8ei and found DISTINCT, not duplicate — a related edge now records the pair. m8ei fails this spec IN ISOLATION about one run in four; this bead passes it 4/4 in isolation and fails it only within the suite, and additionally records that which engine loses varies. Same file and same nominal line, two different defects.

STALE — re-measure before fixing. Commit 2bfe9c34 (2026-08-11) rewrote e2e/multi-tab-input.spec.ts entirely, changing the locator constant to .nocx-tab-title, replacing the snapshot comparison and restoring a missing await; line 13 is now the test declaration rather than an assertion. Neither this bead nor m8ei has been re-measured since.

title: Keyboard handling is gated on a CSS class instead of the authoritative active state
description:
`terminal-content.ts:280` gates keyboard handling on `target.classList.contains('active')`
— a CSS class read as control flow.

The authoritative value already exists. `Tab.setActive` (tabs.ts:91-92) sets `this._active`
and then toggles the class on the very next line. The fix reads the class rather than the
state, so ownership is re-derived from presentation.

Three reasons this matters more than style:

1. **It crosses the nocx-njrx migration boundary.** `tabs.ts` sets the class and WILL be
   rewritten in Solid. `terminal-content.ts` reads it and stays imperative under AD-6.
   That is the single seam most likely to break silently during the migration: a Solid
   rewrite that names the class differently, or stops setting it on the same element,
   breaks keyboard input in a file the migration never touched, with no type error.
2. **ADR-0012 forbids exactly this shape.** It states that state crosses the terminal
   boundary through explicit imperative methods, never by inspecting markup.
3. **`'active'` is a bare string in eight places across four files** — sidebar.ts,
   tabs.ts, tab-strip.ts (four occurrences), terminal-content.ts — with no shared
   constant. A rename in one file silently changes behaviour in another.

WHY IT SHIPPED ANYWAY, so nobody re-argues it: `TabContent` exposes only `mount`,
`viewportChanged`, `focus` and `dispose`. There is no activation hook, so the worker had
no explicit channel to use. Blocking a P0 input fix on widening that interface was the
wrong trade; fixing it properly afterwards is the right one.

## Steps to Reproduce

Not a runtime symptom today. To see the coupling:

```bash
grep -rn "'active'" --include=*.ts frontend/src | grep -v test
sed -n '88,95p' frontend/src/tabs.ts        # the authoritative _active, and the class
sed -n '278,282p' frontend/src/terminal-content.ts   # the class being read back
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- `TabContent` gains an explicit activation signal — for example
  `setActive(active: boolean): void`, delivered by the presentation layer the same way
  `viewportChanged` already is — and `TerminalContent` keeps its own flag from it.
- `terminal-content.ts` no longer reads any CSS class to decide whether to handle input.
- The e2e coverage from nocx-4ff.28 still passes, and a unit test asserts the handler is
  inert for a non-active content instance.
- Whatever remains of `'active'` as a string is presentation only. If a shared constant is
  worth introducing for the rest, say so; if not, say why.
- Coordinate with nocx-njrx: if the Solid migration is already underway on `tabs.ts`, this
  seam change belongs to that work rather than beside it.
notes: In scope for the shell rewrite: keyboard handling gated on a CSS class is the same defect class as the sidebar reading DOM for state. The ownership table (nocx-82l9.7) names the authoritative active-tab slice; this bug is fixed against that slice, not against .active.
close_reason: BaseTabContent records the active flag when setVisible is called, and TerminalContent's keyboard handler reads it instead of classList.contains('active'). The class remains for styling. Verified: 777 unit tests, and multi-tab-input, click-focus and command-editor pass 12/12 in both engines. Note: the ownership table specified this fix and nobody applied it — the bead read as handled because it was described.

title: Dead code: createRegistry() in input-target.ts has no production caller
description:
Found while reviewing nocx-njrx on 2026-07-26. Standalone deliberately: input-target.ts stays imperative under AD-6, the SolidJS migration never touches it, and this must be fixed on its own merits rather than ride along with a migration.

createRegistry() in frontend/src/input-target.ts has no caller outside tests. TerminalContent instantiates ShellInputTarget directly (terminal-content.ts:178) and calls submit() on it (line 199). The InputTargetRegistry abstraction from ADR-0004 section 3 is unused.

The tests are what hid it — a test calling createRegistry looks exactly like a real caller to a linter. Our deadcode gate (nocx-ckoy.1) is Go-only, which is why nothing flagged it.

Decide, do not just delete on sight: either the registry is the intended design and something should be using it, in which case wire it and say where; or ADR-0004 section 3 describes an abstraction the product did not need, in which case delete the code and amend the ADR so the document stops describing something that is not there. 'Clean-only: no dead code' in AGENTS.md points at deletion, but the ADR makes it a decision rather than a chore.
acceptance_criteria: createRegistry is either reachable from the composition root or deleted; if deleted, ADR-0004 section 3 is amended to match; frontend tests referencing it are updated or removed; gates green.

title: Delete the frontend spikes — 1,657 lines nothing imports
description:
Free reduction of the migration surface, isolated in its own directories, takeable by anyone at any time.

frontend/src/spike/dom-scrollback.ts (810) and frontend/src/spikes/gutter-spike.ts (476) plus gutter-spike.test.ts (371) are referenced by nothing outside themselves. Measured 2026-07-26: grep for importers returns only the spike files and the spike's own test.

They are also absent from the epic's own accounting — the description totals 4,731 migrating + 4,344 staying = 9,075, against 10,593 real non-test lines under frontend/src. The spikes are most of that gap, so removing them makes the epic's numbers true as well as making the work smaller.

Note the two near-identical directory names, src/spike/ and src/spikes/ — both go.

OWNS FILES: frontend/src/spike/, frontend/src/spikes/. Nothing else.
acceptance_criteria: Both directories are gone; build, typecheck, lint, vitest and the e2e suite are green; no remaining file references them.
notes:
WAVE-1 OWNERSHIP RULING 2026-07-27 (coordinator). The bead said 'OWNS FILES: src/spike/, src/spikes/. Nothing else.' Measured, that is not enough to satisfy its own acceptance criterion 'no remaining file references them'. Two references live outside those directories: frontend/spike.html (its only content is a script tag for /src/spike/dom-scrollback.ts) and frontend/eslint.config.js:13 (ignores 'src/spike/**'). Ruling: spike.html is ADDED to this bead's ownership — nothing else references it. The eslint ignore entry is NOT: nocx-njrx.1 owns that whole config file and is rewriting it in parallel, so the stale ignore is removed by the coordinator after both branches land. An ignores entry pointing at a deleted directory is harmless in the interim.
REVIEW 2026-07-27 (coordinator). Worker diff accepted: 1,844 lines deleted (1,657 TS + 187 HTML), vitest 26 files/539 tests -> 25/517, delta exactly gutter-spike.test.ts. Merged as f4a88a2.

One inaccuracy in the worker's report, corrected by the coordinator rather than sent back: it stated 'the only code-level reference is eslint.config.js'. Not so — the ROOT directory spike/dom-scrollback/ (24 tracked files, the nocx-4ff.17 spike artifact) held five Playwright drivers (validate.ts, validate.mjs, perf-test.mjs, screenshots/capture.mjs, screenshots/capture-dynamic-padding.mjs) that all navigate to VITE_URL/spike.html — the page this bead deleted. They could no longer run at all. Deleted in a3f1ceb (863 further lines), keeping REPORT.md, DESIGN-NOTES.md and the screenshots as the record of the spike's findings, with the report amended to say the code is gone and why. That directory was never in this bead's ownership list, which is why the worker did not look there.
close_reason: Both spike directories and frontend/spike.html deleted (1,844 lines); coordinator additionally removed 863 lines of orphaned Playwright drivers in the root spike/dom-scrollback/ that could no longer run, keeping REPORT.md and the screenshots as the record. Gate on the merged trunk: typecheck, eslint --max-warnings 0, 544 unit tests, build, prettier all green; e2e 18/18 webkit and 19/20 chromium, the single chromium failure being a pre-existing flake reproduced on origin/main and filed separately.

title: [epic] The sidebar is a real multi-view panel, with a local file tree as its first view
description:
The sidebar panel becomes a real multi-view surface, modelled on Orca's sidebar, with a
working local file tree as its first view.

(It was "the LEFT panel" until nocx-yhc7p moved the panel and its activity bar to the
window's trailing edge. Only the word describing WHERE it sits changed; nothing about
what this epic delivers did. The Orca path below still says right-sidebar because that is
Orca's directory name, not a claim about ours.)

## Where this came from

The sidebar shell exists (nocx-8yg.9, closed 2026-07-24): activity bar plus collapsible
panel, Ctrl/Cmd+B, persisted collapse state. It was built early and deliberately —
"cheap now, avoids restructuring". Its intended MVP content was the SSH host list, which
the owner descoped at the time into nocx-eab. What shipped was the shell plus a
placeholder view labelled "Sessions" that nothing was ever designed behind. Owner
clarified 2026-07-26: the intent is a panel like Orca's.

Reference: /home/dev/repos/orca, src/renderer/src/components/right-sidebar/.

## Scope measured, not guessed

Orca's file explorer alone is **41 non-test files, ~6,900 lines**, and that is only the
explorer — the whole sidebar directory is 458 files / 4.1 MB. What those 41 files buy:
drag-and-drop, undo/redo, virtualised rows, an fs-watcher reconcile loop, keyboard
navigation, batch deletion with classification, auto-reveal, name-filter projection, a
selection model, and a background context menu.

nocx's frontend is vanilla TypeScript with no framework; Orca's is React. A 1:1 port is
not on the table. This epic must therefore define the MINIMUM USEFUL SLICE and name
everything it is not doing, or it becomes an area rather than a deliverable and never
closes — the exact failure that forced nocx-6ek and nocx-k0xk to be split.

## What the reference screenshot actually contains

- An activity icon row: files, blocks, git, tasks, plus a panel-toggle.
- A project header with the repo name and per-view actions (collapse-all, refresh, overflow).
- A filter box, "Find files", with a Names / Contents segmented toggle.
- A file tree: folders then files, git status markers in the gutter (`M`), an ignored/
  excluded entry rendered dimmed and italic (`build`).

## In scope

- The panel hosts SEVERAL named views, switched from the activity bar, each owning its
  own header actions. Today `SidebarImpl` supports one panel view and mixes in
  `action: 'tab'` entries that have no panel content at all — that mixing is the direct
  cause of nocx-rp2j.
- A local file tree view for the active tab's cwd: expand/collapse, lazy directory
  listing, click to reveal, respect for .gitignore.
- The name filter with its Names/Contents toggle, at least for Names.
- Git status markers, read-only.

## Explicitly out

- Remote / SFTP browsing. That is nocx-9le.5 and stays there.
- Drag-and-drop, undo/redo, batch delete, rename, background context menu — the bulk of
  Orca's 6,900 lines. File MUTATION is out entirely for this epic; the tree is read-only
  plus reveal.
- Contents search. The toggle may ship disabled with the Names half working.
- The blocks / git / tasks views from the screenshot. This epic delivers the multi-view
  MECHANISM plus ONE view; further views are their own beads.

## Decide first, in an ADR, before any code

1. **Does a file tree belong in a terminal at all?** This is not in docs/vision.md's
   roadmap, which orders the work editor core -> command blocks and shell integration ->
   terminal core, terminal UI and SSH client -> vault -> Warpify. A file explorer competes
   with every one of those for the same frontend. vision.md section 5 does not list it.
   The wedge is stated as "renders agent TUIs flawlessly AND is comfortable to live in,
   with no cloud" — an argument that it serves the second half is available but must be
   made, not assumed.
2. **Virtualisation.** A tree over a large repo without virtual rows will jank. Orca
   needed `FileExplorerVirtualRows`. Decide whether the first slice virtualises or caps
   the visible node count, and say which.
3. **Where the tree state lives.** This lands squarely on nocx-ycet — a second surface
   keeping its own private copy of "active cwd" is the pattern that epic exists to end.
4. **Which cwd.** Per active tab, or per window? Tabs can sit in different directories,
   and OSC 7 already reports cwd per tab.

## Relationships

- nocx-i74e (the "Sessions" placeholder means nothing) is resolved BY this epic — the
  placeholder becomes a real view or is removed. nocx-rp2j (empty CONNECTIONS panel at
  cold start) is caused by the same one-view-plus-tab-actions mixing.
- nocx-eab (SSH host list in the panel) becomes one of the views this mechanism hosts.
- nocx-vxqj (UI kit) owns the tree row, filter box and toolbar as components; this epic
  must consume that kit rather than hand-roll a third vocabulary.

## Success Criteria

The activity bar switches between at least two real panel views with no empty-panel state
at cold start; a local file tree renders the active tab's cwd, expands and collapses
directories lazily, hides .gitignore'd entries or marks them dimmed, filters by name, and
shows read-only git status markers; every control comes from the UI kit; tree and cwd
state is read from the shared store rather than a private copy; and the ADR recording the
four decisions above is merged before the first line of implementation.
