close_reason: c25c4922. skillReadFinding and skillWriteFinding (internal/assistant/execute.go) and the exported SkillScanFinding (kernel.go) are deleted; skillReadResult.Finding, skillWriteResult.Finding, ApprovalRequest.Finding and transport's agentApprovalRequested.Finding are all *skill.Finding. No wire change, asserted by the over-the-wire tests rather than the diff: TestAgentApproval_SkillWriteCarriesClassifierAndFinding (ws_agent_approval_test.go:638) drives a real skills.create approval through the socket and validates the raw notification against agent.approvalRequested.schema.json (additionalProperties: false) — PASS before and after; likewise TestSkillsPreview_OverTheWireConformsToContract. go test ./internal/assistant/ ./internal/skill/ ./internal/transport/ ok; go vet clean. Nothing blocked the exported one: internal/transport already imports internal/skill in ws_skill_handlers.go, and gob registers only the outer ApprovalRequest — a pointer-to-struct field is encoded structurally, verified by a throwaway encode/decode round trip.

title: A host with an underscore cannot be granted: IDNA refuses it and nothing decided whether it should
description:
Task 2 made destination scopes structured and normalizes hosts through IDNA. idna.Lookup refuses an underscore in a hostname, so http://build_server:8080 cannot be stored as a destination scope. IP literals bypass IDNA, so 127.0.0.1 is unaffected.

Underscores are illegal in hostnames per the RFCs and common in internal DNS anyway. Whether nocx accepts them is a deliberate product decision, not something to discover when a person cannot grant their own build server.

Reported by the Task 2 worker.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The decision is made and written down: either an underscore host is accepted with the reason, or it is refused with an error message that says why and what to use instead.
- A test pins whichever was chosen.

title: A comment says session.run continuations classify as mutate-destructive; they classify as delegate
description:
internal/agenttools/registry.go:425-426 says WorstEffect classifies session.run continuations as mutate-destructive. It classifies them as delegate: effectOrder ranks delegate 6, above cross-boundary 5 and mutate-destructive 2 (internal/content/resources.go:113-131).

Found by the Task 1 worker, in a file it did not own. The same error was in the spec and is corrected there; this is the copy that stayed in the code.

Comment-only. It is filed rather than fixed in passing because the comment states a behaviour nocx-jxq97 may deliberately change, and the two should be read together.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read internal/agenttools/registry.go:425-426.
2. Read effectOrder in internal/content/resources.go:113-131.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The comment says what the code does, or is deleted if nocx-jxq97 changes the behaviour it describes.

title: Approve checks the managed root before it knows which skill it is approving
description:
`Store.Approve` calls `requireManagedRoot()` before it knows which skill it is approving
(internal/skill/store_doc.go). Approving writes nothing to the managed root —
`recordApprovalDigest` hashes the skill's own directory and writes `skills.json` — so the
check was already vestigial for managed, and since nocx-qja4m.1 it names the WRONG root
for an installed skill: with a symlinked `managed-skills`, approving an installed skill
fails with "skill root is a symlink".

Consequence today is nil: app.go always wires a managed root, and a symlinked one means
everything skill-related is broken anyway. Filed rather than fixed in passing because
removing a guard from a function with no unit coverage of its own deserves its own
reasoning, not a ride along an unrelated diff.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Make `<ConfigDir>/managed-skills` a symlink to a real directory.
2. Place a skill in `<ConfigDir>/installed-skills` and approve it.
3. It fails with a message about a root the operation does not touch.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Approve's precondition is about the skill being approved, not about a root the call does
  not write to — or the guard is gone, with a comment saying what it was for.
- A test approves an installed skill while the managed root is a symlink and asserts it
  succeeds.
- A test asserts Approve still refuses a provenance that has no approval to record
  (authored, builtin).
close_reason: Guard removed from Approve in internal/skill/store_doc.go:523, replaced by a comment naming what it was for and why it does not belong (the only write is the document, which DocumentPath puts beside the first filesystem root's parent, not under the managed root). The three requireManagedRoot callers in write.go are untouched. Six tests in store_doc_test.go, including the bead's own case — an installed skill approved while managed-skills is a symlink, which reported 'skill root is a symlink' before the change. Each asserts the document state after the call; refusals assert no write happened. Commit a0444425.

title: pre-commit golangci-lint failed once and did not reproduce
description:
2026-09-03, committing internal/app/session_reconcile_fault_test.go (a new test file, no production
change). The pre-commit hook printed "FAIL: golangci-lint" and refused. The identical command the
hook runs — golangci-lint run --build-tags=gtk3 ./... — was then clean, and an immediate retry of the
same commit passed with no change to the tree.

WHAT IS NOT KNOWN, and it is the important part: whether this was a linter flake or a real finding.
The hook's output was truncated at the observing end (tail -3), so the actual diagnostic was never
read. Do not assume flake on this record alone.

Context that may or may not matter: two agents had been running concurrently in this worktree
immediately before, one of them committing, so the golangci-lint cache may have been contended.

FOR THE NEXT OCCURRENCE: capture the hook's FULL output before doing anything else. That is the one
thing this record is missing and the only reason it is not actionable.

## Steps to Reproduce

Not reproduced. Seen once.

## Acceptance Criteria

A second occurrence with the full diagnostic captured, and then either a named defect or a named
cause for the flake. Closing this on "did not happen again" is not a reason a stranger can check.

title: Task 13: revoking an answer says what happens to the work already running
description:
Plan task 13. Grants already minted stay alive, so revocation has a time and the person chooses it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A change or forget affecting live runs says how many and offers apply-to-future-runs against also-stop-the-runs-using-it.
- Future-only leaves running work alone: asserted at both ends, the run finishes under the old answer and the next run gets the new one.
- Stopping terminates those runs through the existing terminalization path, with the reason naming the revoked answer.
close_reason: Merged as the nocx-r4fh8-revoke-time merge (worker 92bf6ff5). A change or forget affecting live runs says how many and offers apply-to-future against also-stop; affecting none, it asks nothing and applies. THE READING OF 'runs using it' IS THE PRECISE ONE: content.ChangedByRuleWrite builds one representative invocation per selector the write touches — the stored rule's AND the incoming rule's, because a change can move the selector — and compares DecisionForInvocation with and without the write across all seven rows, on the run's OWN frozen policy and fence, through the same evaluator the enforcement uses. A rule the run never matched, one a stricter answer shadows, and one under a refusing row all decide nothing and are counted out. The cheap reading is rejected IN WRITING at runsUnreachedByRuleWrite: it is a count of the registry wearing a permission's clothes, and a person learns within a day that the number means how many runs exist. ORDER: the policy write first, the stop second — if the write fails nothing is stopped and the interval closes where it opened; the other order can destroy work for a revocation that then fails to land, and no sentence makes that true. Mutation (criterion 7): removing mode != runsStop made future-only stop too, and the test failed with 'run 1 was stopped by a forget that said it would leave it alone'. Wiring stays inside internal/transport — the worker corrected my brief here: app.go needs no edit, since pendingRuns and agentPolicy are both fields of the same *WSServer, and the stop goes through the SAME agentHandlers agent.cancel uses rather than a partially-filled one built beside it. Merged tree green: transport (303s), content (211s), assistant, app under -race; contracts:check, tsc --noEmit, 6225 frontend tests.

title: Task 13: revoking an answer says what happens to the work already running
description:
Plan task 13. Grants already minted stay alive, so revocation has a time and the person chooses it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A change or forget affecting live runs says how many and offers apply-to-future-runs against also-stop-the-runs-using-it.
- Future-only leaves running work alone: asserted at both ends, the run finishes under the old answer and the next run gets the new one.
- Stopping terminates those runs through the existing terminalization path, with the reason naming the revoked answer.

title: ws_api_cancel.go's interval comment still says the deferred drop is what closes the token's interval
description:
Split out of nocx-pgp9c.8 during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh so that bead could be closed as fixed without losing its second criterion.

The defect pgp9c.8 and nocx-dbqmx both named was fixed by commit 39d223df (under nocx-f9har): internal/transport/ws_api_handlers.go:515 now drops the cancel token BEFORE enqueueing the result, rather than in a defer that ran after the response was written. The defer at :330 survives deliberately, as cleanup for the paths that never reach :515.

What did not follow is the prose. internal/transport/ws_api_cancel.go:15 still explains the interval as holding 'until the exchange has SETTLED, whichever way it settled, because the drop is deferred in the same function'. The deferral is no longer the reason the interval closes on time; it is the fallback. Two lines, and it is exactly the kind of comment a later reader would trust.
acceptance_criteria: The comment at internal/transport/ws_api_cancel.go:15-20 either states what now closes the interval — the explicit drop before the result is enqueued — or says what the remaining defer is for. No behaviour change.

title: A capped directory is never polled: re-enumerating it every tick computes a digest the cap will refuse
description:
Carried forward from nocx-rkk9 when that bead was closed as superseded during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh. Every other clause of rkk9's remainder found a home — local fsnotify went to nocx-9stiv, remote poll jitter and the backoff ladder to nocx-8hdia (already shipped at internal/transport/ws_files.go:334-433), and the visible-degrade badge landed early inside nocx-708q. This one had none, and would have been lost with the bead.

The clause, in rkk9's words: a directory that is over the entry cap must NOT be polled, because polling it re-enumerates every entry on every tick only to compute a digest the cap will then refuse. Measured during the sweep: grep for entryCap in internal/transport/ws_files.go returns nothing, so the cadence work does not yet know about the cap.
acceptance_criteria: A directory over the entry cap is not enumerated by the poll loop at all, and a test asserts the poll does no work for it — not merely that the result is refused after the enumeration.

title: main() is a 1670-line composition root with no test seam
description:
frontend/src/main.tsx is one `main(): void` invoked at module scope, so the
composition root cannot be exercised by any unit test: importing it runs the
whole application against a webview shim it has no way to satisfy.

Measured while fixing nocx-xhm9e, whose entire defect lived at a single line
of that function — an opener lambda that dropped the profile's port. The
existing frontend/src/main.test.ts is named for the file but does not import
it; it rebuilds a Dispatcher-and-sidebar arrangement of its own and asserts
the disposal contract on that. So there is no seam today, and the arity guard
that closed nocx-xhm9e had to be a TYPE-level one for that reason.

That guard is the right answer for arity and only for arity. Every other
wiring mistake at this root — a client handed to the wrong constructor, a
callback wired to the neighbouring method of the same shape, a provider
registered under the wrong kind set — is still unreachable by anything but
e2e.

WOULD BE DONE WHEN: main.tsx exports the wiring as something a test can call
with fakes (or the root is split so the quick-connect providers are assembled
in a module of their own), and one test asserts a provider list built from the
real assembly rather than from a hand-written opener.

title: Portal root JSDoc teaches the render-into-a-shared-host pattern that wipes siblings
description:
`frontend/src/ui/overlay/portal.ts` documents its usage as
`render(() => <MyOverlay />, getPortalRoot())`. Solid's `render()` disposer ends
with `element.textContent = ''`, so the first overlay to dispose wipes every
other overlay portaled into the shared root.

No live defect today — the sole consumer (`overview/overview-controller.ts:95`)
appends its own host first — but the documented example is the exact shape that
caused nocx-3hv2t, where the clipboard banner rendered straight into `#panes`
and its disposer removed every terminal pane. A doc example is a template; this
one templates the bug.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Follow the `@example` block in `frontend/src/ui/overlay/portal.ts` for two
   overlays: `render(() => <A />, getPortalRoot())` and
   `render(() => <B />, getPortalRoot())`.
2. Dispose A.
3. B is gone from the DOM too — `getPortalRoot()` was emptied.

## Expected Behavior

The JSDoc example shows the safe shape: create a host element, append it to the
portal root, render into the host, and remove the host after disposing the Solid
root.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The `@example` in `portal.ts` creates a per-overlay host and renders into it.
- The doc states in one line why passing the shared root to `render()` is wrong.
close_reason: Portal root JSDoc now shows the host-per-overlay form with its teardown and states why getPortalRoot() must never be passed to render(). Landed on main in 02db8abc alongside nocx-3hv2t.

title: Report the atlas-merge repaint hole upstream to xterm.js
description:
nocx-4z5hv fixed the symptom at our seam: XtermRenderer subscribes to the
addon's onAddTextureAtlasCanvas and schedules the post-frame repaint the
library assumes will happen anyway.

The defect itself is upstream, in @xterm/xterm 5.5.0
(src/browser/renderer/shared/TextureAtlas.ts). _createNewPage() merges four
pages, rewrites the texture coordinates of every glyph it moved IN PLACE, and
then only sets `_requestClearModel = true`. That flag is read by
WebglRenderer.renderRows at the TOP of a frame, while the merge happens later
in that same frame inside _updateModel. So the frame that broke is never
repaired, and nothing is scheduled: no refreshRows, no animation frame,
nothing marked dirty. If no further output arrives, the corruption is
permanent until something unrelated repaints.

Minimal upstream fix: have the merge request a redraw (the renderer already
has _requestRedrawViewport) rather than only recording an intention.

Also worth reporting: `_requestClearModel` is never reset to false, so after
the first merge every subsequent frame is a full-viewport rebuild.

Deliberately not blocking anything. Our seam is correct independent of the
upstream outcome -- a library liveness assumption we cannot verify is one we
have to close ourselves -- so an upstream fix would make our repaint redundant
and harmless, not removable by default.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An issue is opened on xterm.js describing the merge/schedule window, with
  the file and function named and the one-frame reasoning spelled out.
- The issue links a minimal reproduction or explains why one needs a real GPU
  and 16+ atlas pages.
- The issue id is recorded here, and in the comment on
  XtermRenderer._scheduleRepaintAfterFrame.
- Out of scope: upgrading xterm in this repo. That is a separate decision and
  must be taken on evidence that a newer addon actually closes the window.

title: The pet layer paints over a floating panel
description:
`.pet-layer` is z-index 2 and `.ui-floating-panel` is z-index 1, so the animal
can be drawn over a panel rather than under it. The design says a panel covers
the pet, and it does not.

Found by review on 2026-09-02, statically. Which surfaces actually overlap the
pet's area has not been checked in a browser, so the fix should start there
rather than from the numbers.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a surface that renders `.ui-floating-panel` over the terminal.
2. Wait for the pet to walk under it.
3. The animal is painted on top.

## Acceptance Criteria

- With a floating panel open over the terminal, no part of the animal is
  drawn on top of it.
- The animal is still drawn above the terminal's own layers.
- Asserted in the e2e suite, on a real stacking context rather than by
  reading the two numbers.

title: Watching a long command has phases
description:
The animal settles once and holds one posture for however long the command takes, so a two-second command and a two-minute one look identical.

Count how long it has been attending and cross a few thresholds once each: settle by 5s; lie or sit quietly to 20s; change posture once around a minute; after that, a stretch or a scratch and back to watching. No output is read -- only the clock.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A command lasting over a minute produces at least one posture change, and a short one produces none.
- Each threshold fires once per command, never on a loop.
- Still no sleeping and no leaving the ledge while attending.
close_reason: Vigil counts its own seconds and crosses three thresholds once each: settle at 5s, quiet posture at 20s, one gesture at 60s, then deliberately still for the rest of the command. No output read. Agent's gesture is a groom, not the scratch that answers a failed command. No sleeping and no leaving the ledge while attending. Committed b4ef2ce1.

title: A contact shadow under the feet
description:
Nothing connects the animal to the thin line it is standing on, so at a glance it floats over the block rather than resting on it.

A pixel-hard strip or ellipse, 30-45% of the body width and one or two pixels tall, fully visible on a ledge, gone the moment it leaves the ground, back and slightly wider just before it touches down. No large blur -- this is pixel art.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The shadow is present exactly when the animal is grounded.
- It is drawn by the overlay, not by the pack, so every colour gets it.
- It never appears under a pet standing on the window floor with nothing to cast onto.
close_reason: Two-pixel hard-edged strip on the world layer beside the sprite, so it travels with the animal without inheriting squash or tilt. Drawn by the overlay, so every colour gets it. None on the window floor. Returns before contact, widening 36->42% over the last fifth of a second; time to contact computed in pet.ts where the fall already sweeps for its ledge. Committed 403464c7.

title: Noticing that you came back
description:
The animal has its own boredom but knows nothing about the person's. Someone returning to a terminal they left ten minutes ago is the most legible moment a screenmate has, and it is currently indistinguishable from any other second.

Track the user's idle time separately from the cat's: after a few minutes away, damp running and jumping; on return, wake, stretch, and rejoin the ordinary menu after a second or so. Typing is a SESSION, not a keystroke -- the first key after a pause opens it, later keys only extend it, and the animal looks over once rather than per character.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Returning after five minutes produces exactly one waking sequence.
- Typing a hundred characters produces at most one reaction.
- Nothing happens on window focus or blur alone.
close_reason: Human idleness tracked apart from the cat's, fed by main.tsx's existing activity owner as a second consumer rather than second listeners; the vault's 3s throttle untouched because the pet defines its own session. One glance per absence, a hundred keys produce one reaction, focus/blur alone do nothing. Running and jumping damped after five minutes away. The waking stretch takes its length from chosenHold. Committed 403464c7.

title: The pet stops looking like a sticker
description:
The animal walks, jumps, reacts and watches. What it does NOT yet do is
move like a creature: it switches clips instantly, travels at a constant
speed regardless of the gait it is drawing, runs in mid-air, and picks its
next occupation without remembering the last one. Those four are what a
person reads as "a sticker with a state machine".

Reviewed against the implementation on 2026-09-02; the ranking is by effect
over cost, and the cheap half is most of the effect.

## Success Criteria

A person watching the pet for one minute cannot point to a moment where it
moved mechanically. Proved by a deterministic simulator over hundreds of
seeds plus one e2e scenario per motion phase, asserting:

- No reaction clip is ever cut mid-cycle: a one-shot clip plays to its last
  frame before anything else is chosen.
- A walking pet's foot does not slide: at the gait's contact frames the
  world position of the foot moves less than one source pixel per frame.
- No activity repeats immediately, except sitting, lying, sleeping and
  watching.
- No more than two conspicuous events (jump, run, turn, reaction) per minute
  of unattended behaviour.
- The animal is never drawn running while in the air.
- Over five minutes on a landscape with three reachable ledges, the 95th
  percentile of seeds leaves the ledge it started on.

## Deliberately out

Sounds. Speech bubbles. Reacting per keystroke or per output line. Any
appetite, health, streak or currency. Semantic parsing of shell commands.
Dragging the animal with the mouse -- it would end the guarantee that the
layer is transparent to the terminal, and change the genre from an ambient
creature to a toy on top of a working tool.
acceptance_criteria: See Success Criteria

title: Bring your own pet: a pack format and an importer
description:
A user-supplied pack in an open format (`nocx.pet/v1`: JSON manifest plus a PNG
atlas), plus importers that translate a Shimeji or eSheep pack into it.

This is where the licence question stops being ours. The good art in this
genre forbids redistribution -- vscode-pets had to delete its cats from
GitHub at the artist's request -- but if the pack reaches the person from its
author and nocx only READS a folder, nocx is not the distributor. The line is
who hands over the file, not who clicks.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A person can point nocx at a folder and see their own animal, with nocx
  having downloaded nothing.
- The import treats the folder as untrusted input: magic bytes rather than
  extensions, PNG only, no SVG, no `DOCTYPE` or entities, bounded manifest
  size, frame count, pixel budget and durations; staged then renamed;
  nothing from the folder is executed.
- The imported pack is copied into the managed appdir, never read in place.
- The importer says plainly that nocx grants no licence to the pack.
- A Shimeji `actions.xml` is translated into a restricted internal form, with
  no expression evaluation of any kind, and an unknown condition raises a
  diagnostic rather than defaulting to true.

## Deliberately out

A catalogue, a gallery, or any button that fetches a pack. That would make us
the distributor again.

## Depends on a decision

Reading a user's PNG needs a path ADR-0036/0037 do not currently allow.

title: TestLoader_EOFMidFrameNamesBootstrapInterrupted loses its login marker when the master closes under it
description:
Observed once on CI, run 33607389397, job ci-backend (with-secret-service), on
the merged tree of PR #170:

    --- FAIL: TestLoader_EOFMidFrameNamesBootstrapInterrupted (0.01s)
        carrier_exec_test.go:432: the session ended without emitting
        "NATIVE_LOGIN_RAN"

It passed on a rerun of the same commit, and the SIBLING matrix variant
(no-secret-service) passed it on that same commit and the same package list —
so this is the test, not the Secret Service axis and not the merge.

The shape is the one bd memory `a-flaky-go-test-in-this-repo-is` names: the
test closes the PTY master and only THEN waits for two markers on the pipe
(`s.master.Close()` followed by two `s.waitFor`). After the master closes, the
child can lose the race to print `NATIVE_LOGIN_RAN` before it is torn down —
so the marker is a MOMENT the test hopes to catch rather than an observable it
can wait on.

That memory also gives the diagnostic that applies here: a failure that eats
its whole window is a starved machine, and one that fails in 0.01s is a LOST
EVENT. This failed in 0.01s.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `go test -race -tags gtk3 -count=1 ./internal/shellintegration/` in the CI
   image, repeatedly — it is rare, once in the runs looked at.
2. `-count=20` on a loaded machine is the likelier reproduction.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The test waits on an observable that survives the master's close, or the
  ordering is made deterministic so the marker cannot be lost.
- Whatever the fix, it does not weaken what the test asserts: that a truncated
  frame is NOT executed (no STAGE1_RAN) and the native login still runs.
- `-count=20` under load is green.
notes: Backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh: nocx-d3vv5 was closed as a duplicate of this bead (same test, same single assertion, same failure text — internal/shellintegration/carrier_exec_test.go has exactly one s.waitFor(nativeLoginMarker), which d3vv5 cited at :429 and this bead at :432). Its evidence is copied here rather than discarded, because it puts a SECOND mechanism on the table that is recorded nowhere else: d3vv5's captured output carries '/bin/sh: 4: id: not found' and '/bin/sh: 4: [: Illegal number:', i.e. a DEGRADED ENVIRONMENT inherited from the whole-module run, whereas this bead describes a 0.01s lost event. Same assertion, two candidate causes — check which one is actually firing before fixing. Also measured during the sweep: carrier_exec_test.go makes ZERO calls to internal/waittest, while 95 other Go test files already import it.
close_reason: Fixed, and the bead's own instruction — 'same assertion, two candidate causes, check which one is actually firing before fixing' — was followed. Reproduced 2026-09-04 in CI's container image on a full-package go test -race: 0.01s, output 'NOCX1 LOADER_READY / NOCX1 OUTCOME interrupted' and NO degraded-environment lines ('id: not found', 'Illegal number') anywhere in the run. So the LOST EVENT was firing, not nocx-d3vv5's degraded environment. Cause: startLoader gives the child Setsid+Setctty with the pty slave, so it is a session leader whose controlling terminal is that pty; closing the master sends SIGHUP to it, and a non-interactive /bin/sh dies on SIGHUP by default — racing the native login it is supposed to reach. Fix: the child ignores SIGHUP ('trap \'\' HUP; ' prefixed to the launcher), because the hangup is the HARNESS'S ARTEFACT and not the scenario — what the test is about is a frame that stopped arriving, which in the product is an ssh channel reaching EOF and hangs nothing up. An ignored disposition survives the exec, so the whole loader runs under it, and nothing the test asserts moves: a truncated frame is still not executed and the native login still has to run. -count=20 of TestLoader_* in CI's image is green, and so is the whole package. Left standing for whoever sees it next: nocx-d3vv5's SECOND candidate — a degraded environment inherited from a whole-module run — was not observed here and is not addressed by this fix; if the failure returns with 'id: not found' in the output, it is that one and not this. internal/shellintegration/carrier_exec_test.go:418. Commit 8b1c3b15.
