title: Quote tool-call argument values that carry spaces
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Ask the assistant something in a pane whose tab title has spaces (e.g. "* Claude Code").
2. Let it call session.read.

Observed: the call reads `session.read session=* Claude Code id=att-cf87…` —
nothing says which words belong to `session`, because the pairs are joined by
spaces and the value carries them too.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A value containing whitespace is quoted in the title; one without is not.
- Session names, which are people-written tab titles, are the case this is for.
- Nothing is truncated — the title is still what the ⋮ menu copies.
close_reason: Fixed and covered on fix/assistant-bugs

title: What we cost a host has one owner and a ceiling
description:
Owner, after the Files poll was measured: "нам нужен какой-то глобальный
throttler, который ограничивает наше воздействие на локальный и удаленный
сервера."

## The gap, verified

Every bound in this codebase is a CONCURRENCY bound. There is no rate bound
anywhere — grepped for rate / throttle / budget / token bucket across
`internal/`, nothing.

- `capability.Gate(GateFilesystem, 1, 8, 1s)` (`internal/transport/ws.go:1527`)
  — one filesystem call in flight, queue 8, 1s wait.
- `control.NewSemaphore("control", laneCapacity)` — the shared control lane.
- `fsLaneCap` — concurrent in-flight SFTP calls per lease
  (`internal/ssh/ssh_fsconn.go:194`).
- `discovery.Scheduler` — a genuine cadence policy, but only for Ports.

A capacity-1 semaphore does not reduce two requests per second to one; it
serializes them. That is exactly why the Files poll at 500ms produced no
visible contention and still walked every watched directory twice a second.

And the gates are keyed BY DOMAIN — filesystem, git, ports. So three panels
can each be within their own gate while together hammering ONE remote host,
and nothing sees the sum. "What we cost a host" is a quantity that currently
has no owner.

## What a person gets

Opening several panels against a remote host does not degrade that host or
their connection, and the app can say what it is spending rather than leaving
them to guess why their server got slow.

## The mechanism is deliberately NOT decided here

Two candidate shapes, and the first child bead is the ADR that picks one.

- A token-bucket `Admission` in `internal/transport/control`, composed via the
  existing `NewComposite`. The package's own doc pre-authorizes exactly this:
  "a new kind of resource is added by constructing another Admission and
  wiring it, with zero edits in this package" — and `Rejection.RetryAfter`
  already exists in the contract.
- A central SCHEDULER owning cadence the way `internal/discovery/schedule.go`
  does for Ports, so nothing is ever refused because nothing is ever
  over-issued. Refusing background work is safe; a scheduler that never has to
  refuse is better still — but it only governs PERIODIC work, and the epic
  must say what happens to everything else.

Constraints the choice has to satisfy, whichever it is:

1. **Keyed by target host, not by domain.** One budget for the local machine,
   one per remote profile. What identifies the host at the point of admission
   — binding id, profile id, ssh pool key — and whether that mapping already
   has an owner, is part of the ADR.
2. **Background and user-initiated are different classes.** A watch tick, a
   poll, a discovery sample may be deferred or refused; a poll is an
   invalidation hint and skipping one is harmless. An expand, a "Show next", a
   Refresh press, a file open may NOT be. A throttler that refuses a click is
   a defect, not a protection. How that class travels to the admission point
   without every call site growing a boolean it can lie about — and without
   branching on `Name()`, which the package forbids — is the hard part.
3. **Local and remote may not deserve the same mechanism.** Locally the cost
   is lstats and page cache; remotely it is round trips over one SSH
   connection with its own lane cap. The ADR says whether one mechanism spans
   both or they only share a vocabulary.
4. **Refusals are visible in the product.** AGENTS.md: a soft degrade the UI
   contradicts is how a feature that does not exist survives a release. If we
   are throttling, the panel says so.
5. **Numbers are derived, not invented** — from the cadences already stated
   for Ports (10s periodic) and Git (5s), in the form
   `internal/discovery/schedule.go:13-43` uses, where each timer exists for a
   written reason.

## This does not replace the cadence work

A throttler bounds damage; cadence removes work. If the Files poll stayed at
500ms and a limiter refused nine calls in ten, we would have built a
busy-loop that manufactures refusals. `nocx-8hdia` lands first and is what
actually reduces load; this epic is what stops the next panel from repeating
it and gives the quantity an owner.

## Deliberately out

- Per-panel cadence (that is `nocx-8hdia`).
- Throttling the terminal data plane. AD-1 keeps PTY bytes off the control
  plane and this must not become a reason to touch them.

## Success Criteria

- An ADR in `docs/decisions/` picks the mechanism and records what was
  rejected and why.
- One place answers "what are we currently spending against this host", for
  the local target and for each remote profile, and every background producer
  goes through it — Files watching, Git polling, Ports sampling.
- Background work over budget is deferred or refused with a retry hint;
  user-initiated work is never refused by this mechanism, and there is a test
  asserting exactly that under a fully exhausted budget.
- Sustained refusal is visible in the panel, not only in `slog`.
- A test drives several panels against one target and asserts the aggregate
  stays under the stated ceiling — the thing no per-domain gate can assert
  today.
notes:
REVISED after adversarial review (codex, 2026-08-31). The NEED stands; the
proposed wiring was wrong in a way that would have made it decorative.

THE WIRING WAS WRONG. Composing a throttling Admission into the transport
control plane would govern ONE of the three producers. Verified:
  - Files polling calls h.List DIRECTLY from its retained goroutine
    (ws_files.go, filesPollPath), never through the FilesystemBindingOperation.
  - Ports sampling calls its provider directly from the scheduler's own loop
    (schedule.go:380, schedTarget.loop -> sampleTriggered).
  - Only Git polling re-enters through git.status and its operation
    (ws_git.go:715).
So the epic as first written would have throttled Git and nothing else. That
is the single most important correction here.

THE KEY IS NOT 'HOST'. There is no such identity at any acquisition point.
bindingId is one capability; profileId is saved configuration and consent
(several profiles can reach one host, a direct connection has none);
endpointId is domain-local and hashes configured material; HostKeyFingerprint
is reused across clusters and jump routes. The identity of the actually shared
resource is the SSH poolKey — host, port, user, credential principal, jump
route (internal/ssh/pool.go:155) — which is unexported and owned by the pool,
deliberately. So a remote aggregate bound belongs BESIDE poolEntry in
internal/ssh, keyed by poolKey. That is a budget per authenticated route, not
per physical host, and that is the honest boundary: two targets behind one
bastion share a bottleneck, one target over two routes does not.

Do NOT build a transport-level registry that reverse-maps bindings and
profiles to guessed hosts.

LOCAL DOES NOT SHARE THE POLICY. One 'local' bucket would mix CPU, page-cache
pressure and filesystem latency with remote channel starts. Same vocabulary at
most, separate policy — and once fsnotify lands (nocx-9stiv) ordinary local
directory polling disappears anyway, which may leave local with nothing to
bound.

A BUCKET IS THE WRONG PRIMITIVE. It limits STARTS, not cost — a ten-entry
directory and a 5000-entry SFTP directory spend one token each. It is bursty
by construction. And refusing a poll throws away intent that could simply be
coalesced and performed later. The right primitive is a per-target
AUTOMATIC-WORK ARBITER: one automatic operation in flight, a coalescing
capacity-one trigger, demand work first, the next automatic start armed only
after the previous returns, and a demand request able to cancel an in-flight
automatic ReadDir through its context. Ports already is this shape
(schedule.go:380) — this generalises it rather than inventing a second answer.

VISIBILITY REQUIREMENT SOFTENED, DELIBERATELY. 'Every throttled poll is
visible' was wrong: a routine scheduling delay is not a degraded feature and
must not badge. AGENTS.md forbids a degrade the UI CONTRADICTS. So surface
only when a DECLARED freshness threshold is missed, a watch is lost, or
fallback polling is active.

SEQUENCING: this epic is now gated on MEASUREMENT. nocx-8hdia (visibility,
baseline diffing, cadence, one-path dispatch) and nocx-9stiv (fsnotify) remove
the work; they may remove enough of it that the aggregate never approaches a
ceiling worth enforcing. Take this epic when a measurement of aggregate
per-poolKey activity, after those land, shows cross-domain bursts that no
single domain can see. Not before.

title: cwd on macOS is still unanswered, and the two remaining routes both have a price
description:
Left open by nocx-k6p18.10, which established that it cannot be reached the cheap way and
made the product say so honestly instead.

The evidence for the no: macOS's KERN_PROC carries no working directory in any of its
subdivisions, kern.proc.cwd is FreeBSD's, and proc_pidinfo(PROC_PIDVNODEPATHINFO) is a
libSystem symbol rather than a syscall number — so x/sys/unix cannot reach it at all.

TWO ROUTES REMAIN, both with a real price:

  1. Hand-written //go:cgo_import_dynamic plus per-arch asm trampolines to proc_pidinfo.
     Duplicates the machinery x/sys generates, and is verifiable only on a Mac.
  2. Accept cgo for the helper, and re-argue the ~2.8 MiB size constraint that refused it.

THE MEASUREMENT THAT DECISION NEEDS IS ALREADY DONE, which is why this is worth filing
rather than leaving as a shrug: the sysctl inspector cost +17.8 KiB on darwin/arm64 (0.63%,
2.760 -> 2.778 MiB) with ZERO new dependencies, because x/sys/unix was already in the
helper's darwin graph through internal/pty. Whatever cgo would cost is measured against
that, and against the reason the size limit exists at all — the helper is a survival
component that must stay compatible across generations and is deployed to machines we do
not own.

Not urgent. It is filed so the answer is chosen rather than defaulted into.
acceptance_criteria: Either the helper reports a real cwd on macOS, or the decision to leave it unavailable is taken deliberately with the cost of both alternatives written down. 'unavailable' is an acceptable permanent answer; an undecided one is not.
notes:
COST ESTABLISHED 2026-09-02 (coordinator). Not yet decided; this records what the
decision is actually between, because the code used to state a reason that was
wrong.

WHAT WAS WRONG. Two comments -- inspect_darwin.go and proto/session_service.go --
said cgo was "refused by D3's size argument (~2.8 MiB against ~40 MiB)". D3 says
nothing about cgo. It argues for a THIN PRODUCT and never mentions a toolchain.
The number was stale too: after nocx-k6p18.20 split the SSH client out, the
largest stripped target is 4,212,352 bytes against a 5 MiB ceiling. Corrected in
4d3d6362; the comments now point here.

WHAT THE DECISION IS ACTUALLY BETWEEN. Reading another process's cwd on macOS
needs proc_pidinfo(PROC_PIDVNODEPATHINFO), a libSystem symbol, so it needs cgo.
Nothing forbids that. What it costs is the BUILD, twice over:

1. ORIGIN. A cgo darwin target must be compiled on a Mac. nocx-6de7c decided the
   helper artifacts have ONE origin; this splits that into one origin per
   platform. GitHub Actions has macOS runners, so this is a pipeline change and a
   provenance change, not an impossibility -- but it IS the decision, and it is
   the part that outlives the feature.

2. FLOOR. With cgo the deployment floor stops being Go's own and becomes whatever
   -mmacosx-version-min the runner's SDK picks by default. That has to be pinned
   explicitly and asserted in CI, or the helper silently stops running on older
   macOS the first time GitHub bumps its image -- and it would be discovered by a
   user on a remote host, not by us.

WHAT IS NOT AN ARGUMENT. That macOS-as-a-remote-host is rare: that was an
unmeasured guess by the coordinator, and the owner rejected it. Do not reintroduce
it.

THE ALTERNATIVE THAT IS ALREADY SHIPPED. cwd arrives as an explicit "unavailable"
Diagnostic, so the product can say "we do not know where this shell is" rather
than showing where it started (nocx-k6p18.10). That is honest and it is not
nothing. The question this bead answers is whether knowing beats saying we do not
know, at the price of the two costs above.

Third option, considered and not taken: shelling out to lsof. It forks a process
per inventory row on a host we do not own, and makes a diagnostic depend on a tool
being present.

title: Decide deliberately whether a name filter may run before the entry cap
description:
DEFERRED — records a decision, so it is not re-made by accident.

A directory over `entryCap` (10_000 local, 5_000 remote) is refused outright
with `ErrTooLarge` and is not listed or polled at all (design D14). It is
therefore unsearchable: the name filter has nothing to match against.

A `nameFilter` applied BEFORE the cap would make such a directory searchable.

The argument against, and why it is currently the answer: the cap guards the
COST OF ENUMERATION, not the size of the response. The refusal happens at
`local.go:200` / `sftp.go:329`, before the per-entry metadata loop and before
the digest — which is exactly the expensive part. Filtering does not make
that enumeration cheaper, and the full-directory `rev` needs every accepted
entry anyway. So filtering before the cap would spend precisely the cost the
cap exists to refuse.

Changing it means changing what D14 means, deliberately, in the design — not
inside a filter bead.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Either the cap keeps its current meaning and this bead closes as
  "deliberate, recorded"; or D14 is amended in the design document first and
  this bead implements the amended rule.

title: Filter names on the wire, in the transport, when a projection's size is measured to hurt
description:
DEFERRED OPTIMISATION — take it on measurement, not on principle.

Once the filter fetches a truncated directory whole (nocx-708q.8), the cost
that remains is loopback bytes and rows held in a projection: up to `sizeCap`
8 MiB for a directory at the ceiling. A `nameFilter` parameter on `files.list`
would cut that to the matches.

What it does NOT buy: round trips. Both providers enumerate the whole
directory before slicing (`internal/filesystem/local/local.go:177`), so the
expensive half — a remote SFTP `ReadDir` — costs the same either way. And the
WebSocket is 127.0.0.1 (`ws.go:1615`), so the bytes saved are loopback bytes.

What it COSTS: a round trip per distinct query rather than one per filter
session, because every keystroke is a new result set. Through a filesystem
gate of capacity 1, queue 8, wait timeout 1s (`ws.go:1527`), against list
timeouts of 10s local and 30s remote. On a laggy SFTP link that is refusals
while the person types.

So the trigger for doing this is a MEASURED case where a projection's size
hurts — not a hypothetical one.

## The shape, when it is taken

Filter in the TRANSPORT, over the complete provider listing — request
`{offset: 0, limit: MaxInt}` from the provider, filter the sorted result once,
then apply the requested filtered offset and limit. NOT in both providers:
two implementations of "does this name match" that have to agree about case
folding is the second-answer defect AGENTS.md names.

Semantics that must be written into the contract, because they change:
- `total` — the count of MATCHING entries in the complete directory.
- `offset` — an index into the matching subsequence, not the directory.
- `hasMore` — whether another MATCH follows this page.
- `rev` — still the digest of the COMPLETE unfiltered directory. Not
  negotiable: a match-only digest is incomparable with the watcher's map, and
  it would fail to invalidate when a non-matching entry is RENAMED into a
  match.

Note there is no generated TS params type to regenerate — `frontend/src/
generated/files.list.ts` is generated from the RESULT schema only, and params
are built by hand in `files-client.ts:34`. What moves together is the params
schema, the OpenRPC reference, the Go struct, `validateFilesListRaw`
(`ws_files.go:111`) and the client signature.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Not started until a measurement names the directory and the cost.
- If taken: filtering lives in the transport, once; the contract states the
  conditional meanings of `total`, `offset` and `hasMore`; `rev` stays the
  unfiltered digest; a contract test covers a filtered result over the real
  socket.

title: The released fixture writes a file no released build wrote
description:
Measured by nocx-lmb6v.7 on a scratch probe, 2026-08-31, and deliberately NOT asserted in
the parity test — because it would have been red for the fixture's reason rather than the
product's, which is the wrong test.

  fresh:             auto_vacuum = 2  (INCREMENTAL)
  fixture-migrated:  auto_vacuum = 0

Open sets PRAGMA auto_vacuum=INCREMENTAL before the first table, and its own comment
(nocx-rtg0.11) says it cannot be changed afterwards without a full VACUUM — so on any
EXISTING file that line is a silent no-op. A real released 14 build ran the same line at
creation, so the 0 measured here is the FIXTURE's artefact, not a live product defect.

That is itself the finding: aReleasedSchema14Database reproduces the DDL faithfully — it
was diffed byte-for-byte against the schemaV1 constant at the right commit — and does not
reproduce the engine posture. A fixture that differs from what the version actually wrote
is a fixture that can pass a test the real file would fail, or fail one it would pass.

THE LATENT PRODUCT RISK BEHIND IT is the same class as nocx-lmb6v.7 itself: a per-file
setting where the fresh and upgraded populations diverge permanently, with nothing to
notice. auto_vacuum happens to be safe here. Nothing asserts that it is, and nothing
enumerates which other pragmas have that property.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a database through Open. PRAGMA auto_vacuum reports 2.
2. Migrate aReleasedSchema14Database forward through Open. It reports 0.
3. Nothing fails.

## Fix

Either the fixture is written by, or made to match, what the released build produced; or
the suite names the settings it does not reproduce and says why each is safe to differ.
Then, separately, enumerate the per-file settings that can diverge between fresh and
upgraded and decide whether any needs a parity assertion of its own.
acceptance_criteria: A released-schema fixture reproduces the engine posture a real build of that version produced, or the test suite states which settings it does not reproduce and why that is safe. Separately: whether fresh and upgraded databases can diverge permanently on a per-file pragma is answered, either way.
close_reason:
Committed as 15736af4 on omp/lmb6v-10-fixture (first omp worker of the session, run through herdr). Merged and re-tested on the integration tree: go test ./internal/content/ ok 27.0s.

LANDED IN BRANCH ONE: the fixture now reproduces the engine posture rather than only the DDL. aReleasedSchema14Database prepends PRAGMA auto_vacuum=INCREMENTAL and PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL before its first table, exactly as Open does, with the reason in the code: omitting either made it a schema-faithful but engine-different fixture, and an upgraded file could then pass a parity test for the wrong reason.

AND IT DID THE ENUMERATION, which was the half with lasting value. Four per-file settings audited in a SEPARATE test rather than bolted onto the parity comparator, so that comparator keeps checking schema shape and cannot fail because a fixture omitted a creation-time pragma:
  auto_vacuum  — can differ permanently after the first table; the store never inspects it after creation, so a mismatch would be silent. Both populations must be 2.
  page_size    — can differ permanently when chosen before the first table; this build leaves the default, so both must be 4096.
  encoding     — same shape; both must be UTF-8.
  journal_mode — file state, but Open normalises it to WAL on every open, which is what makes it safe for both populations.

The distinction that makes the list a list rather than one example: connection-scoped settings (busy_timeout, foreign_keys, temp_store) are deliberately EXCLUDED and the type says so, because they cannot outlive the connection that set them and so cannot diverge between populations.

Nothing was found that can diverge unsafely, which is the answer the bead asked for either way.

title: ADR-0021 still records the rebuild as decided behaviour, and the surface it promises is gone
description:
Found by nocx-lmb6v.4, 2026-08-31, which deliberately did not fix it — and was right not to:
AGENTS.md says re-deciding a settled question inside another change is how it stops being
settled.

docs/decisions/0021-secrets-in-the-prompt.md asserts the rebuild twice:

  line 48   "The store rebuilds on a schema change and logs how many rows it discarded;
             there is no migration"
  line 157  "A schema change rebuilds the store and says what it discarded" — bolded, and
             adding that "'your history was discarded' is a fact the user is entitled to
             rather than something to infer from an empty panel"

nocx-lmb6v.1 replaced the rebuild with a migrate-or-refuse ladder, and nocx-lmb6v.4
removed the discard sentence because nothing could ever raise it. So the second passage
now promises a surface that does not exist, and the first describes a protocol that was
replaced. The gap pre-dates nocx-lmb6v.4; nocx-lmb6v.1 did not amend the ADR.

FORM MATTERS HERE, and it is the owner's standing instruction: old documents and ADRs are
not rewritten. An ADR records a decision that was correct when taken, and this one was —
the store WAS local and disposable. What is owed is a superseding record saying the
premise expired when content.db stopped being disposable, which is the same sentence
nocx-lmb6v's own description already carries.

Also worth checking while there: whether anything else in docs/decisions/ asserts the
rebuild. This one was found by accident rather than by a sweep.
acceptance_criteria: The record of the current system no longer asserts a behaviour that does not exist. Done as a SUPERSEDING note or a short new ADR, not by rewriting the old one — the old decision was correct when it was taken, and the record of it stays.
close_reason:
ADR-0054 is the superseding record; ADR-0021 is unedited except for one pointer line, and the SCOPE of that line is the finding worth keeping.

The obvious move was "Status: Superseded" on 0021. That would have been wrong: 0021 is about masking secrets in the prompt, and it remains the authority on durable command text, redaction segments and vault-secret resolution. Only its two schema paragraphs expired. So the line reads "Schema lifecycle: superseded by ADR-0054" and 0054 says in its own Consequences which half of 0021 still governs. A supersession that takes the whole document would have quietly retired three live decisions to correct one dead one.

0054 records what nocx-lmb6v.1 decided rather than deciding anything: an ordered migrate-or-refuse ladder, one rung per supported edge, the stamp moving only after the change commits, a newer-stamped file refused rather than rebuilt or judged by an older binary, and a rung landing together with its shape guard in the same change. It states plainly that there is no rebuild path and no "history was discarded" surface in the current system — which is the sentence that makes the stale promise visible as stale.

THE SWEEP THE BEAD SAID HAD NEVER BEEN DONE IS DONE, and its result is the reason the bead asked for it. Sixteen documents assert a rebuild or a discard. Fifteen are still true about something else entirely: disposable projections rebuildable from the ledger (0019), the mirrored-layer approach discarded in 0010, alternate-buffer contents (0029), idle connections dropped on a generation change (0038), window position discarded on a display mismatch (0048), a coordinator rebuilt twice in CI (0052), and so on. Exactly one — 0021 — is stale.

That ratio is the argument for sweeping by CONCEPT rather than by phrase, and for recording the true hits alongside the stale one: the next person who greps "rebuild" will get fifteen false positives, and now there is a list saying so.

The Go comment sweep found only historical explanations, current migration behaviour, and the intentional SQLite table-rebuild mechanics of the 14->15 rung. No stale whole-ContentDB rebuild claim, so no bead was filed — an absence that was looked for rather than assumed.

Merged as 9aac2bb4.

title: A database whose stamp lies about its shape fails with a sentence about corruption, not migration
description:
Noted by nocx-lmb6v.1, 2026-08-31.

A database stamped 14 whose tables are not schema 14's walks the ladder, is stamped
forward, and then fails at schemaV1 with something like `no such column: session_id`.

Nothing is destroyed and the degrade IS visible — it reaches Settings through
HistoryDegradeOpenFailed like every other open failure. The defect is only the wording:
the sentence a person gets is about a missing column, which reads as corruption, when the
actual fact is that the stamp and the contents disagree.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Take a content.db and edit its user_version to a rung the ladder knows, without
   changing its tables to match.
2. Open it. The walk runs, the stamp advances, and schemaV1 fails on a column.
3. Settings shows the raw SQLite error.

## Fix

Check the stamp against the shape before walking, and refuse with the two facts named.
Cheap now that there is one place the walk begins.
acceptance_criteria: A file whose user_version does not describe its tables is refused with a sentence a person can act on, naming what was expected and what was found. Nothing is destroyed, which already holds.
close_reason:
A file whose user_version does not describe its tables is refused BEFORE any rung runs, and the sentence names the objects that differ:

  content: refusing database stamped schema 14: expected schema 14 shape 30be8a0c…, found shape 3e9dc943…; missing index "entries_by_env", index "entries_by_pane", … table "entries"; stamp and contents disagree, and no rows were discarded

Two rounds, and the first one is worth recording because it satisfied the words and not the thing. Round one refused with two sha256 digests and nothing else — "expected shape 761c70…, found shape a3f2…" — and its test asserted the message CONTAINED "expected schema 14" and "found shape", which two hashes satisfy. A test asserting substrings the implementation was written to contain cannot report that the sentence is useless. The bead exists because `no such column: session_id` reads as corruption; a pair of hashes reads as nothing at all.

Round two also fixed the larger defect: validateOnDiskSchemaShape returned nil for any version it had no pinned shape for, so the protection was exactly two versions wide (14 and 15) and silently absent for the current one and every future one. That is the same silhouette as nocx-lmb6v.8, fixed by the same worker an hour earlier — a validator that says yes to the case it cannot judge. Now: a migratable rung with no historical shape is refused as a programming defect, and the expected shape for the CURRENT schema is DERIVED from schemaV1 at run time rather than pinned, so no second constant tracks what schemaV1 already says. That constant would have been the counter nocx-lmb6v.5 removed.

VERIFIED BY THE COORDINATOR, by mutation, because the worker's pre-fix evidence was a compile error (`too many arguments in call to validateOnDiskSchemaShape`), which proves nothing about whether a test catches anything:

  drop the missing-shape refusal  -> TestMigratableRungWithoutHistoricalShapeIsRefused:
      "schema-shape validation accepted a migratable rung without a historical shape"
  make schemaShapeDifference return ""
                                  -> TestAStampedSchema14DatabaseWithAnotherShapeIsRefusedBeforeMigration

Production tree byte-identical after each revert. `go test -race ./internal/content/...` green on the merged tree (213s).

ACCEPTED WITH ONE RESIDUAL, recorded rather than hidden: the `!ok` branch still ends in `return nil` for a version that is in neither the pinned set nor the ladder. It is unreachable today — a version above schemaVersion is refused by the direction check (nocx-7qunp) and one below the first rung is refused by the ladder — but it is the same shape as nocx-lmb6v.8, defended by "unreachable today". If that branch ever becomes reachable it will accept silently.

title: effectiveSize has two names and one of them is wrong
description:
Found while implementing nocx-eidfb.3, 2026-08-31.

session.output's effectiveSize is THE SIZE THE SESSION RUNS AT NOW. frontend/src/ipc.ts
names it "the size the recovered bytes were produced at". Those are different facts, and
they differ whenever the session was resized during the recorded span, or when a teardown
returned it to the default after the bytes were printed.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start a session, produce output, resize the window so the session's size changes.
2. Reclaim the pane. The recovered bytes were produced at the OLD size; effectiveSize
   reports the NEW one.
3. The renderer draws the old bytes at the new grid, which is exactly the wrong-width
   render nocx-eidfb.3 exists to prevent — now caused by the field meant to prevent it.

## Fix

Decide which fact the field is, name it that on both sides, and check every reader. If
BOTH facts are needed, they are two fields — this is the two-owners-for-one-concept shape
AGENTS.md names, and the two agree everywhere anyone has looked.
acceptance_criteria: One name for one field, and it says which of the two facts it is. Every reader is checked against the corrected meaning.

title: One schemaVersion integer governs a file three subsystems share
description:
Discovered while implementing nocx-7qunp, 2026-08-31, and it is filed under the
migration epic because that is where it becomes load-bearing.

content.db holds three subsystems' state — the ledger, the layout (tabs and panes), and
the api runs — behind ONE schemaVersion. Any one of them bumping it refuses or discards
for all three. Today that is fine, because the whole file is disposable.

It stops being fine at the same moment nocx-lmb6v does. Once the file is the only copy
of work, a layout-only change forces the migration ladder to carry a step for the ledger
and the api runs too, and an older binary refuses over a bump that touched nothing it
owns. The failure is not data loss; it is that the version number stops meaning anything
specific, which is how a migration chain becomes impossible to reason about.

Not a defect today. It is the thing that will make the tier-2 shared-database story
awkward, and the cheapest moment to decide it is while the ladder is being designed
rather than after it has steps in it.
acceptance_criteria: Either the ledger, the layout and the api runs stop sharing one version integer, or the design says in the code why one integer is correct for all three and what a bump by one of them costs the other two.
close_reason: Answered together with nocx-lmb6v.5 in commit 6035c0cf — see that bead's closing note for the full argument. The short form: ONE COUNTER FOR ONE FILE is correct, so this bead is answered by stating it in the code rather than by changing anything. The unit of the decision is the file, because Open must answer open/migrate/refuse once for the whole of it; a per-subsystem version would need a per-subsystem refusal, and nothing can express one, since ContentDB is a single interface carrying all three repositories and opening one half is a store reporting itself healthy while a third of it is missing. This bead's stated cost — a layout-only bump forcing a rung the other two do not need, and an older binary refusing over a bump that touched nothing it owns — is real, small, and correct: that binary cannot know the new shape is compatible with its own reads, and guessing is what the ladder exists to stop.

title: Refusing a newer database is a cliff with no way down
description:
Discovered while implementing nocx-7qunp, 2026-08-31. Refusing is right; being unable
to do anything about it is the part that is not finished.

Run a newer nocx once, downgrade, and durable history is permanently off. The sentence
in Settings is correct and names the version to update to, and that is the whole remedy
the product offers. The only other way out is to find content.db on disk and rename it,
which is not a thing this product should ask a person to do.

The tension is real and must not be resolved by making the refusal softer: the point of
nocx-7qunp is that the older binary does not get to decide the fate of rows it cannot
read. A person deciding is different from a binary deciding. So the affordance is an
explicit choice, shown with what it costs, and it moves the file aside rather than
dropping it.

Related to nocx-lmb6v but distinct: migrations answer the upward direction, and this is
the downward one, which no migration chain can answer.
acceptance_criteria: A person who has downgraded can act from inside the product: they are told which database is refused, where it is, and are offered a deliberate choice — start fresh, keeping the old file aside — without leaving nocx to rename a file by hand. Doing so never silently destroys the newer database.

title: The server on a host opens in a browser, and it is the same nocx
description:
Tier 2's second half. Once a host owns durable tabs, the server there is a real
entry point and not only a store, so it should be reachable without installing
anything.

CLOSER THAN IT LOOKS. cmd/nocx-server already runs the shipped coordinator
headless — no wails, no GTK, no display — and already speaks the ordinary
WebSocket protocol to a browser-hosted frontend: the whole Playwright suite
stands it up beside vite and drives it (AGENTS.md, e2e/run-in-container.sh).
So the transport and the frontend are already exercised in CI against a real
browser. What is missing is that the server does not serve the built assets
itself, plus everything below.

WHAT IS NOT FREE, and is the actual work: authenticating a web user. Reaching
the helper is same-UID trust, which is exactly what a browser is not. The
server authenticates the person and then, as a trusted process under that
account, reaches the helper. That boundary is the epic.

DELIBERATELY OUT: a public deployment story (TLS termination, a hostname, a
reverse proxy). This is reachable-on-your-own-network, and says so.
acceptance_criteria: From a machine with no nocx installed, open the browser at a host running nocx-server, and see the tabs that are open there. Type into one, and the desktop app attached to the same host sees the same bytes. Closing the browser does not end the session.
notes: Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-31-level-2-the-server-on-the-host-design.md

title: The splash's minimum second is a tax on e2e run time
description:
The connection splash holds for at least 1000 ms from startup — the owner's
requirement, and the right one. Its side effect: while it holds the top layer
the document beneath is inert, so every e2e spec that types must wait it out.
Across 350+ specs that is minutes per run, paid forever.

The option deliberately NOT taken now: letting the e2e stand zero the minimum.
It buys only speed and costs honesty — the run would stop exercising the path
that ships. And the wait is needed either way, because the splash is modal even
at a zero minimum until the first connection arrives.

Revisit if run time becomes the bottleneck. The only acceptable form then is
the stand setting the minimum, with `e2e/connection-overlay.spec.ts` remaining
the one place that asserts the real delay.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Measured how many seconds the splash wait actually adds to a full both-browser
  run, before and after.
- If the answer is to parameterise the minimum, the overlay spec still asserts
  the shipped value, and that is visible from its text.

title: Classifying a path link pages its whole parent directory
description:
## What happens

Clicking a path link asks main.tsx's pathKind() what the path is. It answers by listing
the PARENT directory in pages of FILES_PAGE_SIZE (50) and scanning each page for the
entry, looping until it finds it or the listing runs out. A link to a file in a large
directory therefore costs one round trip per 50 siblings before the viewer opens:
/usr/bin/something is roughly twenty files.list calls, and over an SSH binding each one
is a network round trip.

Nothing is wrong on screen — the panel is not touched and the viewer opens correctly.
The cost is latency on the common case (a link to a file), paid to answer a question
that only matters for the rare case (a link to a directory).

## Why it is written that way

There is no stat on the wire. files.reveal is the platform file manager (Finder), not a
classification, and files.read answers only for regular files. Paging the parent is the
only classification files.* currently offers, and it was the right call for the fix that
introduced it (nocx-tsqfx): reveal-as-probe was worse, because it moved the panel before
knowing the answer.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Print a path to a file in a directory with a few thousand entries — ls /usr/bin/env in
   a session, or any build output naming a file in node_modules.
2. Cmd-click the link.
3. Watch the files.list traffic: the parent is paged from offset 0 until the entry is
   found, before the viewer opens.

## Two ways out, and the second is the real one

a) Bound the probe: give up after N pages and answer 'unknown', which already falls
   through to openViewer — the pre-fix behaviour, so an unbounded directory costs a fixed
   ceiling and degrades to what shipped before.
b) Put the question on the wire: a files.stat (or a kind field on an existing single-path
   result) answers in one call and is what the panel wants anyway. This is the one that
   removes the loop rather than capping it; it needs a contract, so it is the larger half.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Clicking a link to a regular file in a directory of any size issues a bounded number of
  files.* calls, and the bound does not grow with the directory.
- A test states the bound by exercising it: a parent whose listing pages past the bound
  still opens the file's viewer, and the panel is not touched.
- A link to a directory still reveals it in the Files panel — the behaviour nocx-tsqfx
  bought is not traded away for the bound.
- If (b) is taken: the new shape has a JSON Schema in contracts/, generated renderer
  types, and an over-the-wire conformance test.
close_reason: Landed on the epic branch in bdfec709 + d857800c (+ the successor nocx-hp8p2.1 in 4cdf8eaa). files.stat answers path classification in one call on BOTH providers — filesystem.Provider's own doc states the symmetry rule — so a link to a file in a large directory no longer pays one files.list per 50 siblings, which over SSH was one network round trip each. The reveal hint died with the loop that produced it and was removed rather than left compiling as an always-undefined parameter.

title: The palette row's second destination has no keyboard route
description:
The snippets palette offers "copy this to the clipboard" as an icon at each
row's trailing edge (nocx-8rtr.2). It is reachable by MOUSE only.

The row is a listbox `role="option"` and the roving focus belongs to the
filter field — the surface takes `onMouseDown` preventDefault on the row for
exactly that reason. A focusable control inside an option breaks that, so the
icon carries `tabIndex={-1}` and is out of the tab order. Its accessible name
is correct ("Copy \"<title>\" to the clipboard"), so a screen reader reading
the row's contents finds it; nothing lets a keyboard ACTIVATE it.

Not invented in nocx-8rtr.2 on purpose: quick-connect has no secondary-action
concept at all — no Meta+Enter, no Shift+Enter, no `secondaryAction` — so any
chord added here is inherited at once by the server list, the command palette
and the secret picker, and each of them then has to answer what it means
there. That is a decision about the shared surface, not about snippets.

## Acceptance Criteria

[ ] A keyboard user can reach the row's secondary action without leaving the
filter field, and the binding is defined once for every quick-connect variant
[ ] Every variant that shows rows says what its secondary action is, or shows
none — no variant advertises a key that does nothing
[ ] An e2e drives the copy from the keyboard alone

title: The AppImage gate's teardown kills a coordinator path the coordinator no longer uses
description:
scripts/appimage/verify-in-container.sh tears the run down with
pkill -9 -f "$APPDIR/usr/bin/nocx". Since the coordinator cutover (nocx-gpyxp)
the daemon runs from a versioned copy under the profile data directory
($HOME/.local/share/nocx/bin/nocx-server-<version>-<sha256>) rather than from
the AppDir, because the AppImage FUSE mount dies with the window. That pattern
therefore matches the window and not the daemon.

It does not affect the gate: the cwd observation happens before teardown, and
the container exits with the script, so the stray daemon dies with it. It is a
teardown that no longer says what it means, and the next person to reuse the
script outside a container inherits a surviving process.

Found by the worker fixing nocx-k2q5l, which is the same cutover arriving at
the same file by a second door.

## Steps to Reproduce

grep -n "pkill" scripts/appimage/verify-in-container.sh, then compare the
pattern with internal/update/serverbin: the installed coordinator path is under
the data directory, not under $APPDIR.

## Acceptance Criteria

Teardown terminates the coordinator the run started, and says so in a comment
that names why the daemon is not under the AppDir.

title: Решить, попадают ли memories в бэкап-снапшот бэклога
description:
## Summary

`bd export` без флагов не включает memories, и сегодняшний трекнутый
`.beads/issues.jsonl` — тоже. После перехода на `refs/beads/snapshot`
(см. `.internal/specs/2026-08-29-beads-jsonl-untrack-design.md`) паритет
сохраняется, то есть это не регресс.

Но снапшот теперь и есть единственная страховка на случай подвисшей истории в
`refs/dolt/data`, а `bd remember` — рабочий инструмент проекта (117 memories на
2026-08-29). Значит вопрос «теряем ли мы их в аварии» стал реальным, тогда как
раньше был теоретическим.

Решить: `bd export --include-memories` в снапшоте, или отдельный реф, или
осознанно не бэкапить. Аргумент против: справка `bd export` называет memories
потенциально чувствительным agent context, а реф уезжает на публичный remote.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Решение записано (бид с type=decision или ADR, если размен того стоит).
- Если решено включать — `.githooks/pre-push` изменён и снапшот содержит memories.

title: secret-panel-position.spec.ts asserts bounds that ordinary layout variation crosses
description:
On CI run 33245784702 (job `ci-e2e (webkit)`, PR #121's merged tree):

    Error: expect(locator).toBeVisible() failed
    Locator: getByRole('dialog').filter({ hasText: 'New Endpoint' })
             .locator('#endpoint-header-0-value')
    Expected: visible   Timeout: 10000ms   Error: element(s) not found
    at e2e/secret-panel-position.spec.ts:298:26

The step before is `dialog.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add header' }).click()`,
so the click either did not land or the row it adds was not rendered within 10s.

`ci-e2e (chromium)` passed the same spec on the same tree, and the job passed on
rerun of the identical commit. PR #121 does not touch the API workbench or the
endpoint dialog at all, so this is a pre-existing webkit-only intermittent that
the stack's CI merely surfaced.

Possibly related, possibly not: the frontend unit file for the same surface,
`src/api/api-workbench.test.tsx`, timed out once in a local full-suite run on
the same tree ("the open-a-folder ask says the same thing, in both states", 30s
timeout) while passing on CI. That file carries 276 tests and takes ~312s, so it
may simply be the slowest thing in the suite rather than evidence of a shared
cause. Worth checking together before assuming they are one bug.

## Steps to Reproduce

Intermittent. Seen once in CI run 33245784702; green on rerun at the same commit
and green on chromium. `PW_PROJECTS=webkit e2e/run-in-container.sh
e2e/secret-panel-position.spec.ts` is the local loop, with the AGENTS.md caveat
that the container's WebKit is not CI's for layout-sensitive specs.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The "Add header" step waits on an observable that the click actually
  succeeded, rather than on the new field appearing within a fixed 10s.
- The spec passes on webkit across at least 20 consecutive container runs.
- Whether it shares a cause with the api-workbench unit-file slowness is
  answered explicitly, either way.

## Second occurrence, different test, different browser (2026-08-29)

CI run 33261386104, job `ci-e2e (chromium)`, on the same PR #121 tree
(`b4125fda`):

    e2e/secret-panel-position.spec.ts:209
    expect(gap).toBeLessThanOrEqual(16)
    Expected: <= 16   Received: 17.5
    at expectAnchoredToField (e2e/secret-panel-position.spec.ts:209:15)
    at e2e/secret-panel-position.spec.ts:221:5
      -> "a field panel is inside the viewport, and its rows own their own point"

So this file has now failed twice in one day, in two different tests and two
different browsers: `:291` on webkit (the added header field never appeared) and
`:213` on chromium (the panel sat 1.5px further from its field than the
assertion allows). Neither branch that surfaced them touches the secret panel or
the endpoint dialog.

Two failures of one file in two browsers is no longer "a webkit quirk": the file
asserts pixel geometry and DOM arrival with fixed bounds, and both bounds are
tight enough that ordinary layout variation crosses them. Treat the file as one
defect, not two tests.

Raising 16 to a larger number is NOT the fix — the assertion is about the panel
being anchored to its field, so the number has meaning. Either measure the same
fact in a way that does not depend on sub-pixel rounding, or assert the anchor
relationship directly.
notes:
2026-08-29, четвёртый случай — и он снимает слово «intermittent» с chromium-половины.

Прогон 33267520267, ci-e2e (chromium), SHA 22f5a7cb (main 4a6ebcf0 + ветка
fix/nocx-hgtt0, диф которой — один Go-тест в internal/git/helper и до фронтенда
не дотягивается):

  ✘ secret-panel-position.spec.ts:213 «a field panel is inside the viewport,
    and its rows own their own point»
  expectAnchoredToField, строка 209: expect(gap).toBeLessThanOrEqual(16)
  Received: 17.5

Ключевое: 17.5 — ровно то же значение, что в случае lucky-forest сегодня же.
Не «около 17», не разброс — то же число дважды, на разных деревьях.

Флейк по времени даёт РАЗБРОС: медленная машина промахивается на разную
величину. Одно и то же значение с точностью до десятой — это не шум, а вторая
устойчивая геометрия: панель встаёт в одно из двух законных положений, и
утверждение допускает только одно. 17.5 против потолка 16 — это дельта 1.5 px,
подозрительно похожая на границу, разделитель или округление, а не на «не
успело».

Это ровно та форма, которую координатор нашёл в import-спеках (nocx-b0k9a):
шесть тестов безусловно кликали кнопку, которой в одной из двух законных форм
диалога нет. Там тоже сначала выглядело нестабильностью.

Поэтому предлагаемый первый шаг: не перезапускать и не поднимать порог до 18, а
выяснить, ЧТО даёт вторые 17.5 — какие два положения панели законны и почему
expectAnchoredToField знает лишь об одном. Поднятие порога закрепит симптом и
уничтожит улику: одинаковое значение перестанет наблюдаться.

Webkit-половина бида (:291, «Add header» не отрисовал поле) этим не
объясняется — там другой отказ, и её стоит держать отдельно, пока не доказано,
что причина общая.
2026-08-29, проверка гипотезы «хост != инпут» по коду: для ЭТОГО поля она не
работает, и арифметику надо искать в другом месте.

ПРОВЕРЕНО чтением:
- `#endpoint-key` рендерится `SecretTextField` (endpoints-section.tsx:1110).
- `SecretTextField` передаёт `anchor: inputEl` (api/secret-text-field.tsx:87),
  где `inputEl = document.getElementById(props.id)` (там же, строка 73).
- Спек меряет `document.getElementById(id)` (secret-panel-position.spec.ts:179).

Значит якорь и измеряемый элемент — ОДИН И ТОТ ЖЕ узел. Хост не обёртка, и
разницы «инпут против хоста» здесь нет вовсе.

- ANCHOR_GAP_PX = 6 (floating-panel.ts:33), и обе ветки дают ровно 6:
    above: panel.bottom = rect.top - 6      -> |field.top - panel.bottom| = 6
    below: panel.top    = rect.bottom + 6   -> |panel.top - field.bottom| = 6

То есть без вмешательства зазор обязан быть 6, а не 17.5.

ГИПОТЕЗА (не проверена запуском): 17.5 даёт ОГРАНИЧЕНИЕ, а не якорение.
floating-panel.ts:424: `top = Math.max(0, Math.min(top, maxTop))`, где
`maxTop = Math.max(0, window.innerHeight - height)`. Когда панель не помещается
ни сверху, ни снизу, `top` прижимается к `maxTop`, чтобы нижний край остался в
окне — и тогда панель НАЕЗЖАЕТ на поле, а измеренное расстояние перестаёт быть
шестёркой. Наблюдаемые 17.5 = 6 + 11.5 сходятся и так.

Существенно, что это поведение НАМЕРЕННОЕ и задокументировано на месте,
floating-panel.ts:399-402: «a panel taller than the space on both sides of the
field still lands with top >= 0 and its bottom edge inside the window».

Тогда дефект не в раскладке, а в самом тесте: expectInsideViewport и
expectAnchoredToField в этом режиме противоречат друг другу по построению.
Код отказывается от шестипиксельного якорения ИМЕННО ради того, чтобы удержать
панель в окне, а тест требует обоих одновременно. Отсюда и константа: прижатие
детерминировано высотой окна и высотой панели.

ПРОВЕРКА, дешёвая и решающая: в момент отказа сравнить panel.bottom и
viewport.height. Равенство означает прижатие, то есть подтверждает эту версию;
неравенство её убивает. Оба числа уже есть в measure(), их достаточно
напечатать.

Если версия верна, правка — в утверждении, а не в раскладке: якорение
проверяется только когда панель помещается, а прижатый случай получает своё
утверждение («нижний край в окне, верх не отрицателен»).

2026-08-29, chromium-половина ЗАКРЫТА правкой в #141 (коммит fe8b1553). Причина
оказалась не той, что предполагала записка выше.

Прижатие (clamp) было ПРАВДОПОДОБНОЙ, но неверной версией, и предыдущая сессия
сама отметила, что 6 + 11.5 = 17.5 — это арифметика, подогнанная под уже
наблюдённое число, а не вывод. Проверка равенства panel.bottom и
viewport.height, которую записка называла решающей, версию не подтвердила.

Настоящая причина: анкерная панель размещается ИЗ СВОЕЙ ВЫСОТЫ, а высота в
момент вычисления ещё не окончательна. applyGeometry сначала выставляет ширину,
строки перетекают под неё, и всё, что после этого меняет список, меняет высоту
снова. Панель оставалась там, где помещалась РАНЬШЕ. Значение поэтому и было
устойчивым: перетекание детерминировано, а не «не успело».

Правка: панель наблюдает собственный бокс через ResizeObserver, пока открыта, и
пересчитывает положение через уже существующий onViewportChange — тот же путь,
который отвечает на «то, от чего зависит положение, сдвинулось». Наблюдатель
вешается и отключается вместе с viewport-слушателями, то есть только у открытой
панели, и только у анкерной: attachViewportListeners вызывается из enterLayer,
а тот выходит первой строкой при anchor === undefined.

В спеке порог НЕ поднимался. В сообщение отказа добавлен весь замер
(JSON.stringify(m)), чтобы следующее падение называло свою геометрию — улика,
которую записка выше справедливо требовала сохранить.

CI на #141: 8/8, обе e2e-половины (chromium и webkit) зелёные.

Webkit-половина (:291, «Add header» не рисует поле) НЕ тронута — бид остаётся
открытым ровно за неё. Спек на webkit сейчас зелёный, поэтому отказ либо
относился к другому месту файла, либо требует своих условий: прежде чем закрывать,
нужно воспроизвести именно его, а не считать общую зелень доказательством.
Backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh: kept open deliberately when its two apparent siblings were closed. nocx-brf45 (the 16px anchor tolerance) shipped as commit 78657366 and nocx-rthz7 was closed as brf45's duplicate — but THIS bead is a different assertion in the same file and is NOT fixed: e2e/secret-panel-position.spec.ts:366 still clicks the Add header button and then waits on a fixed 10s budget for #endpoint-header-0-value with no observable that the click landed. Its chromium half was already closed by fe8b1553; the webkit half is what remains. Same spec file is not the same defect.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
Hypothesis with arithmetic, for whoever takes this — NOT yet proven, and stated so it can be refuted cheaply.

The repeating 17.5 (twice, to the tenth, on two different trees) says a second stable geometry rather than scatter, as worktree-silver-cloud-e7cf argued. Here is a candidate for what the two geometries are.

The test and the code do not measure the same rectangle:

  e2e/secret-panel-position.spec.ts, measure(): fieldEl = document.getElementById(id)
    — the <input> itself, and m.field is ITS rect.
  frontend/src/ui/floating-panel.ts, applyAnchoredPosition(): host = this.anchor?.()
    — and the panel is placed at host.bottom + ANCHOR_GAP_PX (below) or
      host.top - ANCHOR_GAP_PX - height (above). ANCHOR_GAP_PX = 6.

So when the panel opens BELOW, expectAnchoredToField computes panel.top - input.bottom, while the code guaranteed panel.top - host.bottom = 6. If the host is a wrapper that extends ~11.5px past the input (a description line, the field's padding), the measured gap is 6 + 11.5 = 17.5 — the exact number observed, and constant because it is a layout constant, not a delay.

When the panel opens ABOVE, the arithmetic runs the other way (host.top is above the input's top because of the label), so that placement can measure within 16 and pass. Two legitimate placements, one assertion that only holds for one — the same shape as nocx-b0k9a, where six specs asserted a dialog state the dialog never promised.

First step, and the reason not to raise the ceiling to 18: the ceiling would make the symptom stop being observed while the mismatch stayed, and the constant 17.5 is the evidence. Establish what anchor() returns for the secret field, then either measure the same element the code anchors to, or assert the property that actually matters — the panel touches the field it belongs to, above or below, with the gap the component promises.

The webkit half of this bead (:291, 'Add header' rendering no field) is a different refusal and this does not explain it; keep them apart until a common cause is shown.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
RETRACTION of my earlier comment: the wrapper-vs-input hypothesis is WRONG for this field. Verified by reading, not by argument:

  frontend/src/api/secret-text-field.tsx:73  inputEl = document.getElementById(props.id)
  frontend/src/api/secret-text-field.tsx:87  anchor: inputEl
  e2e/secret-panel-position.spec.ts:179      fieldEl = document.getElementById(id)

The anchor and the measured element are THE SAME NODE. There is no wrapper, so there is no 11.5px of description line to add, and with ANCHOR_GAP_PX = 6 both placements give exactly 6. My arithmetic reached the observed 17.5 by fitting a plausible decomposition to a number I already had, without checking the premise it rested on — which is the error this bead is about in the first place. Do not follow that comment.

worktree-silver-cloud-e7cf's version is the live one and it is stronger, because the behaviour it names is DELIBERATE and documented at the point of code:

  floating-panel.ts:424  top = Math.max(0, Math.min(top, maxTop)), maxTop = innerHeight - height
  floating-panel.ts:399  'a panel taller than the space on both sides of the field still lands
                          with top >= 0 and its bottom edge inside the window'

When the panel fits neither above nor below, the clamp keeps it on screen and the six-pixel gap is given up ON PURPOSE. In that mode expectInsideViewport and expectAnchoredToField cannot both hold: the code trades the gap for the viewport, and the spec demands both. The constant 17.5 follows from the clamp being deterministic in window height and panel height, not from a delay.

So 'a wrong assertion rather than a flake' still stands — the assertion is wrong somewhere else than either of us first thought.

Decisive check, one line of diagnostics: at the moment of failure compare panel.bottom with viewport.height. measure() already returns both. Equal means clamped and the version is confirmed; unequal kills it.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
MEASURED, not argued. Reproduced locally under container chromium with the full measurement printed in the failure (that diagnostic is worth keeping regardless of the fix):

  panel:    top 317.5   bottom 361.5      -> rendered height 44
  field:    top 378.03  bottom 410.03
  viewport: 1280 x 720
  gap = |378.03 - 361.5| = 16.53

BOTH earlier hypotheses are dead, and the numbers kill them:
- Clamping (worktree-silver-cloud-e7cf): panel.bottom is 361.5 against a viewport height of 720, and panel.top is 317.5, not 0. Nothing is clamped; the panel is nowhere near either edge.
- Wrapper vs input (mine): already refuted by the anchor chain, and these numbers add nothing to it.

THE ACTUAL CAUSE. The panel opened ABOVE, so floating-panel.ts computed
    above = rect.top - ANCHOR_GAP_PX - height,  height = this.root.offsetHeight
Solving with the observed numbers: 378.03 - 6 - height = 317.5, so height was ~54.5 AT POSITIONING TIME. The rendered panel is 44 tall. It shrank by ~10.5 after it was placed, and the placement was never recomputed — so the panel sits ~10.5px further from its field than the six pixels the component promises.

That is a real (cosmetic) product defect, not a test defect: the position is computed from a height the panel no longer has.

AND THE NUMBER IS NOT A CONSTANT. Local chromium gives 16.53, CI gives 17.5. The two CI observations that matched to the tenth were a coincidence of one environment, and the reasoning built on 'a repeating constant means a second stable geometry' does not hold — I argued it too. The threshold 16 sits inside that spread, which is why this passes or fails on rendering metrics.

So raising the ceiling is even more clearly wrong than it looked: it would hide a placement that is genuinely ~10px off.

Two candidate fixes, and they are not equivalent:
- PRODUCT: recompute the anchored position after the content settles (or measure after the rows render), so the six-pixel promise is kept. Fixes the defect the test is pointing at.
- TEST ONLY: assert what the component actually promises. Weaker, and it would leave the panel visibly mis-placed.

The failure message now carries the whole Measured object, so the next occurrence names its own placement instead of a bare number.

title: The summoned answer list stops following its tail on WebKit
description:
On CI run 33245784702 (job `ci-e2e (webkit)`, PR #121's merged tree) the summon
composer's scroll assertion failed:

    expect(received).toMatchObject(expected)
      - "atBottom": true      + "atBottom": false
        "seated": true
      - "tailVisible": true   + "tailVisible": false
    Timeout 5000ms exceeded while waiting on the predicate
    at e2e/ask-about-full-screen-program.spec.ts:596:8

`ci-e2e (chromium)` passed the same spec on the same tree, and the job passed on
rerun of the identical commit — so it is a webkit-only intermittent, not a
regression of the branch that surfaced it (#121 touches assistant cancellation
and key ownership, not the answer list's scroll).

The assertion is the end of "freezes, answers twice with one composer, thaws,
and quits normally": after the SECOND answer, the composer must be seated, the
answer list scrolled to the bottom, and the tail visible. Two of the three were
false for the whole 5s window, so the list was not following its tail rather
than merely being late.

`_mutateSummonAnswers` decides whether to keep following by testing
`scrollTop + clientHeight >= scrollHeight - 2` BEFORE the mutation and restoring
`scrollTop = scrollHeight` after it. On WebKit a fractional or stale
`clientHeight` during the freeze/thaw transition would make that predicate read
false, and the list then deliberately does not follow — which matches the
observed `atBottom: false, tailVisible: false` exactly.

## Steps to Reproduce

Intermittent. Seen once in CI run 33245784702; green on rerun at the same
commit, and green on chromium. `PW_PROJECTS=webkit e2e/run-in-container.sh
e2e/ask-about-full-screen-program.spec.ts` is the local loop, with the caveat
from AGENTS.md that the container's WebKit is not CI's for layout.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The follow decision does not depend on a fractional/stale metric read at a
  moment: either it is taken from an observable the transition cannot make
  temporarily false, or the spec waits for the transition to be complete before
  asserting.
- The spec's final assertion passes on webkit across at least 20 consecutive
  container runs.
- If the cause turns out to be product rather than test, the fix is in
  `_mutateSummonAnswers`, not in the spec's timeout.

title: The secret panel's 16px anchor tolerance flakes in CI (17.5px observed)
description:
## What happened

2026-08-28, PR #120, `ci-e2e (chromium)`: 229 passed, 1 failed.

    e2e/secret-panel-position.spec.ts:213
      expect(gap).toBeLessThanOrEqual(16)
      Expected: <= 16
      Received:    17.5

A rerun of the same job at the same commit passed. The branch under test
touched six files, all of them the terminal pane's summon stack — no dialog, no
floating panel, no shared box model. So the assertion moved without the product
moving.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the e2e suite on CI, chromium project.
2. `e2e/secret-panel-position.spec.ts:213` fails intermittently on the gap
   assertion at `expectAnchoredToField`, reporting a gap just over 16.
3. Re-run the same job at the same commit; it passes.

## Why it matters

`expectAnchoredToField` encodes "the panel touches its field" as a fixed pixel
budget:

    const gap = Math.min(
      Math.abs(m.field.top - m.panel.bottom),
      Math.abs(m.panel.top - m.field.bottom),
    )
    expect(gap).toBeLessThanOrEqual(16)

The 16 arrived with 8c133301 and is a margin, not a fact about the product. A
gap of 17.5 and a gap of 16 are the same thing to the person reaching for the
panel; the difference is a rounding boundary somewhere in the dialog's layout.
So the test currently reports a defect it did not find, which is the failure
mode that trains people to re-run a red suite instead of reading it.

AGENTS.md already bans a test that depends on a duration, for the same reason:
"a spec that needs a slow machine to pass is broken on a fast one too; it has
only not been caught yet." A spec that needs a particular sub-pixel rounding is
the same shape on the space axis.

## The thing to decide, not to assume

What the assertion is actually for. If it exists to catch "the panel detached
from its field and drifted across the dialog", the honest bound is a fraction of
the panel or field box, not a constant — and it should be derived, with the
derivation said out loud. Widening 16 to 24 buys one flake and leaves the next.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The anchoring assertion states what it measures against something that scales
  with the layout, not a hardcoded pixel count, and says why that bound.
- The spec passes on a run whose measured gap is 17.5, and still fails when the
  panel is genuinely not anchored to its field.
close_reason: Duplicate of nocx-brf45, which the fix commit names. Both quote the identical failing statement — expect(gap).toBeLessThanOrEqual(16) in expectAnchoredToField, Received 17.5 — in e2e/secret-panel-position.spec.ts. One assertion, one defect, filed twice. Closed during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh.

title: The file tree and the listening ports of a remote host, in the product
description:
Design .internal/specs/2026-08-28-the-nocx-server-design.md C, section 8. The two remaining reserved service names beside the live git service. The frame protocol, deploy, consent and uninstall already exist (internal/helper/{proto,host,client,deploy,consent}); this is the operations and their bounds.

title: A file reached through a symlink opens a second viewer tab when the link came from terminal output
description:
openFileViewer deduplicates on the provider's CANONICAL path, so two names for one file are one tab. A viewer opened from a TERMINAL LINK cannot supply that: the canonical identity only comes back in the files.read result, and the opener has not read anything yet — it hands the pane its target and the pane does the reading.

frontend/src/terminal-links/open.ts therefore passes the LEXICAL absolute path as `canonical`. Ordinary paths dedup exactly, because lexical and canonical agree; a path reached through a symlink does not, so clicking /x/link.ts after the Files panel opened /x/real.ts gives two tabs claiming to be different files.

Rejected for the first cut: reading the file in the opener to learn `canonical` before opening the pane, which buys correct dedup for a second full read of every clicked file. The likely fix is the other direction — let the pane report its canonical identity once the read lands and have PaneManager settle the singleton key then — which also fixes the same gap for anything else that opens a viewer without having listed the file first.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `ln -s real.ts link.ts` in the session's cwd.
2. Open real.ts from the Files panel.
3. Cmd+click `link.ts` in terminal output.
4. Two viewer tabs are open on one file; expected one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- With a symlink and its target reached one from the Files panel and one from a terminal link, exactly one viewer tab exists.
- No extra files.read is issued per click to achieve it.

title: A terminal link is not detected across a wrapped row, and never inside a path with a space
description:
Two limits the link grammar (frontend/src/terminal-links/detect.ts) ships with, both deliberate for the first cut and both worth closing.

SPACES. The path token set excludes space, so a path containing one is detected only up to the space. Guessing where an unquoted path ends mis-detects more often than it helps, so the first cut refuses; a QUOTED path is a shape we could honour exactly, and probably should.

WRAPPED ROWS. The live xterm policy is asked per grid row (renderers/xterm.ts, provideLinks) and reads that row's text alone, so a path long enough to wrap is two half-paths and neither resolves. The frozen DOM surface already gets this right — serializeRange joins wrapped rows into one .term-line — so the two surfaces DISAGREE on a wrapped path today. That is exactly the drift terminal-links/end-to-end.test.ts exists to catch, and it does not yet cover it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. In a narrow pane, run a command whose output prints a path long enough to wrap the grid, e.g. `echo /very/long/.../file.ts:12` sized past the column count.
2. Hold Cmd and hover the path WHILE THE COMMAND IS STILL RUNNING (the live region, not the frozen block). No link covers the whole path; at most each half is offered.
3. Separately: `ls -l ~/'My Documents'` and Cmd+click a path containing a space — only the segment before the space is linked.

## Acceptance Criteria

- detectLinks over a quoted path containing a space yields ONE span covering the quoted path, and an unquoted one still stops at the space.
- The live policy joins wrapped rows via IBufferLine.isWrapped, so a wrapped path is one link with the same span the frozen surface finds.
- end-to-end.test.ts gains a wrapped-row case asserting the two surfaces agree on it.

title: agent-ask webkit specs flake under full-suite load
description:
In a full e2e run one webkit test in e2e/agent-ask.spec.ts fails; run the file alone in
webkit and all 8 pass in 34 seconds. Measured on wA-integration, 2026-08-27.

The failure moves between tests across runs — :579 'a second ask while the first streams'
in one full run, :520 'custom headers ride the completion AND the connection check' in the
next two — which is the signature of flakiness rather than a regression: a regression
fails in the same place.

The message is always the same shape: locator('.mark-affordance .ui-button') resolves to
the 'Mark block' button, and then 'element is not visible' for the whole 30s, ~56 retries.
So the button exists in the DOM and never becomes visible in time. Nothing in the secret
panel work touched .mark-affordance; it is the block surface.

AGENTS.md: a test may not depend on timing — wait on an observable state change, never on
a duration. A spec that needs a fast machine passes only until the machine is busy, which
is exactly what a full parallel suite makes it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. e2e/run-in-container.sh  (full suite, both browsers)
2. One webkit agent-ask test fails on '.mark-affordance .ui-button' never becoming
   visible.
3. PW_PROJECTS=webkit e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/agent-ask.spec.ts — 8 passed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The reason the button stays invisible under load is named, not worked around with a
  longer timeout.
- The spec waits on the state that makes the affordance appear, not on a duration.
- Ten consecutive full-suite runs with no agent-ask failure, or the flake reproduced
  deterministically first and then fixed.

title: The sleep sweep dropped the process kill on one fail-open timeout path, so a hung shell outlives its test
description:
While restoring the diagnostics nocx-td6d4.8 asks for, the shellintegration worker
found a second thing the sweep took: in internal/shellintegration/channel_exec_test.go,
assertNoTransportFailsOpen used to kill the shell before failing.

Before (commit 6106c6fe):

    if !strings.Contains(snapshot(), sentinel) {
        _ = cmd.Process.Kill()
        t.Fatalf("native prompt %q never appeared without a transport; output=%q", ...)
    }

After (commit 9a736ee8) the loop became testwait.WaitForTimeout, which fatals from
inside the helper — and the Kill went with the loop. What is left on that path is the
deferred ptmx.Close(); the child most likely takes SIGHUP from the pty master closing,
but nothing on this path kills it any more, and "most likely" is what the explicit
Kill existed to replace.

The same function's OTHER timeout path, twenty lines down, still has its
`_ = cmd.Process.Kill()` before t.Fatal — so the two paths in one function now
disagree, which is the tell that this was collateral and not a decision.

This package already has form for exactly this shape: nocx-dsie, "a shellintegration
test fixture leaks both socketpair ends into the shell it starts".

## Steps to Reproduce

    git diff -U10 6106c6fe..9a736ee8 -- internal/shellintegration/channel_exec_test.go

Read the hunk around assertNoTransportFailsOpen: the removed block carries
`_ = cmd.Process.Kill()`, the testwait call that replaces it does not, and the
`select` twenty lines below still kills on its own timeout.

To see it live, make the sentinel unreachable (change the expected prompt text) and
run the test on a host that has GNU bash 3.2; the wait fatals and the shell is left
to the pty close rather than to an explicit signal.

## Acceptance Criteria

The fail-open timeout path kills the shell it started before it fails, or the file
says in a comment why closing the pty master is sufficient here and why the sibling
path below still kills explicitly. Both paths in assertNoTransportFailsOpen agree.

Deliberately out: auditing the rest of the suite for processes that outlive their
test. This restores one thing the sweep removed.
close_reason: Landed as ab57edf0. Restored as one t.Cleanup at the pty rather than two Kills at two call sites: the wait fatals from inside testwait, so that path cannot host a Kill at its call site at all, and a cleanup also covers any path added later. The Kill in the sibling select is removed, so one place owns the shell's death and the two paths agree. Counterfactual measured before restoring: with the sentinel made unreachable so the wait burns its full 10s, no process with NOCX_SESSION_ID=chansess survives either with or without the cleanup — on Linux the deferred ptmx.Close() does deliver SIGHUP. So this does not fix an observable leak here; it restores explicitness on bash 3.2 / macOS, the platform this test actually fails on and the one not measured.

title: A failed live read is reported as 'readScreen', a tool that no longer exists
description:
The owner read his own failure message on 2026-08-26 and asked «то мы же его удаляли» — the
tool called `readScreen` was folded into `session.read` (nocx-2ryxf), and the sentence he was
shown named the dead one.

The sentence is composed in ws_readscreen.go:191 — `fmt.Errorf("readScreen: %w", err)` — and
four sibling lines (122, 125, 131, 183) do the same. The renderer adds its own:
`ReadScreenRangeError` prefixes 'readScreen: ' (frame/capture-identity.ts:44). The file's own
header explains that `agent.readScreenRequest` / `agent.readScreenResolved` deliberately stay
transport identifiers, "distinct from the model-facing session.read tool name" — that
argument is sound for wire method names nobody reads, and it does not extend to a sentence
that reaches a person and a model.

Both readers are misled by it. The person is told about a tool the product no longer has.
The model is told a name that is not in its tool list, in the result of the call it just
made, which is the one place a name must match.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Make a live read fail (see nocx-2ryxf.3 — a `top` running is enough).
2. Read the turn: "the assistant's session.read call did not finish: readScreen: request
   timed out waiting for the renderer". One failure, two names for one tool.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

• No sentence a person or the model can read names `readScreen`. The wire method identifiers
may stay as they are — the header's argument holds for them — but every error string that
escapes to a result or a surface names the tool the caller actually called.
• Asserted by a test that fails a live read and matches the sentence, so the next rename
cannot leave the old word behind again.
close_reason: merged into feat/ai-assistant as 3508d953, full pre-commit gate green (containerised go test -race and vitest, contracts, tsc, linters, prettier)

title: A file named 1 is tracked at the repo root and something still appends shell errors to it
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

From a clean feat/orchestration worktree:

    git status --short          # reports ` M 1`
    cat ./1                     # nocx-loader: 1: printf: printf: I/O error
    git show HEAD:1             # empty — the tracked version has no content

The file is tracked: it was committed empty in f43a7523 and touched again in
0d167c43. The append happens during a run; it was already present before the
nocx-eoijp session started, so it is not that work.

## Why that line names its own writer

That is dash s error format — `$0: <line>: <cmd>: <message>` — and `$0` is
`nocx-loader`, the shell-integration carrier: `carrierLoaderTemplate` in
internal/shellintegration/carrier.go builds a command whose argument region is
` nocx-loader ...` (carrier.go:599, asserted by carrier_test.go:140).

So a loader run had its stderr pointed at a file called `1` rather than at
fd 2 — a `2>1` where `2>&1` was meant. A plain grep for `2>1` across the tree
finds nothing, so the redirect is either composed at runtime or lives outside
the tree (a harness, a hook, a devharness invocation). The template itself
contains `exec 2>&1 @FD@<&-` and `exec 2>/dev/null`; read it with the
substitution applied before concluding the writer is elsewhere.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than deleting quietly

An untracked stray is noise. A TRACKED one that a run keeps writing to leaves
`git status` dirty after an ordinary run, which is how an unrelated change gets
committed by accident alongside it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The writer is named: the code path that redirects stderr to a file called
  `1` is identified and shown, not guessed.
- That redirect is corrected, and a run that previously appended to `1` no
  longer creates or writes any file at the repository root.
- The file is deleted from the tree, and `git status` is clean after a run.
close_reason: Fixed in beff10c6: the writer was the shell-integration carrier loader, whose 'exec 2>&1' arrived as 'exec 2>1' because the bash JSON decoder wrote octal escapes without the leading zero that printf %b needs. The redirect is correct now, the file is deleted from the tree, and TestBashNestedJsonUnescape pins the adjacency cases that caused it.

title: The block menu's mark item is the only lower-case item in the menu
description:
Owner review 2026-08-26. The ⋮ menu reads "ask about this block", "Copy command",
"Copy output", "Copy all", "Do not wrap" — one item in sentence case among four in

## Steps to Reproduce

2. The first item is lower-case; every other item is capitalised.

## Acceptance Criteria

title: The claude driver is tested at 120 columns only
description:
Every capture in internal/agentdriver/testdata/captures was taken at 120x40, and the driver's strongest anchor is a FULL-WIDTH rule: the input box is recognised by two rows that are nothing but the horizontal rule, edge to edge. A narrow pane is therefore untested geometry, and the failure direction is not obviously safe — if a narrow TUI wraps or shortens those rules, the input box stops being found and every pane in that geometry answers 'unknown', which every caller treats as busy. A worker in a narrow pane would then never be typed into and its indicator would say nothing useful.

The captures README says this in its own 'what these do not cover'. It needs a capture at a narrow width and either a rule that holds there or an honest bound written into the driver.
acceptance_criteria: A capture at a narrow width (60 columns or less) classifies into the same states as the 120-column corpus, or the driver states the geometry it is valid for and says so to its caller.
close_reason: Measured, not reasoned about. The full-width-rule anchor holds at 60 and 80 columns, so idle classifies as free text at both; the approval dialog holds at 60 too, which was the case that mattered — its option rows wrap at that width but the driver anchors on the cursor, which sits on the first option, which does not wrap. Three captures joined the corpus and the README now names which geometries are covered instead of claiming none but 120 is. One false alarm on the way: the first narrow dialog capture was taken without --permission-mode manual, so no dialog was ever drawn and the red test blamed the driver for its own fixture.
