delays DOM visibility while keeping validation immutable, so it cannot catch it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- After an async reveal, the gate re-reads validity before focusing and announcing: a test whose
  reveal hook makes the form VALID asserts the gate stops -- no toast, no focus, and the submit
  is allowed or cleanly abandoned, whichever is chosen and written down.
- A test whose async reveal changes WHICH field is first asserts the gate focuses and announces
  the new first field, not the stale one.
- The synchronous path keeps its current behaviour, asserted unchanged.
close_reason: The gate re-reads the whole verdict after the async reveal. When the reveal makes the form valid the submit is ALLOWED, and the reasoning is recorded in the code. The unreachable firstErrorField() ?? first fallback came off as dead code. Merged as 8dd6097c.

title: Step 2: offer visual companion just-in-time
close_reason: No visual-only question arose during clarification; will offer at the UI design section if one does.

title: the wire says whether an observed process name was cut, rather than the renderer restating the kernel's field width
description:
session.integrationChanged carries detail.observedProcess as a bare string. Whether that string is whole or was cut to the process table's field width is knowable only where it is read — darwin's p_comm, internal/procwatch commLen = MAXCOMLEN = 16 — and the renderer now restates that 16 in frontend/src/integration/status.ts to decide whether to mark the name as possibly short (nocx-aimo).

Two numbers for one fact is the AD-8 shape. It is harmless while darwin is the only platform that observes an exec, and it drifts the moment a second one does: Linux's comm is 15 bytes plus a NUL, so the renderer would mark whole names and miss cut ones on the same build.

The fix is on the wire, not in the renderer: the observing side already knows whether it truncated, so detail gains a boolean (or observedProcess gains a sibling) and the renderer stops guessing. That is a contract change plus the Go side that satisfies it, which is why it is not folded into a wording fix.
acceptance_criteria: The renderer decides 'this name may be cut' from a field on the wire, and no length constant lives in frontend/src/integration/status.ts.

title: An empty file named '1' is tracked at the repo root
description:
0d167c43 committed a zero-byte file literally named '1' at the repository root. It is a shell-redirect artifact — someone wrote '> 1' or '2>1' instead of '2>&1' — not anything the build reads.

Found while resolving the PR #61 merge: it showed up as a staged addition in the merge and had to be distinguished from the merge's own changes before the resolution could be trusted, which is the actual cost of it being there.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. 'git ls-tree origin/main -- 1' from the repo root prints a blob.
2. 'git log --oneline -- 1' names 0d167c43 as the only commit that touched it.
3. Nothing imports, embeds or reads it: 'grep -rn' for it finds no reference.

## Acceptance Criteria

The file is deleted and 'git ls-files' at the repository root lists no single-character numeric filename. If something turns out to depend on it, the dependency is named here instead and the bead is closed as deliberate.
close_reason: Duplicate of nocx-o8p1l and already fixed. Both name one behaviour: a zero-byte file literally named 1 at the repository root, committed by 0d167c43 as a 2>1-for-2>&1 slip and read by nothing. Removed by commit 17483de9. This bead's acceptance criterion is met exactly as written and was re-verified during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh: git ls-files lists no single-character numeric filename, and ls ./1 reports no such file.

title: scripts/ci-frontend.sh cannot run from a git worktree; e2e/run-in-container.sh already can
description:
A git worktree keeps no .git DIRECTORY — it keeps a .git FILE pointing at <main-repo>/.git/worktrees/<name>, which is outside the bind mount. scripts/ci-frontend.sh mounts only the worktree, so the container answers 'fatal: not a git repository: <gitdir>' at its first git command and the whole frontend job dies before a check runs.

e2e/run-in-container.sh already solved this: it mounts the common git dir at its own absolute path, read-only, and only when .git is a file. Agents on this repo work from worktrees, so 'make ci-full' cannot complete for any of them until the frontend job learns the same trick.

## Acceptance Criteria
- scripts/ci-frontend.sh runs to completion from a git worktree.
- It still runs unchanged from an ordinary checkout (no mount added when .git is a directory).
close_reason: Shipped, and a duplicate of nocx-yqg0 which names the same behaviour. scripts/ci-frontend.sh:141 now mounts the git common dir, and the comment above it at :140 cites this bead by name: the runner was the one script that never learned e2e/run-in-container.sh's arrangement, so make ci-full could not complete from a worktree at all. Commit 43a65d22. Verified in the tree during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh: the git_flag block is present and an ordinary checkout is unchanged because git_flag stays empty when .git is a directory.

title: completion.spec.ts's 'erasing the line closes the panel' fails on macOS WebKit and passes in the container
description:
e2e/completion.spec.ts:329 presses Control+a then Backspace to erase the line and asserts the completion panel closes. On macOS WebKit it fails: the panel stays open, because Control+a is not select-all there — the editor treats it as the readline 'move to start of line' binding, so Backspace deletes one character and the line is not erased.

Measured 2026-08-12 on macOS 15 with PW_PROJECTS=webkit, and measured on the SAME machine against a tree with nocx-wwz0 stashed, so it is not the login-shell change: it fails identically with the bash tier. The other seven tests in the file pass on macOS, including the ones that depend on the command-existence snapshot.

It is the mirror of the divergence AGENTS.md already names — the container's Linux WebKit is not the shipped macOS WKWebView — with the platforms swapped, and the fix is to erase the line the way a user on that platform would rather than to assert a keybinding that only one platform has.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. On macOS: PW_PROJECTS=webkit npx playwright test e2e/completion.spec.ts
2. 'erasing the line closes the panel entirely — no footer-only panel' fails; the dropdown is still visible.
3. The same spec passes in e2e/run-in-container.sh and in CI.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The spec erases the line by a means that works on both engines (a key the editor binds the same way, or repeated Backspace to an asserted-empty line), and still fails if the panel is left showing only its footer.
- It passes on macOS WebKit and in the container.

title: a user cannot pin which shell nocx starts; the resolver has no setting to consult
description:
internal/loginshell resolves the login shell from the OS account record, then $SHELL, then a candidate list (nocx-wwz0). There is deliberately NO explicit user setting in front of that chain, because none exists in internal/settings today and inventing the storage, the contract shape and the Settings control inside a P0 bugfix would have been the wrong place to decide them.

The gap is real for two shapes of user: someone whose account record names a shell they do not want nocx to start (a chsh they regret, a managed fleet that pins one), and someone who wants an integrated tier on a machine whose login shell has none — pinning zsh rather than accepting a conventional fish session.

The resolver already takes its lookups as injected options, so a setting is one more source at the front of Resolve, not a redesign. Where it does NOT belong is a second derivation somewhere else: the point of that package is that this question has one owner.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A user can name the shell a local session starts, and it is honoured over the account record.
- The setting rides the same contract discipline as the rest of settings (a JSON Schema in contracts/ and generated renderer types).
- An empty or unset setting resolves exactly as today, proven by the existing loginshell table.
- A setting naming a shell that is not on the machine falls through rather than handing the user a tab that dies on exec.

title: scripts/ci-frontend.sh cannot run from a git worktree, so one of the four CI jobs is unrunnable there
description:
## Summary

e2e/run-in-container.sh solves this and says so in a comment: a git worktree
keeps a .git FILE pointing at the common git dir, so a container that mounts
only the worktree gets `fatal: not a git repository`; the script mounts the
common dir at its own absolute path (`git rev-parse --git-common-dir`).

scripts/ci-frontend.sh has the same bind mount and none of that handling. Its
container script runs `git config --global --add safe.directory /work` under
`set -euo pipefail`, git resolves the repo from /work, fails, and the whole
job exits 128 before the first gate.

Agents in this repo routinely work in .claude/worktrees/*, where this makes
the `frontend` job — one of the four AGENTS.md names as the gate — unrunnable
without hand-editing a copy of the script.

## Steps to Reproduce

    git worktree add /tmp/wt-demo
    cd /tmp/wt-demo && ./scripts/ci-frontend.sh

    === frontend job on node:24-bookworm — 4 cpus ===
    fatal: not a git repository: <main>/.git/worktrees/wt-demo

Confirmed 2026-08-12 from .claude/worktrees/agent-a67ea18675eeb5540. The
workaround is a copy of the script with the common git dir mounted, after
which the whole job passes (143 files, 2547 tests, plus the root gates).

## Acceptance Criteria

- scripts/ci-frontend.sh run from a worktree completes the job, using the same
  git-common-dir mount e2e/run-in-container.sh already derives.
- Behaviour from an ordinary checkout is unchanged (the extra flag is empty
  there, exactly as in the e2e script).
- scripts/ci-linux.sh is checked for the same gap in the same pass.
close_reason: Shipped. Same behaviour as nocx-7wkc, filed twice the same day; this was the fuller writeup with the repro transcript. scripts/ci-frontend.sh:141 mounts the git common dir via git rev-parse --git-common-dir, commit 43a65d22. Its third criterion is satisfied by inspection: scripts/ci-linux.sh runs no git inside the container and mounts only the repo read-only, so it never had the gap. Verified during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh.

title: the POSIX sh tier emits no command snapshot and, unlike its other omissions, does not say why
description:
## Summary

nocx.posix carries a deliberate list of what the minimal tier cannot do and
why — no C marker, no authenticated lifecycle channel, no answer to a
refresh_request — and each omission is argued in the file. The OSC 636
command-existence snapshot is now a fourth omission with no such note: bash
has it (nocx-cbtc era) and zsh has it as of nocx-qduc, so a dash/busybox-ash
host is the only integrated environment where the completion dropdown never
learns a command name, and nothing in the repo says so.

Unlike the other three, this one is not obviously unimplementable. The
snapshot needs a PATH scan and one emission from a prompt, and the 'exactly
once' latch the other tiers keep in a shell variable could be the presence of
the staged file itself (the emit removes it) — a POSIX prompt expansion runs
in a fork that cannot write state back, which is what rules the other
omissions out, but not this one.

## Steps to Reproduce

    grep -n 636 internal/shellintegration/scripts/nocx.posix   # nothing

Open a session on a host whose shell is dash: markers, cwd and blocks work;
tab completion reports command names as unavailable for the life of the tab.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Either the POSIX tier emits the hello and the snapshot under the same
  protocol and the same caps as bash and zsh, proven by an exec test against a
  real dash, or nocx.posix states the omission and the reason in the same
  voice as the three it already states.
- Whichever is chosen, the shipped script version is bumped (scripts.go), or
  the change reaches no installed host.

title: the shells' random-nonce fallbacks are broken in different ways when /dev/urandom is unreadable
description:
## Summary

Two fallback paths that only run on a machine without a readable /dev/urandom,
both wrong, both in the same concept (mint a hex nonce):

1. nocx.zsh __nocx_lc_fence builds its fallback with zsh's [##16] arithmetic
   flag, which renders hex in UPPER case, and then validates the result
   against `^[0-9a-f]{64}$`. The check can never pass, so __nocx_lc_fence
   returns non-zero, no complete envelope is sent and no render fence is
   written — the block never freezes.
2. nocx.bash __nocx_gen_nonce falls back to four %04x draws of $RANDOM, which
   is 16 hex characters where the /dev/urandom path produces 32. The frontend
   accepts 1..128 hex (command-snapshot.ts NONCE_RE) so it works, but the two
   paths of one function disagree about the width of what they mint, and the
   Go test helper insists on 32.

Found while writing the zsh snapshot's own nonce generator (nocx-qduc), which
lower-cases its [##16] output for exactly this reason and draws eight times so
the fallback keeps the urandom path's width.

## Steps to Reproduce

    zsh -fc 'code=127; print -r -- "${(l:2::0:)$(( [##16] code ))}"'   # 7F, not 7f

and read nocx.zsh's __nocx_lc_fence regex against it. For the bash half:

    bash -c 'printf "%04x%04x%04x%04x" 1 2 3 4 | wc -c'                  # 16, not 32

Neither path is reachable on a machine with /dev/urandom, which is why both
have survived: AGENTS.md's rule is that every 'returns an error when…' needs a
paired 'and on a normal machine it succeeds', and here it is the fallback that
has no test at all.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The zsh fence fallback produces a value its own validator accepts, asserted
  by a test that drives the fallback (e.g. by making the urandom read fail).
- Both shells' nonce fallbacks mint the same width as their primary path.
- Each fallback has a test; a machine with /dev/urandom is not evidence.

title: The footprint surface shows the local installation too
description:
shell.footprint.status lists remote installed facts only. The LOCAL install
(internal/app/app.go calls EnsureInstalled, which writes ~/.nocx and appends
gate lines to the user own rc files) is invisible there.

Raised while designing consent for the remote footprint (nocx-i5yl): the
owner decided local installation stays consent-free — installing nocx on
your own machine is the consent — but invisible is a different matter. The
local footprint is the one that edits your dotfiles.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The footprint surface shows the local installation: what was written under
  ~/.nocx and which rc files carry a gate line.
- Removing it is offered on the same terms as the remote one, and the action
  text does not claim to remove more than it removes.

title: The control-plane executor emits no telemetry: active work, rejections, duration and cancellations are uninstrumented
description:
ADR-0024 names four observability signals for the bounded control plane — active work, admission rejections, duration by non-secret method name, and cancellations — and none of them is instrumented. Only the wire surface exists: a refused request answers -32004 and a refused notification emits control.saturated, both visible to the user, neither counted anywhere an operator could read.

Found by the ADR worker checking the brief against the code rather than transcribing it, and left visible in the ADR instead of describing telemetry the code does not emit.

Why it matters: the bounds this epic introduced (lane capacity, conflict wait timeout, conflict queue depth, outbound queue depth) were chosen from measurement and reasoning, not from production data. Without counters nobody can tell whether a bound is generous, tight, or being hit constantly — and the first symptom of a bound set too tight is a user seeing 'Control plane busy', which is exactly the outcome this epic worked to make rare.
acceptance_criteria: The four signals are emitted through the logging interface (log/slog behind the interface, never ad-hoc printing), carrying the admission Name and a non-secret method name and NEVER any request parameter — any control frame may carry a secret. A test asserts a rejection increments its counter and that no parameter reaches the log record.

title: Session lane tombstones are never deleted, so the map grows for the life of the server
description:
## Summary

nocx-sfv6.6 (28f789f) gives each session a resize lane, and a lane that outlives its session becomes a tombstone that is never removed from the map. That is deliberate and the reasoning is sound: the tombstone is the single authority refusing later resizes for a dead session, and deleting it reopens the race the gate exists to close — a resize from a second connection that passed state.has and registry.Get before the close could create a fresh open lane for a session the close already removed.

The cost is that the map grows by one small entry for every session ever opened, bounded only by the server's lifetime. On a desktop terminal with heavy tab churn that is slow but genuinely unbounded.

## Steps to Reproduce

Open and close tabs repeatedly against one backend and watch the lane map in internal/transport/ws_session_ops.go: entries accumulate and are never removed. There is no user-visible symptom short of a very long-lived process.

## Why it was not fixed in place

Bounding it safely means knowing when no connection can still hold a stale reference to that session id — a grace period tied to connection lifetime, or an epoch, or moving refusal authority somewhere that does not need a per-session entry. That is a design question rather than a line change, and getting it wrong silently restores the race.
acceptance_criteria: Tombstone retention is bounded by something other than server uptime, and a test proves the race the tombstone closes is STILL closed under that bound — a resize that passed its checks before a close, arriving from a second connection after the tombstone would have expired, is still refused. Removing the bound without that test is not acceptable.

title: An unreproduced -race flake in the export/vault suite, seen once during nocx-sfv6.2
description:
## Summary

The worker implementing nocx-sfv6.2 reported one early -race run failing and never reproducing. Filed rather than dropped because an unreproduced race is the one that comes back in CI.

## Steps to Reproduce

None known — that is the defect report. What was attempted: on the merged result (a4e134d) the coordinator ran

    go test -race -count=3 ./internal/export/... ./internal/profile/... ./internal/content/... ./internal/vault/...

All green: export 6.6s, profile 2.2s, content 10.9s, vault 27.4s. The original failure was seen once by the worker before the restore operation reached its final shape, and the worker did not capture the output.

## Context

If it recurs, the useful fact is that it was already present with RestoreImport in place and predates the control-plane executor wiring (nocx-sfv6.5). Two further caveats from the same worker, both deliberate and both pre-existing rather than introduced: real-store conversation restore still refuses atomically (a stub until agent mode), and store Close has a teardown-only drain window.
acceptance_criteria: Either a reproduction with the failing goroutine pair named, or a recorded decision that it was a one-off in a since-changed test. Closing with 'could not reproduce' alone is not acceptable — state how many runs were attempted and at what -count.

title: Docs: sync architecture.md and the distribution design to the shipped release pipeline
description: release.yml changed substantially on 2026-08-08 (sign/publish split, build -> build-macos, webkit2_41, AppImage icon) and release/v0.1.0 was deleted. Documentation audit and correction.
close_reason: Done in f1dbc1a. architecture.md: the Build & CI bullet names build-macos and build-linux and all four artefacts (it had described a macOS-only release while the next line said Linux ships); two new bullets state that a release is a tag not a branch, where the version actually comes from, and that sign verifies against the shipped keyring. The two release/** mentions are gone. The 'gate that cannot be side-stepped' claim is narrowed to pull requests and now says why main has no push trigger. Distribution design: dated revision note per the file's own convention, a build-linux section, sign/publish split, artefact naming for both platforms. Verified: prettier clean, no release/** left in docs, README install instructions re-read and still accurate. ci.yml deliberately untouched — nocx-286m carries that decision.

title: The release/** CI trigger and its docs describe a branch the release model does not use
description:
The docs half is DONE (2026-08-08): docs/architecture.md no longer mentions release/** in either place, and the distribution design spec records that a release is a tag on a commit reachable from main, never a branch.

What remains is the FUNCTIONAL half, which is a decision rather than a correction: .github/workflows/ci.yml still carries `push: branches: ['release/**']` and a header comment explaining it. No such branch exists — release/v0.1.0 was deleted on 2026-08-08 — so the trigger currently matches nothing.

Do not just delete it. Decide:
- If maintenance lines are wanted later (a 0.1.x branch while main moves on), keep the trigger and say in the comment what it is FOR, so it stops reading as part of the release path.
- If they are not part of the model, remove the trigger and its comment.

Worth noting either way: with release/** gone, ci.yml has NO push trigger at all. That is correct and deliberate — main is PR-only by rule with an owner exception for direct pushes, and a release is gated by release.yml calling ci.yml on the tagged commit, not by anything watching main.

title: The macOS release job is called 'build', so a failure does not say which platform
description: release.yml had 'build' (macOS) next to 'build-linux'. The unqualified name is left over from when macOS was the only target; after ADR-0007 added the AppImage it reads as 'the build' and a red job does not say which platform broke. Renamed to build-macos, with publish's needs updated. Safe to rename: main has no required_status_checks pinned to the old name (nocx-xx56 tracks adding them).
close_reason: Done on main (aa2d325). build -> build-macos, publish's needs updated; both names appear correctly in runs 31245783245 and 31246707047. nocx-xx56 should add required checks under the new names.

title: design: a user-triggered readiness request so 'press Tab again' can be true
description:
## Summary

Deferred deliberately, with the reasoning captured while it is fresh.

nocx-z9s9.16 established that a bash shell idle in readline can emit nothing on
its own — measured on 5.2 and 5.3, a trap does not run until the user submits
something. So the first prompt's grace is the only automatic delivery point for
the OSC 636 snapshot, and under heavy load a job can still miss it. That tab
then has no command names until the user happens to run something.

The encoder fast path shrank the pipeline from ~104ms to ~41ms against a 250ms
bound, which makes the miss rare. It does not make it impossible, and the
product's honest message now tells the user to run a command.

## The option not taken

Bind a reserved sequence in the shell with 'bind -x', and have the renderer send
it to the PTY when completion is pending and the session is known PROMPT_READY.
The handler checks the staging file and emits synchronously from inside readline
— while the interactive shell owns the terminal, which is a stronger safe
interval than any check-then-write from a background job. 'press Tab again in a
moment' becomes literally true.

## Why it is not a bugfix

It crosses the input boundary: the renderer would be sending bytes to the shell
that the user did not type. ADR-0004 §70 treats one-shot user-initiated delivery
as a distinct category from keyboard ownership, so it is not obviously
forbidden — but it is a design amendment and must be decided as one, not slipped
into a defect fix.

Open questions: preserving a user's existing binding; emacs vs vi keymaps;
choosing a sequence that cannot collide with terminal or user input; bindings
changed after the integration loads; nested and remote integrations; proving a
64 KB OSC emitted from a bind -x handler cannot corrupt readline's buffer or
redisplay.
acceptance_criteria: A design decision is recorded (ADR or an amendment to ADR-0004) on whether the renderer may send a reserved readline sequence to request the snapshot, with the input-boundary implications named. If accepted, a fresh tab gets command names on the user's second Tab regardless of load.

title: CommandSnapshotStore.reset() has no production caller
description:
## Summary

`frontend/src/command-snapshot.ts` ends with

    reset(): void { this.nonce = null; this._names = null }

and nothing outside its own unit tests calls it. The store anchors its nonce on the first hello and discards every later one by design ("exactly one hello per session" — the forgery defence). `reset()` is the only way to release that anchor, so as written the anchor is permanent for the life of the store.

Whether that matters depends on whether a store instance can ever outlive its session — one per renderer today (xterm.ts:167), so possibly never. Either it can, and a re-established session loses completion permanently with no way back; or it cannot, and this is dead code that reads like a safety valve. Both want the same first step: establish which, and then either wire it or delete it.

Found while chasing nocx-z9s9.14. It is NOT the cause of that one — measured and ruled out.

## Steps to Reproduce

    grep -rn "\.reset()" frontend/src --include=*.ts | grep -i snapshot   # only its own tests

## Acceptance Criteria

- Established whether a CommandSnapshotStore can outlive the session whose nonce it holds.
- reset() either has a caller that needs it, or is gone.

title: 17 files outside frontend/ have never been prettier-checked
description:
The pre-commit hook ran prettier as `cd frontend && npm run format:check`, so only frontend/ was ever checked, while the repository root carries its own .prettierrc.json, .prettierignore and format:check script. Running the root one reports 17 files: three .internal/ specs, eleven contracts/*.schema.json, and ADRs under docs/decisions/.

Found while fixing nocx-yv37 (a syntactically broken e2e spec passing every gate). That fix gates e2e/ specifically; formatting 17 unrelated files inside it would have made the diff unreviewable, which is why this is separate.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `npm run format:check` from the repository root is clean.
- The pre-commit hook runs the root check rather than the frontend-scoped one, so the drift cannot restart.
- Nothing outside formatting changes: the reformat commit touches no behaviour and its diff is whitespace and quoting only.
close_reason: Fixed. .githooks/pre-commit:215 builds PRETTIER_FILES from git diff --cached and runs prettier --check over them from the ROOT with no cd into frontend, falling back to npm run format:check when nothing is staged. Commits 3e02347d, whose subject is 'run prettier from the root, where its config always lived (nocx-pvjj)', and 493541f1. Measured during the backlog sweep nocx-e1xzh: npm run format:check over the whole tree reports all matched files clean. NOT a duplicate of nocx-srnk, though both are the same SHAPE — the hook's own comment at :228 records that the two checkers were widened by different commits five weeks apart, and says that two checkers with one widened is how a gate keeps half its ground.

title: Say that a wildcard known_hosts entry was preserved when trusting a key
description:
Trusting a changed key now narrows a matching wildcard line rather than deleting it (nocx-9224, 9030eb7): '*.example.com' becomes '*.example.com,!db.example.com' so sibling hosts keep their trust. That is the right behaviour and it edits a file the user maintains by hand, in a way no mainstream tool does — ssh-keygen -R deletes matching entries, and OpenSSH refuses to edit at all.

An unannounced edit to a hand-maintained file is where surprise turns into suspicion, and host keys are the one area where a user's suspicion is the feature. The dialog should say what was done.

## Acceptance Criteria

After accepting a changed key where a wildcard entry was narrowed, the product says so — naming that the wildcard was kept for other hosts. Nothing is said when no wildcard was involved.

title: Profiles and groups are the only state with no change notification, so the list re-reads
description:
The product already pushes state changes: exit, inputStalled, vault.changed, settings.changed and files.changed all have subscribers (ipc.ts:290,301; vault-observer.ts:25; settings-observer.ts:34; files/files-client.ts:67). Profiles and groups have none.

That gap is why connections.tsx:1660 calls loadAll() after every save, even though profiles.create already RETURNS the created profile (ws.go:1869) and the surface already holds it as 'saved'. A second window editing connections sees nothing until it re-reads, and a create-then-list sequence exists at all only because there is nothing to subscribe to.

This is the finishing of an existing pattern, not a new architecture — targeted invalidation like settings.changed, not a replicated state protocol.

## Acceptance Criteria

A profile or group change made in one window is reflected in another without that window re-reading on a timer or a user gesture. The connections surface stops calling loadAll() after a save it already has the result of.

title: ProfileClient is eight families in one class, so no boundary can hold the ordering contract
description:
frontend/src/profiles.ts ProfileClient carries ~40 methods across eight unrelated families: profiles, groups, settings, export/import, connection secrets, sshConfig, the connection probe and trust, and sessions.status. Every method is a pure pass-through — 'return this.call(name, params)' — with no state, no caching and no invariant of its own.

That combination is why 'which call sequences depend on ordering' was unanswerable when PR #64 was reverted for removing the control plane's implicit ordering. A boundary that only renames the wire cannot hold a contract, and forty methods of eight domains in one class means any of them could depend on any other. Splitting into domain clients gives each invariant a place to live next to the calls that hold it.

Not scope for nocx-u687: the backend registry fixes the same 'one object knows the product' smell on the Go side, and this is its renderer half.

## Acceptance Criteria

No renderer client class spans more than one backend module. Each surface imports the client for the domain it uses and no others.

title: Record the jump-route host-key identity as ADR-0023
description:
The decision from nocx-shat — a jump route gets its own opaque known_hosts identity, derived from routing alone — lived only in a commit message. It is hard to reverse (entries are already written under it; changing the derivation orphans them and re-prompts every jump route) and surprising without context (the entries are unreadable by a human and unusable by ssh).

## Acceptance Criteria

docs/decisions/0023 states the decision, why profile-keyed trust and a readable composite identity were both rejected, and what a later change to the derivation would cost.
close_reason: docs/decisions/0023-a-jump-route-is-its-own-host-key-identity.md

title: Contract tests still wait 2s for a notification that is merely late
description:
internal/transport/ws_contract_test.go kept three hard 2-second waits after password_requester_test.go replaced its own with wantWithin=30s. That constant's comment names this exact failure: 'the whole file used to say 2 seconds, and the container gate duly failed at exactly 2.00s on a notification that was merely late (nocx-yht3)'.

Seen once while merging the #64 split: TestConnectionsPasswordRequest_OverTheWireConformsToContract failed at exactly 2.00s under a full 'go test -race ./...' run, and passed in four subsequent runs. Nothing measures latency here — the wait is for an event the implementation hands over without doing work — so the deadline only ever answers 'did it arrive at all'.

Fixed in the same commit as the merge; this bead records it so the next 2-second wait somebody adds has something to find.

## Steps to Reproduce

Run 'go test -race ./...' on a loaded machine. TestConnectionsPasswordRequest_OverTheWireConformsToContract intermittently fails with 'read notification: i/o timeout' at 2.00s.

## Acceptance Criteria

No wait in internal/transport uses a bare 2-second deadline for an event the code produces immediately; they use wantWithin.
close_reason: The three 2-second waits in ws_contract_test.go now use wantWithin, the constant password_requester_test.go already introduced for exactly this.

title: A commit from the panel runs hooks in the tab's live environment, not a resolved one
acceptance_criteria: A hook that passes in the terminal passes from the panel. The resolved environment is cached once at backend start and cannot contain a direnv, a virtualenv, a Nix shell or an export made inside that tab; the shell would have to report it. Until then the panel states which environment hooks run in.

title: Merge conflicts as a surface, not a status letter
acceptance_criteria: A conflicted file can be resolved from the product. Today it shows as U, is not stageable, and stage-all/unstage-all refuse while it exists - deliberately, because git add -A marks it resolved with the markers still in the file and bare git reset deletes MERGE_HEAD.

title: Syntax highlighting inside the unified diff
acceptance_criteria: Diff text is highlighted by the file's language as well as by +/-, without a second highlighter fighting the decoration layer.

title: Side-by-side diff, as an option beside unified
acceptance_criteria: The diff tab can render two columns. The git.diff contract was shaped so this arrives as new optional fields rather than a schema break.

title: Stage a hunk, not a file
acceptance_criteria: A single hunk or line can be staged from the diff. Needs a patch editor.

title: Switch and create branches from the Git panel
acceptance_criteria: A branch can be checked out and created from the panel header. Checkout with a dirty tree is a stash-or-refuse decision the design must name, and checkout changes the reality underneath an agent running in the terminal right now.

title: Sync the branch: push, pull, publish, and Create PR
acceptance_criteria: A user can push, pull and publish a branch and open a pull request from the panel, and one primary control says which of those is appropriate now. Needs remote authentication and a which-action-now resolver; orca's is several hundred lines with its own suite.

title: Upgrade vite 5 to 7 so esbuild understands the ES2024 target
description:
Every vite build and every vitest run prints: 'Unrecognized target environment "ES2024" [tsconfig.json] ../tsconfig.json:16'. esbuild 0.21.5 — the version vite 5.4 pins with '^0.21.3' — tops out at es2023; es2024 first lands in esbuild 0.24.

The warning is cosmetic (esbuild falls back to its default target), but it prints on every build and test run, and output nobody trusts is output nobody reads.

esbuild is transitive, so it moves when vite moves. Checked compatible: vitest 3.2.7 declares vite '^5 || ^6 || ^7', vite-plugin-solid 2.11.13 declares up to ^9, and vite 7's engines want node ^20.19 || >=22.12 (dev machine is on v24).

vite 7 brings esbuild 0.25. Note vite 7 changes the default build target to baseline-widely-available, which is a real behaviour change for the shipped bundle and is why this needs the full gate plus e2e in CI, not just a local build.

## Acceptance Criteria

npm run build and npm test print no esbuild target warning; the frontend suite, the typecheck, a production build and the e2e suite are green in CI.
close_reason: Merged to main while splitting PR #64 into per-concern branches.

title: The connections list scroll chain has no regression guard
description:
nocx-dzi1 was a broken flex height chain: .cm-root and .ui-collection-view claimed no height, so .ui-collection-view__body never got a bounded one and the list clipped instead of scrolling. The fix is four CSS declarations with nothing asserting them — jsdom computes no layout, so no test here can go red when someone drops min-height: 0 again.

ui/scroll-ownership.test.tsx documents this limitation and works around it by asserting the structural invariant from injected CSS rather than from layout. The same shape would work for the surface chain: assert that every element between the page scroll owner and the scroll owner declares flex and min-height, which is exactly what broke.

## Acceptance Criteria

Removing 'min-height: 0' from .cm-root, or 'flex: 1 1 auto' from .ui-collection-view, makes a frontend test fail.
close_reason: Guard added: connections.scroll-chain.test.tsx walks the real DOM chain and asserts the shipped CSS. Verified red on removing min-height: 0 from .cm-root and flex: 1 1 auto from .ui-collection-view. 6d3e8bf

title: Step 2: offer visual companion just-in-time
close_reason: No visual question arose; all questions were conceptual/scope. Companion never offered.

title: Committed Wails bindings drift from the Go source
description:
## Summary

frontend/wailsjs/go/main/WailsApp.d.ts and .js are generated artefacts that are committed, and they had fallen behind: main.go:97 declares LogFilePath() and the committed bindings did not list it. Running `wails dev` regenerates and changes them, so the drift shows up as unrelated diff noise in whatever branch happens to run the app next.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The committed bindings match what `wails dev` generates from the current Go source.
- Either a gate notices the drift, or the reason it is safe to leave ungated is written down.

title: filesystem.CanExpand is a Go twin of the kit's isExpandable, reachable only from tests
description:
Found by the deadcode ratchet during nocx-708q, and it is the nocx-rtg0 shape:
internal/filesystem/openability.go CanExpand has no caller outside tests.
golangci-lint's `unused` is silent because it IS referenced — by three test
files — which is exactly why reachability from main() is a different question
and why that gate now exists.

The interesting part is not that it is unreachable. It is WHY.

"May this row be expanded" is decided in two places: CanExpand in Go, and
isExpandable in frontend/src/ui/tree-row.tsx. The frontend one is live — the
tree calls it on every row. The Go one is not, because expansion is a UI act:
the backend never expands anything, and List's "not a directory" case is
answered by syscall.ENOTDIR from the OS, not by this table.

So this is two answers to one question, agreeing today and free to drift. That
is the pattern AGENTS.md names in its "look for the existing answer" section and
that the 2026-08-05 ssh-context defect cost a session to.

Note the asymmetry with its sibling: CanOpen IS used, by both providers, and
must be — the backend enforces openability from freshly-read metadata at call
time, because a symlink can be retargeted between a list and a read. Opening is
a backend decision; expanding is not.

It is baselined by hand in .githooks/deadcode-baseline.json with this reason
written in, rather than deleted in a rush, because removing it means rewriting
three assertions in packages that were already reviewed and accepted.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. node .githooks/check-deadcode.mjs — CanExpand is in the baseline, added by
   hand with its reason.
2. grep -rn "CanExpand" internal/ — three test files, zero production callers.
3. grep -rn "isExpandable" frontend/src — the live twin.

## Acceptance Criteria

Exactly one of:
- CanExpand is deleted and the three assertions that used it are rewritten to
  express the same thing without it, OR
- a production caller exists that genuinely needs the backend to decide
  expandability, and the reason it is not a duplicate of isExpandable is written
  at the code.

Either way its baseline entry, and the paragraph explaining it, go with it.
acceptance_criteria: Either CanExpand is deleted and its three test assertions rewritten, or a production caller exists with a written reason why it is not a duplicate of the kit's isExpandable; the baseline entry and its note are removed either way.

title: files.reveal has no Wails seam — it answers -32601
description:
Shipped in nocx-708q: the method, its schema, its handler and its guards all
exist. The guard is real and tested — files.reveal is refused on a REMOTE
binding by the backend, not only hidden in the UI, because a UI-only guard is
one bug away from being no guard. What does not exist is the native call that
opens the OS file manager, so on a local binding it answers -32601.

frontend/src/generated/files.reveal.ts is a baselined dead export for exactly
this reason, with a note saying it should be deleted if this never lands.

The design's rule (§4): absent on a remote tab, not disabled. Absence is what
tells the user the capability does not apply to that machine; a disabled control
suggests it might.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Right-clicking a row on a LOCAL tab and choosing "Show in Finder" opens the OS
  file manager with the entry selected.
- The item is ABSENT from the menu on a remote tab, and the backend still
  refuses the call if it is made.
- src/generated/files.reveal.ts leaves the dead-export baseline.
acceptance_criteria: Show in Finder opens the OS file manager on a local tab; the item is absent (not disabled) on a remote tab and the backend refuses it anyway; the generated type leaves the dead-export baseline.

title: Lock the whole app, as a mode the user chooses
description: Owner's question on 2026-08-02: should we lock the whole application rather than just the vault? As a default it is too heavy for a terminal — no comparable tool does it. As an option it is right and cheap: on a shared machine it is exactly what is wanted, and it gives a simpler mental model than 'some things prompt and some do not' for the people who choose it.
acceptance_criteria: A setting turns on app-level locking: while locked nothing is readable and no session runs, and one unlock opens everything for the session. Off by default — a terminal exists to type a command now, and a prompt before the first prompt taxes the commonest action to protect a background feature.

title: nocx.bash leaks the command snapshot into the environment under `set -a`
description:
## Context

The OSC 636 hook (landed in 8d9408f) accumulates the full `compgen -c` list — ~12 KB of the user's aliases, functions, builtins and PATH — in the shell global `__nocx_payload`. A user rc running under `set -a` auto-exports every assignment, so that list would land in the environment of every child process and be readable from `/proc/<pid>/environ`.

The session nonce is already protected against this (`export -n __nocx_snapshot_nonce` at source time), and the nonce is the security boundary, so this is the lesser of the two. But the design brief said the command list must never be persisted or logged because it fingerprints the user's working environment, and an exported variable is exactly that kind of exposure.

Reported by the implementing worker as a known residual, not found in the field.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Put `set -a` in ~/.bashrc before the nocx integration is sourced.
2. Open a nocx tab and let two prompts pass, so the snapshot is built and emitted.
3. Run `env | grep __nocx_payload` — or read /proc/self/environ from any child.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `__nocx_payload` is `local` to the function that builds it, or explicitly `export -n`'d, so it never appears in a child's environment even under `set -a`.
- A test in scripts_exec_test.go sources the hook under `set -a`, runs the snapshot to completion, and asserts the payload appears in no exported variable.
- The other `__nocx_snap*` variables are checked in the same test; they carry no secret today, but the assertion should name what is allowed rather than what is not.

title: Insert path: quote for the target shell dialect, not only POSIX sh
description:
Insertion quotes for POSIX sh and refuses control characters (a newline is legal in a Unix filename and becomes a second command at the prompt). Guessing a dialect is worse than declaring one, so nocx-708q declares POSIX and this bead adds the rest.
Deferred out of nocx-708q by the design in .internal/specs/2026-08-01-file-manager-design.md (nocx-gglz). Depends on the file manager existing.
acceptance_criteria: A path inserted into fish, PowerShell or cmd is quoted for THAT shell; a path that cannot be quoted safely for the detected shell is still refused rather than mangled.

title: Files panel: virtualised tree rows
description:
nocx-708q ships a page plus 'show next N' instead of virtualisation, deliberately (D3). File this when the page size starts hurting — Orca needed FileExplorerVirtualRows, so it probably will.
Deferred out of nocx-708q by the design in .internal/specs/2026-08-01-file-manager-design.md (nocx-gglz). Depends on the file manager existing.
acceptance_criteria: A directory page renders in constant DOM size regardless of entry count, and scrolling a large tree stays smooth. Measured, not asserted.

title: Files panel: read-only git status markers in the tree gutter
description:
Wanted by nocx-708q originally, cut from its first slice: no git surface exists anywhere in the backend, and on a remote filesystem this means running git over SSH. Needs its own backend design.
Deferred out of nocx-708q by the design in .internal/specs/2026-08-01-file-manager-design.md (nocx-gglz). Depends on the file manager existing.
acceptance_criteria: A tracked file modified since HEAD shows a marker; an ignored entry is dimmed; markers are read-only and never block the tree from rendering when git is absent or the directory is not a repo.

title: File viewer: syntax highlighting
description:
The viewer ships as plain monospaced text because CodeMirror is not in the project. It arrives with nocx-2gf.
Deferred out of nocx-708q by the design in .internal/specs/2026-08-01-file-manager-design.md (nocx-gglz). Depends on the file manager existing.
acceptance_criteria: An opened source file is highlighted by language, read-only, in both local and remote viewers; an unknown extension falls back to plain monospace without error.

title: Files panel: recursive name search, not a filter over loaded nodes
description:
nocx-708q deliberately shipped no filter rather than a half one: a filter over lazily-loaded nodes silently fails to find files that exist, which is worse than no control at all. A recursive walk is real work and on SFTP it is a chain of round-trips, so it is its own bead.
Deferred out of nocx-708q by the design in .internal/specs/2026-08-01-file-manager-design.md (nocx-gglz). Depends on the file manager existing.
acceptance_criteria: Typing in the search box finds files anywhere under the root, including in directories never expanded, on BOTH providers; the remote implementation bounds its walk and reports when it stopped early. Tested with a match that exists only in an unexpanded directory — the case a filter over loaded nodes cannot pass.

title: editor.ts and style.css cite nocx-6w4z for a change that bead is not about
description: Found while answering a W1 worker question on 2026-08-01. The hide()/reservation removal in frontend/src/editor.ts (the comment block ending 'the jump comes back and is the smaller of the two problems') and the matching note in frontend/src/style.css both cite (nocx-6w4z). That bead is titled 'Switching strip orientation marks every inactive tab as having activity', which is a different defect. Either the comments cite the wrong id or the work landed under a bead that does not describe it. Low value on its own; it costs real time when someone traces a deliberate decision back to its reasoning and lands on an unrelated bug — which is exactly what happened here. Find the right id or file one retroactively and correct both comments.
acceptance_criteria: Both comments cite a bead whose title describes the reservation removal.
close_reason: The two comments are gone: the reservation was reinstated as CommandEditor.suspend() (nocx-i4h04), and the note that replaces them names THIS bead as the miscitation instead of repeating nocx-6w4z. The decision itself — the reservation removed once, deliberately, for a strip of dead canvas the owner reported twice — is now written where it is acted on, which is what this chore asked for.

title: Per-entry streaming notifications on the control plane
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §6.5. Server-to-client notifications exist (exit, settings.changed, vault.changed) but are BROADCASTS. An agent turn needs per-entry streamed chunks — ledger.chunk {entryId, seq, data} — with ordering and backpressure of its own.

Filed now, ahead of agent mode, so that epic does not discover a missing transport capability mid-flight. The binary data plane stays PTY-only: wrapping model tokens in binary frames would put a second protocol on a plane whose entire contract is 'these bytes go to a terminal'.
acceptance_criteria: Chunks for two concurrent entries interleave on the wire without corrupting either. A slow consumer applies backpressure rather than growing an unbounded buffer. The data plane carries no non-PTY payload.
close_reason: Per-entry streaming: the capability had already shipped as agent.runDelta under nocx-x8s2.2 (runId, entryId, ascending seq, text, with a schema, contract tests, a persisted counterpart and a renderer that routes by run and entry), so no second notification was built. What this bead delivered is the half that had not shipped: its three criteria as assertions, and the one of them that was false. The delta emit discarded TryNotify's error, so a refused frame on a slow consumer became a hole in the live view that read as a complete answer. The refusal is now counted, the count rides the terminal agent.runState as a field absent when zero, and the block says part of the answer was dropped and the whole of it was saved. Merged b28ec295.

title: Output is data: lenses, diffs, and reports
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §10.11, §10.12. Deferred — the seams (derived text, derivedFrom, cites edges) are built by earlier epics; this epic spends them.

Lenses: registered transformers deriving views over derived text — JSON tree, failing tests, compiler diagnostics, changed files, URLs — including as a per-block inspector panel rather than a separate surface (a separate surface would be a second vocabulary for one concept, which is the defect two kit epics were spent unwinding).

Diff of two runs: 'what changed between the run that worked and the one that did not'. Diffing raw VT is meaningless — cursor moves and colour resets swamp the signal — so this is a capability derived text creates rather than exposes.

Export as markdown: the local-first answer to a cloud share link, honouring sensitivity.

Paste provenance: the cites edge only. NOT a clipboard history surface — see §14.
acceptance_criteria: A JSON payload in output can be browsed as a tree without leaving the terminal. Two runs of the same command can be diffed on their derived text. An entry exports as markdown with its environment, status and duration, and a sensitive entry refuses without an explicit override.

title: Settings and key-material secrets now appear in the Secrets list
description:
## Steps to Reproduce
1. Store private key material on a connection.
2. Open Settings → Secrets.

## Expected
The list shows what the surface says it shows — passwords and key passphrases.

## Actual
Key-material and settings-owned secrets surface too, because the inventory is now built from the vault's own records rather than from credential password/passphrase references. Reported by the worker implementing ADR-0016; a consequence of the change, not a defect in it.
acceptance_criteria: Decide what Secrets lists now that the vault knows everything it holds, and make the page's description match.

title: A secret's derived label is empty when the credential has no username
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a credential with a name but no username, save a password on it.
2. Settings -> Secrets.
3. The row reads "SSH password for" — nothing after "for" — then "1 connection".

## Why

The label rule in internal/vault/inventory.go composes "SSH password for <user>@<host>:<port>"
for a single-use secret and "SSH password for <user>" for a shared one. With no username both
collapse to a dangling preposition.

Minor: the row is still identifiable by its usage count and its store. But the point of a
derived label is that the user never has to invent one, and an empty one makes them guess
anyway.
acceptance_criteria: A password on a credential with no username produces a label a human can act on — naming the connection or the host rather than trailing off. A test covers the no-username case, which is the one the current rule does not.

title: Import a key from a host you are already connected to
description:
Asked during the Secrets/Vault design review and deferred there deliberately.

Two readings, and only one is coherent. Recording a PATH on a remote host is meaningless: our SSH client runs locally, so a path on the far side is not something it can open — that only makes sense for jump-host semantics, which is a different feature (nocx-wzc4 territory). READING the key off the host into our vault is coherent and technically possible, since we already hold a session.

Deferred because the cost is out of proportion to the gap it closes:

- It needs a dedicated non-interactive exec channel. Reading key material out of the user's interactive PTY is forbidden by AD-6 (the backend never sniffs the byte stream) and would also leave the private key in the scrollback.
- A remote file browser (SFTP, or exec plus ls, with permissions, symlinks and error states) exists nowhere in the product today.
- nocx-25k9.16's paste path already covers the case at the cost of one extra step: cat the key on the host, paste it here.

Worth checking before this is ever built: whether the real need behind it is agent forwarding rather than moving key material at all. That is a different and cheaper feature.
acceptance_criteria: From the key input, an option reads a private key off a host the user already has a session with and stores it in the vault. The bytes travel a dedicated non-interactive exec channel, never the interactive PTY, and never reach the renderer or the scrollback. The user is shown what will be read and from where before it happens.

title: Auto-seal goroutine has no exit path
description:
The auto-seal goroutine started in vault.New (internal/vault/vault.go:109) has no exit path: its for/select loop has no quit case and Vault has no Close. In production that is one goroutine for the process lifetime, which is harmless. In tests every testVault() creates one, so the vault suite leaves dozens blocked on channels, each holding its Vault alive.

Not urgent and not user-visible. It becomes visible the day someone adds a goleak check, or if the app ever constructs more than one Vault.

## Steps to Reproduce

    grep -n 'go v.autoSealLoop' internal/vault/vault.go
    grep -n 'func (v \*Vault) autoSealLoop' -A 40 internal/vault/vault.go   # no quit case

## Acceptance Criteria

Vault owns the goroutine's lifetime: a Close (or a context passed to New) stops the loop, tests call it, and a goleak assertion in the vault package proves nothing outlives a test. If the decision is instead that a process-lifetime goroutine is correct here, say so in a comment at the loop and close this as wontfix — but decide it rather than leaving it implicit.
close_reason: Fixed in cdc21e7: Vault.Close stops the auto-seal goroutine and seals, is idempotent, and the App holds it as interface{ Close() } and calls it after the transport stops. The test measures a goroutine delta across a batch of twenty and was verified to fail without the fix (22 outlive Close). testVault now registers t.Cleanup(v.Close) so the suite stops leaking.

title: Step 2: offer visual companion just-in-time if a visual question arises
close_reason: Visual companion not offered: no mockup/layout question arose — all forks were conceptual (platform availability, key hierarchy, seal scope). V2 (Vault page) will revisit if a layout question comes up.

title: Evaluate Stryker for TypeScript mutation testing
description:
## Why

Sibling of nocx-u4b, which chose gremlins for Go. The frontend has 990 tests and no measure of
whether they assert on behaviour or merely execute it.

## Candidate

StrykerJS. There is no serious competitor for TypeScript — the alternatives are unmaintained.
It matters that it ships @stryker-mutator/vitest-runner, because this repo runs Vitest, and
that it has an incremental mode, because the cost is otherwise prohibitive.

## Constraint, same as nocx-u4b

Mutation testing reruns the suite once per mutant. The frontend suite is ~12s for 990 tests,
and a file the size of connections.tsx generates hundreds of mutants. This CANNOT go in the
pre-commit hook — that hook was deliberately brought from 67s to 3-29s (nocx-ro3h) and putting
this in it would undo that and more. A separate make target, run on demand, scoped.

## Where to point it first

Pure functions with real branching, where a surviving mutant means something specific:

- `frontend/src/profiles.ts` — parseQuickConnect and decideSaveRoute. decideSaveRoute has 8
  tests for a pure router; whether they pin the routing or just execute it is exactly the
  question this tool answers.
- `frontend/src/connections.tsx` — the largest surface, and the one where a silently wrong
  branch costs the most.

## What it will and will not buy — record this honestly

It measures the quality of tests that EXIST. Most defects found while reviewing worker output
in the 2026-07-29 session were tests that were ABSENT, and for those the mutation score is
uninformative — you do not need mutation testing to notice zero tests, you need to read the
diff.

The one case it would have caught: `ComputeCredentialUsage` returned a nil slice where the
wire contract required an empty array. The Go test asserted `len(refs) == 0`, which passes for
both, so `[]ProfileRef{} -> nil` is a mutant that would have survived and pointed straight at
it. That class — an assertion too weak to distinguish two states the wire distinguishes — is
what this is for.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A make target runs Stryker over a named scope, not the whole frontend.
- Surviving mutants are triaged into beads or dismissed with a stated reason.
- The score is used as a finder, not a gate. A number in CI becomes a target, and the cheapest
  way to raise it is assertion-free tests that kill mutants incidentally — which is worse than
  no measure at all.

title: A one-off ssh_config importer, labelled as producing a detached copy
description:
## Acceptance Criteria

Spec section 4.

- An importer sits alongside the Tabby one in Export / Backup / Import.
- It is labelled honestly: it produces a DETACHED COPY, not a synchronised view. An imported
  record freezes one evaluation of a positional config, and later edits to an earlier wildcard
  block, an Include, a Match condition or alias ordering silently do not reach it.
- The live source remains the default path. This exists for people who want to take ownership
  of a host, not as the way aliases normally appear.
close_reason: A one-off importer sits beside the Tabby one under Export / Backup / Import, labelled as producing a detached copy. It stores the RESOLVED hostname, deliberately unlike adoption which stores the alias: a detached copy is meant to freeze one evaluation of a positional config, which is exactly what the label warns about. Collision policy is skip-by-name-or-host, stated and tested. Coordinator removed a second renderer-side id minting here too. Noted and left: the collision check string-matches the backend error text, which is the fragility the typed-error work (nocx-3isn) exists to remove.

title: light.css: semantic colours fall below any usable contrast floor
description:
Measured while adding the theme catalogue (nocx-7o42): light.css puts
--color-success at 2.69:1 on --color-canvas, and .nocx-chip-ok paints chip TEXT
with it. --color-accent is 4.22:1, below AA for text.

The theme-catalogue contrast gate deliberately excludes the semantic tokens for
this reason — fixing them means redesigning light.css, which did not belong in a
commit that adds themes.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Switch the theme to Light in Settings → Interface.
2. Run a command that exits 0 and look at the green exit chip (.nocx-chip-ok),
   which paints its text with --color-success (#16a34a) on --color-canvas
   (#e6e8ed) — 2.69:1, against a 4.5:1 requirement for text.

## Acceptance Criteria

- light.css --color-success, --color-warning and --color-danger each reach 4.5:1
  on --color-canvas and --color-surface.
- TEXT_TOKENS in frontend/src/theme-catalogue.test.ts is widened to cover the
  three semantic tokens, and the whole catalogue passes.

title: The connection list is a type register smaller than the navigation beside it
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Settings -> Connections.
2. Compare the settings rail on the left with the connection list next to it.

Expected: two columns of navigable rows read as the same kind of thing.
Actual: at base 14px the rail is `--font-size-md` (14px) and the connection row
name was `--font-size-sm` (12.25px), with its second line at `--font-size-2xs`
(10.5px). The right-hand list read as a footnote to the left-hand one.

## What made it a defect rather than a choice

`.ui-settings-rail` sets its size and says why: "this surface primary navigation
rather than fine print". The connection list is the same job on the same screen
and made the opposite choice with no reason recorded — so nothing said which of
the two was right, and both looked deliberate.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The connection row name matches the settings rail: body size.
- The second line is one step down, not two.
- The group caption is not smaller than the rows it heads; it separates itself
  with weight and colour.
- Nothing in the list sits below `--font-size-sm`.
close_reason: The connection list is body-sized like the settings rail beside it, its second line one step down, and nothing in it below sm. The rail's own rule already said why — primary navigation rather than fine print — and the list had made the opposite choice with no reason recorded.

title: The vertical strip's width is draggable and remembered
description:
The strip is a fixed 240px (`tab-strip.css`). Two lines of text per row make that a real constraint: a deep cwd or a long `user@host` ellipses at a width the user cannot change, and a narrow window has no way to reclaim the space.

The width is a preference, so it belongs with the others: a setting the strip reads, not a number in a stylesheet. The mechanism already exists — settings are declared in `internal/settings/settings.go`, delivered through the snapshot, and applied live by `SettingsObserver`; `tab.placement` is the working example.

The drag itself is the part with edges: a splitter between the strip and the panes, a minimum below which rows stop being readable, and the terminal's resize — the panes must re-fit as the strip moves, which is the same viewport path a window resize takes.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Dragging the strip's inner edge resizes it live, and the terminal grid re-fits as it moves rather than after it stops.
- The width persists across a restart, and is clamped to a documented minimum and maximum.
- The setting reaches the strip through the settings snapshot, not through a second storage path.
- Nothing about the horizontal strip changes.

title: Each tab row carries a glyph for the kind of session it is
description:
Warp puts a round icon at the head of every row — a shell prompt for a terminal, an avatar for an agent session. It reads faster than the title, because the kind of a session is what you scan for first.

We have the fact already (`descriptor.surfaceType`) and the icon vocabulary is thin: `src/ui/icons/` holds three glyphs today. This is mostly deciding the set — local shell, SSH, service surface (Settings) — and drawing them in the same Lucide-derived style the existing icons use, at a size that comes from the type scale rather than a number.

Not the avatar: an agent session's picture is a network resource and a whole different question.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every row in the vertical strip shows a glyph naming its kind, and the glyph differs between a local terminal, an SSH session and Settings.
- The glyphs live in `src/ui/icons/` and are exported from its barrel, like every other icon.
- The row's layout does not shift when a glyph is absent or slow — the slot is reserved.
- No raw `px` font-size or hard-coded colour is introduced (the CSS gates stay at zero).

title: Quick-connect selected row may not show its accent fill — re-check on a fresh load
description:
Reported on 2026-07-27 from a screenshot. The rule is present in the stylesheet (accent fill, canvas text) and the screenshot may predate a reload, so this may be nothing.

Re-check on a running page before treating it as a defect. Filed rather than dropped because 'the rule is present' is exactly what was true of every defect in nocx-u7wq, all of which were valid CSS that did not apply.

title: Form row spacing in the connections form — gap may not be reaching the fields
description:
Reported on 2026-07-27 and NOT measured. The suspicion is that `gap` on `.cm-form-section` does not reach the fields because of an intervening wrapper, but nothing was verified — treat the cause as unknown.

Measure before fixing. This surface is being rewritten by the kit migration (nocx-pp3y), so check whether the symptom still exists before spending time on it.

title: Focus survival after a tab reorder is unverified
description:
Reported honestly by the nocx-82l9.5 worker rather than left silent: node identity across reorder is asserted with isSameNode and passes, but focus is not. jsdom shows focus loss that may be an artefact of its incomplete focus model, and no e2e spec covers focus after reorder, so neither result is evidence.

Low priority because reorder is a deliberate drag gesture and the tab is clicked to begin with — but it is exactly the kind of regression a keyboard user would hit and nobody would report.
acceptance_criteria: An e2e spec in both engines focuses a tab button, reorders the strip by drag, and asserts document.activeElement is still that button. The jsdom unit test is not sufficient — its focus model is incomplete, which is why this gap exists.
close_reason: Focus did NOT survive a drag reorder in either orientation on either engine: Solid's <For> clears focused state when reconciliation moves a node via insertBefore, even keyed by id — node identity surviving was necessary and not sufficient. Fixed by saving and restoring activeElement across reorder. Coordinator fixed two flakes in the new spec, both the same cause: fixed timeouts instead of polling the observable outcome. Five consecutive clean runs, 4/4.

title: Probe bead for JSON shape
description:
probe

## Acceptance Criteria

probe
close_reason: probe bead, deleting

title: [epic] Transport runtime modes: dev-verbose, production-quiet
description:
Homeless child of nocx-k0xk given its own epic: nocx-772 is not a quality gate and not dev tooling, it is a feature of the transport.

Suggested by the owner while diagnosing origin/host rejections: show rejection detail only in dev and CI, and rate-limit rejections in production. The concept does not exist yet — the nearest thing is nocx-hl3's OriginPolicy, already injected per runtime mode (LoopbackOriginPolicy for development, PinnedOriginPolicy for production), so the distinction exists in one place and needs generalising rather than inventing.

DONE WHEN: the transport has an explicit runtime mode, verbose auth logging appears only in dev/CI, rejections are rate-limited in production, and the mode is set at the composition root rather than sniffed.
acceptance_criteria: the transport has an explicit runtime mode, verbose auth logging appears only in dev/CI, rejections are rate-limited in production, and the mode is set at the composition root rather than sniffed.

title: [epic] Secret lifecycle hygiene: orphan collection and redaction
description:
Carved out of nocx-6ek. Unclaimed, and needs design before implementation — recorded so it is visibly deferred rather than quietly forgotten.

- nocx-dm0: the credential delete cascade is best-effort by design (ADR-0011 section 4 prefers a brief unreachable orphan over metadata pointing at a missing secret), so orphans accumulate and nothing collects them. The janitor needs a design first: when it runs, what it may delete, and how it proves a secret is unreferenced.
- nocx-23v: mask known secrets in rendered scrollback, the command ledger and clipboard export. A large feature on its own — it beats Tabby (vault, no redaction) and Warp (redaction, no vault) by combining both.

DONE WHEN: orphaned secrets are collected by a mechanism whose safety argument is written down, and a secret injected from the vault never appears in scrollback, ledger or clipboard.
acceptance_criteria: orphaned secrets are collected by a mechanism whose safety argument is written down, and a secret injected from the vault never appears in scrollback, ledger or clipboard.

title: [epic] Windows and Linux support
description:
macOS is the first and only target today (docs/vision.md section 8), but ADR-0007 commits to cross-platform auto-update, so the other platforms are a stated direction rather than a maybe. This epic is where that direction accumulates instead of leaking into macOS-shaped epics as stray P3 children.

- nocx-6ek.1: storage.NewOSPaths returns 'unsupported platform' for any GOOS outside linux/darwin, so app.New() cannot start on Windows at all. ADR-0011 names only the XDG and Application Support layouts. Decide deliberately: add the %AppData%/%LocalAppData% layout, or state the refusal as intentional and record why.

DONE WHEN: the platform question is answered deliberately — either nocx starts and stores its data correctly on Windows and Linux, or the refusal is documented as a decision with its reasoning, and no epic elsewhere carries a stray cross-platform child.
acceptance_criteria: The platform question is answered deliberately — either nocx starts and stores its data correctly on Windows and Linux, or the refusal is documented as a decision with its reasoning, and no epic elsewhere carries a stray cross-platform child.
close_reason:
Closed on its own DONE WHEN, which reads: 'the platform question is answered deliberately — either nocx starts and stores its data correctly on Windows and Linux, or the refusal is documented as a decision with its reasoning, and no epic elsewhere carries a stray cross-platform child.'

The second branch is now taken. Owner decision, 2026-07-26: Windows is not planned. Recorded with its reasoning on the epic's only child, nocx-6ek.1, which is closed rather than dropped — the question was answered, not abandoned.

The Linux half needed nothing: it already works. platform_linux.go implements the updater's Platform seam, AppImage release builds ship in CI (nocx-mbu), and storage.NewOSPaths handles the XDG layout. The epic paired the two platforms because ADR-0007 committed to cross-platform auto-update, but only one of them was ever missing.

CARRY-FORWARD, and it is a real one: ADR-0007 still commits to cross-platform auto-update, which now overstates the intent. That decision record should get a superseding note rather than a quiet edit — the same standard applied to ADR-0001 when wterm was removed. Flagged to the owner; not done here, because amending a decision record is the owner's call.

title: storage.NewOSPaths refuses to run on Windows
description:
internal/storage/paths.go returns 'unsupported platform' for any GOOS outside linux/darwin, so app.New() cannot start on Windows at all. That is the honest behaviour for today (ADR-0011 names only the XDG and Application Support layouts, and macOS is the first target), but ADR-0007 commits to cross-platform auto-update, so Windows is a stated direction. Decide deliberately: either add the %AppData%/%LocalAppData% layout, or record in ADR-0011 that Windows is out of scope for persistence.

## Acceptance Criteria
Either Windows path roles resolve, or ADR-0011 states Windows is out of scope and the error message points at that decision.
close_reason:
Answered deliberately, which is what this bead asked for: Windows is NOT a supported platform, and the refusal in storage.NewOSPaths is intentional rather than an oversight.

Owner decision, 2026-07-26: Windows support is not planned. The bead offered two branches — add the %AppData%/%LocalAppData% layout, or state the refusal as intentional and record why — and this is the second.

Reasoning, so a future reader does not treat this as a gap to fill: nocx is macOS-first (docs/vision.md section 8) with Linux working today (platform_linux.go, AppImage release builds). Windows is a third path with its own storage layout, its own bundle-swap semantics for the updater, its own signing story and its own terminal/PTY behaviour — a cost nobody is currently buying. The code already refuses rather than half-working, which is the honest failure mode: app.New() cannot start on Windows at all, so there is no silent misbehaviour to discover later.

Not permanent, just not planned. Reversing it means adding a Platform implementation behind the existing seam (nocx-kv0) and a Windows branch in NewOSPaths — the seams are in place, so the decision is cheap to revisit if the answer changes.

title: Runtime modes for the transport: gate verbose auth logging and rate-limit rejections
description:
Suggested by the owner while diagnosing the origin/host rejections: show rejection details only in dev/CI.

The concept does not exist yet. The nearest thing is nocx-hl3's OriginPolicy, which is already injected 'per runtime mode' (LoopbackOriginPolicy for development, PinnedOriginPolicy for production) — so a mode distinction is implied but never named. Wiring log verbosity to the same switch would be coherent, and pinning the production Origin is the natural moment to introduce it.

Deliberately NOT done now, and the reasoning should survive:

Production is the one environment where the failure cannot be reproduced. In dev and CI a developer can attach a debugger, add output and re-run; on a user's machine the log is all there is. A rejected upgrade in production means either a bug or a real attack, and both need the Origin and Host that were rejected. Hiding them there removes the evidence exactly where it is irreplaceable. This is not hypothetical: the first version of that log omitted the values on 'attacker-controlled text' grounds, and 36 rejections per CI run were misread as suite flakiness for hours.

What IS worth building here:
- a named runtime mode (dev / CI / production) with the origin policy and log verbosity both keyed off it, rather than two independent switches;
- rate limiting on rejection logs. Log growth under a rejection flood is the real operational concern, and it is solved by capping frequency, not by discarding the fields that make a log useful.

If verbosity does get gated, keep Origin and Host in production and gate something else — the useful distinction is probably per-request detail versus an aggregate counter, not detail versus nothing.

title: STORE-7: export, import and backup as distinct modes
description:
ADR-0011 section 7. With a keychain in the middle there is no honest 'back up everything' unless the app reads secrets back out. So: configuration export (profiles, groups, credential metadata, settings; secret references present but unresolved); portable encrypted export (explicit, user-authenticated, encrypted under a new passphrase — not part of normal persistence); same-machine backup (documents + content.db, plus a plain statement that secrets stay in the OS keychain); import (metadata first, then the user maps existing credentials or supplies missing secrets).

Private content — conversations, command history — is never silently included in a portable export. It is frequently more sensitive than the host metadata beside it.
acceptance_criteria: Each mode exists separately and states what it does and does not carry. No mode silently exports private content or resolved secrets.
close_reason:
STORE-7 core landed: internal/export implements the four ADR-0011 §7 modes as distinct operations — configuration export (SecretID references present, material never), portable encrypted export (NaCl secretbox + Argon2id from x/crypto, no new go.mod dependency, private content only on explicit opt-in), same-machine backup (reports content.db absent rather than failing, since internal/content is still a stub), and import (metadata first, reports unresolved credentials, never invents or resolves a secret). Each mode states what it carries and what it omits as data the UI can display, not as a source comment. 18 tests.

The guarantee is structural: internal/export does not import credential.SecretStore at all — the only mention in the package is a doc comment — so no mode can resolve a secret even by mistake. Verified independently, along with go.mod/go.sum being unchanged.

Closing on the acceptance criteria as written, which are about the modes and their guarantees. The user-facing surface is NOT here: there are no export RPCs and no UI entry points yet. That is filed separately so it stays visible in bd ready.

title: Design: scrollback separator visibility when there are no frozen blocks
description:
Open question Q4 from spike/dom-scrollback/DESIGN-NOTES.md, left unresolved when nocx-4ff.18 closed.

The separator between the DOM block stack and the live xterm region is shown only when at least one frozen block exists, and hidden during alt-screen (frontend/src/scrollback/controller.ts:210). On a fresh session — and again after every clear — there are no blocks, so the live region touches the top of the scrollback area with no boundary. Whether that reads as clean or as disorienting is a taste call the owner has not made.

Options: keep the current conditional behaviour; always show the separator so the live region always has a lid; or show a lighter always-on rule that gains contrast once blocks exist.

Decide live in the browser dev loop against a real session, then record the choice here.
acceptance_criteria:
• The owner picks one of the three behaviours against a running session (fresh, after clear, with blocks, in and out of alt-screen).
• The chosen behaviour is implemented in _updateSeparator() and covered by the existing controller tests.
• DESIGN-NOTES.md Q4 is updated from open question to resolved.

title: SSH sessions miss COLORTERM=truecolor — TUIs fall back to 256 colors over SSH
description:
